name: Espoon Kuninkaankartano
Settlement_Description: <b>Inn:</b> Royal manors (fi: kuninkaankartano, sw: kungsgård)  were obliged to provide accommodation for travelling officials. Information to be amended.

name: Forsby (Pernaja)
Settlement_Description:
Permanent agricultural settlement in Pernaja (sw. Pernå) area and Eastern Nyland (sw. Östra Nyland) dates to the Swedish colonisation in the latter half of the 13th century when new farms were founded amongst earlier 12th and 13th century area of usufruct and colonisation from inner Häme. The parish organisation of Eastern Nyland dates at the latest to the first quarter of the 14th century. King Magnus Eriksson donated the rights of patronate of Porvoo parish and its two chapels of Sipoo (sw. Sibbo) and Pernaja to the Cistercian Abbey of Padise in present Estonia in 1351. The bishop and Cathedral Chapter of Turku reclaimed the rights in 1428. Independent parish at the latest since 1363. The first wooden church was built in the late 13th century or early 14th, pope Bonifacius IX supported the maintenance of the church with indulgences in 1398. After a stone sacristy constructed in 1410s, a vaulted stone church and vestibule were built in the turn of the 1430s and 1440s.

<b>Inn:</b> Forsby alehouse is mentioned in 1543. It was run by Peder Hindersson. Alehouses in Pernaja paid taxes to the king and Vogt (fi. vouti, sw. fogde), 4½ and 13½ öres respectively.
Fair_Description:
King Gustaf I granted the burghers of Helsinki in 1553 the rights for three fairs in Eastern Nyland in Helsinki, in Pernaja (sw. Pernå), and in Pyhtää (sw. Pyttis). In 1584 the official fair dates in the Eastern Nyland were Midsummer in Sipoo (sw. Sibbo), Visitation of Mary (2 July) and Excaltation of the Cross (14 September) in Porvoo, St Michael (29 September) in Pernaja and St Laurentius (10 August) at Pyhtää (sw. Pyttis) church. The same year burghers of Porvoo and Helsinki were granted joint rights for trading with peasants of the eastern half of Pernaja parish at the St Bartolomeus free fair in Vähä-Ahvenkoski in Pyhtää, whereas peasants from the western half of Pernaja were obliged to trade in Porvoo only. Previous traditional local fairs in Mustijoki (sw. Svartså) and Kulloonmäki (sw. Kullo) in Porvoo, Pikku Pernajanlahti (sw. Lillpernåviken) in Pernaja and elsewhere were prohibited. After intense litigation over local fairs both Porvoo and Helsinki were in 1602 and in 1607 respectively confirmed right to trade in the four annual fairs at Porvoo, Pernaja and Pyhtää so that burghers of Helsinki had free right to trade in confirmed fairs east of Porvoo and those of Porvoo west of Helsinki. Pyhtää Bartholomeus fair is cited in an almanac in 1616, but Pernaja Michaelmas fair not. Fair in Pyhtää was held in Vähä-Ahvenkoski and those of Pernaja at Koskenkylä (sw. Forsby) bridge on the Great Coastal Road, where they were held in 1708. The fair site in Pikku-Pernjanalahti is unknown. The fair was held either close to the 16th century rivermouth or in Ilola (sw. Illby) alongside the Great Coastal Road. A short lived castle was located at Husholmen close to the mouth of Ilolanjoki (sw. Illby å) river in Pikku-Pernajanlahti (sw. Lillpernåviken) from the late 1380s to ca. 1400.

Annual summer and early autumn fairs in Sipoo, Pernaja and Pyhtää and the summer fair in Porvoo Saksala may have been organised in the context of ecclesiastical feasts of respective parish churches. In addition to the tar which had a growing status as an export article since the latter half of the 16th century, all the summer fairs were also connected to spawning seasons of Salmon, whitefish and Baltic herring, where summer fairs of Sipoo (24 June) and Porvoo in Saksala (1-2 July) of Julian calendar corresponded July the 4th and 12th in Gregorian calendar which was the high season of Salmon and right after the early spawning of Baltic herring which took place in the inner archipelago of the Gulf of Finland. Julian dates for autumn fairs at Pyhtää parish church (10 August), Vähä-Ahvenkoski (24 August), Porvoo (14 September), and Pernaja (29 September) correspond Gregorian calendar dates of 20 August, 3 and 24 September and 9 October, all of which occurred during the high season of whitefish migration and the autumn spawning of Baltic herring in the outer archipelago.
Toll_Description: The 1/32 duty worth of all goods intended for sale in towns and fairs and brought to the site by peasants was collected in Pernaja Forsby since 1622.

name: Walsrode
Settlement_Description: Around 986 Count Wala founded a monastery of canonesses (from 1225: Benedictine nuns), next to which a market settlement developed. The settlement received borough ('weichbild') privileges after the Brunswick law in 1383/88.

name: Kausala
Settlement_Description: <b>Inn:</b> An inn was established in Kausala in the end of the 16th c. In 1642, Sipi Pekanpoika is mentioned as the innkeeper.

name: Berlaar
Settlement_Description: First mentioned in c. 1155, in a copy from 1243.

name: Ahtiala
Settlement_Description: <b>Inn:</b> An inn was established in Ahtiala in 1642, and Jyri Markunpoika was appointed as the innkeeper.

name: Oostburg
Settlement_Description: In the period 879-918, a castle ('burcht') was built at the site of Oostburg as a defence against attacks by Norsemen. The first mention in written records dates from 949.
Town_Description: Oostburg was first mentioned as town in 1174. It must have been  granted town rights before 1187 by Philip of Alsace, count of Flanders. After a flourishing in the 13th century, the town shrunk significantly and lost its urban character.
Fair_Description: In 1297/8 (Jan.) count Gui de Dampierre granted a fair for three days starting St. Laurentius (August 10).
Toll_Description: Oostburg was one of the toll stations of the Zwin toll of the count of Flanders after 1252. A toll-account dated 1380 is preserved, combined with a.o. Damme. And another dated 1485 on beer with a.o. Sluis and Cadzand. In 1502, a "knight toll" ('riddertol') is mentioned in Oostburg, that was abolished that year because of the construction of the canal Brugse Vaart.

name: Vuolenkosken silta ja lautta
Bridge_Description: Vuolenkoski bridge on the Northern route of Upper Viipuri Road was burned down in the Russian attack of 1592, and again in the internal conflict of the realm between duke Karl and Finnish nobility in Finland in 1599. The bridge was maintained by Hollola judicial district in Häme and Lapvesi judicial district under Viipuri castle. Häme was exempted from the bridge in the time of king Johan III (1568-92). The bridge was not rebuilt in the beginning of the 17th century but replaced with a ferry because of low use the road. In the late 16th century, the bridge is said to have been 200 fathoms long (sw. fathom = 1,78 m, ca. 356 m). The Northern and Southern routes of Upper Viipuri Road were organised into a common road between Viipuri and Häme castles at the latest in the first quarter of the 15th century, but the organisation of the maintenance may date to mid-14th century. The Northern route via Vuolenkoski appears to have been more important in the 16th century, whereas in the 17th the Southern road was the main route. In 1556 king Gustaf I ordered either of the routes demolished, apparently without consecutions.
Ferry_Description: The ferry operated 1600-1914 near the former bridge in Siltasaari and after that closer to the falls until it was replaced with a bridge in 1936.

name: Kuortti
Settlement_Description: <b>Inn:</b> An inn was established in Kuortti in 1650. It continued to serve until 19th and early 20th centuries.

name: Espoo
Settlement_Description: <b>Inn:</b> According to a list from 1545-1550, in Espoo parish there was an alehouse that served travellers both by land and sea. Exact location unknown.

name: Zomergem
Settlement_Description: Earliest mention in the ninth century in a copy dating from 941.

name: Forsbyn silta (Pernaja)
Bridge_Description: The earliest bridge site on Great Coastal Road in Pernaja Koskenkylä may have been located ca. 100 m South from the later bridge. The bridge is documented in an early 18th century map and was maintained in the 18th century by Pernaja parish. The earliest bridge on the site may date to the first organisation of the maintenance of the Great Coastal Road as a uniform land route between Turku and Viborg in the 1340s and 1360s.

name: Antvorskov
Settlement_Description: The village of Antvorskov was first mentioned in 1231, but is significantly older. The settlement had no church but was part of the parish of Skt. Peders Landssogn.

name: Hölttä
Settlement_Description: <b>Inn:</b> Hölttä village was previously located less than a kilometre southwards from the Great Savo Road. An inn was established there in 1639.

name: Uusikylä
Settlement_Description: <b>Inn:</b> Uusikylä is mentioned as a place for accommodation in the travel account of Duke Johan of Finland from 1556. It would also be a possible place for a bailiff (fi. vouti, sw. fogde)  in Jaakko Teitti's list in 1556. The tavern was then owned by the bailiff (fi. vouti, sw. fogde) Augustinus Finne. Official inn was established in 1584, and Paavo Juhonpoika was appointed as the innkeeper. Uusikylä inn had many owners: 1592 Tuomas Heikinpoika and Juhani Heikinpoika the following year, 1595 Juhani Maununpoika and Tuomas Heikinpoika (again) in the following year. In 1597 the inn was hosted by Lasse Paavonpoika, 1598-1600 Juhani Matinpoika, and 1600 Tuomas Heikinpoika (again). In 1620s, there was a transport organiser (sw. skjutsrättare, fi. kyytirättäri) in Uusikylä.  In 1642, Heikki Heikinpoika was the innkeeper. The tavern ordinance from 1651 mentions that Heikki Erkinpoika in Uusikylä is the only innkeeper in Nastola, and he is the richest innkeeper in Upper Hollola district. Uusikylä was in the intersection of Upper Wiborg Road and local roads going north and south, so innkeeping must have been lucrative.

name: Vuolenkoski
Settlement_Description:
Permanent agricultural settlement in Vuolenkoski dates to the 13th century. The village is first cited in 1472. Late medieval bridge on Upper Viipuri Road in Siltasaari cited in 1592 and 1599, when destroyed. Ferry 1600-1936. 

<b>Inn:</b> Food and drinks might have been served by the bridge and later the ferry. An official inn was established in 1642, and Jyri Hannunpoika was appointed as the innkeeper.

name: Morby (Espoo)
Settlement_Description: <b>Post house:</b> In 1638, the Royal Steward Bernhardt Steen von Steenhausen established a post house in the village of Morby in Espoo. It was located in the Nyby house.

name: Melby
Settlement_Description: The village of Melby was first mentioned in 1295, but is older. The parish church is from either the 12th or 13th century.

name: Sairila
Settlement_Description: <b>Inn:</b> Sairila served as a royal manor (fi: kuninkaankartano, sw: kungsgård) in 1557-1571. Royal manors were obliged to provide accommodation for travelling officials. Later, it served as an administrative center and a place for rural court gatherings until 1630, when it became again a state-owned manor (fi. latokartano, sw. ladugård). In 1650, Sairila manor was given to Löwen family.

name: Visulahti
Settlement_Description: <b>Inn:</b> An inn was established in Visulahti in 1572.Visulahti parish constable (fi: nimismies, sw: länsman) ran a tavern in his house in 1639.

name: Juva
Settlement_Description: <b>Inn:</b> There was a medieval tavern in Juva parish village, serving both lay and ecclesiastical travellers. An inn was established in 1572.

name: Unaja
Settlement_Description: Permanent agricultural settlement in Unaja village dates to the 13th century. Assisted by a favourable location at the end of a deep inlet from the sea and alongside the common road between Turku and Ulvila, the village hosted a trading post and possible burgher community predating Rauma town in 1413, when it paid the crown an annual tax of 50 marks. At the same time the tax for Ulvila was 20 and for Turku 600 marks. In the 1560s the village had 15 peasant farms.

name: Vauranoja
Settlement_Description: <b>Inn:</b> Three farmers from Loimaa were travelling home from Turku in 1645, when they stopped in an alehouse between Raatikainen and Haverinkylä villages. The location might be in Vauranoja village.

Ferry_Description: See ferry in Krimpen aan den IJssel.

name: Lauttakylä
Settlement_Description: Permanent agricultural settlement in Huittinen (sw. Huittis) goes back to the Iron Age. Ecclesiastic parish was formed in the early 13th century. Huittinen (sw. Huittisby) village on the eastern bank of Loimijoki river is first cited in 1390. Lauttakylä (literally Ferry village) on the opposite bank in the west is in the 16th century cadasters cited under Huittinen, but is of medieval origin. The name Lauttakylä referring to the ferry on the common road between the two villages is documented first time in the surviving material in 1620.
Bridge_Description: Lauttakylä ferry crossing Loimijoki on the common road from Huittinen to medieval Ulvila (sw. Ulvsby) and Pori (sw. Björneborg, est. 1558) towns is first cited in 1629. It was renovated in 1634 and again in 1650. The ferry was replaced with a floating bridge at the latest in 1644 when the structure of the bridge is included in the map of Huittinen village. The ferry was very likely of medieval origin. Both the ferry and the floating bridge were maintained by Huittinen parish.

name: Ylistaro
Settlement_Description:
Permanent agricultural settlement in Kokemäki (sw. Kumo) goes back to the Iron Age. The medieval parish organisation in Satakunta dates to the early 13th century with precursors in the latter half of the 12th century. Ylistaro village, which was located south of Kokemäenjoki river on the common road between Huittinen and Ulvila was in the 15th century among the most important villages in the parish. A storage house on the village plot was already in the late Middle Ages maintained as a place of worship and pilgrimage of bishop Henrik of Finland, who according to the tradition had slept in the outbuilding the night before his martyrdom in Köyliö on 20 January (ca. 1156). The dendrochronological dating of the preserved logs of the building varies between the winter seasons 1472/73-1623/24. St. Henry's Chapel, completed in 1857 to protect the remaining structure, is Finland's first museum building built with public funds. A large gathering of people in Ylistaro at the time of the feast of St Henrik is documented on 18 January 1439 when the agreement ending the peasant revolt in Ylä-Satakunta area was sealed with the seal of the peasant community (land) of Satakunta. A common building (Sw. soknae stuvae, fi pitäjäntupa) maintained by the parish in Ylistaro is cited as the meeting place of the parish court in 1452 and demolished in 1555. 

<b>Inn:</b> Medieval trading posts likely had private alehouses and taverns to serve travelling merchants and farmers. During court gatherings in Ylistaro common building (Sw. soknae stuvae, fi pitäjäntupa) there were most likely private entrepreneurs serving food, drinks, and lodging. There was also a house called Kesti (ger. Gast) in Ylistaro, which refers to innkeeping. The house is mentioned in a will by Henrik Jaspersson in 1538, when he donated the farm to Antti Tolva's daughter, Anna. She might be the same Anna Kassari who paid the house's taxes in 1540. After Anna, the house owners were Kadrin Kesti, and after 1554, Erich Gest, who also had a nickname <i>Sluk</i>, Glutton. Kesti farm was annexed to Uotila farm in 1585. Pekka Matinpoika from Uotila served as a parish constable (fi: nimismies, sw: länsman) and innkeeper in Ylistaro in 1651-1654. His father was a parish constable as well, and Kesti/Uotila might have served as an inn also during his time. Parish constables were obliged to keep a tavern in the late 16th and early 17th centuries. In 1651, Uotila inn's treasury was stolen when the family was brewing ale. Others served drinks in Ylistaro village as well: in 1636, Mats Jacobsson and Henrik Andersson were selling drinks during church service, and the case was sent to ecclesiastical court. In the same year, serving of drinks was made a monopoly of the official inns.
Fair_Description: King Magnus Eriksson confirmed the inhabitants of the borough of Ulvila (villanis Vlsby) the annual right to trade in the borough of Kokemäki (ad villam Kwma) from January the 13th to Easter in 1347. In 1365 king Albrekt of Mecklenburg chartered the town with rights in align to the town law of king Magnus Eriksson and confirmed the burghers the right to trade in Kokemäki. The trading site may have been located in Ylistaro village, or less than a kilometre downstream in Villiö on the northern side of the river. Villiö is first cited as a village in 1362 and hosted many sessions of parish court of Kokemäki from the 1460s to the 1490s. In the closing decades of the 15th century some of the sessions were held in the rural merchant guild house of Kokemäki, which in 1492 was in Villiö.

name: Gloms
Settlement_Description: <b>Inn:</b> An inn was established in Gloms in 1653.

name: Pyhtää (Kirkonkylä)
Settlement_Description: Permanent agricultural settlement in Pyhtää (sw. Pyttis) area and Eastern Nyland (sw. Östra Nyland) dates to the Swedish colonisation in the latter half of the 13th century when new farms were founded amongst earlier 12th and 13th century area of usufruct and colonisation from inner Häme. The parish organisation of Eastern Nyland dates at the latest to the first quarter of the 14th century. Independent parish at the latest since 1380. Stone church in the 1460s. The border between Sweden and Russia was in 1743–1809 in Ahvenkoski. <b>Inn:</b> There were several alehouses in Pyhtää in 1543, when they paid taxes to the crown and the Vogt (fi. vouti, sw. fogde). "Aniala i Pyttis" (Anjala in Pyhtää) is mentioned as a place for overnight accommodation in the travel account of Duke Johan of Finland from 1555.

King Gustaf I granted the burghers of Helsinki in 1553 the rights for three fairs in Eastern Nyland in Helsinki, in Pernaja (sw. Pernå), and in Pyhtää. Sipoo (sw. Sibbo), Pyhtää and Porvoo fairs were confirmed as the privilege of Helsinki burghers in 1576. In 1584 burghers of the newly re-established Porvoo complained to the authorities, that right after the sea and rivers were free of ice, burghers of Helsinki arrived to trade with peasants of the region at the Old Royal Manor (in Saksala) and elsewhere despite of the official fair dates which were Midsummer in Sipoo (sw. Sibbo), Visitation of Mary (2 July) and Excaltation of the Cross (14 September) in Porvoo, St Michael (29 September) in Pernaja (sw. Pernå) and St Laurentius (10 August) at Pyhtää (sw. Pyttis) church. Previous traditional local fairs in Mustijoki (sw. Svartså) and Kulloonmäki (sw. Kullo) in Porvoo, Pikku Pernajanlahti (sw. Lillpernåviken) in Pernaja and elsewhere were prohibited. Pyhtää Bartholomeus fair in Vähä-Ahvenkoski is cited in an almanac in 1616, but the continuation and character of Pyhtää Church fair after 1584 is unknown.

Annual summer and early autumn fairs in Sipoo, Pernaja and Pyhtää and the summer fair in Porvoo Saksala may have been organised in the context of ecclesiastical feasts of respective parish churches. In addition to the tar which had a growing status as an export article since the latter half of the 16th century, all the summer fairs were also connected to spawning seasons of Salmon, whitefish and Baltic herring, where summer fairs of Sipoo (24 June) and Porvoo in Saksala (1-2 July) of Julian calendar corresponded July the 4th and 12th in Gregorian calendar which was the high season of Salmon and right after the early spawning of Baltic herring which took place in the inner archipelago of the Gulf of Finland. Julian dates for autumn fairs at Pyhtää parish church (10 August), Vähä-Ahvenkoski (24 August), Porvoo (14 September), and Pernaja (29 September) correspond Gregorian calendar dates of 20 August, 3 and 24 September and 9 October, all of which occurred during the high season of whitefish migration and the autumn spawning of Baltic herring in the outer archipelago.

name: Partala
Settlement_Description: <b>Inn:</b> A royal manor (fi: kuninkaankartano, sw: kungsgård) was established in Partala farm in 1556. Royal manors were obliged to provide accommodation for travelling officials. It is also mentioned in Jaakko Teitti's list in 1556 as a possible place for a bailiff (fi. vouti, sw. fogde). Later, Partala farm served as the parish constable (fi: nimismies, sw: länsman). The inn is mentioned in 1639, but parish constables were obliged to keep tavern also before.

name: Lammainen
Settlement_Description:
Permanent agricultural settlement in Nakkila and Harjavalta goes back to the Iron Age. Lammainen (sw. Lammais) stream in Kokemäenjoki was since the early 13th century important fishing ground for salmon and whitefish, where the bishops of Turku had a fishery as early as in 1347. Lammainen village is first cited in 1412. According to a 1414 contract of bishop Magnus II Tavast of Turku with his three tenants in Pirkkala region, Lammainen was also a staple and storage point for the bishop’s fur and other revenues collected in Ylä-Satakunta region. In the contract the three tenants commit each to transport bishop’s freights once a year with sledges from Sastamala to Lammainen, i.e. using the winter way from Sastamala via Äetsä and Kokemäki to bishop’s storage facilities next to the fisheries.

<b>Inn:</b> Medieval gathering places could have private alehouses and taverns to serve travelling merchants and farmers. Pirilä farm on the other side of Kokemäenjoki river got its name from a Middle Low German name for porridge or gruel, so it might have served as a medieval tavern. There are also many Kilta("Guild")-names in the area, which could refer to a medieval guild house, or more broadly to a place of gathering and feast, also after the Middle Ages. Lammainen is mentioned in Jaakko Teitti's list in 1556 as a possible place for a bailiff (fi. vouti, sw. fogde) In 1640, an official inn was established in nearby Torttila village.
Fair_Description: Pori was in 1602 and 1604 granted rights to three annual fairs, one of which took place in the town on apostle Bartolomeus (24 August). The other two fairs took place in Pirkkala in Harju at Candlemas (2 February) and on St Laurentius (10.8.) in Ulvila (Nakkila) Lammainen (some 25 kms upstream from Pori and 20 kms downstream from Kokemäki). Lammais fair is first cited in 1604 and it took place in the high season of whitefish. The tradition of mid-August fish fair in Harjavalta was alive in the 1860s but was extinguished in the end of the 19th century because of log-floating.

name: Heikkilä
Settlement_Description: <b>Inn:</b> An inn was established in Heikkilä in 1639.

name: Salmenkylä
Settlement_Description: Permanent agricultural settlement in Vehkalahti area dates to the 13th century. Vehkalahti parish was established at the latest in the 1340s. The farm of the Vehkalahti parish constable (sw. länsmän, fi. nimismies) was in Salmi village in 1598-1603, 1616, 1620-22 and 1627-29. <b>Inn:</b> An alehouse is mentioned in Vehkalahti in a 1545-1550 list. It served travellers both by land and sea. Parish constables were obliged to keep a tavern in the late 16th and early 17th centuries, so the Vehkalahti constable probably served as a tavern as well.

name: Kaihunmäki
Settlement_Description: <b>Inn:</b> An inn was established in Kaihunmäki in 1649.

name: Nuutilanmäki
Settlement_Description: <b>Inn:</b> An inn was established in Nuutilanmäki in 1649.

name: Brandö
Settlement_Description: <b>Post house:</b> In 1638, the Royal Steward Bernhardt Steen von Steenhausen established six post houses in Åland, along the route from Stockholm to Turku. One of the post houses was located in Brandö.

name: Toivola
Settlement_Description: <b>Inn:</b> Toivola is mentioned in Jaakko Teitti's list in 1556 as a possible place for a bailiff (fi. vouti, sw. fogde). It was the first great village when travelling from Häme. In 1585, Hemminki Matinpoika Toivonen, is mentioned as the innkeeper, and in 1588, Matti Pietarinpoika. The inn rights travelled between houses, and in 1612, innkeeping was given to the parish constable (fi: nimismies, sw: länsman). Toivola inn was established again in 1639, and it continued to serve until the end of the century.

name: Sannainen (Taivassalo)
Settlement_Description: <b>Post house:</b> In 1638, the Royal Steward Bernhardt Steen von Steenhousen established a post house in the village of Sannainen in Taivassalo.

name: Haistilan lautta
Ferry_Description: Ulvila (sw. Ulfsby) Haistila ferry on a common road over Kokemäenjoki river. First mentioned in 1641 when a new ferry was built on the site. Rebuild in 1651, 1656 and 1682. In 1645-47 the ferryman sold beer to travellers on a commission by a farmer in Ravani hamlet. The site was the only permanently maintained crossing on Kokemäenjoki rivermouth area before a ferry (1811) and a floating bridge (1855) were introduced in Pori. In 1641 Haistila ferry was maintained by peasants of Ulvila parish. The crossing was free of charge in 1807, but a fee was introduced some time before 1840. The ferry was taken into the custody of the state in 1921 and was abandoned in 1953. Considering the role of Haistila village as the site of the parish court in Ulvila in 1470, 1473 and 1550-52, the ferry is likely have been first organised at the latest in the latter half of the 15th century.

name: Lapväärtti
Settlement_Description: <b>Inn:</b> Närpiö parish constables (fi: nimismies, sw: länsman) were usually located in Lapväärti. Lapväärti is mentioned in Jaakko Teitti's list in 1556 as a possible place for a bailiff (fi. vouti, sw. fogde). Ture Pedersson Bielke, Swedish nobleman and castellan of St. Olaf's Castle in Savo, stopped to change horses and dine in Lapväärti in 1557. Parish constable Eskil Eskilsson is mentioned as an innkeeper in 1617. In 1624, Jöns Olofsson was appointed as the innkeeper, Jöns Mickelsson in 1632, and Lasse Matsson in 1649. In 1654, the innkeeper was parish constable Erik Jönsson, who is still mentioned in office in 1666.

name: Knuuttila
Settlement_Description: <b>Inn:</b> An inn was established in Knuuttila farm in Kauhajoki in 1627. In 1641, the innkeeper was Niilo Knuutinpoika Knuuttila. Knuuttila also had the first distillation pan that is mentioned in Kauhajoki in 1661.

name: Karleby
Settlement_Description: Permanent agricultural settlement in Kaarlela (sw. Karleby) area dates to the colonisation of the late 13th century and the beginning of the 14th. Karleby was founded as a chapel of Pedersöre parish in the first half of the 15th century and established as an independent parish some time in between 1486–1511. A stone church was built in the second third of the 16th century. After the founding of Uusikaarlepyy (Nykarleby) parish (1607) and town (1617/1620), the parish and town (1620) of Karleby was called Gamlakarleby. The traditional Finnish name of the town is Kokkola. The oldest harbour of the area was located North of Karleby church in Tervaholma.
Fair_Description: Trade in the most important traditional trading posts at major river mouths in the Gulf of Bothnia area was regulated at the latest in 1420, when the crown furnished them with storage houses, started to collect toll, and prohibited other traditional trading sites alongside the Bothnic coastline. One of these was very likely near Karleby chapel church, which was established in the early 15th century. The oldest harbour of the area was located near the church in Tervaholma. Burghers of Oulu had since 1610 the sole right of trading between Kemi and Karleby, but their rights in Karleby and Kalajoki were cancelled when the new town of Gamlakarleby was established in 1620. Since the annual fair in Kokkola was in 1642 ordained to be held on St Bartholomeus (24 August), in 1650 on St Olaf (29 July) and in 1652 again on St Bartholomeus, the medieval fair may have been either of these feasts or consisted of a longer period between them.
Toll_Description: Karleby has very likely been one of the “new havens” of the Gulf of Bothnia area, which the crown furnished with storage houses and started to collect toll in 1420.

name: Iitiä
Settlement_Description: <b>Inn:</b> Iitiä is mentioned in Jaakko Teitti's list in 1556 as a possible place for a bailiff (fi. vouti, sw. fogde). The village was already under bailiff Mats Matsson.

name: Espoo (Church)
Settlement_Description: <b>Inn:</b> Olof, vicar in Espoo parish, was compensated from the yearly taxes because he had served food, drink and accommodation to travellers. Gustaf II Adolf of Sweden confirmed the compensations to the new vicar Johan Martini in 1624.

name: Lusi
Settlement_Description: <b>Inn:</b> Lusi is mentioned in Jaakko Teitti's list in 1556 as a possible place for a bailiff (fi. vouti, sw. fogde). Parish constable (fi: nimismies, sw: länsman) Paavo Sipinpoika ran a tavern from 1587 until 1589, and both his sons Tuomas and Hannu served as constables and innkeepers (1594-1600 and 1601-1615 respectively). After that, the paris constable office was cancelled, but opened again in 1639, when Count Per Brahe the Younger, Governor-General of Finland, established the Lusi inn again. In the same year, people of Asikkala parish were ordered to clear stones from Kuorehkoski rapid near Lusi, so people could travel to Savo by boat. In 1646, Mikko Hannunpoika is mentioned as the parish constable and the innkeeper, and the inn continued to operate also later.

name: Männäinen
Settlement_Description: Permanent agricultural settlement in Kalanti (before 1936 Uusikirkko, sw. Kaland, Nykyrka) area goes back to the Iron Age. The parish is first mentioned in 1411 but was established very likely in the first half of the 13th century. Stone church was built between 1430 and 1450. On 17 May 1616 King Gustaf II Adolf ordained a town to be established in Männäinen in Uusikirkko parish, where the weekly Saturday market attracted burghers from towns and surrounding hinterland as far as Häme. Focused on the trade of wooden vessels made in the area. Männäinen Saturday market is the only weekly market known from Early modern rural Finland. The location of the new town of Uusikaupunki (sw. Nystad) was soon changed to a more suitable site by the sea, where e the town was officially established on 19 April 1617. The weekly market remained in Männäinen, which was frequented by the burghers of Uusikaupunki until 1642.
Fair_Description: In 1616 Männäinen also hosted annual summer fair of old on St Olaf (29 July), which continued as a local fair after the foundation of Uusikaupunki. Very likely of medieval origin the fair was arranged on the feast of one of the two known patrons of Kalanti church (Virgin Mary and St Olaf). The site for the weekly market and annual fairs was located ca. one kilometer downstream from the parish church on the banks of Männäistenjoki river.
Toll_Description: The 1/32 duty worth of all goods intended for sale in towns and fairs and brought to the site by peasants was collected in Männäinen since 1622.

name: Ravani
Settlement_Description:
Ragvaldsby (Ravani) was founded during the Swedish colonisation at the latter half of the 13th century or early 14th. A yeoman farmer held the office of Parish Constable (fi. Nimismies, sw. Länsman) of Ulvila parish in 1583. 

<b>Inn:</b> The first inns In Ravani may date to the 15th century. Ulvila parish constables, who lived in Ravani, most likely served as innkeepers as well. An official inn is cited in Ragvaldsby in 1633. In 1642, Sippola farm served as the inn, and Arvi Pietarinpoika was the innkeeper. In 1655, two accused thieves were seen drinking in many places between Pori and Ravani.

name: Raholammi
Settlement_Description: <b>Inn:</b> An inn was established in Raholammi farm in Jalasjärvi in 1650s. Esko Jaakonpoika was appointed as the innkeeper.

name: Lapua
Settlement_Description:
Permanent agricultural settlement in Lapua (sw. Lappo) dates to the late 14th and early 15th centuries. A chaplain was ordained in 1555, independent parish was established in 1581.

<b>Inn:</b> There might have been an inn already during the 16th c. in Härsilä village ca. 1,5 km northwest by Lapua river. It was established in 1640s at the latest. In 1641, an inn was established by Lapua church, and Tuomas Niilonpoika was appointed as the innkeeper. In 1663, officials in stated that only the inns in Härsilä, Stroka and Ylijepua are needed in Lapua area, and tried to close the inns in Kuhalammi, Toppari, Hemminki and Ylinurmo. It was thought that their owners had established inns only to receive tax exemptions and freedom from military service.
Fair_Description: The trading areas of Vaasa (1606) and Nykarleby (1620) towns hosted of old peasant fairs in three parishes of Lapua, Vöyri and Isokyrö, of which burghers of Vaasa were granted sole rights to St Henrik (20 January) and St Laurentius (10 August) fair in Isokyrö, and Nykarleby to Candelmas fair (2 February) in Lapua, and St Margaret (20 July) and St Mary (8 September?) fairs in Vöyri. Burghers of Vaasa were further granted the right to visit St Margaret fair of Vöyri in 1624. In the early 17th century local fair was also held at St Michael (29 September) in Lapua. The fair site was very likely somewhere near the place where Nurmo river flows to Lapua river.
Toll_Description: The 1/32 duty worth of all goods intended for sale in towns and fairs and brought to the site by peasants was collected in Lapua fair since 1622.

Ferry_Description: In 1236 in both settlements named Krimpen (Krimpen aan den Lek and aan den IJssel) ferries are first mentioned. In 1448 two ferries are found in Krimpen aan den Lek, probably one to Slikkerveer across the river Merwede and one to Elshout (nowadays Kinderdijk) across the river Lek. In 1370 a ferry to Ridderkerk is mentioned as a fief from the seigniory of the Lek, but it is uncertain whether this refers to the ferry in Krimpen.

name: Jyränkö
Settlement_Description: <b>Inn:</b> Sipi Laurinpoika served as a parish constable (fi: nimismies, sw: länsman) and an innkeeper in Jyränkö at least from 1587. He was one of the richest men in Eastern Häme, and he kept also a tavern in Heinola parish village. He is not mentioned in duty after 1599. Niemelä farm served as an inn in 1649, when Jyränkö ferry is also mentioned. The ferrymen were Perttu Tuomaanpoika Karhu and Tuomas Eerikinpoika, who had the right to collect grain for their upkeep from farmers in Asikkala parish and everyone in 3 miles radius (ca. 18 km).

name: Ulvila
Settlement_Description: Permanent agricultural settlement in Kokemäenjoki rivermouth area and Ulvila (sw. Ulvsby) dates to the Iron Age with additional layer of Swedish colonisation on the coast from the late 13th and early 14th centuries. The river valley was visited by Gotlandic and since the 13th century German merchants, who established rural guild houses to Kokemäki and traded with local and inland population with salmon, whitefish and furs. In the 13th century the rivermouth area had several economic and ecclesiastic nodes, one of which was located next to the later Ulvila vicarage in Liikistö ca. 1 km upstream of the medieval town. The location of the parish church stabilised in the beginning of the 14th century to its present site in Ulvila, where merchant burials in the early wooden church were in the late 13th and early 14th century furnished with limestone slabs. The parish church served both the rural and town population until 1550 and was built from stone in the 1490s.
Town_Description:
The oldest known charter of the town of Ulvila (sw. Ulvsby) is from 1365, but the area hosted an economic and ecclesiastical node of local population and merchants already in the turn of the 14th century. The burgher community of the town was formed after the initiative of the crown in the 1340s and 1350s, when the merchants who had previously settled alongside the river were relocated to the town. Ulvila is first cited in 1344 in a confirmation of land transaction, which in 1347 was said to have been corroborated in the presence of parishioners, townspeople (lat. civitatenses), and rector of the parish in the Guild house of St Gertrud of Ulvila. King Magnus Eriksson confirmed the inhabitants of the borough of Ulvila (lat. villanis Vlsby) the annual right to trade in the borough of Kokemäki (lat. ad villam Kwma) from January the 13th to Easter in 1347. The same year bishop of Turku consecrated Ulvila graveyard. A year later the Royal headman of Finland ordered merchants still living in the countryside to pay their taxes to Ulvila and prohibited burghers to move out of the town. One of the last merchants to resettle in the town may have been Andreas Vari, who in 1355 sold his farm in Forsby in Kokemäki to the bishop of Turku to move to Ulvila. King Erik Magnusson confirmed the rights of the inhabitants of Ulvila in 1357. In 1365 king Albrekt of Mecklenburg chartered the town with rights in align to the town law of king Magnus Eriksson and confirmed the burghers the right to trade in Kokemäki and Gulf of Bothnia area. The trading rights of Ulvila were modified in 1491, when merchant sailing to foreign cities and elsewhere was allowed excluding Gotland, but all exports of victualies had to go to Stockholm or Turku only. In 1502 all export of Öregrund, Östhammar, Gävle, Ulvila and Rauma to foreign cities was banned. The charters of 1491 and 1502 were confirmed in 1504, and in 1512 with export rights. King Gustaf I restricted the export of Ulvila to Stockholm and Turku only, banned all export of Ulvila, Rauma and Turku outside of Stockholm in 1531, but confirmed the rights in 1533. Gustaf I ordered the burghers of Ulvila to move to the newly established Helsinki in 1550. The burghers were allowed to return in the mid-1550s but were eventually settled in 1558 in the new town of Pori (sw. Björneborg). An important motive for the new site was postglacial land uplift, which hampered sailing to Ulvila. The northernmost chartered town in the Swedish realm throughout its existence to 1550, Ulvila’s plotland covered the area from north of the parish church alongside Kirkkojuopa brook to river Kokemäenjoki. The site of the market place or public buildings other than the church are not known. No maps or early modern surveys of the town area has survived. The approximate size before the year 1550 is known through later inventories and archaeological surveys. The common Bothnic coastal from Haistila ferry and further north to Korsholm traversed the town. The population of Ulvila has been estimated to ca. 450 in the 1540s, when the size of its tax to the crown were half of that of Rauma and one sixth of Turku.
<b>Ulvila Royal manor:</b> After the annulation of the town Ulvila Royal Manor active in 1551–58 was established in the area. The manor consisted of Ulvila vicarage and other landed properties and served as the administrative centre of Satakunta to 1556, after that a smaller bailiwick to 1558, when the manor was relocated to Pori. Duke Johan spent several winters with his court in Ulvila and Pori Royal manor during the time of his Duchy in Finland 1556–63. 
<b>Inn:</b> Ulvila Royal manor served accommodation also for traveling officials.
Fair_Description: The dates of annual fairs in Ulvila are not known. King Magnus Eriksson confirmed the inhabitants of Ulvila the right to trade in Kokemäki annually from the eight days after Epiphany (13 January) to Easter. King Albrekt of Mecklenburg renewed the rights in 1365. Pori was in 1602 and 1604 granted rights to three annual fairs, one of which took place in the town on apostle Bartolomeus (24 August) and is cited in almanacs in 1585 and 1598. The other two fairs took place in Pirkkala in Harju at Candlemas (2 February) and on St Laurentius (10.8.) in Ulvila (Nakkila) Lammainen (some 25 kms upstream from Pori and 20 kms downstream from Kokemäki).

name: Vöyri
Settlement_Description:
Permanent agricultural settlement in Vöyri (sw. Vörå) dates to the Iron Age. After the 13th century and early 14th century Finnish and Swedish colonisation the area was split ecclesiastically to inland Finnish speaking chapel under Isokyrö and coastal Swedish speaking chapel of Mustasaari parishes. Vöyri is first cited as an administrative parish in 1478, and cited as an independent ecclesiastical parish in 1494.

<b>Inn:</b> An inn might be located by the church, since churches usually had taverns in the Middle Ages and 16th-17th-centuries. Ture Pedersson Bielke, Swedish nobleman and castellan of St. Olaf's Castle in Savo, stopped to change horses by the Vöyri church in 1557.
Fair_Description:
The trading areas of Vaasa (1606) and Nykarleby (1620) towns hosted of old peasant fairs in three parishes of Lapua, Vöyri and Isokyrö, of which burghers of Vaasa were granted sole rights to St Henrik (20 January) and St Laurentius (10 August) fair in Isokyrö, and Nykarleby to Candelmas fair (2 February) in Lapua, and St Margaret (20 July) and St Mary (8 September?) fairs in Vöyri. Burghers of Vaasa were further granted the right to visit St Margaret fair of Vöyri in 1624. In the early 17th century local fair was also held at St Michael (29 September) in Lapua. Since 1643 the right to attend fairs in Vöyri and Isokyrö were held by burghers of both towns. In 1650 burghers of Nykarleby were further granted sole right to hold a local fair on St Nicolaus (6 December) for four days in Vöyri. After continuous litigation, fairs in Vöyri and Isokyrö were granted free for all towns in 1682. Since the late medieval chapel church of Vöyri was dedicated to St Margaret and St Anna (15 December), and the medieval parish church of Isokyrö to St Laurentius, St Margaret fair in Vöyri and St Laurentius fair in Isokyrö may have been of early 16th century or earlier medieval origin.
According to Johannes Qvist (1909), Vöyri fairs were held on Herrholmen island in the mouth of Vöyrinjoki river, where an old fair place is marked on a map from 1845. The rivermouth was apparently an important stopover on the coastal sailing route as early as in 12 July, 1367, when King Albert of Mecklenburg received a delegation of peasants from the Satakunta region at the Vöyri harbor (apud portum Vøra) and issued an order concerning the demolition of the castle in Kokemäki. The date is just a week before the later 17th-century. Because of the isostaitic uplift, the 17th century fair site may have been more inland upstream the river. Winter fair took in the 19th century place near the church.
Toll_Description: The 1/32 duty worth of all goods intended for sale in towns and fairs and brought to the site by peasants was collected in Vöyri fair since 1622.

name: Nurmo
Settlement_Description: <b>Inn:</b> Perttu Vilpunpoika Luukko, a lay member of the court (fi. lautamies, sw. nämbdeman), was appointed as a travel organiser (fi. kyytirättäri, sw. skjutsrättare) in Nurmo in 1620s. He might have served accommodation as well. An inn was established in Penttilä farm in 1642, and Kreki Tapaninpoika Penttilä was appointed as the innkeeper. Penttilä farm was large, and could thus serve as an inn. In 1663, officials stated that only the inns in Härsilä, Stroka and Ylijepua are needed in Lapua area, and tried to close the inns in Kuhalammi, Toppari, Hemminki and Ylinurmo. It was thought that their owners had established inns only to receive tax exemptions and freedom from military service. Luukko 1945 claims that Ylinurmo means here the inn of Antti Tapaninpoika in Penttilä farm.

name: Olhava
Settlement_Description: <b>Inn:</b> Olhava village had a transport organiser (fi. kyytirättäri, sw. skjutsrättare) serving Ii parish constable. An inn was established in 1640s at the latest.

name: Böle (Siuntio)
Settlement_Description: <b>Post house:</b> In 1638, the Royal Steward Bernhardt Steen von Steenhausen established a post house in the Heicka house, located in the village of Böle in Siuntio. The post houses located on the coastal road typically served their purpose for a long time. In the village of Böle, there was postal service activity throughout the entire period of the post house system from 1638 to 1816.

name: Lauroinen
Settlement_Description: <b>Inn:</b> An inn was established in Lauroinen in 1642, and Knuutti Klemetinpoika Seppä was appointed as the innkeeper. Knuutti served also as a parish constable (fi: nimismies, sw: länsman).

name: Lekkerkerk
Ferry_Description: A ferry between Lekkerkerk (Out-Leckerlant) en Nieuw-Lekkerland crossing the river Lek is first found in 1326. It was part of the seigniory of the Lek and the ferry was a fief from the count of Holland. Both villages made up one parish.

name: Porin kuninkaankartano
Settlement_Description: <b>Pori Royal manor (sw. Björneborgs kungsgård):</b> When duke Johan founded Pori, he established in 1559 a new Royal manor on the riverbank East of the town on a location where he planned to build a residential castle. The castle newer materialised, but the site was furnished with a new main building and other facilities translocated from Ulvila Royal manor. The manor served as a centre of various administrative and economic entities in Satakunta to the beginning of the 17th century, but its activities came to an end after the reorganisation of provincial administration in 1635 when the area was attached to the new Province of Turku and Pori. <b>Aborch castle:</b> The site of the Royal manor or its near surroundings may have in the turn of the 15th century been occupied by a wooden castle, which Jakob Abrahamsson (Djäkn) or Bo Jonsson (Grip) had founded in the rivermouth area in the 1370s or 1380s, possibly after 1387 when Jakob was granted the right to build fortifications in his domains. The only source of the castle is the 1395 contract between Jakob and the heirs of Bo Jonsson, where Jakob ceded Turku and Kastelholm castles with their bailiwicks, Wartholm castle with its bailiwick in Uusimaa and the castle of Aborch with its bailiwick in Satakunta and the castle of Vreghdenborch to Bo’s son Knut and widow Margareta Dume. The castle was demolished in the opening years of the 15th century after Kunt had ceded Turku castle and his wooden castles in Finland to Queen Margaret before the Easter of 1399.  The castle may have existed in 1390 when the bailiwick of Satakunta was in control of Jakob’s brother Mårten Abrahamsson. The location of Aborch has been contested in the scholarship since the 19th century with suggested sites in Kokemäki Forsby Linnaluoto, Kokemäki Isoluoto and Liikistö, but together with several other contemporary fortifications built in the time of Bo Jonsson and Jakob Abrahamsson in 1371-95, it must have been part of a larger initiative to furnish important rivermouths and inner archipelago sailing routes with castles.

name: Oravainen
Settlement_Description: <b>Inn:</b> Ture Pedersson Bielke, Swedish nobleman and castellan of St. Olaf's Castle in Savo, stopped to change horses by Oravainen church in 1557. In 1627, Mårten Erikson (Mårtens) was appointed as the innkeeper in Oravainen. In 1641, Carl Ifwarsson (Karls) was appointed as the innkeeper together with Åke Persson Grannas from Miemoinen. In 1651, Oravainen inns were hosted by the parish constable (fi. nimismies, sw. länsman) Bertil Ruuth and Karl Karlsson (Karls, previous innkeeper's son?), and in 1656-1657 Åke Persson was the innkeeper again. In 1657, Oravainen innkeepers were Karl Karlsson and Mats Bertilsson (Bertils) from Kovjoki village. They were also in charge of postal services.

name: Valmarinniemi (Kemi)
Settlement_Description: According to local tradition the oldest market site in Kemi was close to Valmarinniemi. Kemi is first cited in 1329, when it was together with Saloinen a chapel of Pedersöre parish. The earliest parish church was in Valmarinniemi where ten cremation burials from mid-eleventh century to the end of the 14th and a total of 157 inhumation burials from early 14th century to the latter half of the 15th were documented in 1981. In Kemi, site of annual fair was since the 15th century in Haminasaari, an island in river Kemijoki opposite the parsonage and Keminmaa early 16th century stone church where the parish church was relocated from Valmarinniemi sometime between the 1450s and 1517.
Fair_Description: The dates of fairs in Valmarinniemi area are unknown, but they have very likely followed the salmon season from midsummer to early August.

name: Keltti
Settlement_Description: Permanent agricultural settlement in Keltti dates to the 15th or late 14th century. The oldest village in the area is Ruotsula from where the settlement spread to Keltti on the western side of the river. The ferry site over the eastern branch of Kymijoki river at Keltti was in use until 1812. Keltti ferry site was in 1743-1808 located on the border between Sweden and Russia and was fortified form both sides of the river. <b>Inn:</b> An inn was established both in Keltti and Ruotsula (across the Kymijoki river) villages in 1584. Nuutti Simonpoika Ulvi was appointed as innkeeper in Ruotsula. In 1642, Paavali Matinpoika is mentioned as the innkeeper in Keltti.

name: Haapakrouvi
Settlement_Description: <b>Inn:</b> Esko Eskinpoika Kangas established an alehouse by the Lapuanjoki river in the 1640s. It served food and drink to travellers, no accommodation. The alehouse got the name Haapakrouvi ("Aspen inn") and was in service for more than hundred years. Haapakrouvi was located by water and winterways, so there were a lot of customers. During the 17th c., there were complaints how farmers can't afford to pay taxes because they drink all their money in Haapakrouvi, and one farmer's wife from Alanurmo complained that his husband drinks his money in the alehouse.

name: Helsinki Vanhakaupunki
Settlement_Description: Permanent agricultural settlement in Vantaanjoki (sw. Vanda å) rivermouth area and Eastern Nyland (sw. Östra Nyland) coast dates to the Swedish colonisation in the latter half of the 13th century when new farms were founded amongst earlier 12th and 13th century area of usufruct and colonisation from inner Häme. The parish organisation of Eastern Nyland dates at the latest to the first quarter of the 14th century, in Porvoo (sw. Borgå) and Helsinga possibly already to the third quarter of the 14th century. In 1351 King Magnus Eriksson donated the rights of two fisheries in Vantaanjoki river to the Cistercian Abbey of Padise in Estonia together with the patronate of Porvoo parish and its two chapels of Sipoo (sw. Sibbo) and Pernaja (sw. Pernå). The bishop and Cathedral Chapter of Turku reclaimed the ecclesiastical rights for the patronate in 1428. A stone church replaced the older wooden church in the 1450s.
Town_Description:
King Gustaf I founded Helsinki (sw. Helsingfors) in 1550 at the mouth of Vantaanjoki (sw. Vanda å) river on the site of medieval Forsby village (cited 1417). Same year the king ordered all the burghers of Ulvila (sw. Ulfsby), Rauma (sw. Raumo), Tammisaari (sw. Ekenäs) and Porvoo move to the newly established town. In 1550 Helsinki Royal Manor was also established on an island in the middle of the rivermouth, from where its activities were relocated to Itä-Viikki east of the river in 1555. In 1640 the town was relocated to its present site in Vironniemi. After the reorganisation of the provincial administration in 1634, Helsinki was the residence town of the Governor of Uusimaa and Häme province. The province was split temporarily in two in 1640-48. The outline of the town is included in a map from ca. 1645.
The King established Helsinki to draw Dutch shipping and Russian transit trade from Tallinn to the new town, but the venture failed and was abandoned after Tallinn came under Swedish rule in 1561. An important turn in the trading privileges in the Swedish realm took place in 1614, when a system of towns with staple rights (Sw. stapelstad, Fin. tapulikaupunki) and inland towns (Sw. uppstad, Fin. maakaupunki, ylämaakaupunki) was created in the new trading and shipping ordinance. Towns with staple rights were divided to first- and second-class staples. The burghers of both classes had the right to export, i.e. to sail to foreign towns and destinations (active rights in foreign trade), whereas only towns of the first class had the right of imports, i.e. the right of receive and unload foreign vessels in their harbours (passive rights in foreign trade). Modified in 1615 and 1617 the ordinance restricted the trade of foreigners in Swedish towns and searched to bar the traditional peasant trade to regional hubs in the realm. In Finland only Turku (sw. Åbo) and Viipuri (sw. Viborg) held the status of a first-class staple (active and passive rights) continuously from 1614. Other towns with provisional first-class rights from 1614 were Helsinki and Porvoo. Both enjoyed full first-class staple to 1623, when their toll was rented to the city Reval and foreign import shipping in the Gulf of Finland area was only allowed to Reval and Viipuri. Helsinki and Porvoo regained their full staple rights in 1628 with a continuation in 1636. After being relocated to the present site in 1640 Helsinki retained its full rights until the abolition of the staple right system in 1879.
Fair_Description:
Burghers of Helsinki were in 1553 given rights to three annual fairs of which one was held in the town, and the two others in Pernaja and Pyhtää parishes. In older scholarship the fair in Helsinki was attributed to the feast of St Eusebia or Eusebius, but the misinterpretation is based on 19th century false reading of an 18th century source and the actual date of the 1553 fair is not known. When king Johan III in 1584 ordained the midsummer fair (24 June) at Sipoo (sw. Sibbo) to be relocated to Helsinki, he also confirmed a winter fair to be held in the town on 
Epiphany (6 January). In the 1650s the burghers applied the date of the winter fair to be changed first to Candlemas (2 February) and to Apostle Paul (25 January) in 1680. 

In 1584 burghers of the newly re-established Porvoo complained to the authorities, that right after the sea and rivers were free of ice, burghers of Helsinki arrived to trade with peasants of the region at the Old Royal Manor (in Saksala) and elsewhere despite of the official fair dates which were Midsummer in Sipoo (sw. Sibbo), Visitation of Mary (2 July) and Excaltation of the Cross (14 September) in Porvoo, St Michael (29 September) in Pernaja (sw. Pernå) and St Laurentius (10 August) at Pyhtää (sw. Pyttis) church. The same year king Johan III granted burghers of Porvoo and Helsinki joint rights for trading with peasants of the eastern half of Pernaja parish at the St Bartolomeus fair in Pyhtää, whereas peasants from the western half of Pernaja were obliged to trade in Porvoo only. Previous traditional local fairs in Mustijoki (sw. Svartså) and Kulloonmäki (sw. Kullo) in Porvoo, Pikku Pernajanlahti (sw. Lillpernåviken) in Pernaja and elsewhere were prohibited. The king also relocated Sipoo Midsummer fair to Helsinki and confirmed a fair to be held on Michaelmas (29 September) in Espoo (sw. Esbå) Bobäck, where burghers of Helsinki were allowed to trade with peasants of the neighbouring province of Raasepori. Rights in Espoo were confirmed in 1594 when the date was cited as St Mary (8 September). Possibly an older local peasant fair, the Bobäck fair took place at the end of the Espoo bay alongside the Great Coastal Road. After relocation to Pikkala bridge on the same road in 1723, the fair was organised on Apostle Matteus (21 September). Helsinki burghers were in 1594 also granted rights to apostle Matteus (21 September) fair in Inkoo. Burghers of Helsinki are also known to have held fair in Sipoo on St Mary (8 September) in the early 17th century.

After intense litigation throughout the last quarter of the 16th century Porvoo and Helsinki were in 1602 and in 1607 confirmed right to trade in the four annual fairs at Porvoo, Pernaja and Pyhtää. Burghers of Helsinki had free right to trade in confirmed fairs east of Porvoo and those of Porvoo west of Helsinki. Fair in Pyhtää took place in Vähä-Ahvenkoski and those in Pernaja at Koskenkylä (sw. Forsby) bridge on the Great Coastal Road, where they were held in 1708. In 1639 burghers of Helsinki were further granted the right to visit annual tar fair in Porvoo on 1 July. Already in 1614 Helsinki had seized the sole right to hold fair in Janakkala Turkhauta on 1 September, which were traditionally frequented by burghers from Porvoo. Since 1654 Turkhauta fair was organised on 14 September. Helsinki weekly market was confirmed in 1626 to be held on Saturday.
Toll_Description: The 1/32 duty worth of all goods intended for sale in towns and fairs and brought to the site by peasants was collected in Helsinki Vanhakaupunki from 1622 to 1640.

name: Kurittula
Settlement_Description: <b>Inn:</b> An inn was established in Kurittula in 1586, and Sipi Olavinpoika Tuomola was appointed as the innkeeper.

name: Pedersöre
Settlement_Description: Permanent agricultural settlement in Pedersöre dates to the Swedish colonisation of the late 13th century and the beginning of the 14th. Pedersöre is cited as an independent parish together with Mustasaari and Närpiö in 1348, when their inhabitants were given right to trade with victuals between themselves. Jakobstad (fin. Pietarsaari) town north of Pedersöre kyrka was founded in 1652 by Ebba Brahe who controlled the area as a fief from the crown and named the town after her late husband Jakob de la Gardie. <b>Inn:</b> A royal manor, Pinonäs, was formed near Pedersöre in 1556, but served only until 1561. Ture Pedersson Bielke, Swedish nobleman and castellan of St. Olaf's Castle in Savo, stayed overnight in the manor in 1557. Royal manors provided accommodation for travelling officials as well. In 1643, an inn was established in Pedersöre parish village, and Mårten Jönsson was appointed as the innkeeper.
Fair_Description: Trade in the most important traditional trading posts at major river mouths in the Gulf of Bothnia area was regulated at the latest in 1420, when the crown furnished them with storage houses, started to collect toll, and prohibited other traditional trading sites alongside the Bothnic coastline. Among these have apparently been Pedersöre and its 14th century chapel Saloinen both of which developed into merchant towns in 1652 (sw. Jakobstad) and 1649 (sw. Brahestad, fin. Raahe). In 1616 all trade in Ostrobothnia was centred to Oulu and Vaasa (sw. Vasa), but burghers of Stockholm, Turku, Rauma and Pori were granted the right for annual fair of two weeks in Pedersöre and Saloinen starting from St Olaf’s (29 July). When the town of Nykarleby (fin. Uusikaarlepyy) was established in 1620, Pedersöre was together with Nykarleby, Lapua and Vöyri (sw. Vörå) parishes attached to its trading area, which had been previously controlled by Vaasa (est. 1606). The annual St Olaf summer fair (29 July) in Pedersöre was transferred to Nykarleby in 1624 and ordered to last for three days. The burghers of Nykarleby continued to hold fairs in Pedersöre harbour area three times a year, two of which were in 1621 cited as St Peter (29 June) and St Laurentius (10 August). A traditional date for winter fair in the area may have been St Paul (25 January). Pedersöre medieval church may have been dedicated to St Peter.
Toll_Description: The 1/32 duty worth of all goods intended for sale in towns and fairs and brought to the site by peasants was collected in Pedersöre fairs since 1622.

name: Ojaniemi
Bridge_Description: Ferry over Kyrönjoki river existed in 1610. The ferry was replaced with a bridge in the mid 1620s.
Ferry_Description: Ferry over Kyrönjoki river existed in 1610. The ferry was replaced with a bridge in the mid 1620s.

name: Herdecke
Settlement_Description: The settlement was built next to an abbey founded in 810. In 1355 the settlement received market privileges.

name: Virttaa
Settlement_Description: <b>Inn:</b> Virttaa has been an important hub between Finland proper and Southern Satakunta region in 16th and 17th c. It is mentioned as a place for accommodation in the travel account of Duke Johan of Finland from 1556. Also Ture Pedersson Bielke, Swedish nobleman and castellan of St. Olaf's Castle in Savo, stayed overnight in Virttaa in 1557. Their host was the parish constable (fi: nimismies, sw: länsman) Heikki Mikonpoika from Mikkola farm, who served as the parish constable in 1550-52, 1557-60, 1562-67 and 1570. After that, the parish constabe office moved away from Virttaa, but private accommodation and official inns are found also later. Eskeli Tätilä served accommodation to a nobleman travelling in crown's behalf in 1579, and Jaakko Kankuri ("Weaver") hosted Johan de la Gardie, governor of Finland, in 1623, after he had fell down from his horse. Official inns are known from 1621 onwards, and Heikkilä farm served as the inn for the most of the 17th c. Pauli Heikkilä is mentioned as the innkeeper in 1642.

name: Lohtaja
Settlement_Description:
<b>Inn:</b> Ture Pedersson Bielke, Swedish nobleman and castellan of St. Olaf's Castle in Savo, stayed overnight at Lohtaja parish constable's (fi: nimismies, sw: länsman) farm in 1557. Lohtaja also had a transport organiser (sw. skjutsrättare, fi. kyytirättäri), who helped Kaarlela parish constable. In 1630s, an inn was established in Lohtaja parish village in Jukkola farm, hosted by assistant vicar Erik Granberg. Granberg gave up innkeeping in 1646, and Matti Ollinpoika Nissilä was appointed as the innkeeper. Erik Granberg established later, in 1651, an alehouse to Rauma together with parish constable Kristoffer Hannunpoika and Joonas Hilli.

The inn in Lohtaja parish village changed often owners. After Nissilä farm, the inn moved to Niemelä farm and Gabriel Jaakonpoika, who gave up the inn after his house burned. After that, the inn responsibility was shared with Matti Juhonpoika Nissilä and Juho Juhonpoika Kyrölä, who are mentioned in office in 1662. Kyrölä farm continued to serve as an inn until 1673, when Matti Juhonpoika Kyrölä gave up the inn after his father died. Lohtaja inn then moved to Mikko Matinpoika Junttila, and Junttila farm served as the inn until the end of the Swedish reign in Finland (1809).

name: Tervajoki (Vähäkyrö)
Settlement_Description:
<b>Inn:</b> An inn was established in Tervajoki in 1641, and Simo Kempus was appointed as the innkeeper. Governor closed the tavern in 1652.

<b>Post house:</b> Oluf Jönsson appointed Simo Kempus as the postmaster of Vähäkyrö Tervajoki and handed him the postmaster's mandate in 1643.

name: Niemandsvriend
Toll_Description: A toll for sailing transport on the river Merwede, where the rivers Waal and Maas meet, belonging to the count of Holland in Niemandsvriend is first mentioned in 1241 or 1242. It was relocated in 1354 to Woudrichem. In Niemandvriend remained a guard-house. A toll tariff is preserved and edited for the years 1357/1358.
Ferry_Description: A ferry at the tollstation Niemandsvriend, belonging to the count of Holland, is first mentioned in 1331. It must have disappeared when the Grote Waard on the opposite side of the river was flooded in the flood of St Elisabeth of 1421.

name: Sorkkinen
Settlement_Description: <b>Inn:</b> Martti Yrjänänpoika from Lähteenoja farm is mentioned as the innkeeper in Sorkkinen in 1586. There have been many innkeepers (or ale sellers) in Sorkkinen, and it would need more research to found out their status and relationships between them. In 1640, there was a fight in Jöran Anderssons inn/alehouse. In 1642, the official inn was located again in the Lähteenoja farm. In 1652, there was a fight in Klemet Jacobsson's tavern, and in 1656, in Klemet Sigfridsson's tavern. Heikki Meltser was the innkeeper in 1666. Assistant priest Johan Laihiander run the official tavern in 1679. Germund Mattson from Katila farm was the innkeeper in 1682, but the practical work was done by her wife's sister, Margeta Matsdotter. She was sentenced to a small fine for having an illegitimate child, whose accused father was one of the clients of the inn. The official inn moved from Katila farm to Soupas farm in the south in the 1680s.

name: Kalajoki
Settlement_Description:
Permanent agricultural settlement in Kalajoki area dates to the late 13th or early 14th century. 

<b>Inn:</b> Ture Pedersson Bielke, Swedish nobleman and castellan of St. Olaf's Castle in Savo, stopped to change horses in Kalajoki in 1557.
Fair_Description: Trade in the most important traditional trading posts at major river mouths in the Gulf of Bothnia area was regulated at the latest in 1420, when the crown furnished them with storage houses, started to collect toll, and prohibited other traditional trading sites alongside the Bothnic coastline. One of these so called “new havens” may have been in Santaniemi Plassi in Kalajoki. Burghers of Oulu had since 1610 the sole right of trading between Kemi and Kokkola (Karleby) including Santaniemi fair, but the rights for winter fair on St Henrik (20.1.) were transferred to the new town of Kokkola (Karleby) in 1621. In 1622 the king granted the burghers of Kokkola and Oulu the right to trade in Kalajoki fairs on 18 May (feast of St Erik) and Laurentius (10.8.), but the rights remained in Kokkola. Kalajoki fairs were proclaimed free for all burghers in 1638, which was confirmed in 1640. In 1710 the annual fairs were organised in the Eve of St Henrik (19 January), 19 August and on apostle Matthew (21 September). In the 1650s the tar fair was said to cover a period of three weeks.
Toll_Description: The Swedish crown started to collect toll from the new regulated harbours and market posts in Bothnian river mouths in the beginning of the 1420s. The 1/32 duty worth of all goods intended for sale in towns and fairs and brought to the site by peasants was collected in Kalajoki since 1622.

name: Söderby (Taivassalo)
Settlement_Description: <b>Post house:</b> In 1638, the Royal Steward Bernhardt Steen von Steenhousen established a post house in the village of Söderby in Taivassalo.

name: Kalajoki
Bridge_Description: The bridge over Kalajoki on the Bothnian Coastal Road existed in the beginning of the 1650s.

name: Isokyrö
Settlement_Description:
Permanent agricultural settlement in Isokyrö (sw. Storkyro) dates to the Iron Age. In the 12th century the area became under new colonisation from Satakunta. An independent parish was established in the latter half of the 13th century and cited in 1443 and 1477. The late medieval stone church was built in the 1510s and 1520s.

<b>Inn:</b> Gustav II Adolf of Sweden travelled in 1614 from Vaasa to Isokyrö through Hämeenmetsä (Kyrönkangas forest) to Southern Finland. In 1626, he travelled the same route to north. Isokyrö inn might have operated in the vicarage, since vicar Isak Brenner asked in 1650 if the villagers could give victualities to him in return for accommodating travellers.
Fair_Description: The trading areas of Vaasa (1606) and Nykarleby (1620) towns hosted of old peasant fairs in three parishes of Lapua, Vöyri and Isokyrö, of which burghers of Vaasa were granted sole rights to St Henrik (20 January) and St Laurentius (10 August) fair in Isokyrö, and Nykarleby to Candelmas fair (2 February) in Lapua, and St Margaret (20 July) and St Mary (8 September?) fairs in Vöyri. Burghers of Vaasa were further granted the right to visit St Margaret fair of Vöyri in 1624. In the early 17th century local fair was also held at St Michael (29 September) in Lapua. Since 1643 the right to attend fairs in Vöyri and Isokyrö were held by burghers of both towns. In 1650 burghers of Nykarleby were further granted sole right to hold a local fair on St Nicolaus (6 December) for four days in Vöyri. After continuous litigation, fairs in Vöyri and Isokyrö were granted free for all towns in 1682. Since the late medieval chapel church of Vöyri was dedicated to St Margaret and St Anna (15 December), and the medieval parish church of Isokyrö to St Laurentius, St Margaret fair in Vöyri, and St Laurentius and St Henrik fairs in Isokyrö may have been of early 16th century or earlier medieval origin. Isokyrö fair site was very likely close to the church where a thick cultural layer has been documented in archaeological excavations
Toll_Description: The 1/32 duty worth of all goods intended for sale in towns and fairs and brought to the site by peasants was collected in Isokyrö fair since 1622.

name: Salzwedel
Settlement_Description: A castle existed since the 9th or 10th century, around which the settlement developed. It flourished due to its location on the salt road between Lüneburg and Magdeburg. First mentioned in 1112.
Town_Description: The settlement is first mentioned as oppiudum in 1197, but the acquisition of town privileges probably occurred bewteen 1207 and 1233. Salzwedel possessed a town right of its own, which was influenced by the town law of Lüneburg. As member of the Hanse in 1263-1518 it adopted the Lübeck town law.
Fair_Description: The privileges of the cloth merchants in 1360 mention two fairs in Salzwedel, on St Dionysius  and Sunday before Pentecost. In 1496 a new fair is granted by Margrave Johann on Laetare Sunday and the following Monday.
Toll_Description: Toll and safe conduct. A toll register from 1314 shows the fees to be paid. In 1506 a dam and bridge toll is added for the maintenance of the roads. In 1650, Salzwedel was allowed to levy the bridge and dam toll from cargoes of grain. The growing trade with lumber and working stones caused the dilapidation of the bridges and dams, so it was allowed that the council collected the bridge and dam toll from such commodities as well.

name: Arnum
Settlement_Description: The village of Arnum was first mentioned in 1355, but is significantly older. The settlement had no church but was part of the parish of Højrup Church.

name: Olavinlinna Castle
Settlement_Description: <b>Olavinlinna (sw. Nyslott, Olofsborg) Castle:</b> Olavinlinna Castle was founded in 1475 by the knight and former regent of Sweden Erik Axelsson (Tott), who ruled Viipuri Castle and its subordinate bailiffs in 1457–81. The castle was built in a strategic location in Kyrönsalmi, where it could be used to control water, land, winter and portage routes in the narrow passage between Pihlajavesi and Haukivesi. The castle was completed in 1485, the forecourt in the late 1400s. The bailiwick was separated from Vyborg Castle into its own entity under the central administration in 1535. The castle's facilities and defensive fortifications were expanded and modified several times in the 16th century, but its importance as a border castle ended with the Treaty of Stolbova in 1617. In 1638, the city of Savonlinna (sw. Nyslott) was founded on the site of the settlement on the west side of the castle. When the Province of Viipuri was divided into Vyborg and Savonlinna Provinces in 1641, the administrative centre of Savonlinna Province became Olavinlinna Castle until the province was reunited with the Viipuri Province in 1650. After the Peace of Uusikaupunki (sw. Nystad) in 1721, the Castle remained in Sweden, but came in 1743 into Russian possession in the Treaty of Turku, after which it was modernised in the 1780s with a bastion system. An extensive restoration was carried out in the castle in 1961–75.

name: Pyhäjoki
Settlement_Description: <b>Inn:</b> Ture Pedersson Bielke, Swedish nobleman and castellan of St. Olaf's Castle in Savo, stopped to change horses in Pyhäjoki in 1557. Pyhäjoki parish is established in the 1570s, and its constables were located either in the southern Eteläkylä village or eastern Pohjankylä village. An inn was established in Eteläkylä village in 1631, and Prusi Heikinpoika Maijala was appointed as the innkeeper. Many new inns were established in the same year because of clearing and renovating work in the Ostrobothian Coastal Road.

name: Pirkkala
Settlement_Description: <b>Inn:</b> In 1575, there was a transport organiser (fi. kyytirättäri, sw. skjutsrättare) in Pirkkalankylä (Pirkkala village).

name: Bydgoszcz
Town_Description: Town privileges granted by Casimir III.
Toll_Description: Bydgoszcz is mentioned as a toll station as early as 1252.

name: Tesjoki
Settlement_Description:
Permanent agricultural settlement in Pyhtää (sw. Pyttis) area and Eastern Nyland (sw. Östra Nyland) dates to the Swedish colonisation in the latter half of the 13th century when new farms were founded amongst earlier 12th and 13th century area of usufruct and colonisation from inner Häme (sw. Tavastland). The parish organisation of Eastern Nyland dates at the latest to the first quarter of the 14th century. Independent parish at the latest since 1380. Stone church in the 1460s. The border between Sweden and Russia was in 1743–1809 in Ahvenkoski. <b>The royal manor of Tesjoki (sw. Tessjö),</b> also known as Holmgärd, was founded in the late 13th or early 14th centuries on an island at the mouth of the Taasianjoki River (sw. Tessjöån) to support the colonization settlement. Strategically located, the Manor sat on the Great Coastal Road and guarded the bridges on both sides of the island. In 1351, King Magnus Eriksson handed over the royal manor to the Bishop of Turku as part of the arrangements for the patronage of the parish of Porvoo. The manor was reclaimed by the crown in the early 1360s and was since the beginning of the 15th century in the control the nobility including an enfeoffment in 1523–28. 

<b>Inn:</b> The king's and bishop's manors were used as lodgings for those who moved on the affairs of the crown and the diocese. An official inn was established in Tesjoki in 1621. 

<b>Post house:</b> In 1638, the Royal Steward Bernhardt Steen von Steenhausen established a post house in the village of Tesjoki in Pyhtää. According to research literature, Tesjoki is known as a traditional post house village along the coastal road.

name: Härkälä
Settlement_Description: <b>Inn:</b> There has been a transport hub or a tavern in Härkälä village in mid-1540s. An inn is mentioned in 1572. The inn rights circulated between the farms, but the rights established in Kurkila farm, which served as the inn during the 17th and 18th centuries.

name: Groeningen
Settlement_Description: Groeningen originated as hamlet between 300 and 600. Groeningen is first mentioned in the fifteenth century. This small triangle of farms, became a larger settlement.

name: Saloinen
Settlement_Description: Saloinen is first cited in 1329, when it was together with Kemi a chapel of Pedersöre parish. Independent parish was established in the beginning of the 15th century. The earliest church was located on Kirkkoluoto islet in a narrow inlet of the Gulf of Bothnia south from the later harbour and relocated to the later site in 1622. The church was consecrated to St Olaf. The oldest site for the annual fair was in Satamalahti and after that in Markkinaniemi in Satamakangas. The town of Raahe (Brahestad) was first founded as Salo in Satamalahti in 1649, but was soon relocated to Fantinniemi and named in 1652 after governor-general Per Brahe the younger who had established the town. Settlement is here dated to 1329 and located in Markkinaniemi, where the fair and harbour may have been since ca. 1420.
Town_Description: The town of Raahe (sw. Brahestad) was first founded as Salo in Satamalahti in 1649, but was soon relocated to Fantinniemi and named in 1652 after governor-general Per Brahe the younger who had established the town. The first plan of the town area dates to the year 1650.
Fair_Description: Trade in the most important traditional trading posts at major river mouths in the Gulf of Bothnia area was regulated at the latest in 1420, when the crown furnished them with storage houses, started to collect toll, and prohibited other traditional trading sites alongside the Bothnic coastline. In 1459 all trade in these legal trading posts was restricted to Stockholm and Turku only, but without any result. The oldest site for the annual fair was in Satamalahti and after that in Markkinaniemi in Satamakangas, where the fair may have been relocated in 1420. Burghers of Oulu had since 1610 the sole right of trading between Kemi and Kokkola (Karleby).One of the most important annual fairs were held in Saloinen (later Raahe) at St Olaf’s feast (29 July) where burghers of Stockholm, Turku, Rauma and Pori were the same year granted rights for two weeks together with St Olaf’s fair in Pedersöre. Turku and Oulu disputed each other’s rights for Saloinen until 1642, when the fair was relocated to Oulu and set to cover eight days from St Laurentius (10 August). A smaller annual fair designed for local peasants was allowed in Saloinen whatever day they saw the best. The annual fair of Raahe was in 1668 set to St Laurentius, which may hint about a longer period of fairs related to fishing similar to Pedersöre.
Toll_Description: Saloinen has very likely been one of the “new havens” of the Gulf of Bothnia area, which the crown furnished with storage houses and started to collect toll in ca. 1420. The 1/32 duty worth of all goods intended for sale in towns and fairs and brought to the site by peasants was collected in Oulu since 1622.

name: Kokkola
Settlement_Description:
Permanent agricultural settlement in Kaarlela (sw. Karleby) area dates to the colonisation of the late 13th century and the beginning of the 14th. Karleby was founded as a chapel of Pedersöre parish in the first half of the 15th century and established as an independent parish some time in between 1486–1511. A stone church was built in the second third of the 16th century. After the founding of Uusikaarlepyy (Nykarleby) parish (1607) and town (1617/1620), the parish and town (1620) of Karleby was called Gamlakarleby. The traditional Finnish name of the town is Kokkola. The oldest harbour of the area was located close to Karleby church in Tervaholma.

<b>Inn:</b> Ture Pedersson Bielke, Swedish nobleman and castellan of St. Olaf's Castle in Savo, stopped to change horses in Kaarlela vicarage in 1557.
Town_Description:
King Gustaf II Adolf founded Kokkola (sw. Gamlakarleby) town and gave the first town privileges in 1620. The town was originally to be located west of Karleby church, but a better harbour favoured its relocation to the later site west of Kaupunginsuntti inlet. Since 1617 towns in the Gulf of Bothnia area allowed to export their goods only to Stockholm and Turku. In 1636 the crown prohibited all foreign shipping to towns, harbours, or other places north of Turku and Stockholm, including Åland. The first plan of the town was made in the early 1620s, the two oldest surviving plans for enwidening the town area are from the years 1649 and 1651.
<b>Post office:</b> The Kokkola post office is likely to have been founded in 1644, as matters related to the hiring of a postmaster are mentioned in the provincial accounts from that time. The first postmaster is reportedly believed to have been Gabriel Roth, who served as a mayor and judge.
Fair_Description: The annual fair in Kokkola was in 1642 ordained to be held on St Bartholomeus (24 August), in 1650 on St Olaf (29 July) and in 1652 again on St Bartholomeus. Burghers of Kokkola were in 1621 granted the sole rights to the annual winter fairs in Kalajoki Santaniemi previously held by burghers of Oulu. in 1622 Kokkola and Oulu burghers were confirmed the right for two fairs in Kalajoki and together with other towns in Ostrobothnia the right for two annual fairs in Ii and Kemi each.
