Kalajoki fairs were proclaimed free for all burghers in 1638, which was confirmed in 1640.
Toll_Description: The 1/32 duty worth of all goods intended for sale in towns and fairs and brought to the site by peasants was collected in Kokkola since 1622.

name: Kastelholm
Settlement_Description: The ecclesiastical parish organisation in Åland (fi. Ahvenanmaa) goes back to the late 12th and early 13th century. Sund parish is first cited in 1352, but it was very likely established already in the beginning of the 13th century. A bailiwick of its own, Åland made part of the area under Turku castle since the early 14th century. The strategically important <b>Kastelholm Castle</b> was founded as the military and administrational centre of the bailiwick some time in 1384–88 by the seneschal and Bo Jonsson (Grip) who controlled all the castles and bailiwicks in Finland from 1374 to his death in 1386. The castle served as the administrative centre of the entire bailiwick to 1556, after which it made part of the duchy of Johan in 1556–62 and was enfeoffed to Queen Dowager Katarina Stenbock in 1569–99. When Åland since 1635 made part of the province of Turku, Kastelholm remained in modified use until it was destroyed by fire in 1745.

name: Penttilä
Settlement_Description: <b>Inn:</b> Penttilä farm in Pirkkala parish was owned by Duke Johan of Finland, so he stayed there in his travels in 1556.

name: Salo
Settlement_Description: <b>Inn:</b> Salo parish constable (fi: nimismies, sw: länsman) was established in the 1540s. The same family, Juusola, served as constables in many generations. During the period, parish constables were also obliged to keep a tavern, and Salo parish constable had a transport organisator (fi. kyytirättäri, sw. skjutsrättäre) in Siikajoki. Ture Pedersson Bielke, Swedish nobleman and castellan of St. Olaf's Castle in Savo, stayed overnight at Salo parish constable in 1557. In the late 1620s, Juho Juhonpoika Juusola started running a tavern after loosing his office as a parish constable, and Juusola farm continued to serve as an inn until the early 18th c.

name: Emkarby (Finström)
Settlement_Description: <b>Post house:</b> In 1638, the Royal Steward Bernhardt Steen von Steenhausen established six post houses in Åland, along the route from Stockholm to Turku. One of the post houses was located in the village of Embarky in Finström.

Ferry_Description: Ferry between Nieuwerkerk and Ouderkerk aan den IJssel, first mentioned in 1326. It was probably situated in Kortenoord in Nieuwerkerk, but another possible location is Hitland opposite Ouderkerk.

name: Balve
Town_Description: The Cologne archbishop Dietrich II. von Mörs granted town privileges in 1430 based on the Arnsberg rights.

name: Eckerö
Settlement_Description: <b>Post house:</b> In 1638, the Royal Steward Bernhardt Steen von Steenhausen established six post houses in Åland, along the route from Stockholm to Turku. One of the post houses was located in Eckerö.

name: Liminka
Settlement_Description: <b>Inn:</b> Ture Pedersson Bielke, Swedish nobleman and castellan of St. Olaf's Castle in Savo, stayed overnight in Liminka vicarage in 1557. Liminka parish constable, who was obliged to keep a tavern, was located in either the vicarage, Limingankylä village, or Oulunsalo village. In 1557, Liminka parish constable had transport organisers (fi. kyytirättäri, sw. skjutsrättare) in Lumijoki, Oulunsalo and Oulunsuu villages. In early 17th c., Arvola farm served as the inn, and Heikki Matinpoika is mentioned as the innkeeper in 1640s and 1654. His son Matti Heikinpoika continued as an innkeeper, but lost his right in 1668 because of excessive drinking, negligence, and poverty, and the inn was moved to Ojanperä farm.

name: Krimpen aan de Lek
Settlement_Description: First mentioned in 1064 (in a falsification from the first half of the 12th century).

name: Grubben
Settlement_Description: The castle was first mentioned in 1237. In 1308 it was in possession of the Lord of Millen. The castle was destroyed in the 16th century and not rebuilt. The ruins are nowadays known as the 'broken castle' (Gebroken Slot).
Toll_Description: River toll on the Meuse of the Lord of Millen (first mentioned in 1308), from 1328 the Lord of Bergh, from ca. 1392 the Lord of Wevelinghoven and from 1473 the Lord of Gemen. From the second half of the 14th century it was probably levied in Venlo; before the fourteenth century it was possibly partly levied in Venlo. Last mentioned in 1515.

Ferry_Description: A ferry to Kralingen is first mentioned in 1333. In 1668 Rotterdam acquired the seigniory Kralingen with half the ferry, the other half remained property of IJsselmonde.

name: Kortenoord
Settlement_Description: Earliest mention in 1487 when a brickyard is located here. The road between Kortenoord and Rotterdam is called 's-Gravenweg (1371).

name: Rijsoord
Settlement_Description: First mentioned with a parish church in 1336.
Fair_Description: On 23 July 1339 Count William IV granted his clerck Gerard Alewijnsz. a weekly market on Monday and two fairs of eight days each in Rijsoord in the Zwijndrechtse waard near the river Waal. They took place on the eve of St. Mary Magdalene (21 July) and on the Feast of the Eleven thousand Virgins (21 October), with market right like in Alblas, three days before and after the dates. He also granted toll exemption for those living in the newly diked land. On 14 July 1340 count William granted Tielman Jan Heren Gillysz. a weekly market and a free fair during 14 days in his 'achtendeel' (eighth part) of Zwijndrecht named Rissoirde. Who attended this fair would be exempted from tolls with the goods bought or sold there.
Bridge_Description: In 1543 a bridge was built crossing the river Waal with consent of emperor Charles V. The bridge was situated next to the church. During four years a toll was levied in order to pay the costs.
Ferry_Description: A ferry to Dordrecht, first mentioned in 1332, was replaced by a bridge crossing the river Waal in 1543 with consent of emperor Charles V.

name: Kralingse Veer
Ferry_Description: The ferry from Kralingen to IJsselmonde is first mentioned in 1333. In 1668 Rotterdam bought the seignory Kralingen including half of the ferry. The other half remained in possession of IJsselmonde.

name: Kempele
Settlement_Description: <b>Inn:</b> An inn was established in Kempele in 1640s, and Perttu Tuohinoja was appointed as the innkeeper. Tuohinoja/Tuohino farm continued to serve as an inn at least until the end of the 17th century.

name: Maansilta (Karjaa)
Bridge_Description: Karjaa Maansilta (sw. Karis Landsbro) over Mustionjoki river (r. Svartå) on the Great Coastal Road, is mentioned in 1639–40 and 1659, when it was destroyed by floods. The bridge was rebuilt in 1688. Very likely of medieval origin, the bridge was because of its name (Lands bridge) organised to the care of two or more parishes form different judicial districts. In 1803, the bridge was a total of 83 ells (ca. 49.3 m) long.

name: Slikkerveer
Ferry_Description: The ferry station Slikkerveer was connected with Krimpen aan de Lek across the Merwede. It is first mentioned in 1423, but a ferry in Krimpen aan de Lek is already mentioned in 1236, although this might also be the ferry across the Lek. See the ferry in Krimpen aan de Lek.

name: Grubbenvorst
Toll_Description: In 1308 knight Willem van Millen stated the tariff of the toll Roermond had to pay at 'Gribben' (Grubbbenvorst) and Venlo for their ships. Untill 1328 the toll was property of this knight Van Millen, from then till about 1392 from the lord of Bergh, then till 1473 from the lord of Wevelinghoven and after that of the lord of Megen.In 1517 the secretary of the counts of Berg stated that he on request of the magistrate of Roermond investigated the toll at 'Grebbenfoirste'. When se married the lord van den Berghe Elysabeth van Mille († 1355) would have brought in home and seigniory of Grebben, which included halff the toll at Venlo. In 1498 Roermond complained at the countess of Bentheim and Steinfurt who lived at the house of Grubbenvorst that the citizens had to pay toll at Grubbenvorst and Venlo, despite their privileges. In 1520 the count of Schauenberg and Steinfurt (nephew of the duke of Gelre) complained that citizens of Roermond passed the toll at Grubbenvorst without payment. This is granted till proof to the contrary.

name: Mårtensby
Settlement_Description: <b>Inn:</b> Jören Bonde owned an alehouse in Mårtensby village in 1543. The alehouses in Sipoo and Helsinki parishes paid their taxes for ale selling in natura by delivering hops to Wiborg castle and the king's estate in Porvoo. The village was located south of Vantaanjoki River.

name: Utajärvi
Settlement_Description: <b>Inn:</b> An inn might have been established in Utajärvi already in the 1630s.

name: Tongelre
Fair_Description: Before 1340 Tongelre had a fair and in 1340 a cloth-hall.

name: IJsselmonde
Settlement_Description: First mentioned in 1125-1130 (in a copy of ca. 1420).

name: Pikkusilta (Ahvenkoski)
Bridge_Description: The Greater (Isosilta) and Smaller (Pikkusilta) bridges at the westernmost branch of Kymijoki river in Ahvenkoski are first cited in 1555, when Jakob Teitt included them in his map of the bridges in Kymijoki delta area. The earliest bridges on the site may date to the first organisation of the maintenance of the Great Coastal Road as a uniform land route between Turku and Viborg in the 1340s and 1360s. Isosilta bridge was in the beginning of the 17th century maintained by the early 14th century parishes of Swedish colonisation in Central and Eastern Uusimaa, but in the 1720 also by the Western Uusimaa parishes of Inkoo and Espoo because of their old duty in the bridge. The organisation of the maintenance goes back to the period from the 1340s to the 1360s when the area was part of uniform administration under Viipuri castle. The smaller bridge in Ahvenkoski was on the Swedish Russian border in 1743-1809. The maintenance of the supporting stone structures of Isosilta were heavily disputed in 1608 and the bridge was in bad condition in 1638. In the late 17th century Isosilta was together with Pyhtää Church bridge (fi. Kirkonkylän silta) Sutela Larger bridge (fi. Isosilta) and Kymijoki Huumanhaara bridge financed by a special tax collected from the judicial districts of Viipuri province and Porvoo area. Pikkusilta and Isosilta were demolished in 1928 after a new bridge was built over Savukoski. The opening of Merikoski hydroenrgic power plant in 1933 raised the water level in the area for several meters.

name: Kajaanin linna
Settlement_Description: Permanent agricultural settlement in Paltamo and Oulunjärvi area dates to the colonisation from Savolax in the 1550s. The administrative centre of the area was a Royal Manor close to Vuohenginkoski stream in Kajaaninjoki river in 1555–58. The building of Kajaani castle (sw. Kajaneborg) was started in 1604 after the orders of king Charles IX, but the stronghold was left unfinished in 1619. After Queen Christina enfeoffed a large area in Northeast Finland to the Lord High Steward and Governor-General Count Per Brahe the younger in 1649, Kajaani became the centre of administration of his dominion there. Brahe established the town of Kajaani in 1651 and rebuilt the castle as an administrational residence in 1661–66. The fief was revoked in the Great Reduction in 1681. The castle was demolished by the Russian army in 1716.

name: Beek (Aarle)
Settlement_Description: First mentioned in 1286. In historical sources the village Beek is often mentioned in combination with nearby Aarle: Aarlebeek. In modern times merged with Donk as Beek en Donk.
Fair_Description: An undated register from the abbey Tongerlo (Westerlo, B.) (circa 1556) contains a list of fairs in the region Kempen and Peel. 'Aerlebeke' then has two fairs: 1) Tuesday after Mid-Lent, 2) Sunday after visitationis Mariae (March 30) till the first Tuesday after that.

name: Toruń
Staple_Description: In the late 14th century, the city attempted to create a staple market, which led to conflicts with Cracow. Both cities gave up their staples in 1391, but as Cracow started to force merchants to offer their wares on the market in 1398, Toruń received new rights from the Grand Master, which included a staple with limitations to the streets to be used for commodities exported from Poland (wax, furs, metals and spices) and imported cloth from England. When the staple lost importance after the peace of Thorn in 1411, it was reinstated in 1428 and now included corn; confirmed in 1448 with the inclusion of river transport, and again by King Casimir in 1457 after Toruń became Polish. The staple was cancelled after 1466, with the exception of the obligation to travel only on roads leading through town. Attempts to reinstate the staple led to many conflicts with other cities, until all obligations were annulled in 1496. There were renewed attempts to establish a staple in the 16th century, which was confirmed by the Pope in 1516. The King decided in 1533 that ships on the Vistula heading upstream had to unload in Toruń, although the full staple was not acknowledged. A renewed obligation to travel via Toruń from Danzig to Poland was instated, but cancelled in 1537 again, with the exemption of fish. In the 17th century, only the fish staple still existed.

name: Krimpen aan den IJssel
Settlement_Description: First mentioned in 1277 (in a copy from 1329).

name: Brugge
Settlement_Description: A castle was built as a defence against the Normans by count Baldwin of Flanders or his predecessor around 840-875. A settlement developed with a harbour on the sea inlet Sinkfal (later Zwin). It is called "portus" and "oppidum" in the 10th and "colonia" in the 11th and early 12th century.
Town_Description: Town privileges ('keure') were granted by count William of Flanders on 6 April 1127. The city developed into one of the primary economic centres of northwestern Europe in the 13th to 15th century.
Fair_Description: On 14 August 1200, Bruges became one of the five grand fairs in Flanders. The fair started on Sunday after Easter and lasted a month. In the 14th century it gained prominence among the fairs in Flanders and became an important international exchange venue. In 1508/'9 (Jan.) emperor Maximilian and archduke Charles granted a free fair starting January for six weeks.
Toll_Description: The most important toll in Bruges was the comital toll on shipping on the Zwin sea inlet. Citizens of the city were temporarily exempted in 1127. After the closing of the Zwin in Damme in 1180 and the silting of the waterway, the toll was primarily levied at the outports Damme, Monnikerede, Hoeke, Mude and Sluis (see there). Pawn tariffs from the late 15th and early 16th century show the decline of trade on the Zwin. Moreover, there also existed a large and a small toll in the city, of which the former was levied on long-distance trade and the latter was a local toll on produce from the surrounding region to supply the city. Citizens from Bruges were exempted from all tolls in Flanders in 1302. The oldes toll-account is dated 1553/4, the next one  only 1606 and later.
Staple_Description: First privileges of the low German merchants in Bruges date from 1252. The ordinance of the aldermen from 1285 forces citizens to bring all cloth from within a range of 3 miles around the city to Bruges. 1309: Staple for wax, furs, copper and other commodities. The general staple was confirmed by Count Louis II in 1323, with the exception of dried fish, corn, salt, pitch, tar and shipbuilding materials, which are also allowed to be unloaded in Damme, Houcke and Monikerede. Exclusive staple for English wool in 1340-1353. A Hanseatic residence ("Kontor") was established in 1347. During conflicts, the Hanseatic staple was moved to Dordrecht in 1358-1359 and 1388-1392, and to Bergen op Zoom (for wool) in 1388-1392. In the 14th century, Bruges had growing problems in enforcing the staple, in favour of the cities Sluis, Antwerp, Middelburg, Utrecht and Amsterdam. In 1530, the Hanseatic Kontor was finally moved to Antwerp, leaving only a staple for Spanish wool (established in 1490, confirmed in 1531 and 1540) in Bruges.

name: Ventola
Settlement_Description: <b>Inn:</b> Ventola had a parish constable (fi: nimismies, sw: länsman), who ran a tavern in his house in the early 17th c.

name: Oosterhoogebrug
Bridge_Description: A "high bridge" across the canal Damsterdiep (dug in 1424) is already mentioned in 1427, and most likely refers to the bridge later named Oosterhoogebrug (there were also "high briges" north and west of the city of Groningen) since the 17th century. However, there might already have been a bridge across the Hunze river at this place in 1370 before the Damsterdiep was dug.

name: Kajaani
Settlement_Description: Permanent agricultural settlement in Paltamo and Oulunjärvi area dates to the colonisation from Savolax in the 1550s. The administrative centre of the area was Royal Manor close to Vuohenginkoski stream in Kajaaninjoki river in 1555–58. Oulujärvi parish was founded in 1559, when its church was built on Manamansalo island and the area’s administration was attached to Ostrobothnia. The church and the much of the settlement were destroyed by Russians in 1578–80. After the official annexation of the area to Swedish realm in the peace of Teussina in 1595 the settlement was in 1599 organised into Paltamo parish (sw. Kajaneborg socken), the first two wooden churches of which stood at Kirkkoniemi in Paltaniemi in 1599–1716. The parish was split to Paltamo and Sotkamo parishes in 1647. The building of Kajaani castle (sw. Kajaneborg) was started in 1604, but the stronghold was left unfinished in 1619. After Queen Christina enfeoffed a large area in Northeast Finland to the Lord High Steward and Governor-General Count Per Brahe the younger in 1649, Kajaani became the centre of administration of his dominion there. Brahe established the town of Kajaani in 1651 and rebuilt the castle as an administrational residence in 1661–66. The enfeoffment was revoked in the Great Reduction in 1681.
Fair_Description: The burghers of Oulu were granted the right of two annual fairs in Kajaneborg parish in 1625. Of these the summer fair was to be held at midsummer (24 June) in Paltaniemi and the winter fair on 15 December in Särismäki. Paltaniemi midsummer fair was relocated to Kajaani in 1650 where annual winter fair was ordained to Candlemas (2 February). The summer fair in Paltaniemi-Kajaani region may have had a longer tradition before the Finnish and Swedish colonisation of the area in the 1550s. In 1555 the Russian Karelian merchants had a waypoint on their portage trail between Ladoga and Bothnian rivermouths in Vuohenginkoski stream where the castle was statrted in 1604, and after that in 1606 in Nuasjärvi SSE from Kajaani.
Toll_Description: The 1/32 duty worth of all goods intended for sale in towns and fairs and brought to the site by peasants was collected in the fair since 1650.

name: Doeveren
Bridge_Description: At the bridge (location uncertain, between Doeveren and Baardwijk) over the river Oude Maas a toll was raised on the road to the Langstraat. The bridge must have been there around 1400. In the village Doeveren at the north bank of the river Oude Maas was an outpost for the toll from Heusden situated. This one is found in accounts dated 1378-93.

Ferry_Description: Ferries crossing the river Hollandse IJssel and Lek in both settlement called Krimpen (Krimpen aan den IJssel and aan den Lek) are first mentioned in 1236. In 1561 a ferry to Keten (Capelle-West) is found. There might also have been a ferry to the Stormpolder, but this part was only embanked in the years 1287-1300, so it cannot already have existed in 1236.

name: Luhtiala
Settlement_Description: <b>Inn:</b> Parish constable (fi: nimismies, sw: länsman) Diedrich Schlüter ran a tavern in his house from 1636 on.

name: Groningen
Town_Description: Groningen was never officially granted town rights by a land lord. However, Groningen had several town-like features and developed into a town between the eleventh and thirteenth century. By the thirteenth century the town was already walled ('ommuurd'). The earliest document from a city government dates from 14 November 1245.
Fair_Description: Possibly from the twelfth century onward, a 'vrijmarkt' took place in the town of Groningen around the Feast of Saint Otger (10 September). In 1250 a flowering horse-fair is mentioned in a chronicle of the convent Bloemhof at Wittewierum. In 1434, five additional fairs were instituted: on Laetare Sunday, Quasimodo Sunday, Saint Vitus (15 June), Saint James (25 July) and Assumption of Mary (15 August). In 1436, another fair was instituted on Saint Michael (29 September). From 1446 onward, cloth merchants were allowed to sell their goods for a longer period in the cloth hall, namely one day before and two days after the market day, except during the 'vrijmarkt' around Saint Otger. It is not clear whether this held true for all other markets. The 'vrijmarkt' was extended during the sixteenth century, until it lasted until the 2nd of October. In 1609, the duration of this fair was limited to 7-13 September.
Toll_Description: A toll on oxen en horses was collected at the Poelepoort. First known yields in the oldest preserved city-account dated 1526/'7. Unknown when it was installed.
Staple_Description: From 1430 onwards, the town attempted to dominate the economy of the Frisian coastal area between Ems and Lauwers. It acquired full staple privileged for all commodities from the Ommelanden and a beer monopoly in 1500. This led to conflicts with Emden and Appingedam, which organised fairs. The States General recognized the forced offering of commodities for sale on the market in 1559, but the duration was limited to one or two hours. In 1599, all foreign commodities except horses and cattle were exempted from staple obligations. For domestic commodities, the staple obligations existed mainly for corn, butter and cheese. The staple is still mentioned in 1649, but seems to have collapsed shortly afterwards.

name: Antwerpen
Settlement_Description: Earliest mention in the eighth century in a tenth-century copy. Next mention from 692-726, in a copy dating from 1191.
Fair_Description: On 24 April 1298 a horse fair on Saturday for all Brabant is granted by the duke of Brabant. In 1325 two fairs are found: on Pentecost (26 May) and St. Bavo (1 October). Both fairs lasted for six weeks. In the fifteenth century, the fairs in Antwerp became large international fairs, not in the last place as main markets on the continent for English cloth merchants, who had been denied access to the markets in Flanders. A comital cloth hall is first found in 1226, in 1250 half of the revenues are donated to the town. In 1317 all of the revenues and the building were given to the town and it was rebuilt in 1324.
Staple_Description: In 1259 several towns (Brussel, Tienen, Aarschot, Herentals, Turnhout, Oisterwijk, Den Bosch, Breda, Hoogstraten, Lier, Zierikzee and Leuven) declared that the saltstaple had been in Antwerp forever. Malines citizens were freed from staple obligations for fish, salt and oats in Antwerp in 1356, which led to decades of conflict between both cities, ended in favour of Antwerp in 1415. Staple of fatty products for Holland in 1358. 1407: Staple of English cloth merchants. 1409: Privileges of the Hanse, partial relocation of Hanseatic activities from Bruges to Antwerp. In 1416 the staple for herring was relocated from the St. Jansvliet to the Holenvliet. 1444 Staple of Middelburg trading guilds. 1452: Hanseatic staple of Rhenish wines, together with Dordrecht. 1491: Staple for alum from Tolfa. 1540: Agreement with Scotland for a staple of Scottish salt and fishes. An agreement with the Hanse made the city the principal Hanseatic residency in the Netherlands in 1563.

name: Bjerning
Settlement_Description: The village of Bjerning was first mentioned in 1292, but is significantly older. The parish church is from either the 12th or 13th century.

name: Blankenbach
Settlement_Description: First mentioned in 1332. The settlement previously existed a little further to the north, it fell desolate and was then rebuilt in the 16th century on the current site.

name: Afferde
Settlement_Description: The place was first mentioned in 1042.

name: Bodum
Settlement_Description: The village of Bodum was first mentioned in 1344, but is significantly older. The settlement had no church but was part of the parish of Løjt Church.

name: Bommerlund
Settlement_Description: The settlement of Bommerlund was first mentioned in 1543, but is significantly older. The settlement had no church but was part of the parish of Bov Church.

name: Brauerschwend
Settlement_Description: First mentioned in 1273. In 1320 a 'Vorwerk' is named.

name: Angermünde
Settlement_Description: Originated as an Ascanian fortress built at the southern shore of the Münde lake between 1232 and 1250, first mentioned in 1263 as part of the name Henricus de Angermunde.
Town_Description: A town was founded by the Margraves John I and Otto III between 1230 and 1267. Mentioned as civitas in 1284; in 1286 the Angermünde town law was granted to Stolpe, in 1440 to Arnswalde.

name: Braniewo
Settlement_Description: Most likely used to be an old prussic settlement, a castle of the Teutonic Order was built in 1240 and destroyed by the Old Prussians in 1242, a new german settlement was founded in 1250 and destroyed in 1260, what is now known as the historic district was built in 1276
Town_Description: Town law was granted in 1254 by the first Warmian Bishop, Anselm, the now historic town district was granted a handfast of Lübeck town law in 1284 by Bishop Heinrich Fleming from Lübeck, the new town district was founded on Lübeck town law in 1342 by Bishop Hermann of Prag

name: Bredebro
Settlement_Description: The village of Bredebro was first mentioned in 1550 but is significantly older. The settlement had no church but was part of the parish of Brede Church.

name: Apeldoorn
Settlement_Description: Earliest mention in 790-793, in a copy dating from 1170-1175. Next mention is in the beginning of the thirteenth century.
Toll_Description: A land toll owned by the landlord, the duke of Guelders, was levied near Apeldoorn.

name: Arpke
Settlement_Description: The village was first mentioned in 1166.

name: Burguffeln
Settlement_Description: First mentioned in 965 and located near a castle.

name: Coesfeld
Settlement_Description: First mentioned in 809. An earlier mention of Coesfeld as in monte Coisio from 779 is a falsification.
Town_Description: Bishop Hermann II. granted town privileges like Munster in 1197.

name: Behlendorf
Settlement_Description: Village and the associated manor Klein Behlendorf, both first mentioned in 1194.

name: Berggießhübel
Settlement_Description: Originally a small estate and knights estate. In the 15th century the place benefited from flourishing mining.
Town_Description: In 1554 town privileges are first attested.

name: Besenthal
Settlement_Description: The settlement was first mentioned in 1230.

name: Delbrück
Settlement_Description: First mentioned in 1219. Never grew beyond a settlement, but had market- and duty free. This was confirmed in 1591.

name: Bibow
Settlement_Description: The village is first mentioned in 1247.

name: Bethen
Settlement_Description: The settlement was first mentioned in 1362. It is first mentioned as pilgrimage centre in 1448, because of a miraculous pietà image, although the first pilgrimages probably already took place at the time of creation of the image between 1380 and 1400.

name: Bierutów
Toll_Description: The toll is first mentioned in 1324.

name: Bērze
Settlement_Description: The Manor was first mentioned in 1599.

name: Bulduri
Settlement_Description: The manor existed in the 17th century.

name: Bischofsmühle
Settlement_Description: Water mill near Schwerin, first mentioned in 1191.

name: Drengsted
Settlement_Description: The village of Drengsted was first mentioned in 1455, but is significantly older. The settlement had no church but was part of the parish of Døstrup Church.

name: Boechout
Settlement_Description: Earliest mention in 974. Next mention in 1003.

name: Borne (Twente)
Settlement_Description: Earliest mention in 1206, in a fifteenth-century copy.

name: Eckelshausen
Settlement_Description: In 1320 Volpert von Hohenfels imposed the village of Eckelshausen with an annual pension, which he received back as a castle loan.

name: Eifa
Settlement_Description: First mentioned before 1057. Still referred to as a village in 1476.

name: Eltingmühle
Settlement_Description: A water mill at the Eltingsmühlebach in the dispersed settlement ('bauerschaft') Schmedehausen is first mentioned in registers in 1498/99, but must have existed since the High Middle Ages.

name: Elfershausen
Settlement_Description: First mentioned in 1253 as 'villa'. In 1345 referred to as deserted, but again as a village in 1347.

name: Breesen (Tribsees)
Settlement_Description: The village is first mentioned in 1232.

name: Ensted
Settlement_Description: The village of Ensted was first mentioned in 1231, but is significantly older. The parish church is from either the 12th or 13th century.

name: Bremervörde
Settlement_Description: The settlement developed next to a 12th-century moated castle that was built by duke Lothar of Saxony at a ford in the Oste river. After 1219 it became the main castle of the archbishops of Bremen. The settlement acquired borough ('weichbild') privileges after Hamburg model in the 14th century.
Fair_Description: A fair on Ascension Day was moved from Bevern to Bremervörde in 1582. Merchants were offered two days of safe conduct after the fair.
Toll_Description: A toll of the archbishop of Bremen is first mentioned in 1225, when citizens of the town Bremen were exempted from the toll. In the 15th and 16th century, there were conflicts with Bremen citizens, who misused their exemption to drive cattle through Bremervörde for foreigners. In this time, it is mostly mentioned as toll and safe conduct for oxen.

name: Favstrup
Settlement_Description: The village of Favstrup was first mentioned in 1452, but is significantly older. The settlement had no church but was part of the parish of Tyrstrup Church.

name: Bündorf
Settlement_Description: Probably developed during the Frakisch colonization, first written mention in 1012, when Henry II. confirms the possession of Boian villa (Bojandorf) to the church of Merseburg. Mention of a castrum in 1266.

name: Freckenhorst
Settlement_Description: The settlement emerges west of the Freckenhorst Abbey; a 'Wigbold' in the late Middle Ages. First mentioned 851.

name: Werlaburgdorf
Settlement_Description: A family of Burgdorf is first mentioned in 1142, the village itself in 1147. The name Werlaburgdorf - after the early medieval royal palace Werla, which was located in the vicinity - was only adopted as late as 1958.
Toll_Description: A toll in Werlaburgdorf is mentioned in 1301 and 1354.

name: Kożuchów
Settlement_Description: The area was given to the knight Dietrich Stang in 1285 by the Pomesanian diocesan chapter with the right to found a town
Town_Description: The town was founded by the knight Dietrich Stange, so it had to have happened before 1320, the oldest handfast, with Kulm town law, is dated 1331

name: Fronhausen
Settlement_Description: First mentioned in 1159. 1321 still called a village.

name: Fulda
Settlement_Description: A Benedictine monastery was founded in 744. The settlement at the monastery mentioned around 852.
Town_Description: Receipt of town charter under Abbot Marquard I (1150-1165); In 1019 Fulda was given market, customs and minting rights.

name: Øster Gasse
Settlement_Description: The village of Øster Gasse was first mentioned around the year 1300, but is significantly older. The settlement had no church but was part of the parish of Skærbæk Church.

name: Gejlå
Settlement_Description: The settlement of Gejlå was first mentioned in 1543, but is significantly older. The settlement had no church but was part of the parish of Holbøl Church.

name: Czersk
Toll_Description: Mentioned as toll station in c. 1349, where 3 gr. and 4 den. had to be paid for each horse.

name: Cröbern
Settlement_Description: In 1350 referred to as curia, abandoned in 1982 for a lignite open-cast mine.

name: Krosno Odrzańskie
Settlement_Description: A Polish castle is mentioned in 1005 in the context of battles between Henry II and Boleslaw I. A church existed in 1065, mentions of viticulture by German immigrants since 1154. a Slavic fishing settlement existed between the church and the river, later there was also a German market settlement.
Town_Description: The town was founded in the beginning of the 13th century by the Duke of Silesia, most likely Henry I (1201-1221). Mentioned as civitas in 1249, possessed Magdeburg town law since 1317.

name: Zheleznodorozhnyy
Settlement_Description: A castle of the Teutonic Order was built in 1325 to replace the Prussian castle, a settlement grew close to it
Town_Description: The Grand Master Konrad von Jungingen elevates the place to a town with Kulm town law in 1398

name: Gołdap
Settlement_Description: House and yard of a ducal private (Wildschütze) in 1551, ducal sheep farm with adjoining village
Town_Description: The founding was planned for 1565, founded between 1566 and 1570 along the remains of two villages, organised by a locator and the ducal councilman Kaspar von Nositz, Duke Albrecht Friedrich signed the documents in 1570 and granted Kulm town law

name: Dieren
Settlement_Description: Earliest mention in 838, in a eleventh century copy.

name: Diersbüttel
Settlement_Description: The village was first mentioned in 1302.

name: Dieskau
Settlement_Description: The lords of Dieskau gain Dieskau as a fiefdom around 1200.

name: Grebenau
Settlement_Description: First mentioned in 1265. The documents before 1057 can not be assigned with certainty to this Gerebenau or to the one in the Schwalm-Eder district.
Town_Description: Ludwig V of Hesse-Darmstadt granted town and market rights in 1605.

name: Großenlüder
Settlement_Description: First mentioned in 822. Around 900 called 'ville'. Near the settlement were three castles, which are completely vanished today.

name: Dobre Miasto
Settlement_Description: First mentioned in 1325, the settlement was founded by the locator Wilhelm von Wormitt on the order of the Warmian bishop Eberhard von Neiße
Town_Description: Bishop Heinrich von Wogenap grants a handfast with Kulm town law to the civitas in 1329

name: Hagen
Settlement_Description: Mentioned at the end of the 11th century, but possibly much older.

name: Eckendorf
Toll_Description: A land toll was levied here in 1194. The Count of Are/Neuenahr was initially the owner. From 1446/47 it was the Archbishop of Cologne. The annual yield was approx. 6 gulden in 1446/47.

name: Haiger
Settlement_Description: First attested in 778. Around 900 there was a Frankish royal court.
Town_Description: It is unclear exactly when the settlement was raised to town. In 1357 still referred to as a village, but in 1400 as a city. A document about the city rights is missing.

name: Halle (Westfalen)
Settlement_Description: First mentioned in 1146. In 1346 the settlement got granted 'Weichbildrechte' and was called a free 'Wigbold' in 1488.

name: Hanau
Settlement_Description: The name appears as early as 1143. A castle probably existed before that, but it is first mentioned in 1234. At the beginning of the 13th century, a settlement was built south of this castle.
Town_Description: The settlement is only mentioned by name in the course of its city charter in 1303. Before that it is called 'oppidum'.

name: Harmuthsachsen
Settlement_Description: First mentioned in 1195. 1334 still called a village.

name: Elden
Settlement_Description: Earliest mention dates from 855 in a copy dated around 900.

name: Hasselbach
Settlement_Description: First mentioned in 1273. 1363 called a village.

name: Herborn
Settlement_Description: First mentioned in 1251 as 'villa'. Perhaps there was a seat of a royal court here.
Town_Description: In 1251 the settlement received the right to fortification and a market. The sovereign is used as the town lord. Mentioned 'civitas' in 1296, referred to as 'oppidum' in 1329 and as a city in 1332.

name: Herne
Settlement_Description: First mentioned as 'Kirchdorf' in the 9th century at the intersection of old trade routes.

name: Bad Hersfeld
Settlement_Description: Originally a student of Boniface founded a hermitage here in 736/743, but it had to be given up again in 744. Benedictine abbey founded between 769 and 775, near which a settlement was built.

name: Esperstedt
Settlement_Description: Mention in the Breviarium sacti Lulli, Tab. II.

name: Hirschberg
Settlement_Description: The place grew under the protection of the castle of the Counts of Arnsberg, which was built in the 12th century. The settlement was first mentioned in 1308.
Town_Description: In 1308 the town was given town privileges of Eversberg by Count Wilhelm von Arnsberg, which were confirmed in 1364.

name: Olsztynek
Settlement_Description: A castle of the Teutonic Order was built around 1350 alongside a village from 1343
Town_Description: The Grand Master Winrich von Kniprode grants founded the town in 1359 with Kulm town law

name: Høm
Settlement_Description: The village of Høm was first mentioned in 1380, but is significantly older. The settlement had no church but was part of the parish of Seem Church.

name: Frauenwald
Settlement_Description: A chapel of St Nicholas in the Thuringian Forest was donated to Veßra monastery in 1218. A Premonstratensian ladies' convent is mentioned in 1323 and 1406, but must have disappeared soon after.
Toll_Description: A toll registry from the 16th century shows the fees that had to be paid in Frauenwald on the way across the Thuringian Forest, which are edited by Straube. Toll revenues are also mentioned in 1529/30.

name: Frenswegen
Settlement_Description: The Augustinian Monastery was founded in 1394 by several distinguished counts and benefactors. Due to its numerous possessions, including farms and from 1578 even the castle in Nordhorn, the monastery received great prestige and grew to be an institution of economic importance. It was closed in 1809.

name: Franzhagen
Settlement_Description: The settlement Lalkau is mentioned in 1230, and abandoned in the 15th century. Between 1572 and 1592, a manor was built by the wife of Duke Franz I of Lauenburg, called Franzhagen.

name: Hovslund
Settlement_Description: The village of Hovslund was first mentioned in 1474, but is significantly older. The settlement had no church but was part of the parish of Øster Løgum Church.

name: Vreren
Settlement_Description: Earliest mention in 1078, in a thirteenth century copy.

name: Hungen
Settlement_Description: First mentioned in 782 in a deed of gift. Maybe goes back to a Roman settlement.
Town_Description: In 1361 town privileges were granted. Then called town in 1403.

name: Hüsten
Settlement_Description: First mentioned in 802, in connection with the Werden monastery.
Town_Description: In 1360 the majority of Hüsten was liberated and granted Arnsberg rights.

name: Friedberg
Settlement_Description: Around 1170 a castle is mentioned, where the town is planned to be laid out until 1200 and was first mentioned in 1216.
Town_Description: For 1216 'Burggravius ​​et castrenses' are mentioned. 1219 'cives' and 1220 'civitas'. The town has had royal charter since 1232.
Toll_Description: A toll station is mentioned in 1364, a road toll ('Wegegeld') in 1367.

name: Immenhausen
Settlement_Description: Nobles von Immenhausen mentioned since 1143. The town itself is mentioned as a subject of dispute in 1282.
Town_Description: Town privileges can be proven from 1298. The town is mentioned as an 'oppidum' in 1303 and 1331.

name: Ippinghausen
Settlement_Description: First mentioned around 1120. Deserted in the 15th and early 16th centuries. However, settled again in the first half of the 16th century.

name: Hjordkær
Settlement_Description: The village of Hjordkær was first mentioned in 1196, but is significantly older. The parish church is from either the 12th or 13th century.

name: Geeste
Settlement_Description: The village was first mentioned in 890.

name: Graditz
Settlement_Description: The village is first mentioned in 1240. A folwark is mentioned in 1529.

name: Geesthacht
Settlement_Description: First mentioned around 1216. The village belonged to Hamburg and Lübeck jointly between 1420 and 1867.
Toll_Description: In 1216, Hamburg was exempted from the toll in Geesthacht. Likely, this was an im- and export toll for commodities like wood and salt that where shipped on the Elbe river. The toll is once again mentioned when Geesthacht was pawned to Lübeck in 1370.

name: Gildehaus
Settlement_Description: The settlement was called Nyenkerken until the 14th century, after the local church of St Anne. Between the 13th and the 19th century, the settlement was an exporter of the local sandstone.

name: Kinderhaus
Settlement_Description: First mentioned in 1333. There was possibly a leprosy house there.

name: Gloine
Settlement_Description: Mentioned 1187 as the property of Leitzkau monastery. Later property of the archbishopric of Magdeburg and later the district of Loburg. In 1645 reported thoroughly deserted. Bought in 1898 by the German military for the establishment of a military training area.

name: Kirchberg
Settlement_Description: First mentioned in 1226. A castle was built near the settlement in 1366, which was already destroyed by Heinrich II. of Hessen in 1370.

name: Kleinalmerode
Settlement_Description: First mentioned in 1150. Still called a village in 1361, abandoned in 1376, but named as a village again in 1398.

name: Kleinenglis
Settlement_Description: First mentioned between 775 and 786. In 1374 still called a village.

name: Kliplev
Settlement_Description: The village of Kliplev was first mentioned in 1231, but is significantly older. The parish church is from either the 12th or 13th century.

name: Grebehna
Settlement_Description: First certain mention in 1350. An earlier mention of an Arnoldus de Gribene in 1219 probably refers to Grieben near Tangermünde. Merged with Zwochau in 1950.

name: Grenzburg
Settlement_Description: Watchtower with boom barrier in the enclosure ('landwehr') of Güstrow. The enclosure is first mentioned in 1270, the year of construction of the tower is unknown. Later converted into a farm that was leased from the town.

name: Korbach
Settlement_Description: First mentioned in 980. The settlement emerged from a Saxon 'Edelhof', which later became a Carolingian street fortress and imperial court.
Town_Description: When the place received the Soest town charter in 1188 by the bishop of Paderborn, it was probably already a town. According to chroniclers of the 16th century, it was founded in 1073.

name: Krauthausen
Settlement_Description: First mentioned in 1141. Destroyed several times during the 30 years war.

name: Kluczbork
Settlement_Description: An Old Prussian fortress was built on the casltle hill with a dependant  settlement, the Teutonic Order unter Otto von Braunschweig conquered the fortress in 1240, their settlement was then destroyed by the Old Prussians, in 1253 reclaimed the Teutonic Order the castle but had to give it up again in 1263 only to conquer it once more around 1270, afterwards it was the see of the Komtur of Natangen unti 1277, it was given to the bishop of Riesenburg in 1497 who let it decay, until it wasn't defensible anymore in 1507
Town_Description: A privilege from the landmaster Heinrich von Plotzke in 1315 created a town with Kulm town law

name: Groß Schwechten
Settlement_Description: First mention of the church in Schwechten in 1200.

name: Lang-Göns
Settlement_Description: A 'villa' is mentioned in 817. 1233 the settlement is named.

name: Gülzow
Settlement_Description: The vilalge is first mentioned in 1226.

name: Golczewo
Settlement_Description: A castle to the south of Gülzow was first mentioned in 1304.

name: Hadmersleben
Settlement_Description: 961 Otto II. confirms the foundation of Hadmersleben monastary (MGH DD OII nr. 2, S. 11f.). First mention of the castle in 1144.
Town_Description: One of the settlements of Hadmersleben is referred to as civitas in 1399.
Fair_Description: In 1565, two fairs were granted by archbishop Sigismund.

name: Harku
Settlement_Description: Manor and village that were first mentioned in 1241.

name: Hämerten
Ferry_Description: Hämerten maintained a small passenger ferry.

name: Hessisch Lichtenau
Settlement_Description: Created by merging several villages. First mentioned in 1289.
Town_Description: Landgrave Heinrich I founded the town probably before 1289. 'Nova civitas' mentioned for 1289.

name: Lichtenau
Town_Description: An exact award of town privileges is not documented, but it must have been a town before 1350.

name: Lingelbach
Settlement_Description: The settlement is first mentioned in 1458.

name: Haster Turm
Settlement_Description: Watchtower in the enclosure ('landwehr') of Osnabrück next to a bridge over the river Nette, first mentioned as "turris in Harst" in 1383.

name: Lüdinghausen
Settlement_Description: A church is mentioned around 800. Next to it, there grew the 'Wigbold' Lüdinghausen.
Town_Description: The actual city development took place in 1308. Before that, however, there were some attempts to fortify the settlement, against the will of the bishop, which is why it had to be torn down again. In 1314 the bishop again forced the fortifications to be destroyed, which is why Lüdinghausen is considered a city by name, but has no urban rights.

name: Lustrup
Settlement_Description: The village of Lustrup was first mentioned in 1233, but is significantly older. The settlement had no church but was part of the parish of Ribe Church

name: Ełk
Settlement_Description: The village was founded in 1425 by the Teutonic Order close to its castle

name: Herzberg am Harz
Settlement_Description: Count Werner of Lutterberg built a hunting house in 1029, below which a settlement developed. In the second half of the 16th or the first half of the 17th century, Herzberg acquired borough ('flecken') privileges, an exact year is unknown.
Toll_Description: A toll in Herzberg is first mentioned shortly after 1421, but probably existed already in 1315.

name: Hettstedt
Settlement_Description: 1046 Mention in a gift certificate by Henry III. to Meißen monastery (MGH DD H III, nr. 157, S. 198f.).The mining industry facilitates building a castle in Hettstedt, which is desterted again around 1575.
Town_Description: Reference to the settlement as "civitas" in 1283, later as "stad" in 1334. First mention of a council in Hettstedt in 1385.
Fair_Description: In 1453 two fairs were known, additional fairs were granted in 1679 and 1697.

name: Marburg
Settlement_Description: In 1138 the knight Ludwig de Marburg is mentioned first. The mention of a Marburg mint in 1194 presupposes that a market settlement must have existed beforehand.
Town_Description: Orders under city law by Bishop Ludwig von Münster have been documented since 1311.

name: Hilter am Teutoburger Wald
Settlement_Description: The village was first mentioned in 1171.

name: Medebach
Settlement_Description: Before 1144, free 'Tafelgut' of the Archbishop of Cologne. Who also made the settlement an 'oppidum' in 1144.

name: Nieder Erlenbach
Settlement_Description: First mentioned between 768 and 778. Still designated as a village in 1376. Around 1400, the village was protected by a castle and surrounded by a moat.

name: Meschede
Settlement_Description: First mentioned in 913 and called 'Dorp' in 1368.
Town_Description: In 1457 the place received freedom and restricted rights, but  was probably not yet a city. Arnsberger law and privileges were confirmed in 1508.

name: Horn (Hamburg)
Settlement_Description: First mentioned in 1309. A boom barrier is mentioned here in 1465.

name: Hünfeld
Settlement_Description: Charlemagne donated the 'campus hunae' in 781 to the Fulda monastery. A 'Hörigensiedlung' is first mentioned in 1049.
Town_Description: Called 'civis' in 1295 and 1308, 'oppidum' in 1299 at the latest. In 1310 King Heinrich VII granted Gelnhausen town rights.

name: Hünighausen
Settlement_Description: First mentioned between 1107 and 1128. The village was demolished in 1932.

name: Mörshausen
Settlement_Description: The first confirmed mention of the village dates back to 1209. Evidence from the 9th century cannot be clearly assigned.

name: Igavere
Settlement_Description: The village that belonged to the Manor of Ellistfer was mentioned in 1220.

name: Młynary
Settlement_Description: A yard of the Teutonic Order was founded before 1414
Town_Description: Close to the yard of the order, the komtur of Elbing, Hermann von Öttingen, founded a town between 1320 and 1329, the founding documents do not survive, but have been renewed with Kulm town law in 1338 by the komtur von Elbing, Siegfried von Sitten, and endorsed by the Grand Master Konrad von Jungingen in 1404

name: Neuhof
Settlement_Description: First mentioned in 1239. Neuhof combines the villages of Ellers, Opperz and Neustadt.

name: Kalkar
Fair_Description: In 1486 there are two fairs: 1) May 1 and 2) Sept. 21. A cloth hall is first mentioned in 1319. In 1503 there were 42 brewers.

name: Neder Geestrup
Settlement_Description: The village of Neder Geestrup was first mentioned in 1348, but is significantly older. The settlement had no church but was part of the parish of Agerskov Church.

name: Niedermarsberg
Town_Description: The original award of town privileges is not known. However, there is a falsified document on the awarding of Dortmund town privileges 962. In 1104 the place is known as 'oppidum'.

name: Nørby
Settlement_Description: The village of Nørby was properbly first mentioned in 1519, but is significantly older. The settlement had no church but was part of the parish of Løjt Church.

name: Krylovo
Settlement_Description: A 'Wildhaus' was mentioned in 1366, a castle of the Teutonic Order in 1368, a settlement of Old Prussian farmers formed between 1370 and 1378
Town_Description: The place was intended to become a town in 1405, the founding documents with Kulm town law were signed by the Grand Master Ulrich von Jungingen in 1407

name: Ober Erlenbach
Settlement_Description: First mentioned between 768 and 779. However, the area was already settled in Roman times. This is evidenced by finds of pottery, coins and building foundations from the time of Antoninus Pius. The place itself probably goes back to a Frankish settlement from the 6th-7th century.

name: Olfen
Settlement_Description: First mentioned in 889. In 1589, Prince-Bishop Ernst von Münster is said to have had given 'Wigbold' rights. As a 'Wicbold' mentioned again in 1592, 1601 and 1790.

name: Klein Thurow
Settlement_Description: The oldest evidence from 1194 only mentions Thurow; a division between Groß and Klein Thurow is first made in 1332.

name: Ostbevern
Settlement_Description: The place originally belonged to Bevern until the parish was divided into East and West Bevern in the middle of the 13th century.Ostbevern was first mentioned in 1279.

name: Koknese
Settlement_Description: From the 11th to the 13th century there was a castle owned by Russian aristocracy that were expelled in 1208. Thereupon, Bishop Albert built a new castle (1209) around which a fortified borough ('Hakelwerk') settled.
Town_Description: The fortified borough ('Hakelwerk') near the castle acquired town law by Riga in 1277 and was a member of the Hanseatic League.

name: Pasłęk
Settlement_Description: A house of the Teutonic Order is mentioned in place of a Prussian castle in 1297
Town_Description: The land master of the Teutonic Order, Meinhart von Querfurt, grants a handfast with Kulm town law in 1297, the town was likely founded before that, so it's possibly the renewed founding document

name: Kyritz
Settlement_Description: The market settlement developed close to a castle, first mentioned in 1232.
Town_Description: Stendal town privileges were granted by the noble family of Plote in 1237.

name: Recklinghausen
Settlement_Description: First mentioned in 1017, but goes back to a Carolingian castle. In 1236 the place was called 'oppidum'.
Town_Description: Town rights were granted around 1230 and expanded in 1236.

name: Rennertehausen
Settlement_Description: First mentioned in 1274. Still called a village in 1577.

name: Liebstedt
Settlement_Description: In 956 Otto I donated property in Liebstedt to Quedlinburg monastery. In 1331 the moated castle belonged to the Teutonic Order.

name: Leimbach (Fulda)
Settlement_Description: First mentioned in 1061. Abandoned in the 16th century at the latest; the church is last mentioned in 1579.

name: Rom
Settlement_Description: The vilage is first mentioned in 1310.

name: Rüthen
Settlement_Description: The settlement was first mentioned in the second third of the 12th century and the town was founded around 1200, which got its name from the nearby Altenrüthen.
Town_Description: After completion of the 'fundatio' and 'plantatio' of the town, the Archbishop of Cologne granted town rights, which were extended by the citizens.

name: Ruttershausen
Settlement_Description: The village was first mentioned in 1256. Count Johann I of Nassau built a castle in 1367, which was destroyed again by Landgrave Heinrich II in 1370.

name: Sachsenberg
Settlement_Description: First mentioned by name in 1251. The Archbishop of Cologne and the Abbot Corveys planned to build a town near Lichtenfels Castle in 1230, which can be traced to Sachsenberg.
Town_Description: In 1262 the place was called 'oppidum' and was given a town seal.

name: Salmünster
Settlement_Description: The settlement was named as a parish at the end of the 9th century.
Town_Description: Granting of the rights and freedoms of the Wetterau imperial towns in 1320.

name: Loenen aan de Vecht
Settlement_Description: Earliest mention in 953, in a eleventh century copy. Next mention in 975, in a twelfth century copy.
Fair_Description: Around 1540 there is a consented horsefair. Emperor Charles V then forbade illegal horse-fairs in the Sticht of Utrecht.

name: Loenen (Veluwe)
Settlement_Description: Earliest mention in 838, in a eleventh and twelfth century copy. Next mention in 1247.

name: Loobu
Settlement_Description: Village and manor, which were in the possession of the Teutonic Order from the 15th to the 16th century.

name: Fårhus
Settlement_Description: The village of Fårhus was first mentioned in 1648, but is significantly older. The settlement had no church but was part of the parish of Bov Church.

name: Łowicz
Toll_Description: Mentioned as toll station in a document from c. 1349, where 1 gr. for each horse had to be paid.

name: Lubaczów
Toll_Description: Mentioned as toll station in c. 1349, where 1 gr. had to be paid for each horse.

name: Sępopol
Settlement_Description: A castle of the Teutonic Order was built in 1319 in place of an old Old Prussian castle
Town_Description: The grand master Heinrich Dusemer granted the founding documents of the town in 1351 with Kulm town law, it was mentioned as opidum in 1485

name: Lüdenscheid
Town_Description: Around the middle of the 13th century, the Count von der Mark granted town rights. In 1278 it is listed as an 'oppidum'. In 1517, the town rights were temporarily withdrawn because of the participation in riots.
Toll_Description: The Count of the Mark levied a land toll in 1395. In 1444, 3 denarii per draught horse and 1 denar per pack horse had to be paid. Annual revenues are not known.

name: Lüdershagen
Settlement_Description: The church village is first mentioned in 1288.

name: Lüdershausen
Settlement_Description: Castle and village, first mentioned in 1262. In the 15th and 16th century mostly pawned to Lüneburg.
Bridge_Description: The ferry was replaced by a bridge across the Neetze in 1618.
Ferry_Description: A ferry across the Neetze is attested in 1352; it was replaced by a bridge in 1618.

name: Lychen
Settlement_Description: A German castle settlement, a bigger Slavic settlement had been destroyed before. First mentioned at the foundation of the town in 1248.
Town_Description: Margrave John I granted the brothers Daniel and Eberhard of Parwenitz the right to found a town in 1248.

name: Maarssen
Settlement_Description: Earliest mention in 918-948, in a eleventh century copy. Next mention in 1127.

name: Machelen
Settlement_Description: Earliest mention in 1179, in a copy form the middle of the fourteenth century. Next mention in 1125.

name: Magdeborn
Settlement_Description: First mention in 969 in a donation charter of king Otto I to the archbishopric of Merseburg as castle ('Kastell') Magdeborn. In 1980 deserted due to a lignite mine.

name: Małogoszcz
Toll_Description: A toll station is mentioned in 1136.

name: Markranstädt
Settlement_Description: The village was founded near the Medieval settlement of "Altranstädt" in 1170/80.
Town_Description: In a bill of sale Markranstädt is first mentioned as little town "Städtchen".
Fair_Description: The former famous wool market in Markranstädt developed from the nearby sheep husbandry of Alt-Zelle monastery.

name: Sendenhorst
Town_Description: The place was elevated to a town in 1315.

name: Sensenstein
Settlement_Description: The castle was mentioned 1373, but an older watch tower is said to have stood in its place.

name: Siegen
Town_Description: Since around 1170 coins were minted with the inscription "Sigenensis civitas", town rights had to exist before. In 1224 a new Siegen was founded around 700 m to the east, next to a castle, into which the citizens of the old town moved.

name: Mehlem
Toll_Description: The Archbishop of Cologne levied a land toll around 1385. Tariffs are not known. From 1471 to 1472, 7½ mark and 4 shillings were collected. Mehlem was a secondary toll station of Königsdorf in 1455.

name: Sjølund
Settlement_Description: The village of Sjølund was first mentioned in 1452, but is significantly older. The settlement had no church but was part of the parish of Vejstrup Church.

name: Metelsdorf
Settlement_Description: The village is first mentioned in 1230.

name: Sølsted
Settlement_Description: The village of Sølsted was first mentioned in 1230, but is significantly older. The settlement had no church but was part of the parish of Abild Church.

name: Sontra
Settlement_Description: First mentioned in 1232 and still called a village in 1358.

name: Spandet
Settlement_Description: The village of Spandet was first mentioned in 1323, but is significantly older. The parish church is from either the 12th or 13th century.

name: Namysłów
Toll_Description: Merchants from Cracow complained in 1435 about the toll in Namysłów.

name: Sztum
Settlement_Description: An Old Prussian castle was destroyed in 1236 and a castle of the Teutonic Order was built between 1326 und 1335, it became the see of a komtur in 1331, then in 1333 the see of a bailiff and a chapel in 1413, later it was mentioned as a yard of the Teutonic Order
Town_Description: Founding documents with Kulm town law were given in 1416 by the Grand master Michael Küchmeister von Sternberg, endorsed in 1754

name: Nauen
Settlement_Description: Findings from the Stone Age, as well as Germanic and Slavic times. Priests in Nauen are mentioned in 1186 and 1197.
Town_Description: The Margraves of Brandenburg acquire the land in 1292 and grant the right to build a town hall. First mentioned as town in 1305. Additional privileges are granted in 1315 and 1317. Brandenburg town law is mentioned in 1429.
Fair_Description: Two fairs were held in Nauen in the Middle Ages, after the construction of the town hall in 1302. In 1345 one fair is explicitly mentioned.
Toll_Description: A toll was levied by the town on the causeway constructed north of the town ('Dammpfennig'); it was sold in 1326 to the cathedral chapter in Brandenburg. Engel et al. mention Nauen as a royal main toll station only since 1805.

name: Bad Nauheim
Settlement_Description: The place was listed for the first time before the middle of the 12th century in the property register of the Fulda monastery, and only appears again in the 13th century.

name: Neuengamme
Settlement_Description: The settlement was first mentioned in 1212. A church is named in 1261.

name: Sovetsk
Settlement_Description: A castle was built in 1365, another in 1406 with an adjoining Old Prussian settlement, towards the end of the Teutonic Order, a market hamlet grew, a Franciscan monastery was built
Town_Description: Duke Albrecht grants town law in 1552
Staple_Description: In 1543 grain barges travelling through Tilsit obliged to offer their goods for sale for three days

name: Neustadt bei Coburg
Settlement_Description: First mentioned as market settlement in 1248.
Toll_Description: Toll station of the counts of Henneberg, mentioned in an urbarium in 1317. It was located on the route of safe conduct Coburg-Saalfeld.

name: Trendelburg
Settlement_Description: Comes from the village of Trende, 1 km upstream and mentioned in 1203. In 1303 the village was relocated to Trendelburg. Called a city in 1304, but it is unclear whether town privileges were officially granted.

name: Mimoň
Toll_Description: A toll station in Mimoň is first mentioned in 1371. In the second half of the 15th century Johann of Dieczin and Dippold of Ryzemburg were in conflict about ownership of a part of the toll. Before 1659 the toll was moved to Svébořice/Schwabitz because traders circumvented Mimoň.

name: Nordgoltern
Settlement_Description: The settlement Goltern, which was subdivided into Groß- and Nordgoltern, was first mentioned in 1160. Nordgoltern as a separate settlement was mentioned in 1320.

name: Vellern
Settlement_Description: First mentioned at the end of the 11th century.

name: Bad Vilbel
Settlement_Description: First mentioned in 774. Developed on the traces of Roman and Germanic settlements.

name: Oldenburg (Holstein)
Settlement_Description: Slavic fortification, built in the second half of the 7th century. It became seat of a bishop in 968. After the destruction of the fort in 1148/49, the market settlement next to it developed into the new centre.
Town_Description: Adolf IV of Schauenburg granted Lübeck town privileges around 1233, confirmed in 1260 and 1392.
Fair_Description: Oldenburg acquired market freedom for a fair on St Michael's Day in 1392. In the 16th century, fairs were also held on Palm Sunday and St Vitus.

name: Oldendorf (Zeven)
Settlement_Description: First mentioned in 1254 in a donation to the monastery Zeven. In the 15th century, the settlement must have been abandoned; it was resettled with farmers by the monastery Zeven.

name: Walburg
Settlement_Description: First mentioned in 1229. Between 1283 and 1289, a predecessor foundation of the town of Lichtenau may have existed here, which mentions 'civitatis de Walberc' on a seal in 1289. However, it is mentioned again as a village in 1322.

name: Oldemorstoft
Settlement_Description: The settlement of Oldemorstoft was first mentioned in 1472, but is significantly older. The settlement had no church but was part of the parish of Bov Church.

name: Waltrop
Settlement_Description: First known mention in 1147. Previously said to have been in the 9th century but not secured.

name: Wanfried
Settlement_Description: First mentioned in the 9th century. In the 13th century as a 'villa', later called 'Flecken'.
Town_Description: In 1608, Landgrave Moritz granted town rights.

name: Warstein
Town_Description: Archbishop Siegfried of Cologne founded the town in 1276. 1287 Warstein is named as 'oppidum'.

name: Winterberg
Town_Description: Around 1250 the town received town rights and was fortified. These rights were confirmed in 1357.

name: Plzeň
Toll_Description: The toll of Plzeň was leased in 1327 and 1360.

name: Vodder
Settlement_Description: The village of Vodder was first mentioned in the later half of the 13th century, but is significantly older. The parish church is from either the 12th or 13th century.

name: Płoty
Settlement_Description: First mentioned in 1277, when it became a town. Before a Slavic settlement with a fortification existed. The find of 10th-century Arabic coins suggests that it must have been a significant trade location at that time.
Town_Description: Lübeck town privileges granted by the knight Dubislaw von Woedtke in 1277, so the town must have been founded before that year.

name: Põlgaste
Settlement_Description: The village and the associated Manor were first mentioned in 1628.

name: Zādzene
Settlement_Description: The manor was first mentioned in 1449.

name: Quetzdölsdorf
Settlement_Description: First mention in a gift certificate by the margrave of Meißen to the Cistercian convent Marienkammer (register of the record-directory of the convent of St. George's of Glaucha at Halle a.S. (printed in v. Dreyhaupt).

name: Quitzöbel
Settlement_Description: Former Slavic settlement which was occupied by the family of Quitzow after 1147.

name: Rethem
Settlement_Description: The castle of Rethem was first mentioned in the 13th century; next to it, three settlements developed. The central settlement was characterised as town ('stat') in 1382 and as borough ('weichbild' or 'flecken') since 1388.
Toll_Description: Water and land toll, first mentioned in the 14th century. The oldest toll tariff, like in Celle, is known from the time around 1560. In this year, the duke of Brunswick-Lüneburg redeemed the toll from the town of Lüneburg, which had held it as a pawn since 1389. The tariffs were raised later, according to a 1576 complaint from Bremen.

name: Rhens
Toll_Description: In 1376, the Archbishop of Cologne levied a land toll. Tariffs and revenues are not known.

name: Rogoźno
Toll_Description: Merchants complained about raised toll tariffs in Rogoźno in the 16th century.

name: Ropczyce
Toll_Description: The toll in Ropzcyce was given to the church in Gorzyce in 1515.

name: Ridala
Settlement_Description: Parish, first mentioned in 1215. A village with the same name is first mentioned in 1798.

name: Rucksbruch
Settlement_Description: The exact location of the toll station in Rucksbruch is unknown.
Toll_Description: The toll station in the Rucksbruch already existed in medieval times, either from 1355 or 1427. It was moved to Tanne in the 1710s due to the bad condition of the road.

name: Saalburg
Settlement_Description: A fortification Saalburg, which is first mentioned in 1216, was constructed at the Saale crossing at the old trade route Nuremberg - Leipzig.
Town_Description: Referred to as oppidum in 1313. The town was fortified in 1367. Acquisition of Gera town rights in the 14th/15th century; the oldest town privileges date from 1495.

name: Salem (Neukalen)
Settlement_Description: The village is first mentioned in 1314.

name: Sandomierz
Toll_Description: Mentioned as toll station in c. 1349 with tariffs for horses, cloth and other commodities.
Staple_Description: Unimportant staple, confirmed in the Polish Staple Law of 1565

name: Rødekro
Settlement_Description: In 1642 a small house was build at Rødåen, which was turned into an inn, the inn was located at the border of the shire.

name: Schauen
Settlement_Description: First mention in 973, when Schauen is confirmed as property of the chathedral chapter of Magdeburg. In the 13th century, a ministerial family of Schauen is known.

name: Sooden
Settlement_Description: The salt deposits in Sooden were already mentioned in the 8th century under the name "Westera". The name Sooden ist known from 1093 onwards. The village was united with Allendorf in 1929.

name: Skalmierzyce
Toll_Description: Attested as toll station in 1363 and 1393.

name: Kalundborg
Settlement_Description: Castle founded by the powerful magnate Esbern Snarre, a brother to bishop Absalon of Roskilde, around the year 1170, at Hærvig Fjord. Possibly there already was a smaller permanent settlement, something which is indicated by archeological finds dated to the early 12th century.
Town_Description: A registration of towns on Zealand and the surrounding island (Danish: Købstadslisten) from 1241 in King Valdemar’s Cadastre define Kalundborg as one of the richest towns in Zealand. Oldest known privileges were granted by king Christopher III the Bavarian (1440-1448) in 1443, but Kalundborg obtained town rights much earlier. Presumably, Kalundborg was granted its first town rights in the late 12th century. Oldest town privileges as well as many other documents, however, were lost when the town archive burned in 1495. Town privileges renewed that same year. In 1239 a Franciscan monastery was founded. Members of town council and mayors are known from the 14th century. Earliest mention of town hall is from 1442. Relatively early the original central part of Kalundborg centered around the church was fortified, i.e. surrounded by a town wall. In the later middle ages a strong castle to the east replaced the first castle to the west, and the town spread outside the town wall. This new part of town was known as “Kordel”. Throughout the medieval period Kalundborg was the dominant town in northwestern Zealand and one of the wealthiest towns on the island. Kalundborg was also one of the political centers of Denmark, as kings often visited the town. During the early-modern era, however, the town's status declined. The town also suffered during the Count's Feud (Danish: Grevens Fejde) 1534-1536, and was occupied by Swedish troops during the Dano-Swedish wars in the late 1650ties.
Fair_Description: In 1633 the number of annual fairs in Kalundborg were limited to two. Thus, it is reasonable to presume that Kalundborg had at least three annual fairs before 1633. However, these fairs are not mentioned in the preserved sources.
Toll_Description: A royal toll on seafaring was implemented by king Christoffer II (1320-1326 & 1329-1332), probably around 1320. When Christoffer lost the throne in 1326, the toll was abolished.

name: Staritz
Settlement_Description: The village is first mentioned in 1119.

name: Starygród
Toll_Description: The monastery of Lubin owned the toll in Starogród on the street between Toruń and Wroclaw, according to a confirmation from 1294.

name: Vaalimo
Settlement_Description: <b>Inn:</b> An inn was established in Vaalimo in 1649, and Pietari Äikäs was appointed as the innkeeper.

name: Suislepa
Settlement_Description: Village and crown land that was first mentioned in 1583. At the end of the 18th century Neu Suislep (Uue Suislepa) was created, but is now merged with Alt Suislep (Vana Suislepa).

name: Sülbeck (Leine)
Toll_Description: A toll in Sülbeck is mentioned in 1619 and 1629.

name: Teglingen
Settlement_Description: First mentioned in the 9th century. The name goes back to a court, which was mentioned regularly until the 18th century.

name: Teschendorf (Burg Stargard)
Settlement_Description: First mentioned as part of the name Toppenikus de Teskendorpe in 1356.

name: Teuven
Settlement_Description: First mention probably in 720, in a 13th-century copy.

name: Tirza
Settlement_Description: The church, that belonged to to parish of Tirsen-Wellan, was built by the brothers Johann and Fabian von Tiesenhausen in 1589.

name: Tongeren
Settlement_Description: Earliest mention in c. 390, in a sixth and ninth century copy.
Fair_Description: Tongeren was situated on the Roman road ('heerbaan') between Maastricht and Tienen. In 980 emperor Otto II donated the toll on merchandise traded in the town to the bishop. In 1455 the toll was pawned by the prince-bishop for 50 years to the town. In 1250 a cloth-hall is found. Until 1497 the fair was on the day of church consecration (May 9), after that on the Sunday after Sept. 9.

name: Beverungen
Settlement_Description: Beverungen is first mentioned between in a donation to the monastery of Corvey around the middle of the 9th century. Around 1330, the bishop of Paderborn erected a castle here.
Town_Description: A town and bridge were planned around the time that the castle was built, ca. 1330. However, town privileges were first granted in 1417, although the settlement was mostly referred to as borough ('wikbold') afterwards. The bridge was only built in 1902.

name: Raddenfort
Settlement_Description: First mentioned in 1428. According to the Schmettau map of Mecklenburg-Schwerin, the old village was located northeast of the modern settlement.

name: Borgentreich
Settlement_Description: First mentioned in 1280 but previously grown together from older villages.
Town_Description: In 1283 and 1312 mentioned as 'civitas'. The town privileges got renewed in 1330.

name: Trzygłów
Settlement_Description: The village was first mentioned in a document in 1297.

name: Turnhout
Fair_Description: A market existed in 1311 as Turnhout was situated on the road from Antwerp to the Rhineland. Maria van Brabant granted two fairs in 1363 (Apr. 18) on Saturday and Sunday mid May and on Saturday and Sunday after St. Luke (Oct. 18). A cattle-staple for the surrounding countryside was also expanded. In 1487 a free market and two free fairs were confirmed.

name: Uudeküla
Settlement_Description: The village was first mentioned in 1564.

name: Varrel
Settlement_Description: A hamlet ('bauernschaft') was first mentioned in 1289. In 1381, the monastery Heiligenrode founded the manor Varrel, which came to the count of Oldenburg after the Reformation in 1581.
Toll_Description: A toll station in Varrel is mentioned in the first half of the 17th century. It might have gone back to the acquisition of the manor Varrel by the counts of Oldenburg in 1581, possibly as a subsidiary toll station of Delmenhorst, which was circumvented by the road through Varrel. Some undated toll tariffs still exist.

name: Vaassen
Settlement_Description: Earliest mention dates from around 800-850, in a copy dating from 1170-1175.Next mention in 1118-1127 was forged in 1180-1190, in a fourteenth century copy.

name: Stolpe (Parchim)
Settlement_Description: The village is first mentioned in 1274.

name: Valkenswaard
Settlement_Description: Earliest mention in the first quarter of the thirteenth century.

name: Witnica
Settlement_Description: An old village with German farmers, a Slavic fishing village before. Made into a town in 1935.

name: Willah
Settlement_Description: First mentioned in a register of the castle Bremervörde between 1498 and 1500. The settlement consisted of a single farm.

name: Wallenhorst
Settlement_Description: The place was first mentioned in 851.

name: Varbuse
Settlement_Description: Manor and village that were mentioned in 1627.

name: Warta
Toll_Description: Attested as toll station in 1369. A bridge toll of 3 denars for each loaded wagon from Sieradz was granted in 1513, to pay for the maintenance of roads and bridge in the town area; in 1526 it was raised to 4 denars.

name: Weener
Settlement_Description: First mentioned in the 10th century, although a manor of the monastery Werden an der Ruhr existed already in the 9th century. A church is mentioned around 1000.

name: Weferlingen
Settlement_Description: Referred to as borough ('Flecken') in 1239. The place was part of the bishopric of Halberstadt, which had to defend its claims against Magdeburg, Braunschweig and Brandenburg.

name: Wermelskirchen
Toll_Description: The Duke of Berg levied a land toll in 1398. Tariffs and annual revenues are not known.

name: Wietmarschen
Settlement_Description: The Benedictine monastery Marienrode was founded in 1154 by Bishop Frederick of Münster, next to which a settlement developed. The monastery was in operation until 1811.

name: Spitz sluse
Lock_Description: A lock in the canal between the Elbe and the Schwerin lake, which was built between 1568 and 1572, is displayed as "Spitz sluse" on a map of the canal by Daniel Frese from 1605.

name: Wipperfürth
Toll_Description: In 1398, the Duke of Berg levied a land toll in Wipperfürth. 4 Turnosgroschen had to be paid for each foder of wine. A charge of 1 Turnosgroschen was levied per horse. In 1470/72 the toll was leased out for 68 guilders a year.

name: Wirdum
Settlement_Description: The settlement is first mentioned in the 8th or 9th century.

name: Witterda
Settlement_Description: First mention in a charter in 1143.

name: Woensdrecht
Settlement_Description: Earliest mention in 1249, in a copy dating from 1669.

name: Woensel
Settlement_Description: Earliest mention in 1107, in a thirteenth century copy.

name: Woltersdorf (Plaue)
Settlement_Description: Mention in 1562 as Woltirstorff, property of the lords of Wedel since olden times.

name: Wustermark
Settlement_Description: First mention of the settlement in 1212. A castle may have existed, two inns are attested in 1355.
Toll_Description: A margravial toll on the road to Wustermark was pawned to the town Brandenburg in 1424, 1446 and 1458.

name: Zellerfeld
Settlement_Description: Foundation of the monastery Cella in the mid-12th century. It is first mentioned as "ecclesia de Cella" in 1191. After mining activities stopped around 1350, the monastery was abolished in 1432. Mining started again in 1526.
Town_Description: Mentioned as mining town ('freie Bergstadt') in 1532, merged with Clausthal in 1924.
Fair_Description: A fair on the Sunday before St Michael existed since 1613.

name: Zollenspieker
Settlement_Description: The new toll station Zollenspieker/Eislingen was possibly built with the stones of the castle Riepenburg, the previous location of the toll station, which was demolished in 1512. According to a drawing from ca. 1600, there existed a double building with a ferry landing pier and boardwalk.
Toll_Description: The Hamburg toll station Eislingen on the Elbe river, also called Zollenspieker, was moved in the early 16th century from Riepenburg to the current Zollenspieker because of changes in the mouth of the Ilmenau river (see Riepenburg). From 1584, the toll was levied in cooperation with Lübeck. At the end of the 16th century, Lüneburg negotiated reduced toll fees with Hamburg. The toll was abolished with the Elbschifffahrtsakte of 1821.
Ferry_Description: Ferry across the Elbe to Hoopte.

name: Oud-Zuilen
Settlement_Description: Earliest mention is probably from 1169. Next mention of 'Sulen' in 1200. Zuilen became known as Oud-Zuilen after the settlement Nieuw Zuilen was founded in the mid-20th century.

name: Melsungen
Settlement_Description: There is evidence of a settlement dating back to the 10th century, perhaps 973.
Town_Description: The town was founded in the 13th century. 1267 'civitas' and 'burgenses'.

name: Zwijndrecht (Antwerpen)
Settlement_Description: First mentioned in a thirteenth century copy from a document from 847. Next mention in 1114.

name: Bad Zwischenahn
Settlement_Description: The area has been settled since the 9th century. The place was first mentioned in 1134.

name: Eschebrügge
Settlement_Description: On the map <cite>Comitatus Bentheim et Steinfurt, auctore Joanne Westenberg</cite> (made before 1638), <q>Escherbrug</q> is displayed as a fortification on the border between the county Bentheim and the Dutch province of Overijssel. The name must refer to a causeway through marshy terrain rather than an actual bridge.

name: Veere
Settlement_Description: Veere was first mentioned in 1282 as Campvere, suggesting that the settlement developed around a ferry to Kampen (Noord-Beveland).
