The name Vere is first attested in 1283-1284. Before 1296 international wool trade already took place in the settlement. A chapter in the church is known for the years 1467/1469-1572.
Town_Description: On 31 May 1355, Veere is mentioned as a town when it receives the right to pursue the manufacturing of cloth, together with various other towns on Walcheren. Furthermore, a statute from the same period contains regulations not unsimilar to town rights.
Staple_Description: Despite obstruction of Middelburg the lord of Veere succeeded in relocation of the Scottish staple in 1541 from Middelburg to Veere.

name: null
Toll_Description: In 1510, citizens of Bodenwerder were exempted from the Weser toll in Grohnde, which was levied by Evert von Münchhausen, who had been enfeoffed with the toll, before. The Weser toll is further mentioned in a 1584 complaint from Bremen, but not in a list of Weser tolls in a charter of the monastery Hardehausen from 1597.

name: Schlieme
Settlement_Description: In the 13th century, Brun von Hagen received the farm Schlieme as a fief from the count of Bruchhausen. In 1563, it is referred to as noble farm ('meierhof').
Toll_Description: A toll in Schlieme is leased to Dietrich Behr in 1563 and mentioned in a 1584 complaint from Bremen, but not any more in a list of Weser tolls in a 1597 charter of the monastery of Hardehausen. Probably, the river tolls in Schlieme and nearby Dreye were merged in the meantime, as accounts of the administrative region of Syke list incomes from these tolls separately in 1572, but combined in 1586. According to the 1572 account, the toll in Schlieme had higher revenues than the one in Dreye.

name: Schöppenstedter Turm
Settlement_Description: Watchtower in the defensive enclosure ('landwehr') of Braunschweig. The oldest evidence for this part of the landwehr dates from 1387.

name: null
Harbour_Description: The Oker was made navigable between Wolfenbüttel and Schladen in 1575, and up to Oker in 1577.

name: null
Lock_Description: A lock near Dorstadt was constructed in 1575 as part of a project to make the Oker navigable between Wolfenbüttel and Schladen. The basin was 20 feet deep.

name: null
Bridge_Description: A bridge across the Oker was first mentioned in 1527.

name: Hessendamm
Toll_Description: Toll of the bishop of Halberstadt at the Hessendamm, which was built in 1343.

name: null
Harbour_Description: The significance of the Elbe harbour in Lauenburg grew considerably after the opening of the Stecknitz canal in 1398, as cargoes had to be transshipped here because of the different ship sizes on the canal and on the Elbe. Skippers of Lauenburg acquired a transport monopoly for all commodities being transported on the canal that were to be transported further on the Elbe in 1417.

name: Wendenturm
Settlement_Description: Watchtower of the defensive enclosure ('landwehr') of Braunschweig. The oldest evidence for this part of the enclosure dates from 1387.

name: Döhrener Turm
Settlement_Description: Watchtower in the enclosure ('landwehr') of Hannover.

name: Roter Turm
Settlement_Description: Watchtower at the bridge across an arm of the Leine river, constructed in 1440, demolished in 1646.

name: Klus (Blomberg)
Settlement_Description: Klus was part of the dispersed settlement Hiddenhausen and is first mentioned individually in 1519. Its name is derived from a hermitage. The inn Litzenkrug was located here as well, which was built before 1670 and belonged to the watchtower of the town Blomberg, named "to Meien", on the Winterberg.

name: null
Bridge_Description: In 1422 the ferry across the larger, eastern river branch was replaced by a wooden bridge.
Ferry_Description: The ferry is replaced by a wooden bridge in 1422.

name: null
Harbour_Description: The river Jeetze connected Salzwedel with the Elbe and Hamburg, and shipping on the river was significant for the economic development of the town. It is first mentioned in 1248.

name: Groß Nenndorf
Settlement_Description: The settlement was first mentioned as a property of the monastery of Fulda in the 10th century. It consisted of two parts: Groß and Klein Nenndorf, of which the former was first separately mentioned in 1374. Both settlements were united into Bad Nenndorf in modern times.

name: Marx
Settlement_Description: The village church, dedicated to St Mark, dates from the 13th century.

name: Almrich
Settlement_Description: Originally called Altenburg, after a castle which stood here before the foundation of Naumburg. First certain mention in a charter from 1140, but an earlier mention from 1009 of a castle at the Saale river might also refer to Altenburg. In 1168 the castle was destroyed and a village remained.

name: Thüringer Pforte
Bridge_Description: The toll in Sachsenburg was paid north and south of the bridgehead.

name: Mālpils
Settlement_Description: A castle was first mentioned in 1413. It was probably built in 1386.

name: Lõimetsa
Settlement_Description: The Manor and the belonging hamlet ('Hof') were mentioned in 1583.

name: Berkenthiner Schleuse
Lock_Description: The year of construction of the flash lock near Berkenthin is unknown, but it already existed before the construction of the Stecknitz-Delvenau canal from 1391. A reconstruction of the lock is known among others in 1618.

name: Hohenstiege
Settlement_Description: A brick kiln was founded in 1597 and disappeared in 1807. Moreoever, an inn is mentioned at this place, belonging to the manor Padelügge.

name: Kuhmühlenbrücke
Settlement_Description: First mentioned in 1247 as "the mill of lord Hartwic", which was known as the Kuhmühle from the middle of the 15th century.
Bridge_Description: In relation to the mill mentioned in 1247, a "new bridge" across the Eilbeck is mentioned as well. Before there was a ford here. The Eilbeck also formed part of the defensive enclosure ('landwehr') of Hamburg.

name: null
Toll_Description: In 1281 Schoonhoven obtained toll-exemption from the bishop of Utrecht for the tolls in the Sticht Utrecht, in 1322 from the count of Holland.The comital toll for sailing transport was relocated from Ammerstol to Schoonhoven in 1398. It was owned by the Count of Holland. In the years 1424-26 the toll was relocated to Slijker veerstal at the end of the river Lek. In the 15th century the toll became subordinated to the toll in Gorinchem and they were usually leased out together. The Provisional Representantives of Holland decided to abolish the toll in 1795. Toll administration (1432-1433, 1478-1481, 1481-1483, 1483-1484, 1483-1484, 1484-1486, 1487, 1518) is published in <cite>Bronnen voor de economische geschiedenis van het Beneden-Maasgebied</cite>. A 'tolboeck' with a specified tariff and list of exempted places, dated 1521 is preserved in Utrecht. A not edited tariff for this toll and the toll in Gorinchem dates from the first half of the 16th century. Administration for later years (1770 -1793) is preserved in the National Archives, 3.01.28 Rekenkamer ter Auditie en Opvolgende Colleges, inv. no. 5419 - 5434.
Harbour_Description: A harbour crane is first mentioned in 1365.

name: null
Harbour_Description: The harbour on the Saale river in Calbe was located on the castle meadow. Among others it was used by the Staßfurt saltworks as transshipment point for firewood in the 16th century.

name: null
Harbour_Description: The Trave was navigable until Oldesloe, and the town was therefore an important transshipment point for the traffic between the North and the Baltic Sea.

name: Kuressaare
Settlement_Description: In the second half of the 14th century the castle Arensburg was built, residence of the bishops of Ösel-Wiek. A fortified borough ('Hakelwerk') was built in the same century..
Town_Description: The settlement near the castle was granted Riga town rights in 1563.

name: Bad Tennstedt
Settlement_Description: First mention in charter in 772. The settlement developed around two castles. In the 12th century it developed into a market borough ('Marktflecken').
Town_Description: Referred to as town (civitas) in 1275. A town law exists since the 13th century.

name: null
Harbour_Description: Together with Lauenförde on the opposite side of the Weser, Beverungen profited from its location on a river crossing, and became a transshipment point, especially for iron towards Bremen in the 16th and 17th centuries.

name: Ørbæk
Settlement_Description: The village of Ørbæk was first mentioned in 1231, but is significantly older. The parish church is from either the 12th or 13th century.

name: Ostorf
Settlement_Description: The village is first mentioned in 1282.

name: Keldernæs
Settlement_Description: The village of Kildernæs was first mentioned in 1560, but is significantly older. The settlement had no church but was part of the parish of Stokkemarke Church.

name: Tirsted
Settlement_Description: The village of Tirsted was first mentioned in 1329, but is significantly older. The parish church is from either the 12th or 13th century.

name: Kettinge
Settlement_Description: The village of Kettinge was first mentioned in 1498, but is significantly older. The parish church is from either the 12th or 13th century.

name: Fugelsang
Settlement_Description: The village of Fuglsang was first mentioned in 1403, but is significantly older. The settlement had no church but was part of the parish of Toreby Church.

name: Stokkemarke
Settlement_Description: The village of Stokkemarke was first mentioned in 1231, but is significantly older. The parish church is from either the 12th or 13th century.

name: Birket
Settlement_Description: The village of Birket was first mentioned in 1418, but is significantly older. The parish church is from either the 12th or 13th century.

name: Kirkerup
Settlement_Description: The village of Kirkerup was first mentioned in 1259, but is significantly older. The parish church is from either the 12th or 13th century.

name: Hevosoja
Settlement_Description: <b>Inn:</b> Travellers stayed overnight in Hevosoja in 1571.

name: Maasbommel
Town_Description: On 15 August 1312, Reginald I, count of Guelders, confirmed the town privileges of Maasbommel.
Ferry_Description: A ferry across the Meuse is first mentioned in 1332.

name: Asperen
Settlement_Description: Earliest mention in 893 (in a copy from 1222).
Town_Description: Earliest mention as a town (‘die porte tot Asperen’) on 11 January 1314.  It then obatined toll-exemption form the count of Holland. It is presumed that Otto of Heukelum, lord of Asperen, had the town build around 1314, and granted town privileges. Asperen was being walled before 1377.
Fair_Description: In 1468 three fairs are known: 1) Symonis et Jude (Oct. 28), 2) Eastern, 3) Laurenty (Aug. 10). The watertoll collected during these markets is only small because the river Linge is dammed upstream of Tiel and as a result is verry narrow and shallow. The duration of the fairs is not known. In 1556 the account of the steward of the count of Holland mentions five fair-tolls and a watertoll, which is then leased together with two ferrys, one at Asperen and one crossing the river Linge.

name: null
Harbour_Description: The Hoendiep canal was not directly connected with the other canals in Groningen. A mooring place for ships was located outside the Aa gate, as can be seen on old maps of the town.

name: Arrild
Settlement_Description: The village of Arrild was first mentioned in 1300, but is significantly older. The parish church is from either the 12th or 13th century.

name: Hjerpsted
Settlement_Description: The village of Hjerpsted was first mentioned in 1340, but is significantly older. The parish church is from either the 12th or 13th century.

name: Trøjborg
Settlement_Description: The castle of Trøjborg was first mentioned in 1347, in a letter written by duke Valdemar. In 1404 the castle was sold to Queen Margrethe I. The castle was owned by the nobel Rantzau family during most of the 16th and 17th century.

name: Almsted
Settlement_Description: The village of Almsted was first mentioned in 1245, but is significantly older. The settlement had no church but was part of the parish of Notmark Church.

name: Himmark
Settlement_Description: The village of Himmark was first mentioned in 1483, but is significantly older. The settlement had no church but was part of the parish of Svenstrup Church.

name: Espe

name: Vrejlev Kloster
Settlement_Description: The Premonstratensian monastery of Vrejlev was first mentioned in 1253 and again in 1268 and 1335. At the time of the Danish Reformation in 1536 the monastery was dissolved, and the monastery and its properties went to the king.

name: Magleby (Langeland)
Settlement_Description: The village of Magleby was first mentioned in 1231, but is significantly older. The parish church is from either the 12th or 13th century.

name: Snoghøj
Ferry_Description: The ferries across Lillebælt, the narrow strait between Funen and Jutland, was among the most important in Denmark, and the connection between Snoghøj in Jutland and the town of Middelfart on Funen was the center of this traffic. When a stable ferry connection was a reality is uncertain, but it was certainly in place by the 13th century. In the later middle ages and early modern period the ferry became important in the export of oxen from Funen to the markets in northern Germany and Flanders

name: null
Bridge_Description: A bridge is shown on the oldest known town seal from the 14th century. The seal is probably a reference to a bridge near the town across the river, Djursåen. The exact location of the bridge is uncertain. An engraving in Resen’s Atlas Danicus from c. 1675 shows a bridge across Djursåen south of the town. A royal fee (Danish: bropenge/brokorn) had to be paid to cross the bridge, first mentioned in 1602.

name: Borna (Leipzig)
Settlement_Description: Originally a Slavic fortification, later a German settlement from the 12th century. First certain mention in 1251.
Town_Description: In 1264 first mentioned as 'town'. The foundation of the town probably took place in the beginning of the 13th century. In 1298 a burgomaster is mentioned.
Fair_Description: In 1544 Borna had applied for a fair, which was not explicitly denied, despite protests from Leipzig. In 1637 the town owned at least one fair, but it's unknown if this was the same fair as mentioned in 1544. In 1677 a fair on Sunday after St. Margaret's day was moved to Monday after the first Sunday after Trinitatis.
Toll_Description: Important Ernestinian station of safe conduct south of Leipzig, where the road from Nuremberg via Hof and Zwickau and the road from the Ore Mountains merged. Accounts are preserved since 1483, regulations and tariffs ('Geleitsordnung') remain from 1514/15 and 1548.

name: Kuusisto
Settlement_Description: Kuusisto bishop's castle. To be amended.

name: null
Bridge_Description: A bridge across the river, Sakskøbing Å, is mentioned in 1523, but is most likely older.

name: null
Bridge_Description: The land between Doesburg and Ellecom-Dieren went through wetlands. Before the end of the sixteenth century, there was a ford between Doesburg and Ellecom. At high water levels, a bridge located next to it could be used. Around 1597, this ford was no longer usable. The maintenance of the bridge was a cause of conflict for several years, but traffic managed to find a temporary route around it. The bridge was replaced by a ferry in 1672. In 1698, it was replaced by a bridge again.   The chosen location of the ford/bridge on the map may not be exactly right for the period 1350-1650.

name: null
Toll_Description: A toll ('bruggeld'/'weggeld') had to be paid to pass the bridge.
Bridge_Description: The bridge was maintained by the lord of Keppel.

name: Arnemuiden
Settlement_Description: Arnemuiden is first mentioned in 1223. The settlement was originally located at the mouth of the Arne river, but it drowned and was rebuilt slightly more inland around 1460.
Town_Description: Arnemuiden was granted town privileges by William I, Prince of Orange, on 15 June 1574. In 1816, Arnemuiden was also elevated to city rank.
Fair_Description: In 1574/5 (Jan. 26) William of Orange granted a weekly market on Tuesday and a fair. The dates of the fair should be choosen so that they didn't hamper other fairs in the towns of Walcheren.

name: Schmalkalden
Settlement_Description: The settlement Smalacalta is first mentioned when it was given to Fulda monastery in 874.
Town_Description: First mention as a town in 1227, although it was likely already a town before. In 1335 the town rights of Gelnhausen were granted by count Berthold VII. In 1360 half of the town was sold to Hesse. The interests of the landlords were represented by the sheriffs ('Schultheißen'), of which one was appointed by Henneberg and one by Hesse since 1396.
Toll_Description: Toll tariffs of Schmalkalden remain from 1489. The toll belonged to the town council.

name: Holstebro
Settlement_Description: Probably a permanent settlement at the beginning of the 13th century. With its location at a popular ford and later bridge across a relatively large river, Storåen, the settlement was a gathering place for people and goods at an early stage.
Town_Description: The town is first mentioned in 1274. The settlement, however, had an urban character prior to this year. Citizens (civis) first mentioned in 1391, mayor in 1443 and town council in 1481. The oldest preserved town privileges granted by king Christian III (1536-1559) in 1552, because the town’s older documents were lost in a fire that same year. The town benefited from its location at a significant river, Storåen.
Fair_Description: The fairs at Holstebro were among the most important in Jutland. The most important commodities were oxen, which was exported to Germany and Flanderns via other fairs in Jutland (Ribe and Viborg for example). On an engraving of the town of Holstebro in Resen’s Atlas Danicus from 1677 a marketplace is shown north from the town. In 1540 the town lost one of its privileged fairs, but it was reestablished again in 1552.

name: Kalundborg Færge
Ferry_Description: The ferry across the sea of Kattegat between Aarhus and Kalundborg was one of the most important ferry routes in Denmark throughout the middle ages and early modern period. The German chronicler Adam of Bremen probably already c. 1075 mentioned a ferry between the town of Aarhus in Jutland and Kalundborg. Often the island of Samsø between Jutland and Zealand was used to split the trip in two parts. In the 1490ties, for example, the nobleman Mourits Nielsen Gyldenstierne used the ferry between Kalundborg and Aarhus via Samsø, and in 1511 bishop Niels Clausen of Aarhus did the same.

name: Parchim
Settlement_Description: The land of Parchim is first mentioned in 1170. It was an originally Slavic castle, next to which a German merchant settlement developed around 1200.
Town_Description: Founded by Lord Heinrich Borwin II. of Mecklenburg in 1225-1226 with its own town law, which was endorsed multiple times until the 18th century. The new town (Neustadt) was built in 1249 and merged with the old town in 1282.
Fair_Description: A fair on Sunday Invocavit in Parchim is mentioned in an almanac printed in Neudamm (Dębno) in 1598.
Toll_Description: In 1359 citizens from Perleberg enjoyed reduced toll tariffs in Parchim for herring that they brought to Brandenburg with wagons.

name: Aalborg Færge
Ferry_Description: Aalborg was founded at the most narrow part of Limfjorden; an obvious place to cross the fjord by boat. When the first ferry connecting the region of Vendsyssel with Aalborg was established is, however, not known. Presumably, a royal privileged ferry between Aalborg and Vendsyssel was in place in the 13th century. The ferry is, however, not documented before the 15th century. On the northern side of Limfjord opposite Aalborg the ferry landed near the settlement of Sundby.

name: Storebro
Bridge_Description: The place name “Holstebro” (Holstatbro) is first mentioned in a charter from 1274, and reveals how the bridge most likely was present at that time. The oldest known medieval town seal also shows a bridge. The bridge is directly mentioned in 1526. Because of the changing course of the river through time, it is possible that the medieval bridge was at a different place than now. But according to images and maps from the 17th century, the bridge was placed where it is today.

name: Neuenkirchen (Weser)
Settlement_Description: A new church was built around 1100, which gave the settlement its name. It is shown on a map of the 12th century; a priest is first mentioned in 1240.
Fair_Description: A fair on the second Sunday before St Michael's Day was granted in 1588.

name: Koerhuis
Settlement_Description: The ‘Koerhuis’ was a guard post in the enclosure (‘landweer’) of Salland, which was supposed to protect, among other things, the trade route. The enclosure had probably been initiated by bishop and land lord John of Arkel. The Koerhuis lost its military function after 1543. In the mid-seventeenth century, it became a toll station, and later an inn.

name: null
Bridge_Description: According to the travel diary of Henning Brandis from 1495, the Fuhse valley was crossed with a causeway and a bridge.

name: null
Bridge_Description: 'Schipbrug', a pontoon bridge which has functioned since 1603.
Ferry_Description: A ferry was in function until the construction of a pontoon bridge in 1603. From 1287 onward, the ferry was owned by the chapter of Saint-Peter (Sint-Pieter) in Utrecht. In 1601, it was acquired by the town of Arnhem. A land toll owned by the landlord, the duke of Guelders, linked up to the ferry, stimulating trade-related traffic to enter Arnhem.

name: null
Bridge_Description: In the 14th century, a stone bridge is known which led from the Brücktor across the Elbe on the town side to the marsh. In 1440 a wooden bridge is constructed, which had only little openenings for ships to pass through.

name: Westochtersum
Settlement_Description: The settlement Ochtersum is first mentioned in 1237, the church was built around 1260.

name: Westerholt
Settlement_Description: A village was first mentioned in 1420.

name: Vogelsberg
Toll_Description: Secondary station of safe conduct of Erfurt. Mainly rural goods passed thorugh here, even though it gained some meaning with the rising copper trade from Mansfeld. Annual revenues are known since 1517.

name: null
Bridge_Description: The name of the hamlet Schevenbrügge indicates that a "crooked" bridge crossing the Kattbeck stream must have existed in 1633/34 at the latest.

name: Hennigsdorf
Settlement_Description: The settlement was probably founded from Spandau or transferred to German jurisdiction.

name: null
Toll_Description: The dukes of Brabant and Limburg and the duke of Gelre made an agreement in 1380 about the tolls on the Meuse.  The new tolls at Grave, Gennep, Megen en Batenburg will be abolished. Only those in function for over fifty years will be maintained. Around 1525 the toll at Cuijk was relocated to Grave. In 1574 the tollkeeper of Grave however is found in Kuik.Grave obtained toll-exemption over land and water in 1290 from count Floris V in Holland and Zeeland. In 1364 the lord of Cuijk gave toll-exemption in the Land of Cuijk for their own goods over land and water. In 1387 the duke of Gelre gave toll-exemption. Toll-accounts of Cuijk collected at Grave dated 1572-'75 are preserved. For the years 1584-1602 toll-accounts of Middelaar collected at Grave are preserved. Toll-exempt are then: Roermond, Venlo, Nijmegen, 'Bossche' en Grave. Tariffs are equal to the toll of 'Stevensweerde'.
Ferry_Description: First mentioned in 1381. The ferry was in private ownership, split between multiple people. This ferry was moved when the Menno van Coehoorn fortress was build in 1699.

name: Maribo
Settlement_Description: Originally the village of Skemminge, which in 1416 was granted town privileges
Town_Description: In 1416 the Danish king Erik of Pomerania (1396-1439) granted town privileges to the village Skemminge and the newly founded Brigittine monastery. The settlement was renamed Maribo after the monastery. In 1418 the pope confirmed the town name. The new town was centered around the monastery as the town square was established next to the monastery, and the monastery dominated the town throughout the middle ages. In 1449 a mayor was mentioned for the first time, and in 1453 the monastery was granted legal rights (Danish: Birkeret). A town law is known from 1488, and in 1495 a town bailiff and town scribe are mentioned. Late medieval town hall at the town square was rebuilt in 1613. Maribo was, however, one of the smallest and poorest towns on Lolland during the late medieval period, but experienced a certain level of economic growth in the early-modern era.
Fair_Description: Maribo was an important market town on the island of Lolland, and the town or monastery held several annual fairs in the late medieval period and early modern era. The first privileges to held fairs were probably granted by king Eric the Pomerania (1396-1439). There were also several fairs at localities near Maribo. In 1633 king Christian IV (1596-1648) relocated the fairs traditionally held in the villages of Halsted, Saltvig, Tågerup and Olstrup to Maribo. The character and age of these relocated fairs are not known. The town of Maribo, however, did not have the strength to keep the new fairs, so three years later the king moved three of the fairs to the towns of Nysted and Rødby. In the early 17th century  Maribo had six annual fairs, which all had a local character.

name: Bolbrücke
Bridge_Description: The bridge Bolbrugge across the Mühlenteich connected the town with the mainland. It is first mentioned in 1340.

name: Kloster Neuendorf
Settlement_Description: Founded not long before 1232 as a Cistercian convent. It was prosperous until the 15th century, in the aftermath of the Reformation it became protestant. In 1579 the monastery is officially dissolved but a convent of nuns is established, which was dissolved in 1810.

name: Aalborg
Settlement_Description: Archeological excavations have revealed a viking age seasonal market. Around 1000 AD a church was built, and Aalborg now seems to have been a permanent settlement with an urban character.
Town_Description: Around 1040 the Danish king Hardeknud (1035-1042) minted coins in Aalborg. Characterized as a town (“civitas”) by the German chronicler Adam of Bremen around 1075 . According to the so-called main piece in King Valdemar’s Cadastre from 1231, Aalborg was royal property (Danish: Kongelev). The royal castle of Aalborghus was mentioned for the first time in 1340, but probably established in the 13th century. The king’s bailiff (Danish: Foged) is documented in 1293. Existing town privileges were confirmed and expanded in 1342 by king Valdemar IV Atterdag (1340-1375). Mayors, a town council and citizens (villani) are known from the middle of the 14th century onwards. At the beginning of the 13th century the medieval town square (Danish: Gammeltorv), where well-established, and in 1232 a Franciscan convent was founded. Also in the 13th century Aalborg was fortified with a palisade, moats and earthworks. Before 1431 a town hall was built at the medieval town square. A new town hall was built shortly before 1499, but burned down in 1530, and was not rebuilt before after the Count's Feud (Danish: Grevens Fejde) 1534-1536. The medieval castle of Aalborghus was also destroyed during the war, and a new castle was built closer to the harbour. Aalborg benefited from its central role in trading networks between Norway and Germany. From the 13th century onwards German merchants played an important role in the network. The trade with herring caught in Limfjorden was particularly important to Aalborg, and during the late medieval period the town competed with smaller urban settlements in the region such as Nibe to control the herring trade. Around 1600 Aalborg almost had a monopoly on the trade with fish from Limfjorden, and the town experienced growth until the Dano-Swedish wars around the middle of the 17th century. Throughout the medieval period and early modern era Aalborg was one of the most important towns in Jutland.
Fair_Description: From around 1400 onwards the rich herring fishing in Limfjorden became more important. The fishing trade generated economic activities and several fairs were established. In general, the town of Aalborg tried to dominate and even monopolize the trade in the regions around Limfjorden, something which can be illustrated with the ongoing conflicts between the small urban settlement of Nibe and Aalborg. Already in the early medieval period at least one annual fair must have been held in Aalborg, but the age, character and date of this fair is unknown. In the later medieval period Aalborg had at least two annual fairs, but shortly after 1650 only one annual fair took place in Aalborg.
Toll_Description: At least from the middle of the 14th century onwards Aalborg was one of the most important royal tolls in Denmark. The origin of the toll is, however, unclear. In the middle of the 14th century toll was collected on herring, horses and oxen and other commodities exported from Aalborg. Toll lists from the years 1517-1519 have been preserved, and at this time German merchants had to pay a higher toll than the local Danes. During one of the Dano-Swedish wars, the Torstenson War 1643-1645, a toll building in Aalborg was destroyed. It was rebuilt already in 1651.

name: Middelfart
Settlement_Description: Archaeological evidence of a 10th century settlement. The settlement and later town of Middelfart was located at the obvious place to cross the narrow strait of Lillebælt between Jutland and Funen.
Town_Description: Middelfart was registered as royal property (‘patrimonium’) in King Valdemar’s Cadastre c. 1231. Around 1300 Middelfart was probably counted among the towns of Denmark. A town council was first mentioned in 1362, and in 1425 mayors, a town bailiff, citizens and a town court. Oldest known privileges was granted by King Hans (1481-1513) in 1496. Throughout the medieval period and the early modern era Middelfart benefited from its location at the  obvious place to cross the strait of Lillebælt.
Fair_Description: Presumably, Middelfart held two annual fairs, but their date, character and age are unknown. The first documented annual fair is from 1650, when an annual fair was moved from the settlement of Fjelsted to Middelfart.
Toll_Description: When Middelfart became a toll station is uncertain. Due to the town’s ferries, however, royal tolls may have been collected early in the medieval period. Documented as a toll station in 1573, when Middelfart became one of the toll stations on Funen from where oxen had to be exported by sea.
Ferry_Description: The ferries across Lillebælt, the narrow strait between Funen and Jutland, was among the most important in Denmark, and Middelfart was the center of this traffic. The place name Middelfart reflects the original settlement's location at the most narrow part of Lillebælt, and that this was the obvious place to cross the strait. When a stable ferry connection was a reality is uncertain, but it was certainly in place by the 13th century. In the later middle ages and early modern period the ferry became important in the export of oxen from Funen to the markets in northern Germany and Flanders.

Lock_Description: A lock in the canal between the Elbe and the Schwerin lake, which was built between 1568 and 1572, is displayed in Banzkow on a map of the canal by Daniel Frese from 1605.

name: Lund (Skive)
Settlement_Description: The village of Lund was first mentioned in 1584, but is significantly older. The parish church is from either the 12th or 13th century.

name: null
Lock_Description: A lock in the canal between the Elbe and the Schwerin lake, which was built between 1568 and 1572, is displayed as "Stuken sluse" near Stuck on a map of the canal by Daniel Frese from 1605.

name: null
Bridge_Description: Saalfeld was located on a ford in the river Saale. A stone bridge was constructed in the 13th century.

name: Kolby Kås
Ferry_Description: A ferry between Jylland and Zealand with the possibility to go via Samsø was probably established by the late 11th century, when a ferry connecting Aarhus to Zealand was mentioned for the first time by the German chronicler Adam of Bremen. In August 1494 the nobleman Mourids Nielsen Gyldenstjerne sailed from Kalundborg to Koldby, where he stayed for three days before he continued with the ferry from Koldby to Aarhus.

name: Angstedt
Settlement_Description: First mentioned in 1282. An older mention from 869-891 is uncertain. In 1924 the village was merged with nearby Gräfinau.
Toll_Description: Toll regulations from 1566 settled the fees that had to be paid in Angstedt.

name: Wachtendonk
Toll_Description: The Duke of Guelders levied a land toll for the first time around 1430. From 1473 to 1543, the Duke of Cleves held the toll. Tariffs and revenues are not known.

name: Raahe
Town_Description: The town of Raahe (sw. Brahestad) was first founded as Salo in Satamalahti in 1649, but was soon relocated to Fantinniemi and named in 1652 after governor-general Per Brahe the younger who had established the town. The first plan of the town area dates to the year 1650.

name: Kongebro
Ferry_Description: The ferries across Lillebælt, the narrow strait between Funen and Jutland, was among the most important in Denmark, and Middelfart was the center of this traffic. The place name Middelfart reflects the original settlement's location at the most narrow part of Lillebælt, and that this was the obvious place to cross the strait. When a stable ferry connection was a reality is uncertain, but it was certainly in place by the 13th century. In the later middle ages and early modern period the ferry became important in the export of oxen from Funen to the markets in northern Germany and Flanders.

name: Korsør
Settlement_Description: Archaeological evidence of trading activities in the Viking Age at the fjord estuary, where the town of Korsør was established in the later middle ages. Ferries between Funen and Zealand probably also departed from the estuary in the viking and early medieval period. There was however no permanent settlement before the 14th or early 15th century. Around 1400, before Korsør officially was granted town rights, ships from Lübeck sailed to Korsør.
Town_Description: In the eastern bottom of the fjord the town and royal castle of Tårnborg was established in the early medieval period. In the 13th century Tårnborg was damaged by warfare, and in the following 14th century Korsør on the opposite western side of the fjord began to develop. A new royal castle was built at the estuary near the coast of Storebælt, and a permanent settlement with an urban character developed around the castle. In 1425 king Erik the Pomeranian (1396-1439) granted the citizens of Korsør the same town rights as the citizens of Roskilde and Kalundborg. King Erik also ordered Tårnborg demolished, and that the inhabitants of Tårnborg, Vemmelev and Hemmeshøj parishes should trade in the new town of Korsør and no other places. Hereby Korsør took over the town rights from Tårnborg and eventually the inhabitants were relocated from Tårnborg to Korsør. Mayors of Korsør are mentioned for the first time in 1441. Throughout the late medieval period and early modern era the small town of Korsør benefited from the ferry connecting Zealand with Funen; the most important ferry route across Storebælt.
Fair_Description: It is uncertain if Korsør had any annual fair in the medieval period. During the early modern era, however, the town was granted the right to several fairs. These attempts to try to stimulate the trading activities is probably a reflection of the town’s ongoing struggle to control the trade within the region, i.e. western Zealand.

name: Oss
Settlement_Description: Oss is first mentioned in a twelfth-century copy of a document dated 6 May 1069. This document also mentions a church in the settlement.
Town_Description: Oss was granted town privileges on 14 October 1399 by Joanna, duchess of Brabant.
Fair_Description: Before 1340 Oss already had a fair. In 1340 a cloth-hall is known. In 1399 it obtained the right for a weekly market.

name: null
Lock_Description: A lock in the canal between the Elbe and the Schwerin lake, which was built between 1568 and 1572, is displayed as "Steinsluse von Döms" ('stone lock of Dömitz') on a map of the canal by Daniel Frese from 1605.

name: Sondershausen
Settlement_Description: First mention in a charter in 1125, but the beginnings of the settlement are probably much older with roots in Frankish times. The castle Spatenburg was situated above Sondershausen and probably built in 1075 by emperor Henry IV. The role of castle was transferred to the castle in the town in the 14th century.
Town_Description: First referred to as "oppidum" in 1304. The coat of arms of the town are first attested in 1347, when the town was referred to as "stat" and its inhabitants as "Borger" (citizens). The oldest recorded town law dates from 1555, in which it is mentioned that the first bylaws were developed in the first half of the 15th century.

name: null
Harbour_Description: Shipping on the Wakenitz between Lübeck and Ratzeburg has been attested since 1188. The Wakenitz harbour in Lübeck must have been located near the Hüxter gate.

name: Vammaskoski
Bridge_Description: Vammaskoski bridge crossing Vammaskoski stream on a major common road in Sastamala (former Ala-Sastamala and Tyrvää) was in 1680 maintained by the whole of Ylä-Satakunta judicial district, excluding Kyrö parish, which had been declared free of the maintenance in 1623. In 1624 that time (wooden) structure of the bridge had been under maintenance for 18 years (from 1606). The arrangement of the maintenance is of 15th century or early 16th century origin, not later than mid-16th century. Sillankorva (Bridge’s End) farm next to the bridge is cited first in the sources in 1520. The brigde may have been preceded by a ferry.

name: Skælskør
Settlement_Description: Presumably a village on a peninsula in the fjord. From the peninsula it was relatively easy to cross the fjord using a ford, and soon the settlement spredt to the opposite site of the fjord.
Town_Description: When the first town privileges were granted is uncertain, but Skælskør was a royal town by 1241, when it was listed as such in King Valdemar’s Cadastre. A copy of older privileges was written in 1441. During the 13th century a castle was located in or near the town. Citizens documented in 1328. At least from the late 14th century Skælskør was frequently visited by German merchants, in 1399, for example, ships from Lübeck sailed to the town. In the 15th century the Carmelites founded a monastery in Skælskør. Throughout the medieval and early modern period Skælskør competed with the neighboring towns of Slagelse and Korsør.

name: Loiman silta
Bridge_Description: Loima bridge crossing Loimijoki river on the common road from Turku to Huittinen (sw. Huittis) and Northern Satakunta region is first cited in 1585. The bridge was destroyed by flooding in 1607, and again renovated in 1643 when the costs were taken care by the whole of Ala-Satakunta judicial district. Further renovations took place in 1658 and 1675. In 1675 the bridge is cited as a Landsbro (Land’s bridge), which may hint to the organisation of its maintenance in the late 14th century before the introduction of judicial districts (fi. kihlakunta) in the first decade of the 15th century. The bridge is included on a 1641 map of Huittinen parish.

name: Ilmenau
Settlement_Description: The moated castle and the adjoining settlement were located at the long-distance trade route Erfurt-Nuremberg. They are first mentioned in 1204.
Town_Description: The town was founded around 1300. First mentioned as such ('stet') and acquisition of town privileges in 1341.
Toll_Description: A station of safe conduct and toll was installed in Ilmenau by Count Boppo of Henneberg in 1558. A toll regulation remains from 1642.

name: null
Ferry_Description: Due to its location at the most narrow part of Limfjorden just opposite the town of Aalborg, a ferry connecting the region of Vendsyssel with mainland Jutland departed from Sundby. The age and character of the ferry from Sundby to Aalborg is, however, uncertain. Presumably a royal ferry was established in the 13th century.

name: Hien
Settlement_Description: Earliest mention probably dates from the second half of the ninth century, in a copy dated between 1150 and 1158. Mentioned as 'apud Hian' at the end of the eleventh century.

name: Linnansilta (Hämeen linna)
Bridge_Description: Linnansilta -bridge between Ojoinen manor and Häme Castle and Hämeenlinna town was in the 16th century maintained by Asikkala parish as part of their obligations to the Castle. The organisation of the maintenance was very likely done in the 14th century.

name: Grieth
Toll_Description: The Duke of Kleve levied a river toll on the Rhine here from 1472 to 1485. The toll was in Büderich before and after that. The same tariffs therefore apply as in Büderich. In 1481, 5200 guilders were collected. Actually, the toll was to be moved to Grieth as early as 1336 - but this did not happen. The transfer of the customs in 1472 was justified by the fact that toll evasions were increasing in Büderich.

name: Cölln (Berlin)
Settlement_Description: In the 13th century, increased trade seems to have increased the meaning of the settlements of Berlin and Cölln at the Spree crossing. There is no secure proof of a Slavic predecessor settlement.
Town_Description: The first written indication of Cölln is given in the mention of its provost in 1237. Since its first mention, Cölln can be seen as a town, it is referred to as civitas in 1261. The exact date of the awarding of town rights has not survived, as well as earlier mentions, which may have been destroyed during a town fire in 1380. In 1244, the provost of Berlin is first mentioned, who is also referred to as provost of Cölln in 1247, which may be seen as proof that both towns can be seen as twin towns at the time. Participation at the Hanseatic Diets 1359, 1430 and lastly 1443, in 1518 they were forced by their territorial lord to quit the alliance.

name: Rodenberg
Settlement_Description: A castle is mentioned around 930, which was located on the "alter Rodenberg" and belonged to the counts of Roden-Wunstorf. At the end of the 13th or beginning of the 14th century, Count Adolf of Holstein-Schaumburg erected a moated castle, next to which a settlement developed, that acquired borough ('flecken') privileges  before 1375.
Town_Description: Town privileges were granted in 1615 by Count Ernst of Schaumburg.
Fair_Description: In the town privileges of 1615, Rodenberg received the right to organise three fairs, on the days of St Philip and James, St James and All Saints.

name: Göttingen
Settlement_Description: First mentioned in 953 in a donation charter of Emperor Otto I to the monastery of St Maurice in Magdeburg.
Town_Description: It is unknown when exactly the town rights were acquired, probably in the early 13th century. First mention as "civitas" around 1230.
Fair_Description: In Göttingen trade regulations of the year 1398, four fairs are mentioned, taking place on St Walpurga, Corpus Christi, St James and St Simon and Juda. The Corpus Christi fair was founded in 1380.
Toll_Description: Fee for safe conduct for commodities moved through town, owned by the Duke of Brunswick, and toll for all commodities sold and bought in Göttingen, except those intended for the nobility and clerics, perishables and retail. Already in 1380, the height of the toll was defined by the civic council. Extensive toll registers exist from the first half of the 15th century. The toll was levied at the town gates.

name: null
Bridge_Description: A bridge across the Unstrut built on stone pillars is first mentioned in 1207.

name: null
Toll_Description: Toll on the Elbe river in Dömitz. For details, see Dömitz main node.

name: null
Harbour_Description: Boizenburg was an important transshipment point in the salt trade route between Lüneburg and Wismar. Salt from Lüneburg was transported on the Elbe to Boizenburg, where it was transshipped onto the land route to Wismar. The importance of Boizenburg in this system declined in the late 14th century, when the salt trade was increasingly diverted to Lübeck. A skippers' guild with c. 30 persons is known from 1516.

name: null
Harbour_Description: Aardenburg had a harbour that connected the town with the Zwin estuary and the sea via the Ee river. The harbour was moved to the west of town when the waterway was reconstructed in 1244. The harbour boomed in the 13th, but silted up in the 14th century and lost its significance.

name: Nørresundby
Settlement_Description: The small fishing settlement is mentioned for the first time in the 13th century when the king donated the village to Vitskøl monastery.

name: Gerdrup Bro
Bridge_Description: Probably a late medieval bridge across the river of Hove Å north of the village. Another possibility is that the bridge was located about 1 kilometer south of the village, or that there were two bridges near the village of Gerdrup.

name: Grønbæk
Settlement_Description: The village of Grønbæk was first mentioned in 1231, but is older. The parish church is from either the 12th or 13th century.

name: Lauenau
Settlement_Description: The village Schwedestorf is first mentioned in 973/1059. Next to it, the dukes of Brunswick-Lüneburg built the castle Lauenau, which is first mentioned in 1307. It was usually pawned to the counts of Schaumburg. The castle was destroyed in 1519, but rebuilt in 1568-72. The settlement next to the castle was first mentioned as borough ('bleck'/'flecken') in 1527. In 1575 it received borough privileges, which were renewed in 1649.

name: null
Ferry_Description: Documented from the early 16th century, but may be older.
Harbour_Description: The character of the medieval harbour is unknown. But on a map produced by the Swedish officer Eric Dahlberg during the Swedish occupation of Rudkøbing in the 17th century a jetty is shown.

name: Otterndorf
Settlement_Description: Around 1100, duke Lothar of Saxony is said to have raised the settlement, which probably existed before the 11th century, to a borough ('flecken'). A church is first mentioned around 1261. The settlement functioned as central market place for the Hadeln region.
Town_Description: The settlement acquired Stade town privileges around 1400, which were modified in 1541.
Fair_Description: Fairs in Otterndorf are already mentioned in the town privileges of 1541, but were probably older. They were specified in 1567 as two three-day fairs, which were held in the churchyard on 8 days before St Vitus and 8 days before St Michael. A cattle market was connected to the latter. In 1570, a horse fair on the Dispersion of the Apostles was added. The venue for the fairs was moved to the town hall, the current Marktstraße, in 1582.

name: Brunkau
Settlement_Description: The settlement is first mentioned in 1238, but had been deserted for a long time by 1375. In 1538 the land was first used again for animal husbandry, an outlying estate ('Vorwerk') was established in 1544, and in 1608 a village is mentioned again.

name: Freiburg (Elbe)
Settlement_Description: First mentioned as castle of the bishop of Bremen in 1154. The moated castle was destroyed by Henry the Lion in 1177.
Town_Description: Archbishop Hildebold of Bremen granted the settlement town privileges in 1271.

name: Neuhaus (Oste)
Settlement_Description: A castle built in 1404 by the archbishop of Bremen Otto von Braunschweig. It was destroyed in 1420, but rebuilt in 1435 by archbishop Balduin. The settlement developed into a borough ('flecken') by the 16th century.

name: Geversdorf
Settlement_Description: First mentioned in 1230. The church is first mentioned in 1233.

name: Lamstedt
Settlement_Description: The parish of Lamstedt is first mentioned in 1115, but was much older.

name: Randbøl
Settlement_Description: The village of Randbøl was first mentioned in c. 1330, but is significantly older. The parish church is from either the 12th or 13th century.

name: Kranenburg (Oste)
Settlement_Description: A castle was built around 1375 by Curd Camermeister and Bartold Kint, high officials of Bremervörde, possible at the location of an older castle.

name: Altmörbitz
Toll_Description: Secondary station of safe conduct ('Beigeleitsstelle') of Altenburg. Annual revenues are known since 1509/10, tariffs and regulations ('Geleitsordnung') date from 1548.

name: Cadenberge
Settlement_Description: First mentioned in 1146/48. A church is first mentioned in 1337.
Fair_Description: Fairs in Cadenberge are first mentioned in 1448, but further details before the 18th century are not known.

name: Belum
Settlement_Description: First mentioned around 1230. The St Vitus church was probably built in the 14th century. However, the settlement seems to have existed since early Saxon times.

name: Lehe
Settlement_Description: Settled by Frisians around 1000. Around 1200 a stone church was built. The settlement is first mentioned in 1273/78 and developed into a market borough ('marktflecken'). Incorporated into Wesermünde in 1924, later known as Bremerhaven.
Fair_Description: The Bremen council granted the right to hold two three-day fairs in Lehe in 1588, on Sunday Cantate and Sunday after St Bartholomew. In 1620, three fairs are mentioned, on Sunday after St George, Sunday after Trinity Sunday and Sunday before All Saints' Day.

name: Stotel
Settlement_Description: Around 1220 a castle was constructed in Stotel; an older one was destroyed in 1213. It was seat of the counts of Stotel until ca. 1350.
Toll_Description: A toll of the archbishop of Bremen was pawned to the town Bremen in 1362. In 1365, citizens of Bremen were exempted from toll payments.

name: Derikum
Toll_Description: Secondary toll station of the land toll of Neuss, which is attested for the period 1560-1793. It was also often called Norf after the neighbouring village.

name: null
Bridge_Description: The existence of a bridge can be derived from the sources before 1340.
Lock_Description: One of seven locks in the Fulda river between Kassel and Hersfeld, which were built by landgrave Moritz of Hesse-Kassel in a campaign to make the Fulda navigable. Regulations from 1613 specify the lock fee at 2 Alben. At each lock, it was checked whether the toll for the cargo had been paid in Kassel.

name: Wilsum
Settlement_Description: According to most literature, the earliest mention of Wilsum dates from 1213; according to Jager, the earliest mention dates from 1170. Its church was built in the mid-eleventh century.
Town_Description: It is assumed that Wilsum was granted town privileges by the bishop of Utrecht before 1321. On 24 February 1321, its town privileges were codified.

name: Bad Bederkesa
Settlement_Description: First mentioned in 1159 in connection with the Lords of Bederkesa. Around 1200 a wooden castle was built and in 1287 the settlement was characterised as a borough ('flecken'). The settlement came into possession of Bremen in 1421,
Fair_Description: A fair for commodities and wood took place on Tuesday before St Michael. It is first attested in 1724, but probably it was granted around 1588, when the settlement belonged to Bremen, similar to the fairs in Lehe and Neuenkirchen.

name: null
Harbour_Description: As seen on a map from Braun and Hogeberg of 1590, the harbour place "Zu den Stiegen" was accessible directly from the market place. Due to its location on small old Rhine arms, it was only usable for smaller boats.

name: null
Ferry_Description: A ferry between Scherpenisse, Sint Maartensdijk and Duiveland is first mentioned in 1360. A ferry across the Pluimpot near Scherpenisse is mentioned in 1399. It was discontinued after the Pluimpot was dammed a little to the north in 1556, since this created an overland connection between the districts ('ambachten') of Sint Maartensdijk and Scherpenisse.

name: Scherpenisse
Settlement_Description: First mentioned in 1204, in a copy from ca. 1208.

name: Mindrebro
Bridge_Description: The bridge Mindebro, downstream from the old bridge across the Aarhus Å, was first mentioned in 1634.

name: Ritzebüttel
Settlement_Description: The settlement Ritzebüttel is first mentioned in 1325 (with an earlier uncertain mentioned of 1310), but earlier terp settlements already existed before the area was diked in the 11th century. Around 1300, the lords Lappe erected the castle Steenborch, which was first mentioned in 1342. It was acquired by Hamburg in 1394, as a means to control the mouth of the Elbe river. Ritzebüttel was merged with Cuxhaven in 1872.

name: Altenbruch
Settlement_Description: First mentioned in 1280. The double-towered church of St. Nicholas was built in the 13th century and served as beacon for ships on the Elbe.
Fair_Description: In 1632 the fair on Good Friday, which had been organised for some years, was moved to Thursday after Easter. In 1640 it was mentioned to have a duration of 14 days.

name: Schnöggersburg
Settlement_Description: Founded in 1694 and named after the forester. In the following years it was an inn, forester's office and sheep farm until it was bought by the state in 1931 and integrated into a military training area.

name: Midlum (Wursten)
Settlement_Description: The church of Midlum was built in the 12th and expanded in the 13th century. In 1219, a Benedictine nunnery was founded here, but moved to Altenwalde in 1282.

name: Blumenthal (Bremen)
Settlement_Description: The knights of Oumund built the Blomendal castle in the 13th century, which was destroyed in 1305 and rebuilt at another location in 1354. The castle belonged to the town of Bremen since 1430.

name: Ebersdorf (Saale)
Settlement_Description: The settlement was first mentioned in 1396.

name: Schwanewede
Settlement_Description: A Borchardus de Svanewede is first mentioned in 1203. The family owned a castle in the village, which was destroyed in a feud with Bremen around 1300, but rebuilt later.

name: Meyenburg (Bremen)
Settlement_Description: A moated castle was first mentioned in 1309. Next to it, a village developed.

name: Elsfleth
Settlement_Description: The settlement is first mentioned as meeting place of representatives of the Bremen council and the Frisian land of Rüstringen in 1220 and 1291. A church was built in 1285 at the latest.
Toll_Description: Toll on the Weser river, which was levied by the Count of Oldenburg from 1623 onwards, initially in Brake. In 1624, the toll was moved to Elsfleth, although a secondary toll station remained in Brake. The town of Bremen did not accept the levying of the toll and managed to avoid toll payment of Bremen ships with naval and diplomatic measures, until the town was finally forced to acknowledge the toll in 1653. Toll registers for the years 1624-1627, 1653-1661, 1663-1668 and single years in the 1670s are kept in the Niedersächsisches Landesarchiv Oldenburg.

name: Klüden
Settlement_Description: First secure mention in 1472; earlier mentions might refer to Kläden.

name: Blätz
Settlement_Description: First mention in 1359, but the settlement was probably deserted after 1366. In 1562 it is used again as a farmin estate. A village only re-emerges in 1794.

name: Rødby
Settlement_Description: Rødby was probably established as a village during the Viking Age in the indland part of Rødby Fjord, which was drained and cultivated in the year 1878. Due to its location as the most southern tip of the Danish realm and on the direct route between Eastern Denmark, in particular Zealand and nearby islands, and Germany, Rødby developed into an important harbour with ferry routes to Germany.
Town_Description: In the medieval period Rødby was a hybrid between a village, a borough (Danish: Flække) and a town. Both peasants and merchants lived in Rødby. Mentioned as a royal estate in the so-called main list of King Valdemar’s Cadastre from 1231, and in the following centuries alternately described as both a borough and a town. King Christian I (1448-81) granted Rødby rights to trade with Germany in 1405, and in 1454 Rødby was granted the same privileges as other boroughs on Lolland. In 1528 the citizens of Rødby were granted trading privileges, and in 1555 the citizens were also granted free oxen export. Still Rødby was considered a borough. Until the 17th century the toll officer served as the king's representative, it was not before 1682 Rødby had its own bailiff and council. Already in 1634, however, Rødby was characterized as a town in a royal charter.
Fair_Description: In 1636 the fairs from the villages of Tågerup and Sædding were relocated to Rødby. The character and date of these fairs are uncertain.
Toll_Description: Rødby was one of the most important royal toll stations throughout the late middle ages and early-modern period. The collection of toll was first mentioned in 1471 but appears to be older. Toll accounts are preserved from the period 1518-1522. The toll station was probably located at Dragsminde, where possible remains of a toll building have been found. The collecting of tolls declined in the 17th century.

name: Neubrandenburg
Town_Description: Margrave Johann of Brandenburg commissioned the knight Herbord von Raven to found the town in 1248 with Brandenburg town law. In the 14th and 15th century, it was the primary residence of the dukes of Mecklenburg-Stargard.
Toll_Description: In 1366 Neubrandenburg bought back the "small and big" tolls that the town of Friedland had possessed in Neubrandenburg since 1276. Citizens of Friedland remained exempted from toll payments and other duties, whereas Neubrandenburg still had to pay toll in Friedland.

name: Menz
Settlement_Description: In the 13th century a castle and a village were founded as a border protection. First mentioned in 1290.

name: Renko
Settlement_Description: <b>Inn:</b> In Jaakko Teitti's list in 1556 as a possible place for an official, Vogt (fi. vouti, sw. fogde). An inn might be located by the church.

name: null
Toll_Description: <li> Emperor Otto II donated the imperial toll in Deventer to the bishop of Utrecht in 975. This Bishop's toll ('Bisschopstol') was first leased to the town in 1354, from 1401 on eternally.  As result of the Reformation the ownership of the toll went over to the Province of Overijssel. The toll was abolished in 1799. The 'Bisschopstol' was a market toll levied at the town gates ('Bisschopstol te Lande') and on the IJssel river ('Bisschopstol te Water'). see node 1417. The central toll station for the Bishop's toll and other tolls on river transport was (at least from around 1541) located at the gate 'Zandpoort'. The procedure of levying was the same as for the Katen Toll, see below. Toll registration is preserved for the years 1577, 1583-1585, 1591 and 1684/85 in Collectie Overijssel locatie Deventer 0691 Schepenen en Raad van de stad Deventer, periode Republiek.<li>The Katen toll (Kathen, Caten, Cathen, Caeten, Coter tol) for sailing transport was a toll founded before 973. That year is was granted by Emperor Otto II to the Elten Abbey. In origin it was a levy on fishing, but it developed in a toll on ships and transported goods. This must have taken place after the last half of the 12th century when navigability of the IJssel increased after storm floods. The toll was levied at Katerveer, the location of the ferry between Zwolle and Hattem. From 1241 the Katen toll went in leasehold to the city of Deventer. The levying ended in 1799 as result of the decree of October 1st 1798 on the abolition of tolls on inland transit, by the Executive Authority of the Batavian Republic. Yields of the toll are edited for the years 1460-'79. It is unknown when the levying of the toll was moved to Deventer. Possibly it took place in the second half of the 16th century influenced by the political troubles with Spain and the insecurity during these years. The Tarif list of 1541 speaks about levying of the toll in Deventer. In 1579 a little house in Deventer is rented for the Katen toll and the toll is levied by the gatekeeper of the Zandpoort in Deventer. He also levies the Bisschop toll, the harbor dues and the Salt toll. This combination of functions is confirmed 1594 and later supplemented with the Rudder toll and the Welle due, (Het Welle geld). A description from 1583 shows that all ships, upstream and downstream the IJssel river are obliged to moor on the Welle, to pay toll or to show their exemption. This procedure is confirmed in 1696. The documents from 1799 concerning the termination of the Deventer tolls, shows that there still (or again?) was a toll collector in the Katerveer regio levying toll from the ships loaded downstream Deventer to Katerveer. A document from 1584 seems to indicate that also at that moment the Katen toll was levied on two locations. Toll registration is preserved for the years 1577, 1583-1585, 1591 and 1684/85 in Collectie Overijssel locatie Deventer 0691 Schepenen en Raad van de stad Deventer, periode Republiek.<li> Rudder toll (Roertol, Rodertol) was only levied on ships that were docking at the Welle and on ships from a group of towns with freedom on the Katen- and the Bishop's toll. It is not clear from when this levy had to be paid. It started before 1473 The Rudder toll was abolished in 1799.<li> Ships using the quay called the 'Welle', had to pay 'Wellegeld', in 1479 described as 'laede gelde op der Wellen'.  It is not clear from when this levy had to be paid. According to a printed Ordonnantie of 1696 The Wellegeld is payed when loading or unloading a (part of a) shipload. The Wellegeld was continued after 1799.
Harbour_Description: A harbour on the IJssel in Deventer is first mentioned in 877. A harbour crane is shown on the town map of Jacob van Deventer (16th century) at the end of the current Kranensteeg ('crane alley').

name: Dreitzsch
Toll_Description: Secondary station of safe conduct ('Beigeleit') of Triptis in the district ('Amt') Arnshaugk. Revenues are known from 1541 onwards.

name: null
Ferry_Description: Ferry to Tangermünde, first mentioned in 1376.

name: Hulshorst
Settlement_Description: Earliest mention in 1294/95. Archeological evidence suggests habitation from the eleventh/twelfth century onward. In the period 1350-1650, Hulshorst consisted of a scattered number of farms, mainly along the roads Oudeweg and Harderwijkerweg (former Bovenweg).

name: Poortvliet
Settlement_Description: First mentioned in 1200, in a copy from 1308.

name: Neuhausen (Erzgebirge)
Settlement_Description: The settlement came into existence near the castle Purschenstein and is first mentioned in 1495.

name: Eibergen
Settlement_Description: Earliest mention in 1188, in a thirteenth century document. Another mention dates from 1246.

name: null
Lock_Description: Between 1644 and 1646, a lock was built at the watermill Nieuwe Molen, as part of attempts to make the Berkel river navigable. Tariffs for using the locks were set in 1646.

name: null
Harbour_Description: In 1591, when plans were made to improve the navigability of the Berkel river, it was navigable between Zutphen and Borculo. Significant river traffic for earlier periods is unlikely.

name: null
Toll_Description: The Zutphen toll for sailing transport was a ducal toll founded before 1196. In the 'Town letter', dated between 1191 and 1196, it is mentioned that freedom of shipping toll was granted to traders that visited the Zutphen market. The location of the toll is not completely sure. Most likely is that the toll was levied from the approach of the bridge (built in 1487) at the town side. In 1490 it has been shown that the Zutphen market toll for sailing transport was levied at this location. Until 1487 there was a ferry at the same location, possibly the jetty for the ferry was the place the toll was levied. Toll registration for the years 1382, 1394 – 1395 (also in print see: Westermann 1939), 1424 1544 - 1567, 1573 - 1575, 1581-1583 (1582 is analysed), 1598 - 1605, 1610 – 1611 1612 -1613, 1614 – 1615, 1617 – 1618, 1621 – 1623, 1624 – 1649, 1655 – 1656, 1666 - 1672, is preserved in Gelders Archief, 0012 Gelderse Rekenkamer. Toll registration for 1801 - 1805 and 1809 (part.) is preserved in: Gelders Archief, 0016 Gewestelijke besturen in de Bataafs-Franse tijd. Toll-accounts for the years 1388-'99 have been analysed by Weststrate (in particular for wine). A tariff for Utrecht dated 1399 is edited.
Harbour_Description: On the maps of Zutphen of Jacob van Deventer (mid-16th century) and from the Atlas van Loon (1649), a harbour crane is drawn next to the bridge on the IJssel river front.

name: null
Harbour_Description: In front of the Rhine gate, the large harbour place of the town Neuss was located. The town map of Braun and Hogeberg from 1590 shows a ship crane here, which is first attested in 1400. According to a description from 1670, larger Rhine barges could not get closer to town on this Rhine arm.

name: null
Ferry_Description: A ferry between Neuss and Düsseldorf is first mentioned in 1262. On the Neuss side, it was connected to the farm Kothausen at the Heerdter Busch. Since 1315 the ferry was owned by the Clarist monastery in Neuss.
Harbour_Description: Due to changes in the course of the Rhine in the Middle Ages, Neuss became located on old Rhine arms that slowly silted up, making it ever more difficult for ships to get close to the town. In situations with low water levels, the ship crane of Neuss, normally located near the Rhine gate, was even moved to the Rhine shore near the ferry to Hamm, as is for example shown on a drawing from 1621.

name: Lavinto
Settlement_Description: <b>Inn:</b> Local official (fi: nimismies, sw: länsman, eng. sheriff) was obliged to run a tavern in his house (Ollila) in the late 16th c. In 1565, the farmers of Turkhauta and Puujaa were given fines for not bringing horses to the inn. Lavinto inn is no longer mentioned in 1623 list of taverns in Hattula region.

name: null
Bridge_Description: A wooden bridge was renewed in 1573 and had to be renovated again in 1589; it was built from oak. It was destroyed during the Thirty Years' War in 1636, but rebuilt almost immediately.

name: null
Ferry_Description: The ferry privileges of Neuss were divided in two parts by the end of the 13th century. Next to the ferry in Hamm, another ferry was connected to the farm Hüchelheim near Grimlinghausen.

name: null
Toll_Description: Until about 1810 Arnhem was the location for some tolls:<ul><li>The first toll for sailing transport is the Great Guelders toll of Arnhem. It is first mentioned in 1195, but was moved to Lobith in 1222. After Lobith was lost to Cleves in 1473, the duke of Guelders re-instated the toll station in Arnhem in or after 1492. In combination with the tolls of Nijmegen, Tiel, Zaltbommel, IJsseloord and Zutphen and the tolls on river Meuse, these were the Great Guelders tolls. Toll administration 1543 - 1567, 1574-75, 1586-1604, 1617/18, 1623/24, 1626/28,1636/40, 1655/63, 1663/79, 1688/90 and 1739/41 is preserved in Gelders Archief, 0012 Gelderse Rekenkamer. Toll administration 1801- 1810 is preserved in: Gelders Archief, 0016 Gewestelijke besturen in de Bataafs-Franse tijd. </li> Yields of the toll and the number of passing ships up- and downstream for the years 1543-'57 are edited.<li>The second toll for sailing transport is the Anholt toll, "Anholtse tol". It was situated in Arnhem from 1618. This toll was the result of the temporarily removal of the toll of the Duchy of Guelders from Lobith to IJsseloord in the war time between 1372 -1379. 1384 the Duke of Guelders recieved permission from the Holy roman emperor to levy this toll in addition to the one of Lobith permanently at IJsseloord, as 'IJsselorde' tol. The toll moved temporarily (1472) for a short while to Huissen. In 1434 Duke Arnold gave the toll over in pledge (and in 1472 in property) to his brother Willem van Egmond, reason that the name was during many years Arnoldian or Egmondian toll. From 1561 the toll was owned by the Lord of Anholt, so it became the name Anholt toll. Caused by the troubles of the Dutch Revolt the toll was levied temporarily (1588 - 1597) in respectively Büderich, Reeser Schanz and Rijnberk. Then it came back to IJsseloord. Because the toll house at IJsseloord was permanently threatened by the river, from 1618 the levying of the toll took place from the tower above the guardhouse near the Sabelspoort bridge in the town of Arnhem. In 1816 the toll was transferred to the Kingdom of the Netherlands.Toll administration is preserved: for the years 1401-02, 1403-06, 1407-08, 1415-16, 1417-19 and 1424-25 in Gelders Archief, 0001, In: Graven en hertogen van Gelre, graven van Zutphen  registers from 1688 - 1756 in Fürstlich Salm-Salmsche Archiv (FSSA), Schloss Anholt, Anholt, Germany, In: Archiv Arnheimer Zoll: III Zollrechnungen und Zollbücher, Tolregisters van de ontvangers van de Arnheimer Zoll, inv.nrs. 31, 36-40, 43-59.</li> <li>The Market toll, 'Merckttol'', this toll for sailing transport was founded before 1249, the year is was levied for the Hospital of St. John. In 1782 is noted that the market toll was levied three times a year for a period of 21 days.  the fist time from 11/12 March, the second time the 7th September and the third time the 10th November. The toll was collected then in combination with the Anholt toll.</li></ul>
Harbour_Description: The grain market of Arnhem was moved to a new location outside the Rijnpoort (Rhine gate), near the river. Earliest mention of the grain market on this location in 1428. The quay was broadened; in 1440, decisions were made for a new harbour here, and paving the road. In 1449, a crane was being build. Cranage had to be paid if one used the crane. This crane was out of use between 1499-1525 because it had been destroyed. Officially, Arnhem had no grain staple, but around the mid-fifteenth century, from 1437-1439 onward, the town de facto forced people to offer their load of grain for sale in Arnhem when passing by on the river Rhine. In 1603, the harbour was made safer.

name: Syke
Settlement_Description: Archaeological excavations have shown that a refuge castle must have existed around 800. First mentioned around 1250. At the end of the 13th century, a castle is built. The settlement is characterised as borough ('flecken') in 1520, but only acquired the corresponding privileges in 1718.

name: Bruchhausen(-Vilsen)
Settlement_Description: The castle of Bruchhausen, first mentioned in 1189, was residence of the lords of Bruchhausen, later inherited by the counts of Oldenburg, and sold to the count of Hoya in 1326. The settlement developed into a borough ('flecken') at the beginning of the 15th century. It merged with nearby Vilsen in 1929.
Toll_Description: A toll of the counts of Hoya in Bruchhausen was pawned to Heinrich Starke in 1545. After complaints from Bremen in the 1590s, it was mentioned that the toll had existed for a long time.

name: Vilsen
Settlement_Description: First mentioned in 1227. The settlement acquired borough ('flecken') privileges in the 15th century, which were confirmed in 1577. It merged with nearby Bruchhausen in 1929.

name: null
Toll_Description: In the years 1552-1564 the toll of IJsseloord was collected at Doesburg.
Harbour_Description: The harbour of Doesburg, on a side branch of the river IJssel, was originally located at a narrow strip of land called "werf". The harbour was moved to the area Contre-Escarpe when new fortifications were constructed in 1607.

name: Blankenstein (Saale)
Settlement_Description: First uncertain mention in 1392, first certain mention in 1444.

name: null
Toll_Description: At least from 1487 onward, a toll was levied for crossing the bridge.
Bridge_Description: In front of the gate called 'Waterpoort' a bridge crossed the river. During the Eighty Years' War, the bridge was removed for several years and replaced by a ferry.
Ferry_Description: During the Eighty Years' War, the bridge was replaced by a ferry for several years.
Harbour_Description: Shipping on the Oude IJssel was made possible in 1582, when the water mill in Keppel was demolished. According to a document from 1590, shipping took place at that time between Doesburg and Doetinchem. Shipping in the other direction, to Bocholt and Anholt, was made possible with construction works in 1592.

name: Naantali
Settlement_Description: Permanent agricultural settlement in Naantali (sw. Nådental) area dates to the 13th century. The villages were part of Raisio (sw. Reso) parish. The council of the Swedish realm founded in 1438 a Bridgettine abbey in Finland. After initial phases elsewhere the abbey was finally located to Ailoinen in Raisio in 1442. Active since 1444 the Abbey was consecrated in 1462. The Abbey’s landed property was confiscated in 1557, but the convent remained partially active until 1591. King Karl IX ordered the convent buildings to be demolished in 1608.
Town_Description:
In the context of the relocation of the Abbey to Pyhäjoki in 1441 the council of the realm furnished it with the right to establish a town to its sustention in accordance with the rights of other towns in the realm. Like in Vadstena, the town was designed to support the monastery's economy. The rights of the town attached to the abbey in its new location in Ailoinen were confirmed by king Christopher in 1443. The following year, the king confirmed the abbey's right to freely export the products of its farms and import food and other goods, but this did not apply to the town burghers, who had to pay customs duties in Turku on their exports and imports. The town council of Naantali was active in 1464. In 1523, king Gustav I confirmed the privileges of the town separate from the monastery. The city's burghers had little independent opportunity for their own foreign exports and imports in the 16th and 17th centuries, and traffic mainly ran on ships owned by the burghers of Turku. There is information about the trading activity of the burghers of Naantali in the Gulf of Bothnia from the early 16th century, but no more after that. The town did not have rights to foreign trade after 1614. The population of the town was at the end of the Middle Ages ca. 200. The oldest map of the town is a survey of Hans Hansson in 1649.

<b>Inn:</b> Naantali abbey charter of foundation from 1441 stated that the abbey is not to be burdened with travellers, but a trading place is to be established next to it, and private alehouses and taverns established there to serve pilgims and other travellers. This most likely happened. In late 16th and early 17th centuries, the townspeople complained that there weren't enough taverns and they were heavily burdened with serving food, drinks, and accommodation. According to a statute from 1638, there was supposed to be two inns in every town, but this does not seem to be the case in Naantali, and sometimes there were none. In 1648, Akseli Liinakankuri ("Linen weaver"), member of the town council, was appointed as the innkeeper, and afterwards the office moved from one burgher to another.
Fair_Description: Naantali Ash Wednesday (4 February – 10 March) fair on the first week of Lent is first documented in 1506 when the election of the lagman of Northern Finland was arranged next to the Abbey, where according to the bishop of Turku the common people of the land gathered at that time of the year. King Gustav I ordered the fair to be discontinued at the request of the Turku burghers in 1531, but without success and they are mentioned in the almanacs of 1585 and 1595. The date of the market at the beginning of Lent seems to have been in use already in 1452 and 1453, when judges, clerics, members of the nobility, burghers of Turku and peasants were present in Naantali in large gatherings on Ash Wednesday. The Ash Wednesday fair was very likely held on ice between the Abbey and the town. The late medieval date for the annual autumn market may have been the feast of Saint Birgitta (7 October), for which day the burghers of Naantali requested a second annual market during the reign of Queen Christina (1632–54). The request was granted after a new application in 1660, but due to overlapping fairs in other towns, the fair was set on Michaelmas (29 September). The market day of Naantali was in 1619 Saturday.
Toll_Description: The 1/32 duty worth of all goods intended for sale in towns and fairs and brought to the site by peasants was collected in Naantali since 1622.

name: null
Harbour_Description: The Bocholter Aa was made navigable in 1592. This allowed shipping between Bocholt and Doesburg via the Oude IJssel.

name: null
Harbour_Description: The Issel river was cleaned of obstacles in 1592; this allowed shipping between Anholt and Doesburg via the Oude IJssel.

Bridge_Description: The ferry was replaced by a bridge in 1616.
Ferry_Description: A ferry across the Rhin river was the reason for the addition 'fehr' (ferry) to the name of Bellin. The ferry is first attested in 1402.

name: Haastrecht
Settlement_Description: Haastdrecht is first mentioned in a twelfth-century copy of a 1108 text. The settlement originated around 1100 at the point were the river Vlist flows into the river Hollandse IJssel.
Town_Description: Cox argues that Haastrecht must have been granted town privileges before 24 May 1301. Possibly, this grant was received from Willem (II) Berthout, bishop of Utrecht.
Fair_Description: A cattle-fair in Haastrecht is first atttested in 1366 in the first week of June, in 1416 a horsefair is mentioned. Annual yields are preserved and edited for the years 1440-1593 (maximum in 1564). In the Enqueste of 1494 Haastrecht mentions keeping horses and cows as a means of subsistence. In the second half of the 16th century the horsefair had more importance then the three ones in near Gouda. The fairday was St. Odulphus (June 12). Duration unknown. A manual of the toll-keeper of Geervliet dated 1562 mentions the horse-fair in 'Astre' (Haastrecht) on June 10 in a calendar of many horse-faires. In 1594 the horsefair in Delft with St. Odulphus was put forward from June 10 to June 7, because of competetion by the fair in Haastrecht on June 11.

name: Rauman kuninkaankartano
Settlement_Description: <b>Rauma Franciscan Friary:</b>The Franciscan Friary on the northern bank of Raumajoki river and outside the town area is first cited in 1449. The stone church was built in 1515–20. Friary was closed in 1538. <b>Rauma Royal Manor:</b> The manor was established in the former premises of the Franciscan Friary in 1556 as an administrative centre of a bailiwick of Rauma, Laitila and Kalanti parishes. It served as such until 1563 and sporadically even later. The manor was an important centre of horse breeding from the 1560s to the early decades of the 17th century and hosted a shipyard from the 1570s to the beginning of the 17th century.

name: null
Toll_Description: Hermann of Gommern and his sons donated the Cistercian convent Plötzky among others a toll on the Elbe river as it "had been since old times" in 1330. The toll had therefore probably existed longer. It does not appear in later records, which might have been related to Plötzky's location at an old river arm, which function was gradually taken over by the main arm of the Elbe, the "Stromelbe", in the late Middle Ages.

name: Kloster Donndorf
