Settlement_Description: A convent of Cistercian nuns was founded around 1250. It was badly damaged during the Peasant's War and dissolved in 1541. A school was founded in the former monastery in 1561, which served as pre-school for the school in Pforta.

name: null
Bridge_Description: In 1369 the town of Kahla acquired the right to confiscate rafts that damaged the bridge across the Saale or the mill weir.

name: Tammerkosken silta
Bridge_Description: Tammerkoski bridge is first mentioned in 1556, but the important crossing on common road from Häme to Satakunda and Gulf of Bothnia area may have existed already in the Middle Ages. The bridge was maintained by four medieval and one 16th century parishes of Ylä-Satakunta district. The original bridge site was some 50 m North from the present Hämeensilta bridge.

name: null
Harbour_Description: A harbour in Ruhrort is already attested in the Middle Ages, but was no ideal loading point. Ships had to anchor on the Rhine or Ruhr until the construction of harbour quays in the 18th century.

name: IJsseloord
Toll_Description: The IJsseloord toll for sailing transport is one of the Great Guelders tolls. It is one of the continuations of the Lobith toll after this toll was deprived for the Guelders duke and became Clevish in 1473. (See also Great Guelders toll Arnhem). Originaly the toll was levied at the bifurcation of the river Rhine into the branches Nederrijn and IJssel. In an early 16th century right of the toll both streams are indicated as: the Rhine passing Arnhem downstream towards the Grebbe till the border between the Sticht of Utrecht and Gelre and the IJssel up till Doesburg. The toll house was threatened by the water so levying became difficult. In or short after 1472 the toll was possibly briefly moved to Huissen. The toll was temporarily situated in Doesburg from 1552 - 1564. In 1562 the toll was sold to the lord of Anholt. From 1564 on, the levying of the toll was combined with that of the the Great Guelders toll of Arnhem. Edited are the years 1394/95 and analysed the years 1388-'99, in particular for wine. A tariff for Utrecht dated 1399 is edited. Yields of the toll and the number of passing ships up- and downsteam for the years 1543-48 are edited. The accounts of the 1570's are also analysed. Until 1585 the location of the toll varies between Arnhem and IJsseloord. After that year the toll was officially located in Arnhem but in practice levied near the Westervoort ferry. Toll administration for the years 1392-1426 is preserved in the archives of the dukes and counts of Gelre, for the years 1480-88 in the archive of the counts of Salm-Salm at Anholt (with a tariff from the lord of Egmond dated 1540), and for the years 1543 - 1567, 1573 - 1576, 1598 - 1599, 1601 - 1604, 1608 - 1617, 1619 - 1649, 1655 - 1679, 1688/90 and 1739-1741 in Gelders Archief, 0012 Gelderse Rekenkamer. Toll administration 1801- 1805 and 1809 (part.) is preserved in: Gelders Archief, 0016 Gewestelijke besturen in de Bataafs-Franse tijd.

name: null
Bridge_Description: The Oder bridge in Crossen is first attested in 1477.

name: null
Harbour_Description: A good and well protected natural harbour. The character of the medieval harbour, however, is not known. A small wharf is seen on a copper engraving of Nykøbing Sjælland in Resen’s Atlas Danicus from 1675. When the wharf was originally built is uncertain.

name: null
Toll_Description: A toll on the Weser river in Landesbergen is mentioned in a Bremen complaint from 1584, as well as in a 1597 charter of the monastery Hardehausen.

name: null
Ferry_Description: The Ruhr river could be crossed with a ford near Mülheim. A ferry is first mentioned here in 1408, which belonged to the Count of Broich, but was usually pawned. It was planned to replace the ferry by a bridge as early as 1443, but an actual bridge is only attested in ca. 1750.

name: null
Ferry_Description: The ferry between Cologne and Deutz is among others mentioned in 1488.

name: Diepenau
Settlement_Description: A castle was built by the count of Hoya at the border with the diocese of Minden around 1380. Next to it a settlement developed, which was first mentioned in 1462 and received borough ('flecken') privileges in 1486.
Toll_Description: A toll in Diepenau is mentioned in 1581 as existing since old times. It probably goes back to the foundation of the castle around 1380.

name: Müsleringen
Settlement_Description: The place was first mentioned in 1235.

name: Rothentor
Settlement_Description: Farm at the location where the street between Wismar and Schwerin and Gadebusch crossed the Wismar defensive enclosure ('landwehr'). First mentioned in 1469.

name: Greven (Ems)
Settlement_Description: The place was a Frankish settlement and church village, which was first mentioned around 890. A market is attested in the 13th century.
Fair_Description: A fair in Greven is first attested in the 13th century. It is mentioned again in 1403, when it took place on Monday after St Bartholomew. It was predominantly a market for cattle, horses and other animals. The fair attracted visitors from the wider region, as far as Nijmegen and Cologne. A second market on the 3rd of May was added in 1746.

name: null
Lock_Description: A new lock was constructed near Marienwerder in 1506.

name: Gehrden
Settlement_Description: Mentioned as borough ('oppidum') in 1298; the settlement acquired borough ('flecken') privileges in 1647.

name: Lenzer Fähre
Ferry_Description: The ferry across the Elbe near Lenzen was sold by the Bülow family of Gartow to the town Lenzen in 1438. It might have been in possession of the Knights Hospitaller in Gartow before (possibly since 1360). The ferry originally crossed the Elbe near Pevestorf; it was moved to Holtorf in 1695-1699.

name: Rötha
Town_Description: First mentioned as town in 1291, usually referred to as borough ('städtlein', 'flecken') afterwards.

name: null
Harbour_Description: The navigability of the river Pleiße must have started near Rötha.

name: null
Harbour_Description: A fee for vessels on the river Pleiße is mentioned in a register of the margraves of Meißen from 1378. Probably this indicates a regular supply of the town of Leipzig via the river. The landing place for these ships must have been located directly northwest of the old town.

name: Enumatil
Bridge_Description: The settlement developed next to a bridge ('til') across the Hoendiep, from which the name was derived.

name: Halte
Settlement_Description: Originally a folwark of the monastery of Knights Hospitalers Muhde. It was secularised in 1561.
Toll_Description: The count of Eastern Frisia installed a toll station in Halte around 1580, which led to complaints from the bishop of Münster, who claimed that it conflicted with a toll treaty from 1572. After a verdict of the Imperial Chamber Court in 1583 the toll was temporarily not levied on ships from Münster. Later complaints from Münster and Emden show that the toll continued to be levied against high tariffs, despite multiple verdicts of the Imperial Court.

name: Lobith
Settlement_Description: First mentioned in 1222 when the toll privileges were granted. The toll house was extended into a castle and ducal residence around 1307.
Toll_Description: River toll, located until c. 1540 on the bifurcation of the Rhine and Waal rivers. It belonged to the Count of Guelders, who moved it from Arnhem to Lobith in 1222. In 1307, a new toll house was built because of changes in the course of the Rhine. The toll was temporarily levied in Emmerich between 1355 and ca. 1359. In 1479, Lobith castle became property of the Duke of Cleves (Kleve). Although probably not formally entitled to collect tolls, the Duke of Cleves had tolls levied at Lobith. The Duchy of Gelre, which was certainly formally entitled, had the Lobith toll - an important source of revenue - levied as the Great Toll of Gelre at each of the three western Rhine arms: at Wageningen (later Arnhem/IJsseloord), Nijmegen and Doesburg (Zutphen). So in fact there were two ‘Lobith tolls’. The information on the three branches of the Great Toll of Gelre is continued under the nodes Arnhem, Nijmegen and Zutphen.The Toll administration 1306 - 1459 (1550) is preserved in Gelders Archief: 0001 Graven en hertogen van Gelre, graven van Zutphen and 0012 Gelderse Rekenkamer. The oldest accounts for 1294/5 have been edited, which show that the toll amounted to 30% of the total revenues of the count of Guelders. Accounts for 1306, 1404 and 1408 have been analysed by Jappe Alberts. Toll-accounts for the years 1388-'99 have been analysed by Weststrate (in particular for wine). The accounts for 1394/5 have also been edited. A tariff for Utrecht, dated 1399, is also edited. The yields for the years 1404-'59 (with gaps) are presented in a graph.Here we continue with the Clevian toll of Lobith.Until at least 1556 (Map Jacob van Deventer) the toll of Lobith was at the bifurcation of the River Rhine into Waal and (Neder-) Rijn. But already in 1540 was concluded that the bifurcation moved more south to the place where from 1586 on the Schenkenschans divided the Rhine into the two branches. Levying toll for small ships still took place in Lobith, bigger ships payed at an alternative small toll house at ‘s Gravenweerd, later in Grieth and still later at Schenkenschanz. From about 1597 ‘s Gravenweerd was the toll station again, but from 1689 to 1708 Schenkenschanz was the toll station again. From 1711 on levying of the toll took place near the Christinaschanz north of the Rhine. The toll house was the basis for the for the present-day village of Tolkamer.
Ferry_Description: This ferry, known as the 'Tolhuisveer' ('Toll house ferry'), is first mentioned in 1394. From at least the fifteenth century onward, the ferry had three owners: half of it was owned by the Chapter of Elten, a quarter by the lords of Grondstein, and a quarter by the lords of Bergh. Around 1660, the ferry was impeded by the 'Gelderse Rekenkamer', after which it ceased to exist after a couple of years.

name: null
Bridge_Description: The "long bridge" and causeway across the Aue are first mentioned in 1303. They were part of the defence system ('landwehr') of the town of Braunschweig.

name: Ottersleben
Settlement_Description: First mention in a donation charter in 937.

name: Woeste Hoeve
Settlement_Description: The inn 'Woeste Hoeve' is presumably one of the oldest still existing inns on the Veluwe. It was located on the crossroad of the road between Arnhem and Deventer, and the Hesseroad between Steenderen and Barneveld. The town account of Zutphen of 1469 mentions 'den wech na Wuesterhuve'.

name: Gendt
Town_Description: Town privileges granted in 1233, by Otto II, count of Guelders and Zutphen.
Fair_Description: In 1493 (Sep. 3) the duke of Gelre granted a fair to Gent in the 'ambt Averbetuwen', starting Sept. 1.

name: null
Ferry_Description: In 1409 the citizens of Belgern hand over their share of the ferry to Buch monastery.</br>In 1474 Buch monastery loans half the ferry to ferryman Wenzel for life. In the following time, the ferry seems to only have been passed over to private persons. There was a large raft ferry and a small boat ferry.

name: null
Bridge_Description: A bridge in Freden is mentioned in 1413.

name: null
Bridge_Description: A bridge and causeway across the Schunter near Lehre is mentioned in 1488.

name: Schwarzer Kater
Settlement_Description: Inn at a crossing west of Dahlen. Crossing of the 'Hohe Straße' and the 'Hainstraße', here called 'Heustraße'.

name: null
Bridge_Description: A wooden bridge is first mentioned in 1577.

name: null
Toll_Description: A bridge and ferry toll were due in Torgau, as well as a toll on wares that were shipped on the Elbe river (LHASA, MD, d. 49, Nr. 2, Amt Torgau 1510, p. 348–354.). The toll is also attested in four travel accounts of skipper Gottfried Kleeditz from Pirna from 1671-1674.
Bridge_Description: Between 1422 and 1428 a wooden bridge across the Elbe was constructed in Torgau by the order of prince electorate Friedrich I.

name: null
Toll_Description: Mentioned as toll station on the river Elbe in the beginning of the 17th century. The toll is also mentioned in four travel accounts of skipper Gottfried Kleeditz from Pirna from 1671-1674.

name: null
Toll_Description: A toll on the Elbe river is first mentioned in 1362. The regulation of safe conduct from 1566 settles the fees taken from rafts as well as boats. In four travel accounts of skipper Gottfried Kleeditz from Pirna in 1671 to 1674 the toll on the Elbe river is mentioned as well.

name: null
Toll_Description: In the Dessau regulations of safe conduct from 1549, the fees for rafts and ships on the Elbe were fixed. The toll also appears in four travel accounts of skipper Gottfried Kleeditz from Pirna from 1671-1674.

name: null
Toll_Description: A toll in Aken is first mentioned in 1295, probably an export toll, possibly also a transit toll on the river Elbe. Regulations of safe conduct from the 16th century list the fees due on the Elbe river. The toll is also mentioned in four travel accounts of skipper Gottfried Kleeditz from Pirna in 1671-1674.

name: null
Toll_Description: In a report from 1577 a river toll in Barby is mentioned, of which the tariffs were doubled. The toll also appears in four travel accounts of skipper Gottfried Kleeditz from Pirna from 1671-1674.

name: Teichel
Settlement_Description: First mention in a donation charter in 1076.
Town_Description: First mention as town in 1417, the settlement must have been granted town privileges by the counts of Schwarzburg. In 1535 bylaws are mentioned, which refer to older bylaws, which are based on those of Rudolstadt. Nevertheless, Teichel always retained a village-like character.

name: Eisenberg (Thüringen)
Settlement_Description: In 1171 the construction of town fortifications is reported (at the same time as Leipzig and Freiberg).
Town_Description: Before 1219 a new town is founded, in 1256 the citizens own the town sigil. The first recording of town rights stems from 1563 but they were probably adapted in the 15th century.

name: null
Toll_Description: First mention of a toll on the Elbe river in Jerichow in an exemption charter for the citizens of Magdeburg in 1430. In 1432 Wolmirstedt, Rogätz and Jerichow are mentioned as toll stations in a letter of conflict between the council of Magdeburg and the archbishop. Further mentions occur in 1460, 1480-1490 and 1492. Toll regulations remain from the 16th century. The toll is also mentioned in four travel accounts from skipper Gottfried Kleeditz from Pirna in 1671-1674.

name: Stadtroda
Settlement_Description: A Cistercian nun convent was founded by the lords of Lobdeburg between 1228 and 1247.
Town_Description: A citizen of the settlement is first mentioned in 1251. A planned town was founded on a hill on the left bank of the Roda river, around the "Alter Markt". It is first referred to as town in 1333 and granted town rights in 1340. The common law was recorded in the 15th century. A council is mentioned in 1403, a burgomaster in 1434. A second market developed in the valley, which acquired equal rights as the old market in 1523.

name: Turenki
Settlement_Description: <b>Inn:</b> An inn was established in Turenki in 1622.

name: null
Toll_Description: A toll on the Elbe river is first mentioned in a possibly falsified charter of 1136, when Magdeburg citizens received a reduced tariff. Further mentions of the toll in 1373, 1377 and 1385, it is differentiated between the land (town) toll and the water (Elbe) toll. Further mentions in 1414, 1428 and 1458 when the exemption of toll of the citizens of Tangermünde is mentioned. The toll is also mentioned in four travel accounts of skipper Gottfried Kleeditz from Pirna in 1671 to 1674.

name: null
Bridge_Description: A drawbridge across the Unstrut is destroyed by mercenaries in 1631.

name: null
Toll_Description: The toll of Sandau, first mentioned in 1425, was also levied on the Elbe river, at least in the 17th century, as it is mentioned in four accounts of skipper Gottfried Kleeditz from Pirna in 1671-1674.
Ferry_Description: A ferry across the Elbe is first mentioned in 1272.

name: Hardisleben
Settlement_Description: First mention in 1230 in the charter book of Pforte monastery.

name: null
Lock_Description: The map of Mecklenburg included in the atlas of Janssonius from 1622 shows a lock south of Vietow in the Schaale canal, which was built in 1564.

name: null
Lock_Description: The map of Mecklenburg included in the atlas of Janssonius from 1622 shows a lock north of Vietow in the Schaale canal, which was built in 1564.

name: Vyborg Castle
Settlement_Description: <b>Viipuri Castle:</b>Viipuri Castle was established by a Swedish expedition to the area previously in the control of the principality of Novgorod in 1293. The castle is documented in 1295 and 1308. After the stabilisation of the border with Novgorod in 1323 the fortress became one of the most important strongholds in the Swedish realm with the castellan’s extensive powers over the economy, jurisdiction, and defence of the area in the bailiwicks of Viipuri, Olavinlinna (sw. Olofsborg, Nyslott), Kymenkartano (sw. Kymmene) and Porvoo (sw. Borgå). The castle’s role controlling the Swedish-Russian border was greatly diminished after the peace of Täyssinä 1595 (sw. Teusina) and Stolbova in 1617. Since 1635 it served as the residence of the new provincial administration and governor of Viborg and Nyslott’s province until 1710 (1721). The castle and its fortifications were modified several times for different purposes since the Middle Ages. Duke Johan of Finland stayed in the castle during his travels in 1555. The castle was heavily restored in the 1890s.

name: Kritzowburg
Settlement_Description: Farm at the point where the street between Wismar and Güstrow crossed the defensive enclosure ('landwehr') of Wismar. First mentioned in 1474.

name: Bülower Burg
Settlement_Description: Watchtower with boom barrier in the enclosure ('landwehr') of Güstrow. The enclosure is first mentioned in 1270, the tower itself in 1373. Later converted into a farm that was leased from the town.

name: Weida
Settlement_Description: First mention in a record in 1122 as part of the name of a witness.
Town_Description: First mention as a town in 1209, but it probably became a town in the middle of the 12th century. Town rights were granted in 1377 by Heinrich XV, but older town rights probably existed.

name: null
Harbour_Description: In the 1630s the Winschoterdiep canal was dug, which allowed river traffic between Groningen and Winschoten. Regular barge ('trekschuit') services were offered since 1654 at the latest.

name: Eutzsch
Settlement_Description: First mentioned in a possibly falsified charter from 966. First secure mention in 1004.

name: Oschersleben
Settlement_Description: Allegedly first mentioned in 814, first secure mention in 994. A castle was built in the 12th century and first mentioned in 1205. A market settlement developed next to it.
Town_Description: Town privileges probably granted at the end of the 12th century. First mentioned as "civitas" in 1235. The first record of a council remains from 1322. In 1376 it was characterised as borough ('Weichbild') and had a town hall. The jurisdiction remained in the hands of the castle, however.
Fair_Description: Three fairs and cattle markets are confirmed in Oschersleben in 1650 and two cattle markets are added before the fair after Reminiscere and another on St. Bartholomew's day.

name: Hughevliet
Settlement_Description: First mentioned in 1174. The exact location of the settlement is unknown, as it ceased to exist in 1404 when it drowned due to a storm surge.
Town_Description: Town rights were probably granted in the thirteenth century. The town disappeared in a storm surge in 1404.
Fair_Description: Hughevliet received the right to hold a fair and a weekly market in 1355 (August 2) from count Louis of Flanders.
Staple_Description: A staple for herring and fish was granted in 1355 (August 2) by count Louis of Flanders, starting 14 days before St. Bavo (Oct. 1) and during the 'herring time'.

name: Salmen silta
Bridge_Description: Salmi bridge in Vehkalahti parish is first cited in 1555, when Jakob Teitt included it in his map of the bridges in Kymijoki delta area. The earliest bridge on the site may date to the first organisation of the maintenance of the Great Coastal Road as a uniform land route between Turku and Viborg in the 1340s and 1360s. The present (2025) bridge was built in 1904 and was listed as part of National Road Heritage in 1982.

name: Kottmann
Settlement_Description: Crossing of the defensive enclosure ('landwehr') of Vreden near the farm Kottmann. The boom barrier was first mentioned as "Lewer Hecke" in 1543.

name: Salmer
Settlement_Description: Near the farm Volmer, the road crossed the 16th-century defensive enclosure ('landwehr') of Vreden.

name: Seeste
Settlement_Description: First mentioned in the 13th century. It was a dispersed settlement ('Bauerschaft'), which was divided into two part Ober- and Nieder-Seeste.

name: Arle
Settlement_Description: First mentioned in the early 12th century.

name: Hage
Settlement_Description: First mentioned in 1400, but there already existed a wooden church here in ca. 1200.

name: null
Toll_Description: "Beyond the toll station at the Rußningsbach in direction of Bila" a traveler had to pay for safe conduct.

name: null
Lock_Description: The map of Mecklenburg included in the atlas of Janssonius from 1622 shows a lock near Blücher in the Schaale canal, which was built in 1564.

name: null
Lock_Description: The map of Mecklenburg included in the atlas of Janssonius from 1622 shows a lock near Kogel in the Schaale canal, which was built in 1564.

name: null
Lock_Description: The map of Mecklenburg included in the atlas of Janssonius from 1622 shows a lock near Pamprin in the Schaale canal, which was built in 1564.

name: null
Ferry_Description: The settlement Vehra was named after the ferry that was situated here.

name: null
Toll_Description: After the Aller river had changed its course between 1618 and 1630, the toll levied on river traffic in Ahlden was now levied in Hudemühlen.

name: null
Bridge_Description: A bridge across the Innerste near Marienburg is mentioned in 1571.

name: null
Lock_Description: The mouth of the Wilster Au river in the Stör was closed with a flood gate in 1438. It was replaced by a chamber lock in 1925.

name: Plaue (Gera)
Settlement_Description: First mentioned in 1222. The settlement consisted of a village with a church and a castle.
Town_Description: Town rights were probably granted in the first half of the 14th century. In 1335 market rights after the Mühlhausen model were granted. Referred to as town ('stat') in 1346.
Toll_Description: A toll in Plaue is mentioned in 1336. In 1342 king Louis IV revoked this toll, which he had granted to the lords of Schwarzburg-Arnstadt before. However, from 1626 toll regulations with tariffs are known. It is unknown whether the toll was levied in the centuries inbetween.

name: null
Lock_Description: The mouth of the river Kremper Au in the Stör was closed with a flood gate in 1636. The barrier was moved to the dike in Borsfleth in 1756.

name: Bothenheilingen
Settlement_Description: Heilingen is first mentioned in 775-786, Bothenheiligen as separate settlement in 1143.

name: Wethau
Settlement_Description: The name of the settlement is first mentioned in 1146, the name of the district as early as 976.

name: null
Toll_Description: <li> The origin of the oldest Kampen toll for sailing transport, sometimes also called ‘Bisschops tol’ is not clear. Archieval evidence confirms that the toll existed in 1292 and was levied by the Bishop of Utrecht who also governed the Oversticht to which Kampen belonged. But in a dispute with the town of Zwolle around 1520 about a toll on the river Zwarte Water, the Kampen government claims that the toll had been levied for 300 years, so from about 1220. As stated under Node 3541 Kampen “Town”: It is, …., likely that town privileges have been granted by Wilbrand of Oldenburg, bishop of Utrecht, between 1230 and 1233. Possibly the toll was founded in this period too.However the toll was leased to the town of Kampen in 1327 and in 1402 the toll was sold to the town of Kampen. The levying of the toll has ended in 1799 as result of the decree of October 1st 1798 on the abolition of tolls on inland transit by the Executive Authority of the Batavian Republic.The toll was situated in the toll house that was built immediately south of the bridge at the town side. It's renewal in stone is mentioned in 1394.In 1416 the fleet of Kampen counted 120 ships; more then in all other harbours of the Northern Netherlands together.<li> As a temporary toll and as compensation for the damage suffered by neutral Kampen and Deventer ship owners and merchants during the war between the Wendish cities and the Dutch, Kampen levied the Pound toll 'Pondtol'. The levy was paid from all goods from Holland, Zeeland and West Friesland.The levy began in September or October 1439 and ended in August 1441.The complete toll register has been published in print.<li> Kampen also levied Paalgeld from at least 1334 to 1527 from ships coming from the sea. It was a levy for navigational aids placed in the Vlie between the isles of Vlieland and Terschelling to ports further south in Zuiderzee. In 1527 Amsterdam took over the levying and payed Kampen for its part of the application of the navigational aids. It is unclear whether Baakgeld, which was levied by Kampen for much the same reason, was combined with Paalgeld.<li> Another temporary toll for sailing transport is the Kampen toll on the Zwarte Water estuary. It was introduced by Kampen in 1512 as trade from Zwolle avoided the increasingly silting IJssel and sailed to the Zuiderzee via the increasingly navigable Zwarte Water. The toll was ended in 1522 after years of armed conflict between the two cities.<li> In 1292 laat de bisschop van Utrecht de tollenaar te Kampen weten dat de burgers van Utrecht daar tolvrijdom hebben. In 1328 laat de bisschop weten dat burgers van Kampen vrij van tol en weggeld zijn in Twenthe. Uit ca. 1340 dateert een (uitgegeven) tollijst van Kampen voor inwoners van Westfalen, Keulen, tussen Maas en Rijn, Oost-Friesland (uitgezonderd Staveren), Holland, de Wendische steden, Denemarken, Zweden, Noorwegen, Engeland en Vlaanderen. In 1343 liet de tollenaar te Staveren weten dat hij en zijn opvolgers geen tol zouden heffen van Kampense burgers. Uit de jaren 1439-'41 zijn registers bewaard en uitgegeven van de pondtol die te Kampen werd geheven op goederen uit Holland, Zeeland en West-Friesland. Al in de 14e eeuw onderhield Kampen de bebakening op de Zuiderzee en de vaarwegen via Vlie en Marsdiep naar de Noordzee (1323 oudste vermelding). Daartoe werd paalgeld geheven (1334 oudste vermelding). In de loop van de 15e eeuw gaat Amsterdam zich daar mee bemoeien. In 1499 wordt overeengekomen met Amsterdam dat Kampen gedurende 6 jaar 28 zeetonnen zal leggen en onderhouden, waarvoor paalgeld wordt geheven. In 1527 draagt Kampen het recht van de paalkist over aan Amsterdam. Door Amsterdam zal in Kampen een ontvanger worden aangesteld. Kamper schepen met Kamper goed blijken al in 1514 vrij van paalgeld te zijn, wat in 1527 ook nog met Amsterdam wordt overeengekomen. Rekeningen van het tol-, paal- en bakengeld te Kampen zijn bewaard vanaf 1553 (met hiaten). Een tarief uit 1561 is uitgegeven. Bestudeerd zijn de jaren 1562, 1567, 1573 en 1577. Maar dit is een IJsseltol en laat vooral Friese schippers zien die meest goederen vanuit Deventer naar Holland brachten. In 1593 blijken Amsterdam, Weesp, Muiden en Naarden daar tolvrij te zijn.
Ferry_Description: Mid 16th century there is a regular marketboat to Amsterdam with 12 or 13 caravels.
Harbour_Description: Kampen was an important harbour on the mouth of the IJssel river. The quay of the IJssel (IJsselkade, also known as the 'Welle') was the most prominent location for loading and unloading ships and boats. A crane is first mentioned in 1342 and replaced in 1475 by a new one. It was located near the Stadsbrugplein (the square near the bridge over the IJssel). The crane was demolished in 1851. Perpendicular to the quay there existed jetties. The northern part of the IJssel quay at the neighbourhood known as 'de Hagen' was used as a shipyard in the 16th century. To the north of the city there existed a harbour as well, which is mentioned in 1456 and is nowadays known as the 'Oude Buitenhaven'.

name: Brunnepe
Settlement_Description: Earliest mention in 1329, but the settlement has been inhabited before. The inhabitants of the village were scattered around several centers. The diked core of the village was called 'Oerd', 'Oord' or 'Oerde'. In 1672-73, the village was destroyed by the French army.

name: Vanhankaupunginkoski
Bridge_Description: The two bridges connecting Helsinki town and the Royal Manor to Hämeentie road and the road leading to Great Coastal Road in Malmi were built together the founding of the Manor and the town in 1550-51. In the mid 17th century the bridges were maintained by Helsinge and Siuntio parishes.

name: Schipborg
Settlement_Description: Earliest mention of 'Borc' in 1298-1304.  Earliest mention of 'Schipbork' in 1634.

name: Kranichfeld
Settlement_Description: First mentioned in 1143. The settlement was surrounded by four castles and was the centre of the lordship Kranichfeld, which was divided in two since 1172, resulting in a double governance of the settlement and frequent changes of ownership. In the 15th century it was sometimes characterised as borough ('Flecken').
Town_Description: The settlement was granted town privileges by its two owners, the lords of Schwarzburg and Mörsberg, in 1651.

name: Pyhäjoki bridge (S)
Bridge_Description: The two bridges on the Bothnian Coastal Road over Pyhäjoki river are included in an early 1650s map. The northern bridge had stone foundations already in the 17th centruy

name: Oulujoki
Ferry_Description: Oulu parish agreed in 1629 to maintain a ferry over Oulujoki river. The first brdge was built in 1866-69. The exact site of the ferry will be amended.

name: Pohjoinen
Settlement_Description: <b>Inn:</b> An inn was established in Pohjoinen in 1637, and Matti Niisiuksenpoika was appointed as the innkeeper.

name: Porras (Tuulos)
Settlement_Description: <b>Inn:</b> An inn was established in Porras in 1639, and Yrjö Laurinpoika was appointed as the innkeeper. The inn continued to operate until 1647.

name: Okerla
Settlement_Description: <b>Inn:</b> Niilo Pätiäinen was the innkeeper in Okerla village. In 1610, he received tax exemptions because his barn had burned down.

name: null
Bridge_Description: A bridge across the Eider must have existed in 1220 at the latest, as the village Brügge was named after the bridge.

name: null
Toll_Description: The regulations of safe conduct mention a bridge toll that had to be paid by wagons and cattle herders.

name: Auvaismäki
Settlement_Description: <b>Inn:</b> There has been a farm named Krouvi ("Tavern") in Auvaismäki village in the 16th c. It didn't serve as a tavern at the time nor later, so the name must refer to a medieval tavern.

name: Karkku
Settlement_Description: <b>Inn:</b> Karkku vicarage is mentioned as a place for accommodation in the travel account of Duke Johan of Finland from 1556. Karkku village is mentioned in Jaakko Teitti's list from the same year as a possible place for a bailiff (fi. vouti, sw. fogde). Karkku parish constable (fi: nimismies, sw: länsman) hosted Ture Pedersson Bielke, Swedish nobleman and castellan of St. Olaf's Castle in Savo, in his travels in 1557. In 1639, an inn was established in Rikala/Rikainen village nearby, and parish constable Sipi Eskonpoika Rikala was appointed as the innkeeper.

name: Kerälä
Settlement_Description: <b>Inn:</b> Kerälä farm served as a parish constable (fi: nimismies, sw: länsman) and a tavern for a couple of years in the turn of the 16th and 17th c.

name: Vilajoki
Settlement_Description: <b>Inn:</b> The Säkkijärvi parish constable was in Vilajoki village. It is mentioned as a place for overnight accommodation in the travel account of Duke Johan of Finland from 1555.

name: Pyterlahti
Settlement_Description: <b>Inn:</b> The Virolahti parish constable was in Pyterlahti village. It is mentioned as a place for overnight accommodation in the travel account of Duke Johan of Finland from 1555. In 1590, Virolahti parish constable was moved to another farm in the village, but the old constable continued as a tavern.

name: Reinfeld
Settlement_Description: Cistercian monastery, founded in 1186. After its abolition, a castle was built. The associated settlement developed into a borough ('flecken') around 1600.

name: Oberheldrungen
Toll_Description: The secondary station of safe conduct ('Beigeleit') in Harras is moved to Oberheldrungen in 1570.

name: null
Bridge_Description: A bridge across the Saale is first mentioned in 1445, located near the Saaltor gate. In 1547 the bridge was moved to the current position at the end of the Ludwigsstraße.

name: Blaue Warte
Settlement_Description: In 1438 archbishop Günther promises the council of Wanzleben that he will erect and man watchtowers around the town.

name: Vitsiälä
Settlement_Description: <b>Inn:</b> Parish constable (fi: nimismies, sw: länsman) Hans Kåck (Kekkonen) was appointed as the innkeeper in 1601.

name: Syrjäntaka
Settlement_Description: <b>Inn:</b> Syrjäntaka is mentioned in Jaakko Teitti's list in 1556 as a possible place for a bailiff (fi. vouti, sw. fogde).

name: Laitila (Hämeenkyrö)
Settlement_Description: <b>Inn:</b> Laitila inn was established in 1586 at the latest. Hämeenkyrö parish constable (fi: nimismies, sw: länsman) Mikko Laurinpoika Laitila ran the tavern in his farm. Laitila strait had also a bridge, which was an important hub between regions. Laitila farm served as a tavern until 1671, and after that the tavern moved to Tuokkola.

name: Tenhiälä
Settlement_Description: <b>Inn:</b> Tenhiälä had a parish constable (fi: nimismies, sw: länsman), who ran a tavern in his farm Seppälä in the late 16th c. to early 17th c.

name: Friedrichstadt
Town_Description: Friedrichstadt was founded by duke Friedrich III of Holstein-Gottorf to attract religious Dutch refugees (Remonstrants) with religious freedom and economic privileges. First negotiations took place in 1619, and actual building activities started in September 1621. A town law was constituted in 1631. Despite initial economic success, the town remained insignificant.
Fair_Description: In a charter from 1620, the future town Friedrichstadt was granted the right to hold two annual fairs, horse and cattle markets and a weekly market.
Toll_Description: A note about town finances from 1633 mentions a road toll.

name: Virojoki (Virolahti)
Settlement_Description: <b>Post house:</b> In 1638, the Royal Steward Bernhardt Steen von Steenhausen established a post house in the village of Virojoki in Virolahti.

name: null
Toll_Description: The ferry toll was moved from Süderstapel to Friedrichstadt in 1635.
Ferry_Description: A ferry to Dithmarschen appears in a note about town finances from 1633.
Harbour_Description: Sea harbour on the Eider river south of the sluices.

name: null
Bridge_Description: A bridge across two arms of the Leine river, consisting of a "short" and a "long" bridge, is first mentioned in 1445. Before, there existed a ford here.

name: Tuovila
Settlement_Description: <b>Inn:</b> Tuovila village had an inn in the 17th c. In 1633, an inn was established also in the nearby Helsingby village, and Jöns Klemetsson was appointed as the innkeeper.

name: Bierkade
Harbour_Description: The canal Bierkade was dug in the 1610s as part of the defensive canal around the village. A crane was located here at the end of the Kranestraat.

name: Tervajoki
Settlement_Description: <b>Inn:</b> Tervajoki is mentioned as a place for overnight accommodation in the travel account of Duke Johan of Finland from 1555.

name: Pernaja
Settlement_Description: <b>Inn:</b> There has probably been an alehouse already in the 14th century near the medieval church in Pernaja, but the first alehouse is mentioned in 1543. It was run by Matts Buske, who is also known as parish constable, still in office in 1564. In 1556, also Mårten (Jopsson?) run an alehouse in the church village. In 1578, parish constable Mårten Larsson served food and drink to 43 sailors on their way to Russia. In 1610, Evert Horn stayed at Pernaja vicarage while some of his men were accommodated at the parish constable's farm. Mats Sigfridsson was appointed as tavern keeper in Pernaja church village in 1621. In 1640, Clas Baij had an alehouse in the church village.

name: Moritzberg
Settlement_Description: A chapel was founded in 1025 and devoted to St Maurice in 1028; connected to it was a nunnery, which was turned into a collegiate church with 16 canons in 1068. Around the monastery a settlement developed in the 11th century. It developed into a borough ('flecken') in the 15th century.

name: Siechenhof (Mühlhausen)
Settlement_Description: The infirmary near the Lengenfeld watchtower is already mentioned in 1283. It is still mentioned in the descirption of the proper road of safe conduct from 1609. In 1802 it is referred to as a popular resting station for wagoners.

name: Heilig-Geist-Spital Eisleben
Settlement_Description: The infirmary of the Holy Ghost is attested since 1373, but was probably founded in the 13th century.
Bridge_Description: A letter from 1594 mentiones a bridge near the infirmary.

name: Henne (Naumburg)
Ferry_Description: According to Sixtus Braun and his town history of Naumburg, the council of Naumburg already owned the ferry in 1354. It was officially given to it by the cathedral chapter (of St. Peter and Paul in Naumburg) in 1447. The ferry to Halle ('Hallesche Fähre') in Naumburg was situated at the inn "Zur Henne", which is first mentioned in 1800.

name: Auf den Steinen
Toll_Description: A land toll of the duke of Berg at "auf den Steinen", levied on the ferry traffic, is first attested in 1393.
Ferry_Description: A Rhine ferry between Düsseldorf and Neuss at Hamm is first mentioned in 1262. On the Hamm side, it was located at "auf den Steinen" (on the stones).

name: Hohenschemsbrücke
Bridge_Description: Bridge across the Werse, first mentioned in 1280.

name: Sudenburg
Settlement_Description: A suburb south of Magdeburg is first mentioned in 965, it was closely connected to the cathedral immunity. A parish church of Sudenburg is first mentioned in 1288. A Carmelite monastery was founded in 1338.
Town_Description: Sudenburg acquired town privileges in 1368 and was a distinct town from Magdeburg, although it remained small in comparison to the old town and new town of Magdeburg. According to early modern views of town and the town seal, it was fortified with walls. Partially destroyed during sieges of Magdeburg in 1551 and 1631, it was completely demolished during modernisations of Magdeburg's fortifications in 1812. A new settlement Katharinenstadt or Neu-Sudenburg was constructed along the road towards Halberstadt.

name: Hees
Settlement_Description: Earliest mention in 1196 in relation to the foundation of St Jans Hospital. A wooden chapel, belonging to St Stephen's Church (Stevenskerk) in Nijmegen, already existed around 800. Around 1250, a chapel of stone was built on the current location of the Church of St Peter (Petruskerk, Schependomlaan 85), which was replaced by a new one around 1430, and by a church around 1550.

name: null
Harbour_Description: The river Oste was navigable for larger ships until Bremervörde, although due to shallow waters near Bremervörde, some cargoes had to be transshipped onto smaller vessels at landing places downstream before being transported to Bremervörde.

name: Løvel Bro
Toll_Description: In the late medieval period and early modern era, and probably earlier, a fee (Danish: bropenge/brokorn) was paid to cross the bridge. In 1560 the king granted the toll to the nobleman Laurits Skram of Hastrup. After his dead in 1587 the income from the bridge was granted Henrik Below of Spøttrup.
Bridge_Description: A medieval stone bridge, or perhaps several bridges, across the river of Skalks Å from the 13th century onwards. Archeological excavations during the 20th century revealed an advanced construction as well as a stone from with a medieval inscription. According to the inscription the stone bridge was built by king Eric, probably king Eric Plovpenning (1241-1250). Another possibility is that the bridge was built during the reign of king Eric Glipping (1259-1286). The bridge was first mentioned in 1454. In 1627 and 1628 the bridge was repaired, only to be completely destroyed during the Dano-Swedish wars in the late 1650ties. Throughout the late medieval period and early modern era the bridge played a key role in the export of oxen from northern parts of Jutland.

name: Sundhausen
Settlement_Description: First mention in 775/786 in the Breviarium sancti Lullii of Hersfeld monastery (Tab. I).

name: null
Bridge_Description: A water mill at the river Neetze is first mentioned in 1314. At this time at the latest, a bridge and causeway must have existed as well. Before there was a ford.

name: Lübscherbaum
Settlement_Description: Boom barrier in the defensive enclosure ('landwehr') of Hamburg on the road to Lübeck, first mentioned in the 15th century.

name: Schlagd
Harbour_Description: The river harbour of Kassel was located at the Schlagd, the shore of the Fulda near the old market place. In the 1570s, storage houses were built here.

name: null
Bridge_Description: Bridges across the Haune and Fulda  are mentioned in 1310 and 1368.
Harbour_Description: Around 1600, landgrave Moritz of Hesse-Kassel launched construction works to make the Fulda river navigable between Kassel and Hersfeld, which was realised in 1601. Later ordinances secured the navigability.

name: null
Bridge_Description: A wooden bridge across the Werra existed from the 13th century. It was replaced by a stone bridge in 1606.

name: null
Bridge_Description: A bridge across the Werra is first mentioned in 1326. According to an engraving of Merian from 1655, it consisted of three stone arched bridges across three arms of the river.

name: Schweinitz (Jessen)
Settlement_Description: First mention in 1182. Originally a Slavic settlement; in the 12th century there existed a castle, next to which a settlement developed.
Fair_Description: In 1484 a fair and a weekly market are granted.
Toll_Description: Tables of fees ('Geleitstafeln') remain from 1510 and 1531/32.

name: Paulusbroedersluis
Bridge_Description: A stone bridge at the Oudezijds Achterburgwal is shown on the city map by Cornelis Anthonisz from 1544. It was (re-)built in stone in the early 16th century as part of a campaign to improve the east-west connection within the city.

name: Tenhola
Settlement_Description: <b>Inn:</b> According to the alehouse taxation list from 1556, there was one alehouse in Tenhola. No exact location is known. It could be the church alehouse, which is mentioned in the 17th c., but it was popular to sell drinks near the church already earlier. Also Tenhola vicarage served travellers by the road: in 1577, vicar Thomas Laurentii complained how he lives next to a busy road and is obliged to serve food, drinks and lodging to soldiers and other travellers. Also the Tenhola villagers complained in 1573 that the king's and noblemen's servants and soldiers burden them with transportation and accommodation. Those living by the road received tax exemptions for their troubles.

name: Näse (Perniö)
Settlement_Description:
Permanent agricultural settlement in Perniö (sw. Bjärnå) dates to the Iron Age. Independent parish was established in the early 13th century and is mentioned in 1350. The earliest church was veryt likely located in Yliskylä, whereas the site of the later church along the Great Coastal Road dates to the early 14th century. The stone church was built between 1460 and 1480.
<b>Näse Royal Manor</b> (r. Näse kungsgård): King Gustav I relocated the older medieval manor in Vanhakartano (sw. Helgå) to Muntolannokka at the confluence of the Perniö and Kisko rivers in 1556. The manor came into possession of the nobility in 1640 and was moved to its later location near Latokartano in 1690. The route of the Great Coastal Road passed through the Näse and Vanhakartano area until the first quarter of the 17th century, when a new section of the road was built from Pakapyöli to Perniö Maansilta bridge.
Fair_Description: The earliest record of the Perniö Laurentius (10 August) fair is from 1599, but since Apostle Laurentius is cited as the patron saint of Perniö stone church built in 1460–80 it is of medieval origin. The fair site was located between Näse manor and the Perniö river at the latest in the 1550s, in the Middle Ages possibly in Vanhakartano area. In 1647, the fair site was downstream from Näse on Broända farm’s land. The Perniö fair was one of the four fairs in Finland proper (Männäinen, Mynämäki, Salo, and Perniö) regularly visited by the burghers of Turku in the 17th century. Local fair was held in Perniö in the 18th century also on Michaelmas (29 September).
Toll_Description: The 1/32 duty worth of all goods intended for sale in towns and fairs and brought to the site by peasants was collected in Perniö fair since 1622.

name: Deetzer Warthe
Settlement_Description: The defensive trench ('Landwehr') of Deetz was already mentioned in 1238. A watchtower was erected in 1409. Since 1703 an inn existed, from which toll was collected at least since 1745.

name: null
Bridge_Description: The bridge across the Hörsel near Eisenach was probably constructed during the 12th century.

name: Oderbrück
Bridge_Description: A bridge across the Oder is first displayed on a map of the Harz area from 1530.

name: Hubeturm
Settlement_Description: Watchtower in the defensive enclosure ('landwehr') of Einbeck, first mentioned in 1436. It was demolished in 1800.

name: Wiebrechtshauser Turm
Settlement_Description: Watchtower in the defensive enclosure ('landwehr') of Northeim, built around 1400. It was demolished in 1829.

name: Barnum
Toll_Description: In 1277, Wesel was exempted from payment of the toll on river traffic in Barnum, which was levied by the duke of Cleves.

name: null
Harbour_Description: Haltern was transit point for many commodities between Münsterland and the Rhine river system. A harbour crane is attested in 1597.

name: Haus Ostendorf
Toll_Description: Toll on river traffic of the lords of Ostendorf as vassals of the bishop of Münster. Since 1494 in possession of the lords of Raesfeld. There are many records of attacks on skippers from Wesel here.

name: Haus Vogelsang
Toll_Description: Toll on the Lippe river at the house Vogelsang, which was only levied on ships that moored there.

name: Varkenssluis
Bridge_Description: The wooden bridge called Peter Jacobssoensbrugge is first mentioned in 1432. In the beginning of the 16th century it was rebuilt in stone as part of a campaign to improve the east-west traffic axis through the city.

name: Maye
Ferry_Description: Ferries in Dreischor are first mentioned in 1343/44. A ferry to Dirksland in Overflakkee is first mentioned in 1431-42. From 1470/71 the ferries to Duiveland and Overflakkee are mentioned to depart from a place called Maye; the Overflakkee ferrymen were sailing to Herkingen and/or Oude-Tonge.

name: Simpelveld
Settlement_Description: Earliest mention in 1155, in a thirteenth century copy.

name: Nousiainen
Settlement_Description:
One of the most important pilgrimage routes in medieval Finland was St Henrik’s path (fi. Sant Henrikintie), which led from Nousiainen Church to Köyliö since the early 14th century and may have followed an older 12th century wintertime route from Nousiainen and Mynämäki region to Yläne, Köyliö and Kokemäki areas. Since the route was not a common road maintained by peasants, but a pilgrimage path used in the summer, the route has not been included in Viabundus database. St Herik’s path led from Nousiainen Church to Haanoja in Mynämäki, from where it branched off so that the main route led parallel to the Raasinjoki River to Yläne Church and further alongside Lake Pyhäjärvi to Köyliö.

<b>Inn:</b> Nousiainen church tavern for pilgrims ("kirke herbergh"), where one could get food, drink, and lodging, is mentioned in 1459. Churches usually had alehouses also in the following centuries.

name: Heenvliet
Settlement_Description: Heenvliet is first mentioned in a fourteenth-century copy of a 1254 text.
Town_Description: In 1388 Heenvliet obtained toll-exemption from the count of Holland. Heenvliet was granted town rights on 20 March 1469 by Adriaan, lord of Cruyningen, of Heenvliet and of Woensdrecht. However, Heenvliet never really developed into a town.
Fair_Description: In 1469 the lord of Heenvliet, burgrave of Zeeland, granted a town-right togeter with a weekly-market and fair.
Ferry_Description: A ferry to Geervliet, at the opposite bank of the river Bernisse, is first mentioned in 1379.
Harbour_Description: In 1584 the lord of the town ordained an excise to be levied from each animal sold on the fair to finance the maintenance of the harbour.

name: Taivassalo
Settlement_Description: <b>Inn:</b> Farmer Airich Krovi is mentioned in Taivassalo in 1556. There is no exact location for his tavern, but it could be located by the church. Churches usually had taverns in the Middle Ages and 16th-17th-centuries.

name: Kvis (Kirkkonummi)
Settlement_Description: <b>Post house:</b> In 1638, the Royal Steward Bernhardt Steen von Steenhausen established a post house in the village of Kvis in Kirkkonummi. According to research literature, the post boy from Kvis also transported mail along a side route to Porkkala and received an additional tax relief of 6 thalers for his duties.

name: null
Ferry_Description: A ferry across the Gouwe between the islands Schouwen and Duiveland is first mentioned in 1313. The "Gouweveer" to Zierikzee, belonging to Capelle, is first mentioned in 1469. Ferry services stopped when a dam was built between Schouwen and Duiveland in 1610.

name: Koliseva
Settlement_Description: <b>Inn:</b> An inn was established in Koliseva during the 17th century at the latest.

name: Vianen (Duiveland)
Ferry_Description: A ferry between St. Maartensdijk and the island Duiveland is first mentioned in 1360, a ferry to Stavenisse in 1376. Sandberg assumes that the landing place in Duiveland was Vianen. Ferries from Vianen in the ambacht Ouwerkerk to the island Tholen are also mentioned in the 16th century. The ferry to Stavenisse was not in use in 1509-1599 because Stavenisse was flooded, and is first mentioned again in 1603.

name: null
Ferry_Description: A ferry from Stavenisse to Duiveland and Zierikzee is first mentioned in 1376. The ferry ceased to exist in 1509, when the island of Stavenisse was flooded. After renewed land reclamation in 1599, a ferry between Stavenisse and Vianen in Duiveland is mentioned again in 1603.

name: null
Ferry_Description: A ferry between the polders Oud- and Nieuw-Vossemeer was created directly after the reclamation of the latter polder in 1567.

name: null
Ferry_Description: A ferry between the polders Oud- and Nieuw-Vossemeer was created directly after the reclamation of the latter polder in 1567.

name: Sint Annaland
Settlement_Description: The polder with the same name was reclaimed from the sea in 1476; the settlement is first mentioned in 1493.

name: Botshoofd
Toll_Description: A special dam toll was levied next to the ferry fee for the construction and maintenance of the ferry dams (constructed in ca. 1500). Inhabitants of Vossemeer were exempted from the toll, but were obliged to maintain the dams on both sides. Later the dam toll was integrated into the ferry tariff.
Ferry_Description: A ferry across the Eendracht between "an die Hicke" and "Kijckuut" is first leased in 1494. In the 16th century, Botshoofd became the place of departure. Ferry services stopped in 1886.

name: null
Ferry_Description: A ferry across the Eendracht between "an die Hicke" and "Kijckuut" is first leased in 1494. Ferry services stopped in 1886.

name: Yerseke
Settlement_Description: The earliest mention from 966 was recorded around 1000, handed down in a 15th-century copy. Next mention in 980, also in a 15th-century copy.

name: Hansweert
Ferry_Description: A ferry to Flanders from Hansweert is mentioned in 1521, but must have been older. In 1591, Kalfsteert is mentioned as destination, but the latter place was flooded around 1600. The ferry was moved to Walsoorden-Waarde; from the 18th century, it sailed to Hansweert again.

name: Veikars
Settlement_Description: <b>Inn:</b> Ture Pedersson Bielke, Swedish nobleman and castellan of St. Olaf's Castle in Savo, stopped to change horses in Veikars in 1557. An inn was likely established already in 1574, at the latest in 1633, when Simon Hendersson Pörn was appointed as the innkeeper.

name: Ammerbrücke
Bridge_Description: A bridge across the Unstrut at this site was probably built in the 13th century.

name: null
Toll_Description: A transit toll in Wesel is first mentioned in 1188/1193 in complaints from the monastery Cappenberg that its exemption from the toll in Wesel was being disregarded, upon which the count of Cleves forbade the levying of toll on ships and wagons from Cappenberg. Later sources indicate that the toll was only levied on the transshipment ("upslach") of cargoes between ships and land vehicles. In the 16th century, this was only applied on commodities that left the town after having been transshipped. Wesel citizens were exempted from toll payments. Despite protests from the town, the duke of Cleves enforced the levying of the toll on commodities that stayed in Wesel in the 1580s as well; a new toll regulation from 1586 only mentions commodities which were transported further on the land route, however.
Harbour_Description: Wesel was an important transshipment point on the Rhine and Lippe rivers. Harbour infrastructure is attested from 1355, when a crane was brought from Neuss to Wesel. A harbour basin was built in an old Lippe arm in 1525, but had silted up again by 1600. A crane ship to facilitate loading and unloading of ships on the waterfront of the Rhine was built in 1524, but burnt down in 1535. A new crane from 1537 was destroyed by Spanish troops in 1588. It was rebuilt in 1590/91. A register of crane fees is extant for 1623.

name: Schakerloo
Ferry_Description: A ferry from the district ('ambacht') Schakerloo to Reimerswaal is first mentioned in 1371. It was eternally pawned to the town Tholen in 1462, but disappeared with the abandonment of Reimerswaal in 1631.

name: Walsoorden
Ferry_Description: After Kalfsteert had disappeared in the water around 1600, the ferry to Zuid-Beveland was moved to Walsoorden, where it is first mentioned in 1640. The ferry was pawned in 1646, when it sailed to Waarde. From the 18th century, it sailed to Hansweert.

name: Breskens
Settlement_Description: In 1487, Philip of Cleves, Lord of Ravestein, was granted the privilege to reclaim the mud-flats Breskenszand from the sea. The project was only executed in 1510, and the polder became a privileged lordschip ('heerlijkheid'). It was inundated in 1583, but reclaimed in 1610.
Ferry_Description: In the 18th century, the ferry of Vlissingen sailed to Breskens. A precise destination for the ferry from Vlissingen to Flanders, which existed since ca. 1300, is not mentioned earlier. Probably the settlement known as Ter Ouder Vere / Ten Oerde / Nieuwerhaven was the destination of the ferry before it drowned in 1583. Afterwards the ferry was probably moved to Breskesn, as is assumed by Horsten.

name: Varrelgraben
Settlement_Description: Settlement at the stream Varrelgraben on the border between Bremen and Delmenhorst territory, first mentioned in 1338. It often functioned as a meeting place for negotiations between Bremen and Oldenburg.
Bridge_Description: A bridge across the Varrelgraben must have been built at the latest around 1311, when Bremen and the count of Delmenhorst agreed that the road between Delmenhorst and Bremen was to be maintained for traffic.

name: Limmen
Settlement_Description: First mentioned in 918-948, in an 11th-century copy.

name: Krommenie
Settlement_Description: First mentioned in 1317. The name is derived from the water Krommenie, which is first mentioned in 1276. In 1398 it obtained together with West-Zaanden (Zaandam) toll-exemption from the count of Holland.

name: Molletjesveer
Ferry_Description: A ferry crossing at this point became required after the canal Nauernasche Vaart was dug. The licence for the ferry was granted in 1634.

name: Etelänkylä
Settlement_Description: <b>Inn:</b> The inn in Kalajoki parish village moved to Etelänkylä in 1644 at the latest, where it was hosted by the assistant vicar Joosef Matinpoika, head of Heusala farm.

name: Urjala
Settlement_Description: <b>Inn:</b> Count Per Brahe the Younger, Governor-General of Finland, stopped by Urjala parish constable (fi: nimismies, sw: länsman) farm in Kankaanpää village when returning to Turku in winter 1639-40.

name: Aardenburg
Settlement_Description: In 170, a Roman castellum was situated at the site of the modern-day town of Aardenburg. The first mention in written records dates from 966.
Town_Description: In the 11th and 12th century, Aardenburg developed into a town. It was granted town privileges before 1187 by Philip of Alsace, count of Flanders. The charter has not survived, but the privileges were renewed in 1330. By 1299, Aardenburg had an earth wall, a moat and four town gates. It was a significant trading and cloth manufacturing centre, but the town lost its economic significance and urban character from the 14th century onwards. The walls and gates were removed in 1581 and the countryside flooded in 1583 during the Dutch revolt. The town was reconstructed as a fortress in 1620-1625.

name: null
Harbour_Description: The Oker river was made navigable between Schladen and Wolfenbüttel in 1575, and between Schladen and Oker in 1577.

name: null
Settlement_Description: Based on archaeological evidence, an inn may be located just outside the core of Hees and about a thirty minutes' walk from Nijmegen, along the 'Hooge Weg', the road between Nijmegen and Wijchen. It existed from the end of the fourteenth century until it probably burned down around the middle of the fifteenth century - possibly during the siege of Nijmegen in 1473.

name: null
Ferry_Description: The ferry between Nijmegen and Lent has existed from at least the beginning of the eight century onward. Originally, it was owned by the land lord. During the Middle Ages, it was owned by a partnership of ecclesiastical and secular lords, among which the provisors of the Holy Spirit. In 1592, the town council of Nijmegen became the ferry's owner. The ferry was leased out to multiple leaseholders. Due to war, the ferry's exploitation was very limited between 1585 and 1591. In 1657, the ferry was replaced by a cable ferry, invented, and exploited as well, by Hendrick Heuck. In 1563, the ferrymen and town council of Nijmegen complain about multiple illegal ferry activities upstream near Ooij, and downstream near Oosterhout.

name: null
Toll_Description: <ul><li>The Imperial toll “Rijkstol”, after 1560 called “Stads Rijkse tol” = (Imperial toll of the town), for sailing transport on the Waal river at Nijmegen is first mentioned in 1145. It will have been founded between 1112 and 1145. From 1228/29 to 1356, the Count of Cleves was the owner of the toll. He moved it to Griethausen in 1356 as a Cleves toll. From1357, the Imperial toll was levied by the Duke of Guelders. In the first half of the 15th century partially and from 1498 completely, the toll was pawned (but de facto owned, by) to the city of Nijmegen, who kept it until its abolition in 1810. No tariffs are known from the years before 1357. In 1357, 6 turnosgroschen had to be paid. More detailed lists of tariffs date from the first half of the 16th century. Toll-accounts for the years 1388-'99 have been analysed by Weststrate (in particular for wine). A survey of toll-exemptions is published. A graph of the 'Rijkstol' (1510-1650) is published. Yields of the 'Rijkstol' are edited for the years 1550-1600. Toll administration is available for the years 1583, 1624-1625, 1630-1656, 1678-1703, 1729-1730, 1731-1732, 1747-1748, 1763-1764, 1803-1808.Regionaal Archief Nijmegen: 1 Stadsbestuur Nijmegen 1196 – 1810, Inv. No. 1931-1948</li><li>The second toll is the Great Guelders toll of Nijmegen. The Duke of Gelre founded it in 1492, just like the tolls in Arnhem and Zutphen, as the continuation of the Lobith toll that was seized by the Clevish in 1479. Until the Habsburg take over in Gelre in 1543 the toll was usually referred to as “Lobith toll”. Afterwards it was the Great Guelders toll of Nijmegen. From 1585-1591, because of the Spanish occupation of Nijmegen, the toll was levied at ‘s Gravenweerd, an isle in river Rhine at the bifurcation of the river Rhine into the branches Nederrijn and Waal. The toll was abolished in 1810 and replaced by de Droit de navigation. Toll administration is available for the years 1543-1579, 1591-92, 1598-1606, 1625-1629, 1636-1641, 1648-49, 1655-56, 1658-1672, 1674-1679, 1688/90, 1702/03, 1739-1741. Gelders Archief 0012   Gelderse Rekenkamer, Inv. No. 2416 – 2490.</li> Yields of the toll and the number of passing ships up- and downstream are edited for the years 1543-'57.<li>The third toll of Nijmegen are the Market tolls. They were founded before 1317According to a 18th century source the first Market toll was levied from 29th of April to 19th of May inclusive and the second one from 29th of September (Michaelis) to 19th of October inclusive, so both during 21 days. The tariff was one third of the normal tariff of the Great Guelders toll of Nijmegen. This toll also was abolished in 1810.Toll administration is available for the years 1621-1624, 1636-1640, 1658-1675, 1675 – 1678.Gelders Archief 0012   Gelderse Rekenkamer, Inv. No. 2491 - 2494.</li> </ul>
Ferry_Description: See harbour and ferry in Lent
Harbour_Description: A wharf with a crane was situated just outside the town gate called 'Kraanpoort', at the end of the main street from the river Waal into town, the 'Grotestraat'. The Grotestraat is one of the oldest streets of the town. Archeological research shows the presence of a wharf or harbour in the tenth and eleventh century. In 1420, the wharf was extended from 170 to 400 metre. The 'Kraanpoort' gate is first mentioned in 1382, just as the crane. The ferry bridge was located near the 'Kraanpoort' as well. Before 1422, the ferry bridge was probably located a little more eastward. Graphs of the farming out of the crane (1510-1595), the ferry (1595-1650) and the harbour (1605-'40) is edited. A small harbour was located west of the town, perpendicular to the river Waal, between the river and the town gate called 'Hezelpoort'. Between 1601 and 1604, this harbour was moved and enlarged inside the town walls, parallel to the river Waal.The skipper owed a levy for use of the harbour in favour of the town of Nijmegen.

name: Jääsken lautta
Ferry_Description: The ferry site at Jääski church over Vuoksi river is first cited in 1626 together with another ferry downstream in Kuukauppi. A third ferry over Vuoksi is cited 1638 in Siitola. The oldest of the three ferry sites was Kuukauppi, which was maintained by the whole Jääski judicial district and located on an important common road between Viipuri and Saviniemi Royal Manor. Annual tax collected from Jääski judicial district for the Vuoksi ferryman is cited in 1565–66 and 1580. Two ferrymen are known from Jääski parish village: Lautturi-Matti (Matti the ferryman) in 1635 and Lautturi-Mikko in 1642-1646.

name: null
Bridge_Description: Originally the narrow part of the fjord could be crossed by a ford. A bridge across the fjord was first mentioned in 1413, but is probably from the 14th century, maybe the 13th century. A bridge is also shown on the medieval municipal seal. A bridge in the town center is shown on a map of the town in Erik Pontoppidan’s Danske Atlas from the 1760s. Most like this was also the location of the medieval bridge.
Ferry_Description: Presumably relatively stable ferry routes connecting Zealand with the islands of Funen and Langeland departed from Skælskør. The ferry to Funen from Skælskør was not as popular as the route departing from Korsør.
Harbour_Description: The character of the medieval harbour is uncertain. But the narrow part of the fjord was a good natural harbour. According to a map of the town in Erik Pontoppidan’s Danske Atlas from the 1760s the town bridge also functioned as a pier. Perhaps this was also the case in the Middle Ages. German ships frequently used the harbour.

name: null
Ferry_Description: A "new" ferry across the Oste in Geversdorf is first mentioned in 1423. It connected Geversdorf with Itzwörden.

name: null
Toll_Description: Onezhitsy was toll station for boats sailing into Swedish territory on the Luga river.
Harbour_Description: A document from 1633 suggests, that Onezhitsy was a harbour where commodities had to be transshipped from smaller to larger vessels.

name: Tannroda
Settlement_Description: First mention in 1115. The castle around which the village developed was probably built in the 12th century. The settlement is mentioned as town in 1403 and as borough ('Flecken') in the 16th century. The council only held administrative privileges, no jurisdiction.

name: null
Harbour_Description: Duke Albrecht granted the construction of a harbour in 1403 'uyter zee inder meente' (in the Zuiderzee with a connection to the town). Via the Karnemelksloot there was a connection with the river Vecht. In 1533 emperor Charles V granted the construction of a harbour mouth.

name: Nieuwe Brug
Bridge_Description: The "new bridge" across the harbour was built in the late 14th century. In the 16th century it was partly built in stone, but had wooden movable parts to let ships pass.

name: Bushuissluis
Bridge_Description: A wooden draw bridge was built as part of the first extension ('eerste uitleg') of the city in 1585.

name: Zeeland
Settlement_Description: Earliest mention in 1376, in a copy dating from 1677.

name: Bevern (Bremervörde)
Settlement_Description: Bevern was first mentioned as a farm of the monastery Heeslingen in 986. Around 1500, ten farms and seven cottages in the village belonged to the monastery Zeven. One remaining farm was acquired by the monastery later as well.
Fair_Description: A fair on Ascension day took place in Bevern before 1582, when it was moved to Bremervörde.

name: Hezelpoort
Harbour_Description: A small harbour was located between the river Waal and the town gate named Hezelpoort. Between 1601 and 1604, this harbour was moved and enlarged inside the town walls, parallel to the river Waal.

name: Schloß Broich
Toll_Description: The settlement of Broich itself probably had a land toll, which is documented in 1250. This was probably levied by the Lord of Broich. Tariffs and revenues are not known. It is possible that it was a land toll at the Ruhr crossing, but its existence after 1250 can no longer be proven. It was not until the 18th century that a land toll was again established in Broich.

name: Hirvikoski
Settlement_Description: <b>Inn:</b> An inn was established in Hirvikoski in 1642, and Jaakko Jaakonpoika Knuutila was appointed as the innkeeper. The inn was located by the winter road.

name: Landsberg
Settlement_Description: First mentioned as "civitas holm" in 961 in a donation charter of Otto I to the monastery of St Maurice in Magdeburg. A castle was built in 1170-1186, alongside which a small settlement developed.
Town_Description: In 1442 the settlement is referred to as town.
Fair_Description: In the years 1604-1612, Leipzig objected to the foundation of a new fair in Landsberg, which would conflict with the staple privileges of Leipzig. Eventually Leipzig agreed to the existence of the fair, under condition that the fairs and staple of Leipzig would be respected.
Toll_Description: Secondary station of safe conduct of Delitzsch, as mentioned in the regulations of safe conduct from the 16th century, in which the tariffs for wagons and horses are also recorded.

name: null
Bridge_Description: A bridge across the Meuse is first mentioned in 1106, when a battle took place here.

name: Säivi
Settlement_Description: <b>Inn:</b> An inn was established in Säivi in the 1640s.

name: null
Toll_Description: The archbishop of Magdeburg levied a toll on the use of the ship alley ('flutrinne'), which is mentioned in 1364.
Lock_Description: The mill weir in Calbe provided an obstacle for ships. For this reason, a narrow channel ('schiffsgasse', 'flutrinne'), possibly with a flash lock, was constructed to circumvent the weir. It is first mentioned in 1150. A mention of wooden locks from 1366 probably also refers to this channel rather than an actual lock. A pound lock was only built in 1564, facilitating river traffic.

name: null
Toll_Description: The toll in Lenzen was - at least from 1558 onwards - also levied on traffic on the Elbe river. According to 18th-century maps, the toll house was located on an old river arm. For more details, see Lenzen.

name: null
Harbour_Description: Geesthacht was a harbour for produce of the Vierlanden, as well as wood from the Sachsenwald.

name: null
Lock_Description: A pound lock in Bernburg was built in 1560. Possibly, there existed a shipping canal with a flash lock ('flutrinne') to circumvent the mill weir (first mentioned in 1219) here before.

name: null
Lock_Description: The pound lock in Alsleben was probably built around 1560.

name: Süderstapel
Toll_Description: Toll of the dukes of Schleswig-Gottorf on the Eider river, originally levied in Tielen, but moved to Süderstapel in 1594. Detailed toll tariffs exist for the years 1614 and 1632. Toll registers from the 17th century show that predominantly grain and wood was shipped on the river.

name: null
Bridge_Description: A bridge across the Eider river was already part of the castle when it was constructed around 1150, and is often mentioned in sources from the second half of the 12th century. A bridge is still depicted on the view of the town by Braun and Hogenberg from 1584, but around 1600 it was replaced by a causeway with a lock.
Harbour_Description: After the construction of a causeway in front of the castle around 1600, commodities transported on the Eider river were forced to be transshipped in Rendsburg.

name: Mooksche veer
Ferry_Description: Ferry in use well before 1557. Around 1598, the ferry was temporarily out of use.

name: null
Bridge_Description: In 1450, a copper (?) bear is cast for the construction of the bridge across the Mulde. In a depiction of Eilenburg of 1550, the bridge is shown as a bridge on poles ('Pfahlbrücke').

name: null
Toll_Description: With the construction of the lock, the town Rathenow lost the fee on the use of the town canal, but shared a new lock toll with the Elector Joachim II. A shipping toll is first mentioned in 1559.
Lock_Description: A round lock was constructed between 1548 and 1559 outside the town of Rathenow. It was replaced by a pound lock in 1610-1741.

name: null
Bridge_Description: The Stresow bridge is mentioned in 1433.

name: Mühlendamm
Bridge_Description: Bridge at a former ford, which formed the earliest connection between the twin towns Berlin and Cölln. Water mills are first attested in 1285, a mill weir ("Mühlendamm") in 1298. It provided an obstacle for ships.

name: null
Bridge_Description: The construction of the "long" bridge (today the Rathausbrücke) began in the 13th century. It was the second-oldest Spree crossing between Berlin and Cölln.
Harbour_Description: Berlin was an important transshipment harbour, where predominantly wood and corn from Brandenburg were loaded onto vessels that could sail via the Spree, Havel and Elbe rivers to Hamburg.

name: null
Toll_Description: At places along the Havel and Spree in which locks had been constructed, a lock toll was collected for the maintenance of the locks. However, they were as high as other tolls which generated purely financial income.
Lock_Description: The mill weir ('Mühlendamm') between Berlin and Cölln provided an obstacle for ships. A flash lock circumventing the obstacle is first mentioned in 1432. It was probably located near the later Stadtschleuse, in the canal surrounding the town of Cölln. Later a pound lock was built, first mentioned in 1578, but a predecessor was probably built around 1550.

name: Berltsum
Settlement_Description: Berlikum is known to have existed around 900, located near the Middelzee (a former estuary of the Wadden sea).
Town_Description: Berlikum is first mentioned as a town in 1355 and is known to have had city-like features in the fourteenth-century.

name: Stroka
Settlement_Description: <b>Inn:</b> An inn was established in Stroka in 1641, and Simo Vilpunpoika Stroka was appointed as the innkeeper. Stroka farm was on the other side of the Lapuanjoki river, so it might have served primarily waterway travellers. In 1663, officials in stated that only the inns in Härsilä, Stroka and Ylijepua are needed in Lapua area, and tried to close the inns in Kuhalammi, Toppari, Hemminki and Ylinurmo. It was thought that their owners had established inns only to receive tax exemptions and freedom from military service.

name: Ylijepua
Settlement_Description: <b>Inn:</b> An inn was established in Ylijepua in 1646, and Erkki Simonpoika Grötas was appointed as the innkeeper.

name: Kuivaniemi
Settlement_Description: <b>Inn:</b> Kuivaniemi village had a transport organiser (fi. kyytirättäri, sw. skjutsrättare) serving Ii parish constable. An inn was established in 1640s at the latest.

name: Vuono
Settlement_Description: <b>Inn:</b> An inn was established in Vuono in the 1640s.

name: Simo
Settlement_Description: <b>Inn:</b> Simo village had a transport organiser (fi. kyytirättäri, sw. skjutsrättare) serving Ii parish constable. In 1560 and 1573, local farmers were fined for hitting the transport organiser. In 1573, he was Antti Ruikka. An inn was established in 1640s at the latest, and Ruikka farm served as an inn until the end of the century.

name: Uikhoven
Settlement_Description: The settlement is first mentioned in 1298.
Toll_Description: A toll in 'Uyckhoven' is one of the six small tolls of Maastricht in 1357, when these were enfeoffed by the duke and duchess of Limburg to Thierri de Hornes, lord of Perwez. The toll in 'Oudichoven' is mentioned in 1362 when the steward of the duke of Brabant leased out seven tolls on the river Meuse. According to Slanghen, however, this toll was domanial property of the lord of Valkenburg, together with the toll levied in Geulle.

name: Heimburg
Settlement_Description: Emperor Henry IV founded the castle Heimburg around 1070, together with Harzburg castle. Property of the lords of Heimburg in the 12th century, then the lords of Blankenburg-Regenstein in the last third of the 13th century, until only a steward resides on the castle since 1344. Beneath the castle the settlement of Heimburg develops, which is referred to as borough ('Fleck') in 1434.
Toll_Description: In a pawn charter of 1434 the toll in Heimburg is mentioned.

name: null
Harbour_Description: Before ca. 1200, Bevensen seems to have been an important trading site at the Ilmenau river. Afterwards, the Ilmenau was used upstream from Lüneburg until Bevensen, occasionally also until Uelzen, mostly for the transport of firewood for the Lüneburg saltworks.

name: Simoniemi
Settlement_Description: <b>Inn:</b> Simoniemi village had a transport organiser (fi. kyytirättäri, sw. skjutsrättare) serving Ii parish constable. An inn was established in 1640s at the latest. Rajanen farm usually served as the inn in Simoniemi.

name: Sangi
Settlement_Description: <b>Inn:</b> An inn was established in Sangi in the 1640s.

name: Sittard
Town_Description: Town privileges were granted between 10 and 30 April 1243 by Walram II 'the good', lord of Monschau, and his mother Elisabeth van Bar. A chapter is founded in 1299 by the bishop of Liège. A hospital is also first mentioned in 1299. The town privilege of 1243 also mentions a market. A market hall is found in 1326 ('theatrum'), which is mentioned in 1329 as 'domus pannorum', but was not used exclusively for the cloth trade. Market dates are, however, unknown.
Toll_Description: The Duke of Jülich levied a land toll in 1494. Exact tariffs are not known. Between 1494 and 1495, 24 gulden were collected. In 1496 Johan Noillman was ordered to construct and maintain a road paved with stone through town from the junction of the roads to Limbricht and Einighausen and the junction of the roads to Broeksittard and Wehr. In return he acquired the right to levy toll on this road.

name: null
Harbour_Description: The Ilmenau river upstream from Lüneburg was used as a waterway, mainly for transporting wood. In 1348, the town received the privilege to make the river navigable until Uelzen. The landing place for the vessels must have been located in the vicinity of the water mill, since the mill weir prevented ships from reaching the main harbour of the town.

name: null
Toll_Description: In the context of making the Ilmenau river navigable for wood transports to Lüneburg, a draw bridge was to be built near Medingen in 1343. In return, the monastery was allowed to levy a toll on the wood transported on the river.

name: null
Harbour_Description: The harbour of Harburg was used to ship corn and wood, but due to the constant attempts of Hamburg to prevent shipping on the southern Elbe because of the Hamburg staple from the 15th century onwards, it never gained prominence.

name: null
Toll_Description: In 1435 a bridge toll of the marshal of Kranenburg is attested. In 1573 there is mention of a road toll of 4 Pfennig for a wagon and 1 Pfennig for a pedestrian, as well as a new toll, of which the latter was forbidden by the Archbishop of Bremen. Levying of the road toll was discontinued when the bridge was destroyed in 1628. A toll on shipping on the Oste was levied as well. In the late 17th century, a chain across the river forced ships to halt for toll payment. Before 1628, the bridge must have fulfilled the same function.
Bridge_Description: A draw bridge across the Oste, which allowed passage to larger ships, was destroyed by imperial troops in 1628. Its construction might go back to the construction of the castle around 1375. A new bridge was built in 1659 further downstream near Hechthausen.
Ferry_Description: Before construction of the bridge and after it was burned down in 1628, a ferry must have existed near Kranenburg. It must have been replaced by the new river crossing at Hechthausen in 1659 at the latest.

name: null
Toll_Description: The town Werden acquired the right to levy a bridge toll to pay for the maintenance of the bridge in 1387. After 1479, the duke of Mark introduced a bridge toll for citizens of the town as well, who had been exempted before.
Bridge_Description: A bridge across the Ruhr is first mentioned in 1065. It was destroyed by floods in 1399 and 1533. At the latter occasion, it was replaced by a ferry for five years. According to a view of town by Braun and Hogeberg from 1572, the bridge was made from stone and had seven arches.
