Above the second pillar on the town side, there was a gate building, where the bridge toll was probably levied. The bridge was again destroyed by floods in 1642 and replaced for a ferry for the following two centuries.
Ferry_Description: A ferry replaced the bridge during its reconstruction in 1533-1538 and after its final destruction in 1642.
Harbour_Description: In 1033, it is mentioned that the Ruhr river is navigable until Werden abbey. Probably, this was true for later centuries as well.

name: Wiedensahl
Settlement_Description: An old Saxon manor existed around 500. A settlement was founded in the 13th century and first mentioned in 1253, which developed into a market borough ('flecken').

name: Marttila
Settlement_Description: <b>Inn:</b> An inn had been established in Marttila farm probably in the 1650s, and it was hosted by Matti Jaakonpoika. In 1663, officials stated that no one travelled to Seinäjoki village, where the farm was located, and thus the tavern rights were cancelled.

name: Säräisniemi
Settlement_Description: <b>Inn:</b> Parish constable (fi: nimismies, sw: länsman) Antti Eerikinpoika was appointed as the innkeeper in 1634. He was later appointed also as the bailiff (fi. vouti, sw. fogde) of Kajaani barony. Son Jeremias Antinpoika continued innkeeping after his father.

name: Vatsiainen
Settlement_Description: <b>Inn:</b> An inn was established in Luukas farm in Vatsiainen in 1635.

name: Laatu
Settlement_Description: <b>Inn:</b> An inn was established in Laatu in 1623.

name: Peltoniemi
Settlement_Description: <b>Inn:</b> Ilmajoki parish constable (fi: nimismies, sw: länsman) was located in Peltoniemi village from 1571 onwards. Parish constables were obliged to keep a tavern in late 16th c. In 1641, Sakari Jaakonpoika from Talvitie ("winter road") farm was appointed as the innkeeper. The road turns in Peltoniemi from Kyröjoki river towards Ylistaro.

name: Teuva
Settlement_Description: <b>Inn:</b> An inn was established in Teuva in 1637, and Jaakko Niilonpoika from Riippi farm was appointed as the innkeeper.

name: Paltaniemi
Settlement_Description:
Permanent agricultural settlement in Paltamo and Oulunjärvi area dates to the colonisation from Savolax in the 1550s. The administrative centre of the area was Royal Manor close to Vuohenginkoski stream in Kajaaninjoki river in 1555–58. Oulujärvi parish was founded in 1559, when its church was built on Manamansalo island and the area’s administration was attached to Ostrobothnia. The church and the much of the settlement were destroyed by Russians in 1578–80. After the official annexation of the area to Swedish realm in the peace of Teussina in 1595 the settlement was in 1599 organised into Paltamo parish (sw. Kajaneborg socken), the first two wooden churches of which stood in Kirkkoniemi at Paltaniemi in 1599–1716. The parish was split to Paltamo and Sotkamo parishes in 1647 The building of Kajaani castle (sw. Kajaneborg) was started in 1604. The town of Kajaani (sw. Kajana) was established in 1651.

<b>Inn:</b> Medieval trading posts likely had private alehouses and taverns to serve travelling merchants and farmers. An official inn was established in Paltamo parish village in 1634, and Pekka Sivonen was appointed as the innkeeper.
Fair_Description: The burghers of Oulu were granted the right of two annual fairs in Kajaneborg parish in 1625. Of these the summer fair was to be held at midsummer (24 June) in Paltaniemi and the winter fair on 15 December in Särismäki. Since no real other information on the latter exists, Särismäki fair may have been a proposed new fair to be held some 50 kms SWW from Kajaani at Saarismäki, where the portage trail and possible winter way from Savolax via Vieremä to Oulujärvi crossed the Maanselkä watershed. Paltaniemi midsummer fair was relocated to Kajaani in 1650 where annual winter fair was ordained to be held on Candlemas (2 February). The summer fair in Paltaniemi-Kajaani region may have had a longer tradition before the Finnish and Swedish colonisation of the area in the 1550s. In 1555 the Russian Karelian merchants had a waypoint on their portage trail between Ladoga and Bothnian rivermouths in Vuohenginkoski stream close to the place where the castle was started in 1604, and after that in 1606 in Nuasjärvi SSE from Kajaani.
Toll_Description: The 1/32 duty worth of all goods intended for sale in towns and fairs and brought to the site by peasants was collected in the fair since 1625.

name: Vahee
Settlement_Description: <b>Inn:</b> An inn was established in Vahee in 1642, and Matti Knuutinpoika was appointed as the innkeeper.

name: Mellilä
Settlement_Description: <b>Inn:</b> An inn was established in Mellilä in 1642, and Yrjö Rekonpoika Kyröläinen was appointed as the innkeeper. The inn was located by the winter road.

name: Sonnila
Settlement_Description: <b>Inn:</b> An inn was established in Sonnila in 1640, and it served long as the tavern in Ylistaro parish.

name: Mankoinen
Settlement_Description: <b>Inn:</b> A medieval guild hall was located either in Mankoinen village, Hintikkala village in the island west, or in Harolanluoto island in southwest, which has also been called as Killansaari ("Guild Island"). No exact date or location of the hall is known, but it is certain that in 13th-14th c. there has been some kind of gathering place here.

name: Raision silta
Bridge_Description: Raisionjoki bridge on the common road from Turku to Masku and further North was in 1638 maintained by Raisio and Masku parishes. The arrangement was of medieval origin, possibly from the 14th century.

name: Aakerfähr
Ferry_Description: The existence of a Ruhr ferry at this place is attested in a 1359 Duisburg town account, but it is likely to have been much older. Due to frequent changes in the course of the river, the ferry was frequently moved, changing hands between Meiderich and Duisburg, who kept half of the ferry fees. The other half of the revenues belonged to the duke of Cleves.

name: Bierbruch
Toll_Description: A toll of the bishop of Hildesheim on the "Bruch vor Sarstedt" is first mentioned in 1384. The bishop cancelled levying of the toll in favour of Hildesheim citizens in 1393.

name: null
Ferry_Description: A comital ferry to Spaardam crossing the IJ is found in 1315.

name: null
Harbour_Description: After the construction of the Schaale waterway in 1564, Dutzow on the northern shore of the lake Schaalsee became a transshipment point for transport, mainly of salt, between the Baltic Sea harbour of Wismar and the Elbe river.

name: Hämeenkyrö
Settlement_Description: <b>Inn:</b> Knight Arvid Klausson Djekn got sick during his travel to Ostrobothnia, so he prepared his will in "Kyrw", which is usually understood as Hämeenkyrö. Hämeenkyrö inn was usually located in Laitila (southward by the strain), but when Matti Sipinpoika from Tuokkola farm (near the church) served as the parish constable (fi: nimismies, sw: länsman) in 1639-40, the tavern was located there. The tavern moved from Laitila to Tuokkola in 1671.

name: Onkkaala
Settlement_Description: <b>Inn:</b> There has been a tavern in Onkkaala from mid-16th c. to 18th c.

name: null
Lock_Description: A lock in the canal between the Elbe and the Schwerin lake, which was built between 1568 and 1572, is displayed near Plate on a map of the canal by Daniel Frese from 1605.

name: null
Harbour_Description: The town of Rostock maintained a barge service with Bützow, which was rented out in 1433.

name: Laitikkala
Settlement_Description: <b>Inn:</b> An inn was established in Laitikkala in mid-16th c. In late 16th c., Erkki Olavinpoika Kokkola acted as the innkeeper and parish constable (fi: nimismies, sw: länsman).

name: null
Harbour_Description: When the king acquired Præstø in 1353 the settlement appears to have functioned as a harbour. Presumably a natural harbour, which was frequently used by German ships. The character of the harbour in the middle ages and early modern era is uncertain. On a map of the town in Erik Pontoppidan’s Danske Atlas from 1767 two piers are shown; the age of these constructions are not known.

name: Drübeck
Settlement_Description: Founded as a Benedictine convent in 877, the monastery remains as a protestant convent until today.

name: null
Harbour_Description: Tesovo was a transshipment point between land transport and water transport on the Oredezh and Luga rivers.

name: null
Lock_Description: A lock in the canal between the Elbe and the Schwerin lake, which was built between 1568 and 1572, is displayed in Grabow on a map of the canal by Daniel Frese from 1605.

name: null
Lock_Description: A lock in the canal between the Elbe and the Schwerin lake, which was built between 1568 and 1572, is displayed in Neustadt on a map of the canal by Daniel Frese from 1605.

name: null
Ferry_Description: The ferry between Deutz and Cologne is among others mentioned in 1488.

name: Korvensuun Isosilta
Bridge_Description: Korvensuu Isosilta (Great Bridge) crossing Laajoki river on the Great Postal Road was in the beginning of the 17th century maintained by Vehmaa and Taivassalo parishes of Vehmaa judicial district and Mynämäki parish of the neighbouring Masku judicial district. The maintenance of the bridge was of medieval origin, possibly from the early 15th century or second half of the 14th.

name: Walbeck
Settlement_Description: First mention in a record from 959. In 992 a monastery of Benedictine nuns was founded in Walbeck. The monastery was dissolved in 1525.

name: Wiederstedt
Settlement_Description: First mention of the village in 944. A convent of Augustinian nuns, consecrated to the Virgin Mary, was moved from Hettstedt to Wiederstedt before 1259. It was originally a hospital, converted into a convent before 1248.

name: Volewijck
Ferry_Description: The ferry on the peninsula Volewijck to Amsterdam is first mentioned in 1308. See Amsterdam for further details.

name: Vianen
Settlement_Description: According to Van Berkel & Samplonius, Vianen is first mentioned about 1270. Cox states this more specifically as 1 December 1271.
Town_Description: Town privileges were granted on 22 September 1336 by Willem of Duivenvoorde, lord of Oosterhout, and Heilwich of Duivenvoorde, lady of Vianen and Oosterhout. That year Vianen also obtained toll-exemption in Holland.
Fair_Description: In 1271 (Dec. 2) the bishop of Utrecht granted Vianen two fairs. He enfeoffed knight Zweder van Beusichem the right to organise the two fairs in the judicial area where his castle in Vianen was located. In 1335 (Dec. 18) Willem van Duivenvoorde granted 'Vyanen aan de oever' (the new settlement on the river Lek) three fairs and a weekly market. Dates: 1) St. Jamesday (July 25?), 2) St. Severinusday (Jan. 8) and 3) Sunday till Midlent. The marketright lasted 14 days. On All Saints and All Souls cloth is cut in the town, on the Sunday after Midlent and the day after that as well. In 1561/2 the market-toll was levied from horses and other goods and registered for only 7 stuivers.

name: Oudewater
Settlement_Description: The first mention of Oudewater dates from 1239. It gains importance as a fortified border settlement/town. A hospital is first mentioned in 1419.
Town_Description: Town rights were granted by Henry I, count of Vianden. Neither the grant itself, nor any copies, have survived; therefore, the exact date of the grant is unknown. Based on source material from the seventeenth and eighteenth century, Cox states that these privileges may have been granted in 1257.
Fair_Description: The establishment of a staple in 1326 (see sub staple) confirmes the existence of a market. The comital account of 1343/'4 mentions a fair with St. John (June 24) and a butter measure. In 1363 the fair of St. Michelsday (Sept. 29 sept.) is found. In 1387 (July 13 juli) duke Albrecht farmed the tolls for 5 years to the town. A charter dated 1410 mentions the horse-fair starting six days after St. John midsummer (June 24), duration 14 days, 3 days before St. John the cross was erected. In 1413 (May 13) duke Willem donated the market-tolls to the town. All goods are toll-exempt, except for the horses. King Philip II granted in 1564 (Sept.) a horse-fair on June 6 juni, just like count Willem in 1413 did. The tariff was doubled to match that in Gouda. This town was heared in advance just like Schoonhoven, IJsselstein and Woerden about possible harming.
Toll_Description: In 1310 the abbey of Rijnsburg obtained free passage at the episcopal toll on ships in Oudewater. A tariff from the count of Holland for the toll in Woerden, dating 1337-'45, indicates that the toll in Oudewater levied at the lock there must have been usurpated by the count of Holland, somewhere since 1310 (as in Woerden).
Staple_Description: The count of Holland ordained in 1326 that alle goods grown in the Land van Woerden had to be traded in Oudewater. Possibly this was a reaction on the fact that inhabitants of the Sticht of Utrecht were forbidden to bring their goods in the Land van Woerden. This stapleright was certified in 1351 and then it was specified for butter.
Harbour_Description: The silting up of the river Hollandse IJssel (as a result of the upstream damming in 1285) increasingly troubled shipping to and from the harbour of Oudewater. In 1494, the town complained that the river trade had disappeared since the time of Charles the Bold (1467-1477) and that maintenance of the harbour was very costly.

name: Neue Turmwarte
Settlement_Description: Watchtower, mentioned in 1461. The name alludes to an older predecessor.

name: Horstbergwarte
Settlement_Description: Watchtower, part of the ditch system that stretched all the way to the Neue Turmwarte.

name: Austbergwarte
Settlement_Description: Watchtower, in the 15th century it was a watchtower for Blankenburg.

name: Sargstedter Warte
Settlement_Description: Watchtower built in the 15th century by Halberstadt monastery.

name: null
Toll_Description: At places along the Havel and Spree where locks had been constructed, a lock toll was collected for the maintenance of the locks. However, they were as high as other transit tolls.
Lock_Description: A pound lock in Fürstenwalde is constructed in 1588, which facilitated transportation to Frankfurt (Oder). Before that year, the mill weir (first mentioned in 1298) might have included a simple flash lock.

name: Pommerœul
Fair_Description: In 1354 (Oct. 31) the countess of Hainaut granted a weekly market and a fair the Sunday after Sacramentsday (Friday after Eastern).

name: Enghien
Settlement_Description: A castle was built by the lords of Enghien in the 11th century. Next to it a settlement developed.
Town_Description: Enghien was fortified in the 14th, possibly already in the 13th, century.
Fair_Description: Two free fairs were granted by duke Philip the Good around 1457.

name: Schellinkhout
Settlement_Description: Schellinkhout is first mentioned around 1311/1312. Schellinkhout was granted town privileges on 21 December 1402 by Albert (‘Albrecht’) of Bavaria, count of Holland. In 1414, the villages Wijdenes and Oosterleek were added to the ‘stede’ Schellinkhout. These settlements, however, never developed an urban character. The granting of town rights was part of an administrative reorganization in which a number of smaller settlements were granted town rights in order to provide them with a certain degree of self-government which replaced the need for the count of Holland's bailiffs ('baljuws'). The settlements kept their own separate settlement governments. In 1429, the town privileges were withdrawn and on 6 January 1430, Wijdenes and Oosterleek were separated from the ‘stede’ Schellinkhout (and were granted their own town privileges). The town rights of Schellinkhout itself were restored sometime between 1442 and 1450.
Fair_Description: In 1402 (Dec. 21) duke Albrecht granted Schellinkhout the town privileges of Medemblik with a free fair eight days before and after St. Odulphusday (June 4) and a weekly market on Thursday. A weigh-house is also found in 1402.
Staple_Description: In 1452 it was prohibited for citizen to export dairy before it was weighed at the weigh-house.

name: Porvoo Gammelgård
Settlement_Description: Permanent agricultural settlement in lower Porvoonjoki (sw. Borgå å) area and Eastern Nyland (sw. Östra Nyland) dates to the Swedish colonisation in the latter half of the 13th century when new farms were founded in an area previously part of usufruct and emerging colonisation settlement from inner Häme. The parish organisation of Eastern Nyland dates at the latest to the first quarter of the 14th century, in Porvoo (sw. Borgå) possibly already to the third quarter of the 14th century. The parish and rector of Porvoo is first cited in 1327. The bailiwick of Porvoo (sew. Borgå fögderi) was since the beginning of the 15th century placed permanently under Viipuri castle (sw. Viborg) and administered by a bailiff of a new <b>Royal Manor (sw. Gammelgård)</b> first cited in 1413. The new Manor was founded separate of the possessions of an older Crown Manor in the area possibly established in the combination of the first castle, or after it. The oldest Crown Manor and the new 15th century Royal Manor may have also controlled the Saksala (sw. Saxby) fair located upstream of the castle and the later medieval town frequented by inland peasants and merchants of Porvoo and Helsinki as late in the 17th century.

name: Korsholm
Settlement_Description: Permanent agricultural settlement in Mustasaari area dates to the Swedish colonisation of the late 13th century and the beginning of the 14th. Korsholm castle is first cited in the testament of Bo Jonsson (Grip) in 1384 and had a bailiwick attached to it in 1388. Because of its Middle Low German name of “Krytzeborch” documented in 1384, the castle may have been first established as a fortification in the opening years of the reign of king Albrekt of Mecklenburg after 1364, but it was likely either founded or developed into an administrative centre only in the 1370s by the seneschal and magnate Bo Jonsson who was ordained as the headman of Finland in 1371 and controlled all castles and bailiwicks in Finland and much of Sweden proper from 1374 to his death in 1386. The castle and the later early 16th century Royal Manor served as the administrative centre of Gulf of Bothnia area north of Kvarken until 1441, and after that periodically and since 1525 to 1634 that of Ostrobothnia or the southern part of it. <b>Inn:</b> Korsholma (royal manor) is mentioned in Jaakko Teitti's list in 1556 as a possible place for a bailiff (fi. vouti, sw. fogde). Ture Pedersson Bielke, Swedish nobleman and castellan of St. Olaf's Castle in Savo, stayed overnight in Korsholma in 1557.

name: null
Toll_Description: Hausberge was a toll station at the Weser river, mentioned in a 1584 complaint from Bremen and in a 1597 charter of the monastery Hardehausen.

name: null
Bridge_Description: A bridge across the Ruhr in Wetter is first mentioned in 1605. This was a wooden construction on ten pillars.

name: Monnickendam
Settlement_Description: Monnickendam is first mentioned in 1288. A hospital is first mentioned in 1420.
Town_Description: Monnickendam is granted town rights on 2 and 27 March 1356 by William V, count of Holland.
Fair_Description: In 1342/'3 the town had already three fairs: with 'crucen' (Crossday, Sept. 14), the 'middle' and the 'last' fair. The town right of 1356 (March 27) stated this data: 1) Sunday after Ascension, 2) Sunday after St. Margareth (July 13 juli), 3) Sunday after the decapitation of St. John the Baptist (August 29). The toll was property of the count and its successors. In 1574 (May 10) Monnickendam was granted by Philip II two leather-fairs. The cattle-fair which they had of old on August 30 was relocated to Oct. 11 (the day after Victoris). This will have become a fat cattle-fair. The dates are: Monday before 'palin' (Palm Sunday?) and Monday after St. John 'uitgaande oogst' (at the end of the harvest) (August 29).
Ferry_Description: A ferry is first mentioned in 1342 in the comital account. The destination is not given, probably Katwoude at the other bank of the Purmer Ee (or Amsterdam?).
Harbour_Description: In 1443 and 1483/4 the king granted free trade in Denmark, Sweden and Norway. In 1470 the king granted free access to the harbour of Bergen in Norway. In 1564 (Febr. 27) the magistrate was granted to make a lock next to the town with which ships could better reach the harbour.

name: Zaandam
Settlement_Description: Zaandam came into existence when the Hogendam or Zaanderdam was built not long before 1288, which closed off the Zaan river from the IJ. It is first mentioned in 1316. Around the dam and its locks, a village developed with inns that boomed in the 16th and 17th centuries due to the growth of shipping and industry along the Zaan river. In the 17th century, Zaandam became divided in Oost-Zaandam and West-Zaandam, which were merged into a single village Zaandam only in 1811. Zaandam was elevated to a town on 1 January 1812 by Emperor Napoleon.
Ferry_Description: In 1399 the ferry between Westzaan and presumably Amsterdam is found, when this and a.o. the sluice in the 'Noirtdamme' (the northern dam) there are sold by the count to four citizens of Amsterdam. Ferry services between Zaandam and Amsterdam were regulated in 1631: four skippers for each settlement were allowed to operate on the route and tariffs were fixed. In 1683, ferry services were extended to 12 skippers.
Harbour_Description: A harbour developed on the western side of the dam in the 16th and 17th century during the economic boom of Zaandam. It served as transit harbour for regional as well as international ships. Extensive harbour structures on the IJ side of the dam were built in 1636 and 1650, which were connected with the sea. Larger sea-going vessels could not anchor in the harbour and had to use the mouth of the Zaan river as roadstead.
Lock_Description: When the Hogendam was constructed around 1288, two wooden sluices were built for draining purposes. Probably, these were passable for smaller vessels. From 1544 to 1547, one of them was replaced with a pound lock from stone, which allowed larger vessels to pass, which made the Zaan the main waterway from Amsterdam to northern Holland. However, the lock was bridged and built over, so that its capacity remained limited. The fee for use of this large lock was 10 stuiver; the town of Alkmaar enjoyed the right of free passage. The second "Wormer Sluis" or "Kleine sluis" was renewed in 1549, and protests from various villages in 1588 after it was announced that the lock would be closed show that there was a high demand for two passages for ships in the dam. In 1608, an "overtoom" (a construction for dragging ships across a barrier) was constructed to allow sea-going ships built at the Zaan shipyards to enter the IJ. A third sluice was built in 1612 in connection with the draining of the Schermer and Beemster lakes.

name: Alphen aan den Rijn
Settlement_Description: Alphen goes back to the Roman castellum Albaniana, located opposite the mouth of the Aar in the Rhine. It was first mentioned around 300, in a 7th-century copy. The castellum developed into the settlement Alphen in the Middle Ages.

name: Beverwijk
Settlement_Description: Beverwijk is first mentioned in an eleventh-century copy of a document dated 918-948. In the thirteenth-century it gains some importance as a place for transhipment. In 1302 the oldest cloth-hall in Holland is found here, which was teared down in 1397.
Town_Description: Beverwijk was granted town rights on 11 November 1298 by John I, count of Holland and Zeeland.
Fair_Description: In the townright of 1298 two fairs are found. The first one on the 'Scheiding der Apostelen' (July 15) and the second one the day before St. Michelsday (Sept. 28), each for one week. According to the (18th-century) 'Tegenwoordige Staat' the town obtained in 1303  a privilege for a leather-fair. There is no proof for this. This spring-fair seems to have developed to a leather-fair. Moreover the landlord's decision to change the start of the fair in 1547 was instigated by the fact that Beverwijk had become the only leather-fair in Holland and Utrecht. The autumn-fair remained unchanged and was sometimes called Bamis-fair, as the local patron St. Bavo had its holy day during the fair-week on October 1. On this fair cattle, dairy and corn were traded. In 1547 (July 30) the town obtained two leather-fairs. In all this was the restauration of the two old fairs. The start of the first fair was quickly changed because the two months between the two fairs was too short to prepare leather. The first fair started now the first Saturday-evening after Eastern. Guicciaridini also stressed in his description of the Netherlands dated 1566 that Beverwijk had two famous leather-fairs. Shoemakers and leatherdressers from Holland, Overijssel and Friesland attended the fairs with ships. The town was well situated at the IJ according to Guicciardini, but the depth  of this water was 'veel verloopen' (shallowed). In 1595 the magistrate promised the comital steward of Kennemerland to pay yearly 2 pounds for the market-tolls of the two fairs.

name: null
Harbour_Description: The Schuitendiep was dug around 1400 and extended to Zuidbroek in 1628 and Winschoten in the 1630s. The Damsterdiep was dug in 1424 and connected Groningen with Appingedam and Delfzijl. Regular barge ('trekvaart') services took place on both canals from the middle of the 17th century; the barges moored in Groningen in the vicinity of the Steentil bridge, as can be seen on 17th-century maps of the city.

name: Edam
Settlement_Description: According to Van Berkel & Samplonius, Edam is first mentioned in 1342-1343. Cox states that there is an earlier mention dating from 1310. A hospital is first mentioned in 1392.
Town_Description: Edam was granted town privileges on 19 November 1357 by William V, count of Holland.
Fair_Description: The townprivilege of count William V also granted three fairs: 1) starting 8 days before Palm Sunday, 2) 8 days after St. John in the summer (June 24), 3) the third sunday after St. Bavo (Oct. 1), each during 8 days. The municipal account dated 1560/'1 mentions incomes of the autumn-fair and the Easter-fair. In 1585 a meath-hall and a fishmarket were built.
Harbour_Description: In the town privileges of 1357, Edam acquired the right to construct a new harbour, that connected the Purmer lake with the Zuiderzee. It became an important sea harbour for the hinterland of northern Holland. In 1412 (May 1) it obtained toll-exemption at the tolls of Spaarndam and Beverwijk. In the Enqueste dated 1494 they state they had at the time of duke Charles the Bold (before 1477) 40 'maer'ships, of which only six are left over and 30 'reyn'(Rhine)ships for the catch of herring before 1477, of which only two now are left over. They a.o. built ships and trade eastward over water.

name: Löwenberg
Settlement_Description: Founded in 1200-1250 at a road crossing, first mentioned in 1269. The settlement was protected by a castle that was mentioned in 1375. The settlement itself was characterised as borough ('Flecken', 'oppidum') since 1270.

name: Aggersund
Toll_Description: In 1516 a royal toll on oxen exported from the regions of Vendsyssel and Thy was introduced. Aggersund was one of the toll stations.
Ferry_Description: One of the most important ferry connections across Limfjorden, which was located at one of the most narrow parts of the fjord. The age and character of the ferry is uncertain, but most likely established in some form during the Viking age. During the late medieval period the ferry across the narrow strait of Aggersund was central to export of oxen from the regions of Thy and Vendsyssel. The ferry was, for example, used by the nobleman Mouritz Nielsen Gyldenstierne in the 1490ties. In the late 16th century 6-7 ferrymen living of the northern shore were responsible for the ferry connection.

name: Hvam bro
Bridge_Description: Presumabely the bridge is from the late medieval period. Not documented, however, before the 1620s.

name: Vielsen
Settlement_Description: Fortified main court of the Bishop of Paderborn with a deserted settlement, which at times was directly passed by the Hellweg. Archaeological finds prove a settlement since the 9th century, called a parish since 1216, to which the Sälzer settlement to the north also belonged. As a bulwark on the border to the archbishopric of Cologne, Vielsen was secured in 1247 with a tower hill fort (Motte), which was destroyed in 1256 and not rebuilt. The rural settlement remained till 14th century, the parish church was moved to Salzkotten.

Town_Description: The exact date of granting of town rights is unknown because the corresponding charter is missing. In 1232 the settlement is mentioned as 'oppidum' with walls, in 1279 Frankfurt town privileges are confirmed.
Toll_Description: In 1344, Gerlach Herr von Limburg levied a land toll and a fee for safe conduct on land. He pledged the income from an older toll to Archbishop Baldiun of Trier.

name: Sint Jansbrug
Bridge_Description: Together with the Visbrug, this was the oldest bridge in Leiden. They are first mentioned in 1204.

name: Druzhba
Settlement_Description: Prussian castle on the 'Zickelberg' has been reinforced in 1256 after being seized by the Teutonic Order, was destroyed again four years later and again rebuilt in 1272, afterwards a settlement grew
Town_Description: The Grandmaster of the Teutonic Order, Konrad von Jungingen grants the Magdeburg-Kulm town law, endorsed in 1663 by the Great Elector

name: Alte Lahnbrücke
Toll_Description: A bridge toll on the old wooden bridge is mentioned in 1286. A bridge toll also financed the construction of the new stone bridge from 1315 onwards. The toll house was located at the outer bridge tower.
Bridge_Description: The first wooden bridge crossing the Lahn river was built in c. 1160-1180. After it was destroyed by ice drift in winter 1305/1306 the town ordered the construction of a new stone bridge in 1315, although it was only completed in 1345, and in 1373 the old wooden bridge is still mentioned in existence. The bridge had to be repaired in 1555, 1657, 1948 and 1982/1983.

name: Olsztyn
Settlement_Description: Castle of the diocesan chapter of Pomesania built before 1353, when there existed a mill and a settlement
Town_Description: Town probably existed before 1348, founding documents were granted in 1353 by the diocesan chapter of Pomesania, Kulm town law, mentioned as civitas seu opidu in 1353 and opidum in 1378

name: Aller
Settlement_Description: The village of Aller was first mentioned in 1273, but is significantly older. The parish church is from either the 12th or 13th century.

name: Uckerath
Toll_Description: The Duke of Berg levied a land toll from 1440. Tariffs are not known. In the years 1440/41 and 1441/42 a lease of 12 mark can be recorded.

name: Mariager
Settlement_Description: Perhaps a small village prior to the foundation of Mariager monastery.
Town_Description: The town of Mariager grew around a Birgittine monastery probably founded in the 1430s, and sanctioned by the pope in 1446. The monastery soon developed into one of wealthiest and most important religious institutions in Denmark. In 1449 Mariager monastery was granted trading rights and a free harbour. The same year a bailiff (Danish: Foged) in Mariager is mentioned. In 1457 a town council was mentioned, and in 1486 a town bailiff and a town scribe. At the time of the Reformation in 1536 Mariager was recognized as a borough. In 1592 king Christian IV (1588-1648) granted Mariager the same rights and freedoms as the neighboring town of Hobro.
Toll_Description: In 1592 the toll previously collected in Hadsund was moved to Mariager.

name: Douai
Fair_Description: Late 10th century count Arnulf II granted toll- and marketrights. A fair is found in 1076. Market-tolls are found in 1247 and 1251. A free fair was granted by countess Margareth of Flanders in 1265 (Apr. 11) starting the Sunday before Ascension (Thursday after the 5th Sunday after Eastern) till Pentecost.
Toll_Description: Tariffs of tolls dated 1247 (levied by the castellan) and 1251 (market) are edited.
Staple_Description: Guicciardini mentions around 1560 a grain-staple and export in particular to Mechelen.

name: Ath
Staple_Description: In 1458 Ath received the staple for linen in Hainaut. In 1542/3 emperor Charles refused renewal of this right.

name: Dordrecht
Settlement_Description: The first mention of Dordrecht dates from 1064, in a falsified copy from the first quarter of the twelfth century. The next mention dates from about 1151-1155.  A chapter in the church is known for the years 1367-ca. 1572.
Town_Description: Dordrecht was granted town rights in July 1220 by William I, count of Holland. However, it is probable that Dordrecht already held town(-like) privileges before 1200. In 1200, Dordrecht is mentioned as 'oppidum' and as 'stede'.
Fair_Description: A cloth hall is first mentioned in 1310. In 1331 a fair of lord Daniel (van der Merwede) in his manor in Dordrecht is found with St. Bonifatius-eve (June 4). The duration of this fair is found in 1560: 8 days between St. Bonifatius (June 5) and St. Odulphus (June 12). Since 1424 this was combined with a toll, excises and market-stalls.  This was a fief held from the lord of Voorne and since 1371 from the count of Holland.In 1342 (Nov. 26) count Willem IV granted the town two fairs, each for 14 days with report of the taxes to be paid by the merchants. The dates: 1) 26st day after Easter when people sing: 'Resurrexstio Domini' and 2) 10th day after St. Bavo (Oct. 1) with preservation of the rights of the lord Van der Merwede. In 1379 (Oct. 18) duke Albrecht ordained that the Bamisfair was moved to the first Friday after St. Victorsday (Oct. 10) as there were problems with the visit of merchants on the 'toog'-(display)days before the Bamisfair (possibly regarding the Bamisfair of Antwerp). In 1414 (Sept. 3) duke Willem stated that Dordrecht would be exempt of tolls on all fairs. In 1404 merchants of Dordrecht are first seen on the fairs of Frankfurt.
Toll_Description: A toll on sailing ships is first mentioned in 1220, but is probably older.  In the oldest list of fiefs of count Floris V dated 1282-'84 the 'Hulctol' is found (a hulk is a seaworthy type of ship), fief of the lord of Wassenaer. In 1289 (March 1) he gave this toll to the town of Dordrecht. Afterwards this toll is unknown. Exemption from tolls for Easterlings in 1313 who brought their wares directly to Dordrecht; preferable tariffs for Hanse merchants in 1358 and between 1388-1392 while the Kontor in Bruges was displaced. A tariff for merchants from Prussia and Westfalen is dated 1340. A general tariff is preserved and edited for the years 1356-1358, accounts of the toll for the years 1380-1385. A list with exempt places, abbeys and convents at the tolls of Dordrecht and Geervliet is s.d. (first half of 16th century). A special account for all imported wines is dated 1565/6.
Staple_Description:
Count John of Holland established a staple market for oats in 1298, which was extended to all commodities on Merwede and Lek in 1299, confirmed in 1304. From 1388 compulsory market for all ships coming from the east to the Maas. Staple for Rhine whine of eight days in 1324, which became a general wine staple in 1401. The staple obligations became hard to enforce after the St Elizabeth's flood (1421), after which Dordrecht became located on an island, making it easier to bypass the city. In 1441, commodities coming downstream with destinations elsewhere had to be transferred to other ships, but did not have to be offered for sale any more. Hanseatic staple for Rhenish wines in 1452, together with Antwerp. Staple for wine and salt for Holland and Friesland in 1453. In the 16th century, there were growing conflicts with other cities about the staple, which led to Middelburg being freed from staple obligations in Dordrecht in 1533. The staple was still confirmed by the emperor in 1540, but restricted in the following year: only corn, legumes, salt, wine, lime, coal, millstones and iron transported on Lek, Merwede and Maas had to be brought to Dordrecht. Despite ever growing conflicts and violations of the staple, it remained in place until 1670.In 1377 it was ordained that all peat dug in the Grote Waard had to be traded at the market in Dordrecht. In 1442 the same was stated for all dairy-products from Zuidholland. In 1520 the socalled 'Octrooi Serviel' was granted by king Charles V which caused that of the remaining 40 villages around the town in Zuidholland after the St. Elisabethsflood, 25 were forced to market their agricultural products in Dordrecht, the other 15 only had to pay excise of beer and were obliged to help deepen the harbour in Dordrecht. In 1553-'57 a trial layed by the other towns in Zuidholland (Schoonhoven, Gorcum en Rotterdam) and some local lords against this market-right was pending but in 1562 it was lenghtened for another 25 years. In 1589 however it was abolished. 
Guicciardini mentions a staple for grain supplied of Gelre, Kleve, Gulik and other southern regions around 1560.

name: Altenbauna
Settlement_Description: Mentioned as Bunon in 1015. It was the seat of a landgrave's office and court.

name: Altastenberg
Settlement_Description: First mentioned in 1533. After 1536 some huts were built on the Lichtenscheid, where a settlement formed.

name: Altmorschen
Settlement_Description: First mentioned in the first half of the 9th century.

name: Belœil
Fair_Description: In 1516 a free weekly market and two fairs were granted by the count of   Valkenburg (Faucquemont) to the baron de Ligne.

name: Kivennapa
Settlement_Description: <b>Inn:</b> An inn was established in Kivennapa in 1605, and Hannu Unnukainen was appointed as the innkeeper.

name: Wolfhagen
Settlement_Description: The settlement is first mentioned in 1231. Landgrave Ludwig of Thuringia erected a castle here around 1226.
Town_Description: Next to the castle a settlement developed, which acquired town privileges in 1264.

name: Arnsbach
Settlement_Description: First mentioned in 1245. Called a 'villa' in 1314 and 1347.

name: Attendorn
Settlement_Description: First mentioned in 1072, from the 9th century there was already a parish church. It lies at the crossroads of two old long-distance trade routes.
Town_Description: In 1222 Attendorn received town privileges of Soest.

name: Mons
Fair_Description: A flax-market en a linnen-hall are found in 1265. Market-tolls are found between 1256-86. The count of Hainaut granted in 1290 (April) two fairs: with Pentecost and with Allsaints (de la Toussaint: Nov. 1). The first one lasted eight days. The last one existed already in the 12th century, it started with St. Martin and lasted 11 days. On Nov. 2 St. Waudru was commemorated, foundress of the abbey, this was a day of pilgrimage. In 1331 a weekly horsemarket was granted. These privileges were confirmed in 1337 and 1346. In 1607 (Dec. 7) the fair with Pentecost was relocated to the second Monday after Quasimodo (first Sunday after Eastern).

name: Babenhausen
Settlement_Description: Founded in the 8th / 9th century at the latest.
Town_Description: In 1295 the settlement was granted Frankfurt town privileges.

name: Barciany
Settlement_Description: In Old Prussian times a castle of the Barten county, later in 1357 a castle of the Teutonic Order, moved in 1325 and destroyed in 1455, close to the new castle a settlement grew, mentioned as Städtlein in 1473
Town_Description: Granted town right in 1628 by the elector Georg Wilhelm, population became citizens/burghers, Kulm town law, mentioned as a city in 1630

name: Halle (Zenne)
Settlement_Description: Earliest mention in 1152. Countess Aleid of Holland of Hainaut donated a miraculous statue of Maria in 1267, which gave birth to a flowering pilgrimage.

name: Kippenbrug
Bridge_Description: In 1324 a second bridge was built across the Rhine with permission of the count of Holland, probably replacing a ferry. The bridge was known as Vrouwenbrug, and later as Kippenbrug. Initially the use of the bridge was only allowed for agricultural traffic, due to circumvention of the toll on the older Visbrug, but from the middle of the 14th century this rule disappeared.

name: Soignies
Settlement_Description: Mid seventh century Saint Vincent founded a convent close to the river Zenne, which gave birth to the town.
Fair_Description: There were two fairs and a large marketplace in the late Middle Ages. Drapery was flourishing.

name: Belecke
Town_Description: Town privileges under Soester rights were granted in 1296 by the Cologne archbishop Siegfried II.

name: Haven
Harbour_Description: The harbour just outside of the Zijlpoort was dug in 1576.

name: Warmond
Settlement_Description: First mentioned in 918-948, in an 11th-century copy.

name: Ringerbrügge
Bridge_Description: On the map <cite>Comitatus Bentheim et Steinfurt, auctore Joanne Westenberg</cite> (made before 1638), <q>Ringer brugge</q> is displayed near the village Ringe. It must have indicated a bridge across the Leegraben. Its age is unknown.

name: Northeim
Settlement_Description: Northeim probably originated in Frankish times. It is first mentioned around 780-802.
Town_Description: The settlement acquired town privileges in 1252 from Duke Otto the Child. The town privileges of Göttingen were granted in 1266.
Fair_Description: Three three-day fairs are mentioned in Northeim in 1336, "as they have taken place since old times" on the Sundays after St John, St Bartholomew and St Andrew. It is unclear when these fairs were founded, but probably not later than the year the settlement received the Göttingen town privileges in 1266. After 1336, a fourth fair on Sunday after Estomihi was added.
Toll_Description: The Benedictine monastery acquired toll privileges in 1141. In 1492, the town received permission from Duke Wilhelm of Brunswick to levy a road toll for 20 years to fund the improvement of the road to Hammenstedt. It was also levied at the other roads leading out of town and remained in existence after 20 years. In 1502, a ducal road toll was added by Duke Erich, which was levied at the town gates as well.

name: Nörten
Settlement_Description: Nörten was the seat of the law court of the nearby castle Hardenberg, which belonged to the archbishop of Mainz.
Town_Description: Town, market and fortification privileges were granted in 1360, but from the late 15th century onwards, Nörten is usually referred to as borough ('flecken').
Toll_Description: A toll is first mentioned in 1357, then already existing for a while. In the town privileges of 1360, it is determined that the archbishop of Mainz had the right to levy a toll of 1 shilling in the Göttingen currency of each horse pulling a wagon or cart through town. In 1478, an additional road toll for the maintenance of the street is installed.

name: Angerstein
Settlement_Description: The place was first mentioned in 1082.

name: Bovenden
Settlement_Description: First mentioned in 949. In the 16th century the settlement became a borough ('Flecken').

name: Weende
Toll_Description: A new toll station of the dukes of Brunswick-Lüneburg was installed in Weende in 1501, but destroyed by Göttingen citizens. Between 1504 and 1512, a toll was effectively levied in Weende.

name: null
Bridge_Description: The often wet valley of the Leine is relatively narrow south of Nörten, and was therefore often used as a river crossing point. A bridge is already mentioned in 1055.

name: Harste
Settlement_Description: First mentioned between 822 and 826. There existed a moated castle of the dukes of Brunswick here, which was first mentioned in 1294.
Toll_Description: In 1413, the duke of Brunswick leased the toll and safe conduct in Harste and Göttingen to Albrecht Lange.

name: Barterode
Settlement_Description: The place was first mentioned in 1093.

name: Varlosen
Settlement_Description: The settlement was first mentioned in 1093.

name: Bühren
Settlement_Description: The settlement was first mentioned between 826 and 876.

name: null
Bridge_Description: The Werra bridge in Münden is first mentioned in 1329. It was rebuilt in stone with seven arches in 1397-1402. A bridge toll was mentioned in the 15th century.

name: Holtensen
Settlement_Description: The settlement was first mentioned in the middle of the 13th century.

name: Hann. Münden
Settlement_Description: The older settlement Altmünden west of the Fulda river is first mentioned around 800; the newer settlement on the opposite shore in 1049.
Town_Description: Possibly a planned town was founded around the middle of the 12th century at the confluence of the Werra and Fulda in the Weser river. It is first mentioned as the town Münden around 1182-85.
Staple_Description: The basis for the Münden staple was its location at the confluence of the Werra, Fulda and Weser rivers. Natural and man-made barriers in the river arms forced transshipment to other vessels for further transportation on one of the three rivers. The town was granted a staple privilege by the duke of Brunswick-Lüneburg in 1247, although the document is probably a falsification made during a conflict with Kassel in 1319 about the salt trade. The staple privilege was confirmed by emperor Rudolf II in 1597. The shipping regulations from 1653 mention the right of Münden skippers to sail past the town, whereas skippers from other towns were obliged to unload their cargo in Münden. Moreover, the Münden skippers sought to acquire a privilege for shipping between Münden and Kassel. The staple led to numerous conflicts, mostly with Kassel, in the 16th and 17th centuries. Although the staple privilege does not discern between river and land traffic, it seems that it was only applied to river traffic.

name: null
Bridge_Description: The bridge across the Leine in Göttingen is first mentioned in 1285. A box for collecting transit fees was placed on the bridge in the 15th century.

name: Vorwerk Heißental
Settlement_Description: The folwark was built in the 17th century near the settlement of Heistendal, which had been abandoned in the 15th century and was first mentioned in 1251.

name: Jühnde
Settlement_Description: First mention of the settlement in 960. A castle is first mentioned in the 13th century, the St Martin's church in 1271.

name: Wiershausen
Settlement_Description: The settlement was first mentioned in 990.

name: Grone
Settlement_Description: Northeast of the current Göttingen quarter Grone on the street to Harste, there existed the royal palace Grone and a connected settlement named Burggrone, which are first mentioned in 915 and 1101 respectively. The castle was destroyed by Göttingen citizens in 1294 and again in 1387, after which Burggrone was abandoned. The later village and current quarter Grone developed from the farm Altgrone, which belonged to the palace and is first mentioned in 1118-1137.

name: Olenhuser Warte
Settlement_Description: Watchtower in the defensive enclosure ('landwehr') of Göttingen, built on a hill north of the road. The road was closed off with a boom barrier.

name: Dransfeld
Settlement_Description: Perhaps a settlement developed around a church of St Martin, founded in the 9th century. Dransfeld was first mentioned in 960.
Town_Description: Traditionally, it is assumed that town privileges were acquired in or before 1305, but it is likely that the settlement was only a borough ('flecken') at that point. Full Münden town privileges were granted by Duke Otto of Brunswick in 1368.

name: Wellersen
Settlement_Description: First mentioned between 1015 and 1036. In the Middle Ages a village, nowadays only a manor. It is unknown whether the village was only partially abandoned or that it disappeared completely with the manor being built later.

name: Niederscheden
Settlement_Description: The settlement Scheden, first mentioned in 1046, was divided into Niederscheden and Oberscheden, of which the former was first mentioned separately in 1317. In modern times, both settlements have grown together again.

name: Volkmarshausen
Settlement_Description: First mentioned between the 8th and the 9th century. In 1345, a boom barrier was built here as part of the defensive enclosure ('landwehr') of Münden.

name: Reinser Turm
Settlement_Description: Watchtower of the defensive enclosure ('landwehr') of Einbeck, close to the former village Reinsen, built in 1407. It was first mentioned in 1454. Demolished in 1800.
Toll_Description: A toll of the Amt Salzderhelden, which was levied at the Reinser Turm, was first mentioned in 1548.

name: Strodthagen
Settlement_Description: At the Sülberg in Strodthagen there existed a regional law court, which was moved later into the settlement and is still mentioned in the 16th century as local court.
Toll_Description: The toll is mentioned in charters from 1394 and 1395 and was still levied in the 18th century.

name: Pilshäger Warte
Settlement_Description: Watchtower, erected by duke Otto I the Evil of Brunswick-Göttingen between 1383 and 1394.

name: Moringen
Settlement_Description: First mentioned in 1002-1003. There was a royal court here, and from 1158 a castle of the Dukes of Brunswick-Lüneburg.
Town_Description: The date of acquisition of town rights is unclear. Already in the middle of the 14th century, there existed an urban community; Uslar town privileges are reiterated in 1384.
Fair_Description: Moringen acquired the right to hold a fair four times: in 1390 on St Margaret, founded by duke Otto I of Brunswick-Göttingen; in 1432 on St Michael, founded by Otto II; in 1582 on the Presentation of Mary, founded by duke Erich; and in 1684 on Sunday Judica, founded by duke Ernst August.
Toll_Description: A "new" toll in Moringen is pawned by duke Erich of Brunswick-Calenberg to Cord von Mandelsloh in 1514.

name: Hulst
Settlement_Description: A chapel in Hulst is first mentioned in a 14th-century copy of a document from 1108.
Town_Description: Hulst was granted town privileges around 1180.
Fair_Description: The existence of a fair in Hulst is known from statutes from before 1482, which mention that cloth not produced in Hulst was only allowed to be sold during the free fair.
Toll_Description: The toll in Hulst was leased by the count of Flanders to three persons in 1306. Toll regulations are known from 1317, when the toll was owned by the Lord of Asse. Citizens from Hulst that were born as free Flemings were exempted, as were citizens from Axel, Hugersluis, Biervliet, Saaftinge, St. Jansteen, Kallo, Rupelmonde, Sluis, Damme and Nieuwpoort, knights, the clergy, lombards and other groups. Toll was levied on ships, cargo and animals. Transit trade was charged only half tariffs. In 1473 the toll came into possession of the Lords of Herzele and Roubaix. A tollaccount on hopped-beer from the Vier Ambachten levied in the harbours of Hulst and a.o. Terneuzen dated 1439/40 is preserved.

name: Biedenkopf
Town_Description: First mentioned as a town in 1254. The exact year of the town charter is not known.

name: Gladebeck
Settlement_Description: First mentioned between 1015 and 1036. A castle of the dukes of Brunswick existed here possibly since 1318, first mentioned in 1447. It must have dilapidated in the late 16th century.

name: Einbeck
Settlement_Description: First mentioned in the time of Emperor Conrad II (1024-1039) as "predium" (estate) of count Udo of Katlenburg. The monastery of St Alexander was founded before 1085. South of it, a market settlement developed in the late 12th century.
Town_Description: Einbeck was mentioned as "civitas" in 1203 und 1239. A council is first mentioned in 1252, a town wall in 1264, and a "new" market in 1266. Braunschweig town privileges were granted in 1279.
Toll_Description: The safe conduct in Einbeck was changed into a road and bridge fee in 1417.

name: Diemardener Warte
Settlement_Description: Watchtower ('warte') was part of the enclosure ('Landwehr') of Göttingen, built in 1409. It still exists today.

name: Klein Lengden
Settlement_Description: First mentioned in the 8th or 9th century as 'Lengidi'. At first there was only Lengden, since 1022 a distinction was made between Groß- and Klein Lengden.

name: Wittmarshof
Settlement_Description: First mentioned in 1022. Originally called Wittmarshausen, it is mentioned to have been (partially?) abandoned in the 15th century. In the 16th century, the name Wittmarshof appears, which is probably related to its resettlement as folwark.

name: Gelliehausen
Settlement_Description: The settlement was first mentioned in a forged document from the 12th century.

name: Fegebankswarte
Settlement_Description: Watchtower of the defensive enclosure ('Landwehr') of Heiligenstadt, built in 1479. Plenary diets ('Landtag') of the Eichsfeld were held here. Demolished in the third decade of the 19th century.

name: Heilbad Heiligenstadt
Settlement_Description: Heiligenstadt was founded as a missionary-centre and as a King's Court during the 9th and 10th century. Marketplace in the 11th century.
Town_Description: Archbishop Siegfried II. of Mainz gave town privileges in 1227.
Fair_Description: Heiligenstadt owned four fairs in 1460, two more were added later.
Toll_Description: In 1294 the archepiscopal rights for tolls and safe conduct were moved from Beuren to Heiligenstadt.

name: Niedergandern
Settlement_Description: The settlement Gandern, first mentioned in 1118-1137, was divided into the three parts Nieder-, Hohen- and Kirchgandern, of which Niedergandern is first mentioned separately in 1294.

name: 's-Heerenberg
Town_Description: Town privileges granted on 8 September 1379 by Willem I, count of Bergh and lord of Bylant, knight. In 1494, the inn of Johan Splynter is mentioned.
Toll_Description: In 1376 the lord of Berge granted the town van den Berge a toll-right on the dikes and roads up to a maximum of 2 brabants per coach en 1 per cart, with exemption for the servants of the lord.

name: Hvalpsund
Ferry_Description: The age and character of the ferry connection between the region of Himmerland and the peninsula of Salling is uncertain. But a ferry probably existed in the 15th century, perhaps earlier. In 1532 the brothers Las and Christian Christiansen were granted a royal privilege to the ferry, a right they took over from their father. In 1549 the king ordered the nobleman Herman Skeel to build a ferry house at Hvalpsund and to keep a good ferryman and ferries for the crossing.

name: Aachen
Settlement_Description: First mentioned in 769, Aachen was the primary residence of the Carolingians and place of coronation for over 30 German kings.
Town_Description: Aachen was granted town rights, as well as market and mint rights, as "caput civitatum" (head of towns) and as "caput et sedes regni Theutonici" (head and seat of the German kings) on 8 January 1166 by Emperor Frederick Barbarossa. The document became known as the "Karlsprivileg" and made the town to a free imperial city.
Fair_Description: Emperor Frederick granted two fairs in 1166 (Jan. 9): Sunday Invocavit (Sunday before Eastern) during 15 days and eight days before St. Michael (Sept. 29) till 8 days after that.

name: Haagse Schouw
Ferry_Description: The ferry 'Dodinsveer' at the Dodinxlaan across the Rhine is already mentioned as a fief of Wassenaar in 1282/1284. A ferry house was first mentioned when the ferry was leased in 1619; it was rebuilt in 1629. Plans to replace the ferry with a bridge date from 1628, but were only realised in 1801.

name: Aligse
Settlement_Description: Evidence for earlier mentions in 826-872 and 1022 is based on falsified documents.

name: null
Toll_Description: A toll was collected in Wegeleben in order to maintain the stone bridge, it was confirmed in 1651.
Bridge_Description: At some point there was a stone bridge across the Bode in Wegeleben.

name: Aalst (Vlaanderen)
Settlement_Description: Earliest mention in 866, in an 18th-century copy, as "villa" in possession of the abbey of Lobbes. Situated on the left bank of the river Dender and on the medieval road Bruges-Cologne (possibly earlier the Roman road Boulogne-Cologne). The lords of Aalst built a castle in the 11th century.
Town_Description: The settlement was fortified in the late 11th century. At the end of the 12th century it was acquired by the counts of Flanders. A new town wall was built in c. 1200. A town hall ('schepenhuis') was built in the first quarter of the 13th century.
Fair_Description: In 1351 (Sept. 26) the count of Flanders granted two free fairs, both during 14 nights. The first starting 8 days before Sacramentsday and 8 days after that. The second on (8 days before?) St. Bavo (Oct. 1) and 8 days after that.

name: Wassenaar
Settlement_Description: Earliest mention in 1200, in a copy dating from 1305.

name: Abja
Settlement_Description: Manor that was first mentioned in 1551.

name: Ackendorf
Settlement_Description: In 1121 given as property to St. Lorenz' monastery near Schöningen. Probably of Slavic origin.

name: Aderstedt
Settlement_Description: The royal court in Aderstedt was acquired by the bishopric of Halberstadt in 1063 and became property of Ilsenburg monastery in 1086.

name: Gaujiena
Settlement_Description: The castle was built in the 13th century. Later, there was also a fortified borough ('Hakelwerk') nex to the castel.

name: Aerzen
Settlement_Description: Castle of the lords of Everstein, first mentioned around 1200. In 1293, we hear for the first time of a settlement ('oppidum') near the castle. It received borough ('flecken') privileges in 1589.
Toll_Description: Count Hermann of Everstein confirmed in 1385 that Hameln remained exempted from the toll in Aerzen as before.

name: Almricher Furt
Ferry_Description: A ferry across the Saale river in Tauschwitz is mentioned in 1323. According to Bergner, there existed a bridge or boardwalk before, mentioned in 1291 as "ponti in Wentzendorff, que contra Salam protenditur", but Böhme argues that Wenzendorf was more probably located opposite Bad Kösen, so that this mention probably refers to the bridge there and that a bridge near Tauschwitz/Almrich never existed.

name: Haga Kungsgård
Settlement_Description: Haga Royal manor was established in 1556 and served as a centre of Saltvik, Finström, Sund and Kumlinge bailiwicks in 1556-62 and again 1564-1621.

name: Agathenburg
Settlement_Description: The village was originally called Lieth, and first mentioned as such in 1199. The village was renamed Agathenburg when a manor house was built here with the same name in 1652.

name: Ageri
Settlement_Description: Village and Manor were mentioned in 1447.

name: Ahrbeck
Settlement_Description: Because of the likeliness of confusion with nearby Arpke, of which the name shares the same onomastic origin, the first certain mention of Ahrbeck can only be attested in 1406.

name: Ahrensbök
Settlement_Description: A chapel with a miraculous statue of the Virgin Mary existed in Ahrensbök around 1300, and is first mentioned in 1328. It became a pilgrimage destination. A Carthusian monastery was founded in 1397. The monastery was secularised in 1542, the settlement was abandoned and turned into a folwark in 1593.

name: Ahrenswohlde
Settlement_Description: First mentioned in a register of the castle Bremervörde between 1498 and 1500. At the time, the settlement consisted of three farms and two cottages.

name: Aidu (Viljandi)
Settlement_Description: The village was first mentioned in 1583. A hamlet ('Hof') was built between 1638 and 1688.

name: Aidu (Jõgeva)
Settlement_Description: The village and the Inn were first mentioned in 1583.

name: Aken
Settlement_Description: First mentioned with the name Waltherus de Aken in 1219. The Ascanian electorate princes and the dukes of Saxony owned a residence in Aken.
Town_Description: First mention as a town in 1271.
Toll_Description: A toll in Aken is first mentioned in 1295. In 1447, the castle and the town of Aken are pawned, including toll and ferry. In 1485 the burnt down town of Aken is granted exemption from toll and ferry fees on the Elbe for six years. In the 16th century, escorts ('Geleitsleute') are mentioned several times in the fiefdom ledgers ('Lehnsbücher') of the archbishops of Magdeburg.
Staple_Description: Aken loses its staple rights to Magdeburg

name: Alansi
Settlement_Description: The village was first mentioned in 1241. In 1417, the village including the hamlet ('Hof') and mill were given to Jacob Ronne. Shortly after that the hamlet in Alansi lost its importance.

name: Albersdorf
Settlement_Description: First mentioned in 1281. The village church dates from ca. 1230.

name: Aldekerk
Toll_Description: In 1436, the Duke of Geldern levied a land toll whose revenues are not preserved. The toll was later abolished due to a complaint by the town of Geldern.

name: Aldenhoven
Settlement_Description: First mention in a possibly falsified document from the last quarter of the 11th century. The place was fortified at the end of the 14th century.
Toll_Description: The Duke of Jülich levied a road toll in 1501. It is known that the annual income in 1501 and 1510/11 was 3 Mark and 6 Shilling. The toll was probably leased.

name: Alfeld
Settlement_Description: First mentioned in ca. 1019-1022. The settlement developed at a ford at the Leine river, which was secured by a castle (first mentioned in 1358).
Town_Description: Acquired town privileges between 1220 and 1258 and became the second-most important town in the diocese of Hildesheim.
Fair_Description: In 1501, two two-day fairs were mentioned in Alfeld, which took place "according to old custom" on St Nicholas and Sunday Letare. These probably went back to the time that Alfeld became a town. In 1456 three additional fairs were added, on St Vitus, St Gallus and on Sunday before All Saints' Day. The Vitus and Gallus fairs were extended with three-day cattle markets in 1619.

name: Alfhausen
Settlement_Description: First mentioned in 977. Around 1350 Alfhusen was called 'villa'.

name: Algermissen
Settlement_Description: First mentioned between 980 and 982. The settlement consisted of the two parts Groß and Klein Algermissen until the modern period.

name: Allaži
Settlement_Description: In 1562 Heinrich von Dohna received the area as a fief. Thereupon a manor house and a village developed.

name: Allendorf (Sauerland)
Town_Description: Made into a town by archbishop Friedrich von Saarwerden in 1407.

name: Türi-Alliku
Settlement_Description: Hamlet ('Wirtschaftshof') of the Teutonic Order, which was mentioned in 1429.

name: Aluvere
Settlement_Description: The village was sold to the Teutonic Order in the 15th century and thus belonged to the manor of 'Sommerhusen'.

name: Allmenhausen
Settlement_Description: First mention in a donation charter to Jechaburg monastery by Archbishop Adalbert I from 1133.

name: Almelo
Town_Description: From 1346 onward, Almelo gradually grew into a place with town-like characteristics. Town privileges were probably granted by Evert van Heeckeren and Beatrix II, lord and lady of Almelo, before 3 July 1376, probably between ca. 1363 and 1376.
Fair_Description: In 1346 (March 7) the bishop of Utrecht granted Arend van Almlo two free fairs, each for two days. Dates: 1) St. Georges-eve and -day (April 22/23), 2) St. Matthew apostle-eve and day (Febr. 23/24).

name: Alphen
Settlement_Description: Earliest mention in 709, in a copy dating from 1191. Next mention in the twelfth century.

name: Aldrup
Settlement_Description: Dispersed settlement ('bauerschaft'), first mentioned in the 9th or 10th century.

name: Bonames
Settlement_Description: First mentioned in 1039 as a 'locus'. 1292 called a 'ville'.

name: Alsleben (Saale)
Settlement_Description: A castle and a monastery were built in the 10th century. First mentioned in 961.
Town_Description: The year in which the town rights were granted is unknown. However, Alsleben was referred to as "town" in 1479.

name: Alstätte
Settlement_Description: First mentioned in a confirmation charter of bishop Werner of Münster of 1151. Mentioned as belonging to Münster cathedral in 1176.

name: Vecaduliena
Settlement_Description: The manor was first mentioned in 1354 as 'pagast Adolene'.

name: Alt Bukow
Settlement_Description: First mentioned as Buchowe in 1192. The adjective Alt ('old') was added after the foundation of the town Neubukow around 1250.

name: Hummuli
Settlement_Description: The area is mentioned in 1226, the manor was only built after 1470.

name: Alt Mölln
Settlement_Description: "Mulne" was first mentioned in 1188. The original Slavic settlement was probably located at the mouth of the Delvenau in the Mölln lake, near the current street "Ohlendörp". It was moved to Altmölln before 1194, when it was first mentioned, already with the addition "old".

name: Alt-Wolfsburg
Settlement_Description: The castle Wolfsburg on a crossing of the Aller river is first mentioned in 1135, and expanded by the von Bartensleben family after 1300.

name: Dąbie (Szczecin)
Settlement_Description: The hillfort Badam was destroyed by the Polish in 1121. The duke of Pomerania donated the adjoining settlement to the monastery of Kolbatz in 1176, but it went back to Pomerania in 1226.
Town_Description: Duke Barnim I granted the Magdeburg town law in 1260, changed to Lübeck town law in 1293 but returned to the former one in 1297.
Toll_Description: Duke Otto granted Altdamm the right to levy a toll on commodities in 1310.

name: Altencelle
Settlement_Description: A castle Celle is first mentioned before 1007, possibly in 983. The settlement acquired town privileges around 1249, but was moved 3 km downstream the Aller river in 1292, to the current location of Celle. Thereupon the original settlement became known as Altencelle ('old Celle').

name: Altenkirchen
Settlement_Description: Can be traced back to the founding of a parish church. This 'Antiqua Ecclesia' was however first mentioned in 1314.
Town_Description: In 1314 it was granted town rights. From the 15th century onwards, it was first an administrative seat and from the 17th century onwards the seat of the county of Sayn-Altenkirchen.

name: Altenstaßfurt
Settlement_Description: Probably location of a moot of the Eastern Saxonians, called in by Charlemagne.970 salines in Ostersalzhusen (district of Staßfurt) are given to Thankmarsfelde monastery by archbishop Gero of Cologne and his brother margrave Thietmar. Altstaßfurt thus gained market rights. 1035 the market is moved from Altstaßfurt to Nienburg

name: Altenweddingen
Settlement_Description: Given to St. Moritz' monastery by Otto I. in 937. In 1338 it is mentioned as deserted, but a family of Weddinge is reported to reside here into the 16th century.

name: Altenzaun
Settlement_Description: First secure mention in 1238; earlier mentions from 946 and 1150 can not clearly be connected to Altenzaun.
Ferry_Description: Altenzaun maintained a small passenger ferry.

name: Altgandersheim
Settlement_Description: Originally, the settlement was called Gandersheim until the foundation of the monastery of Gandersheim (the current Bad Gandersheim) in 852, whereupon the old settlement became known as Alt ('old') Gandersheim.

name: Altharen
Settlement_Description: Haren was sold to the bishop of Münster in 1076, who built a castle there. The name Haren was later transferred to the younger settlement on the river Ems, which developed in the 13th century. The old settlement thereupon came to be known as Alt-('old')haren.

name: Altenbreitungen
Settlement_Description: The settlement Breitungen, first mentioned in 933, consisted of three separate villages Alten-, Frauen- and Herrenbreitungen. Altenbreitungen is first mentioned in 1137. In 1950 it was merged with Frauen- and Herrenbreitungen into one village called Breitungen.

name: Borghorst
Settlement_Description: First mentioned in a charter in 967, when a women's convent was founded here. Sometimes mentioned as borough ('Wigbold') around 1512.

name: Altenberge
Settlement_Description: The parish village is first mentioned in 1142.

name: Althof
Settlement_Description: First mentioned in 1171, Althof was the location where the Cistercian monastery Doberan, called after a nearby Slavic village, was founded in 1171. After the destruction of the monastery in 1179, it moved into the village Doberan. The original location remained as a farm of the monastery that became known as Alt ('old') Doberan, later as Althof.

name: Altkalen
Settlement_Description: The castle Kalen was bestowed upon the monastry Dargun in 1174, a church was mentioned in 1232. Lord Borwin of Mecklenburg tried to establish a town in 1244 without succes. It was relocated by Lord Waldemar in 1281 as Neukalen. At the original location, the village Altkalen remained.

name: Hof Altona
Settlement_Description: Inn and farm, first mentioned in 1388.

name: Ambla
Settlement_Description: The place with a church was built in the 13th century. It was mentioned for the first time in 1253. The church was probably built by the Danes in 1221-23.

name: Alt Ruppin
Settlement_Description: A castle was constructed in the 12th century, first mentioned in 1256, which served as the seat of the counts of Lindow-Ruppin from the first third of the 13th century until their demise in 1524. The adjoining settlement developed as a borough in the 13th century, but only gained town rights in 1840. Merged with Neuruppin in 1994.

name: Altwigshagen
Settlement_Description: The settlement was first mentioned as part of the name 'dominus Henricus de Swerin dictus Oldogheshagen' in 1295. Location of an important castle, which fell into ruin in the 15th century.

name: Alverdissen
Settlement_Description: First mentioned in 1151. A planned town was founded by the count of Sternberg around 1300, but it never received full town privileges. It is characterised as town in 1410, but only as borough ('weichbild') in 1464.

name: Allzunah
Settlement_Description: The settlement developed from the glassworks Franzenshütte, which were founded in 1691.

name: Embūte
Settlement_Description: The Teutonic Order built the old castle between 1245-50. However, it may have been built later, in 1265. Until 1583 it was the domain of the bishop.

name: Amelinghausen
Settlement_Description: First mentioned in 1236. From ca. 1300 seat of an administrative division ('vogtei'), later a law court is attested.

name: Amelungsborn
Settlement_Description: Cistercian monastery, founded between 1123 and 1135. According to the Annales Cistercienses, the monks moved in in 1135. The monastery became Lutheran in 1568.

name: Amersfoort
Settlement_Description: Amersfoort is first mentioned in 1028. It developed from a bishop's court that is first mentioned in 1203. A hospital is first mentioned in 1378.
Town_Description: Town privileges granted before 12 June 1259 by Henry I van Vianden, bishop of Utrecht.
Fair_Description: In 1331 the town obtained permission from the bishop of Utrecht for another two fairs next to the existing one with St. Gallen (Oct. 16): 1) with Eastern, 2) with St. Bartholomeus (August 24). In 1432 merchants from Amersfoort are first found on the fairs at Frankfurt. In 1478 (Febr. 22) a free fair for horned cattle with safe-conduct for the visitors was obtained from the bishop. Regular income from the market and year-toll and from the toll on the road outside the Rode poort (gate) and Slijkpoort and from the year-toll and toll on the road at the Kamp- and Bloemendaalse poort are found in the town-accounts dated 1464-'72. In 1562 the king collected 90 pounds at the   Kamp- and Bloemendaalse gates and 80 pound at the Slijk- and Utrechtse gates.
Toll_Description: A toll of the bishop of Utrecht in Amersfoort is first mentioned in accounts from 1325/26, but must have existed since the 13th century. It was a fair toll as well as a transit toll for land transport.

name: Ammensen
Settlement_Description: The village was first mentioned in 1093.
Toll_Description: A toll of the dukes of Brunswick-Lüneburg in Ammensen is mentioned in 1412, 1502 and 1567.

name: Ammern
Settlement_Description: First mention in 897. Archaeological finds indicate dense settlement in Germanic and Frankish times. Possibly it was an important manor.

name: Amöneburg
Settlement_Description: In 721 a monastery was founded by Boniface, but traces of habitation date from the 7th century. A castle is first mentioned in 1165.
Town_Description: Town foundation probably at the beginning of the 13th century by the Archbishop of Mainz. Since 1260 mentioned as 'civitas'.

name: Oudeschans
Settlement_Description: The fortress ('schans') Bellingwolderschans was constructed in 1593. Later it became known as Oude Schans.

name: null
Harbour_Description: A harbour was first mentioned in 1449, but is probably as old as the town itself. The character of the harbour is unknown. A pier is shown at the south side of the mouth of a small river, Helligånds Å, on a copper engraving of Nykøbing Mors in Resen’s Atlas Danicus from 1677.

name: null
Bridge_Description: In its beginnings, the bridge was exclusively used by Pforte monastery. The bridge was probably built between 1172 and 1195, but is first mentioned in the sources in 1289 as "bridge of Wenzendorf" (Wenzendorf was probably a village opposite Bad Kösen, which was deserted later). In 1393 a wooden bridge is mentioned, which is reconstructed in stone in 1404 at the latest. It was probably last referred to as bridge of Wenzendorf in 1347. The Chronicle of Sixtus Braun from 1393 first refers to the bridge as Kösen bridge. In 1890 the historical bridge was destroyed by floods and a new bridge was opened to public traffic in 1893.

name: Voorburg
Settlement_Description: Earliest mention in 918-948, in an eleventh century copy.

name: Anholt
Settlement_Description: In the 12th century the lords of Zuylen built a castle near which the settlement grew. It was first mentioned in 1234.
Town_Description: Town privileges were granted in 1349 by Dietrich of Zuylen.
Toll_Description: The Lord of Batenburg-Anholt levied a land toll from 1475. The exact localisation as well as revenues are not known.

name: Anloo
Settlement_Description: Earliest mention in 1139, in a sixteenth century copy.

name: Ankum
Settlement_Description: The settlement is first mentioned as 'locus' in 977. The fortified parish church is first attested in 1169. From the end of the 12th century often mentioned as 'villa'.
Fair_Description: A fair in Ankum is first clearly attested in 1580, but possibly goes back to the 13th century.

name: Annaburg
Settlement_Description: The settlement was originally called Lochau, first mentioned in 1339. In 1528 it is called small town ('stetlein'). After the construction of the castle Annaburg, named Anna of Denmark, the wife of Elector August, in 1572-1575, the settlement became known after the castle.

name: Annarode
Settlement_Description: First mention of the village in 1400.

name: Emburga
Settlement_Description: In the 13th or 14th century, a castle was built probably by the Teutonic Order.

name: Annikvere
Settlement_Description: Village that belongs to the Manor of Oberpahlen castle, first mentioned in 1583.

name: null
Toll_Description: In 1421, toll rights were granted to Herdecke, which according to the document had existed "since time immemorial". The aforementioned bridge toll was presumably levied as early as 1392. In 1421, Duke Adolf of Kleve-Mark transferred the bridge toll to Herdecke Hospital. Tariffs  and revenues are not known.
Bridge_Description: Written evidence for the existence of a Ruhr bridge in Herdecke first appears in the 13th century, when it became property of the Herdecke monastery. At the end of the 14th century, the bridge belonged to the counts of Cleves-Mark. In 1410, the bridge was apparently destroyed, since a new bridge with stone pillars was to be built, which only happened in 1421. The bridge was destroyed by floods in 1514 and rebuilt afterwards.

name: Vegesack
Settlement_Description: An inn "Zum Vegesack" is mentioned around 1500. At the end of the 16th century, a settlement developed around the harbour basin.
Harbour_Description: Because large ships had ever greater trouble reaching the harbour of Bremen due to the silting up of the river Weser, a new harbour basin in Vegesack was planned in 1618. The plans were realised between 1619 and 1622. However, travel accounts of the Utrecht antiquarian Aernout van Buchel from 1587 and 1591 attest that the harbour of Vegesack was used as a landing place for sea-going ships on the way to Bremen already before the construction of the harbour basin.

name: Apen
Settlement_Description: Around 1200, a castle existed in Apen, and from 1550 a fortress, which became an administrative and market centre.
Toll_Description: A butter toll in Apen is first mentioned in 1275, but possibly older. Additional tolls were levied on wagons and ships, as well as cattle driven through the village. The toll belonged to the Counts of Wildeshausen, later Oldenburg. Toll registers exist a.o. from 1428 and 1565.

name: Sevel
Settlement_Description: The village of Sevel was first mentioned in 1330-48 and again in 1467, but is significantly older. The parish church is from either the 12th or 13th century.

name: Stadtlengsfeld
Settlement_Description: First mention of the castle Lengsfeld in 1137.
Town_Description: In 1359 the settlement was granted market rights. It probably became a town at the end of the 14th century.

name: null
Bridge_Description: A bridge across the Werra in Frauenbreitungen is first mentioned in 1137.

name: Brilon
Town_Description: Raised to a town in 1220 and granted Soester rights.

name: Aabenraa
Settlement_Description: Presumably founded in the 12th century in the bottom of Aabenraa Fjord, where a small river, Mølleåen, runs into the fjord.
Town_Description: A castle, Aabenraahus, was constructed at the end of the 12th century, presumably by Duke Valdemar, the later king Valdemar II of Denmark (1202-1241). The castle is believed to have been decommissioned in the beginning of the 1400s, when a new castle, Brundlund, was constructed. Town law was granted by king Valdemar II the Victorious (1202-1241) probably in the period 1234-1241, and confirmed in 1335 by a new town lord, Duke Valdemar V of Schleswig. King Valdemar II likely also granted Aabenraa the first town privileges, but the oldest preserved privileges is from 1435. In the 1500s the town privileges were confirmed and expanded. In 1576 and 1610 the town was devastated by fire.
Harbour_Description: A wharf is mentioned in the oldest town law, probably from the first half of the 13th century, and the port of Aabenraa is mentioned again in 1257. A late medieval wharf was restored in 1609. The port was frequently used by Hanseatic ships, for example from Lübeck in 1399.

name: Apollensdorf
Settlement_Description: The village is first mentioned as Boldewinsluch in 1293.

name: Appels
Settlement_Description: Earliest mention in 707, in a copy dating from 941. Next mention in 1145.

name: Appingedam
Settlement_Description: First mentioned in 1224, but Appingedam probably already existed around 1000. Archaeological research shows evidence for habitation during the mid-twelfth century along the Damsterdiep where later Appingedam was located; around 1200, Appingedam had a market function.
Town_Description: Appingedam developed urban qualities in the 13th century with the establishment of a law court and market. With the privileges officially confirmed on 24 May 1327 in the 'buurbrief', Appingedam can be considered to have become a town.
