The 'buurbrief' also mentions the control of measures and weights three times a year, which indicates the existence of a weigh-house.
Fair_Description: The so-called ‘buurbrief’ of 1327 mentions stipulations which point at trading activities in Appingedam around that time: the control of measures and weights on three days per year, and the control of coin forgery and clipping. This has let some authors believe that fairs were held on these days: mentioned are court days after the octave of Easter, after the Nativity of Mary (September 9) and on the octave of Epiphany (January 13). However, Benders’ extensive study shows that fairs in Appingedam probably took place at different dates. <br> At least from the early fifteenth century onward, merchants from Groningen sold cloth at Appingedam. Probably, this already took place during the first half of the fourteenth century, or even during the thirteenth century. The first explicit mention of a fair in Appingedam dates from 1308, but it is unclear when it took place. Benders deduces this fair as the fair (‘kermis’) related to the celebration of the consecration of the church of Saint Nicholas (‘Nicolaaskerk’), a fair which is first mentioned in a charter of a guild (‘gildebrief’) in 1449. Based on stilistic characteristics, this church has been dated back to the first half of the thirteenth century, and was dedicated to Saint Nicholas in 1238. In 1504, Georg, duke of Saxony etc granted the rights for four fairs and a weekly market on Wednesday. Benders rejects earlier doubts about the actual existence of this piece: in 1536 or halfway the sixteenth century, Appingedam asked the emperor for its confirmation. However, clear evidence that all four actually took place is still lacking, just like indications for their success. Benders suspects that the Friday after the Sunday after Eastern (Friday after Quasimodo Sunday) has been the consecration day of the Nicholas Church. According to the charter of 1504, the fair on this day lasted eight days. <br>The charter of 1449 mentions another ‘kermis’: the fair of the monastery church of the Augustinians. The monastery was founded around 1325. According to a source dating from the beginning of the sixteenth century, this fair (‘Broederkermis’) lasted for eight days from the Sunday after the Feast of the Cross (the Sunday after September 14), and linked up to the free fair in Groningen (which took place fourteen days around September 8, ending on September 15). In 1504, the ‘Broederkermis’ was moved to the Saturday fater the Feast of the Cross; it is indicated that it lasted eight days. According to the history written by Johan Rengers van Ten Post (1542-1626), the most important fair of Appingedam took place on September 21 (eight days before Saint Michael), and lost much of its importance from 1536 onward, when the fair of Groningen was extended with eight days. <br>The two other fairs mentioned in 1504 took place on the day before the Assumption of Mary (August 14) and the day before St. Ursula and the Eleven Thousand Companions (October 20). The fair on August 14 lasted eight days, the duration of the fair on October 20 is unknown.

name: Arnstein
Settlement_Description: First secure mention of the castle in 1159. It has been the property of the counts of Mansfeld since 1387. The castle was already mentioned as ruinous in 1736.

name: Arcen
Fair_Description: In 1503 (Sept. 26) the duke of Gelre granted on request of the lord of  Arcen two free fairs for cattle and trade with safe-conduct and a weekly market on Wednesday. Dates fairs: 1) first working-day after St. Marcusday evangelist (April 25) during two days, 2) first working-day after St. Luke evangelist (Oct. 18) also for two days. With a conduct and tariff.
Staple_Description: Recurrent pretensions that the staple here was older then in Venlo. In 1413 en 1434 the duke of Gelre took side of Venlo. In the years 1514-'38 there was a quarrel about this between Venlo and the lord of Arcen and Zaltbommel. In 1541 the skippers of Nijmegen stated they had always loaded grain at Arcen without payment in Venlo.

name: Arendsee
Settlement_Description: In 1184 a benedictine monastery was founded in close proximity to a village.
Town_Description: It is uncertain whether the place received any town rights. Though, the place was reffered to as 'oppidum' in 1289 and 1381. However, in 1445 the town is still mentioned as a 'Flecken'.
Fair_Description: In an official schedule from 1719, Osterburg, Arendsee and Bismark each held six fairs. It can be assumed that some of these had existed for a while to this point.

name: Arensburg
Settlement_Description: Around 1300, a castle was constructed to control the pass near Steinbergen, first mentioned in 1385. Possibly, the 12th-century castle Steinburg stood at the same location.

name: Arneburg
Settlement_Description: Around 925 Henry I erected the castle Arneburg at the border to the Slavic area of settlement; it is first mentioned in 978. The castle was destroyed at the end of the 10th century, but rebuilt by Henry II in 1006.
Town_Description: The settlement is mentioned as 'civitas' as early as 997, and again in 1338. Formal privileges were not granted. In the 14th century there was a town council and court. In later times the settlement is usually referred to as borough ('Flecken') or small town ('stedtlein').
Fair_Description: In 1672 three fairs and cattle markets were granted, on Thursday and Friday after Quasimodogeniti and after Galli, as well as a fair on 27th June. It can be assumed that some of these had already existed before the Thirty Year's War.
Toll_Description: The citizens of Stendal are granted exemption from the toll at the castle Arneburg as early as 1160. In 1345 exemption from toll and safe conduct is granted to the citizens of Stendal, Salzwedel, Osterburg, Tangermünde, Seehausen, Werben, Havelberg and Arneburg. Further mentions of the toll during the pawning of Arneburg in 1414 and 1416, 1441 and 1452. In 1482 first mention of a wagon toll, further in 1487 as a road toll. In 1492 the toll is mentioned as belonging to the margrave.

name: Aschersleben
Settlement_Description: In the 9th century mentioned as the property of Fulda monastery, given to the property of Ilsenburg monastery in the 1086 and since the 11th century property of the counts of Ballenstedt.
Town_Description: In 1266 the place received Halberstädt town rights that were given by Henry II. from Anhalt. The town was member of 'the Hanse' between 1426 and 1518.
Fair_Description: The exact dates of the fairs in Aschersleben are unknown.

name: Arnhem
Settlement_Description: Earliest mention dates from 893. Before the 13th century domains in Arnhem were in possession of the monasteries of Prüm and Elten and the count of Guelders.
Town_Description: Shortly before 1200 a merchant settlement developed on the shore of the Rhine, which acquired town privileges on 13 July 1233 from Otto II, count of Guelders. A town council is mentioned in 1291, a burgomaster in 1339.
Fair_Description: Three fairs are mentioned in 1240, their dates are known from 1294/95. In 1459, and additional cattle fair was granted. Since the middle of the fourteenth century or even earlier, the dukes of Guelders had been pawning or leasing out the cashing of all three Arnhem fairs to private persons, and since 1372 to the town of Arnhem itself. Around the middle of the fourtheenth century, town accounts of Deventer mention a fair in Arnhem 'in festo Palmarum' or '(in) Palmis', which could refer to the Mid-Fast fair.Fairs took place on the 'Nieuwe Markt' (New Market), the present-day 'Korenmarkt', which was in function from the second quarter of the thirteenth century, whereas the weekly market took place on the old market. Cloth was the most important commodity traded on the fairs in Arnhem, followed by wine and salt.
Toll_Description: A land toll ('weggeld'), owned by the landlord, the duke of Guelders, was levied at all four mayor town gates: the Sabelspoort, Rijnpoort, Velperpoort, and Sint-Janspoort. The toll at the Rijnpoort (Rhine gate) linked up with the ferry, which stimulated trade-related traffic coming from the ferry to enter Arnhem. Most traffic used the Rijnpoort; profit from the Sint-Janspoort was quite low.
Staple_Description: Officially, Arnhem had no grain staple, but around the mid-fifteenth century, from 1437-1439 onward, the town de facto forced people to offer their load of grain for sale in Arnhem when passing by on the river Rhine. The grain market was located outside the Rhine gate, near the harbour.

name: Arnsberg
Settlement_Description: The settlement is first mentioned in 1082, but goes back to the castle "Alte Burg", which is already named in 1060.
Town_Description: The duke Gottfried III. granted Arnsberg in 1237 the town privileges of Lippstadt and urban freedom. Additionally the town expanded.

name: Choszczno
Settlement_Description: A Slavic or German settlement probably existed before it was first mentioned as Hoscno in 1234.
Town_Description: Founded in 1284 by the Ascanians. Mentioned as civitas in 1291, called new town ("nyeve stad") in 1310. The Angermünde town law was confirmed in 1441.

name: Arpsdorf
Harbour_Description: The Stör river was sometimes used for shipping up to Arpsdorf.

name: Aruvalla
Settlement_Description: Village and Manor that were first mentioned in 1417.

name: Artlenburg
Settlement_Description: The name goes back to the Ertheneburg, an early 9th-century castle erected on a crossing of the Elbe river, first mentioned in 1106. It was demolished in 1181 after the retreat of Henry the Lion of Saxony. The castle was succeeded by the settlement Artlenburg on the southern shore, although there has been much discussion about whether this was also the original location of the castle or whether it was located on the opposite shore of the river. Artlenburg is later mentioned as borough ('oppidum'); a ducal manor house was mentioned in 1414, which also served as inn for the ferry.
Toll_Description: A toll in Artlenburg is first mentioned in 1163. In 1188 Emperor Frederick I exempted Lübeck from tolls in the duchy of Saxony, except for Artlenburg, where each wagon had to pay 5 penny for crossing the river. This situation was confirmed in 1226. Although an agreement between the dukes of Lauenburg and the town of Lüneburg from 1335 states that the salt toll from Lauenburg was to be moved to Artlenburg because of a change in salt transport routes from Lüneburg, it seems that this change never took place, or only for a short time, and the toll in Artlenburg remained limited to a ferry toll.
Ferry_Description: The ferry is first mentioned in Arnold of Lübeck's <cite>Chronica Slavorum</cite>, who narrates that duke Bernhard of Saxony wanted to move the ferry to Lauenburg after the destruction of the Erthenburg, but after the wishes of Lübeck, the emperor decided that it should stay at the original location.

name: Aruküla
Settlement_Description: The village was mentioned in 1582 and belonged to the manor Rathshof.

name: Aschaffenburg
Settlement_Description: First mentioned between 496 and 506 as Alemannian hilltop settlement.
Town_Description: Town privileges were granted in 1161 and 1173.

name: Aschendorf
Settlement_Description: The village was first mentioned in 849.
Toll_Description: A toll of the bishop of Münster in Aschendorf is mentioned in 1576, when it was pawned. Annual revenues are known from the years 1591-1605. In 1645, a toll collector could not be found because of decreased revenues due to the Thirty Years' War.

name: Aschenhütte
Settlement_Description: Glassworks, which came into existence at the middle of the 16th century.

name: Aizkraukle
Settlement_Description: A castle of the Teutonic Order was built in 1213. A manor and a fortified borough ('Hakelwerk'), which was first mentioned in 1526, were built nearby.

name: Assen
Settlement_Description: The monastery Mariënkamp was moved from Coevorden to Assen around 1259. The monastery was abolished around 1600, after which Assen became a regional centre of government. Granted the rank of city by Royal Decree, 13 March 1809.
Town_Description: Rond 1500 liep er waarschijnlijk al een doorgaande noord-zuid route via Assen van Halen (verder zuid naar Beilen/Meppel) naar Rhee (verder noord naar Vries en Groningen). Tevoren liep die alleen via Rolde.

name: Astfeld
Settlement_Description: First mentioned in 1153. Around 1448, Astfeld was abandoned. Resettlement of the area probably took place south of the medieval settlement.

name: Athenstedt
Settlement_Description: First mention in 1219 as villa Atenstede.

name: Buchenau
Settlement_Description: The settlement 'Bechenowe' is first mentioned in 1238 but possibly goes back to a deserted settlement.

name: Lēči
Settlement_Description: The manor was first mentioned in either 1466 or 1507.

name: Atzendorf
Settlement_Description: Mention in a gift certificate by Otto I. to the monastary of St. Mauritius in Magdeburg (MGH DD O I, nr. 74, S. 153f.).

name: Augustów
Toll_Description: A toll station was established in Augustów in 1569.

name: Auma
Settlement_Description: An Albert of Auma is first mentioned in 1248, but the castle itself only in 1328.
Town_Description: The small town ('Städtchen') at the castle is first mentioned in 1331, and might have acquired town privileges at the end of the 13th century. The settlement was fortified around 1360. In 1378 it was referred to as civitas. A council charter is attested in the second half of the 15th century. The town had local significance only, its economy was primarily based on agriculture.

name: Aurich
Settlement_Description: Around 1150, the parish church of St Lambert was built, around which a market settlement developed. The settlement was first mentioned around 1250 in Frisian judicial sources.
Town_Description: Sometimes mentioned as town from 1491 onwards. The first town rights were granted in 1539 by Count Enno II of East Frisia.
Fair_Description: The cattle and horse fairs in Aurich were important for merchants from the Netherlands and Westfalia in the 15th and 16th century. No less than 7 fairs are mentioned in the 16th century, although only the most important one is kwown with a date, the so-called "silent" market on Laetare.
Toll_Description: Toll on cattle, from which merchants from Groningen were temporarily exempted in 1427. The toll fee was raised from 1 to 5 Krumstert for each piece of cattle for foreign traders in 1548. In 1602, the count of Oldenburg complained about an increase in the toll fees at the Imperial Chamber Court. A document from 1641 attests that this toll was no longer levied for persons from Oldenburg at the time.

name: Ústí nad Labem
Toll_Description: A toll in Ústí nad Labem is first mentioned in 993; it probably was a toll on the Elbe river. According to a report of skippers from Pirna from 1577, the grain toll tariffs in Ústí nad Labem had tripled in eight years time.

name: Baarle
Settlement_Description: Earliest mention of Baarle in 1237. After parts of the village were given to the lord of Breda by the duke of Brabant, the village was divided into two administrative units: Baarle "onder den Hertog" for the Brabant parts, and Baarle "onder Nassau" for the Breda parts. This division became a national border in the Treaty of Westfalia (1648) and exists until today.
Toll_Description: The Hanseatic settlement ('Kontor') in Bruges complained about a raise of the toll tariff in Baarle in 1468.A memorandum from 1436 makes mention of a tollpost of the toll from Breda being in Baarle.

name: Baarn
Settlement_Description: Baarn developed as a settlement in the eleventh century. Its first mentions in historical sources dates from 1308.
Town_Description: Baarn exists as a settlement since the 11th century. Town privileges granted between 21 October 1346 and 14 February 1390, by John ('Jan') of Arkel.

name: Baasrode
Settlement_Description: Earliest mention in 821, in copy dating from circa 1300.

name: Bäbelitz
Settlement_Description: The village is first mentioned in 1236.

name: Baben
Settlement_Description: First secure mention in 1281; possibly in 1215 within a name, even though it cannot be proven that the person actually came from Baben.

name: Babimost
Settlement_Description: One of the oldest settlements and parishes in the area, developed close to a castle that already existed in 1000. The village passed into the possession of the monastery Obra in 1257.
Town_Description: Mentioned as oppidum in 1329. King Wladislaw II granted the Magdeburg town law before 1397, Sigismund I granted more privileges in 1539.

name: Bacharach
Toll_Description: (1) From 1225/26 the Count Palatine levied a river toll on the Rhine. Only short interruptions of customs operations are to be assumed, f.e. 1269 to 1272 and 1317 to 1320. In 1360/80, the river toll was united with the "Ruderzoll" that was levied by the Archbishop of Cologne.The annual yield amounted to 7000 pound Heller in 1316/17. For exact tariffs see the source listed below.(2) Together with the river toll, an escort fee was levied by the Count Palatine.

name: Badbergen
Settlement_Description: First mentioned in 1175. In 1249, the settlement is called 'villa'.

name: Baddeckenstedt
Settlement_Description: The main farm of the castle Wohldenberg was located in Baddeckenstedt.

name: Badingen
Settlement_Description: Became property of the bishopric of Brandenburg in 1270, but the settlement and a castle already existed in early German times. Referred to as little town (oppidulum; 'Städtchen') in 1459.

name: Badra
Settlement_Description: First mention in 1157 (MGH DF I 187). Mentioned in a donation charter to Walkenried monastery in 1197.

name: Bække
Settlement_Description: The village of Bække was first mentioned in King Valdemar's Cadastre c. 1231, but is older. The parish church is from either the 12th or 13th century.

name: Bāliņi
Settlement_Description: A village called 'Balem' was first mentioned in 1560 and belonged to the Idwen ('Idus') Manor. Today, the single hamlet belongs to the village 'Vērsis'.

name: Bamberg
Settlement_Description: First mentioned in 902. Settlement is archaeologically attested since the Merovingian period. Seat of a diocese since 1007.

name: Banteln
Settlement_Description: The place was first mentioned in 997.

name: Barbis
Settlement_Description: The village was first mentioned in 1384.

name: Barchel
Settlement_Description: First mentioned in 1340. There were 7 farms and one cottage in Barchel around 1500.

name: Jägerbrücke
Bridge_Description: A stone bridge in Arnsberg was built by Elector Salentin in 1575. It was destroyed by floods in 1619. A new wooden bridge was only built in 1655.

name: Wiegendorf
Toll_Description: Secondary station of safe conduct ('Beigeleitsstelle) of Weimar, which was pawned from 1489 until at least 1528. Accounts remain from 1530-1569, according to which the village was also frequented by long-distance trade. Regulations of safe conduct with tariffs date from 1535/36.

name: Banzendorf
Settlement_Description: The village is first mentioned in 1365.

name: Bardowick
Settlement_Description: First mentioned around 785. Otto I granted the place market, mint and toll privileges in the 10th century. After the destruction of the town in 1189 at the latest, Bardowick lost its importance as trade centre to Lüneburg.

name: Barenburg
Settlement_Description: A moated castle to guard a street crossing was presumably built in 1247 by the count of Hoya. A borough ('flecken') probably came into existence in the 15th century, and is first mentioned in 1530.

name: Barendorf
Settlement_Description: The village was first mentioned in 1158.

name: Bargloy
Settlement_Description: Mentioned around 1000 in a tax register of the monastery of Corvey.

name: Bargteheide
Settlement_Description: Parish village with regional market function, first mentioned in 1314.

name: Belm
Settlement_Description: The place was first mentioned in 1150.

name: Barneveld
Settlement_Description: Earliest mention dates from 1174 in a possibly falsified seventeenth-century copy. Barneveld is at least mentioned from 1307 onward.

name: Barnstorf
Settlement_Description: The name of the settlement is first mentioned in an 890 tax register of the abbey of Werden, but the settlement is clearly older. Moreover, it had borough ('flecken') privileges, but it is unknown when these were granted.

name: Barßel
Settlement_Description: The place was first mentioned in 1330.

name: Bartelsdorf
Settlement_Description: The settlement was first mentioned in 1230.

name: Bartoszyce
Settlement_Description: A castle of the Teutonic Order was built in 1241.
Town_Description: First mentioned as a town in 1326, but it was officially founded by Grand Master Luther of Braunschweig in 1332 with Kulm town law.

name: Barsikow
Settlement_Description: The village is first mentioned in 1433.

name: Castrop
Settlement_Description: Castrop was originally a farm, which in 1236 became the property of the counts and later dukes of Kleve. In 1484 the settlement around the courtyard received a freedom privilege for court and parish.
Town_Description: The settlement got town privileges in 1470.

name: Barth
Settlement_Description: Developed from an old castle. The Land of Barth is first mentioned in 1159, in 1225 a Petrus burchravius de Bart.
Town_Description: Lord Jaromar II of Rügen granted the Lübeck town law in 1255.

name: Bartolfelde
Settlement_Description: The village was first mentioned in 1222.

name: Barum
Settlement_Description: The village was first mentioned in 1140.

name: Baruth
Settlement_Description: A castle and adjoining borough existed already in Slavic times.
Town_Description: Granted town law by the Elector Johann Georg I in 1616.

name: Barwice
Settlement_Description: First mentioned in 1286, already as town ('civitas').
Town_Description: The town ('civitas') Barwitz is first mentioned in 1286. It developed along the old salt road to Kołobrzeg (Kolberg). A church was built around 1300. The town was in possession of Reimer Podewil and Hans Hechthausen in 1389. Lübeck town law is attested in 1409. It belonged mainly to the house of Münchow in 1479 and jointly to the Houses Münchow, Glasenapp, Wolde and Zastrow in 1523.

name: Mieszkowice
Town_Description: Founded by the Ascanian Albrecht III at a previously uninhabited location, first mentioned in 1298 as civitas. The town had the Strausberg town law.
Toll_Description: Elector Joachim I granted the town the right to levy a drawbar toll for foreign waggoners and carters to fund the maintenance of the dams and bridges in 1513.

name: Basdahl
Settlement_Description: First named on October 11, 1297 as the place of the peace treaty between Archbishop Giselbert of Bremen and Duke Otto of Brunswick. In the 14th to 16th century, the land diets of the bishopric Bremen were held at the Hohlen Grund at the Steingraben (probably a dolmen) on the road between Basdahl and Kuhstedt.

name: Bassen
Settlement_Description: The stream Bicina, which allegedly gave Bassen its name, is possibly first mentioned in a description of the borders of the diocese of Bremen from 787. The settlement itself is first mentioned in 1259.

name: Oberhof
Toll_Description: Regulations of safe conduct date from 1540, and are based on an older document from 1505. Another toll tariff dates from 1568.

name: Isserstedt
Settlement_Description: First mentioned in 780-802. The knights of Isserstedt, who are first mentioned in 1174, owned a castle here. It was destroyed in 1452.

name: Bassum
Settlement_Description: A house of canonesses was founded between 846 and 850; mentioned as Benedictine nun monastery from 1207 onwards. The monastery was rewarded royal privileges shortly after its foundation and was the only landowner in Bassum. In 1542, the monastery became a Lutheran ladies' foundation ('damenstift'). The settlement belonging to the monastery acquired limited borough ('weichbild' or 'flecken') privileges in the 16th century.
Toll_Description: A toll in Bassum is first mentioned in 1380, which was leased to the lords of Diepholz in 1407. There is a likely connection with the acquisition of the county Altbruchhausen by the counts of Hoya in 1388, and the rebuilding of the castle Freudenberg in Bassum in 1379, at which occasion also minting took place, which is attested until the 17th century. It is unknown whether the toll was also levied during the same time frame.

name: Bov
Toll_Description: A transit toll was installed in Bov in 1554. It belonged to the district ('amt') of Flensburg.

name: Baumgarten (Altmark)
Settlement_Description: First mention of a noble family of Bomgarden in 1157.

name: Baunach
Town_Description: Baunach acquired Bamberg town privileges in 1328.

name: Bauska
Settlement_Description: In the 14th century a castle of the Teutonic Order was built, near which a fortified borough ('Hakelwerk') was built.

name: Bautzen
Settlement_Description: A castle and the eldest church were probably founded in the 10th century. Before that, the area was inhabited by Slavs. In the northwest of the castle a 'suburbium' settled, which secured the ford crossing the river Spree.
Town_Description: In 1213 the town hall was erected. First mention of the town privileges in 1240. The town was situated along the Via Regia which favoured the economical developement.

name: Bawinkel
Settlement_Description: Mentioned in the early 10th century. Consisting of four farms at that time, later two more were added.

name: Bayreuth
Toll_Description: Toll station on the route between Nuremberg and Saxony since 1283.

name: Untersuhl
Settlement_Description: The village is first mentioned in 1261. In the village stood a watchtower that controlled the Werra crossing. In 1615 the tower was transformed into the village church.
Toll_Description: Secondary station of safe conduct of the Amt Gerstungen. Revenues are recorded since 1537.

name: Consrade
Settlement_Description: First mentioned in 1260. The name indicates that the village was a German foundation without Slavic predecessor. It belonged to the monastery Reinfeld from the 13th to 16th century.

name: Bebra (Rotenburg an der Fulda)
Settlement_Description: First mentioned in the beginning of the 9th century in the Breviarium Sancti Lulli.

name: Beckum (Werse)
Town_Description: Borough ('weichbild') privileges granted in 1220; characterised as "civitas" in 1224. Town privileges were possibly granted around 1231.

name: Beekbergen
Toll_Description: A land toll owned by the landlord, the duke of Guelders, was levied near Beekbergen.

name: Gredstedbro
Toll_Description: From the middle of the 16th century the river of Kongeå became an important toll boarder between Jutland and the duchies. Thus, Gredsted Bro became an important toll station, especially toll was collected from the export of oxen.
Bridge_Description: The age and character of the bridge is unknown. The place name is an explicit reference to a bridge, so a bridge was probably built in the early medieval period.

name: Beelitz
Settlement_Description: A burgward of Belizi was granted to the archbishopric Magdeburg by Emperor Otto III in 997, although it is unclear whether it refers to Beelitz or Belzig. A Slavic castle became Ascanian after 1150, a Gerhard von Belitz is mentioned in 1204. The newly founded town near the castle is referred to as oppidum in 1247. It gained some meaning as a place of pilgrimage in the context of the legend of the Holy Blood.
Town_Description: First mentioned as civitas in 1307. Since 1321 Beelitz is mentioned as one of the towns of the Mark Brandenburg. In 1341 town rights are confirmed for the first time. After 1350 the Ascanian castle was probably demolished when the town was fortified.
Fair_Description: In 1654 two free fairs exist, which might have been granted earlier.
Toll_Description: Toll station of the Margrave of Brandenburg, mentioned in 1433.

name: Beese
Settlement_Description: First mention in 1284; the stream of Beese is also mentioned early (1287). In 1420 and into the 16th century mention as little town ('Stedeken').

name: Benitz
Settlement_Description: The village is first mentioned in 1270.

name: Beeskow
Settlement_Description: Slavic settlement can be attested from the 10th century. On an island in the Spree river, a German castle was founded to control the Spree crossing. First mentioned in 1272.
Town_Description: The knights of Strele, first mentioned in 1202, founded the planned town around 1260. Magdeburg town law granted in 1285.
Staple_Description: In 1321 Beeskow was granted staple rights for rafted lumber on the Spree.

name: Beestland
Settlement_Description: The village is first mentioned in 1178.

name: Beetzendorf
Settlement_Description: The records which mention Beetzendorf in 1204 are lost today; the first remaining mention therefore occurs in 1304. In 1375 it is mentioned as a castle borough ('Burgflecken').

name: Behrensen
Settlement_Description: The place was first mentioned in 993.

name: Beilen
Settlement_Description: Earliest mention in 1139, in a sixteenth century copy.

name: Beinum
Settlement_Description: The place was first mentioned in 1209.

name: Białogard
Settlement_Description: A slavic castle mound from the 6th century became a town-like settlement in the 11th century and was was conquered by the Polish duke Boleslaw III in 1102.
Town_Description: The term ‘civitatem Albam’ first appears in 1107. The Pomeranian duke Bogislaw IV granted the German settlement Lübeck town law in 1299. A ducal castle was built in 1315 on the castle mound and later became the see of a castellan.
Staple_Description: Duke Bogislaw IV granted staple privileges for furs, wax and timber in 1307.

name: Belgern (Elbe)
Settlement_Description: There was probably a settlement before 900 which was situated around the church. It is first mentioned in 973. Later a castle to control the border was erected. The settlement developed into a market place.
Town_Description: Referred to as 'oppidum' around 1300. However, the year of the founding is uncertain. In 1572 town statutes were confirmed.
Toll_Description: In 983 emperor Otto I. gives the toll on the Elbe river in Belgern to the chapter of Meißen. In the late Middle Ages secondary station of safe conduct ('Nebengeleit') of Wettin in the system of safe conduct around Leipzig.

name: null
Ferry_Description: A ferry is mentioned near the castle Neuermühlen in 1603.

name: Bellingwolde
Settlement_Description: Earliest mention in 1438, in a copy.

name: Frauenbreitungen
Settlement_Description: The settlement Breitungen, first mentioned in 933, consisted of three separate villages Alten-, Frauen- and Herrenbreitungen. Frauenbreitungen was originally known as Königsbreitungen, after a Frankish royal court, and is first mentioned in 1073. A nunnery is first mentioned in 1165, after when it became known as Frauenbreitungen. In 1950 it was merged with Alten- and Herrenbreitungen into one village called Breitungen.

name: Bemmel
Settlement_Description: Earliest mention end of the twelfth century. Mention in 1178 might be falsified. Another mention in 1189 in a copy of ca 1485.

name: Benneckenstein
Settlement_Description: First mentioned in a letter of enfeoffment in 1319. In 1344 count Henry IV. of Honstein erected castle Benneckenstein around which a village developed. Frederick the Great granted town rights in 1741.
Bridge_Description: Mention of a Benickenbrugge (Benicken bridge) across the Rappbode in 1250-1260.

name: Bad Bentheim
Settlement_Description: Settlement near a castle, first mentioned around 1050. In the 16th and 17th century, the village had town-like characteristics, but town privileges were only granted in 1865.

name: Zbąszyń
Toll_Description: A toll station in Zbąszyń is attested since the first half of the 13th century.

name: Bentwisch
Settlement_Description: The village is first mentioned in 1235.

name: Beroun
Toll_Description: Part of the incomes of the toll in Beroun were given to the monastery of Prague castle by king Wenceslaus III (before 1306).

name: Berchem
Settlement_Description: Earliest mention in 1186, in a fourteenth century copy.

name: Berge (Gardelegen)
Settlement_Description: In 1327 the homestead of Berghe is given to count Otto of Braunschweig. Mention as village in the 15th century.

name: Bennungen
Settlement_Description: First mention in a charter by Henry V in 1112.

name: Darup
Settlement_Description: The parish village is first mentioned between 1188 and before 1300. An earlier mention of Dotharpa from 779 is based on a falsification.

name: Bergen an der Dumme
Settlement_Description: Castle of the lords of Bergen, which came to the lords of Lüneburg around 1203. The corresponding settlement was characterised as borough ('blek', 'stadtlein').
Toll_Description: In 1435, the dukes of Brunswick-Lüneburg set the rate to be paid for safe conduct in Lüchow and Bodenteich for citizens of Salzwedel at the same height as that in Bergen. Between 1548 and 1574, the toll collector Herman Schradt is mentioned in Bergen. Toll tariffs are known from the 16th century (StAB).

name: Bergen op Zoom
Settlement_Description: Bergen op Zoom is first mentioned in 966.
Town_Description: Town privileges were granted between ca. 1198 and 25 February 1212 by Godfried II, lord of Breda and Schoten. A hospital is first mentioned in 1246.
Fair_Description: In 1314 a cloth-hall and a weekly market on Monday are found and a weighhouse is built in 1355. Before 1337 there were already two fairs. In 1338 a cloth-fair is mentioned. In 1365 two fairs were arranged by the lord of the town: the famous free Eastern- and 'Koude'(Cold/Winter)-fairs (although named like this already in 1359) during 6 weeks, including 2 weeks for the journey there and back. The Koude-fair started 2 weeks after All Saints (Nov. 1), the Eastern fair 2 weeks after Maundy Thursday. In 1349 and 1356 the German emperor and the duke of Brabant granted free traffic through Brabant and Limburg, which afterwards was confirmed. In 1486 the emperor granted free travel to the fairs of Bergen in all his empire. In 1490 the period in which the merchants were protected on the way back of the Koudefair in the seigniory was enlengthened till Jan. 24 and in 1495 even during the whole year. This caused many protests from the towns in Flanders and was thus raised in 1498. In 1501 the freedom of the Eastern-fair was enlengthened 1 week and for the Koude-fair 3 weeks. This two fairs made a cycle with those in Antwerp with Pentecost and St. Bavo (Oct. 1). Origins and numbers of merchants from the Netherlands are visualised on a map for the period 1432-89. Socalled 'Craam' (market-stalls)-accounts are preserved and analysed for the years 1481-1542. In it are found the names and origin of the merchants and their goods and taxes. After 1530 the fairs were in decline as a result of the floods of 1530 and 1532 which hampered access of the harbour. As a result of the floods the Honte was better navigable, which was profitable for Antwerp. The important market for madder was relocated to Zierikzee.
Toll_Description: The landtoll in Brabant was partly collected in Bergen op Zoom. Yields of this comital landtoll are published for the years 1531-'85.
Staple_Description: Between 1388 and 1392, the Hanseatic wool staple was moved from Bruges to Bergen op Zoom. In 1474/'5 the staple of the English cloths is here.

name: Bergheim
Toll_Description: (1) The Duke of Jülich levied a land toll from 1375, after public peace in the same year. In 1389, a horse fee and a fee for safe conduct was included into the land toll. The annual yield in 1389/93 amounted to 1864 Mark per year. In 1398/99 it was 1553 Mark, in 1434 it was 833 Mark and in 1500/01 it was 1565 Mark per year. Around 1500 the fee for safe conduct was collected by an escort servant.(2) Furthermore, a road toll was levied by the Duke of Jülich from 1434. The exact tariffs are not known. The yield taken over half a year amounted to 8 Mark and 9 Shilling in 1434/35. In 1500/01 it was 34 Mark and 6 Shilling per year.

name: Bergholz
Settlement_Description: Former Slavic settlement, in 1228 an early German castle is constructed. The German settlement must have emerged around the same time, the village church can be proven since 1257. A manor lay nearby, its first lord can be proven in 1249.

name: Burgau
Settlement_Description: First mention in 1216. In 1486 the districts of Burgau and Jena were joined.
Toll_Description: A toll in Burgau is first mentioned in 1466. The safe conduct in the district of Burgau was collected together with that of Jena. The accounts of safe conduct in Burgau show that the amount of traffic was clearly related to the fairs of Leipzig and Naumburg and was especially significant for timber transports. Tariffs exists for the year 1538. A toll on timber rafting on the Saale river was also due in Burgau, from which the monastery of Pforta was exempted.

name: Berkhof
Settlement_Description: The place was first mentioned in 1393.

name: Barlinek
Town_Description: In 1278 Margraves Albrecht III and Otto V commissioned the knight Heinrich Toyte to found a town with Magdeburg town law, intended as an Ascanian fortress against Pomerania.

name: Bernau bei Berlin
Town_Description: Foundation of the town in 1230 at the earliest. In 1296 referred to as civitas.
Toll_Description: In 1532 Elector Joachim I permitted the town to levy a dam and road toll ('damm- und deichselpfennig') for the maintenance of the streets and causeways.

name: Vorbasse
Settlement_Description: The village of Vorbasse was first mentioned in 1330-48 and again in 1456, but is significantly older. The parish church is from either the 12th or 13th century.

name: Bernburg
Settlement_Description: First mention of the castle Brandanburg in a donation charter of Emperor Otto I to the Monastery of St Maurice in Magdeburg in 961. Archaeological evidence shows early medieval fortifications on the castle hill. A civic settlement developed in the valley along the main street that crossed the Saale with one or more fords.
Town_Description: The town consisted of the old and new town in the valley (Talstadt), which received town privileges after Magdeburg model in 1278, but were formally united only in 1561. The Bergstadt around the castle hill was raised into a town between 1442 and 1457 and was merged with the Talstadt in 1825.
Toll_Description: A toll in Bernburg is first mentioned in 1239, but it could refer to the bridge toll only. In 1537 the toll from Neundorf (Anhalt) is moved to the district of Bernburg. A regulation of safe conduct of 1563 settles the bridge and road toll.

name: Berneau
Toll_Description: Toll station in the second half of the 14th century.

name: Hörschel
Settlement_Description: The settlement is first mentioned in 932.

name: Markröhlitz
Toll_Description: Station of safe conduct on the road between Naumburg and Merseburg/Halle. It was levied together with the safe conduct in Freyburg. Twin safe conduct ('Doppelgeleit') of Freyburg. Revenues are known for the years 1449-1459 and 1479-1485. Regulations of safe conduct for the district of Freyburg from 1621 mention Markröhlitz as secondary station of safe conduct and list the fees for cargo and cattle.

name: Pełczyce
Settlement_Description: German settlement and a Slavic village next to a former fortification, mentioned in 1290 when a monastery was founded.
Town_Description: Mentioned as a civitas in 1290 and 1315, the year of foundation is not known. The town later became dependent of the castle built after 1315.

name: Bersenbrück
Settlement_Description: First mentioned in 1221; in 1231 the settlement was called 'villa'. In the same year, a Cistercian nunnery was founded. The monastery was a large landowner until it was closed in 1787.

name: Bērzaune
Settlement_Description: The settlement was owned by the Tiesenhausen-Family in 1229. The first written reference can be dated back to the 14th century. A castle was built in 1382.

name: Berßel
Settlement_Description: First mention as a villa in a gift certificate to Ilsenburg monastery in 1018.

name: Berstadt
Toll_Description: Mentioned as toll station of Fulda in 1357.

name: Pszczew
Settlement_Description: Originally a Pomeranian moated castle, mentioned in 1259 as a German settlement belonging to the bishop of Poznań, still mentioned as a village in 1350.
Town_Description: Already a town in 1412, a bailiff mentioned in 1435. The only remaining charter is the renewal of the founding privileges by the bishop of Poznań Johannes Lubranski after a fire in 1508.

name: Žebrák
Toll_Description: Mentioned as royal Bohemian toll station in 1391.

name: Bettmar (Hildesheim)
Settlement_Description: A watchtower of the defensive enclosure ('landwehr') of Hildesheim was built in Bettmar in the 15th century.

name: Bettmar (Vechelde)
Settlement_Description: The place was first mentioned in 1146.

name: Betzendorf
Settlement_Description: Earliest mention from ca. 1300. According to a 1450 register, the village consisted of 9 half farms ('plog') and 5 cottages.

name: Beuren
Settlement_Description: The village of Beuren is first mentioned in 1128. Foundation of a monastery before 1200. In 1550 the monastery is abandoned, after it had suffered heavy damages during the Peasants' war.
Toll_Description: Toll and safe conduct are moved to Heiligenstadt in 1294.

name: Beveren
Settlement_Description: Earliest mention in 1112, in a copy dating from c.1175.

name: Bevern
Settlement_Description: First mentioned in 822-826. The Renaissance country house ('schloss') of Bevern was constructed in 1603-1612.

name: Iława
Settlement_Description: There are traces of pre-Teutonic Order settlements close to the town
Town_Description: Founded in 1305 by Sieghard von Schwarzburg, the komtur of Christburg, new handfast granted in 1317 by Luther von Braunschweig, the Komtur of Christburg, the founding documents were expanded in 1333 by Günther von Schwarzburg, Kulm town law was granted

name: Bias
Toll_Description: Mentioned as a toll station and station of safe conduct in 1419, 1454 and 1479.

name: Biederitz
Settlement_Description: The tithe of Bidrici is mentioned as given to St. Moritz' monastery in Magdeburg when the bishopric of Brandenburg was founded.

name: Bielefeld
Settlement_Description: First mentioned between 856 and 866 in the possession of the monastery Corvey.
Town_Description: Münster town privileges were probably granted in 1214 and confirmed in 1287 and 1326.
Fair_Description: Three fairs are attested in Bielefeld: on the day before and after St John's Day (1338), on the day before and after St Leonard (1485) and on the day before and after St Michael (16th century).
Toll_Description: In 1224 the counts of Ravensberg acquired the right to levy a toll in Bielefeld.

name: Bielsk Podlaski
Toll_Description: Toll station from the late 15th to the mid-16th century.

name: Bienenbüttel
Settlement_Description: The first certain mention of the settlement is dated to 1238. An earlier mention as Biangibudiburg from 1004 could belong to Buntenburg near Lüneburg.

name: Bierbergen
Settlement_Description: The village was first mentioned in 1151.

name: Biesdorf
Settlement_Description: First mention of Biesdorf in 1375. It was a knightly residence until 1665.

name: Dillenburg
Settlement_Description: The place was based around the castle founded in 1240, which was on the long-distance trade route Frankfurt-Siegen-Cologne

name: Bilderlahe
Settlement_Description: The village was first mentioned in 1254. It was destroyed in 1519 together with the nearby castle Wohldenstein and rebuilt in 1523, when it became a seat of regional administration ('amt').

name: Billerbeck
Settlement_Description: First mentioned by name in 834. But a church was mentioned as early as 809.
Town_Description: In 1302 town privileges got granted and named as an 'oppidum' in 1312.
Toll_Description: The toll of Billerbeck was moved to Nienborg and Gronau at the beginning of the 16th century.

name: Binder
Settlement_Description: The village was first mentioned in 1153.

name: Bingen
Settlement_Description: A copy of the 11th century suggests a first mention of the settlement around 107. A castle called Klopp was built in the 13th century.
Toll_Description: There were two land tolls in Bingen owned by the Archbishop of Mainz: 1) A toll for cattle was probably levied from 1190 or 1194/98. In 1368 this was leased out for 200 guilders.2) The 'Gaupfortenzoll' was first mentioned in 1247. In 1390, 50 pounds Heller were collected.In addition, a river toll was probably levied around 1250. A transit toll on the Rhine in the 14th and 15th centuries, however, can be ruled out. It was probably only a fee for the ferry.

name: Birkenwerder
Settlement_Description: Founded probably around 1230 from a rampart nearby, which had been settled from the Bronze Age until the early German phase.

name: Birkesdorf
Toll_Description: From 1289, the Count of Jülich levied a land toll, which was localised in Velden until 1274. In the 'landfrieden' of 1375, a certain tariff per horse was fixed. For more detailed information see source. In 1375 and 1389/93, an fee for save conduct and a 'landfrieden'-toll were levied in addition to the existing tolls. In 1350 the revenue amounted to about 120 marks. In 1398/99 about 1897 marks.

name: Biskupiec
Settlement_Description: Built before 1389 as a fortress against the Lithuanians, no older settlement found
Town_Description: Mentioned as 'civitas Bischofsburg'; Bishop Heinrich III. Sorbom of Ermland grants the Kulm town law in 1395 to the civitas

name: Bilzen
Settlement_Description: Earliest mention in circa 1050, in a copy from the end of eleventh century.

name: Bischofswerda
Town_Description: In 1361 Bischofswerda was referred to as 'town' for the first time. In 1416 referral as 'oppidum'.

name: Bismark
Settlement_Description: Presumably a castle or a castle mound existed, which are not mentioned in the records. Town rights were never officially granted, despite being referred to as town in 1375 and having a town hall in 1413 - in the 15th/16th century the settlement was alternatly referred to as borough ('Flecken') or little town ('Stetlein').
Fair_Description: In an official schedule from 1719, Osterburg, Arendsee and Bismark each held six fairs. It can be assumed that some of these had existed for a while to this point.

name: Bissendorf (Wedemark)
Settlement_Description: The place was first mentioned in 1285.

name: Bissendorf (Osnabrück)
Settlement_Description: The village was first mentioned in 1160.

name: Bladel
Settlement_Description: Earliest mention in 1173-end of the thirteenth century

name: Blankenburg (Harz)
Settlement_Description: In 1123 Blankenburg is first mentioned. The settlement beneath the castle is mentioned as oppidum in 1195.
Town_Description: Since 1389 a council is proven in the town, in 1380 the village is granted Goslar rights, market- and coin privileges.

name: Blankenese
Settlement_Description: The settlement was first mentioned in 1301 and was built at a pier of the Elbe ferry.
Ferry_Description: Ferry to Buxtehude and Cranz. A landing pier for the ferry is first mentioned in 1301. It was also an important river crossing for oxen in the 15th and 16th century, although many merchants preferred the ferry in Zollenspieker because of the high prices of hay in Blankenese.

name: Blatzheim
Toll_Description: The land toll in the possession of the Archbishop of Cologne weas levied from 1425. In 1425, 285 guilders were recorded as revenue, although the period of the revenue is unclear.

name: Blumenhagen (Pasewalk)
Toll_Description: Shortly after 1524, a toll station was installed in Blumenhagen.

name: Bleckede
Settlement_Description: Duke Wilhelm of Lüneburg tried to develop the village Bleckede into the town Löwenstadt in 1209. The project failed, and in 1258, the settlement is mentioned under its old name Bleckede as borough ('flecken'). A castle is first mentioned in 1271.
Toll_Description: A land and water toll of the duke of Saxony-Lauenburg is attested from 1248. It was acquired by the duke of Lüneburg in 1308. The castle was often pawned without the toll, although the toll is mentioned in 1492 as belonging to the town council of Lüneburg. In the latter year, the toll fees are indicated as 4 Gulden, 1 loaf of bread and 2 buns for each ship. Toll registers exist from the year 1503 onwards.

name: Bleckenstedt
Toll_Description: Road toll of the dukes of Brunswick-Wolfenbüttel at the Damm (causeway) of Bleckenstedt, first mentioned in 1540/1.

name: Opheusden
Settlement_Description: First mention from probably the second half of the 9th century, in a copy from 1150-1158.
Toll_Description: A tariff for the land toll in Opheusden remains from the beginning of the 15th century.

name: Blerick
Settlement_Description: Earliest mention in circa 365, in a thirteenth century copy. Next mention in probably  802-822, in a copy dating from 1150-1158. Next mention in 1213.
Toll_Description: The Duke of Guelders possibly levied a fee for safe conduct here from 1355/61. In the tariff of the toll in Venlo, Blerick and Kessel were mentioned as secondary toll stations.

name: Bledzew
Settlement_Description: Originally a small Slavic settlement, given to the Cistercian Abbey of Semmritz in 1312 by Margrave Waldemar of Brandenburg. A new abbey was built in the early 15th century, and the entire convent of Semmritz moved to Bledzew in 1578.
Town_Description: The Polish king Kasimir IV granted the Magdeburg town law between 1458 and 1485 at the request of the abbot, renewal of the rights in 1565 and 1619.

name: Blexhaus
Settlement_Description: The settlement was first mentioned in 1546, but goes back to the family name 'Blexen', which is already mentioned in 1506. Around 1570, an inn is mentioned here.

name: Westerblokker
Settlement_Description: Earliest mention in 1289. In 1414, Westerblokker, Oosterblokker and Westwoud were granted town privileges by William VI, count of Holland. Together, these settlements became the ‘stede’ Westwoud. These settlements, however, never developed an urban character. The granting of town rights was part of an administrative reorganization in which a number of smaller settlements were granted town rights in order to provide them with a certain degree of self-government which replaced the need for the count of Holland's bailiffs ('baljuws'). The settlements kept their own separate settlement governments.

name: Blankenhain
Settlement_Description: In 1252 the village is first mentioned. A castle is mentioned in 1279.
Town_Description: In 1424 Blankenhain is mentioned as town. During the 15th century it is continuously referred to as town and market.

name: Domnovo
Settlement_Description: A castle of the Teutonic Order was mentioned in 1324, a settlement grew close to the castle hill, but the castle itself was destroyed in 1460
Town_Description: First granted town law in 1400, mentioned as a town for the first time in 1427, the handfast was renewed by Konrad von Egloffstein in 1480 with Kulm town law

name: Blokzijl
Settlement_Description: Earliest mention of a sluice in 1375. There existed three sluices for drainage of the surrounding countryside in the Zuiderzee, around which a settlement developed for the transshipment of peat to Holland. In 1438 there is still only mention of one house ('Blockes Huys'), but a larger settlement must have developed soon after. The name Blokzijl first appears in 1524. In 1581 the settlement was rebuilt into a fortress. Town-like privileges were granted by prince Maurice from 1589 onwards. Town privileges were granted by prince William III, 19 October 1672. Contemporaries objected these privileges, and they were revoked within several years.
Toll_Description: In 1504/5 the bishop of Utrecht levied a toll 'up den groeten zyl [Blokzijl] end up die zuetwende' with a yield of 56lb. (libra=pounds), in 1507/8 38lb. In 1518, 1529/1530 and from 1542 onwards a toll on peat was levied at the lock ('groote Zyll'), as established in a deed of bishop Philip of Burgundy. Accounts are preserved for the years 1565/1566 and combined with the toll at Zwartsluis for 1568. Steenwijk was exempted from toll payments. Yields of the toll are edited starting 1609 and of a peat-impost starting 1634.
Harbour_Description: Between the fifteenth and the seventeenth century Blokzijl was a port of transshipment at the Zuiderzee for peat from Steenwijk and the surrounding countryside. A skipper's guild was founded in 1490. A harbour basin was dug around 1550. After the construction of the canal Steenwijker Diep, which was finished in 1632, it was possible for larger ships to sail to Steenwijk, and transshipment in Blokzijl was no longer necessary.

name: Blomberg
Settlement_Description: First mentioned between 1230 and 1255. The settlement goes back to a castle built around 1200.
Town_Description: A charter from 1283 attests that Blomberg had Lippstadt town privileges. They were probably granted around 1260. After the destruction of the town during the Soest feud of 1447, the town was rebuilt and became a pilgrimage destination.

name: Bobbau
Toll_Description: The regulation of safe conduct of Bobbau states, that safe conduct in Bobbau is taken of those who travel from Dessau to Steinfurt or from Köthen to Bitterfeld and Delitsch or vice versa. Who was already promised safe conduct in Jeßnitz or Ragun may not gain it in Bobbau. Who travels to the fairs in Leipzig from Bobbau is given a permit, upon which he may pass free of payment if he returns via Bobbau. (LHASA, DE, Z 10, Nr. 27, Land Register über den Dessauischen Anteil 1547/49.)

name: Bobbin
Settlement_Description: The village is first mentioned in 1248.

name: Bobrowniki
Toll_Description: Mentioned as toll station in ca. 1349.

name: Bochnia
Toll_Description: A toll is first mentioned in 1267.

name: Bocholt (Münsterland)
Settlement_Description: First mentioned in 779 but might be much older. Called 'villa' in 1142.
Town_Description: The settlement got 'Weichbildrechte' in 1201. In 1222 the bishop of Munster granted town privileges.

name: Bochum
Settlement_Description: First mentioned in 1041. However, the oldest part of the city dates from the 9th century.
Town_Description: A charter from 1321, in which the settlement is called 'oppidum', has often been interpreted as a town privilege. However, Bochum remained a minor town or borough ('minderstadt') and seems to have acquired the status of a full town only in 1437.

name: Bockenem
Town_Description: Raised to a town by the counts of Woldenberg in 1300. The town was sold to the bishop of Hildesheim in 1314.

name: Bocklemünd
Toll_Description: The Archbishop of Cologne levied a fee for save conduct and a land toll here from 1389. In 1396, 2 to 3 white pfennigs per horse had to be paid. An average of 837 Mark per year was collected through this toll. In 1455, Bocklemünd served as a secondary toll for Königsdorf.

name: Böddensell
Settlement_Description: First mention around 1150 or 1160, after 1311 it was deserted, only to be re-settled in around 1500.

name: Bornum am Harz
Settlement_Description: The place was first mentioned in 1132.

name: Bodenburg
Settlement_Description: Settlement at a castle of the lords of Steinberg, after 1359 in possession of the dukes of Brunswick. Bodenburg is mentioned as borough ('flecken') in 1545.
Toll_Description: Around 1439 the bishop of Hildesheim started to levy a wine toll, like in Marienburg and Lamspringe.

name: Bad Bodenteich
Settlement_Description: First mentioned in 1130. Since 1290 a castle is mentioned; in 1323 the place became a borough ('weichbild').
Toll_Description: Toll of the dukes of Brunswick-Lüneburg, first mentioned in 1323. In 1435, the rate for safe-conduct for citizens of Salzwedel in Bodenteich was set at the same height as that in Bergen. Toll tariffs are known from the 16th century (StAB).

name: null
Toll_Description: Weser toll station, first mentioned in 1387. In lists of the Weser tolls in a 1584 Bremen complaint and a 1597 charter of the monastery Hardehausen, it is not mentioned anymore. The toll could have been related to the existence of a castle ('slot') in Bodenwerder, which is mentioned between 1399 and 1442.
Bridge_Description: A bridge across the Weser is mentioned already in 1289, but it was often destroyed by floods and drift ice, among others in 1573 and 1595.
Ferry_Description: When a bridge was not existing, the traffic was moved across the river by ferries.
Harbour_Description: According to the data from the Rinteln toll registers, Bodenwerder was the town most active in river transport between Minden and Hameln.

name: Boitzen
Settlement_Description: Mentioned in 1306 when property of the monastery Zeven in Boitzen had been damaged.

name: Boizenburg
Settlement_Description: In Slavic times the centre of the land Boizenburg, first mentioned in 1158. The old fortress was replaced by a new German fortress in 1170. A merchant settlement developed near the castle around 1180.
Town_Description: First mentioned as civitas in 1241. Citizens are mentioned in 1255. Lübeck town law was granted by the dukes Guncelin and Helmold of Schwerin in 1267. The town was pawned multiple times in the 14th century. The local economy mostly depended on the trade in wood, agricultural products and locally caught fish.
Fair_Description: An almanach from 1598 printed in Neudamm (Dębno) lists three fairs in Boizenburg: on Sunday Reminiscere and Exaudi and Simon and Jude's Day.
Toll_Description: A toll of the lords of Schwerin, later the dukes of Mecklenburg, in Boizenburg is first mentioned in 1216. In 1241, Hamburg was exempted from payment of the river toll on the Elbe in Boizenburg, as well as citizens from the duchy of Saxony, Lauenburg, Artlenburg and Altengamme for transporting their own grain in 1260. In the 1360s, there were complaints of Lüneburg citizens that they had to pay tolls for herring, from which they claimed to be exempted. It was declared in 1369 that they were only due for toll payments for salt, and not for herring and other commodities that they transported from Lübeck. In the 15th century, a toll of 2 shilling was levied for each wispel (unit of volume). A toll register from 1470/71 has been analysed by Nissen.

name: Vreschen-Bokel
Settlement_Description: First mentioned between 1260 and 1275. The addition 'Vreschen' appears for the first time in 1428 to distinguish the settlement from Bokel in the community of Wiefelstede.

name: Bornsen
Settlement_Description: The first certain mention dates from 1309. An earlier uncertain mention dates from ca. 1252.

name: Bölhorst
Settlement_Description: First mentioned in 1397. However, it is possible that the name of Hinrik Balhorst, who is listed in a 1381 town register of Minden, refers to a variant of the name of the settlement.

name: Bolków
Toll_Description: Citizens from Wrocław were exempted from the toll in Bolków in 1366.

name: Boalsert
Harbour_Description: Regular barge ('trekvaart') services were offered on the route Leeuwarden-Bolsward-Workum from 1648 onwards.

name: Born
Settlement_Description: The alleged first mention in the records in 1187 by Hermes and Weigelt seems to have nothing to do with the settlement Born. This settlement was founded as an outlying estate ('Vorwerk') in 1745. The inn mentioned by Bruns-Weczerka can only be assumed by the end of the 18th century.

name: Alkmaar
Settlement_Description: According to Van Berkel & Samplonius, Alkmaar is first mentioned in the first half of the eleventh century. Cox, however, claims that the earliest mention dates from 922-939. A market is mentioned in 1132, and Alkmaar is called an 'oppidum' in 1166. A hospital is first mentioned in 1341.
Town_Description: Alkmaar is granted town rights on 11 June 1254 by William II, count of Holland. However, in 1426, Alkmaar lost its town privileges (and its military defences). The defences were re-established in 1451. In 1456, the town rights were re-granted, but these (and the city gates and walls) were lost again in 1491. The town rigts were again restored in the sixteenth century.
Fair_Description: A 'forum' (market) in Alkmaar is found between 1132 and 1174 and in 1215, as appears from the Annales Egmundenses, the yearly toll was property of the abbot of Egmond. In 1277 the toll outside the fair is mentioned. In 1339 (Dec. 8) count Willem IV granted three fairs to the citizens, each of 3 weeks: 1) Midlent, 2) St. Jacobsmisse (July 25), 3) Bamis (Oct. 1). Merchants from Flanders, Brabant, Denmark a.o. had to pay toll of cattle and cloth and furthermore the '100e penning' (1%). That year the count also gave a toll for the Oostfriezen on the fairs. In 1365 the fair after Easter was moved to the Monday after the octave of Easter. In 1379 (Sept. 22) duke Albrecht granted a fourth fair starting 3 days before St. Matheusday (Sept. 21) till 4 days after with equal freedom and rights as the fair with Low Sunday (Sunday after Easter).The comital account dated 1524 mentions tolls of three fairs: 1) Easter fair for 8 days, 2) St. Bartholomeusfair (August 24) for 12 days and 3) St. Mathysfair (Sept. 21) for 8 days. In particular those of 'Overmase' (south of the river Maas) had to pay toll. Tol was levied from cattle and linen cloth. As a result of damage by war and the fact that local lords around the town had raised fairs with lower tolls in 1526 (May 4) emperor Charles V gave permission to levy a lower toll during 12 years. The comital account of 1544 stated that the right of the horse-fair was equal to that in Gouda, Valkenburg, Voorschoten and Vlaardingen. King Philip II granted in 1575 (March 3) two leather fairs. Alkmaar was not as good situated as other towns in West-Friesland and Waterland, which resulted in the fact that artisans as shoemakers did not establish easily because of lack of materials. The decaying trade would improve by the new leather fairs like in Hoorn, Purmerend and Beverwijk. Dates: Monday after Low Sunday and the day after St. Matheus (Sept. 22).
Staple_Description: In 1347 the count prohibited the weekly markets in the villages in  Kennemerland and Westfriesland and ordained that the bailiff would assure that the weekly market at Alkmaar was attended.

name: Bonn
Settlement_Description: Before the Romans could establish their military camps, the Ubii settled in the area of today's Bonn. In the 1st century Bonn served as a legionary suburb, a so-called 'civil vicus' ('Zivilvicus'). Under Frankish rule, Bonn rose to become an important marketplace and after 1288 became the residence of the Cologne electors.
Fair_Description: In 1166 a May-market was granted for 3 days. Of old a fair was organised here at the Joh's cross near Dietkirchen on June 23-29.
Toll_Description: Three tolls were levied in Bonn by the Archbishop of Cologne:1) The river toll on the Rhine was levied 1244-1254, before 1282, 1293-1302 and from 1306. The tariff was 12 pfennigs in 1293. In 1367 the customs were leased for 4 years for 30600 guilders a year. In 1371/74 the revenues added up to an average of about 16839 guilders a year. In 1473, the toll was moved to Remagen for a few weeks.2) From 1302 onwards, the escort fee was probably levied together with the Rhine toll.3) A land toll was established before 1282, but was not attested again until the beginning of the 15th century. In 1454/60, 70 marks were estimated for the cattle fee.

name: Bönnien
Settlement_Description: The village was first mentioned in 1143.

name: Boppard
Settlement_Description: The settlement originated at the end of the 3rd century.
Town_Description: In 1216, the town received its first town seal.
Toll_Description: An identification of the toll in the year 991 is not certain, which is why the first mention is in 1074. It was a river toll on the Rhine in the possession of the empire. From 1282, the toll was pledged to the Counts of Katzenelnbogen. In 1344 there was also a toll by Kurtrier. In the 14th and 15th centuries, the customs changed hands frequently. The tariff for the Rhine toll was 2½ pfennigs per ship in 1212. In 1282, there was a temporary surcharge of 6 pfennigs per foder of wine.In 1314 the tariff for the Kurtrier toll was 4 Turnosgroschen per foder of wine.In 1413 about 7340 guilders could be collected, in 1422/23 about 5193 guilders. For more detailed information, see source.

name: Borculo
Town_Description: Town privileges granted on 1 May 1375, by Gijsbert of Bronkhorst and Borculo, and his wife Henrica of Borculo-Dodinkweerde.

name: Bordesholm
Settlement_Description: The monastery of Augustinian Canons in Neumünster was moved to an island ('holm') in the lake near the village Eiderstede before 1327/28. It became a pilgrimage destination because of the veneration of the relics of St Vicelin. The monastery was secularised in 1565/66.

name: Borgloon
Settlement_Description: Earliest mention in 1078, in a thirteenth century copy.

name: Borger
Settlement_Description: Earliest mention in 1327, in a copy dating from 1471.

name: Bösel
Settlement_Description: First mentioned in 1330/52. The village consisted of 13 farms in 1450.

name: Bossow
Settlement_Description: The village is first mentioned in 1391.

name: null
Toll_Description: Toll on the Weser river, which is mentioned in a 1584 complaint from Bremen. Toll accounts exist from the year 1565 onwards (Landesarchiv NRW, Detmold). These have been analysed by Korinth.

name: Bornhöved
Settlement_Description: The village was founded in the second half of the 12th century. It was a meeting place for regional diets until 1480.

name: Bornum (Hannover)
Settlement_Description: The settlement was first mentioned in 1304.

name: Börry
Settlement_Description: The settlement was first mentioned in 968.

name: Borstel (Stendal)
Settlement_Description: In 1150 the tithe in Borstel was given to the bishopric of Halberstadt.

name: Borstel (Winsen)
Settlement_Description: First mentioned in 1117. According to 17th-century registers, the village consisted of 5 farms ('plog') or 4 farms and a half farm.

name: Borxleben
Settlement_Description: First mention in the Breviarium Sancti Lulli in the 8th/9th century.

name: Bösdorf
Settlement_Description: Mention in the beer-privilege of Oebisfelde as property of Oebisfelde.

name: Bourtange
Settlement_Description: First mentioned in 1573. Located on the only passage through the extensive Bourtange moor, a fortress ('vesting') was constructed here between 1580 and 1593 to control the traffic.
Toll_Description: According to documents pertaining to the toll in Leerort, a road toll was levied in Bourtange.

name: Brackede
Ferry_Description: A ferry between Brackede and Boizenburg is first mentioned in 1209.

name: Brake (Lemgo)
Settlement_Description: A castle with adjoining settlement was first mentioned in 1306, but it is archaeologically dated back to the end of the 10th century.

name: Brakel
Settlement_Description: First mentioned in 836 in the "Translatio Sancti Viti" as a station on the way to Corvey. Presumably, a main farm at the Hellweg existed here, which later became the nucleus of the medieval town.
Town_Description: The town was founded in 1229 at the latest by the Lords of Brakel, who already owned a castle to the west of the church (and from 1232 onwards also the Hinnenburg). Minting of coins is proven since 1220, a town wall is attested in 1304. In 1385, the town's sovereignty passed to the bishops of Paderborn. Because of the population influx and increase, the 'novum oppidum' was built around 1340 and mentioned 1383.

name: Breukelen
Settlement_Description: Earliest mention in 1130-1161, in a copy probably from circa 1420.Next mention in 1139.

name: Bramsche
Settlement_Description: First mentioned in 1097. The village developed to a borough ('flecken') until the 16th century.
Toll_Description: In an agreement between the town of Osnabrück and the cathedral chapter from 1532, the "new toll" in Bramsche and Venne was cancelled. Probably, the toll had been installed by the recently deceased bishop Erich von Braunschweig-Grubenhagen (1508-1532), whose financial politics had led to complaints and revolts in Osnabrück in 1524/5.

name: Bad Bramstedt
Settlement_Description: First mentioned as "villa Bramstede" in the 13th century; the settlement acquired borough ('flecken') privileges in 1448. They were confirmed in 1533, 1627 and 1652.
Fair_Description: According to ordinances of the borough ('amtsbuch') from ca. 1530, a cattle market took place during Lent. It remained important into the 17th century and took place around a Roland statue. Heinrich Rantzau also mentions a fair on 22 July in 1597.
Toll_Description: In 1487, the council of Lübeck complained to the Danish queen Dorothea about the levying of a toll in Bramstedt, which had not been levied before.

name: Zwochau
Settlement_Description: The village is first mentioned in 1158.
Toll_Description: Secondary station of safe conduct of Delitzsch, as recorded in regulations of safe conduct from the 16th century.

name: Brand
Settlement_Description: First mentioned in 1441. From 1548 the settlement is referred to as borough or small town ('Flecklein', 'Städtlein'). Merged with nearby Erbisdorf in 1912 as the town Brand-Erbisdorf.

name: Brandenbaum
Settlement_Description: Border crossing in the Lübeck enclosure ('landwehr'). There was a draw bridge and a boom barrier, first mentioned in 1256, as well as a village, which was "founded recently". In 1410, an inn is mentioned as well.
Bridge_Description: A draw bridge over the enclosure ('landwehr') ditch is first mentioned in 1256.

name: Brockensen
Settlement_Description: A first mention in the 10th century is uncertain.

name: Errested
Settlement_Description: The village of Errested was first mentioned in 1292, but is significantly older. The settlement had no church but was part of the parish of Bjerning.

name: Elbląg
Settlement_Description: There are relics of germanic settlements in pre-roman Iron Age, the imperial era as well as prussian-viking time, signs of a prussian trading post from 890 may have been a pre-settlement. The Teutonic Order founded the place on the mouth of the Elbing on the Vistula Lagoon in 1236 or 1237
Town_Description: A town was founded by the Teutonic order in 1237, Lübeck merchants settled there, the town was granted Lübeck town law by Wilhelm von Modena in 1240, but the documents do not survive, the eldest copies are from between 1263 and 1267, a handfast from 1246 granted restricted Lübeck town law, but it was extended in 1288, 1339 and 1343, the municipal ordinance made it an official town in 1808 and again later in 1853
Staple_Description: The staple existed already in 1388, when it was confirmed that the town was the only import harbour for english cloth; English merchants were only allowed to buy corn and wood from Prussia and Poland in Elbing. The staple was expanded in 1393 to include the export of corn, malt, tar, pitch, ash, tin, lead, timber and wood from the entire region between the Vistula and the Curonian Lagoon. Soon after, the entire system must have collapsed in favour of Danzig: in 1411 the Grand Master of the Teutonic Order moved the staple of Danzig temporarily to Elbing. A request of Elbing to instate a staple on the Diet of Prussian estates in 1440 shows that by that time, nothing was left of the Elbing staple.

name: Brandenburg (Havel)
Settlement_Description: A Slavic settlement is first mentioned in 928. Foundation of a bishopric in 948 under Otto I, but lost to the Slavs afterwards. Premonstratensian Canons settled in Parduin (the current old town) around 1147. Reconquered by the margrave of Brandenburg and the archbishop of Magdeburg in 1157. They resided on the cathedral island.
Town_Description: The old town (formerly the village Parduin) developed into a town after 1157. Toll privileges are granted in 1170 for the 'cives nostri Brandenburgensis'. The new town is first mentioned in 1196. In the middle of the 13th century, Magdeburg town rights are attested, although it is unknown when they were granted. In 1263 council members are mentioned in the old and new town; both parts were were formally merged in 1718.
Fair_Description: At the end of the 15th century two fairs in old and new town, one additional fair in the new town. At the end of the 16th century 6 fairs in the old town and 5 in the new town.
Toll_Description: In 1424, 1446 and 1458 the margravial toll in both towns Brandenburg (old town and new town), as well as the toll on the streets between Plaue, Pritzerbe and Wustermark and between Brandenburg and Werder was pawned to the town of Brandenburg.
Staple_Description: In a treaty of the Elector Frederick with the Neustadt in Brandenburg from 1455, a three-day staple is mentioned for merchants who wanted to travel through the "Arche". Since 1564 there was also an entrepot in the old town.

name: Brandlecht
Settlement_Description: Castle of the counts of Bentheim, first mentioned in 1313. It was destroyed by troops from Münster in 1360 and rebuilt afterwards.

name: Brasschaat
Settlement_Description: Earliest mention in 1267, in a fifteenth-century copy.

name: null
Toll_Description: In 1454 known ('Ten Bryell') as an outpost of the toll of the count of Holland at Geervliet.
Ferry_Description: Ferries to Rotterdam, Dordrecht and Zwartewaal are first mentioned in 1332. In 1365 a ferry to Maassluis is known. And in 1378 ferries to Staalduinen and Vlaardingen.
Harbour_Description: The old harbour in Brielle was located on the north side and within the town-walls. In the 14th century famous for its herring catch. A crane is first attested in 1414. The connection with the Meuse was via de Voornse Goote. This water was also used as a sluice to deepen the harbour. However this water silted up and was dammed upstream in 1473. A plan to construct a new canal to Oud Helvoet towards the Haringvliet was not carried out because of financial problems in the early 16th century. Skippers recolated more and more to the north bank of the Meuse to the towns Rotterdam, Vlaardingen, Schiedam and Delfshaven. In 1565 two buizen (herringboats) and 20-22 boats remained. Vitelli counted in his report for the duke of Alva1567 30 boats for the catch of cod, 9 or 10 boats harboured then at Zwartewaal.

name: Braunlage
Settlement_Description: Braunlage is mentioned in 1518 as forestry settlement, and in 1531 with ironworks. It developed into a market borough ('marktflecken') in the 17th century.

name: Brickwedde
Settlement_Description: First mentioned at the end of the 12th century. The settlement was possibly founded in Frankish times.

name: Braunschweig
Settlement_Description: Braunschweig is first mentioned in the dedication charter of the St Magnus church from 1031.
Town_Description: The town consisted of the five initially independent boroughs ('weichbilde') Altstadt, Hagen, Neustadt, Altewiek and Sack, which merged with each other and appeared as the single town Braunschweig in the course of the 14th century. The oldest town rights of Altstadt were granted in 1204.
Fair_Description: The three most important fairs in Braunschweig, on St Walpurga, New Year's Day and St Giles, were first attested in 1385. Three smaller fairs are attested in 1439, on Sunday Jubilate (the dedication day of the church of the Paulinian fathers), Sunday Rogate (dedication day of the Franciscans) and the day of St John. In the late 15th century, the town tried to raise its markets to large international fairs after the example of Leipzig. A privilege was granted in 1497; the New Year's market was moved to the period between 9 and 19 December and the Walpurga market to Friday after Ascension Day. Further extensions came with the market privilege of emperor Maximilian in 1505, when both fairs were extended to 10 days and the New Year's market moved to the day after the Immaculate Conception. However, the great ambitions were never realised, and the three large fairs were reduced to 6 days again in 1521, with the Ascension Day market being moved to two weeks after Easter.
Toll_Description: A ducal toll in Braunschweig on foreign commodities sold in town is first mentioned in 1204. If the commodities were transported through town without halt, the merchant did not have to pay; if he stopped and rested only half of the toll. The tariffs were specified in the toll regulations around 1300. Since the mid-14th century the toll was pawned to the town authorities, and completely acquired by them in 1412 and 1428. Extensive toll tariffs and other regulations date from 1503, 1548 and 1597. The toll booth was located directly west of the town hall of the new town; payment of the toll was controlled at the nine town gates.

name: Brauweiler
Toll_Description: From 1389 the Archbishop of Cologne levied a fee for safe conduct and a land toll here. The tariff in 1396 was 2 to 3 white pfennigs ('Weißpfennige') per horse, depending on the load. The annual amount added up to an average of 117 marks in 1389/93.

name: Breckerfeld
Toll_Description: The count of Breckerfeld charged road toll in 1499. The tariff was fixed at 1 Heller per carriage. The annual revenue in 1499 was 20 guilders, which was to be used to repair the roads.

name: Valenciennes
Settlement_Description: First attested in 693 with a palatium as centre of a fiscus.
Fair_Description: In 1264 a fair is known. Market-tolls between 1256-86.

name: Breda
Settlement_Description: Breda is first mentioned in a sixteenth-century copy of a document dated 1152. Core of the settlement used to be around the current Vismarkt and Havermarkt next to the harbour, as the location and orientation of the Grote Kerk still attests.  A chapter is founded in 1309.
Town_Description: Town privileges were granted ca. 1198-before 25 February 1212 by Godfried II, lord of Breda and Schoten.
Fair_Description: In 1290 'cauchidegeld' is known: levied to maintain the roads from incoming wagons, horses and cattle. In 1355 the magistrate obtained from the lord of the town the right of the weighhouse and the hall for the butchers near the corn-market . A tariff (called 'oude caerte') of the exises is dated 1397 and edited. Here a.o. a wine-crane is mentioned and 'caudsidegeld' levied from horses. An edited tariff dated circa 1436 from the lord of Breda for his toll levied on land and on water names 'weggeld' (tax on road) levied from incoming or outgoing traffic at the Gasthuisgate, toll from cattle and gooses and from ships. Then two fairs are found: with Bamis (Oct. 1) and Sinxen (Pentecost). Another tariff of cauchide is also edited and dated 1467 and concerns also the toll and 'weggeld' (tax on roads). Steenbergen, Oudenbosch, (Oud-)Gastel, Van der Hoeven, Loenhout and Hoogstraten had a special tariff in the marktets. Loenhout and Hoogstraten had to pay all three taxes if they just passed through Breda on their way to Holland with goods. In the Meierij van Den Bosch were freed from tolls except during the markets: Den Bosch, Eindhoven, Oorschot, Beke, Helmond, Tilburg, St. Oedenrode, Oosterwijk, Oss en Waalwijk. A third edited tariff dated circa 1475 also concerns the weighhouse, measures ('maten' from a.o. coal, salt and grain) and the crane.From 1313 at the latest Breda had two fairs. One of which was the Sinxenmarkt, for two weeks starting the day after Pentecost. The Sinxenmarkt continued to be held at least up to 1756. The other is the Bamismarkt, which was held for two weeks after the holy day of saint Bavo on the 1st of October. The Bamismarkt stopped being held in 1653.
