Toll_Description: An edited tariff from the toll belonging to the lord of Breda levied on land and on water dated circa 1436 notes that there is only a single toll in the Land van Breda, one preferably paid in Breda itself but which also had two outposts in Gilze and in Baarle. Those from the Land van Hoogstraten had to pay watertoll for what they got from outside the Land van Breda en transported through it. Those from the Meierij van Den Bosch and from Bergen op Zoom were freed from this toll but had to pay 'weggeld' (tax on the roads). Those from Antwerpen had to pay this toll but who lived inside the 'borcht' (the old town?) not. Those from Turnhout, Weelde and Poppel had to pay toll for the 'houtscat' (wood) and other goods they exported from the Land van Breda.The toll must have predated Breda becoming a city. Furthermore, the location of the toll was probably the Tolbrug over the Mark, which would likely have extracted a toll from both foot traffic and ships that passed it.In 1581 Breda obtained a privilege of Philip II that it became a free city (like Tienen, Diest, (Zout)Leeuw en Nijvel) and never again had to contribute to the toll of Brabant,
Staple_Description: In 1355 magistrate and inhabitants of Breda obtained from the lord of the town the right called 'opslag' (storage of goods) in the freedom of the town. In 1397: in the parish. In 1404: in the Land van Breda.

name: Brzeg
Settlement_Description: Fishing village on the left shore of the Oder, first mentioned in 1235.
Town_Description: The town was founded between 1246 and 1250 according to German law and acquired Magdeburg town privileges in 1327. Ducal residence between 1311 and 1675.
Toll_Description: A toll is first mentioned in 1316.

name: Dronryp
Settlement_Description: Earliest mention in 1132 in a falsification dating from the second half of the thirteenth century. The next mention probably dates from 1243.

name: Marsum
Settlement_Description: Earliest mention in the thirteenth century.

name: Bückwitz
Settlement_Description: The village is first mentioned in 1308.

name: Brest
Toll_Description: Brest was the most important toll station from Lithuania to the west in the 16th century.

name: Brielle
Settlement_Description: Brielle is first mentioned in 1257. A hospital is first mentioned in 1293. A chapter in the minster church is found in the years 1300/1310-1572.
Town_Description: Town privileges granted 30 November 1330 by Gerard, lord of Voorne, but at least from 1306 onward already indicated as a city. In 1368 Brielle and the Land of Voorne received from the king of Sweden the privilege for a 'vitte' (trading-post) on Schonen (southern point of Sweden) with its own guardian.
Fair_Description: The 'Tegenwoordige Staat' dated 1744 states that count Floris V in 1280 granted marketrights to the town, this is however without evidence. In 1332 a cloth-hall, meat-hall and weigh-house, shoemakers- and 'marsemans' (pedlars)-marketstalls and stalls for people from abroad are found, which indicates the existence of a fair. In 1346 the cross of the fishmarkt is erected which also shows that. In 1445 a fair on  Saterday before St. Catharinday (Nov. 25) during 8 days, of which there are 4 'wercke toechdagen' (display-days). In 1552 (April) Brielle requested splitting of the fair. The town was since 1400 a 'koopstad' (town for merchants) with lots of 'hulcken' and 'koopvaarders' (ship types), where many skippers of the Baltic and Scotland arrived and many herringbusses from Holland or Waterland. The fair in November was late in the year as the skippers of the big boats and the 'stierluiden' (captains) and partners of the busses were at home. As a result of the silting up of the harbour and the embankment of the Gote in 1470 to get cornland the ships 'armeren' (be at anchor) now in Amsterdam and Walcheren and the busses in Holland. Brielle nowadays had only 10 busses and some smaller fishboates to catch herring. The inhabitants were forced to live from agriculture. Therefore the fair had to be half when the harvest of corn was (in August). As this caused no injury for the towns in east-Voorne the privilege was granted. The fair would be as of old 8 days (in August?, Dijkman: Nov.) and another 5 days with a horse-fair starting 8 days before the fair in the seigniory 'Suytlant or Blenckvliet', this meant the Monday after this fair in September (Zuidland was called of old Westenrijk and had a horse-fair since 1439). The toll per horse was 2 stuiver brabants.
Staple_Description: The staple for all herring brougt in via the mouth of Meuse was situated here. A grainstaple for the surrounding countryside (Oudorp, Nielant en Oestdijck) is obtained in 1477 (August 18) from Mary of Burgundy. All grain had to be brought at the weekly market of Brielle.

name: Wrocław
Staple_Description: In 1274, Henry IV of Silesia limited the staple for entire Silesia to Breslau; confirmed 1409. However, most of the times the staple was difficult to enforce due to conflicts with Poland. An agreement between Frankfurt (Oder) was made in 1490, that merchants were only allowed to cross the Oder at Frankfurt or Breslau. The Enforcement of this agreement was complicated by counter-measures of the Polish king. Merchants from Poland, Russia, Prussia, Lithuania and Masovia were prohibited to trade further than Frankfurt and Breslau in 1507. The staple of Breslau was confirmed by the Emperor 1510, but the following Polish trade boycott forced the city to refrain from its staple rights between 1515 and 1530. The staple disappeared at the end of the 18th century.

name: Emsdetten
Settlement_Description: The settlement originated in the 9th or 10th century near a church and was first mentioned by name in 1178.

name: Ernsthausen
Settlement_Description: First mentioned around 1130. In 1482 it fell in ruins, but in 1577 the settlement was called a village again.

name: Erwitte
Settlement_Description: The place was at the crossroads of two long-distance trade routes; it was a parish with a royal court. First mentioned in 822.

name: Esch
Toll_Description: The Count of Blankenheim-Gerolstein levied a land toll in 1490.

name: Wąbrzeźno
Town_Description: Acquisition of town rights in c. 1331.

name: Groß Briesen
Toll_Description: In 1550 it was ordained that wagoners travelling from Müllrose to Cottbus had to pay toll in Briesen.

name: Brietlingen
Settlement_Description: The place was first mentioned in 1004.

name: Brinkum
Settlement_Description: The place was mentioned for the first time in 1158.
Toll_Description: A toll of the counts of Hoya is first mentioned around 1380. It is still mentioned in a charter from 1562, in which the count of Hoya lowers the fares for the citizens of Arsten and Habenhausen (in Bremen territory) to dig peat around Brinkum, and obliges them to pay these fares at the comital toll house in Brinkum and to use only the toll road through the Kattenturm to get there. Further details of the toll are only known from the late 17th century onwards (Niedersächsisches Landesarchiv Hannover).

name: Britz (Berlin)
Settlement_Description: First mention at the end of the 12th century.

name: Brockel
Settlement_Description: A priest from Brockel is mentioned as owner of a part in the Lüneburg saltworks in a register of 1379-1381.

name: Freyburg (Unstrut)
Town_Description: The town is first mentioned by name in 1203. It is erected in the shadow of the castle Neuenburg, built around 1076. Its foundation was probably planned. It is referred to as a town several times during the 13th century, even though there is no evidence that town rights were ever granted. First mention of a council in 1410, fist mention of a town constitution in 1446.
Toll_Description: Station of safe conduct on the road from Naumburg to the North. It was levied together with the safe conduct in Markröhlitz. Revenues are known for the years 1449-1459 and 1479-1485. Safe conduct regulations from 1621 of the district of Freyburg list the fees and mention Karsdorf, Nebra, Schönewerda and Markröhlitz as secondary stations of safe conduct.

name: Broich
Toll_Description: In 1389, the Duke of Jülich levied a lfee for save conduct and a land toll here. Fees for horses and save conduct were collected here. Depending on the load, the tariff was 2 to 3 white pfennigs ('Weißpfennige') per horse. The annual revenue in 1389/93 was on average 79 marks per year, in 1510/1511: 375 marks.

name: Brome
Settlement_Description: The castle and settlement were first mentioned around 1202/3. The settlement was usually characterised as borough ('flecken').
Toll_Description: A toll of the dukes of Brunswick is first mentioned in 1321, and again in 1409.

name: Bronkhorst
Town_Description: Earliest mention as 'stedeke' in a charter of 1371. Town privileges granted on 13 March 1482, by Gijsbert VII of Bronkhorst and Borculo.

name: Brual
Settlement_Description: First mentioned when a castle was destroyed here in 1345.

name: Brück (Köln)
Toll_Description: The Duke of Berg levied a land toll in Brück. Tariffs and revenues are not known. Established in 1411 as a secondary land toll of Mühlheim, in 1487 of Dünnwald.

name: Brudersdorf
Settlement_Description: Originally a Slavic village called Dobimuisle, first mentioned in 1178. In the 13th century the name changed to Brudersdorf, probably because Cistercian monks from Dargun built a chapel in the village, which became parish church in 1309.

name: Brüel
Settlement_Description: First mentioned as a village in 1222. The nearby 13th-century castle complex belonged to the noble house Plessen.
Town_Description: Reimar of Plessen raised the settlement to a small town ('Stedeken'), most likely with Parchim town law, in 1340.

name: Brücken
Settlement_Description: First mention in the Breviarium sancti Lulli before 775/786. The settlement received market rights in 1518.

name: Eschwege
Settlement_Description: In 974 Emperor Otto II gave the royal court of Eschwege, which was on the southern bank of the Werra, to his wife; The imperial abbey was probably founded in the 10th century; Development into a city from the middle of the 13th century

name: Grüner Jäger
Settlement_Description: Alexander von Weltzien founded an inn in the forest, called "der grüne Jäger" in 1689.

name: Brumby
Toll_Description: A station of safe conduct is attested in 1486.

name: Brummen
Settlement_Description: Earliest mention dates from 794, in a tenth century copy.

name: Bründeln
Settlement_Description: The year of first mention was 1191.

name: Brunsen
Settlement_Description: The settlement was first mentioned in 1148.

name: Brunshausen
Settlement_Description: The settlement was first mentioned in 852, when a house of canonesses was founded. After the canonesses had moved to Gandersheim in 881, a new Benedictine monastery was founded before 1106/11, which became a nunnery between 1192 and 1206. In 1655 the monastery became Lutheran, and was abolished in 1810.

name: Brussel
Settlement_Description: Earliest mention in 966, in a fifteenth century copy.
Fair_Description: In 1486/'7 (Jan.) the Roman king Maximiliaan granted two free fairs, with Ascension and with St. Luke (Oct.18), each for 10 days.
Toll_Description: The grand toll of Brussels (grant tonniv de Broussele) belonging to the duke of Brabant is found in 1299.

name: Brüssow
Settlement_Description: A castle probably existed in Slavic times, a small German settlement with a church is mentioned in 1259.
Town_Description: The knight Heinrich von Stegelitz was granted the right to built a court house in 1259, later the town law of Prenzlau and Magdeburg was granted. In 1299 the village was characterised as civitas when it was merged with Alt-Borstow.
Toll_Description: A market toll was granted to knight Heinrich von Stegelitz in 1259.

name: Most
Toll_Description: The town acquired the privilege to levy a toll for the maintenance of the fortifications in 1338.
Staple_Description: The staple privilege from 1273 contained obligations to use specific routes only. Corn staple for the surrounding countryside. Special staple privileges for salted fish were issued in 1515.

name: Brześć Kujawski
Toll_Description: Mentioned as toll station in a document from c. 1349, where 6 gr. 8 den. had to be paid for each horse. In 1390 King Władysław of Poland ordained that the toll tariffs in Sieradz, Kalisz, Pyzdry and Poznań were to be the same as those levied in Piotrków Trybunalski, Łęczyca, Przedecz and Brześć.

name: Büchen
Settlement_Description: The village was first mentioned in 1230.

name: Buchladen
Settlement_Description: A law court with the name Bocla is first mentioned in 1213. The name of the forester's lodge Buchladen is first mentioned in 1823. It is questionable whether there already existed a settlement in the Middle Ages

name: Buberow
Settlement_Description: The village is first mentioned in 1438.

name: Buckau
Settlement_Description: First mentioned in 937 in a donation charter of Otto I to the monastery of St Maurice in Magdeburg (MGH DD OI, nr. 16, 103 - 105).

name: Bückeburg
Settlement_Description: Around 1300, a moated castle was built by the counts of Schaumburg, which was first mentioned in 1304. The attached settlement acquired Stadthagen borough ('flecken') privileges from count Adolf VII of Schaumburg in 1365.
Town_Description: Town privileges were granted in 1609 by count Ernst of Schaumburg.

name: Buckow (Berlin)
Settlement_Description: Since there are no rights of the Mark in Buckow, it can be assumed that the village was founded before it became territory of the margraves in the Teltow-war 1239 - 1245.

name: Primorsk
Settlement_Description: Heinrich von Strittberg, the bishop of Samland, was given a village by the Teutonic Order in 1264, he built a fortified bishop's see and gave land to settlers in 1268, the first attempt of a town founding in 1299 was not successdul
Town_Description: Bishop Siegfried took over the town's founding in 1305, granted Kulm town law, the founding documents were endorsed in 1475 by elector Johann Sigismund

name: Büderich
Fair_Description: A fair is first mentioned in 1270, but without a date. In 1319 a four-week fair on the Nativity of Mary (September 8) is mentioned. This was one of the most important fairs in the lower Rhine area.
Toll_Description: Next to the Rhine toll in Büderich (see harbour), a land toll was levied by the Duke of Cleves in 1417/1446. Tariffs are not known. First evidence from 1446, but probably already established in 1417.

name: Buke
Settlement_Description: A church called 'Buke' was first mentioned in 1231.

name: Buļļuciems
Settlement_Description: The place was first mentioned in 1450. A little further west there was probably a ferry with which you could cross the river Aa.

name: Bülow
Settlement_Description: The village is first mentioned in 1232.

name: Bümmerstede
Settlement_Description: First mentioned in 1310. Münster troops from Vechta burned the village to the ground in 1454.

name: Bunde
Settlement_Description: The settlement is first mentioned in 1428, but the village church dates from between 1230 and 1280. The settlement developed into a borough ('flecken') in the 15th century.

name: Thierschneck
Toll_Description: Lesser known station of safe conduct with an uncommonly high transfer of wares. Several conflicts between Ernestingian and Albertinian escorts are recorded. A registry of safe conduct ('Geleitstafel') from 1535/36 is preserved (ThHStA Weimar, Reg. Bb 171, Capitalrechnung der Ämter zu Thüringen, Vogtland und Franken 1535/36.).

name: Bunschoten
Settlement_Description: First mention in 1249. Around 1200 an agrarian settlement had developed, after the region was cultivated ('ontgonnen') in the twelfth century.
Town_Description: Bunschoten was granted town rights sometime between 1336 (last mention as parish village) and 1355 (first mention as town), by John IV of Arkel, bishop of Utrecht. The town was fortified with ramparts and palisades. An extension of the town privileges was granted by Floris of Wevelinkhoven, bishop of Utrecht, on 11 August 1383. The privileges were confirmed in 1398, 1414, 1439 and 1457. However, after becoming part of Holland in 1427 Bunschoten was sacked by troops from Utrecht in 1430, subsequently went into decline and remained little more than a farming village.
Fair_Description: Tolls of fairs are found in the accounts of the bishop dated 1337-'79 (afterwards not anymore, although preserved with gaps: the next account is dated 1426). But the toll is still mentioned in a lawsuit dated 1394. In 1377 the tolls are collected with St. Margaret (July 13) and St. Matthew (Sept. 21).

name: Büren
Settlement_Description: First mentioned in 1015. A castle of the lords of Büren was constructed in c. 1150.
Town_Description: The town was probably founded before 1194 by the lords of Büren near their castle. Before 1220 the city was expanded based on the Lippstadt model with a new town; a market and mint existed since c. 1250. Before 1252 a second new town was founded, which was unsuccessful.

name: Burg (Bremen)
Settlement_Description: A castle likely existed on the crossing of the river Lesum in the 13th century, next to which a settlement developed. The castle was reconstructed in 1350.

name: Burg (bei Magdeburg)
Settlement_Description: The origin of the place lies in an early medieval settlement, probably from the time of Henry I. In the 10th century there was a castle guard and a settlement in close proximity. First written mention in the foundation of the bishopric of Brandenburg, when its tithe mentioned as belonging to St. Moritz' monastery in Magdeburg.
Town_Description: Town hall and marketplace point towards a trading enclosure, which probably held town rights from the beginning. Dating based on the emergence of the "jus Burgense" in the middle of the 13th century. Revisions of the town rights e.g. 1474, 1558, 1576 and 1598.Since 1262 Burg had purchased a freedom of tax and trade in Magdeburg.
Fair_Description: The first market privilege was granted in 1562, with fairs on the Assumption of Mary and St Dionysius. Another fair was added between 1635 to 1657 on Simon and Juda's day.
Toll_Description: In 1489 the town of Magdeburg complained to the escort  ('Geleitsmann') of Burg that safe conduct fees had been collected from two citizens, even though they were supposed to be exempted from such payments. The toll station of Burg is also mentioned in 1493.

name: Burgdamm
Settlement_Description: Between 1388 and 1390, a causeway ('damm') was constructed to cross the marshes of the Lesum river between the newly erected Lesum bridge in Burg and the dry sandy moraine north of it. A settlement developed on the north end of the causeway and took over its name.

name: Waltershausen
Settlement_Description: First mention in 1209, when landgrave Hermann I protested against the market in Friedrichsroda. A foundation in Frankish times seems possible.
Town_Description: First mention as town in 1357, town rights were granted in the 14th century. In 1441 the town privileges are confirmed.
Toll_Description: 1410 Waltershausen is granted safe conduct and toll privileges like Gotha.

name: Burgdorf
Settlement_Description: A castle of the bishop of Hildesheim with a connected settlement was mentioned between 1260 and 1279.
Town_Description: The settlement developed into a borough ('flecken') or town without acquiring town rights. A council and seal is first mentioned in 1398.
Fair_Description: Before 1578, two fairs existed in Burgdorf. It is unknown since when these existed, possibly since the moment the settlement became a town or borough ('flecken') around 1400. A third fair was added in 1578, and a fourth carnival fair in 1614. In 1619, the dates and locations are specified: the fairs on Carnival and St Gallus took place in front of the Uetzen and Celle gates east of the town, and the fairs of St George and St Vitus in front of the Hannover gate west of the town.
Toll_Description: In 1354, the bishop of Hildesheim cancelled the toll and fees for safe conduct in Burgdorf. In the early 16th century, citizens from Braunschweig transshipped their commodities intended for Bremen on ships in Essel, thereby circumventing the toll in Celle. For this reason, the duke of Brunswick raised the toll tariff in Burgdorf, which led to Bremen complaints in 1526-1529.

name: Burlage
Settlement_Description: Around 1140 a Benedictine monastery was founded. The drainage of the surrounding moors in the 14th century favoured its economic situation to a certain extent, but the monastery did not own many lands or tithes. After it had become Lutheran in 1543, monastic life in Burlage ended in 1672.

name: Burtnieki
Settlement_Description: The year of first reference is unclear, but is dated between 1306 and 1366. A castle was built on the southern shore of the lake, which the Russians burned down in 1560.

name: Buttlar
Settlement_Description: First uncertain mention as Butelir in 811. First certain mention in 1170.

name: Butzbach
Toll_Description: Emperor Charles IV set the tariffs for the toll and safe conduct in Butzbach in 1349 and 1356.

name: Bützow
Settlement_Description: Mentioned in 1171 as terra Butissowe, where a Slavic fortress existed.
Town_Description: A town must have come into existence in the early 13th century, and is first mentioned in 1229. Town privileges (presumably of Schwerin) were granted in 1236 and confirmed in 1371, 1449 and 1603.

name: Burgwalde
Settlement_Description: First mention in 1318. In the 15th century it was deserted for a time but it must have been inhabited again by the middle of the 16th century.

name: Frieda
Settlement_Description: First mentioned in 974. At times, documented from 1444, the village was desolate.

name: Friedewald
Settlement_Description: A castle is first mentioned in 1302 where a settlement developed. Later still referred to as a 'Flecken'.

name: Kassinurme
Settlement_Description: Village and manor were first mentioned in 1560.

name: Buxtehude
Settlement_Description: First mentioned in a donation charter of Otto I to the monastery of St Maurice in Magdeburg in 959. The original settlement was located in the vicinity of the Altkloster (old monastery), which was founded in 1196.
Town_Description: Archbishop Giselbert of Bremen founded the Neustadt ('new town') north of the original settlements in the 1280s; the town acquired Stade town privileges in 1328. The name of the original settlement was transferred to the new town in the mid-15th century.
Fair_Description: The oldest fair in Buxtehude, on St Lawrence's day, took place since 1287. A fair on St Martin's day appears in 1420. A horse market was founded in 1474, which often took place in combination with a fair on St Peter and Paul's day. In 1511, the horse market was moved to Wednesday before Palm Sunday, while the fair on St Peter and Paul remained in existence until 1573. In 1531, a fair was added on Thursday and Friday before Palm Sunday, which was moved to  the week after Judica in 1583. A Pentecost fair is mentioned in 1559. In the 16th century, the fairs had a duration of at least 3 days, with the horse market one week and the St Martin's fair 14 days.
Toll_Description: A toll of the archbishop of Bremen in Buxtehude is first mentioned in 1376. In 1385, after complaints about exceptional levying of toll on the Elbe, it is guaranteed that no toll shall be levied on shipping on the Elbe. It is therefore likely that the toll in Buxtehude was a fee on local im- and exports. Moreover, a pound toll for the fight against piracy was levied in Buxtehude in the 1360s, like in Hamburg and Stade.

name: Calau
Settlement_Description: Developed near an old Slavic settlement, protected by a German castle. It is first mentioned in 1279, then already as town.
Town_Description: First mentioned in 1279 as civitas. Town privileges were probably granted earlier by Margrave Dietrich (1210-1221) or Henry of Meißen (1221-1288). The Magdeburg town law was certified in the 15th century.

name: Cheine
Settlement_Description: First mentioned in 1270, when the village was acquired by the monastery Neuendorf.

name: Chełm (Bochnia)
Toll_Description: A toll is first mentioned in 1260. A new toll for the improvement of the road to Cracow was installed in 1521.

name: Calbe
Settlement_Description: First mentioned in 936 in a donation charter to Quedlinburg monastery. It was located near a castle, first mentioned in 961, at a river crossing on the road Magdeburg-Halle. Around 965 a royal court was mentioned and since 968 it belonged to the archbishopric of Magdeburg. A market settlement developed in the 10th and 11th century.
Town_Description: Acquisition of market and town rights in the 12th century, probably around 1160. A civic judge ('schultheiß') is mentioned in 1168 and councillors in 1289.
Toll_Description: In 1364 the bishop levied a toll on the passage of ships around the mill weir on the Saale river (see there). A toll station in Calbe is further attested by several conflicts with citizens of Magdeburg about toll exemption in 1432, 1486 and 1487. Toll regulations exist from the 16th century.

name: Calbitz
Toll_Description: A safe conduct station in Calbitz on the road to Leipzig is mentioned in 1498.

name: Kalefeld
Toll_Description: A toll is first mentioned in 1318.

name: Calvörde
Settlement_Description: Calvörde came into existence at a former ford at the Ohre river, which was secured by a castle. First mention in 786, in a 12th-century falsification. First secure mention in 1196.
Town_Description: Mention as a borough ('Flecken') in the 13th century, referred to as town in 1345.
Toll_Description: In 1621/22, Gardelegen complained about the new tolls of the Duke of Brunswick in Calvörde.

name: Celle
Settlement_Description: Mentioned at the old location Altencelle as early as 983. The town was moved to the present location in 1292.
Town_Description: Celle was moved from its previous location at Altencelle ('old Celle') in 1292, and received the Lüneburg town privileges; in 1301 those of Braunschweig. Celle was the principal residence of the Dukes of Lüneburg between 1433 and 1705.
Fair_Description: In 1353, three three-day fairs are mentioned in Celle: on Sunday before St Walpurga, St Maurice and Sunday before St Martin. The fair of St Maurice is moved to the Sunday after the Ascension of Mary in 1412.
Toll_Description: Land and water toll and safe conduct of the dukes of Brunswick--Lüneburg. The toll in Celle is already mentioned in the town privileges of the Braunschweig borough ('weichbild') Hagen in the early 13th century as the only toll at the waterway between Braunschweig and Bremen. Toll registers are available from 1379, see Peters 1913. In the years 1455-58, we first hear from different toll fees for commodities transported by Celle and Braunschweig citizens; the latter have to pay the double toll amount. The oldest known tariff dates from ca. 1560.
Staple_Description: The town of Braunschweig received freedom of shipping on the Aller and Oker rivers in 1459, but the Dukes of Lüneburg owned the pre-emptive right on a third of the corn shipped through Celle. Moreover, skippers were forced to offer the corn on the market for a while. The town attempted to expand the staple towards to include other commodities in the second half of the 16th century. In 1618, Bremen citizens acquired the right to buy corn up- and downstream from Celle, which effectively ended the staple.

name: Chełm
Toll_Description: Mentioned as toll station in c. 1349, with tariffs for horses, cloth and other commodities.

name: Dzierzgoń
Settlement_Description: A castle of the Teutonic Order was built in 1248 and a settlement grew close to it, it was mentioned as opidum in 1254, but destroyed between 1260 and 1273.
Town_Description: Founding documents were granted by the Komtur Helwig von Goldbach in 1288, but it was already mentioned as a civitas between 1260 and 1273, documents were endorsed and expanded in 1290 by the landmaster of the Order, Meinhard von Querfurt, the handfast was renewed in 1451 by the Grand master Ludwig von Erlichshausen with Kulm town law.

name: Chüttlitz
Settlement_Description: First mention in 1340. The village apparently was deserted by 1420 but resettled in 1503.

name: Gardeja
Settlement_Description: A settlement on old-Prussian remains belonging to the knight Dietrich Stange before 1285, the Cistercian Order of Pelplin unsuccessfully planned a new monastery in 1285, mentioned as a village in 1323
Town_Description: Founded by the bishop of Pomesania in 1328, the founding documents are lost, the oldest handfast survives from 1334 with Kulm town law, after being destroyed by a fire in 1554 it was rebuilt in 1559

name: Clausthal
Settlement_Description: Around 1530, mining activities in Clausthal were started (again).
Town_Description: Clausthal is first mentioned as mining town ('freie Bergstadt') in 1554. It was merged with nearby Zellerfeld in 1924.

name: Cremlingen
Settlement_Description: First mentioned in 1296. In the vicinity of the church, shards from the 3rd-7th centuries were found, which indicate earlier habitation with an urn cemetery.

name: Cloppenburg
Settlement_Description: Before 1297, the castle Cloppenburg was built by the counts of Tecklenburg near the village Krapendorf.
Town_Description: Cloppenburg first received borough ('weichbild') privileges in 1411, and in 1435 the town privileges of Haselünne.
Fair_Description: A fair in Cloppenburg is first mentioned in 1535.
Toll_Description: In a Cloppenburg register from 1474/5, the income from the toll in Cloppenburg is listed as 46 Mark 5 Shilling. Probably, this was a road toll on the "flämische Straße" (Flemish street) from Bremen to Flandern. It is unclear when it was first levied.

name: Coburg
Settlement_Description: First mentioned in 1056. The settlement was founded as planned town around the beginning of the 11th century next to the older settlement Trufalistat. It is located at an old road from Bamberg to Frankfurt. A new castle was constructed around 1200.
Town_Description: In 1331 Coburg was granted Schweinfurt rights and an own jurisdiction. Since 1540 residence of the dukes of Saxony-Coburg-Gotha.
Toll_Description: The regulations of safe conduct from 1492 describe the extent of the safe conduct in Coburg as well as the fees that were due. A cart had to pay 9 pennies, a Jew on foot 24 pennies and a horse 1 pound and 6 pennies. The income from these fees belonged to the toll collector, whereas the fees for wagons and their cargoes and wagoners belonged to the territorial lords.

name: Coevorden
Settlement_Description: First mentioned in 1141 as part of a name ('Fredericus de Cuvorde'). Coevorden is located on a sand ridge ('zandrug') in the Bourtange Moor. This made it not only into a military strategic location, but also into an important trading point, as every traveller from Groningen to Munster needed to pass through Coevorden.
Town_Description: Town rights were granted at 31 December 1407 by Frederick of Blankenheim, bishop of Utrecht. Town privileges may have been granted earlier (before 1395); however, by 1407 the document that proofed this had been lost.
Fair_Description: In 1541 three fairs were instituted in Coevorden: one on the Monday before Pentecost, one on Saint Odulf (12 June), and one on Saint Giles (1 September). The fair of Saint Giles probably already existed before 1440; the institution of the fair in 1541 thus probably was a re-institution.
Toll_Description: A toll of the bishop of Utrecht is first mentioned in a conflict with count Otto of Bentheim in 1187. In 1402 the bishop declared that he would improve the road between Ane and Coevorden, which was impassable in winter. The three towns in Salland will pay for the construction works, whereas the bishop will fund the eternal maintenance of the road with a road toll with the same tariff as in Gramsbergen, of which the citizens from the three towns will be exempted.

name: Connewitz
Settlement_Description: First mention in 1277 in the name Borzlaus de Kunawiz.

name: Coppenbrügge
Settlement_Description: First mentioned in the 10th century. Around 1300, a castle was built here, whereupon the settlement developed into a borough ('burgflecken').

name: Coswig (Sachsen)
Settlement_Description: The settlement Coswig was first mentioned in 1350 with a moated castle. It was raised to a town in 1939.

name: Vejrup
Settlement_Description: The village of Vejrup was first mentioned in 1291 and again in 1330-48, but is older. The parish church is from either the 12th or 13th century.

name: Coswig (Anhalt)
Settlement_Description: The settlement in a castle district was first mentioned in 1187.
Town_Description: In 1215 the town is referred to as oppidum. In 1315 town rights are attested, probably based on Magdeburg rights.
Toll_Description: A toll on the river Elbe in Coswig is first mentioned in 1362. The regulations of safe conduct from 1566 mention two land and road tolls as well as safe conduct and the water toll.
Staple_Description: The regulations of safe conduct from 1566 state that rafters had to offer their wares for three days in Coswig, unless they paid the toll right away.

name: Cottbus
Settlement_Description: A German castle was built in the late 10th century, which went back to a Slavic fortification. A market settlement developed in its vicinity, first mentioned in 1156, then already a town.
Town_Description: Exact date of foundation unclear. First mentioned as a town in 1156, formal introduction of the Magdeburg town law in 1409.

name: Cranz
Ferry_Description: Around 1400, Cranz replaced Urenfleth as landing place for the ferry across the Elbe river. The latter settlement was flooded, its location unknown.

name: Creußen
Settlement_Description: The counts of Schweinfurt owned a castle in Creußen around 1000, which is first mentioned in a chronicle in 1003.

name: Cuijk
Settlement_Description: Earliest mention dates from 365 in a thirteenth century copy. Cuijk is mentioned as 'Kuik' around 1050 in an eleventh century copy.
Fair_Description: At the end of the 15th century a market-toll is attested starting 3 days before St. Martini (Nov. 11) during 14 days. An early 16th century source mentions two fairs: 3 days before St. Martini in the summer called translacionis (July 4) and 3 days before St. Martini in the winter (Nov. 11, both for 14 days. An early 16th century manual of the toll-keeper in Venlo with the market-tolls on the Maas has this tariff: per ship 1 vlaamse plak. One account dated 1572 (juli 1- nov. 30) from this market-toll is preserved.

name: Kuringen
Settlement_Description: Earliest mention in 1076, in a thirteenth century copy.

name: Dahlen
Settlement_Description: The settlement developed from the merger of the German villages Wolffersdorf, Dittersdorf and Zissen. It is first mentioned in 1188.
Toll_Description: Secondary station of safe conduct ('Beigeleitsstelle') of Oschatz.

name: Dahlenburg
Settlement_Description: According to a Slavic chronicle from the 13th century, this was a Slavic castle, erected between 860 and 900. The settlement is first mentioned in a charter in 1172.

name: Dahlinghausen
Settlement_Description: The settlement was first mentioned in the 12th century.

name: Dahme
Settlement_Description: A German castle was built on Slavic remains, the earlier settlement was called Altstadt ('old town'), a German market settlement developed close to it. First mentioned in 1186.
Town_Description: The town was probably founded by the lord of the castle, first mentioned as civitas in 1265.
Toll_Description: Mentioned as toll station for traffic with surrounding villages in 1265.

name: Dalchau
Ferry_Description: In 1486 a ferry in Dalchau is mentioned.

name: Gevelsberg
Settlement_Description: First mention of the Cistercian monastery there in 1225. Then pilgrimage site.

name: Giershagen
Settlement_Description: First mentioned in 949. In the 16th century the original place name "Upsprunge" was replaced.

name: Gießen
Settlement_Description: First mentioned in 1197. A castle was built in 1150.

name: Dąbrówno
Settlement_Description: In 1316 the castle Ilien was the see of an 'Ordenspfleger' and it was close to three Prussian castle mounds
Town_Description: The komtur of Christburg, duke Luther von Braunschweig founded the town in 1326

name: Damgarten
Settlement_Description: Originally a Slavic settlement, probably close to a cultic site on the temple hill. First mentioned as villa in 1225.
Town_Description: Lord Jaromar II of Rügen granted the Lübeck town law in 1258, as a border defence against Mecklenburg. Merged with nearby Ribnitz in 1950.

name: Damme (Osnabrück)
Fair_Description: A fair in Damme is first mentioned in 1435, when it was the scene of a violent conflict between visitors from Osnabrück and Münster. It is mentioned again in 1580.

name: Damnatz
Settlement_Description: First mentioned in 1330/52. In 1450, the village consisted of 12 farms and 8 half farms.

name: Danndorf
Settlement_Description: First mentioned in 1150. The settlement was partially abandoned in the 14th century, destroyed in 1464 and resettled in 1539.

name: Dannenberg
Settlement_Description: The settlement developed next to a castle, which was possibly constructed around 800. The castle is first mentioned in 1162, when a count Volrad of Dannenberg as vassal of duke Henry the Lion appears in the sources.
Town_Description: The settlement is first mentioned as 'urbs' in 1202. In 1293 at the latest, Dannenberg owned town privileges. The Lüneburg town law was granted in the 16th century.
Fair_Description: In 1293 at the latest, a three-day fair was held in Dannenberg. More details are mentioned in 1365, when a fair in the week after Easter was granted, next to an already existing fair on the Birth of Mary.
Toll_Description: Land and water toll of the dukes of Brunswick-Lüneburg, pawned to the Bülow family. It was first mentioned in an agreement between Friedrich von Bülow and Salzwedel in 1474. Toll fees are known from the 16th century (StAB).
Harbour_Description: Dannenberg was an important skipper's town for the river traffic on the Jeetzel.

name: Dankmarshausen
Toll_Description: Secondary station of safe conduct of the Amt Gerstungen. Revenues are known since 1537.

name: Schipbekerhuizen
Harbour_Description: In the 19th century, two harbour basins are attested near the farms Berendsen and Schoman (Schipbekerhuizen) on the road between Diepenheim and Goor. Possibly, this was the 16th-century harbour for the Schipbeek canal, that was dug by the town of Deventer in 1399-1402. According to an 18th-century register, the harbour in Schipbekerhuizen also served as transshipment point for the land traffic to Germany.

name: Hem
Settlement_Description: Hem is first mentioned around 1312. On 2 February 1414 Hem, together with Venhuizen, was granted town privileges by William (‘Willem’) VI, count of Holland. These settlements, however, never developed an urban character. The granting of town rights was part of an administrative reorganization in which a number of smaller settlements were granted town rights in order to provide them with a certain degree of self-government which replaced the need for the count of Holland's bailiffs ('baljuws'). The settlements kept their own separate settlement governments.

name: Großwelsbach
Settlement_Description: Welsbach is first mentioned in 1195, Großwelsbach as distinctive settlement in 1216.
Toll_Description: Station of secondary safe conduct ('Beigeleitsstelle') of (Großen)Gottern, as mentioned in the regulations of toll and safe conduct for the Amt Langensalza and Thamsbrück from 1516.

name: Gdańsk
Settlement_Description: First mentioned in 997 as fishing village and castle of the princes of Danzig. The castrum Gdansk was mentioned in 1148 as a settlement belonging to the castle; a market settlement of German merchants is attested in 1178.
Town_Description: Prince Swantopolk (1220-1266) granted the German town law to the market settlement in 1224. Lübeck town law was granted in 1263, Magdeburg town law in 1295, Kulm town law in 1343. The settlement was first mentioned as a "civitas" in 1236.
Staple_Description: The origins of the Danzig staple are unclear, but in 1411, the staple was moved temporarily to Elbing by Grand master Heinrich von Plauen (HR I, 6 n 12). Apparently, the staple system of Elbing collapsed in favour of Danzig around 1400. In 1425, Danzig declared that it wanted to construct a building where guests could offer clothing. From 1441, there are clear attempts to force merchants to offer their commodities on the market, and in 1451 and 1482, Polish and Lithuanian merchants complained about the prohibition of trading between non-citizens. After Danzig was confiscated by Poland (1454), King Casimir confirmed the prohibition to travel between the sea and the hinterland without a stop in Danzig. In 1584, the staple for English cloth was moved to Elbing; in 1628, Danzig regained the exclusive import rights on foreign cloth.

name: Dardesheim
Settlement_Description: Probably a Frankish settlement from the 8th century, that developed into a market borough ('Marktflecken') during the 13th and 14th century. Town rights were granted much later, only in the 18th century.

name: Dassel
Settlement_Description: First mentioned between 826 and 877. A church is mentioned around 1022.
Town_Description: The settlement is characterised as borough ('weichbild') in 1310. It received Alfeld town privileges in 1315.

name: Dassow
Settlement_Description: Dassow goes back to a Slavic settlement and castle from the 10th century. A land of Dassow is first mentioned in 1158, the settlement itself in 1219. It developed into a market borough ('marktflecken') and is first mentioned as such ('oppidum') in 1451.
Fair_Description: A fair in Dassow is first mentioned in 1628, when it led to protests from the Parkentin family. According to late 18th-century sources, it took place on the first Tuesday of November.

name: Datterode
Toll_Description: A toll station was installed in 1583 after merchants circumvented the toll station in Ulfen by traveling via Datterode.

name: De Meern
Settlement_Description: Earliest mention is from a copy dating 1217.

name: Deelen
Settlement_Description: Earliest mention dates from the end of the thirteenth century.

name: Deetz (Zerbst)
Settlement_Description: The village is first mentioned in 1314, in a 15th-century copy.

name: Deetz (Altmark)
Settlement_Description: Until 1238 the settlement was owned by the counts of Osterburg, which means that it has existed before.

name: Dehnsen
Settlement_Description: The settlement was first mentioned in 1146.

name: Dellbrück
Settlement_Description: First mentioned in 1448. The name is derived from a bridge across a canal ('delf').

name: Delden
Settlement_Description: First mentioned in 1036 (in a copy from the second half of the 14th century). Originally a dispersed settlement.
Town_Description: In 1322, New Delden was founded as a fortified settlement south of the original settlement. The inhabitants of old Delden were relocated here, with their old privileges. In 1333, Jan III of Diest, bishop of Utrecht, granted the town privileges of Oldenzaal to Delden.

name: Delitz am Berge
Settlement_Description: Mention in the Hersfeld Zehntverzeichnis (No. 122). Seat of a ministerial family in the 14th century.

name: Seemühl
Settlement_Description: First mentioned in 1298. The name of the settlement is derived from a water mill. In 1630 an inn is mentioned.

name: Delft
Settlement_Description: Delft is first mentioned in a 1420 copy of a document from the period 1130-1157. It originated near the court of a count. A hospital is first mentioned in 1252. A breadhouse and a meathouse were granted by the count in 1295. A cloth hall is first mentioned in 1316 (an old and a new one in 1334), a weighhouse in 1342. The 'scroede ambocht' also mentioned in 1342 indicates that there was a crane.
Town_Description: Delft was granted town privileges on 15 April 1246 by William II of Holland. Cox argues that Delft already was a town-like community before that time, as the grant is the result of an initiative by towndwellers.One of the smaller ‘Kamers’ (departments) of the VOC (Verenigde Oost-Indische Compagnie, Dutch East India Company, founded in 1602) was located in Delft.
Fair_Description: The town-privilege of 1254 mentions two fairs: with St. Odulphus (June 12) and the other without a date (in 1316 with St. Gillismis: Sept. 1). The marketfield is found in 1315 and then property of the count. In 1436 it is granted to the town. In 1405 merchants of Delft are first found on the fairs of Frankfurt. A manual from the toll-keeper of Geervliet dated 1562 with a calendar of horsefairs mentions the horse-fair in Delft on June 9. In 1580 king Philip II granted a seed-fair starting August 25  for 6 days. The mayors said that Rotterdam recently obtained a seed-fair starting August 12. The seed was desended from Overmaas and the isle of Overflakkee and because of this the trade in Delft was halved.Dated circa 1594 a tariff for the horse- and dairyfair is preserved. Merchants from Flanders, Henegouwen, Brabant, Zeeland, Gelre, Gulik and 'Zuidholland' (the region around Dordrecht) are found in it. The towns and villages in 'Noordholland' (present Zuid-Holland above the Meuse) are free but had to give 1 groot for wax and toll-letter. Waalwijk was freed by trial but also had to pay 1 groot for wax. Permission from the comital audit-office had to be obtained to start the horse-fair two days earlier (3 days before Odulphusday: June 11). The date was now five days before St. Oel (Olevaer? July 29). This had to be published in almanacs, as the horse-fair in Haastrecht hampered the one in Delft too much. For the St. Gillisfair (Sept. 1) or dairy-fair a tariff  is registered. The toll-keeper was situated outside the Ketelgate to collect the 'keizersmarktgeld' (market-toll of the emperor) levied of butter and cheese.

name: Eisenach
Settlement_Description: First mentioned in 1150. The settlement developed near the castle Wartburg as a market village on long-distance trade routes in Hesse.
Town_Description: In 1189 the settlement was referred to as civitas. The landgraves of Thuringia stimulated town development since the 12th century. Between 1384 and 1387 the town rights were recorded in the "Eisenach law book" ('Eisenacher Rechtsbuch').
Fair_Description: Around 1300, there were three fairs in Eisenach, although it can be assumed that the fairs were established earlier. In the regulations of safe conduct of 1517/18 four fairs are mentioned, without dates.
Toll_Description: In Eisenach, a market toll and a fee for overland safe conduct ('Feldgeleit') were due, which was determined by the mode of transport and the amount of the load. In 1341 the safe conduct was leased. Revenues are known from 1480 onwards. Fees and regulations ('Geleitsordnung') date from 1517/18. Secondary stations of safe conduct existed in Creuzburg, Marksuhl, Schweina and Mihla.

name: Delligsen
Settlement_Description: An inn is mentioned in Delligsen in 1567.
Toll_Description: A "minor" toll in Delligsen on the street between Alfeld and Höxter/Uslar is mentioned in 1548, where it is specified that it is levied only on hops (4 pounds for each wagonload), pikes brought from Uslar to Hildesheim (1/2 pound per bundle) and on horses bought on the market (2 pounds each). The total revenues are estimated at 8 or 9 guilders in good years. The toll is reiterated in 1567 and 1587.

name: Neunheilingen
Settlement_Description: First mention of Heilingen in 775-786, Neunheilingen as separate settlement first in 1150.

name: Delmenhorst
Settlement_Description: The settlement developed in the 13th century next to a castle of the counts of Oldenburg. The castle is first mentioned in 1254, the settlement in 1285.
Town_Description: Acquisition of Bremen town privileges in 1371. However, until the 17th century, the settlement is often characterised as borough ('flecken').
Toll_Description: The toll in Delmenhorst is first mentioned in the town privileges of 1371. The count of Oldenburg ceded the toll to the town of Bremen in 1380. Bremen citizens were exempted from the toll in 1461.

name: Dendermonde
Fair_Description: In 1393 (Sept.) a free fair was granted by Philip the Bold to restore war-damage. In 1398 (March) this fair was confirmed: it started the first Tuesday after St. Luke (Oct. 18), safe-conduct was given 8 days before and after. Confirmation by emperor Charles in 1550 of a free fair donated by duke Philip of Burgundy in 1397 with St. Luke (Oct. 18) during 3 days.

name: Denekamp
Settlement_Description: Earliest mention in the late tenth century, another mention in the twelfth century.

name: Denklingen
Toll_Description: The Duke of Berg levied a land toll here in 1435. It is mentioned again in 1555. More precise tariffs or revenues have not been preserved.

name: Dennewitz
Settlement_Description: The settlement is known since 1174 and was part of the initial property of Zinna monastery.

name: Derben
Settlement_Description: Mention as Derwen at the end of the 14th century.

name: Steinhagen (Vorpommern)
Settlement_Description: The village is first mentioned before 1278.

name: Derenburg
Settlement_Description: In the 10th and 12th century, a castle (Derenburg), which was erected in 925 by Henry I., constituted the centre of the settlement. The castle was destroyed in 1126 and the following village settled in its place.
Town_Description: A year or date of the awarding of town rights is unknown. The village is referred to as civitas in 1289, however.

name: Dessau
Settlement_Description: In the Early Middle Ages Dessau probably was a Wendish fishing village. First mention in a record in 1213. Dessau was a market place in the 12th century.
Town_Description: Since 1382 Dessau was referred to as town and was granted Magdeburg rights. An exact date of the awarding of the town rights is not known.
Fair_Description: A third fair is prevented in the town of Dessau in 1573 due to protests of Leipzig.
Toll_Description: The safe conduct was calculated by the horses that pulled a wagon. If someone had loaded herrings and crossed the Mulde river, this person had to pay an additional fee per ton of herring. In 1549 four road tolls and safe conducts are mentioned and the former method of raising fees confirmed.
Staple_Description: Each raft loaded with lumber or planks had to anchor on the Elbe river at Dessau for "three sunshines". In 1549 this staple right is mentioned again in the regulations of safe conduct.

name: Diekholzen
Settlement_Description: The first mention dates back to the 11th century.

name: Detern
Settlement_Description: First mentioned in 1409. The settlement is characterised as borough ('flecken') in the late 16th century.
Fair_Description: In ca. 1596, count Edzard of East Frisia granted a fair in Detern. A date is not mentioned.
Toll_Description: Around 1599, the count of East Frisia introduced a toll connected to the fair in Detern. This led to complaints from Oldenburg in 1602, after which the Imperial Chamber Court ruled that the toll was to be discontinued. After repeated complaints, a document from 1641 attest the discontinuation of the toll.

name: Detmold
Settlement_Description: A place ('locus') called Theotmalli is first mentioned in Frankish annals in 783; a church in 1023. The settlement itself is first mentioned in 1263.
Town_Description: The town was probably founded shortly before 1265 by the Lord of Lippe and received Lippstadt town rights. From 1357 it is listed as a town.
Fair_Description: A market privilege from 1361 confirmed the already existing fair on St Vitus, which was probably founded after Lippstadt example with two days of market freedom before and after. A second fair on Sunday before St Martin is granted in 1469. The two fairs were confirmed and a weekly market on Wednesday was added in 1603. A year later, St Martin's fair was moved to St Andrew's Day. Both fairs were also cattle markets.

name: Dettmannsdorf
Settlement_Description: The village is first mentioned in 1293.

name: Wałcz
Settlement_Description: The Slavic fishing village Walcz existed before the foundation of the town. Next to it a fortification was located. Another village Cron is first mentioned in 1249.
Town_Description: The town was founded in 1303 by the margraves Otto, Konrad, Johann and Waldemar of Brandenburg. The documents were endorsed multiple times by the Polish kings.

name: Deutz
Toll_Description: In 1386, the Archbishop of Cologne levied a transhipment toll on goods unloaded from the ship. A fee of 4 pfennigs was charged for a barrel of wine or per wagon. Unfortunately, annual revenues have not been preserved.

name: Deventer
Settlement_Description: Deventer was founded as a Carolingian missionary centre at a river crossing by St Lebuinus before 774. As such it is first mentioned in the <em>Vita Ludgeri</em> from 840-849 (in a copy from around 1000). In 877, it is called "portus" (a settlement with a harbour).
Town_Description: In 956, Deventer is called a town ('urbs'); in 960 Deventer is called a 'civitas'. In 1123, Holy Roman Emperor Henry V granted a privilege to the town ('stad') of Deventer. Successive bishops of Utrecht will probably have granted additional town privileges which resulted in the town privileges granted to Zwolle in 1230.
Fair_Description: At least from 1340 onward, four fairs were organized in Deventer. One around St John in the summer (24 June), one around St Jacob (25 July), one around St Giles (1 September), and one around St Martin and St Lebuinus (11 and 12 November). In 1386, a fifth fair was granted around Laetare. The duration of these fairs in the second half of the fifteenth century was eight days before and after, only the one with St. John started 14 days before that. In 1522 (May 15) emperor Charles V granted a sixt fair for beasts.
Toll_Description: <ul><li> Emperor Otto II donated the imperial toll in Deventer to the bishop of Utrecht in 975. This Bishop's toll ('Bisschopstol') was first leased to the town in 1354, from 1401 on eternally. The toll was abolished in 1799. The 'Bisschopstol' was a market toll levied at the town gates ('Bisschopstol te Lande') and on the IJssel river ('Bisschopstol te Water'). The central toll station for the Bishop's toll on land traffic was located at the gate 'Bergpoort'; the central toll station for the Bishop's toll and other tolls on river transport was (at least from around 1541) located at the gate 'Zandpoort'. See for 'Bisschopstol te Water' Node 11135. <li>

name: Dieckhorst
Settlement_Description: First mentioned in 1433. A castle (first mentioned in 1479), later a manor, was located on the left shore of the Aller. On the opposite shore a settlement developed.

name: Meinbecker Turm
Settlement_Description: Watchtower, erected in 1479 as part of the "Neue Landwehr" (new defensive line) east of Lüneburg. The tower guarded the place where the road crossed the little creek Dieksbeck with a little bridge or ford. The road was barred by a chain and would only have been opened by the guard. There was a well between two houses. The whole area was protected by palisades. Probably given up before 1580. In 1774, the place is still marked as "alte Thurm" (old tower) on the map of the Kurhannoversche Landesaufnahme.

name: Diepenheim
Settlement_Description: First mentioned in 1118. The early mentions probably refer to the lordship of Diepenheim rather than the settlement. A castle is first mentioned in 1169, next to which the settlement developed.
Town_Description: Earliest mention of Diepenheim as a town on 14 June 1379. Town privileges were possibly granted by the bishop of Utrecht as lord of Diepenheim between circa 1340 and 1379.

name: Diepholz
Settlement_Description: Between 1120 und 1160, the castle Diepholz was built, which protected the settlement next to it and gave it its name. The settlement is characterised as "oppidum" in 1356.
Town_Description: Town privileges of Osnabrück were granted by lord Johann of Diepholz in 1380. They were only partially confirmed in 1655 by the Duchy of Brunswick-Lüneburg, whereupon Diepholz was degraded to the status of borough ('flecken').
Fair_Description: Diepholz acquired the right to hold two fairs in 1525, on three days before and after St Dionysius and Our Lady. In 1577, they were replaced by two new cattle fairs, on Monday after Palm Sunday and the day after St Matthew. In 1614, only the fair on St Matthew still existed.

name: Diest
Toll_Description: A toll and tax called 'doorgang' (passage through) is found since 1423. This was probably levied from oxen and cattle. In 1467 the bailiff (schout) of Diest was ordained by the duke of Brabant to prevent evading this toll in Brabant.
Staple_Description: Lier was already reconfirmed in its privilege for a cattle-staple in Brabant in 1469 by duke Charles the Bold. But was opposed by Diest in 1475, who said to have the oldest oxen-fair. In 1477 the duke of Gulik informed Kampen that the oxen-fair in Diest was restored and that safe-conduct was given. In 1485 the staple was moved to Diest by Maximiliaan but in 1498 Lier won a lawsuit. In 1503 Diest granted safe-conduct for merchants with cattle from Deventer, Kampen, Zwolle and other inhabitants of the Oversticht, although Lier tried to prevent that. Den Bosch also opposed the market at Lier at least since 1555.

name: Diestedde
Settlement_Description: The parish of Diestedde is first mentioned in 1136.

name: Dietkirchen
Settlement_Description: The settlement probably goes back to a Bronze Age settlement, which was probably already fortified. In the 6th century a monastery and a church developed. The collegiate monastery St. Lubentius is mentioned for the first time in 841.
Toll_Description: The Count of Katzenelnbogen levied a toll here in 1445. It is not precisely recorded whether it was really a land toll - but it is probable. Tariffs are not known. The annual revenue in 1445/46 was ½ gulden and 13½ heller.

name: Dziwna
Settlement_Description: Nowadays Dievenow consists of four independent villages: West Dievenow - probably the oldest part of the settlement - East Dievenow, Berg Dievenow and Wald Dievenow.
Toll_Description: Dievenow was mentioned as a toll station in 1243. Further information about the toll is missing.

name: Dilschhausen
Settlement_Description: First mentioned between 780 and 802. In 1259 called 'villa'.

name: Dinant
Fair_Description: In 1070 Henry IV donated the bishop of Liège the mint-, market- and tollrights and the castle.

name: Dinslaken
Fair_Description: Before 1478 a fair is known on Nov. 11 with 3 days before and after safe-conduct. A weekly market took place on Monday-Wednesday.
Toll_Description: The Count of the Mark levied a land toll in 1397. Tariffs and revenues are not known.

name: Grebenstein
Settlement_Description: First mentioned in 1272 in the context of a castle at Grebenstein.
Town_Description: Was granted town privileges in 1324. The new town was founded in 1356 and united with the old town in 1370.

name: Greifenstein
Settlement_Description: The settlement developed near a castle and was first mentioned in 1237.

name: Dissen
Settlement_Description: First mentioned in 895, it probably originated as a late Carolingian royal court. The settlement is characterised as 'oppidum' in 1284 and was the seat of a law court. In 1556 it is mentioned as borough ('wigbold') and became seat of a regional district ('Vogtei') in the Prince-Bishopric of Osnabrück. The settlement acquired town rights in 1951.

name: Ditterke
Settlement_Description: The place was first mentioned in 1208.

name: Döbeln
Settlement_Description: Castle and adjoining settlement of the 10th century, first mentioned in 981.
Town_Description: The town was founded shortly after 1200.
Fair_Description: In the 16th century, there was a cattle market in Döbeln, which held some meaning for the Middle German region as well as the Erzgebirge. In the middle of the 16th century, tolls were raised in the electorate of Saxony and the Habsburg area and the electorate of Saxony was avoided by cattle traders, which led to concerns that the fair might decline.
Toll_Description: A toll in Döbeln is first mentioned in 1445. The town council bought the toll in 1460.

name: Gouda
Settlement_Description: Gouda was first mention in a (+/-) 1420 copy from a text dated 1143. It originated from a castle. In the eleventh and twelfth century, cultivations ('ontginningen') took place on the banks of the River Gouwe close to this castle. A port was constructed after 1250, after which Gouda grew into an important trade settlement.  A hospital is first mentioned in 1315.  A weighhouse and cloth hall are mentioned in 1356.
Town_Description: Gouda was granted town rights on 19 July 1272 by Floris V, count of Holland. In the 1350s, fortifications were added to the town.
Fair_Description: Fairs in Gouda are first mentioned in 1336 and 1356, taking place on St James's and St Lambert's Day. In 1381 they were characterised as horse and cloth markets. In 1501, the two fairs on St James and St Matthew were extended from three to six days. In 1505 a third fair was added on Saturday after Letare. A market toll was levied during market times, since 1410 only from horses. A tariff levied of old dated 1436 (June 6) is edited. In it several ship types are found, wagons and horses and barges from the Sticht (of Utrecht) and Gelre. The account of the comital steward of Gouda dated 1446 states that exempt of the market-tolls are citizens of Gouda, Schoonhoven, Middelburg, Goes, Schiedam, Woudrichem, Montfoort, Eethen en Meeuwen in Brabant and all people living in the socalled Blois territory. In 1465 Vlissingen, Tholen and Zierikzee are added. Citizens of Gouda were since 1407 (as a reward for the support to the count in his battle with the lord of Arkel, like many other towns in Holland and Zeeland) exempt of market-tolls levied in Woudrichem, Heusden and Middelburg. Heusden is not found in the list of exempt places on the fairs in Gouda. A manual of the toll-keeper of Geervliet dated 1562 mentions horse-fairs in Gouda on Febr. 11 and March 11 in a calendar of many horse-fairs.

name: Dobbertin
Settlement_Description: Around 1220, a Benedictine monastery was founded at Dobbertin, which shortly afterwards became the seat of a convent of nuns. The monastery was the centre of medieval expansion efforts and was able to steadily increase its possessions in the course of the 13th century.

name: Richtenberg
Settlement_Description: The church village is first mentioned when it was donated to the monastery Neuenkamp at its founding in 1231.

name: Dobele
Settlement_Description: The 'Semgallenburg' (castle) was conquered by the Teutonic Order in 1289. The order built a new castle in 1335. In 1444 a fortfied borough ('Hakelwerk') was mentioned.

name: Döbrichau
Settlement_Description: The village is first mentioned in 1241.

name: Driehausen
Settlement_Description: First mentioned in 1182 as separate settlement. From the 16th century, it was considered a part of Schwagstorf.

name: Doberlug
Settlement_Description: A Sorbian village is first mentioned in 1005. In 1165 the Cistercian monastery Dobrilugk is founded. After the secularisation of the monastery in 1541 it was turned into a castle. The settlement was granted town privileges by Duke Christian I of Saxony-Merseburg in 1664. Merged with Kirchhain in 1945.

name: Berka (Werra)
Settlement_Description: First mentioned in 775-786 in ownership of the monastery Hersfeld. In the beginning of the 16th century Berka was called market borough ("Marktflecken"). Town rights were only granted in 1847.
Toll_Description: In 1283 toll rights of the Thuringian landgrave are mentioned. Station of safe conduct mentioned in 1509.

name: Dongen
Settlement_Description: Earliest mention in 1288, in a copy dating from 1349.

name: Doesburg
Town_Description: Earliest mention as oppidum probably in 1204 or 1230. Granting of town privileges on 19 September 1237 by Otto II, count of Guelders. A burgomaster and town council is mentioned in 1329.
Fair_Description: At least from 1294/95 onward, Doesburg had a fair. Another fair was granted in 1340. Both fairs existed until at least 1655.
Toll_Description: The Doesburg Market toll for sailing transport was levied first during the week of the St. Gallus fair (October 16th). From 1340 onward, with the introduction of the second annual fair, a toll was levied during the week of the St. Margraret's fair (July 13th). After shifting this fair to St. George's Day (April 23th) the toll was levied during the week of this fair. The toll was levied on behalf of the count of Guelders and Zutphen.

name: Doetinchem
Town_Description: Doetinchem probably already had a market and merchants in the second half of the 11th century. Town privileges were granted after 22 October 1229 and before 11 November 1231, by Otto II, count of Guelders and Zutphen. The oldest seal dates from 1236. The burgomaster and council received the right to fortify the town in 1282. Town privileges were confirmed by count Reginald I on 4 December 1312.
Fair_Description: Doetinchem had at least since 1294/95 a fair on St. Catharine’s Day (25 November). The duration of this fair is unknown.

name: Dohna
Toll_Description: Secondary station of safe conduct ('Beigeleitsstelle') of Pirna.

name: Döhren
Settlement_Description: The village was first mentioned in 1042.

name: Dokkum
Settlement_Description: First mentioned as a settlement existing in 754 in a fourteenth-century copy of an early ninth century document.
Town_Description: First mentioned as a town on 8 March 1298.

name: Dölitz
Settlement_Description: First mentioned as manor in 1262, since 1451 knightly manor.

name: Dollern
Settlement_Description: First mentioned in possession of the monastery Katlenburg in a charter from 1105. Earlier settlement since before 800 can be assumed.

name: Dommelen
Settlement_Description: Earliest mention in 1297, in a eighteenth century copy.

name: Dommitzsch
Settlement_Description: Originally a Slavic village with a fortification, first mentioned in a falsified charter from 965. First certain mention in 979/981. A German settlement developed next to it.
Town_Description: The date of acquisition of town privileges is uncertain. In 1465 Dommitzsch was mentioned as town.
Toll_Description: Secondary station of safe conduct ('Nebengeleit') of Wettin in the system of safe conduct around Leipzig.

name: Domnitz
Settlement_Description: In 1137 a monastery farmyard ('Klosterhof') was founded in Domnitz, showing that the settlement already existed earlier.

name: Doorn
Settlement_Description: Earliest mention in 918-948, in a eleventh century copy. Next mention in 1126, in a falsification which probably dates from the twelfth century.

name: Doornspijk
Settlement_Description: Earliest mention dates from 796, in a tenth century copy.

name: Franzburg
Settlement_Description: Lord Witzlaw I of Rügen founded the Cistercian monastery Rosetum sanctae Mariae, later known as Neuenkamp, in 1231. A settlement developed around the monastery. After the Reformation the ducal castle Franzburg was built on the secularised monastery grounds before 1587.
Town_Description: The town Franzburg was founded by Duke Bogislaw XIII of Pomerania near the castle of the same name. Privileges are known from 1587, 1588, 1612 and 1626.

name: Dodewaard
Settlement_Description: Earliest mention dates from the late eleventh century.

name: null
Harbour_Description: Aalborg benefited from a good natural harbour due to the town locality at a river estuary and beach meadows. The knowledge of the medieval port is, however, limited. It was placed in the small river, Østerå. Bulwarks were constructed in the 13th century. Smaller vessels could be loaded at a bridge across the river, Ladebro, while larger ships had to anchor in the fjord outside the harbour. In the late medieval period the port was expanded. Throughout the medieval period and early modern era Aalborg was one of the most important ports in Jutland. From the early 14th century onwards, German ships often used to port, for example from Lubeck in 1366 and 1399.

name: Hämeenlinna
Settlement_Description: Permanent agricultural settlement in Hämeenlinna (sw. Tavastehus) area goes back to the Iron Age. The earliest parishes in Häme (lat. Tavastia, sw. Tavastland) were established at the latest in the second quarter of the 13th century. The site of Hämeenlinna town (est. 1639) north form the castle may have been preceded by temporary or permanent settlement already in the 15th century.
Town_Description:
Queen Christina founded Hämeenlinna (sw. Tavastehus) after the initiative of Governor-General of Finland Per Brahe and gave the first town privileges in 1639. The area of the town was regulated before 1650 and slightly enlarged towards north in the 1650s. The town centre was moved to its later location after the fire of 1739 in 1777–84. In the last quarter of the 1700s, the castle was surrounded by modern bastion system that extended to the former town area. A large barracks area was built on the site of the town in several stages from the late 1840s to the late 1910s. The residence and of the governor of the province of Uusimaa and Häme (sw. Nyland and Tavastehus län) was in Häme castle since 1635. The province was split in two in 1640–48, after which the residence of the combined provinces was removed to Helsinki in 1648.

<b>Post office:</b> According to sources, the official founding year of the Hämeenlinna post office is unknown. In this context, the founding year of the postal route is used in the database. The postal route to the city was established in 1638, when postage rates for mail traveling from Helsinki to Hämeenlinna were defined. Hämeenlinna received its own postage rates in 1643, becoming equal to other offices. The postmaster in 1649 is known to have been the castle clerk Jonas Peerson
Fair_Description: Hämeenlinna was in 1650 confirmed two annual fairs on Epiphany (6 January), and 1 September, of which the latter was in the same year changed to St Olaf (29 July). The apostle Jakob’s fair (25 July) in Renko of the mid-17th century and likely of medieval origin was in 1670 translocated to Hämeenlinna and combined to St Olaf’s fair there together with the annual Saturday before Pentecost fair of Hattula.
Toll_Description: The 1/32 duty worth of all goods intended for sale in towns and fairs and brought to the site by peasants was collected in Hämeenlinna.

name: Dormagen
Settlement_Description: The settlement has been documented since Roman times.
Toll_Description: 1) The Duke of Jülich levied land toll and fee for save land conduct here from 1389. The escort money was collected by a special servant in the 15th century, so that toll and escort money existed independently of each other. Depending on the load, 2 to 3 white pfennigs per horse were collected as fee for save conduct. In 1389/93, an average of about 623 marks per year was collected. In 1398/99 it was about 420 marks.2) In addition, the duke levied road toll in 1434, which was collected by a publican. In 1495, the tariff was 1 light shilling per wagon.

name: Dörnhagen
Settlement_Description: First mentioned in 1253, in 1303 called a 'villa'. 1346 probably desolate.

name: Dornitz
Settlement_Description: In 1484 Dornitz is sold to the lords of Ammendorf by the archbishopric of Magdeburg. Before it was owned by the counts of Alsleben.

name: Reichmannsdorf
Toll_Description: Mentioned as secondary station of safe conducht ('Beigeleitsstelle') of Gräfenthal in 1728.

name: Dörpen
Toll_Description: A toll of the bishop of Münster in Dörpen is mentioned in 1576, when it could not be leased. Likewise, in 1645 a toll collector could not be found as revenues had decreased due to the Thirty Years' War.

name: Amsterdam
Settlement_Description: In 1275 count Floris V granted the people living around the dam in the river Amstel toll exemption. This is the first time that 'Amstelledamme' is found in historical sources. This dam was situated at the current square called Dam and was probably built around 1270
Town_Description: Town privileges were officially granted after 21 May 1300 and before 5 August 1301. Extended town privileges were granted on 9 December 1342. In 1368 Amsterdam received from the king of Sweden the privilege for a 'vitte' (trading-post) on Schonen (southern point of Sweden) with its own guardian. The largest of six 'Kamers' (departments) of the VOC (Verenigde Oost-Indische Compagnie, the Dutch East India Company, founded in 1602) was located in Amsterdam.
Fair_Description: It is unknown when Amsterdam obtained market rights. In 1304, the market rights were withdrawn by William III of Holland, the eldest son of the count of Holland. It is unknown when market rights were regained, but this happened definitely in the fourteenth century. A weigh-house is first mentioned in 1392. In the fifteenth century, there were at least two fairs. In 1422 the first merchants from Amsterdam visited the fairs of Frankfurt. Until the beginning of the seventeenth century, the fairs took place on the Dam and the Damrak.
Toll_Description: In 1275 the people who lived at the Amestelledamme (dam in the river Amstel) obtained toll-exemption from the count of Holland. Probably shortly before 1323 a toll on all imported beer from Hamburg and the Baltic via the Zuiderzee was located by the count of Holland in Amsterdam at the entrance of the 'rout binnendunen' through Holland. Accounts ('particulen') of the beertoll are preserved and edited for the years 1352-1354 and 1364-1366. Yields are preserved and edited for the years 1343-'69. From 1469/70 the accounts of the stewards of Amstelland mention a toll on 'vreemd bier' (imported beer). In an unedited account dated 1531/2 it is said that inhabitants of Amsterdam were free of this toll as those exempted from the toll at the Spaarndam. In 1557 Amsterdam purchased this right from the count (king) of Holland, Philip II. In the 14th century Kampen took care of buoying the Zuiderzee and the tidal inlets. In the course of the 15th century Amsterdam took over this role more and more. 'Bakengeld' (buoy-money) is first found in 1413 after duke Albrecht situated a new toll in the Zuiderzee or the Marsdiep. The Hanse opposed this toll. In 1452 duke Philip of Burgundy granted the raising of the harbour-money or 'paalgeld'. In 1474 an ordinance stated the levying of 'paalgeld' from goods of the Hansa for two years. In 1527 Kampen renounced the right to place the buoys in the Vlie, Marsdiep and other tidal inlets where paalgeld was levied, to Amsterdam. Goods of Kampen however would be free of this tax (this was the case already in 1514). Yields of the paalgeld are edited and analysed for the 1530-'72 and show a considerable increase of the shipping in the periode circa 1545-1565. Around 1550 there are 'paalmeesters' (collectors of the paalgeld) for Amsterdam in Hoorn and Enkhuizen. This caused opposition. Tariffs of the paalgeld dated 1514 (especially for England), 1556 and 1560 are almost corresponding. In 1573 king Philip II granted after advice of William of Orange and the Estates the right of the paalgeld to Enkhuizen.
Staple_Description: The count of Holland ordained shortly(?) before 1323 that all beer imported via the Zuiderzee from Hamburg and the Baltic had to be traded in the ports of Amsterdam and Medemblik. Afterwards Medemblik is never mentioned again. The staple was important both for the early development of Amsterdam as for the utilisation of the 'route binnendunen' through Holland. The famous worldstaple-market which Amsterdam supposedly was during the Golden Age, is altered by Lesger in a gateway to the Dutch hinterland with moreover a news- and information-staple then a staple for goods.

name: Dorsten
Town_Description: The Cologne archbishop Konrad von Hochstaden awarded Dorsten the town privileges of Dortmund on June 1, 1251
Toll_Description: 1) The archbishop of Cologne confirmed the river toll in Dorsten that his predecessor had introduced in 1332. The toll was divided into two parts in 1334: one part belonged to the archbishop, the other part to the town. The toll was raised from 1 Rader albus to 1/2 Taler in 1557, despite many protests. Citizens from Dorsten only had to pay the old fee of 1 Rader albus after 1577. More exact toll tariffs are known from 1625.2) The Archbishop of Cologne also levied a bridge toll in 1371.

name: Dortmund
Settlement_Description: First mentioned between 880 and 890. The origins of the settlement are unknown. 939 it is called 'urbs' and in 979 'oppidum'.
Town_Description: The exact date when the town was established is unknown, because a town fire in 1231/32 destroyed the relevant charters. In 1236 Emperor Frederick II confirmed the old privileges, which are believed to have been issued between 1138 and 1152. The town is first mentioned as a Free Imperial City in 1232 and was an important member of the Hanse.
Fair_Description: In 1232 King Henry VII granted Dortmund a second fair next to the already existing one from Ascension Day until Pentecost. The new fair took place on 14 days after St Michael's Day (29 September).
Toll_Description: Both the county of Dortmund and the city of Dortmund levied a land toll in 1074. In 1241, half of the fees and the county itself, then in 1431 completely, fell to the town of Dortmund. According to the tariffs of 1330/40, fees were only levied in February and from the end of March to the end of April. 1330/40 resulted in a tariff of 4 pfennigs per wine carriage (detailed tariff: RÜBEL, Urkundenbuch II, no.456). In 1390 an annual yield of 9 marks 10 shillings, in 1391 one of 10 marks and 7½ shillings and in 1392 one of 11 marks and 12 pfennigs could be achieved. For further yields see source.

name: Dösen
Settlement_Description: First mentioned in 1305 as Dosene, as part of a name.

name: Drawiny
Bridge_Description: The settlement is mentioned after a bridge across the Drawa. Duke Mestwin of East Pomerania and the margraves of Brandenburg formed an alliance here in 1273.

name: Düshop
Settlement_Description: The place was first mentioned in 1383.

name: Drawsko Pomorskie
Settlement_Description: A settlement developed near an old Slavic fortification, first mentioned in 1273.
Town_Description: The Margraves of Brandenburg Otto IV, Konrad and his children, granted the knight Arnold von Goltzen and his brothers the right to found a town in 1297.

name: Dranse
Settlement_Description: In 1233 property in Dranse is given to Amerlunxborn monastery. The monastery sells its property in 1430.

name: Drebkau
Settlement_Description: Probably first mention as Trebetz in 1301, first secure mention as Drebekowe in 1353.

name: Drensteinfurt
Settlement_Description: First mentioned in c. 851. The village developed around the church of the farm Steinfurt. It is mentioned as a town-like settlement ('Wigbold') in 1428.

name: Dresden
Settlement_Description: The town developed from a Sorbian port settlement; by c. 1150 there was fortress with a settlement.
Town_Description: Niemeyer dates the town’s foundation to 1200/1210; town fortifications existed in 1216. Today’s Dresden-Neustadt to the north was buit in the 17th century.
Toll_Description: A toll in Dresden is first mentioned in 1343. Probably this was only a toll on the land road, not on river traffic. The regulations of safe conduct recorded in 1716 are a copy of the regulations from 1547. They also include land and water safe conduct regulations from 1630.
