Staple_Description: In 1455, Elector Frederick II of Saxony moved the staple right of Brüx (Most), which had been conquered by Bohemia, to Dresden. Salt, fish, honey and other commodities which were transported through Saxony to Bohemia, had to be offered for sale in Dresden. However, enforcing merchants to travel through Dresden proved to be difficult, and the road via Freiberg was still often used. The staple was confirmed in 1603, with special mention of corn and wood for the supply of the town.

name: Dreilützow
Settlement_Description: First mentioned in the tithe register ('Zehntregister') of Ratzeburg in 1230.

name: Bad Driburg
Settlement_Description: In 753, a "castrum Iuberg" is mentioned for the first time in the Frankish imperial annals and refers to the Iburg, located 1 km southwest of the town center on a mountain spur. The beginnings of the settlement of Driburg probably date back to the 12th century. The earliest mention is found on a coin minted in 1215.
Town_Description: Driburg is first referred to as a "civitas" around 1250. The exact date of the granting of town rights is unknown, but councilors and a town wall are attested in 1290 at the latest. In 1345 the town rights were confirmed by the bishop of Paderborn. The town was an important station on the Hellweg and on the pass of the same over the Eggegebirge.

name: Drieberg Dorf
Settlement_Description: The village is first mentioned in 1275.

name: Sulechów
Settlement_Description: Originated as a castle settlement from the times of the early Piasts. First mentioned in 1319, already a town.
Town_Description: The town was established around 1250 by the Silesian dukes, first mentioned as castle and town ('Haus und Stadt') in 1319.

name: Drezdenko
Settlement_Description: The Polish fortification Drzn was first mentioned in 1092, later it became the seat of a castellan. A Slavic settlement existed next to it.
Town_Description: First mentioned as a town in letters from 1317. In 1373 it was characterised as castle and borough ('castrum et oppidum') and in 1526  as town ('Stad' and 'Stedichen').
Toll_Description: The toll on water and land of Drezdenko is first mentioned in 1317.

name: Drönnewitz
Settlement_Description: The originally Slavic village is first mentioned in 1228.

name: Großentaft
Settlement_Description: First mentioned in 815. In the 12th century, there was a 'Wasserburg' in the lower part of the village, and another, younger "Salzburg" to the north. There was probably a third castle, called "Hirtstor". All the castles have disappeared today.

name: Ośno Lubuskie
Settlement_Description: A German market settlement developed near an old settlement, with subsequent enlargement eastwards with two markets. First mentioned in 1252, then already a town.
Town_Description: Founded in 1252 by the bishop of Lebus.
Toll_Description: A toll is first mentioned in 1434.

name: Dzelda
Settlement_Description: In 1253 the Celde manor belonged to the bishop.

name: Amsterdamse Verlaat
Lock_Description: In 1436 a new lock  was constructed in the Lage Gouwe, in order to improve the shipping capacity of the Gouwe river through the city. It was still under construction in 1442. The lock functioned as a northern counterpart of the old lock in the city centre (Donkere Sluis), in fact creating a large pound lock of 380 m. The construction was funded by Haarlem, Leiden, Amsterdam, Gouda, Alkmaar, Hoorn, Medemblik and Edam.

name: null
Harbour_Description: A harbour is mentioned for the first time in 1378, but the character of the medieval harbour is not known. In 1580 the king donated oak trees to repairs of an old wharf. The wharf was also repaired in 1635 and 1649. In 1658 the wharf was about 30 meters long.

name: Grünberg
Settlement_Description: A castle was built in 1180, where a settlement formed immediately.
Town_Description: Mentioned in 1186 as a castle suburb, unclear whether city rights exist. Listed as a 'Flecken' in 1195, named as 'civitas' in 1222.

name: Düderode
Settlement_Description: A falsified charter from the 16th century contains a first mention for the year 935.

name: Duderstadt
Settlement_Description: King Henry II donated property in Duderstadt to his wife Mathilde in 927 and 929. This royal farm - later mentioned as ducal farm - was located around the current St Servatius's church. East of it, around the current Gropenmarkt, a market settlement developed.
Town_Description: First privileges are attested in 1247; the first town seal in 1255. The Brunswick town privileges were confirmed by duke Henry the Admirable of Brunswick-Grubenhagen in 1279.
Fair_Description: Duderstadt had 4 fairs, the dates of which are unknown. In 1638, they were extended with horse and cattle fairs.

name: Dutzow
Toll_Description: In 1434 it is mentioned that a toll was levied in Dutzow since times of old. The revenues financed the maintenance of causeways, which were constructed in 1352.

name: Duiven
Settlement_Description: Earliest mention in 838, in an eleventh century copy.

name: Dülken
Toll_Description: The Duke of Jülich levied a road toll in 1387. In 1517 the annual revenue was 5 marks.

name: Düsseldorf
Town_Description: Town privileges granted by the counts of Berg in 1288.
Fair_Description: Duke William of Jülich and Berg granted Düsseldorf a fair on St Albin's day (22 June) and a weekly corn market on Wednesday in 1482.
Toll_Description: 1) The Duke of Berg levied a river toll on the Rhine in 1374/77. In 1380, 6 turnosgroschen were collected per foder of wine. In 1386, it was 12 Turnosgroschen per foder of wine. For more detailed tariffs and yields, see source. In 1427 the annual yield was about 6782 gulden, in 1428 about 4810 gulden and in 1429 5507 gulden.2) In 1398/99 the Duke of Berg levied a fee for free conduct on the river. Rates and revenues have not been preserved.3) The duke also levied a land toll in 1476. 4) In 1395 he levied a road toll. One shilling had to be paid per carriage with heavy goods such as wine, fish or cloth.

name: Schiffahrt
Toll_Description: The Münster cathedral chapter levied a toll at the bridge from 1521, with the same tariffs as the toll at the bridge in Schöneflieth.
Bridge_Description: A bridge across the Ems is mentioned in accounts of the cathedral of Münster between 1509 and 1630. It was destroyed in the Thirty Years' War; a planned reconstruction of the bridge in 1652 did not take place. Only in 1822, a new bridge was built.
Ferry_Description: A ford existed at the Ems river at this place, which was crossable by foot in summer. A ferry operated here as well, which gave the location its name. A document from 1341 suggests that the ferry at that time was located in Gimbte, and it must have moved to the location near Fuestrup before 1446.

name: null
Toll_Description: A toll on the Meuse is first found in 960. Merchants from Nijmegen were exempted from the toll, as confirmed in 1388. In 1480 Maastricht was freed by the bishop of Liège from the toll on the Meuse in Liège. Three tolls are found in 1671: the one on the bridge, the 'alkijn'toll (?) and the toll on 'steen- en smeekolen' (forge and coal).
Harbour_Description: It is assumed that a harbour on the Meuse in Liège existed at least since the late 10th century, due to the development of the city in that period. At least landing places for vessels on the river are mentioned in 985 in Dinant, Namur, Huy and Maastricht, which all belonged to the bishopric of Liège. The main harbour was located on both sides of the Meuse bridge, as shown on early modern views of the city. The part upstream was called Sur-Meuse and downstream Goffe. Here existed loading stations for foreign wines (mentioned in 1332) and salt (1369). Numerous other smaller landing places, some of them in use for other commodities, were located along the many shores of the various branches of the river.

name: Ebendorf
Settlement_Description: Mentions in 950 and 965 when the tithe in Ebendorf is given to St. Moritz' monastery in Magdeburg. Since 1363 the counts of Falkenstein hold some of their judgement days ('Dingtage') in Ebendorf.

name: Eickhof
Settlement_Description: Fortified manor or castle, first mentioned in 1285.

name: Gudensberg
Settlement_Description: The settlement goes back to a court mentioned in the 10th century. A castle of the Counts of Gudensberg is attested from 1121, besides the place developed.
Town_Description: The exact development of the town is unknown as there is no document. However, the place might be fortified at the end of the 12th century and is mentioned in 1254 as 'oppidum'.

name: Gusev
Settlement_Description: The church village Pifferkeim grew out of the Kulligkehmen around 1554 and later became Gusev

name: Dülmen
Town_Description: In 1311 the settlement was granted town privileges of Munster.
Fair_Description: Two single-day fairs were granted in 1311, on Peter and Paul's and St Victor's Day. Two additional fairs were granted in 1326, on New Year's Day and Sunday before St John the Baptist.

name: Düna
Settlement_Description: Abandoned between 1337 and 1372, with the exception of a manor; resettled in 1935.

name: Daugavpils
Settlement_Description: Daugavpils was founded by the Russians in 1577, after they had destroyed the old castle and town of Dünaburg, 20 km upstream.

name: Vecdaugava
Settlement_Description: Bishop Albert founded a Cistercian monastery on the right bank of the Düna in 1202. This was built in 1205-1208. Over time it was expanded into a fortress. In 1305 the Teutonic Order bought it.

name: Dünebroek
Settlement_Description: Monastery of the Knights Hospitaller, founded before 1319. It was abolished in 1529, although the first Protestant service in the church only took place around 1550; the former monastic property was leased in 1580. The buildings were still extant in a dilapidated state in the 17th century; they were demolished in 1810.
Toll_Description: A road toll was levied near Dünebroek; an "old toll house" is first mentioned in 1719, but it is unknown when it was introduced. Possibly, the toll was levied after the monastery's secularization.

name: Dungelbeck
Settlement_Description: The village was first mentioned in 1053.

name: Dünninghausen
Toll_Description: The bishop of Münster relocated the toll of Dünninghausen in 1390.

name: Dünnwald
Toll_Description: The Duke of Berg levied a land toll in 1487. The tariff was 3 white pfennigs per ohm of wine or per horse with dry goods.

name: Durbe
Settlement_Description: The place was first mentioned in 1230 and fell under control of the Teutonic Order in 1253. In the 15th century a fortified borough ('Hakelwerk') was built, which burned down in 1435.

name: IJsselhavensluis
Lock_Description: A lock in the mouth of Gouda's harbour was allegedly constructed in 1615 to prevent the harbour from silting. However, a city map of Blaeu from 1649 still displays an open entrance to the harbour, so it could be that it was constructed later in the 17th century.

name: Diesdorf
Settlement_Description: First mention in 1112. In 1161 a monastery of Augustinians was founded, which was converted into a worldly chapter of nuns in 1551.

name: Ebern
Settlement_Description: The settlement probably originated in the 8th century. First indirect written evidence of the settlement in 1151, but is is first mentioned explicitly in 1216.

name: Eberswalde
Settlement_Description: Many stone and bronze age findings as well as a Slavic castle mound. A German castle was mentioned in 1261 and a market settlement developed close to it, first mentioned in 1276. A church is mentioned in 1294 and a merchant house in 1300.
Town_Description: Acquisition of town privileges around 1300 from Margrave Albrecht III. Eberswalde was additionally known as "Neustadt" ('new town'), which became a fixed addition to the town name in the 14th century.
Toll_Description: The toll of Niederfinow was moved to Eberswalde in 1317.
Staple_Description: The transshipment point between land traffic and shipping on the Oder was moved from Niederfinow to Eberswalde in 1317, including the obligation to use roads leading through Eberswalde. However, a real staple, including the obligation to offer transported commodities on the local market, was not established.

name: Ebstorf
Settlement_Description: Around 1160 the first founding of a Premonstratensian monastery in Ebstorf is presumed. A second foundation probably took place in 1190, when Benedictine nuns from Walsrode moved to Ebstorf. The monastery owned land in the surrounding villages and parts of the saltworks in Lüneburg (mentioned in 1224). In 1565 the monastery became Protestant.

name: Rønne
Settlement_Description: Originally a fishing village. Permanent settlement in the 13th century, when the church of Rønne was built.
Town_Description: In 1327 Rønne was characterized as a town for the first time. In 1345 the town paid an annually town tax (Danish: Midsommergæld) to the town lord. Mayors and citizens are mentioned from the 15th century onwards. In most parts of the medieval period the town as the whole island of Bornholm belonged to the Danish archbishops of Lund in Scania. After the Danish reformation in 1536 Rønne came under the king. Throughout the middle ages the town benefited from the rich herring fishing in the Baltic Sea. Especially merchants from Greifswald visited the town, and in the 14th century a guild for the Greifswald merchants was founded in Rønne. The town was probably the largest of all towns on Bornholm both in the medieval period and afterwards

name: Echte
Settlement_Description: First mentioned in the 8th or 9th century.

name: Ychten
Settlement_Description: Earliest mention in 1245, in a  thirteenth century copy.

name: Ebeleben
Settlement_Description: In 1198 a noble family of Ebeleben is mentioned. It is only later mentioned as a settlement. The village only became a town in 1928.

name: Eķengrāve
Settlement_Description: The manor was first mentioned in 1526.

name: Eckhorst
Settlement_Description: Manor in posession of Lübeck citizens, first mentioned in 1306. An inn is mentioned in 1447.

name: Edderitz
Settlement_Description: The village is first mentioned in 973.

name: Eeklo
Settlement_Description: Earliest mention in 1220, in a 17th-century copy.

name: Eersel
Settlement_Description: Earliest mention in 712- 713, in a copy dating from 1191. Next mention in 1102-1105, in a twelfth century copy.
Fair_Description: Before 1316 Eersel had a fair. In 1544 Eersel obtained the right for a weekly market. An undated register from the abbey Tongerlo (Westerlo, B.) (circa 1556) contains a list of fairs in the region Kempen and Peel. 'Eerselle' has then four fairs: 1) first Sunday after Quasimodo (first Sunday after Eastern) till the first Tuesday after that, 2) Sunday before festum assumptionis Mariae (Aug. 15) till the first Tuesday after that, 3) Sunday after 'St. Mertten' (Nov. 11) till the first Tuesday after that, 4) Wednesday before Mid-Lent.

name: Edersleben
Settlement_Description: First mention in the Breviarium sancti Lulli before 775/786.

name: Schönewerda
Settlement_Description: The settlement of Schönewerda was founded on an island in the Unstrut in the 12th century. It is first mentioned in 1177, together with a water mill. The nearby village Eßmannsdorf is older (first mentioned in 786), but was only merged with Schönewerda in the 20th century. According to some authors the settlement acquired town and market rights in 1310 and lost them again in 1628, but this cannot be proven.
Toll_Description: Schönewerda is mentioned as secondary station of safe conduct ('Beigeleitsstelle') of Freyburg in regulations from 1621, where fees had to be paid for cattle.

name: Egeln
Settlement_Description: In the 9th century a castle was constructed by Henry I. which was the centre of a burgward settlement in the 10th century. Thanks to a crossing of two roads in Egeln a road market developed early.  In the 12th/13th century a market borough ('Marktflecken') developed.
Town_Description: First mention as civitas in 1251. Town rights can be proven for 1365. The town probably earned town privileges earlier (possibly when market rights were granted in 1250).
Toll_Description: An escort ('Geleitsmann') can be proven in 1494-1497 in Egeln.

name: Eggenstedt
Settlement_Description: Mention of Eggenstedt 1143 as the property of Gottesgnaden monastery near Calbe.In 1563 the number of inhabitants of Eggenstedt had shrunk to 10-12, the settlement decayed during the 30-year-war.

name: null
Bridge_Description: A bridge across Suså is first mentioned in 1420. There can, however, be little doubt that it was considerably older.

name: Eggersdorf (Bad Salzelmen)
Settlement_Description: The village is first mentioned in 1205.

name: Eggershausen
Settlement_Description: The place was first mentioned in 1323.

name: Ehrenburg
Settlement_Description: Castle of the counts of Hoya, first mentioned in 1427. The related settlement was characterised as borough ('flecken').
Toll_Description: The toll in Ehrenburg was pawned in 1525.

name: Eichenbarleben
Settlement_Description: In 1140 mention in a buying record, mention of a ministerial family in 1283, which had a manor here.

name: Eickenrode
Settlement_Description: The place was first mentioned in 1295.

name: Eickhorst
Settlement_Description: First mentioned in the second half of the 13th century.

name: Eidapere
Settlement_Description: Manor that was first mentioned in 1530.

name: Eilenburg
Settlement_Description: In the 10th century a castle was built that was mostly destroyed during a Slavic uprising. The settlement at the castle, however, remained. It is already referred to as town ('urbs') in 981.
Town_Description: The acquisition of town rights probably occurred at the beginning of the 13th century.
Fair_Description: Over decades the town of Eilenburg requests a second fair, but always fails due to the resistance of Leipzig. The date of the first fair is unknown.
Toll_Description: An uncommonly detailed regulation of safe conduct lists the toll on the transportation of several commodities in 1524 (ThHStA Weimar, Reg. Cc 676, Geleitsrechnung Eilenburg 1524/25, p. 2–6.).

name: Eilensen
Settlement_Description: The place was first mentioned in 1118.

name: Eilum
Settlement_Description: A first mention from 888 is debatable; the next mention of the settlement dates from 1121. Urn graves north of the current village hint at earlier habitation around 400/500.

name: Eime
Settlement_Description: A first mention in the second half of the 10th century is uncertain. The settlement is attested as borough ('flecken') in 1550.

name: Eimen
Settlement_Description: The village was first mentioned in 1183.

name: Eimersleben
Settlement_Description: First mention probably in 1043, next secure mention around 1150.

name: Zalk
Settlement_Description: Earliest mention in 1213. The predecessor of the St. Nicolaaskerk (St Nicholas Church) possibly dated from the eleventh century. The current tower dates from the end of the twelfth century.

name: Eindhoven
Settlement_Description: Assumably, Eindhoven was founded between 1212 and 1232. The first mention of Eindhoven can be found in a sixteenth-century copy of a document dated 1232.
Town_Description: Eindhoven was granted town rights in 1232 by Henry I, duke of Brabant. Eindhoven was surrounded by a stone wall and had a moat.
Fair_Description: In 1232 or 1233 Eindhoven obtained the right for a weekly market from te duke of Brabant. Before 1340 Eindhoven had a fair and a cloth-hall, in 1340 a weigh- and meat-house. In 1419 three fairs and a weekly market are mentioned. An undated register from the abbey Tongerlo (Westerlo, B.) (circa 1556) contains a list of fairs in the region Kempen and Peel. 'Eijndoven' then has five fairs: 1) first day after 'Jaers'-day (Jan. 1), 2) first Tuesday before 'Pallemen'-day (Sunday before Eastern), 3) Tuesday before Sacraments-day (Friday after Eastern), 4) first Tuesday after St. Jacobs-day (July 25), 5) first Tuesday after the Sunday before festum nativitatis Mariae (Sept. 8). In 1572 the town had a weigh-house for butter.

name: Markt Einersheim
Toll_Description: Emperor Charles IV granted the toll and safe conduct in Einersheim to the noble Lutz von Hohenlohe and his heirs in 1349.

name: Mníšek
Toll_Description: The Bohemian toll station was pawned to Saxony in 1425.

name: Einum
Settlement_Description: First mentioned in the 8th or 9th century in a register of possessions of the monastery Corvey.

name: Oulun Kastelli
Settlement_Description: Permanent settlement in Liminka and Oulu area dates at the latest to the turn of 13th and 14th centuries. In 1375 a castle of Swedish Crown was built to that time rivermouth in Kastelli. Novgorod laid siege to the castle in 1377. The castle did not establish itself as an administrational centre and it was either destroyed, demolished or left in oblivion in the turn of the 14th and 15th centuries.

name: Lutherstadt Eisleben
Settlement_Description: First mention between 780 and 802. In 994 the market borough ('Marktflecken') earned market-, coin- and tollrights.
Town_Description: Around 1180 mentioned as civitas. In 1286 the town wall is mentioned in a record. Around 1500 a new town is established.
Fair_Description: In 1522 Leipzig complained about the fairs ein Eisleben, who claimed that the fairs there would benefit Leipzig, since wares in Eisleben had to pass through Leipzig first. They had also owned their fairs since 100 years already. In 1690 the fairs on the Sundays Reminiscere, after St. Viti, St. Gallus and St. Mauritius were moved to the following tuesdays.
Toll_Description: Station of safe conduct of the counts of Mansfeld

name: Eitze
Settlement_Description: First mentioned in the year 860 in the wonders at the grave of bishop Willehad in Bremen. First mention in a charter in 1220.

name: Elberfeld
Toll_Description: The Duke of Berg levied a land toll, possibly already before 1496.

name: Elbingerode
Settlement_Description: Resting place at the route between Wernigerode and Nordhausen, since 1220 mentioned as village. 1298 first mention of a castle in Elbingerode.

name: Loket
Toll_Description: A transit toll is mentioned in 1351.

name: Aldskoat
Settlement_Description: In 1299, a women's monastery of the Teutonic Order was founded in Oudeschoot. The monastery was abolished in 1580.

name: Schweina
Settlement_Description: The brook Schweina is first mentioned in 933. The settlement is mentioned in 1183.
Toll_Description: Since the safe conduct in Eisenach was avoided by some by taking the route Vacha – Salzungen – Schweina – Waltershausen, a secondary station of safe conduct was established in Schweina in 1508/09.

name: Großensee (Berka)
Toll_Description: Seulingssee was a secondary station of safe conduct of the amt Gerstungen. Revenues are known since 1537.

name: Bad Salzungen
Settlement_Description: The settlement developed near saltworks and is first mentoned in 775 as site of a Carolingian royal court.
Town_Description: The town was probably founded by the lords of Frankenstein in the 13th century. Acquisition of town rights probably before 1289. At the beginning of the 14th century the town was subject to Fulda town rights.

name: Elburg
Town_Description: It is generally assumed that town privileges were granted to Elburg between 1220 and 1271, probably by Otto II, count of Guelders; possibly around 1233. The town was probably located along the Zuiderzee shore southwest of the current town, but threatened by floods. For this reasons, duke William of Guelders ordered his steward ('rentmeester') Arent thoe Boecop to rebuild and fortify the town slightly more inland in 1392. The new town was being build with a chessboard street pattern from 1393 onwards, and walled in 1396. Only the Ellestraat is a remnant of the old town and therefore differs slightly from the regular street pattern. In 1397 the bishop of Utrecht granted permission to rebuild the church of St Nicholas within the town walls.
Fair_Description: In 1397, Duke William I of Guelders granted two fairs, each lasting 8 days before to 8 days after the fair date. Its ‘market freedom’ was based on the example of Arnhem.
Staple_Description: At least since 1530 Elburg has the right to direct the oxen driven over the Veluwe to its fair. In 1557 it stated to have a privilege for this from the count of Gelre and that it relates to the oxen transported around St. Galli (Oct. 16) across the Veluwe to Brabant.

name: Ellamaa
Settlement_Description: Originally a village near the Soinitz manor. In 1515 the estate was called "Hellenbeke". From 1580, however, it is referred to as a village again.

name: Ellamaa
Settlement_Description: Around 1500 there was a little estate.

name: Ellecom
Settlement_Description: Earliest mention in 1128-1139. Archaeological research shows that around 1100, a wooden chapel arose on the location of the Saint Nicholas Church (Nicolaaskerk).

name: Elm
Settlement_Description: First mentioned in a donation charter between 1111 and 1116.

name: Eldena (Mecklenburg)
Settlement_Description: Bishop Gottschalk founded the Cistercian nunnery Eldena between 1229 and 1235. The exact date of foundation is unknown. The monastery was abolished in 1558 and became the administrative centre of the region ('Amt').

name: Eldena (Greifswald)
Settlement_Description: The settlement was first mentioned in a donation document from 1193/99. In 1199, Cistercians founded a monastery in Eldena, which was approved by Pope Innocent III in 1204. A village developed shortly afterwards.

name: Obersuhl
Toll_Description: Secondary station of safe conduct of the Amt Gerstungen. Revenues are known since 1537.

name: Elmshorn
Fair_Description: In the description of Schleswig and Holstein of Heinrich Rantzau from 1597, it is mentioned that three fairs were held in Elmshorn: a horse market on Thursday after Quadragesima, a fair on the Dedication day of the church on Sunday after Trinitatis, and a fair on 21 September, which was also a horse and cattle fair.

name: Escharen
Settlement_Description: Earliest mention  dates from the beginning of the thirteenth century.

name: Elspeet
Settlement_Description: Veen et. al. (2016) presume permanent habitation of Elspeet from ca. 1250 onwards. Neefjes and Bleumink (2015) consider earlier habitation a possiblity, possibly from the tenth century onwards. There is consensus that habitation and cultivation of land intensified during the thirteenth century in this area. From the thirteenth century onwards, habitation centered around a church dedicated to St. Paul. Nowadays, this is the ‘Hervormde Kerk’ located at Nunspeterweg 3.

name: Elst
Settlement_Description: Earliest mention dates from 726 in an eleventh century copy.
Fair_Description: Elst had one fair from at least 1294/95 onward, on the Day of the Assumption of Mary (August 15) and the day before that. At least in the sixteenth century, this was a horse fair. In 1545 the day after St. Laurentius (August 11).

name: Elstertrebnitz
Settlement_Description: First mentioned as a manor in 1079, later as a knightly manor (1548).

name: Elze
Settlement_Description: Founded as Carolingian missionary centre. First mentioned between 826 and 876, characterised as village in 1190 and developed into a borough ('flecken') in the 14th century.
Town_Description: Already in 1360, a council and seal are mentioned. A town hall was built in 1546, town privileges acquired in 1579.

name: Ērģeme
Settlement_Description: The castle was first mentioned in 1323.

name: Falkenhagen (Mark)
Settlement_Description: First mention in 1313, in the 14th century referred to as oppidum, once as town in 1369, after that as little town ('Städtlein') and borough ('Flecken').

name: Emden
Settlement_Description: Emden arose from a Frisian trading settlement, where a Carolingian missionary church was erected around 800.
Town_Description: While Emden was occupied by Hamburg in 1433-1439 and 1448-1453, the settlement acquired urban character and institutions. However, town privileges were never granted.
Fair_Description: In 1440, it is first mentioned that fairs were organised in Emden. In 1497 they were specified as two eight-day fairs, taking place eight days before Laetare Sunday and eight days after St Michael.
Toll_Description: - Toll on the river Ems, first mentioned in 1224. Toll reductions were introduced in 1457 for citizens of Groningen, who were freed from staple and toll obligations in Emden; in 1493 for Hamburg beer; and in 1497, reduced toll rates are mentioned for merchants from Münster. East Frisians were exempted from the Ems toll as well. The toll rates were doubled in 1541.<br/>- The 1494 staple privileges contained a so-called 'ruderzoll' for large see-going vessels that entered the harbour of Emden in cases of emergency, but were not obliged to stay in the town for a certain time.<br/>- New tolls were introduced in 1595 for imported commodities belonging to East Frisians, or being transported further to East Frisia. They were cancelled between 1603 and 1605. Citizens from Emden were exempted from these tolls in 1610.
Staple_Description: The staple right was officially granted in 1494, but already practised in times that the town was controlled by Hamburg (1433-1439, 1448-1453). Merchants from Groningen were initially freed from staple obligations in Emden, but the 1483 prohibition to export corn, butter and cheese from East Frisia was also strictly implemented towards Groningen. Under Count Edzard of East Frisia in 1506-1514, Groningen merchants were privileged again. Emperor Charles V removed the Emden staple in favour of Groningen in 1548, but it was still practised, and his successor Ferdinand I declared Charles's decree invalid in 1558. In the following years, Emden's staple was acknowledged by Hamburg, Osnabrück and Münster. Emden was staple port of the English Merchant Adventurers in 1560-1564, 1580-1587 and 1599-1602. The staple was practised without many conflicts until the 1680s, afterwards often restricted and finally abolished in 1765.

name: Emmerich
Settlement_Description: The place was first mentioned in 828. A cloth-hall is first found in 1353.
Town_Description: Town rights were granted in 1233. A town council is mentioned in 1316, a burgomaster in 1334.
Fair_Description: In 1294 two fairs are mentioned: 1) Sept. 14 and 2) Nov. 1. Before 1450 three fairs are mentioned, next to Sept. 14 (duration 7 days) on Sunday after June 24 (3 days) and on Oct. 28 (2 weeks). In 1450 the September and June fairs were relocated to Apr. 26 (duration 3 days) and June 6 (7 days). Weekly markets from Tuesday to Thursday and Friday to Sunday are mentioned before 1233.
Toll_Description: The monastery of St. Maria in Utrecht levied a river toll on the Rhine here in 1318. A toll was mentioned for the first time as early as 1142. This was probably a market fee. Fees on river and land traffic, documented in 1233, were also market-related. In 1324, a preferential tariff of 4 pfennigs per foder of wine applied to citizens from Duisburg. A right and tariff dated 1393 with the freedom of Nijmegen was confirmed, which was also valid for the other towns of Gelre. Free were goods owned by citizens on their own or foreign ships, foreign goods on these ships were taxed. It states further that Cologne, Neuss and Kaiserswerth are free 'upverdich' (upstream) but not 'uytverdich' (downstream). Dusseldorf, Uerdingen, 'Berck' (Rheinberg), Dorsten, Recklinghausen, Dortmund, Soest and  the 'Mercksen' towns are not free. Towns of old belonging to Gelre and Kleef situated between Roer and Linge are free. Tiel and Grave as not of old belonging to Gelre and Duisburg and Culemborg are not free. Wesel, Kleve and Xanten are half free, but should not be as they were not of old belonging to Kleef. In 1436/37 the annual yield was about 650 gulden, in 1489/90 579 gulden. Accounts are preserved and partly digitised for the years: 1436/7, 1489/90, 1493/4, 1495-1507, 1509, 1511, 1515, 1522, 1533, 1626-29, 1636. The river toll was moved to Schenkenschanz around 1635.

name: Eemnes-Binnen
Settlement_Description: Cultivation of land west of Ter Eem/Eembrugge resulted in the settlements Eemnes-Binnen en Eemnes-Buiten. Earliest mention of 'Emnesse' dates from 1269. Especially after ca. 1300, people settled here. Both places and the area west of the river Eem fell under the jurisdiction of Ter Eem. In 1439, Eemnes-Binnen became independent of Ter Eem.
Town_Description: Town privileges granted in 1439 by Rudolf of Diepholt, bishop of Utrecht.

name: Eemnes
Settlement_Description: Cultivation of land west of Ter Eem/Eembrugge resulted in the settlements Eemnes-Binnen en Eemnes-Buiten. Earliest mention of 'Emnesse' dates from 1269. Especially after ca. 1300, people settled here. Both places and the area west of the river Eem fell under the jurisdiction of Ter Eem. In 1352, the northern part of the area west of the river Eem, was split off Ter Eem: Eemnes-Buiten became independent.
Town_Description: Town privileges granted by John ('Jan') of Arkel, bishop of Utrecht, in 1352. In 1356, Eemnes-Buiten became part of Holland.

name: Eschborn
Settlement_Description: First mentioned in 766 as part of a donation to the monastery Lorsch.

name: Emsbüren
Settlement_Description: First mentioned as Buren in 1151, although the settlement is der Ort ist probably older and contained one of the manors donated to the holy Liudger before 849. Market borough ('marktflecken') since the 14th century. The connection with the river Ems in the name is first attested around 1490.

name: Endorf
Settlement_Description: First mentioned in a charter in 934 as Emmundorp.

name: Äntu
Settlement_Description: A manor was first mentioned in 1277. In 1558 it was occupied by the Russians.

name: Engelskirchen
Toll_Description: Toll station of the Count of Berg

name: Emstek
Settlement_Description: The settlement is first mentioned in a charter of king Otto I from 947.

name: Emmen
Settlement_Description: Earliest mention in 1139, in a 16th century copy.

name: Mamonovo
Settlement_Description: There used to be an Old-Prussian sacrificial altar where the city stands today, probably alongside a castle and a castle mound, the first german settlement later grew into a village, but was destroyed during the uprising of the old Prussians in 1260, the Old Prussian fortress was captured and destroyed in 1272 by the Counts Günter and Dietrich von Regenstein, the german settlement was rebuilt in the 14th ct.
Town_Description: The handfast is lost but the town was likely founded in 1301 with Kulm town law, it was mentioned as a civitas in 1330, new privileges were granted in 1522 and 1560

name: Enger
Settlement_Description: First mentioned in 948. The settlement acquired borough ('weichbild') rights in the late Middle Ages.

name: Enkhuizen
Settlement_Description: The earliest mention of Enkhuizen dates from 1305. In 1397 the count donated his rights on the weighhouse to the town for the benefits of the poor.
Town_Description: Enkhuizen was granted town rights on 27 January 1356 by William V (duke of Bavaria and count of Holland). In 1368 Enkhuizen received from the king of Sweden the right for a 'vitte' (trading-post) on Schonen (southern point of Sweden) with its own guardian. One of the smaller ‘Kamers’ (departments) of the VOC (Verenigde Oost-Indische Compagnie, Dutch East India Company, founded in 1602) was located in Enkhuizen.
Fair_Description: In 1356 (Jan. 27 jan.) duke William V granted town rights to Enkhuizen with the right for a fair 4 days before St. John decapitation (St. Jansdag decollacio= Aug. 29), duration 14 days ('uitgaande oest'= at the end of the harvest), with tolls and rights like the duke had in Medemblik ('Medemleke'). The market-cross should be put upright 4 days before the start of the fair. In 1462 (May 2) duke Philip of Burgundy replaced the fair held on the Sunday before Crossday (Sept. 14) to the Sunday after St. Michelsday (Sept. 29), because in Sneek (Friesland) a fair was organised on the first date. Duration of the fair will be 15 days. In 1494 a free weekly market on Thursday was granted by Maximiliaan and Philip the Fair. On 13 April 1564 the town declared that the fair admitted in 1356 was not organised for a long time as a result of poverty of the welfare of the town as a result of the war with the Guelders and Frisians. The date of that fair was not suitable as the adjacent villages lived from the herring sailing and the villagers were then at sea. The town asked at the same time staff with the recovery of the harbour, walls and dikes. The king  is asked to replace the fair and the foundation of the market-cross to 8 days before St. Jacob till 8 days after that, with safe-conduct during 14 days. In 1565 (May) king Philip II granted a fair for 8 days, the 2 'toondagen' (days of display) were the 2 working days before St. Margareth (July 13). In 1575 (Oct. 20) the king granted three leather-fairs, the dates are: 1) Monday before Midlent, 2) the day after St. Margareth (July 14) and 3) 14 days before All-Saints (14 days before Nov. 1).
Staple_Description: In 1573 king Philip II granted the staple for all salted (dogh)fisch brought in via the Vlie or Marsdiep.

name: Ensen
Toll_Description: The Duke of Berg levied a land toll in 1487. Since Ensen was a secondary toll station of Dünnwald, the same tariffs applied as there. In 1488, the annual revenue was 316 marks 10 shillings.

name: Eppegem
Settlement_Description: Earliest mention in 966, in a fifteenth century copy. Next mention in 1146-1152, in a copy dating from circa 1265.

name: Eppendorf
Settlement_Description: First mentioned around 1140. The village church, mentioned in a document from 1267, is said to have existed since 840. In 1343, an inn is mentioned together with the toll station.
Toll_Description: A road toll is mentioned in Eppendorf in 1343.

name: Vacha
Settlement_Description: The settlement developed at an important Werra crossing and is first mentioned in 802-817.
Town_Description: The elevation to town occurred in 1186 at the latest by abbot Konrad of Fulda. It was subject to Fulda town rights. Around 1260 ditches, ramparts and walls, as well as the town castle Mendelstein were constructed.
Fair_Description: In 1508 two fairs are mentioned, in 1576 seven.
Toll_Description: Trade caravans heading for Frankfurt were taken into Hessian safe conduct in Vacha since the town was pawned to Hesse in 1399.

name: Lidzbark Warmiński
Settlement_Description: Originally an old Prussian castle and settlement, a castle of the Teutonic Order is mentioned in 1241 but was destroyed by the Old Prussians in 1242, it was rebuilt in 1260 as the castle of a bishop, as such it was captured by the Old Prussians during their riot and remained in their possession until 1273
Town_Description: Eberhard von Neiße, the bishop of Warmia, grants the Kulm town law to the village next to the Bishop's castle in 1308

name: Hellevad
Settlement_Description: The village of Hellevad was first mentioned in 1340, but is significantly older. The parish church is from either the 12th or 13th century. Hellevad watermill was mentioned in 1550, and its presence created a ford, making it possible to cross Surbæk.

name: Escheburg
Settlement_Description: The place was first mentioned in 1319.

name: Erfurt
Settlement_Description: Erfurt developed at the site of a ford ('furt') in the Gera river. The area was already settled in the Palaeolithic. In the 8th century centre of a Catholic bishopric, as well as Carolingian royal court ('Pfalzort'), it is first mentioned in 742.
Town_Description: Erfurt appears as trade centre in 805 and had urban characteristics since the 10th century. Expanded into a town since the early 12th century; in 1167 it is referred to as civitas. A university was founded in 1392.
Fair_Description: Erfurt hosted two large international fairs, the first of which was a four-week spring fair after Misericordia Domini granted in 1331. A second fair of three weeks on Trinity Sunday was added in 1473. Both fairs were reduced to two weeks in 1497. Additionally, Erfurt held several free markets which were less prestigious than the large fairs.
Toll_Description: Merchants from outside Thuringia hat to pay a fee of 4 pennies for wagons and 2 pennies for carts for entrepot ('Niederlagegeld') in Erfurt in 1289. They had to pay the same fee when they loaded their wares again. The transit toll was probably higher. Around 1495 the fee of entrepot had been changed to a fee of 6 pennies for every entrepot and wagonload of every foreign trader. The toll was paid in the toll station on the cathedral plaza. Regulations of safe conduct from 1315 and 1441 (in a copy from 1533) remain.
Staple_Description: The town legitimised its staple policy by the capitulary of Charlemagne of 805. It exercised a toll policy with staple characteristics in the law ('weistum') of 1289, to which later prescribed roads for the East-West-traffic between the Thuringian Forest and the Harz were added. The staple was abolished with the instalment of a staple in Leipzig in 1507, which led to resistance in Erfurt. The town tried to regain its staple in vain until the 17th century. Weight ordinances from 1631 and 1738 show that the town exercised a limited staple policy, in the sense of a pre-emptive right by its citizens.

name: Helsa
Settlement_Description: First mentioned in 1058. 1353 still called a village.

name: Hamburg
Settlement_Description: Precarolingian refuge fort of the Saxons north of the Elbe, bishopric since 831, archbishopric since 834. A market settlement outside of the fortress is first attested in 845.
Town_Description: The archiepiscopal old town (Altstadt) became a town no later than the mid-12th century. The new town (Neustadt) was founded by Duke Adolf III of Schauenburg and received Lübeck town privileges in 1188. Both parts were united around 1215.
Fair_Description: The oldest fair in Hamburg was the market of St Felicianus in the old town, which probably went back into the 11th century. The town privileges of the new town from 1188 mention two fairs on St Vitus and the Assumption of Mary. In 1365, emperor Charles IV founded a large three-week Pentecost fair, which was not well received and cancelled in 1383, five years after his death. An eight-day horse fair was founded on the Sunday after Lent in 1435, four additional four-day horse fairs were added in 1471: on three weeks before Sunday Estomihi, Sunday Oculi, Palm Sunday and All Apostles' Day.
Toll_Description: Four tolls existed in Hamburg:<br/>1) the Count, Priest or Schaumburg toll of the territorial lords was first mentioned in 1188 and in 1460 half went to the Danish royal house and from 1640 in its entirety. The levying of the toll was, however, in the hands of the town, to whom it was regularly pawned. Payment of the toll was handled at the town gates and at the harbour entrance; merchants from Bremen, Brandenburg, Meißen, Magdeburg, Braunschweig and Saxony were exempted.<br/>2) The Werkzoll, first mentioned in 1309, was raised by the council of Hamburg to finance navigation beacons for the isle of Neuwerk and the Lower Elbe; it was privileged by the Emperor in 1628. It has been mentioned that the toll was originally levied at the island of Neuwerk in the mouth of the Elbe itself, but this was probably an attempt by the city of Hamburg to legitimise its staple claims for the entire Lower Elbe river. <br/>3) A toll for securing the sea lanes from pirates and robbers was raised as a pound toll first in 1362, then from 1424 with some breaks until 1528. From 1541 the toll was raised in cooperation with Lübeck; in 1552 the toll was imposed unilaterally by Hamburg and converted into a grain toll after complaints from Lübeck in 1557. After the foundation of the Admiralty in 1623 a new toll for the defence of the sea lanes was introduced, which was almost exclusively levied on the shipping with Portugal and Spain.<br/>4) The Land and Elbe toll for trade heading inland by both water and land; toll records are edited by Pitz. Registers from the Land and Elbe toll and the Admiralty toll have survived from the 17th century; they were partly assessed by Reißmann. Pound toll records from 1485-6 have been edited as well.
Staple_Description: First attempts to establish a staple can be seen in the toll tariffs of 1236, where it is recorded that merchants were exempted from toll payment when they offered their commodities for sale on the market in Hamburg. In the following centuries, ever more trade limitations were taken; the town law of 1458 first contained an obligation for merchants to offer butter, cheese, fish and corn for sale on the local market for three days. The staple was confirmed by king Christian I of Denmark in 1480 and by the emperor in 1482. Merchants from Brandenburg were exempted from the staple between 1518 and 1555, but had to sell 2/3 of their grain in Hamburg afterwards. A threat for the staple was posed by the possible circumvention of town via the southern Elbe arm, which Hamburg tried to prevent from the 14th century. This led to conflicts with Brunswick-Lüneburg, Stade and Buxtehude in the 16th and 17th centuries. Despite a verdict of the imperial chamber court from 1619 that traffic on the southern Elbe should be free, the emperor confimed the staple privileges in 1621, and in 1628 Hamburg's control over the southern Elbe as well. After the mid-17th century, the staple was ever more difficult to enforce and finally abolished in 1748.
Harbour_Description: Until the construction of a new crane on the inner harbour in the 16th century, the only crane was that on the square adjacent to the town hall. This crane is first mentioned in 1291, but was probably older. Lighter boats transported commodities to here from the larger sea-going ships in the lower and inner harbours.

name: Ērgļi
Settlement_Description: Settlement existed since the middle of the 14th century. A castle called 'Erlaa' was built in 1397.

name: Erlangen
Town_Description: Acquisition of Auerbach town privileges in 1383.

name: Ermelo
Settlement_Description: Earliest mention dates from 855 in a copy made around 900. Earliest mention of the Oude Kerk (Old Church) in 1006.

name: Ermsleben
Settlement_Description: A castle near a prehistorical settlement was constructed at the end of the 12th or at the beginning of the 13th century. The village developed into a market borough ('Marktflecken').
Town_Description: In 1298 the village is already referred to as oppidum, but there are no further mentions concerning the town rights. In 1530 Karl V. grants market rights.
Fair_Description: In 1530 emperor Karl V. grants two fairs to Ermsleben, which didn't help the citiy's economy at all and could not prevent its dwindeling population.

name: Erndtebrück
Settlement_Description: First mentioned as knight's castle in 1296.
Toll_Description: The toll station in Erndtebrück is confirmed with a royal charter in 1349. It was renewed in the 16th and 17th century.

name: Erpe
Settlement_Description: Earliest mention in 972, in copy from the middle of the eleventh century. Next mention in 1088.

name: Ertvelde
Settlement_Description: First mentioned in a 12th-century copy of a document from 1167.

name: Erxleben (Magdeburg)
Settlement_Description: First mention at the end of the 10th or beginning of the 11th century; further mention in 1021. In 1170 a noble family which carried the name of Erxleben emerges in the records, probably in connection with the castle that is first mentioned in 1273, but probably existed before. A settlement existed alongside the castle and was closely tied to its events. The castle held garrisons from Magdeburg and Braunschweig; served as waypoint and station between Helmstedt and Magdeburg.

name: Erxleben (Altmark)
Settlement_Description: First secure mention in 1200; possibly already in 1145.

name: Eschenrode
Settlement_Description: First mention as Haskenroht as the property of Marienthal monastery.

name: Eschershausen
Settlement_Description: The settlement probably already existed in the 8th century. In the second half of the 14th century the settlement became a borough ('flecken'). Town rights were granted in 1833.
Toll_Primary_Owner: Edelherr von Homburg; Herzog von Braunschweig
Toll_Description: A toll station of the lords of Homburg in Eschershausen is first mentioned in 1384; it is included in a 1587 list of tolls in the duchy of Brunswick as well.

name: Ezemaal
Settlement_Description: Earliest mention in 1066, in an eighteenth century copy.

name: Eschweiler
Settlement_Description: A Carolingian court is mentioned in 828. Town privileges were only granted in 1858.

name: Herstelle
Settlement_Description: The settlement possibly goes back to a Carolingian fortification near an important river crossing; it was first mentioned in 1036. A castle of the bishop of Paderborn was first mentioned in 1163. The settlement near the castle acquired a market in 1171, and was mentioned in 1399 as town.
Toll_Description: Herstelle was listed as a toll station on the Weser river in a complaint from Bremen from 1584.
Ferry_Description: River crossing between Herstelle and Würgassen. It cannot be determined whether this was a ford or a ferry. According to Herbst (1926), the crossing had the character of a ford, as there existed a settlement on both sides of the crossing, since wagoners had to wait here for a while during floods before they could cross the river.

name: Essel
Toll_Description: Land and water toll. In 1389 the dukes of Brunswick-Lüneburg proclaimed that the same toll shall be levied on the Leine river in Neustadt that is levied on the Aller in Essel, namely for each fuder corn, flour or beer one Hannover shilling. According to a Hildesheim complaint from 1456, the fare for the land toll was doubled from one to two pennies. A 1507 agreement between Hannover and Celle regulated the fares for toll and safe conduct in Essel. Probably, this regulation concerned the toll in Neustadt, as Essel is not located at the Leine.

name: Essen
Settlement_Description: A first mention around 870 is debatable. Around the middle of the 9th century, bishop Altfrid of Hildesheim founded a women's monastery, around which the settlement developed.
Town_Description: A civic community appears in a charter from 1244, in which permission is granted to fortify the town. However, the town never became completely independent from the monastery.
Fair_Description: Abbess Theophanu of the Essen monastery received the right to hold a one-week fair on the feast of St Cosmas and Damian in 1041. By the 13th century, the fair had been reduced to two days and was overshadowed by the fair on St Kilian, the dedication day of the Münster church, and in the 14th century by the August market around the Assumption of Mary. Two smaller two-day fairs existed around the St George's Day and the feast of the 11,000 Virgins.

name: Essen (Oldenburg)
Settlement_Description: First mentioned between 968 and 978. There is said to have been a law court here at times, which suggests that the settlement had the character of a borough ('flecken' or 'weichbild').

name: Bad Essen
Settlement_Description: The place was first mentioned in 1074.

name: Estebrügge
Settlement_Description: The settlement goes back to the settlement Eschete, which developed on both sides of the river Este during the cultivation of the region Altes Land in the 12th century. The church is first mentioned in 1200. Estebrügge proper is named after the bridge over the Este, which is first mentioned in 1335 and was the only fixed river crossing until 1875.
Fair_Description: A fair in Estebrügge is first mentioned in 1595 and took place in September.

name: Estedt
Settlement_Description: First mention as the property of Calbe monastery, which is given to St. Lorenz' monastery.

name: Etingen
Settlement_Description: In 961 Otto I. gives Adinga to the archbishopric of Magdeburg.

name: Eula
Settlement_Description: Referred to as villa in 1090, in 1206 mentioned as manor.

name: Pont d'Amercœur
Toll_Description: A toll of the Duchy of Limburg was levied on the bridge. According to an account from 1389, the toll had been given by duchess Johanna of Brabant to lord Oiste of Charnoir.

name: Eutritzsch
Settlement_Description: First written record of the settlement in 1335 as Udericz, mentioned in 1378 as part of the administrative district of Leipzig. In 1890 the independent municipality was incorporated into the town of Leipzig.

name: Evere
Settlement_Description: First mentioned in a end thirteenth-century copy from a document from 1120.

name: Evessen
Settlement_Description: First mentioned in 965. The settlement might originally have consisted of two parts, the Osten- and Westendorf.

name: Eyendorf
Settlement_Description: Mentioned in a register of the diocese of Verden of ca. 1252.

name: Eystrup
Settlement_Description: A Saxon settlement already existed before the 9th century.

name: Eythra
Settlement_Description: Emperor Otto II. gave Eythra to the prince-bishopric ('Hochstift') of Merseburg, since it had had been illegaly revoked by margrave Thietmar. The village had to move to a brown coal opencast mine in 1982 and after operations were ended, was flooded.

name: Väo
Settlement_Description: Originally a village and town estate east of Reval. In 1402, Väo was bought by Reval.

name: Sokolov
Settlement_Description: First mentioned in 1279. The settlement was founded in the 13th century on the route Prague-Cheb-Nuremberg. It had a moated castle and a parish church, which is first mentioned in 1290.

name: Etterwinden
Settlement_Description: Uncertain mention in 958, first certain mention in 1292.

name: Fahrbinde
Settlement_Description: The village is first mentioned in 1333.

name: Kärkna
Settlement_Description: The monastery was built before 1234. It was a Cistercian monastery. In 1558 it was conquered and destroyed by the Russians.

name: Falkenberg (Mark)
Toll_Description: According to a 1549 complaint from Eberswalde, a barrier had been placed here and a toll ('niederlagsgelder') was levied.

name: Złocieniec
Settlement_Description: First mentioned in 1311, a castle in 1317. It was most likely a borough ('flecken') already before 1333.
Town_Description: The Brandenburg town law was granted in 1333 by Lüdeke and Hasse von Wedel.

name: Falkenhagen (Falkensee)
Settlement_Description: Founded around 1200, first mentioned in 1330 as property of the convent in Spandau. The village is merged with Seegefeld as Falkensee in 1923, which gains town rights in 1961.

name: Sokola Dąbrowa
Toll_Description: Attested as toll station in the 16th century.

name: Fallersleben
Settlement_Description: First mentioned in 942, then already with a church. The village was characterised as borough ('weichbild'; later 'flecken') from 1344.
Fair_Description: Three fairs were granted to Fallersleben in 1573: on Misericordia Sunday, Sunday after St Lawrence and 14 days after St Martin.
Toll_Description: A toll of the Duke of Brunswick is mentioned in 1409.

name: Bad Fallingbostel
Settlement_Description: First mentioned in 990. A church in Fallingbostel existed in 1239.

name: Farmsen
Settlement_Description: The place was first mentioned in 1151.

name: Farnstädt
Settlement_Description: First mention in the tithe register of Hersfeld monastery in the late 9th century.

name: Farsleben
Settlement_Description: In 1197 Ammensleben monastery held a third of the village. Unsure, if it is the same settlement that is mentioned in a record in 946 as being given to Quedlinburg monastery as a gift, since it is not mentioned again.

name: Rokin
Harbour_Description: After a dam was built in the Amstel river and a settlement developed, the area south of the dam became the harbour for river traffic. In the early 16th century a quay was built, which is shown on the oldest map of the city from 1544. Room had to be made for the quay by reducing the parcels lining the waterfront. The name Rokin, first attested in 1559, is derived from this action of "moving back" ('Ruck in') the houses.

name: Hochheim
Settlement_Description: First mentioned in 754 during the transfer of Bonitafius's remains from Mainz to Fulda.

name: Hofgeismar
Town_Description: The place was granted town privileges between 1220 and 1230, which were confirmed several times between 1354 and 1646. A 'nova civitas' is mentioned in 1234 and a mint master in 1210.

name: Hofheim
Settlement_Description: The settlement was mentioned in 1294, in the vicinity there are Roman remains of a stone fort built in 83 AD.
Town_Description: In 1352 Philipp von Falkenstein was allowed by Charles V to convert the village, called a 'villa' since 1294, into a town.

name: Fegetasche
Settlement_Description: The charterhouse of Ahrensbök acquired an eel weir at the Holsten bridge in 1429 and erected an hermitage with a chapel of St Anthony, which was enlarged in 1485. On the other side of the bridge, an inn at the toll station is first mentioned in 1596. The later name of the inn, "Fegetasche", first mentioned in 1649, probably does not refer to the toll payment, as is often suggested.
Toll_Description: Toll station of the counts of Holstein, connected to Plön. As the town Plön is not directly located on the main street, the toll was levied at the Holsten bridge on the border of the town area. The beginnings of the toll are unknown; a 1390 charter that guaranteed the freedom to use the streets for citizens from Plön has been interpreted to suggest exemption from toll payments. The fees to be paid were raised in line with other tolls in Holstein in 1474, but in comparison to the other toll stations, the Plön toll had only modest revenues. Lübeck citizens were exempted from toll payments. Toll registers are available for the years 1490-1518. Levying of the toll was discontinued in 1838.
Bridge_Description: The "Holsten" bridge, mentioned in the town privileges of Plön of 1236, crossed the Schwentine near the later inn Fegetasche. It formed the eastern border of the town area of Plön.

name: Kiviloo
Settlement_Description: The manor ('Hof') was first mentioned in 1322. It was situated near Kiviloo (1241: Kiulo). The castle 'Fegefeuer' was not completely built in 1474, but was already mentioned.

name: Fehrbellin
Settlement_Description: First mentioned in 1216, started as a small settlement close to the castle, that was first mentioned in 1305.
Town_Description: First mentioned as civitas in 1294, later in 1471 called opidum.

name: Vestiena
Settlement_Description: The manor was first mentioned in 1452.

name: Feldbergen
Settlement_Description: The settlement was first mentioned in 1218.

name: Lemvig
Settlement_Description: Founded around 1200, based on the age of the church. A borough (Danish: Flække) in most of the middle ages. In the late medieval period, however, Lemvig was characterized as a privileged borough.
Town_Description: A major rebuilding of the church in the 1400ties as well as other factors suggests urban growth in the late medieval period. Citizens of Lemvig mentioned in 1412. Described as a borough (Danish: Flække) in 1471. Town hall mentioned in 1479, when it burned down. Up until the 17th century Lemvig benefited from a rich fishing in Limfjorden.

name: Højrup
Settlement_Description: The village of Højrup was first mentioned in 1340, but is significantly older. The parish church is from either the 12th or 13th century.

name: Viljandi
Settlement_Description: The castle of the Livonian Brothers of the Sword was built in 1224 after they had conquered the Estonian castle 'Viliende'. A town developed next to the castle.
Town_Description: In the 13th century the city received Riga town privileges and later became a member of the Hanse.

name: Fermersleben
Settlement_Description: First mentioned in 937 in a gift certificate by Otto I. to the monastary of St. Moritz in Magdeburg (MGH DD OI, nr. 16, S. 103 - 105).Until the 10th century, Fermersleben should have been situated on the bank of the Elbe until it changed its course. Until the 18th century, the cut-off meander would have carried water.
Ferry_Description: In 1150 the ferry in Fermersleben is given to Berge monastery.

name: Fettehenne
Toll_Description: Countess Margarethe von Berg levied a land toll in 1377. A fee of ½ Weißpfennig per horse had to be paid.

name: Kivi-Vigala
Settlement_Description: A church was built in the 14th century. The Castle of Fickel was probably built around 1400, but was first mentioned in 1453. A Borough ('Flecken') around the church did not appear until the 20th century.

name: Finkenberg
Settlement_Description: First mentioned in 1351, characterised as farm (libera curia) in 1354. A mill is mentioned in 1355. Nowadays disappeared.

name: Finsterwalde
Settlement_Description: First mentioned in 1282. Originated as a market settlement near a castle from the 13th century, which was first mentioned in 1301.
Town_Description: Finsterwalde probably became a town in the 13th century.

name: null
Harbour_Description: A harbour is first mentioned in 1449. It was probably a natural harbour throughout the medieval and early modern period.

name: Hohenhorst
Settlement_Description: The dispersed settlement ('Bauerschaft') is first mentioned in 1142.

name: Fischbeck (Weser)
Settlement_Description: A monastery of canonesses was founded in Fischbeck in 955. After the Reformation it was converted into a Lutheran ladies' house in the 1560s, and recatholicised during the Thirty Years' War in 1629-1633.

name: Fischbeck (Elbe)
Settlement_Description: First mention in 1172. Probably part of the castle district of Kabelitz, since 1337 property of the bishop of Havelberg, since 1562 of the lords of Bismark.

name: Fischbek
Settlement_Description: First mentioned in a Kiel town register of 1264-1289.

name: Flemhude
Settlement_Description: First mentioned in the Kiel town register of 1264-1289; the church was built around 1242. The village name signifies a landing place of Flemish traders on the Eider river.
Harbour_Description: The Eider was navigable until Flemhude, which made the settlement an important transshipment port between the North and Baltic Sea in the High Middle Ages.

name: Horstmar
Settlement_Description: First mentioned at the beginning of the 11th century.
Town_Description: In the second half of the 13th century, town privileges were granted by the Bishop of Münster. Called 'oppidum' in 1297.

name: Friens
Settlement_Description: Earliest mention in the thirteenth century.

name: Flensburg
Settlement_Description: A permanent settlement with an urban character developed around the Church of St. John in the 12th century, probably around 1150. Flensburg benefited from its location in the bottom of Flensburg fjord near Hærvejen/ Ochsenweg.
Town_Description: Around 1190 a Saint Canute Guild (Danish: Sankt Knuds Gilde) in Flensburg was taken under royal protection, and at this time Flensburg must be considered as a town. Flensburg is mentioned in King Valdemar’s Cadastre in 1231, and the town was granted a town law in 1284 by Duke Valdemar IV. It was confirmed by Duke Eric II in 1314. At this time a town council had also been established. A Franciscan monastery was founded in 1263. In the early 15th century a royal castle, Duborg, was built northwest of the town as part of the ongoing conflict between Denmark and different counts of Holstein. The town wall is probably from the middle of the 14th century, when Flensburg was in the hands of count Nicolaus of Holstein. Throughout the late medieval period and in the early modern era Flensburg played an important role in the export of oxen from Denmark.
Toll_Description: Probably first mentioned in King Valdemar’s Cadastre in 1231. Tolls on different goods are mentioned in 1300. Citizens from Flensburg were exempted from the toll in 1337 and 1354. The toll was probably mainly levied on ships that visited the harbour of the town. Lists of toll tariffs exist from 1314, the 14th century, 1480 and 1594. Throughout the middle ages and the early pre-modern period Flensburg was an important toll station.
Harbour_Description: A natural harbour located in the bottom of Flensburg Fjord. From the 13th century onwards one of the most important ports in Denmark. Wharf in the bottom of the fjord in the medieval period. The port of Flensburg was central to trade between continental Europe and the Baltic Sea.

name: Flieden
Toll_Description: A toll for each horse laden with commodities had to pay toll to the monastery of Fulda in Flieden since 1357.

name: Forchheim
Settlement_Description: Border settlement of the Frankish realm before 805. Carolingian royal palace in the 9th century.

name: Lichterfelde
Settlement_Description: The village is first mentioned in 1310.

name: Frankenberg
Settlement_Description: First mentioned in 1243. The castle was built in 1233/34.
Town_Description: Acquisition of town privileges before 1243; In 1335 a new town was founded, which in 1556 was merged with the original town of Frankenberg.

name: Hønkys
Settlement_Description: The village of Hønkys was first mentioned in 1477, but is significantly older. The settlement had no church but was part of the parish of Egvad Church.

name: Forst
Settlement_Description: First mentioned in 1346, then already a town. Originated as German merchant settlement near a castle that secured a crossing of the Neiße river.
Town_Description: First mentioned as town in 1346. The Magdeburg town law was renewed in 1428.

name: Frjentsjer
Settlement_Description: Earliest mention in 1085. This document, however, is a falsification dating from around 1200. Another early mention dates from 1216.
Town_Description: A document from 25 July 1417 notes several town-like features; however, town rights are not mentioned. According to Cox, town privileges gradually developed between the late fourteenth century and 1474.
Fair_Description: The duke of Saksen granted the town in 1502 (March 26) a weekly market on Wednesday and two free fairs and abolition of excises. Dates of the fairs: 'Sanddt Veyts tage' (June 15) and: the 'nechsten tag nach Aller Selenn tage' (Nov. 3).

name: Frielingen
Settlement_Description: The settlement was first mentioned in 1357.

name: Frankfurt am Main
Settlement_Description: First mentioned in 794 in a document of Charlemagne. In 815 it became a the seat of a Carolingian royal palace. A Celtic settlement is said to have existed way before, which was conquered by Germans and was inhabited by the Romans in Augustan times.
Town_Description: A market town developed around the second half of the 12th century. It was mentioned as "oppidum" in 1142, and as "civitas" in 1226. In 1372 it became a free imperial city.
Fair_Description: The fairs in Frankfurt are first mentioned in 1227. They became large international fairs, attracting visitors from as far as France, Flanders, northern Italy and northern Germany. In 1240, Emperor Frederick II granted safe conduct for visitors of the fairs. The exact dates of the fairs were first mentioned in 1349. The oldest one was the Our Lady's or autumn fair ('Frauenmesse'); in 1330 a Lent fair was added.

name: Homberg
Settlement_Description: A castle is mentioned for the first time in 1162.
Town_Description: The city was founded in 1231 at the latest. 'Villicitatio et burgenses' mentioned in 1254.

name: Struer
Harbour_Description: Struer functioned as a harbour for the town of Holstebro from around 1500, and probably also before. No urban settlement until centuries later.

name: 's-Gravenvoeren
Settlement_Description: The settlement Voeren is first mentioned in 878 and consisted of multiple villages, of which 's-Gravenvoeren is considered the most prominent one.

name: Sint-Martens-Voeren
Settlement_Description: Earliest mention of the settlement Voeren in 878. It consisted of multiple villages.

name: Borken
Settlement_Description: First mentioned in the 9th or 10th century. Characterised as 'villa' in 1201-1203.
Town_Description: Between 1222 and 1226, the place was granted town privileges of Munster.
Fair_Description: A four-day fair from the day before St Michael until St Remigius is attested since 1249, a second fair from the day before St George until St Liudger since 1297. A third one-day fair on the day before Corpus Christi was added in 1594.

name: Frombork
Settlement_Description: Around 1270 a castle was built on the remains of an old Prussian settlement. It was first mentioned in 1278.
Town_Description: Originally planned as a town. Councillors and citizens are mentioned in 1287, a major in 1304. The Warmian cathedral was relocated from Braunsberg to Frauenburg. A town charter with the Lübeck town law was granted by the Warmian bishop Eberhard von Neiße in 1310.
Toll_Description: A new toll was levied in violence of the conditions of a treaty in 1467.

name: Saldus
Settlement_Description: The area was already populated from the 9th to the 13th century. In 1253 it was assigned to the Teutonic Order, that built a castle in the 1370s. A fortified borough ('Hakelwerk') existed in the 16th century.

name: Wschowa
Toll_Description: Listed as one of the five most important toll station in Greater Poland in the 16th century.

name: Gerstungen
Settlement_Description: First mentioned in 1015-1020. A market is assumed to have existed since the first half of the 11th century, the triangular shape of the market square points at an early foundation. Gerstungen was a royal court in the 11th century. In 1311 a moated castle is attested, the settlement is called opidum (borough) in the same year.
Fair_Description: Gerstungen had four fairs in 1604, on Wednesdays after Candlemas, Trinity Sunday, St. Bartholomew and St. Martin. All fairs were followed by a horse market.
Toll_Description: First mention of a toll in Gerstungen in the town rights of Eisenach from 1283. Revenues of the safe conduct of the Amt Gerstungen exist since 1522/23. Secondary stations of safe conduct existed in Untersuhl, Obersuhl, Dankmarshausen and Seulingsee (Großensee). Tariffs and regulations (Geleitsordnung) date from 1539/40.

name: Fredeburg
Settlement_Description: Watchtower in the Mölln enclosure ('landwehr') of the town of Lübeck, which was constructed around 1350. Fredeburg consisted after a drawing from 1594 of a tower guarded with a palisade, and three boom barriers - two from Lübeck and one from Mecklenburg.

name: Freiberg
Settlement_Description: The place grew out of the village of Christiansdorf; after the laying down of old town in 1170, the town developed into an important trading and mining town in the high medieval period.
Town_Description: The old town probably received its market, town and mining rights when it was founded in 1170; rights renewed at the end of the 13th century and 1433. From 1223 the term ‘civitas’ is used.
Fair_Description: Margrave Henry III of Meißen granted a 14-day fair to Freiberg in 1263.
Toll_Description: The toll and safe conduct of Freiberg came into possession of the town council in 1323.
Staple_Description: The staple of Freiberg is first mentioned in 1381. The foundation of the Dresden staple led to conflicts with Freiberg about bypassing Freiberg (1466). The staple was confirmed by the Elector of Saxony in 1470.

name: Bad Freienwalde
Settlement_Description: Originated as a German settlement in between two Slavic fishing villages, probably belonging to Pomerania in the late 12th century, first mentioned in 1316.
Town_Description: Exact date of founding is unknown, it was confirmed as a so called 'offene Stad' with a fair in 1364, mentioned as oppidum in 1373 and as civitas in 1375, called a 'stedeken' in 1477.
Toll_Description: A toll of the Uchtenhagen family, who owned the town, appears in a document from 1465. Citizens from Berlin-Cölln and Frankfurt were exempted, unless they were transporting commodities from other persons. A fish toll is mentioned as well.

name: Freren
Settlement_Description: First mentioned in a donation charter of the monastery of Corvey. The settlement possibly goes back to a missionary centre founded by the holy Liudger.

name: Fresendorf
Settlement_Description: The village was founded by the Rostock patrician family Frese, first mentioned in 1289.

name: Fretzdorf
Settlement_Description: In the second half of the 13th century, Fretzdorf fell into the property of the margraves.

name: Freudenberg
Settlement_Description: The place originated near a castle which was first mentioned in 1389.
Toll_Description: A toll in Freudenberg is mentioned in 1442-47, toll revenues in 1463.

name: Freyenstein
Settlement_Description: First mentioned in 1263. An old town close to the former castle mound was destroyed during border wars between Werle and Brandenburg.
Town_Description: Margrave John founded the town in 1287 with Brandenburg town law and exemption from tolls. Temporarily reduced to the state of a borough ('flecken') by the aristocratic rulers, fight for the re-establishing of former rights in the 18th century.

name: Strzelce Krajeńskie
Town_Description: Built between 1260 and 1270 by Margrave Konrad of Brandenburg as a fortress against Poland. It was destroyed in 1272 and rebuilt, mentioned as "civitas" in 1286.

name: Altfriedland
Settlement_Description: Mention of a Cistercian convent in 1271, in a record from 1300 an oppidum Vredeland is mentioned. Referred to as little town ('Städtchen') until 1565, but never overcame its status as village.

name: Friedrichsfelde
Settlement_Description: In 1288 Rosenfelde is first mentioned in the records. In 1319 it becomes property of the town of Berlin, which consigns it to the family of Ryke, who resides there until 1601/02. It is renamed to Friedrichsfelde only in 1699.

name: Friesack
Settlement_Description: An Ascanian castle existed in 1216, by 1256 in the possession of the noble family of Jerichow. A settlement developed close to the castle, mentioned as "hus und stat" ('castle and town') in 1327.
Town_Description: The town regulations were granted in 1571 and 1616 by the noble rulers.

name: Uebigau
Settlement_Description: First mentioned in 1251. Probably there existed a slavic settlement in the 7th century, which included a fortification upon which a castle was built by the lords of Ileburg in 1285.
Town_Description: Mentioned as civitas in c.1303. Town privileges were probably granted around 1300. Uebigau had Magdeburg town rights.
Toll_Description: Secondary station of safe conduct ('Beigeleitsstelle') of Liebenwerda. Annual revenues are known from 1464 onwards, although they remain absent for some years ('vacat'). Tariffs and regulations ('Geleitsordnung') date from 1505.

name: Friesoythe
Settlement_Description: A castle  of the counts of Tecklenburg was built in the 13th century. At the end of the century, a market settlement is attested, which is mentioned as "oppidum" in 1308.
Town_Description: Friesoythe was fortified after 1338 and had a council constitution in 1366/67 at the latest. Probably the town had town privileges of Osnabrück, from the 17th century of Lemgo.
Fair_Description: In the first half of the 14th century, various fairs are mentioned in Friesoyte, on many different days. For these fairs, letters of safe conduct are issued for merchants from Osnabrück. However, it is unclear how long these were organised. In 1369, a fair is still mentioned on Thursday after St John, but in an overview of fairs in Friesoythe from 1497, none of the 14th-century fairs is still mentioned. In their place there are two eight-day fairs, on St Giles and on the day of the Eleven Thousand Virgins. These must have disappeared in the course of the 16th century as well, and two new fairs are founded in 1565, on St Matthew and on the day of the Ten Thousand Martyrs. The importance of these markets was probably limited.
Toll_Description: A wagon toll of the bishops of Münster, which was levied at the town gates, as well as a shipping toll are mentioned in the 15th century. In 1573 and 1592, there were problems finding a person interested in leasing the toll. This suggests that the toll revenues were limited.
Harbour_Description: The river Soeste was navigable up to Friesoythe.

name: Frohburg
Settlement_Description: First mentioned as castle in 1198; earlier mentions from 1149 and 1172 belong to another settlement.
Town_Description: Developed into a town shortly after 1200. A burgomaster is mentioned in 1229 and the settlement is first characterised as "oppidum" in 1233. Usually referred to as minor town ('Städtchen', 'Städtlein').

name: Frohse
Settlement_Description: Originally a Slavic settlement. First mentioned in 936 in a donation charter to the monastery of Quedlinburg. Later often a place of royal residence. The settlement had a town hall, constitution and administrative bodies, but always stayed under the jurisdiction of the archiepiscopal lesser judge ("Möllenvogt"). 1202 is the year of the construction of the two parish churches in the "Old new town". A town council is mentioned in 1396. However, the settlement remained a borough ('flecken').
Toll_Description: A toll on horses and wood in Frohse is mentioned in 1230. In an enfeoffment from 1365, we hear of a toll on the Elbe river in Frohse, but this might be a writing error. In the 15th century there is regular mention of a little toll of Frohse on the Elbe.

name: Füchtorf
Settlement_Description: The first reference can be dated back to the 11th century.

name: Fürstenberg (Havel)
Settlement_Description: First mentioned in 1278 as settlement close to a castle.
Town_Description: First mentioned as civitas in 1318. The first town privilege dates from 1532, but was most likely a renewal of older privileges. It followed the Neubrandenburg town law.

name: Fuhlsbüttel
Settlement_Description: The settlement was first mentioned in 1283.
Harbour_Description: Harbour on the Alster river. It is known that Hamburg ships sailed to Fuhlsbüttel, where goods were transshipped to land transport, in 1584. In 1618, the Lübeck council was informed that due to closure of the Steindamm, travellers to Hamburg should use the waterway between Bergstedt and Poppenbüttel or Fuhlsbüttel.
Lock_Description: A lock in the Alster river was constructed in 1527 as part of the construction works for the Alster-Trave canal.

name: Fuestrup
Settlement_Description: The village was first mentioned in the 11th century.

name: Iserlohn
Settlement_Description: First mentioned as a mint between 1030 and 1050.
Town_Description: In 1278, town privileges were confirmed after Dortmund law. However, the first awarding of town privileges can no longer be verified. Called 'oppidum' around 1232.

name: Fürstenau
Settlement_Description: The settlement developed near the castle that was erected in 1344 by Gottfried von Arnsberg, bishop of Osnabrück. It was built as a planned town with limited borough ('weichbild') privileges, which were reiterated in 1402 by bishop Heinrich von Holstein.
Town_Description: Fürstenau acquired Osnabrück town privileges in 1642.
Toll_Description: According to the privileges of 1402, half of the toll in Fürstenau belonged to the bishop of Osnabrück, the other half to the settlement. The toll probably goes back to the time that the castle was built, around 1350. The situation of 1402 was reiterated in 1516 and 1620. The toll was levied predominantly on cattle that was bought in the settlement and its surroundings.

name: Gettorf
Settlement_Description: First mentioned in 1259. The local Church of St George was a pilgrimage destination from the 1460s until the Reformation.

name: Fürstenberg (Oder)
