Settlement_Description: A German castle, most probably with a Slavic predecessor, gave the region the name Vorstenbergh in the 13th century. A Slavic settlement is evidenced in 1411.
Town_Description: The town was probably founded late in the 13th century, mentioned as civitas in 1293 and 1300, as oppidum in 1316. The Magdeburg town law was approved with small changes in 1331 and endorsed in 1335 and 1371. The town acquired complete and eternal exemption of all tolls in Brandenburg in 1350, confirmed in 1374. Since 1961 part of Eisenhüttenstadt.
Toll_Description: Toll station on Oder shipping of the margraves of Brandenburg, mentioned in 1288 and 1316. Merchants from Guben were exempted, but when they travelled on ships of others, they had to pay the half of the toll tariff.

name: Fürstenberg (Weser)
Settlement_Description: The castle Fürstenberg is first mentioned as a fief of the Duchy of Brunswick in the middle of the 14th century.
Toll_Description: A toll in Fürstenberg is mentioned in registers from the years 1539, 1541, 1544, 1546 and 1587.

name: Boleszkowice
Settlement_Description: A german village was probably founded after 1252, mentioned as oppidum (borough) in 1337. An urban law was only introduced in 1809.

name: Fürstenwalde
Settlement_Description: Small Slavic settlement, in possession of Brandenburg around 1250. First mentioned in 1272, already as town.
Town_Description: Founded between 1252 and 1258 by the Margraves John I and Otto III of Brandenburg. The town rights are confirmed in 1285.

name: Fürth
Toll_Description: A toll station in Fürth was established in the first half of the 15th century.

name: Darnewitz
Settlement_Description: The village is first mentioned in 1253 when a priest Engelbertus de Dernewitz is mentioned.

name: Fürstensee
Settlement_Description: The margraves of Brandenburg had a castle in Fürstensee, where a document is dated in 1283.
Toll_Description: In 1561 it is mentioned that the toll of Strelitz is levied in Fürstensee, which suggests that most traffic circumvented Strelitz. Fürstensee is once again mentioned as toll station in 1569.

name: Gaarden
Settlement_Description: The settlement Gaarden developed from the villages Hemminghestorpe (first mentioned in 1232) and Wulvesbrooke. In 1286, there were 10 farms, 4 cottages and a mill. The name Gaarden for the entire settlement is first attested in 1389.

name: Gadesbünden
Settlement_Description: The name Gadesbünden is probably derived from "godesbunde", which suggests that the settlement developed from a monastic grange of the monastery of Bassum.
Toll_Description: In 1377, the count of Hoya installed a toll in Gadesbünden of one Turnosgroschen for each horse. In 1380, the toll station is moved to "Stotebrucke" (UB Lüneburg II:945), which however is called "Scotemburge" in a 1382 charter (Hoyer UB I:256); the latter is confirmed in 1583. This location cannot be identified with certainty. In Stöcken near Rethem on the same street, there exists a side street called "Stoßbrücke", but it is not located in the former county of Hoya. "Scotemburge" is identified by Erler as Stoltenburg, a former island in the Weser near Drakenburg, but this identification is rather uncertain as well. Moreover, in the latter case, the toll would have been transformed into a water toll on the Weser river, but it does not appear in any of the Weser toll lists from the 16th century.

name: Gägelow (Wismar)
Settlement_Description: The village is first mentioned in 1230.

name: Gagzow
Settlement_Description: The village is first mentioned in 1293-1300.

name: Ganderkesee
Settlement_Description: First mentioned in 860 in the Vita St Willehadi. Bishop Adalbert of Bremen founded a church with a law court ('sendkirche') here in 1050. The settlement developed into an important market place in the Middle Ages.

name: Bad Gandersheim
Settlement_Description: Originally a small village to the northwest of the later town. The monastery of canonesses, founded in 852 in nearby Brunshausen, moved to Gandersheim in 881. The monastery settlement acquired market privileges around 990.
Town_Description: Gandersheim acquired town privileges in the 13th century; these were reiterated in 1330.
Toll_Description: The monastery Gandersheim acquired the right to levy a transit toll for merchants travelling between the Rhine and Elbe and Saale rivers in 877. According to an overview of tolls in the duchy of Brunswick-Wolfenbüttel from 1582, the toll in Gandersheim was calculated by weight of the cargo.

name: Gangelt
Settlement_Description: First mentioned around 828, when the place was in the possession of the king.
Town_Description: In the 14th century, the town was referred to as an 'oppidum'.
Toll_Description: The Duke of Brabant-Limburg levied a land toll in 1396. Around 1400, the toll was pledged several times. In 1420 the toll passed to the Lord of Heinsberg, in 1483 to the Duke of Jülich. Tariffs and revenues are not known.

name: Jablonné v Podještědí
Toll_Description: A toll of the lord in Jablonné v Podještědí is mentioned in the city rights of 1466, together with a road toll ('Deichselpfennig') for the maintenance of the roads of the town, which is said to have been levied since hundred years. Likely the toll existed at least since a charter from 1361 which declared the road via Jablonné v Podještědí to be the official road between Prague and Zittau.

name: Jels
Settlement_Description: The village of Jels was first mentioned in 1231, but is significantly older. The parish church is from either the 12th or 13th century.

name: Gardelegen
Settlement_Description: In the Early Middle Ages Gardelegen already was a village with a castle from the 10th century. The first secure mention dates from 1121. In 1196 it was donated to the archbishop of Magdeburg.
Town_Description: Developed as a town at the end of the 12th century. Referred to as civitas in 1241. Magdeburg town rights can be attested in c.1290; since 1358 member of the Hanse.
Fair_Description: In 1579 the privileges for Gardelegen's four fairs are renewed. The Mid-lent-fair is cancelled and a new fair on Monday after Michaelis is established. The other fairs took place on Monday after Invocavit, after Palmarum and after Peter and Paul's day . Each fair lasted four days, with a cattle market at the beginning of the fair. The Palmarum fair was moved to Tuesday after Quasimodogeniti in 1664, because it desecrated the Holy Week.
Toll_Description: In 1483 the town of Gardelegen is granted a dam- and road fee from loaded wagons and half the fee from unloaded wagons in order to maintain the roads. In 1533 a secondary statio of the toll in Gardelegen is established in Wegenstedt.

name: Garrelsweer
Settlement_Description: Earliest mention in 1057, in a copy dating from fourteenth century.
Fair_Description: In 1057, Henry IV, King of the Romans, gave the counties of Hunsingo and Fivelgo to archbishop Adalbart of Bremen and Hamburg, with the right to institute fairs in Winsum and Garrelsweer with mintage and toll rights. Possibly, the river Fivel still carried so much water that its estuary near Garrelsweer still formed an open connection to the sea. Because of silting up between probably 1050 and 1200, Garrelsweer lost its central position. Appingedam is seen as its successor as a market place.

name: Garoza
Settlement_Description: The manor was given as fief in 1556.

name: Garsena
Settlement_Description: Mention of lords of Corzene in 1286.

name: Gartow
Settlement_Description: A castle of the lords of Gartow is first mentioned in 1225. The adjoining settlement was referred to as a minor town or borough ('stedeken') from 1360; between 1360 and 1438 there was a monastery of the Knights Hospitaller in Gartow.

name: Walsleben
Settlement_Description: The village is first mentioned in 929.

name: Garmerwolde
Settlement_Description: Earliest mention in 1288, in a sixteenth or seventeenth century copy.

name: Pisz
Settlement_Description: A house belonging to the Teutonic Order was built in 1342, destroyed in 1351, rebuilt and again destroyed in 1455, a fishing settlement grew close to the castle
Town_Description: A handfast exists from 1367, the first attempt at a town founding with Kulm town law by the Grand Master Ludwig von Erlichshausen in 1451 was unsuccessful, most likely because of the 13 year war in the 15th ct., the people have been called citizens in 1553 and the place was mentioned as a hamlet in 1566, new inquieries after town law were loud in 1595, but elector Friedrich Wilhelm only granted Kulm town law in 1645

name: Gehlenbeck
Settlement_Description: A farm in Gehlenbeck is mentioned in ca. 1100.

name: Gartz
Settlement_Description: Site of a Slavic fortress, later the seat of a castellan in 1236.
Town_Description: Duke Barnim I of Pomerania granted the Magdeburg town law in 1249.
Toll_Description: A toll on the Oder river was moved to Gartz in 1321. In 1339 the town received the right to levy a road toll of 1 Pfennig for each horse for the maintenance of the roads. It was raised to 4 Pfennig in 1345 and 6 Pfennig in 1480.
Staple_Description: Duke Barnim proclaimed in 1271 that only citizens of Gartz were allowed to buy corn in Stettin, and limited the right to ship corn outside the town. In 1325 and 1328, Gartz acquired the right to hold back commodities intended for Stettin, if cargoes destined for Gartz were held back in Stettin, and merchants travelling between Stettin and Schwedt had to use the road through Gartz. A full staple privilege with a compulsory duration of one day for corn, beer, venison, butter and cattle was granted in 1397; a three-day staple for beer and wine followed in 1464.

name: Geel
Settlement_Description: First mentioned in a copy dating circa 1243 from a document dating circa 1155.

name: null
Ferry_Description: A ferry in Leerdam, likely to Asperen, is mentioned in 1504.

name: Marksuhl
Settlement_Description: This borough ('Marktflecken') probably already belonged to the property of Fulda monastery before 900. It belonged to castle Altenstein, later to the district of Creuzburg. Duke Johann Ernst had a castle constructed here in 1587-1591.
Toll_Description: The secondary station of safe conduct ('Beigeleitsstelle') of Eisenach in Marksuhl was only established in 1508/1509, after a new road from Westfalia and Hessia to Frankia was used. The regulations of safe conduct ('Geleitsordnung') of 1535 and 1553/54 list the fees for several commodities. Revenues for the safe conduct, with a separate safe conduct for cattle ('Viehgeleit') are known since 1535/36.

name: Gasthuis
Settlement_Description: Earliest mention in 1450. The hamlet is named after the hospital ('gasthuis') of St Servatius, which was founded here before 1350, on the road between Maastricht and Aachen.

name: Garz
Settlement_Description: Former Slavic settlement; in the first decade of the 13th century the German village was founded, which is first mentioned in 1334.

name: Geertruidenberg
Settlement_Description: Geertruidenberg is first mentioned in written records in 1213. However, a trade settlement existed at the place long before 1213. In 1399 duke Albrecht granted the magistrate to prohibit traffic otherwise then through the town. Of old the route was along 'ons land van de Grote Waard in Zuidholland' to Breda. A hospital is first mentioned in 1410.
Town_Description: Town rights were granted on 21 September 1213 by William I, count of Holland. Between 1323-1325 a castle is built near Geertruidenberg and a stone wall may have been added to the town in 1319 (although it is possible that Geertruidenberg was already walled before that year).
Fair_Description: Geertruidenberg obtained town rights from the count of Holland in 1213 (Sept. 21), including the right to hold three fairs. In 1275 (Jan. 22) a fourth fair was added. Dates are then: July 5-12, July 17-24, Sept. 1-8 and Oct. 11-18. In 1398 (Sept. 17) duke Albrecht granted a cattle-market on Wednesday as there was little trade en because of the location on the border between Holland and Brabant. This market  had tolls like in Diest and Antwerp. In 1581 (Apr. 24) king Philip granted three free fairs for horses and beasts, each during 4 days, in stead of the four fairs of old, to restore war-damage. The dates: 1) Thursday after 'Beloken Pasen' (Sunday after Eastern), 2) Monday before Margareth in July, 3) the day after Lambertus (Sept. 18). In 1583 (Oct. 29) it was decided to have a cattlemarket Thursday after Bamis (Oct. 1).
Toll_Description: A probably combined market-toll, a toll on traffic overland to Brabant and a toll on ships dates back prior to 1213. Since 1330/1 known as a comital toll (in 1475 with limitation: "streckende tot Randenrode": see: Lage Zwaluwe). A tariff is preserved and edited, dated 1357 or 1358. In 1454 known ('Sanct Gertrudenberch') as an outpost of the toll of the count of Holland at Geervliet.

name: Geffen
Settlement_Description: Earliest mention in 1246, in a fifteenth century copy.

name: Gehrenrode
Settlement_Description: The village was first mentioned in 1228.

name: Gelchsheim
Toll_Description: Emperor Charles IV granted the toll and safe conduct in Gelchsheim to the noble Lutz von Hohenlohe and his heirs in 1349.

name: Geisleden
Settlement_Description: First mention in 1022, when property in Geisleden is donated to the monastery in Heiligenstadt. A noble family of Geisleden is attested.

name: Gefell
Settlement_Description: The settlement was probably founded in the 11th century from the castle Kirchberg. It is possibly first mentioned in 1211; first certain mention in 1303.
Town_Description: Acquisition of town privileges in 1364. A town constitution remains from the 15th century.

name: Kamen
Settlement_Description: First mentioned in the 11th century. Around 1243 a sovereign castle existed near the settlement.
Town_Description: Town privileges were granted to the settlement between 1243 and 1248, which were expanded in 1346.

name: Geldern
Settlement_Description: The settlement was first mentioned in possession of the abbey of Werden in the early 10th century. In the 11th century it became the seat of the counts of Guelders; a comital castle must have existed in 1095 at the latest, but is first mentioned only in 1237.
Town_Description: In the 13th century, the settlement was mentioned as a town.
Fair_Description: It is unclear when the fairs in Geldern were first granted, they are first mentioned in 1343/44
Toll_Description: 1) The Duke of Guelders levied a land toll here in 1393/94. Tariffs are not known. In 1397 the annual revenue was 26 gulden and 14 groschen.1469/70 this was leased out for 12 gulden.2) In 1462, the duke levied a fee for save conduct on land. The annual yield in 1462/63 was 2 marks and 6 shillings.3) In 1386, the duke also levied a road toll. The average annual yield from 1386 to 1399 was about 48 marks 3 shillings and 7 pfennige.

name: Geldrop
Fair_Description: In 1371 the lord of Geldrop granted four fairs and a weekly market on Friday. An undated register from the abbey Tongerlo (Westerlo, B.) (circa 1556) contains a list of fairs in the region Kempen and Peel. Geldrop then still has four fairs: 1) Sunday before St. Brigitten (Febr. 1) till the first Tuesday after that, 2) second Sunday after Quasimodo (the first Sunday after Eastern) till the first Tuesday after that, 3) Sunday before nativitatis Johannis Baptistae (June 24) till the first Tuesday after that, 4) Sunday before  Remigii (Sept. 1) till the first Tuesday after that.

name: Gelnhausen
Settlement_Description: Presumably the place comes from a Carolingian settlement; in the High Middle Ages the political and economic boom took place.
Town_Description: Barbarossa founded the imperial town with a palatinate.

name: Gembloux
Fair_Description: In the 11th century a fair in the autumn is known and a hall is built.

name: Burg Gemünden
Settlement_Description: First mentioned in 1274 as a castle. The settlement received market privileges with a weekly market, jurisdiction and fortifications in 1372. Mentioned as village in 1390.

name: Genemuiden
Settlement_Description: Earliest mention dates from 14 January 1275, when town privileges are granted to Genemuiden.
Town_Description: Town privileges were granted by Jan I of Nassau, bishop of Utrecht, on 14 January 1275.

name: Geseke
Settlement_Description: In the 6th/7th century a settlement with pottery existed. First mention in 833, when there probably was a royal court with a chapel. In the middle of the 10th century foundation of a ladies' monastery.
Town_Description: In 1220 the archbishop of Cologne granted the town rights (Rüthen rights). After 1294 the construction of a mighty city wall with six gates began. In the 13th century, a fully formed citizenry existed; a municipal seal has been handed down from 1237. Despite membership in the Hanseatic League, Geseke remained a farming town for a long time.

name: Nazza
Settlement_Description: The settlement is first mentioned in 1229, the brook with the same name already in 1014.

name: Haßfurt
Toll_Description: Mentioned as toll station in a register from 1506-1507. Revenues are known for the years 1529-1539.

name: Pulheim
Toll_Description: The Duke of Jülich levied a road toll in 1500. Tariffs and revenues are not known.

name: Gennep
Town_Description: On 6 January 1371, town privileges were confirmed by Reginald (Reinoud) of Brederode, lord of Gennep, and Joanna (Johanna) of Gennep. Town privileges have thus been granted before 1371.
Fair_Description: In 1385 a market toll is mentioned of the lord of Gennep is mentioned. In 1464 there existed a weekly market on Wednesday, from sunrise to sunset. At the end of the 15th century a market toll is attested on 14 days after St Gall (October 16) and before 1532 on St Lucas (October 18) for 14 days. In 1588 two fairs are mentioned on March 26 and October 1, with safe conduct 3 days before and after. A toll manual of the toll-keeper of Venlo dated early 16th century with the market-tolls on the Maas river states this tariff:  a ship up- or downstream with goods: 3 'oude groot', after payment shout: 'orloff' (permission) and then free to pass.

name: Gent
Settlement_Description: Earliest mention in first quarter of the eighth century in a tenth-century copy.
Fair_Description: Around the year 1000 a fair with St. Bavo (Oct. 1) is known. Probably this fair was much older. It lasted al least till 1199. Possibly it was first organised outside the city-walls near the St. Baafs abbey. In 1199 market-tolls are levied at the Brabant-gate, at the Drongen-gate, at the bridge near St. Jacob, the socalled 'Wasselintol' and inside the center of the town.In 1453 (Oct. 13) duke Philip the Good granted two fairs of each 14 days during 7 year with Lent and in the beginning of August, while paying him 1/4 of the excises.
Staple_Description: In 1251, a staple between Aardenburg and Ghent was prohibited. It was prohibited to manufacture cloth within five miles of Ghent in 1314; in 1338 to trade woad within the same area, and yarn within three miles. A corn staple was introduced in 1343, whereby half of the corn from the region around the city had to be stored within the town. Conflicts with Ypres because of the corn staple were solved in favour of Ghent in 1424, and it was further enforced in 1484. Further fixation of the grain stapel in 1484: a quarter of the corn shipped through the city and all corn grown in Flanders had to be offered to the local population for 8-14 days. In 1486 and 1514, the staple was reiterated. The forced offering of commodities for sale was abolished in 1540, but in in its place came a forced transshipment between Scheldt and Leie, and in 1547 for the Sassevaart. The staple was reinstated in 1587, with the exception of all commodities intended for personal use of the merchants.

name: Genthin
Settlement_Description: The village emerges from a Slavic settlement named Plote, first mentioned in 1144, which today is a part of Genthin (Altenplathow). Here existed a German knightly manor with a moated castle. Establishment of a market in 1160. The settlement Genthin itself is first mentioned in 1171, probably founded by Dutch or Flemish immigrants. It is a market borough ('Marktflecken') since 1413. The settlement is called 'oppidulum' (small town) in 1459 and borough ('Flecken') in 1562.
Fair_Description: Since 1539 markets privileged by cardinal Albrecht took place in Genthin.
Toll_Description: Mention of Plote as a toll station together with Jerichow in 1432, but it is possibly confused with Klietznick here. Genthin is, however, also mentioned as toll station in 1512.

name: Jersika
Settlement_Description: In 1209 the area was conquered by the Teutonic Order. The castle was destroyed in 1239.

name: Gera
Settlement_Description: First mention of the land of Gera in 995. In Slavic times there already was a castle. The minting of coins is attested in 1180. In c. 1200 the settlement was still referred to as "villa".
Town_Description: Gera developed into a town in the 13th century. The settlement is referred to as "oppidum" and citizens ('cives') are mentioned in 1237. Town privileges are first attested in 1292 and show influence of Magdeburg town law. The oldest remaining town rights date from 1487.

name: Gesmold
Settlement_Description: A first mention between 1027 and 1037 is uncertain. The settlement is first mentioned reliably in 1160.

name: Kastel
Settlement_Description: The settlement goes back to the Roman fort 'castellum matiacorum', which was built between 4 and 9 AD. A triumphal arch built around 19 AD was excavated within the site. In Frankish times, the settlement was fortified again and used as a royal court. Between 1194 and 1198, the settlement was mentioned as a 'villa'. In 1349, Emperor Charles IV decreed that no new fortress was to be built.
Town_Description: First mentioned as a town in 1237.

name: Wendelstein
Settlement_Description: The castle was inherited in 1322. It was probably extended in 1332. The castle was damaged in the 30 Years' War and decayed until 1958.

name: Giebichenstein
Settlement_Description: The castle Giebichenstein is first mentioned in 961 and referred to as "civitas" or "urbs". After the advent of Halle (first mentioned in 1064) it lost much of its importance, but it remained the administrative centre for the region and residence of the archbishop of Magdeburg. In 937 it acquired toll and mint rights, but these were moved to Halle around 1064.
Toll_Primary_Owner: Erzbischof von Magdeburg, Rat von Halle

name: Gieboldehausen
Settlement_Description: The settlement was first mentioned in 1003. A castle of the dukes of Brunswick was pawned to the archbishop of Mainz in the 14th century. The settlement is mentioned as borough ('flecken') since 1450.
Fair_Description: The privilege for two fairs is granted in 1607 by emperor Rudolf II.
Toll_Description: The toll in Gieboldehausen, belonging to the dukes of Brunswick, was acquired by the lords of Minnigerode in 1518. Around 1600, the duke tried to acquire the toll again. A toll house in the village is mentioned in 1596.

name: Gielow
Settlement_Description: The village is first mentioned in 1228.

name: Giessendam
Settlement_Description: Earliest mention in 1230. In 1382 Giessen-Oudekerk was seperated from Giessendam.
Toll_Description: A dam with a lock is found here (Outgiesin) in 1281 (Oct. 20). In 1416 there are complaints about the comital tollkeeper in Giessendam who collected illegaly toll on horses and other merchandise from Goes.

name: Gietelo
Settlement_Description: Earliest certain mention in 1299. The settlement 'Getlo' mentioned in 1050 might also refer to Gietelo.

name: Gifhorn
Settlement_Description: Gifhorn came into existence at an important crossing of the Aller river, where a castle is first mentioned in 1196. The settlement next to the castle was granted market privileges by duke Johann of Lüneburg in 1275. Mentioned as "oppidum" in 1332; borough ('weichbild') rights were granted in 1364; characterised as borough ('flecken') in 1544-1640.
Toll_Description: A toll station of the dukes of Brunswick-Lüneburg in Gifhorn is first mentioned in 1303/1330. Toll tariffs are known from the 16th century (StAB).

name: Gispersleben
Settlement_Description: First mention in a record from 1143 as Gispotisleyben, but it probably existed already in prehistoric times. Later half of the village was property of the counts of Gleichen.

name: Gittelde
Settlement_Description: First mentioned in 965, at which time there already existed a market, toll and a royal mint. The settlement is mentioned as borough ('flecken') in 1496.

name: Pont des Arches
Bridge_Description: A stone bridge across the Meuse was constructed under bishop Reginhard (1025-1037). It was destroyed by floods in 1409, after which a new stone bridge was constructed between 1421 and 1446. It was destroyed again by floods in 1643 and subsequently rebuilt.

name: Gitter
Settlement_Description: First mentioned in the 8th or 9th century. After the saltworks in nearby Salzgitter were developed around 1300, the original village Gitter acquired the addition "auf dem Berge".

name: Glandorf
Settlement_Description: The place was first mentioned in 1074.

name: Glimmen
Settlement_Description: Earliest mention in the twelfth century.

name: Gliesmarode
Settlement_Description: First mentioned in 1031. In Gliesmarode, there stood a watch tower of the defensive enclosure ('landwehr') of Braunschweig, for which the oldest evidence dates from 1387.

name: null
Bridge_Description: A bridge across the Dinkel "near Spechtholte" is first mentioned in 1365.

name: Gnandstein
Settlement_Description: Mentioned as manor in 1228, around 1402 as knightly manor.

name: Gniezno
Toll_Description: Prussian merchants complained to Poland about a raise in toll tariffs in Gniezno in 1452.
Staple_Description: Around 1440, the town started to force merchants to offer their commodities for sale on the market.

name: Gnetsch
Settlement_Description: The village is first mentioned in 1209.

name: Goch
Settlement_Description: First mentioned in the second half of the 11th century. A cloth-hall is first found in 1370.
Town_Description: Referred to as a town from 1261.
Fair_Description: Before 1294 a fair on St Victor (10 December) is mentioned. In 1424 two fairs were added, on St Walburgis (1 May) and the first Monday in September.
Toll_Description: The Duke of Geldern and the town of Goch levied a road toll before 1372. Tariffs and revenues have not been handed down.

name: Bad Godesberg
Toll_Description: The Archbishop of Cologne levied a land toll in 1331. This included road toll and carriage toll ('Karrenzoll'). In 1470, 4 denarii per ox had to be paid. In 1381/82, an annual average of 156 mark 4 shillings in road toll was collected. In 1382/83 it was 85 mark 2 shillings. In 1381/82, 206 mark were collected per year, in 1382/83 209 mark per carriage. In the 15th century, there was no longer a distinction between road toll and carriage toll.

name: Godow
Settlement_Description: The village is first mentioned in 1398.

name: Goingarijp
Settlement_Description: Earliest mention in the thirteenth century.

name: Groß Godems
Settlement_Description: The village is first mentioned in 1291.

name: Kullamaa
Settlement_Description: The parish of Goldenbeck is mentioned in 1364.

name: Göldenitz
Settlement_Description: The village is first mentioned in 1332.

name: Goldenstedt
Settlement_Description: The first mention of 1080 is recorded in a 14th-century copy.

name: Goldewin
Settlement_Description: The village is first mentioned in 1341.

name: Kuldīga
Settlement_Description: Between 1242 and 1245 a castle was built, which was named Jesusborg.
Town_Description: The fortified borough ('Hakelwerk'), which originated in the 14th century, received town rights of Riga in 1347. It was Hanseatic town since 1368. In the Middle Ages, the town was an important transshipment point from water to land vehicles.

name: Gollmenz
Settlement_Description: First mention in 1350, mention as knightly manor in 1445/47.

name: Goleniów
Settlement_Description: A Slavic settlement is first mentioned in 1218-1233.
Town_Description: Duke Barnim I of Pomerania founded the new town ('novella civitas') Vredeheide with Magdeburg town law in Gollnow in 1268. The old name Gollnow remained in existence, however. Lübeck town law was later granted in 1314 by Duke Otto I.
Fair_Description: A fair on Sunday Judica in Goleniów is mentioned in an almanach printed in Neudamm (Dębno) in 1598.

name: Groß Bützin
Settlement_Description: The village is first mentioned in 1235.

name: Golm
Settlement_Description: First mentioned in 1308. An inn in Golm is mentioned in 1584.

name: Goldenstädt
Settlement_Description: The village is first mentioned in 1285.

name: Kirtorf
Settlement_Description: A 'villa' is mentioned between 780 and 802. The settlement itself is first named in 917/18.

name: Golßen
Settlement_Description: First mention in 1276 as Golsyn. In 1301 a castle is mentioned.
Town_Description: The settlement gained the character and rights of a town in the course of the 14th century: a castle borough is mentioned in 1346, as town in 1397 and 1401. The significance of the town remained limited: in 1454 it is characterised as small town, in 1530 as borough ('Flecken'). Formal town rights only with the Prussian "Städteordnung" of 1832.

name: Golzow (Brandenburg)
Settlement_Description: A castle probably existed since the 2nd half of the 12th century and is first mentioned in 1219. The village of Golzow is referred to as borough or small town ('Stadechen') in 1335 and 1451, but never acquired town rights.
Toll_Description: Already mentioned as toll station in 1335. The town of Brandenburg was exempted, as well for a new barrel toll that is mentioned in 1473. In 1525 it was decided that only citizens of Brandenburg and the chapter there were exempted from the toll.

name: Gommern
Settlement_Description: Since 948 a German settlement with castle district ('Burgward'), before a Slavic settlement; gained borough rights ('Marktfleckenrecht') in the 16th century.

name: Goor
Settlement_Description: Earliest mention dates from 1027-1054 (in a copy from the second half of the twelfth century).
Town_Description: Town privileges were granted by Henry (Hendrik) van Vianden, bishop of Utrecht on 16 September 1263.
Fair_Description: In 1283, Goor acquired the right to hold two fairs, on the first Sunday after Peter and Paul's day, as well as the two days before and after, and on St Andrew's day. A weekly market on Monday was added in 1390. In 1565 (May 16 mei) the stadtholder of Overijsel granted Goer a fair on April 27 in stead of St. Peter and Paulsday (June 29) because there were many fairs in the surrounding towns then.
Toll_Description: In the confirmation of town privileges from 1390, a road toll is mentioned since times of old ('van olden tyden'), the revenues of which were used to maintain the gates and bridges of the town. In a document from 1779, outposts of the toll are mentioned in Markelo, Enter and Zeldam.

name: Gordemitz
Bridge_Description: Maintenance of the bridge had to be undertaken by the town of Leipzig.

name: Gorinchem
Settlement_Description: Gorinchem is first mention about 1200 (document is fourteenth-century copy). In the thirteenth century, it was a trade settlement near a castle. A chapter in the church is found in the years 1378-1572.
Town_Description: Gorinchem was granted town privileges on 11 November 1382 by Otto, lord of Arkel. A hospital is first mentioned in 1321. During the reign of William VI, count of Holland (r. 1404-1417), the castle near Gorinchem was demolished and a smaller castle was built in the town itself.
Fair_Description: Before 1382 already six fairs exists, including a cloth-fair, a cattle-fair and a horse-fair. A tariff dated 1387 for the watertoll of the fair with 'Sinxen' (Pentecost-fair) is edited. A tollregister dated early 16th century with the market-tolls on the Maas mention: 8 days before Pentecost during 14 days with a tariff. In 1553 five market-tolls are found (together 30 pound worth) and a watertoll on the river Merwede (46 pound) (to compare: the combined toll on sailing ships of Gorinchem and Schoonhoven with its outposts is then farmed for 12500 pound). In 1565 the second horsefair starts the first Tuesday in Lent, duration 4 days with freedom equal to the first fair. A manual of the toll-keeper of Geervliet dated 1562 mention a horse-fair in Gorinchem on July 5 in a calendar of many horse-fairs. In 1580 (August 24) king Phliip II granted a free horse-fair on 28/29 September with two days before and after freedom as a compensation for the heavy burdens of the war and the cut dikes. In 1596 there are nine fairs: 1) a horsefair starting the first Tuesday in Lent, duration: 4 days, 2) Midlent starting Friday before Sunday when people enter the Holy church, till the end of May, duration 2 weeks, 3) Pentecost starting the third Friday before that, duration 2 weeks, 4) horsefair starting the third day of July on St. Maartensday-eve translation (July 3), duration 4 days, 5) horsefair on Sept. 28 and 29 with St. Michelseve (Sept. 29) starting, except on Sunday, duration 2 marketdays and 2 days before and after, 6) Bamis (Oct. 1) 2 weeks starting the Friday before Bamis, 7) Thursday after St. Victor (Oct. 10?) a cattle-fair starting the Tuesday before the Thursday, duration 4 days, 8) cattle-fair with All-Saints starting the Friday before, duration 2 weeks, 9) cloth-fair on Monday after St. Maartensmis (Nov. 11), duration 6 days starting the Saturday before the Monday.

name: Gorschendorf
Settlement_Description: The village is first mentioned in 1314.

name: Gortel
Settlement_Description: Earliest mention in the fourteenth century.

name: Góry
Toll_Description: Mentioned as toll station in a document from c. 1349, where 1 gr. had to be paid for each horse.

name: Görzke
Settlement_Description: A castle with a castle district were probably the origins of this settlement.
Town_Description: In 1283 the term civitas can be found, the systematic foundation of the town by the margraves of Brandenburg probably occurred around 1250. Mention of a council in 1355, in 1378 a mayor and a council are mentioned. During the 30-year war the place was mostly destroyed and lost its town privileges.
Toll_Description: Electoral Brandeburg gains the rights of safe conduct.

name: Gorzyce (Sandomierz)
Toll_Description: Mentioned as toll station in c. 1349, where 1/2 gr. for each horse and 12 gr. for each cart had to be paid.

name: Goslar
Settlement_Description: Founded by king Henry I around 922; first mentioned in 1005.
Town_Description: The development of the market town Goslar was driven by the exploitation of the Rammelsberg mines. Goslar already had town-like characteristics in the 11th century. Official representatives of the market settlement are mentioned in 1108, and it was characterised as "civitas" in 1131. The first town right exists from 1320, which codified the privileges granted by Emperor Frederick II in 1219. Goslar became Free Imperial City in the first half of the 14th century.
Fair_Description: It is known that fairs were organised in Goslar, for example in 1429, 1444 and 1466, but dates are not known before the 16th century. Only in an almanac printed in Neudamm (Dębno) from 1598 two fairs are mentioned in Goslar, on Sunday Jubilate and Holy Innocent's Day.

name: Gostynin
Toll_Description: Mentioned as toll station in a document from c. 1349, where 2 gr. 4 den. had to be paid for each horse.

name: Groß Denkte
Settlement_Description: First mentioned in 947. However, a settlement already existed in the neolithic and Roman period.

name: Gößnitz
Settlement_Description: First mentioned in 1291. The advantageous position in the network of long-distance trade led to a economic boost in the 15th century. The village only gained town rights in 1718.

name: Gotha
Settlement_Description: The existing settlement became a royal court in the 8th/9th century, which owned a castle in the 11th centruy; because of its advantageous position in the traffic network the settlement developed into a market village, which mostly traded grain in the 16th century.
Town_Description: Around 1168 Gotha was owned by the landgraves of Thuringia, who promoted road construction. Awarding of town rights probably around the end of the 12th century (1180/1189). Gotha had Gotha Eisenach town rights.
Fair_Description: The toll- and regulations of safe conduct from the 16th century mention fairs in Gotha, during which the toll is doubled.
Toll_Description: Toll- and regulations of safe conduct remain for the town of Gotha from the 16th century (ThStA Gotha, Kammer Stadt Gotha 66 Nr. 222).

name: Gottorf
Settlement_Description: A castle was built by the bishop of Schleswig after 1161; owned by the dukes of Schleswig since 1268.
Toll_Description: The royal Danish toll station at Gottorf was one of the transit tolls with the highest revenues. Total revenues for 1485 amounted to 2352 Lübeck mark; in 1491 2813 Lübeck mark and in 1519 4154 Lübeck mark. Detailed toll registers are available for the years 1484-1704, with lacunae for some years (Landesarchiv Schleswig-Holstein, Schleswig and Rigsarkivet, Copenhagen). These have been analysed by Schwetlik, Wiese and Enemark.

name: Govelin
Settlement_Description: First mentioned in 1360. The settlement consisted of 3 farms.

name: Grabow (Elde)
Settlement_Description: The settlement developed out of a 12th-century Slavic castle. A german castle was first mentioned in 1186, a parish in 1230-1235.
Town_Description: Founded by the Duke of Dannenberg for military reasons. The founding privilege from 1252 is a forgery, but the privileges are confirmed in 1317. The town is mentioned as a civitas with Lübeck town law in 1354, and as oppidum in 1355.
Toll_Description: Lübeck was exempted from the toll in Grabow by Duke Albrecht of Mecklenburg in 1354.

name: Grabow (Wendland)
Settlement_Description: First mentioned in 1330/52. In 1450, the village consisted of 11 farms, which were later turned into two noble manors (the Ober- and Untergut) and a folwark.

name: Mihla
Settlement_Description: Old royal property, which was donated to the newly founded Hersfeld monastery in 780-802. Renaissance castles were constructed in the 16th century.
Toll_Description: A toll station is mentioned in 1249. Later a secondary station of safe conduct ('Beigeleitsstelle') of Eisenach/Creuzburg. Revenues are recorded from 1549/50 onwards.

name: Gryfice
Town_Description: The town was founded without a prior settlement with Lübeck town law before 1262 by duke Wartislaw III. The founding was endorsed in 1264 by Barnim I, at which occasion it is first mentioned in the sources.

name: Gräfenhainichen
Settlement_Description: Foundation of the settlement in the High Middle Ages, initially as a fief of Anhalt. First mentioned in 1285.
Town_Description: The year of the awarding of town rights is unknown. However, in 1454 existing town rights were confirmed, which leads to assume that privileges were granted at the beginning of the 14th century.
Toll_Description: A regulation of safe conduct remains from 1550 (LHASA, MD, d. 16, Nr. 17 1a, Erbbuch des Amtes Gräfenhainichen 1550).

name: Gräfentonna
Settlement_Description: First mention in 845 as the property of Fulda monastery. It served as the residence of the counts of Tonna, later the counts of Gleichen. It was granted market rights in 1785.

name: Gräfinghausen
Settlement_Description: First mentioned in ca. 1260. The settlement probably already existed before the 9th century.

name: Gramsbergen
Settlement_Description: Earliest mention of the settlement dates from 1227. A castle was built in 1339.
Town_Description: Gramsbergen is mentioned as a town ('stedeken') in a charter of 13 August 1442. The small town was closely related to the lord of Gramsbegen, who hold the right to inn taxes from its inhabitants, and who appointed the members of the town government.

name: Gramzow
Settlement_Description: A village is first mentioned in 1168. Duke Bogislaw I founded a Premonstratensian monastery in 1177/78.
Town_Description: First mentioned as a town in 1288, in 1586 only as borough ('Flecken').
Fair_Description: The fair in Gramzow is moved to Vierraden in 1733.
Toll_Description: There's a large and small toll in the town. In 1592, the toll is mentioned as old.

name: Gräfinau
Settlement_Description: First mention in 1282. In 1924 Gräfinau was merged with neighbouring Angstedt.

name: Grasdorf (Leine)
Settlement_Description: The settlement was first mentioned in 1235.

name: Grasdorf (Innerste)
Toll_Description: In the town accounts of Hildesheim from 1444, there are records of toll being paid in Grasdorf.

name: Grathem
Settlement_Description: Earliest mention in 1116, in a sixteenth century copy.
Fair_Description: In een clearing dated mid 14th century(?) about the market-right of Grathem the fair is dated the day before and after St. Severinusday (July 6).

name: Graudupes
Settlement_Description: Private property of the Teuring family from Goldingen, which was first mentioned in 1616.

name: Grave
Settlement_Description: Grave presumably originates from 1133 or later, as an allodium of the lords of Cuijk (Van Kuyc). Earliest mention dates from 1214. A hospital was founded in 1294. Around 1300, there was a wine house, and in 1326 a clothmakers' hall.
Town_Description: According to Cox, town privileges were presumably granted before 1279, by John I of Cuijk. According to Rutte, however, town privileges were granted in 1308 by Otto of Cuijk. In 1323, Otto of Cuijk grants Grave in fee to the duke of Brabant. On 15 December 1400, the town acknowledges duke William I of Guelders as its lord. The church was founded briefly before 1300 by John I.
Fair_Description: All fairs in Grave were specialized markets. On the two fairs which already existed in 1456, horses and cloth were traded. The two new ones instituted in 1456 by Arnold, duke of Guelders, on the request of the town council, were meant specifically for cattle and horse trading.
Staple_Description: The duke of Burgundy (who pawned the duchy of Gelre) granted magistrate and inhabitants of Grave a privilege in 1473 (March 27) that all 'koopbier' (beer for the market) in the Land of Cuijk had to be brewed in Grave.

name: Gryfino
Settlement_Description: A Slavic agricultural settlement with a market; a German merchant settlement developed in its vicinity. First mentioned in 1254 when it became a town.
Town_Description: Duke Barnim I of Pomerania granted the Magdeburg (later the Lübeck) town law in 1254.

name: Gransee
Settlement_Description: Founded near a Slavic fortress and settlement. First mentioned in 1262, already as town.
Town_Description: Margrave John I of Brandenburg founded the town as market settlement and defence against Mecklenburg and granted the Brandenburg (Magdeburg) town law and exemption of tolls in 1262.
Toll_Description: Gransee had a toll and market tax in 1285.

name: Kuhmoinen
Settlement_Description: <b>Inn:</b> Kuhmoinen village had a transport organiser (fi. kyytirättäri, sw. skjutsrättare) in the 1640s. In 1641, there was also an inn in Tapiala village.

name: Iso-Äiniö
Settlement_Description: <b>Inn:</b> An inn was established in Iso-Äiniö in 1639, and Tuomas Yrjönpoika was appointed as the innkeeper.

name: Greußen
Town_Description: The oldest bylaws are known from 1556, although these refer to older bylaws. Keyser assumes that these were the bylaws of Clingen from 1353. Since Greußen was referred to as villa in 1268, the bestowal of town rights must have taken place afterwards.
Toll_Description: In 1389, the council of Greußen raises the toll on woad from Mühlhausen.

name: Groß Dahlum
Settlement_Description: First mentioned in 1022. A castle mentioned in 1191 could not be reliably located.

name: Grevenbroich
Town_Description: The place was given town rights around 1300.
Toll_Description: The Count of Kessel levied a land toll here in 1273. From the beginning of the 14th century, the place came into the possession of the Count of Jülich. It is therefore unclear whether the toll continued to exist. Tariffs and revenues are not known.

name: Grevenkrug
Settlement_Description: First mentioned in 1392. The settlement is not named after an inn ('krug').

name: Grevesmühlen
Settlement_Description: The village is first mentioned in 1230. It became the seat of the local administrative unit ('vogtei') Gnewesmolen before 1242.
Town_Description: Grevesmühlen is mentioned as oppidum in 1262 and as civitas in 1267, but it must have become a town earlier. Lübeck town privileges are first attested before 1356 and were confirmed in 1359.
Fair_Description: An almanac printed in Neudamm (Dębno) in 1598 mentions two fairs in Grevesmühlen: on Sunday Letare and the Assumption of Mary.
Toll_Description: A new toll was granted to the dukes of Mecklenburg by Emperor Frederick in 1471, which led to protests from Wismar, Rostock and Lübeck. Lübeck was exempted from the toll in 1473.

name: Griebo
Settlement_Description: The village is first mentioned in 1200. Originally located more to the South, it was moved to its current location due to changes in the course of the Elbe river in the 14th century.

name: Grimlinghausen
Toll_Description: The Archbishop of Cologne levied a land toll here from 1386. Exact tariffs are not known. Presumably 4 white pennies ('Weißpfennige'/Albus) had to be paid for every horse. Revenues were 20 mark in 1386/87, 22 in 1392/93, 80 in 1442/43 and in 1444/45. Additionally, in 1479 Grimlingshausen was mentioned as a secondary toll station of Neuss. Accounts from 1583-4 show that the revenue was very low; presumably it was abandoned afterwards because of insignificance.  In 1630, the toll is no longer mentioned.

name: Ilmoila
Settlement_Description: <b>Inn:</b> An inn was established in Ilmoila in 1637, and Matti Joosepinpoika was appointed as the innkeeper.

name: Grimmen
Settlement_Description: Settlement of the late Iron Age; later probably a Slavic settlement, from ca. 1220 German. First mentioned in 1267.
Town_Description: Acquisition of Lübeck town law in 1287 at the latest. A town council is mentioned in 1306.

name: Joachimsthal
Settlement_Description: A glassmaker's settlement existed since 1577, which was revived in 1601.

name: Grobina
Settlement_Description: An important sea trading centre in the early Middle Ages. In 1245 there was a castle, which was destroyed in 1262. In 1464 the already existing fortified borough ('Hakelwerk') was expanded.

name: Horodok
Toll_Description: Mentioned as toll station in c. 1349, where 2 gr. for each horse had to be paid.

name: Groenlo
Town_Description: Mentioned as 'cives de Gronlo' in 1251. Earliest mention as a town in 1273. Town privileges received on 1 December 1277 by Reginald I, count of Guelders.
Fair_Description: Around 1440, a market took place in Groenlo of which it is unknown how old it was, and whether it concerned a daily or weekly market, or a fair. The market had a local function: it was visited by inhabitants of the neighbouring small principality of Borculo.

name: Muurame
Settlement_Description: <b>Inn:</b> Pertti Erkinpoika, Muurame parish constable (fi: nimismies, sw: länsman) ran a tavern in his house in 1600. Two other farms were ordered to help him.

name: Grolloo
Settlement_Description: Earliest mention probably in the twelfth century.

name: Gröningen
Settlement_Description: In 936 a court (curtis) is mentioned. In 1371 the settlement is granted borough rights ('Weichbildrechte'). From 1369 to 1648 it served as a residence to the bishops of Halberstadt, the bishopric's seat remained in Halberstadt. In the Middle Ages, the settlement split into  Wester-/Klostergröningen, Südgröningen (Sudendorf) and Nordgröningen. Since the sources usually only refert to Gröningen, a distinction remains difficult. Since the 16th cenutry, the village owned a council constitution, but it was nevertheless referred to as borough ('Flecken') up into the 17th century.
Fair_Description: In 1641 Gröningen is granted two fairs.

name: Groß Ammensleben
Settlement_Description: First mention in 950. A lord of Groß Ammensleben is first mentioned in 1087. Foundation of an abbey in 1120, which was converted into a Benedictine monastery in 1129. It never seems to have gained much significance.

name: Lielauce
Settlement_Description: The manor was mentioned in 1561 as a fief.

name: Langförden
Settlement_Description: First mentioned between 870 and 900. A church was built in the 11th century. In 1498, there lived ca. 35-37 persons in the village.

name: Groß Berkel
Settlement_Description: First mentioned around 1066-1081, initially only as Berkel. To make a distinction with nearby Klein Berkel (first mentioned in 1241), the settlement became known as Groß Berkel in the 16th century.

name: Groß Beuster
Settlement_Description: First mention in 1246 as part of a noble family.

name: Pärnäsaari
Settlement_Description: <b>Inn:</b> Count Per Brahe the Younger, Governor-General of Finland, stopped in Laukaa parish constable (fi: nimismies, sw: länsman) Klemetti Daavidinpoika's farm in Pärnäsaari when returning to Turku in winter 1640. His company had two meals which he paid 10 silver <i>dalers</i> to the constable.

name: Iecava
Settlement_Description: The manor was first mentioned in 1272.

name: Großflintbek
Settlement_Description: The village Flintbek - first mentioned in 1223 - was divided into Groß and Klein Flintbek, of which the former is first mentioned separately in 1328.

name: Groß Förste
Settlement_Description: The settlement Förste was first mentioned in the beginning of the 12th century. It consisted of two parts, Groß and Klein Förste, of which the former was first mentioned separately in 1283.

name: Freden
Settlement_Description: First mentioned in the 12th century. The parish church of St George is mentioned in 1068. A castle is first mentioned in 1158, later it is presumed that there was a fortification of the bishop of Hildesheim near the church, to guard the river crossing.

name: Groß Fullen
Settlement_Description: First mentioned around 1000 in plural, which indicates that already at that time, Fullen encompassed two distinct settlements, which developed into Groß and Klein Fullen.
Toll_Description: A road toll ('wegegeld') of the bishop of Münster was mentioned in Fullen in 1576, when it could not be leased. In the 17th century, half of the toll was owned by the town Meppen.

name: Groß Grabow
Settlement_Description: The village is first mentioned in 1441.

name: Groß Grenz
Settlement_Description: First mentioned in 1278. The addition "Groß" ('large') developed soon after to discern the village from nearby Klein Grenz.

name: Groß Grönau
Settlement_Description: Mentioned in the tithe register of Ratzeburg from 1230. The St Willehad church dates from the 13th/14th century.

name: Groß Hesepe
Settlement_Description: First mentioned around 1000, where a distinction between Groß and Klein Hesepe is not yet made.

name: Dzelmes
Settlement_Description: 'Villa Pepholt' is mentioned as the original name of the settlement in 1257.

name: Groß Lüsewitz
Settlement_Description: The village is first mentioned in 1344.

name: Groß Methling
Settlement_Description: The church village is first mentioned in 1269.

name: Möringen
Settlement_Description: First mention in 1200; mention of an inn in 1375 and 1472.

name: null
Bridge_Description: The bridge across the Ifta marked the border of safe conduct between Hessia and Saxonia.

name: Groß Oesingen
Settlement_Description: Originally named Oesingen. The addition "Groß" ('large'), to distinguish the settlement from Klein ('little') Oesingen, is attested since the end of the 15th century.

name: Groß Reken
Settlement_Description: Wolfhelm, bishop of Münster, donated land around Reken in 889.

name: Groß Ringmar
Settlement_Description: The settlement is first mentioned in the list of contributors to the construction of the Weser bridge in Bremen, ca. 1250.

name: Bad Salzelmen
Settlement_Description: The important saltworks of Groß Salze were first mentioned in 1170. The nearby settlement Elmen (first mentioned in 1124) was merged into Groß Salze in 1894; it was renamed Bad Salzelmen in 1926.
Town_Description: A register of the council ('Rathandelsbuch') of 1291 suggests that Groß Salze was referred to as town at the time and had Magdeburg town rights.
Toll_Description: The castle Schadeleben in Groß Salze was built between 1310 and 1313, where a salt toll was levied. The castle, including the toll and safe conduct, was pawned several times later, among others in 1388.

name: Groß Sarau
Settlement_Description: Already when it is first mentioned in 1230, a division of the settlement between 'Sarowe' and 'Slavicum Sarowe' is made, which points at a German and a Slavic settlement. An inn is attested here in 1466.

name: Groß Schwaß
Settlement_Description: The village is first mentioned in 1328.

name: Groß Quassow
Settlement_Description: The village is first mentioned in 1346.

name: Küstelberg
Settlement_Description: First mentioned in 1177. A monastery is mentioned from 1302.

name: Groß Schwiesow
Settlement_Description: The village is first mentioned in 1284.

name: Groß Stavern
Settlement_Description: The place was first mentioned in 890.

name: Groß Stöckheim
Settlement_Description: First mentioned in 1051. Traces from habitation from the Roman imperial period have been found.

name: Großharthau
Settlement_Description: Village and manor, first mentioned in 1241.

name: Großbeeren
Settlement_Description: Probably founded in the context of the colonisation of the Teltow by the Ascanians since the Middle of the 13th century. Mention as Berne in 1297. In 1344 the settlement was given to the family of Berne, who stayed in possession of the settlement until their demise at the beginning of the 19th century.

name: Großwoltersdorf
Settlement_Description: The village is first mentioned in 1326.

name: Spanbroek
Settlement_Description: According to Cox, Spanbroek is first mentioned in a 1300-copy of a 1256 document. Van Berkel and Samplonius take a slightly later date, 1290 (in a thirteenth- or fourteenth-century copy). In 1414, the settlements Spanbroek, Opmeer, Obdam and Hensbroek were granted town privileges by William VI, count of Holland. Together, these settlements formed the ‘stede’ Spanbroek. These settlements, however, never developed an urban character. The granting of town rights was part of an administrative reorganization in which a number of smaller settlements were granted town rights in order to provide them with a certain degree of self-government which replaced the need for the count of Holland's bailiffs ('baljuws'). The settlements kept their own separate settlement governments. For political reasons, the 'stede' lost its privileges in 1426. By 1434, the territory was divided between several lords. In 1456, 'stede' Spanbroek received its own town privileges, separate from the 'stede' Obdam-Hensbroek.

name: Großenhain
Settlement_Description: Slavic fortress and settlement in place before its foundation in the 12th century as a fortress of the margraves of Meißen.
Town_Description: Town foundations laid down around 1200; development into an important weaving town by the 15th and 16th centuries. Town privileges confirmed in 1464.
Fair_Description: In 1545 Leipzig protests against a new fair in Großenhain. The town's council answers that it wasn't aware of a new fair and the other fairs had been held since the olden times.
Toll_Description: A toll of the Margrave of Meißen in Großenhain is first mentioned in 1323, as well as in in 1399 and 1404. Safe conduct of the Duke of Saxony is mentioned in 1490. Extensive regulations of safe conduct remain from 1547 (SHStA Dresden, Loc. 40 085, Hain Nr. 116 b, Erbbuch des Amtes Großenhain 1547, p. 731–780v).
Staple_Description: Staple for woad in the duchy of Saxony, granted in 1477. The rival Görlitz succeeded in repressing the staple rights for ten years, but staple was reinstated in 1490. Only woad that was unsold after four weeks could be taken onwards to Görlitz. In 1523 the council of Großenhain decided that only one quarter of the woad should be offered for sale in their town; the staple was intensified in 1592 and 1607.

name: Suuremõisa
Settlement_Description: In the Medieval times there was an estate of the Teutonic Order ('Deutscher Orden') north of today's settlement. The farmers settled further south in 1626, where the former fields of the estate were. After the Teutonic period, it first became a Danish, then a Swedish and later a Russian domain.

name: Königsdorf
Toll_Description: 1) Even before 1314, Dietrich Luf of Cleves levied a land toll. From 1314 this was in the possession of the Archbishop of Cologne. In 1396, 2 to 3 alb. per horse had to be paid, depending on the load. In 1430, 4 shillings per horse had to be paid. In 1314 the annual income was about 5 mark. In 1395 only the road toll was collected. In 1455 Blatzheim, Bocklemünd, Brüggen (Erft), Lövenich, Mehlem, Merheim and Widdersdorf were secondary toll stations.2) In 1395, the Archbishop of Cologne levied a road toll. In the same year, a tariff of 2 heller per wagon had to be paid. In 1454/60, 40 mark per year could be collected.

name: Großgrabe (Mühlhausen)
Settlement_Description: First mention in 997 in a donation charter to the monastery of St Victor in Mainz by emperor Otto III.

name: Großfahner
Settlement_Description: Already settled in prehistory, archaeological finds suggest beginnings in the early Stone Age. First written mention in 876.

name: Großmühlingen
Settlement_Description: First mentioned in 936 in a donation charter to Quedlinburg monastery. A castle is first mentioned in 1318. Independent county until 1659.

name: Großörner
Settlement_Description: Mentioned in 973 in an exchange of estates between Fulda monastery and the archbishopric of Magdeburg. In 1337 Großörner is referred to as Alten-Örner, but the name did not establish itself.

name: Großringe
Settlement_Description: The settlement Ringe is first mentioned in 1329, both parts Groß- and Kleinringe separately in 1456.

name: Großwudicke
Settlement_Description: First mention possibly in 1397 as Weddig.

name: Großzöbern
Toll_Description: Secondary station of safe conduct ('Beigeleitsstelle') of Gräfenhainichen (LHASA, MD, d. 16, Nr. 17 1a, Erbbuch des Amtes Gräfenhainichen 1550).

name: Gruna
Settlement_Description: First mention of Gruna in 1456. Deserted because of lignite mining in 1980.

name: Grundzāle
Settlement_Description: Until 1489, the manor belonged to the Grundeis family.

name: Grumbach
Toll_Description: In 1547 the counts of Henneberg erected a blockhouse and a tollbar in Grumbach.

name: Großwechsungen
Settlement_Description: First mention in 1155 in an exchange of property between Fulda and Walkenried monasteries.

name: Großtöpfer
Settlement_Description: First mentioned in 1195. The village was property of castle Stein (Bischofsstein) and home to a family which named itself after it.

name: Grünhagen
Settlement_Description: First mentioned in 1252. The settlement was called Boytelendorp before the 14th century.

name: Grünhof
Settlement_Description: Folwark, which was constructed not long after 1557.

name: Zaļenieki
Settlement_Description: The manor was first mentioned in 1566.

name: Gubin
Settlement_Description: First mentioned in 1211. Archaeological finds date from 1400BC to 200AD.
Town_Description: Henry, Margrave of Meisen and Ostmark granted the Magdeburg town law in 1235, mentioned as civitas since 1286. Divided into a Polish (the old town) and a German part since 1945.
Toll_Description: A toll collector is mentioned in 1511.

name: Häädemeeste
Settlement_Description: In the 16th century, a harbour was built. A village settled around this harbour. At the same time, a hamlet ('Hof') was built, which was owned by the Mayor of Pernau in 1624.

name: Sallingsund
Ferry_Description: The age and character of the ferry across the strait of Sallingsund is uncertain, but a ferry route was probably in place in the 13th century. In 1529 peasants on the island threatened to not pay taxes to either the bishop or the king before they got a new ferry, which the bishop in Viborg granted. In 1632 local nobles complained that that travelers had nowhere to seek shelter, so the ferry yard (Danish: færgegård) “Plagen” on the island of Mors and the inn “Pinen” on the Salling side must be after 1632. In the later medieval period and early modern era the ferry played an important role in the export of oxen from Mors to Salling.

name: Güntersberge
Settlement_Description: In 1326 a castle was mentioned. During the 14th century the settlement was referred to as borough ('Flecken'), which requested a confirmation of its rights and privileges in 1531.
Town_Description: In 1539 privileges, that are similar to those that existed in Harzgerode, were given. However, the term 'borough' ('Flecken') was still used after that.

name: Gütersloh
Settlement_Description: First mentioned in 1110 as a parish ('Kirchspiel'). But a settlement seems to have existed before 1000.

name: Gutow
Settlement_Description: The village is first mentioned in 1226.

name: Hardheim
Toll_Description: Toll station of the count of Wertheim

name: Haaksbergen
Settlement_Description: Earliest mention in 1188 in a document dating from the end of the thirteenth century.

name: Gumpelstadt
Settlement_Description: First uncertain mention in 907, first certain mention in 1015.

name: Gundersleben
Settlement_Description: First mention in 780-802. Further mention in 927 in a donation charter of emperor Henry I.

name: Gutengermendorf
Settlement_Description: The village is first mentioned in 1420.

name: Den Haag
Settlement_Description: The earliest mention of 's-Gravenhage dates from 1242, in a copy from 1390. The settlement developed near a court of the count of Holland, which was founded in the 13th century. A chapter in the church is found in the years 1367-1572. Although the settlement had town-like features and was sometimes considered a town by contemporaries, it was only elevated to town rank on 25 November 1806 by Louis Bonaparte, king of Holland.
Fair_Description: In the comital account of 1334 market-tolls are found. In the account dated 1343/'4 the toll of 'St. Katrijnenmisse' (Catharina) is mentioned (Nov. 25). In 1407 count Willem VI replaced a fair from July 25 juli to May and granted a free horse- and cattlefair in May during 14 days. Right (tariffs) and freedom should be as in Delft.In 1537 a new 'wagenveer' (location for carts with regular destinations) was made at  the St. Anthonisbridge (Wagenstraat), previously this was at the Voorhout. Here wagons from Delft, Rijswijk and Voorhout were found. In 1562 a toll with a tariff was installed to finance the costs for the pavement of the Noordeinde. Toll was levied from wagons and carts belonging to fishermen and merchants from Amsterdam, Hoorn and Enkhuizen and those from the 'Zijde' (the fishing villages at the Noordzee). Fish, game and poultry was transported to Brabant, Luik, Maastricht and Cologne. In 1581 (Jan. 8) (or 1580 Dec. 28?) admission for a fair of horses, cattle and other goods was obtained. Date: 8 days before Mayday, duration 14 days. The fair of 1406 (sic: 1407) and other privileges were decayed because of the Guelders and had long not been organised. As a result of the war there was poverty. The fair was granted on the same date. In 1597 (March 15) the Estates of Holland gave permission to organise the horse- and cattle-fair after the horse-fair of Valkenburg.

name: Habaja
Settlement_Description: Manor and village that was first mentioned in 1417.

name: Habbrügge
Settlement_Description: The name of the settlement indicates a plastered ford.

name: Haabersti
Settlement_Description: In 1265 it was referred to as a village in the borderland of Reval. In the 16th/17th century the village became property of Reval.

name: Hachenburg
Toll_Description: The Count of Sayn levied a land toll here before 1327. In the following decades, the toll rights were further granted: among others, Reinhard von Westerburg held them from 1340 and Heinrich Beyer von Boppard from 1372. Under Beyer of Boppard in 1372 and 1402, ½ gulden per carriage was paid. Under Westerburg in 1402, 1 guilder per carriage. In 1511, the Sayner customs were leased out for 150 gulden.

name: Hachmühlen
Settlement_Description: The village was first mentioned in 1217.

name: Hadamar
Settlement_Description: First mentioned in 832. In 1190 a curia is mentioned. The settlement is named as 'villa' in 1231 and 1287.
Toll_Description: The Count of Katzenelnbogen levied a gate toll in 1453. Accounts from 1430 and 1431 still mention a fair/market toll. Tariffs are not known. In 1453, 5 Turnosgroschen were collected in the year.

name: Hagenah
Settlement_Description: First mentioned when count palatinate Frederick II donated 3 farms in Hagenah to the monastery of St George in Stade before 1132. In a register from 1535, 4 farms and a cottage are mentioned. In hist travel account, Samuel Kiechel mentions for 1586 a "krueg oder wirtshaus" (inn or tavern).

name: Haderslev
Settlement_Description: Originally a marketplace at Starup on the southern shore of Haderslev Fjord east of the later medieval town of Haderslev. The latter developed into a permanent settlement during the 12th century. The settlement and later the town of Haderslev benefited from its strategic location at a section of Hærvejen/Ochsenweg, and at the shortest route across the peninsula of Jutland between the Baltic Sea, accessible from the town via Haderslev Fjord, and the important town of Ribe at the North Sea cost.
Town_Description: Presumably the town of Haderslev is indirectly mentioned by the chronicler Saxo (“Hatheri oppidum”) in his Gesta Danorum, finished c. 1208. Royal income from “Haderslev District” (Danish: Haderslev Herred) is listed in the so-called main piece of King Valdemar’s Cadastre from 1231, and probably this is a reference to the town. Around 1250 a Dominican priory was established, and by then Haderslev certainly had a clear urban character. First town law granted by Duke Valdemar IV in 1292. About a century later, in 1397, count Gerhard of Schleswig reconfirmed existing town rights. During the medieval and early-modern period Haderslev was in general an important town that alternately belonged to the king of Denmark or the dukes/counts in the region. A royal castle, Haderslevhus, known from the 14th century. Various kings and queens made regular use of the castle. In the middle of the 16th century Haderslev became residence of duke Hans the Elder, who rebuilt the castle of Haderslevhus, now also known as Hansborg. The castle was burned during the Dano-Swedish wars in the 17th century, which also heavily damaged the town.
Toll_Description: A royal toll was collected in Haderslev by 1231 according to the so-called main piece in King Valdemar’s Cadastre. Tolls on many different goods are also listed in the town law from 1292. Toll records from the year 1539 have been preserved.
Harbour_Description: First mentioned in 1253. From the second half of the 13th century onwards the harbor was one of the most important in this part of Jutland. Danes from both the hinterland and other regions within the kingdom as well as German merchants frequently used the harbor; in 1399, for example, ships from Lübeck sailed to Haderslev. During the late medieval period the harbor had a wharf.

name: Pinen (Oddesund)
Ferry_Description: The age and character of the ferry across the narrow strait is uncertain. A ferry is mentioned in 1578, but is probably significantly older. It was also possible to cross the strait using a ford, but according to a document from 1574, this could be very dangerous. In the later middle ages and early modern era oxen from the region of Thy was exported to the markets in Holstebro, and from there taken further south. In the 16th century the income from the ferry was important to the stewards (Danish: lensmænd) of Ørum.

name: Habichtswald
Settlement_Description: Manor ('schultenhof'), first mentioned in 1494. In 1545 it was deserted, but later it was reoccupied.

name: Hagen (Altmark)
Settlement_Description: First mention in 1329/30. There is a mention in 1215, but this may only refer to a field name. Until 1542 property of Dambeck monastery.

name: Hagenohsen
Settlement_Description: Came into existence as settlement near the castle Ohsen on the right shore of the Weser. The settlement was first known as Nordohsen, later as Hagenohsen.

name: Hagenow
Settlement_Description: A village existed since Wendish times, east of which a German village was founded. A parish priest and knights are mentioned in 1190-1195. Attested as village in 1230-1327.
Town_Description: Became a town after it got into possession of Mecklenburg in 1358. First mentioned as oppidum in 1370, and as a town in 1420. Full town privileges were only granted in 1754.

name: Hahnenburger Schleusen
Harbour_Description: Already before the construction of the canal between Stecknitz and Delvenau, salt was transported on the river Stecknitz to Lübeck. It had arrived on the land route to Mölln, where it was transshipped.
Lock_Description: Between 1391 and 1398 the city of Lübeck constructed a canal between the Mölln lake and the Delvenau river. At the connection of the canal with the lake, where a fall of 5m had to be compensated, a system of 4 flash locks was constructed. An additional small lock, the "Möllner Kehle", was constructed in 1601.

name: Hakenberg
Settlement_Description: First mention in the records in 1200.

name: Hakendover
Settlement_Description: Earliest mention in 1138, in a thirteenth century copy.

name: Halberstadt
Settlement_Description: The settlement is first mentioned in 781 and became seat of a bishop in 827. Mint, market and toll rights were granted in 989.
Town_Description: In 1105, the bishop confirmed the "iura et statua civilia". Court, police and administration emerged during the following years. In 1184 Halberstadt already adapted the town rights of Goslar. In the first third of the 13th century the first council forms after several conflicts with the episcopal town lord. 1241 a town hall is mentioned for the first time.
Fair_Description: In 989 emperor Otto III. grants market privileges to the settlement.

name: Haldensleben
Settlement_Description: The settlement was first mentioned in a document during Otto I. regency in 966. Althaldensleben was the original settlement. After 1150 Neuhaldensleben was built to the north. Both places were united in 1938.
Town_Description: Magdeburg town rights granted in a foundation record in 1223.
Toll_Description: Awarding of a road toll for the town by archbishop Wilbrand in 1249, with which the town was supposed to fund road construction, the expansion of the gates and the erection of wall towers.The toll in Haldensleben is further mentioned in the 16th century, when a complaint is filed that the toll stations of Oebisfelde, Neuhaldensleben, Wolmirstedt, Dreileben, Wanzleben and Calbe collect less toll because of Magdeburg's toll excemption.In 1549 a listing of the yearly income from the safe conduct of the district of Haldensleben remains.

name: Haldern
Toll_Description: The Archbishop of Cologne probably levied a land toll before 1299. From 1392 onwards, there is no longer any mention of a toll in Haldern. Tariffs and revenues are not known.

name: Halen
Settlement_Description: Earliest mention in 741, in an eleventh century copy. Next mention in 1107, in a thirteenth century copy.

name: Halfweg
Settlement_Description: Earliest mention 1680, in a reprint in 1745.
Harbour_Description: Due to the existence of three sluices between the Haarlem Lake and the IJ, the tow canal ('trekvaart') between Amsterdam and Haarlem, which was built in 1631, was interrupted in Halfweg. Passengers had to change barges here.

name: Halle (Saale)
Settlement_Description: Numerous prehistorical finds are witness to an early settlement of the region. Mention of castle "Halla" on the eastern bank of the Saale in 806, its location is not known. The second mention of Halle in 1064 indicates a growing independence from Giebichenstein, the former political centre. A market settlement developed in the 11th century around the booming saltworks.
Town_Description: Town privileges after the fashion of the Magdeburg town law must have been granted before 1170. First explicit referral to the settlement as a town in 1177. It only received a full autonomous town status in 1310, but lost part of its autonomy after the archbishop conquered the town in 1478 and made it his residence.
Fair_Description: A fair in Halle is first mentioned in 1128. Probably this was the fair on the Nativity of Mary, which is mentioned a century later. A second fair on New Year's Day appears in 1464 during a conflict with Leipzig about conflicting fairs.
Toll_Description: The archiepiscopal coin and toll were moved from Giebichenstein to Halle around 1064. The monastery Paulinzella was exempted from the salt toll in Halle in 1154, in 1176 the Merseburg monastery of St Peter and one year later the entire diocese of Merseburg. In 1281 the town acquired the income from the tolls. The toll was levied at the town gates, as mentioned in 1182. Escorts ('Geleitsmänner') are attested at the Steintor and Galgtor gates in 1499.

name: Hallenberg
Settlement_Description: The settlement Merklinghausen in the Nuhne valley was first mentioned in 1147, but possibly belonged to the abbey of Deutz since its foundation in 1002. Between 1248 and 1253, the castle and town Hallenberg were founded on an elevation next to the village by Arnold von Hochstaden; it was first mentioned in 1259.
Town_Description: Town privileges were confirmed in 1338 and extended in 1354 by the town right of Rüthen-Brilon.

name: Hallerburg
Settlement_Description: A castle in Hallerburg was built around 1350; a settlement developed next to it. The castle was destroyed in 1519.
Toll_Description: A toll in Hallerburg is mentioned in 1455.

name: Haljala
Settlement_Description: In the 13th century, the village belonged to the church.

name: Haltern am See
Settlement_Description: The settlement itself is first mentioned in 1017, but goes back to roman colonization.
Town_Description: In 1288 the settlement was given 'Wigboldsrechte' by Bishop Everhard von Munster.
Toll_Description: The toll in Haltern was divided into two parts: one for the bishop of Münster and one for the town. In 1557, the tariff was raised from 1 Rader albus to 1/2 Taler, but the old tariff was restored after complaints from towns on the Rhine.

name: Boven-Hardinxveld
Settlement_Description: Earliest mention of Hardinxveld ('Herdingfelde') in 1105. In 1399 Hardinxveld, subjects of the lord of Brederode, obtained toll exemptions from the count of Holland. The addition 'Boven' ('upper') is attested in 1899, to discern the village from Neder-Hardinxveld, nowadays merged with Giessendam.

name: Hameln
Settlement_Description: Hameln, which consisted of more than one settlement, is first mentioned in the 9th century, but was considerably older.
Town_Description: A planned town with Minden town privileges was founded around 1200.
Fair_Description: Fairs in Hameln are first mentioned around 1240, among others on St Peter and Paul's Day. In the oldest town register from ca. 1350, three fairs are mentioned: on St Boniface, St Michael and "tho der hoighen kerkemisse", probably on All Saints' Day. The dates were changed in 1556: the St Michael and All Saints fair took place on Monday after the feast days, and the fair on St Boniface was replaced by two new ones, on Monday after Letare Sunday and on the second Monday after Trinity Sunday.
Staple_Description: In practice, there existed a forced transshipment in Hameln for a long time because of the barrier of the Hamelner Loch (see harbour). A formal staple right, however, is first attested in 1627, and it is uncertain whether it was ever really enforced.

name: Hamfelde
Settlement_Description: The settlement Hamfelde, first mentioned in 1230, developed on both shores of the Bille. Because this became the border between Lauenburg and Stormarn, it was divided into two administrative units.

name: Hamm (Lippe)
Settlement_Description: After the nearby castle and town of Nienbrügge were destroyed, Count Adolf von der Mark founded a settlement in "Hamm" in 1226.
Town_Description: Since its foundation, the settlement has been mentioned as an 'oppidum' and 'civitas' and got Lippstadt rights approved in 1279.
Toll_Description: The Count of the Mark probably levied a land toll in 1347/91. From 1456, half of the yields fell to the town of Hamm. Tariffs and revenues are not known. A road toll was levied from 1612 onwards.

name: Hamm (Hamburg)
Settlement_Description: First mentioned in 1212. A boom barrier is mentioned here in 1465.

name: Hammenstedt
Settlement_Description: First mentioned in the 8th or 9th century.

name: Hammer (Kiel)
Settlement_Description: The settlement of five farms probably goes back to Malugesdorf, which is mentioned in the 13th century. In 1288, the name Hammer appears for the first time.

name: Czarne
Settlement_Description: A border castle (Wildhaus) of the Teutonic Order was relocated here in the late 14th century, a village developed next to it.
Town_Description: The Kulm town law was granted in 1395 by grandmaster Konrad von Jungingen. It was endorsed in 1411.

name: Bullerup
Settlement_Description: The village of Bullerup By was first mentioned in 1383, but is significantly older. The settlement had no church but was part of the parish of Agedrup Church.

name: null
Harbour_Description: A harbour in Ringkøbing is first mentioned in 1368, but is older. Probably, it was a natural harbour, where ships anchored near the beach in the fjord. To some extent Ringkøbing served as port of shipment for other towns in the region such as Viborg and Holstebro.

name: Haren (Groningen)
Settlement_Description: Earliest mention in 1249, in a  copy from circa 1789. The next mention dates from 1323.

name: Miłomłyn
Settlement_Description: A house of the Teutonic Order was built before 1335
Town_Description: The komtur of Christburg, Dietrich von Altenburg, founded the town in 1335 with Kulm town law, the handfast was renewed in 1438 after the old one was lost in a fire.

name: Hanerau
Settlement_Description: Around 1180, a castle was built by count Adolf III of Holstein as border defense against Dithmarschen.
Toll_Description: A toll in Hanerau is levied from the mid-15th century, first mentioned in 1461, but then already existing for some years. In 1474, the toll in Hanerau is confirmed and set at the same level as the other tolls in Holstein. The toll was also levied at other streets to Dithmarschen, at the castle Lindhorst (Keller) and since 1601 in Hohenhörn.

name: Hannover
Settlement_Description: First mentioned around 1150; there are traces of permanent settlement from ca. 1000. The settlement was fortified in the second half of the 12th century.
Town_Description: Hannover developed into a town in the 1230s; the Minden town privileges were confirmed in 1241.
Fair_Description: Fairs in Hannover are first mentioned in 1399, taking place on the feast of St James and Maundy Thursday.
