According to a 1444 letter from Hildesheim, there also existed a fair of St Simon and Jude at the time, which was to be replaced by a fair on St Walpurga and the day before and after, with the addition that no other free fair was to take place in Hannover. St Walpurga's fair is mentioned again in 1453, when Hildesheim complained about hindrance of their citizens during the said fair. However, in 1445 there is also mention of a fair of St Giles in Hannover.
Toll_Description: Next to a market toll, which was levied by the duke of Brunswick-Lüneburg, there existed a transit toll for the town area. This belonged to the duke as well, but in practice it was levied by the town authorities since 1293, who in return acquired part of the revenues. In the middle of the 15th century, the toll was acquired by the town; customs for many commodities were raised around the same time.

name: Hamberge
Settlement_Description: First mentioned in 1231. The local church is mentioned in 1340.

name: Haapsalu
Settlement_Description: A bishop's castle in Hapsal was the residence of the bishops of Oesel-Wiek from 1265/66 until the middle of the 14th century. The Fortified Borough ('Hakelwerk') was built in the 13th century next to the castle.
Town_Description: The Fortified Bourough received town rights in 1279. The town rights of Riga were granted in 1294. Later, in 1581, town rights of Reval were granted.

name: null
Harbour_Description: The Sieg river was navigable until Siegburg until the 19th century and reached town via the Mühlengraben, which is first mentioned in 1183-85. A small harbour is known in front of the Cologne gate in the 16th century.

name: Åsum
Settlement_Description: The village of Åsum was first mentioned in 1339, but is much older. Probably etablished in the iron age.

name: Harburg
Settlement_Description: Moated castle of the archbishop of Bremen, first mentioned in 1133-1137. In the following time, the castle was often destroyed and changed hands. A settlement at the castle was first mentioned when it received borough ('weichbild') privileges in 1288.
Town_Description: The settlement acquired borough ('weichbild') privileges in 1288, and Lüneburg town privileges in 1297, which were confirmed in 1458. However, the settlement was characterised only as borough ('flecken') for a long time.
Fair_Description: A fair on Monday before St Philipp and James in Harburg is mentioned in an almanac printed in Neudamm (Dębno) in 1598.
Toll_Description: A toll in Harburg was mentioned when the castle was pawned to Lüneburg in 1369, and to Lüneburg, Hamburg, Lübeck and Hannover in 1397. It was most likely a fee on exports of grain and wood on the Elbe.

name: Hardenberg
Settlement_Description: Earliest mention dates from 1229-1230. Hardenberg came into being near by a castle which had been established around 1227. Inhabitants of near by Nijenstede, a place with limited town privileges, moved to Hardenberg over time.
Town_Description: On 18 September 1362, Jan IV of Arkel, bishop of Utrecht, renews the town privileges of Nijenstede, and moves them to Hardenberg. He grants additional town privileges, including the same rights as the citizens of the town of Zwolle.
Fair_Description: According to the 1362 town privileges, Hardenberg had the right to hold a weekly market and four annual fairs: on St Gertrude, Sunday before St Walpurga, St Peter in chains, and St Victor. The market freedom lasted from 8 days before to 8 days after the event, and market stalls were allowed to remain in place for 4 days. The dates were changed in 1789.
Toll_Description: The bishop of Utrecht received the right to levy a toll at his castle in Hardenberg from Emperor Charles IV in 1364. He exempted his servants in Twente from toll payments in Hardenberg and Nieuwebrug in 1391 and in 1395 the citizens of Oldenzaal. The toll is also mentioned in an account of Duke Frederick of Schleswig-Holstein from ca. 1500.

name: Schloß Hardenberg
Toll_Description: The Lord of Hardenberg levied a land toll in the village of Hardenberg, presumably in 1487. Tariffs and revenues are not known.

name: Bad Harzburg
Settlement_Description: A settlement below the castle Harzburg is first mentioned in 1338 as "Neustadt unter der Harzburg".

name: Harderwijk
Settlement_Description: Earliest mention in 1231, when Harderwijk received town privileges. A dispersed agrarian settlement is known from the 12th century.
Town_Description: At the end of the 12th century, large floods had created the Zuiderzee and Harderwijk became located on the sea shore, leading to its rapid development as a harbour town. Town privileges were granted on 11 June 1231, by Otto II, count of Guelders and Zutphen.
Fair_Description: In 1294/95, Harderwijk had one fair on Pentecost. In 1424, the town received a second fair held from Sunday Reminiscere to Laetare Sunday. An urban degree from 1431 ordained that merchandise coming to this fair was free of paying toll. At least around 1524, there was an additional oxen fair on October 6th.
Toll_Description: Toll had to be paid on land and water. An urban degree from 1431 states that people from Frisia, Hattem, Staveren, Sloten en Kuinre did not have to pay land toll (‘weggeld’). The same was applicable to ‘those of whom the aldermen of Harderwijk knew that they were free of charge’. The latter phrase was also mentioned for shipping tolls. A degree of 1437 stated that beasts from people from Frisia were free of charge, just like ‘sleden’ (sledges). The tariffs on land and water ordained in 1431 can be found in Berns’ edition of the urban degrees.
Staple_Description: A renewed privilege in 1443 for a fish staple in Harderwijk for all fish brought ashore between Muiden and Kampen was given by the duke of Guelders as a reaction on the fish staple of Naarden in Holland from 1442. However, there is no evidence that a formal fish staple existed before that year, although there was a fee levied on fish brought ashore ('numeratio piscium'), which was given to the town council by the count in 1302. A tariff exists from 1431. The staple had only limited success, as the revenues from the fish trade declined after 1442.

name: Åsum bro
Bridge_Description: Originally a ford across the river of Odense Å at the village of Åsum on the main route between the towns of Nyborg and Odense. A bridge was first mentioned in the 1570ties, when the merchants of Odense needed easier access to the town’s new harbour at Munkebo. A wooden bridge is depicted on a copper engraving of Odense in Civitates orbis terrarum by Georg Braun and Frans Hogenberg (1588). Peasants from 19 parishes in the region were obligated to maintain the important bridge, which in the 17th century was partly built of stone and partly of wood.

name: Harns
Town_Description: According to Cox, the earliest mention as a town dates from 1317. Van Berkel & Samplonius claim that Harlingen was granted town privileges in 1234.

name: Bad Lippspringe
Settlement_Description: The village was first mentioned in 1346, but goes back to a Saxon settlement. Charlemagne had 776, 780, 781 and 804 stays in this settlement. In 1312 a castle is mentioned, near which a suburbium was created, which is first mentioned in 1434.

name: Harmstorf
Toll_Description: A Lüneburg toll in Harmstorf is mentioned in 1441, and in 1495 together with nearby Jesteburg.

name: Harmöle
Settlement_Description: Mill, first mentioned in a late 13th-century addition to a document from 1188.

name: Harpendorf
Settlement_Description: The village was first mentioned in 1178.

name: Harsewinkel
Settlement_Description: First mentioned around 1050 and grown near a church. In 1592 called a 'Wigbold'.

name: Harsleben
Settlement_Description: First mention in a charter at the end of the 11th century. A castle referred to as old castle ('Alte Burg') is known.

name: Hartha
Settlement_Description: First mentioned in 1223. A manor and village in the 13th century, which developed into a small town in the 14th.

name: Hartmannshausen
Settlement_Description: First mentioned at the end of the 14th century.

name: Užava
Settlement_Description: In 1253, the area fell to the Teutonic Order. A manor that was built by the Teutonic Order was mentioned in 1443.

name: Marslev
Settlement_Description: The village of Marslev was first mentioned in 1339, but is significantly older. The parish church is from either the 12th or 13th century.

name: Köörtilä
Settlement_Description: <b>Inn:</b> Köörtilä village might have had an inn already in the Middle Ages. In 1589, the farmers complained how they live close to busy summer and winter roads, which causes them much trouble with food, drink and travel arrangements.

name: Haselünne
Settlement_Description: A farm owned by the monastery of Corvey is mentioned in 1107. An earlier mention in the 11th century is questionable. The church was possibly erected around 800.
Town_Description: In 1271, the bishop of Münster confirmed the town privileges that were originally granted by the Counts Hermann and Otto of Ravensberg before 1220.
Fair_Description: Various fairs are mentioned in Haselünne in the early 14th century: on Sunday Laetare and 1 August (1307), 11 March (1319), and Petri ad Vincula (1324). These were mainly visited by merchants from Osnabrück. It is unclear how long these existed; in 1497, only one fair is still mentioned, the eight-day fair on Laetare, which possibly goes back to the 1271 town privileges.
Toll_Description: The toll probably came into existence at the end of the 12th century, and was owned by the counts of Ravensberg in the 13th century. Later it belonged to the bishop of Münster. In 1569, the towns of Deventer, Kampen and Zwolle complained that a bridge toll was levied against all customs and rights. The lease of the toll is known from the same year and 1578. In 1594, 1626 and 1645, there were complaints about decreased revenues because no oxen were transported through Haselünne anymore, among others due to wars.

name: Hasenburg
Settlement_Description: The Hasenburg was the first and most important watchtower of the Lüneburg enclosure ('landwehr'), built in 1397 on the road to Munster and Soltau. The road crossed the Mühlenbach with a bridge, which could be closed with a barrier. The tower was renewed in 1484. The guard of the tower also checked the payment of excises for foreign beer. An inn at the tower is mentioned in 1562.

name: Aizpute
Settlement_Description: The original castle of Hasenpoth fell to the Teutonic Order in 1245, after which a new castle was built on the left bank in 1249.
Town_Description: In 1378 the founding charter was issued. The town received Rigian town rights as well as mayor and council.

name: Hasport
Settlement_Description: First mentioned in 1637 as a farm on the "Annen-Heyde".

name: Haßbergen
Settlement_Description: The village was first mentioned in 1025.

name: Hasselfelde
Settlement_Description: In 1043 and 1052 King Henry III issued charters in Hasselfelde, but a village probably didn't exist yet. In 1209/27 three villages named Hasselfelde are mentioned, most probably today's districts Hagen, Mittel- and Osthasselfelde. In 1346 the village is once referred to as town, otherwise mostly as borough ('Flecken').

name: Hasselt (Zwolle)
Settlement_Description: A settlement probably came into being around 1180 and was first mentioned on 22 July 1227.
Town_Description: Town privileges were probably granted by Henry (Hendrik) I of Vianden, bishop of Utrecht, in 1252.
Fair_Description: In 1396 the bishop of Utrecht pawned the toll of the fairs for 16 years to the aldermen of Hasselt for the benefit of the town. In 1403 this was changed to long lease. In 1423 the town obtained a privilege, like the three towns, to drive the oxen through the roads of the 'land' (Oversticht) without taxes. In 1531 emperor Charles V confirmed the episcopal privileges for three fairs dated 1357 and 1402/3.

name: Hassenhausen
Settlement_Description: First mentioned in the tithe register of the monastery Hersfeld from 860-890.

name: Hattem
Town_Description: Charter of town privileges has not been preserved. Generally, one assumes the granting of town privileges between 25 September and 31 October 1299, by Reginald I, Count of Guelders.
Fair_Description: In 1353, Duchess Alianora (second wife of Reinald (Reginald) II), Lady of the Veluwe, granted two fairs to Hattem.
Toll_Description: A landtoll is located here. Accounts are preserved for the years 1420-24, 1451-53.

name: Lepplax
Settlement_Description: <b>Inn:</b> An inn was established in Lepplax in 1642, and Mårten Grelsson Abbor was appointed as the innkeeper.

name: Haustenbeck
Settlement_Description: The village Haustenbeck was founded in 1659 by Count Hermann Adolf of Lippe-Detmold as a stopover on the road through the Senne heath. In 1939 it was deserted for an expansion of a military proving ground.

name: Howiek
Settlement_Description: The settlement is first mentioned between 1260 and 1270.

name: Havelberg
Settlement_Description: Settlement with castle of Slavic origin. Foundation of a bishopric in 948 by Otto I, destroyed in 983. A Premonstratensian cathedral chapter was founded at the castle around 1150.
Town_Description: The founding of the town was endorsed by Frederick I in 1179.
Fair_Description: A fair on Sunday Quasimodogeniti in Havelberg is mentioned in an almanac printed in Neudamm (Dębno) in 1598.
Toll_Description: A river toll in Havelberg is first mentioned in 1259 (see harbour). A toll is also mentioned when Havelberg was pawned by margrave Ludwig in 1335. A toll collector is mentioned in 1473.

name: Heede
Settlement_Description: Although first mentioned in 1212, the settlement is probably much older. It is traditionally believed that St Liudger founded a chapel here.
Fair_Description: Reyner von den Bele is mentioned in 1378 as owning a quarter of the market toll in Heede; other quarters are mentioned in 1420 and 1426. The fair in Heede is mentioned in 1482 as one of the free fairs in Emsland (next to Meppen, Haselünne and Haren). A date, however, is not known.
Toll_Description: A toll of the bishop of Münster in Heede is mentioned in 1576, when it could not be pawned. Similarly in 1645, no toll collector could be found because the revenues had become very low due to the Thirty Years' War. A list of annual revenues is known from the years 1591-1604.

name: Heerde
Settlement_Description: Earliest mention in 838, in a eleventh century copy.Next mention dates from 1176, in a seventh century copy.

name: Heeslingen
Settlement_Description: Heeslingen is first mentioned when a monastery of canonesses was founded around 961. The monastery was moved to Zeven in 1141.

name: Heer
Settlement_Description: Earliest mention in 1176, in a eighteenth century copy.

name: Finow
Settlement_Description: First mention of the farm, mill and inn in "Hegermole" in 1294. The name suggests that it was a fortification at a Finow crossing. Acquired town rights in 1935, under the name Finow.
Toll_Description: A toll station in Hegermühle is mentioned in 1355.

name: Heide
Settlement_Description: First mentioned in 1434. Between 1447 and 1559, the settlement was the chief village of the peasant's republic Dithmarschen.
Fair_Description: A market in Heide is first mentioned in 1467, which seems to have been a weekly market. Heinrich Rantzau mentions a fair on Sunday Judica in his 1597 description of Schleswig and Holstein. This fair is also mentioned in an almanac printed in Neudamm (Dębno) in 1598.

name: Heikethalwarte
Settlement_Description: Watchtower, erected around 1280, destroyed in 1425, re-erected in 1452. According to Schmidt (1891) erected in 1454.

name: Heiligenhafen
Settlement_Description: A planned town was established shortly after 1250.
Town_Description: First mentioned as a town in 1262; Lübeck town privileges were probably granted by Adolf IV of Holstein, confirmed by Gerhard II in 1305.
Toll_Description: A toll of the counts of Holstein is mentioned in 1325 and 1328, when citizens of Heiligenhafen were exempted from it. The toll was mainly an export toll for corn shipped from Holstein through the harbour of Heiligenhafen.

name: Heiligenkirchen
Settlement_Description: The settlement is first mentioned in the <cite>Vita Meinwerci</cite> in 1024. According to legend, the settlement goes back to a chapel founded by Charlemagne in 783.

name: Heiligenstedten
Settlement_Description: First mentioned by Adam von Bremen in the late 11th century, who described the foundation of a church around 830.

name: null
Toll_Description: Permission for levying a bridge toll by the town Neustadt of 8 shilling for each last of corn was granted in 1562 and renewed in 1595 and 1601.
Bridge_Description: A bridge in Neustadt is mentioned when the Hospital of the Holy Ghost was founded next to it in 1344, but probably goes back to the foundation of the town in 1244.

name: Heisede
Settlement_Description: First mentioned between 826 and 876. Since the evidence for Heisede could also apply to a homonymous place near Gronau, it is not always clear to which place it pertains.

name: Helfta
Settlement_Description: First mention in the tithe register of Hersfeld in the late 9th century. A a castle from the 9th century is known, which was used as a royal court in the Early Middle Ages. The Cistercian convent from Mansfeld was moved to Helfta in 1259. It had some importance until the Peasant's War in 1525.

name: Helme
Settlement_Description: At the beginning of the 14th century a castle was built. A settlement developed around it during medieval times. The castle was destroyed in 1658. A manor was built around the same time as the castle.

name: Buttstädt
Settlement_Description: First mentioned before 775/786. Referred to as villa in 1067. Village and market place since 1199.
Town_Description: Referred to as town since 1331, in 1392 town rights of Weißensee were granted.
Fair_Description: The cattle fairs in Buttstädt belonged to the largest in middle Germany. Three dates are known since 1479: on St Michael's day, All Saints and St John the Baptist.

name: Helmstedt
Settlement_Description: A missionary church was founded around 800 near the village Helmonstedi (first mentioned in 802), which developed into the Benedictine St Ludger monastery. The later town developed around the current market place in the 12th century. West of it, the monastery of Augustinian Canonesses Marienberg was founded in 1176. Between the monastery and the walled town, the planned suburb Neumark was located, which is first mentioned in 1249.
Town_Description: Helmstedt is first mentioned as "civitas" in 1228. Town privileges were confirmed in 1247.

name: Helmstorf (Tessin)
Settlement_Description: The village is first mentioned in 1345-1348.

name: Helvoirt
Settlement_Description: Earliest mention in 1192. There is evidence for two inns that have both been here from at least 1438 until the nineteenth century. The first one is located on Oude Rijksweg 20 and was called De Zwarte Leeuw ("The Black Lion"). The second one was located on De Dijk 2, called Den Engel ("The Angel").

name: Lüne
Settlement_Description: The Benedictine nunnery Lüne was founded in 1171 by Hildeswidis von Markboldestorp, under the supervision of the Benedictine monastery of St Michael in Lüneburg. In 1573, the monastery became a Lutheran ladies' foundation ('damenstift').

name: Hemmendorf
Settlement_Description: When it was first mentioned in 822, Hemmendorf was in possession of Corvey. Later, the settlement developed into a borough ('flecken').
Toll_Description: Hemmendorf is first mentioned as toll station of the lords of Homburg in 1384.

name: Hendrieken
Settlement_Description: Earliest mention in 1079, in a seventeenth century copy.

name: Herk-de-Stad
Settlement_Description: Earliest mention in 1107, in a thirteenth century copy.

name: Herentals
Fair_Description: The fair started Monday after St. Bavo (Oct. 1), safe-conduct was 14 days before and after that.
Toll_Description: The accounts of the 'grote landtol' or 'weggeld van Brabant' mention an new toll levied in Herentals on linen from Flanders, which was bleached here.

name: Henri-Chapelle
Toll_Description: A toll belonging to the Duchy of Brabant-Limbourg in Henri-Chapelle is mentioned in accounts from 1389 onwards, with annual revenues.

name: Herbern (Greven)
Settlement_Description: Dispersed settlement ('Bauerschaft'), first mentioned in the 9th or 10th century.

name: Herford
Settlement_Description: The imperial abbey Herford was founded in 789.
Town_Description: The old town received town rights around 1170. A judge and leader of the community are mentioned in 1191. The characterisation 'civitas' appears between 1219 and 1226. The new town was founded around 1224 and remained independent until 1634.

name: Herzford
Settlement_Description: A first mention as Hriasforda in 890 is very uncertain.

name: Herwijnen
Settlement_Description: Earliest mention in 850 in a eleventh-century copy.

name: Herve
Town_Description: Duke Walram IV of Limbourg granted privileges ('vrijheidscharter') around 1270 and the settlement had a strong castle, but never developed into a town of much importance.
Toll_Description: A toll station of the duchy of Brabant-Limbourg in Herve is attested in accounts from 1389 onwards.

name: Herrnburg
Settlement_Description: First mentioned as castle in 1191. A village is first mentioned in 1399.
Toll_Description: A toll of the duke of Saxony-Lauenburg in Herrnburg is first mentioned in 1261.

name: Herrenbreitungen
Settlement_Description: The settlement Breitungen, first mentioned in 933, consisted of three separate villages Alten-, Frauen- and Herrenbreitungen. Herrenbreitungen is first mentioned in 1049 and was originally known as Burgbreitungen. A Benedictine monastery is first mentioned in 1112. Merged with Alten- and Frauenbreitungen into one village called Breitungen in 1950.
Toll_Description: Toll regulations from the 16th century settle the fees that had to be paid in (Herren-)Breitungen.

name: 's-Hertogenbosch
Town_Description: Town rights were granted in May 1195 by Henry I, duke of Brabant. In 1363 the king of Denmark granted Den Bosch a 'vitte' (trading-post) situated at Schonen (most southern point of Sweden) in the Baltic, with rights as Kampen.
Fair_Description: On the market-place opposite of the town hall was a hall where a cloth-hall (first mentioned 1287), meat-hall (1310) and a bread-house (till 1339) are found. The weigh-house (1299) was situated next to the town hall. The cattle-market must date before 1200 but is ony found in 1464. The fishmarket is mentioned in 1299. In 1374 inhabitants of Den Bosch are first present on the fairs at Frankfurt. In 1403 (Sept. 25) duchess Johanna granted two new fairs. Dates: 1) Monday after Midlent for 3 days, safe-conduct: Saturday before to the Sunday after the fair, 2) day after St. Bartholomeus (August 23) and two days after that, with safe-conduct till St. Gillis-eve (August 31). The duchess would collect the tolls. In an excise-ordinance dated 1444 two new fairs are mentioned. In the same ordinance the socalled 'vestgeld' levied for the safe-conduct from the waggons or chariots is found, with a tariff. Leuven, Diest, (Maas)Tricht and Gorcum had to pay this. Nijmegen had to pay for the cattle they sold in Den Bosch, but the cattle they only passed through the town was free. The inhabitants of the Meierij of Den Bosch, Turnhout, Hoogstraten, St. Geertruidenberg, Baarle, Breda, Land of Breda, Tiel, (Zalt)Bommel, Heusden and the Land of Heusden were free. Duke Philip stated in 1465 that the fair which started till then the day after St. Luke till Severijnsday (Oct. 19-22) should furthermore start the day after Severijnsday (Oct. 23) during a week. This as the fair coincided with the one granted by the duke in Arnhem. In 1540 (July) emperor Charles granted a free fair for meager cattle on Tuesday and Wednesday in the Holy week (before Eastern). According to an old town-history there would have been even seven fairs in Den Bosch. In the years 1535-'39 some 57000 waggons passed the Vughter-gate yearly. That is 230 per day, assuming 260 working-days per year.
Toll_Description: The landtoll in Brabant was partly collected in Den Bosch. Income was rising up to 1468/9, after that it stagnated. In 1480 with 1815lb. at a maximum for the 15th century, this level was only after 1506 reached again. Around 1500 there were many problems regarding competency, in 1530 the collection was suspended and in 1533 it was leased for 12 years to Den Bosch, afterwards this was enlengthed many times. Delegates of the comital council tried to recover 2/3 of the yields on the countryside. The Meierij was finally obliged to pay after a lawsuit for the Council of Brabant. Yields of this comital landtoll are published for the years 1531-'85.
Staple_Description: In 1585 the governor prince of Parma granted a staple for oxen and horned cattle like Lier had and a free weekly market for meager and fat cattle. In 1587 king Philip II confirmed this right but also for Lier in Brabant. Lier was already reconfirmed in its privilege for this staple in Brabant in 1469 by duke Charles the Bold. But was opposed by Diest in 1475, who said to have the oldest oxen-fair. In 1503 Diest granted safe-conduct for merchants with cattle from Deventer, Kampen, Zwolle and other inhabitants of the Oversticht, although Lier tried to prevent that. Den Bosch also opposed the market at Lier at least since 1555.
Ferry_Description: 's-Hertogenbosch and the surrounding area often flooded during autumn and winter, due to flooding of the river Meuse, and the smaller rivers Aa and Dommel. Small ferries came into function when the elevated access roads flooded. This started out as private enterprises, but at least from the end of the seventeenth onward, the town council of 's-Hertogenbosch controlled these ferries. The ferries were located at the Orthenpoort, Sint-Janspoort, Vughterpoort, Grote Hekel, Kleine Hekel, and Hinthamerpoort. The hydraulic situation did not change much until 1875, when the 'vestingwet' (a law for fortified towns) was repealed.

name: Hildernisse
Settlement_Description: Earliest mention in 1094-1095, in a fifteenth century copy. This village  drowned in 1570.

name: Hessen
Settlement_Description: First mentioned in 966. Since 1129 the lords of Hessen are mentioned as the owners of the castle and the village.

name: Hessisch Oldendorf
Settlement_Description: A first mention around 1160/70 is uncertain; first certainly mentioned around 1247. The planned town was probably founded in the 1230s.
Town_Description: Lippstadt town privileges were granted in 1405.
Fair_Description: In 1462, older market privileges in Oldendorf were confirmed. This concerned the large seven-day fair on Monday before St Michael. In 1563, two other fairs were granted on the Mondays after Oculi and after Exaudi, for which the timeframe was set to three days before and after the said days.
Toll_Description: The toll levied on land and river traffic was moved from Großenwieden to Oldendorf in 1588. Because the old river arm on which Oldendorf is located was closed in 1616, the toll was moved to Rumbeck, but it came back to Oldendorf in 1638 at the latest during the 30-Years' War. Toll registers exist in NLA Bückeburg, L1 Nr. 6372-6379, 6386-6390.

name: Herzberg (Mark)
Settlement_Description: The village is first mentioned in 1365.

name: Heumen
Settlement_Description: Earliest mention dated in 1188, but it is uncertain whether this year is correct. Knights of Heumen are mentioned multiple times in the thirteenth century.

name: Hilleshagen
Settlement_Description: Earliest mention in 1227. It was located on the old route between Aachen and Maastricht. According to a register of the Lord of Wittem from 1471 there existed a hospital here.
Toll_Description: According to the so-called Spechtboek (a fief register of the Duke of Brabant) from 1374-1381 a road toll was levied in Hilleshagen.

name: Iļķene
Settlement_Description: In 1463, the land with the ferry, inn and fishing was given as a fief. David Hilchen bought the land in 1599.
Ferry_Description: The ferry is first mentioned in 1463.

name: Hildesheim
Settlement_Description: Emperor Louis the Pious founded the diocese of Hildesheim near a merchant settlement in 815. The settlement received market privileges around 1000.
Town_Description: Around 1146, Hildesheim is already characterised as 'civitas'. A town hall is first mentioned in 1217, and in 1300 the old town granted itself town rights. The new town, which was founded around 1220, formed a union with the old town since 1583, but both parts were only formally united in 1803.
Fair_Description: The town rights of 1300 mention three fairs, on the Annunciation, the Ascension of the Virgin Mary, and on St Michael's day. According to the stand fees in the town accounts from 1379 onwards, the Annunciation fair was the most visited of the Hildesheim fairs. A fourth fair on St Gotthard is mentioned in 1310. In 1460, the old fairs were replace by two six-day fairs, for a trial period of four years: the fair of St Michael remained, and a new fair took place on Misericordia Sunday. Apparently the trial was a success, because in 1476, the two fairs were reiterated for the period of 12 years with slight modifications. After that period and before 1523, the situation must have changed again, since it is mentioned in the latter year that there were four three-day fairs in the town, which had been held since times of old: next to the fairs of St Michael and Misericordia Sunday, the Annunciation fair had been revived and a new fair on Wednesday after Pentecost was added.
Toll_Description: A toll of the bishop of Hildesheim is first mentioned in 1382, when it was pawned to Aschwin von Meienberg. In 1389 it was pawned to Gunzel von Lutter.

name: Malbork
Settlement_Description: The Teutonic Order started building a castle in 1274
Town_Description: The town close to the castle was given a handfest with Kulm town law in 1276 by Conrad von Tyrbech, a second handfast followed in 1304

name: Hylpen
Town_Description: First mentioned as a town on 25 July 1368.

name: Inčukalns
Settlement_Description: The manor and the surrounding land were mentioned as fiefs in 1436.

name: Höchst
Settlement_Description: First mentioned in 790. In the area of ​​the old town there was an earth fort built in Augustan times.
Town_Description: In 1355, Karl IV authorizes the Archbishop of Mainz to fortify his villages and make them towns under Frankfurt law.

name: Hindenberg
Settlement_Description: The village is first mentioned in 1365.

name: Hohemeile
Settlement_Description: The inn Tannenkrug dates back to the 14th century. Later it was a post station between Lübeck and Wismar named Hohemeile. A forester's lodge was built in 1862, the inn was discontinued in 1864.

name: Hohen Schwarfs
Settlement_Description: The originally Slavic village was first mentioned in 1305. The addition Hohen ('high', first mentioned in 1323) was added after the foundation of the German settlement Klein ('little') Schwarfs.

name: Hohenfinow
Settlement_Description: First mention of castle Vinow in 1258. Due to its location at trading routes between Berlin and Frankfurt/Oder it developed quickly, but this development came to a sudden end when the trade route was moved to Eberswalde in 1317. Hohenfinow was last referred to as little town in 1547. The village deteriorated in the Thirty Years' War and only recovered around 1666.

name: Hohengöhren
Settlement_Description: First mention in 1337, mention of a knightly manor.

name: Hohenhameln
Settlement_Description: First mentioned in 1146. The settlement was the seat of a regional court ('gogericht'). Next to the village, a market borough ('marktflecken') was founded in the 14th century.
Fair_Description: Fairs in Hohenhameln were probably held since the founding of a market borough in the 14th century. Dates are not known before 1695, when three two-day fairs were granted.

name: Hohenheida
Settlement_Description: First mention in 1399 as Windysche Heide.

name: Hohenhörn
Toll_Description: After the construction of the "new road" to Dithmarschen, the toll of Hanerau was also levied in Hohenhörn since 1601.

name: Hoheneiche (Saalfeld)
Toll_Description: Hoheneiche is mentioned as secondary station of safe conduct of Saalfeld in 1728.

name: Hohenseeden
Settlement_Description: First mention in 1144 as property of Berge monastery.

name: Hohen Sprenz
Settlement_Description: First mentioned as Sprentze in 1270. The addition Hohen ('high') was added to discern it from nearby Klein ('little') Sprenz. Probably the addition Groten / Maior ('great') also refers to Hohen Sprenz.

name: Hohenthurm
Settlement_Description: In 1244 a noble family is mentioned. In 1347 Hohenthurm became property of Magdeburg.

name: Hohen Wangelin
Settlement_Description: The village is first mentioned in 1244.

name: Holtorf (Nienburg)
Settlement_Description: A settlement probably already existed before the 9th century.

name: Hohenwestedt
Settlement_Description: First mentioned in 1217. A church was founded in the 12th century and the village became an important regional centre. At least one inn existed in the village in 1601.
Fair_Description: A fair must have taken place soon after the founding of the parish on St Peter and Paul's Day. In the 16th century, a new fair was added on Friday before Palm Sunday. The market privileges were confirmed by King Christian IV in 1596. The dates of both markets, however, are only known from a letter from 1777.

name: Hohenzethen
Settlement_Description: The settlement was first mentioned in 1289.

name: Hohenziatz
Settlement_Description: First mentioned in a record by Otto III in 992. Belonged to the castle district ('Burgward') of Loburg in 1187, afterwards property of the archbishopric of Brandenburg and later of Ziesar.
Toll_Description: Toll station of Magdeburg on the road to Brandenburg.

name: Hohnsen
Settlement_Description: It is uncertain whether the Hainanhusen mentioned in 955 refers to Hohnsen; first mentioned with certainty as Hodenhusen in 1185/87.

name: Hoikendorf
Settlement_Description: The village is first mentioned in 1230.

name: Pamppala
Settlement_Description: <b>Inn:</b> An inn was established in Pamppala in 1649, and Pärttyli Susi was appointed as the innkeeper. His son Yrjö was rude to travellers, so the inn moved to Väärämäki for a short time, and then back to Pamppala.

name: Pieniężno
Settlement_Description: The Old Prussians held an older fortress and an adjoining village, a german settlement existed close by in 1282
Town_Description: The German settlement was turned into a town in 1295 by the locator Dietrich von Lichtenfeld, a town parson is mentioned in 1304, the final founding documents of the civitas with Kulm town law were given in 1312 by the territorial sovereignty, the Warmian diocesan chapter

name: Holleben
Settlement_Description: First mentioned in the tithe register of Hersfeld from the end of the 9th century. In 1091 it was the centre of a castle district ('Burgward'). The village developed into a town-like settlement with a market, town hall, Jew's toll and ferry during the Middle Ages. The economic prosperity of the village came to an end during the Thirty Years' War and a plague.
Toll_Description: Secondary station of safe conduct ('Beigeleitsstelle') of Lauchstädt, mentioned in 1600 as located on the road from Merseburg and Weissenfels to Halle.

name: Hollenstedt
Settlement_Description: The place was first mentioned in 947.

name: Hollingstedt
Settlement_Description: Hollingstedt is mentioned in the Schleswig town law of ca. 1200 as North Sea harbour of Schleswig at the Treene. Archaeological finds show that there was a transshipment point here since the 11th century.

name: Holstre
Settlement_Description: Hamlet ('Hof') owned by the Teutonic Order, first mentioned in 1424.

name: Waardenborg
Toll_Description: Road toll of the bishop of Utrecht at Waardenborg castle, first mentioned in 1383 when the toll fees were set for inhabitants from Twente. From 1444 to 1487 the toll was pledged to the town of Deventer. In 1528 Charles V, the Holy Roman Emperor took over the power of the bishop of Utrecht. He decided to demolish the castle as happened in the following years.

name: Holten (Dinslaken)
Fair_Description: Two fairs are mentioned in 1478: 1) April 22; 2) September 9. In the same year, the weekly market was moved from Saturday to Thursday. Two horse fairs were granted in 1582.

name: Höltenklinken
Settlement_Description: Originally the settlement Klein-Rümpel, mentioned in 1420. It was succeeded in the 16th century by the manor Klinken and the associated village Höltenklinken.

name: Kuusvesi
Settlement_Description: <b>Inn:</b> An inn was established in Laukaa in 1600, and Matti Leinonen from Kuusvesi was appointed as the innkeeper. From Laukaa, there were many local waterways and winter roads to east, west, and north.

name: Stevensweert
Settlement_Description: First mentioned in 1221. The settlement centred around the 13th-century church of St Steven was located on a river island ('weerd'). A castle is mentioned in 1244. The village was reconstructed as a fortress ('vesting') by the Spanish in 1633.
Toll_Description: In 1561 the levying of a toll of safe conduct on carts and ships near Stevensweert is declared before the magistrate of Roermond. Children of someone who had levied toll for a long time declared that a barrel with grain was taken from ships with grain from burghers from Roermond, as was made public under the gate of the castle. Between 1582 and 1613 the toll was levied in Roermond, and accounts have been preserved with the tariff of 1609. A toll list dating from 1593 has also been preserved. Only Grave and ’s-Hertogenbosch were exempted; it is unclear whether burghers from Nijmegen obtained toll freedom as well.

name: Mengeringhausen
Settlement_Description: The settlement is first mentioned in 1234 as a 'villa', in 1239 and 1299 as an 'oppidum'. A castle was built around 1300, but it was not mentioned until 1388.
Town_Description: In 1301 the old town received town privileges, the new town in 1392. In 1500 a new privilege was granted again for both of them and in 1587 it was confirmed.

name: Holtsee
Settlement_Description: First mentioned in a Kiel town register of 1264-89.

name: Bad Holzhausen
Settlement_Description: The place was first mentioned in 1033.

name: Hoorn
Settlement_Description: According to Cox, Hoorn is first mentioned in 1298. Van Berkel & Samplonius, however, state that the 1298 mention is a forgery dating from 1424. The following mention they note, dates from 1312. A hospital is first mentioned in 1347. Revenues from a weighhouse belonging to the count are first found in 1344.
Town_Description: Hoorn was granted town rights on 26 March 1357 by William V, count of Holland. One of the smaller ‘Kamers’ (departments) of the VOC (Verenigde Oost-Indische Compagnie, Dutch East India Company, founded in 1602) was located in Hoorn.
Fair_Description: In 1343 cattle is sold by 'Oosterlingen' (merchants from the Baltic) on the market of Hoorn to comital servants. In 1389 duke Albrecht granted Danish traders to visit the market with oxen and horses while paying a toll. In 1446 (March) a dairy-fair was granted by duke Philip of Burgundy with St. Laurensdag (August 10) for three days. The two existing fairs with Palm-eve and Pentecost-eve had little revenues and huge costs as a result of competition from neighbouring fairs, which caused poverty. In 1449 duke Philip of Burgundy ordained after complaints from Alkmaar (there would be no tax collecting in Hoorn and the fair was 8 days before the fair in Alkmaar) at the Court of Holland that the dairy-fair was forbidden. In 1450 however Hoorn still announced this fair even in Flanders, so the landlord had to act again.In 1564 Hoorn requested the Secret Council in Brussel admission for a free leather-fair. The town said to have high costs of dikes and little negotiation. In the town lived many shoemakers and some traders in fells. According to Hoorn in Holland there was only in Beverwijk a leather-fair. The town asked and obtained from Philip II, after advice from the steward of Kennemerland and the audit office, in December admission for no less than three free leather- and fell fairs. These would not hamper Beverwijk because of the distance and dates. The dates are: 1) Monday after Lent-eve, 2) Thursday after Pentecost, 3) the day after St. James (July 26 juli), each with a duration of 3 days. In 1575 (Nov. 1) Philip II granted another privilege for a leather-fair, the day after All Saints (Nov. 2), duration 3 days before and after. In 1582 (August 25) the mayors of Hoorn obtained from prince William of Orange a free fat and lean cattlefair on 15-18 November. In autumn mechants from Denmark, Eiderstedt, Friesland and Overijssel arrived, and income for Hoorn was derived mostly from shipping.

name: Holzminden
Settlement_Description: First mentioned in 826. The original settlement was possibly located in Altendorf, because in the 11th century, both Altendorf ("Aldenthorpe") and two settlements named Holzminden ("Holtisminni duo") appear in the sources. Altendorf was merged with Holzminden in 1922.
Town_Description: A town was founded around 1200 by the counts of Everstein; it received town privileges in 1245.
Fair_Description: Duke Julius of Brunswick-Wolfenbüttel granted Holzminden in 1588 the right to hold 3 fairs. These took place on St Martin's Day, Cathedra Petri, and Pentecost.
Toll_Description: A toll of the duke of Brunswick-Wolfenbüttel in Holzminden is first mentioned in 1539. It was levied on land and river traffic, of which the latter was far more significant. According to a note in 1584, those who already paid toll in Holzminden were exempted from the toll in Fürstenberg. The earliest toll registers date from 1601/1602, which were analysed by Rothe.

name: Bad Homburg vor der Höhe
Settlement_Description: The place goes back to the Dietigheim settlement, which was first mentioned between 769 and 782. The reason for the settlement was probably the nearby salt springs, which were already used in Roman and Frankish times. At the end of the 12th century a castle was built near the village.
Town_Description: The elevation to a town is set between 1318 and 1335. In 1361 it was first called a town.

name: Hönebach
Settlement_Description: First mentioned in 1363. An inn was built in 1566, despite protests of Saxony and the landgrave of Hesse, who feared that it would be a hideout for bandits.

name: Honerdingen
Settlement_Description: The place was first mentioned in 1382.

name: Holtwick
Settlement_Description: The parish village is first mentioned in the 9th or 10th century.

name: Hoog-Soeren
Settlement_Description: Earliest mention in 814-815, in a copy dating from 1170-1175. Next mention in 1025, in an eighteenth century copy.

name: Hoogeveen
Settlement_Description: Earliest mention of 'Nie Echten' in 1634.Earliest mention of 'Hoogeveen' in 1648,

name: Hooghalen
Settlement_Description: Earliest mention in a copy dating from  1217. Next mention dates from 1334.

name: Branti
Settlement_Description: The manor was first mentioned in 1424.

name: Hoogkarspel
Settlement_Description: Hoogkarspel is first mentioned probably circa 1312. On 20 April 1403, Hoogkarspel was added to the ‘stede’ Broek, which already consisted of Grootebroek, Bovenkarspel and Lutjebroek. Grootebroek and Bovenkarspel had been granted town privileges on 2 August 1364 by Albert ('Albrecht'), governor ('ruwaard') of Holland. In 1402, Hoogkarspel had been added to this ‘stede’. These settlements, however, never developed an urban character. The granting of town rights was part of an administrative reorganization in which a number of smaller settlements were granted town rights in order to provide them with a certain degree of self-government which replaced the need for the count of Holland's bailiffs ('baljuws'). The settlements kept their own separate settlement governments. The 'stede' lost its privileges in 1426, but these were partly regranted in 1429, and fully restored in 1436.

name: Hoog-Keppel
Settlement_Description: First mentioned in the mid-12th century. The addition "Hoog-" or "Olden-" appears later to discern the village from Laag-Keppel near the castle Keppel.

name: Hoogstraten
Settlement_Description: Earliest mention in 1210, when the settlement received limited town privileges ('vrijheidsrechten'). However, it must have already existed before the 13th century. The name refers to a location on an important road, probably the road to Breda.
Toll_Description: Outpost of the Brabantse Landtol on the route to the fairs of Bergen (op Zoom).

name: Hoopte
Ferry_Description: Ferry to Zollenspieker, moved here in the 16th century due to the relocation of the Ilmenau estuary.

name: Marttila (Uusikylä)
Settlement_Description: <b>Inn:</b> An inn was established in Marttila in 1639.

name: Horn (Lippe)
Settlement_Description: First mentioned between 1107 and 1128 in possession of the monastery Corvey.
Town_Description: Lippstadt town privileges were granted before 1248.
Toll_Description: Horn is mentioned as toll station in 1482.

name: Hornburg
Settlement_Description: A settlement Hornberc is already mentioned in 890 in the Hersfelder Zehntverzeichnis. The foundation of a monastery occurrs at the beginning or the middle of the 12th century, in 1535 it is secularized.

name: Dobra (Bad Liebenwerda)
Toll_Description: Secondary station of safe conduct ('Nebengeleit') of Liebenwerda. Annual revenues are known from 1464, but for many years they remain absent ('vacat') and for other years only display a low amount. According to the tariffs and regulations ('Geleitsordnung') from 1505, fees were only paid on cattle driven through the village during the fairs in Kirchhain and Herzberg.

name: Stadt Hornburg
Settlement_Description: A castle is first mentioned in 994, but possibly goes back to Frankish times. Next to it, a settlement developed.
Town_Description: The exact date on which town privileges were granted is unknown, possibly in 1525. After 1378, the settlement is characterised as borough ('flecken'), and as town from 1552.
Fair_Description: The bishop of Halberstadt granted two free fairs in 1552, on the day of St Walpurga and on Sunday before St Martin.

name: Horndorf
Settlement_Description: The place was first mentioned in 1299.

name: Horneburg (Altes Land)
Settlement_Description: A castle was built by the archbishop of Bremen in 1255. Next to the castle a settlement developed.

name: Horodło
Toll_Description: Mentioned as toll station in c. 1349, where 4 gr. had to be paid for each horse.

name: Horodyszcze
Toll_Description: A dam toll for the maintenance of the road was granted in 1539.

name: Hötensleben
Settlement_Description: First attested in the 9th century. In 1251 a castle is mentioned.

name: Hovestadt
Settlement_Description: The place was first mentioned in 1231.
Toll_Description: The Archbishop of Cologne levied a toll in 1438. This was probably a land toll.

name: Bad Berka
Settlement_Description: First mention as a church village in 1119. It was the seat of the counts of Berka, who died out before 1273 and whose castle was destroyed in 1277.
Town_Description: 1414 first mention as town, but it is also still called a village and a borough ('Flecken') until the 18th century. In 1592 the town was granted bylaws.

name: Kaukalampi
Settlement_Description: <b>Inn:</b> An inn was established in Kaukalampi in 1639.

name: Hützel
Settlement_Description: The village was first mentioned in 1267.

name: Huy
Fair_Description: In 985 emperor Otto III donated the bishop of Liège the mint- and tollrights. In 1189 a 'forum pecudum' (marketplace for beasts) is found in Huy. A cloth-hall is found in 1209. The first time a fair is known here is in 1249 but likely this was already in the first half of the 12th century the case.

name: Höxter
Settlement_Description: Archaeological findings show a continuous settlement of the place at the Weser since the 7th/8th century. The first mention of the "villa regia (...) Hucxori" was in 823 in the course of its donation to the Corvey Abbey. The first fortification was built in the 9th century.
Town_Description: The exact date of acquisition of town privileges is unclear. A market near the Weser bridge is mentioned in 1115. The first town fortification was built around 1150, was destroyed by the Corvey abbots and rebuilt in 1152. Even before 1200 there was a town seal. In the 13th century, the citizens of Höxter were increasingly emancipated from Corvey Abbey. In 1225 councilors are mentioned for the first time. After 1256 Höxter received the city rights of Dortmund.
Fair_Description: The seven-day fair around the holiday of Simon and Jude, which was granted before or around 1300 by the abbot of Corvey, was the most important fair in Höxter. Two other fairs are known as well, on Cathedra Petri and Cantate Sunday. In 1514, it was ordained that all commodities had to be offered for sale on the market for three days before they were allowed to be sold elsewhere in town.

name: Kirchhuchting
Settlement_Description: The settlement Huchting was divided in three parts: Kirch-, Mittels- and Brokhuchting, of which the former two are the oldest parts. In Kirchhuchting, the church was located, which was probably founded in the 12th century. It is first mentioned separately in 1288.

name: Huckingen
Toll_Description: The Duke of Berg levied a land toll in 1471. Tariffs and revenues have not been handed down.

name: Huckstorf
Settlement_Description: The village is first mentioned in 1314.

name: Hudemühlen
Settlement_Description: The castle Hodenhagen was destroyed in 1289. A new castle was built in nearby Hudemühlen.

name: Hulja
Settlement_Description: The manor was built in the 13th or 14th century. A village developed next to it.

name: Hüls
Toll_Description: The Archbishop of Cologne levied a land toll in 1364.

name: Hummeldorf
Settlement_Description: First mentioned in a register of the monastery of Werden from ca. 890.

name: Hummelo
Settlement_Description: Earliest mention dates from 828, in a eleventh century copy.

name: Hundorf
Settlement_Description: The village was originally called Lyzcowe, first mentioned in 1171, then already with the alternative Latin name Alta Villa ('high village'), in Low German Honthorp (1186).

name: Psie Pole
Toll_Description: A toll station is first mentioned in 1266.

name: Psary
Toll_Description: A toll station was installed in 1436, abolished in 1504, but reinstated in the 17th century.

name: Härkälä
Settlement_Description: <b>Inn:</b> An inn was established in Härkälä in 1642. It was at the intersection of a local road from Asikkala to Great Savo Road and the northern route of Upper Wiborg Road.

name: Hunteburg
Settlement_Description: Castle, built by bishop Gottfried of Osnabrück in 1324, next to which a settlement developed successively.
Toll_Description: Toll station of the bishop of Osnabrück after 1334. An agreement with Diepholz in 1388 concerns the toll on fish caught in the Dümmer lake, furthermore the fish carts were exempted from toll.

name: Hüselitz
Settlement_Description: First mention in a personal name in 1251. Further mention in records from 1345.

name: Bad Iburg
Settlement_Description: First mentioned as castle in 753, but possibly goes back to the Merovingian period. In the 11th century, the bishop of Osnabrück built a castle, under which a settlement developed. A Benedictine monastery was founded around 1080/81, flourished economically at the end of the 15th century and was closed in 1803. The settlement itself was first mentioned as 'villa' between 1219 and 1237.
Town_Description: Listed as 'oppidum' with civic rights in 1254. From 1359 the town privileges were partly based on those of Osnabrück.

name: Ichtershausen
Settlement_Description: Foundation of a church in 1133, which was transformed into a Cistercian convent in 1147.

name: Iden
Settlement_Description: First mention in a name in 1308; mention of the village in 1334.

name: Ihleburg
Settlement_Description: Given to Berge monastery in 1117, in 1300 a family of Ilborch is mentioned.

name: Īle
Settlement_Description: The manor was probably built shortly after 1530.

name: Drylts
Town_Description: The earliest possible year that IJlst was granted town privileges is 1268. Cox states that IJlst is first mentioned as 'oppidum' in 1315.

name: Ildehausen
Settlement_Description: The village was first mentioned in 1147.

name: Illeber Brücke
Bridge_Description: The Illeben bridge constituted the border of the Erfurt escort area.

name: Ilmjärve
Settlement_Description: The place was first mentioned in 1510.

name: IJsselmuiden
Settlement_Description: Earliest mention in 1133. The medieval church (located at Dorpsweg 53) has probably been built around 1200.

name: Ilfeld
Settlement_Description: First mentioned in 1103. A Premonstratensian monastery was founded before 1190. After the Peasants' War and the Reformation the monastery was converted into a Latin school in 1546.

name: IJzendoorn
Settlement_Description: Earliest mention in 850-865 (possibly 855) in a copy dated between 1170 and 1175.

name: Villähde
Settlement_Description: <b>Inn:</b> An inn was established in Villähde in 1642, and Matti Niilonpoika was appointed as the innkeeper.

name: Immenrode
Settlement_Description: The village was first mentioned in 1086.

name: Immervad
Bridge_Description: The current stone bridge is from 1787, but the 18th century bridge probably replaced an older wooden bridge. When a bridge was first built across the river is, however, uncertain. As Immervad was  part of the prehistoric route system of Hærvejen/Ochsenweg through Jutland a bridge was probably built during the medieval period, when it replaced a ford. The place name of "Immervad" is a reference to a ford.

name: Inowłódź
Toll_Description: Mentioned as toll station in c. 1349, where 2 gr. had to be paid for each cart.

name: Inowrocław
Toll_Description: First mentioned as toll station in 1252. Prussian merchants complain in 1452 about a raise in toll tariffs.

name: Chernyakhovsk
Settlement_Description: Developed around a castle of the Teutonic Order that was built around 1336. There existed a Prussian settlement before.
Town_Description: Margrave George Friedrich von Anspach, duke in Prussia, granted town privileges based on the Kulm town law to the market settlement in 1583.

name: Inciems
Settlement_Description: The Inzeem manor was mentioned in 1625 as property of the Treyden castle.

name: Iprump
Settlement_Description: Mentioned in the 14th century as a dispersed settlement.

name: Irxleben
Settlement_Description: First secure mentions in the 14th century; before there were older mentions but Irxleben can't be clearly distinguished from other settlements in the surroundings.

name: Tönnishäuschen
Settlement_Description: The dispersed settlement ('bauernschaft') Isendorf is first mentioned in the 11th century. After a chapel of St Anthony was built on a crossroads in the settlement (first mentioned in 1499), this part of Isendorf became known as Tönnishäuschen.

name: Iserbegka
Settlement_Description: The village is first mentioned in 1376/87.

name: Westkapelle
Settlement_Description: The earliest mention of Westkapelle dates from a twelfth-century copy of a document dated between 1102-1105, but it is known that a church was built in Westkapelle before 1050. Economically, the early settlement relied on agriculture and fishery.
Town_Description: Westkapelle was granted town rights in May 1223, but never fully developed into a town. In 1341 it obtained toll-exemption from the count of Holland. A hospital is first mentioned in 1398.
Fair_Description: Duke Albrecht granted on Nov. 4 1361 a free fair starting the Nativity of the Virgin Mary (Sept. 8), duration 4 days. With rights and freedom as in the other towns of Walcheren. In 1477 (May 6) this privilege was renewed by Mary of Burgundy as it was decayed by the salt air.

name: Jameln
Settlement_Description: First mentioned in 1360. In 1450, the village consisted of 4 farms, a cottage and a farm with a mill.

name: Itzehoe
Settlement_Description: A fortification was built at a bend in the Stör river by the Saxon duke Magnus Billung around 1000. A merchant settlement developed on the opposite shore, the St Lawrence chuch was probably dedicated in the 11th century.
Town_Description: Adolf IV of Schauenburg granted Lübeck town privileges in 1238 and built a planned new merchants' town (Neustadt) on a peninsula, which was joined with the old town in 1303.
Fair_Description: It is not known how old the fairs in Itzehoe are. A "new market" on Monday after Epiphany was first mentioned in 1400. Other presumably older late medieval fairs were the fair on "Bürgertag" (citizen's day) on 7 or 8 September, to which a horse fair was connected, and the oxen fair on St Gallus. The latter was one of the most important markets for oxen driven from Jutland, which was held on the premises of the monastery. The oxen fair on St Gallus and the horse fair on Bürgertag were extended to 8 days in 1655. In 1489, five fairs were added: 3 weeks before Carnival, 8 days before Carnival, Sunday before Reminiscere, Thursday before Palm Sunday, and 8 days before St James, the latter being also the day the regional court took place in Itzehoe. A second horse fair in the early modern period took place 3 days before Sunday Letare.
Toll_Description: A transit toll is first mentioned in 1492. In the 16th and 17th century, Lübeck claimed the right to be exempted from the toll for the import of cloth from Emden through Itzehoe.
Staple_Description: In 1260, counts Johann and Gerhard of Holstein obliged all skippers sailing on the Stör to offer their commodities for sale on the market in Itzehoe. The staple was enforced by a barrier in the Stör ("Störbaum"), first attested in 1572, which prohibited sailing past town.<br/>Citizens of Krempe were exempted from staple obligations for salt, corn and timber in 1271, but the enforcement of the staple often led to conflicts between both towns in the following centuries. The staple privileges were confirmed against Krempe interests in 1496, but Krempe was exempted from the staple for beer and timber transports in 1540. Further exemptions were introduced in 1575 for the noble Rantzau family, in 1607 and 1609 for timber and cheese transported from and to Wilster, and in 1627 for timber from Glückstadt. In 1638, a prohibition for foreigners to trade with each other was introduced.

name: Itzum
Settlement_Description: First mentioned in the 12th century. A watchtower of the Hildesheim enclosure ('landwehr') was built in Itzum in 1442.

name: Ivangorod
Settlement_Description: In 1492, Ivan III built a castle called Ivangorod on the right bank of the river. Since then, it was distinguished between the Russian and Estonian part of the town.

name: Jackerath
Toll_Description: In 1389, the Duke of Jülich levied a land toll and a fee for save conduct. At first there was only a fee for save conduct mentioned, later only land toll. Depending on the load, 2 to 3 white pfennigs ('Weißpfennig'/Albus) per horse had to be paid as escort fee in 1389/93. Further tariffs are not known. The annual yield in 1389/93 averaged 139 mark, in 1398/99 113½ mark.

name: Jakobidrebber
Settlement_Description: First mentioned in 980 as "Thriburi", which refers to three farms. In 1281, separate parts of the settlement east and west of the Hunte river are mentioned. From the 16th century, the eastern part is known after the patron saint of the local church, St James.

name: Jagel
Settlement_Description: First mentioned at the end of the 12th century.

name: Jahmen
Settlement_Description: The village is first mentioned in 1235.

name: Isselburg
Fair_Description: In 1486 two fairs are mentioned: 1) May 6, 2) November 23, both during two days.

name: Jēkabpils
Settlement_Description: The settlement originated in the 17th century and only received Magdeburg town rights in 1670. The place already was a transshipment point from water to land in the 16th century.

name: Jarosław
Toll_Description: Mentioned as toll station in c. 1349, where 1 gr. had to be paid for each horse.

name: Jastrowie
Settlement_Description: Originally a Slavic settlement, mentioned as a Polish royal village in 1363.
Town_Description: The town privileges and the Magdeburg town law were granted in 1602 by Peter Potulicki and endorsed in 1603 by King Sigismund III of Poland.

name: Jeddingen
Settlement_Description: Mentioned in a register of the diocese of Verden between 1237 and 1246.

name: Jędrzejów
Toll_Description: A toll station is mentioned in 1363.

name: Jõelähtme
Settlement_Description: A village that was first mentioned in 1241. In 1482, there was an estate.

name: Jeggau
Settlement_Description: Probably came into the property of the hospital in Gardelegen around 1300. Mention in a name in 1429. A secure mention occurs in 1472.

name: Joala
Settlement_Description: The village was first mentioned in 1497. A manor was built at the end of the 17th century.

name: Jelling
Settlement_Description: Original an iron age village. In the middle and second half of the 10th century Jelling became a very important political and memorial site for Danish royal power. Amongst other things two high mounts and the longest ship setting (350 meters) in Viking Age Scandinavia were erected. Two runestones described how the monument were erected by king Gorm and his son king Harald Bluetooth. For unclear reasons the monument lost its political importance soon after it was constructed. Throughout the middle ages and early modern era the stone church, which was also a part of the original royal monument, functioned as parish church for the village of Jelling.

name: Jemgum
Settlement_Description: First mentioned in the 10th century. Before 1240 a monastery of the Knights Hospitaller was founded here, which was expanded several times in the following centuries and acquired modest property. The monastery was closed around 1528.

name: Soest (Westfalen)
Settlement_Description: First mentioned in 836. A Merovingian cemetery in the urban area indicates earlier habitation of the area. Soest was allegedly already a well populated town in the 9th century.
Town_Description: The town law of Soest first appears in 1144, its origins probably dating back to around 1100. It was granted to Lübeck in 1158 and thus became model for many town foundations in the Baltic region.
Fair_Description: Markets in Soest developed since Merovingian times and are mentioned after the 11th century. Next to weekly markets, annual fairs were organised on St Ulrich (4 July, the dedication day of St. Patrokli church), the Birth of St Mary, and All Saints' Day, according to a mention in 1417. A complaint from 1504 suggests a regional importance for the markets in Soest, although it remains unclear whether they were significant for bulk trade or remained mere retail markets.
Toll_Description: From 1306/08, the Archbishop of Cologne was the owner of a land toll and a fee for safe conduct on land. In 1444, the toll fell to the Duke of Kleve-Mark. In 1360, 4 denarii per foder of wine had to be paid. In 1306/08, 30 mark were collected.

name: Jäneda
Settlement_Description: The manor and village were mentioned in 1353. The Bishop of Reval gained land from the Teutonic Order on which he built up the settlement.

name: Jerichow
Settlement_Description: First mention as church village and castle in 1144, when a monastery of Premonstratensian canons was founded here. Before that a Slavic fortification and a nearby suburbium existed at the bank of the Elbe river. The monastery was moved 1km north to its current location in 1148, because market activity in the village disturbed the religious life of the monastery.
Town_Description: Town rights after Magdeburg rights were probably granted between 1259 (first mention as 'oppidum') and 1336 (reconstruction of the settlement after destruction by floofds) by the lords of Jerichow. The settlement, however, always remained a borough ('Flecken') and was also referred to as such in later times.

name: Nidzica
Settlement_Description: A castle of the Teutonic Order was first mentioned in 1376 later the see of a 'Pfleger' of the Order
Town_Description: The town was founded by the Grand Master Winrich von Kniprode in 1381, after it was lost, the handfast was renewed in 1420 by Grand Master Michael Küchmeister with Kulm town law, mentioned as a 'Städtlein' in 1679 and a 'Stadt 2ter Klasse' in 1723

name: Jessen
Settlement_Description: Development as suburbium in the shadow of a castle at the Elster. In 1290 the castle is first mentioned, which means that hte 12th century can be seen as the time in which the settlement developed.
Town_Description: Citizens are mentioned before 1378. In 1350 referred to as civitas.
Toll_Description: Secondary station of safe conduct ('Nebengeleit') of Wettin in the system of safe conduct around Leipzig. The regulations heavily refer to long-distance trade goods, which gives Jessen the character of a main station of safe conduct.

name: Jevenstedt
Settlement_Description: First mentioned in the Visio Godeschalci of ca. 1190.

name: Jõhvi
Settlement_Description: The village was first mentioned in 1241. A parish was probably established around 1250. Since 1491 there was a manor for a bailiff of the Teutonic Order from Narva.

name: Jõgisoo
Settlement_Description: Manor and village, which was first mentioned in 1241.

name: De Jouwer
Settlement_Description: Earliest mention in  the thirteenth century.

name: Jüchen
Toll_Description: The Duke of Jülich levied a road toll here in 1434/35. Tariffs and revenues are not known.

name: Jülich
Toll_Description: In 1249, the Count of Jülich levied a land toll and a fee for safe conduct. In the same year, Flemings had to pay 12 denarii per barrel of wine. Around 1300, 12 to 15 denarii per barrel had to be paid. For more exact tariffs, see source. In 1389/93, about 557 mark a year were collected as escort fee. In 1398/99, 924¼ mark were collected as land toll.

name: Jürgenstorf
Settlement_Description: The village and manor is first mentioned in 1411, but it must be older. The base of the church tower dates from the 14th century.

name: Judenbach
Settlement_Description: First mention in 1279. The name of the settlement is probably not derived from Jewish settlers, but from the old German name Judo.
Toll_Description: Toll station of the safe conduct from Eisfeld.

name: Jüterbog
Settlement_Description: A slavic settlement and castle mound existed that are mentioned in 1007. They were conquered by archbishop Wichmann of Magdeburg in 1157, afterwards a German castle with a chapel and a village. A Flemish settlement was mentioned later.
Town_Description: In 1174 a German town was founded with Magdeburg town law, it was destroyed in 1179 by Henry the Lion and later rebuilt with a new market place.
Fair_Description: Since 1376 two big fairs are known, others were added in 1497 and 1623.
Toll_Description: Toll station and safe conduct of the Archbishop of Magdeburg, first attested in 1285.

name: Kabelitz
Settlement_Description: Probably a former Slavic settlement. Mention in the context of a "castrum Marienborch" in 946, around which a settlement "urbs Marienburg" developed (mentioned in 1145), which can probably be equated with Kabelitz, as records from 1150 and 1157 suggest. The castle district ('Burgward') seems to have consisted of several settlements in the 10th century, which mostly seem to have dissolved in the course of the 12th century. Only in the 15th century the scattered settlements seem to have bounded together in villages, one of which was Kabelitz. The settlement became property of Jerichow monastery.

name: Kabli
Settlement_Description: The village was first mentioned in 1638.

name: Kahala
Settlement_Description: In 1560 the village was burned down by the Russians.

name: Kahala
Settlement_Description: The village, which was first mentioned in 1241, belonged to the 'Kolk' manor.

name: Kantküla
Settlement_Description: This village was first mentioned in 1419.

name: Ķeipene
Settlement_Description: The manor was first mentioned in 1457.

name: null
Lock_Description: A lock in the canal between the Elbe and the Schwerin lake, which was built between 1568 and 1572, is displayed as "Foien kercker sluse" near Maliß on a map of the canal by Daniel Frese from 1605.

name: null
Lock_Description: A lock in the canal between the Elbe and the Schwerin lake, which was built between 1568 and 1572, is displayed as "Gam sluse" on a map of the canal by Daniel Frese from 1605.

name: Kaiserswerth
Toll_Description: 1) The empire levied a river toll on the Rhine here in 1174, which was often pawned. Other owners included the Archbishop of Cologne, the Count of Jülich and the Count of Berg. In 1348, 6 Turnosgroschen had to be paid for each foder of wine from ships coming from Duisburg. In 1368 it was 16 Turnosgroschen per foder of wine. For further tariffs see source. In 1400/01, approx. 5784 guilders were collected per year, in 1406/07 8460 Rhenish guilders and in 1408/09 approx. 14300 Rhenish guilders. 2) In addition, in the period from 1425 to 1431, Gerhard von Kleve levied a fee for safe river conduct. Rates and revenues are unknown. It is also questionable whether it was more of a punitive levy or whether it was collected continuously.3) A land toll was also levied in 1424. The ownership is similar to the Rhine toll mentioned above. Tariffs and revenues are not known.

name: Kalbe
Settlement_Description: In 983 a Benedictine convent was destroyed by Slavic rioters. In 1196 a castle is mentioned as the seat of a burgward, of which half is given to the archbishopric of Magdeburg.
Town_Description: Around 1200 town foundation, possibly planned. First referred to as town in 1324. A council is only mentioned in 1497. In the 16th and 17th century merely referred to as borough ('Flecken').
Fair_Description: In an official schedule from 1719, Kalbe held two fairs. It can be assumed that one or both of these had existed for a while to this point.
Toll_Description: The town lords of Kalbe are granted a dam toll under the condition that they use it in order to maintain the roads and grant safe conduct to travelers.

name: Pausa
Settlement_Description: First mention in 1263, it is unclear whether it was based on a Slavic settlement.
Town_Description: In 1350 mention as civitas, but it was always a rather uninportant rural town.

name: Kahla
Settlement_Description: First mention around 860 as property of Fulda monastery. A castle existed that became property of the lords of Lobdeburg since 1283. A church is mentioned in 1227.
Town_Description: The lords of Lobdeburg-Leuchtenburg supported the development of a planned town between 1287 and 1299. In 1299 citizens are mentioned. The oldest town law dates from 1455.

name: Nieder Ense
Settlement_Description: First mentioned between 1016 and 1020. The earlier mentions are problematic in that they do not differentiate between Ober- and Nieder-Ense.

name: Kalisz
Toll_Description: A toll in Kalisz is first attested in 1258. In 1390, King Władysław of Poland ordained, that the toll tariffs in Sieradz, Kalisz, Pyzdry and Poznań were to be the same as those levied in Piotrków Trybunalski, Łęczyca, Przedecz and Brześć.
Staple_Description: The staple rights from 1469 contained precise street ordinances; Wares from Prussia to Wroclaw must be carried through Kalisz; Wares to other Silesian centres could also be transported via Poznań.

name: Kallenhardt
Settlement_Description: The place originally bore the name 'Ostervelde', which was mentioned in 1072. A settlement was founded there, which was called 'opido' around 1297 and was systematically expanded into the town of Kallenhardt.
Town_Description: Kallenhardt received Rüthen town privileges in 1543.

name: Kalēti
Settlement_Description: The manor was first mentioned in 1509.

name: Kalisz Pomorski
Settlement_Description: Prehistoric settlement is attested by archaeological finds. A castle complex was built in the mid-13th century. A settlement developed nearby.
Town_Description: The settlement was conquered by the Margraves of Brandenburg at the turn of the 14th century and received Brandenburg town privileges in 1303.
Staple_Description: Staple privileges for pitch and ash were granted in 1303.

name: Kalitsa
Settlement_Description: The village, which was mentioned in 1558, belonged to the 'Erwita' manor.

name: Kalli
Settlement_Description: In 1560 the area was granted as fief. An estate was built between 1624 and 1638.

name: Kalve
Toll_Description: A toll in Kalve is mentioned in registers of the official responsible for the water management ('watergraaf') from 1399 onwards. It was levied on peat ships on the canal to Axel, possibly also on the Moervaart. It was usually leased out. In 1488-1492, the tenant of the toll was exempted from lease payments because of the war between emperor Maximilian and the Flemish cities.

name: Kammerbusch
Settlement_Description: Mentioned as fortified outwork ('vorwerk') of the castle of knight Heinrich von Borch, which was destroyed in 1311, but only in later historical accounts of his actions (1771). First mention in a charter in the Bremervörde register of ca. 1500. At the time, it consisted of one farm, belonging to the von Borch family.

name: Kämmerich
Settlement_Description: The village is first mentioned in 1262.

name: Kamień Pomorski
Settlement_Description: A castle was built around 800, mentioned in 1107 during a battle of the polish ruler Boleslaw against Pomerania. Residence of the Pomeranian Dukes from 1124 until the 13th century.
Town_Description: After the settlement around the castle was destroyed in 1273 by Brandenburg, a new settlement was built. Duke Barnim I granted Lübeck town law in 1274.

name: Kampe
Settlement_Description: In 1473, three families are reported in the hamlet ('bauerschaft').

name: Kampen
Settlement_Description: The earliest mention dates from 9 July 1227. Archaeological finds indicate habitation from the twelfth century onward. It has been suggested that the town was founded by merchants from the Rhineland as a transshipment port at the mouth of the IJssel river.
Town_Description: It is not known for sure whether Kampen has been granted town privileges. Possibly, those privileges may have developed from customary law, and afterwards been acknowledged and confirmed by the landlord. It is, however, likely that town privileges have been granted by Wilbrand of Oldenburg, bishop of Utrecht, between 1230 and 1233.
Fair_Description: In 1382, Floris van Wevelinkhoven, bishop of Utrecht, granted the rights for three fairs: one around the fourteenth day after Eastern, one around St Martin of Tours Translation Day (4 July), and one around St Victor (10 October). A fair around Pentecost was already in place before 1382.

name: Kanaküla
Settlement_Description: A village, that belonged to the Tignitz Manor.

name: Kandava
Settlement_Description: In 1245 the old castle was conquered by the Teutonic Order. A new castle was built around 1300, where a fortified borough ('Hakelwerk') developed. In the 17th century the settlement was referred to as borough ('Flecken').

name: Stolzenfels
Toll_Description: A river toll on the Rhine was levied here in various periods. The toll was first documented in 1331 and was initially levied until 1349, later from 1362 to 1412. The original owner was the Archbishop of Mainz. Later, the toll went into the possession of the Archbishop of Trier. In 1345, 15 turnosgroschen were collected per foder of wine, from 1345 to 1349 7 turnosgroschen per foder, and in 1368 27 turnosgroschen per foder of wine. From 1333 to 1334, approximately 11463 pounds Heller were collected. In 1331/34 this toll was established as a secondary toll of the Kurmainzer Oberlahnsteiner toll on the Rhine. Later, the Koblenz river toll was also collected at this location. In 1412, the toll was moved to Engers.

name: Kapellen
Toll_Description: The Duke of Guelders levied a land tariff in 1397. Exact tariffs are not known. In 1397, however, 12 guilders of lease were collected.

name: Karksi
Settlement_Description: A castle was built in the 13th century, but was burnt down in 1297. It was the domicile of a bailiff in medieval times. A Manor was built nearby, which was owned by the Teutonic Order until 1561.

name: null
Bridge_Description: In 1547 the bridge was moved to the current position at the end of the Ludwigsstraße in order to better defend the town during the Schmalkalden war.

name: Creuzburg
Settlement_Description: First mention of the castle Creuzburg at a ford in the river Werra in 973, together with the villages of East and West Milingen, which were later assimilated into Creuzburg.
Town_Description: Elevated to town by landgrave Ludwig II or Ludwig III (between 1170 and 1189). Around the same time fortification of town and castle. The term "civitas" can be found before 1189. Town rights were probably based on the rights of the Hessian-Thuringian towns at the Werra, Eisenach or Gotha.
Fair_Description: In the regulations of safe conduct ('Geleitsordnung') for Creuzburg from 1535/36 two fairs are mentioned, on the rogation days and on St Gall's day. There is no indication of their lenghth.
Toll_Description: Secondary station of safe conduct ('Beigeleitsstelle') of Eisenach. Revenues are recorded from 1478 onwards. The fees for the safe conduct in Creuzburg are listed in the regulations for safe conduct ('Geleitsordnung') from 1535/36.

name: Porvola
Settlement_Description: <b>Inn:</b> Porvola is mentioned in Jaakko Teitti's list in 1556 as a possible place for a bailiff (fi. vouti, sw. fogde).

name: Niedervellmar
Settlement_Description: Vellmar was first mentioned between 775 and  786. Since 1107 Ober- and Niedervellmar are mentioned separately for the first time, which is why it is unclear to which Vellmar early documents refer. Niedervellmar itself was mentioned in 1240.

name: Nieheim
Town_Description: Town privileges granted by Bishop Bernhard IV of Paderborn (1228-1247), extended in 1282.

name: Karuse
Settlement_Description: Medieval parish, first mentioned in 1240. It belonged to the Teutonic Order ('Deutscher Orden') from 1242 to 1561, making it one of the oldest parishes in Estonia.

name: Karze
Settlement_Description: The place was first mentioned in 1468.

name: Strib
Settlement_Description: Strib was a very small settlement without a church. It was first mentioned in 1553, but is probably older. When the town of Fredericia on the opposite side of the strait of Lillebælt was etablished in the middle of the 17th century, the settlement of Strib grew. Due to the strategic position at Lillebælt a medieval castle was located near the settlement.
Ferry_Description: A ferry between Strib and the town of Fredericia on the opposite side of the strait of Lillebælt was etablished in the middle of the 17th century, when Fredericia was founded.

name: null
Harbour_Description: After 1244 a canal was dug between the rivers Gouwe and Oude Rijn, which gave way to the development of a small harbour in Gouda. A crane was first mentioned in 1429, when it was donated by the town magistrate to the hospital. The crane was situated in front of this hospital along the Oosthaven, close to the lock. Possibly the crane was mainly used for lowering the mast of ships that passed through the lock.

name: Vilkkilä
