Settlement_Description: <b>Inn:</b> An inn was established in Vilkkilä in 1637. Two years later, Sipi Jaakonpoika is mentioned as the innkeeper.

name: Mikołajki
Settlement_Description: The church village was first mentioned in 1444 as a yard of the Teutonic Order

name: Bergeijk
Settlement_Description: First mentioned in 1137, in a 13th-century copy.

name: Kaugurciems
Settlement_Description: The fishing village was first mentioned in 1634.

name: Košice
Town_Description: Kassa was referred to as a royal town in 1347.
Fair_Description: King Louis I permitted two annual fairs on the 28th of July 1347: one on St. Michael and the other on Holy Trinity. In 1355, the fair of St. Michael was abolished so that the fair on Holy Trinity, that was referred to as the fair on Corpus Christi during the 14th century, came in its place. Sigismund granted an annual market on St. Elizabeth in 1392.King Louis II, who reigned from 1516 to 1526, also granted the holding of two annual fairs: one on the feast on the Discovery of the Holy Cross and the other on Mary's Ascension.
Toll_Description: Košice was a thirthies custom duty station from the 13th century.
Staple_Description: On the 28th of July 1347, King Louis I issued a privilege that requested every passing merchant to stop in town when a market could be held every day. Due to misinterpretations, Louis I confirmed and specified that former staple right in 1361. This stated, that all merchants of Russia, Poland and their provinces had to deposit their goods in the town of Košice, so that they were not allowed to distribute their goods beyond Košice. On the 25th of February 1368, Louis I allowed Polish merchants to freely enter the country as far as Košice. Though, they had to pay the old tolls. Polish merchants had to deposit and sell their goods in Košice for three days. If no merchants wanted to trade with them, they were permitted to leave the town on the fifth day and sell their goods anywhere in the Kingdom and beyond. On the 2nd of January 1399, Sigismund demanded inland and foreign merchants, especially those from Transylvania and Nagyvárad, to also deposit and sell their goods in Košice. Goods that were illegally passed around the town were confiscated. It is likely that the staple right only applied to merchants travelling to or from Poland. That is supported by a document from 1423 given by Sigismund.

name: Kaseküla
Settlement_Description: There was a small village that was mentioned in 1601. Nowadays it is part of the village Selja.

name: Werrabrücke
Bridge_Description: Built by landgrave Ludwig in 1223, the Werra bridge in Creuzburg is the oldest preserved stone bridge north of the Main.

name: Kassebohm
Settlement_Description: The village is first mentioned in 1233.

name: Kassel
Settlement_Description: Developed from a Frankish fortification of the 10th century.
Town_Description: Town privileges granted around 1180, Kassel is first characterised as "civitas" in 1189. Town privileges were confirmed in 1239. The new town on the opposite shore of the Fulda appears in 1283, the "Freiheit" around 1330; the three parts were united in 1378.
Fair_Description: Since 1336, three fairs are known to have taken place on the Altmarkt in Kassel: on Sunday Invocavit, St James and St Martin.
Toll_Description: Toll on commodities, introduced by Landgrave Moritz after the Fulda river had been made navigable between Kassel and Hersfeld. In an ordinance from 1613, the toll duties were set at the rate established in 1604. At each lock in the Fulda, it was checked whether the toll had been paid.
Staple_Description: A staple in Kassel with a forced stay of three days was introduced in 1336, in a conflict about the older staple of Münden.

name: Kasterer Tollhaus
Toll_Description: The Duke of Jülich collected a road toll here from 1398/99.

name: Katase
Settlement_Description: The village was first mentioned in 1419.

name: Nørre Ønlev
Settlement_Description: The Church of Ønlev was first mentioned around 1280, and was destroyed during the first half of the 15th century. The village of Nørre Ølev was first mentioned in 1535, and was at that point a part of the parish of Rise Church, as it did not have its own church.

name: Katlenburg
Settlement_Description: The castle Katlenburg was built in the 11th century on the rivers Rhume and Katel; it was turned into an Augustinian monastery by Dietrich III of Katlenburg in 1105. The monastery was secularised after 1534. The village belonging to the monastery was originally called Duhm.
Toll_Description: A road fee is first mentioned in 1604.

name: Kazimierz Dolny
Toll_Description: Mentioned as toll station in c. 1349, where 8 gr. had to be paid for each horse.

name: Kazimierz
Toll_Description: A toll station is attested in 1318.

name: Kehtna
Settlement_Description: The village was first mentioned in 1417. During the 15th century the village had several estates.

name: Ķekava
Settlement_Description: Estate near the mouth of the Ķekava river. A church named after the castle Dahlen (Dole) on the river island of the same name was also built here at an unknown date, which was mentioned as being deteriorated in 1630.

name: Keila
Settlement_Description: Originally a small village, first mentioned in 1241. It was sold to the Teutonic Order in 1433. Listed as a village until 1549. In the 15th/16th century a small settlement or a fortified borough ('Hakelwerk') was built close to the church, which was granted town rights in 1938.

name: Ronni
Settlement_Description: <b>Inn:</b> An inn was established in Ronni in 1642, and Esko Eskonpoika Eskola was appointed as the innkeeper. Later, his son served as an innkeeper as well.

name: Kempten
Toll_Description: The Archbishop of Mainz levied a land toll and a fee for safe conduct here from 1441. Tariffs and revenues are not known.

name: Kerpen
Toll_Description: In 1475, the lord of Kerpen levied a land toll. Per hundredweight ('Zentner') of iron 4 alb. (Albus) had to be paid. Yields are not known.

name: Kärbla
Settlement_Description: In 1511 there was an estate called 'Kerffel'.

name: Bürgel
Settlement_Description: First mention in 1133 as the foundation of a Benedictine monastery.
Town_Description: The town of Bürgel, which was founded by the monastery, is first mentioned 1234 and lay on the right bank of the Gleiße. In 1307 it is referred to as civitas. A council is first mentioned in 1360. The monastery is dissolved in 1526 and its property as well as the town are made a electoral-saxonian district.

name: Paakkola
Settlement_Description: <b>Inn:</b> An inn was established in Paakkola in 1642.

name: Kenz
Settlement_Description: First mentioned as part of the name Reimarus de Kenitze in 1256. The village itself is first mentioned in 1316. The village was a place of pilgrimage due to a miraculous image of the virgin Mary in a linden tree.

name: Nottuln
Settlement_Description: First mentioned in 834. Already in 803 an Augustinian monastery was founded.

name: Oberbeisheim
Settlement_Description: Mentioned as 'villa' around 800. Fallen desolate in 1415 and uninhabited for a long time, but mentioned again as a village in 1575/85.

name: Kessel (Maas)
Settlement_Description: Kessel originated in the Roman period and is first mentioned in 950; this document, however, is a forgery. The subsequent mention dates from 1107.
Town_Description: Kessel was granted town privileges some time between 1279 and 1291 by Reginald I, count of Gueldres. Kessel, however, hardly developed into a town.
Fair_Description: In 950 Roman king Otto I gave his vassal Ansfried the rights on a fair and mint in Kessel ('Cassalo sito in pago Masalant'). It is uncertain if this is Kessel. In 1312 Kessel obtained the right for a fair and weekly market, but this privilege was probably never issued. In the 15th century a market is found however. Kessel was situated on the landroute from Cologne tot Antwerp but this traderoute became only important in the course of the 14th century.
Toll_Description: Next to the river toll on the Meuse, the Duke of Guelders also levied a fee for safe conduct on land in Kessel; the town is mentioned in 1355/61 as a secondary location for the toll of Venlo. Tariffs are not known.

name: Kestla
Settlement_Description: The village belonged to the manor of 'Alt-Isenhof'.

name: Kettelstorf
Settlement_Description: Possibly first mentioned between 1133 and 1137. There is an earlier mention around 1006 that is uncertain.

name: Kiiu
Settlement_Description: The village was first mentioned in 1241. At the end of the 14th century, a castle was built that lasted until the 20th century.

name: Kessin
Settlement_Description: Kessin castle was first documented during the expansion efforts of Lothar von Süpplingenburg in 1121. It was last mentioned in 1170. The church village Kessin is first mentioned in 1219. It is uncertain if the castle was located at the same location as the later village.

name: Dingelstädt
Settlement_Description: The first mention of the settlement can be dated at the beginning of the 9th century, which is preserved in a copy of a charter from 1150. Since 1309 location of a judicial court. In the Late Middle Ages it became a market borough ('Marktflecken'). Lifted to the status of town only in 1859.
Fair_Description: The privilege for two fairs on St Gertrude's day and on Sunday after St John the Baptist was granted in 1607 by emperor Rudolf II, after Dingelstädt had requested market privileges in 1560. In 1662 Dingelstädt was granted a third and fourth fair, after the economy had been completely destroyed during the Thirty Years' War.

name: Lumiala
Settlement_Description: <b>Inn:</b> Lumiala village is close to Linnalevonvuori hill, which is mentioned as a permanent resting place in 1470.

name: Obermarsberg
Settlement_Description: The existing Sachsenfest Eresburg was taken by Charlemagne in 772. Which was destroyed in 1115 by Count Friedrich von Arnsberg.
Town_Description: An exact award of town privileges is not known. However, the place was already referred to as a city around 820, 915 and 938.

name: Oberrad
Settlement_Description: First mentioned in 1151. The village was included in the Frankfurt Landwehr and received its own moat in 1441. Incinerated in the course of the siege of Frankfurt in 1552.

name: Obervellmar
Settlement_Description: Vellmar was first mentioned between 775 and  786. Since 1107 Ober- and Niedervellmar are mentioned separately for the first time, which is why it is unclear to which Vellmar early documents refer. Obervellmar itself was mentioned in 1299.

name: Kiel
Settlement_Description: First mentioned in 1232. Before the foundation of the town, there already existed a merchant settlement at this place.
Town_Description: Count Adolf IV of Holstein founded "Holstenstadt tom Kyle" as a planned town between 1238 and 1242. Johann I of Holstein granted Lübeck town privileges in 1242. Kiel was pawned to Lübeck between 1469 and 1496.
Fair_Description: The most important fair in Kiel was the one-week so-called 'Kieler Umschlag', which must date to 1431 at the latest, but was first mentioned in 1469. It became the most important international capital market for the nobility of northern Germany and Denmark in the 16th and 17th century. There are many different dates known for the fair, among others on St Martin, St Michael, the Presentation of Jesus, Easter, Ascension Day, Pentecost or Christmas. From the 16th century onwards, it usually took place in the week after Epiphany. In some years, it was also held in other towns such as Rendsburg and Oldesloe. The Umschlag was discontinued in 1911, but revived as a funfair in 1975. Next to the Umschlag, there existed three other one-week fairs in the early modern period, after Sunday Invocavit, Monday after St Peter and Paul, and on Monday after St Francis.

name: Keikkala
Settlement_Description: <b>Inn:</b> Uoti Eeronpoika Hommonen from Keikkala village is mentioned as a tavern owner in 1653, when he hosted the court gathering in his tavern. He might be the same farmer that was appointed as the tavern owner in Keikkala village in 1649.

name: Kreuzebra
Settlement_Description: First mention in 817; one of the oldest villages in the Eichsfeld.

name: Hohengandern
Settlement_Description: First mentioned in 1297. Formerly part of the Eichsfeld of Mainz, it was pawned off to the family of Hanstein in the 14th century. The manor in Hohengandern was still in the property of the family of Hanstein in the early 20th century.
Toll_Description: Hohengandern was a main toll station since 1624. Safe conduct zones ended here.

name: Kurhila
Settlement_Description: <b>Inn:</b> An inn was established in Kurhila in 1585. Abraham Mikonpoika is mentioned as the innkeeper in 1639-1645. Kurhila village was also later the place for an inn in Asikkala parish.

name: Ķimale
Settlement_Description: The area 'Kiemala' was first mentioned in 1230. In 1253, the settlement came into the possession of the Teutonic Order.

name: Kindelbrück
Settlement_Description: Mention in the Breviarium sancti Lulli in the 8th/9th century.
Town_Description: Albrecht from the house of Wettin bestowes civil rights upon the inhabitants of Kindelbrück.
Fair_Description: In the oldest bylaws of the town (shortly after 1400) mention fairs, their date and exact number are unknown however.
Bridge_Description: The toponym Kindelbruccun in the Breviarium sancti Lulli alludes to a bridge across the Wipper at the end of the 8th century for the road from Erfurt to the salines of Bad Frankenhausen and consequently to Magdeburg.

name: Kirberg
Toll_Description: The Count of Diez probably levied a land toll and later a fee for safe conduct on land before 1349. In 1349, the toll was confirmed. Tariffs from that time are not known. From 1355, Count Johann von Nassau and Daniel von Langenau levied so-called imperial surcharges ('Reichszuschläge'). This meant that 1 guilder had to be paid in addition per load. Von Langenau demanded 1 turnosgroschen extra per horse as fee for safe conduct on land.

name: Kirch Rosin
Settlement_Description: The village is first mentioned in 1228.

name: Kirch-Steinbek
Settlement_Description: First mentioned as 'Stenbeke' in 1212. 1239 the place was mentioned as 'Kirchsteinbek'.

name: Kirchwelver
Settlement_Description: The settlement Welver is first mentioned in 1179. Foundation of the Cistercian woman's monastery Welver in 1238/40. The settlement around the monastery became known as Kirchwelver.

name: Rahja
Settlement_Description: <b>Inn:</b> Ture Pedersson Bielke, Swedish nobleman and castellan of St. Olaf's Castle in Savo, stopped to dine in Rahja in 1557. Later, an inn was established in the village, and in 1637, Pekka Erkinpoika from Alajoki farm is mentioned as the innkeeper. Alajoki farm hosted the inn until 1675, when the inn moved to Roukala.

name: Kirchdorf
Settlement_Description: The settlement is first mentioned in 1380. According to local legend, the church goes back to a foundation of a countess of Hoya, by way of thanks for helping her free her travel wagon when it was stuck in the snow. If this is true, the countess in question could have been the wife of count Heinrich II, in which case the foundation must have taken place shortly after the middle of the 13th century.

name: Kirchedlau
Settlement_Description: Former property of the counts of Alsleben, who sold the village to the lords of Ammendorf.

name: Kirchgellersen
Settlement_Description: The settlement Gellersen, which consisted of three parts, was first mentioned before 1117; the village of Kirchgellersen separately after 1236. According to 17th-century registers, the village consisted of 2 farms ('plog'), 2 or 3 half farms and 4 cottages.

name: Kirchhain (Hessen)
Town_Description: Landgrave Heinrich II granted town charter between 1344 and 1352. First referred to in 1352 as town and 'oppidum'.

name: Tuusjärvi
Settlement_Description: <b>Inn:</b> Tuusjärvi is mentioned in Jaakko Teitti's list in 1556 as a possible place for a bailiff (fi. vouti, sw. fogde), but nearby Lusi was more central to the area.

name: Kirchhatten
Settlement_Description: Originally mentioned as "Hahtho" (Hatten) in 860, since 1260/80 called Kirchhatten.

name: Salaspils
Settlement_Description: In 1380 the Teutonic Order built a castle on the right-hand bank of the Düna. In 1577 it was destroyed by the Russians.

name: Kirchhorst
Settlement_Description: The village was first mentioned in 1368.

name: Kirchweyhe
Settlement_Description: The settlement was first mentioned as 'Weinethe' in 1253.

name: Kirumpää
Settlement_Description: In 1322 the castle was called 'castrum' and served to protect against raids from the east. In 1369 it was taken by the Russians. The nearby village was burned down. The castle was destroyed in the mid-17th century.

name: Kissenbrück
Settlement_Description: First mentioned in a register of possessions of the monastery of Corvey (822-836). Location of a Frankish royal court until its dissolution in the 13th century. Regularly characterised as borough ('weichbild') from 1331, although the corresponding privileges were probably older.

name: Kitzingen
Staple_Description: In 1498 raftsmen sailing down the Main were obliged to offer their wares for three days in the town.

name: Klatzow
Settlement_Description: The exact year of the first mention is not known. However, from the beginning of the 13th century until 1245, Klatzow was the seat of the Benedictine monastery of Verchen, which had been founded at the end of the 12th century. Eventually, the monastery moved to Verchen.

name: Kirchheilingen
Settlement_Description: First mention of Heilingen in 775-786, of Kirchheiligen as distinct settlement in 833.

name: Berkeler Warte
Settlement_Description: Watchtower in the defensive enclosure ('landwehr') of Hameln (first mentioned in 1385) near the village Klein Berkel.

name: Klein Dannewerk
Settlement_Description: The settlement is named after the Danish defensive wall Danewerk, which was built between the late 7th and the late 12th century. The settlement is first mentioned in 1231, and divided into two villages Klein and Groß Dannewerk, which are first mentioned separately in 1412.
Toll_Description: A station of the Gottorf toll on the ox road (hærvejen) was located in Klein Dannewerk. For more information, see Gottorf.

name: Klein Engersen
Settlement_Description: First mention in 1238, further mentions in the 15th and 16th century together with Groß Engersen.

name: Klein Fullen
Settlement_Description: First mentioned around 1000 in plural, which indicates that already at that time, Fullen encompassed two distinct settlements, which developed into Groß and Klein Fullen.

name: Klein Grönau
Settlement_Description: In the 1280s, Lübeck citizens founded a hospital of St George near Grönau (the current Groß Grönau). A chapel was built in 1409. The currently still existing hospital buildings were built in 1479/1480. In modern times, the settlement at the hospital became known as Klein Grönau.

name: Klein Hesepe
Settlement_Description: First mentioned around 1000, where a distinction between Groß and Klein Hesepe is not yet made.

name: Mazjumpravas muiža
Settlement_Description: The manor was first mentioned in 1257.

name: Klein Methling
Settlement_Description: The village was first mentioned in 1235.

name: Klein Neuleben
Settlement_Description: The village Klein Mist was first mentioned in 1211. In 1956, it was merged with Groß Mist and renamed into Neuleben.

name: Olpe
Settlement_Description: The settlement goes back to a main courtyard of the Cologne church, which was first mentioned in 1120. The village itself is said to have arisen only at the beginning of the 14th century.
Town_Description: Received 1311 town rights after those of the citizens of Attendorn. Confirmation 1368.

name: Åstorp
Settlement_Description: The village of Åstorp was first mentioned in 1440, but is significantly older. The settlement had no church but was part of the parish of Taps Church.

name: Clus
Settlement_Description: House on the border between the bishopric of Minden and the county of Schaumburg, first mentioned in 1558 as "Klues up den Helwege vor dem Santfoerde".

name: Klein Nenndorf
Settlement_Description: The settlement was first mentioned as a property of the monastery of Fulda in the 10th century. It consisted of two parts: Groß and Klein Nenndorf, of which the latter was first separately mentioned in 1401. Both settlements were united into Bad Nenndorf in modern times.

name: Klein Oschersleben
Settlement_Description: First mention in a donation charter to the bishopric of Halberstadt in 1086.

name: Väike-Maarja
Settlement_Description: The exact foundation of the parish is unfortunately not known. This may have happened in the 13th century. The village near the church was first mentioned in 1499. At the end of the 19th century, the place grew as a borough ('Flecken').

name: Klein Schwarfs
Settlement_Description: First mentioned in 1375, Klein Schwarfs was a German settlement which was named after the older Slavic settlement (Hohen) Schwarfs. Since the addition Hohen (first attested in 1323) for the original settlement was made after the foundation of Klein Schwarfs, the latter settlement must have been founded before 1323.

name: Klein Schwaß
Settlement_Description: The village is first mentioned in 1219.

name: Colditz
Town_Description: Colditz is first mentioned as civitas in 1265.
Toll_Description: The regulations of safe conduct settle the fees due in the town as well as on the Mulde river when it is high enough to use as a waterway. The station of safe conduct is especially important for cattle trade from Poland; every year toll was paid on thousands of cows and oxen.

name: Klein-Kreutz
Settlement_Description: Mention of Wendish- i.e. Klein Kreutz in 1275 when the Ascanians sell property to Lehnin monastery. In 1324 the settlement is given to the new town in Brandenburg.

name: Klingenberg am Main
Toll_Description: Toll station of the archbischop of Mainz.

name: Kleinenberg
Town_Description: It is unknown when Kleinenberg became a town, but it is first mentioned as 'oppidum' in 1249.

name: Kleinkayna
Settlement_Description: Großkayna is first mentioned in 1286. Kleinkayna was devastated in 1966 for coal mining.

name: Kleinringe
Settlement_Description: The settlement Ringe is first mentioned in 1329, both parts Groß- and Kleinringe separately in 1456.

name: Øster Løgum
Settlement_Description: The village of Øster Løgum was first mentioned in 1359, but is significantly older. The parish church is from either the 12th or 13th century.

name: Kleve
Fair_Description: Before 1319 there was a fair on August 24, before 1431 another on Febr. 22 (8 days before and after) and in 1431 a third one on Oct. 22 (three days before and after). In 1572 a horse-fair was granted. A cloth-hall is first found in 1374.
Toll_Description: The Count of Cleves levied a land toll before 1319, which he granted to Borgart van Vonderen as a fief until 1320. Tariffs are not known. In 1320, around 10 Brabant mark were collected.

name: Kleverhof
Settlement_Description: First mentioned as Glewe in 1314. The settlement was renamed to Kleverhof in the 18th century.

name: Klietz
Settlement_Description: First mentioned as castle district ('burgward') of the bishop of Havelberg in 1145.
Toll_Description: A toll station in "Clitzk" is mentioned together with the tolls in Sandau and Jerichow in negotiations on the diets of princes in 1480-1490. Weissenborn has assumed that this refers to the village Klietznick near Jerichow, but the interpretation of the toll station in Klietz is more likely.

name: Kloster Zinna
Settlement_Description: A Cistercian monastery was established in 1170-1171. The corresponding village Zinna was first mentioned in 1258, but probably lent its name to the monastery. It is deserted today. The monastery was secularised in 1553. King Frederick the Great of Prussia established a town in 1764-1777.

name: Klink
Settlement_Description: The village is first mentioned in 1345.

name: Klimmen
Settlement_Description: Earliest mention in 968, in a falsification dating from 1138. Next mention in midden of the eleventh century, in an eighteenth century copy.
Toll_Description: A 'small toll on the street' in Klimmen is mentioned in the comital accounts of Valkenburg from 1395 onwards, with annual revenues. It was subordinate to the 'big' toll in Valkenburg.

name: Klostermansfeld
Settlement_Description: Klostermansfeld is probably older than the settlement Mansfeld. Property in the surroundings was possibly exchanged as early as 973. The monastery may have already existed in 1042, when the name Klostermansfeld may have emerged. Albrecht the Bear and count Hoyer IV brought monks of the then already existing monastery with them on their pilgrimages to Jerusalem in 1158 and 1173.

name: Klötze
Settlement_Description: The settlement developed next to a castle, first mentioned in 1311. In 1334 referred to as borough ('Flecken'). Referred to as small town ('Städtchen') in the 14th century.
Toll_Description: Mention of the toll in Klötze, owned by the dukes of Braunschweig-Lüneburg, in 1409.

name: Klus (Magdeburg)
Settlement_Description: In 1479 the inn is mentioned and is the namesake of the adjoining causeway ('Straßendamm') to Magdeburg.

name: Kluß
Settlement_Description: Farm at the location where the street between Wismar and Sternberg crossed the Wismar defensive enclosure ('landwehr'). First mentioned in 1467, when a chapel ('klause') was rebuilt here, which gave the farm its name.

name: Knesselare
Settlement_Description: Earliest mention in 1128, in a sixteenth century copy.

name: Cobbel
Settlement_Description: Unclear, whether it was already mentioned in the property index of Corvey monastery in 1053, but secure mentions in 1136, 1164, 1180 and 1227.

name: Könnern
Settlement_Description: King Henry II. gives Könnern, former property of the county of Alsleben, to the archbishopric of Magdeburg.
Town_Description: Around 1300 the place develops to a town, an Easter and Christmas market are granted.
Fair_Description: Next to the Bartholomäimarkt there were also Easter and Christmas fairs in Könnern, it is unclear when the privilege was granted though.

name: Wołczyn
Toll_Description: Merchants from Cracow complained in 1435 about the toll in Wołczyn.

name: Oksenvad
Settlement_Description: The village of Oksenvad was first mentioned in 1404, but is significantly older. The parish church is from either the 12th or 13th century.

name: Koblenz
Settlement_Description: The settlement was first mentioned between the second and fourth centurie. The Franks conquered the place around 500 and a Frankish royal court was established here around 550. In 882, the settlement was destroyed by the Normans.
Town_Description: In 1276, a town council was mentioned.
Toll_Description: 1) Until 1018, the empire levied a river toll on the Rhine here. This was levied from 1000/1018 to 1302, 1309 to 1343 and from 1350 to 1362. A tarif roll from 1140 exists. The Archbishop of Trier held the toll from 1018 to 1042. From 1042 to about 1300, the monastery of St. Simeon in Trier held it. From about 1250 to 1267 and from 1300 onwards, the property went back to the Archbishop of Trier. In 1309 and 1314, 6 Turnosgroschen had to be paid for each foder of wine. From 1317 to 1321, 12 Turnosgroschen had to be paid per foder of wine, in 1345 15 Turnosgroschen and in 1358 already 17 Turnosgroschen. In 1267, 500 to 800 marks could be collected. From 1345 to 1348 the toll was leased for 655 pounds turnosgroschen (equivalent to 13100 guilders) a year.2) The Archbishop of Trier collected a fee for safe conduct on the Rhine from 1250 to 1267. The annual revenue in 1267 was about 40 mark.3) Parallel to the Rhine toll, there was a river toll on the Moselle, which was paid together with the river toll on the Rhine until about 1336. The owner and early tariffs are therefore identical. In 1354, 12 Turnosgroschen had to be paid per foder of wine, in 1430 1 Gulden per foder of wine.In 1336/37 and 1338/39 the annual rent was 40 pounds turnosgroschen. In 1344/46 59 pounds Turnosgroschen and in 1358/61 120 pounds Turnosgroschen could be collected.4) In addition to the two river tolls, a land toll was also levied. Before 1000, 4 denarii per pack animal had to be paid. Annual revenues are not known.
Staple_Description: Archbishop John II of Trier gave Koblenz staple rights between Boppard and Engers; specified in more detail in 1480. Cattle and grain from the Bonn-Wetzlar-Bingen-Wittich region and fish caught in the Rhein between Platzenborn and Oberlahnstein needed to brought to market in Koblenz.

name: Koguva
Settlement_Description: The Schmul family was provided with land and was responsible for messenger and ferry services across the 'kleine Sund' from 1532 until the 20th century.

name: Kohala
Settlement_Description: The village was first mentioned in 1241 and belonged to the the 'Tolks' manor.

name: Kohlenbissen
Settlement_Description: Kohlenbissen is possible the same settlement as "Marcolvissen", which was mentioned in 1259.

name: Kohila
Settlement_Description: First mentioned in 1241. In 1438, there was an estate called Kogell, which was situated on an island in the river.

name: Kołobrzeg
Settlement_Description: Two settlements developed near saltworks in the 6th or 7th century, with a small castle nearby, which was extended during the middle of the 9th century. The settlement is first mentioned in 975. Boleslaw Chrobri of Poland made it into a bishopric under the archdiocese of Gniezno (Gnesen) around 1000.
Town_Description: The German settlement received Lübeck town privileges in 1255 from Duke Wartislaw of Pomerania and the bishop of Kammin.
Fair_Description: A fair on Sunday Invocavit in Kołobrzeg is mentioned in an almanac printed in Neudamm (Dębno) in 1598.

name: Kolín
Staple_Description: King John of Bohemia stated in 1310, that he had once moved the staple of Kolín to Nymburk, but would now move it back. The privilege was renewed in 1327. In 1363 it was decided that Kolín would have a wood staple on the river Elbe.

name: Winsum
Settlement_Description: Earliest mention in the tenth or eleventh century. In 1276, a dominican monastery was established in Winsum. In 1581, the monastery was abandoned.
Fair_Description: In 1057, Henry IV, King of the Romans, gave the counties of Hunsingo and Fivelgo to archbishop Adalbart of Bremen and Hamburg, with the right to institute fairs in Winsum and Garrelsweer with mintage and toll rights. The right to mint coins was used.

name: Köln
Settlement_Description: Mentioned as the birthplace of Agrippina 50 A.D. Since the middle of the 5th century under Frankish rule.
Town_Description: Already in the Middle Ages, Cologne was a spiritual centre and town of pilgrimage. In 1388 the university was founded. A town council or regiment probably existed already in the 13th/14th century. Niemeyer does not mention the granting of town rights before 1475. Cologne was referred to as a free imperial town in 1475.
Toll_Description: 1) Cologne levied a river toll on the Rhine from 1317 to 1321. This also existed in 1363 and from 1475 to 1494. In the period between 1317 and 1321, 6 Turnosgroschen per foder of wine had to be paid. From 1475 to 1494 the tariff was 2 guilders and 2 turnosgroschen per barrel of wine. In the years 1317 to 1320, 1400 pounds 14 shillings and 5 turnosgroschen could be collected. This corresponds to about 9338 guilders a year. For other annual revenues, see Pfeiffer. 2) In 1103 a gate toll was also levied. Around 1360 1/3 of the revenue went to the town and 2/3 to the Archbishop of Cologne. In the 12th century only special tariffs are known. In 1453, 3 heller had to be paid for a loaded carriage across the Rhine. At the end of the 14th century, 4 heller had to be paid per wine carriage. For other tariffs see Pfeiffer. Annual revenues are not known.3) Road toll was collected in 1262 parallel to the gate toll. Tariffs are therefore similar.
Staple_Description: Developed probably shortly before 1169, but original plans not always enforced. Confirmed in 1259, 1349 and 1355; revoked in 1356. Staple rights were probably not exercised after 1300. In late 1300s renewed attempts for the imposition of a staple; wood must remain in the town for one day; the Fishmonger ordinances of 1397 forced foreigners to seller their fish to the merchants of Cologne; ordinances of 1407 stipulated that wine, wood, fish, salt and iron should be offered for sale in the city; regulations regarding these matters became stricter throughout the 15th century. The Ordinances of the Merchant Store and the Old Market of 1486 contained new regulations for the staples for meat, oils and fats, iron, steel, lead and leather. Attempts at end of the 15th century to enforce staple rights in the trade of cattle, cloth and wool. The unloading of goods while travelling along the lower Rhine banned in 1497, but not mentioned in the imperial staple privileges for 1505. The staple after 1505 appears to decline, but is re-enforced in 1525/6. The bypassing of the staple via Neuss, Bonn and Mülheim encouraged the council in 1603 to forbid the unloading of goods along the Rhine in both directions. From 1616 there were exemptions for stone from Andernach. Staple confirmed once again by the emperor in 1635; after the Thirty Years’ War the staple was gradually transformed into a requirment to transfer wares and was finally dissolved with the Rhine Shipping act of 1831.

name: Chojna
Settlement_Description: Most likely a Pomeranian castle with a Slavic settlement, the village was first mentioned in 1244.
Town_Description: First mentioned as civitas in 1270. It had Magdeburg town law.

name: Plauen
Town_Description: Heinrich IV. of Weida founded a new town around 1230/40 which was referred to as 'civitas'.
Fair_Description: A fair in Plauen is mentioned in the regulations of safe conduct from 1506 and 1532, in which a toll had to be paid on the day of the fair on St John the Baptist.
Toll_Description: The safe conduct in Plauen controlled the road from Hof and Nürnberg to Leipzig. Revenues are known since 1471 and fall apart in a safe conduct fee for wagons, a toll for cattle, safe conduct for riding horses and a safe conduct fee on the bridge. Tariffs are known from 1506 and 1532/33.

name: Pasym
Settlement_Description: Probably grew out of the church village Heinrichswalde
Town_Description: Founded by the Grand Master Konrad Zöllner von Rothenstein with Kulm town law in 1386

name: Kölzow
Settlement_Description: The village is first mentioned in 1233.

name: Hradec Králové
Toll_Description: Hradec Králové acquired the right to levy a toll on all incoming and outgoing wagons in 1364, to fund the construction of new town walls.
Staple_Description: A staple privilege was granted to Hradec Králové by king Albert in 1307.

name: Hoogwoud
Settlement_Description: The name Hoogwoud is first mentioned in a copy of a document dating from 1289. This, however, concerns the 'ambacht' Hoogwoud. The first mention of the settlement dates from from c.1312. On 2 February 1414, Hoogwoud, together with Aartswoud, was granted town privileges by William VI, count of Holland. Hoogwoud and Aartswoud combined formed the ‘stede’ Hoogwoud. These settlements, however, never developed an urban character. The granting of town rights was part of an administrative reorganization in which a number of smaller settlements were granted town rights in order to provide them with a certain degree of self-government which replaced the need for the count of Holland's bailiffs ('baljuws'). The settlements kept their own separate settlement governments. The town privileges of the 'stede' were withdrawn on 13 August 1426, but were re-granted on 29 March 1450.

name: Kaliningrad
Settlement_Description: The first castle of the Teutonic Order was built on the remains of an Old Prussian castle, a marketsettlement of craftsmen and farmers grew next to it, their church is documented since 1256, the first settlements were destroyed between 1262 and 1263
Town_Description: After the settlement was rebuilt, the Landmaster of Prussia, Konrad von Thierberg, granted the Kulm town law in 1286
Staple_Description: Imposition of ordinances and rules for the compulsory inspection of ash, tar, pitch and honey and also a reduced staple for wood in the 1390s. An agreement in 1466 made arrangement for a staple for ash, which must have been lost shortly after 1476. Mandate of Grandmaster Albert of Brandenburg ordered merchants from Lithuania, Maosvia, Moscow, Gdansk and Torun to offer their wares for sail when travelling through Königsberg, but was forbidden in the treaty of Krakow in 1525. Trade outside of the town forbidden in 1529, and livestock from Lithuania and Samogitia should be kept at market for three days. A mandate of 1565 ordered merchants of Bartenstein, Rastenburg, Friedland, Wehlau, Tilsit, Memel and Insterburg to bring their wares solely to market in Königsberg; repeated in 1622.

name: Königsbrück
Toll_Description: The yearly income from the safe conduct was documented in 1564 (SHStA Dresden, Loc. 8634, Bl. 246–248v.).

name: Kontich
Settlement_Description: Earliest mention in the tenth-eleventh century.

name: null
Ferry_Description: Revenues of the ferry across the Elbe near Prettin are known from registers of the district ('Amt') Torgau from 1497/98 onwards.

name: Königslutter
Settlement_Description: Emperor Lothar III converted an early 11th-century monastery of canonesses into a Benedictine monastery in 1135, next to which the settlement Lutter developed. A ducal castle was constructed around 1200. The addition "Königs-" ('royal') to the placename first appears in the 14th century.
Town_Description: A market in Königslutter is mentioned in 1318 and the settlement is characterised as borough ('weichbild') in 1344 and 1359. Between 1400 and 1409, it received Braunschweig town privileges. More extensive privileges were granted in 1474 and 1589.
Fair_Description: In 1621, duke Friedrich Ulrich granted Königslutter a second retail and cattle fair on Sunday before St Gallus, next to the already existing one on St Peter and Paul. It is unknown how old the latter fair was, but it was probably connected to the annual pilgrimage to Königslutter on 29 June, which is first mentioned in 1291. With the pilgrimage becoming more popular in the 15th century, there were frequent complaints about fair-like situations on the monastery premises, which disturbed religious services. Thereupon trading on the grounds of the monastery was forbidden.

name: Lubniewice
Settlement_Description: A German village developed close to a fortress after 1241, first mentioned in 1322.
Town_Description: First mentioned as a town in 1367, a constitution didn't exist until 1808.

name: Königswinter
Toll_Description: 1) The Archbishop of Cologne levied a river toll on the Rhine in 1291/92 and 1424/25. Tariffs are unknown in 1291/92. In the 15th century Königswinter was a toll station of the Linz river toll on the Rhine. Tariffs are therefore the same - in 1424/25 6 alb. had to be paid per barrel of wine. 2) The Archbishop of Cologne levied a land toll in 1300. Tariffs are not known. In 1405 the annual yield was about 20 mark.

name: Konin
Toll_Description: A toll station in Konin is attested since 1328.

name: Konju
Settlement_Description: A village is first mentioned in 1444. It was owned by the Teutonic Order in the 15th century. The manor was built in 1635 under Swedish occupation.

name: Kopki
Toll_Description: Mentioned as toll station in c. 1349, where 1/2 gr. had to be paid for each horse.

name: Marzahna
Settlement_Description: The village is first mentioned in 1354.
Toll_Description: Secondary station of safe conduct ('Beigeleit') of Wittenberg. Regulations of safe conduct remain from 1513. Revenues are known since 1459/60.

name: Ogkeln
Toll_Description: Secondary station of safe conduct ('Nebengeleit') of Wittenberg. Revenues are known since 1536. Regulations and tariffs ('Geleitsordnung') are attested in 1550.

name: Korbeek-Lo
Settlement_Description: Earliest mention in 1107, in a copy from the middle of the thirteenth century.

name: Koorküla
Settlement_Description: The village 'Kuerkull' was granted as a fief in 1487. The manor 'Korküll' was built near the village.

name: Karlino
Settlement_Description: First mentioned in 1240. An earlier Slavic fortification and settlement are presumed.
Town_Description: Supposedly founded as a town in 1240. Mentioned as civis in 1299 and castrum in 1308. Lübeck town law was granted by the bishop of Kammin. The date is not recorded, but the privileges were endorsed in 1500.

name: Cornau
Settlement_Description: Originally a moated castle of the lords of Diepholz from the mid-11th century, first mentioned only in 1369. Borough ('flecken') privileges were confirmed in the mid-16th century by duke Christian Ludwig of Brunswick-Lüneburg.

name: Kose
Settlement_Description: A village was mentioned in 1241, a mill and a farm in 1346. In 1525 there was only an inn left. From 1642 the village belonged to the Meks manor.

name: Kościan
Toll_Description: The toll station of Kościan, first attested in 1387, was one of the most significant tolls in Greater Poland. The town also received the right to levy a bridge tax in 1474.

name: Oelsnitz
Settlement_Description: The settlement was situated around the Voitsberg castle, which was built in 1240. The settlement probably had market rights since its foundation.
Town_Description: The expansion of the town took place in the middle of the 14th century. In 1357, the town received town rights.
Fair_Description: The regulations of safe conduct of the district ('Amt') Voigtsberg from 1542 mention fees that were due on the fairs in Oelsnitz on St. Michael's day, mid-Lent and St. Kilian's day.
Toll_Description: The regulations of safe conduct of the district ('Amt') Voigtsberg from 1542 mention a bridge toll, as well as fees that were due on the fairs. Probably these refer to the tolls and fairs in Oelsnitz. Revenues are known from 1447 onwards.

name: Koserow
Settlement_Description: The village was first mentioned in a document in 1347, but is much older.

name: Koszalin
Settlement_Description: Duke Bogislaw II. donated the village to the Cistercian abbey Belbuck in 1214. An earlier castle complex is presumed, based on a mention from 1313.
Town_Description: Bishop Hermann von Gleichen granted Lübeck town law in 1266. It is mentioned as castrum in 1281.

name: Kossow
Settlement_Description: The village is first mentioned in 1276.

name: Köthen
Settlement_Description: 1115 mention of an "oppidum" Köthen, near which a battle against the Slavs took place.From 1180 - 1212 duke Bernhard of Saxony had coins minted with "kotene civitas", which indicates the existence of a fortified market. One can assume an earlier, slavic settlement.From 1396 a castle can be proven in Köthen.
Town_Description: Since the beginning of the 14th century, Köthen is referred to as "civitas" in the records and a sheriff, councilmen and jurymen are mentioned. Jurisdiction stays with the town lord, however.
Fair_Description: In 1643 Leipzig prevents the establishment of two additional fairs in Köthen.
Toll_Description: A regulation of safe conduct remains from 1563 (LHASA, DE, Z 10, Nr. 48, Amtsregister und Anschlag des Amtes Köthen.).

name: Kowal
Toll_Description: Mentioned as toll station in a document from c. 1349, where 2 gr. had to be paid for each horse (formerly 1 gr.).

name: Kaunas
Staple_Description: Attempts to erect a staple in the 15th century. The Hanseatic Kontor in Kaunas gained its freedom in 1441 and concentrated Lithuanian trade in the city. The mercantile ordinances of c. 1470 stipulated that that merchant wares should remain in Kaunas for three days and fobade trade with guests. In 1492 any remaining markets in Samogitia for foreign merchants were abolished; from 1541, markets allowed if they held the appropriate privilege from the king.

name: Krempelsdorf
Settlement_Description: Krempelsdorf was of Slavic origin; in the 13th century it is said that there was a Slavic and a German part. The settlement belonged to Lübeck since 1226. At the beginning of the 15th century, there were two farms, which were owned by Lübeck councillors.

name: Kraków
Staple_Description: In 1306 the town was made the staple for wares from Hungary, especially metal. After conflicts with the Hungarians, salt transported from Torun to Sandek is excepted. Citizens of Wroclaw exempt from the Krakow staple; in 1354 trade with guests forbidden. Decres of the Polish King of 1372 and 1389 making Krakow the staple market for all merchants coming to Poland (except those from Sandomir and Lublin) lead to several conflicts with Torun. In 1391 both towns removed themselves from the staple, but in 1398 merchants of Krakow forced once again to the offer their wares in the town. The important stapel for the copper trade from Hungary and for Baltic wares was confirmed in the Polish Staple law of 1565.

name: Cracau
Settlement_Description: Settlement of Slavic origin; from 1158 and 1166 detailed accounts on the settlement of Dutch colonists remain. In 1164 it is conquered by archbishop Wichmann. Destroyed several times during the 30-year-war.

name: Krakow am See
Settlement_Description: Grew out of a Wendish town close to a castle; a German village was founded to the north of it. It is first mentioned in a charter of 1298, but existed at least since 1235-1277.
Town_Description: According to a note in a charter of 1298, Krakow was granted Schwerin-Güstrow town privileges by Lord Nikolaus I of Werle (1235-1277). The privileges were endorsed multiple times in 1366-1375, Güstrow town law endorsed in 1437.

name: Kranenburg (Niederrhein)
Toll_Description: The Count of Cleves levied a land toll in 1381. Tariffs and revenues are not known.

name: Krefeld
Fair_Description: Emperor Charles IV granted the right to organise two fairs of seven days on 13 October 1373: on St Blasius (13 February) and Sunday after St Vitus (15 June).
Toll_Description: The Count of Moers and the town of Moers levied a land toll in 1373. In 1373, 1 Turnosgroschen per horse had to be paid.

name: Kreischau
Settlement_Description: Manor and village, first mentioned in 1251.

name: Kremmen
Settlement_Description: Early Ascanian fortress close to a Slavic and a German settlement with church and market, first mentioned in 1216.
Town_Description: Town probably founded around 1232. In 1298 the town privileges of were endorsed by the margrave. In 1459, it is only mentioned as oppidum (borough).

name: Krimulda
Settlement_Description: The castle was built as a branch castle of Treyden Castle in 1231. A manor was built near this castle.

name: Kreyenbrück
Settlement_Description: A farm at the bridge across the Hunte might have existed before 1428.
Bridge_Description: Bridge across the Hunte. It was originally called Klusbrücke after the family Klüsener, who lived here in 1538. Around 1630, they were replaced by the family Kreye, after whom the bridge became known as Kreyenbrück.

name: Krogaspe
Settlement_Description: First mentioned in the town register of Kiel from 1264-1289. The settlement is characterised as 'villa' in 1230 and as village ('dorp') in 1393.

name: Kronach
Toll_Description: Emperor Charles IV granted bishop Leupolt of Bamberg the right to levy a fee of safe conduct from each loaded wagon in Kronach in 1357.

name: Kröpelin
Settlement_Description: The settlement existed since Wendish times. A church village is first mentioned in 1177, a mill in 1219.
Town_Description: Made into a town between 1232 (last mention as village) and 1250 (first mention as oppidum) by Lord Borwin Heinrich III of Rostock. Mentioned in 1280 as civitas. Lübeck town privileges were endorsed multiple times, e.g. 1347, 1378, 1588.

name: Bagrationovsk
Settlement_Description: A castle of the Teutonic Order was built by Arnolph von Eylenstein under the Grand Master Werner von Orseln (1325-1330), later the see of a 'Pfleger', a parson is mentioned in 1348
Town_Description: After a general privilege was granted in 1348 for many settlements, people asked after a town privilege, which was granted in 1585 by Duke Georg Friedrich in 1585

name: Kröppelshagen
Settlement_Description: The place was first mentioned in 1334.

name: Krapa
Settlement_Description: The exact date of mentioning is unclear. During the 14th century, the manor belonged to the Kropfen-Family. In 1625, it was abandoned but was resettled in 1681.

name: Kropstädt
Settlement_Description: First mention in 1347 as Liesenitz, a former castle that overlooked the road leading from Treuenbritzen to Berlin. After being destroyed in 1358, it was rebuilt as Kropstädt castle in 1567. A municipality of Kröpstedt only developed after 1560.

name: Krummesse
Settlement_Description: First mentioned in 1194. Since the second half of the 14th century, parts of the village belonged to Lübeck.

name: Krzeszów
Toll_Description: Mentioned as toll station in c. 1349, where 1 gr. had to be paid for each horse.

name: Krzywiń
Toll_Description: Mentioned as toll station in the 13th century.

name: Winschoterhogebrug
Settlement_Description: A fortress ('schans') was constructed near the bridge across the Pekel-Aa around 1625.
Bridge_Description: The fortress was constructed near the high (=fixed) bridge across the Pekel-Aa. It is unknown how old it was.

name: Kückhoven
Toll_Description: In 1490, a land toll was levied here. Holders, tariffs and revenues are not known.

name: Kuddewörde
Settlement_Description: First mentioned in 1230. A monastery of Augustinian hermits was founded here in 1497, and already abolished in 1524.
Toll_Description: Because travellers circumvented the toll station in Trittau by taking the route via Kuddewörde, a toll was also levied in Kuddewörde, starting before 1558.

name: Kuhstedt
Settlement_Description: First mentioned around 1187. From the 15th century, the settlement consisted of 7 farms.

name: Kuijõe
Settlement_Description: The manor is first mentioned in 1688.

name: Kuimetsa
Settlement_Description: In 1241 first mentioned as a village, which was owned by the Cistercian monastery of St Michael in Reval (Tallinn). In 1345 a farm was mentioned, which was burned down by Russians in 1560.

name: Kuinre
Town_Description: On 22 March 1385, Herman, lord of Cuynre has granted town-like privileges to Cuynre. In 1407, it is mentioned that Kuinre sealed a charter with a town seal ('Stadt Segel van Kuynre'). In 1436 and 1448, the weighhouse on the dike ('zeedijk') is mentioned.
Fair_Description: Kuinre had a fair in 1385 but the dates are unknown. In 1448 there was a fair during 4 days with All-Saints (Nov. 1) and a weigh-house on the dike. In 1508 (Dec. 13) the bishop granted a free market for the sale of beer, bread, dairy and other foods.
Toll_Description: In 1377 the lord of Kuinre stated that Kampen only had to pay 'roedertol' (paid for the ship, not the cargo). Kuinre was primarily an export harbour for butter and peat. In 1407 the bishop of Utrecht acquired the seigniory of Kuinre with support of the towns of Deventer, Kampen and Zwolle and granted the inhabitants of this towns freedom of toll and 'weggeld' (taxes levied on the roads) in and passing through this seigniory. In 1412 Hasselt was freed from the toll by the bishop of Utrecht. Only one account is preserved and dated 1427/'8, drawn by the castellan of Kuinre for the bishop and the IJssel-towns, and states 166 guilders of toll-yields. An 'olde tolcedel' with a tariff of the seigniory Kuinre compiled by the castellan of the lord of Utrecht (the bishop) dated [14]74 was copied anno [15]19. Freed from this toll are then: the lord for his own goods, Deventer, Kampen, Zwolle, Hasselt, Vollenhove, 'Geelmuyden' (Genemuiden), 'Stellinckwerff' (Stellingwerven), Schoterland, 'Dongewerffstadt' (Doniawerstal), 'Ooster Sengerlandt' (Oosterzeeingerland, later also: Lemsterland) and the neighbours of Kuinre and Veenhuizen if they don't make 'verwapeninge' (alienation of goods). Accounts of the peat-toll, combined with the one levied in Blokzijl, are preserved for the years 1561-'66.

name: Kuivastu
Settlement_Description: Referred to as a village around 1645. In the Medieval times, however, it was the centre of its own administrative area.

name: Kulna
Settlement_Description: The village is first mentioned in 1219.

name: null
Harbour_Description: The Winschoterdiep canal was dug in the 1630s, which allowed water traffic with Groningen. Regular barge ('trekschuit') services were offered in 1654 at the latest.

name: Cumlosen
Toll_Description: A toll on the Elbe in Cumlosen is first mentioned in negotiations about reducing the tolls on the Elbe from 1476. The toll tariff was 4 Lübeck shilling, 1 loaf of bread and 3 buns for each ship. The toll is still mentioned in four travel accounts of skipper Gottfired Kleeditz from Pirna from 1671-1674.

name: Kunersdorf
Settlement_Description: First mention in 1340; a nearby castle mound can be traced back to Slavic times.

name: Curau
Settlement_Description: First mentioned in 1220. The church is first mentioned in 1286. The village belonged mainly to the Hospital of the Holy Ghost in Lübeck. An inn is mentioned in 1447.

name: Ķoniņciems
Settlement_Description: One of the villages of the 'Curonian kings' with special privileges, which it received in 1439.

name: Kurtna
Settlement_Description: A Manor and village which was first mentioned in 1471.

name: Kuusna
Settlement_Description: The village near an old quarry was named in 1558.

name: Kostrzyn nad Odrą
Settlement_Description: Belonged to Greater Poland in the Middle Ages. A German market settlement came after 1232, mentioned as oppidum in 1261, when it was acquired by Brandenburg.
Town_Description: Magdeburg town law was likely granted by margrave Albrecht III shortly before 1300. Mentioned as civitas in 1317 and 1372, as opidum in 1323.
Toll_Description: A toll is first mentioned in 1338, when it was pawned for three years. A river toll on the Oder is mentioned in 1345. Citizens from Bärwalde (Mieszkowice) and Schönfließ (Trzcińsko-Zdrój) were exempted from the toll in 1356, and an older similar privilege was confirmed for Königsberg (Chojna) in 1371 as well. A bridge toll is mentioned in 1436, and a privilege from 1482 allows a bridge and dam toll of 4 pennies for each wagon. In 1457, parts of the revenues of the river toll were owned by the Benedictine women's monastery of Guben.
Staple_Description: In 1424, Poles were exempted from the staple in Kostrzyn.

name: null
Harbour_Description: In 1351 Montfoort obtained toll-exemption from the count of Holland and in 1379 from the bishop of Utrecht for the tolls in the Sticht of Utrecht.

name: Sijbekarspel
Settlement_Description: Earliest mention in circa 1312. In 1414, Sijbekarspel and Benningbroek were granted town rights by William VI, count of Holland. Together, these settlements formed the ‘stede’ Sijbekarspel. These settlements, however, never developed an urban character. The granting of town rights was part of an administrative reorganization in which a number of smaller settlements were granted town rights in order to provide them with a certain degree of self-government which replaced the need for the count of Holland's bailiffs ('baljuws'). The settlements kept their own separate settlement governments. For political reasons, the town rights were withdrawn in 1426. The privileges were temporarily regranted in 1428 and 1452, before they were permanently restored in 1456.

name: Laag-Keppel
Settlement_Description: Origin as a settlement near the castle of Sweder van Voorst, which was probably built around 1350. Earliest mention of 'Borch Keppell' dates from 1361.
Town_Description: Market privileges are granted on 14 April 1361 by Emperor Charles IV to Sweder of Voorst for his 'opidum'. Additional town privileges granted to Laagkeppel in 1374, 1404 and 1425. It concerns a town of the type 'minderstadt'.
Fair_Description: In 1361 (April19) the emperor granted on instigation of the archbishop of Cologne the lord of Keppel (Sweder van Voorst) a fair and a weekly market for his new town next to his castle Keppel, with safe-conduct for the visitors.
Toll_Description: Laag-Keppel was located near a ford where the IJssel could be crossed. This ford was part of the road between Zutphen and Emmerich; a toll was levied here. It is unknown from which moment onwards toll has been levied.

name: Bad Laasphe
Town_Description: The settlement had town rights from the second half of the 13th century. From 1277 'civitas', from 1295 'oppidum'. It was not until 1438 that it received the Wittgenstein town privilege.

name: Polessk
Settlement_Description: The Teutonic Order built a castle to protect Königsberg against the Lithuanians in 1258, which was destroyed in 1277 and rebuilt in 1280. A settlement developed the 13th century, which received privileges in the 15th century.
Town_Description: First mentioned as town ('Stadt') in 1626. The Great Elector Frederick William granted town privileges in 1642.

name: Læborg
Settlement_Description: The village of Læborg was first mentioned in the middle of the 14th century, but is older. The parish church is from either the 12th or 13th century.

name: Laer
Settlement_Description: The parish village is first mentioned in the 11th century.

name: Laarne
Settlement_Description: Earliest mention in 1040, in a copy from the second half of the twelfth century.

name: Neman
Settlement_Description: The Teutonic Order built a castle in place of an old Prussian fortress in 1289, it was repeatedly destroyed, but between 1397-1409 fortified as one of the strongest military fortresses of the Order and kept that position of importance, a settlement existed close ot the castle, the founding of a town was planned for 1410 but took long to realise

name: Lage (Kommende)
Settlement_Description: Probably goes back to a Frankish foundation. Since 1221 it was owned by the counts of Tecklenburg. A monastery of the Knights Hospitaller was first mentioned in 1260 (probably founded in 1245 by Count Otto von Tecklenburg). In the 14th century the monastery became an important place of pilgrimage. The monastery was closed in 1811, but a Catholic institution remained.
Fair_Description: Two fairs came into existence in the 14th century in the context of the pilgrimage to the Holy Cross in Lage, on the day of the Birth of John the Baptist, the patron saint, and on the Dedication day of the church on the Exaltation of the Holy Cross. These fairs were visited among others by merchants from Osnabrück.

name: Lage (Lippe)
Settlement_Description: The settlement is first mentioned with a priest in 1274. The village developed into a borough ('weichbild') in the late 15th century and received legal privileges and a seal in 1495. Full town privileges were only granted in 1843.
Toll_Description: A toll station in Lage is mentioned in 1395 and 1532.

name: Lahde
Settlement_Description: The place was first mentioned in 1168.

name: Laiuse
Settlement_Description: The parish was established in 1319. In 1406 a castle of the Teutonic Order was built nearby, which was occupied by Russians in 1558. 1622 conquered by Sweden, later destroyed.

name: Jõgeva
Settlement_Description: Originally a manor with hamlets ('Hof'), which were mentioned in 1601. At the end of the 19th century a fortified borough ('Hakelwerk') was built near the manor, which later received town rights.

name: Laitse
Settlement_Description: First mentioned in 1219. In 1365 it was given to the Teutonic Order. Around 1800 the village was abandoned.

name: Lamspringe
Settlement_Description: A monastery of canonesses in Lamspringe was first mentioned in 872, and later converted to a Benedictine nun monastery. It became Lutheran in 1568 and was closed in 1803. The connected settlement was characterised as a borough ('flecken'/'blek') from 1426 and received corresponding privileges in 1499.
Toll_Description: In 1439 the bishop of Hildesheim began to levy a wine toll, as well as in Marienburg and Bodenburg.

name: Lędyczek
Settlement_Description: Originally a fortification, later a small border castle of the Teutonic Order, mentioned in 1447. The settlement acquired urban character in 1775, but was still characterised as market borough ('marktflecken') in 1789.

name: Landegge
Settlement_Description: A castle was built here in 1178 to guard the road.
Fair_Description: A market with market toll in Landegge is first mentioned in 1238, which attracted visitors from places as far as Reiderland and Dortmund. Between 1303 and 1345, three dates for fairs are mentioned, on Pentecost, St John and the Nativity of Mary.
Toll_Description: A road toll in Landegge is mentioned in 1483, when half of it was given to the town Meppen by the bishop of Münster.

name: Landen
Settlement_Description: Earliest mention in circa 1050. Next mention in 1080, in a middle thirteenth century copy. Next mention in 1116.

name: Landesbergen
Settlement_Description: The settlement is first mentioned around 1200, a family von Landesbergen already in ca. 1160.

name: Gorzów Wielkopolski
Settlement_Description: Developed from a late Slavic settlement. First mentioned in 1257 when it became a town.
Town_Description: The knight Albert of Luge was certified to found the town "Landisberch Nova" by Margrave John I in 1257. The town acquired Magdeburg town law after ten years.
Staple_Description: The first mention of a staple in a charter from 1257 is probably a later addition; furthermore mentioned in 1391 and 1400. In 1424, Poles are exempted from the staple. In 1539, the use of the road via Landsberg for transit traffic was prohibited in favour of Frankfurt, and the staple limited to commodities transported downstream from Poland. In the other direction, there existed no staple obligations.

name: Gorzów Śląski
Toll_Description: Merchants from Cracow complained in 1435 about the toll in Gorzów Śląski.

name: Pikasilla
Settlement_Description: A bridge was built near an old castle and first mentioned in 1398 as site of negotiations between the Teutonic Order and the bishop of Tartu. Later a village with an inn developed.

name: Langelsheim
Settlement_Description: The settlement was first mentioned around 1016.

name: Langenberg (Gera)
Settlement_Description: A castle district and a nearby village are attested in 1060. In 1505, when Langenberg was already a borough ('Flecken'), it was granted its first privileges ('Ortsrecht'). Langenberg was only elevated to town in 1933.

name: Langenhagen
Toll_Description: A toll station of the dukes of Brunswick-Lüneburg is first mentioned in 1501. A register of toll revenues exists from 1602/1603 and has been analysed by Rothe.

name: Langenlehsten
Settlement_Description: The village was first mentioned in 1194.

name: Langwedel
Settlement_Description: Construction of a castle by the archbishop of Bremen around 1222; first mentioned in 1226.
Toll_Description: Toll of the archbishop of Bremen. Bremen citizens were exempted from the toll in 1226. In 1366, the castle including the toll was pawned to the town Bremen. A raise of the toll fares led to complaints from Hannover in 1427. The toll was pawned to Lüneburg in 1435 for six years. Its revenues amounted to almost 90 Taler in 1567/8. Toll revenues are also recorded in a register from 1616/1617.

name: Lasfelde
Settlement_Description: The first mention of 1174-1195 concerns a forest, but it is likely that the settlement already existed at that time as well.

name: Lastrup
Settlement_Description: The parish of Lastrup is first mentioned in 1223, although the hamlet ('bauernschaft') existed already before that date.

name: Langewiesen
Settlement_Description: The settlement is first mentioned in 1198. The settlement acquired the character of a borough ('Flecken'). Statutes date from 1611, but town privileges were only granted in 1855.

name: null
Harbour_Description: After the Schuitendiep canal had been extended to Zuidbroek, the first ship from Groningen arrived here in 1628. In the 1630s, the canal was extended to Winschoten. Regular barge ('trekschuit') services were offered in 1654 at the latest.

name: Latferde
Settlement_Description: First mentioned in the 1222. A mention of the settlement "Lofurdi" in a register of the monastery Corvey from 822 probably refers to Lafferde near Peine.
Toll_Description: Road toll in the 17th century, first mentioned in 1620.

name: Bad Lauchstädt
Settlement_Description: First mentioned in the Hersfelder Zehntregister around 899. Borough ('Flecken') in 1519. In the course of the 14th and 15th century, the settlement gained several privileges, such as the privilege of jurisdicition in 1519. In 1608 borough rights ('Weichbildrechte') are confirmed by Johann Georg of Merseburg.
Toll_Description: The extensive regulations of safe conduct from 1600 confirm earlier regulations (LHASA, MD, U 10 XXIII Nr. 1.).

name: Lauenburg
Settlement_Description: The castle Lauenburg was built in 1181/1182 by duke Bernhard I of Ascania. After 1227, a settlement developed near the castle.
Town_Description: In the mid-13th century, the settlement probably became a town. A town council and citizens are attested at the end of the 13th century.
Toll_Description: A toll of the dukes of Saxony-Lauenburg is first mentioned in 1248, with specifications of the toll tariffs. Citizens from Hamburg were exempted from the toll in 1252. The toll in Lauenburg was especially levied on salt exported from Lüneburg towards Lübeck and towns upstream on the Elbe. According to a 1492 description, each ship had to pay 8 Gulden, 1 rye bread and a loaf of bread in Lauenburg.

name: Lębork
Settlement_Description: First mentioned in 1230, then a Slavic town-like settlement. The emergence of a German settlement between 1313 and 1341 is assumed.
Town_Description: Dietrich, burgrave of Altenburg and grandmaster of the Teutonic Order gave the town with Kulm town law to Rutcher von Emmerich in 1341. Town privileges were renewed in 1507.

name: Lauenförde
Settlement_Description: Lauenförde came into existence next to a castle, which is first mentioned in 1348. The settlement was mentioned as borough ('flecken') in 1447, but as village in the 16th century.

name: Laiküla
Settlement_Description: The village has existed since medieval times (probably the 13th century). An estate was built in 1688.

name: Lihula
Settlement_Description: The parish of Leal was mentioned in 1241. Beside the castle, which was built in 1211, a village/Borough ('Flecken') settled, which was destroyed again in 1298. It was rebuilt and developed itself in to a place with some churches and monasteries in the 16th century. Borough rights ('Fleckenrechte') were only granted in 1945.

name: Langebro
Bridge_Description: In 1460 a bridge across a narrow part of the outlet of Kerteminde Fjord south of town was mentioned for the first time, but the bridge is probably older. The bridge was called “Langebro” in 1496, and the name probably reflects the considerable length of the bridge.
Ferry_Description: In the 16th century a ferry route presumably connected Kerteminde to Zealand. The ferry was, however, not as important as other ferry routes between Funen and Zealand.
Harbour_Description: Kerteminde Fjord was a good natural harbour used by both Hanseatic merchants and merchants from the neighboring town of Odense. Around 1600 bulwards were erected to protect the harbour, and in 1635 a wharf is mentioned. One of the most important harbours on the island of Funen in the 16th and 17th century as the merchants from Odense used the harbour, especially during winter.

name: Ryn
Settlement_Description: A castle of the Teutonic Order was built in 1337 and became the see of a komtur in 1393, a mill was built in the beginning of the 15th ct. and a village grew around 1485, with craftsmen settling, the market hamlet was burned down by the Tartars in 1657

name: Lehre
Settlement_Description: First mentioned in the 8th or 9th century.

name: Lebus
Settlement_Description: Culturally important place for a wide region since early Slavic times, a Polish fortress consisting of three castles is mentioned in 1109. Nearby a German market settlement was founded by the Silesian Piast dynasty shortly after 1225.
Town_Description: Mentioned as civitas in 1226. The German town law was granted in Silesian times, probably before 1250. Lebus lost much of its significance after the founding of Frankfurt in 1253. It is only mentioned as oppidum (borough) in 1354 and 1355, 1406 as Städtchen (small town).
Toll_Description: A toll on the Oder river is first mentioned in 1222. In 1371 it is mentioned that Königsberg (Chojna) was exempted from this toll since times of old. In 1356 citizens from Schönfließ (Trzcińsko-Zdrój) and Bärwalde (Mieszkowice) were exempted as well.
Harbour_Description: Important transshipment point between the Oder river and land transport in the early 13th century. After the founding of Frankfurt with its staple in 1253, Lebus lost significance as harbour.

name: Łęczyca
Toll_Description: Mentioned as toll station in c. 1349, where 6 gr. had to be paid for each horse. In 1390, King Władysław of Poland ordained, that the toll tariffs in Sieradz, Kalisz, Pyzdry and Poznań were to be the same as those levied in Piotrków Trybunalski, Łęczyca, Przedecz and Brześć.

name: Liedikas
Settlement_Description: The village was first mentioned in 1486.

name: Beek (Xanten)
Toll_Description: The Count of Kleve levied a transshipment toll in 1366. Moreover, the river toll on the Rhine of Griethausen was levied in Beek from 1385 to 1400/01.

name: Hagestein
Settlement_Description: Hagestein is first mentioned in 1228. A castle was located in the village. After this castle and the town were demolished in 1405, a new castle was build from around 1546. It was accompanied by a modest settlement.
Town_Description: Town rights were granted to Hagestein on 11 November 1382 by Otto, lord of Arkel. In 1405 the town and castle were sieged, captured, and demolished.

name: Leer
Settlement_Description: A missionary church was erected by Liudger around 790, next to which a market borough developed. Borough ('flecken') statutes are first known from 1585 and the settlement acquired urban characteristics, although formal town privileges were granted as late as in 1823.
Toll_Description: A toll of the counts of East Frisia is mentioned in 1577 complaints from Emden. In 1640, Emden merchants complain about a new toll on flax and wine in Leer.
Harbour_Description: Leer was an important harbour on the rivers Ems and Leda in the 16th century, although it suffered from the staple privileges of Emden. The importance of the harbour for the borough is indicated by the fact that the market, which originally took place at the Kaakskpütte, moved to the waterfront, where a weigh house was erected in the middle of the 16th century. In the late 16th century, a ferry with Emden is mentioned, which was privileged to skippers from Emden and Leer.

name: Rhadern
Settlement_Description: First mentioned between 1015 and 1046. 1473, as well as in the 16th century deserted, but settled again from 1567.

name: Riederhöfe
Settlement_Description: The place was first mentioned in 1193. All that remains of the Großer Riederhof today is a late Gothic gate building from 1492.

name: Rise
Settlement_Description: The village of Rise had its own parish church, build around 1335, but the settlement is significantly older.

name: Leerort
Settlement_Description: A castle was built by the Frisian nobleman Focko Ukena around 1420, which was destroyed in 1431. A new castle was erected by Hamburg in 1432 as protection of the trade routes against pirates. Later the castle was acquired by the Cirksena family and became the administrative centre of the region. From 1611 to 1744, the fortress was occupied by Dutch troops.
Toll_Description: During the Dutch occupation of Leerort, the admiralty of Dokkum moved the toll of Bourtange to Leerort and changed it into a toll on shipping on the Ems river in 1621. A list of toll fees from that year is still extant. The toll was finally abolished after many complaints from the count of East Frisia and the town of Emden in 1653.

name: Leersum
Settlement_Description: Earliest mention in the eleventh century.

name: Leese
Settlement_Description: The settlement was first mentioned in 1183.
Toll_Description: An insignificant toll is attested here in 1583.

name: Leisnig
Settlement_Description: Castle and castle district of the 10th/11th century, first mentioned in 1046.
Town_Description: The original market settlement was founded shortly before 1215 at the location of Altleisnig. It was mentioned as civitas in 1278. The town was moved to the current location in 1286.
Toll_Description: In Leisning, safe conduct was paid in today's districts Clennen, Fischendorf and Börtewitz. A toll was due for rafts on the Mulde river.

name: Ljouwert
Settlement_Description: First mentioned on a coin from 1038-1057.
Town_Description: Leeuwarden never officially received town rights. However, Leeuwarden was recognized as a town by other cities. The earliest mention of this dates from 31 October 1285.
Fair_Description: In 1453 there are three fairs: 1) Thursday to Saterday after Eastern 2) St. Margaret (July 13/Schuur: July 20!?), 3) St. Matthew (Sept. 21). The last two fairs were there of old, the first seems new. A weighhouse is found in 1486 but dates probably back before 1435.
Toll_Description: In 1533 (1531? on instigation of the stadtholder) with permission of the Court of Frisia the magistrate installed a toll for 3 years on the new Zwartenweg(road) which connected Leeuwarden eastern (in the direction of Ryptsjerk) with the Wolden and Groningen. This road replaced the old one via Lekkum and Miedum. In 1535 the Landen (countryside) protested against this. Leeuwarden removed without consultation the bridge at Miedum and so made this route unusable. The Court gave order to repair the bridge but extended the levying of the toll on the new route. The countryside opposed this. In 1554 this was not yet solved.
Harbour_Description: In the 17th century, Leeuwarden became the centre of regular barge ('trekvaart') services with Franeker and Harlingen (1646, with five departures daily in both directions), Dokkum (1647), Bolsward and Workum (1648), Groningen (1656) and Sneek (1661).

name: Kerteminde
Settlement_Description: A fishing village around 1200. Mentioned for the first time in a will in 1350, when a merchant from Lübeck donated to the church in Kerteminde. The will is evidence of Hanseatic activity at a relatively early stage.
Town_Description: King Erik the Pomeranian (1396-1439) granted Kerteminde the same town rights as Svendborg and Faaborg in 1413. The previous year Kerteminde was pawned to the bishop of Roskilde. Mayors are documented in 1493, and town hall in 1602. From the second half of the 16th century, merchants from Odense used the harbour in Kerteminde during winter.

name: Bad Belzig
Settlement_Description: It is uncertain whether the castle district center Belizi, mentioned in 997, refers to Beelitz or Belzig. In the 12th century, an Ascanian castle emerges there, mentioned in 1161. A market settlement developed in the 13th century, referred to as oppidum in 1269. A council is mentioned in 1506, but it was only granted full town rights in 1702.
Toll_Description: Northernmost Ernestinian main station of safe conduct. Revenues are known since the mid-15th century. Secondary stations ('Nebengeleite') were located in Brück, Groß Marzehns, Niemegk, Ragösen and Lütte.

name: Leimbach (Mansfeld)
Settlement_Description: Mentioned in 973 in an exchange of estates between Fulda monastery and the archbishopric of Magdeburg. (MGH OII no. 64, S. 74-77) Earlier already mentioned in the Hersfelder Zehntverzeichnis.
Town_Description: On 10th august 1530 elevation of the marketplace to town on demand of count Hoyer VI. of Mansfeld-Vorderort.
Fair_Description: Count Hoyer IV. (1484 - 1540)  obtained town-, fair-, and weekly market rights for Leimbach, which were later confirmed by emperors Ferdinand I. and Maximilian II.

name: Leipzig
Settlement_Description: Developed from an originally Slavic settlement since c. 800, first mentioned in c. 1015. The settlement developed on the early trade routes of the 'Hohe Straße' and 'via imperii/Salzstraße'. Centre of a castellany since the 10th century.
Town_Description: A planned town was founded around 1170 by Margrave Otto of Meißen with Halle-Magdeburg town rights. Because of its fairs and the favourable traffic situation, Leipzig became an important trading centre between Nuremberg and the towns of the Hanse, copper trade in Hungary and mining in the region of Mansfeld. In 1409 a university was founded. Severe damage was inflicted during the 30 Years' War and Leipzig was occupied by the Swedes in 1632-1633 and again in 1642-1650.
Fair_Description: In a document from between 1156 and 1170 a protected zone for the annual fair was imposed around the town of Leipzig, which is the first evidence for fairs in Leipzig. In 1268 a document refers to the fair at Leipzig being visited by foreign merchants, who were under the protection of local territorial lords during fair times. In the 15th century the three eight-day fairs of Leipzig on New Year's Day, Sunday Jubilate and St Michael's Day became large international trading venues. They were confirmed in 1497 by Maximilian I, including a safe conduct of three weeks, and in 1507 extended by a ban zone ('Bannmeile') of 15 miles around the city and a staple. Since the 16th century the fair of St Peter and Paul in Naumburg was aligned with the Leipzig fair calendar (see Naumburg (Saale)).
Toll_Description: A special safe conduct in Leipzig was in place eight days before and after the fairs. During this time, the citizens of Leipzig had to pay the fees as well, where they would normally be exempted. In 1558 the safe conduct, including the secondary station in Taucha, is pawned off by the Elector to the council of the town of Leipzig. The council was supposed to maintain roads, paths, dams, ditches, bridges and footbridges from the revenues.
Staple_Description: The staple requirements appears first in the market privileges of Emperor Maximilian in 1507. However, other records indicate that the staple existed before, e.g. citizens were forbidden to trade outside of town within a designated zone. Such prohibitions are already known from the last decades of the 15th century. The staple was valid within a protected zone ('Bannmeile') of 15 miles around the town. Confirmed by Pope Leo X in 1514 and renewed in 1521 by Emperor Charles V. A complete enforcement of the staple was, however, not possible: conflicts with Erfurt, Halle, Magdeburg, Dresden and Prina ensued, all of whom wished to keep their staple rights. In the Seven Years’ War the Leipzig staple finally deteriorated.

name: Litoměřice
Toll_Description: A toll in Litoměřice is first mentioned in 993; it was probably a toll on the Elbe river. A tariff from 1057 shows that it was levied according to the size of the vessel. It was owned by the duke of Bohemia, and half of it was given to the church of St Stephen in Litoměřice, as confirmed in 1218. A salt toll is mentioned in 1377. Merchants from Pirna reported in 1577, that the water toll tariffs in Litoměřice had tripled within eight years. In the early 17th century, two tolls existed in town: one belonging to the emperor, the other to the city.
