Staple_Description: A staple is first mentioned in 1306. In 1325 King John of Bohemia recognised the right of compulsory exchange; in 1341 exceptions were made for ships from Ústi nad Labem carrying fresh fish and lead, and in 1351 for ships from Melnik, who carried grain and other wares down the Elbe or salt towards Litoměřice. In 1391 the staple rights were confirmed, but in 1409 the staple obligations were abolished for grain in return for a duty. For other commodities, the staple remained in place.

name: Leinefelde
Settlement_Description: First mention of the village in 1227. Leinefelde was elevated to town in 1961.

name: Roager
Settlement_Description: The village of Roager was first mentioned in 1291, but is significantly older. The parish church is from either the 12th or 13th century.

name: null
Harbour_Description: Narva developed as a significant harbour in the Hanseatic trade with Novgorod, because it was the nearest harbour on the Baltic Sea from Novgorod and was located on the border between Livonia and Russia.

name: Leitzkau
Settlement_Description: In the Early Middle ages the place served as a rally point for armies marching into the East, the earliest mentions stem from records written in Leitzkau to that regard. In 1114 a stone building was erected and Leitzkau was possibly the first makeshift centre of the bishopric of Brandenburg. In 1390 the settlement is referred to as oppidum. <br/> In 1138/39 an order of Premonstratensian Canons was established at the settlement. Beginning at the end of the 14th century, the convent, that didn't earn much property during the Middle Ages, decayed. In 1600, the convent was converted into a Renaissance castle.

name: Lelle
Settlement_Description: A Manor and later an estate that was first mentioned in 1559.

name: Lembruch
Settlement_Description: A castle was erected by the lord of Diepholz around 1275, which was first mentioned in 1305.

name: Lielvārde
Settlement_Description: In 1201, the already existing castle was given as a fief. In 1255, a second castle was built, which was repeatedly occupied by the Teutonic Order. In 1514 the archbishop founded a monastery of St. Anthony.

name: Lemförde
Settlement_Description: A castle in Lemförde is first mentioned in 1316, but probably built around 1248. A charter from 1349 mentions Lemförde for the first time not explicitly as castle, which suggests that at that time, a significant settlement had developed. Lemförde acquired borough ('weichbild') privileges in 1427. The settlement was characterised as "wigbold" in 1457 and "flekken" (borough) in 1530, and as "Städtlein" (small town) in 1624.
Fair_Description: in 1694 it is mentioned, that a "Kirchmeße und Kramermarck" (dedication day festival and retail market) had taken place since old times before the Thirty Years' War. It is unclear how far back the fair went, possibly into the 14th century.

name: Lemgo
Settlement_Description: The name Limga is first mentioned as the name of a region in 1005. There existed multiple settlements in the area before a town was founded.
Town_Description: The town of Lemgo was founded around 1190 by the Lords of Lippe. It received town privileges in 1245.
Fair_Description: Lord Simon I of Lippe granted three fairs to the new town ('Neustadt') of Lemgo in 1330, on the Day of St Philip and James and Walburga (1 May), the Exaltation of the Cross (14 September) and St Nicholas (6 December). A weekly market as it already took place in the old town was granted as well. An almanac printed in Neudamm (Dębno) in 1598 mentions two fairs in Lemgo: on Sunday Letare and on St Nicolas.
Toll_Description: A toll of the counts of Lippe is mentioned in Lemgo in 1403, 1405 and 1471.

name: Lemke
Settlement_Description: The village was first mentioned in 1241.

name: Lviv
Settlement_Description: First mentioned in a chronicle for the year 1256.
Toll_Description: Mentioned as toll station in c. 1349, among others for carts and herring.
Staple_Description: Beginnings are unclear. In 1379 a staple for various wares was confirmed, which were guaranteed in a treaty between Lemberg, Waldimir and Luzk. A provision of King Louis of Poland in 1380 stipulated that merchants from Hungary and Poland should offer their wares for sale for 14 days; renewed in 1387 with the addition of salt to the list of goods that should be offered for sale. A privilege of 1444 forbade foreign merchants from travelling east or west via Lemberg; confirmed in the Polish Staple Law of 1565.

name: Zuidbroek
Settlement_Description: Earliest mention of 'Broke' in 1273. Earliest mention of 'Suthabroke' in 1283, in a sixteenth or seventeenth century copy.

name: Rotenburg an der Fulda
Settlement_Description: A castle was built around 1150, and an old town was laid out almost 50 years later. Mentioned in 1197 as 'villicus'.
Town_Description: The town was founded around 1200 and named as such in 1248. 1259 'civitas'.

name: Limbaži
Settlement_Description: A castle was built even before 1318. During the 14th century, a fortified borough ('Hakelwerk') developed between the lake Duhnesee (today: 'Dunezers') and the medieval castle.
Town_Description: The fortified borough ('Hakelwerk') received town rights by Riga in 1385. The town was member of the Hanseatic League. The town had access to the sea due to the tributaries of the river Salis and had its own harbour.

name: Lemsel
Settlement_Description: First mention in 1350. 1428 mention as a knightly manor.

name: Lengerich (Emsland)
Settlement_Description: A settlement was first mentioned in 891.

name: Lennep
Fair_Description: A cattle and horse fair was granted in 1571.
Toll_Description: The Count of Berg levied a land toll in 1371. In 1398, an additional 4 turnosgroschen per foder of wine and 1 turnosgroschen extra per horse had to be paid. In 1495, the annual amount was around 20 guilders.

name: Sappemeer
Settlement_Description: Earliest mention in 1660. The settlement was called after a lake with the same name, which was dredged in 1617-1618.
Harbour_Description: In the 1620s, the Schuitendiep canal was extended to Zuidbroek, where the first ship from Groningen arrived in 1628. Regular barge ('trekschuit') services were offered since 1654 at the latest.

name: Lengröden
Settlement_Description: The manor of Lengröden was first mentioned in 1432.

name: Lengerich (Westfalen)
Settlement_Description: First mentioned in 1147. The settlement was a church village in the county of Tecklenburg. It received town privileges in 1727.
Toll_Description: A toll station of the counts of Tecklenburg is first mentioned in 1441.

name: Lenči
Settlement_Description: The manor and village were first mentioned in 1590.

name: Leschede
Settlement_Description: The place was first mentioned in 1330.

name: Lethe
Settlement_Description: Archaeological excavations showed that a castle was constructed in the first half of the 15th century. Herbord von Dorgeloh is first mentioned as inhabitant in 1471.

name: Leuschentin
Settlement_Description: The village is first mentioned in 1338.

name: Leuvenum
Settlement_Description: Earliest mention dates from the end of the thirteenth century.

name: Levenhagen
Settlement_Description: In 1280, Bishop Hermann von Kammin confirmed the patronage of the church in Levenhagen and the ownership of the village itself to the Eldena monastery.

name: Liepāja
Settlement_Description: Originally a small fishing village 'Liwa', the harbour/port of which was first mentioned in 1253/67. In 1291 there existed 'castrum Lyva'. It was first mentioned as a settlement in 1413. After the settlement was destroyed by Lithuanians in 1418, it was rebuilt and referred to as a market place.

name: Niederfreden
Settlement_Description: First mention of Freden around 1226. The settlement under the castle Lichtenberg consisted of two parts, Nieder- ('lower') and Ober- ('upper') Freden, of which the former is first mentioned separately around 1274. Both villages were merged with Lichtenberg under the name of the castle in 1856/57.

name: Liebenberg
Toll_Description: A toll is mentioned in 1364, when it was moved to Müncheberg. However, this could have been a temporary measure, as Liebenberg is later still mentioned as toll station of the Margraves of Brandenburg, e.g. in 1433, 1456 and 1469.

name: Liebenburg
Settlement_Description: Bishop Siegfried of Hildesheim started the construction of the castle Liebenburg near the settlement Lewe in 1292. It came into the possession of the dukes of Brunswick-Wolfenbüttel in 1523.
Toll_Description: A toll of the bishop of Hildesheim in Liebenburg was cancelled in 1354.

name: Liebenwalde
Settlement_Description: Slavic settlement and castle mound. An Ascanian fortress was built in the beginning of the 13th century. A provost is mentioned in 1244. The settlement is characterised as small town ('Stetichen') in 1449.

name: Lieberose
Settlement_Description: First mentioned in 1272, characterised as oppidum with a castle in 1301.

name: Liepe
Settlement_Description: In 1233 the surroundings of Liepe are mentioned as former Slavic territory. In 1267 two villages of Lipa are mentioned. In 1375 only one of those villages seems to have remained.

name: Lier
Fair_Description: In 1309 (Sept. 8) duke Jan II granted Lier the cattle-staple for Brabant and its cattle-fair. Before this the staple was situated in the village Wespelaar next to Leuven. At first it was foremost a fair for sheeps in connection with the local important drapery. But when the drapery perished in the second half of the 15th century it was tiring changed to a horned cattle-fair, in particular oxen. However there was more and more competition from Diest and Hoogstraten. In 1468 the cattle-fair privilege was confirmed by Charles the Bold but with a yearly payment. In the last quarter of the 15th century some 7000-10000 oxen were traded. In 1567 Guicciardini told that Lier had a famous oxenfair lasting from 'St. Jansmis' (June 24) till 'Martensmis' (Nov. 1) one day per week. In the slaughter-time some 11000-14000 oxen were traded per day.
Staple_Description: In 1309 (Sept. 8) duke Jan II granted Lier the cattle-staple for Brabant and its cattlefair. Before this the staple was situated in the village Wespelaar next to Leuven. In 1485 the staple was moved to Diest by Maximiliaan but in 1498 Lier won a lawsuit. In 1564 (May 20) king Philip II confirmed the staple for oxen. In 1566 Guicciardini told that Lier had a famous oxenfair lasting from 'St. Jansmis' (June 24) till 'St. Martensmis' (Nov. 1) one day per week.

name: Liesborn
Settlement_Description: According to tradition first recorded in the 14th century, the abbey of Liesborn was founded in 799 by Charlemagne. Although it is likely that a settlement indeed existed around this time, the monastery was more probably founded around 855, which is also attested by archaeological finds. It is first mentioned in a charter in 1019. Originally a noble ladies' convent, it was converted into a Benedictine abbey in 1130, that existed until 1803.

name: Linau
Settlement_Description: First mentioned in 1230. In the 13th and 14th century, there was a castle of the knights of Scharpenburg in Linau, who disturbed the land traffic in the region. The castle was destroyed by a coalition of Hamburg, Lübeck, the count of Holstein and the duke of Lauenburg in 1350.

name: Lindau
Settlement_Description: Around 1322, bishop Otto II of Hildesheim erected a new castle in Lindau, where an older castle had existed before. The accompanying settlement was first characterised as borough ('flecken'/'oppidum') in 1496.
Toll_Description: A toll and safe conduct of the duke of Brunswick was mentioned in 1477, when a citizen of Schwarzburg had circumvented it. The toll might go back to the foundation of the castle around 1322. It still existed in the 17th century.

name: Linden (Wolfenbüttel)
Settlement_Description: First mentioned in 1007. Archaeological finds suggest that a settlement existed already in the 1st to 4th century.
Toll_Description: Toll of the dukes of Brunswick. A toll collector is first mentioned in 1316; the toll was pawned in 1349. It is moved to the Gotteslager in Wolfenbüttel before 1630.

name: Lindena
Settlement_Description: First mention in 1234 and property of the Cistercian monastery of Dobrilugk.

name: Lindenau
Settlement_Description: First mention of a Didericus of Lindinouwe in 1182.

name: Lindlar
Toll_Description: The Duke of Berg levied a land toll in 1470. Tariffs are not known. In 1470/72 the toll was leased out for 20 mark a year.

name: Lingen
Settlement_Description: Lingen came into existence near a ford in the Ems near the current Altenlingen ('Old Lingen'). The settlement is first mentioned in 1150 as "Aldenlingen", which indicates that already at that time, the centre of the settlement had moved to the new Lingen further south. A first mention as "Liinga/Linga" in 975 is very questionable.
Town_Description: Lingen acquired toll, mint, market and court privileges in 1227 and was built as a planned town. In 1306, the settlement was first mentioned as 'civitas'. Town privileges were granted in 1401.
Toll_Description: Lingen received toll privileges in 1277. A toll in Lingen is also attested in accounts of duke Frederick of Schleswig-Holstein from ca. 1500.

name: Linsburg
Settlement_Description: The settlement is characterised as "villa" in 1203. Duke Erich of Calenberg built a hunting castle in the 16th century, where there already existed a hunting lodge before.

name: Linse
Settlement_Description: First mentioned in the 8th or 9th century.
Toll_Description: A toll in Linse is mentioned in toll lists of the years 1539, 1540 and 1587.

name: Linum
Settlement_Description: Became property of the bishops of Havelberg in 1294.

name: Martenshoek
Settlement_Description: Earliest mention in 1652, in a copy dating from 1768.

name: Lindow (Neubrandenburg)
Settlement_Description: First mentioned in 1298. An inn in Lindow is mentioned in 1584.

name: Linne
Settlement_Description: Linne is first mentioned in an eleventh-century copy of a text dating from 943.
Town_Description: Linne developed into a town in the period 1180-1225. It was granted town rights some time between 1255 and 24 November 1258 by Elisabeth of Sprimont, lady of Linne. The development of Linne into a town was halted before the end of the thirteenth century.
Fair_Description: Prior to 1294 Linne possibly already had a fair.

name: Lipiany
Settlement_Description: Developed near a Pomeranian castle, administrative centre of the land Lippehne.
Town_Description: Mentioned as civitas (town) since 1302, but only named oppidum (borough) in 1337. Nothing is known about town privileges.

name: Lochem
Settlement_Description: Earliest mention dates from 1059, in a falsified charter of ca. 1180-1190.
Town_Description: Town privileges granted on 9 July 1233, by Otto II, count of Guelders and Zutphen.
Fair_Description: Before 1294 two fairs are known here. In 1564 king Philip II granted Lochem a weekly market on Friday and two fairs: 1) Saturday before Judica (=Sunday before Eastern), 2) Saturday before St.Victor (Oct. 10).

name: Lubast
Settlement_Description: The village is first mentioned in 1356.

name: Lippstadt
Settlement_Description: Lippstadt was founded by the counts of Lippe around 1184 as a planned town on the shore of the Lippe river.
Town_Description: Lippstadt must have been granted town privileges after Soest model around 1220.
Fair_Description: A confirmation of town privileges from 1244 included the right to hold a fair, including market freedom of two days before and after the fair. The oldest fair probably took place on St Martin's Day. In 1553, a fair that formerly took place on 9 September was moved to the second day of Christmas and in 1574 to Innocent's Day. In 1580, four fairs are attested: next to the two already mentioned, there were fairs on St Michael and Thursday after Sexagesima. Given the fact that the fairs took place in autumn and winter, it is likely that mainly agricultural products and cattle were traded there.
Toll_Description: Although an export tax on corn existed since 1366, the town acquired a privilege to levy a toll on merchant's commodities only in 1449. Moreover, in 1481 a toll was introduced on cattle sold in town and on carriages passing the bridges, to cover the maintenance of the town walls and the bridges.

name: Leśnica
Toll_Description: A toll is mentioned in 1266 and 1338.

name: Lißdorf
Settlement_Description: First mention in the tithe register of Hersfeld monastery from 860-890.

name: Lisse
Settlement_Description: Earliest mention in 918-948, in a eleventh century copy. Next mention in 1198.

name: Listerfehrda
Settlement_Description: The village is first mentioned in 1395.

name: Littel
Settlement_Description: The place was first mentioned in 1350.

name: Lohu
Settlement_Description: In the years 1216 and 1220 the place was a camp for soldiers from Riga. The nearby 'Lone' Castle, around which the village developed, was conquered in 1223.

name: Löbejün
Settlement_Description: First mentioned in 961. In the 10th century it was the centre of a castle district ('Burgward'), around which the village developed.
Town_Description: Elevated to town by archbishop Günther in 1430.
Fair_Description: From 1562 three fairs were organised in Löbejün: on Tuesday after Judica, Tuesday before the Visitation of Mary and Tuesday before St Simon and Jude's Day.

name: Bad Lobenstein
Settlement_Description: Lobenstein is first mentioned as part of the name Otto de Lobenstein in 1250. The castle was possibly built by the lords of Lobdeburg.
Town_Description: Citizens ('civibus') are mentioned in 1278 and the settlement is characterised as town in the same year. A burgomaster and council are attested in 1411. The oldest known town statutes from 1500 are based on the town law of Gera and were confirmed in 1543, 1568, 1593 and 1657. They also contain market privileges. In 2005 the addition "Bad" was added to the name.

name: Lübbecke
Settlement_Description: Originally a Saxon settlement, first mentioned in 775.

name: Loburg
Settlement_Description: The settlement developed near the castle and the castle district ('Burgward'), which were constructed for the control of the Ehle crossing. In 1246 the village was referred to as oppidum.
Town_Description: 1246 the town was mentioned in a record, it can be assumed it already held the status of town in 1207, when a farmstead is mentioned in its direct vicinity. In 1558 a council is mentioned.

name: Löcknitz
Settlement_Description: Early Slavic settlement with a fortification at the crossing of Randow river (originally called Lochnitza until ca. 1700, first mentioned in 1216), became a German castle around 1400. The settlement is first mentioned as villa in 1267.
Toll_Description: Toll station of the territorial lords; Prenzlau was exempted from the land and water toll in 1348.

name: Ten Boer
Settlement_Description: Earliest mention in a copy dating from 1301.

name: Koluvere
Settlement_Description: A bishop's place was built in the 13th century (around 1227) and was converted into a castle in 1424. The village developed next to the castle.

name: Lohe
Settlement_Description: At the first mention of the settlement, seven free farmers are mentioned.

name: Lohe (Uetersen)
Settlement_Description: First mentioned in 1285; characterised as "villa" in 1385.

name: Löhsten
Settlement_Description: The village is first mentioned in 1251.

name: Lohusuu
Settlement_Description: The fishing village probably already existed in the 15th century, but was only mentioned in 1601.

name: Loitz
Settlement_Description: First settlement probably a Slavic village with a fortification. First mention in 1242 when a town was founded.
Town_Description: Detlev of Gadebusch granted Lübeck town law in 1242, Lord Witzlaw II of Rügen ratified the privileges in 1299.

name: Lommel
Settlement_Description: Earliest mention in 1227. In 1422 Lommel obtained market-rights for a weekly market. Around 1420 the duke of Brabant granted the income from the weigh-house to the citizens militia.

name: Löningen
Settlement_Description: The settlement is first mentioned in 1149 as farm of the monastery Corvey. Probably the St Vitus church already existed in the 9th century. The settlement became a borough ('wiek') or minor town ('minderstadt') in the 14th century.

name: Lünzen
Settlement_Description: First mentioned in a register of the diocese of Verden between 1237 and 1246.

name: Loon op Zand
Toll_Description: Prior to 1230 a toll of Venloon must have been property of Dirk van Altena as part of his seigniory of Drunen. In 1232 he sold the toll to the duke of Brabant. In 1387 the lord of Loon op Zand only obtained the right to levy a toll on the traffic passing his newly acquired seigniory. The toll station was moved several times during time. That was due to political changes but also as a result of the damming up of the river Maas and the extraction of peat (the digging of the socalled Loonse 'turfvaart' -canal for peat-transport- and the rise of the region Langstraat).The Hanseatic settlement ('Kontor') in Bruges complained about a new toll in Loon op Zand in 1468.

name: Lopau
Settlement_Description: A Ludolfus from Lopau is first mentioned in a Lüneburg town register in 1293. The village consisted of three farms. It was abandoned in the 1970s to make place for a military training area.

name: Lößnig
Settlement_Description: First mention in 1040, mention as a manor in 1156-68, mention as a knightly manor since 1445/47.

name: Lossow
Settlement_Description: A bronze-age rampart was abandoned around 500 BC. Around 800 AD a Slavic settlement developed, at the end of the 10th century a small Polish castle was erected.

name: Giżycko
Settlement_Description: House of the Teutonic Order was mentioned in 1340, the first settlement from the first half of the 15th ct. grew into a 'Zinsdorf', craftsmen began settling in the 16th ct., which soon became a market borough.
Town_Description: Founding documents were signed by duke Johann Sigismund of Prussia in 1612, they features Kulm town law

name: null
Bridge_Description: The bridge was probably completed along with the town walls and gates around 1320, to allow entrance to the town. The bridge connects to the Veenpoort.

name: Leuven
Settlement_Description: Earliest mention in 884, in an eleventh-century copy. Next mention in 1015 is a forgery from the first quarter of the twelfth century. Next mention in circa 1050, is in a late eleventh century copy.
Fair_Description: A wel attended fair in Leuven is mentioned in a chronicle written by a canon of the abbey in Ninove in 1152.
Toll_Description: Headquarter of the Brabantse (land)toll. A tariff of the 'old' toll of the duke of Brabant and the old 'geleide' (conduct) of goods passing through the town to be paid by people from outside of Brabant, is partly older then 1287 when Gorcum was freed of it. The part of the tariff called 'new' toll must be dated before 1303. This tariff is edited, together with later 15th-17th century versions. In 1479 a toll collector is mentioned. In 1523 (June 1) this tariff was renewed from a board hanged on the wall of the 'tolkamer' (toll-office) of Leuven which was 80-100 years old and is called old 'geleide' or 'nuwen ' (new) toll of Brabant.

name: Lübben
Settlement_Description: Lübben developed out of a German or Slavic settlement along the main trade route to Prussia and Poland.
Town_Description: A foundation charter is missing. The settlement was mentioned as urbs around 1150 and stood under the protection of the burgrave, who was first mentioned in 1208. The Magdeburg town law was granted in ca. 1220.
Toll_Description: The town acquired the right to levy a toll on foreign commodities in 1497.

name: Lübbenau
Settlement_Description: First mention around 1301. The settlement is characterised as borough ('oppidum') in 1315. A castle is mentioned in 1319. A formal elevation to town status is not probable.

name: Lübberstedt
Settlement_Description: First mentioned in a register of the diocese of Verden from ca. 1252. According to a register from 1563/4, the village consisted of 7 farms and 1 cottage.

name: Lübberstorf
Settlement_Description: The village is first mentioned in 1235.

name: Lübbow
Settlement_Description: First mentioned in 956. The village consisted of 7 farms in 1450.

name: null
Harbour_Description: The character of the medieval harbour is unknown. A pier was first documented in the 17th century, but is probably much older. The harbour was frequently used by Hanseatic ships, for example from Lübeck in 1399.

name: Manker
Settlement_Description: The village is first mentioned in 1365.

name: Lubin
Toll_Description: Duke Johann of Silesia moved the toll of Prochowice to Lubin in 1324.

name: Lublin
Toll_Description: Mentioned as toll station in c. 1349, with tariffs for horses, cloth and other commodities.
Staple_Description: The stipulation that Russians and Lithuanians could not travel via Lublin when they headed westwards is first noted in an agreement between Gdansk and Krakow in 1493; confirmed in the Polish Staple Law of 1565.

name: Lübow
Settlement_Description: The village is first mentioned in 1219.

name: Lübsche Burg
Settlement_Description: Farm and watchtower at the point where the street between Lübeck and Wismar crossed the Wismar defensive enclosure ('landwehr'). First mentioned in 1363.

name: Lübz
Settlement_Description: First mentioned in 1224, the nearby castle Eldenburg in 1308. It was originally inhabited by Slavs, later by Germans.
Town_Description: Could not have been made a town before 1456. Lübz is first mentioned as a town in 1506 when the privileges were endorsed.

name: Lüchow
Settlement_Description: Castle of unknown age. In 1144, a count of Lüchow is first mentioned, the settlement itself in 1158.
Fair_Description: A market is first mentioned in 1395. According to a register of the department of Lüchow and Warpke (between 1548 and 1574), two fairs were held annually in Lüchow, on Oculi and Exaltation of the Holy Cross.
Toll_Description: Already in 1191, a water toll is mentioned in nearby Plate. In 1435, the fee for safe conduct for citizens of Salzwedel is set to the same amount of Bergen and Bodenteich. A register of the Lüchow district of 1548-1574 mentions that citizens of Lüneburg and Wustrow are exempted from toll in Lüchow, as well as those from Dannenberg partly during fairs in their home town. Toll was levied on water and road traffic, among others on wood, pots, vegetables, fish, horses and cattle. Toll fees are known from the 16th century (StAB).

name: Lucienvorde
Settlement_Description: The village existed since the 9th century (first mentioned between 826 and 876), but was abandoned in the 15th century. The village church, dedicated to St Stephen, remained and was renewed as St Peregrinus in 1596 and demolished in 1829.

name: Lürschau
Settlement_Description: First mentioned in the Heimskringla in the 12th century.

name: Luckau
Settlement_Description: A castle with a church settlement existed around 1200, a German market settlement came into being before 1250. First mentioned  in 1276.
Town_Description: The town was a German foundation before 1250. It is first mentioned as civitas in 1297. The Luckau town law was adapted from Magdeburg town law.
Staple_Description: In 1382 the town received staple privileges for all commodities. It principally served to strengthen the control the town exercised over its surroundings.

name: Luckenwalde
Settlement_Description: Traces of habitation from the Roman imperial age, later Slavic settlement. A German castle is first mentioned in 1216. In 1285 the settlement is characterised as borough ('oppidum'), when it became property of Zinna monastery.
Town_Description: In 1430 town-like privileges are granted. In 1471, a mayor, a council and councillors are mentioned, as well as a town hall in 1480. However, Luckenwalde was never granted town rights.
Fair_Description: In 1562 two fairs are granted to Luckenwalde, which probably held more regional meaning. Another fair is added in 1678.

name: Løgumkloster
Settlement_Description: A Cistercian abbey founded in the 1170s. The monastery was dissolved in the middle of the 16th century as a result of the Danish Reformation.

name: Lühnde
Settlement_Description: The church of Lühnde was mentioned in 1117.

name: Luko
Settlement_Description: The village is first mentioned in 1307/52.

name: Liège
Fair_Description: A market toll is mentioned in 1250. In 1339 two fairs are known, each during an octave (8 days): on the birth of St. Lambert (Sept. 24) and with the feast of his translation (of his relics) (April 28). In 1350 the two fairs are combined by the bishop into one fair in the period Sept. 24-Oct. 1.
Staple_Description: In 1369 the salt-staple is situated here.

name: Schlüchtern
Settlement_Description: Originated near a monastery founded around 880. The settlement is called in 993. In 1278 already an independent place, in 1550 and 1572 still mentioned as 'Flecken'.
Town_Description: First mentioned as a town in 1562.

name: Lünen
Settlement_Description: A church is mentioned in 1018, around which the settlement developed.
Town_Description: It is unknown when the oldest town privileges were granted. A market is mentioned in 1262, a law court and council in 1265 and a town seal in 1299.
Toll_Description: The Count of Dortmund levied a land toll before 1335/41. From 1347, the toll fell to the town of Dortmund. In 1347, 2 denarii per barrel of wine and 1 denar per horse had to be paid. Annual revenues are not known. In 1195, a market toll in Lünen is also mentioned.

name: Lüsen
Settlement_Description: First mentioned in 1360. In 1450 the village consisted of 6 farms and a cottage.

name: Luso
Settlement_Description: The village is first mentioned in 1307.

name: Lütau
Settlement_Description: The place was first mentioned in 1230.
Toll_Description: The duke of Saxony-Lauenburg levied a road toll for the maintenance of the road in Lütau, which led to complaints from Lübeck and other towns in 1466, 1486 and 1503, who claimed that the toll should only be levied if it would actually lead to improvement of the road.

name: Lutter am Barenberge
Settlement_Description: The place was first mentioned in 1000 as "Lutterun". A castle of the bishop of Hildesheim probably already existed around this time, which was often-contested throughout the centuries between the bishop of Hildesheim and the duke of Brunswick-Lüneburg. It was finally acquired by the latter in 1523, who made it an administrative seat; the settlement became a borough ('flecken').

name: null
Toll_Description: A bridge toll appears in accounts of the district ('amt') Voigtsberg from 1447 onwards.
Bridge_Description: A bridge toll appears in accounts of the district ('amt') Voigtsberg from 1447 onwards.

name: Lütte
Toll_Description: Secondary station of safe conduct ('Nebengeleit') of the district ('Amt') Belzig, where it first appears in the accounts in 1489, with minor revenues. A separate "garlic safe conduct" ('Knoblauchgeleit') in Lütte is mentioned from 1527 onwards.

name: Maasland
Settlement_Description: Ealiest mention in 918-948, in a eleventh century copy. Next mention in 1083, in a falsification from circa 1125.
Toll_Description: In 1454 known as an outpost of the toll of the count of Holland at Geervliet.

name: Maassluis
Settlement_Description: First mentioned in 1367. Maassluis originated at a lock ('sluis') in the sea dike around the Maasland region. Maassluis was elevated to town rank on 26 August 1814 by William I, king of the Netherlands.
Ferry_Description: A ferry to Brielle is first attested in 1365.
Harbour_Description: Maaslandsluis was part of Maasland. In the 16th century already some fishermen lived near the lock, at the end of this century this was a fast growing community. In 1555 harbour-heads and beacons were made for the fishermen. The Estates of Holland saw this harbour as an important chain in the traffic from Holland to Voorne and Zeeland via the ferry to Brielle. As a result the lock was fortified in 1571 (a 'schans' was made) against attacks by the Beggars. In 1614 the Estates gave permission to levy a tax during 24 year on fish in order to enlarge the harbour and erect a crane. With socalled 'hoekers' (boats) cod was caught. Usually some 50 boats for haddock  were harboured here but in 1636 only 10 as a result of hijackers from Dunkirk.

name: Maarheeze
Settlement_Description: Earliest mention in 1223, in a thirteenth century copy.

name: Mahlerten
Toll_Description: A toll in Mahlerten is first mentioned in 1371. Hildesheim complained in 1459, that a toll was levied on wagon cargoes, which had not been levied before.

name: Mahlsdorf
Settlement_Description: First mention in 1345, it housed two knightly manors.

name: Mainz
Settlement_Description: By the end of the 1st century BC, Mainz was already serving as a Roman camp. First written evidence from 44 AD as 'Mogontiacum'.
Town_Description: Mainz was first referred to as a 'civitas' in 297 AD. In late Roman times, Mainz was the capital of a Roman province and served as a royal court under the Frankish rule. From 1244 to 1462 Mainz was a free imperial town.
Staple_Description: Beginnings are unclear; first documentary mention of a staple comes from the 1470s, including obligation to exchange and offer wares for sale; recognised by the emperor in 1486 and official confirmed in 1495. A tightening of the staple in 1534 led to conflict with the Count Palatine from 1542. During the Thirty Years’ War the staple was suspended, but was back in force by 1641 at the latest. The staple was dissolved in 1831 with the Rhine Shipping Act.

name: null
Toll_Description: The regulations of safe conduct from 1513 also specify the toll on the Elbe, while the account books from 1444 to 1545 provide annual revenues for the toll. Returning and loaded boats were exempt from the toll in Wittenberg. Furthermore, the regulations of safe conduct do not mention rafts, which gives Wittenberg the impression of being a start or end point for trade within the electorate of Saxony. The river toll is also mentioned in four accounts of the skipper Gottfried Kleeditz from Pirna from 1671 to 1674.

name: Malburgen
Settlement_Description: The hamlet was first mentioned in 1118, in a possibly falsified copy from the 13th century.

name: Maldegem
Settlement_Description: Earliest mention in ca. 930, in a copy from the mid-11th century.

name: Mansfeld
Settlement_Description: Estate given to the archbishopric of Magdeburg by Fulda monastery (MGH OII no. 64, S. 74-77). This record probably refers to Klostermansfeld, which held most of the surrounding estates.
Town_Description: Mentioned as "vallis Mansfeld" in the Halberstädter Archdiakonalsmatrikel from 1400. In 1408 it is known to have been surrounded by walls. It must have owned town and market rights before that though.
Fair_Description: The counts of Mansfeld bestow a cattle- and two annual fairs upon the city.

name: Mariakerke
Settlement_Description: Earliest mention in the ninth century, in a copy dating from 941.

name: Mariaweiler
Toll_Description: The Duke of Jülich levied land toll in 1571. A first mention around 1431 could be refuted. Tariffs and revenues are not known.

name: Marienau
Settlement_Description: The gamekeeper's settlement Ouhagen came into existence in the 13th century; its pilgrimage chapel acquired an indulgence in 1298. In 1310, the Carmelite monastery Marienau was founded here; abolished in 1565.

name: Alūksne
Settlement_Description: The castle was built by Burkhard von Dreyleben on an island. A settlement developed soon afterwards and was referred to as a fortified borough ('Hakelwerk') in 1516/34.

name: Marienburg
Settlement_Description: A castle was constructed by the bishop of Hildesheim in 1346-1349.
Toll_Description: The bishop of Hildesheim started levying a wine toll in Marienburg around 1439.

name: Marienfelde
Settlement_Description: In 1375 the settlement can be found in the property of the Knights of St. John of Jerusalem, before had been in the property of the Order of the Temple. The area had been settled in the Bronze age and by Germanic peoples but remained unsettled during Slavic times. In 1435 it was given to Berlin-Cölln together with Tempelhof.

name: Schwelm
Settlement_Description: Mentioned around 900. Called 'villa' or 'curtis' around 950. The settlement grew up at the church, mentioned in 1085, and was granted market privileges in 1493.
Town_Description: The town rights were first granted in 1496, but were withdrawn in 1501 after complaints from the peasantry. In 1590 town rights were granted again.

name: Schwerte
Town_Description: In 1367 the town was given expanded city rights, but was fortified as early as 1242.

name: Marienhafe
Settlement_Description: Marienhafe is mentioned in the law of the region Brokmerland from 1300 as 'wic', which characterised a settlement with special legal protection during market times. The church was built in the 13th century. The village had access to the sea from 1362 at the latest, although the bay silted up again later.

name: Kwidzyn
Town_Description: The Landmeister of the Teutonic Order Hermann Balke founded the town Marienwerder in 1233 with Kulm town law. The privileges were renewed in 1336 and 1505.

name: Marienwohlde
Settlement_Description: The settlement was originally called Pezeke, first mentioned in 1230. After the Bridgettine monastery Marienwohlde, founded in 1412, moved to Pezeke, the settlement became known after the monastery. The monastery became a local pilgrimage destination in the 15th century. After destruction of the monastery in 1534, the nuns resided in Lübeck. The monastic properties were secularised by the duke of Saxony-Lauenburg in 1558.

name: Märkisch Buchholz
Settlement_Description: The castle Buchholz is first mentioned in 1301, the adjoining settlement in 1336, in 1346 as parish. Mentioned as a town in 1449, but later only borough ('Stedlein' in 1518 and 'Flecklein' in 1554). Market privileges were granted in 1579. Town right was not granted until the modern period.
Toll_Description: In 1449 and 1494 a toll and safe conduct are mentioned in Märkisch Buchholz. The lords ('Schenken') of Landsberg, who resided on castle Teupitz, owned the land toll in Teupitz, as well as the bridge and dam tolls in Königs Wusterhausen and Märkisch Buchholz.

name: Mirosławiec
Settlement_Description: Probably founded as town without pre-existing settlement.
Town_Description: The Brandenburg town law was most likely granted in 1303. Further privileges were granted in 1314 by the brothers Heinrich and Johann von Wedel. These were endorsed in 1565.

name: Markkleeberg
Settlement_Description: First mention as manor in 1212, since 1515 mention as knightly manor.

name: Markoldendorf
Settlement_Description: Near the settlement Oldendorf, of which the church is first mentioned in 1142, a market settlement was founded on the opposite shore of the Ilme river in the 13th century, which was called Markoldendorf. The regional court was moved before 1395 to the new settlement, where the courts took place until the late 16th century. Markoldendorf was made into a borough ('flecken') and fortified in 1637.

name: Geisa
Settlement_Description: Abbot Bertho II. of Fulda founded the market settlement next to the old settlement and had it fortified.
Town_Description: Elevated to town in the first half of the 14th century. The town rights were probably similar to the town rights in Fulda.

name: Wittenburg
Settlement_Description: Originally one of three castle districts of the Polabian territory, since the middle of the 12th century probably occupied by Germans. A district of Wittenburg is mentioned in 1154, an adjoining church village in 1194.
Town_Description: Founded by the counts of Schwerin with Lübeck town privileges, first mentioned as town in 1226. The privileges have been endorsed multiple times afterwards.

name: Abbekerk
Settlement_Description: Earliest mention in circa 1312. In 1414, Abbekerk, Lambertschaag, Twisk and Midwoud were granted town rights by William VI, count of Holland. Together, these settlements formed the ‘stede’ Abbekerk. These settlements, however, never developed an urban character. The granting of town rights was part of an administrative reorganization in which a number of smaller settlements were granted town rights in order to provide them with a certain degree of self-government which replaced the need for the count of Holland's bailiffs ('baljuws'). The settlements kept their own separate settlement governments. The stede lost its town privileges in 1426. These were temporarily restored in 1436 and 1452. In 1456, the restoration of the privileges was made permanent.

name: Lutherstadt Wittenberg
Settlement_Description: Originally a fishing village from the 11th or 12th century, first mentioned in 1187.
Town_Description: Duke Albrecht II granted town rights in 1293. Wittenberg was the residence of the Ascanian dukes in the 14th century. In 1317 councillors, a mayor and a citizenry appear in the records.
Toll_Description: First mention of a toll in 1423 in a certificate from duke Friedrich the strident to duchess Barbara, widow of elector Rudolf III. The safe conduct in Wittenberg shows the high amount of trade traffic from north to south and east to west. The regulations of safe conduct also settle the tolls on the Elbe and the bridge toll, while the account books from 1444 to 1545 further mention income from the ferry and cattle tolls. Regulations of safe conduct remain from 1513. Secondary stations of safe conduct existed in Kemberg, Schmiedeberg, Elster, Marzahna, Eckmannsdorf, Mellnsdorf and Ogkeln.
Staple_Description: In 1415 King Sigismund gave Duke Rudolf of Saxony staple privileges in his castle and city of Wittenberg; this privilege was confirmed by King Friedrich II for the Dukes Friedrich and Wilhem in 1444. Staple rights were again confirmed in 1478, but proved difficult to enforce.

name: Maszewo
Settlement_Description: A castle borough with a church was mentioned in 1233. A Slavic castle mound  vanished before 1334.
Town_Description: Already mentioned as borough ('oppidum') in 1274. The newly founded settlement received Magdeburg town privileges in 1278 from bishop Duke Hermann von Gleichen of Kammin. In 1286 Lübeck town law was granted. It has been mentioned as civitas since 1289. The privileges were endorsed in 1501 by Duke Bogislaw X.

name: Mątwy
Toll_Description: A toll in Mątwy at the crossing of the Notec river is already mentioned in the first half of the 13th century.

name: Maua
Settlement_Description: First mention in 1259. The seal of Maua shows a ferryman, which suggests that there used to be a ferry at the Saale ford near the village.

name: Mechelen
Fair_Description: In 1409 (Apr. 15) the duke granted two free fairs as of the failing economy, each for 8 days. The first on Monday after Asecension and the other on the Monday after Sept. 27 (Cosmas and Damiaen). The French king granted safe conduct for the visitors. In 1415 (Jan. 21) these were however relocated by the emperor to Antwerp. After ten days new fairs were granted: a fair in Spring on Monday before Candlemas (O.L.V. Lichtmis) and a Summermarket on the Monday after july 25 (Jacob and Christoffel). In 1415 emperor Sigismund gave Mechelen the privilege of holding two yearly markets in compensation for the moving of the staple to Antwerp.
Staple_Description: In 1301 and 1358 free fairs for oats, salt and fish were confirmed by the dukes. In 1356 Mechelen was freed from the staple in Antwerp. In 1369 the Antwerp staple for fish, salt and oats was moved to Mechelen. The rights were disputed by Antwerp and Brussels till in the 15th century.

name: Medingen
Settlement_Description: The settlement was originally called Zellensen, first mentioned in 1252. After the Cistercian nun convent Medingen moved here from Altenmedingen in 1336, the settlement took over the name of the monastery. Possessions were lands primarily located near Altmedingen, as well as parts of the Lüneburg saltworks. In 1554 the monastery became a Protestant ladies' foundation.

name: Meerane
Settlement_Description: Castle and castle village of the 12th century, first mentioned in 1174. In the 15th century market settlement.
Town_Description: The village was referred to as oppidum in 1361. In 1565 Georg of Schönburg granted the town bylaws.

name: Meerlo
Settlement_Description: Earliest mention in 1134, in a falsification from circa 1180-1190. Next mention in 1213.

name: Meesiger
Settlement_Description: The village is first mentioned in 1245.

name: Mehderitzsch
Settlement_Description: The village is first mentioned in 1251.

name: Meijel
Settlement_Description: First mentioned in 1303, the settlement Meijel developed around a road through the Peel high moor region and grew into a semi-independent lordship ('vrijheerlijkheid'). The original settlement, known as Luttel Meijel and later Hof, was located near a well of St Willibrord on the border with Deurne. More southerly, a parish church was built around 1425. There were one or more inns in the village.
Toll_Description: A toll of the lord of Meijel on the border between Deurne and Meijel was first mentioned as "Kijeboem" in 1483. The toll station was located a bow shot away from the well of St Willibrord in the area known as Luttel Meijel.

name: Meinerzhagen
Toll_Description: The Count of Mark levied a land toll in 1444. The toll was established on the model of the toll in Lüdenscheid. The tariff was therefore also 3 denarii per draught horse and 1 denar per pack horse.

name: Oulunsuu
Settlement_Description: <b>Inn:</b> An inn was established in Oulunsuu in 1631, and Antti Kiviniemi was appointed as the innkeeper. Many new inns were established in the same year because of clearing and renovating work in the Ostrobothian Coastal Road. In 1640s, Matti Saarela served as the innkeeper.

name: Meißen
Settlement_Description: In the 10th century a German royal castle was constructed, below which a moated castle and a settlement developed. Bishopric since 968.
Town_Description: Foundation of a town probably around the middle of the 12th century. The town right was closely related to the Magdeburg town law.
Fair_Description: The fair on Saturday after Letare was moved from Lommatzsch to Meißen in 1475.
Toll_Description: A toll of the bishop of Meißen is first mentioned in 983. In the regulations of safe conduct of 1547 the fees on the water, by land and for cattle are settled (SHStA Dresden, Loc. 37997 Meißen 9f., Erbbuch des Amtes Meißen 1547, p. 338–339).

name: Delfzijl
Settlement_Description: First mentioned in 1303. Delfzijl originated near three locks built in 1272. The settlement was granted town rights at 7 May 1819 by William I of the Netherlands.
Ferry_Description: A ferry to Emden operated at least from the mid-16th century. In 1584, a Johann Tyen is mentioned, who had been operating the ferry for more than two decades.
Harbour_Description: Delfzijl functioned as the sea harbour for the town Groningen, especially after the Damsterdiep canal connected both places with a waterway in 1424.

name: null
Toll_Description: A bridge toll is mentioned in the account books from 1451 onwards. The high incomes from the bridge toll probably show the close relations between Wittenberg and the surrounding agricultural settlements.
Bridge_Description: The bridge across the Elbe was constructed on orders of Elector Friedrich in 1428.
Ferry_Description: A ferry is mentioned in a certificate from Friedrich the Strident to duchess Barbara, widow of prince electorate Rudolf III, in 1423. The account books from 1444-1545 still mention income from the ferry, although a bridge had been built by that time, so it must have remained in operation alongside the bridge.

name: Melbeck
Settlement_Description: The village was first mentioned in 1296.

name: Klaipėda
Settlement_Description: A Kurish wooden fortress from the early 13th century was conquered by the Livonian Brothers of the Sword in 1252, who built Memelburg castle here.
Town_Description: A town was founded next to the castle in 1253. It acquired Lübeck town privileges in 1258 and Kulm town law in 1475.
Staple_Description: Memel began to oblige merchants from Königsberg to staple their wares in the city from 1522. Princely mandate in 1580 forbade any exports by see; repeated in 1619 and 1622.

name: Melle (Osnabrück)
Settlement_Description: First mentioned in 1169 and characterised as "oppidum" in 1350. Melle received borough ('wigbold') privileges in 1443.
Fair_Description: The borough ('wigbold') privileges of 1443 also contained a market privilege. A fair is explicitly mentioned in 1580. A date is not known.
Toll_Description: A toll is mentioned in the borough privileges of 1443; it is still mentioned in the 1570s.

name: Mellerup (Aabenraa)
Settlement_Description: The village of Mellerup was first mentioned in 1411, but is significantly older. The settlement had no church but was part of the parish of Bjolderup.

name: Mellin
Settlement_Description: First mention in 1360; in 1375 it already is deserted, but the village is mentioned again in 1521.

name: null
Lock_Description: One of seven locks in the Fulda river between Kassel and Hersfeld, which were built by landgrave Moritz of Hesse-Kassel in a campaign to make the Fulda navigable. Regulations from 1613 specify the lock fee at 2 Alben. At each lock, it was checked whether the toll for the cargo had been paid in Kassel.

name: Kemberg
Settlement_Description: Located in a former Slavic area, Kemberg was possibly founded by Flemish colonists between 1150 and 1200. The settlement is first mentioned in 1306. In 1332 a provost is mentioned.
Town_Description: In a charter by duke Rudolf of Saxony from 1346 referred to as "our town". In 1488 the town rights were confirmed.
Toll_Description: Secondary station of safe conduct ('Beigeleit') of Wittenberg. Regulations of safe conduct remain from 1550. Annual revenues are known since 1485.

name: Meppel
Settlement_Description: First mentioned in 1141 (in a early fifteenth-century copy, possibly a falsification). Meppel was granted city rank at 15 March 1809 by Louis Napoléon Bonaparte, king of Holland.
Fair_Description: Since 1460, two fairs took place in Meppel. One of them took place in April, and lasted for 15 days. The second took place around Saint Lambert (17 September). In 1560, this fair was moved up to September 14th.

name: Meußließen
Settlement_Description: First mentioned in 1296-1297. In 1450, the settlement consisted of 3 farms, 1 half farm and a cottage.

name: Meppen
Settlement_Description: Missionary centre for the Emsland, in possession of the monastery Corvey in 834. It was, however, probably founded before 793. The settlement acquired toll and mint privileges in 945, and market rights in 946.
Town_Description: Fortification privileges granted by the bishop of Münster in 1360, extended in 1374. In 1387 the settlement acquired the right to have a court as well.
Fair_Description: From the early 14th century, fairs are mentioned in Meppen, for which Osnabrück merchants received safe conduct. The only consistent fair was that of St Michael, which according to a list of 1440 drew visitors mainly from Frisian territory. In 1497 the main fair is mentioned to be held at St Simon and Jude. Two cattle markets and a weekly market on Wednesday were added in 1482. After their importance had declined, the cattle fairs were re-founded in 1578.

name: Merchtem
Settlement_Description: Earliest mention in circa 1040, in a copy dating from middle of the eleventh century. Next mention in 1117.

name: Weidenpesch
Toll_Description: In 1389, the Archbishop of Cologne levied a fee for safe conduct on land and a land toll. Depending on the load, 2 to 3 alb. fee for safe conduct per horse had to be paid. In 1389/93, the annual yield averaged about 250 mark a year. In 1454 up to 8 alb. per horse had to be paid as land toll. Together with the toll in Lövenich, about 200 guilders could thus be collected. In 1455 Merheim was a secondary toll station of Königsdorf.

name: Märjamaa
Settlement_Description: The parish of Merjama probably already existed at the end of the 13th century.

name: Meriküla
Settlement_Description: Around 1527 a hamlet ('Hof') was built near the village of Koerawerre, which was referred to as 'Merreküll' in 1533.

name: Merseburg
Settlement_Description: First mention of the settlement in the Hersfelder Zehntverzeichnis (HZV A 212, HZV B 243). In the 10th cenutry, Merseburg becomes royal court and in 968 episcopal seat.
Town_Description: The royal privilige of market, coin and toll had to be granted before 981 and was confirmed in 1004. First mention of a council and burghers in 1289. Several privileges and registers are destroyed in a town fire in 1444, the "jurisdiction and freedom" of the town are restored in the same year. A more independent town constitution is achieved only after 1435, since the town was very dependent on the bishops.
Fair_Description: A fair took place until 1323, when a fire destroyed several booths on the market and foreign traders stayed away. It was not re-established, due to the growing influence of the fairs in Leipzig.
Toll_Description: The safe conduct in Merseburg also had special regulations during the time of the fairs in Leipzig; during this time, every passerby had to pay a fee until the fair ended, after that, the regular fees only had to be paid once if one returned in the course of four days.

name: Merzen
Settlement_Description: First mentioned in a document in 977. The settlement was possibly founded in Frankish times.

name: Międzyrzecz
Settlement_Description: One of the oldest settlements of the Land of Poznań, as border fortification often contested. A monastery was most likely founded in 997 and first mentioned in 1005.
Town_Description: Mentioned as civitas (town) in 1248. The oldest known town privilege with Magdeburg town law was issued by the Polish king Kasimir IV in 1485.

name: Meßdorf
Settlement_Description: First mention in a name in 1215; first mention of the village in 1281.

name: Mäo
Settlement_Description: The hamlet ('Hof') of the Teutonic Order was mentioned in 1558.

name: Meyenburg (Brandenburg)
Settlement_Description: A castle with adjoining borough ('Flecken') is first mentioned in 1285.
Town_Description: Founding of a town probably around 1300, first mentioned as town in 1332. Official town privileges were only granted in 1809.
Toll_Description: Meyenburg is mentioned as station of safe conduct in 1334, and as toll station in 1585.

name: Middelaar
Toll_Description: A toll on sailing ships from the count of Gelre on the Meuse is found in Middelaar (Mook). Accounts are preserved for a small range of years between 1390-1405. The accounts for 1394/5 are edited. A tariff for this toll and the one in Ravenstein dated 1394 is edited.  In 1394 the duke of Gelre and Julich gave the citizens of Roermond toll-exemption regarding the halff of this toll and the one in Mook, with a tariff (edited). The toll on sailing ships amounted to 650 scild. There was also a road-toll at Mook which amounted to 60 guilders or 32 scild.

name: Międzyrzec Podlaski
Toll_Description: A secondary toll station is attested in the second half of the 16th century.

name: Stříbro
Toll_Description: A pavement toll ('Pflastermaut') for travellers is mentioned in 1382.

name: Milicz
Toll_Description: A toll in Milicz is first mentioned in 1249.

name: Moers
Toll_Description: The Count of Moers levied a land toll here before 1317, which was, however, referred to as road toll. Rates and revenues are not known.

name: Miltenberg
Settlement_Description: The place was mentioned for the first time in 1225, but it is much older.
Town_Description: In the 13th century the settlement developed into a town.
Staple_Description: Emperor Charles IV supposedly gave the town staple privileges in 1368, but the charter has been lost. Merchants from Nuremberg were obliged to carry their goods to Miltenburg by land and load them into ships there. As the Nurembergers sometimes shipped their wares to Bamberg and Würzburg under fake marks, an agreement was reached between the Archbishop of Mainz and the city of Nuremberg, and in 1521 ships from Bamberg were held and unloaded in Miltenberg. In 1539 the staple was disestablished in return for Nuremberg credit, but was installed again in 1547. Emperor Charles V stipulated in a law of 1555 that the staple should be disestablished. In 1562 the agreement reached stipulated that Nurembergs could enjoy free shipping rights in return for a yearly payment of 200 golden gulden. The Nurembergers were only to load their goods in Bamberg, but from 1685 they could also do the same in Kitzingen and Würzburg. An ordinance of 1818 ended the market and exchange rights for Miltenberg.

name: Mockrehna
Settlement_Description: The village is first mentioned in 1015 in the chronicle of Thietmar of Merseburg.

name: null
Lock_Description: A dam closed off the Delf from the Ems river in 1272, in which three sluices ('zijlen') were constructed.

name: Minden
Settlement_Description: Fishing and shipping settlement near a ford on the Weser river, where a bishopric was founded by Charlemagne around 800. The settlement acquired toll, market and minting privileges in 977.
Town_Description: Minden developed into a town around 1230, with Dortmund town privileges. It is unknown on which date these privileges were exactly granted.
Fair_Description: In the 15th century, three fairs are mentioned in Minden: on the Nativity of the Virgin and St Gorgonius, on St Martin and on Candlemas. Of these fairs, at least the fair of St Martin can probably be traced back to the market and toll privilege of 977. In 1528, the number of fairs was reduced to two. Next to the fair of St Martin, a new fair was held on St Walburga. These fairs still exist today as the Autumn and May fairs.
Toll_Description: Toll privileges were granted in 977; in 1155-1206 the toll is still mentioned, among others in a conflict about tolls with Hameln. Possibly, the toll was levied since the 13th century at the harbour (Schlagde), until it was moved to Petershagen in 1377.
Staple_Description: Staple for corn and timber. Already around 1200, citizens from Hameln were exempted from toll, if they ended their journey in Minden. Skippers on the Werre were obliged in 1457 to offer their commodities on the market in Minden. In 1530, the free transport of firewood was prohibited. In Bremen, complaints that shipments of corn were being withheld in Minden are known from 1532, which led to a centuries-long conflict between both towns. The staple privileges were confirmed by the emperor in 1627, although it was enforced relatively mildly in the 17th century. The staple was finally abolished with the "Weserschifffahrtsakte" of 1823.

name: Jelgava
Settlement_Description: In 1265 a castle was built by the Teutonic Order.
Town_Description: A fortified borough ('Hakelwerk') was mentioned in 1345. Town rights by Riga were granted in 1578.

name: Mittelhausen
Settlement_Description: First mention as propert of Hersfeld monastery in 775-786. Important, interregional judicial court until 1346.

name: Mittenwalde
Settlement_Description: Ascanian castle, likely built on a Slavic castle mound, first mentioned in 1239. A market settlement grew close by, named as a parish and the see of an archdeaconry in 1255.
Town_Description: No mention of an official founding, probably some time after 1240. Mentioned as civitas and stad in 1307. Magdeburg town rights can be assumed since 1430.
Fair_Description: In the 15th and 16th century, three fairs and cattle markets are known in Mittenwalde.
Toll_Description: Toll and safe conduct station. The town Luckau was exempted from the safe conduct in Mittenwalde in 1361. In 1495 a wagoner was accused of circumventing the toll in Mittenwalde. Further mention in 1653.

name: Bad Schmiedeberg
Town_Description: First referred to as civitas in 1350, mention of a town hall in 1379.
Toll_Description: Secondary station of safe conduct ('Beigeleitsstelle') of Wittenberg. Annual revenues are known since 1485. Tariffs are known from regulations of safe conduct from 1550.

name: Mirow (Burg Stargard)
Settlement_Description: Commandry of the Knights of St. John, built in 1226. Since 1587 residency of Duke Karl von Mecklenburg. The settlement acquired borough ('flecken') privileges around 1600.

name: Stangmoseled
Settlement_Description: It is not known when the village of Stangmoseled is first mentioned. The settlement had no church but was part of the parish of Vejstrup Church.

name: Möckern (Magdeburg)
Settlement_Description: First mention in 948 as a castle district that paid tithes to the monastery of St Maurice in Magdeburg. A village developed near the castle.
Town_Description: Town-like settlement since the Middle Ages. If and when town rights were granted is unknown. Since 1375 referred to as town and the settlement enjoyed a certain independence.

name: Madona
Settlement_Description: The manor was mentioned in 1461 as a fief.

name: Mödrath
Toll_Description: 1) From 1389 onwards, a fee for safe conduct and a land toll were levied here. In 1389 and 1401, the Archbishop of Cologne is documented as the owner of the toll. However, the exact ownership situation is unclear. From 1470 the toll fell to the Duke of Brabant. In 1396, 2 to 3 alb. per horse had to be paid, depending on the load. The annual yield in 1389/93 averaged about 442 mark a year. In 1470/71 about 39 guilders could be collected per year, in 1498/99 about 53 guilders. 2) The Duke of Brabant also levied a road toll in 1470. Tariffs are not known. In 1470, 1 gulden 7 alb. were collected. These were used for work on the bridge over the Erft.

name: Moordrecht
Toll_Description: Toll for sailing transport first mentioned in 1250; last mentioned in 1284. It was owned by the duke of Holland. Probably relocated to Gouda before 1325.
Ferry_Description: A ferry between Moordrecht and Gouderak is first mentioned in 1348. In 1402 it was ordained that no other ferry or bridge should be located in between the churches of Haastrecht and Moordrecht without permission of the vassal.

name: Moerkapelle
Settlement_Description: Earliest mention around 1540 on the map of Jacob van Deventer of the province Holland as a small chapel with: 'Moer'.

name: Moryń
Settlement_Description: First mentioned in 1263, a church village existed in 1265. Margrave Otto rebuilt the early 13th-century German castle in 1365, but it was dilapidated by 1399.
Town_Description: Town foundation after German law, mentioned in 1306 and 1360 as civitas. It was supposed to be made into a village before 1433, but the town resisted.

name: Morąg
Settlement_Description: A house of the Teutonic Order was founded around 1280.
Town_Description: The town was founded by the commander of Elbing, Hermann von Öttingen, between 1320 and 1331 with Kulm town rights. The founding documents were renewed in 1331 when the new municipal administrator ('Erbschulz') was installed.

name: Staufenberg
Settlement_Description: First mentioned between 1205 and 1216. At the beginning of the 12th century, a castle was built by the Counts of Ziegenhain. In 1353, two settlement parts, old and new town, are mentioned.
Town_Description: In 1409 it was designated as a town, but it probably became a town in the 14th century. A medieval town charter has not been preserved. It was also walled in and provided with a gate tower in 1401. In 1605, the town rights and freedoms were confirmed by Landgrave Ludwig.

name: Mol
Toll_Description: Deventer complained in 1466 about the levying of a toll in Mol.

name: Möllenbeck (Altmark)
Settlement_Description: First secure mention in 1238; an earlier mention in 1209 cannot be confirmed.

name: Möllenkotten
Toll_Description: The Count of the Mark levied a land toll here in 1466. Tariffs and revenues are not known.

name: Mölln
Settlement_Description: First mentioned in 1188. Mölln developed as a transshipment place on the salt route between Lüneburg and Lübeck. Originally, the settlement was located at the current street Ohlendörp. A planned town was built around the current church from ca. 1200.
Town_Description: Lübeck town privileges granted by king Valdemar II of Denmark in 1202. The town was under the jurisdiction of Lübeck between 1359 and 1683.
Toll_Description: A toll of the counts of Lauenburg was first mentioned between 1220 and 1226. During the time the town was pawned to Lübeck (1359-1683), so was the toll. The toll was especially levied on herring exported from Lübeck.

name: Mannare
Settlement_Description: Around 1500 there was a small estate called 'Mannafer'.

name: Mönchengladbach
Toll_Description: 1) Before 1304, a land toll and a fee for safe conduct were still levied here. In 1304, the Count of Kessel is mentioned as the owner. In 1389 the toll fell to the Duke of Jülich. In 1389/93, 2 to 3 alb. per horse had to be paid, depending on the load. In the years 1389/93, an average of 105 mark per year could be collected. 2) The Duke of Jülich levied a road toll even before 1387. Rates and revenues are not known.

name: Monheim am Rhein
Toll_Description: 1) The Duke of Berg levied a temporary river toll on the Rhine against merchants from Guelders in 1425/26. In 1490/91 the river toll of Düsseldorf was temporarily moved to Monheim. In 1425/26, 24 Turnosgroschen had to be paid for each foder of wine.2) The Count of Berg levied a land toll in 1257. In 1555, 3 alb. had to be paid per foder of wine. Between 1434 and 1440 the toll was mortgaged for 60 guilders a year.

name: Steinheim (Westfalen)
Settlement_Description: First mentioned in 963. Village in the 12th and 13th centuries.
Town_Description: Fortified in 1275 and raised to town.

name: Montfoort
Settlement_Description: Montfoort is first mentioned in 1204. It originated as a market settlement near a castle that was built about 1163.
Town_Description: Montfoort was granted town rights at 28 May 1329 by Zweder I de Rover, Burgrave of Montfoort. By 1353, Montfoort had been fortified with a stone wall and a moat.

name: Liiva
Settlement_Description: Independent parish since the 13th century, which by 1200 already belonged to the 'Doppelgau' of the area with Peude.

name: Moritz
Settlement_Description: First mentioned in 1259. The church belonged to St. Lawrence's monastery in Magdeburg since 1275, in 1306 it was given to Plötzke monastery.

name: Morl
Settlement_Description: Seat of the family of Mordal.

name: Morna
Settlement_Description: A manor, which was in the possession of the Teutonic Order until 1561.

name: Mörsen
Settlement_Description: Around 1280 the settlement consisted of a single farm.

name: Mortsel
Settlement_Description: Earliest mention in 1158, in a fifteenth century copy.  Next mention in 1159.

name: Mosel
Settlement_Description: First mentioned as manor in 1248, mention of several knightly manors in 1552.

name: Neukloster (Mecklenburg)
Settlement_Description: The settlement was originally called Cuszin, first mentioned in 1170. In 1219, the monastery Sonnenkamp (Campus Solis) moved from Parchow to Cuszin; the village thereupon assumed the name Neukloster ('new monastery').

name: Müden (Aller)
Toll_Description: A toll booth is first mentioned in 1543. Around 1800, Müden was an ancillary toll station of Celle.

name: Müden (Örtze)
Settlement_Description: First mentioned in 1022. According to a register from 1563/4, the village consisted of 5 farms and 3 half farms.

name: Müggenburg
Settlement_Description: Farm at the point where the street between Wismar and Rostock crossed the defensive enclosure ('landwehr') of Wismar. First mentioned in 1599.

name: Mühlen Eichsen
Settlement_Description: A mill in the parish Eichsen is first mentioned in 1230. Around it a village developed.

name: Mühlengeez
Settlement_Description: The village is first mentioned in 1306. It developed from a mill near the village Karcheez (=Kirchgeez).

name: Mühlsdorf
Settlement_Description: The village is first mentioned in 1307/1352.

name: Mühlstedt
Settlement_Description: The village is first mentioned in 1282, in a 14th-century copy.

name: null
Toll_Description: There was a toll on the lower bridge.
Bridge_Description: Two bridges led across the Weiße Elster.

name: Mühlberg (Thüringen)
Settlement_Description: First mention in 704 as Mullenberge. Mentioned as property of the archbishop of Mainz in 1137 and 1144, who enfeoffed the village several times.

name: Elster
Settlement_Description: First mentioned in 1187. In 1428 a market is mentioned. Since then referred to as little town ('Städtchen') and borough ('Flecken').
Toll_Description: Secondary station of safe conduct ('Nebengeleit') of Wittenberg in the system of safe conduct around Leipzig. Regulations of safe conduct remain from 1513. Annual revenues are known since 1459/60.

name: Greiz
Settlement_Description: First mention in 1209. First mention of the castle and church of St Mary in Greiz in 1225.
Town_Description: First mention of the town in 1359, although it was probably founded at the end of the 13th century. The oldest town privileges date from 1527, the oldest town law only from 1672.

name: Muiden
Settlement_Description: Van Berkel & Samplonius state that Muiden is first mentioned in an eleventh-century copy of a document dated between 918 and 948. Cox, however, claims that Muiden's earliest mention dates from the period 777-866.
Town_Description: Muiden received several town(-like) privileges from the bishops of Utrecht from 1122 onwards, but an official grant of town rights is unknown.  Muiden is first mentioned as a town in 1258. On 5 June 1817 Muiden is elevated to the rank of city by Royal Decree.
Fair_Description: See sub tolls. From 1308 onwards comital market-tolls at 'Muden' are collected by the steward of  Amstelland. Dates or duration are unknown. In 1565 king Philip II granted a free weekmarket on Wednesday.
Toll_Description: In 953 the emperor gave his probably combined toll on sailing transport and market-toll to the bishop of Utrecht. In 975 the toll was partly relocated to Utrecht. The toll in Muiden is last found in 1244. The toll was situated at the mouth off the river Vecht, connecting the Zuiderzee (formerly: Almere) and Utrecht. In 1320 Muiden obtained toll-exemption from the count of Holland. In 1399 together with Weesp at the tolls of Spaarndam and Beverwijk (which belonged previously to the count of Blois).
Bridge_Description: The oldest preserved account of the steward of Amstelland dated 1308 mentions a toll-bridge across the sluice. In 1403 duke Albrecht granted the right to collect a toll on the bridge with a tariff (carts, charriots and animals) as was previously given by his ancestors. In 1515 this was confirmed by king Charles because the big wooden bridge was burned six or seven years before by the Guelders (and a ferry was installed) with permission to collect a toll on the bridge for ten years, of which he collected a tenth part. In 1525 this was renewed for ten years by the emperor and an agreement with the town of Naarden was made for a fee of 25 guilders yearly. In 1536 it was renewed again for ten years. In 1565 a double toll was granted for a period of 25 year as of poverty.
Harbour_Description: In 1424 Haarlem was freed from paying 'bakengeld' (tax on beacons). Every ship entering the harbour of Muiden had to pay yearly 1 oude vlaamse groot. Exempt were those from towns which had older privileges (like Haarlem). In 1565 the town claimed to be with Vlaardingen the oldest town in Holland and the poorest. The beautiful harbour was only utilised for fishing on the Zuiderzee. The magistrate asked king Philip II permission to levy a.o. double bakengeld during 25 years, but this was denied as of trade interests.

name: Nedlitz
Settlement_Description: Part of the archbishopric of Magdeburg since 963. Village and castle were completely destroyed during the 30-year war.

name: Mülheim (Rhein)
Toll_Description: 1) The Duke of Berg levied a land toll in 1383. In 1383 about 10 gulden, in 1388 about 30 gulden and in 1403 already 100 gulden could be collected per year. In the years 1411, 1414, 1436 and 1444, the respective annual revenue was around 100 gulden. For other revenues, see source. From 1411 to 1478, Brück, Rheindorf and Wiesdorf were secondary toll stations of Mülheim.2) In 1489 the Duke of Berg levied transhipment toll. In 1489/90, 852 mark were collected in about six months. Mülheim was a secondary toll station of Dünnwald.

name: Mülheim an der Ruhr
Toll_Description: The Lord of Broich probably levied a land toll from 1342 onwards. In 1588, however, the toll was confirmed directly for the first time. Earlier mentions may refer to Broich. Tariffs or revenues are not known.

name: Müllrose
Settlement_Description: Slavic fortification close to a German village. First mentioned when it became a town.
Town_Description: Founded by Margrave Otto III around 1260 with Berlin town law, endorsed in 1275. The settlement was later only called opidum (borough), not bigger than a village in 1405.
Toll_Description: A toll station is mentioned in 1473.

name: Liedakkala
Settlement_Description: <b>Inn:</b> Kemi parish constable was located in Liedakkala village from the 1540s onwards. Parish constables (fi: nimismies, sw: länsman) were obliged to keep a tavern in the 16th c.

name: Müncheberg
Settlement_Description: Duke Henry of Silesia gave land to settlers from the Cistercian monastery Leubus around 1224. The settlement was originally known after the monastery, but the name soon changed into Müncheberg.
Town_Description: Acquisition of town privileges in 1245, however still mentioned as oppidum (borough) in 1253 and 1352.
Toll_Description: A toll station of the Margraves of Brandenburg is first mentioned in 1348. In 1364, the toll of Liebenberg was (probably temporarily) moved to Müncheberg.

name: Münchehof
Settlement_Description: The settlement was probably an outpost of the monastery Walkenried.

name: Münchhausen (Hessen)
Settlement_Description: First mentioned around 1130. 1577 still called a village.

name: Munster
Settlement_Description: First mentioned in 1379. The name Munster is probably derived from Monasterium, 'monastery', but there is no evidence for the existence of a monastery in the settlement.

name: Namur
Fair_Description: In 1265 Namur had a fair but likely this was already the case in the 12th century.

name: Münster (Westfalen)
Settlement_Description: The foundation of Münster was related to missionary activities of St Ludger. A monastery was founded in 793, and a diocese in 799. The settlement is first mentioned by name in 819. A market settlement developed next to the cathedral.
Town_Description: Around 1170 Münster was was first characterised as town. Town privileges were granted gradually. After the anabaptist rebellion of 1534/5, town privileges were temporarily suspended, but re-conferred in 1541 and 1553.
Fair_Description: The two most important fairs in Münster were connected with the annual diocesan synods, hence they were called 'Send'. Although the Send as market is first mentioned only in 1525, it was much older. The synods are first mentioned in 889; around 1282/1290 their dates were recorded as the Mondays after Sunday Letare and the day of St Gereon and St Victor - from 1652 on the Tuesdays after these days. According to Kerssenbroick's history of the Anabaptist rebellion (ca. 1570), the fairs started on Monday midnight and lasted three days. Two other five-day fairs took place on St Peter and Paul's Day and St Jerome's Day (Dedication day of the Cathedral), but were less significant than the Send fairs. Especially the fair of St Jerome is not mentioned anymore after 1538/1550 because of its insignificance. Additionally, Kerssenbroick mentions three cattle markets, which were held in front of the St Liudger and Jüdefeld gates.

name: Münsterdorf
Settlement_Description: The small monastery Wellen was founded in the 9th century. The connected settlement became known as Münsterdorf, first mentioned in 1189. The names Wellen and Münsterdorf were used synonymously until the 18th century, Wellen usually in a clerical context or when referring to the manor.

name: Mustla
Settlement_Description: The village was first mentioned in 1241. In 1433 it was owned by the Teutonic Order.

name: Mylau
Settlement_Description: The castle was erected around 1200. A settlement (suburbium) in close proximity to the castle developed in the 12th and 13th century.
Town_Description: Town priviliges were probabaly given in the middle of the 14th century. In 1367 the place was first referred to as 'town'.

name: Roringer Warte
Settlement_Description: The watchtower ('Warte') was part of the enclosure ('Landwehr') of Göttingen, which was probably completed in 1407/08.
Bridge_Description: Next to the tower there was a bridge across a moat.

name: Naarden
Settlement_Description: Naarden is first mentioned in the tenth century. In 1355 the freedom of the town was enlarged 30 roods (ca. 100 meters) 'ter tye wart': in the direction of the Y. In 1396 a bigger enlargement followed at the expense of Muiderberg.
Town_Description: After the demolition in 1351 Naarden got comital permission to be rebuild close to the old place. Town privileges were granted on 10 June 1353 by William V, count of Holland. Before that, Naarden already is mentioned as 'stede' and has several town-like features, such as a 'schepenbank' - a court of aldermen. Naarden (also) received town rank by Royal Decree in 1817.
Fair_Description: In 1377 (March 20) Naarden obtained the right to organise two fairs and one weekly market (on Thursday) from duke Albrecht. In 1381/2 (Jan. 3) the dates of the fairs were altered: 1) Thursday after Low Sunday (Sunday after Easter) en 2) with Eleven thousand virgins day (Oct. 21), each during 8 days with 3 days before and after the erection of the cross.
Staple_Description: In 1342 Naarden obtained the right from the count of Holland Willem IV that all fish brought ashore in Holland, Kennemerland and (West-)Friesland and all fish catched between Muiden and Kampen (i.e. the rivers Vecht and IJssel) on the Zuiderzee had to be marketed in Naarden. In 1356 this staple-privilege was renewed by count Willem V and in 1395 by duke Albrecht, although without mentioning the previous rights but with staple-freedom for Naarden. The last renewing was given by duke Philip of Burgundy in 1442. A tariff, dated 1342, is preserved and edited. Two staple-accounts are preserved for the years 1457 and 1459 and analysed.In 1376 Naarden obtained the right to organise two fairs and one weekly market from duke Albrecht. For the weekly market it was ordained that all inhabitants of the surrounding country (Gooiland) had to market their goods there. The privilege was confirmed in 1382.

name: Narva
Settlement_Description: The settlement developed on an old and important trading route at the beginning of the 13th century. In 1277, a Danish castle was mentioned for the first time, which was probably built around 1256.In 1492, Ivan III built a castle called Ivangorod on the right bank of the river. Since then, it was distinguished between the Russian and Estonian part of the town.
Town_Description: At the end of the 14th century the village developed into a town and was referred to as 'civitas' in 1329. Town privileges by Lübeck and Reval were confirmed in 1345. In 1347, Narva belonged to the Teutonic Order.

name: Natruper Turm
