Settlement_Description: Watchtower in the enclosure ('landwehr') of Osnabrück. The defensive system was built around 1347, while the watchtower itself is first mentioned as "new gate" in 1383. A possible explanation for the addition "new" is that first a tower near the Bärenteich, located a little to the south, was used for defensive purposes, which was acquired by the town in 1353.

name: Lunstädt
Settlement_Description: Lunstädt and Nahlendorf are first mentioned in the tithe register of Hersfeld from the end of the 9th century. Both villages were hardly separated and can be seen as a double village ('Doppeldorf'). In 1937 Nahlendorf was incorporated into Lunstädt, which was in turn incorporated into Roßbach in 1950.

name: Nowogard
Settlement_Description: Originally a Slavic castle mound. Around 1260 a German settlement was established, in possession of the bishop of Kammin when it was first mentioned in 1268 as village or borough ('villa sive oppidum').
Town_Description: Mentioned as small town ('Stettlein') in 1274 and in 1290 as town ('civitas'). Lübeck town law was granted in 1309.

name: Naumburg (Hessen)
Settlement_Description: The place goes back to Naumburg Castle, which was first mentioned in 1182. The settlement itself is named 1206/07.
Town_Description: In 1230 'civitas' are mentioned and there is a town seal. 1256 the place is called 'oppidum'.

name: Naunhof
Settlement_Description: Mention as castrum in 1210. 1378 referred to as villa, the castle seems to have been deserted by then.
Town_Description: In 1406 mention as a small town ('Städtchen') that was independent until 1548, when it was incorporated into the district of Grimma.

name: Nebenhof
Settlement_Description: The Overste-Pepermöle ('upper pepper mill') near the Holsten gate was acquired by the city of Lübeck in 1310. Later, the mill disappeared and a farm with the name Nebenhof remained in the 18th century.

name: Neerijnen
Settlement_Description: Earliest mention in 996, in a twelfth century copy. Next mention probably in circa 1200, in a fourteenth century copy.

name: Neerwinden
Settlement_Description: Earliest mention in 976. Next mention in 1139, in a middle thirteenth century copy.

name: Neetze
Settlement_Description: First mentioned in 1205. According to lists from 1450, 1564 and 1669, there were 8 farms and 20-30 cottages in the village.

name: Negenborn
Settlement_Description: The settlement was abandoned in the 15th century, but re-populated from 1490.

name: Neheim
Settlement_Description: First mentioned in 1202 but was probably founded in the 12th century.
Town_Description: In 1358 the town was granted the town rights of Lippstadt. 1360 a privilege for a free fair. The town rights were confirmed by archbishops of Cologne in 1369 and 1372 and re-established in the 16th century, like the rights of Arnsberg.
Toll_Description: The Count of Arnsberg levied a land toll and bridge toll even before 1314. From 1368, the Archbishop of Cologne was the owner of the toll. Tariffs and revenues are not known.

name: Neiden
Settlement_Description: The village is first mentioned in 1249.

name: Nereta
Settlement_Description: The bogland 'Nerfter Moor' was mentioned in the 14th century. In 1561 a manor is mentioned as well.

name: Neritz
Bridge_Description: A bridge across the Beste is mentioned several times in the 16th century.
Lock_Description: Lock in the Beste river, which was constructed as part of the construction works for the Alster-Trave canal from 1526 onwards. It had to be renewed as early as 1530. Shipping on the canal was discontinued around 1550.

name: Niedernetphen
Toll_Description: Netphen is mentioned as toll station in 1463 and 1470.

name: Nettelstedt
Settlement_Description: The village was first mentioned in 1033.

name: Neuhardenberg
Settlement_Description: Founded in the first third of the 13th century.
Toll_Description: Toll station mentioned in 1348. Citizens from Eberswalde were exempted for their own commodities that were transported by their own horses in 1445. Exemptions were also issued for Wriezen in 1461 and confirmed in 1491.

name: Verijärve
Settlement_Description: Before 1558 the area ('Wacke') Kasseritz belonged to the Neuhausen castle. In the 17th century the farm Neu-Kasseritz was founded in the village Verijärve; later it became a post station.

name: Neuenbau
Settlement_Description: The village is first mentioned in 1672.

name: Neubukow
Settlement_Description: Established around 1250 close to the castle Bukow.
Town_Description: First mentioned in 1260 as "novum opidum Bukowe", it was the seat of the bailiwick of Bukow. Lübeck town law is attested in 1435, but no charters of privileges remain. Usually referred to as borough or small town ('städtlein', 'oppidum').

name: Neuburg
Settlement_Description: A castle called Neuburg was probably built around 1171. By 1331, a small settlement had developed.

name: Dębno
Settlement_Description: A village is mentioned in 1261, a knightly manor in 1337.
Town_Description: Margravine Katharina of the Neumark settled tradesmen in the village and probably raised it to a town in 1562. Mentioned as a small town ('Städtlein') in 1614.

name: Neuendorf
Settlement_Description: The village is first mentioned in 1357.

name: Neuendorf
Settlement_Description: A village is first mentioned in 1271 and was deserted in the 16th century. From 1608 onwards it was a manor.

name: Neuenhaus
Settlement_Description: The moated castle Dinkelrode was first mentioned in 1328, next to which a settlement developed.
Town_Description: The town was founded by Count Bernd I. of Bentheim. It received the Münster town privileges in 1369.
Toll_Description: In 1370, Neuenhaus acquired the right to levy a transit toll for wagons for the maintenance of the bridges, as well as a ship toll on herring, butter, cheese and salt.

name: Neuenkirchen (bei Bassum)
Settlement_Description: The place was first mentioned in 1255.

name: Ādaži
Settlement_Description: The castle Neuermühlen of the Teutonic Order was mentioned in 1297. In 1656 it was destroyed. There was also an associated manor. The castle was not located in the modern village Ādaži, but near the later manor Bellenhof, which was first mentioned in 1781.

name: Neuflemmingen
Settlement_Description: The settlement developed from an inn at the road, which is first mentioned in 1704.

name: Neugattersleben
Settlement_Description: First mention of the castle in 1291.

name: Valtaiķi
Settlement_Description: In 1253, the region fell into the possession of the Teutonic Order. The castle already existed in 1338.

name: Vastseliina
Settlement_Description: Burchard von Dreileben founded the castle in 1342, which rose to one of the strongest castles in the country by 1379. In 1702, however, it was destroyed. A manor and a suburbium were developed next to the castle.

name: Jaunkrimulda
Settlement_Description: The manor was first mentioned in 1566 as a gift.

name: Neuhof
Settlement_Description: The settlement was abandoned and was acquired by the monastery Walkenried in 1248, which resettled it as a folwark.

name: Neukalen
Settlement_Description: First mentioned in 1281 when the town of Kalen was moved here. Before, there existed a Slavic village named Bugelmast.
Town_Description: Lord Waldemar of Mecklenburg refounded the town Kalen (the current village Altkalen) as Neukalen at a new location with all the old privileges in 1281. The Lübeck town law was endorsed multiple times.

name: Neukammer
Settlement_Description: First mentioned in 1329, the settlement was already deserted in 1349. Its church became a pilgrimage site until it was demolished in the middle of the 16th century.

name: Niederdehme
Settlement_Description: The place was first mentioned in 1088.

name: Stare Czarnowo
Settlement_Description: The village was first mentioned in a property confirmation for the Kolbatz monastery in 1255, which shows that the village was formerly called Cirnowe and that it already paid the church tithe in the 13th century. In 1242 the Kolbatz monastery probably founded a market borough ('Marktflecken') there, and in 1274 it is referred to as an 'oppidum'. Duke Bogislaw IV withdrew the market rights from the settlement in 1283.

name: Neumünster
Settlement_Description: A monastery of Augustinian canons was founded after 1127 at the church of Wippendorf-Faldera. The monastery was moved to Bordesholm around 1330. The settlement developed into a borough ('flecken') in the late Middle Ages.
Fair_Description: A fair on eight days before the Decapitation of St John the Baptist is mentioned by Heinrich Rantzau in his 1597 description of Schleswig and Holstein.
Toll_Description: Toll station of the counts of Holstein. Queen Dorothea of Denmark installed a new toll in Neumünster in 1492. Only one toll register before the 18th century is still extant, from the year 1501.

name: Vasknarva
Settlement_Description: The castle of the Teutonic Order was built in 1349, but was soon destroyed by Russians. This was followed by reconstruction in 1427-1442.

name: Neukloster (Buxtehude)
Settlement_Description: In 1286 the Benedictine nun monastery in Neuenkirchen (founded in 1274) moved to Bredenbek, which was renamed after the monastery. The nuns adopted the Cistercian habit, but still lived according to the Benedictine rule. In 1499 the monastery burned down, but was rebuilt in 1519. Having remained Catholic during the Reformation, the convent died out after the Swedish occupation in 1645 until 1705.

name: Großenehrich
Settlement_Description: Mention in a donation charter to Fulda monastery in 772. Mention as borough ('Flecken') in 1469, as market borough in 1500.
Town_Description: Referred to as town in 1521, until the end of the 16th century simultaneous mention as market borough. Since 1521 a council is known.

name: Neuruppin
Settlement_Description: Founded as town in the early 13th century, probably at the location of an old village. First mentioned in 1238.
Town_Description: The town was probably founded by the lords of Ruppin (the Counts of Arnstein) close to the castle Ruppin (Alt Ruppin) between 1214 and 1238. The town was granted Stendal town law by Günther of Arnstein in 1256. A town wall was built in the 14th century.
Fair_Description: A fair on Sunday Invocavit in Ruppin is mentioned in an almanac printed in Neudamm (Dębno) in 1598.

name: Nybøl
Settlement_Description: The village of Nybøl was first mentioned in 1400, but is significantly older. The parish church is from either the 12th or 13th century.

name: Neuss
Settlement_Description: The Roman fortress Novaesium was founded around 16 BC on the shore of the Rhine. In the vicinity a trading settlement developed that became the old town of Neuss. In Carolingian times a castle is mentioned here.
Town_Description: Neuss is first characterised as "oppidum" in 1170 and probably became a full town around 1200. The oldest town seal dates from 1245. Various privileges were granted in the next centuries. Among others, Neuss was granted the privileges of a Hanse town in 1475 by emperor Frederick III.
Fair_Description: It is unknown when the fairs in Neuss originated. In the 14th century, there were three fairs, on St Walpurga, St John and St Remigius. A fourth one on St Bartholomew was added before 1419. The four fairs were confirmed by emperor Frederick III in 1475, who also granted a fifth fair on St Martin. All fairs were to last four days before and after the said dates. The St Walpurga fair, which coincided with the feast on the dedication day of the church of St Quirinus, attracted most visitors, together with St John's fair in the 15th and 16th centuries.
Toll_Description: 1) Already in 877, an Imperial toll for ships hauled upstream on the Rhine existed in Neuss. Pfeiffer claims that this toll was market-related. A Rhine toll of the bishop of Cologne is mentioned in 1138. The towns of Cologne and temporarily Rees were exempted from the toll. The Rhine toll was moved to Zons because of changes in the course of the river in 1372. In 1243, at least 6 denarii per ship had to be paid. In 1236 about 1200 Cologne mark were collected, in 1256 about 800 Cologne mark. For further tariffs and revenues, see Pfeiffer. <br/>2) A market toll is mentioned in 1138 and 1169, and in 1203 a transit toll for land traffic of the bishop of Cologne. At least between 1389 and 1393, a horse toll was levied by the bishop, and a toll for safe conduct was granted by king Wenceslaus in 1396. In 1396, 2 to 3 alb. per horse had to be paid, depending on the load. In the years 1389/93, an average of about 2152 mark per year could be collected. Half of the land toll was acquired by the town of Neuss in 1455; in 1463 completely. In 1455, about 700 Rhenish guilders were collected. Elaborate details about the practice of levying the toll are known from testimonies written during a 1478-1479 conflict about the toll between Düsseldorf and Neuss. To prevent circumventing of the toll station, the toll was levied at many secondary toll stations around town as well. Detailed list of toll tariffs are known from 1601 and 1618.<br/>3) The town of Neuss also levied a road toll in 1373. However, the Archbishop of Cologne declared this to be illegitimate, which is why its existence after 1373 is not known.

name: Neustadt am Rübenberge
Settlement_Description: The counts of Wölpe founded a castle around 1215, next to which a settlement developed.
Town_Description: According to the name "nova civitas", which Neustadt was already called in 1215, the settlement possibly was already a town at the time. There exists no charter of town privileges, although the use of the Bremen town rights has been attested.
Toll_Description: In a 1389 charter, the dukes of Brunswick-Lüneburg proclaim that the same toll that is levied on the Aller river in Essel, will now be levied on the Leine in Neustadt, namely of each fuder grain and each fuder beer one Hannover shilling. No other tolls will be levied between Hannover and Rethem. A 1507 agreement between Hannover and Celle regulated the fares for toll and safe conduct in Essel. Toll receipts for the journey from and to Hannover were copied into a register of the town Hannover for the years 1507-1515. Likely, these refer to the the toll levied in Neustadt, as Essel is not located on the Leine.

name: Neustadt in Holstein
Settlement_Description: Before the foundation of Neustadt in 1244, there might have existed a fishing settlement.
Town_Description: Founded as the planned town Neukrempe by Count Adolf IV of Holstein and provided with Lübeck town privileges in 1244. The Hospital of the Holy Ghost was founded in 1344.
Fair_Description: A fair was held in Neustadt eight days after St Michael's Day, among others mentioned by Heinrich Rantzau in 1597. It was probably connected to the Dedication Day of the local church. The date was changed in 1701.

name: Neustadt am Rennsteig
Settlement_Description: First mention in 1454. Despite the name Neustadt, the settlement never was a town.

name: Neustadt (Magdeburg)
Settlement_Description: After a 'new town' (first mentioned in 1209) had developed north of the old town Magdeburg, it was destroyed in 1213 and incorporated into the old town. Afterwards a new 'new town' came into being around 1230.
Town_Description: Around 1230 the new town was walled. Citizens are mentioned around 1250, judges in 1300. In 1886 the independent town was merged with Magdeburg.
Toll_Description: Mention of a toll in the context of a quarrel between the archbishop and the town of Magdeburg in 1432.

name: Neustadt-Glewe
Settlement_Description: Neustadt was founded near the Slavic village Glewe, where a castle and settlement of the counts of Schwerin is attested in the late 12th century.
Town_Description: Founded by the Duke of Schwerin in 1248, mentioned as civitas in the 13th century.
Toll_Description: Toll revenues of the toll station in Neustadt are known from 1558 until 1561.

name: Nowe Miasteczko
Toll_Description: Mentioned as toll station, in existence for more than 40 years, in 1452.

name: Neuwallmoden
Settlement_Description: A castle was bought by the bishop of Hildesheim and the town of Goslar in 1307; the settlement probably developed as a consequence. The castle and the settlement were destroyed in 1368, with only the inn Wallmerhol on a border remaining. The village was resettled in the 16th century.

name: Neuwarmbüchen
Settlement_Description: The settlement was first mentioned in 1476.

name: Neuzelle
Settlement_Description: A Cistercian monastery was founded in 1268, even though monks probably only resided there since 1281. The monastery was prominent in the 15th century; after the Reformation it became protestant.

name: Nichtewitz
Settlement_Description: The village is first mentioned in 1251.

name: Nieder-Ingelheim
Toll_Description: In 1254, Werner IV of Bolanden probably levied a river toll on the Rhine and/or a land toll in the village of Ingelheim. The castle, which probably served as a customs post and was close to the Rhine, was destroyed in 1254. It can also be assumed that a land toll was collected on the Mainz-Bingen road. Tariffs or revenues are not known.

name: Oisu
Settlement_Description: Manor and village that were first mentioned in the 15th or 16th century.

name: Nonnenmühle
Settlement_Description: The mill belonging to the village Krickow, later known as Nonnenmühle, is first mentioned in 1290.

name: Niederbreisig
Settlement_Description: A settlement possibly dates back to Celtic times and became increasingly important in the Middle Ages. In 1969, Bad Niederbreisig, Oberbreisig and Rheineck were united to form Bad Breisig, which received town rights in 1970.
Toll_Description: In 1363, the abbess of Essen levied a land toll, the so-called "schmaler Zoll". In 1397, this passed into the possession of the Duke of Jülich. In 1397 the tariff was set at 4 white pfennigs ('Weißpfennige') for 100 pigs. The annual yield is not known. A river toll on the Rhine planned for 1302 was not established.

name: Niedereimer
Settlement_Description: The settlement Eimer was first mentioned in 1191. It was divided into two parts Nieder- and Obereimer, which are first mentioned separately in 1207.

name: Niederfinow
Town_Description: In 1308 the settlement is referred to as civitas, but in 1334 only as oppidum, after the toll station and harbour at the Finow was moved to Eberswalde in 1317. In the 15th century it is steadily referred to as town or civitas, and regained some meaning in trade, but great damages during the Thirty Years' War degraded the town to a village. Its town privileges were still confirmed in 1558, 1689 and 1713, even though it is only referred to as borough ('flecken') since 1573.
Fair_Description: Two fairs were held in Niederfinow, that were later moved to Oderberg.
Toll_Description: The toll station is moved to Eberswalde in 1317.

name: Niederheimbach
Toll_Description: The Mainz cathedral chapter levied a river toll on the Rhine in 1369. In the same year, 2½ Turnosgroschen had to be paid for each foder of wine. Annual yields are not known.

name: Niederklobikau
Settlement_Description: First mention in the tithe register of Hersfeld monastery from the end of the 9th century. Property of Wimmelburg monastery since 1215. In the 15th century the village was sold to the bishop of Merseburg.
Toll_Description: Secondary station of safe conduct of Merseburg.

name: Nymburk
Staple_Description: Staple rights for salt from northern Germany in 1401; confirmed in 1412.

name: Nienburg (Weser)
Settlement_Description: A castle of the bishop of Minden on a crossing of the Weser river is first mentioned in the 11th century; residence of the counts of Hoya in 1215-1582.
Town_Description: Town privileges were granted before 1235. From 1225, Nienburg is characterised as "civitas". Attested as "villa" in 1215.
Fair_Description: In the early modern period, eleven retail fairs are mentioned, which were connected with markets for cattle, timber and shoes. Three dates are known: Friday before Laetare, Monday and Tuesday after the Exaltation of the Holy Cross (the "Krüzemarkt") and a fair for horses and cattle on Wednesday and Thursday after St Simon and Juda. It is unknown when they were founded.

name: Niendorf (Teterow)
Settlement_Description: First mentioned in 1282 as alternative name for the village Tessekow (Teschow). From 1314, both names refer to separate villages.

name: Niendorf (Rostock)
Settlement_Description: The village is first mentioned in 1230.

name: Treysa
Settlement_Description: A settlement is mentioned in the 8th century. Mentioned as a 'villa' in 1229 and as a village in 1233.
Town_Description: 1270 referred to as 'oppidum' and given a town seal. The settlement was probably previously raised to a town under Count Friedrich I. von Ziegenhain (1186-1229). However, the privileges were not confirmed until 1445.

name: Niemegk
Settlement_Description: A borough developed next to a castle that was first mentioned in 1161.
Town_Description: No documents known about the foundation of the town, but apparently town privileges and a coat of arms were granted in 1228. The Wittenberg town law was apparently granted in 1349. A council exists since the second half of the 14th century.
Toll_Description: In 1349 and 1373 mention of a wagon toll. Secondary station of safe conduct ('Nebengeleit') of Belzig, mentioned from 1489 onwards in the accounts of safe conduct.

name: Savonlinna
Settlement_Description: Permanent agricultural settlement in Savonlinna (sw. Nyslott) area goes back to the 13th century. After the peace of Nöteborg in 1323 the region was left on the Novgorodian side of the Swedish border, where the castellan of Viipuri (sw. Viborg) founded the new casle of Olavinlinna (sw. Nyslott, Olofsborg) in 1475. The settlement made part of Juva parish established in 1442 and since 1510 the independent Sääminki parish.
Town_Description:
On the west side of Olavinlinna Castle, the so-called castle's malm (sw. Nyslotts malm) was inhabited in the 1500s at the latest. The initiative to establish a town on the site was made in 1638 by General-Gouvernor of Finland Per Brahe, who first proposed the establishment of two annual markets and then granted the first privileges of the town in 1639. Originally called as Savo New town (sw. Savlax Nystad) or New Castle’s malm (sw. Nyslotts malm), the name stabilised later to Savonlinna (sw. Nyslott). Th eearliest surviving town plans are from 1641–43. When the Province of Viipuri was split into Viipuri and Savonlinna provinces in 1641, the castle became the administrative centre of Savonlinna Province. The town privileges renewed by Per Brahe in 1649 were officially confirmed in 1653. Savonlinna Province was reunited with Viipuri Province in 1650. Because the Savo trade, which was in the hands of the burghers of Vyborg, passed through Lappeenranta throughout the 17th century, the importance of the town remained small, and its rights were cancelled in 1683. The town was re-established only in 1784.

<b>Inn:</b> The first inn in Savonlinna was in parish constable's (fi: nimismies, sw: länsman) farm by the Olavinlinna malm in 1639. The inn operated until the 1660s, and for twenty years, there was no inn in Savonlinna town. In 1687, Olli Heikinpoika established a new inn. He built a new house for it, which had several rooms for travellers. 

<b>Post office:</b> The first post office in Savonlinna was in operation from 1644 to 1743. It is mentioned in postal accounts only in 1668, but according to available sources, it was likely established in 1644. According to provincial records, in 1644, wages were paid for postal transport to the postmaster of Savonlinna, Lauri Martinpoika (Lars Mårtensson), and to about twenty postmasters.
Fair_Description: Since the earliest town privileges have not survived, the dates of the town's early annual fairs are unknown. In 1643 an annual fair was proposed to be established on the day of the Apostles St. Peter and St Paul (29 June) in Savonlinna, the significance of which remained small compared to the autumn fair in Lappeenranta.
Toll_Description: The 1/32 duty worth of all goods intended for sale in towns and fairs and brought to the site by peasants was collected in Savonlinna.

name: Bad Nieuweschans
Settlement_Description: The fortress Langakkerschans (later known as Nieuweschans) was built on the border between Groningen and East Frisia in 1628.

name: Nijkerk
Settlement_Description: Earliest mention dates from 1333-1334. The village was destroyed in 1412. The following year, its inhabitants received town privileges; the settlement was rebuild.
Town_Description: Town privileges granted on 27 March 1413 by Reginald IV, duke of Guelders.

name: Niemcza
Toll_Description: A toll station is first mentioned around 1305.

name: Tyrstrup
Settlement_Description: The village of Tyrstrup was first mentioned in 1315, but is significantly older. The parish church is from either the 12th or 13th century, and was replaced in 1862-63.

name: Thamsbrück
Settlement_Description: The name of the settlement is first mentioned in 780-802. It was either deserted before the foundation of the town or it was assimilated into the new town. A castle was built in the 13th century.
Town_Description: Around 1193 landgrave Herman I of Thuringia probably granted market and town rights. The settlement is first mentioned as "civitas" in 1206. In the late 13th century, a town council is attested, which consisted mostly of knights. The town was integrated into Langensalza in 1994.

name: Heldburg
Settlement_Description: First mention in a donation charter to Fulda monastery in 837.
Town_Description: The foundation of the town goes back to 1390, in 1396 a council constitution ('Ratsverfassung') is known. Until the middle of the 15th century it is referred to as borough ('Flecken') and little town ('Städtchen') interchangeably. In 1423 Hildburghausen town rights, in 1457 Coburg town rights are known.
Toll_Description: Toll station of the district Heldburg, from which the oldest account dates from 1546.

name: Königsee
Town_Description: Probably acquired town rights in the first half of the 13th century by the counts of Schwarzburg. In 1257 citizens (cives) are mentioned, in 1287 town rights are mentioned. In 1365 town rights are based on the bylaws of Stadtilm from 1350. Since 1342 a council is known.

name: Burghorn
Settlement_Description: The earliest mention dates from 1456. Burghorn is founded as a polder. Burghorn is granted town privileges between 1 January and 18 November 1462 by Willem van Schagen, lord of Burghorn. The settlement never developed an urban character. The granting of town rights was part of an administrative reorganization in which a number of smaller settlements were granted town rights in order to provide them with a certain degree of self-government which replaced the need for the count of Holland's bailiffs ('baljuws'). Burghorn eventually merged into Schagen.

name: Nijmegen
Settlement_Description: Earliest mention in 98-117. Around 98, emperor Trajanus granted market privileges and the title Ulpia Noviomagus to the settlement. In the second century, possibly in 161, town privileges were granted. In the second half of the eight century, a royal palace ('palts'/ 'pfalz') was built.
Town_Description: Nijmegen is mentioned as 'oppidum' in 1204. Town privileges similar to the town privileges granted to other free imperial cities are granted to Nijmegen by Henry VII, on behalf of his father, Frederick II, Holy Roman Emperor, on 31 August 1230. The palace and the city were acquired by the count of Guelders Otto II in 1247, who moved the central market place next to the newly founded parish church of St Stephen. A burgomaster and councillors are first mentioned in 1282. Most taverns and inns were located in the Grotestraat: the street between the town square and the town gate to the river Waal which was located next to the crane and called 'Kraanpoort'.
Fair_Description: In Nijmegen, two fairs already existed before 1294/95. In the sixteenth century, an oxen fair was added on St. Victor's Day. Two horse fairs were instituted during the Gueldern Wars. Those fairs existed for three years only, between 1540 and 1543. In Nijmegen, three days of each fair were dedicated to cloth trade.
Staple_Description: Statutes from 1468 (in the 'keurboek') mention a staple on woad. It was related to the wool-dyeing which flourished in the fourteenth century, and died out in the fifteenth century. The related cloth hall is first mentioned in 1382, and lost its function at least before 1542, when it was remodeled. Gorissen suspects that this staple has been of limited importance.

name: Pyari
Settlement_Description: Manor and hamlet ('Hof') owned by the Teutonic Order. First mentioned in 1429. The farm got its name from its owner, Hans Ninigal.

name: Nõmme
Settlement_Description: The farm, village and mill Nömme are first mentioned in 1796.

name: Magdala
Town_Description: The town was founded between 1284 and 1288 by the counts of Orlamünde. It is referred to as civitas in 1288 and had a council constitution in 1290. The town was destroyed in 1452 and recovered only slowly.

name: Noordbroek
Settlement_Description: Earliest mention of 'Broke' in 1273. Earliest mention of  'Nortdabrock' in 1478.

name: Noordlaren
Settlement_Description: Earliest mention in a copy dating from in 1254.

name: Norden
Settlement_Description: The village of Norden developed from the merger of the two hamlets Ekel and Lintel, which are first mentioned in 785.
Town_Description: A central market place was established in the first half of the 13th century. Norden is documented in 1255 as the centre of the land of Norden and must have had a town-like character at that time. In 1455 the town had two mayors, in 1498 it had a town seal and in 1535 town regulations are known. However, a year for the acquisition of town rights is unknown.
Fair_Description: Fairs in Norden are first explicitly mentioned in 1440 in a letter of safe conduct. They are also mentioned in the town regulations of 1535. Dates are only known later: the fair of St James in the mid-16th century, the Pentecost market in 1598, and the large three-day autumn cattle fair ('Beestmarkt') on the day before St Martin. All of these fairs must have been older.
Toll_Description: A toll of the counts of East Frisia was levied in Norden. In 1497, it was specified that commodities for which toll had already been paid in Norden were exempted from toll in Emden. For each horse or piece of cattle 1 Krummstert had to be paid. A more specific list of toll fees for various commodities is known from 1629. A toll register exists for the years 1596-1599.

name: Põltsamaa
Settlement_Description: In the 13th century, a fortified borough ('Hakelwerk') was built around the castle and church, although the origins of the settlement are much older. In the 15th and 16th centuries it became a borough ('Flecken').

name: Nordhorn
Settlement_Description: The old village Nordhorn, current Altendorf, possibly goes back to an 9th-century missionary centre. A local law court existed here since 1319.
Town_Description: The borough ('weichbild') to the southwest of the old village received the same town privileges as the town Schüttorf in 1379; they were reiterated in 1417.
Toll_Description: A privilege of the Count from 1416 permitted Nordhorn to introduce a road toll "for the utility and improvement of the town". It was levied on wagons passing through town. As the many bridges in town demanded a great deal of maintenance, a separate bridge toll was introduced in 1613.

name: Nordkirchen
Settlement_Description: The settlement came into being at a farm of the abbey of Werden. The family Morrien had a castle here after 1350. Because of enlargement of the castle in 1533, the village was moved to its current location.

name: Nortorf
Settlement_Description: First mentioned around 1190, but the settlement probably came into being between 500 and 800. A church was founded in the mid-12th century, after which the settlement developed into a large craftsmen village.

name: Usingen
Town_Description: The transition from village to town is fluid. In 1326 the place was last called a village, in 1362 citizens were mentioned for the first time. Accordingly, the place developed into a town during this period. It is first mentioned as a town in documents in 1377, a city seal before 1394.

name: Nordhausen
Settlement_Description: The first mentions of 927 and 929 refer to a Liudolfing stronghold near today's cathedral. The early medieval settlement was far removed from any natural traffic corridors. Former Carolingian-Ottonian royal court. In the middle of the 10th century, a marketplace developed nearby.
Town_Description: Nordhausen was declared a free imperial city before 1220, probably around 1180.
Fair_Description: Two fairs are known in Nordhausen since the 12th century, on the Exaltation and Elevation of the Holy Cross. A horse and cattle market took place at the square Pferdemarkt (horse market), which is attested in 1491.

name: Nossen
Settlement_Description: A knight called Petrus de Noßin was mentioned in 1185. The village was first mentioned in 1264. The settlement surrounded a castle,  which came into the possession of the monastery Altzella in 1430, at which time the settlement was characterised as small town ('städtlein'). Town privileges were granted in 1664.

name: Nõo
Settlement_Description: Parish, which was etablished in the 14th/15th century. A Borough ('Flecken') only developed in the 19th century.

name: Nuland
Settlement_Description: Earliest mention in 1299, in a seventeenth century copy.

name: Nunspeet
Settlement_Description: Earliest mention of the church and settlement 'Nunspiet' in 1313. There is discussion whether farms were already present here before 1200, but there is consensus that habitation and cultivation of land in this area intensified during the thirteenth century. At least from the thirteenth century onwards, the centre of the settlement Nunspeet was formed by the church, the present-day 'Oude Kerk' or 'Hervormde Dorpskerk' located at Dorpsstraat 12.From the seventeenth century onwards, 'De Roskam' served as an inn on the route between Amersfoort and Zwolle.

name: Nurmiži
Settlement_Description: The manor was first mentioned in 1561.

name: Nürnberg
Settlement_Description: The place was founded in the 11th century and had market rights from the beginning.
Town_Description: In 1219, Nuremberg was mentioned as a 'free imperial town'. In the late Middle Ages, i.e. between 1470 and 1530, the town was able to become an important trading centre due to its convenient location.

name: Nüxei
Settlement_Description: At the first mention in 1420, the hamlet is mentioned as abandoned. It must have been resettled before the next mention in 1557. There existed an inn here, which became a toll station at the Thuringian border after the Thirty Years' War.

name: Bārta
Settlement_Description: The manor was first mentioned in 1252. A church was situated there in 1560.

name: Oberhaverbeck
Settlement_Description: Haverbeck is first mentioned in a register of the diocese Verden of ca. 1252. The distinction between the two parts Ober- ('upper') and Nieder- ('lower') Haverbeck is from a later date.

name: Oberlangen
Settlement_Description: The elongated settlement Langen, first mentioned around 1000, was divided into Ober- ('higher') and Nieder- ('lower') langen.

name: Oberlind
Settlement_Description: The village probably already existed at a ford in the 9th century. A "Wignandesford" is mentioned in 1162, which was probably located at the Steinach near Oberlind. In 1225 the village is first mentioned as property of Saalfeld. Town rights were only granted in 1931.

name: Oberlungwitz
Settlement_Description: This abandoned area was settled around 1100. The founder of this village built a property, which was reused as a manor until 1273. Town privileges were granted in 1936.

name: Obermörmter
Toll_Description: The Count of Cleves levied a land toll in 1319. Tariffs and annual revenues are not known.

name: Obersickte
Settlement_Description: The settlement Sickte is first mentioned in 888 and was divided into the two parts Ober- and Niedersickte, of which the former is first mentioned individually in 1308.

name: Oberwesel
Toll_Description: From 1253 to 1269, the empire levied a river toll on the Rhine. In 1435, the Archbishop of Trier briefly established a toll. Tariffs and annual revenues are not known.

name: Ochsenzoll
Toll_Description: Toll station on the Ochsenweg ('oxen road') on the border between Hamburg and Holstein territory. A toll was levied here between 1612 and 1867.

name: Otepää
Settlement_Description: In 1116, an Estonian castle in Otepää was mentioned. This was conquered by Germans in the 13th century. Bishop Hermann I then built a new castle to serve as the center of the Dorpat diocese. It was destroyed at the end of the 15th century. A settlement next to the castle developed in the 13th century and gained economic importance in medieval times. However, it was completely destroyed in 1558.

name: Oderberg
Settlement_Description: A hospital of St Mary was built around 1210 near a Slavic village. The Ascanian Albrecht II built a castle in 1214; a German castle borough developed nearby, a bailiff is mentioned in 1231. A Premonstratensian monastery that was founded in 1231 was merged with the hospital into the new Cistercian Monastery Mariensee in 1258.
Town_Description: A plebanus civitatis is mentioned in 1259, and the settlement is mentioned as civitas in 1301, as opidum in 1317 and 1393. It must have become a town before 1259, but nothing is known about the acquisition of town privileges.
Toll_Description: Margrave Jost von Mähren decided in 1401, that citizens from Guben were subjected to the same toll tariffs in Oderberg as those from Frankfurt.
Staple_Description: Staple rights from 1313 valid only for trade upstream; merchants from Frankfurt were exempted, and in 1317 merchants from Berlin-Kölln too. In a confirmation from 1415, the staple appears as a simple transit fee.

name: null
Harbour_Description: Harbour for the regular passenger barge services ('trekvaart') to Haarlem, dug in 1631.

name: Oberröblingen
Settlement_Description: First mention of Röblingen in the tithe register of Hersfeld monastery from c. 830-850. Oberröblingen as distinct from the settlement Niederröblingen is first mentioned separately in 1134. A church is mentioned in 1154.

name: Odoorn
Settlement_Description: Earliest mention in 1327, in a copy dating from 1471.

name: Ohrum
Settlement_Description: Settlement at an important ford on the Oker river, first mentioned in Frankish royal annals of 747.

name: Oidrema
Settlement_Description: Village and manor from the 16th century. In 1534, it was the administrative center of the area.

name: Oebisfelde
Settlement_Description: First mention presumably between 1014 and 1037. Several fortifications were erected against Slavic settlement. At the beginning of the 11th century the settlement was property of Corvey monastery.
Town_Description: Referred to as civitas in 1226, mention as oppidum in 1262. In 1448 the town privileges were confirmed.
Fair_Description: Oebisfelde owned four fairs in 1523, some were ware- and others were cattle fairs. In 1783 another ware- and cattlemarket was granted, until 1887 the number of markets was raised to 12. Some ware markets were replaced by cattle markets, however.
Toll_Description: A toll was already given in 1485, further mentions occur in 1503 and 1533. In the course of the 16th century, the toll stations in Oebisfelde, Neuhaldensleben, Wolmirstedt, Dreileben, Wanzleben and Calbe complain that their income was reduced due to the toll exemption of Magdeburg.

name: Oelde
Settlement_Description: First mentioned in 875. Fortified in the 14th century and characterised as borough ('wigbold') since the 16th century.

name: Oerel
Settlement_Description: The village was first mentioned in 937; the church was built around 1100. Oerel was the seat of a regional court. There were 6 farms and 2 cottages here around 1500.

name: Oegstgeest
Settlement_Description: Earliest mention in 918-948, in an 11th century copy. The parish of Oegstgeest was also known as Kerkwerve in the 11th century.

name: Ødsted
Settlement_Description: The village of Ødsted was first mentioned in c. 1330, but is older. The parish church is from either the 12th or 13th century. Near the village there may also was another church in the middle ages until the middle of the 16th century.

name: Oleśnica (Wrocław)
Toll_Description: The toll station in Oleśnica was installed in the second half of the 13th century.

name: Oederan
Settlement_Description: Farmers and miners settled in this area around 1180. Mining is said to have been mentioned as early as 1216.
Town_Description: Oederan gained greater economic importance due to its location on an old Bohemian street, so that there was constant growth. Several marketplaces were created and city rights were granted before 1286 (around 1250). In 1583 Mining town.
Toll_Description: Station of secondary safe conduct of Chemnitz, as mentioned in regulations of safe conduct from 1551.

name: Volkmarsen
Town_Description: The settlement was raised to a town by the Corvey Monastery. 1233 called 'oppidum'.

name: Oesede
Settlement_Description: First mentioned in documents between 836 and 891.

name: Ohepalu
Settlement_Description: The village was first mentioned in 1241 and belonged to the manor of 'Heinrichshof'.

name: Oisterwijk
Settlement_Description: The earliest mention of Oisterwijk may date from before 1167. According to Van Berkel & Samplonius, however, it is uncertain whether this is the first mention of Oisterwijk. The subsequent mention they have recorded dates from 1214 (Cox records a mention from 1212).
Town_Description: Town rights were granted on 25 November 1230 by Henry I, duke of Brabant. There might have been an earlier grant, but Cox states that no consensus exists among historians on that point.
Fair_Description: In 1340 Oisterwijk had a weigh-house, in 1441 a cloth-hall. The duke of Brabant granted in 1355 (March 13) a weekly market on Wednesday and two fairs of each eight days. The first fair on May 1 and the second on the eve of St. Simon and Jude (Oct. 27). With rights and liberties as in Den Bosch.

name: Oker
Settlement_Description: Already in the 10th century, mining activity took place on the Rammelsberg. The existing ironworks were united in 1527 by the Duke of Brunswick into the Frau Marien Saigerhütte, next to which a settlement of previously itinerant miners developed. A watchtower of Goslar, the Okerturm, is first mentioned in 1530.
Toll_Description: Toll was levied at the Okerturm watchtower.
Harbour_Description: The Oker was made navigable up to the Okerturm in 1577.

name: null
Harbour_Description: Harbour for the the barge services ('trekschuit') to Amsterdam; the tow canal was dug in 1631.

name: Oldebroek
Settlement_Description: Earliest mention in 1277, in a fifteenth century copy.

name: Medemblik
Settlement_Description: The earliest mention of Medemblik in writing occurs in the eleventh-century copy of a document dated 918-948. Cox states that Medemblik originated in the late seventh or early eighth century. It gained governmental and economic importance as it was located on the shipping route through the Vlie between Dorestad and Almere. Furthermore, there were royal and episcopal residences in the area.
Town_Description: Medemblik was granted town rights on 25 March 1289 by Floris V, count of Holland. In 1402 a hospital is first mentioned.
Fair_Description: The town-privilege of 1289 mentions a fair with St. Bonifatius (June 5 ) duration 14 days. The toll will be from the count and its successors. The comital account dated 1343/'4 mentions a fair with St. Odulphus (June 12).
Toll_Description: A toll for sailing transport in Medemblik at the Almere lake was partly given by king Otto III to count Ansfried, before 985 it was a fief. Possibly this was later relocated to Muiden. In 1311 however the bisshop of Utrecht made an agreement with Kampen about mutual toll-tariffs. In 1323 a toll on imported beer from the Baltic and the Sticht van Utrecht was installed in Medemblik by the count of Holland. But is since never found again.
Harbour_Description: On the map of Jacob van Deventer (mid 16th century) the harbour intersects the town as a small canal. Two heads of the harbour are situated in the sea but offer little mooring. Vitelli counted in his report for the duke of Alva in 1569 15 or 16 ships of 70-80 'last' named 'boeiers' with destinations like Hamburg, Danzig and 'Oostland' (Baltic) and 60 small fishboats including 5 or 6 bigger ones. In 1599 the 'Nieuwe haven' (new harbour) south of the old town is finished together with defensive works. The start for this enlargement was already in 1577.

name: Oldenburg (Oldenburg)
Settlement_Description: Residence of the counts of Oldenburg from ca. 1150.
Town_Description: Bremen town privileges were granted in 1345, but the settlement already had an urban character before: fairs and burghers are first mentioned in 1243, a magistrate court around 1300, and a council and town seal in 1307.
Fair_Description: Two fairs in Oldenburg are mentioned in an agreement between Oldenburg and Bremen from 1243, on St Vitus and St Margaret. These two markets are also mentioned in 1307, together with a fair on St Lambert (17-9), and in the town privileges from 1345, no less than seven fairs are mentioned. However, it is the question whether these were organised for a long time: in the 15th century, only St Vitus's and St Margaret's fairs are still mentioned. In the "Verordnung wegen der Oldenburger Krahmer-Marckte" from 1608, it is mentioned that there were four traditional fairs. However, older evidence for the two additional markets, on St Michael and Quasimodogeniti, is not known.
Toll_Description: An agreement from 1243 grants merchants from Bremen exemption from tollsin Oldenburg and free conduct. Oldenburg citizens complained in 1383 that the Count had increased the tolls to be paid by citizens from Bremen, Wildeshausen and Friesoythe. More specific toll amounts are known from the 15th century (1428) for beer, salt, oil, corn and other commodities.
Staple_Description: An agreement with Bremen limited the trade of merchants from Bremen and Westfalia in Oldenburg to the fairs on St Vitus and St Margaret. This restriction was removed in 1278, but there still existed the obligation for external merchants travelling through town to offer their commodities for sale on the market.

name: Oldendorf (Luhe)
Settlement_Description: First mentioned in 1406; a water mill is mentioned in 1511.

name: Oldenrode
Settlement_Description: The settlement was first mentioned in 1302.

name: Oldenstadt
Settlement_Description: Bishop Bruno of Verden founded a house of canonesses before 973, around which a settlement developed. In 1133/37 the monastery was converted into a Benedictine monastery by monks from Corvey. Around 1260 the settlement was moved 2 km to the west bank of the Ilmenau and became the town of Uelzen. The monastery remained at the original location and became known as Oldenstadt. It owned several properties in and around Uelzen as well as shares in the Lüneburg saltworks. The monastery was abolished after the Reformation in 1529.

name: Oldenzaal
Town_Description: Borough ('wigbold') privileges were granted by bishop Otto III of Utrecht between 1 February 1233 and 27 March 1249. Later Oldenzaal must have acquired full town rights, although the exact year is unknown.
Fair_Description: Oldenzaal acquired market privileges from the bishop of Utrecht in 1049. It included the right to hold a weekly market on Thursdays and a five-day fair around the Dedication day of the church (21 September).

name: Vonsild
Settlement_Description: The village of Vonsild was first mentioned in 1436, but is significantly older. The parish church is from either the 12th or 13th century.

name: Bad Oldesloe
Settlement_Description: Oldesloe came into existence near saltworks, which are first mentioned before 1152. The church existed in 1163 at the latest.
Town_Description: Oldesloe received town privileges in the 13th century, possibly before 1249. An exact date is unknown.
Fair_Description: Heinrich Rantzau mentions in his 1597 description of Schleswig and Holstein that a fair was held eight days after St John the Baptist. It is also mentioned in an almanac printed in Neudamm (Dębno) in 1598. In some years, the fair Kieler Umschlag was also held in Oldesloe. See Kiel for more information.
Toll_Description: Toll of the counts of Holstein, first mentioned in 1175. Lübeck citizens were exempted from the toll in 1226 (confirmed in 1247), but were still required to pay a fee for safe conduct. Bremen citizens were also exempted from the toll in 1347, 1396 and 1494. Because these exemptions greatly reduced the toll revenues, a "new" toll was installed in 1474, whereby the fee for safe conduct was raised to the height of the old toll. Dutch towns complained to Lübeck in 1479 about the raise of toll tariffs from 4 to 7 shilling, equally on the Stecknitz canal. Bremen and Hamburg complained in 1511 about illegal toll levying in Oldesloe. Between 1340 and 1495, the toll was often partially or completely pawned to Lübeck.

name: Oldisleben
Settlement_Description: First mention in 1089 in the foundation charter of a Benedictine monastary by Kunigunde of Weimar-Orlamünde. The settlement is probably older. Occasionally mentioned as town in the 13th century (1245, 1255), but it never developed into more than a market borough ('Marktflecken').

name: Olst
Settlement_Description: Earliest mention of 'Holsto' in 947. Earliest mention of 'Olst' in 1235.

name: Alt Olvenstedt
Settlement_Description: In 826-53 Corvey monastery already owned property in Olvenstedt. The church in Olvenstedt is already mentioned in the 10th century. Since 1287 a noble family can be proven in Olvenstedt.

name: Ommen
Settlement_Description: Earliest mention dates from before 13 June 1133. Ommen came into being around 1100 near a ford in the Overijsselse Vecht.
Town_Description: Town privileges were granted by Otto III of Holland, bishop of Utrecht, on 25 August 1248.
Toll_Description: A toll in Ommen existed in 1432.

name: Ommerschans
Settlement_Description: A fortification ('schans') in the marshes near Avereest was built by the estates of Overijssel in 1596.

name: Ontika
Settlement_Description: Manor and village, which were property of the Teutonic Order in the 15th and 16th centuries.

name: Oordegem
Settlement_Description: Earliest mention in 1160, in a twelfth century copy.

name: Oosterbeek
Settlement_Description: Earliest mention in 834 in an eleventh century copy. The next mention dates from 1028 in a copy dating from circa 1530.

name: Eastersee
Settlement_Description: Earliest mention in 1132,  in a falsification of the second half of the thirteenth century.

name: Ostendorf
Settlement_Description: The settlement was first mentioned in 1146.

name: Ootmarsum
Settlement_Description: Earliest mention dates from 919-977 or 962-977 (in a fifteenth century copy).
Town_Description: On 1 July 1325, Jan III of Diest, bishop of Utrecht, granted town privileges similar to other towns in the area called Overijssel. Before 1325, Ootmarsum had 'Wigboldrecht', a limited type of town rights which is mainly found in Westphalia.
Fair_Description: In 1314, the bishop of Utrecht granted the right to hold a weekly market and a three-day fair on Sunday after the Nativity of Mary.

name: Opatów
Toll_Description: Mentioned as toll station in a document from c. 1349, where 3 gr., previously 1 gr., had to be paid for each horse.

name: Opoczno
Toll_Description: King Casimir decided in 1344 that the tolls that had been levied for a long time in Piotrków Trybunalski and Rozprza now had to be paid in Opoczno. In c. 1349 2 gr. had to be paid for each horse and 2 den. for each cart.

name: Opole
Toll_Description: The toll in the town is first directly mentioned in 1254, but possibly existed already in 1169.

name: Oppin
Settlement_Description: Mention as early as 952 in the context of an exchange of property. A noble family of Oppin in known.

name: Kerkdorp
Settlement_Description: The settlement was originally known as Oosterwolde, which is first mentioned in 1265. The village was replaced to the south in the 19th century and the church demolished. The settlement at the original location became known as Kerkdorp.

name: Ophemert
Settlement_Description: Earliest mention in 800-850, in a copy dating from 1170-1175.

name: Oranienburg
Settlement_Description: A castle of the margraves of Brandenburg was built around 1200, the adjoining village is mentioned in 1217, mentioned as small town ('stedeken') in 1350. Only acknowledged as town in the first half of the 18th century. Originally called Bötzow, the settlement changed name after it was acquired by Luise Henriette of Orange in 1650.

name: Oschatz
Settlement_Description: Before 929 the settlement was situated in close proximity to a castle and its rampart, which later became the manor. Around 1150 the old market was created.
Town_Description: The expansion of the town took place in the 13th century. In 1246 the place was first mentioned as 'town' ('Stadt').
Toll_Description: A toll station of the Margrave of Meißen is mentioned in 1399 and 1404, a safe conduct of the Duke of Saxony in 1490. Regulations of safe conduct remain from 1516 and 1552.

name: Nedlitz
Settlement_Description: The Havel-passage between lakes Lehnitz- and Jungfern has been guarded since the Bronze Age. Later, a Slavic settlement is formed, which is then absorbed into a German village.
Ferry_Description: First mention of the ferry in Nedlitz in 1323; it was the only direct connection between Potsam and Spandau. The ferry existed well into the 19th century.

name: Spaarndam
Toll_Description: The charter first mentioning Spaarndam in 1253 includes toll tariffs. Together with the toll of Gouda, this was one of the tolls belonging to the count of Holland on the main sailing route ('route binnendunen') through Holland. Both tolls were combined in the 15th century: those who had already paid toll in Spaarndam were exempted from the toll in Gouda and the other way around. A toll account dated 1391/2 is preserved and edited. Yields are (incomplete) preserved and edited for the years 1356-1600. After a raid by the Geldersen in 1517 the toll was collected in Haarlem.
Ferry_Description: A comital ferry to Assendelft crossing the IJ is first mentioned in 1315.
Lock_Description: A dam that closed off the Spaarne from the IJ already existed in 1253, when count Willem II of Holland announced the plan to build a lock for ships. The plan was not realised and the entire dam destroyed by floods before 1286. A new dam with a lock was mentioned in 1305, and the lock fees were set in 1316 to the same tariff as in 1253.

name: Osternburg
Settlement_Description: The settlement was first mentioned on 6 December 1404 in a sale contract.

name: Osnabrück
Settlement_Description: First mentioned in ca. 772. The cathedral, which belonged to the bishopric founded by Charlemagne, was probably dedicated in 787. The merchant settlement acquired market, toll and minting privileges in 1002.
Town_Description: Characterised as "civitas" since 1147. Emperor Frederick I granted town privileges to Osnabrück in 1171.
Fair_Description: The oldest fairs in Osnabrück went back to the market privilege of 1002. Before 1190, two four-day fairs are mentioned, the "Herrenmesse" of the Dedication of the cathedral on St Crispin and Crispinian, and on mid-Lent. From 1190, a third fair, the "new fair" was held on the Exaltation of the Holy Cross, which disappeared in the late 15th century. The large fairs were especially important as markets for the locally produced cloth, and attracted visitors from as far as Bremen, Lippstadt, Dortmund, Wesel, Xanten and Deventer. Smaller fairs of a single day were held on the dedication days of the churches of the Franciscan, Dominican, Augustinian and Teutonic knights' monasteries.
Toll_Description: The bishop of Osnabrück levied a market toll since the foundation of the market. A third part of the toll which was levied on the "new" fair on the Exaltation of the Holy Cross was ceded to the cathedral chapter in 1190. The toll of the fair on the cathedral square is mentioned in 1242 as "thelonium cimiterii". From 1359 the toll was mostly leased out, with the exception of the toll on salt. The latter was finally also leased to the burgomaster in 1487. The citizens of Osnabrück were exempted from toll payments between 1388 and 1424.

name: Ossendrecht
Settlement_Description: Earliest mention in 1187, in a copy dating from 1277.

name: Osteel
Settlement_Description: The church in Osteel was built between 1260 and 1285. The village itself was first mentioned in 1387.

name: Øster Nykirke
Settlement_Description: The village was first mentioned in c. 1330, but is older. The parish church is from either the 12th or 13th century.

name: Osterburg
Settlement_Description: Former Slavic settlement. In the 10th cenutry probably castle village. In 1196 property in Osterburg is given to the archbishop of Magdeburg.
Town_Description: In 1164 the village is first referred to as "urbs".
Fair_Description: In an official schedule from 1719, Osterburg, Arendsee and Bismark each held six fairs. It can be assumed that some of these had existed for a while to this point. Ware markets, fairs and cattle markets are mentioned earlier.
Toll_Description: In 1287, the old city of Osterburg is referred to as toll station.

name: Osterhausen
Settlement_Description: In 772, 777 and 780, Charlemagne donated royal chapels in Osterhausen to Hersfeld monastery.

name: Osterholz (Scharmbeck)
Settlement_Description: The Benedictine nunnery Osterholz was founded east of Scharmbeck in 1182. In 1550 the monastery became Protestant, with a short return of Catholic nuns during the Thirty Years' War. In 1650 the monastery was closed.

name: Ostercappeln
Settlement_Description: First mentioned around 1200. In the 16th century the settlement developed into a borough ('weichbild'), but is still characterised as 'villa' in 1512.

name: Osterlinde
Settlement_Description: The attribution of the placenames "parvo", "negheren" and "lütken" ('little') Linden to Osterlinde is not entirely certain; these could possibly refer to Westerlinde.

name: Ostróda
Settlement_Description: A castle of the Teutonic Order was first mentioned in 1332. In 1341 it was a commandery.
Town_Description: Founded with Kulm town law between 1327 and 1330 by the Grand Master Luther von Braunschweig. The founding documents are lost, but a first renewal from 1335 and a second from 1348 exist.

name: Osterode am Harz
Settlement_Description: First mentioned in 1136; a castle is first mentioned in 1153.
Town_Description: Osterode became a town in 1239 at the latest. Goslar town privileges were granted in 1293. The town became an important centre for mining activity in the Harz mountains.
Toll_Description: A toll in Osterode is mentioned in 1334. In the 17th century, it probably did not exist anymore.

name: Osterwieck
Settlement_Description: Possibly founded as a missionary centre after 800, Seligenstadt is first mentioned in 974, when it acquired toll, market and mint rights. It is believed that this settlement was later renamed to Osterwieck, which first appears in the 11th century.
Town_Description: The settlement is first referred to as "civitas" in 1215, and in 1310 as "oppidum". A new town around the Church of St Nicholas emerged in the 13th century, which was formally merged with the old town around St Stephen's Church in 1488.
Toll_Description: Toll privileges date back to 974. In 1456 toll was collected illegally from a citizen of Hildesheim.

name: Ostheim (Butzbach)
Settlement_Description: First mentioned in 1265. Earlier evidence cannot be attributed without doubt.

name: Oosthuizen
Settlement_Description: Earliest mention in the twelfth century, in a copy dating from circa 1420.

name: Osterholz (Elbe)
Settlement_Description: First mention of the settlement in 1337.

name: Ostritz
Settlement_Description: The old town, that was mentioned in 1245, was situated in close proximity to a castle. There was also a market place. The location on the road between Görlitz and Zittau favored trade.
Town_Description: In 1241 the place was first referred to as 'oppidum'.

name: Ottendorf-Okrilla
Toll_Description: Station of secondary safe conduct ('Beigeleitsstelle') of Radeberg.

name: Otterloo
Settlement_Description: Earliest mention in 838, in a eleventh century copy.

name: Parey
Settlement_Description: Given to the bishopric of Havelberg by Emperor Otto I in 946.

name: Ottersberg
Settlement_Description: The castle Boberg was built by vassals of the archbishop of Bremen around 1180. After some decades, the castle was renamed Ottersberg after the nearby village Otterstedt. A chapel was built near the castle, next to which a settlement developed. It was characterised as borough ('flecken').
Fair_Description: Three cattle and horse market were renewed after the Thirty Years' War in 1690, on Wednesday before Carnival, Wednesday before the Holy Week and Wednesday before St Michael. It is unknown whether they were held before the war as well.
Toll_Description: A toll in Ottersberg, from which Bremen citizens were exempted, is mentioned in 1562, but was probably older. In a register from 1586/7, revenues from an oxen, horses, salt and general toll are listed. The modest amounts suggest only limited traffic through Ottersberg.

name: Otterstedt
Settlement_Description: The Lords of Otterstedt first appeared in the 12th century.

name: Oud-Alblas
Fair_Description: A fair or market (market-toll) is first mentioned in 1331. Starting 1350 it is called a summer horse-fair at St. Peterseve ad vincula (evening before August 1). In 1445 bailiff and dikereeves of Nieuw-Lekkerland hand over the seigniory Alblasserdam with a.o. the condition to be toll-exempt in future on the fair there. A manual of the toll-keeper of Geervliet dated 1562 mentions the horse-fair in Alblasserdam on July 25 in a calendar with many horse-fairs.

name: Oud-Diemen
Settlement_Description: Earliest mention in 1226. The village was originally called Diemen. In the 19th century the nearby settlement Diemerbrug became more important and assumed the name Diemen, whereafter the old village became known as Oud-Diemen.

name: Ousterhaule
Settlement_Description: Earliest mention in the thirteenth century.

name: Overasselt
Settlement_Description: Earliest mention in the first quarter of the thirteenth century. In 1258, Overasselt is mentioned as 'de Assele Superioris'.

name: Overschie
Settlement_Description: Earliest mention in the first half of the eleventh century .

name: Paatna
Settlement_Description: The village was first mentioned in 1241 and belonged to the manor of Peuth.

name: Pada-Aruküla
Settlement_Description: Manor and village (Pada-Aruküla) were first mentioned in 1241.

name: Padelügger Baum
Settlement_Description: Boom barrier in the Lübeck defensive enclosure ('landwehr'), which was named after the neighbouring manor Padelügge. The enclosure was constructed around 1300.

name: Parila
Settlement_Description: Manor owned by the canons of Hapsal (Haapsalu), first mentioned in 1500.

name: Alde Ouwer
Settlement_Description: Earliest mention in the thirteenth century.

name: Neustadt an der Orla
Settlement_Description: First mention in the records as <i>nova civitas</i> in 1287.
Town_Description: The town was founded by Otto IV of Lobdeburg-Arnshaugk in 1287, possibly at the site of earlier Slavic settlements. The town experienced an economic bloom in the second half of the 14th century. A town council governed the settlement from c. 1365. It acquired legal sovereignty in 1411 and 1483. A market toll was acquired in 1411.

name: Wersen
Settlement_Description: First mentioned in the 11th century, in a copy from 1479.

name: Paderborn
Settlement_Description: Location of a Carolingian palace since 776; in 777 mention of the Salvator church; since 805/06 seat of a diocese. The palace and the cathedral were surrounded by a fortification from the beginning, a wooden-earth construction, which was replaced by a wall in 777. Around 900 the place was called 'oppidum'.
Town_Description: The settlement received market, toll and mint privileges in 1028 at the latest. In the 13th century, the town freed itself of the overlordship of the bishop and acquired legal freedom, which was recorded in a charter in 1327. A town council is mentioned in 1238.
Fair_Description: Paderborn acquired market privileges in 1028. The oldest fair was that of St Gallus, which is mentioned in 1327 as taking place in front of the western town gate according to old custom. It was mainly used for agricultural products. A second fair of St John appears in the early 16th century; it was replaced by bishop Erich in 1521 with two new fairs, on the Chair of St Peter and on Mary Magdalene. Both fairs had three free market days before and after the fair day. In the town accounts from 1575, two other fairs, on Annunciation Day and St Nicholas, are mentioned; they might have been introduced after 1521.
Toll_Description: There were three tolls in Paderborn:<br/> 1) The market toll of the bishop, granted in 1028, was a tax on bought and sold commodities in town. Before 1301, the toll was acquired by the noble Schilder family, in the service of the bishop, and the toll became known as the Schilderzoll. It was probably levied in the Schildern alley, which might have been named after the family and the toll. In the 15th century, the toll was sold to Paderborn citizens and in 1491 to the town. Afterwards it was turned into a road toll.<br/> 2) The "small toll" belonged to the family Endehachte, who sold it to the cathedral treasurer in 1311. Further details are not known.<br/> 3) A fee for safe conduct, called "gheleyde", owned by the lords of Lippe at the beginning of the 14th century. It was sold to bishop Heinrich III in 1367. According to a 16th-century document, this toll was levied on commodities bought by foreigners in Paderborn territory and transported through town. Inhabitants of the territory were exempted from the toll. Some registers of this toll exist from the 16th century.

name: Padise
Settlement_Description: The monks of Dünamünde owned land here in the 13th century. A chapel was built in 1281. In 1305 a Cistercian monastery was founded, which could only be inaugurated in 1448 due to uprisings. In 1559 the monastery was closed.

name: Paistu
Settlement_Description: End of the 13th century a church was built, which was first mentioned in 1329. The pastorate was probably established at the same time.

name: Brieži
Settlement_Description: The village was mentioned in 1637 and belonged to Kokenhof.

name: Penningsveer
Ferry_Description: A ferry in Spaarnwoude across the Liede to Haarlem is first found in 1398. In 1472 it was pawned a.o. domain rights to the city of Haarlem. In 1492 this contract was ended. One account is preserved and dated 1496. The 30 neighbours (inhabitants) of Spaarnwoude paid yearly 2 stuiver per person. A person on a coach: 1 penning holl., a coach: 1 duit, a bale cloth: 1 oort, a horse with a rider: 1 duit, a chariot: 1 duit, an empty coach, loaded with hay on the way back: 1 duit.  In 1521 it is called the ferry of the Liede and was leased by emperor Charles V to Haarlem for 12 years with the obligation to make a lock. In that same year, the ferry was replaced by a dam, probably to prevent the use of the Liede as a waterway. The name Penningsveer must be of later date.

name: Westhofen
Settlement_Description: The settlement is first mentioned in 1255.
Town_Description: The privileges were confirmed in 1401. The place was previously mentioned as freedom and fortified around 1300.

name: Wetter (Hessen)
Town_Description: Town ready since the end of the 12th century, citizens are mentioned from 1223. A council constitution before the oldest wisdom is documented in 1239. 1309 called 'oppidani'.

name: Wetter (Ruhr)
Settlement_Description: First mentioned in 1214. Nearby, the sovereign castle of the Counts of the Mark was built between 1243 and 1273.
Town_Description: In 1355, urban privileges, which probably existed earlier, were first documented.

name: Papenburg
Settlement_Description: Watchtower in the Lüneburg enclosure ('landwehr'), which was built around 1400. In 1562 an inn was also documented. Around 1830 the inn burned down and was abandoned.

name: Rubene
Settlement_Description: The parish existed before 1208. The associated church was first mentioned in 1543.

name: Papendrecht
Ferry_Description: A ferry to the seigniory Merwede is first mentioned in 1330.

name: Pape
Settlement_Description: In 1253 the settlement was assigned to the Teutonic Order.

name: Parchau
Settlement_Description: Property of Berge monastery in 1191, even though St. Nicholai in Magdeburg held property here since 1188.

name: Parchen
Settlement_Description: In 1144 property of Berge monstary. Mention of a Theodoricus of Parchen as a liege of the archbishop pf Magdeburg  in 1196. A romanic church suggests an existence of the settlement in earlier times. Later construction of a castle.
Town_Description: Referred to as oppidum in 1368, in 1389 as "little town" ("Städtchen").
Fair_Description: In 1389 Archbishop Albrecht III granted the settlement two fairs, on St John and St Simon and Jude.

name: Gadebusch
Settlement_Description: Originally (since the 8th century) a Slavic settlement and fortification. In the 12th century it became a German seat of administration ('vogtei'), first mentioned in 1154 as provincia Godebuz. A German occupation of the castle is attested in 1181.
Town_Description: The settlement acquired privileges in 1225 from Lord Borwin of Mecklenburg, and full Lübeck town privileges in 1271 from Lord Heinrich I the Pilgrim. The privileges were confirmed multiple times.
Toll_Description: Gadebusch enjoyed exemption of tolls up to the Elbe river since 1225. Bruns and Weczerka mention Gadebusch itself as toll station, but provide no further details or references. If this is true, it might refer to a situation that existed in the 18th century.

name: Donkere Sluis
Bridge_Description: The lock was covered by a stone bridge, which forced ships to lower their masts when passing the lock. Possibly the bridge was too narrow for wagons, because it was ordained in 1623 that these should use the nearby Hoornbrug.
Lock_Description: A lock in Gouda is first mentioned in 1321, in a complaint about the narrowness of the lock, but it must have existed from the time that the Gouwe became a navigable waterway in the mid 13th century. At the lock a fee was levied called 'sluisgeld', first mentioned in 1344 at the time of count Jan van Beaumont, lord of the town. After the death of his grandson count Guy of Blois in 1397, this right returned to the count of Holland. Revenues are available for the years 1356-1600. The limited capacity of the lock led to numerous complaints: strict regulations were issued in 1452 and 1466 to prevent problems. New locks were created at the eastern and western side of town in 1536 and 1576, which allowed circumvention of town, but the use of these was only allowed for local traffic and warships; thoroughgoing commercial shipping still had to use the old lock in the middle of the city. Accounts of the 'sluisgeld' are preserved for the years 1548/9, 1557/8, 1577/8 en 1579/1580. The name Donckere Sluys ('dark lock') is first attested in 1665.

name: Wickendorf
Settlement_Description: First mentioned in a papal charter of 1189.

name: Wicker
Settlement_Description: First mentioned in 927. In 1361, the village was burnt down in the context of the Mainz feud. In 1610 and 1648, further fires severely damaged the village.

name: Wiedenbrück
Settlement_Description: First mentioned in 952 and from then on the mint and market place of the Bishop of Osnabrück.
Town_Description: The old town was founded around 1200, the new town started in 1249.

name: Pasewalk
Settlement_Description: A Pomeranian castle is attested around 1150.
Town_Description: A town was founded around 1230. Magdeburg town law granted around 1250, mentioned in 1276 as civitas.

name: Passendorf
Toll_Description: Station of safe conduct, metioned in a regulation of safe conduct from 1600.

name: Passow (Uckermark)
Settlement_Description: First mention of a castle in 1296, a village develops nearby.
Toll_Description: The castle is a toll station.

name: Pastow
Settlement_Description: The village is first mentioned in 1318.

name: Pattensen (Hannover)
Settlement_Description: A traditional first mention from 986-988 as Pathi probably refers to another settlement.
Town_Description: Pattensen probably acquired town privileges in the 13th century.

name: Patika
Settlement_Description: The village was first mentioned in 1241. From 1280 it was in the possession of the "St. Johannis-Siechenhaus" (probably an old hospital) in Reval. From 1370 to 1505 there was a hamlet ('Wirtschaftshof').

name: Paunküla
Settlement_Description: Village and Manor that were first mentioned in 1241.

name: Paupitzsch
Settlement_Description: First mention of the place in a name in 1288; mentioned with a manor house since 1486 (Neuhaus). Deserted and demolished for a lignite opencast mine in 1976.

name: null
Ferry_Description: A ferry is first mentioned in 1356. The destination is not mentioned, but must have been Stolwijkersluis at the opposite bank of the river Hollandse IJssel, where the land route through the Krimpenerwaard to Schoonhoven started. Revenues of the pawning of this domain of the counts of Blois are edited for the second half of the 14th century and early 15th century.

name: Haarlem
Settlement_Description: Haarlem is first mentioned in an eleventh-century copy of a document dated 918-948. Haarlem became situated at the crossroad of several trade routes and gained importance as an military-strategic location. A hospital is first mentioned in 1282.
Town_Description: Haarlem was granted town rights on 23 November 1245 by William II, count of Holland.
Fair_Description: A toll levied at the fair with St. John (June 24) is found since 1267. A detailed right granted for 10 years (in order to strengthen the town) by count Floris V regarding traded and self produced goods is dated 1274 (Dec. 13). In it cloth from abroad, imported wine and beer from Bremen are found. In 1355 (Sep. 11 sep.) duke Willem V granted a fair wit St. Luke-eve (Oct. 17). The duration of this fair in the 15th century is 14 days. In 1387/8 three fairs are mentioned, only one is dated then: on St. Peter and Paulsday (June 29). In 1558 it is called a oxen-fair on October 10. In the period 1374-'93 the count of Blois owned the market-tolls and a tariff dated circa 1372 is preserved. In it 'gordelgeld' and 'roertol' (ruddertoll) are levied from anybody living south of the river Meuse or in Zeeland or outside Holland. Dordrecht only had to pay halff of both. The fair would be as free as the fair of Daniël van der Merwede in Dordrecht, except for all corn which was for the bailiff and court of justice. Afterwards the fairs are registrated in the comital accounts of the steward of Beverwijk (formerly in the Blois period the steward of the 'Wijk'), e.g. in 1456/'7 with St. John midsummer and St. Luke.In 1508 (Oct.) Maximiliaan of Oostenrijk granted a free horse-fair to compensate the heavy duties of the war. The town asked for three fairs each of 3 or 4 days. Granted were two fairs: 1) 29-31 Jan., 2) 29-31 May, with 6 days before and after for a secured travel to the town. The right would be as in Delft, Gouda, Alkmaar a.o., who had obtained this right earlier. This market however, according to the comital accounts, decayed already in the twenties.
Staple_Description: Haarlem tried, after complaints of towns in the Baltic about the quality of the herring, since 1514 to establish a staple for all exported herring caught by Rotterdam, Schiedam, Vlaardingen, Delfshaven, Den Briel, Goeree, Bommenee and other places. All herring should first be packed and marked in Haarlem, like was the case in Dordrecht and Antwerp. In 1516 (April 26) king Charles granted this staple. Furious protests followed by Delft, Leiden, Amsterdam, Rotterdam, Schiedam and places in Waterland and Westfrisia. This matter continued till after the death of Margaretha of Oostenrijk (1530) and remained undecided.

name: Wiesenfeld
Settlement_Description: The village was first mentioned in 1238 and was at the same time a branch of the Order of St. John.

name: Peckelsheim
Settlement_Description: Originally an old peasant settlement; first mentioned in the early 11th century.
Town_Description: The town was founded with a castle in 1318 and received town rights of Borgentreich, Borgholz and Warburg. 1548 confirmation of town privileges.

name: Peer
Settlement_Description: Earliest mention in 1107, in a thirteenth century copy.

name: Pegau
Settlement_Description: Around 1068 there was a village and a castle belonging to Wiprecht von Groitzsch. Between 1191 and 1196 a monastery was built and founded. Since the end of the 11th century there was a market place. In 1170/90 the place was expanded by a new town.
Fair_Description: Pegau owned two fairs of old, one of which had to be moved in 1700 due to the day of penance ('Bußtag'). In 1454 and 1561 Pegau tried for additional fairs, which were not granted due to intervention from Leipzig.
Toll_Description: A safe conduct collector is mentioned in 1551. A table of fees ('Geleitstafel') remains from 1619.

name: Peine
Settlement_Description: A comital family of Peine is first mentioned in the 12th century.
Town_Description: Gunzelin of Wolfenbüttel founded a planned town next to the castle around 1220. It received town privileges in 1223.

name: Peitz
Settlement_Description: Originally a fishing settlement. A castle was built in the mid-13th century; a German market and church settlement developed next to it. First mentioned in 1301, then already a town.
Town_Description: First mentioned as a town in 1301, then in 1336 and 1423, mostly in donation or sale charters.

name: Penig
Settlement_Description: The village of Altpenig settled on the northern bank. However, in today's existing urban area there was a moated castle. In 1301 Penig received market rights.
Town_Description: Between 1170 and 1329 the town was expanded by the Lords of Altenburg. In 1227 the place probably received town rights. In 1455 they were confirmed by Georg zu Leisnig.

name: Wiesbaden
Settlement_Description: First mentioned as early as 50 AD when it was inhabited by the Romans. Around 500 there was a settlement by the Franks. In 1022 the place is mentioned as a 'villa'.
Town_Description: Is mentioned in 1241 as 'civitas' and in 1242 as 'civitas imperatoria'. Still referred to as 'oppidum' in 1344, it was first mentioned as a town in 1348. In 1393 the town received a letter of freedom confirming the old freedoms and rights. These were partly repealed by the peasant uprising in 1525, but awarded again in 1566.

name: Perila
Settlement_Description: The manor and village were mentioned in 1241. The St. Michaelis monastery in Reval owned the Folwark of Pergel together with the village and mill in 1286.

name: Perleberg
