The inn was closed down a couple of years later, but the location was good and served a lot of travellers, since in 1684, the previous innkeeper's son Pertti Yrjönpoika complained how he has to give rides to people between Toivola and Kuortti. His tavern rights were thus renoved, and Mäkivola inn continued to serve until 1740s.

name: Schevenbrügge
Settlement_Description: Hamlet near a bridge, first mentioned in 1633/34.

name: Schiedam
Settlement_Description: Schiedam is first mentioned in 1204, according to Van Berkel & Samplonius. Cox mentions a later date, 1264. In the river Schie, a dam was built in 1250. Schiedam was a small port town on the trade routes over the rivers Meuse and Schie. However, the port suffered from sedimentation. The importance of the port diminished in the fourteenth century, when Rotterdam en Delft got a connection to the Meuse. A hospital is found in 1276.
Town_Description: Schiedam was granted town rights on 18 March 1275 by Adelaide of Holland (lady of Schiedam).
Fair_Description: In 1270 (May 29) count Floris V granted together with his aunt ex-regentes Aleid a fair in Schiedam. He gave alle visitors safe-conduct and protection in his countship on the fair and weekly-market. In 1346 (August)  countess Margret donated the market-field to the town. In 1468 (St. Bavo) the fair is moved because St. Bavo (Oct. 1) was a holy day. The fair will now start the first working day after St. Bavo, the freedom however starts with St. Bavo. In 1484 (Febr. 22) Maximiliaan of Oostenrijk granted a free horse-fair on the second Friday in March. The market-rights would be equal to those in Delft and Rotterdam. The yields are destined to improve the harbour. In 1488 (Oct. 3) the town obtained (another?) horse-fair starting 'grote Vastenavond' (Shrove Tuesday) during 8 days, with equael tolls as in Delft and Rotterdam. In 1559/'60 (March 8) king Philip II granted two free fairs. The walled town only had herring-catch as a mean of subsistence, which was in decay since (15)52 as a result of the war with France where many busses were lost. This was cause for one-third of the poverty. Dates: 1) July 5 when the herringbusses had to be provided, 2) Oct. 3 when the citizens provided themselves for the winter, each for 14 days. In 1601 (March 27) The Estates of Holland granted a meager cattle-fair on the day after Allsaints (Nov. 2), or when this was a Sunday the day after that.

name: Schinditz
Settlement_Description: First mention in 1378, mention of a manor in 1491/2.

name: Schipluiden
Settlement_Description: Earliest mention in the twelfth century, in a copy dating from circa 1420.

name: Schirmenitz
Settlement_Description: The village is first mentioned in 1130.

name: Brandýs nad Labem
Toll_Description: In 1531 Conrad and Johanna von Krayk gave the toll in Brandýs to the town council, including the obligation to maintain the roads. In the document the toll is said to have existed "since old times".

name: Świdwin
Settlement_Description: Originally a Wendish castle mound and settlement, in possession of the Ascanian margraves from 1266. German settlers were first mentioned in 1280.
Town_Description: The Brandenburg town law was likely granted by margraves Otto IV and Conrad in 1296, but the settlement was already walled in 1292. Characterised as town ('civitas') in 1373. The privileges were renewed in 1378 by Hans von Wedel.

name: Schkeuditz
Settlement_Description: Mentioned in 849 as limes Sorabicus, first mention of the castle in 941. In the 10th century, Schkeuditz was a castle district centre ('Burgwardhauptort') of the Slavs and later taken over by the Germans.
Town_Description: In 1200 the expansion to town began. In 1210 referred to as oppidum, however, certain privileges and rights were only granted in 1436 by bishop Johannes II. In 1557 the town rights were confirmed.
Toll_Description: The regulations of safe conduct were renewed and copied in 1535, which means they existed earlier.

name: Schkopau
Settlement_Description: The settlement was founded in the 9th century. A family of imperial ministeriales were called after Schkopau since 1177 at the latest and died out in 1480.
Toll_Description: The revenues from land and ferry tolls recur in the records of the Trotha family on castle Schkopau since 1477.

name: Schladen
Settlement_Description: Originally a farm of the royal palace Werla, it was reconstructed as a castle by bishop Udo of Hildesheim before 1110.

name: Schlage
Settlement_Description: The village is first mentioned in 1351.

name: Slaný
Toll_Description: King Wenceslaus permitted citizens from Cheb in 1391 to travel via Slaný to Prague; they would have to pay the tolls normally levied in Žebrák in Slaný.

name: Sławno
Settlement_Description: First mentioned in 1186. The settlement developed close to a fortification at a river. A castellan is mentioned in 1223 as well as a church of St Adalbert.
Town_Description: The town was probably founded in 1311. First mentioned as town ('civitas') in 1317 and received Lübeck town law from the Swiencan Jesko.

name: Schleswig
Settlement_Description: The predecessor of Schleswig was Haithabu (Danish: Hedeby), the largest town (emporium) in Viking age Scandinavia. Haithabu was located at the southern side of Slien, a narrow inlet of the Baltic Sea, but in the 11th century Haithabu was abandoned, and Schleswig developed on the opposite northern side of Slien. Already in 948 a bishop of Schleswig is mentioned in an Ottonian charter, but if the bishop actually resided in Schleswig at this point is not clear. The emporium of Haithabu as well as Viking age Schleswig was the main transshipment point in long-distance trade between the North Sea and the Baltic Sea.
Town_Description: First mentioned as a 'civitas' in 1196; The Schleswig town law developed in the late 12th century.
Fair_Description: Heinrich Rantzau mentions three fairs in his 1597 description of Schleswig and Holstein, but does not provide dates. An almanac printed in 1598 in Neudamm (Dębno) mentions a fair on the Beheading of St John the Baptist.

name: Schleusingen
Settlement_Description: The settlement is first mentioned in 1232, but might have been much older given the settlement of the surrounding valleys in the High Middle Ages. The castle Bertholdsburg was built in the 12th century.
Town_Description: First mentioned as town in 1268, but only received town statutes in 1412.
Fair_Description: Market rights and four markets were granted in 1533.

name: Człuchów
Settlement_Description: Wendish refugees were granted the right to settle in 1200 by duke Sambor I of eastern Pomerania. The Teutonic Order bought the lands surrounding it in 1312 and built a castle and in 1332 a commandry.
Town_Description: A charter with Kulm town law was granted by the Grandmaster Heinrich Dusemer in 1348 and was later endorsed by the Polish King Sigismund II.

name: Człopa
Town_Description: Town privileges were likely granted at the end of the 13th century, the town itself was first mentioned in 1350. The town privileges with Magdeburg town law were renewed in 1614.

name: Schlutup
Settlement_Description: First mentioned in 1225. In the fishing village, there was a guarded crossing of the Lübeck border ('landwehr') with Mecklenburg, with an inn and a boom barrier. The watchtower was demolished in 1673, its stones used for the mill gate (Mühlentor) in Lübeck.

name: Schmarsau
Settlement_Description: First mentioned in 1330/52. In 1450, the settlement consisted of 3 farms, a mill and a cottage.

name: Schmithausen
Toll_Description: From 1062/76 until around 1318, there was a river toll on the Rhine in Schmithausen. This was moved to Emmerich after 1318. The Bishop of Utrecht was the owner of the toll, with the monasteries of St. Johannes (1076 to 1085) and St. Maria (since 1085) listed as owners as well. The toll was frequently leased out: before 1228 to the Lord of Schmithausen, since 1228 to the Lord of Lek and since 1351 to the Lord of Culembourg. In 1319, 4 denarii per barrel had to be paid.

name: Schmilau
Toll_Description: A toll station in Schmilau was created in 1583.

name: Schmira
Settlement_Description: First mention in 1243. Property of the counts of Thüringen-Schwarzburg, who enfeoffed the village on several occasions.

name: Schmölau
Settlement_Description: First mention in 1330. In 1375 it is mentioned as deserted, mentioned again in 1458 but it is unclear whether it is active. Surely reconstructed by 1542.

name: Hiltula
Settlement_Description: <b>Inn:</b> An inn was established in Hiltula in the early 17th c.

name: Turakkala
Settlement_Description: <b>Inn:</b> An inn was established in Turakkala in 1649.

name: Piła
Town_Description: The town privileges were probably granted in 1380 by Queen Hedwig, but were destroyed in 1824 in a fire. It is first mentioned in 1456 and called a town in 1506 and 1511. In 1513 Sigismund I of Poland granted the Magdeburg town law.
Toll_Description: Mentioned as Polish border toll station in the first half of the 17th century.

name: Scholen
Settlement_Description: In a 1203 charter, a "Dietrich von Sconenla" appears, around 1370 the settlement itself is first mentioned.

name: Schönberg (Mecklenburg)
Settlement_Description: First mentioned in 1219. Bishop Ulrich of Ratzeburg built a fortified house between 1257 and 1284, which was made into the residence of bishop Marquard in the early 14th century. The settlement was characterised as borough ('oppidum') in the early 16th century, but only received town rights in 1822.

name: Schönberg (Lauenburg)
Settlement_Description: First mentioned in 1389. The settlement was abandoned after 1554. The current village Schönberg is located more to the north.

name: Schönböcken
Settlement_Description: The area around Schönböcken belonged to the town of Lübeck since 1226, and the village must have been founded not long after. It is first mentioned in 1262.

name: Bělá pod Bezdězem
Staple_Description: A staple is first mentioned in 1337 at the renewed foundation of the town and endorsed multiple times. In 1396 it is specified that all commodities brought into town had to stay there for one day and two nights.

name: Schönebeck (Elbe)
Settlement_Description: The settlement was first mentioned in 1194. In 1372 a castle is mentioned at the location of former saltworks. Even though the settlement was planned, it was never granted town rights and was always ruled by a town lord.
Fair_Description: In 1555 Schönebeck is granted the privilege for two fairs and one weekly market, which leads to several conflicts with the town of Magdeburg.

name: Schönberg (Mark)
Settlement_Description: The village is first mentioned in 1365.

name: Lahnaniemi
Settlement_Description: <b>Inn:</b> Lahnaniemi ("Bream cape") could be the same place which is referred to as Lahnamäki and Lahnamaa ("-hill", "-land"). In mid-16th c., there was a transport hub in the village, and in 1572, an inn was established in Lahnamäki. Lahnaniemi could serve as a stopping point on the way to Mikkeli church.

name: Schönhausen (Elbe)
Settlement_Description: First mention of the church in Schönhausen in 1212; sources that claim a mention in 1202 cannot be proven. Mention as a little town ('Stedtchen') in the 16th century, in 1600 characterised as borough ('Flecken'). Mention of a monastery in 1608.

name: Schöningen
Settlement_Description: First mentioned in 747. There was probably a royal court here, since  Pippin, Charlemagne and Otto III. held court in 747, 784, 994 and 995.
Town_Description: Duke Magnus of Brunswick granted town privileges in 1346-48. However, the settlement was already mentioned as 'oppidum' in 1332 and 'civitas' in 1338. The town was fortified in the first half of the 14th century and a ducal castle was built in 1348.

name: Trzcianka
Settlement_Description: The village was first mentioned in 1561. It is mentioned as small town ('Städtchen') in 1679 and received town privileges in 1731.

name: Schöppenstedt
Settlement_Description: The church was founded in 827. The settlement is first mentioned in a charter in 1051 and characterised as "villa" until 1332.
Town_Description: Schöppenstedt is characterised as borough ('weichbild') from 1345, and as town in the 16th century.
Toll_Description: One of the five toll stations in the Amt Wolfenbüttel, first mentioned in 1492.

name: Schöppingen
Settlement_Description: The church of St Brictus was built before 838, when it was first mentioned.
Town_Description: A planned town was founded in the 14th century, first mentioned as borough ('wigbold') in 1396. It is characterised as town between 1435 and 1658, but after 1659 it is usually called 'wigbold' again.

name: Putkilahti
Settlement_Description: <b>Inn:</b> There has been a transport hub or a tavern in Putkilahti village in mid-1540s owned by Olavi Rennare. It is not mentioned after the mid-16th c.

name: Schopsdorf
Settlement_Description: Schopsdorf was a residence of the bishop of Brandenburg was 1327 - 1347. The correlating village was probably already deserted in the 13th century. A new settlement developed around a barbican in 1763.

name: Schorrentin
Settlement_Description: First mentioned in 1305. A document from 1314 speaks of a German and a Slavic village.

name: Schoten
Settlement_Description: Earliest mention in 868, in an 18th-century copy.

name: Śrem
Toll_Description: King Władysław II ordained in 1398 that merchants had to pay toll in Śrem. King Sigismund I allowed a tariff increase from 4 to 6 Pfennig for each merchant's horse in 1539.

name: Skrunda
Settlement_Description: In 1253 the wooded region fell to the Teutonic Order, that built a castle in 1368. In 1429 there was a manor.

name: Schulenhof
Settlement_Description: First mentioned in 1434. The village called Schulendorf was abandoned between 1444 and 1620, a farm ('hof') remained.

name: Schüttorf
Settlement_Description: First mentioned in 1154 in the foundation charter Wietmarschen monastery. In 1184 it was called "curia" and in 1288 "oppidum".
Town_Description: Schüttorf became the first urban settlement in the county of Bentheim in 1295, when it received the town rights of Münster.
Fair_Description: Four six-day fairs are mentioned in Schüttorf in 1465, which were doubtlessly older. Dates are not mentioned.
Toll_Description: According to privileges from 1465, the town levied a road toll at the town gates and on the bridge.

name: Schwalbach am Taunus
Settlement_Description: First mentioned in 1352. Was a comparatively large settlement in the Middle Ages and therefore rose to become a town without any official granting of privileges. Called 'Flecken' around 1600. 1643 granting of the 'Burgfrieden' and confirmation of old rights.

name: Schwanbeck (Dassow)
Settlement_Description: First mentioned in 1292. At that time, there were 14 farms in the village. A tax register from 1525 lists 12 farms.

name: Alt Schwagstorf
Settlement_Description: The village was first mentioned in 1090.

name: Schwanbeck (Friedland)
Settlement_Description: A castle was built in Schwanbeck before 1317, when its demolition was ordered in the peace of Templin.

name: Soikkala
Settlement_Description: <b>Inn:</b> An inn was established in Soikkala in 1584. In 1640s, parish constable (fi: nimismies, sw: länsman) Olli Laurinpoika Puttonen ran a tavern in his house. His neighbour, Nuutti Niilonpoika Soikkanen, served as a transport organiser.

name: Gulbene
Settlement_Description: Around 1340 a castle and church were built. The first written reference dated back to 1416. A fortified borough ('Hakelwerk') developed close to the castle and appeared under the name 'vicus Svaneburgensis' in 1489. The settlement and castle were destroyed by Ivan IV in 1577.

name: Zvārde
Settlement_Description: An inn is mentioned in 1603. The district of 'Schwarden' was first mentioned in 1628.

name: Bad Schwartau
Settlement_Description: Settlement at the Schwartau river. A mill is mentioned in 1215, a leprosy hospital for women in 1258.

name: Ādams
Settlement_Description: The manor existed before 1625. However, the ownership is only known from 1625.

name: Schwarzenbek
Settlement_Description: The village was first mentioned in 1291.
Toll_Description: In 1618, the city of Hamburg complained at the Imperial Chamber Court that the Duke of Saxony-Lauenburg had started to levy anew toll in Schwarzenbek.

name: Schwedt
Settlement_Description: First mentioned in 1265, already as a town. The settlement developed near a 12th-century Pomeranian castle at an Oder crossing.
Town_Description: A town was probably founded around 1250 by the Margrave of Brandenburg, first secure mention of the castle and town in 1265. Confirmation of town rights in 1515.
Toll_Description: The town held a land and water toll, from which Angermünde was exempted in 1350. The toll belonged, together with the town, to the Dukes of Pomerania between 1354 and 1465/74, and to the Margraves of Brandenburg before and after. A bridge and dam toll were added later. In 1563 an old and new toll are mentioned.

name: Schwerin
Settlement_Description: Slavic settlement and castle, first mentioned in 1018. Schwerin became the centre of Christian missionary activity in 1155, seat of a bishop in 1160.
Town_Description: Town privileges granted by Duke Henry the Lion in 1160. In 1266, the old town was extended by a new town. Schwerin became the capital of the duchy of Mecklenburg in 1348.
Fair_Description: A fair in Schwerin is first attested in 1171. It took place on the dedication day of the cathedral, 9 september. Another market took place on 15 June since 1248. Until 1222 a fair was also held on Maundy Thursday.

name: Skwierzyna
Settlement_Description: Probably originally a Slavic fishing settlement, first mentioned in 1251.
Town_Description: The town was founded around 1295, first mentioned as town in 1306. After the town privileges were lost in a fire, they were renewed by King Władysław II Jagiełło in 1406 with Magdeburg town law.
Toll_Description: King Władysław of Poland set the tariffs for the toll in Skwierzyna in 1390.

name: Schwerz
Settlement_Description: First mention in the Chronicon Montis Sereni, the Wettin chronicle of the Petersberg (MGH SS. 23, ed. E. Ehrenfeuchter, Hannover 1874, S. 172).

name: Parkumäki
Settlement_Description: <b>Inn:</b> An inn was established in Parkumäki in 1584. It continued to serve until early 18th c.

name: Świebodzin
Settlement_Description: A castle was apparently built in 1228, mentioned in 1247 and 1303, a market settlement existed next to it.
Town_Description: First mentioned as a town in 1319. Full town privileges were granted in 1469.

name: Sebexen
Settlement_Description: The place was first mentioned in 1139.

name: Seehausen (Altmark)
Settlement_Description: In the 10th century, a border castle probably already existed as protection against the Slavs. Around 1150 the Old city was constructed, around 1170 a New town was established.
Town_Description: Referred to as oppidum in 1196. The town was probably under Magdeburg town rights, while "Seehausen town rights" were given to Pritzwalk in 1256. Member of the Hanse in 1358.
Fair_Description: In an official schedule from 1719, Seehausen, Werben and Arneburg each held three fairs. It can be assumed that some of these had existed for a while to this point.

name: Seehausen (Wanzleben)
Settlement_Description: Important place on the road from Magdeburg to the west (Werla).First record mention 966 in a gift certificate by Otto I to his familiar Mamaco (MGH DD O I, nr. 327, S. 441), it probably existed before that though and was an im portant waypoint on the way to Magdeburg.With the shift of royal courts from Werla to Goslar, Seehausen looses its importance for traffic.
Town_Description: In 1197 Seehausen had the status of a town, in 1563 it is only referred to as borough ('Flecken').

name: Seelow
Settlement_Description: First mention in 1252, probably founded in the first half of the 13th century. Mention as borough ('Flecken') in 1278 and as little town ('Städtchen') in 1308 and 1317. Town privileges were not granted.

name: Joroisniemi
Settlement_Description: <b>Inn:</b> An inn was established in Joroisniemi in 1649, and Pekka Kärri was appointed as the innkeeper.

name: Seesen
Settlement_Description: The settlement, consisting of a royal court and castle, is first mentioned in 973/4 in an imperial charter of Otto II. In the 13th century, a merchant settlement came into existence around the St Andrew's church next to the old settlement.
Town_Description: Seesen is characterised from 1360 as town or borough ('stad', 'blek' or 'oppidum'). A council is attested in 1407, and the settlement received borough ('weichbild') privileges in 1428. Only in 1532, however, Seesen is first counted among the towns in the duchy of Brunswick.
Fair_Description: A fair in Seesen is first mentioned in 1434. In 1640, there were three fairs, to which a cattle fair was added.
Toll_Description: A toll of the dukes of Brunswick is first mentioned in Seesen in 1405, when it was pawned. Toll revenues were limited. According to an overview of tolls in the duchy of Brunswick-Wolfenbüttel from 1582, the toll was calculated according to the weight of the cargo.

name: Bad Segeberg
Settlement_Description: A castle and a monastery of Augustinian canons were founded in 1134. Next to it, a market settlement developed.
Town_Description: Lübeck town privileges granted by Adolf IV. of Holstein in 1244(?), confirmed by the counts Johann and Gerhard in 1260. The town was pawned to Lübeck between 1342 and 1366.
Fair_Description: In his 1597 description of Schleswig and Holstein, Heinrich Rantzau mentions a fair on All Saints' Day.
Toll_Description: Already in 1400, it is ordained that merchants from Lübeck to Neumünster and Rendsburg were obliged to travel via Segeberg. An actual toll station of the counts of Holstein is first mentioned in 1479 in a Lübeck complaint. However, toll revenues were only modest in the 16th century.

name: Sigulda
Settlement_Description: Around 1207/10 a knightly order built a castle, which was one centre of the Teutonic Order in the 14th and 15th centuries. The decay of the castle began around 1600. In 1434 the fortified borough ('Hakelwerk') near the castle was first mentioned. It was probably destroyed by Ivan IV in 1577. A church was first mentioned in 1483 - it was probably built in 1225.

name: Sehnde
Settlement_Description: The place was first mentioned in 1147.

name: Preedi
Settlement_Description: The manor and the associated hamlets ('Hof') belonged to the cathedral in Reval in 1442.

name: Vecsēlpils
Settlement_Description: In 1208, Germans conquered the existing castle ('castrum Selonum'), which became the bishopric from 1218. Another castle of the Teutonic Order was built in 1373. Before 1596 a fortified borough ('Hakelwerk') was built, which was referred to as 'Städtlein'. In 1621, it received market rights.

name: Seligenstadt
Settlement_Description: Emerges from a monastery settlement that merged with the town of Obermühlheim. The monastery is first mentioned in 847.

name: Seljaküla
Settlement_Description: Village with a manor was mentioned in 1517.

name: Selmsdorf
Settlement_Description: First mentioned in 1292. At that time, there were 26 farms in the village. In a tax register from 1525, 23 farms are listed.

name: Pirhiänniemi
Settlement_Description: <b>Inn:</b> An inn was established in Pirhiänniemi in 1584.

name: Zeltiņi
Settlement_Description: The manor was probably built in the 13th century.

name: Silla
Settlement_Description: The village was mentioned in 1489 and belonged to the lands of the 'Uchten' manor. On the other side of the river, two inns are mentioned in 1586.
Bridge_Description: The village was called after the bridge Sembruggen, also known as the "Kohalsche Steinbrücke".

name: Ziemeri
Settlement_Description: The Manor was built even before 1550.

name: Sārnate
Settlement_Description: The latvian region 'Sarnitus' was first mentioned in 1230.

name: Cesvaine
Settlement_Description: In the early 14th century, the archbishop built a castle, which was mentioned in 1426. The castle may not have been built until the end of the 14th century.
Town_Description: A fortified borough ('Hakelwerk'), which was referred to as 'oppidum' in 1441 was built near the castle. The castle and the settlement were both destroyed by the Russians in 1577.

name: Sece
Settlement_Description: The manor was first mentioned in 1556 and was burned down by Russians in 1559.

name: Džūkste
Settlement_Description: The manor of the Teutonic Order was mentioned in 1442.

name: Siebigerode
Settlement_Description: In 1040 Siebigerode is given as part of a dowry. In 1273 it was noticed that the village was deserted. In between the village must have been reconstructed, but by 1646 it had been deserted again. In 1651 it was attempted to be rebuilt again.

name: Sieciechów
Toll_Description: Mentioned as toll station in c. 1349, where 8 gr. had to be paid for each horse.

name: Sieden
Settlement_Description: Settlement near a ford in the stream Siede. The stream is first mentioned in 1241, the settlement in ca. 1380. On the "Kurhannoversche Landesaufnahme" (1764-1784), a toll house is depicted here. However, there is no evidence for a toll in the period before 1650.

name: Siegburg
Settlement_Description: Archbishop Anno II of Cologne founded a Benedictine monastery on the Siegberg around 1064; a small settlement already existed at the site at this time. The monastery received market, toll and mint privileges in 1069.
Town_Description: Siegburg is first mentioned as 'oppidum', 'stat' or 'civitas' in the 1180s and can be considered a town at this point, although town privileges were not granted. The town was fortified in 1220-40.
Fair_Description: The monastery Siegburg received market privileges in 1069; the oldest market is mentioned in 1183-85 to take place on Ascension Day, which was well visited, among others by merchants from Cologne. A second fair of St Servatius is mentioned in 1461, which was moved to Corpus Christi in that year. A third fair, on St Matthew's Day, might have existed since 1491 and was confirmed in 1521/22. A fourth fair, on St Nicholas, was granted in 1600.
Toll_Description: 1) The monastery of Siegburg received toll privileges in 1069; this probably concerned a market toll. Moreover, according to complaints from Cologne in 1438, a "new toll" on land and water, especially for wine, was levied by the Duke of Berg. It was abolished around 1442.<br/>2) In 1357, a bridge toll was levied by the town itself. A fee of 4 old heller per horse had to be paid.

name: Sieradz
Toll_Description: In 1390, King Władysław of Poland ordained, that the toll tariffs in Sieradz, Kalisz, Pyzdry and Poznań were to be the same as those levied in Piotrków Trybunalski, Łęczyca, Przedecz and Brześć.

name: Sierpc
Toll_Description: Merchants from Vilnius complained in 1528 and 1533 about a new toll that was levied in Sierpc.

name: Sierße
Settlement_Description: The place was first mentioned in 1141.

name: Sievershausen
Settlement_Description: The place was first mentioned in 1234.

name: Sildemow
Settlement_Description: The village is first mentioned around 1330.

name: Sillamäe
Settlement_Description: The settlement was first mentioned in 1502.

name: Silvolde
Settlement_Description: Earliest mention in 838, in a eleventh century copy. Next mention dates from 1200.

name: Simmringen
Toll_Description: The count of Hohenlohe complained in 1483, that merchants from Nuremberg had circumvented his toll station in Simmringen.

name: Liberec
Toll_Description: A toll station in Liberec is first mentioned in 1454.

name: Obersimtshausen
Settlement_Description: First mentioned between 1200 and 1220. A distinction between Ober-, Mittel- and Unter-Simtshausen is first attested in 1574.

name: Sinsleben
Settlement_Description: In 964 Gernrode monastery held property in Sinsleben, in following years it was owned by Quedlinburg monastery and the counts of Falkenstein.

name: Sint-Oedenrode
Settlement_Description: Sint-Oedenrode is first mentioned in the twelfth century.
Town_Description: Town rights were granted some time between 9 April 1232 and 2 April 1233 by Henry I, duke of Brabant.
Fair_Description: In 1341 St. Oedenrode obtained a fair. In 1403 the duchess gave the right for a weekly market and for a weigh-house.

name: Sint-Stevens-Woluwe
Settlement_Description: Earliest mention in circa 1040, in a copy of the middle of the eleventh century. Next mention in 1046.

name: Sinzig
Toll_Description: From 1452, a land toll was levied in Sinzig. The Archbishop of Cologne was mentioend as the pledgee. It is probable that there was already a market toll in Sinzig before 1452. In 1490, an additional 1 gold gulden had to be paid for each foder of wine. Annual revenues are not known.

name: Antamoinen
Settlement_Description: <b>Inn:</b> Parish constable (fi: nimismies, sw: länsman) Lasse Antinpoika ran a tavern in his house in 1571.

name: Sint-Odiliënberg
Settlement_Description: Earliest mention probably in the first half of the ninth century, in a seventeenth century copy. Next mention in 858.

name: Joroinen
Settlement_Description: <b>Inn:</b> An inn was established in Joroinen area in 1602. It was located in Antti Auvinen's farm by the common road, and he was given a piece of land so he could better serve travellers.

name: Sliedrecht
Settlement_Description: Earliest mention in 1203, in a copy dating from 1704. The village was originally called Oversliedrecht, to discern it from the original Sliedrecht located at the opposite side of the river. After the latter place drowned in 1421, Oversliedrecht became known as Sliedrecht.

name: Slijk-Ewijk
Settlement_Description: Some identify 'Euuic Silec' as Slijk-Ewijk, but Van Berkel and Samplonius (2018) consider this identification unlikely. According to them, the place is first mentioned in 1573 as 'SlijckEwick'. The tower of the church (Hervormde Kerk, Dorpsstraat 70), however, dates from the twelfth century; the nave from the fifteenth century.

name: Sloten
Town_Description: First mentioned as a town on 27 April 1422. Sloten was walled during the Middle Ages. Further fortifications were added in 1672.
Fair_Description: In 1535 Sloten asked the stadtholder and council for two fairs. The excises of the emperor would improve as a result of consent. In 1537 the advice however is to deny this.

name: Slochteren
Settlement_Description: Earliest mention in the eleventh century.

name: Sittendorf
Settlement_Description: First mention in 1059-1072 in the charter book of Hersfeld monastery. In 1128 the possession of tithes among others from the village "Sidendorph" by Jechaburg monastery was confirmed by archbishop Adalbert of Mainz.

name: Ahvola
Settlement_Description: <b>Inn:</b> <i>Neljännesmies</i> (sw. fjärdingsman, a local official) Jöns Ahvonen kept a tavern by the common road and received victuals for it.

name: Hauklappi
Settlement_Description: <b>Inn:</b> There might have been an inn in Hauklappi already in the 16th century, but an official inn was established in 1649, when Niilo Lappalainen was the innkeeper.

name: Plate
Settlement_Description: Pope Celestine III confirmed the bishopric of Schwerin in 1191, but also a ship or water toll in Plate in a document. A castle also existed, but it was destroyed in 1326.
Toll_Description: In 1191, a ship toll was mentioned in Plate. In 1506, a 'small toll' was also mentioned.

name: Hoornbrug
Bridge_Description: The bridge Hoornbrug was a stone bridge located next to the lock. In 1623 it was ordained that wagons were not allowed to use the wooden bridges over the harbour south of the lock, because they caused too much damage to the bridges, and had to use the Hoornbrug instead.

name: Orlamünde
Settlement_Description: The settlement emerged in the 11th century near the castle of the lords of Weimar-Orlamünde. It is first mentioned in 1040.
Town_Description: Town rights were probably granted by landgrave Frederick II of Thuringia between 1344 and 1349.
Toll_Description: The income from the fees of safe conduct ('Geleitseinnahmen') in Orlamünde is high enough to assume that long-distance-trade passed through here

name: Andernach
Settlement_Description: Mentioned at the end of the 3rd century on the stone of Tongeren. Originally a Roman fortress next to a settlement on the Rhine street. In the Middle Ages it became a Frankish royal farm, donated to the Archbishop of Cologne in 1167.
Toll_Description: (1) The Archbishop of Cologne levied a river toll on the Rhine from 1147 to 1190, in 1235, from 1277 to 1282, from 1287 to 1302 and from 1306 to 1365. In 1365, the toll was relocated to Linz until it was reestablished in Andernach in 1475. Between 1475 and 1485, the annual return amounted to 3000 Gulden. The amount to pay for wine was relatively low, but salt, fish and grains are similar to the tariffs in Bonn. The tariffs can bee seen under the following source below. (2) In 1302 and from 1312, together with the river toll, an escort fee was levied by the Archbishop of Cologne.(3) This unknown toll, probably a transit toll, was levied from 1389 and concerned millstones. The tariff per millstone was 6 Pfennig/Denar. The annual yield amounted to 12 Mark in 1390-95 and 1433.

name: Nysted
Settlement_Description: Presumably founded in the shadow of the royal castle of Ålholm in the 13th century.
Town_Description: Nysted most likely had an urban character in the middle of the 13th century. Franciscan monastery founded in 1286. Town privileges granted by king Eric the Pommerian (1396-1439) in 1409, but privileges may have been granted earlier. The privileges from 1409 decided that all taxes and tolls paid from Nysted to Ålholm castle, in the future, would be replaced by town taxes to the king. Oldest town hall placed at the old square, Gammel Torv, burned down in 1654. Throughout the medieval and early-modern era Nysted benefited from the rich agriculture on the island of Lolland and rich herring fishing. The town, however, remained one of the smallest in Denmark.

name: Jääski
Settlement_Description:
Permanent agricultural settlement in Jääski area dates to the Iron Age. Jääski was together with Savilahti and Äyräpää the three pogosts Novgorod handed over to the Kingdom of Sweden in the peace of Nöteborg in 1323. Jääski is mentioned as an independent parish together with Lapvesi in 1415. Jääski church was originally located West of Vuoksi in Kirkonkylä village from where it as translocated to later site east of Vuoksi some time in the 16th century, at the latest in 1612.

<b>Inn:</b> Noble travellers have stayed in Jääski parsonage in 1591.
Fair_Description: Burghers of Viborg were in 1542 granted sole right for four annual fairs in their trading area of which Vehkalahti St Olaf’s fair (29 July) were also allowed to take place in Viborg town. The other thre fairs were held on apostle Peter (29 June) in Jääski, on the Nativity of Mary (8 September) in Lapvesi and on the Elevation of the Holy Cross (14 September) in Äyräpää. The burghers sole right to all four fairs was confirmed in 1594. Apostle Peter was the medieval patron saint of Jääski church.

name: Groß Marzehns
Settlement_Description: The village is first mentioned in 1388. Mentioned as deserted in 1450 and 1514, it was re-occupied after c. 1545.
Toll_Description: A secondary station of safe conduct ('Nebengeleit') of the district ('Amt') Belzig in 'Mortzens' appears in accounts from 1489 onwards. Straube identifies this place with Marzahna, but this is unlikely, as Marzahna was located in the district Wittenberg. Moreover, in 1513/14 the safe conduct is listed together with the village Klepzig (which is otherwise not mentioned as station of safe conduct), a neighbouring village of Groß Marzehns.

name: Puumala
Settlement_Description: <b>Inn:</b> Puumala vicar Gabriel Carolin established an inn in 1646. Three years later, an inn was established in Puumala strait. It was held by Matti Mikonpoika Penttinen. In 1654, a ferry was established over the strait, and in 1663, a new inn was built with glass windows, a chimney, and a door with iron hinges. The construction was ordered by the innkeeper Tönne Skult, but there were some incoherences with payments. After Tönne, the old parish constable (fi: nimismies, sw: länsman) Paavo Vakkolainen held the inn for over 30 years.

name: Smiltene
Settlement_Description: In 1224, a castle was mentioned, which fell to the Teutonic Order in 1556. In 1428, a fortified borough developed, which was referred to as a 'minor town' ('Weichbild') oder 'oppidulum' in 1553/37.

name: Snits
Town_Description: Sneek was first mentioned as a town on 9 October 1317. In 1492, an earthen wall was built and a moat was added.
Fair_Description: Sneek obtained in 1456 the right for a buttermarket.
Staple_Description: In 1517 Karel van Gelder ordained that no fairs or weekly markets should be organised around Sneek. Nor weavers, pilchards, shoemakers of merchants with heavy trade or heavy balances for butter or cheese.

name: Sochaczew
Toll_Description: Mentioned as toll station in 1501, when toll was levied of merchants travelling from Russia, Lithuania, Mazovia and Moscovy to Poznań, Gniezno and Wrocław, circumventing Lublin.

name: Söder
Settlement_Description: Castle of the bishop of Hildesheim, first mentioned as enfeoffed to the lords of Hagen around 1200. Reconstructed as baroque castle in 1740/42.

name: Laag-Soeren
Settlement_Description: Earliest mention as Laag Soeren in 1830-1855.

name: Soest (Amersfoort)
Settlement_Description: Earliest mention in 1028, in a copy dating from circa 1530.

name: Soestdijk
Settlement_Description: The Soestdijk, a raised causeway through wet territory, was built shortly after 1350 by the bishop of Utrecht to improve the road between Utrecht and Ter Eem. A country house was built at the dike around 1650, which was later transformed into palace Soestdijk.

name: Ruokolahti
Settlement_Description: <b>Inn:</b> Ruokolahti parsonage served travellers in the late 16th c. There has also been inns held by Suni Hannunpoika Härskiäinen and Suikki Vaittinen in Ruokolahti area. In 1638, an inn was established in Rasila farm in Ruokolahti parish village, close to the parsonage. It was held by Pekka Rasilainen and Pertti Heikinpoika.

name: Kukkola
Settlement_Description: <b>Inn:</b> An inn was established in Kukkola in 1585, and Hannu Kukkoinen was appointed as the innkeeper.

name: Store Heddinge
Settlement_Description: Archaeological excavations near the church, which is dated to c. 1150, have located settlement remains from the 12th century. Presumably a royal estate in the 11th and 12th century formed the basis for the founding of a permanent settlement. The settlement was placed in the middle of Stevns, one of the most fertile regions of Zealand.
Town_Description: According to the so-called main piece in King Valdemar’s Cadastre from c. 1231 Store Heddinge was “patrimonium”, i.e. the settlement belonged to the royal family. Another text in the same manuscript, a registration of towns on Zealand and surrounding island from 1241, counted Store Heddinge among the towns of Zealand. Thus, Store Heddinge was considered as an urban settlement around 1240. In the 13th century the town had two guilds. In 1357 townsmen (uillanus) are mentioned for the first time, and in 1415 a town mayor. King Christoffer the Bavarian confirmed town privileges in 1441, and these were later confirmed and expanded in 1454, 1563 and 1628. In 1481 a town bailiff was indirectly mentioned. Throughout the middle ages and early-modern era Store Heddinge benefited from the rich agriculture and fishing possibilities on Stevns. The town, however, remained one of the smallest in Denmark. Store Heddinge suffered heavily during the Dano-Swedish wars in the late 1650ties.

name: Myślibórz
Settlement_Description: A Slavic castle mound and settlement. A farm of the Knights Templar is mentioned in 1260, which later became a castle, which was destroyed in 1349.
Town_Description: Founded by the Margraves between 1262 and 1270, mentioned as a fortified town ('civitas') in 1271.
Toll_Description: Soldin (Myślibórz) acquired the right to levy a bridge toll of two Pfennig on every horse that drew a loaded wagon on the road between Landsberg (Gorzów Wielkopolski) and Stettin (Szczecin) from Elector Joachim in 1514.

name: Solpke
Settlement_Description: In 1473 Solpke is mentioned as the pertinence of Calbe
Toll_Description: A royal secondary station of safe conduct ('Nebengeleitsstelle') of Gardelegen is mentioned in Solpke in 1743.

name: Soltau
Settlement_Description: 937 mentioned in a donation charter from King Otto I. In 1304, a moated castle was built at the mouth of the river Soltau, to where the village of Soltau was relocated in 1383. In 1388, this settlement received borough ('weichbild') privileges and market rights after Celle model.
Toll_Description: A toll of the dukes of Brunswick-Lüneburg is mentioned in 1409.

name: Sõmeru
Settlement_Description: The village was first mentioned in 1615 as possession of the Manor of Noistfer (Purdi).

name: Ihantala
Settlement_Description: <b>Inn:</b> An inn was established in Ihantala in 1585, and Antti Ihantoinen was appointed as the innkeeper. Two years later, Matti Jönsinpoika Ihantoinen was the innkeeper.

name: Hatula
Settlement_Description: <b>Inn:</b> An inn was established in Hatula in 1586, and Pekka Ollinpoika Olkinuora was appointed as the innkeeper.

name: Sõmerpalu
Settlement_Description: Originally a castle, mentioned in 1555 and 1561. However, this has not been preserved. A manor was built in the early 16th century.

name: Sommersdorf
Settlement_Description: The village is first mentioned in 1330.

name: Son
Settlement_Description: Earliest mention in 1107, in a thirteenth century copy.
Fair_Description: Between 1355 and 1406 a fair was installed in Son (and Breugel). An undated register from the abbey Tongerlo (Westerlo, B.) (circa 1556) contains a list of fairs in the region Kempen and Peel. 'Zon' has then three fairs: 1) Thursday after Mid-Lent, 2) Sunday before 'Bertholomei' (August 24) till the first Tuesday after that, 3) Sunday post Simonis (Oct. 28?) till the first Tuesday after that.

name: Sunākste
Settlement_Description: The pastorate and the associated church were first mentioned in 1567.

name: Ortrand
Settlement_Description: A sigil from the 13th century remains. Develops into a marketplace.

name: Maasilinna
Settlement_Description: A castle, which was built in 1345. The former castle in Peude was destroyed in an uprising, so that the residents had to build the new castle as an atonement ('Soneburg = Sühneburg').

name: Sonnewalde
Settlement_Description: A lordship of Sonnewalde appears in 1255, the castle in Sonnewalde is mentioned  in 1301 and was probably built upon a former slavic settlement. A settlement developed at the castle, which was characterised as borough ('oppidum') in 1362 and as small town ('stetel') in 1479.

name: Sonsbeck
Fair_Description: A weekly market is mentioned in 1431 on Tuesday-Thursday.
Toll_Description: The Count of Cleves levied a land toll in 1319. In 1365, about 14 mark were collected per year, and from 1371 to 1395 about 16 mark.

name: Allendorf (Werra)
Settlement_Description: Allendorf is first mentioned in 1229 and was at that time already a town, founded between 1212 and 1218.
Town_Description: Allendorf was founded between 1212 and 1218 near the saltworks of Sooden by the landgrave of Thuringia.

name: Żary
Settlement_Description: Probably originally a Slavic castle. First mentioned in 1260 as town.
Town_Description: Burgrave Albrecht of Dewin likely granted the Magdeburg town law in 1260, mentioned as oppidum and civitas in 1329.

name: Sorgbrück
Settlement_Description: Ann inn at the river Sorge is first mentioned in 1470.
Bridge_Description: A bridge across the Sorge river is mentioned in 1587.

name: Kavantjärvi
Settlement_Description: <b>Inn:</b> An inn was established in Kavantjärvi in 1591, and Pentti Riikonen was appointed as the innkeeper. The inn moved to Kavantjärvi from Kilpeenjoki. In 1649., Kavantjärvi helped the Pullila inn.

name: Tynkkylä (Talikkala)
Settlement_Description: <b>Inn:</b> An inn was established in Tynkkylä in 1589, and Matti Hännikäinen was appointed as the innkeeper. The inn was given victuals from the parish constable's taxes.

name: Pullila
Settlement_Description: <b>Inn:</b> An inn was established in Pullila in 1649, and Pekka Pullinen was appointed as the innkeeper. Kaipola, Kavantjärvi and Noskua villages were ordered to help the inn. Kavantjärvi had served as an inn before, and in late 17th c., the inn moved to Kaipola.

name: Spandau
Settlement_Description: First traces of settlement have been dated to the 8th century and a Slavic castle existed into the 12th century. In 1197 the German castle is first mentioned and first traces of a German settlement could be dated to the beginning of the 13th century. Around 1200 the settlement around the castle mound in Spandau was abandoned and moved further north, where it became a market settlement around the church of St Nicholas.
Town_Description: The charter that grants the settlement next to the castle Brandenburg town rights in 1232 is a forgery; the actual awarding of the town rights presumably occurred around 1240 after a fire.
Toll_Description: Wagoners had to pay a toll as early as 1320 as well as a street toll ('Deichselpfennig') later on.
Staple_Description: A temporary staple in Spandau is mentioned in a complaint of the Elector in 1450.

name: Pangodi
Settlement_Description: Manor, which was owned by King Gustav Adolf.

name: Spechtsbrunn
Toll_Description: Secondary station of safe conduct ('Beigeleitsstelle') of Gräfenthal in 1728.

name: Spithal
Settlement_Description: First mentioned in 1350. The name of the settlement is possibly derived from a leprosy. The ruined church on the graveyard probably dates from the 12th century. In 1450, the village consisted of 8 farms and a cottage.

name: Spremberg
Settlement_Description: Possibly a Sorbian castle in the 10th-12th century. In 1272 a family of Spremberg appears, who founded a German castle and town, which is characterised as borough ('oppidum') in 1301.

name: Staphorst
Settlement_Description: Earliest mention in copies from 1217, 1263, 1283 and 1346. Next mention in 1355.

name: Spielberg
Settlement_Description: First mention in the tithe register of Hersfeld monastery from 830-850.

name: Kuukauppi
Settlement_Description: <b>Inn:</b> Kuukauppi villagers were paid for the serving and accommodation they had given to travelling officials.

name: Springe
Settlement_Description: First mentioned before 1007. The St Andrew's church is mentioned in 1264.
Town_Description: The nearby castle of Hallermund was lost to the dukes of Brunswick-Lüneburg in 1282, whereupon the counts of Hallermund retreated to Springe. Possibly, the settlement was raised to a town soon afterwards. It is first mentioned as "oppidum" in 1324; town privileges exist from 1415.
Toll_Description: A toll of the bishop of Hildesheim in Springe is mentioned when it was pawned to Reineke Holtgreve in 1388.

name: Sprundel
Settlement_Description: Earliest mention in 992, in a falsification of circa 1610. Next mention in 1282.

name: Staaken
Settlement_Description: First mention in the records in 1273, noble residence after it was sold to Spandau in 1295.

name: Stabroek
Settlement_Description: First mention in a copy from 1244.

name: Potsdam
Settlement_Description: First mention 993 in a donation charte by Otto III to Quedlinburg monastery. A Slavic settlement and a Kietz existed next to each other, the castle warden first took residence in the Slavic fortification in the 12th century. Before 1237 a stone castle was erected at the bank of the Havel river.
Town_Description: Developed into a town in the 14th century: mentioned as borough ('oppidum') in 1317, as small town ('städeken') in 1323. In 1345 mention as civitas with a town council. The date of acquisition of town rights is unknown. From the 15th century usually called small town or borough. Became residence of the kings of Prussia in the 18th century, then reverted to full town.
Toll_Description: The castle was the seat of the custums office. The toll station is first mentioned in 1370.

name: Stade
Settlement_Description: The fortress and settlement was first mentioned when it was destroyed by Vikings in 994. Around 1000 the settlement became the seat of the counts of Stade.
Town_Description: King Otto IV granted town privileges in 1209; they were confirmed in 1236.
Fair_Description: Stade acquired the market privilege in 1038; the oldest fair took place on St James's Day. A second fair on Tuesday after Easter is first mentioned in 1593, as well as a horse market on Letare Sunday. A second horse market eight days before Lent was renewed in 1670, but it is unknown when it was first organised. In 1692, St James's fair had a duration of 14 days, the Easter fair 8 days.
Toll_Description: The Archbishop of Bremen introduced a market toll in 1038, and in connection to the 1259 staple privilege a toll on the Elbe traffic at the mouth of the Schwinge (see Stadersand). Moreover, a toll existed on cattle driven through town, as well as a wine toll (mentioned in 1487 and 1530).
Staple_Description: In 1259, Archbishop Hildebrand of Bremen founded the Stade staple, which forced all ships coming from the sea to stay in Stade for 3 tides. The staple led to conflicts with Hamburg, which managed to acquire exemption from the staple in Stade in 1340. In the long run, it proved to be impossible to enforce the staple for other seafarers as well. Next to Hamburg and Buxtehude, Stade was a staple market for grain along the Elbe, as confirmed in a treaty from 1487. Staple of the English Merchant Adventurers in 1577-1597 and 1602-1611.
Harbour_Description: The harbour of Stade was located at the Schwinge river. A crane is first mentioned in 1337.

name: Stadthagen
Settlement_Description: Founded in ca. 1220 by count Adolf III or Adolf IV of Holstein-Schaumburg. A moated castle is first mentioned in 1224, a church in 1230.
Town_Description: Mentioned as "civitas" in a 1244 charter. The town acquired market privileges, among others the right of free trade with Minden and other towns, in 1322. Lippstadt town privileges were confirmed in 1344.

name: Stadtlohn
Town_Description: Town rights were probably granted in the 13th century. Borough ('Wigbold') privileges were granted in 1411 and later confirmed by Bishop Otto IV of Münster.

name: Stadtoldendorf
Settlement_Description: A settlement must have existed long before the foundation of the town, possibly since the 5th century.
Town_Description: The foundation of the town was closely related to the nearby castle Homburg. Holzminden town privileges were granted by Heinrich of Homburg in 1255. Since 1281, the addition "stadt" (town) was part of the place name.
Toll_Description: A toll station is mentioned in toll lists of the years 1539, 1540 and 1587, but probably originated with the lords of Homburg.

name: Stapelmoor
Settlement_Description: The settlement was first mentioned in 1424, but the village church is dated to c. 1300.

name: Kloster Homburg
Settlement_Description: First mentioned in 1073 and as site of a battle between rebelling Thuringians and Saxonians and king Henry IV in 1075. Around 1100 a Benedictine nuns monastery was founded. The former convent of nuns was converted into a monastery of Benedictine monks in 1136. It was destroyed during the Peasant's war and finally sold and demolished in 1544.

name: Stargard
Settlement_Description: First mentioned in 1124. Slavic castle, mentioned in possession of the Knights Hospitaller before 1187. Next to the castle, the seat of regional administration, a German settlement developed.
Town_Description: Duke Barnim I of Pomerania granted Magdeburg town privileges in 1253 (or 1243). Lübeck town law since 1292.

name: Nienhagen
Settlement_Description: In 1267 the provost of monastery Dobbertin sold the farmers of Wolframshagen (modern Altenhagen) a forest where there had been a Slavic village before. On this site the village Nienhagen was founded.

name: Altenhagen (Güstrow)
Settlement_Description: The settlement Wolframshagen is first mentioned as property of the monastery Dobbertin in 1237. After a new village was founded after 1267, the old settlement became known as Altenhagen.

name: Gerdshagen (Güstrow)
Settlement_Description: The village is first mentioned in 1237 as property of the monastery Dobbertin.

name: Alt Schönau
Settlement_Description: The village Schonowe is first mentioned as property of the monastery Broda in 1230.

name: Burg Stargard
Settlement_Description: Originally a Wendish fortification, first mentioned in 1170. It was acquired by the Margraves of Brandenburg in 1236. Next to the castle, a German village developed.
Town_Description: Margrave Otto III of Brandenburg granted Brandenburg town privileges in 1259.

name: Hotokka
Settlement_Description: <b>Inn:</b> An inn was established in Hotokka in 1642.

name: Pero
Settlement_Description: <b>Inn:</b> Pero inn might date already from the 17th century, and it continued to operate until the opening of St. Petersburg railway in 1870.

name: Kuusaa
Settlement_Description: <b>Inn:</b> An inn was established in Kuusaa in 1649, and Antti Raaska was appointed as the innkeeper.

name: Sluis
Settlement_Description: The settlement of Sluis probably came into existence during the second half of the 13th century around a sluice. It is first mentioned in 1290 and already was a town by that time.
Town_Description: The earliest mention of Sluis as a town dates from 30 November 1290. Town privileges of Bruges were granted by Guy of Dampierre, count of Flanders, before that date. The town was officially called Lamminsvliet, but the name Sluis persisted since the 14th century. It quickly gained prominence as harbour for the city of Bruges on the mouth of the Zwin. From 1382, Sluis was a fortified town. From 1387 onwards, it functioned as a navy port of the Burgundian dukes.
Fair_Description: A free fair was admitted in 1387 by Philip the Bold, which was granted by the count of Namur, who moved it from Béthune.
Toll_Description: Sluis must have become a toll station for the Zwin toll of the counts of Flanders in the second half of the 13th century (see also Bruges). An account dated 1328/'9 is preserved, when Sluis is an outpost of the toll at Damme. A toll collector is mentioned in 1368, who had been in office for 22 years. An account dated 1437/'8 from the toll at Damme and Sluis has levies on gutted herring (kaakharing) and beer, of 'petits congés' (? with a tariff) and 'pondgeld' on water and from 'spelleghelt' (on the ballast of ships). Accounts dated 1449-'51 are also combined with the toll at Damme. An account dated 1485-'93 has a levy on 'kaakharing'. Seperate toll-acounts for Sluis are dated 1477-'96 (with gaps) and on beer dated 1384-1492 (many gaps, tariff on Dutch beer dated 1482). In 1473 duke Charles the Bold gave an ordonnance regarding the markets for alum in Sluis, Middelburg, St. Anna ter Muiden and Antwerp. Flemish inhabitants of Lambinvliet were exempted from the Zwin toll in 1293, and in the 14th century also those of other origins. In 1360 privileges were give to the 'Oosterlingen' by the count of Flanders, in 1414 to those of Genua. In 1449 the people of Sluis obtained toll-exemption of the duke of Burgundy as count of Flanders.
Staple_Description: In 1497 the staple for gutted herring ('kaakharing') was granted to Sluis. In 1500 and 1511 Damme opposed this for the 'Grote Raad van Mechelen' (high court at Mechelen).

name: Königstein im Taunus
Settlement_Description: A castle has been documented since 1225, which was probably a foundation of the Staufer dynasty. The adjoining settlement is first mentioned in 1276.
Town_Description: In 1313 the settlement, which was hitherto referred to as 'oppidum', received the town privileges of Frankfurt.

name: Geulle
Toll_Description: A toll in 'Goele' is first found in 1381. The comital account of 1395-96 mentions a revenue of 3 Holland guilders. A toll levied from horses had no revenues at the time because it was leased out together with the toll and horse toll in Rode (Herzogenrath).

name: Malchow (Mecklenburg)
Settlement_Description: In Slavic times a significant fortification, conquered by Germans in 1164, reconquered by Slavs in 1164 and conquered by Henry the Lion in the same year. A new settlement was built here around 1220 by the Dukes of Mecklenburg.
Town_Description: Schwerin town privileges granted in 1235, later those of Güstrow.

name: Kämärä
Settlement_Description: <b>Inn:</b> An inn was established in Kämärä in 1649, and Matti Kämärä was appointed as the innkeeper.

name: Staßfurt
Settlement_Description: Staßfurt developed around saltworks at the southern bank of the Bode, first mentioned in 1145.
Town_Description: Staßfurt acquired market privileges before 1276 - town rights were probably granted around 1265. A castle is first mentioned in 1278, but must have been older. The economy revolved around the saltworks, which required large quantities of wood, which had to be transported via the Saale harbours Nienburg or Calbe.

name: Stauffenburg
Settlement_Description: A castle was probably founded in the 11th century, first mentioned in 1130. It became an administrative centre for the region.

name: Starum
Settlement_Description: Earliest mention dates from the tenth or early eleventh century.
Town_Description: Town rights were granted by Egbert I of Brunswick and Margrave of Friesland, before 1068, or before 1077 by Egbert's son and successor, Egbert II, Margrave of Meissen and Friesland. The current old town of Stavoren is only the easternmost remnant of the original town; the rest was swallowed by the Zuiderzee before the 16th century.
Fair_Description: In 1562 king Philip II granted a fair on October 5 to cover the costs of the maintenance of dikes a.o.
Toll_Description: Staveren had three tolls: an episcopal, a comital and one from the town itself. In 1334 the magistrate donated toll-exemption to Groningen. Possibly this was the marktet-tol. The episcopal toll-keeper is found in an undated list of vassals in the Sticht, like his ancestors had the toll as a fief from the 'Gesticht'. In 1353 the town granted toll-exemption of the usurpated episcopal toll to all free towns in Holland, as long as this was mutual. In 1343 Kampen was already freed from the episcopal toll and mutually Staveren from the Kamper toll. In 1347 an award was made with the comital toll-keeper regarding the toll-payment by citizens of Hamburg. 55 Brewers of Hamburg worked in 1365 in service of Staveren, where a Hamburger Hansa was (as in Amsterdam) of merchants trading with this town. In 1367 an agreement was made by the magistrate with the count of Blois for the payment of a fixed yearly sum to pass his tol at Spaarndam. In 1368 old rights regarding the 'vitte' of Staveren at Schonen (southern point of Sweden) in the Baltic were confirmed by the king of Norway. The 'Stadboek' (book with important privileges of Staveren) contains a 'Waterrecht', which is corresponding with that of Amsterdam.
Harbour_Description: At least in the 16th century, the harbour for sea-going ships was located north of town. Smaller ships could also anchor in the town centre.

name: Steddorf
Settlement_Description: Mentioned in 1306 in the context of damaged property of the monastery Zeven in Steddorf. In 1390 the entire village was sold to the monastery.

name: Steenderen
Settlement_Description: Earliest mention in 1046, in a twelfth century copy.

name: Steenwijk
Settlement_Description: A church must have existed around the year 1000. Steenwijk is first mentioned in 1141 (in a 15th-century copy, possibly a falsification).
Town_Description: Earliest mention as 'opidum' in 1296. Probably, town privileges were granted by John II of Sierck (Jan II van Sierck), bishop of Utrecht before 29 February 1296. In 1523, the town was burned down by troops of the duke of Guelders and the town of Zwolle. The town was rebuild.
Fair_Description: In 1358, Steenwijk was granted the rights for three fairs: one during Lent, one around the Feast of Corpus Christi, and one around St Ursula (21 October). The duration of these fairs is unknown. Documents from 1561, 1562 and 1569 mention four fairs being in practice in Steenwijk. A document from 1587 indicates that 'fairs' (plural) were still in practice around that time.

name: Stegen
Harbour_Description: First attempts to build a canal between Alster and Trave started in 1448. Although construction work was discontinued in 1452 without success, the section Hamburg-Stegen was kept navigable for the transport of lime from Segeberg, which was transferred from wagon to ship in Stegen. Transshipment in Stegen is still attested in 1557.
Lock_Description: Lock between the Alster and the Alster-Trave canal, which was constructed in 1527. Already in 1550, shipping on the canal was discontinued.

name: Steinau an der Straße
Settlement_Description: A castle might have been built around 900. Called 'castrum' in 1287. The settlement is only mentioned in the course of the granting of city rights in 1290.
Town_Description: In 1290 the settlement received town rights and a weekly market. 1401 and 1404 it is mentioned that the town has Frankfurt and Gelnhausen rights.

name: Steinbrück
Settlement_Description: Castle on the border of Hildesheim territory, which was erected in 1370-1383 by bishop Gerhard vom Berge of Hildesheim. It was first mentioned in 1391. The fortifications were demolished in 1643 and the site was turned into a manor.
Bridge_Description: Stone bridge across the Fuhse river, after which the castle was called.

name: Steinburg
Settlement_Description: Moated castle of the counts of Holstein, first mentioned in 1307. The castle was demolished in 1640. A sconce remained; the last remains were demolished in 1763.

name: Steinfeld
Settlement_Description: First mentioned in a charter of the monastery Amorbach of ca. 1000. However, the charter is interpreted as a falsification. In 1548, four farms are mentioned in Steinfeld.

name: Steinfurt
Settlement_Description: Settlement at a ford, first mentioned in 1229.

name: Steinheim am Main
Settlement_Description: The settlement is named 1223 and goes back to a castle that dates back to the 10th century.
Town_Description: In 1320 Frankfurt freedoms and rights were granted.
Toll_Description: Toll station of the archbischop of Mainz.

name: Steinkuhle
Settlement_Description: Toll house and inn. On the border between the princedoms a bit to the north, there was also a watchtower, where the town of Einbeck stationed a guard. The toll house was burnt down in the Thirty Years' War and not rebuilt afterwards.
Toll_Description: The toll was pawned by duke Eric I of Brunswick-Calenberg in 1514.

name: Stendal
Settlement_Description: First mentioned in 1022. In the 10th century there already existed a small village.
Town_Description: The settlement received market and town rights in 1160 according to the Magdeburg Law. In the 13th century the Stendal seafarer guild was founded. Between 1350 and 1515 Stendal was a member of the Hanse.
Fair_Description: Stendal had three fairs, their dates and durations are unknown. During the siege of Magdeburg between 1547 and 1554, the Magdeburg market and staple was moved to Tangermünde, Stendal and Brandenburg. Since 1563 it was allowed to hold cattle and horse markets on two of the Stendal fair days. A fair on Sunday Exaudi is mentioned in an almanac printed in Neudamm (Dębno) from 1598. A new cattle fair on Monday after St Gall was granted in 1643. Another fair was granted in 1672, which took place in the week after second Advent: a cattle fair on Monday, and a commodity market on Tuesday to Thursday.
Staple_Description: The market and staple rights of Magdeburg were moved to Tangermünde, Stendal and Brandenburg in 1547-1554, due to the siege of Magdeburg.

name: Torzym
Settlement_Description: A castle is mentioned in 1317, the adjoining settlement is characterised as borough ('oppidum') in 1385. Town privileges were never granted.

name: Lange Brücke
Bridge_Description: A bridge across the Havel is first mentioned in 1317, but must have disappeared afterwards. A new wooden bridge was built in 1416; in the meantime a ferry is mentioned. The name "long bridge" ('Lange Brücke') is first mentioned in 1564.
Ferry_Description: A ferry is among others mentioned in 1375. It was replaced by the new bridge in 1416.

name: Sternberg
Settlement_Description: The town was founded without a pre-existing settlement between 1238 and 1256.
Town_Description: Lord Pribislaw I of Mecklenburg founded the town with Parchim town privileges between 1238 and 1256. The settlement is mentioned as civitas in the early 14th century.
Fair_Description: A fair on Palm Sunday in Sternberg is mentioned in an almanac printed in Neudamm (Dębno) in 1598.
Toll_Description: Revenues of the toll station in Sternberg are known for the years 1559-1561.

name: Szczecin
Settlement_Description: First mentioned in 1091 as ducal castle. Two German market settlements developed in its vicinity in 1124-1129.
Town_Description: In 1243 the Magdeburg town law was granted by Duke Barnim I of Pomerania after both market settlements were merged.
Toll_Description: A toll erected in 1311 for citizens of the Mark of Brandeburg, who wished to circumvent the Stettin staple.
Staple_Description: First regulations restricting the grain trade in Pomerania to Stettin in 1253 and 1281; staple rights followed in 1283, with obligation to exchange wares and the forbidding of transports on the tributaries of the Oder and the banning of guest trading. Exemptions existed for citizens of Gartz and Greifenhagen and from the Mark of Brandenburg, who after payment of a toll were allowed to pass through Stettin in the same ship. Expansion of staple privileges in 1312. Around the middle of the 15th century a dispute between Stettin and Stargard over the bypassing of the Stettin staple by shipping on the river Ihna was settled in favour of Stettin. Confirmation of the staple followed in 1467, including the stipulation that all wares on ships coming from the sea into the Stettin lagoon and wares entering Stettin overland from the Oder basin should be stapled in Stettin. In 1475 merchants were obliged to store herring in Stettin for three days. Abolition of the staple in 1752, after which Stettin enjoyed only a monopoly over the linseed trade.

name: Haus Steuerwald
Settlement_Description: Around 1510/13, an inn was built by the bishop of Hildesheim, which was later called Haus Steuerwald after the nearby castle Steuerwald, which is first mentioned in 1310. The bailiff of the castle erected a boom barrier here in 1586, which was removed by the town of Hildesheim again afterwards.

name: Stickhausen
Settlement_Description: The castle Stickhausen was erected around 1432 by Ulrich Cirksena, the later count of East Frisia.
Toll_Description: Around 1589, Count Johann II of East Frisia introduced a toll in Stickhausen. In 1599, a bridge and water toll is mentioned in connection to the fair in Detern. It was discontinued after a conflict with Oldenburg in 1641 at the latest. See Detern for further details.

name: Stiege
Settlement_Description: First mentioned as a castle in 1329. It developed into a village until 1599 at the latest.

name: Stockelsdorf
Settlement_Description: Manor belonging to Lübeck citizens, first mentioned in 1303. An inn is mentioned in Stockelsdorf in 1447.

name: Storbeck
Settlement_Description: The village is first mentioned in 1319.

name: Stöcken (Hannover)
Toll_Description: The registers of the Amt Neustadt am Rübenberge from 1425 and 1426 list revenues from the toll in Stöcken.

name: Stalbe
Settlement_Description: The manor was mentioned in 1350 in the course of granting fief.

name: Słupsk
Settlement_Description: First mentioned in 1180, but archaeological finds date back to the 7th century. A castellan was mentioned in 1236.
Town_Description: Duke Swantopolk II granted Lübeck town law in 1265 or 1278.In 1310 Margrave Waldemar of Brandenburg granted the Lübeck town law again to the German market settlement.

name: Stommeln
Toll_Description: 1) In 1389, the Duke of Jülich levied a land toll and a fee for safe conduct on land. For 1389/93 there is evidence of both horse toll and escort fee. Depending on the load, 2 to 3 alb. per horse had to be paid. On average, about 771 mark were collected per year. In 1398/99 it was about 283 mark. Later, this collection point was only referred to as a toll station.<br/>2) The duke also levied a road toll in 1434/35. Tariffs are not known. In 1500/01, 20 mark were collected.

name: Osieczna
Toll_Description: The owner of Osiecznica acquired permission to levy a toll of 2 Groschen for each wagon in 1518.

name: Storkau
Settlement_Description: First mention in 1209 in a name; mention of the village and farmstead in 1337.
Ferry_Description: Storkau maintained a small passenger ferry.

name: Stötterlingenburg
Settlement_Description: In 992 a Benedictine women's monastery was founded within the castle of Stötterlingenburg, but the castle buildings were already gone by 1106. The monastery was secularised in 1565 and was made into the centre of an administrative region ('amt').

name: Straach
Settlement_Description: The village is first mentioned in 1390.

name: Straelen
Toll_Description: The Duke of Guelders levied a road toll in 1395. Tariffs and revenues are not known. A market toll was also mentioned from 1326.

name: Strasburg
Town_Description: The town was founded after 1250, a mayor is mentioned in 1267. The town acquired Magdeburg town law, has always been called civitas or town since 1328.

name: Straßebersbach
Toll_Description: A toll collector is mentioned in 1447.

name: Straupitz
Settlement_Description: First mention of a sovereignty of Straupitz in 1294.

name: Strausberg
Settlement_Description: A fortification ('curia') of the margraves of Brandenburg was constructed around 1225. A town was founded next to it.
Town_Description: The market settlement received German town privileges from Margrave John I of Brandenburg in 1232, later the Brandenburg town law is attested. Characterised as town ('civitas') in 1268/84.

name: Strecknitz
Settlement_Description: The manor Strecknitz, belonging to Lübeck, was first mentioned in 1248. Shortly after 1316, the "Grönauer Baum", a boom barrier across the street, was mentioned here. At the end of the 17th century, the fee for opening the barrier was 6 pfennig for wagons. There existed an inn at the barrier as well.

name: Ströbeck
Settlement_Description: First mention in 1004, referred to as borough ('Fleck') in 1470. Within Ströbeck, a watchtower can be found.

name: Strelitz-Alt
Settlement_Description: First a Slavic, then a German village. A castle was built that promoted the development of the village, first mentioned in 1278.
Town_Description: Neubrandenburg town privileges granted in 1349 by the Counts Otto and Ulrich of Fürstenberg. The ducal residence Neustrelitz was founded in 1733. Since 1933 the old town is part of Neustrelitz under the name Strelitz-Alt.

name: Strehla
Settlement_Description: At the end of the 10th century a castle was built in the middle of a castle guard. A suburb developed around this castle.
Toll_Description: Secondary station of safe conduct ('Beigeleitsstelle') of Oschatz. Strehla is mentioned as toll station on the Elbe river in the 17th century.

name: Rantakylä
Settlement_Description: <b>Inn:</b> An inn was established in Rantakylä in 1642, and Niilo Iivonen was appointed as the innkeeper. The inn was located by the winter road over Vuotjärvi lake.

name: Mäkisauru (Perniö)
Settlement_Description: <b>Post house:</b> In 1638, the Royal Steward Bernhardt Steen von Steenhausen established a post house in the village of Mäkisauru in Perniö.

name: Strobus
Settlement_Description: Earliest mention  is probably from circa 1660.

name: Strzelno
Toll_Description: A document from probably 1349 mentions that the toll of Radziejów will be levied in Strzelno for those travellers circumventing Radziejów.

name: Ulbroka
Settlement_Description: In 1528 the area was given as a fief. Thereupon, a manor was built, which was given to the Mayor of Riga in 1562.

name: Suchsdorf
Settlement_Description: First mentioned in 1269. Since the 14th century, the village belonged to the Hospital of the Holy Ghost in Kiel.

name: Hoptrup
Settlement_Description: The village of Hoptrup was probably first mentioned in 1289, byt may very well be older. The parish church was built in either the 12th or 13th century.

name: Südlohne (Oldenburg)
Settlement_Description: The place was first mentioned in 1291.

name: Jaunjelgava
Settlement_Description: The settlement was probably built at the end of the 16th century, but was destroyed around 1600 during the Swedish-Polish wars.
Town_Description: The settlement received town rights for the first time around 1630. In 1647 these were confirmed.

name: Sülfeld
Lock_Description: Lock between the river Beste and the Alster-Trave canal, which was constructed in 1527. Already in 1550, the shipping on the canal was discontinued.

name: Sulingen
Settlement_Description: Around 800, a missionary parish ('urpfarrei') was founded by the diocese of Minden. The settlement is first mentioned in 1029 and is characterised as borough ('flecken') in 1519.
Town_Description: The settlement was first mentioned as town in 1558. A town seal is attested as well. However, formal town rights were first granted in 1929.

name: Sulmierzyce
Toll_Description: Border toll station between Poland and Silesia in the 16th century.

name: Joutselkä
Settlement_Description: <b>Inn:</b> An inn was established in Joutselkä in the early 17th c., and Lauri Nuutinpoika was appointed as the innkeeper. Daniel Hjorth stayed in the inn while delivering a royal letter to Russia. Lauri moved away in 1607, when the inn moved to Sittarossi, but came back to Joutselkä in 1640s. In 1642 Matti Jononen was the innkeeper, and in 1649, Reijo Iivarinpoika and Martti Hänninen.

name: Suntaži
Settlement_Description: The manor was mentioned in 1318 and was owned by the Archbishop of Riga. A castle was built at the same time.

name: Süpplingenburg
Settlement_Description: The castle was built in the 10th or 11th century on a river island west of the current settlement. The settlement was first mentioned in 1106.

name: Sülten
Settlement_Description: The village is first mentioned in 1264.

name: Häntälä (Halikko)
Settlement_Description:
<b>Inn:</b> Halikko parish constable (fi: nimismies, sw: länsman) ran a tavern in his farm. Constables were obliged to keep a tavern in late 16th and early 17th c.

<b>Post house:</b> In 1638, the Royal Steward Bernhardt Steen von Steenhausen established a post house in the village of Häntälä in Halikko.

name: Susteren
Settlement_Description: Susteren is first mentioned in 714, in a copy from 1191, which mentions a church and small convent. In 1312 a chapter is first attested.
Town_Description: Susteren is first mentioned as a town on 26 April 1276. An official charter of town rights is not known to exist. Possibly town privileges were granted by Reginald I, count of Guelders.

name: Świnoujście
Settlement_Description: First mentioned in 1182. An important trading and strategic location for Vikings, Germans and Slavs since the Middle Ages. A church is mentioned in 1336. The settlement only formally became a town in 1765.

name: Tabivere
Settlement_Description: In the middle of the 16th century a hamlet ('Hof') emerged around which a small village settled (mentioned in 1582).

name: Tachov
Toll_Description: Mentioned as Bohemian toll station in 1391.

name: Tahkuranna
Settlement_Description: Around 1500, the hamlet ('Hof'), probably owned by the Teutonic Order, was set up. In 1620 the court was fief.

name: Puurmani
Settlement_Description: Before 1561 the farm belonged to the Falkenau monastery. The manor was crownland property until 1645.

name: Tammiste
Settlement_Description: Manor and estate were first mentioned in 1560.

name: Sonneberg
Settlement_Description: Castle Sonneberg was founded around 1200 and first mentioned in 1207. At the foot of the castle the settlement Altenröthen already existed, but soon disappeared. A new settlement Röthen is first mentioned in 1260, which adopted the name of the castle in the 14th century.
Town_Description: First mention as little town ("stetelyn") in 1317. Town privileges based on the Coburg town law were confirmed in 1349.
Fair_Description: Two fairs and a weekly market are mentioned in 1601.

name: null
Harbour_Description: The waterfalls of Joala in the Narva river prevented direct river traffic from Narva to the south. Cargoes had to be transshipped on the landway in Joala.

name: Tangermünde
Settlement_Description: First mention between 1012 and 1018. The settlement was the centre of a castle district ('Burgward') in the 10th to 12th century. In 1196 property in Tangermünde was given to the archbishop of Magdeburg.
Town_Description: The margraves of Brandenburg promoted the town's development, which was mostly finished around 1200. In 1436 Tangermünde joined the Hanse.
Fair_Description: From 1547 to 1554 the staple and market from Magdeburg are moved to Tangermünde, Stendal and Brandenburg, due to the siege on Magdeburg. </br>Through complaints by Magdeburg in 1668, four fairs are known, two of which take place during autumn. A fair in August and a fair on St. Martin's day are mentioned. In 1686, fairs on Carnival and St. Johannis' day are mentioned.
Toll_Description: A market toll in Tangermünde is first mentioned in 1151. A transit toll is mentioned in 1275, which was also levied on the Elbe river (see harbour). In 1345 the exemption of toll and safe conduct for the citizens of Stendal in Tangermünde was confirmed. The toll is further mentioned in 1373, 1377 and 1385, where it is differentiated between the land (town) toll and the water (Elbe) toll. Further mentions in 1414, 1428 and 1458, when citizens of Tangermünde were exempted. Tariffs remain from 1589 and 1632.
Staple_Description: From 1547 to 1554 the staple and market from Magdeburg are moved to Tangermünde, Stendal and Brandenburg, due to the siege on Magdeburg.

name: Tanne
Toll_Description: The toll station in Rucksbruch was moved to Tanne in the 1710s.

name: Gvardeysk
Settlement_Description: An Old Prussian castle was given to the Teutonic Order in 1265 and subsequently enlarged. The castle was moved in 1280-1290 and later became the see of a commander. For a while it was the residence of Duke Albrecht, who died there in 1567.

name: Tarnów
Staple_Description: Unimportant staple, confirmed in the Polish Staple Law of 1565

name: Tarvastu
Settlement_Description: The parish was mentioned in 1225 and 1234, making it one of the oldest. The first church was built in the 14th century. In addition, there was a castle of the Teutonic Order in Tarwast, which was built at the beginning of the 14th century. It was destroyed at the end of the 16th century.

name: Dorf Tatschow
Settlement_Description: The village is first mentioned in 1350.

name: Taucha
Town_Description: The town was founded in the middle of the 12th century. The town presumably had 'Magdeburg law'.
Toll_Description: Seconday station of safe conduct ('Beigeleitsstelle') of Leipzig.

name: Taurupe
