Settlement_Description: The manor was first mentioned in 1492 and was owned by the Pahlen-Family.

name: Telgt
Settlement_Description: Earliest mention in 806, in a tenth century copy.

name: Telgte
Town_Description: In 1238 Telgte was granted borough ('wigbold') privileges by the bishop of Münster and was later called a town.
Fair_Description: A Kirmes (feast of the dedication of the church) in Telgte is first mentioned in 1483, taking place on the Exaltation of the Holy Cross. Around 1600, an Autumn fair in connection to the feast took place on the Monday after. The market had a strict local importance. In 1616, a cattle market was added on Wednesday after Trinity Sunday, and the Autumn market was moved to the Nativity of Mary. After 1650, two additional markets were added.

name: Teltow
Settlement_Description: The land of Teltow is first mentioned in 1232.
Town_Description: The settlement is first mentioned in 1265, when Teltow received guild rights and toll exemptions. Still mentioned as town ('civitas') in 1317, but since 1351 only as borough ('oppidum').
Fair_Description: Three fairs are mentioned before 1700, especially flax markets.

name: Tempelberg
Settlement_Description: In 1244 the settlement's tithe is given to the Knights Templar.

name: Czaplinek
Settlement_Description: Originally an old Slavic settlement called Czaplin. At the time the area was given to the Knights Templar in 1286, it was mentioned as deserted. The castle Tempelburg, after which the town was named later, was first mentioned in 1291.
Town_Description: Two knights are mentioned as owners of the town in 1334, so it must have been founded before that year with Magdeburg town rights. The privileges were confirmed by King Stephen in 1580.

name: Tempelhof
Settlement_Description: First mentioned in 1247. The settlement was in possession of the Knights Templar, from whom it derived its name. In 1435 the settlement was in possession of the Knights Hospitaller, who sold it to the towns Berlin-Cölln.

name: Templin
Settlement_Description: A Pomeranian castle that became Ascanian around 1230. The settlement is first mentioned in 1270, then already a town.
Town_Description: The date of the foundation is unknown, probably around 1250 by the Margraves of Brandenburg, first mentioned in 1270, always characterised as town.

name: Tecklenburg
Settlement_Description: First mentioned in the 12th century as castle of the counts of Tecklenburg. In 1226 the adjoining settlement is first referred to as 'suburbium'.
Town_Description: In 1388 the settlement was already designated as a town, but only received town privileges in the 17th century.

name: Eembrugge
Settlement_Description: Eembrugge is first mentioned in 1254, the near-by castle 'Huis ter Eem' in 1252. The settlement was located near a ford in the river Eem. A bridge was built there in the late twelfth century. Eembrugge is located on the road between Baarn and Bunschoten.
Town_Description: Eembrugge was granted town privileges sometime between 1336 and 1340 by John ('Jan') III van Diest, bisshop of Utrecht. According to Cox it never fully developed into a town and was destroyed in 1527 by people from Guelders. Van Berkel & Samplonius argue that it was an important town untill its destruction in 1527. The castle was destroyed as well in 1527. After the destruction, habitation moved to the west side of the river Eem.
Fair_Description: A toll of a fair is found in the accounts of the bishop of Utrecht dated 1328-'31 en 1377/'8, afterwards not anymore, although preserved with many gaps: the next account is dated 1426.The toll however is still  mentioned in a lawsuit dated 1394. In 1377/'8 the toll is collected with St. Jacobsmis (July 25).

name: Terborg (Gelderland)
Town_Description: Town privileges granted on 23 April 1419, by Dirk and Hendrik, lords of Wissche (Wisch).

name: Terschuur
Toll_Description: Mentioned as toll station in 1469. In 1555 the toll is farmed out by the steward of the Veluwe for a period of three years 120 carolus guilders yearly. A tollright and tariff dated 1628 (and a printed copy of thus from around 1770) is preserved. All people of Gelre and the inhabitants of Culemborg are free. Carts or charriots from outside Gelre loaded with goods from Gelre or from Gelre but loaded with goods from outside Gelre are not free. The tariff mentions wine and animals and has deviated amounts for oxen from Hattem, Zutphen and Deventer.

name: Teschendorf (Brandenburg)
Settlement_Description: The village is first mentioned in 1271. In 1374 there stood a castle of the bishop of Brandenburg.

name: null
Harbour_Description: According to a document from 1633, Medved' served as transshipment point for the waterway on the Mshaga and Shelon rivers and the Ilmen lake towards Novgorod.

name: Themar
Town_Description: Mentioned as civitas and oppidum in 1317 and 1319. However, the settlement is referred to as borough ('Flecken') in 1452 and as market borough ('Marktflecken') in 1491. After that the term "town" is consistently used.

name: Teupitz
Settlement_Description: First mention of a castle and settlement in 1307. Elevation to town rank only in 1808.
Toll_Description: The lords ('Schenken') of Landsberg, who resided on castle Teupitz, owned the land toll in Teupitz, as well as the bridge and dam tolls in Königs Wusterhausen and Märkisch Buchholz.

name: Theal
Settlement_Description: The parish of Theal was mentioned in 1379.

name: Kloster Thedinga
Settlement_Description: The Benedictine monastery was allegedly founded by the holy Hatebrand, who was abbot of Feldwirth around 1190. However, it is first mentioned in a charter only in 1338. The last time the monastery was mentioned in documents was in 1616, after which the monastery seems to have been closed.

name: Thiede
Toll_Description: A toll of the duke of Brunswick in Thiede is mentioned in 1347, but not anymore in descriptions of tolls in the Amt Wolfenbüttel from the 16th and 17th centuries.

name: Thiene
Settlement_Description: The settlement was first mentioned in 1037.

name: Thölstedt
Settlement_Description: The village was first mentioned in 1211.

name: Tome
Settlement_Description: The village was first mentioned in 1434. In 1442, a manor was built by the Teutonic Order.

name: Thräna
Settlement_Description: First mention in 1181; mentioned as manor in 1243.

name: Mittelsten Thüle
Settlement_Description: The hamlet ('bauerschaft') Thüle, first mentioned in 1270, was stretched out along 6 km and was divided into three parts. The middle part was first mentioned separately in 1411.

name: Tiddische
Settlement_Description: Mentions of the settlement before 1366 (among others as "Didighessen" in 1315) are very uncertain.

name: Tõlluste
Settlement_Description: In 1528 an estate was called Arries. Before that, the place was probably a manor.

name: Thiedenwiese
Settlement_Description: First mentioned in the 10th or 11th century as Tiadikasheim, abandoned probably before 1412. In the 18th century, a post station named Thiedenwiese was installed south of the former settlement.

name: Tienen
Settlement_Description: Earliest mention in 872, a falsification from the twelfth century . Next mention in 1146.
Fair_Description: In 1460 (May 5, granted by duke Philip of Burgundy) and in 1517 it obtained a privilege for a compulsory market for grain and wool for the surrounding countryside (1460: 'the Meierei van Tienen').
Staple_Description: In 1460 (May 5, granted by duke Philip of Burgundy) and in 1517 it obtained a privilege for a compulsory market for grain and wool for the surrounding countryside (1460: 'the Meierei van Tienen').

name: Tilburg
Settlement_Description: The earliest mention of Tilburg can be found in an 1191 copy of an document dated 709. Tilburg was elevated to town rank on 18 April 1809 by Louis Bonaparte, king of Holland.
Toll_Description: The Hanseatic settlement ('Kontor') in Bruges complained about a new toll in Tilburg in 1468.

name: Tielenbrücke
Bridge_Description: Bridge across the Tielenau, first mentioned in the 16th century.

name: Timmaspe
Settlement_Description: Characterised as 'villa' in 1320, and as village ('dorp') in 1538.

name: Timmeitz
Settlement_Description: First mentioned in 1450/51. It consisted of 3 farms at the time.

name: Sternberger Burg
Settlement_Description: The castle near Sternberg was first mentioned in 1316. Archaeological excavations, however, indicate a Slavic predecessor (7th-9th century).

name: Tiefthal
Settlement_Description: First mention in 1074. The settlement was probably founded by St. Peter's monastery in Erfurt, later it became property of the town of Erfurt.

name: Titz
Toll_Description: In 1389, the Duke of Jülich levied a land toll and a fee for safe conduct on land. In 1389/93, both horse toll and escort fees are recorded. Depending on the load, 2 to 3 alb. had to be paid per horse. On average, about 5 mark could be collected per year. In 1398/99 it was 20 mark.

name: Todendorf
Settlement_Description: The village is first mentioned in 1304. The modern village is located east of its historical location.

name: Tödwensche Brücke
Bridge_Description: The bridge was first mentioned in 1438 and belonged to the village Tödwen (Tõdva), which was first mentioned in 1241. There existed inns on both sides of the bridge.

name: Toftlund
Settlement_Description: The village of Toftlund was first mentioned in 1510, but is significantly older. The parish church is from either the 12th or 13th century

name: Tolkmicko
Settlement_Description: Originally an Old Prussian settlement with fortification, later a castle of the Teutonic Order (destroyed in 1454), next to which the town was founded.
Town_Description: Founded as a town by the commander of Elbing Ludwig von Schippen (1296-1300). A charter with Kulm town privileges was issued in 1351 by Grand master Heinrich Dusemer and renewed in 1444 by Grand master Konrad von Erlichhasen.

name: Tollendorf
Settlement_Description: First mentioned in 1330/52. In 1450, the village consisted of 2 farms, 2 half farms and a mill; in 1564 of 6 farms.

name: Tungeln
Settlement_Description: First mentioned in 1160 by biship Philipp of Osnabrück.

name: Tønder
Settlement_Description: Probably a permanent settlement with a certain urban character in the 11th century. Direct access to the North Sea by a river, Vidå, until dikes were built in the 15th and 16th centuries. Maybe founded by people from the nearby settlement of Møgeltønder.
Town_Description: Tønder was most likely founded as a town c. 1100, perhaps even earlier. First mentioned in the middle of the 12th century by the Arab al-Idrisis.  Franciscan monastery established in 1238. Town law granted by duke Abel, the later king of Denmark, in 1243. Town council and town seal are known from the middle of the 13th century, and a town bailiff first appeared in the following 14th century. A castle, Tønderhus, was built around 1270. A medieval town hall was located at the present town square northern side. Tønder had different town lords during the middle ages, as the town soon fell under the king, soon under the dukes. In the later middle ages and also the period after the reformation Tønder played a central role in the Danish export of oxen.
Harbour_Description: Tønder was described as a harbour by the Arab al-Idrisis c. 1130. The medieval river harbour was presumably located at the end of modern day street of Vestergade. The character of the harbour is unknown. When the dikes to the west were constructed in the 15th and 16th centuries, ships could no longer use the harbour, and Tønder began to use Rudbøl as harbour. In the following 17th century the harbour was relocated to Højer.

name: Töpingen
Settlement_Description: A "Holt de Tobinghe" is mentioned as a new citizen in the Lüneburg town register in 1302, which is the first written reference to the village of Töpingen.

name: Torgau
Settlement_Description: The old market and trade settlement was first mentioned in a falsified charter from 965. First secure mention in 973. From the mid-10th century, there existed a castle with adjoining borough.
Town_Description: The town was founded in the late 12th century by the margraves of Meißen. Margrave Henry III the Illustrious granted town privileges between 1255 and 1267. From 1525 the town was the preferred residence of the Ernestinian dukes.
Fair_Description: The fairs in Torgau were confirmed in 1575 and 1641.
Toll_Description: A transit toll on the Elbe in Torgau is first mentioned in 1386, a salt and wine toll in 1432. The regulations of safe conduct in Torgau from 1510 give the exact fees for bulk wares ('Zentnergut') LHASA, MD, d. 49, Nr. 2, Amt Torgau 1510, p. 348–354.)

name: Torma
Settlement_Description: Manor and the associated village and hamlet ('Hof') were mentioned in 1493.

name: Tornau (Stendal)
Settlement_Description: First mention in a name in 1217; first mention of the village in 1238.

name: Tramm
Settlement_Description: First mentioned in 1330/52. In 1450 the settlement consisted of 2 farms.

name: Helmarshausen
Settlement_Description: 944 mentioned for the first time in a deed of gift. At the end of the 10th century a Benedictine monastery was founded, at which a settlement developed. Shortly after its foundation, the abbey of Helmarshausen received market, mint and toll privileges. In the early 12th century, the settlement is characterised as 'oppidum'.
Town_Description: The settlement became a town in the first half of the 13th century, probably in competition with nearby Herstelle, which was owned by the bishop of Paderborn. Town privileges were confirmed in 1241 by the archbishop of Cologne.
Fair_Description: A fair at St. John the Baptist was established in 1223. In 1254 there were three fairs mentioned.

name: Travemünde
Settlement_Description: Count Adolf III of Holstein built a tower here in 1187 to secure the mouth of the Trave river. The settlement was first called Travemünde in 1219, and a fire beacon for navigation is mentioned in 1226. The tower was acquired by Lübeck in 1247, and in 1329 the entire settlement. It was reconstructed as a fortress after 1559.

name: Trebatsch
Settlement_Description: First mention of the name in 1324, further mention of the settlement in 1495.
Toll_Description: The family of Trebatsch held a toll on rafted lumber on the Trebatsh Fließ.

name: Trebbin
Settlement_Description: First mention of Trebbin in 1213 as part of a name, which attests the existence of a castle. The adjoining settlement and market are first mentioned in 1373.
Town_Description: Date of the acquisition of town rights is unknown, they are first attested in the 15th century.
Toll_Description: Station of safe conduct and toll attested in 1375. In 1560 revenues from a dam toll are attested.

name: Trzebiszewo
Toll_Description: Border toll station in the 16th century.

name: Trebitz
Settlement_Description: First mentioned in a falsified charter from 965. First certainly mentioned in 1004 as a castle district ('Burgward'). Occasionally the settlement was characterised as a borough ('Flecken') or a little town ('Städtlein').

name: Trzebnica
Toll_Description: A toll tariff for salt, cloth and beer is known from 1224.

name: Trebnitz
Settlement_Description: In 1252 the manor Trebnitz is bought.

name: Aarle
Settlement_Description: Earliest mention from 1496 but probably older. Subsumed in Aarle-Rixtel during the twentieth century.

name: Trechtingshausen
Toll_Description: A river toll on the Rhine was levied here for several years. The Lord of Hohenfels was the owner of the toll in the periods 1260 to 1269 and 1278 to 1282. Possibly a toll was also levied by the Mainz cathedral chapter in 1369. However, it is unclear whether the imperial grant of toll rights in the same year applied to Trechtingshausen or Niederheimbach. Tariffs from the 13th century are not known. In 1369, a charge of 2½ Turnosgroschen per barrel of wine is recorded.

name: Trollerup
Settlement_Description: The settlement of Trollerup was first mentioned in 1476, but is significantly older. The settlement had no church but was part of the parish of Nørup.

name: Turaida
Settlement_Description: In 1214, Bishop Philipp von Ratzeburg built a castle that was the residence of the Teutonic Order in the 15th century. Only a ruin can be seen since the 18th century.The parish of Treyden was mentioned in 1248 and 1457.

name: Trems
Settlement_Description: First mentioned in 1215. At the mill and settlement Trems, there was a crossing of the Lübeck enclosure ('landwehr'), which was constructed around 1300. It consisted of a boom barrier and a watchtower with a guard.

name: Trzebiatów
Settlement_Description: First mentioned as a Slavic settlement near a castle in 1180.
Town_Description: Founded as a German town with Lübeck town privileges by the dukes Barnim I and Bogislaw IV of Pomerania in 1277, endorsed in 1285.

name: Turbia
Toll_Description: Mentioned as toll station in c. 1349, where 1/2 gr. had to be paid for each horse.

name: Treuenbrietzen
Settlement_Description: A local noble family is attested in 1209, a castle in 1217. In the shelter of the castle a settlement developed, as well as a settlement around St Nicholas' Church in the early 13th century.
Town_Description: In 1290 both settlements are united as town ('civitas'), but earlier privileges must have existed. Since 1324 Magdeburg town rights can be attested.
Fair_Description: In 1521 a cattle market is granted that is merged into a cattle and flax market in 1606. In 1671 five fairs are granted or confirmed, four of which have a preceding cattle-, horse- and flax market.
Toll_Description: In the district of Treuenbrietzen, the fee of safe conduct on wagons with centerload ('Zentnerwagen') was 6, beyond the border 8 pennies.

name: Trzebiel
Town_Description: First mentioned as town in 1301. A castle is mentioned in 1319 and 1336, the town was probably founded by the owner of the castle.

name: Altentreptow
Settlement_Description: A settlement developed close to a Slavic fortification; a church was mentioned in 1175. A Benedictine convent was founded at the end of the 12. century, but was soon relocated.
Town_Description: The founding date is not known, but it was mentioned as civitas in 1245. The town law was confirmed in 1540.

name: Triestewitz
Settlement_Description: The village and manor are first mentioned in 1251.

name: Trittau
Settlement_Description: First mentioned in 1239. A castle was built in Trittau by count Johann of Holstein in 1326. It was pawned to Lübeck in 1375, 1504-1515, and 1524. It was conquered by Lübeck troops in 1534, but returned to Holstein the following year. The castle was demolished in 1775.
Toll_Description: The toll of the counts of Holstein in Trittau is first mentioned in 1457. According to a register of toll revenues from the early 1540s, the toll receipts were usually around 600 Lübeck mark per year.

name: Troisdorf
Toll_Description: Toll station of the dukes of Berg, first mentioned in 1387. It was abolished in 1389, but re-installed around 1400.

name: Trotha
Settlement_Description: In Trotha finds of the Thuringians were recovered, probably a settlement existed since then. During the middle ages a noble family of Trotha existed. In 1900 Trotha was incorporated into Halle.

name: Ramskulla (Pohja)
Settlement_Description: <b>Post house:</b> According to sources, a post office was established in the village of Ramskulla in Pohja no later than 1645.

name: Trzemeszno
Toll_Description: The toll that was levied in Wylatowo for the monastery Trzemeszno was moved to Trzemeszno itself at the end of the 14th century.

name: Mustvee
Settlement_Description: During the 14th century the settlement was a fishing village. It received town rights in 1938.

name: Tuchtfeld
Settlement_Description: First mentioned in the 8th or 9th century.

name: Tukums
Settlement_Description: The area fell to the Teutonic Order in 1253, that built a castle in 1299. A manor was mentioned since 1442. In 1445 a fortified borough was stated.

name: Türi
Settlement_Description: Around 1300 there was a church in whose surroundings a village developed.

name: Tuczno
Settlement_Description: Originally a bailiwick and Slavic settlement, archaeological evidence dates habitation back to the 7th century.
Town_Description: The town privileges were attested in 1306 and the Magdeburg town law was granted in 1331 by the brothers von Wedell.

name: Twello
Settlement_Description: Earliest mention dates from the end of thirteenth century.

name: Twizel
Settlement_Description: Earliest mention dates from the thirteenth century, probably from circa 1240.

name: Twillingen
Settlement_Description: The village was first mentioned in 1301.

name: Twistringen
Settlement_Description: First mentioned in the list of donors to the construction of the Weser bridge in Bremen, ca. 1250. The settlement is doubtlessly older; a parish was possibly already founded before 850.

name: Tykocin
Toll_Description: Lithuanian toll station, mentioned at least in 1526.

name: Ubbakal
Settlement_Description: The small village, which was first mentioned in 1564 belongs to the Manor of Koigi.

name: Uhti
Settlement_Description: Village that was first mentioned in 1299.

name: Uchte
Settlement_Description: A castle of the count of Hoya is built in 1284. Next to it, a settlement developed, which had a burgomaster and council in 1459 and was characterised as borough ('flecken') in 1520.

name: Vaabina
Settlement_Description: Since only the remains of the wall have survived from the earlier castle, it is not possible to date the exact year of construction. However, in 1405 possible owners of the castle are mentioned. In 1522 a manor is mentioned.

name: Ueckermünde
Settlement_Description: A Pomeranian castle and settlement existed in the mid-12th century. The shore of the river Uecker is mentioned as location of a Diet in 1178, the settlement itself in 1223.
Town_Description: Lübeck town law granted around 1260, first mentioned as a town in 1276.

name: Udria
Settlement_Description: The village belonged to the Lagena manor since 1623.

name: Uelsen
Settlement_Description: The church of St Willibrord already existed in 1131, and there was a regional court in the village.

name: Uelzen
Settlement_Description: Around 1260, the settlement at the monastery Uelzen (the current Oldenstadt) was moved to the western shore of the Ilmenau river as a result of a conflict between the dukes of Lüneburg and the counts of Schwerin.
Town_Description: The "new town" Uelzen acquired Lüneburg town privileges from duke Johann of Brunswick in 1270, under the name Lewenwolde.
Fair_Description: Fairs in Uelzen are first mentioned in 1448, on Letare Sunday (mid-Lent) and the Day of St John. In the late 16th century, two additional fairs are mentioned: dedication day, on the Nativity of Mary, and on Invocavit Sunday.
Toll_Description: A toll at the monastery in the old town (Oldenstadt) is first mentioned around 1133/37, when it was given to the monastery by the bishop of Verden. After the foundation of the new town of Uelzen, the toll was owned by the duke of Brunswick, who sold it to the town in 1370. The toll was levied at the town gates from travellers from outside of the principality of Lüneburg, who carried commodities with them.

name: Uerdingen
Toll_Description: 1) The Archbishop of Cologne levied a fee for safe conduct on the Rhine even before 1279. Tariffs and revenues have not been preserved. The levy was abolished in the same year.<br/>2) The archbishop levied a land toll in 1449/53. The annual revenue around the years 1454/60 amounted to about 80 mark.

name: Ikšķile
Settlement_Description: The village where Bishop Meinhard started the Liven mission was first mentioned in 1184. A castle and a church were therefore built in 1185. In 1202 the castle lost its importance and the live began several riots. The Teutonic Order was able to regain the castle in the 14th and 15th centuries. The village was mentioned in 1405. In 1507 there was a fortified borough ('Hakelwerk').

name: Uulu
Settlement_Description: Village and manor house, which originated around 1500. A courtyard was mentioned in 1601.

name: Ulfen
Toll_Description: A toll station existed before 1583, as in that year a toll station was installed in Datterode, because some merchants circumvented the toll in Ulfen by travelling via Datterode.

name: Ulmale
Settlement_Description: In 1350, the settlement was mentioned as fief. In 1442, a manor of the Teutonic Order is documented.

name: Uenglingen
Settlement_Description: Mention as property of St. Ludgeri monastery in Helmstedt in 1238. In 1247 mention of a warden.

name: Spui
Harbour_Description: The canal Haagse Trekvliet was dug in 1345 to create a waterway between Den Haag and the Vliet canal between Delft and Leiden. A harbour was located at the Spui. A crane for wine was built here in 1401 by an officer of the count, who was responsible for his wine cellar ('bottelrie').

name: Unna
Settlement_Description: A church is mentioned in 1019. However, the settlement dates back to the Merovingian period.
Town_Description: 1243 and 1278 called 'villa'. In the course of disputes between the Counts of the Mark and the Archbishops of Cologne at the end of the 13th century elevated to a country town. Awarded the 'Wigboldsrecht' in 1243 and urban privileges in 1290.
Toll_Description: A land toll was first mentioned in 1470. The property realtions are not clear. Presumably the toll was owned by the Count of the Mark or the town of Unna itself. Tariffs and revenues are not known.

name: Uppen
Settlement_Description: At the pass of Uppen a watchtower of the Hildesheim enclosure ('landwehr') was built. Since 1664, the settlement is joined with Achtum.

name: Urbach
Toll_Description: The Duke of Berg levied a land toll in Urbach for the first time in 1411. Tariffs and revenues are not known.

name: Urnehoved
Settlement_Description: The thing for the province of Southern Jutland/Schleswig. An important political institution in the early middle ages. Several kings of Denmark were proclaimed or elected at Urnehoved Thing during the medieval period.

name: Ursel
Settlement_Description: Earliest mention in 1147, in a copy from the end of the thirteenth century.

name: Uetersen
Settlement_Description: Developed out of a 12th-century castle of the knights of Barmstede and a Cistercian nun convent that was founded around 1234.

name: Utrecht
Settlement_Description: A 'castellum' (fort) was built at the location of the present-day Domplein in Roman times. It is first mentioned in 300 (in seventh-, eight- and tenth-century copies of the document). Later, the settlement became an episcopal see and a religious centre. Around 925 when the Vikings were gone the bishop returned from Deventer. In 936 the bishop granted mint-rights and in 953 the revenues from the toll at Muiden situated at the mouth of the river Vecht. In the 11th and early 12th century a vicus called Stathe originated west of the castle of the bischop with the first markets.
Town_Description: Town rights were granted between 1114 and 2 June 1122 by Godebald, bishop of Utrecht. The privileges were extended in the 12th and 13th century.
Fair_Description: Fairs in Utrecht probably originate in the 10th or early 11th century. Four fairs are mentioned in 1127, with a duration of two weeks: on Easter, St John the Baptist, Birth of Mary and St Martin. They were visited by merchants from a large region, especially the Rhineland. By the late 14th century, they had lost importance and were reduced to three days. In 1378, they were replaced by three new fairs: three days after Palm Sunday and St Victor and three days before Ascension Day. These seem to have been predominantly cattle and horse markets. A fourth fair, on St Pontian, was added in 1533 and was more important as a festival than for trading. It was merged with the dedication festival of the cathedral on St Magdalene in 1614. A manual of the toll-keeper of Geervliet dated 1562 mentions the horse-fairs in Utrecht on Febr. 16, March 28, May 24 and August 12, in a calendar of many horse-faires.
Toll_Description: In 975 the bishop obtained permission to relocate the toll at Muiden partly or as a whole to Utrecht. The last option was chosen. Toll privileges were granted in 1122: the charter lists detailed tariffs for visiting merchants from the Rhineland, Frisia and Saxony. Norwegians were exempted from the toll, as well as Kaiserwerth (in 1145), Duisburg (1165) and Tiel (before 1174). Later in the 12th and 13th century merchants from Holland, Zeeland, Flanders, the Meuse-region and England are mentioned.
Staple_Description: In 1542 (Febr. 4) emperor Charles V prohibited horse-fairs in the Sticht of Utrecht, except those in Abcoude and Utrecht.

name: Veldhoven
Settlement_Description: Earliest mention in 1294, in a fifteenth century copy.

name: Valkenburg (Rijn)
Settlement_Description: Earliest mention in 918-948, in a 11th-century copy. A hospital ('leprosarium') is first mentioned in 1295. In 1401 Valkenburg obtained together with Katwijk toll exemption from the count of Holland.
Fair_Description: The fair must have existed in the first half of the 13th century. The village was situated on the old landroute along the coast of Holland, used by merchants from Flanders on their way to Friesland. In 1343 a cloth-hall is mentioned. A toll on the fair with St. Lambert (duration 14 days), including a 'ellemaat' (ell) 'botermaat' (measure for butter) and 'muddepenning' (retribution on the use of measures) belonging to the vicount of Leiden (the lord of Wassenaar) is first found in 1360. The accounts of the steward of the lord of Wassenaer as burgrave, preserved since 1554 with gaps, mention a fair with St. Lamberts-eve (Sept. 16). According to a charter dated 1580 the fair started 8 days before. A manual of the toll-keeper of Geervliet dated 1562 mentions the horse-fair in Valkenburg on September 15 in a calendar of many horse-faires. Guicciardini stated in his book about the Netherlands dated 1566 that the merchants of Wieringen said that the horses on the fair of Valkenburg were excellent.

name: Valaste
Settlement_Description: The village was first mentioned in 1241 and belonged to the Teutonic Order from 1444. From 1624 it was property of the manor of Ontika.

name: Veghel
Settlement_Description: Earliest mention in the beginning of the thirteenth century.

name: Vechelde
Settlement_Description: The settlement was fortified by the dukes of Brunswick-Lüneburg in 1382. Between 1392 and 1671, the castle was pawned to the town of Brunswick.

name: Vechta
Settlement_Description: The counts of Ravensberg constructed a castle "prope Vechtam" at the crossing of the Moorbach in the 12th century.
Town_Description: Acquisition of town privileges unknown, possibly before 1252. In ca. 1180/81, mint and toll rights were granted to the settlement. A charter from 1269 suggests that Vechta had (limited) town privileges at that moment, although it is later still characterised only as borough ('wicbold'); first mentioned as 'civitas' in 1351, the town privileges were confirmed by the bishop of Münster in 1372. In the 15th century, Vechta had the Osnabrück town rights.

name: Veckenstedt
Settlement_Description: In the 9th century a family of Veckenstedt is mentioned, who presumably held residence in a castle in Veckenstedt.

name: Veenhusen
Settlement_Description: The settlement was first mentioned in 1283.

name: Wredenhagen
Settlement_Description: At the end of the 13th century, the Lords of Werle built a castle in Wredenhagen, which was owned by the margraves of Brandenburg in 1316 and was probably first mentioned in that year. A village developed around the castle.

name: Ramsdorf
Settlement_Description: In the 11th century there was an episcopal official court and shortly before 1200 a parish church was founded, where the settlement originated. In 1319 this is called 'villa'.
Town_Description: In 1319 'Wigboldrechte' were granted. In 1384 the place was mentioned as an 'oppidum' and town, in 1427 also called town.

name: Velbert
Toll_Description: The Duke of Berg levied a land toll in 1471. The first mention results from a lawsuit. In 1555 the toll station is no longer mentioned. Tariffs and revenues are not known.

name: Veldhausen
Settlement_Description: First mentioned around 1300. The church in the hamlet ('bauerschaft') Veldhausen was moved to Neuenhaus in 1370, but because the new location was difficult to reach, it was moved back to Veldhausen in 1410-1411.

name: Velp
Settlement_Description: Earliest mention dates from the beginning of the ninth century, in a copy dating from 1170-1175.

name: Venlo
Town_Description: Earliest mention as 'oppidum' in 1272, and in 1339 Venlo is called 'stede'. Town privileges were granted by Reginald II, duke of Guelders, on 1 September 1343. In the same year Venlo was fortified with a town wall. A town hall is mentioned in 1374, burgomasters and councillors in 1394.
Fair_Description: Venlo probably had one fair from at least 1294/95 onward: a fair of sixteen days on Sunday after Invocavit. When Venlo received town privileges in 1343, it received the right to held three fairs of sixteen days: the one on Sunday after Invocavit, one on St Albinus, and one on Sunday after St Lambert. The ducal account of 1343/'4 states: a cloth-hall on the market: 2 mark 6 sol., the 'big' toll (probably the one on the river Maas) farmed out for 240 mark 'goedgeld': 290 mark 7 sol. 4 den., a market-toll with St. Lambertus: 3 sol. 9 den., a summer-toll: 22 sol. 6 den., half the big toll from St. Margareth till the octave of Easter: 119 mark, from then till July: 11 mark 3 sol. On Jan. 1 1617 three fairs, which were not attended fot a long time as a result of the war, were restored: 1) Monday in the 'Vastelavond', 2) St. Albaensday (June 21), 3) the third Monday after St. Lamberti in Sept. (Sept. 17), each during eight days before and after and with safeconduct for the visitors.
Toll_Description: In 1270 the 'kartol' in Venlo levied on traffic with horses and wagons, was commissioned in fief to the count of Julich. Next to the Meuse toll and safe conduct of the Count of Guelders (see description harbour), the town of Venlo levied a road toll in 1366. Rates and revenues are not known.
Staple_Description: Venlo acquired limited staple privileges in the town privileges of 1343. The council tried to impose a monopoly on the river trade between Venlo and Dordrecht for skippers and vessels from Venlo. Until the early 16th century this was indeed the case, but vessels from other cities increasingly circumvented the town. In 1523, the full eight-day staple of Roermond was moved to Venlo during a conflict with that city.

name: Vellahn
Settlement_Description: First mentioned in 1154, characterised as village ('villa') in 1218 and 1327.

name: Wozinkel
Settlement_Description: The village is first mentioned in 1342.

name: Vejen
Settlement_Description: The village of Vejen was first mentioned in c. 1280 and again in c. 1340 , but is significantly older. The medieval parish church was built in either the 12th or 13th century, but replaced by a new church in the late 19th century.

name: Walchow
Settlement_Description: The village is first mentioned in 1445.

name: Porkkala
Settlement_Description: <b>Post office:</b> The exact year of the establishment of the Porkkala post office is uncertain, but according to sources, the office was likely founded by 1640 at the latest. The postal service at the time was reportedly overseen by postmaster Antonius Pape. Mail was transported once a week from Porkkala to Rääveli (Tallinn). The shipmaster's responsibility was to handle the mail delivery for a monthly salary.

name: Mühlberg (Elbe)
Settlement_Description: First mentioned in 1226, but the settlement probably already existed around 1200. The Cistercian nunnery Marienstern was founded in 1228.
Town_Description: Referred to as oppidum in 1230, in 1295 as civitas, when the old and new town were differentiated. In 1363 town rights were granted by Charles IV.

name: null
Toll_Description: A land toll of the bishop of Utrecht was levied at the bridge on the 'Bisschopsweg', first mentioned in an account from 1328/29, but it must have existed since the construction of the bridge. From 1602 onward, a water toll was levied at Eembrugge for ships going from and to Amersfoort.
Bridge_Description: A bridge across the Eem river is first mentioned in 1300. This gave the shortest and most northern connection to Bunschoten en thus between the Nedersticht en Oversticht. In 1542 4 pound was collected which was half for the emperor and half for the inhabitants.

name: Verden
Settlement_Description: The settlement is first mentioned in 782. A royal court of Charlemagne existed here, as well as a bishopric. A cathedral church is attested in ca. 814.
Town_Description: Emperor Otto III granted Verden market, toll and minting privileges in 985. A town council is mentioned in 1235 and town privileges were granted in 1259. Since 1405 at the latest, the town was a Free Imperial City.
Fair_Description: The oldest fair in Verden, on the Dedication day of the cathedral, can be linked to the market privilege of 985. Later Verden became an important centre for the cattle trade. Bishop Barthold founded four fairs in 1477, predominantly for cattle, and advertised them in a letter to the town of Zutphen (HUB X:527). These took place on 14 days before, 8 days and 3 weeks after St Philipp and James (April/May), and 8 days before St Bartholomew. Apparently, the cattle markets in spring were not a big success. In a privilege from 1491, they are not mentioned anymore: next to the Dedication Day fair (14 days before St Walpurga), there were two cattle markets on 14 and 8 days before St Bartholomew. After the Thirty Years' War in 1651, Queen Christine of Sweden revived the three fairs with different dates.
Toll_Description: The town acquired toll privileges in 985. According to 1460 complaints from the towns Brunswick and Celle, the toll tariff on the Aller river in Verden had at that time been increased to a sixfold of the previous tariff. Three years later, the toll was reduced again to 50 percent.

name: Vetschau
Settlement_Description: A parish village is mentioned in 1346, later it becomes a market borough, presumably Slavic. An earlier mention of Veczicz from 1302 cannot be linked to Vetschau with certainty.
Town_Description: King Ferdinand I granted town privileges in 1548-1549 upon request of the local lord.

name: Viborg
Settlement_Description: In the pre-christian part of the Viking Age Viborg appears to have been both an important place of worship and home to the provincial assembly of Jutland, which was one of the most important political institutions in Denmark. A permanent settlement with an urban character existed by the late 10th century.
Town_Description: In the end of the Viking Age and throughout the Middle Ages Viborg was home to the provincial assembly (Danish: Landsting) of Jutland and the island of Funen; one of the most important political institutions in the kingdom of Denmark. Up until 1655 all future kings of Denmark in theory had to be elected at the thing in Viborg. From the middle of the 11th century Viborg was home to a diocese; around 1130 the building of the town cathedral was begun. In the 13th century both a Dominican and Franciscan monasteries were founded, and during the medieval period Viborg also housed several other clerical institutions. At the end of the middle ages the town played a crucial role in the Danish reformation in 1536.In 1070 citizens (“civitas”) of Viborg were mentioned for the first time. Coins were minted from the time of Canute the Great (1016-1035) until around 1330. In the middle of the 12th century the town was fortified, and in the beginning of the 14th century a royal castle was built. A municipal seal is known from c. 1250, and in the 13th century Viborg was probably also granted a town law. The oldest preserved town privileges, which registered and confirmed 38 older privileges, are from 1440. At this time a town hall was located at Gammel Torv, the medieval town square. During the middle ages Viborg was in a dynamic political, economic and cultural center, but the importance of the town declined in the following centuries.
Fair_Description: Due to its central location in Jutland, Viborg was an important market town with several annual fairs. The intense market activity in Viborg was throughout the middle ages and early-modern era related to the provincial assembly. The different fairs were used by both locals and foreigners, especially Germans. Oxen and horses were important commodities at the fairs of Viborg, and were exported to Germany and the Netherlands.

name: Vienenburg
Settlement_Description: The castle Vienenburg was built around 1300 by the count of Wernigerode, first mentioned in 1306. It was sold to the bishop of Hildesheim in 1367 and came to the duke of Brunswick-Wolfenbüttel in 1523.
Toll_Primary_Owner: Graf von Wernigerode / Bischof von Hildesheim
Toll_Description: The privilege of levying a toll was granted in 1323. In 1396, Goslar butchers complained that they had to pay a toll on cattle driven through Vienenburg, of which they claimed to be exempted.

name: Vierde
Settlement_Description: The village was first mentioned in 1337.

name: Vierhouten
Settlement_Description: Earliest mention in 1418 as 'Vierholten', but a small settlement probably already existed before. Veen et. al. (2016) presume permanent habitation from ca. 1250 onwards. Neefjes and Bleumink (2015) consider earlier habitation a possiblity, possibly from the tenth century onwards. There is consensus that habitation and cultivation of land intensified during the thirteenth century.

name: Vierraden
Settlement_Description: A mill is mentioned in 1265. In the beginning of the 14th century a Pomeranian castle was built, first mentioned in 1321. A castle borough ('Burgflecken') is mentioned in 1450.
Town_Description: The Duke of Hohenstein, the feoffee of the castle since 1478, founded a small town ('Stetlin') in 1515 with electoral permission.
Toll_Description: The lordship (later department) of Schwedt owned a bridge- and dam toll in Vierraden, first mentioned in 1481.

name: Vilvoorde
Settlement_Description: Earliest mention in 779, in a copy from around 1191.
Town_Description: Duke Henry I of Brabant granted Vilvoorde a charter of freedom in 1192. The town was completely fortified in the mid-14th century and a ducal castle built in 1375-1380. In the 15th century, Vilvoorde went into decline.

name: Visselhövede
Settlement_Description: First mentioned in 1258. Seat of a bailiff ('vogt') of the diocese of Verden. Around 1450, the settlement acquired borough ('weichbild') privileges from bishop Johann von Asel of Verden.

name: Viuf
Settlement_Description: The village of Viuf was first mentioned in 1325, but is significantly older. The parish church is from either the 12th or 13th century.

name: Vreeland
Settlement_Description: Vreeland is first mentioned in 1265 as an 'oppidum'. It received town privileges in 1265, but these were withdrawn in 1560 by the States of Utrecht.
Town_Description: Vreeland is first mentioned in 1265 as an 'oppidum', when it is founded and granted town privileges by Henry I van Vianden, bishop of Utrecht. Henry has a castle (Kasteel Vreeland) built between 1258 and 1260 for military/strategic purposes. It is situated on the intersection between the river Vecht and a land route. Vreeland was also founded for military and economic reasons, but never fully developped into a town. The town priliveges of Vreeland were withdrawn by the States of Utrecht in 1560.

name: Vries
Settlement_Description: Earliest mention in 1139, in a sixteenth century copy.

name: Tanna
Settlement_Description: First mention in 1232, when a parish priest is mentioned.
Town_Description: In 1495 town rights are granted, which are probably based on Schleiz town rights. Town bylaways remain from 1566 with references to earlier versions.

name: Visé
Fair_Description: The oldest known fair in the Netherlands dated 983 is found till in the 12th century. A charter about the fair dated 1131 appeared to be a falsum dated 1220-1225. Huy had a regional fair.

name: Vilz
Settlement_Description: The village is first mentioned in 1236, but probably already existed in 1178.

name: Vlaardingen
Settlement_Description: Vlaardingen is first mentioned in a mid-fourteenth-century copy of a document dating from about 1018. Van Berkel & Samplonius mention archeological findings from Merovingian and Carolingian times.
Town_Description: Vlaardingen is granted town rights on 14 May 1273 by Floris V, count of Holland.
Fair_Description: The fair must have existed in the first half of the 13th century and is mentioned in the town rights of 1273 without date or duration. The village was situated on the old landroute along the coast of Holland, used by merchants from Flanders on their way to Friesland. In 1276 the lord of Wassenaer donated money off the toll-revenues for the salvation of his father and himself.  In the oldest register with the fiefs of count Floris V dated 1282-'84 the 'teloneum de Vlerdinghen' is found as a fief of the lord of Wassenaer. Circa 1355 it is stated that the fair started Mayday (May 1). A cloth-hall is first mentioned in 1351. The accounts of the steward of the lord of Wassenaer preserved from 1554 onwards with gaps, mention a horsefair in Vlaardingen on St. Peter and Pouwelseve (June 28). A manual of the toll-keeper of Geervliet dated 1562 mentions the horse-fair in Vlaardingen also on June 28 in a calendar of many horse-faires. An account of this horsefair is dated 1581 and analysed.
Ferry_Description: In 1378 a ferry to Brielle is mentioned.

name: Vlotho
Settlement_Description: An early settlement close to the castle at a ford in the Weser river can be dated back to the 12th century.
Town_Description: Town rights were granted around 1250. After 1368, the town was degraded into a market borough ('marktflecken'), and received new town privileges in 1719.
Toll_Description: A toll on the Weser river in Vlotho was levied since 1224. It is mentioned in a complaint by the town Bremen in 1584 and in a document from the Hardehausen monastery in 1597.

name: Rannajõe
Settlement_Description: In the Middle Ages, this area was part of the church's benefices. 1564 an estate was mentioned.

name: Voigdehagen
Settlement_Description: The village is first mentioned in 1282. Until the Reformation the churches in Stralsund were filial churches of the parish of Voigdehagen. A mill is mentioned in 1290.

name: Vojensgård
Settlement_Description: The village of Vojens was first mentioned in 1421, but was significantly older. The village was abandoned in the late 16th century and was originally located east of the modern town of Vojens, at the modern location of Vojensgård.

name: Vrijenberg
Settlement_Description: An inn ('Loener Herberg') is named on the map of the Veluwe by Christiaan Sgrooten (1559). This is probably the inn and farm Vrijenberg, first mentioned in 1603. Jochem Alof is mentioned as inn keeper in 1680.

name: Vught
Settlement_Description: Earliest mention in 1028, in a copy dating from circa 1530.
Fair_Description: A (market-?)toll mentioned in 1028 possibly indicates a fair was existent then. Vught is situated where the rivers Aa and Dommel confluence in the river Dieze. In 1370-80 rights called 'loot and geleide' were levied here. Inhabitants of the Meierij were free of this rights. The fair(s) probably perished afterwards as the town Den Bosch was too close.

name: Vollenhove
Settlement_Description: Vollenhove developed as a settlement near Vollenhove castle. The earliest mention of ‘Fulnaho’ as the name of a forest dates from 944 (in a copy from the second half of the twelfth century). The castle was built in 1165. Possibly since the end of the thirteenth century, but at least before town privileges were officially granted in 1354, a market was held in Vollenhove.
Town_Description: Town privileges were granted by Jan IV of Arkel, bishop of Utrecht, on 13 July 1354. In the beginning of the fourteenth century, there was at least one inn in Vollenhove.
Fair_Description: In 1348 is een jaarmarkt in Vollenhove bekend uit de Deventer stadsrekeningen. Dit moet de Allerheiligenmarkt zijn die mogelijk al in 1284 bestond, maar pas in 1429 als zodanig genoemd wordt. Deze markt duurde 4 dagen en sloot aan op de Zwolse Simon en Judasmarkt rond 28 okt., die in 1309 al langer bestond. Er aan vooraf ging sinds 1357 de Hasselter Gallusmarkt rond 16 okt. Vanaf 1358 kwam de Steenwijker Elfduizendmaagdenmarkt rond 21 okt. er tussenin. In 1380 bestond ook een jaarmarkt met Pasen van 4 dagen. De Vollenhoofse Bartholomeusmarkt (rond 1393 aantoonbaar) was rond 24 aug. en sloot aan op de Zwolse Maria-Hemelvaartmarkt rond 15 aug. Aan de drie bestaande jaarmarkten werd in 1420 (21 febr.) door de bisschop van Utrecht aan de bewoners van het Camp en ambt van Vollenhove en omliggende landen een nieuwe vrije jaarmarkt gegeven binnen de Camp van Vollenhoven op St. Gereoens en Victorsdag (10 okt.) met vrijheden en voordelen als andere jaarmarkten van het Camp. In de tweede helft van de 15e eeuw duurden alle jaarmarkten 14 dagen. Een vijfde jaarmarkt wordt eind 15e eeuw gevonden 8 dagen na St. Jan (24 juni), de duur van alle markten is dan 16 dagen.

name: Voorst
Settlement_Description: Earliest mention in 893 in a copy from 1222. Over time, the river IJssel moved away from Voorst.

name: Voorthuizen
Settlement_Description: Earliest mention dates from 970 in a copy from 1480.

name: Vorchten
Settlement_Description: Earliest mention in 1176, in a seventeenth century copy.

name: Vorden
Settlement_Description: Earliest mention in 1121, in a thirteenth century copy.

name: Vörden
Settlement_Description: Vörden developed near a ford, which was paved by the bishop of Osnabrück already in 1081. The settlement itself is first mentioned in 1341, and a castle in 1370. After the conquest by the bishop of the settlement by the bishop of Osnabrück in 1387, the settlement became a borough ('weichbild'). Characterised as 'oppidum' around 1391.

name: Vordersten Thüle
Settlement_Description: The hamlet ('bauerschaft') Thüle, first mentioned in 1270, was stretched out along 6 km and was divided into three parts. The northernmost part was called Vordersten Thüle.

name: Vorselaar
Settlement_Description: Earliest mention in 726, in a copy dating from 1191 and circa 1222. Next mention in 1117.

name: Vrasene
Settlement_Description: First mentioned in a c.1175 copy of a document from 1149-1166.

name: Vreden
Town_Description: Borough ('Wigbold') privileges were granted at the latest in 1241. According to a later charter, the settlement received town rights in 1252 at the latest.

name: Waardenburg
Settlement_Description: Earliest mention in 1108, in a twelfth-century copy

name: Waarloos
Settlement_Description: Earliest mention in circa 1188, in a copy dating from circa 1243. Next mention in 1218 is a copy.

name: Waddinxveen
Settlement_Description: Earliest mention in 1233, in a copy dating from 1340.
Bridge_Description: A bridge crossing the river Gouwe at the 'Kerkweg' was built somewhere in the (mid?) 16th century. It likely replaced a ferry.

name: Wageningen
Settlement_Description: Earliest mention in 1125, but this is possibly a forgery. It was originally a dispersed settlement located on the hill north-east of the later town.
Town_Description: The town New ('Neo-')Wageningen was founded in the mid-13th century south-west of the old settlement. In 1240 Otto II, count of Guelders, fortified the town with walls and double moats. He granted town ('oppidum') privileges on 12 June 1263. Confirmation of town privileges on 4 December 1312 by Reginald I, count of Guelders, and elevation from oppidum to civitas. The town remained small, however, and mainly served as a border fortification of the duchy of Guelders against the bishopric of Utrecht.
Fair_Description: A weekly market on Thursday is first mentiond in 1263. From at least 1294/95 onwards, Wageningen also had one fair, taking place on St James's Day.
Toll_Description: The ducal land and markets tolls in Wageningen remained unleased in 1428. Accounts from the years 1442-1471 exist of the new and old ducal land toll in Wageningen, which show that the revenues were higher than for other tolls on the Veluwe. Ordinances from 1451 show that the town also levied a road toll ('weggeld') at both town gates.

name: Taagepera
Settlement_Description: The Manor was first mentioned in 1509.

name: Vahastu
Settlement_Description: The village and a manor were first mentioned in 1534. An old castle on a hill near Vahastu hints at an earlier settlement.

name: Vahuküla
Settlement_Description: In 1253 the Teutonic Order left the village 'Wawe' to the bishop of Reval. The village belonged to the manor 'Sitz'.

name: Wahlitz
Settlement_Description: Settlements on the nearby Taubenberg go as far back as the Nelolithic and is constantly settled through the ages. Written mention in 1015, when it is given to St. Mary's church in Magdeburg.

name: Wahn (Emsland)
Settlement_Description: It is uncertain if the settlement Walinoon, mentioned around 1000, is the same as Wahn. The village was demolished in 1941 to make place for an extension of a firing range.

name: Vaimastvere
Settlement_Description: Village and manor were first mentioned in 1527.

name: Vaida
Settlement_Description: A village, that came into the possession of the Teutonic Order ('Deutscher Orden'), was first mentioned in 1241.

name: Walchum
Toll_Description: A toll of the bishop of Münster in Walchum is mentioned in 1576, when it could not be leased. Likewise, a toll collector could not be found in 1645 because revenues were low because of the Thirty Years' War.

name: Waldau (Bernburg)
Settlement_Description: Charlemagne gathered his troops in Waladala in 806 before crossing the Saale river. First mention of Waldau 1049 as the property of Gernrode monastery.

name: Waldheim
Toll_Description: Medieval toll and safe conduct station.

name: Valga
Settlement_Description: The settlement probably already existed in the 13th century. A priest was mentioned there in 1286. The settlement was destroyed by Lithuanians in 1345.
Town_Description: In 1387 the place was already referred to as 'oppidum'. It received town rights from Riga and Dorpat only in 1584.

name: Walkenried
Settlement_Description: A Cistercian monastery was founded in Walkenried in 1127/29. In 1556 it changed to the Protestant denomination, and was secularised in 1648.

name: Walle (Bremen)
Settlement_Description: First mentioned in 1139. On a hill in Walle, the gallows of the town of Bremen were located.

name: Wallendorf
Settlement_Description: St. Peter's monastery had property here since 1091.

name: Wallhausen
Settlement_Description: Important Ottonian an Saxonian imperial palace, several royal stays are documented such as the wedding of Otto, father of Henry I, and Mathilde in 909. Mentioned in 1028 as castle district ('Burgwardbezirk'). During the Late Middle Ages temporary residence of the Teutonic Order, afterwards the village was pawned several times, until the family Von der Asseburg had its residence here from 1414 until 1945.

name: Valle
Settlement_Description: The place was first mentioned in 1542 and was crownland.

name: Valkla
Settlement_Description: Manor and village, which were mentioned in 1241. In 1400 the area was occupied by the Teutonic Order.

name: Wallmerod
Toll_Description: Toll station of the Electorate Trier

name: Wandsbek
Settlement_Description: The settlement was first mentioned in a document in 1296 as a village with five farms ('Hufen') that developed into estates. The moated castle Wandesburg was built in 1568.

name: Wange
Settlement_Description: Earliest mention in 742. Next mention in 1070.

name: Wanssum
Fair_Description: A market-toll is found in the account of the duke of Guelders dated 1343/4. Fairday was St. Michael (September 29).

name: Wanzleben
Settlement_Description: One of the earliest settlements in the environs of Magdeburg that probably exited before 877.Earliest mention of a castle in 968 that controlled the crossing across the Sarre by the road from Magdeburg to Halberstadt.
Town_Description: After the settlement as grown considerably through influx from the surrounding areas, archbishop Peter raises its status to that of town. It is considered immediately responsible to the crown.
Fair_Description: With its town privileges, Wanzleben was granted a fair. While Keyser has it held on Thursday before Ascension day, Bergner cites it as being granted on the first Sunday after "meynden".
Toll_Description: Complaint in the 16th century, when it is stated that the toll stations of Oebisfelde, Neuhaldensleben, Wolmirstedt, Dreileben, Wanzleben and Calbe collect less toll because of Magdeburg's toll excemption.

name: Kumlinge
Settlement_Description: <b>Post house:</b> In 1638, the Royal Steward Bernhardt Steen von Steenhausen established six post houses in Åland, along the route from Stockholm to Turku. One of the post houses was located in Kumlinge.

name: Warburg
Settlement_Description: A castle is first mentioned in 1017. A charter from 1036 first mentions a settlement near the castle.
Town_Description: Warburg originally consisted of two towns: the old and new town. The granting of town privileges is unknown for both. The old town was mentioned as "civitas" in 1195 and had a burgomaster and council by 1245. For the new town, a burgomaster and council are mentioned in 1239. Both towns were united in 1436.
Fair_Description: The oldest fair in Warburg was the fair on St Michael's day in the old town, which was predominantly a grain market. On 15 July 1366, Bishop Henry III of Paderborn granted the town two fairs of three days, and on 31 October in the same year another two. These alternated between the old and new town. In 1372, he permitted both towns each to organise a church consecration fest. Tolls and fares for safe conduct were connected to the fairs, which were pawned to the city by the bishop in 1446.

name: Wardenburg
Settlement_Description: First mentioned in 1218. A castle was built by the count of Oldenburg around 1268, after which the settlement was named, as well as a chapel. The castle was destroyed by troops of the bishop of Münster in 1342.

name: Varudi
Settlement_Description: Manor and village were first mentioned in 1241.

name: Warin
Settlement_Description: First mentioned in 1178, in a 14th-century (falsified?) copy. A church is mentioned in 1233, bishop Hermann of Schwerin built a castle at the end of the 13th century.
Town_Description: First mentioned as a town in 1306, but no written privileges exist, and the settlement is usually called a borough ('oppidum'). However, there is evidence of a town council around 1306.

name: Varja
Settlement_Description: The village was first mentioned in 1241. It was owned by the Teutonic Order since 1472.

name: Warken
Settlement_Description: Earliest mention in 1059 in a falsified copy dating from ca 1180-1190.

name: Warmsdorf
Settlement_Description: Mention in a record of bishop Burchard of Halberstadt, who gives estates to Ilsenburg monastary during their renovations (Codex Diplomaticus Anhaltinus I, 101).1347 mention of castle Warmsdorf in the records, which controls the Wipper crossing.
Toll_Description: In 1496 the toll from Warmsdorf is moved to Neundorf (Anhalt). The toll house is repoted to have been right next to the castle's bridge until 1724.

name: Warnsveld
Settlement_Description: Earliest mention dates from 1121, in a thirteenth century copy. The Saint Martinus Church (Sint Martinuskerk) was probably founded in the eleventh century; it is first mentioned in 1121. The oldes buildings were primarily located south and east of the church. Archaelogical evidence suggests settlement since the ninth century: dendrochronology dates a well around 841.

name: Varangu
Settlement_Description: Manor and village were first mentioned in the 16th century.

name: Warszawa
Toll_Description: Mentioned as toll station in c. 1349, where 3 gr. and 4 den. had to be paid for each horse.
Staple_Description: Merchants started to be forced to offer their commodities on the Warsaw market around 1440.

name: Warlin
Settlement_Description: The village is first mentioned in 1170. An inn in the vilage is mentioned in 1587.
Toll_Description: A toll station is mentioned in 1587.

name: Bardo
Settlement_Description: A border castle is first mentioned in 1096.
Toll_Description: A toll is first mentioned in 1310.

name: Vasalemma
Settlement_Description: First mentioned in 1241. In 1364 it came into the possession of Padis monastery.

name: Wassenberg
Toll_Description: 1) The lord of Wassenberg probably levied a land toll in 1237 or before 1354/55. Among others, the Archbishop of Cologne (1283 to 1296), the Lord of Heinsberg (1310 to 1448/53) and Count Vinzenz of Moers (1453 to 1480/94) were pledge holders. In 1494, the toll fell to the Duke of Jülich. In 1389, 2 shillings per barrel of wine had to be paid. The annual yield in 1354/55 was about 11 mark. <br/>2) The Duke of Brabant-Limburg also levied a fee for safe conduct on land in 1389. 2 shillings per horse had to be paid. The fee was later merged with the land toll.

name: Vastemõisa
Settlement_Description: In 1559 the Teutonic Order owned a hamlet ('Hof') in this place. At the end of the 16th century this hamlet belonged to the fief of the castle in Fellin.

name: Webbekom
Settlement_Description: Earliest mention in 1107, in a copy from the middle of the thirteenth century

name: Wedde
Settlement_Description: Earliest mention in 1316. Around 1360, the noble family Addinga constructed a fortified manor here.

name: Weddingen
Settlement_Description: In 1399, Weddingen became the seat of a monastery of the Teutonic Order, which moved here from Goslar. The church in Weddingen was already in their possession in 1287.

name: Wedel
Settlement_Description: The place was first mentioned in 1212 as a ferry landing.
Fair_Description: Wedel was the most prominent market for oxen driven south from Denmark in the late 16th and 17th century. It is first mentioned in 1553, but already existed at that time. It is often assumed that the market already existed in 1465, when Hamburg attempted to stop the drift of oxen that circumvented the city. However, Poul Enemark argued that the sources do not permit the conclusion that a cattle market in Wedel existed before the mid-16th century. The market took place from mid-March to mid-April or for three to four weeks after Annunciation Day.

name: Weert
Settlement_Description: Weert originated on the crossroad of several trade routes. It is first mentioned in 1062, but this document is a forgery from the late eleventh century. Its subsequent mention dates from 1155. However, both Cox and Van Berkel & Samplonius mention political development around Weert in the late eleventh century. Between 1452 and 1556 the inhabitants of Weert and Nederweert were free of the roadtax ('weggeld') at Eindhoven, as Eindhoven was at Weert. Since at least 1476 Weert had a cloth-hall in Bergen (op Zoom) and since around 1490 one in Antwerp.
Town_Description: Town rights were granted on 5 May 1414 by William VI of Horne (Huis Horne). Further town privileges were added in 1563. During the fifteenth century, Weert flourished socio-economically.
Fair_Description: In 1414 (May 5) the lord of Horn granted three fairs: 1) St. Bonifatius (June 5), 2) St. John's beheading (May 6) and St. Barbara (Dec. 4) and a weekly market on Saturday and the right to levy excises. An undated register from the abbey Tongerlo (Westerlo, B.) (circa 1556) contains a list of fairs in the region Kempen and Peel. 'Weerdt' then still has three fairs: 1) first Tuesday after Grootvastenavond (Tuesday before start of the Lent), 2) Sunday post visitationis Mariae (July 2) till the Tuesday after that, 3) Sunday before conceptionis Mariae (Sept. 8) till the Tuesday after that. In 1563 (Sept. 27) the magistrate was granted three free horse-fairs by the count of Horn, lord of the town. Dates: 1) Thursday and Friday before 'Papenvastelavond' (Lent-eve), 2) two days before Petri and Pauli Apostolorum in June (June 29, so on June 27), 3) Friday and Saturday after the market at Grevinghen (Greven) in Westphalen (August 24) with safe-conduct and each two days before and after.
Toll_Description: Before 1240 the toll at Wessem was relocated to Weert by the lord of Horn. It seems to have changed from a toll on sailing ships to a landtoll. When the roads from Cologne to the west which crossed the Maas river above Wessem became of more importance the development of Wessem decayed and Weert en Roermond grew in importance. In 1452 Weert obtained freedom of 'weggeld' (taxes levied on the roads) at Eindhoven on the route to the fairs of Bergen (op Zoom). In 1480 (Febr. 16) Maximiliaan en Marie decided in a trial before the Court of Brabant between the count of Horn and the tenants of the toll and the 'oude geleide' (old conduct) of Brabant that citizens of Weert were free of tolls of old for their trade to Antwerp and Bergen (op Zoom). On April 11 that year it was stated that citiziens of Weert only had to pay once the 'oude geleide' in Beke (in the Meierij of den Bosch) to the inn-keeper living in the 'Mane'. The tariff of the old and new toll in Brabant dated 1560 has Weert in a list of toll-exempt places and mentions a sentence dated Febr. 11 1500 of the Council of Brabant which stated they had to pay 'geleiderecht' (conduct-right) each time on the route through Beke to Bergen (op Zoom) or through Oistmale to Antwerp or elsewhere: a coach: 12s., a cart: 6s.

name: Weesp
Settlement_Description: Weesp is first mentioned in 1131. It is located at the river Vecht and was a village/town of military-strategic importance. A hospital is first found in 1349.
Town_Description: Weesp was granted town rights on 20 May 1355 by William V, count of Holland. In 1355 military defences were added to the city, and later the town was surrounded by a stone defence wall.
Fair_Description: In 1387 (Jan. 8) duke Albrecht granted a free fair around St.-Victorsday (Oct. 10), four days before and after. Tolls would be as in Naarden and Muiden.

name: Wegenstedt
Settlement_Description: First mention in 1311 in the fiefdom register of Halberstadt. The exact date of foundation is not known.
Toll_Description: In 1533 a secondary station of safe conduct of the toll in Gardelegen is established in Wegenstedt, so travellers could choose between the routes via Oebisfelde or Gardelegen.

name: Veģi
Settlement_Description: The manor was first mentioned in 1560.

name: null
Toll_Description: A toll at 'Stockheim' is one of the six small tolls of Maastricht in 1357, when these were enfeoffed by the duke and duchess of Limburg to Thierri de Horne, lord of Perwez. A toll in 'Stocheym' is named in 1362 when the steward of the duke of Brabant leased out seven tolls on the river Meuse.

name: Widawa
Toll_Description: The toll station of Widawa is first attested in 1266.

name: Weert (Maastricht)
Toll_Description: A 'winage' (wine toll) in Weert is mentioned in comital accounts of Valkenburg from 1395 onwards, with revenues. It was subordinated to the 'big' land toll in Valkenburg.

name: Weisin
Settlement_Description: The village is first mentioned in 1235.

name: Aalsmeer
Settlement_Description: First mentioned probably in the 12th century, in a copy from ca. 1530.

name: Znamensk
Settlement_Description: The Old Prussian built a fortress against the Teutonic Order in 1255, but it was soon conquered by the Order and then in 1280 destroyed during a siege along with the settlement surrounding it
Town_Description: The teutonic Order granted Gottfried Hundertmark the privilege to found the civitas in 1336 with Kulm town law

name: Bobäck
Settlement_Description: Permanent agricultural settlement in Kirkkonummi (sw. Kyrkslätt) goes back to the 12th century. The parish organisation in Western Nyland dates to the early 13th century. The stone church was built in the end of the 15th century or in the early 16th
Fair_Description: In 1584 king Johan III confirmed an annual fair to be held on Michaelmas (29 September) in Kirkkonummi (sw. Kyrkslätt) Bobäck, where burghers of Helsinki were allowed to trade with peasants of the neighbouring province of Raasepori. Rights in Bobäck were again confirmed in 1594 when the date was cited as the Nativity of St Mary (8 September) and the site as Brendeberg’s sund. Possibly an older local peasant fair, the Bobäck fair took place at the end of the Espoo fjord alongside the Great Coastal Road. In the 1560s Bobäck village consisted of nine taxpaying farms. After the fair was relocated to Pikkala bridge on the Great Coastal Road in 1723, it was organised on Apostle Matteus (21 September).
Toll_Description: The 1/32 duty worth of all goods intended for sale in towns and fairs and brought to the site by peasants was collected in Bobäck since 1622.

name: Wehrbergen
Settlement_Description: The village was first mentioned in 1042.

name: Wehre
Settlement_Description: The settlement Wehre consisted of two parts: Ost- or Klein-Wehre and West- or Groß-Wehre. Groß-Wehre, the current village Wehre, is first mentioned separately in the 13th century. Klein-Wehre seems to have been abandoned in the 16th century.

name: Wehrstedt
Settlement_Description: First mention as villa, formerly it lay a little furhter away from Halberstadt at a nowadays detached church.

name: Weiden
Toll_Description: The Duke of Brabant-Limburg levied a land toll in 1312/15. Tariffs are not known. In 1312/15 about 20 pounds were collected, in 1356/57 142 Aachen mark.

name: Weiden in der Oberpfalz
Toll_Description: King Wenceslaus permitted citizens from Cheb in 1391 to travel to Frankfurt via Neustadt and Weiden; fees normally levied in Tachov would have to be paid in Weiden.

name: Weißenberg
Settlement_Description: It was probably an estate in the 12th century.

name: Weißenfels
Settlement_Description: Due to several town fires, most sources on the settlement are lost to us. The settlement was probably founded in 1185 at the bottom of the Wettins' castle.
Town_Description: First mention of a town council in 1280, a town hall and the consecration of the town church are mentioned in 1303.
Fair_Description: In the confirmation of the fair of 1500 an earlier fair is mentioned whose record was lost in a city fire.
Staple_Description: A staple is mentioned in 1185 and possibly in 1075.

name: Güstrow
Settlement_Description: Part of the terra Bisdede in Wendish times. A castle is mentioned in 1226; the settlement grew out of a collegiate chapter that was established close to the castle.
Town_Description: Founded by Heinrich Borwin II, Lord of Rostock (1219-1226) with Schwerin town law, first mentioned as civitas in 1228.
Toll_Description: In 1359 the town acquired the right to levy a transit toll for non-citizens travelling through Güstrow.

name: Aalten
Settlement_Description: First mentioned in 828, in an 11th century copy.

name: Weißensee (Berlin)
Settlement_Description: The settlement was probably first founded in 1230, and first mentioned in 1313. Over time, four noble manors were established in Weißensee.

name: Weißensee (Thüringen)
Settlement_Description: The castle as the nucleus of the town was built as a resting point between the Wartburg and the Neuenburg near Freyburg. It is first mentioned in 1168. In the 12th/13th century it played an important role in conflicts to block the road.The market places of the old market settlement and the planned city were not situated on the axis of the main traffic, which were defined by geographic circumstances.
Town_Description: A systematic foundation of the town can be seen architecturally around the castle at the beginning of the 13th century. It is first characterised as town in 1212.Since 1198 there are market officials, followed by jurymen, a district court and the citizen's rights of the citizens of Eisenach and Gotha in 1265 by landgrave Balthasar.
Fair_Description: In 1646 a chronicler mentiones three fairs in Weißensee, which had been there 'since olden times': Laetare Sunday, Sunday after St. Margaret and the third Sunday after Galli. The fairs are confirmed in 1693 and another fair is added on wednesday and thursday after the third advent. The fairs are still mentioned in 1863.
Toll_Description: A document from 1430 mentions that safe conduct has been given 'since olden times'. Toll station for the main safe conduct by Sachsenburg. In 1558 prince electorate August pawnes off the safe conduct to the council of Weißensee for three years, so that they may maintain paths, roads, dams, footbridges, ditches and bridges.

name: Paide
Settlement_Description: In 1265/66 a castle of the Teutonic Order was built, which served as a residence for the bailiffs. A fortified borough ('Hakelwerk') was built near the castle. The expansion and reconstruction of the castle began in the 14th century.
Town_Description: The fortified borough ('Hakelwerk') received town rights of Riga in 1291.

name: Weißig (Dresden)
Toll_Description: Secondary station safe conduct ('Beigeleitsstelle') of Radeberg.

name: Welplage
Settlement_Description: Hamlet ('bauerschaft'), which probably came into existence in the context of securing of the border between Minden and Osnabrück, possibly not much older than Huntebrück (1324).

name: Weitendorf
Toll_Description: Mentioned as ducal toll station in 1593.

name: Welsede
Settlement_Description: The place was first mentioned in 1224.

name: Lohma
Toll_Description: In the accounts of safe conducts of the district ('Amt') Altenburg, a secondary station of safe conduct ('Beigeleit') is mentioned in Lohma in the years 1526-1529

name: Cēsis
Settlement_Description: The mission of the pagans who settled there began in 1206. Therefore a castle of a knightly order was built in 1207-1210, soon after that a second one was built. It became the main castle of the Teutonic Order. A village developed around the two castles, which burned down in 1221. In 1224/27 a new settlement came into being, which is mentioned as a fortified borough ('Hakelwerk').
Town_Description: Wenden was referred to as a town in 1323. It received town rights of Riga during the first half of the 14th century. It was member of the Hanseatic League. In the 16th century, staple for trade via Marienburg to Pleskau and Novgorod.

name: Wennigsen (Deister)
Settlement_Description: First mentioned at the end of the 12th century or the beginning of the 13th century.

name: Vendzavas
Settlement_Description: The area 'Venelis' was first mentioned in a contract in 1230. Later, a manor was built.

name: Wentorf
Settlement_Description: The village was first mentioned in 1217.

name: Werben
Settlement_Description: Originally a Slavic settlement. A border castle against the Slavs was constructed in the 10th century, first mentioned in 1005.
Town_Description: Referred to as oppidum in 1196, and as civitas in 1225. The town had Magdeburg town rights. Since 1358 member of the Hanse.
Fair_Description: A horse market in Werben on 23 June is mentioned in 1593. In an official schedule from 1719, Seehausen, Werben and Arneburg each held three fairs. It can be assumed that some of these had existed for a while to this point.
Toll_Description: In 1160 citizens from Stendal were exempted from the toll in Werben. In 1429 margrave Johann commanded that the toll, which belonged to the chapel of Arneburg, had to be continued. In 1440 the toll is described more closely as a toll on land and on water, with fees for ships and commodities. In 1487 and 1541 only the road toll in Werben is mentioned, the water toll was possibly abandoned by that time.

name: Virtsu
Settlement_Description: An estate was mentioned in 1459. A castle was built in 1465 to keep a watch on the sea route. It was destroyed in 1533/34. The current village around the harbour was only created at the end of the 19th century.

name: Werl
Town_Description: In 1246 it was mentioned as an 'oppidum'. Archbishop Engelbert II of Cologne confirmed the town rights of Werl in 1271.
Toll_Description: The archbishop levied a land toll here for the first time around 1238/61. In the years there were also several pledge holders. From 1306/08, half the toll fell to the Count of Arnsberg. Tariffs are not known. There was probably a cattle and market toll in Werl. Together with the land toll, the annual revenue in 1306/08 amounted to about 20 mark.

name: Wildenburg
Toll_Description: The lord of Wildenburg levied a land toll before 1396. 2 Turnosgroschen per horse had to be paid.

name: Werne
Settlement_Description: First mentioned in 834. A market place had developed in the late 12th century.
Town_Description: Werne received borough ('wigbold') privileges in 1385 and was fortified after 1400.
Fair_Description: A fair on St Simon and Jude was granted in 1362. It is still mentioned as cattle market in a fair calendar of the land of Münster in 1636.

name: Werneuchen
Settlement_Description: A parson is named in 1247, the settlement is first mentioned as borough ('oppidum') in 1300, but did not fully develop into a town. Only a document from 1315 calls it a civitas, otherwise just oppidum, Städtlein or Flecken. Only officially became a town in 1865.

name: Wernigerode
Settlement_Description: First mentioned in 1121. The settlement was preceded by a village from the 9th century, probably a new foundation of Corvey monastery around 836.
Town_Description: In 1229 Wernigerode was granted town rights. Around 1265-1279 a new town developed, which was affiliated with the old town, but which were joined only in 1528.
Toll_Description: The count of Wernigerode Konrad sells the toll in the old and new city to the town of Wernigerode, so that the town defenses may be financed through it.

name: Werste
Settlement_Description: The village was first mentioned in 1176.

name: Werth
Settlement_Description: First mentioned in 1260. 'Castrum' in 1318, castle in 1369.
Town_Description: In 1426 the place was called a town according to a statute, but was not granted its rights. In 1547 it was named as a 'Wigbold' and in 1574 as a 'Städtlein'.

name: Wesel
Settlement_Description: First uncertain mention in a note of the monastery Echternach, which can be dated to 719-739. The foundation of a church around 800 and the finds of a grave field from the 8th and 9th century indicate that there existed a large settlement at this time already.
Fair_Description: A toll levied with the fair is found in 1241. Before 1430 the Walburgis fair (May 1), 3 days before and after, the fair with St. Matheus (Sept. 21) 3 days before and after, and a fair on Nov. 19, 7 days before and after, the most important fair ('frigidum forum') were founded. A fourth fair was founded in 1431 on June 15. In 1467 (Apr. 29) the St. Vitus horse-fair was granted: 15-18 June with 7 days before and after that.
Toll_Description: 1) The Count of Cleves levied a land toll in 1300. In 1319, 120 mark were collected together with the transhipment toll in Wesel.<br/>2) In 1319, a road toll was also mentioned, which was levied by the town itself. The Count of Cleves granted the privilege for this fee.

name: Rakvere
Settlement_Description: In 1220 the area and the Estonian castle 'Tarwanpe' was conquered by Danes, who built the castle 'Wesenbergh' in the same place in 1252. The city developed alongside the castle.
