Town_Description: The city received 'Lübeck town law' in 1302 and was governed by the Teutonic Order in 1346. In the 16th century, the city came under Russian and later Swedish conquership.

name: Wesendorf
Settlement_Description: First mentioned in 1543. It is very uncertain whether the "Vesendorpe" mentioned in 1278 can be identified with Wesendorf.

name: Wesloe
Settlement_Description: In 1256, the village is mentioned as "recently founded". It was in possession of Lübeck, from the middle of the 14th century privately owned.

name: Wespelaar
Settlement_Description: Earliest mention in 1154, in a copy from the middle of fourteenth century.

name: Veselava
Settlement_Description: The manor was first mentioned in 1602.

name: Westergellersen
Settlement_Description: The settlement Gellersen, which consisted of three parts, was first mentioned in 1117; Westergellersen separately in 1276. According to 17th-century registers, the village consisted of 4 farms ('plog') and 2 half farms or 3 farms and 3 half farms.

name: Westerhüsen
Settlement_Description: The settlement of Westeros is counted to the Northern Thuringian areas (Nordthüringgau) in the founding letter ('Fundationsbrief') by emperor Louis the Pious. Further mention in 840 in the records of Corvey monastery.

name: Westerlinde
Settlement_Description: The village was first mentioned in 1022.

name: Westervoort
Settlement_Description: Earliest mention in 1025, in a eighteenth century copy.

name: Westrem
Settlement_Description: Earliest mention in 1087, in a copy dating from 1775.

name: Wesuwe
Settlement_Description: From the 1379 charter in which Wesuwe was first mentioned, it can be inferred that there existed a parish church already around 1200.

name: Wickensen
Settlement_Description: Originally a folwark of the castle Homburg, which goes back to the Middle Ages. After it came in possession of the dukes of Brunswick-Lüneburg, the administrative centre was moved from the Homburg to Wickensen in 1542.
Toll_Description: A toll station of the dukes of Brunswick in Wickensen is mentioned in toll lists of the years 1539-1544 and 1587.

name: Westhausen
Settlement_Description: First mention in 1146, when property in Westhausen was given to Lippoldsberge monastery. A family of Westhausen is attested.

name: Widdersdorf
Toll_Description: In 1389, the Archbishop of Cologne levied a fee for safe conduct on land and a land toll. At first there is only the fee mentioned, later also the land toll. In 1389/93 there is evidence of both horse toll and escort fee. Depending on the load, 2 to 3 alb. per horse had to be paid. The annual revenue amounted to an average of about 667 mark. In 1455 Widdersdorf was a secondary toll station of Königsdorf.

name: Wiebrechtshausen
Settlement_Description: The place was first mentioned in 1015. Around 1230 a Cistercian nun convent was founded. It was closed shortly before 1612.

name: Wiedelah
Settlement_Description: The moated castle Wiedelah was built between 1292 and 1297 by the knights von der Gowische; in the 14th century it became property of the bishop of Hildesheim. The castle was acquired by the Brandenburg noble family of Quitzow in 1569, who rebuilt it as renaissance palace around 1600.

name: Wiederitzsch
Settlement_Description: First mention in 1091, first mention as "Großwiederitzsch" ('Großen Wederiß') in 1475. Merged with Kleinwiederitzsch as Wiederitzsch in 1904.

name: Wiedersbach
Settlement_Description: First mentioned in 1304. Enfeoffed to the archbishop of Mainz in 1311.

name: Wieluń
Toll_Description: A road toll of 4 denars for each loaded wagon on the roads leading from Wieluń towards Niedzielsko, Ruda and Dąbrowa was granted by the Polish king in 1504.

name: Wiepke
Settlement_Description: First mention in damage accounts from 1420, in which damages from 1412 and 1418 are recorded.

name: Wiesdorf
Toll_Description: The Duke of Berg levied a land toll in 1411. Tariffs and revenues are not known. Wiesdorf was a secondary toll of Mülheim, at the end of the 15th century also temporarily of Büchel.

name: Wijhe
Settlement_Description: Earliest mention in 960, in a sixteenth century copy.

name: Wildeshausen
Settlement_Description: A monastery of secular canons was founded in the 9th century, an "oppidum" is mentioned at the same time. A castle was built around 1150. In 1270, the archbishop of Bremen acquired the power in the town and administrative region of Wildeshausen. The monastery had minting rights in the 13th and 14th centuries.
Town_Description: In 1270, the archbishop of Bremen granted Bremen town privileges to Wildeshausen.
Fair_Description: The most important fair in Wildeshausen was on St Ulrich, which is first mentioned in 1298 and is the only fair which can be attested through the centuries. For Ulrich's fair and for that on St Simon and Jude, invitations were sent to Osnabrück in the 14th century. In 1507, three three-day fairs were installed, because the old ones were not visited any more. Next to the renewed fair on St Ulrich, these took place on St George and on the day of the Eleven Thousand Virgins. The latter two must have disappeared soon after, because in 1529, only two fairs are still mentioned, on St Ulrich and St Dionysius.
Toll_Primary_Owner: Graf von Oldenburg / Hoya / Erzbischof von Bremen
Toll_Description: Originally owned by the counts of Oldenburg. In 1271, citizens of Bremen were freed from toll in Wildeshausen by the bishop. A part of the toll was owned by the counts of Hoya in the 14th century, who sold it to the town of Wildeshausen in 1441. The toll was often leased, from 1541 onwards by Münster, which had acquired the toll. In the 17th century, an additional toll on oxen was levied on Easter.

name: Willershagen
Settlement_Description: The village is first mentioned in 1293.

name: Vilnius
Staple_Description: In negotiations between Gdanks and Krakow in 1493 it is noted for the first time that Russians and Lithuanians wishing to trade in the west were obliged to travel via Vilnius.

name: Wilp
Settlement_Description: Earliest mention in 840-849, in a copy dating from circa 1000. Next mention in 840-864, in a fifteenth century copy. A map from 1551 shows two inns near the church.

name: Leubsdorf
Toll_Description: Secondary station of safe conduct ('Beigeleit') of Triptis in the district ('Amt') Arnshaugk. Revenues are known from 1532 onwards.

name: Bad Wilsnack
Settlement_Description: Mentioned as a church village in 1300, destroyed during a feud in 1383. The parson found three intact hosts in the burned church; the miracle led to the establishment of the settlement as one of the major pilgrimage sites in northern Europe. Mentioned as borough ('oppidum') in 1398, a council and merchant house are mentioned in 1424.
Town_Description: The Wittstock town law and market rights were granted in 1513 by the bishop of Havelberg.

name: Ventspils
Settlement_Description: The area fell to the Teutonic Order in 1253, after which a castle was built in the 13th century. The castle was first mentioned in 1290. In 1244 a fortified borough ('Hakelwerk') was built.
Town_Description: Town right were granted in 1378. In 1440 the town joined the Hanseatic League.

name: Windesheim
Settlement_Description: Earliest mention in 1028, in a copy dating from 1530.

name: Westendorf
Settlement_Description: The settlement was first mentioned in 1383.

name: Winnenthal
Toll_Description: The Duke of Cleves levied a land toll around 1450. Records about tariffs or revenues have not survived.

name: Winsen (Aller)
Settlement_Description: First mentioned in 1107-1128. The castle is first mentioned in 1312.
Toll_Description: The toll of the Duke of Brunswick-Lüneburg is first mentioned in 1409. In a 1507 agreement between Hannover and Celle, it is stipulated that citizens of Hannover have to pay tolls for shipping on the Aller river in Celle, like the toll levied on the land route in Winsen. A toll tariff is known from the 16th century (StAB).

name: Winsen (Luhe)
Settlement_Description: Winsen was mentioned for the first time in 1158. A church was mentioned in 1233. The settlement was referred to as borough ('oppidum') in 1293. In 1299, a moated castle is first mentioned.
Town_Description: In 1322, Winsen received Lüneburg town privileges. The town was often pawned to Lüneburg in the following centuries.
Toll_Description: A charter from 1333 attests a herring toll of the dukes of Brunswick for citizens from Hannover: for each last herring 25 pennies. The toll is still mentioned in 1388.

name: Winterswijk
Settlement_Description: Earliest mention in the eleventh century, in a copy dating from 1493.
Fair_Description: Even though Winterswijk did not have town privileges, it was being granted a one-day fair in 1531 by Charles, duke of Guelders. The day of this fair is unknown.

name: Winzenburg
Settlement_Description: The settlement was originally called Hasekenhusen; a chapel is mentioned in 1140. After the nearby castle Winzenburg was destroyed in 1522, the administrative centre was moved to the folwark Hasekenhusen and the village restructured. It thereupon became known after the former castle.

name: Winschoten
Settlement_Description: First mentioned in the thirteenth century. Winschoten was granted town rights at 7 May 1819 by William I of the Netherlands.

name: Wismar
Settlement_Description: The settlement Alt ('old') Wismar, located east of the current town, was a small Slavic fishing village. German farmers and merchants settled around 1200 in the northern part of the old town around the church of St Nicholas. The settlement was first mentioned with a harbour in 1211.
Town_Description: First mentioned as town in 1229, it was most likely founded in 1226 but the charter has not survived. Lübeck town privileges were confirmed in 1266.
Fair_Description: A fair is first mentioned in 1397. According to regulations from 1604, it lasted from Sunday Exaudi until the Friday before Pentecost. A 'Kauffschlagsmontag' on the first Monday of Lent appears in 1547, is characterised as free fair in 1608 and developed into a three-day fair in the second half of the 17th century.
Toll_Description: Toll of the lords of Mecklenburg, that was acquired by the town of Wismar in 1308-1311 and again in 1375. Toll tariffs exist from 1328 and 1628, when it was converted into a toll on the causeways and bridges of the town; it still existed in 1828.
Staple_Description: Staple for stockfish from Bergen; in 1446 members of the Hanse were only allowed to export flour, malt, and other victuals to Bergen if they brought fish from Bergen back with them to Lübeck, Wismar, Rostock or Stralsund. Regulations from 1435 and 1480 refer to a staple for grain.

name: Wispenstein
Settlement_Description: The family of Steinberg constructed a moated castle here between 1445 and 1451, probably next to an older water mill of the monastery Lamspringe.

name: Wittenberge
Settlement_Description: Originally a Slavic settlement with a castle mound, a German castle of the Lords Gans von Putlitz was likely built after 1136. The village and its ferry were first mentioned in 1226, but this is likely a falsification. First certain mention in 1239.
Town_Description: The town was founded after 1200 by the Gans family, first mentioned as town ('civitas') in 1264. The old privileges were confirmed between 1300 and 1365.
Toll_Description: A toll on river transport on the Stepenitz was installed by margrave Ludwig in 1337, in return for his support of the improvement of the river for shipping. Perleberg citizens were exempted from the toll in 1348. A toll on shipping on the Elbe river is first mentioned in negotiations about the reduction of tolls on the Elbe in 1476. It was pawned to the family Gans of Putlitz, who claimed to have received the right of levying a toll from the emperor in 1208, a statement that is impossible to verify. The toll fee on the Elbe was 7 Gulden, 1 loaf of bread and 1 bun for every ship in 1492. The toll on the Elbe is also attested in four travel accounts of Pirna skipper Gottfried Kleeditz from 1671-1674.

name: Wittingen
Settlement_Description: The place 'Wittingen' is mentioned for the first time in 1014. However, a referral to 'Wittingau' dates back to the 8th century.
Town_Description: Characterised as "civitas" in 1267 and "oppidum" in 1293. In 1369 at the latest, Wittingen had a council, judges and burghers as well as a town seal. However, the settlement was also regularly characterised as borough ('weichbild').
Toll_Description: Wasmod von dem Knesebeck sold a part of the toll in Wittingen to the duke of Brunswick-Lüneburg in 1410. Johann von dem Knesebeck was pawned with a sixth part of the toll in 1444; later a sixth part of the toll was owned by the von dem Knesebeck family as well.

name: Wittmar
Settlement_Description: The charter with the first mention of 965 appears to be a falsification from the 12th century.

name: Wittstock
Settlement_Description: A Slavic fortification is first mentioned in 948. A castle of the bishops of Havelberg since the mid-12th century.
Town_Description: Bishop Henry I of Havelberg raised the settlement into a town around 1245. Stendal town law granted in 1248; they were endorsed in 1275 and later.

name: Witzenhausen
Town_Description: Witzenhausen acquired market and town privileges in 1225. It was characterised as "oppidum" in 1232 and "civitas" in 1247.

name: Wizna
Toll_Description: A Masovian border toll station is attested since 1382.

name: Volodymyr-Volynskyi
Toll_Description: Mentioned as toll station in c. 1349.

name: Wittlage
Settlement_Description: A moated castle was built here between 1309 and 1313 by Osnabrück bishop Engelbert von Weihe.

name: Karjamaa
Settlement_Description: The village is first mentioned in 1796.

name: Wohldenberg
Settlement_Description: Castle of the counts of Wöltingerode, who started naming themselves after the new castle in 1172 or 1153/78.

name: Ēvele
Settlement_Description: The parish and manor were first mentioned in 1562. In 1660, 'Neu-Wohlfahrt' ('Vecjērcēni') was separated.

name: Vuikovychi
Toll_Description: The castellan of Przemyśl received permission to levy a toll of 4 denars for each ox in Vuikovychi in 1525.

name: Wolbeck
Settlement_Description: First mentioned in 1185. The settlement became a borough ('wigbold') before 1310.

name: Woffleben
Settlement_Description: First mention in 927 in a donation charter by Henry I.

name: Dobiegniew
Settlement_Description: A Slavic settlement and manor, which was donated to the convent Ovinsk near Poznań in 1250.
Town_Description: The town Woldenberg was probably founded by the Ascanians around 1298 with Brandenburg town law. First mentioned as town ('civitas') in 1313.

name: Lützen
Settlement_Description: Originally a Slavic settlement, which developed into a market borough ('Marktflecken') on the road between Frankfurt and Leipzig with a German castle in the 13th century. It is first mentioned in 1269.
Town_Description: It is unclear when the village gained town rights. In 1281 a market is first mentioned, in the 14th century the town was walled. In 1330 it is characterised as 'oppidum'.
Toll_Description: Regulations of safe conduct remain from the begining of the 16th century.

name: Wolfenbüttel
Settlement_Description: The castle Wolfenbüttel is first mentioned in 1118. First indications about a settlement near the castle date from the early 14th century. From 1432, the castle was the main residence of the dukes of Brunswick and was reconstructed as a fortress.
Town_Description: Wolfenbüttel acquired market privileges in 1570 and acquired its final form as a renaissance fortress between 1570 and 1626, which consisted of the Heinrichstadt around the castle, the civic settlement Neustadt, and the suburb Gotteslager east of it. Duke Julius attempted to develop the town into the major trading hub Gotteslager from 1582, but the project failed.
Fair_Description: Wolfenbüttel acquired market privileges in 1570 with two fairs, on 9 May and 4 November. When duke Julius tried to raise the town to the major trade hub Gotteslager, he granted four fairs of twelve days, on 14 January, 14 April, 14 July and 14 November. After the failure of the project, the fairs were reduced to two eight-day fairs in spring and autumn again, taking place on 5 May and 5 November.

name: Wolfshagen
Settlement_Description: Mention of the castle in Wolfshagen in 1375.

name: Wolgast
Settlement_Description: Duke Wartislaw I of Pomerania conquered the Slavic castle and market settlement in 1123. A church was built before 1128.
Town_Description: Town privileges were probably granted between 1250 and 1259. Confirmation of the Lübeck town law in 1282. Between 1295 and 1637 residency of the dukes of Pomerania-Wolgast.

name: Valgunde
Settlement_Description: The manor was first mentioned in 1413.

name: Wolken
Settlement_Description: The village is first mentioned in 1178.

name: Wolkenstein
Settlement_Description: In 1323 the place was already called 'oppidum' and probably arose from a 'suburbium', which was situated next to the castle.
Town_Description: In 1434 the place was referred to as 'town'.
Toll_Description: A table of fees ('Geleitstafel') remains from 1591 (SHStA Dresden, Loc. 40099, Wolkenstein Nr. 40b, Erbbuch des Amtes Wolkenstein 1591, p. 477–481).

name: Wolin
Settlement_Description: Extensive prehistorical findings of a pre-german settlement, Slavic and Viking merchant town since the 10th century until the founding of a German town in the 13th century.
Town_Description: Duke Barnim I of Pomerania granted Lübeck town law to the market settlement in the 13th century. First mentioned as a town in 1279, when the privileges were renewed.

name: Valmiera
Settlement_Description: In 1224, the area came to a knightly order who built a fortress out of wood. In 1283/87 there was a castle and a church, around which a settlement developed.
Town_Description: Wolmar was already referred to as a town before 1323. In 1328, the town received town rights of Riga and in 1365 became a member of the Hanseatic League. In 1684, town privileges were revoked.

name: Kõo
Settlement_Description: The village was first mentioned in 1583. A hamlet ('Hof') was built in the 17th century.

name: Zedtlitz
Settlement_Description: First mention as manor in 1190, in 1303 referred to as castrum, since 1548 knightly manor.

name: Wolfen
Settlement_Description: First mentioned in 1304. Until the 19th century a farmer and linen-weaver village with a manor, whose owners often changed. Merged with Bitterfeld in 2007.

name: Juutila
Settlement_Description:
<b>Inn:</b> Jaakko Teitti's list of roads (1556) mentions Marttila's parish constable in Juttila. Parish constables (fi: nimismies, sw: länsman) were obliged to keep a tavern in late 16th c, and during the Russian war in 1570-1595, hundreds of soldiers travelled to and from Häme by the Oxen road. They were accommodated in Marttila parish constable's in Juutila. In the 17th century, the constable office moved to Krouvi.

Juttila is also a probable place for king's estate (fi: kuninkaankartano, sw: kungsgård) before it was moved to Engesholm in 1559. Another possible place in Juva, Marttila. King's estates were used as inns for officials.

name: Wolmirstedt
Settlement_Description: In 1009 a German castle is mentioned in the chronicle of Thietmar of Merseburg from 1012-1018. A village developed next to it. The settlement was until the mid-13th century located on the confluence of the Elbe and Ohre rivers, and was therefore important as a crossing of the Ohre between Magdeburg and Stendal. Residence of the archbishops of Magdeburg since 1342.
Town_Description: First mentioned as town in 1363, later also as small town or borough. A burgomaster and town council are only first attested in 1564.
Fair_Description: A fair on the Nativity of Mary is mentioned in 1558.
Toll_Description: A toll and safe conduct in Wolmirstedt is attested since 1368. In 1405 king Wenzel granted the archbishop of Magdeburg permission to collect toll on any ware that is carried to the market in his towns. In a letter of conflict between the council of Magdeburg and the archbishop from 1432, the settlements Wolmirstedt, Rogätz and Jerichow are mentioned as toll stations, the toll in Wolmirstedt is mentioned as being collected on an (old) Elbe crossing. The toll in Wolmirstedt is further mentioned in the 16th century, when a complaint is filed that the toll stations of Oebisfelde, Neuhaldensleben, Wolmirstedt, Dreileben, Wanzleben and Calbe collect less toll because of Magdeburg's toll exemption.

name: Wöltingerode
Settlement_Description: A monastery was founded in 1174. According to a document from 1188, it was a Cistercian nun monastery, which was converted into an Evangelical women's convent after the Reformation. It was closed in 1809.

name: Vooreküla
Settlement_Description: The village was first mentioned in 1627.

name: Warkum
Town_Description: According to Cox, Workum became a town before 1385. Van Berkel & Samplonius mention 1350.
Harbour_Description: Regular barge ('trekschuit') services were offered on the route Workum-Bolsward-Leeuwarden from 1648 onwards.

name: Orneta
Settlement_Description: First mentioned as a German settlement in 1308, as a parish in 1312.
Town_Description: Bishop Eberhard von Neitze granted Kulm town rights in 1312. First mentioned as a town in 1313. The town charter ('Handfeste') was renewed in 1359.

name: Worringen
Toll_Description: 1) The archbishop levied a fee for safe conduct on water before 1279. Presumably this toll was abolished in the same year in the course of the landfrieden. Revenues and tariffs are not known.<br/>2) In 1287/88, a land toll of the Archbishop of Cologne was also mentioned.

name: Voose
Settlement_Description: The village of the Manor 'Pallfer' was mentioned in 1241.

name: Wöstendöllen
Settlement_Description: The settlement 'Duliun' is first mentioned around 1000. Since the 11th century, it was divided into Ostdöllen ('Astulini') and Norddöllen ('Nordulini'). In 1383 'Wostendolne' is first mentioned.

name: Wriezen
Settlement_Description: Probably originally a Slavic trading place; a German market borough ('oppidum') is mentioned in 1247.
Town_Description: An official town founding is unknown. Mentioned as civitas in 1303, but as oppidum in 1320. Margrave Ludwig granted the Magdeburg town law in 1337.
Toll_Description: Elector Joachim II granted Wriezen the right to levy a road toll ('deichselpfennig') for the maintenance of the dams and roads of the town in 1546.

name: Wrisbergholzen
Settlement_Description: The place was first mentioned in 1125.

name: Wronki
Toll_Description: King Władysław set the toll tariffs in Wronki in 1390.

name: Wunstorf
Settlement_Description: First mentioned in 871. Bishop Dietrich I of Minden founded a nunnery here.
Town_Description: Town privileges granted in 1261 by bishop Cuno of Minden.

name: Suchań
Settlement_Description: First mentioned in 1269 as village in possession of the Knights Hospitaller. A castle was built in 1312. The settlement was mentioned as small town ('Städtichen') in 1487, but town privileges are not known.

name: Würzburg
Settlement_Description: Duchy in the 7th century. Saint Kilian suffered his martyrium in Würzburg in 689. In 742 the bishopric was founded. The place was first mentioned around 700 in a copy of a document. Around the same time, the settlement centre was moved to the right side of the river Main.

name: Wurzen
Settlement_Description: The place emerges from a Slavic settlement with castle. In the middle of the 10th century a German castle was built.
Town_Description: Around 1300 the market settlement was fortified.
Fair_Description: In 1670, Wurzen requested two fairs, which seem to have been granted despite protests from Leipzig.
Toll_Description: Extensive regulations of safe conduct remain from the 16th century (SStA Leipzig, Stadt Wurzen Nr. 932).

name: Wülfingerode
Toll_Description: Wülfingerode is mentioned in a registry of safe conduct from 1610.

name: Wustrow
Settlement_Description: First mentioned in 1217. In the 13th century, the lords of Wustrow built a castle, next to which the settlement developed. It was characterised as borough ('weichbild') in 1352 and 1369.
Town_Description: The settlement was first mentioned as town in 1377, although the town privileges were only confirmed in 1654.

name: Wylatowo
Toll_Description: The toll in Wylatowo that was raised for the monastery Trzemeszno was moved to Trzemeszno itself at the end of the 14th century.

name: Wymeer
Settlement_Description: The settlement was first mentioned in 1319 together with the monastery Dünebroek west of it.

name: Nobiskrug
Settlement_Description: The Inn was first mentioned in 1582.

name: Wyszogród
Toll_Description: Mentioned as toll station in c. 1349, where 3 gr. and 4 den. had to be paid for each horse.

name: Xanten
Fair_Description: Before 1237 two fairs are known: 1) Oct. 10 and 2) Dec. 21 and a weekly market on Saturday.
Toll_Description: In 1142, there is evidence of a ship or river toll in Xanten, which was market-related. In 1314, this was merged into a river toll on the Rhine in Rheinberg. In 1336, a toll privilege was issued to the town of Xanten, granting a land toll that had been levied "since time immemorial". The revenue was to be used for road construction. In 1353 and 1372 the toll rights were confirmed. In 1392, the toll presumably fell to the Count of Cleves.

name: Sabile
Settlement_Description: An old castle already existed in the 9th to the 13th century. In 1253 the land fell to the Teutonic Order that built a new castle around 1282. In 1462/64 there is evidence of a fortified borough ('Hakelwerk') which was referred to as a 'town'. When this fell into disrepair in 1563, the borough ('Flecken') was rebuilt in the 17th century.

name: Zahna
Settlement_Description: First mentioned in 965. Originally a Slavic settlement; in 1198 main settlement of a castle district ('Burgwardhauptort').
Town_Description: Erhard and Heinrich of Wederden granted town privileges in 1326, including toll rights. These were confirmed in 1361 and 1484.

name: Zahrensen
Settlement_Description: The village probably goes back to the Zahrenhusen family; a Lippold of Zahrenhusen is first mentioned in 1231.

name: Zakroczym
Toll_Description: Mentioned as toll station in c. 1349, where 3 gr. and 4 den. had to be paid for each horse.

name: Zaltbommel
Settlement_Description: Earliest mention dates from 850 (in a copy dating from the end of the eleventh century).
Town_Description: In 999, Zaltbommel received toll, mintage and ‘gruit’ privileges, which indicates the existence of a market. In 1195 it is first mentioned as a town. Possibly Otto II, count of Guelders, granted Zaltbommel town privileges in 1231. Reginald II, count of Guelders, granted Zaltbommel town privileges on 13 December 1315 and more extensive town privileges on 19 October 1316.
Fair_Description: In Zaltbommel, two fairs came into existence before 1494/95. In 1492, two additional horse and cattle fairs were granted. In 1538 (Febr. 23) the horsemarket with Lent was replaced, as it coincided with the one in Gorinchem and thus was hampered.
Staple_Description: The duke of Gelre ordained in 1513 that all grain grown in the Tieler- and Bommelerwaard had to be marketed in Zaltbommel.

name: Sianów
Settlement_Description: A castle belonged to the descendants of the Pomeranian nobleman Swenzo in 1311.
Town_Description: Peter von Pollnow founded the town in 1343 with Lübeck town law. It was confirmed in 1348 by the bishop of Kammin and frequently afterwards.

name: Zarnewenz
Settlement_Description: First mentioned in 1292. At that time, as well as in a tax register from 1525, eight farms are registered in the village.

name: Carnikava
Settlement_Description: The manor was first mentioned in 1463.

name: Zboyscha
Toll_Description: A dam toll was granted by the king in 1506, for the maintenance of the road.

name: Zeddam
Settlement_Description: Earliest mention in 1139-1148, in a copy dating from 1211 which might be a falsification. The next mention in 1200.

name: Zehdenick
Settlement_Description: First a Slavic, around 1200 a German castle. First mentioned in 1216, a Cistercian nun monastery is founded around 1250.
Town_Description: Town foundation of the Margraves of Brandenburg. First mentioned as civitas in 1281.
Toll_Description: Mentioned as toll and safe conduct station in 1498.

name: Zeist
Settlement_Description: Earliest mention in 838, in a eleventh century copy. Next mention in 1028, in a copy dating from circa 1530.

name: Zele
Settlement_Description: Earliest mention in 1149, in a copy from the second quarter of the thirteenth century.

name: Zellik
Settlement_Description: Earliest mention in 974. Next mention in 1003.

name: Zerbst
Settlement_Description: Originally a Slavic settlement, which fell into the missionary area of margrave Gero, first mentioned in 948. Castle district ('Burgward') since 1196.
Town_Description: Around 1200 during the German east migration the town was fortified and granted Magdeburg town rights.
Fair_Description: Zerbst presumably had two fairs of some renown in the 14th and 15th century. Their exact length cannot be determined for their early stages. In 1502, 1503, 1545, 1546 and 1595 the fairs were confrimed. In 1514 Zerbst tries for a third fair, which is prevented by Leipzig. Both fairs are held together with cattle markets.

name: Zernien
Settlement_Description: First mentioned in 1360. In 1450, the setttlement consisted of 2 farms.

name: Zeven
Settlement_Description: The settlement was first mentioned in 986. In 1141 the Benedictine monastery of Heeslingen was moved to Zeven. In 1158, the monastery was granted market, mint and toll privileges by Emperor Frederick I. It was abolished in 1647.
Fair_Description: Zeven acquired market privileges in 1158, but a fair 14 days after Pentecost ist first mentioned only in 1740. Older dates are unknown.

name: Zibühl
Settlement_Description: The village is first mentioned in 1322.

name: Zittau
Settlement_Description: Originally a Slavic settlement, which was located on the long-distance route between the Baltic Sea and Bohemia. Later, a German castle with the associated borough close to the castle ('Burgflecken').
Town_Description: The city was founded before 1230. In 1255 the town wall was built. In 1275 the term 'civitas' was used.
Toll_Description: A toll in Zittau originally belonged to the king, but was given as a fief to Heinrich von Liepa in 1310. Parts of the toll were pawned or enfeoffed multiple times, and ultimately acquired by the town, who returned them to emperor Charles in 1357. In 1348 an additional toll of one heller for each horse for the maintenance of roads and bridges was given to the town. The town council rented this toll and the safe conduct of Karlsfried castle in 1364 and in later years from the emperor.
Staple_Description: In 1351 the city secured a ban on the use of an ancillary road bypassing the city via Friedland; revoked in 1383. In 1425 staple for lead from Frauenburg; in 1469 staple for fish.

name: Ziegenhagen
Settlement_Description: The village is first mentioned in 1200.

name: Code
Settlement_Description: The manor was first mentioned in 1543.

name: Sulęcin
Settlement_Description: A Polish castle and settlement, whose owner, Duke Mrochko or Mrotsek, attracted German settlers in 1241. The Slavic was incorporated by the German settlement.
Town_Description: Founded by the Knights Templar. Mentioned as civitas in 1244, but opidum in 1286 and 1351 and villa in 1289, throughout the 14th century usually mentioned as civitas or town.

name: Ziepel
Settlement_Description: Mentioned in 992 as property given to Memleben monastery.

name: Ziesar
Settlement_Description: Castle district centre ('Burgwardmittelpunkt') in Slavic times, mentioned in 949 as property for the newly founded bishopric of Brandenburg. Since 1214 mentioned as residence of the bishop.
Town_Description: In 1337 bishop Dietrich grants Magdeburg town rights.
Fair_Description: Since the 17th century, four fairs are known. In 1697 two cattle fairs are granted.

name: Ziethen (Anklam)
Settlement_Description: The place was first mentioned in a document from 1311.

name: Zilly
Settlement_Description: First mentions of the place since 1172 as property of Ilsenburg monastery. First mention of the noble family of Zilly in 1211. First mention of the castle in 1334.

name: Zinnowitz
Settlement_Description: First mentioned in 1309 in a property record of Krummin Monastery.

name: Nowy Żmigród
Toll_Description: First mentioned as toll station in 1359.

name: Zöblitz
Settlement_Description: Probably a farming settlement that developed into a market place by 1323.

name: Zierke
Settlement_Description: First mentioned in 1408. The nearby lake Zierker See is mentioned in 1346.

name: Zollgrün
Settlement_Description: First mention in 1342. An inn in Zollgrün is attested since 1501.

name: Issersheilingen
Settlement_Description: The settlement Heilingen is first mentioned in 775-786; the part Issersheilingen as distinct settlement in 1279.
Toll_Description: Station of secondary safe conduct ('Beigeleitsstelle') of (Großen)Gottern, as mentioned in the regulations of toll and safe conduct for the Amt Langensalza and Thamsbrück from 1516.

name: Zons
Toll_Description: 1) In 1372 a river toll on the Rhine was mentioned in Zons, which was levied by the Archbishop of Cologne. In the 15th century, 1½ 'oberländische Gulden' and 2 alb. per foder of wine are established as the fee. From 1475 to 1495, an additional 1 turnosgroschen per foder of wine had to be paid. In 1419 to 1420 the annual yield amounted to 7520 guilders, in 1421 to 1422 to 7987 guilders.<br/>2) Around 1425, the Archbishop of Cologne also levied a fee for safe conduct on water, which was collected together with the river toll. <br/>3) Around the same time, the Archbishop of Cologne levied a road toll.

name: Sopot
Settlement_Description: A castle dates back to around 1000. The surrounding villages were given to the monastery of Oliva in 1283 by Duke Mestwin II. of Pommerelia.

name: Zörbig
Settlement_Description: Founded in the 10th century as a German castle as the centre of a castle district ('Burgward'). A rural settlement developed in the surroundings.
Town_Description: Prince electorate Ernst and count Albrecht of Saxony granted town rights in 1470.

name: Zorge
Settlement_Description: The foundation of the settlement goes back into the 13th century. In the 16th century, ironworks were constructed.

name: Zöschen
Settlement_Description: In the 13th century, a ministerial family of Zössen in mentioned. The former Aldindorph is today part of Zöschen and encompassed the church, the upper village and the corresponding buildings.

name: Zuidhorn
Settlement_Description: Earliest mention of 'Hurum' in 1338. Earliest mention of 'Zuuthorm' in 1466.

name: Züllsdorf
Settlement_Description: The village is first mentioned in 1284.

name: Zundert
Settlement_Description: Earliest mention in first-fourth century. Next mention in a falsification from 1157.

name: Schagen
Settlement_Description: Schagen is first mentioned in a ca. 1420 copy of a document dated at the end of the eleventh century. Schagen was granted town rights on 12 May 1415 by William VI, count of Holland. The granting of town rights was part of an administrative reorganization in which a number of smaller settlements were granted town rights in order to provide them with a certain degree of self-government which replaced the need for the count of Holland's bailiffs ('baljuws').
Fair_Description: In 1463/'4 (Febr. 10) the lord of Schagen granted a free weekly market on Thursday and two free fairs: 1) 8 days before and after St. Peter & Paul (29 juni) 2) 8 dagen before and after St. Mary Magdalenaday (22 juli). A weigh-house will only be erected with his consent and only in Schagen in the 'Kerkbuurt'. In 1603 the town obtained from the Staten of Holland a horsefair on 17 juni, 8 days before St. Jan Baptist (Juni 24) with rights as in Voorschoten and Valkenburg. Schagen was situated three miles from Alkmaar, Hoorn and Medemblik and so did not hamper these towns.

name: Pfersdorf
Toll_Description: Toll station of the district Heldburg, from which the oldest account dates from 1546.

name: Zutphen
Settlement_Description: Earliest mention dates from 1101, but archeological research shows that the place where Zutphen is located has at least been permanently inhabited from the sixth or seventh century onwards. From circa 900 onwards, Zutphen was walled and functioned as a central place for a duke or lord. Oldest mention as 'oppidum' Zutphen dates from 1059. Between 1120 and 1138, the county of Zutphen was inherited by the count of Guelders.
Town_Description: Town privileges granted between 15 April 1191 and 30 March 1196, by Otto I, count of Guelders and Zutphen. Zutphen was the first settlement in the county of Guelders to receive town privileges and was the example for many other towns in Guelders. The town was enlarged with the new town ('Nieuwstad') around 1230. In 1243 the town had a stone wall. A town council is first mentioned in 1312. Four administrative units (quarters) were distinguished in Guelders from the 14th century; Zutphen functioned as the capital in the Quarter of Zutphen ('Kwartier van Zutphen'). Het Stuvennest or Stuvenest, in the Melatensteeg, was one of the inns in town. It is being named between 1468 and 1531. Already before 1268, a hospital was located just outside the Spitaalpoort along the road towards Emmerich. The course of the river IJssel near Zutphen was influenced by human activity several times. In 1357, the river was changed by cutting the southern meander. Unintentionally, this activated the old IJssel at Empe again. As a result, the town risked to lose its location close to the main stem. In 1406/1407, the meander directly west of the town was being canalized until the Polbeek estuary. As a result, the branch at Empe and the northern meander across the Mars were cut off. The canalized river was located between short banks.
Fair_Description: A weekly market on Thursday is mentioned in the town privileges from 1194/1195. Zutphen had one fair at least from 1294/1295 onwards. Fair trading in Zutphen decreased from the beginning of the fifteenth century onwards, despite an ongoing increase in the number of fairs. This was among others due to constant competition with the fairs in the town of Deventer. Duke Reginald IV of Guelders granted two new fairs in Zutphen in 1420, to enforce the economic strength of the town, and duke Arnold granted four new fairs on the same dates as the Deventer fairs during a trade boycot of Deventer in 1463-1465, but without lasting success. The Saint Walpurgis fair (1st of May) was the only fair in Guelders with a limited supraregional function. An eighth (cattle) fair on St Gregory was founded in 1522 by Duke Charles of Guelders.
Toll_Description: A land road toll ('weggeld') was levied at three town gates. At the Laarpoort (road towards the east: towards Lochem, Twente and Westphalia), the Spittaalpoort or Hospitaalpoort (road towards the south: towards Doetinchem, Emmerich and Cleves), and the Nieuwstadspoort (road towards Deventer). The gates Olypoort and Veerpoort had become redundant after the course of the river IJssel had been altered in the fourteenth century. Sources from the fourteenth century show that the Laarpoort brought in more than the other gates combined.

name: Zwartsluis
Settlement_Description: Earliest mention in 1398. The settlement developed around a lock ('sluis') that was built in the dammed Meppelerdiep shortly before 1398.

name: Zwenkau
Settlement_Description: Originally a Slavic settlement. In the 10th century a German castle was built, which was surrounded by a settlement, first mentioned in 974.
Town_Description: Already at its first mention in 974, the settlement was referred to as 'civitas'. In 1195 a market is attested. Town rights are only known from 1475, when Bishop Thilo of Merseburg confirmed or renewed them.
Toll_Description: Secondary station of safe conduct ('Beigeleitsstelle') of Pegau, mentioned in 1619.

name: Zwethau
Settlement_Description: First mentioned in a forged charter from 966. First certain mention in 981. At that time, there existed a castle here. Later it is mentioned as village and manor.

name: Sleen
Settlement_Description: Earliest mention of 'Slene' probably in the 12th century. Earliest mention of 'Zuetsleen' (South Sleen) in 1381-1383.

name: Darłowo
Settlement_Description: Archaeological finds prove habitation from the 8th to 12th century. The castle district Dirlova is first mentioned in 1205.
Town_Description: The town Rügenwalde was likely founded by Witzlaw II of Rügen in 1270. In 1271 it is first mentioned as town ('civitas'). The town was destroyed in the late 13th century and subsequently rebuilt. The new town privileges of 1312 include Lübeck town law.
Staple_Description: The privileges of 1312 included a forced stay of 2 days for skippers.

name: Ummerstadt
Settlement_Description: In 837 Fulda monastery was given property in Untrangeuui, which could be interpreted as Ummerstadt. First certain mention as Umerstat in 1223.
Town_Description: In 1290 a citizen ('civis') is mentioned and the settlement is referred to as town since 1317, which leads to the assumption that it was constructed as planned town at the end of the 13th century. Town privileges were confirmed in 1394.
Fair_Description: Two fairs are known since 1394, on St Bartholomew and St Andrew. A weekly market on Thursday already took place before that year.

name: Zwickau
Settlement_Description: A castle and a market probably existed since the 11th century. The area was previously inhabited by Slavs. The place settled near an old river crossing.
Town_Description: Market and city rights were probably given between 1198 and 1221.
Toll_Description: A Bohemian toll in Zwickau is mentioned in 1118. The Ernestinian safe conduct in Zwickau was predominantly based on the transport of mining products.

name: Middelburg (Walcheren)
Settlement_Description: Middelburg originated as a Caroligian castle, built as a defence against attacks from Norsemen. In the late tenth century, it is already said to have been a port. A hospital is first mentioned in 1289.
Town_Description: In May 1217, town privileges of Middelburg are confirmed by Joan, countess of Flanders, and William I, count of Holland. Possibly, earlier town rights were granted by Floris III, count of Holland. The 'Kamer' (department) of Zeeland, the second largest of the six 'Kamers' of the VOC (Verenigde Oost-Indische Compagnie, Dutch East India Company, founded in 1602), was located in Middelburg.
Fair_Description: In 1323 (May 1) count Willem III granted two fairs: 1) St. Mary Magdalena-eve (July 21) duration: 5 days, with an extensive tariff, 2) Sunday after Midlent also for 5 days. An extensive excise ordinance is edited and dated 1325 (Febr. 24). In it a fair and marketfield are found. The oldest town-account dated 1365/'6 mentions the fair with St. Jacobsday (July 25) and an excise levied from the marketfield in 1361. A crane, a meathouse and a cloth-hall are found in 1366/'7, a weigh-house ('balans') in 1376. In the account of the comital steward of Bewestenschelde dated 1429/'30 the tolls on the fair with St. Jacobsday are found. This toll appears to be comital. The town-account dated 1443 mentions the erection of the market-cross on St. Mary-Magdalena-eve at all town-gates. In 1439 it was discussed to enlengthen this fair which was done in 1443 with 4 days. In 1522 (Dec.) emperor Charles V granted a free fair on Febr. 3, with 15 'toon'(display)days, and freedom for 15 days before and after the fair. This in stead of the fair which started the week before Palm-Sunday. With equal rights as on the fair with St. Jacobsday. The town of Bruges opposed against this. In 1523 the fair in the week before 'Palmen' was relocated by Charles V to  Febr. 3.
Toll_Description: In 1304 Middelburg was freed from the staple in Dordrecht. In 1340 Middelburg obtained toll-exemption in Holland. See staple below. In 1473 Charles the Bold stated a decree on the alum-market in Middelburg, St. Anna ter Muiden, Sluis and Antwerp.
Staple_Description: 1347-48 saw the establishment of English and Scottish merchants, with privileges for English merchants following in 1383-88 (yields and amounts of wool are edited). Privileges for merchants from Portugal in 1390. From 1405 efforts made to secure a staple for the entire island of Walcheren that seems to have been merely an obligation to travel through Middelburg for the payment of the pound toll due there. The staple was given up in 1445. In the 16th century new attempts to erect a staple; in 1521 imperial staple privileges for wine, oil, fruit and iron coming from the west over see; in 1522 staple treaty with Scotland for 14 years, after which there were attempts to extend the staple. 1558 saw the establishment of English merchants.

name: Buren
Settlement_Description: Earliest mention dates from 772 (mentioned in a copy from around 1183-1195).
Town_Description: Town privileges granted on 27 June 1395 by Alart, lord of Buren and Beusichem. Buren was located near the castle Buren. The oldest known privileges of Buren concern family rights dating from 1368 and heritage rights dating from 1383.

name: Beusichem
Fair_Description: The (market-)toll in the account of the steward of the Land van Buren and Beusichem on St. Peters and Pauls-eve (July 28) in 1435/'6 was 33 guilders.

name: Adavere
Settlement_Description: The manor was first mentioned in a document by Wolter von Plettenberg in 1510.

name: Rinteln
Settlement_Description: The village Rentene (old Rinteln) is attested at the northern shore of the Weser from the late 11th century. Around 1230, count Adolf IV of Holstein and Schaumburg founded the planned town new Rinteln at the southern shore. The church is first mentioned in 1235.
Town_Description: Rinteln is characterised as civitas in 1238, and acquired Lippstadt town privileges the following year.
Fair_Description: Rinteln acquired market privileges in 1392 and was allowed to hold two seven-day fairs, before and after the second Sunday after Easter and before and after St James's Day.
Toll_Description: Rinteln acquired the right to levy a road toll in 1391: of each wagon 4, of each cart 2, of each horse and cow 1 penny, and of each pig, sheep or goat 1 Heller. The toll collector for the water toll on the Weser river was also responsible for collecting the road toll. Revenues are included in the Rinteln toll registers from 1571 (NLA Bückeburg, see Rothe).

name: Großenwieden
Settlement_Description: First mentioned around 825. A market is attested in the 13th century.
Toll_Description: A toll booth on the Weser river in Großenwieden is first attested as early as 1287.The toll station was moved to Oldendorf in 1588. Toll registers from 1548 are kept in the Niedersächsisches Landesarchiv Bückeburg, L1 Nr. 6358-6373.

name: null
Lock_Description: One of seven locks in the Fulda river between Kassel and Hersfeld, which were built by landgrave Moritz of Hesse-Kassel in a campaign to make the Fulda navigable. Regulations from 1613 specify the lock fee at 2 Alben. At each lock, it was checked whether the toll for the cargo had been paid in Kassel.

Regulations from 1613 specify the lock fee at 2 Alben. At each lock, it was checked whether the toll for the cargo had been paid in Kassel.

Regulations from 1613 specify the lock fee at 2 Alben. At each lock, it was checked whether the toll for the cargo had been paid in Kassel.

Regulations from 1613 specify the lock fee at 2 Alben. At each lock, it was checked whether the toll for the cargo had been paid in Kassel.

Regulations from 1613 specify the lock fee at 2 Alben. At each lock, it was checked whether the toll for the cargo had been paid in Kassel.

name: null
Lock_Description: Fish and mill weir near Spiekershausen with a passage for ships on the left side of the river.

name: null
Lock_Description: Fish and mill weir near Speele with a passage for ships on the left side of the river.

name: Obernkirchen
Settlement_Description: The monastery of Augustinian canonesses Obernkirchen is first mentioned in an 1167 charter. An earlier history since the 9th century is legendary and cannot be proven. The settlement that developed near the monastery is first mentioned in 1171. It received imperial market privileges and limited borough ('weichbild') rights in 1181. A further development of the settlement took place after the secularisation of the monastery by count Otto IV of Schaumburg in 1565, when the settlement received a borough ('flecken') council after the Bückeburg model.
Town_Description: Town privileges granted by count Ernst of Holstein-Schaumburg.

name: Bosseborner Warte
Settlement_Description: Watchtower in the enclosure ('landwehr') of Höxter. The tower proper was located on a hill 200m south of the street. In its place the Bismarckturm was built in 1900.

name: Rumbeck
Toll_Description: The Weser toll station of Oldendorf was moved to Rumbeck in 1616 because of damming of the old river arm near Oldendorf. After 1621, it was moved back to Oldendorf during the Thirty Years' War. Toll registers are extant in the Niedersächsisches Landesarchiv Bückeburg, L1 Nr. 6380-6385.

name: Gieselwerder
Settlement_Description: The lords of Gieselwerder are first mentioned in 1093, who inhabited a castle on a former island ('werder') in the Weser river. A ferry is mentioned here in 1409. The castle was already dilapidated in 1583/87 and consequently almost entirely demolished.
Toll_Description: Water, land and ferry toll, which was leased by the archbishop of Mainz to the landgrave of Hesse in 1462. The toll was also listed in a 1584 complaint from Bremen about the tolls on the Weser. Toll registers exist among others for the years 1637-9 and 1645-6; for the 16th century, only entries for the land and ferry toll are known. Toll tariffs are known only from 1543-45 (analysed by Demandt).

name: null
Lock_Description: Lock in the Aller river in Celle, which was built before 1461 to facilitate shipping between Braunschweig and Celle. Both towns paid half of the construction costs. The lock is displayed on an engraving by Merian from 1654.

name: Vlissingen
Settlement_Description: First mentioned in 1235 (in a copy from 1324). This first mention refers to the settlement that would later be called Oud-Vlissingen. It was located just to the west of the old town and disappeared when defence structures were built during the French period. A hospital is first mentioned in 1271.
Town_Description: Near Oud-Vlissingen, count Willem III of Holland constructed a harbour around 1300, around which the town of Vlissingen developed. It was granted town rights on 2 April 1315. The town was fortified after 1485.
Fair_Description: Duke Albrecht granted Vlissingen in 1368 a free fair starting St. Simon and Judeday apostel (Oct. 28), duration four days. With rights and freedom as in the other towns on the isle Walcheren. In 1395 (April 6) he donated a 'korfharingmarkt': a fair for herring sold per basket, with safeconduct, as there was one previously in Den Briel.
Staple_Description: In 1444 a previously by his predecessors donated privilege was confirmed by duke Philip of Burgundy.  It concerned the herringtoll and the staple for the fish and herring caught and brought ashore between Westkapelle and 'Welsingen' harbour (later known as Rammekens, a fortress built mid 16th century, east of Vlissingen). Conflict with Middelburg led to the compromise whereby wine and fruit from the Walcheren region was taken to Middelburg and fish to Vlissingen.

name: Lubrza
Settlement_Description: Castle and adjoining settlement first mentioned in 1319.
Town_Description: Mentioned as town in 1319 and 1322, called civitas in the beginning of the 16th century. Turned into a borough ('Flecken') after military destruction in 1615. Town privileges were not granted until 1857.

name: Brückfeldwarte
Settlement_Description: Boom barrier and watchtower in the enclosure ('landwehr') of Höxter

name: null
Toll_Description: Bridge toll; it was leased to the monastery Willebadessen in 1300.
Bridge_Description: Located near the monastery of Corvey on the crossing of two important long-distance routes, Höxter was an important point to cross the river Weser. A ferry is first mentioned in 836, and from 1115 onwards a bridge, which was the first bridge known to have been built across the Weser. The original bridge was probably constructed from wood, replaced in 1249 at the latest by a stone bridge with seven arches and a wooden central part, which could be removed in case of ice drift in winter. The bridge was destroyed in 1673 and only rebuilt in 1831.

name: Ölper
Settlement_Description: First mentioned in 1251. In Ölper stood a watchtower of the defensive enclosure ('landwehr') of Braunschweig, which was erected around 1390.

name: null
Lock_Description: A lock in the Leine in Neustadt was built in 1506.

name: Bodenfelde
Settlement_Description: The settlement originally existed as two separate settlements on both sides of the Reiherbach. Economically significant were the saltworks in the village. Attempts to raise the village to a town in 1437 failed due to destructions during feuds.
Toll_Description: In 1270, the duke of Brunswick acquired the toll in Wahmbeck and half of the toll in Bodenfelde. The river toll was moved to Lauenförde in 1534, because ships sailing upstream on the Weser increasingly transshipped their cargo onto the land route in Herstelle. The land toll in Bodenfelde remained.

name: Polle
Settlement_Description: It can be assumed that the place was already settled during the 9th and 10th century. The borough ('flecken') that exists today originated from the castle that was first mentioned in 1285.
Toll_Description: In the first mention of the castle in 1285, a toll of the Counts of Everstein on the Weser is mentioned, which is confirmed in a Bremen complaint of 1584, as well as a charter of the monastery Hardehausen from 1597.

name: Burg Ohsen
Settlement_Description: Castle on the right shore of the Weser, first mentioned in 1259, but probably built around 1200.
Toll_Description: Toll station for the river traffic, mentioned in a 1584 complaint from Bremen, as well as in a 1597 charter of the monastery Hardehausen. The beginnings of the toll are unclear; it is not known whether a toll was already levied here before the castle came to the dukes of Brunswick in 1422. When Ohsen was pawned to Oberhofmarschall Franz Ernst Graf v. Platen in 1681, both a land and a river toll were mentioned.

name: Hamelner Loch
Toll_Description: Conflict about tolls between Hameln and Minden around 1200; bishop Dietmar of Minden arbitrated and declared that citizens of both towns were mutually exempted from toll payments. Hameln acquired the right to levy a ship and bridge toll from duke Albrecht of Brunswick in 1277. The toll is still mentioned in a Bremen complaint from 1584, but not in a Weser toll list in a charter of the monastery of Hardehausen from 1597.
Lock_Description: A weir in the Weser river, the so-called Hamelner Loch, which was first mentioned in 1314 but might have been built at the beginning of the 11th century, provided a considerable barrier for shipping on the river. The 6,30m wide passage for ships in the form of a wooden slipway, the Fiehre, was only passable when the cargo of the ships was unloaded first, which promoted a staple-like situation.

name: Hausberge
Settlement_Description: The castle Schalksburg was first mentioned in 1020, later referred to as Hausberge and demolished in 1723. Next to it, a settlement developed that was characterised as town in 1548 and received market privileges in 1613, but remained a borough ('flecken').
Toll_Primary_Owner: Herr von Schalksberg / Bischof von Minden

name: Stolzenau
Settlement_Description: A castle was built in 1346 by the count of Hoya during a border conflict between Hoya and Minden. The corresponding settlement is characterised as borough ('flecken') from 1459 onwards.
Fair_Description: Three fairs were granted in 1590, on the Mondays after Reminiscere, St John the Baptist and St Lawrence.
Toll_Description: Toll on land and on the Weser river, which was pawned in 1553. Furthermore, it is mentioned in 1576, in a 1584 complaint from Bremen, and in a 1597 charter of the monastery Hardehausen. The toll station probably went back to the founding of the castle. Toll revenues are known for some years around 1600.

name: Schlüsselburg
Settlement_Description: A castle was built by the bishop of Minden in 1335 during border disputes with Hoya. A planned settlement was built in the second half of the 14th century, which received borough ('weichbild') privileges in 1400.
Toll_Description: A toll on the Weser river in Schlüsselburg is mentioned in a 1584 complaint from Bremen, as well as a 1597 list of Weser tolls from the monastery Hardehausen. It probably went back to the foundation of the castle.

name: null
Harbour_Description: Important transshipment point between water and land traffic between Bremen and Braunschweig. On a view of Celle by Merian (1654), we can see that the harbour was located next to the water mill near the castle.

name: Hoya
Settlement_Description: Possibly a settlement of the Angrivarii before, it is first mentioned in the 11th century. A castle is first mentioned in 1213. From 1233, it is characterised as town ('urbs', 'civitas', 'stadt') or borough ('weichbild', 'flecken'). It acquired borough ('weichbild') privileges probably in 1368.
Toll_Primary_Owner: Graf von Hoya / Herzog von Braunschweig-Lüneburg
Toll_Description: In a 1335 treaty between Bremen and Hoya, it is agreed that Bremen skippers enjoy free shipping on the Weser river in return for the payment of a transit toll in Hoya. The toll was pawned in 1543, and mentioned in a 1584 complaint from Bremen and in a charter of the monastery Hardehausen from 1597. Toll revenues are known from the late 16th century.

name: null
Lock_Description: Between 1442 and 1444, locks were constructed in Veltenhof, Ölper and Watenbüttel, so that the Oker was navigable between Braunschweig and the castle Neubrück.

name: null
Lock_Description: Between 1442 and 1444, a lock was constructed near Watenbüttel in order to increase the navigability of the Oker river between Braunschweig and the castle Neubrück.

name: Zeulenroda
Settlement_Description: First mention in 1325, but the settlement probably developed in the middle of the 13th century.
Town_Description: Zeulenroda is granted town and market rights in 1438, probably due to its beneficial location in the traffic network.

name: Dreye
Toll_Primary_Owner: Graf von Hoya / Herzog von Braunschweig-Lüneburg
Toll_Description: Toll of the counts of Hoya, later the dukes of Brunswick-Lüneburg. The monastery of Schinna was exempted from toll payments in Weyhe in 1258. Later - probably before 1370 - the toll was moved to Dreye, where it is mentioned again in the 16th century. It was leased to Dr. jur. Gideon Eggeling in 1571, and to the wife of count Simon of Lippe in 1582. The toll collector in 1574 is named Johann von Redessen (Bodeßen?), who was responsible for collecting the land and water toll. The river toll in Dreye is mentioned in a 1597 charter of the monastery of Hardehausen, but not in a list of Weser toll stations in a 1584 complaint from Bremen; a toll in Schlieme, just a few kilometres upstream, is mentioned instead. Probably both tolls were merged between these years, as accounts from the administrative region of Syke list both tolls separately in 1572, but combined in 1586.

name: Wetenkamp
Toll_Description: A toll of the archbishop of Bremen at the confluence of the Weser and Aller rivers near Thedinghausen already existed in the 14th century. Half of the toll was leased to Bremen burgomaster Dirick Hoyer in the 16th century, and returned to the Bremen cathedral chapter after Hoyer's death in 1569. The toll was moved to Intschede in 1607 because of changes in the course of the Aller. Toll tariffs are known for the early 15th century and 1545; for the years after 1567, toll registers are extant (Niedersächsisches Landesarchiv Stade, analysed by Peters 1913).

name: null
Bridge_Description: The only bridge across the Weser river between Höxter and Minden, which was constructed shortly after 1000. At first it was a wooden bridge, which had to be renovated multiple times. It was replaced by a bridge with stone pillars between 1380 and 1390. A bridge toll is attested in the 14th century.

name: Bremer Schlagd
Toll_Description: A toll on the Weser river in Münden is mentioned in a 1584 complaint from Bremen. Probably, it refers to the harbours fees that were introduced two years earlier.
Harbour_Description: At the confluence of the Fulda and Werra, the harbour for traffic on the Weser was located, which was named Bremer Schlagd after the sea port at the other end of the river. The harbour quays were extended in 1582; at the occasion harbour fees ('Schlachtgeld') were introduced.

name: Varenholz
Settlement_Description: First mentioned in 1176. A castle was built around this time, and is first mentioned in 1323, when it was sold to the lords of Lippe. The settlement developed into a borough ('flecken') in the 16th century.

name: Kasila (Nousiainen)
Settlement_Description: <b>Post house:</b> In 1638, the Royal Steward Bernhardt Steen von Steenhousen established a post house in the village of Kasila in Nousiainen.

name: Kleine Schlachte
Harbour_Description: The so-called "kleine" ('small') Schlachte was located east of the Weser bridge. It served as a harbour for river traffic, contrary to the Schlachte, located west of the bridge, which was the sea port of Bremen. The river harbour appears for the first time on the map of Bremen by Braun/Hogenberg (1588/9) and was constructed from stone shortly before. However, a landing place for timber rafts was probably already existing on this spot in the 13th century.

name: null
Toll_Description: In Rinteln a shipping toll was levied on the Weser river by the count of Schaumburg. The toll registers, which are available from the year 1571 (NLA Bückeburg), give an extraordinary insight in traffic on the river in the late 16th century.
Harbour_Description: The harbour was of minor importance for the town Rinteln. According to Merian's town view of 1647, it was located on the northern shore of the Weser, which was unpaved.

name: null
Bridge_Description: A ferry across the Weser river was probably replaced by a wooden bridge in the 11th century. A bridge toll for foreigners is mentioned in 1232. Around 1340, the bridge rested on stone pillars, until it was replaced by a bridge completely constructed from stone in 1463.
Ferry_Description: A ferry is first mentioned in 1319, but was probably much older. It seems that it operated next to the bridge, which was not usable for heavier traffic before its construction from stone. Afterwards, a ferry was deployed as well in the frequent cases of damage to the bridge.

name: null
Lock_Description: To make the Oker river navigable, the town of Braunschweig made an arrangement with the miller Lütkens in Hillerse to construct a lock in the mill weir. The lock was finalised in 1460.

name: null
Lock_Description: Lock near Wienhausen, built between 1459 and 1461 by the town of Braunschweig to facilitate shipping on the Oker and Aller rivers.

name: null
Ferry_Description: Since the name of the village Schepsdorf, first mentioned in 1313, is derived from a ferry across the Ems, it must already have existed at this time.

name: Schlachte
Ferry_Description: Close to the westernmost lifting crane ('Wippe'), a ferry house was built for the ferry that operated since 1645 to the newly founded Neustadt ('new town') on the opposite shore. The ferry was leased for 25 Bremen marks. The ferrymen were obliged to have three vessels in operation, at least one waiting on each side of the river. Passengers paid 1 Grote per person, but only half the tariff if multiple people were transported at once.
Harbour_Description: The port activities, which originally took place at the Balge river arm, were expanded to include the bank of the Weser river in the course of the 13th century. This developed into Bremen's harbour for sea-going traffic under the name "Schlachte", first mentioned in 1247. Originally, mooring facilities were made of wooden pile work (from which the name "Schlachte" was derived), but stone quays were built in the 16th century. Simple lifting cranes ('Wippen') are first attested in 1489, but were probably older; five of them existed in the 16th century. An additional treadwheel crane for heavy cargo was built in the early 17th century.

name: Balge
Harbour_Description: The Balge, a river arm of the Weser that was located directly next to the market square, was the oldest harbour of Bremen. Due to the limited place, building activities and silting up of the river arm, it gradually lost its significance to the new sea-going harbour at the river front, the Schlachte. However, the Balge regulations of 1399 still indicate a lively traffic at that time, though it must have remained limited to lighter boats. In the 16th century, it had largely lost its importance as a harbour and was closed for regular traffic in 1602.

name: null
Toll_Description: In 1379, a bridge toll is first mentioned. Until the 16th century, it was owned by the counts of Neubruchhausen and later Hoya, from whose lands multiple villages had paid for the construction of the bridge. Still in 1533, the toll was owned by the count of Hoya, but by the 18th century, it was in the hands of the cathedral and six Bremen families.
Bridge_Description: Bridge over both arms of the Weser river, the "kleine" ('little') and "große" ('large') Weser. A wooden bridge is first mentioned in 1244 and was probably built in the early 13th century. Between 1522 and 1531, a large tower, called the "Braut" ('bride'), was constructed on the peninsula between both river arms to guard the bridge. At the occasion, the bridge over the little Weser, which was presumably originally a straight continuation of the large bridge, was reconstructed as a draw bridge a little upstream on the Teerhof peninsula.

name: Intschede
Toll_Description: In 1607, the toll at the mouth of the river Aller in the Weser near Wetenkamp (Thedinghausen) was moved to Intschede because of changes in the course of the river. Toll registers are available in the Niedersächsisches Landesarchiv Stade; for the year 1610/11, they have been analysed by Peters (1913).

name: Afferdsche Warte
Settlement_Description: Watchtower at the crossing of the Hamel river in the defensive enclosure ('landwehr') of Hameln, first mentioned in 1385. The tower is mentioned in 1415 as a stone building.
Bridge_Description: A bridge across the river Hamel is mentioned in 1356 and 1394.

name: Wehrberger Warte
Settlement_Description: Watchtower in the defensive enclosure ('landwehr') of Hameln, which is first mentioned in 1385. The tower was located in such a way that both land and river traffic could be watched over.

name: null
Lock_Description: In 1390, the town of Hannover and the owner of the Bordenau mill weir agreed that the weir should be opened to shipping on the Leine at all times.

name: Bothmer Mühle
Lock_Description: In 1389 the town Hannover agreed with Eberhard von Mahrenholz, the owner of the Bothmer mill, that he would construct a passage for ships on the Leine river in the mill weir. After the establishment of the shipping monopoly of Celle in 1516, the weir was barricaded by Celle. This led to conflicts with the towns Neustadt am Rübenberge and Hannover in 1546-8, which would last until the end of the 16th century.

name: null
Lock_Description: In 1389 the town Hannover arranged with the owner of the mill weir in Grindau, that it had to be opened for ships on the Leine river at all times.

name: null
Lock_Description: In 1390 the town Hannover and the owner of the Dinstorf mill weir agreed that the weir should be opened to ships on the Leine river at all times.

name: null
Lock_Description: In 1390 the town Hannover arranged with the monastery Mariensee, the owner of the mill in Wulfelade, that the mill weir had to be opened to ships on the Leine river at any time. Moreover, the town promised to repair any damage inflicted to the mill weir by passing ships within four weeks.

name: null
Lock_Description: A lock near Veltenhof was built between 1442 and 1444 as part of construction works to increase the navigability of the Oker river between Braunschweig and the castle Neubrück.

name: Marienwerder
Settlement_Description: Foundation of a monastery of Augustinian canons in ca. 1196; the monks were replaced by nuns from the monastery Obernkirchen in 1216. It became a pilgrimage destination. In 1543, the monastery became a Lutheran Ladies' convent. The buildings were destroyed and plunedered during the Thirty Years' War in 1632, and rebuilt after a fire in 1687.

name: Ahlden
Settlement_Description: First mentioned in 1160. The castle of Ahlden was confiscated by the dukes of Brunswick-Lüneburg in 1431. Around this time, the settlement acquired the character of a borough ('flecken').
Toll_Description: With the acquisition of Ahlden by Lüneburg, it became one of the toll stations on the Aller river. An agreement between Hannover and Celle from 1507 defines that for ships sailing from Bremen to Hannover, half of the tolls in the duchy of Celle have to be paid in Ahlden. After changes in the course of the river between 1618 and 1630, the toll was levied in Hudemühlen. Toll revenues are known for the 18th and 19th century.

name: null
Bridge_Description: The bridge across the Aller near Essel became a hindrance for traffic on the river in the 16th century. Plans from 1586 to construct a higher bridge that could be passed by ships were never realised, according to a Bremen complaints from 1608. Instead there existed a hatch, for which one had to get the key from the bailiff ('vogt') in Essel. In order to get there, the marshy terrain separating the river and the settlement had to be crossed, which was difficult especially in winter when the marshes were flooded.
Harbour_Description: Essel was a transshipment point for the land and water traffic, predominantly between Bremen and Braunschweig. Around 1587 the Duke of Brunswick tried to stimulate the settlement as transshipment point, which led to complaints from Celle.

name: Haren (Ems)
Settlement_Description: The settlement, originally a fishing village, adopted the name of the current village Altharen. In the 13th century, the settlement had a church, and a castle of the bishop of Münster is mentioned in 1304.
Fair_Description: Various fairs are mentioned in Haren in the early 14th century, for which merchants from Osnabrück received safe conduct. Of these fairs, the fairs at Pentecost and St John are still mentioned in the late 15th century, together with a new fair on St Giles.
Toll_Description: A toll in Haren is first mentioned as a fief of the count of Tecklenburg in 1236; later it belonged to the bishop of Münster. A list of toll fees for various commodities exists for the year 1631. In the 17th century, half of the toll was owned by the town Meppen.

name: Klapperturm
Settlement_Description: Watchtower of the defensive enclosure ('landwehr') of Einbeck on the street to Dassel, built in 1446. It is the only watchtower of Einbeck that still exists.

name: Bartshäuser Turm
Settlement_Description: Watchtower of the defensive enclosure ('landwehr') of Einbeck, which is first mentioned in 1431. The tower itself is mentioned in 1439. Demolished in 1795.

name: null
Bridge_Description: The small bridge across the Leine between Göttingen and Rosdorf is first mentioned in 1419.

name: Leineturm
Settlement_Description: Watchtower on the crossing of the river Leine near Northeim, which was built in 1399. Since the late 16th century, there was an inn next to the tower. The tower was demolished in 1717.
Bridge_Description: An older wooden bridge was replaced by a stone one in 1497. It was located 100m north of the current river crossing.

name: Stau
Harbour_Description: The "Stau" at the mouth of the Haaren in the Hunte was the harbour of Oldenburg. Shipping traffic is first attested in the 14th century. An additional loading place for the river traffic was located in Donnerschwee, where a toll for ships loading timber is mentioned in 1428, and where pottery was loaded as well. In the course of the 15th century, shipping activity was moved from Donnerschwee to the Stau.

name: Schlagde
Harbour_Description: The construction of a city wall in the 13th century separated the old market, located on the shore of a river arm, from the water. Consequently a harbour at the shore of the Weser was established, which received the name "Schlagde". The harbour was located outside of town; possibly, the Weser toll was levied here before the toll in Petershagen was granted (1377).

name: null
Harbour_Description: The harbour for seagoing vessels in Hamburg was divided into two parts in the mid-14th century: the inner and lower harbour, which were separated with a row of poles that could be closed with a boom barrier. The ships were anchored here - mostly in the lower harbour - and lighter boats transported the cargoes from the ships to the harbour crane on the town hall square, because larger sailing ships could not pass the bridges in town. In the 16th century, the inner harbour was incorporated within the urban defence structure, and a new crane was built here, making the harbour fit as transshipment point between land and water traffic.

name: null
Harbour_Description: In the 15th century, a small upper harbour at the Bille river came into existence, which served the river traffic.

name: Bäckerstraße
Toll_Description: Toll of the dukes of Lüneburg on road traffic in the Bäckerstraße, first mentioned in 1383. Lüneburg citizens were exempted from toll payments. Tariffs are known from 1495. A toll register of ca. 1500 in a town account gives an impression of the traffic through the street.

name: null
Toll_Description: Already in 1396 Lüneburg had attempted in vain to levy a toll on traffic on the Ilmenau river. According to complaints from Hamburg, a toll was levied again in 1465, which was legalised by the emperor in a 1471 privilege. After conflicts with other Hanseatic towns, Lüneburg had to cancel the levying of the toll in 1476.
Harbour_Description: River harbour at the Ilmenau, of which the shores were stabilised with stone quays since the 16th century at the latest. On the eastern side of the harbour, a crane existed since 1346 as well as a storage building ('kaufhaus'), which was enlarged in 1574. A new storage building was erected in 1622. The harbour basin could be closed off with a barrier; additionally a bastion was built to guard the harbour entrance in 1534, which had to be reconstructed after an explosion in 1537.

name: Krapendorf
Settlement_Description: The settlement was first mentioned in 1185. In 1279 the castle Cloppenburg was built near the settlement, which developed into a town that converged with Krapendorf. However, both settlements remained independent until 1855.

name: null
Harbour_Description: In the 17th century, Haren was the centre of the transport with barges ('pünten') on the Ems.

name: null
Harbour_Description: The Vechte was navigable up to Schüttorf with barges until the 20th century. The town was an important transshipment point for sandstone from the Bentheim quarries on its way to the Dutch cities.

name: null
Harbour_Description: Nordhorn was a transshipment harbour for sandstone from the Bentheim quarries on its way to the Dutch cities. The current street Steinmaate is a reminder of this.

name: null
Harbour_Description: The Ems river was navigable with larger ships downstream from Meppen, which made the town a transshipment point for water transport.

name: null
Toll_Description: It is mentioned in 1482 that the town of Meppen would share the profits from the bridge toll, levied by the town alone before, with the bishop. The entire toll income was returned to the town in 1569.
Bridge_Description: A bridge over the Ems was built by the bishop of Münster in 1385. In 1569, it was acquired by the town.
Ferry_Description: A ferry existed here until construction of a bridge in 1385.

name: null
Toll_Description: It is mentioned in 1482 that the town of Meppen would share the profits from the bridge toll, levied by the town alone before, with the bishop. The entire toll income was returned to the town in 1569.
Bridge_Description: The bridge over the Hase was first mentioned in 1398, when Bishop Otto of Münster bought half of the bridge. In the next year, the other half was acquired by the town of Meppen; In 1569, it was owned completely by the town.

name: null
Bridge_Description: Bridge over the Hase. An extraordinary bridge toll is mentioned here in a complaint from Deventer, Kampen and Zwolle in 1569.

name: null
Harbour_Description: The Hase was navigable up to Haselünne

name: null
Lock_Description: Flash lock at the mill in Ohrum, built to regulate the shipping on the Oker in 1577.

name: null
Lock_Description: The Nette (Altenau) was made navigable in 1575, at which occasion a lock was constructed near Wendessen. Shipping on the stream must have stopped around 1610.

name: Donnerburgbrücke
Settlement_Description: Stables for draught horses are mentioned in 1584. Since the 17th century, there existed an inn at the bridge.
Bridge_Description: The bridge is first mentioned in 1385 in a peace agreement between the town Braunschweig and Cordt van der Assenburg. A draw bridge is mentioned in 1584. The current still existing stone bridge dates from 1708 and is called Donnerburgbrücke, after a former inn at the bridge, which came into the possession of Hans Jürgen Donner in 1705.
Harbour_Description: A place for loading stones from the Ösel was created next to the bridge in 1575.
Lock_Description: A lock was built here in the context of making the Nette (Altenau) navigable in 1575.

name: null
Harbour_Description: The Nette (Altenau) was made navigable in 1575, mainly for the transport of stones from the Elm. According to a 1578 source, in which duke Julius promised the transport of building material by ship for the reconstruction of houses after the town of Schöppenstedt had burned down, the Nette was navigable up to Schöppenstedt. Shipping on the stream must have stopped around 1610.

name: null
Toll_Description: A toll of the archbishop of Bremen on the crossing of the river Lesum is already mentioned in 1062. A bridge toll was levied from 1387 onwards, to cover the expenses of the construction of the new bridge. At first, this toll was levied by the town of Bremen, later it was shared with the archbishop.
Bridge_Description: A bridge across the Lesum was built by the town of Bremen around 1388 for the sum of 6000 Mark.
Ferry_Description: In the charter about the reconstruction of the castle from 1350, a ferry is mentioned. This ferry must have existed until the construction of the bridge in 1388.

name: Sulberger Warte
Settlement_Description: Watchtower in the defensive enclosure ('landwehr') of Duderstadt on the Sulberg, first mentioned in annals of the year 1400. In the vicinity, the gallows of Duderstadt were located as well.

name: Liepen (Malchin)
