Settlement_Description: The village is first mentioned in 1247.

name: Fräulein Steinfort
Settlement_Description: Possibly first mentioned as Steynuorde in 1335, but this might also refer to the western neighbour village Steinfort, which was originally called Rutnik.

name: Schaalmühle
Settlement_Description: Mill at the Schaale river, first mentioned in 1279.

name: Giehlermühlen
Settlement_Description: Water mill, farm and inn, mentioned in an itinerary from 1425.

name: Gotteslager
Toll_Description: The toll in Linden was moved before 1630 into the suburb Gotteslager in Wolfenbüttel. According to a description of 1630, the toll in Gotteslager had the highest revenues of the five toll stations in the Amt Wolfenbüttel.

name: Thiedebach
Settlement_Description: Toll station with inn at the stream Thiedebach, which was built by duke Julius of Brunswick-Wolfenbüttel after 1586.
Toll_Description: A toll station was installed here by duke Julius of Brunswick-Wolfenbüttel after 1586.

name: Mattierzoll
Settlement_Description: The town of Brunswick erected a guardtower on the northern side of the causeway that bridged the Große Bruch (Hessendamm) in 1375.
Toll_Description: Toll station of the dukes of Brunswick at the Hessemdamm, which was built in 1343. Since the 19th century, the toll station is known as Mattierzoll, because the toll had to be paid in Mattier (Matthiasgroschen), a coin minted in Goslar since 1471. Detailed toll tariffs and regulations are recorded in an overview of tolls in the duchy of Brunswick-Wolfenbüttel from 1582.

name: Bungenstedter Turm
Settlement_Description: Watchtower on the border between Brunswick and Hildesheim territory, first mentioned in 1461. In the second half of the 16th century, lumberjack Albrecht Gillies constructed a house next to the tower.

name: Holm (Dassow)
Settlement_Description: First mentioned in 1306, when the village was given to the Hospital of the Holy Ghost in Lübeck.

name: Martinsmühle
Settlement_Description: Water mill near Sülsdorf, first mentioned in 1285. A murder stone from 1398 is located nearby.

name: Siechenhaus
Settlement_Description: A hospital for lepers near Dassow was probably built in the 13th century. In 1441, it is first mentioned, when it also accommodated the poor.

name: Sankt Hülfe
Settlement_Description: The village was originally called Nutlo. A first mention as "Stuttele" between 1238 and 1250 is believed to be a writing error. A chapel dedicated to the Holy Wilgefortis is first mentioned in 1378, and became a pilgrimage centre. This resulted in the village becoming known as Sankt Hülfe. The chapel burned down after 1519 and was not rebuilt.

name: Maurine-Mühle
Settlement_Description: Mill at the Maurine river, first mentioned in 1373.

name: null
Harbour_Description: Due to changes in the course of the Ems, the Mühlenbach was enlarged in 1541 to keep allowing smaller ships to anchor near the town. In this area, the former landing place at the bank of the Ems is to be presumed as well.

name: Gleviner Burg
Settlement_Description: Watchtower with boom barrier in the enclosure ('landwehr') of Güstrow. The enclosure is first mentioned in 1270, the year of construction of the tower is unknown. Later converted into a farm that was leased from the town.

name: Warturm
Settlement_Description: Watchtower to guard the border between Bremen and Oldenburg at the Ochtum river, built in the early 14th century. The name is derived from the settlement War(e), which was abandoned in the 14th century. A new toll house and inn was built in 1577, the "Storchennest" (stork's nest). The tower was demolished in 1661, but rebuilt in 1669. After its destruction in 1813, the remains were removed in 1820. The toll house still exists.
Toll_Description: The road toll is first mentioned in 1449, when it was leased to several citizens for 12 years, but it probably existed from the time the road between Delmenhorst and Bremen via Huchting was constructed, as was agreed upon by the counts of Oldenburg and the town of Bremen in 1311. Oldenburg citizens acquired exemption of the toll at the Warturm in 1461. A new toll house was erected in 1577.
Bridge_Description: Bridge across the Ochtum (Warbrücke), first mentioned in 1390.

name: Mittelshuchting
Settlement_Description: The settlement Huchting was divided in three parts: Kirch-, Mittels- and Brokhuchting, of which the former two are the oldest parts. Mittelshuchting is first mentioned separately in 1384.

name: Kattenturm
Settlement_Description: Watchtower of Bremen, built in 1390 to control the crossing of the Ochtum river near Kattenesch, after which village the tower was named. Next to the tower, there was a toll house and an inn. Demolished in 1803. The current settlement, a quarter of Bremen, was later named after the former tower.
Toll_Description: At the Kattenturm, a toll was levied by the town of Bremen.
Bridge_Description: Bridge over the river Ochtum. In 1799, the draw bridge was replaced by a fixed bridge.

name: Stumpfer Turm
Settlement_Description: Watchtower Dörshelf with an inn on a pass on a trade route, first mentioned in the first half of the 15th century. Possibly, it belonged to the town Alfeld to secure the street, later to the noble family of Steinberg-Wispenstein. The tower became known as Stumpfer Turm in the 18th century because of the missing spire.

name: Parczew
Toll_Description: A salt toll is mentioned in 1504 and 1505.

name: Kreuzkrug (Senne)
Settlement_Description: The inn Kreuzkrug was built in 1706 as replacement of the inn Finkenkrug, which had been destroyed during the Thirty Years' War. The inn was moved slightly in 1811 when the new road Gauseköte was constructed.

name: null
Ferry_Description: At least from the mid-16th century, there existed a ferry to Delfzijl. In 1584, a certain Johann Tyen is mentioned, who had operated the ferry for more than two decades.
Harbour_Description: The harbour of Emden was located in a bend of the river Ems, which was cut across 4 km south during a flooding in 1509, creating the island Nesserland. As a result the harbour, now located on a river arm, started to silt up. The town tried to prevent the silting of its harbour and the bypassing of its staple between 1585 and the Thirty Years' War with a pile barrier in the main stream. The harbour in the town was extended in 1538 by raising and reinforcing the peninsula Butvenne between the Ratsdelft and the Falderndelft. Countess Anna ordered the construction of a loading crane on the Bonesse, the eastern shore of the Falderndelft, in 1544.

name: Dörverden
Settlement_Description: Possibly, Dörverden is identical to the "Tulifurdon" mentioned by Ptolemy in 150. This possibility is supported by archaeological finds of graves from pre-Christian times. It was an old regional court ('gogericht'), which was acquired by the bishop of Verden in 1288. The court existed until ca. 1650. The local church is first mentioned in 1340.

name: null
Harbour_Description: Ems harbour in Rheine, which could be reached with the Ems barges ('pünten'). With the development of shipping to Greven after 1550, the significance of Rheine as transshipment point and skipper town grew.

name: null
Bridge_Description: Construction of a bridge over the Dinkel was started when the settlement received town privileges in 1369; the next year, the citizens acquired the right to fetch timber in the surroundings and to levy a toll for the maintenance of the bridge.

name: Mühlenkolk
Harbour_Description: The harbour was located at the current Mühlenkolk, which was connected to the Vechte and Dinkel via the Mühlenbecke.

name: Victorbur
Settlement_Description: Victorbur is mentioned in the law of the region Brokmerland from 1300 as 'wic', which indicates a settlement with special legal protection during market times. The oldest predecessor of the local church was possibly built in the 11th century.

name: Rotenburger Turm
Settlement_Description: Watchtower in the defensive enclosure ('landwehr') of the town Braunschweig, which was erected between 1381 and 1385.

name: Raffturm
Settlement_Description: Watchtower of the defensive enclosure ('landwehr') of Braunschweig, erected between 1384 and 1388.

name: Landwehrschenke
Settlement_Description: Watchtower and inn of the defensive enclosure ('landwehr') of Hannover.

name: Schlagd
Harbour_Description: Wanfried was the end of shipping on the Werra and therefore an important transshipment station between land- and rivertransport.

name: Zum Dicken Weib
Settlement_Description: An inn at the Emmer bridge is first mentioned in 1223; in 1563 it is first referred to with the name "thom dicken wyve".
Bridge_Description: Bridge across the Emmer, first mentioned in 1223 in connection with the inn.

name: null
Bridge_Description: The bridge in Bodenteich is mentioned in 1393, when wagons toppled over there.

name: Eigenroder Warte
Settlement_Description: Watchtower north of Mühlhausen, erected as part of the defensive enclosure of Mühlhausen ('Mühlhäuser Landgraben') in the mid-14th century.

name: Harzburg
Settlement_Description: The castle Harzburg, which actually consisted of two castles on mountain tops, was built by emperor Henry II in 1065-1068. The castle was demolished after the Thirty Years' War.

name: Dambeck
Settlement_Description: First mentioned in 1450/51. An earlier mention from 1330/52 as Dannenbeke is uncertain. In 1450, the village consisted of 3 farms.

name: null
Harbour_Description: Transshipment point for river traffic on the Volkov. Commodities had to be transshipped from sea-going vessels onto shallow river boats.

name: null
Toll_Description: A bridge fee is mentioned in 1400 and 1548. In 1582, an additional toll is established.
Bridge_Description: A bridge across the Leine is first mentioned in 1062.

name: Hitzacker
Settlement_Description: Slavic fortification from the 8th century, later a castle of Henry the Lion and the dukes of Saxony-Lauenburg, which is first mentioned in a charter from 1162.
Town_Description: Hitzacker was already mentioned as "urbs" in 1203, but received the Lüneburg town privileges in 1258.
Toll_Description: Toll on the Elbe river traffic of the dukes of Saxony-Lauenburg, first mentioned in 1248 with references to the toll fees. In the 14th century, the toll often changes hands or was pawned. At the division of the duchy of Brunswick-Lüneburg in 1428, the toll was divided by the dukes of Brunswick and Lüneburg; it came completely to Lüneburg in 1491. In 1492, the toll fees were indicated as 4 Gulden, 1 "pärchin", 1 loaf of bread and 2 buns for each ship. The toll was discontinued in 1872.
Harbour_Description: The harbour of Hitzacker was important for shipping on the Jeetzel river. Commodities that were transported further onto the Elbe sometimes had to be transferred to other ships here.

name: Schnackenburg
Settlement_Description: The settlement came into existence next to a castle, which was possibly built in the 11th century and first mentioned in 1218. The settlement was characterised as borough ('weichbild') in 1351 and as town in 1373, although it remained a borough or minor town.
Toll_Description: Toll on the Elbe of the margraves of Brandenburg, shared with the lord of Mecklenburg in 1321. It was acquired by the dukes of Mecklenburg in 1373 and by the dukes of Brunswick-Lüneburg in 1390/91. Levying of the Mecklenburg part of the toll was moved to Lenzen before 1411. The Lüneburg part of the toll in Schnackenburg was divided between the dukes of Brunswick and Lüneburg after the partition of the duchy in 1409; it came completely to Lüneburg in 1491, but was often pawned to the lords of Bülow. The dukes tried to raise the toll tariffs in 1576, after which various towns complained that the fees had already been doubled. A new raise of the fees was confirmed in 1613.
Ferry_Description: A ferry across the Elbe in Schnackenburg is first mentioned in 1410.
Harbour_Description: Trade relations with Hamburg in Schackenburg are attested from 1288.

name: Kasseler Schlagd
Harbour_Description: The quay at the shore of the Fulda in Münden was the harbour for the traffic on the Fulda river, and it was named Kasseler Schlagd after its most important destination Kassel. In 1582, the landing bridges were extended and harbour fees were introduced.

name: Wanfrieder Schlagd
Harbour_Description: The harbour at the shore of the Werra in Münden was destined for handling shipping on the Werra; it was named Wanfrieder Schlagd after the Werra town where the cargoes were transshipped to land traffic. In 1582, the harbour quays were extended and harbour fees were introduced.

name: null
Bridge_Description: A bridge across the Weser is first mentioned in 1569 as "Lembker bruggen" ('bridge to Lemke'). The bridge was destroyed by Danish troops in 1625 during the Thirty Years' War, temporarily replaced by a pontoon bridge, and rebuilt in 1663.
Ferry_Description: The Weser near Nienburg could be crossed at a ford. Before the construction of a bridge, ferrymen were also active here.

name: Rohrsen (Weser)
Settlement_Description: The settlement consisted of 3-5 households in the 15th and 16th century.

name: Rohrsener Warte
Settlement_Description: Watchtower in the defensive enclosure ('landwehr') of Hameln, first mentioned in 1385.

name: null
Harbour_Description: The harbour on the Este river in Buxtehude was in connection with Hamburg and Wedel an important transshipment point for the crossing of the Elbe river on the road between Flanders and Lübeck and for the transport of oxen between Denmark and the Low Countries.

name: Bad Bevensen
Settlement_Description: The settlement is first mentioned in 1162, but possibly originated in the Lombard period and seems to have been an important trading place before it lost its significance to Lüneburg and Uelzen around 1200. The settlement was usually referred to as borough ('wicbeld').

name: null
Harbour_Description: In the 16th century, there existed a skippers' guild in Winsen, which was obliged to keep the Luhe navigable.

name: null
Harbour_Description: The Ilmenau river was occasionally used as a transport route upstream from Lüneburg, mainly for the shipping of firewood for the Lüneburg saltworks. The Ilmenau privilege of 1348 granted Lüneburg the right to make the Ilmenau navigable between Lüneburg and Uelzen; the section between Medingen and Uelzen was given up in 1562.

name: null
Harbour_Description: Although the river harbour of Kassel was located on the Schlagd in the old town, the towns maps of Michael Müller from 1547 and of Merian from 1646 show a loading place for river barges at the eastern shore of the Fulda just outside of the walls of the new town.

name: null
Toll_Description: In order to pay for the construction of a new bridge in 1346, a bridge toll was introduced for many commodities. The toll also had to be paid by wagons crossing the river at the ford.
Bridge_Description: A wooden bridge across the Fulda existed since the building of the new town on the eastern shore of the Fulda, which was first mentioned in 1283. In 1346, it was complained that the bridge was in a bad state, probably as a result of flooding in 1342, and had to be renewed. Next to the bridge, there also existed a ford at the time. The new bridge was a wooden construction on stone pillars, which was replaced with a massive stone bridge by Landgrave Philipp in 1509-1512, and finally demolished around 1790, with a new bridge constructed on a different site.

name: Wangersen
Settlement_Description: First mentioned in 1105. According to a register from Bremervörde from ca. 1500, the settlement consisted of five farms.

name: null
Toll_Description: The town acquired the right to levy a bridge toll in 1571: for pedestrians one Pfennig, for a horseback rider one Verden Schwar, for a pig or a sheep one Pfennig, and for a wagon one Witten.
Bridge_Description: Verden took its name from a ford or a ferry across the Aller river. However, from 1220 a bridge is attested as well. On a view of the town by Merian from 1653, we can see that this was a summer bridge, which could be partly deconstructed to protect the structure from flood and ice in winter. At these times, the bridge was replaced by a ferry.

name: Stintbrücke
Toll_Description: The Stint toll was called after the place where it was levied, the bridge Stintbrücke across the Balge. This toll of the archbishop was leased to Bremen citizen Johann Uppenhus in 1346. In 1371 it was sold to the inn of St George ('St. Jürgengasthaus') and the hospital of St Rembert.

name: Lengefelder Warte
Settlement_Description: Erected around 1360, this watchtower controlled the Northwest of Mühlhausen, controlling the passage through the Mühlhäuser Landgraben.

name: Dinaburgas pils
Settlement_Description: Castle of the Livonian order, destroyed by the Russians in 1577, who founded a new town 20km downstream (modern Daugavpils).

name: null
Bridge_Description: A bridge across the Weser in Rinteln is first mentioned in 1223. It was destroyed in the Thirty Years' War in 1623. A new bridge could only be constructed in 1654.
Ferry_Description: A ferry is mentioned in 1623 that replaced the destroyed bridge.

name: Sülbeck (Schaumburg)
Settlement_Description: A first mention as "Sullethe" in 1055-1085 might refer to another settlement. First mentioned as "Sulbike" in 1153-1170.

name: Pötritz
Settlement_Description: First mentioned in a document from 1363. The settlement was deserted around 1500, but in 1664 an inn was founded at the same location.

name: null
Toll_Description: A toll on the Elbe river in Schönebeck is first mentioned in 1423. According to treaty from 1562, citizens from Magdeburg were exempted from the toll. Although a description of the bishopric of Magdeburg from 1665 states that the cathedral chapter used to own a river toll in Schönebeck, four accounts of the river merchant Gottfried Kleeditz from Pirna from 1671-1674 attest that the toll was still in existence.

name: null
Bridge_Description: Bridge over the Eder in Fritzlar. The bridge was guarded by a watchtower.

name: Barby
Settlement_Description: First mention in a 961 donation charter to the monastary of  St Maurice in Magdeburg. The placename may allude to an older age. In the 12th century a small territorial lordship was established with a castle. After the comital line of succession ended in 1659, the county of Arnstein-Barby became part of the Electorate of Saxony.
Town_Description: Probably founded as a planned town by the counts of Arnstein-Barby in the early 13th century. A town council is mentioned in 1407. The local economy depended on agriculture and brewery.

name: Rothenhaus
Settlement_Description: Rothenhaus was constructed by Duke Franz II of Lauenburg as toll station in 1609.
Toll_Description: Toll station of the dukes of Saxony-Lauenburg.

name: Palmschleuse
Bridge_Description: In 1613, a bridge over the Delvenau was constructed, because the previous ford had been too problematic to cross.
Lock_Description: Wooden pound lock, built in 1393 as connection between the Delvenau and Elbe rivers as part of the construction of the Stecknitz canal by the city of Lübeck. The lock acquired its current oval form during a reconstruction in 1724. The name is derived from the lock master Palm, who was appointed in 1592.

name: Neuekrug
Settlement_Description: The Neue Krug is first mentioned in 1745.

name: Drasenberg
Settlement_Description: A village is first mentioned in 1303. It was deserted before 1500; in 1493 only single farms on the Drasenberg are mentioned.

name: Winkel
Settlement_Description: Winkel is first mentioned in 1289. Winkel was granted town rights on 12 May 1415 by William VI, count of Holland. The settlement, however, never developed an urban character. The granting of town rights was part of an administrative reorganization in which a number of smaller settlements were granted town rights in order to provide them with a certain degree of self-government which replaced the need for the count of Holland's bailiffs ('baljuws'). Winkel lost its town privileges as a consequence of the Hook and Cod wars, but these rights were regranted on 8 May 1452 by Philip the Good, count of Holland.
Fair_Description: In 1452 krijgen Oude en Nieuwe Niedorp en Winkel hun stadsrecht terug (ontnomen in 1426 i.v.m. steun aan Jacoba van Beieren). Filips de Goede geeft dan ook twee jaarmarkten en een weekmarkt, die dienen gehouden te worden in het aan de Zuiderzeekust gelegen Winkel.

name: Schenkenschanz
Settlement_Description: The bifurcation of the Rhine and Waal rivers, originally located in Lobith, moved a few kilometres upstream around 1540. At the new bifurcation point (on Cleves territory), the fortress Schenkenschans was built by the Dutch Estates General in 1586.
Toll_Description: This toll for sailing transport is the continuation of the toll of Esserden (before 1062) that moved to Schmithausen (1085) and then to Emmerich (1142). Ca. 1635 it moved to Fort 's Gravenweerd /Schenkenschans.Through the years the tollhouse was located at at least two spots. Because the toll was levied at the bifurcation of the river Rhine into the branches Nederrijn and Waal, the registers of this toll are the best source to get an idea of total Dutch-German trade and transport on the Rhine in 17th and 18th century. From 1800-1803 the levying of the toll took place in Arnhem and Nijmegen.  Toll administration 1635 (1630) - 1810 is preserved in Utrechts Archief, 221 Kapittel van Sint Marie te Utrecht inv.no. 1630 - 1712 f.e. 1666-1666 (registers)

name: Badenhauser Landwehr
Settlement_Description: Crossing of the border ('landwehr') between Osterode and Staufenburg, first mentioned in 1438. In 1536, a watchtower and boom barrier are mentioned here; a house for the guard at the barrier was built in 1579.

name: Alte Warte
Settlement_Description: Watchtower in the defensive enclosure ('landwehr') of Osterode, built in the 14th century. The remains were rediscovered in 1965.

name: Kummerow (Malchin)
Settlement_Description: A church at Kummerow was mentioned in a document of Duke Wartislaw III from 1222, confirmed by Duke Barnim I in 1253.
Town_Description: Both dukes confirmed a council and the town of Kummerow in 1255 and 1256. Before 1330, the place is referred to as 'civitas' and 'oppidum'.

name: Stadersand
Toll_Description: With the staple privilege of Stade from 1259, a cargo toll was introduced for commodities on ships that passed the town, as well as a "Ruderzoll", measured by the size of the ship. This led to conflicts with Hamburg, which was exempted from the toll in 1340, as well as Lübeck, Bremen and Lüneburg. In case that circumstances prohibited anchoring of the ship in the mouth of the Schwinge, the toll could also be paid at the archepiscopal toll collector in Hamburg. The cargo toll was cancelled in 1862, the "Ruderzoll" already in 1844.

name: null
Harbour_Description: Because of the bad condition of the roads, transport in East Frisia up to Apen often took place over the water, especially in winter.

name: null
Harbour_Description: Harbour at the Elbe river. In the 16th century, passing ships were often forced to unload their cargo and to bring it to the Lüneburg staple market.

name: null
Toll_Description: The toll in Boizenburg had to be paid by ships on the Elbe river as well as the Schaale canal from 1564. Because Boizenburg was not located directly on those rivers, a toll station must have existed in the vicinity of the ferry. For further details, see Boizenburg.
Ferry_Description: A ferry between Boizenburg and Brackede is first mentioned in 1209.

name: Bleicherode
Settlement_Description: Developed at the foot of the Löwenburg and the Wallburg.
Town_Description: Referred to as oppidum in 1326, as town in 1395. Town rights were probably granted in the first half of the 14th century, but they were lost and renewed in 1572.

name: null
Bridge_Description: A bridge across the Weser in Petershagen is first mentioned in 1407. It is shown as a wooden bridge on an engraving of Merian from 1645; this was a summer bridge, which could be partially deconstructed in winter to protect the construction from damage by floods and ice. Nevertheless, the bridge was destroyed by floods and rebuilt in 1565 and 1596. After a renewed destruction in 1622, the bridge was not rebuilt. This means that the bridge that Merian depicted did not exist at that time anymore.
Ferry_Description: At times when the bridge could not be used and after its destruction in 1622, a ferry was in service.
Harbour_Description: Skippers from Petershagen regularly appear in the toll register of Rinteln.

name: null
Lock_Description: The mill weir in Eschwege had an opening for ships to pass. Vessels built in Wanfried could pass the opening without problems downstream, but upstream only with great difficulty.

name: Hjørring
Settlement_Description: Place name known from the 12th century. In the middle of the 12th century the Danish king Svend Grathe (1146-1157) produced coins in Hjørring, which by then was a settlement with some level of urban activity. The settlement belonged to the crown.
Town_Description: Hjørring was listed as a town in King Valdemars Cadastre about 1231. In 1243 Hjørring was granted town privileges by the Danish king Erik Plovpenning (1241-1250), and hereby became the first official town in the region of Vendsyssel. In 1408 a mayor and citizens were mentioned.
Fair_Description: Hjørring was one of the most important market towns in the province of Vendsyssel. During the medieval period the town must have had at least one annual fair, Saint Knud’s fair (Danish: Knudmesse or Knudsmarked) but the age and character of the first annual fair(s) are uncertain. Several minor fairs relocated to Hjørring from other places in Vendsyssel by King Christian IV (1596-1648) in 1602.  All annual fairs of Hjørring appear to have had a local character.

name: Angeren
Settlement_Description: Earliest mention in the beginning of the ninth century in a copy dated between 1170 and 1175. Mentioned as 'apud Angram' at the end of the eleventh century.
Toll_Primary_Owner: Holy roman emperor (the name of Heinrich IV is in the first source)
Toll_Description: The toll for sailing transport is mentioned for the first time in 1074 and for the last time in 1226. After 1226, it moved to Huissen, where ownership of the toll changed to the Count of Cleves.

name: Ribbeck
Settlement_Description: First mention of the name in 1282, first mention of the settlement in 1335.

name: Fährkrug
Settlement_Description: First mention in 1721 as a ferry inn, in the 19th century a secondary toll station of Werben.
Ferry_Description: A ferry across the Elbe is first mentioned in 1272.

name: Voorde
Settlement_Description: First mentioned in 1238. The settlement was named after a ford in the Eider river.

name: null
Harbour_Description: Although the road was the main artery for Höxter's trade, skippers from Höxter were active in transport on the Weser, as can be seen from the toll accounts of Rinteln.

name: null
Harbour_Description: Vlotho developed into an important skippers' town on the Weser in the 17th century. Harbour structures were however first built in the 18th century.

name: Keller
Settlement_Description: In the 14th century, a fortification was constructed on the border between Schauenburg and Dithmarschen, which became known as (M)eddiksee, after a nearby lake. In the second half of the 16th century, the Rantzau family built the manor Lindhorst here, a dependency of the castle Hanerau. The manor was demolished between 1614 and 1620. Since 1642, the settlement is known as Keller.
Toll_Description: The toll of Hanerau, which was levied since the middle of the 15th century, was also levied at Lindhorst (Keller).

name: Schalentiner Mühle
Settlement_Description: The village Schalentin is first mentioned in 1288. The village was deserted later, only a water mill remaining.

name: Bad Münder
Town_Description: Raised to a market town in an early stage; civic court and council present in the first half of the 13th century. Mentioned as "oppidum" in 1260 and "civitas" in 1302.

name: Nibe
Settlement_Description: In the 13th century and the early 14th century Nibe was a fishing village with a certain level of trading activity, which benefited from rich fishing banks in Limfjorden. Herring from Nibe was imported and sold in Hanseatic towns. Nibe was a royal settlement, and the king granted Nibe certain trading rights, which normally belonged to towns. Hereby Nibe was in opposition to the town of Aalborg a bit further west. In 1536 Nibe was described as a town. In 1545 Nibe was granted the right to a law (Danish: Birkeret) and a bailiff  (Danish: foged). In 1570 Aalborg resisted Nibe’s desire to have permanent craftsmen living. This was however granted in 1587. The ongoing conflict with Aalborg is probably the reason why Nibe was not officially granted town privileges before the 18th century.
Fair_Description: In the 15th century Nibe held at least one annual fair. The age an character of the fair is uncertain. Around 1490 the fair was moved to Aalborg.
Harbour_Description: The character of the harbour is uncertain. Presumably, a natural harbour.

name: Cochstedt
Settlement_Description: First mention in a donation charter by Otto I in 941, but the settlement is probably older and developed from two villages.
Town_Description: Cochstedt was granted town rights in 1535, market rights were probably granted earlier.

name: Børglum
Settlement_Description: An important royal manor in the viking age and a Premonstratensian abbey and the diocese of Børglum or Vendsyssel in the middle ages.  It is uncertain when the abbey and later the diocese was established. The abbey is probably from around 1200, perhaps some decades earlier, and prior to 1220 the bishopric of Vendsyssel was also placed in Børglum. Throughout the Middle Ages, Børglum was a religious, political and economical center in Northern Jutland.
Fair_Description: In the middle ages an annual fair was held in Børglum. The age, character and date of the fair is uncertain. Presumably, an important fair in the region of Vendsyssel from the early middle ages onwards. In 1598 the fair was moved from its original location to a hill (Danish: Årslev høj), which also belonged to Børglum, by then a manor. In 1651 the fair was relocated to the town of Hjørring.

name: Vårdö
Settlement_Description: <b>Post house:</b> In 1638, the Royal Steward Bernhardt Steen von Steenhausen established six post houses in Åland, along the route from Stockholm to Turku. One of the post houses was located in Vårdö.

name: Schneiderkrug
Settlement_Description: The settlement is first mentioned in 1703.

name: Warnemünde
Settlement_Description: The settlement was probably founded by German settlers in the early 13th century. A "Ludolfus de Warnemunde" is first mentioned as Rostock councillor in 1237. The town Rostock acquired the harbour of Warnemünde in 1264, and the entire village in 1323. It is mentioned as borough ('flecken') in the 16th century.
Toll_Description: After Sweden had conquered Warnemünde in 1632, a toll was levied on seagoing ships. 3.5% of the value of the cargo was paid to Sweden, 1% to the Duke of Mecklenburg. Despite heavy protests from Rostock, where the seagoing trade was hindered by the toll, the toll remained in existence. It came to the Duke of Mecklenburg in 1714, and was finally abolished in 1748.
Harbour_Description: Located on one of the streams that connected the Warnow river and Breitling with the Baltic Sea, the harbour of Warnemünde was of primary importance for the town of Rostock, who acquired it in 1264. Around 1500, the Alter Strom through Warnemünde became the primary passage for seagoing ships. The settlement had its own shipping industry, but after conflicts with the Rostock skipper's guild in the 16th century, most skippers moved to Rostock, and the harbour of Warnemünde was predominantly used for fishing vessels.

name: Aggerbrücke
Toll_Description: A bridge toll at the bridge across the Agger of the Dukes of Berg is first mentioned in 1357. They promised to abolish the toll, but in later times it still exists. In the 16th century, the abbot of the monastery of Siegburg was responsable for the levying of the toll. A toll house still existed in 1805.
Bridge_Description: Bridge across the Agger between Troisdorf and Siegburg, first mentioned in 1357 in connection with the bridge toll.

name: Schwaan
Settlement_Description: A Slavic castle is mentioned around 1170. Next to it a German village developed; a parish priest is first mentioned in 1232.
Town_Description: Founded by the lords of Werle, first mentioned as oppidum in 1276. Town privileges were endorsed in 1308, 1526 and 1532.

name: Japenzin
Toll_Description: The toll in Japenzin was first mentioned in March 1301 and given to the town of Anklam on 15 September the same year.

name: Nykøbing Mors
Settlement_Description: Presumably a settlement with and urban character in the 13th century.
Town_Description: Nykøbing (Nova civitas) was characterized as a town for the first time in 1299, and was probably granted town privileges earlier in the 13th century. Dueholm Priory, a Knights Hospitaller monastery, was founded c. 1370 west of the town, and greatly influenced the town’s development during the medieval period. A mayor was first mentioned in 1419, and in 1460 previously granted town privileges were confirmed and expanded. The town benefited from the rich agriculture on the island of Mors and up until the 17th century fishing in Limfjorden.
Fair_Description: As the only town on the island of Mors, Nykøbing was important to the local market activities. Apparently the town held one annual fair, but the age and character of the fair is uncertain. The fair had a local character and took place on September 26, this was at least the situation in the early modern era.

name: Hovsør
Settlement_Description: Hovsør is first mentioned in 1374, but probably an older fishing village.
Town_Description: A borough around 1530, probably in 1532. This year the king promised tax exemption for a period of five years to Hovsør as well as freedom from toll in Denmark, expect for the Scania Market. Hovsør hereby appears to have been considered as a town, but in 1542 the privileges were lost. Hovsør benefited from rich fishing banks in Limfjorden, but also the export of oxen was important.
Harbour_Description: The character of the medieval harbour is not known. Probably a natural harbour within the bay area. During the 15th and 16th century some people moved from the neighboring town of Thisted to Hovsør because of the harbour.

name: Königsberg in Bayern
Toll_Description: Secondary station of safe conduct of Coburg. Revenues are known since 1484 and indicate high amounts of traffic in Königsberg.

name: Alt Wallmoden
Settlement_Description: First mentioned around 941. There existed a farm of bishop Meinwerk of Paderborn. A noble family of Wallmoden is first mentioned in 1154; around 1500 the place is mentioned as castle in the diocese of Hildesheim. In the 14th century, the addition "Alt" ('old') appears, to discern the settlement from the castle Neuwallmoden.

name: null
Bridge_Description: Mentioned as stone bridge (pons lapidus) in 1161.

name: Klietznick
Settlement_Description: First mentioned as belonging to the castle district of Jerichow in 1368.

name: Hobro
Settlement_Description: Based on the age of the church, Hobro was presumably a permanent settlement by the 12th century. The place name “Hobro” probably refers to a bridge across the narrow part of the bottom of Mariager Fjord, where the settlement was located, or perhaps a bridge across the nearby river, Onsild Å.
Town_Description: The place name “Hobro” is first mentioned on a guild seal from around 1300, and at this time Hobro was considered as a town. In 1421 a citizen of the town appeared in a document, and in 1471 Hobro was counted among the boroughs (Danish: Flække) of Jutland. In 1541 mayors and a town council were mentioned.   Older town privileges were confirmed in 1560. A town seal is known from 1584. The central motive of the seal is a bridge, which probably is a reflection of the bridge across Mariager Fjord, and its importance to the town. At this time Hobro was one of Jutland's poorest urban settlements after the Brigittine monastery in the neighboring town of Mariager, an important institution in Hobro as well, had been dissolved.
Fair_Description: The fair at the village of Glenstrup was relocated to Hobro in 1552, and in 1561 the markets previously held in Dybdal and Testrup were also moved to Hobro. This resulted in dissatisfaction among the local peasantry, and in 1578 one of the fairs was moved back to Testrup. In 1608, however, it was decided that all fairs within 2.5 miles of the town had to be held in Hobro. The fairs of Hobro were to be held on May 1th, September 17th and October 9th.

name: null
Bridge_Description: In 1546 an agreement was made between the town Schoonhoven and the lord of Brederode about the 'tolveer and bruggeld' at Meerkerk. The bridge was situated at Lakerveld (across the Oude Zederik). A tariff about the 'bruggeld' specifies persons, cattle corn, hemp and wood.
Ferry_Description: In 1546 an agreement was made between the town Schoonhoven and the lord of Brederode about the 'tolveer and bruggeld' at Meerkerk. The ferry was situated at Lakerveld (across the Oude Zederik).

name: null
Harbour_Description: Important harbour for salt from the local saltworks

name: null
Lock_Description: The weir for the water mill contained a passage for ships. Ships built in Wanfried could pass this downstream without problems, upstream however with great difficulty. A drawing of the passage from 1610 is kept in the Hessian State Archive in Marburg, 4 a Nr. 39/54.

name: Jever
Settlement_Description: First mentioned between 1011 and 1062. Originally possibly a fishing settlement of the Chauki, in the 10th or 11th century fortified with earthworks. In 1039 mentioned as mint of the House of Billung.
Town_Description: Jever was already mentioned as 'oppidum' in 1347 and had a seal. In 1536, the town was re-founded and fortified. The oldest town rights date from 1572.
Fair_Description: Around 1350, Jever is already mentioned as a market settlement. In the following period, its importance must have declined, as the fairs on the old market place are first mentioned again in 1535. In the town rights of 1572, fairs are mentioned on eleven Tuesdays each year and import tolls for these fairs are set. Next to these, there existed two horse fairs and fairs on Carnival and Christmas. In 1602, three additional horse fairs were added. Exact dates are only known from 1729.

name: Esens
Settlement_Description: A church was probably built around 1100, but the settlement is first mentioned only in 1300.
Town_Description: Town rights were probably granted between 1537 and 1540.
Fair_Description: The markets of Esens were provided with safe-conduct in 1440. In the description of Harlingerland by Balthasar Arends, the dates are specified on 14 days after Pentecost and St Bartholomew (called Magnus's fair). In 1572, a third fair was granted and in 1610 another four fairs. However, these disappeared again after a while.

name: Wittmund
Settlement_Description: A missionary church is mentioned in 884, which was demolished in 1164.
Town_Description: In 1567, the market settlement received town rights from the Countess Agnes von Rietberg, which it lost again in the 17th century.
Fair_Description: Market regulations for Wittmund are first known from 1607. Later, the most important markets are defined as the fairs of St John and Our Lady.

name: Dreileben
Settlement_Description: Mention in 996 in the properties that are given to St. Moritz' monastery in Magdeburg by Otto I. Since 1304 center of a small jurisdiction.
Toll_Description: In the course of the 16th century, the toll stations in Oebisfelde, Neuhaldensleben, Wolmirstedt, Dreileben, Wanzleben and Calbe complain that their income was reduced due to the toll exemption of Magdeburg.

name: null
Harbour_Description: In 1356 Weesp got toll-exemption in Holland, Zeeland en West-Frisia. In 1399 duke Albrecht granted Weesp together with Muiden toll-exemption at the tolls of Spaardam and Beverwijk. In 1401 the duke stated that the exemption at Spaardam was like granted to Amsterdam. The Kamper Pondtol (1439-41) mentions 29 skippers from Weesp. In the Enqueste of 1494 they claim to have had 30 'Rijn'(Rhine)ships at the time of Charles the Bold (before 1477) for trade to Deventer (wood) and Zeeland (salt) and now only two are left.

name: Neuenkrug
Settlement_Description: The inn ('krug') is mentioned in several travel accounts from 1425 onwards on the main route from Stade to Bremen. Commendone and Ruggieri mentioned in 1561 that there were only two beds.

name: Lenzen
Settlement_Description: Originally a Slavic castle mound where a battle took place in 929. A German settlement under the lords of Schwerin existed around 1220.
Town_Description: The Salzwedel town law was granted in 1237. Exemptions from toll payments in Brandenburg were granted in 1252. First mentioned as civitas or town in 1373.
Toll_Description: The toll in Lenzen is first mentioned in 1219, when the count of Schwerin acquired the castle as a fief. In 1237, Lübeck is exempted from the toll in Lenzen by the counts of Dannenberg, and once again in 1354 by the dukes of Mecklenburg. In 1411, the Mecklenburg part of the toll in Schnackenburg is moved to Lenzen. It is unclear if this means that a toll was also levied on shipping on the Elbe from this year, or if there was only a road toll in Lenzen. In 1558, the margrave of Brandenburg acquired the right to levy a grain toll on the Elbe as well as on the street.

name: null
Harbour_Description: In 1342 the river Meuse was diverted towards the town on instigation of the magistrate of Roermond to promote trade.

name: Uslar
Settlement_Description: Possibly already settled in prehistoric times. First mentioned as village in 1006-1007. It became a borough ('flecken') in the early 13th century.
Town_Description: First mentioned as "civitas" in 1269. The Göttingen town privileges were granted at an unknown date; reiterated in 1345.

name: Randers
Settlement_Description: King Canute the Holy (1080-1086) minted coins in Randers, which appear to have had an urban character at the end of the 11th century. The settlement was located in the bottom of Randers Fjord and a relatively easy place to cross the river of Gudenå.
Town_Description: In the end of the 12th century Randers had four paris churches and a urban character. Town council and town seal is known from around 1250. A Franciscan monastery was established already in 1236. Oldest known privileges granted by king Erik VI Menved (1286-1319) in 1302. First mention of  mayors in 1379, and of town hall in 1457. The medieval town fortification was rebuilt in 1535. In the 17th century Randers suffered from the plague, fires and the Dano-Swedish wars.
Fair_Description: Randers held several annual fairs from the early medieval era onwards. A couple of the fairs are well documented from the 16th century onwards, but their dates, age and character is, however, uncertain. In 1634 it was decided that two annual fairs were to be held in Randers, but prior to that the town already had at least two annual fairs. The fairs of Randers played a role in the export of oxen from Jutland.

name: Ringkøbing
Settlement_Description: Presumably, originally a fishing village and marketplace in the northeastern corner of Ringkøbing Fjord. Archaeological finds indicate a permanent settlement in the second half of the 13th century.
Town_Description: The urbanization of Ringkøbing was partly caused by the sanding up of the western mount of Limfjorden around the year 1100. Ringkøbing is first mentioned in the 14th century, perhaps already in 1325.  In 1368 Ringkøbing was characterized as “uillam”. Mayors and citizens (Danish: “bymænd”) first mentioned in 1440. In 1443 king Christoffer the Bavarian (1440-1448) confirmed and expanded existing town privileges. The older privileges are unknown, but were probably granted by king Valdemar Atterdag (1340-1375), and it is likely that Ringkøbing’s originally were granted town rights in the late 13th century. A town hall is mentioned for the first time around 1600. In 1656 Ringkøbing was described as a small town, with a few wealthy inhabitants. The town suffered heavily during the wars of the 17th century as well as growing challenges to sail into Ringkøbing Fjord from the North Sea.
Fair_Description: In 1608 Ringkøbing was granted the right to an annual fair on Saint Giles Feast (September 1th). Presumably the fair also took place in the late medieval period. In the second half of the 17th century two annual fairs were held in Ringkøbing.

name: Ebeltoft
Settlement_Description: Presumably a permanent settlement before or in the 13th century.
Town_Description: Granted town privileges by king Erik VI Menved (1286-1319) in 1319. Two years before, in 1317, the town was granted a town law. The law was a copy of the town law of Schleswig, which was used in several towns across Jutland. In the 15th century mayors, town court and town council were mentioned for the first time. First known town hall built in 1576. Throughout the medieval period and early-modern era Ebeltoft was a small town, which struggled with illegale trade in the region.
Fair_Description: In 1552 king Frederik II (1559-1588) moved three annual fairs from the settlement of Fuglslev to Ebeltoft. It is unknown when these small local fairs took place.

name: Crivitz
Settlement_Description: Originally a Slavic settlement and fortification, which became property of the Counts of Schwerin in the late 12th century. First mentioned in 1251.
Town_Description: A town was founded by the Count of Schwerin between 1251 and 1279. It is first mentioned as town in 1302. The town received Schwerin law. The local economy centred on agricultural produce.
Fair_Description: A fair on Sunday Letare in Crivitz is mentioned in an almanac printed in Neudamm (Dębno) in 1598.

name: Oude Haven
Harbour_Description: In 1349 the lord of Schoonhoven ordained the building of a sluice in the dam in the Oude Haven. This would have made a connection to the river Vlist and the Hollandse IJssel. But there is no proof that this plan was excecuted.

name: Dockenhuden
Settlement_Description: Farming village, merged with Blankenese in 1919

name: null
Harbour_Description: Harbour for traffic on the Alster river.

name: Hardegsen
Settlement_Description: The settlement is first mentioned between 1015 and 1036. In 1310, a castle is mentioned.
Town_Description: Town rights were allegedly granted by Duke Otto I the Evil of Brunswick-Lüneburg in 1383, although a charter is not known. Already two years before, Hardegsen is characterised as town. Burgomaster and town council are mentioned in 1409.
Fair_Description: A charter of the baker's guild from 1390 mentions two fairs in Hardegsen, on Sunday before the Ascension of Our Lady and Sunday before St Martin. On these days, bakers from other towns were allowed to offer their produce for sale in Hardegsen.
Toll_Description: A toll in Hardegsen is first mentioned in 1559.

name: Krummesser Baum
Settlement_Description: Watchtower in the Lübeck enclosure ('landwehr'), which was completed around 1300. It existed of a tower with three floors, a palisade, a boom barrier, and an inn. The tower was still existing in 1785.

name: null
Toll_Description: The toll on the Weser in Dörverden is first mentioned in the 1360s. In 1575, it is confirmed that Dörverden belongs to the Bishopric of Verden, although the toll is owned by the Count of Hoya. However, the toll is not mentioned in lists of Weser tolls from 1584 and 1597.

name: null
Toll_Description: The toll in Nienburg is mentioned in 1390 and 1563, in a Bremen complaint from 1584 and in a charter of the monastery Hardehausen from 1597. It was leased out in 1574 for 1000 Joachimsthaler.

name: Gerbstedt
Settlement_Description: Foundation of a nunnery in 985, which was later turned into a convent of Benedictine nuns. The nunnery converted to Protestantism in 1564 and existed until 1805. Since 1404 the settlement near the nunnery is referred to as a borough but it already owns a town hall.
Town_Description: Mentioned as oppidum in 1520. In 1530 town rights are granted by Karl V.
Fair_Description: With the awarding of town rights a fair is mentioned that is moved from its former location near the chapel at the Welfenholz.
Toll_Description: At the beginning of the 16th century the income from safe conduct is recorded.

name: Neundorf (Anhalt)
Toll_Description: The toll from Warmsdorf is moved to Neundorf in 1496. In 1537 the toll is moved again to Bernburg.

name: Engerhafe
Settlement_Description: Engerhafe was mentioned in the 1300 law of the region Brokmerland as 'wic', a settlement with special legal protection during market times. The village church dates from the 13th century.

name: Dreckburg
Settlement_Description: Around 1350, the provost of Paderborn Cathedral had a moated castle built at the gates of Salzkotten, which belonged to the archbishopric of Cologne (Dreckburg = Moorburg). Conflicts repeatedly arose between the two ecclesiastical territorial powers over the Salzkotten brine springs. The rectangular residential tower from the 14th century is now used for residential an cultural purposes.Excavations on the Dreckburg site have uncovered part of the Hellweg. The 7-metre-wide track still showed clear lanes. There was no artificial road surface, but there were accompanying side ditches.

name: Warthe
Settlement_Description: Around 1400, the surrounding countryside belonging to the city of Paderborn was completely surrounded by an enclosure. Approximately at this point there was a watchtower (which no longer exists). There was a hermitage here that served as a hospital for pilgrims and other travellers. In 1578, the hermit was forbidden to have an inn, a jug or any other "suspicious tail". In Prussian times, the toll for the Chaussee was collected here.

name: Gammel Rye
Settlement_Description: The Cisterciean monastery of Øm was founded in 1172. The settlement or village of Ry developed close to the monastery, and here a holy well and relikvies in the church of Saint Søren attracted many pilgrims. The settlement hosted the annual fair of the monastery of Øm, and developed an urban character during the late medieval period.
Town_Description: In 1408 land rent (Danish: grundskyld) was paid to the monastery.  In 1492 Ry was a separate judicial district (Danish: “birk”) and a citizen (Danish: bymand) of Ry is mentioned that same year. In the first half of the 16th century Ry was categorized as a borough (Danish: Flække).

name: Gnoien
Settlement_Description: Originally a Slavic settlement. The Lords of Werle founded a town here around 1250. First mentioned in 1257.
Town_Description: Foundation of a town by the Lords of Werle around 1240. Mentioned as civitas in 1290 with confirmation of the Rostock (i.e., Lübeck) town law. Town privileges have been renewed multiple times.
Toll_Description: A dam toll existed in Gnoien, from which the monastery Dargun was exempted in 1333.

name: Tribsees
Settlement_Description: The settlement developed out of a fortification of the Lords of Rügen. First documented in 1136, since the mid-13th century seat of the stewardship ('Vogtei') of Tribsees.
Town_Description: Town law granted between 1218 and 1267. In 1285 the Lübeck town law in the style of Rostock was ratified by Prince Witzlaw II.

name: Treffurt
Settlement_Description: First mention in 1104. The name of the settlement refers to three fords in the Werra river. The village developed next to the castle Normannstein, built in the 12th century, into a market borough ('Marktflecken').
Town_Description: Date of acquisition of town rights unknown. The settlement was probably fortified before 1336. In 1532 extended market rights were granted by Charles V.

name: Hohenwarthe
Settlement_Description: Between 1309 and 1314 archbishop Burchardt III founded a castle in Hohenwarthe and extracted toll on the Elbe, whereupon the castle was destroyed by Magdeburg citizens.

name: Stock
Ferry_Description: Already at the first mention of Wedel in 1212, a ferry is mentioned. It became an important crossing point for oxen from Denmark on the river Elbe. The transport of oxen through Wedel is attested from the second half of the 15th century. The ferry belonged to the manor Haseldorf, at the current Fährmannssand. Around 1500, the owner of Haseldorf received 6 shilling for every 20 ferried oxen. The remaining revenues belonged to the count of Schauenburg, who deployed 7-8 barges here in the 16th century. However, often the ferry in Zollenspieker was preferred by the oxen traders, due to high hay prices in Wedel and Blankenese and frequent complaints about the ill-treatment of the oxen by the Wedel ferrymen.

name: null
Harbour_Description: Connections with Bremen can be attested from the 13th century onwards. The existence of the "Hamelner Loch" upstream could have stimulated the shipping from Oldendorf.

name: null
Bridge_Description: In 1456 the council of Zerbst supported the construction of a bridge across the Saale in Calbe at the request of the archbishop of Magdeburg. It often had to be repaired or rebuilt after damage by flooding, among others in 1571. The bridge was destroyed by the Swedes during the Thirty Years' War in 1636.
Ferry_Description: Before and after the existence of the bridge, as well as during repairs, a ferry must have operated.

name: null
Ferry_Description: The town acquired the ferry across the river Trebel in 1285, which had previously belonged partly to Prince Wizlaw II of Rügen and partly to Heinrich von Werle. The ferry is mentioned in 1358 as place of an agreement between Brandenburg and Pomerania.

name: Altona
Settlement_Description: The settlement probably originated in the early 16th century as a fishermen's and craftsmen's settlement. The inn Altona was first mentioned in 1537. The settlement became a borough ('flecken') in 1604.
Town_Description: King Frederick III of Denmark granted town privileges on 23 August 1664, which included market rights (five horse fairs) and toll exemptions. This led to conflicts with neighbouring Hamburg.

name: Kloster Gröningen
Settlement_Description: Endowed by count Siegfried in 936. The monastary was run by monks from Corvey. Gröningen monastary belonged to Corvey monastary until the 17th century, even if the monastery proper was dissolved in 1550.

name: De Hongerige Wolf
Settlement_Description: Inn named 'Honrige Wolf' along the so-called 'Bourtangestraße'. It is unclear when this inn came into existence.

name: Uphusen (Emden)
Settlement_Description: The village is first mentioned in 1325, but its church dates from the second half of the 13th century.

name: Westerende Kirchloog
Settlement_Description: This place was first mentioned in 1408.

name: Rispel
Settlement_Description: The place was first mentioned in 1475.
Toll_Description: According to a 1640 complaint from Emden merchants visiting the fairs in Jever, the count of East Frisia had started to levy a toll on commodities in Rispel during the eleven market times in Jever about three years earlier. In 1648, renewed complaints attest that the fees had been raised and the toll was now also levied on cattle.

name: Friedeburg
Settlement_Description: Castle of the chieftain Fredo, later of the counts of East Frisia, which was built in 1359 and demolished in 1763. The attached settlement was originally called Endel.
Toll_Description: A transit toll was introduced by countess Theda of East Frisia at the Friedeburg in 1480; the inhabitants of Dornum were exempted from toll payments. A list of toll fees for various transported commodities from 1637 still exists.

name: Neuenburg
Settlement_Description: Castle, erected in 1462 by Count Gerd of Oldenburg to control the road to East Frisia.
Toll_Description: A toll station of the county of Oldenburg was installed in Neuenburg in 1613.

name: Bockhorn
Settlement_Description: First mentioned in 1220, and developed into a market borough in the 14th century.

name: Dringenburg
Settlement_Description: The settlement is preceded by a castle built in the first half of the 14th century. It was built by Count Konrad I of Oldenburg as a defence against the Frisians.

name: Wiefelstede
Settlement_Description: The settlement is first mentioned in 1059 and has the oldest Romanesque church of Ammerland.

name: Sandhorst
Settlement_Description: First mentioned between 822 and 872. Former summer residence of the Counts of East Frisia.

name: Rattelsdorf
Toll_Description: Secondary station of safe conduct of Coburg, located on the road between Coburg and Bamberg/Nuremberg. Accounts and revenues are known from 1527 onwards.

name: Cappel
Settlement_Description: The Premonstrensian nunnery Cappel was founded in 1139 at the latest by counts Bernhard and Hermann zur Lippe. It was turned into a protestant ladies' house in the 16th century.

name: Bytom Odrzański
Toll_Description: A toll station is mentioned in 1302.

name: Brockenstedter Mühle
Settlement_Description: The settlement is first mentioned in a record in 937. During the Late Middle ages the settlement is abandoned, although the village mill remains until the 1970s.
Toll_Description: In 1657 the toll station of the district of Mahndorf is supposed to be moved here.

name: null
Bridge_Description: A bridge was built in the 12th century, which connected the old town of Quedlinburg with its territories to the East. It made the detour via Ditfurt unnecessary.

name: Sønderborg
Settlement_Description: The settlement developed in the period 1170-1200 in the shadow of Sønderborg castle. The place name of Sønderborg mirrors the settlement's location on the southern part of the island of Als and the castle in relation to the settlement and later the town.
Town_Description: Sønderborg was controlled by different town lords, as it was both in the hands of various dukes and counts as well as kings of Denmark. In 1229, for example, count Albrecht of Orlamünde obtained the island of Als and hereby Sønderborg, by the Danish king Valdemar II (1202-1241). Uncertain when the town was granted town privileges, but probably in the 13th century. Existing privileges were confirmed by king Christian I (1448-1481) in 1461, and in 1487 a mayor was mentioned for the first time. The medieval town hall was replaced by a new town hall in 1611. Throughout the late medieval period and early-modern era Sønderborg struggled with illegal trade activities on the island of Als and conflicting interests with the neighboring towns of Aabenraa and in particular Flensburg. The town suffered heavily during the Dano-Swedish war in the late 1650ties.

name: Nordborg
Settlement_Description: Around 1150 the Danish king Svend Grathe built a castle on a small peninsula in Nordborg lake. In the following century a permanent settlement with an urban character developed around the castle. Nordborg, which was also known as “Købing”, was first mentioned in 1313, and characterized as a borough (Danish: Flække). The place name Nordborg reflects the settlement's location on the northern part of the island of Als. Traders and craftsmen lived in the settlement during the middle ages, but Nordborg was not given official trading privileges before 1680.

name: Hohe Brücke
Bridge_Description: A stone bridge ('Hohe Brücke' or 'Klaustorbrücke') across the Saale was constructed by the city council in 1172. It was demolished in 1840 and replaced by the Elisabethbrücke.

name: null
Toll_Description: A bridge toll is already mentioned in 1293, when monks from Nienburg were exempted. A regulation of safe conduct from 1563 specifies the bridge and road toll.
Bridge_Description: A Saale bridge in Bernburg is first mentioned in 1239 when it is specified that monks from Nienburg monastery are exempted from paying the bridge toll.

name: Bagband
Settlement_Description: The settlement was first mentioned in 1454, although the village church dates from the middle of the 13th century.

name: Aurich-Oldendorf
Settlement_Description: First mentioned in 1431, but the village church dates from the middle of the 13th century.

name: Booneschans
Settlement_Description: Small fortress ('schans') on the border between Groningen and East Frisia. There is unclarity about the date of its construction: 1587 according to some authors, but more likely is a construction around 1593, at the same time as Oudeschans and Bourtange.

name: Ditfurt
Settlement_Description: Former Saxon stronghold above the Bode ford. To the South, a Karolingian royal residence was established.
Toll_Description: Quedlinburg monastery profits from the toll at the Bode crossing in its village of Ditfurt.

name: Donnerschleuse
Lock_Description: The new Niederschleuse was constructed around 1451 (the old Niederschleuse was located near Anker). The lock was later known as Donnerschleuse, after multiple generations of lock keepers from the Donner family in the 17th century. A second lock, the lower Donnerschleuse, was built 200m downstream in the 18th century. Between both locks, the ford on the street between Hamburg and Lübeck was located.

name: null
Harbour_Description: In front of the gate named 'Sabelspoort', a jetty is visible on the map printed by Joan Blaeu in 1649. Blaeu's map is based on a map drawn ten years earlier by Nicolaas van Geelkercken. A harbour on this site only became possible after a meander in the Rhine was cut short in 1530.

name: Huissen
Settlement_Description: Earliest mention in 850-865, in a copy dated between 1170-1175.
Town_Description: Huissen is first mentioned as town in a charter from 1319, with Cleves town privileges. On 13 July 1348, count John of Cleves confirmed the privileges.
Fair_Description: In 1348 two fairs are mentioned, on the 3rd to the 4th Sunday of Lent, and on 13 July with a duration of 8 days before and after, and a weekly market on Thursday-Saturday. In 1584 four fairs are mentioned, on Monday after 10 August, 8 days after 25 November, Ash Wednesday, and on 12 July, with a duration of 2 days before and after for each fair.
Toll_Description: 1) The Rhine toll of the Count of Cleves was moved from Angeren to Huissen in 1242. In 1405, approx. 0.92 guilders ('Gulden') had to be paid for each fuder of wine, then 1 guilder ('Gulden') per fuder of wine in 1486. Annual revenues are known from 1419 onwards. The toll-account of 1578/'80 is analysed. In 1656, the toll was moved to Emmerich. In 1751 a new "Lizent zu Huissen" was founded for the sailing traffic that came from Nijmegen via the river Waal to Arnhem. This ended in 1816 as the Huissen and Malburgen area were incorporated into the Netherlands.2) The Count of Cleves also levied a land toll in 1312, which was pawned until 1418. Originally, the land toll was levied to grain, which was brought to the market in Arnhem. Tariffs and revenues are not known.

name: Krämerbrücke
Toll_Description: Toll collection point at the church of St Giles for the usage of the road and bridge.
Bridge_Description: The Krämerbrücke, first mentioned in 1117, is located at a former ford in the Gera river and was probably built by the Benedictine monks of the monastery of St Peter. The church of St Giles at the bridge head is already mentioned as chapel in 1110. Already in 1156 it is mentioned as built over with houses and shops. A new stone bridge was built in 1325 by the city council. Two wooden pedestrian bridges were built on both sides of the bridge in 1391 to increase its capacity. Today it is the longest bridge lined with houses in Europe.

name: Texel
Settlement_Description: Texel is a Dutch Wadden Island on which several settlements are located. Texel is first mentioned in a 1183-1195 copy from a document dating from 772 or 776.
Town_Description: Texel is a Dutch Wadden Island on which several settlements are located. The island in its entirety was granted town privileges on 26 March 1415 by William VI, count of Holland. Texel lost its town rights in 1426 (for joining the Hook side in the Hook and Cod wars). The privileges were re-granted in 1434, and were lost again in 1491. The town rights were once again restored in 1494.
Fair_Description: In 1383 (April 20) count Guy van Blois granted a free fair three days before and after St. John midsummer (June 24). The freedom of the market stretched from the new bridge till the house of Jan Scoemakers.

name: Bredstedt
Settlement_Description: Bredstedt was first mentioned in the so-called mainpiece in King Valdemar’s Cadastre from 1231, but archaeological finds indicate that the settlement is much older. A chapel was built in Bredstedt in 1462, and in 1510 Bredstedt became a parish. At this time Bredstedt was a village with a certain urban character, something which is reflected in a concentration of craftsmen in preserved tax lists from the years 1479 and 1483. Bredstedt was, however, not considered as a town, but the settlement was characterized as a borough (Danish: Flække/German: Flecken). It was not before 1580 that Bredstedt was allowed a weekly market day. Bredstedt benefited from a location at a section at Hærvejen/Ochsenweg, as well as shipping from the nearby coast.
Fair_Description: In 1530 two annual fairs were granted to Bredstedt. The two annual fairs are also mentioned in 1583. Thus, Bredstedt held two annual fairs from the 16th century. The character and dates of the fairs are, however, uncertain. Heinrich Rantzau mentions a fair in Bredstedt in his 1597 description of Schleswig and Holstein, but does not provide a date.

name: Nowa Sól
Settlement_Description: A salt refinery was founded in 1564.

name: Holzweißig
Toll_Description: Secondary station of safe conduct ('Beigeleitsstelle') of the department of Bitterfeld. Revenues are known since 1496, regulations ('Geleitsordnung') date from 1539/40 and 1550.

name: Soerel
Settlement_Description: According to seventeenth century maps, there was one farm in Soerel. This farm served as an inn, possibly at least from 1418 onwards. It was located on the intersection of two roads: the 'Amersfoortse Weg' between Zwolle and Amersfoort, and the 'Arnhemseweg' between Arnhem and Elburg. The map of the Veluwe by De Man from ca. 1810 shows an additional post house. From 1634 onwards, postillions made use of the land route between the inns 'De Zwarte Boer' and 'Het Soerel'.

name: Miłakowo
Settlement_Description: The place was first mentioned in 1314. A castle of the Teutonic Order was first mentioned in 1354, but has to be older.
Town_Description: First mentioned as town in 1323. The oldest town charter ('Handfeste') with Kulm town law was burned and thus re-issued in 1490 by Grand Master Hans von Tieffen.

name: Bad Frankenhausen
Settlement_Description: First mention before 900 as a Frankish settlement. Mention in a record by Otto III. (MGH DO III 305). Throughout the medieval ages exploitation of salt salines around the place, starting from 1074.

name: Artern
Settlement_Description: First mention in 775/786, when the chapter of St Wigibert in Hersfeld owned property in Artern. A castle at a crossing of the river Unstrut was built in the 12th century.
Town_Description: Town rights granted around 1346 by emperor Louis the Bavarian. Mentioned as civitas in 1430. Saltworks in the town are exploited since the mid-15th century.

name: Stadt Gernrode
Settlement_Description: First known through the castle of margrave Gero, but since his family died out, his seat was changed into a house of canonesses in 959. In 1604 the property was assimilated into imperial property.
Town_Description: The settlement near the nunnery is granted town rights by Abbess Anna of Plauen in 1549.

name: Woggersin
Settlement_Description: First mentioned in the donation charter for the foundation of the monastery Broda in 1170.

name: Weitin
Settlement_Description: First mentioned in the donation charter for the foundation of the monastery Broda in 1170.

name: Memleben
Settlement_Description: First mentioned before 775/786. Popular residency of the early Saxonian kings, dying place of Henry I in 936. Between 976 and 979 foundation of a Benedictine monastery with market, toll and mint rights. In 1015 all privileges and gifts were revoked and Memleben monastery was put under the jurisdiction of Hersfeld monastery. The monastery's history ends in the 16th century during the Peasant's war, when it was looted and afterwards given to the school in Pforta.

name: Schoonhoven
Settlement_Description: Schoonhoven is first mentioned in 1247. A castle was built nearby in the mid-thirteenth century. A hospital is first mentioned in 1325. A weighhouse is first mentioned in 1356, a cloth hall in 1360.
Town_Description: Schoonhoven was granted town(-like) privileges in several steps. It developed into a town from especially 1280 onward, when Floris V, count of Holland, granted town privileges on 3 May 1280. These rights were supplemented with additional rights over the years.
Fair_Description: The town-right of 1280 gave permission to levy market-tolls from visitors. The accouts of the count of Blois, preserved since 1356/'7, show three fairs in Schoonhoven: the 'Hoenkyns'-fair in May (likely in origin a poultry-market), a fair with Assumptio in the 'oest' (harvest): August 15 and a fair with Bamis: October 1.  Already in 1362 the second fair was moved on order of the count of Blois to St. Peters-eve advincula: August 1. As of this the merchants were toll-exempt this year. Since 1398/’9 the Hoenkynsmarkt is without income. In 1412 (June 27) count Willem VI relocated a fair for horses and cattle from Stolwijk (centrally in the Krimpenerwaard) to Schoonhoven. Both had a duration of 14 days and safe-conduct for the visitors. The horse-fair started July 4, the cattle-fair October 17, The comital accounts however, starting again in 1440, have tolls from the 'huentgents' fair of horses (!) and from a cattle-fair. Watertolls are collected on the fairs with St. Maartensday translatio (July 4) and St. Luke (Oct. 18). Since 1399 the dates of the fairs have been moved again. In 1535 the magistrate replied the lord of Batenborch that the two (!) market-tolls once were given by 'a lord of Blois' and that the data were: St. Maarten translatio eve in the summer (July 3) and St. Victorseve (Oct. 9), both fairs lasted 14 days. In 1535 the town obtained permission from king Charles V for a third fair for dairy products. The dates then are: 1) a horsefair starting June 1, 2) a dairy-fair starting 'op die octave van Sinte Pieters ende Pouwelsdach' (July 6), 3) a cattle-fair starting October 17, each for 14 days. After protest of Gouda regarding the new dairy-fair (mostly because of the date, just before the fair with St. John -July 25- in Gouda) even before the highest court in the Netherlands, the socalled 'Grote Raad van Mechelen', this new fair was first in 1540 (although without succes) and ultimately in 1546 abolished. In 1557 the statutes of the town mention a horse-fair on June 1, the 'other' fair on July 4 and the cattle-fair on October 12, each with a duration of 14 days.

name: null
Bridge_Description: In 1589 the wooden bridge across the Unstrut was renewed.

name: Auebrücke
Toll_Description: A toll on the bridge across the Weiße Elster is mentioned in 1152.
Bridge_Description: A bridge across the Weiße Elster is first mentioned in connection to a toll in 1152. A wooden bridge is mentioned in 1364, which was replaced by a stone bridge in 1535. It was demolished in 1886 to make way for the current bridge.

name: Głogów
Staple_Description: Staple for fish, salt and mill stones, confirmed in 1477 and 1511. The staple was under constant pressure from Frankfurt and Breslau, which tried to limit all traffic crossing the Oder river to both towns.

name: Ollendorf
Settlement_Description: First mentioned in the Codex Eberhardi of the imperial abbey Fulda, between 822 and 842. At the end of the Middle Ages the village served as an important crossing of roads and had several features of traffic infrastructure, such as an inn, a wagoner, a blacksmith and a toll house.
Toll_Description: The moated castle was a secondary station of safe conduct at the end of the Middle Ages or even after.

name: Beyersdorf
Toll_Description: Secondary station of safe conduct ('Beigeleit') of the district Bitterfeld. Revenues are known for the years 1530-1541. Beyersdorf is mentioned in the regulations of safe conduct ('Geleitsordnung') from 1539/40, but not in 1550, which suggests that the station was probably abolished in the meantime.

name: null
Harbour_Description: Large quantities of bay salt were transported to Neusalz via the Oder river, where they were refined and transported further on the landways to Silesia.

name: Vestervig
Settlement_Description: The Order of Saint Augustine Monastery, founded around 1110.
Fair_Description: The abbey of Vestervig was central to market activities in the region of Thy. During the medieval period, the monastery held several annual fairs, which also to some extent attracted traders from other parts of Denmark as well as foreigners. In the aftermath of the Danish reformation in 1536, when the monastery was dissolved, three annual fairs were moved from Vestervig to the town of Thisted. In 1573, however, all three fairs were moved back to Vestervig, which by then was a royal estate.

name: Roßleben
Settlement_Description: First mention in the record book of Hersfeld monastery from 830 - 850. It was granted town rights only in 1999.<br/>In 1140 an Augustinian monastery was founded and gained some meaning during the middle ages, it was converted into a convent of Cistercian nuns before 1263 until it slowly declined in the 16th century. The remaining monastery buildings were destroyed during a fire in 1686.

name: Eigenrieder Warte
Settlement_Description: Watchtower to the West of Mühlhausen, controlling the passage through the Mühlhäuser Landgraben, erected in the 14th century.

name: Sollstedter Warte
Settlement_Description: Watchtower of the defensive system around Mühlhausen ('Mühlhäuser Landgraben'), which was established in the mid-14th century.

name: Horsmarer Warte
Settlement_Description: Watchtower, established during the construction of the Mühlhäuser Landgraben.

name: Wietzendorf
Settlement_Description: First mentioned in 1231, when Wietzendorf became its own parish. According to a 1438 register, there were 20 farms in the village.

name: null
Ferry_Description: Ferry to Artlenburg, first mentioned 1181. See Artlenburg for more details.

name: Tellmer
Settlement_Description: The village was first mentioned in 866.

name: Waren
Settlement_Description: Originally a Slavic fishing village, first mentioned in 1218, where a castle was built as the administrative centre of the land of Warne by the Lord of Werle.
Town_Description: Lord Nikolaus I of Werle founded the town with Schwerin town law between 1260 and 1270. It is mentioned as civitas in 1292 and as oppidum in 1331.

name: Lexkesveer
Toll_Description: The Market toll "Markt- or Mercktol" or "Springtol" of Lexkesveer, a toll for sailing transport was levied every year from July 25th (St. Jacob) during 21 days by the toll employee from the Great Gueldres toll in Arnhem. The origin of this toll is not quite clear. Probably, it is the continuation of tolls near the Medieval ferriage or ferry of Lexkes where toll was levied for the Wageningen market tolls. About 1450 and about 1500 these tolls are documented in two 'Tolboucxkens' in which the tarifs of a lot of Rhine tolls are noted. The first period the toll was levied from 14 days before until 14 days after St Johns day, Midsummer. The second period the toll was levied from 10 days before St Jacobs day until 10 days after.  In 1538 a part of the income of this tolls was donated by Duke Willem van Gulik to the town of Wageningen. In 1782 only the second period is still mentioned.Toll registers of this toll are saved in Gelders Archief, 0012 Gelderse Rekenkamer for the years 1739-1774, 1790, 1793 and 0016 Gewestelijke besturen in de Bataafs-Franse tijd for the years 1794 - 1797.
Ferry_Description: A ferry across the Nederrijn is first mentioned in an account from Nijmegen in 1426. It was owned by Nijmegen and Wageningen in the 15th century.

name: Rengelröder Warte
Settlement_Description: Watchtower west of Heiligenstadt, controlling traffic in the Leine valley.

name: Hendungen
Fair_Description: Emperor Maximilian granted three fairs to Hendungen in 1498, on Carnival, St Peter and Paul's Day and Sunday before St Burkhard's Day.

name: Camsdorfer Brücke
Toll_Description: A bridge toll on the Camsdorfer Brücke is first explicitly mentioned in 1480. Possibly the revenues listed in the safe conducts accounts of the district Burgau-Jena in Camsdorf from 1539/40 refer to a fee on the bridge.
Bridge_Description: After the course of the Saale moved to the East in the mid-14th century, a new bridge with seven arches was built in stone between 1377 and 1406. Two additional arches were built in 1575. The bridge was destroyed in the Thirty Years' War in 1637, provisionally restored in wood and destroyed again by floods in 1655, after which it was rebuilt in stone. The bridge was replaced by a concrete construction in 1912.

name: Poitzen
Settlement_Description: First mentioned in the first half of the 15th century. An earlier mention as Pochedissen from 1252 is uncertain.

name: Trauen
Settlement_Description: First mentioned in a register of the diocese of Verden of ca. 1252.

name: Toppenstedt
Settlement_Description: First mentioned in a register of the diocese of Verden of ca. 1252.

name: Sahrendorf
Settlement_Description: First mentioned in a tithe register of Verden from ca. 1252. In 1275, the settlement consisted of 4 farms and a cottage. In the late 15th century, the village was deserted and resettled by the monastery of St Michael in Lüneburg.

name: null
Bridge_Description: A bridge across the Sieg river is first mentioned in 1343.

name: Hanstedt I
Settlement_Description: The settlement was first mentioned in the register of possessions of the monastery of Corvey between 822 and 876. It was also called Hansted on the Schwienau ('Hanstede uppe der Swynouwe') to discern it from other Hanstedts in the region.

name: Lebbin
Settlement_Description: First mentioned in the donation charter for the foundation of the monastery Broda in 1170.

name: Malchin
Settlement_Description: A German settlement was founded by the Lords of Werle around 1220 near a Slavic fishing settlement, first mentioned in 1215.
Town_Description: First mentioned as civitas in 1236. On 7 April the same year, lord Nikolaus von Werle granted Schwerin town rights. Town walls and gates are mentioned in the 1330s.

name: Eisfeld
Settlement_Description: First mentioned in 802-817 as Asifelde. It consisted of a village and a Frankish manor in the valley of the Werra.
Town_Description: The old town was characterised as a borough ('oppidum') in 1319. In 1323 king Ludwig the Bavarian gave permission to construct a town wall around the new town. Market privileges were granted in 1331. Since 1342 the town had Schweinfurt or Frankish town rights and was referred to as "civitas".
Toll_Description: Eisfeld was an important toll station and a secondary station of the safe conduct of Coburg on the road between Nuremberg and Erfurt.
