Revenues of a toll on wagons are known for the years 1485-1550. Tariffs are recorded in regulations of safe conduct from 1666. Furthermore a "small toll" or road toll was collected by the town itself.

name: Oberohe
Settlement_Description: The settlement Ohe is first mentioned in 1450; the part Oberohe ('upper Ohe') in 1668.

name: Rekottila (Paimio)
Settlement_Description: <b>Post house:</b> In 1638, the Royal Steward Bernhardt Steen von Steenhausen established a post house in the village of Rekottila in Paimio. It also served as the constable's house.

name: Oudenbosch
Settlement_Description: Earliest mention in 1275 as a settlement in the Baerlebosch forest. When another settlement Nieuwenbosch was founded in the 14th century, the older settlement became known as Oudenbosch. Between 1421 and 1621 but possibly longer, there was an inn on what's now called de markt.

name: Langendorf
Settlement_Description: First mentioned in 1279. From 1314 the village belonged to Stralsund.

name: Löbnitz
Settlement_Description: First mentioned as part of the name Godeschalcus de Lobeniz in 1319.

name: Kelbra
Settlement_Description: First mention of the church in Kelbra in 1093. In the 10th century a moated castle was built. A Cistercian nunnery was founded in 1251, and destroyed during the Peasants' War in 1525.
Town_Description: First mention as an "oppidum" in 1351, first mention of councillors in 1352.
Fair_Description: Kelbra owned two fairs "since times of old" on St Bartholomew and St George.

name: Engenstein
Settlement_Description: A castle controlled the "High Road" in the Thuringian Forest since the 14th century, first mentioned in 1311. End of the area in which horse hauling services ('Vorspanndienst') were offered from Eisfeld. Location of one of the oldest inns within the department of Eisfeld (surviving date on the building: 1587).

name: Heiligkreuzbrücke
Bridge_Description: At the location of a ford in the Itz river, a wooden bridge was constructed in 1398. It was replaced by a stone bridge in 1465, which was destroyed by floods in 1552. A new bridge was built soon after and again in 1618. It was replaced by a concrete bridge in 1955/56.

name: null
Bridge_Description: The bridge across the Schleuse near Kloster Veßra is mentioned in the safe conduct regulations of Coburg from 1492 as the end of the safe conduct.

name: Buttelstedt
Settlement_Description: First mentioned before 775/786. There was a castle, which is mentioned in 1281, and a market.
Town_Description: The landgraves of Thuringia granted Buttelstedt town privileges most probably before 1334. In 1454 the town possessed the town law of Weißensee. The town is situated at a crossing of the Via Regia, which moves from West to East, and the salt road, which moves from North to South. As a result, the town developed facilities such as a law court, an escort building and a hospital.
Toll_Description: In 1403 the safe conduct of Buttelstädt was sold for one year. Revenues are recorded since 1511. It was a station of safe conduct for Erfurt, as shown in the registry of safe conduct from 1533. It was the easternmost Ernestinian station of safe conduct and the only one between Erfurt and Leipzig.

name: Laeva
Settlement_Description: Manor and village were mentioned in 1295, a hamlet ('Hof') in 1645.

name: Oddesund Nord
Ferry_Description: The age and character of the ferry across the narrow strait is uncertain. A ferry is mentioned in 1578, but is probably significantly older. It was also possible to cross the strait using a ford, but according to a document from 1574, this could be very dangerous. In the later middle ages and early modern era oxen from the region of Thy was exported to the markets in Holstebro, and from there taken further south. In the 16th century the income from the ferry was important to the stewards (Danish: lensmænd) of Ørum.

name: Anna
Settlement_Description: The oldest church in whose proximity the village settled can  be dated to the 17th century.

name: Toolse
Settlement_Description: The Teutonic Order built a castle ('Vredeborch') here in 1471 to protect the harbour against pirates.

name: Piltene
Settlement_Description: The castle was first mentioned in 1309. In 1329, a fortified borough ('Hakelwerk') was built.
Town_Description: Piltene received town rights by Riga in the 15th century.

name: Bad Bibra
Settlement_Description: First mention in the Breviarium Sancti Lulli from 775/786 as Bibaraho. A castle existed since Carolingian times. A Benedictine monastery was founded in 963, which was converted into a convent of Augustinian canons in 1124. The settlement developed into a borough ('Flecken'), which acquired market rights in 1124. It was fortified with a wall in the 15th century, but only acquired town rights in 1829.

name: Kruisstraat
Settlement_Description: First mentioned in 1565. The hamlet is named after its location on the crossing of two roads.

name: Sønder Aggersund
Ferry_Description: One of the most important ferry connections across Limfjorden, which was located at one of the most narrow parts of the fjord. The age and character of the ferry is uncertain, but most likely established in some form during the Viking age. During the late medieval period the ferry across the narrow strait of Aggersund was central to export of oxen from the regions of Thy and Vendsyssel. The ferry was, for example, used by the nobleman Mouritz Nielsen Gyldenstierne in the 1490ties. In the late 16th century 6-7 ferrymen living of the northern shore were responsible for the ferry connection.

name: Simested bro
Bridge_Description: The age and character of the bridge across the river of Simested Å is uncertain. However, remains of an advanced medieval stone bridge were located in 1900. The bridge played a central role in the export of oxen from northern parts of Jutland.

name: Klein Bengerstorf
Settlement_Description: Bengerstorf is first mentioned as Bunsertorpe in the Ratzeburg tithe register of 1230. In a register from 1453 we find for the first time a distinction between the two parts of the village, which became known as Groß and Klein Bengerstorf since 1462. Klein Bengerstorf was probably the original Slavic settlement.

name: Anklam
Settlement_Description: Newly founded around 1242-43, systematically built near a river crossing.
Town_Description: First mentioned as town in 1264, when its citizens were exempted from all tolls in Pomerania. Exact date of acquisition of town privileges unknown, but Duke Bogislaw IV confirmed the rights granted by his father in 1278. The Lübeck town law is certainly attested from 1292.
Toll_Description: In 1286 the town of Malchin received a reduced tariff of the toll in Anklam and tolls elsewhere in Pomerania, which should not be higher than the toll in nearby Demmin. In 1326 the town Altentreptow received excemption from the tolls in Anklam and Demmin from Duke Otto I of Pomerania.
Staple_Description: In 1579, Anklam acquired the right to force merchants to offer their commodities on the local markets for two hours; confirmed in 1679.

name: Nermsdorf
Toll_Description: A secondary station of safe conduct ('Beigeleit') of Buttelstädt in Nermsdorf appears in accounts from 1532 onwards. Separate regulations ('Geleitsordnung') for Nermsdorf are recorded in 1557.

name: Leutra
Toll_Description: Secondary station of safe conduct ('Beigeleit') of the district Burgau-Jena, which first appears in complaints from 1539 that wagons with wood circumvent the safe conduct of Burgau and travel via Leutra instead. Revenues are known since 1541/42.

name: Nesselhof
Settlement_Description: The hospital Nesselhof was founded by the Lazarist Gottfried Walldorf in 1290.

name: Ringsted
Settlement_Description: The place of the provincial assembly (Danish: Landsting) of Zealand and surrounding islands such as Falster, Lolland and Møn. Possible that the town developed in the shadow of a 11th century monastery, but exactly when and how Ringsted was founded is uncertain. It appears obviously, however, that Ringsted was a permanent settlement with an urban character during the 11th century.
Town_Description: As home to the provincial assembly (Danish: landsting) Ringsted was one of the political and juridical centres in the Danish kingdom. Presumably, a Benedictine monastery was founded around 1080, and in 1135 king Eric II Emune (1134-1137) granted the monastery the annual town tax (Danish: Midsommergæld) of Ringsted. A town hall and mayors were mentioned for the first time in 1388, and the oldest known privileges were granted by king Christoffer the Bavarian (1440-1448) in 1441. There is, however, little doubt that Ringsted was granted town rights long before this, probably in the 13th century. In the later middle ages the development of Ringsted stagnated. During the second half of the 16th century the town was devastated by fire on several occasions, and Ringsted also suffered during the Dano-Swedish wars of the following 16th century.
Fair_Description: Due to its central location on the island of Zealand and its political importance Ringsted was also an important market town. Several fairs took place in Ringsted, and these market activities probably date back to the late Viking age. However, the fairs in Ringsted are not mentioned in the written sources before the late medieval period. Horses appear to have been an important commodity at the fairs. Although all the fairs in Ringsted had a local character, they were important on the island of Zealand. In 1516 king Christian II (1513-1523) allowed only four annual fairs on the island of Zealand. A fair in Ringsted was one of these legal fairs. The effect of the king’s initiative is, however, uncertain, as other fairs at least in time continued

name: Oberschleuse
Lock_Description: The (little) Oberschleuse ('upper lock') between the Mölln lake and the Stecknitz river was also known as Erichschleuse, probably after Duke Erich I (1296-1361) of Lauenburg. It is first mentioned in 1336 and therefore the oldest of the three locks in the Stecknitz. A second lock, the "large" Oberschleuse, located ca. 420m from this one, the year of construction is unknown, but it was reconstructed in 1614.

name: Kemnade
Settlement_Description: The monastery of canonesses Kemnade was founded between 959 and 965. The monastery became part of the Benedictine order in 1147. Abolished in 1584.

name: null
Harbour_Description: The barges of the skippers on the Stecknitz canal moored in Lübeck on the quay between the Holsten bridge and Petersgrube. This part of the quay was known as Salzmarkt (salt market) in the 15th to 17th century, after the main commodity shipped on the canal. On the opposite shore we still find the Salzspeicher (salt storehouses) that served as temporary storage for the salt cargoes.

name: Zienburger Schleuse
Settlement_Description: Around the middle of the 15th century, an inn was built at the lock, where beer was served and skippers could spend the night.
Lock_Description: The flash lock connected the Stecknitz canal, dug between 1391 and 1398 by the city of Lübeck, with the Delvenau river.

name: Seeburger Schleuse
Settlement_Description: An inn was built around the middle of the 15th century, where beer was served and skippers on the canal could spend the night.
Lock_Description: Flash lock in the Delvenau river, built during the construction of a canal between the Stecknitz and Delvenau by the city of Lübeck in 1391-1398.

name: Büchener Schleuse
Lock_Description: Flash lock in the Delvenau, built to improve the navigability of the river during the construction of the canal between the rivers Stecknitz and Delvenau by the city of Lübeck in 1391-1398.

name: Niebuhrschleuse
Lock_Description: Flash lock in the Delvenau river, built to improve the navigability of the river during the construction of a canal between the rivers Stecknitz and Delvenau by the city of Lübeck in 1391-1398. The name is derived from the family of lock masters who operated the lock between 1551 and 1725.

name: Dückerschleuse
Lock_Description: Flash lock in the Delvenau river, built to improve navigability of the river during the construction of a canal between the rivers Stecknitz and Delvenau by the city of Lübeck in 1391-1398. It is the only lock of the river that still exists. The name is derived from lock master Hans Düker in the first half of the 17th century.

name: Frauweiderschleuse
Lock_Description: As part of the construction of a canal between the Stecknitz and Delvenau rivers by the city of Lübeck in 1391-1398, the mouth of the Delvenau in the Elbe was moved as well. The Vroweder lock was built in 1396 to maintain enough water depth in the Delvenau during low tides on the Elbe.

name: null
Bridge_Description: A bridge across the Stecknitz near Krummesse is first mentioned in 1469; it was repaired in 1614. During reconstructions of the road from 1650, the bridge was temporarily replaced by a ferry. A bridge is attested again in 1655.

name: null
Toll_Description: A bridge toll is introduced in 1588. The first two years, the revenues were used to cover the construction costs of the bridge; afterwards, half of the toll was paid to the duke of Saxony-Lauenburg, the other half was used for maintenance of the bridge. Toll tariffs are known from 1592 and 1627.
Bridge_Description: A bridge across the Ratzeburg lake is already mentioned in connection to the castle in documents from the 13th century. This was a narrow bridge for pedestrians; wagons with cargo had to go around the lake or be carried across with ships. In 1588-91, a new wider bridge was constructed, which allowed two horse-drawn wagons to pass each other. The bridge was replaced by a stone causeway in 1847.

name: Georgenthal
Settlement_Description: Foundation of a monastery on the heights of the Georgenberg in 1143, which was moved to the valley between 1160 and 1190. During the Peasant's war the convent fled to Gotha and the monastery was used as a quarry. In 1531 the monastic properties were given to the administration ('Kammer') and a department ('Amt') was formed.
Toll_Description: In 1637 the safe conduct from Tambach is moved to the village of Georgenthal.

name: Osterberg
Settlement_Description: First mentioned in 1251. In 1410 a monastery was founded in Osterberg.

name: null
Bridge_Description: A bridge across the Saale in Burgau was built by Hans Münch von Wurghausen in 1491. Three arches were added in 1534. In 1544 the bridge collapsed and traffic was redirected via Camsdorf. The Swedes destroyed the bridge during the Thirty Years' War in 1637. It was only restored with seven arches in 1744.

name: Hammbrücke
Bridge_Description: The bridge across the Schmalfelder Au is first mentioned in 1650.

name: null
Bridge_Description: The bridge across the Krückau in Elmshorn was first mentioned in 1386.

name: null
Bridge_Description: The stone bridge and causeway at the mill in Schwartau are mentioned in 1475 and were mended on various occasions in the 17th century.

name: Großenbroderfähre
Ferry_Description: Ferry to Fehmarn, first mentioned in 1361.

name: Herrenfähre
Ferry_Description: A ferry owned by the count of Holstein was first mentioned in 1190; it could be acquired by Lübeck temporarily in 1247, and definitively in 1329.

name: Wijk bij Duurstede
Settlement_Description: First mentioned in a eleventh-century copy from a document from 948.Settlement history in this region goes back to Roman times, however. Romans built a 'castellum' (fort) in the region. In the Caroligian era an international trade hub, called Dorestad, was located in the area. An enormous amount of archeological evidence from the Dorestad period has been found. Dorestad was first mentioned on paper in 695 and dissappeared from the map in the ninth century (after 843). In 948 a 'villa' is indicated as having been known as 'Dorestad' but now being called 'Wijk'. A chapter in the church is known for the years 1365-1811. A hospital is first mentioned in 1394.
Town_Description: Wijk bij Duurstede was granted town privileges on 12 March 1300 by Gijsbrecht II, lord of Abcoude and Wijk.
Fair_Description: In 1160 a judge for the fairs is mentioned. The municipal rights of 1300 mention a fair and a weekly market, the fair is three days before and after 'Elfduizendmaagdendag' ('Eleven thousand virginsday'= St. Ursula= Oct. 21). In 1406 (Sept. 1)  Willem van Abcoude granted his town Wijk again a fair on Elfduizendmaagdendag, 14 days after St. Gallen (sic: =Oct. 16, can not be right). In 1447 the date is: on the Monday after St. Gallen, in 1484 the Monday after St. Dionysius (Oct. 9). In 1452 Wijk and Amersfoort agreed mutually not to collect toll or 'weggeld' (taxes on the roads or gates).In 1494 (May 20) the bishop of Utrecht granted two fairs: with St. Joris (April 23) and four days before St. John Baptist midsummer (June 24) with freedom three days before and after. Starting 1529 a toll on horses is found in the accounts of the steward of the landlord. In 1597 the dates of four fairs are: 1) three days before and after the second Sunday after St. John (June 24), duration one week, 2) a horse-fair with St. Joris, 3) three days before St. John midsummer, 4) a cattle-fair on te Monday after St. Dionysius.

name: Bad Lauterberg
Settlement_Description: The settlement acquired its name from a castle that is first mentioned in 1183. However, the settlement only developed in the second half of the 15th century with the growth of mining activities. Lauterberg acquired mining privileges ('bergfreiheit') in 1521, but never developed into a mining town ('bergstadt'). In the 17th century, it was a borough ('flecken') with various privileges.
Fair_Description: Lauterberg acquired the right to organise two fairs in 1619.

name: Gouwsluis
Toll_Description: A toll was levied at the Gouwsluis by the lord of Wassenaar, burgrave of Leiden. A tariff dated 1339 is preserved and edited and mentions 'Alfen' as toll place. A tariff for the Hansa is dated 1454 and edited. Another unedited tariff from 1527 includes a list of toll-exempted places. Yet another unedited tariff is dated 1551. Accounts (some incomplete) are preserved for a range of years dating 1547-1580. For a large part of the 16th century, the toll was levied in Gouda.
Lock_Description: The connection between the Gouwe and Rijn rivers is first mentioned in 1244. A flash lock must have existed here around the middle of the 13th century and is first mentioned in 1284. A second pound lock was built next to the old one in 1562 to increase the capacity of the system.

name: null
Toll_Description: After the reconstriction of the bridge, the builder, knight Jürgen of Waldenfels is granted the former ferry fee as bridge toll in 1459. After 1575 the bridge toll is abolished and the maintenance of the bridge and dam had to be paid from the income of the regular horse- and walking fee ('Pferd- und Fußzoll').
Bridge_Description: A crossing of the Havel existed since Slavic times. In 1244 the bridge near Plaue was destroyed during an attack of Magdeburg on Brandenburg and not reconstructed until 1459.
Ferry_Description: After the destruction of the bridge in 1244, a ferry was used as replacement.

name: Brehna
Settlement_Description: The settlement probably derives from a Slavic-Sorbic settlement with a castle. A village developed near the castle and is first mentioned in 1142. A monastery was founded in 1201.
Town_Description: An exact date of the acquisition of town rights in unknown. The settlement is referred to as town since 1274 and was fortified and expanded.
Fair_Description: From 1624-28 Leipzig and Brehna argued over the requested fairs in Brehna; only when Brehna promised to only hold rural fairs ('Landjahrmarkt') and to never establish a staple or depot, the quarrel ended.
Toll_Description: Secondary station of safe conduct ('Beigeleitsstelle') of the department of Bitterfeld. Revenues are known since 1484, regulations ('Geleitsordnung') date from 1539/40 and 1550.

name: null
Ferry_Description: A ferry in Zwijndrecht is first mentioned in 1332.

name: Scharzfels
Settlement_Description: The castle Scharzfels was first mentioned in 1131 and belonged to the Dukes of Brunswick-Lüneburg. It was destroyed by French troops in 1761.
Toll_Description: Below the Scharzfels castle, a toll was levied by the lords of Hohnstein. Citizens from Osterode were exempted from toll payments in 1465, and in 1521 all persons who worked in the Count's mines. The toll was discontinued in 1851. According to Herbst, there was also a toll station in the neighbouring village Scharzfeld, but he does not provide a source for this statement.
Bridge_Description: A bridge over the Oder existed presumably already in the 13th century.

name: Święciechowa
Toll_Description: Mentioned as toll station on the street to Poznań in 1294.

name: Roitzsch
Toll_Description: Secondary station of safe conduct ('Beigeleit') of the district Bitterfeld. Revenues are known from 1528, first in combination with Brehna, but from 1536 separately. Regulations ('Geleitsordnung') date from 1539/40 and 1550.

name: Schmiedehausen
Toll_Description: A safe conduct for wine ('Weingeleit') in Schmiedehausen appears in accounts of the district ('Amt') Camburg between 1548 and 1552, with low revenues.

name: null
Toll_Description: Until 1529 one Bohemian heller was paid for a bushel of grain. The price was afterwards raised to one Bohemian penny. A report from 1577 states that the lords of Anhalt had doubled the toll tariffs in Roßlau. The toll is also mentioned in four travel accounts of the skipper Gottfried Kleeditz from Pirna from 1671-1674.
Bridge_Description: In 1437 there was a first unsuccessful plan to build a bridge across the Elbe near Roßlau. A bridge was finally built in 1583. It was destroyed during the Thirty Years' War in 1631 and only rebuilt in 1680.
Ferry_Description: The Elbe ferry near Roßlau is mentioned in 1349. In 1407 the archbishop of Magdeburg destroyed the mill, the bridge across the Mulde river and the ferry across the Elbe river.

name: null
Ferry_Description: Since 1362 the ferry across the Elbe is first attested, although it probably existed before. In 1447 the castle and town of Aken are pawned, including the toll and ferry. As the result of a flooding, the Elbe couldn't be crossed at Aken in 1433.

name: Magdeburger Warte
Settlement_Description: Watchtower in the defensive enclosure ('landwehr') of Helmstedt, built before 1252.

name: Bad Sachsa
Settlement_Description: The settlement came into being next to the castle Sachsenstein, which was destroyed in 1074. The settlement is first mentioned in 1219.
Town_Description: An exact year in which the settlement became a town is not known. It was mentioned as a borough ('flecken') in 1432; a first town seal is known from 1525.

name: null
Toll_Description: A tariff from the toll dated 1392 is edited. Exempt were a.o. Brussels, Antwerp, Bruges, Damme, Sluis, Leuven and Aachen.

name: Kölleda
Town_Description: Granted town rights in 1392. The settlement owned market rights already before that year.

name: Siestarjoki
Settlement_Description: <b>Inn:</b> Joutselkä Inn moved to Siestarjoki in 1607 and back in 1642 the latest.

name: Riepenburg
Settlement_Description: The toll station and the ferry of Eislingen were protected by the castle Riepenburg, which was consrtucted in the mid-13th century. Since 1455, it is also known as Zollenspieker after the toll station. Because of relocation of the mouth of the Ilmenau, Riepenburg castle was demolished in 1512; possibly, its stones were used for the construction of the new toll station.
Toll_Description: Toll on the Elbe river of the dukes of Lauenburg, first mentioned in Krauel in 1216; the toll station Eyslinghe is first mentioned in 1252, from 1455 it is also known as Zollenspieker. According to a list of toll fees from 1278, Lüneburg was partially exempted from toll payments. The toll was acquired by Hamburg and Lübeck in 1420, who did not acknowledge the privileges of Lüneburg. Subsequently, a project was started by Lüneburg to dig a canal between the Ilmenau and the Elbe near Laßrönne to circumvent the toll station, with limited success. The toll station was moved west in the 16th century after a relocation of the mouth of the Ilmenau river (see Zollenspieker).
Ferry_Description: A ferry at the toll station Eislingen to Stöckte is first mentioned in 1252. It was moved to Zollenspieker/Hoopte when the toll station was relocated in the 16th century.

name: Stöckte
Settlement_Description: First mentioned in a register of the diocese of Verden from c.1252.
Ferry_Description: Ferry to Riepenburg that was first mentioned in 1252. In the 16th century it was moved to Hoopte / Zollenspieker due to the relocation of the Ilmenau estuary.

name: Gronau (Leine)
Settlement_Description: Originally there existed a castle of the bishop of Hildesheim and a settlement (Empne) on the shore of the Leine, which was destroyed during a feud in 1279. The settlement was moved to a river island and reconstructed as the planned town Gronau, first mentioned as such in 1298.
Town_Description: In 1298, bishop Siegfried II of Hildesheim founded the new planned settlement Gronau. The settlement is characterised as town from the start. Its predecessor Empne had already been characterised as "civitas" around 1228.
Fair_Description: According to a 1593 register of the house of Gronau, a fair took place on Sunday Oculi. On this day, a toll was levied of one Goslar penny for all who bought commodities at the market, with the exception of nobles.

name: Ilsenburg
Settlement_Description: A castle in Ilsenburg is given to the bishop of Halberstadt in 998, which is converted to a Benedictine monastery in 1003 and 1018. After its destruction during the peasant's war, the monastery is reconstructed and used as a residence by lords and officials.

name: null
Bridge_Description: A bridge across the Rhume is already mentioned in 1260.

name: null
Bridge_Description: A bridge across the Mulde river is already attested in a contract between Nienburg monastery and the Ascanians from 1239. Around 1400 there was a permanent bridge crossing the Mulde in Dessau.

name: null
Bridge_Description: A bridge across the Mulde between Roßlau and Dessau was constructed in 1584 and destroyed during the Thirty Years' War in 1642. It was only rebuilt in 1680.

name: Lukaszoll
Toll_Description: According to 18th-century maps, the toll station in Vienenburg was located at the crossing of the "high street" between Harzburg and Vienenburg and the "old street" between Oker and Stapelburg. The toll privilege was granted in 1323 (see Vienenburg).

name: Stapelburg
Settlement_Description: A castle was constructed in 1360 by the counts of Wernigerode as toll station and protection of the road above the former village of Wendelburgerode. In the 16th century a village developed underneath the castle.
Toll_Description: The castle was built as a toll station and for the safety of the road.

name: null
Ferry_Description: The ferry across the Saale was maintained by castle Schkopau.

name: Ammendorf
Settlement_Description: The lords of Ammendorf are mentioned in 1155, who resided in a moated castle. In 1264 a Heinrich of Ammendorf founded a monastery in Ammendorf.

name: Neumarkt
Settlement_Description: The Augustinian monastery Neuwerk was founded in 1116. Quickly a village developed near the monastery, mentioned in 1121. It developed into a market settlement in the 15th century and acquired town-like character in the 16th century. The monastery was abolished in 1513. Neumarkt officially became a town in 1723, but was merged with Halle in 1817.
Fair_Description: Two fairs in Neumarkt are mentioned in 1405. Only one fair still existed in 1491, on St Martin's Day. The neighbouring town Halle tried to annex the fair in the 16th century, but it was confirmed by Emperor Charles V in 1521. It existed into the 19th century.

name: Kleinsteinrade
Settlement_Description: Manor at the enclosure ('landwehr') of Lübeck, which must have been founded around 1247. There existed a boom barrier to secure the border here.

name: Stockelsdorfer Baum
Settlement_Description: Crossing of the enclosure ('landwehr') of Lübeck - completed around 1300 - with a boom barrier.

name: Nienwohld
Lock_Description: Lock in the Alster-Trave canal, built in 1527. Traffic on the canal was discontinued around 1550.

name: Rader Schleuse
Lock_Description: A lock in the Alster river near Rade was constructed in 1527 as part of construction works on the Alster-Trave canal.

name: Wohldorfer Schleuse
Toll_Description: A toll was levied by Hamburg, who had acquired Wohldorf in 1437, on wood floated down the Alster. The Hamburg town accounts (Kämmereirechnungen) register revenues from this toll from 1461 onwards.
Lock_Description: Lock in the Alster river, which was constructed in 1527 as part of the construction works for the Alster-Trave canal.

name: null
Harbour_Description: In 1618, the Lübeck council was informed that travellers to Hamburg should use the waterway between Bergstedt and Poppenbüttel or Fuhlsbüttel because of closure of the Steindamm street.

name: null
Bridge_Description: A bridge across the Trave river was first mentioned in 1188.

name: Assens
Settlement_Description: Originally a village. The medieval town parish church was originally built in the 12th century.
Town_Description: The layout of the medieval town indicates that Assens was a planned urban settlement, which was placed at one of the most obvious places to cross the narrow strait of Lillebælt between Funen and Jutland. Assens is registered as royal property (patrimonium) in the so-called main piece in King Valdemar’s Cadastre from c. 1231. The first town privileges were probably granted during the reign of king Valdemar II the Victorious (1202-1241). A municipal seal ("Sigillum de Asnes") is known from the first half of the 14th century, and a mayor was first mentioned in 1397. A Carmelite monastery was founded around 1500. At this time Assens was an important market town, and it came to play an important role in the Danish export of oxen in the late medieval period. The town was fortified in the medieval period, and the fortification was rebuilt during the reign of king Christian IV (1596-1648). The town was attacked and plundered both during the Count’s Feud (Danish: Grevens Fejde) in the 1530ties and during the Dano-Swedish wars of the 17th century.
Fair_Description: In the middle of the 15th century Assens had become one of the centre’s of the important Danish export of oxen. This status was strengthened when the town was granted stable rights. The town had at least one annual fair in the middle of the 15th century, which was held in October.
Toll_Description: The town law of Haderslev mentions toll on various agricultural products from the ferry between Assens and Årøsund/Haderslev. Thus, Assens must also have functioned as a royal toll station in the late 13th century, and most likely also earlier. When Assens was granted stable rights in 1475 the town became one of the most important royal toll stations in Denmark. Toll registers, which most likely are from Assens, are available for the years 1519-1520 (The National Archives/Rigsarkivet).
Staple_Description: Stable rights were granted by king Christian I (1448-1481) in 1475, who ordered that oxen were only allowed to be transported to Assens as well as a few other towns (Ribe, Kolding and the annual fairs in Skanør and Falsterbo). In the middle of the following 16th century Assens lost its staple rights, as other towns on Funen (Fåborg and Middelfart) were now again allowed to export oxen. A few years later, however, the king once again abolished the export of oxen from other towns on Funen than Assens.

name: null
Harbour_Description: Harbour at the Zenne river. After the opening of the canal Brussel-Willebroek in the middle of the 16th century, which circumvented Vilvoorde, the harbour lost its importance.

name: null
Ferry_Description: Ferry connection across the strait of Lillebælt between Assens and Årøsund in Jutland was first mentioned in the town law of Haderslev from 1292, but is probably older, perhaps from around 1200. Throughout the middle ages and early modern era the ferry between Assens and Årøsund was one of the most important routes across Lillebælt, especially from the 15th century onwards when this particular route became central to the export of oxen from Funen. In the years around 1500 about 1.500 oxen were annually exported from Funen using the ferry, and in early years of the following 17th century the annual numbers had increased to 9.000-10.000 oxen. In 1640 the newly established royal postal service between Copenhagen and Hamburg began using the ferry between Assens and Årøsund.
Harbour_Description: Due to the town's location at the eatsern shore of the narrow strait of Lillebælt the harbour of Assens was central to the ferry connection between Funen and Jutland. The character of the medieval harbour is, however, uncertain. A wharf is first mentioned in 1596 but is most likely older. A wharf is also seen on a map of Assens in Resen’s Atlas Danicus from 1677. Assens was an important harbour on Funen, and was often used by both Danish and German merchants. In 1399, for example, ships from Lübeck sailed to Assens. Already prior to Assens becoming a stabletown in 1475, the harbour also played a key role in the export of oxen from Funen and Zealand to Jutland and the further south to northern Germany and Flanders.

name: Kloster Allendorf
Settlement_Description: First mentioned in 1218. A monastery of Cistercian nuns was founded after 1265. In 1525 the monastery was abolished, its buildings used as a quarry after the great fire of Salzungen in 1786.

name: Fåborg
Settlement_Description: Presumably a royal castle before c. 1200.
Town_Description: Faaborg was a privileged town before 1229, and probably got its first town right from king Valdemar II (1202-1241).The town name indicates the existence of a royal castle, and the town is likely to have developed in the shadow of the castle. The castle probably existed in 1377, when a royal steward (Danish: høvedsmand). In 1297 a town bailiff (Danish: byfoged) was mentioned for the first time. The earliest evidence for mayors and town council is from 1402, and around 1500 the town had a town hall. The town court  (Danish: byting) was first documented in 1572, but is much older. Presumably already from the 13th century Faaborg was surrounded by a moat and a rampart with three town gates. The town suffered during the 16th and 17th century due to illegal trade outside the town and the Danish-Swedish wars in the 17th century.
Fair_Description: During the late medieval period Fåborg held two annual fairs, which both had a local character. The exact age and character of the fairs of Fåborg is unknown. At least periodically the fairs played an important role in the export of oxen from Funen.

name: Hundested
Ferry_Description: The exact age and character of the ferry between Rørvig and the settlement of Hundested on the peninsula of Halsnæs is uncertain. It is, however, older than 1553, when it was mentioned for the first time.

name: Tidselbro
Bridge_Description: The age and character of the bridge across the river of Ringsted Å is uncertain. Presumably significantly older than when it was mentioned for the first time in 1638-1639.

name: Tartu
Settlement_Description: The Russians conquered the Estonian settlement in 1030. The castle was then expanded. In 1224-34 the German conquerors built a new castle that served as the centre of the diocese.
Town_Description: In 1248 the town received Riga town rights and also became a member of the Hanseatic League.
Staple_Description: A privilege of King Sigismund III from 1562 obliged every Russian travelling on his way to Livonian ports to offer his wares for sale in Tartu for four days. Foreign merchants wishing to trade in Russia were not allowed to travel further than Tartu.

name: Gröbzig
Settlement_Description: The castle of Gröbzig is first mentioned in 1291. The archbishopric of Magdeburg possibly held rights Gröbzig as early as 1176.
Town_Description: The settlement was first referred to as town in 1401. In 1465 it acquired borough ('Weichbild') rights.
Fair_Description: In 1587 the town was granted the privilege to hold two fairs.

name: Kilen Syd
Ferry_Description: The age and character of the ferry across the narrow strait of Kilen is uncertain. The ferry was first mentioned in 1578, but is most likely significantly older. In the early modern era the responsibility of the ferry was in the hands of the steward (Danish: lensmand) of Ørum. In the period 1589 to 1640 the ferry was replaced by a bridge. When the bridge collapsed in 1640, the ferry connection was reestablished.

name: Großengottern
Settlement_Description: In 802/17 one of the villages of Gottern is referred to as 'in Thuringia' and mentioned as the property of a count Erpfol. Großengottern, formerly Bischofsgottern, is first explicitly mentioned as separate settlement in 1189/1190.
Toll_Description: A station of safe conduct existed in Gottern, which is located by Straube in Großengottern, due its obvious location of the main road between Mühlhausen and Langensalza. However, Eberhardt locates it in Altengottern based on a mention from 1602. The safe conduct in Gottern was farmed out in 1341. Merchants from Mühlhausen complained in 1406 that they had to pay toll in Weberstedt, even though they had already paid it in Gottern. According to the safe conduct regulations of Erfurt from 1441, toll had to be paid for commodities from the direction of Mühlhausen in Gottern, but these commodities were then excempt from the safe conduct in Erfurt on the same day. According to regulations of safe conduct ('Geleitsordnung') of the Amt Langensalza and Thamsbrück from 1516, Gottern was a secondary station of safe conduct ('Beigeleitsstelle') of that region.

name: Bitterfeld
Settlement_Description: First mentioned in 1224. A former Slavic settlement probably existed.
Town_Description: Referred to as town in 1382. In 2007 Bitterfeld was merged with Wolfen as Bitterfeld-Wolfen.
Fair_Description: A fair in Bitterfeld is mentioned in the regulations of safe conduct ('Geleitsordnung') of 1539/40. In 1582 the council of Bitterfeld proclaimed the wish to establish two cattle markets, which would profit from traffic to Buttstedt. Permission would only be granted if surrounding markets would consent. Leipzig's reaction remains unclear, as well as whether the markets ever took place.
Toll_Description: Station of safe conduct. Revenues are known since 1483. The regulation of safe conduct from 1539/40 is uncommonly detailed and contains numerous exemptions, which show the importance of long-distance trade here. Bitterfeld was especially important as a station for cattle driven from Poland, for which a separate safe conduct existed ('Viehgeleit'). Secondary stations of safe conduct existed in Brehna, Roitzsch and Holzweißig.

name: Sömmerda
Settlement_Description: As property of Fulda monastery, Sömmerda probably already existed in the 9th century. It is mentioned in the Hersfelder Zehntverzeichnis in 876. It is first mentioned in the records in 1268, when it is given as a fiefdom. The castle was destroyed in 1312, its location is unknown. Until the 15th century, Sömmerda is referred to as village.
Town_Description: In 1459 it is referred to as borough ('Flecken') and since then a market borough with a kind of town constitution. A town council is known for 1433, a first town hall was first built between 1529 and 1539.
Fair_Description: The first fair privilege for the fair on St. Michael's day was granted in 1546, further privileges followed in 1591, 1684 and 1778.

name: Odense
Settlement_Description: The place name of Odense is a reflection of a sacral status in the pre-Christian era. Presumably, a place of worship and also economical and political center in the Viking Age. The latter is reflected in the ring fortress of Nonnebakken built by king Harald Bluetooth around 980.
Town_Description: Odense was located at a river, Odense Å, that may have been navigable in the Viking Age and early medieval period, but not in the later middle ages. The town was placed at the obvious route used to cross the island of Funen. Odense was first mentioned in a Ottonian charter from 988, issued by emperor Otto III to the bishops of Odense and other Danish towns. Thus, around 1000 AD Odense appears to have had an urban character, but the first time Odense was described as a town was in c. 1075, when the German chronicler Adam of Bremen placed it as the largest town (“civitas … magna”) on the island of Funen. In 1086 the Danish king Canute the Holy (1080-1086) was killed under a rebellion in Odense, and canonized around 1100 as the first royal saint of Denmark. Saint Canute the Holy’s tomb in the town’s cathedral and the status as episcopal sea secured Odense an important religious and political status throughout the medieval period. The town lord was, however, the king of Denmark. The first mention of a royal tax from towns (Danish: Midsommergæld) is from 1137. Townsmen (Danish: bymænd) are documented in 1175, and members of a town council from 1257. The oldest preserved town privileges are from 1335, but Odense was probably granted its first town rights in either the 12th or early 13th century. In 1351 mayors were mentioned for the first time, and a town hall in 1437. During the medieval period several monasteries were established. Three of the town’s monasteries were, a Benedictine Abbey, which may be the first monastery in Denmark, was founded around 1096, and probably in 1239 the Dominicans followed and in 1279 the Franciscians. Throughout the middle ages and early modern era Odense was the largest and dominant town on Funen. The town benefited from the rich agriculture on the island, and its status as the administrative, economical and political center of Funen.
Fair_Description: Due to its central location to both maritime and land-based traffic on the island of Funen Odense was an important market town. This was most likely already the case during the Viking Age, and the town’s status as the trading center of Funen continued throughout the medieval period and early modern era. Apparently, the oldest known annual fair, which also was the most important, was associated with the royal Saint Canute (Danish: Sankt Knudmesse Marked). It was held in the days around July 10th, the day king Canute the Holy was killed in 1086. Around 1600, and maybe also before, three other annual fairs were also held in Odense. In the second half of the 17th century, the number of fairs had been limited to two.

name: Kyrönniemi
Settlement_Description: <b>Inn:</b> Archbishop of Uppsala Laurentius Petri, Bishop of Turku Mikael Agricola, and member of the royal council of Sweden Sten Eriksson Lejonhufwud returned from Moscow after negotiating a peace between Sweden and Russia. In Kyrönniemi, bishop Mikael Agricola died of disease. Rest of the company continued to Vyborg, where they arrived the next day. Kyrönniemi is located by the winter road following the coastline between Vyborg and the Russian border.

name: Mittelpöllnitz
Settlement_Description: The settlement Pöllnitz is first mentioned in 1238, the part of the settlement known as Mittelpöllnitz is first mentioned as separate settlement in 1378.
Toll_Description: A station of safe conduct was based in Mittelpöllnitz. Revenues are known from 1484, mostly together with the safe conduct of Triptis. They indicate a limited regional traffic.

name: Großebersdorf
Toll_Description: Station of safe conduct on the road between Leipzig and Nuremberg via Schleiz and Gera. Although the use of this road had been forbidden by the Ernestinians for long-distance traffic in 1470, the annual revenues from 1485 to 1536 show a considerable amount of traffic.

name: Altengottern
Settlement_Description: First mentioned as Biscofestat in 750-779. The name Altengottern first appears in 997.

name: Nuppola
Settlement_Description: <b>Inn:</b> Travellers between Lappeenranta and Savitaipale stayed overnight in Nuppola.

name: Nebra
Settlement_Description: First mention in the records of Fulda monastery from 822-842. Formerly a Slavic village, later Carolingian royal court. The settlement developed into a market borough ('Marktflecken') in the 11th century.
Toll_Description: Regulations of safe conduct for the district of Freyburg from 1621 mention Nebra as secondary station of safe conduct ('Beigeleitsstelle') of Freyburg, where fees had to be paid for cattle.

name: null
Toll_Description: Already in the 12th century a toll on the Meuse is found.

name: Helmstorf (Harburg)
Settlement_Description: First mentioned in a register of the diocese of Verden from ca. 1277-1295.

name: Hjarbæk
Harbour_Description: Viborg was listed as a legitimate harbour in 1449. The reason that the inland town of Viborg is on the list, is the harbour in Hjarbæk at Limfjorden, north of the town. When Viborg began to use Hjarbæk as Harbour is, however, uncertain. But by the middle of the 15th century, this was not a new situation.

name: Harras
Settlement_Description: First mention in 1252. Seat of the family of Harras.
Toll_Description: A secondary station of safe conduct ('Beigeleit') in Harras is mentioned in 1552. After 1570, it was moved to Oberheldrungen.

name: Reppel
Settlement_Description: Earliest mention in 726, in a copy dating from circa 1222. Next mention in 855-856, in a copy dating from circa 1222. Next mention in thirteenth century.

name: Pärnu
Settlement_Description: From 1242 to 1263 Alt-Pernau was the episcopal centre ('Bischofssitz'). A castle of the Teutonic Order ('Deutscher Orden') was built on the left bank of the Pernau, around which Neu-Pernau settled. In the Medieval times, due to the location on the river, there was extensive trade relations with Fellin and Dorpat as far as Russia.
Town_Description: In the 14th century, the city received town rights of Riga and became a member of the Hanseatic League ('Hansebund').

name: Guthmannshausen
Toll_Description: Station of safe conduct from Erfurt. It lost significance duting the end of the 15th century and the beginning of the 16th century due to the Wettin separation ('Wettinische Teilung') in 1485, in which the department of Sachsenburg went to the Albertines. As a result, traffic could be forced on the road via Sachsenburg, thus circumventing Guthmannshausen and Vogelsberg. Regulations and tariffs are not known, but they were identical to those in Vogelsberg and Buttelstedt. Annual revenues are known since 1517.

name: Bad Langensalza
Settlement_Description: First mention in the Breviarum sancti Lulli from 775-786. The settlement was located near the castle Dryburg of the lords of Salza, which controlled the crossing at the ford of the roads from Gotha to Mühlhausen and from Eisenach to Tennstedt.
Town_Description: After a siege of the settlement by emperor Otto IV in 1212, the lords of Salza received the privilege to develop the settlement into a town. First referral to the town as "oppidum" in 1222. Extensive destruction of the town in 1346. In 1356 the old town was merged with its two suburbs, the Jakobsstadt and the Neustadt ('new town'), under one communal administration, which was corroborated by the construction of a town wall.
Fair_Description: Since 1438 two, since 1484 three fairs are attested.
Toll_Description: According to the regulations of safe conduct from 1516, there was no safe conduct in the department of Salza, only the toll in town. In 1558 the safe conduct was given to the town council with an option of repurchase, in 1663 it was ultimately given to the prince electorate.

name: Wieringen
Settlement_Description: Wieringen is a former island in the Dutch province of Noord-Holland. It is first mentioned in 1150-1158 in a copy of a manuscript dating from the late eighth century - 817. Wieringen remained an island until the first half of the twentieth century.
Town_Description: Wieringen is a former island in the Dutch province of Noord-Holland. Several settlements were located on the island. The island in its entirety was granted town rights on 10 August 1432. Wieringen lost its town rights in 1492, but later these were restored.

name: Hehlen
Settlement_Description: First mentioned in a register of possessions of the monastery Fulda from the 8th or 9th century.

name: Hühnerbusch
Settlement_Description: A water mill at the Schaale river north of the village Blücher is first mentioned in 1456. The name Hühnerbusch first appears in the 18th century.
Toll_Description: A toll house is first mentioned in 1577 and is also shown on a drawing by Daniel Frese from 1587. Not much is known about the toll, but it was probably levied both on the water and land route and was probably abolished in 1840.
Bridge_Description: A bridge across the Schaale river must have been built in 1456 at the latest, when the mill is first mentioned, but is only explicitly mentioned in 1697. A report from 1751 mentions four bridges across the various branches of the river.
Lock_Description: A lock near the water mill is first mentioned in 1460, through which floated timber was transported. It was probably constructed as part of construction works to improve the navigability of the Schaale river for salt transports from Lüneburg, which were only finished in 1564. The lock is shown on a drawing by Daniel Frese from 1587, mentioned as "Blüchers Kist".

name: Sloten
Settlement_Description: First mentioned in the first half of the 11th century. In 1465 the inhabitants obtained the right from duke Philip of Burgundy for a weigh-house together with Osdorp. They had cows and no sowing-land.

name: Hetlinger Turm
Settlement_Description: Watchtower in the enclosure ('landwehr') of the Neustadt in Osnabrück, which was constructed in 1406/09. The tower itself is mentioned in 1493.

name: Steinigerturm
Settlement_Description: Watchtower on the border between Osnabrück and Iburg

name: null
Bridge_Description: A bridge over the Wipperau was first mentioned in 1142, and a bridge toll was possibly levied here.

name: Osthausen
Settlement_Description: First mention in 1271, but it probably already existed in the 8th and 9th century.

name: Unterlauter
Toll_Description: Secondary station of safe conduct of Coburg, its role is not exactly clear. From an account of 1550-1551 it seems that the fees for copper and lead had to be paid here instead of in Coburg.

name: Teutleben
Settlement_Description: First mention at the end of the 8th or the beginning of the 9th century.
Toll_Description: Secondary station of safe conduct ('Beigeleitsstelle') of the Amt Tenneberg, according to tariffs from 1596.

name: Noordwijk
Settlement_Description: Noordwijk is first mentioned in a 1520 copy from a document dating from 889.
Town_Description: Noordwijk was granted town rights on 1 April 1398 by Albert (Dutch: Albrecht) I of Bavaria, count of Holland. However, these town privileges were withdrawn again on 12 March 1399. A hospital is first mentioned in 1341.

name: null
Toll_Description: In 1284, a fee of safe conduct was mentioned for the first time. In 1294/95, a river toll on the Maas is also mentioned, which was of great importance especially in the 14th century. The Count of Guelders and temporarily the Lord of Millen (before 1328/39) was the owner of the toll. Very detailed and edited tariffs date from ca. 1355/61 for Den Bosch, Zaltbommel, Zutphen, Roermond and Tiel. A right and tariff for Venlo and Roermond at the tolls on the Maas river is dated ca. 1375-1400. From the first half of the 15th century tariffs are preserved for the market-tolls on the river Meuse at: Gennep, Cuyk, Ravenstein, Megen, Maasbommel, Lith, Herwaarden, Driel, Heusden, Woudrichem and Gorinchem. And for the rivers Waal and IJssel at Tiel, Nijmegen, Lobith, Emmerich, IJsseloord, Arnhem, Zutphen Deventer and Rhenen. Around 1271, a land toll is also mentioned, but according to the safe conduct tariffs from ca. 1355/61, transit through the town was free as long as the river was not crossed. A transhipment toll is mentioned there as well.<br/>It is likely that in the second half of the 14th and in the 15th century the river toll of Grubbenvorst was levied in Venlo, and partly before as well. An arrangement with the lords of 'Grebben' (Grubbenvorst) and Arcen on passage is dated 1432.
Ferry_Description: Ferry-men of Venlo are found in the oldest account of the duke of Gelre dated 1294/5: 'nautis de Venle'.
Harbour_Description: Over the course of the 13th and 14th centuries, Venlo became a transshipment port. The isle 'De Weerd' in de bend of the river Maas offered a safe and natural harbour. From Holland to Venlo, the river Meuse was well navigable for deep-drawing ships, but upstream, the use of smaller ships with a more shallow draught was necessary.

name: Weberstedt
Toll_Description: Merchants from Mühlhausen complained in 1406 that they had to pay toll in Weberstedt, even though they had already paid it in Gottern. Later a toll station in Weberstedt is not mentioned anymore.

name: Niederschleuse
Lock_Description: The Niederschleuse is one of three flash locks in the Stecknitz river that already existed before the construction of the Stecknitz-Delvenau canal from 1391. It is first mentioned in 1409. A new lock called Niederschleuse was constructed near Lankau in 1451, later known as Donnerschleuse.

name: null
Harbour_Description: The Stör river was navigable until Itzehoe, which made the town an important transshipment point between river and sea trade (via the Elbe and the North Sea) and land transport.

name: Leutenberg
Town_Description: The town was probably founded in the 13th century by the lords of Schwarzburg, first mentioned as town in 1326. Adaptation of Saalfeld town law in 1496.
Toll_Description: Toll station en route of Nürnberg and Leipzig via Saalfeld. It is known through a complaint of an escort from Lehesten, there are no further record on it.

name: Trotz
Settlement_Description: First mention as post station in 1833.

name: Lehesten
Settlement_Description: First mentioned in 1071. The settlement was property of Saalfeld monastery.
Toll_Description: Through a writ by an escort from Lehesten we know that transport form Leipzig to Nürnberg passed through. It may have been a station of explicit long-distnace safe-conduct. A list of fees ('Zolltafel') remains from 1579. In 1728 secondary station of safe conduct of Zella.

name: Anjala
Settlement_Description: <b>Inn:</b> Travellers stayed overnight in Anjala in 1571.

name: Kungsbacka
Settlement_Description: A royal estate named Tölö registered as royal institutional property (‘kongelev’)  in the so-called main piece of King Valdemar’s Cadastre c. 1231. A settlement developed around the royal estate during the 13th and 14th centuries.
Town_Description: Around 1400 Kungsbacka was counted among the towns of Denmark. Citizens (Danish: bymænd) first mentioned in 1408, and in 1462 mayors and a town bailiff (Danish: byfoged). Throughout the late medieval period Kungsbacka benefited from its status as a border town and a royal administrative center. Still, the town remained one of the minor towns in the Danish realm. When the provinces of Halland was handed over to Sweden in 1645 Kungsbacka stagnated, especially after the foundation and dynamic development of Göteborg.

name: null
Toll_Description: The toll in Arneburg was also levied on river traffic on the Elbe (see Arneburg).

name: Ottenstein
Settlement_Description: Castle of the counts of Everstein and adjacent settlement, first mentioned in 1319. An earlier mention of 1192 cannot be verified.

name: Halmstad
Settlement_Description: In the so-called main piece of King Valdemar’s Cadastre from c. 1231 Halmstad was  registered as royal institutional property (‘kongelev’). An urban settlement probably developed in the shadow of a medieval royal castle located near a ford across the river of Nissan in the second half of the 13th century.
Town_Description: Town privileges granted by duke Christoffer of Halland and Samsø in 1307, and a town seal known from around 1300. Dominican monastery founded ca. 1260. In 1322 the town was moved closer to the coast either by King Christoffer II (1320-1326 & 1330-1332) or by duke Knud Porse of Halland and Samsø. In the following years the newly founded town benefited from the support of Knud Porse. Before 1344 the Dominican monastery was relocated to the new town. The new town was for a short period of time known as Broktorp, but soon the town became known as Halmstad. The town’s existing fortification was expanded during the Count’s Feud (Danish: Grevens Fejde) 1534-1536 and again by king Christian IV (1596-1648). After the Dano-Swedish war 1643-1645 Halmstad as well as the rest of the province of Halland was handed over to Sweden.
Harbour_Description: A wharf is documented in 1322, and the medieval port was frequently used by both Danes and foreigners. In 1399, for example, the port was used by German ships from Lübeck.

name: Nurmi
Settlement_Description: <b>Inn:</b> Nurmi is mentioned in Jaakko Teitti's list in 1556 as a possible place for a bailiff (fi. vouti, sw. fogde).

name: Eutin
Settlement_Description: Slavic fortification, where Hollanders settled after 1143. It became a market settlement and a residence of the bishop of Lübeck in 1156/57.
Town_Description: Lübeck town privileges were granted by Lübeck Bishop Johann II of Diest in 1257.

name: Chemnitz
Settlement_Description: The name is derived from a river, at which shore a Benedictine monastery was founded in 1136. A river crossing on the old road to Bohemia existed there. First mentioned in a charter when market privileges were granted in 1143.
Town_Description: Urban character after 1170. From 1254 and in 1308 Chemitz had margravial Meißen town law. The town prospered from 1470 by the growth of mining activity in the Ore Mountains.
Toll_Description: A pavement toll and transit toll was levied on salt wagons in 1431. Revenues of the safe conduct are known from 1483 and 1484. Regulation of safe conduct from 1551 and 1558 (including a salt toll) are known and edited by Straube. Secondary stations of safe conduct existed in Oederan, Schellenberg, Kunnersdorf and Zschopau (mentioned in 1551) and Röhrsdorf (separate regulations from 1548).

name: Siitola
Settlement_Description: <b>Inn:</b> Siitola is the newest of the three ferries across Vuoksi river: others are in Kuukauppi and Jääski. First mention of Siitola ferry is from 1638, when Mulli family and Mäenpää farm were responsible for it. An official inn was established in 1662, althought the ferrymen might have served food and drinks also prior to that. Paavo Pekanpoika Mäenpää was the first innkeeper, and Siitola inn continued to operate for more than 200 years.

name: Burg auf Fehmarn
Settlement_Description: Market settlement next to a castle. The church of St Nicholas was founded in the 13th century.
Fair_Description: Heinrich Rantzau mentions a fair eight days before St Michael's Day in his 1597 description of Schleswig and Holstein.

name: Lund
Settlement_Description: Founded in the late 10th century by king Swein Forkbeard (c. 987-1014) as a settlement with an urban character. The first archaeological evidence of the settlement is from a graveyard at a wooden church dated to c. 990. The settlement was founded at a central junction in Scania, where several main routes within the province crossed.
Town_Description: In the 11th century Lund became a bishopric, and from 1103/1104 the archbishops of Denmark resided in Lund. Up until the Danish Reformation in 1536 the town was the ecclesiastical center of the Danish kingdom: “Metropolis Daniae”. The cathedral of Saint Laurentius was built in the early 12th century, and by the 13th century the town had 22 churches and four monasteries. The town’s lord was, however, the king of Denmark. A royal mint was established around the year 1000, and a royal official (‘Gælkeren’) is known from the 11th or 12th century. At this time the first town law (‘Birkeretten’) was also introduced, and it later spread to towns across Scania. According to the so-called main piece in King Valdemar’s Cadastre from c. 1231 Lund was royal institutional property (‘Kongelev’), and an annual town tax (‘Midsommergæld’) was paid to the king from before 1085. Also, the provincial assembly of Scania, Halland and Blekinge was located in Lund. Mayors, a town council and a municipal seal are not documented prior to the 14th century, but there is no reason to doubt that these civic urban institutions were well established already in the 13th century. As a political and religious center Lund remained one of the most important Danish towns, but during the late medieval period and early modern era Lund lost ground to other dynamic urban communities in the region, in particular Copenhagen and Malmö.
Fair_Description: Lund was one of the most important regional market towns in Scania, and the town held several annual fairs. The age, date and character of the earliest fairs are uncertain, but annual fairs were held in Lund before 1400. At a common meeting in 1504 the towns of Scania decided only to allow a limited number of annual fairs in the province. Two of these legal annual fairs of Scania were held in Lund: “Trehøjemarked” and Saint Laurentius fair. In 1540 only two annual fairs were allowed in Scania, one in Lund and the other in Engelholm.

name: Garding
Settlement_Description: The church was founded in 1109; the settlement was first mentioned in 1187.
Town_Description: Borough ('flecken') with market privileges in 1575, town privileges granted in 1590.

name: Tönning
Settlement_Description: Originally a terp settlement, going back to Carolingian times or earlier, first mentioned in 1187 as central place of Eiderstedt. A church existed around this time as well.
Town_Description: Town privileges granted in 1590 by Duke Johann Adolf of Holstein-Gottorf.

name: Glückstadt
Town_Description: Built as a planned town by the Danish King Christian IV as a stronghold and trade centre as competition for Hamburg. The 'Fundationsbrief' of 1617 granted Lübeck and Hamburg town privileges.
Staple_Description: The Danish king tried to establish Glückstadt as a staple for Icelandic products in competition with Hamburg. In 1623, a branch of the Copenhagen Icelandic trade company was established in the town, and in 1645, it was ordained that all Icelandic products had to be stored in Glückstadt first and sold there. Despite further limitations in the 17th and 18th centuries, the staple was often circumvented.

name: null
Harbour_Description: Kellinghusen is mentioned as a harbour in 1260.

name: Krempe
Settlement_Description: First mentioned around 1234, developed from a settlement at the Krempau river.
Town_Description: Lübeck town privileges were granted in 1240-1250. They were confirmed by count Gerhard I in 1271.
Fair_Description: Heinrich Rantzau mentions in his 1597 description of Schleswig and Holstein that two fairs were held in Krempe: on Sunday before St Margaret and eight days after St Gall.

name: Lütjenburg
Settlement_Description: St Michael's Church was built around 1165. The older Slavic settlement Liucha / Lutilinburg was located nearby, but should not be seen as a direct predecessor of Lütjenburg.
Town_Description: First mentioned as town in 1271. Lübeck town privileges were confirmed in 1275 by count Gerhard of Schauenburg.
Fair_Description: Heinrich Rantzau mentions in his 1597 description of Schleswig and Holstein a fair on St Dionysius.

name: null
Harbour_Description: With the establishment of a trekvaart (tow-canal) on the Vliet canal between Leiden and Delft in 1636-1638, the Vliet was extended to the Galgenwater at the west side of the city.

name: Heldrungen
Settlement_Description: First mention of a settlement named Heltrunga in 847, at another location. The current settlement developed near a moated castle that is mentioned in 1004. It was rebuilt into a fortress in 1512.
Town_Description: Town rights were granted in 1530 by emperor Charles V.

name: Fähre (Schwerin)
Ferry_Description: The ferry across the Stör river near Schwerin is first mentioned when a treaty was signed here between the Count of Schwerin and the Duke of Pomerania in 1331.

name: null
Ferry_Description: A ferry across the river Lek is found in 1394. In 1561/2 the ferry was leased out by the steward of Brederode for 221 pounds (seventh of eigth year period) and again for two years for 292 pounds yearly.
Harbour_Description: In 1336 the town obtained toll-exemption from the count of Holland. In 1414 the lord of Vianen, burgrave of Utrecht, and the maid of Ameide gave toll-exemption both on land and water in Ameide and Meerkerk. A crane on the harbour-head of Vianen was leased out by the steward of Brederode in 1561/2 for 57 pounds (second of three years period). The right for this crane in the seigniory stretched from Amerongen to the Ysseldam.

name: Langennaundorf
Toll_Description: Secondary station of safe conduct ('Nebengeleit') of Liebenwerda. Annual revenues are known from 1464 onwards, but for many years remain empty ('vacat') or records only low amounts. In the regulations of safe conduct from 1505 it is mentioned, that fees were only levied on cattle driven through the settlement during the fairs of Herzberg.

name: null
Toll_Description: Toll station at the castle of Lauenförde, which was moved here from Bodenfelde in 1534, because skippers increasingly transshipped their cargo on the land route in Herstelle.

name: Trelleborg
Settlement_Description: A Viking age fortress and later a permanent settlement, which belonged to the king.
Town_Description: By the middle of the 13th century Trelleborg had an urban character. Citizens were first mentioned in 1257 and again in 1316. A town council and a town bailiff (Danish: foged) are documented in 1359. A Franciscan monastery was established in 1267. By the middle of the 14th century Trelleborg was partly protected by a town wall, which was destroyed by an army from Lübeck in the 1360ties. The town of Trelleborg was relatively small and was very dependent on the rich fishing of herring in the Baltic Sea. When the fishing began to decline in the 15th century the town also stagnated.

name: Zschopau
Settlement_Description: A castle had stood there since the mid-12th century to protect the 'Salzstraße' and its ford near Zschopau from Halle to Bohemia.The town was expanded after 1200.
Toll_Description: Station of secondary safe conduct ('Beigeleit') of Chemnitz, as mentioned in the regulations of safe conduct from 1551.

name: Pößneck
Settlement_Description: First mentioned in 1252. The oldest parts of the town are based on an 9th-11th century Slavic settlement with a fortification, next to which a market settlement developed in the 12th century.
Town_Description: Planned town foundation, first mentioned as such in 1324. Since 1351 in possession of the town rights of Saalfeld. It flourished in the 15th century because of leather and cloth production. The town rights were lost in 1525 due to the Peasant's War, but regranted in 1527.
Fair_Description: Pößneck was granted fair privileges by King Ruprecht of Bohemia in 1409. In 1660, Pößneck is granted a Christmas fair.
Toll_Description: Safe conduct in the district of Pößneck is handled under the same regulations as in the district of Saalfeld in 1728.

name: Skanör
Settlement_Description: Originally a seasonal market on the peninsula of Falsterbonäset in the southwestern corner of Scania. First mentioned in the 12th century as an annual fair, which developed due to the rich fishing of herring in the strait of Øresund. According to the so-called mainpiece in King Valdemar’s Cadastre from c. 1231 Skanör was royal property (Danish: kongelev).
Town_Description: During the 13th century a permanent settlement with an urban character began to develop at Skanör. Around 1230 a royal castle was built, and in the 13th century the settlement had at least two parish churches. Municipal seal (“Secretum ville Schanør") documented from c. 1300, and during the 14th century mayors, a town council and a town bailiff (Danish: byfoged) are also mentioned for the first time. In 1410 queen Margrete confirmed existing town privileges. The town was relatively small and was dependent on the rich fishing of herring in Øresund. When the fishing began to decline the town also stagnated.
Fair_Description: The annual fair at Skanör sprung from the rich fishing in Øresund during autumn, when schools of herring passed through the Sound. International trade related to the fishing of herring probably began in the 12th century, and around 1200 the market was concentrated at Skanör. In the early 13th century the fishing and trading spread from Skanör to Falsterbo and from around 1300 also to other towns in the region around Øresund. During the 14th and 15th century towns such as Malmö, Ystad, Landskrona, Trelleborg and Dragør (on the island of Amager) came to dominate the annual fairs of Scania. In the 13th century both fairs on the peninsula of Falsterbo had an international character, and were visited by merchants from towns across northern Europe, especially from northern Germany. Merchants from Lübeck and other German towns came to Skanör and Falsterbo to sell their own products such as salt, cloth and beer and to buy salted herring. At the fairs both Danish and foreign towns were given their own plots (Danish: fed; German: Vitten), where they could implement their own jurisdiction, conduct trade and where the herring was processed. At Skanör towns such as Rostock, Stralsund, Wismar, Kiel and Lübeck had their plots, and at Falsterbo western merchants from England and Netherlands concentrated. In the late 14th century, however, the Germans forced the English and Dutch traders out of the fairs, and even more than before, German merchants now dominated the fairs. In the year 1399, for example, toll records from Lübeck revealed that 1218 ships from Lübeck visited the different fairs in Scania. During the period 1398-1400 the town of Lübeck imported c. 76.000 barrels of salted herring from the fairs. The fairs also attracted fishers and traders in large numbers from Denmark, in particular from the region around Øresund, and from the middle of the 13th century onwards many Danish towns were granted specific rights at the fairs. The fairs were controlled by the king of Denmark, but during the 14th century they were periodically in the hands of the king of Sweden as well as German political agents. The most important commodity was herring, but a broad variety of goods were bought and sold at the Scania fairs, as the fairs functioned as transit markets for products from the North Sea regions and the Baltic areas. The fairs of Scania were an important source of income for the king of Denmark, who collected various tolls at the different markets, and tried to regulate the market activity by legislation, the so-called ‘Motbogen’/’Modbogen’.  During the 15th century the Scania fairs began to decline. Fishing and export of herring was still important, but the fairs lost their function as a place of exchange of goods between the Baltic and the North Sea. By the end of the 16th century the Scania fairs were no longer among the most important annual fairs of northern Europe.
Toll_Description: Probably from the late 12th century royal tolls were collected at the annual fair at Skanör. Toll on the export of herring and imported German beer and several other goods are known from the 13th century onwards. In general foreigners (i.e. in general Germans) had to pay a higher toll on herring as well as other goods than Danes. The toll was probably collected by the royal steward at Skanör castle.
Staple_Description: Stable rights were granted by king Christian I (1448-1481) in 1475, who ordered that oxen were only allowed to be transported to Skanör as well as a few other towns (Kolding Assens, Ribe and the annual fairs in Skanør and Falsterbo). When Skanör lost these stable rights are uncertain.

name: Mellnsdorf
Settlement_Description: The village is first mentioned in 1330.
Toll_Description: Secondary station of safe conduct ('Nebengeleit') of Wittenberg in the system of safe conduct around Leipzig. Regulations of safe conduct from 1550 are attested. Revenues are known since 1485.

name: Skinders Bro
Bridge_Description: The exact age of the bridge is unknown. As part of the prehistoric route system of Hærvejen/Ochsenweg through Jutland a bridge was built in the early middle ages or before.

name: Eckmannsdorf
Settlement_Description: The village is first mentioned in 1354.
Toll_Description: Secondary station of safe conduct ('Nebengeleit') of Wittenberg in the system of safe conduct around Leipzig. Regulations of safe conduct remain from 1550. Revenues are known since 1478/79.

name: Ystad
Settlement_Description: Due to the rich fishing of herring and the trade that followed, a settlement began to develop in the 12th century. In the following 13th century the settlement got a permanent character and a church was built.
Town_Description: When Ystad was granted town privileges is uncertain, but a town council was mentioned for the first time in 1290ties. A Franciscan monastery was founded already in 1267. Throughout the medieval period, and especially in the 14th century, Ystad benefited from the rich fishing of herring in the Baltic Sea, and the trade that followed. The fishing and trade attracted many Germans, and a German guild in Ystad is documented in 1380. In 1599, when the fishing of herring had stagnated and was no longer a lucrative business, Ystad was granted the right to export oxen.
Fair_Description: The rich fishing of herring each autumn attracted people and trade to the coast at Ystad. In the 14th century the market activities in Ystad grew in importance, and the town developed into one of the most important of the international markets in Scania. Like the other annual fairs in Scania the fishing market in Ystad probably took place from August 15th to October 9th. As other Scania fairs, the one in Ystad lost its importance during the 16th century.

name: Wöllmen
Settlement_Description: First mention of a manor in 1347
Toll_Description: Station of secondary safe conduct of Eilenburg.

name: Åhus
Settlement_Description: Near the medieval town of Åhus archeological excavations have located a Viking Age permanent marketplace. Uncertain if this market and predecessor to the medieval town nearby should be seen as an emporium. The existence of the Viking Age marketplaces are, however, evidence of the region’s role in trade in the Baltic region and beyond.
Town_Description: Around 1150 Åhus belonged to the archbishop of Lund, who probably was the town’s lord until the Danish Reformation in 1536. Town seal known from second half of the 13th century and citizens were first mentioned around 1300. In the first half of the 14th century, Åhus was surrounded by a strong town wall. A Dominican monastery was founded in 1243, and a German guild before 1358. The latter is a reflection of the significant role of Åhus in the Baltic trade in this part of the medieval period. Later the town stagnated and was attacked and plundered by Swedish troops.
Fair_Description: Åhus was an important market town in eastern Scania. However, the date, age and character of the town’s annual fair(s) are not known. At a common meeting in 1504 the towns of Scania decided only to allow a limited number of annual fairs in the province. One of these legal annual fairs of Scania was held in Åhus.
Bridge_Description: Late medieval bridge, Ströme Bro, across the river of Helge Å. The age and character of the bridge is uncertain. In 1481 king Christian I (1448-1481) ordered the citizens in Åhus to maintain the southern part of the bridge while the peasants of Villands shire (Danish: Villands herred) had to maintain the northern half. The bridge was demolished in 1614 to clear the passage for ships on Helge Å to the newly founded town of Kristianstad.

name: null
Toll_Description: King Christian IV of Denmark started to levy a toll from all passing ships on the Elbe in Glückstadt in 1630: for each mast 1 Rosenobel, from each Schiffspfund of the cargo 1 Thaler, and 1.5 percent of the entire value. After complaints of Hamburg, the toll was discontinued in 1645, although the Danish king tried to re-introduce it in 1675.

name: Vainikkala
Settlement_Description: <b>Inn:</b> Vainikkala is mentioned in Jaakko Teitti's list in 1556 as a possible place for a bailiff (fi. vouti, sw. fogde). The village was already under bailiff Mats Matsson.

name: Wahrenbrück
Toll_Description: Secondary station of safe conduct ('Beigeleit') of Liebenwerda. Annual revenues are known from 1464 onwards, tariffs and regulations ('Geleitsordnung') from 1505.

name: Hohenleipisch
Toll_Description: Secondary station of safe conduct ('Beigeleitsstelle') of Liebenwerda. Annual revenues are known from 1464 onwards, tariffs and regulations ('Geleitsordnung') date from 1505.

name: Kirkeby
Settlement_Description: The village of Kirkeby was first mentioned in 1348, but is significantly older. The parish church is from either the 12th or 13th century

name: Vä
Settlement_Description: A village before the medieval period. A Premonstratensian monastery established in the 1160ties, which was moved to the settlement of Backaskog in the 13th century. The settlement of Vä was registered as royal institutional property (‘kongelev’) in the so-called main piece of King Valdemar’s Cadastre c. 1231.
Town_Description: Vä was counted among the towns of Denmark in the 13th century. Privileges to town-dwellers (‘uillanos’) of Væ were granted in 1250, and extended in 1253, 1268 and 1293. In 1340 members of the town council and citizens were documented. During the wars between Denmark and Sweden in the 16th century Vä was attacked several times, and in the Kalmar War (1611-1613) the town was plundered and almost destroyed by Swedish troops. Thus, in 1614 king Christian IV (1596-1648) repealed the town’s privileges as part of the foundation of the new town of Kristianstad north from Vä.
Fair_Description: Vä held at least one annual fair. However, the date, age and character of the town’s annual fair(s) is not known. At a common meeting in 1504 the towns of Scania decided only to allow a limited number of annual fairs in the province. One of these legal annual fairs of Scania was held in Vä. Apparently the annual fair in Vä was declared illegal by king Christian II (1513-1523) in 1516.

name: null
Ferry_Description: The ferry was mentioned in 1532 and 1534.

name: Sölvesborg
Settlement_Description: A royal castle of Sölvesborg, which probably was built in the early 13th century, in Blekinge close to the province of Scania. A settlement with an urban character developed near the castle in the 13th and 14th centuries.
Town_Description: Sölvesborg was probably granted town privileges during the 13th century. The oldest known town privileges were, however, from 1445 when king Christoffer the Bavarian confirmed the existing town rights. Citizens were first mentioned in 1436, and in the 1480ties a Carmelite monastery was founded. In the medieval period the town and castle was an important royal stronghold in the border region between the Danish provinces of Scania and Halland and between the kingdom of Denmark and the kingdom of Sweden.

name: Horne
