Settlement_Description: The village of Horne was first mentioned in 1231, but is significantly older. The parish church is one of only seven round churches in Denmark, from either the 12th century.

name: Kværndrup
Settlement_Description: The village of Kværndrup was first mentioned in 1348, but is significantly older. The parish church is from either the 12th or 13th century

name: Bøjden
Settlement_Description: The village of Bøjden was first mentioned in 1588, but is significantly older. The settlement had no church but was part of the parish of Horne Church.

name: Tranekær
Settlement_Description: The village of Tranekær was first mentioned in 1231, but is significantly older. The parish church is from either the 12th or 13th century.

name: null
Bridge_Description: A bridge across the Schaale river in Zahrensdorf is shown on a drawing by Daniel Frese from 1587. It must have been built at the latest during construction works that improved the navigability of the river for Lüneburg salt transports, which were finished in 1564.

name: Oldersum
Settlement_Description:
The village was first mentioned in 1381. There were two castles here, of which one was rebuilt after they were destroyed by Hamburg at the end of the 14th century.
A travel account of Friedrich Duke of Württemberg from 1592 mentions a tavern in Oldersum.

name: Døllefjelde
Settlement_Description: The village of Døllefjelde was first mentioned in 1362, but is significantly older. The parish church is from either the 12th or 13th century.

name: Horst (Venlo)
Fair_Description: The duke of Gelre granted two cattle-fairs in 1501: 1) 4/5 May, 2) the third day after St. Lambert (Sept. 17) during two days, Both with safe-conduct four days before and after the dates. With a specified tariff for the beasts and for wool and neckerchiefs.

name: Nørreballe
Settlement_Description: The village of Nørreballe was first mentioned in 1619, but is significantly older. The settlement had no church but was part of the parish of Østofte Church.

name: Wetzlar
Town_Description: In 1180 the settlement was raised to an imperial town by emperor Friedrich I.  Mentioned as 'civitas' in 1225.

name: Besse
Toll_Description: In 1586 Besse acquired the right to levy a road toll to pay for the maintenance of the stone road and seven bridges.

name: Wüstmark
Settlement_Description: The village is first mentioned in 1356.

name: Våbensted
Settlement_Description: The village of Vognsted was first mentioned in 1231, but is significantly older. The parish church is from either the 12th or 13th century.

name: Herrested
Settlement_Description: Royal property according to the so-called main piece of King Valdemar’s Cadastre from 1231. The character and age of settlement is uncertain, but probably established before the medieval period.
Town_Description: Existing town privileges, originally granted by king Valdemar II the Victorious (1202-1241), were confirmed by king Eric Glipping (1259-1286) in 1270. These privileges were reconfirmed on several occasions during the first half of the 14th century until 1353. By 1415 Herrested had lost its town privileges, and was no longer considered as a town. Apparently an attempt to turn the settlement of Herrested into a town had failed.

name: Koskela
Settlement_Description:
<b>Inn:</b> Travellers stayed overnight in Koskela in 1582. The place might be the same as Kellari-Matti ("Cellar-Matti"), who, in 1593, received tax exemptions and 80 logs to rebuild the buildings that the soldiers had burned down by accident the year before. Cellar family, or Kellersvens, could have run an alehouse also earlier, since in Lappee rural court gathering in 1549 there was a local official (fi. neljännesmies, sw. fjärdingsman) Mons Kellarsven. He housed the court gathering in Koskela the next year. Mons Kellarsven had previosly served in Vyborg castle, so his surname could refer to his tasks in the castle, or he could have continued serving drinks in Koskela as well.

An official inn was established later, and the parish constable (fi: nimismies, sw: länsman) Risto Sirkkunen ran a tavern in his house in 1654. It might be the same farm that the Cellar/Kellersven family had previously owned.

name: Magleby (Møn)
Settlement_Description: The village of Magleby Møn was first mentioned in 1370, but is significantly older. The parish church is from either the 12th or 13th century.

name: Staverden
Settlement_Description: Earliest mention of 'apud Staveren' in 1290. On 3 June 1291, Reginald I, duke of Guelders, is granted permission by King Rudolf I of Habsburg to found the town of 'Stavera'.
Town_Description: 25 March 1298, Reginald I, duke of Guelders, granted town privileges to Staverden. Staverden, however, never grew into an actual town, but remained a castle with several farms.

name: Damsholte
Settlement_Description: The village of Damsholte was first mentioned in 1664, but is significantly older. The parish church is from either the 12th or 13th century.

name: Elmelunde
Settlement_Description: The village of Elmelunde was first mentioned in 1370, but is significantly older. The parish church is from either the 12th or 13th century.

name: Toreby
Settlement_Description: The village of Toreby was first mentioned in 1231, but is significantly older. The parish church is from either the 12th or 13th century.

name: Ottestrup
Settlement_Description: The village of Ottestrup was first mentioned in 1186, but is significantly older. The parish church is from either the 12th or 13th century.

name: Toksværd
Settlement_Description: The village of Toksværd was first mentioned in 1331, but is significantly older. The parish church is from either the 12th or 13th century.

name: Skelby (Sjælland)
Settlement_Description: The village of Skelby Sj was first mentioned in 1292, but is significantly older. The parish church is from either the 12th or 13th century.

name: Bredevoort
Settlement_Description: Earliest mention in 1188. In the 13th century, Bredevoort is walled and has a moat.
Town_Description: In 1388, Bredevoort is named as a town ('stat'). Possibly, William of Jülich, duke of Guelders (1371-1402), has granted town privileges. Bredevoort is a town of the type 'Borgmannenstad': privileges were granted to the 'borgmannen' (D: Burgmanschaft).

name: Hittfeld
Settlement_Description: First mentioned in 1004. A wooden predecessor of the current church might have been constructed in the 9th century.

name: Wörlitz
Settlement_Description: First secure mention in 1004, possibly as early as 966, but the authenticity of the record is contested. Possibly a centre of a castle district ('burgward').
Town_Description: In 1440 referred to as town, but after that also mentioned several times as borough ('Flecken'), market borough, little town ('Städtlein') or town.

name: null
Ferry_Description: A ferry to Zwijndrecht is first explicitly mentioned in 1373, but might have existed before, since the placename indicates a river crossing.

name: Mechelen (Limburg)
Settlement_Description: In 1215 the duke of Limburg donated his 'curiam nostram Mechele' to the commander of the Knights Hospitallers in Cologne. This court is first mentioned in 1133. Prior to 1243 a commandry of the Hospitallers was built in Mechelen. Due to a fire they moved to Aachen in 1585.
Fair_Description: A privilege for a cattle fair was given by the dukes of Brabant on 20 August 1362. It lasted eight days before and after St. Michael (29 September) and was a free market, although the inhabitants of Limburg, Dalhem and Herzogenrath were obliged to trade their cattle there.

name: Fuglebjerg
Settlement_Description: The village of Fuglebjerg was first mentioned in 1370, but is significantly older. The parish church is from either the 12th or 13th century.

name: Bisserup
Settlement_Description: The village of Bisserup was first mentioned in 1370, but is significantly older. The settlement had no church but was part of the parish of Holsteinborg Church.

name: Tuohikotti
Settlement_Description: <b>Inn:</b> Travellers stayed overnight in Tuohikotti in 1571.

name: Leiderdorp
Settlement_Description: First mentioned in 918-948, in an eleventh century copy. The settlement was originally called Leiden, but as that name became attached to the settlement near the castle that developed into the city of Leiden, the village became known as Leiderdorp.

name: Oinen
Settlement_Description: <b>Inn:</b> An inn was established in Oinen in 1642, and Eero Mikonpoika Nikula was appointed as the innkeeper.

name: Sallerup
Settlement_Description: The village of Sallerup was first mentioned around 1200, but is significantly older. The settlement had no church but was part of the parish of Køng Church.

name: Vester Egesborg
Settlement_Description: The village of Vester Egesborg was first mentioned around 1370, but is significantly older. The parish church is from either the 12th or 13th century.

name: Herbsleben
Settlement_Description: First mention in 780-802. Even though the village is referred to as town several times during the 16th century, it was never actually granted town rights and by the end of the century is only called borough ('Flecken').
Fair_Description: On 15 June 1331 emperor Ludwig granted permission to hold a fair on St Bartholomew's day and a weekly market in Herbsleben.
Toll_Description: Toll station at an important crossing of the river Unstrut. In 1375 the castle and its belongings are pawned, <em>except</em> the safe conduct. In 1424 an escort ('Geleitsmann') is mentioned. In 1545 renewal of the requirement that wagoners coming from the Thuringian forest on their way to Herbsleben, Weißensee and onwards have to travel via Erfurt. Regulations of safe conduct ('Geleitsordnung') and a table of fees ('Geleitstafel') remain from 1554. Revenues are known for 1549-1554, which mention a regular and a "small" safe conduct.

name: Ørslev
Settlement_Description: The village of Ørslev was first mentioned in 1400, but is significantly older. The parish church is from either the 12th or 13th century.

name: Skibinge
Settlement_Description: The village of Skibinge was first mentioned in 1297, but is significantly older. The parish church is from either the 12th or 13th century.

name: Bogense
Settlement_Description: Bogense probably originated as a trading place and harbor for the royal estate of Harridslevgaard. Around 1200 Bogense was a permanent settlement with an urban character.
Town_Description: Bogense was granted town privileges during the reign of king Eric Glipping (1259-1286). In 1288 existing town privileges were confirmed by king Eric Menved (1286-1319). Mayors and town councils are known from 1420. Oldest town hall avoided a devastating fire in 1575, only to be destroyed in one of several fires in Bogense during the 16th century. During the 16th century and in particular in the following 17th century Bogense stagnated and developed into one of the poorest towns on the island of Funen.

name: Bårse
Settlement_Description: The village of Bårse was first mentioned in 1231, but is significantly older. The parish church is from either the 12th or 13th century.

name: Haraldsted
Settlement_Description: The village of Haraldsted was first mentioned in 1231, but is significantly older. The parish church is from either the 12th or 13th century. In 1131 duke Knud Lavard was murdered in the forrest of Haraldsted and burried at Haraldsted Church.

name: Mern
Settlement_Description: The village of Mern was first mentioned in 1231, but is significantly older. The parish church is from either the 12th or 13th century.

name: Grebbeberg
Toll_Description: Situated on the border of Gelre and Sticht of Utrecht on the northern bank along the old overlandroute of the Rhine. In 1640 part of the road-toll of the Oversticht of Utrecht owned by the lord of Amerongen (first mentioned there in 1289). In 1561 this toll was pawned by king Philp II to the lord of Amerongen. But since when the outpost at the Grebbeberg was part of this toll is uncertain. In 1603 however also founded as an outpost by the Estates of Utrecht of the water-toll at Wijk bij Duurstede. In 1623 this toll was leased out for 23 guilders (existed there till 1812).

name: Snesere
Settlement_Description: The village of Snesere was first mentioned in 1231, but is significantly older. The parish church is from either the 12th or 13th century.

name: Culemborg
Settlement_Description: Earliest mention on 4 July 1281. The origin and development of Culemborg as a town-like place are being dated around 1300.
Town_Description: Town privileges granted to the burghers (‘poorters’) at Culemborg by Johan van Bosinchem, lord of Culemborg, on 6 December 1318. A chapter in the church is found for the years 1421-ca. 1578.
Fair_Description: Al voor het stadsrecht van 1318 werden er twee jaarmarkten gehouden, want de poorters worden daarin vrij gesteld van de tollen. In 1423 worden tot dan gesproken van drie vrije jaarmarkten. In 1446 wordt de St. Johanspaardenmarkt ingesteld, dat jaar wordt dat in 20 plaatsen bekendgemaakt, het volgende jaar nog eens in 15. Dan zijn er vier jaarmarkten: 1): paardenmarkt van vrijdag voor halfvasten tot zaterdag de volgende week, 2) magere ossen, beesten, schapen en varkensmarkt van dinsdag na beloken pasen tot de eerste dinsdag in mei, 3) paardenmarkt en kermis: zondag na Pinksteren gedurende 8 dagen, de paardenmarkt op maandag, 4) vette beestenmarkt van 21-23 oktober, de weekmarkt is op dinsdag, van maandagmiddag tot woensdagmorgen, is ook een vrijmarkt. In 1568 worden genoemd: een tol van de paardenmarkt met Palmen en St. Jansmisse: deze markten zijn vergaan, een tol op St.Victorsdag (10 okt.), eertijds (in 1494 daarop teruggezet) op St. Lucasdag, nadien verzet aangezien men dacht dat bekwamer was.

name: Heukelum
Settlement_Description: Earliest mention dates from 996 (copy from the second half of the twelfth century).
Town_Description: Descriptions as a town date from 1070 (‘stedeken’), 1329 (‘stadt’), and 1393 (‘poerte van Huekelem’). It is presumed that Heukelum has been granted town privileges by Otto, lord of Heukelum, before July 1393. In 1399 it obtained toll-exemption from the count of Holland.

name: Bad Düben
Settlement_Description: In Asorbic times a fishing and boatmen's village; in the 10th century castle and castle district ('Burgward') of the margraves and corresponding castle borough ('Burgflecken'); after 1200 construction and extension of the town (end of the 15th century).
Toll_Description: Secondary station of safe conduct in between Wittenberg and Leipzig.

name: Wellsee
Settlement_Description: The village was first mentioned in the Kiel town register of 1264-1289, in an entry dated ca. 1275. The settlement took its name from the nearby lake.

name: null
Harbour_Description: Originally the harbour was located on the shore of the Eider river. In 1613, the harbour was enlarged and dug directly into the town.

name: null
Harbour_Description: As the only town on the Eider river until the foundation of Friedrichstadt, Rendsburg was an important transshipment point on the transit trade between the North and Baltic Sea. Especially the role of transit harbour for Eckernförde gained prominence in the 15th and 16th centuries. Moreover, Rendsburg was the central harbour for the export of wood from the regional forests. A fee had to paid for (un)loading the Eider barges at the quays. Around 1600, a causeway was constructed, which forced the transshipment of cargoes which were further transported on the Eider.

name: Jaala
Settlement_Description: <b>Inn:</b> An inn was established in Jaala in 1642, and Erkki Martinpoika was appointed as the innkeeper.

name: Døstrup
Settlement_Description: The village of Døstrup was first mentioned in 1291, but is significantly older. The parish church is from either the 12th or 13th century.

name: Skast
Settlement_Description: The village of Skast was first mentioned in 1292, but is significantly older. The parish church is from either the 12th or 13th century.

name: Søby
Settlement_Description: The village of Søby was first mentioned in 1277, but is significantly older. The parish church is from either the 12th or 13th century.

name: Stadsbrug
Toll_Description: Toll had to be paid to cross the bridge. A toll plate with tariffs from 1628 has been preserved in the Stedelijk Museum Kampen.
Bridge_Description: The town of Kampen built a wooden bridge over the river IJssel in 1448. It was destroyed and rebuild several times. From 1598 onward, it became a pontoon bridge. In 1638, it changed to a bridge with a permanent cross-river connection.

name: Ammerstol
Settlement_Description: Ammerstol is first mentioned in a 1320 copy of a document from 1221.
Town_Description: Ammerstol was granted town rights on 16 May 1320. Economically, Ammerstol relied on the salmon fishery.
Fair_Description: In 1327 Ammers obtained the right for a weekly market on Wednesday from the count of Holland.
Toll_Description: This toll for sailing transport is first mentioned in 1221. It was owned by the count of Holland. The tollhouse was situated just opposite of the outlet of the river Ammers in the river Lek. In 1321 it obtained toll-exemptrion from the count of Holland, like the citizens of the town Dordrecht. In 1398, the count of Holland relocated the toll to the town of Schoonhoven which is situated about 4 km upstream.  From 1397 onward Schoonhoven fell under his jurisdiction. In the previous years Schoonhoven had developed into a serious town and although Ammerstol received town rights, it stayed a rather small village. A tariff list written between 1355 and 1358 is published.
Ferry_Description: A ferry between Ammerstol and Groot-Ammers crossing the river Lek is first mentioned in 1356. Yields for the lease of this domain of the counts of Blois for second half of the 14th century are published.

name: Kimola
Settlement_Description: <b>Inn:</b> An inn was established in Kimola in 1642, and Tuure Tuomaanpoika was appointed as the innkeeper.

name: Bagenkop
Settlement_Description: The village of Barnkop was first mentioned in 1587, but is significantly older. The settlement had no church but was part of the parish of Magleby Church.

name: Spodsbjerg
Settlement_Description: The village of Spodsbjerg was first mentioned in 1472, but is significantly older. The settlement had no church but was part of the parish of Longelse Church.

name: Lindelse
Settlement_Description: The village of Lindelse was first mentioned in 1231, but is significantly older. The parish church is from either the 12th or 13th century.

name: null
Toll_Description: The Wijk bij Duurstede toll for sailing transport was the continuation of the toll of Rhenen.The Rhenen toll moved to Wijk bij Duurstede around 1470 on behalf of Bishop David of Burgundy. A long term conflict about the location of the toll resulted in a temporary displacement of the toll back to Rhenen from 1546-1557. But after the last year the toll definitely was levied in Wijk bij Duurstede. Toll administration (1623,1770-1799, 1800-1805) is preserved in Utrechts Archief, 37 Financiële instellingen van de landsheer en van de Staten van Utrecht en daarop volgende gewestelijke besturen, inv. no. 324, 1471-1501 and 2858-2865. And 218-1 Bisschoppen van Utrecht, inv.no. 10, fo. 235v-237. Tariff lists (1486, 1545) are published. In 1449 Wijk obtained toll-exemption from the bishop of Utrecht for the tolls in the Sticht Utrecht.

name: Amerongen
Settlement_Description: Earliest mention in 1126, in a falsification which probably dates from the twelfth century.
Toll_Description: A road toll in Amerongen is first mentioned in 1289, when Gijsbert of Abcoude acknowledged that 3/4 of the toll belonged to the provost of Utrecht cathedral. Later it must have been acquired by the bishop of Utrecht, in whose accounts it appears in 1426/27. In 1542 the toll is farmed out for 93 carolus guilders and is especially collected between St. John midsummer [June 24] and Victoris [Oct. 10] as then the Guelders and other people from abroad passed with peat. In 1561 the toll is pawned by king Philip II to the lord of Amerongen. In 1563 the toll is also collected at Sterkenborch, at Woudenberch and on the road at Lunteren. In a tariff and records from the 17th and 18th century, it appears that the toll was also levied on various outposts on the border with Guelders: at the Grebbeberg, at the ferry in Rhenen, in Elst and in Scherpenzeel.

name: Marstal
Settlement_Description: The village of Marstal was first mentioned in 1533, but is significantly older. The parish church is from either the 12th or 13th century.

name: Urajärvi
Settlement_Description: <b>Inn:</b> An inn was established in Urajärvi in 1639, and Nuutti Matinpoika was appointed as the innkeeper.

name: null
Bridge_Description: In 1452 the water board of Rijnland granted a bridge instead of a ferry over the river Rijn at Leiderdorp. The bridge was used by the people of Zoeterwoude to attented church at Leiderdorp. In 1563 the bridge was pawned by the lord of the village to the neighbours for 25 years for 25 carolus guilders annually. Later a ferry returned, but from 1664 a bridge existed again.
Ferry_Description: Until the construction of a bridge in 1452, a ferry existed at the Rijn in Leiderdorp.

name: Oudegein
Toll_Description: A toll levied by the bishop of Utrecht on shipping on the Vaartsche Rijn at Gein was first mentioned in 1200. A source from 1244 specifies this toll as a fee for the cargoes that were transshipped here with a crane and the ships that were dragged across the dike via a portage ('overtoom'). After the Hollandse IJssel was closed off from the Lek river at Hoppenesse in 1286 and a "nieuwe vaart" was dug to connect the Vaartsche Rijn and the Lek river in 1289, the toll was also levied in Vreeswijk.
Lock_Description: The Vaartsche Rijn canal met with the dike Randijk at Oudegein. Originally, ships and their cargoes had to be dragged over the dike here via a portage ('overtoom'). After the Hollandse IJssel had been closed off from the Lek river in 1286, minimising the risk of inundations, a lock in the Randijk (first mentioned 1331) gave the canal its current name Doorslag.

name: Frankfurt (Oder)
Settlement_Description: A marketplace existed (perhaps from 1226) in the vicinity of the Church of St Nicholas before the settlement’s foundation as a town in 1253.
Town_Description: Town foundation and provision of town rights by Margrave John I of Brandenburg in 1253.
Toll_Description: In the town privileges of 1253, Margrave John I also installed a toll in Frankfurt, which was levied on land and water traffic. Exact toll tariffs are registered in a town register of 1516.
Staple_Description: The mention of the staple in the foundation charter of the town from 1253 is probably a later addition. A privilege by the Margrave of Brandenburg from 1351 limited the land and river traffic to routes through Frankfurt; other river crossings were prohibited. A treaty with Breslau from 1490 limited the crossing of the Oder by merchants to Breslau and Frankfurt, but proved difficult to enforce because of Polish counter-measures. In 1507, merchants from Poland, Russia, Lithuania, Masovia and Prussia were prohibited to trade further than Frankfurt and Breslau. The staple privileges were confirmed in 1510 and 1512, but could not be reinforced in the wake of the collapse of the staple of Breslau in 1515. However, both staples were reinstated in 1530 and confirmed in 1555, 1624 and 1643. The street via Landsberg was not allowed to be used by transit traffic. The prohibition of shipping on the Oder South of Frankfurt from 1459 was cancelled in 1555 for salt transports; all other commodities had to be transported on the land route. The staple was abolished in 1752, having been reduced to a monopoly on the linseed trade.

name: Venebrugge
Settlement_Description: First mentioned in 1253. The name refers to a causeway through the moor on the border between the county Bentheim and the diocese Utrecht (Oversticht). On the Utrecht side, there was a fortification, on the Bentheim side there was an inn.

name: Marköbel
Settlement_Description: First mentioned in 839. At the site of the village, a fortress was located in Roman times.
Town_Description: Ulrich III of Hanau acquired a charter from Emperor Charles IV in 1368, in which he granted Marköbel the town privileges of Hanau.

name: Bromme
Settlement_Description: The village of Bromme was first mentioned in 1248 . Accordring to the maps of The Royal Danish Academy of Sciences and Letters a bridge across the river of Tuse Å was located here in the 18th century. Whether a bridge existed here in the late medieval period and early modern era is uncertain. If this was not the case Bromme was located at an obvious place to cross the river using a ford.

name: Vester Åby
Settlement_Description: The village of Vester Aabye was first mentioned in 1304, but is significantly older. The parish church is from either the 12th or 13th century

name: Havrebjerg Bro
Bridge_Description: A combined watermill and bridge near the settlement of Havrebjerg. The age and character of the bridge is uncertain. It is, however, older than 1454, when it was mentioned for the first time.

name: Vårby bro
Toll_Description: A fee was paid to cross the bridge (Danish: bropenge/brokorn).
Bridge_Description: The exact age and character of the bridge is uncertain. The bridge was first mentioned in 1618-1619, but is probably older. Presumably, a bridge existed in the16th century, perhaps even earlier.

name: Ollerup
Settlement_Description: The village of Ollerup was first mentioned in 1372, but is significantly older. The parish church is from either the 12th or 13th century

name: Falsled
Settlement_Description: The village of Falsted was first mentioned in 1472, but is significantly older. The settlement had no church but was part of the parish of Svanninge Church.

name: Sandager
Settlement_Description: The village of Sandager was first mentioned in 1468, but is significantly older. The settlement had no church but was part of the parish of Gislev Church.

name: Vesivehmaa
Settlement_Description: <b>Inn:</b> Vesivehmaa is one of the traditional inns in Asikkala area. The inn might date from earlier, but it is first mentioned in 1585. After 1641, there was also a transport organiser (sw. skjutsrättare, fi. kyytirättäri) in Vesivehmaa.

name: null
Ferry_Description: A ferry across the river Vecht is mentioned in 1376/1385. In 1525 there are two ferries: a big one and a small 'Neer'veer. In 1821 a bridge is built.

name: Sotjala
Settlement_Description: <b>Inn:</b> Parish constable (fi: nimismies, sw: länsman) accommodated travelling soldiers in 1564. Parish constables were obliged to keep a tavern in late 16th c. and early 17th c, so he might also have served other travellers.

name: Spanjaardsbrug
Toll_Description: The Lord of Wassenaar levied a toll at the bridge; the toll house was demolished in 1574 to make place for the fortification. In 1619, Leiden leased the bridge for 18 guilders per year. The tenant was allowed to levy a fee of a half stuiver for each ship that passed the bridge with raised mast, and double the amount at night.
Bridge_Description: A bridge across the river Zijl where it connected with the Oude Rijn must have existed for a long time before 1407, when Leiden received permission to enlargen the bridge. The town Leiden paid 2/3, and the water board of Rijnland 1/3 for the maintenance of the bridge. A fortification ('schans') was built here as defence against Spanish troops during the siege of Leiden in 1574, hence the bridge became known as Spanjaardsbrug.

name: Piipanoja
Settlement_Description: <b>Inn:</b> An inn was established in Piipanoja in 1634, and a man named Maunu was appointed as the innkeeper.

name: Galsted
Settlement_Description: The village of Galsted was first mentioned in 1510, but is significantly older. The settlement had no church but was part of the parish of Agerskov Church.

name: Tyrisevä
Settlement_Description: <b>Inn:</b> An inn was established in Tyrisevä in 1586, and Eskel Eskelinpoika Läykki was appointed as the innkeeper. The inn was located close to winter and summer roads.

name: Schönhagen
Settlement_Description: Schönhagen is mentioned in 1588 as a "new village, built only 18 years ago". This should probably be interpreted as a reconstruction of large parts of the village after a fire or other disaster, as the village is first mentioned in 1418.

name: Küheturm
Settlement_Description: Watchtower of the defensive enclosure ('landwehr') of Northeim, built in 1442. The remains became part of the hotel Rücking.
Bridge_Description: The bridge over the Rhume in Northeim was constructed in 1285 as a joint enterprise by the town and the Benedictine monastery. In 1395, the bridge is mentioned as "pontem longum", and was reconstructed shortly before 1432. A cross was placed on the bridge in 1424, where donations for the maintenance of the bridge were collected. In 1568, the bridge was reconstructed in stone.

name: null
Ferry_Description: A ferry across the Weser near Lippoldsberg is first mentioned in 1409. Earlier, there existed a ferry near Bodenfelde, which was mentioned already in 1120 and was owned by the monastery of Helmarshausen.

name: Lippoldsberg
Settlement_Description: The count of Northeim returned the fief of Lippoldsberg to the archbishop of Mainz in 1090 for the foundation of a monastery of Benedictine nuns.

name: Raalte
Settlement_Description: Earliest mention in 1123 in a falsification of the second half of the twelfth century.

name: Welleringhausen
Settlement_Description: First mentioned in 1194. It was characterised as village ('dorf') in 1382.

name: Skjellerup
Settlement_Description: The village of Skjellerup was first mentioned in 1259, but is significantly older. The parish church is from either the 12th or 13th century.

name: Katbjerg
Settlement_Description: The village of Katbjerg was first mentioned in 1259, but is significantly older. The settlement had no church but was part of the parish of Mariger.

name: Udby
Settlement_Description: The village of Udbye was first mentioned in 1203, but is significantly older. The parish church is from either the 12th or 13th century.

name: Corvey
Settlement_Description: The Benedictine Abbey of Corvey was founded in 822 as an imperial monastery and obtained mint and toll privileges in 833. South of the abbey a settlement with St. Paul's church developed. By the 12th/13th century a town with a market and a bridge over the Weser (1229) had established here, which was in strong competition with the nearby town of Höxter. Regularly referred to as "civitas", it had its own civic court and council. The town was destroyed in 1265 by Bishop Simon of Paderborn. It was mentioned for the last time as "oppidum" in 1438 and finally fell desolate. The monastery itself was destroyed in 1634 – except for the Carolingian westwork – and rebuilt after the Thirty Years' War. Since 1803 it has been in secular use as „Corvey Castle“. In 2014 it was declared a UNESCO World Heritage Site.

name: null
Bridge_Description: Since 1306 there seems to have been a wooden bridge at this Werra-crossing, which was damaged often and destroyed by a flood in 1496. From 1549-1551 a stone bridge was built, from which the keystone is still intact. In 1552 massive floods forced the re-construction of two of the vaults. In 1881 an iron bridge was constructed.

name: Bad Grund
Settlement_Description: First mentioned on 26-9-1317 as forester's settlement of lumberjack Reinecke de Fundo. Later it became a miner's settlement.
Town_Description: Bad Grund acquired mining privileges ('bergfreiheit') in 1532, and a first town seal in 1535. A judge and council are mentioned in 1553. It owned the privileges of a miner's town ('freie bergstadt'), which were reiterated until the 18th century.

name: Lautenthal
Settlement_Description: Mining activity in the valley of the Laute is first attested in 1330. After iron ore was discovered at the Kranichsberg in 1538, the miner's settlement Lautenthal developed.
Town_Description: Lautenthal presumable acquired mining privileges ('bergfreiheit') in the 1560s, as it is listed as a mining town ('bergstadt') in 1568. In 1613, the town privileges were extended.
Fair_Description: With the market privilege of 1613, a weekly market and a fair on St Simon and Jude were founded.

name: Salon silta
Bridge_Description: Isosilta (fi. Great bridge, sw. Salo stora bro, 1792) over Uskelanjoki river in Salo may date to the first organisation of the maintenance of the Great Coastal Road as a uniform land route between Turku and Viborg in the 1340s and 1360s. The bridge is included in the 1650s map of the Piikkiö and Halikko districts. The length of the bridge was in 1798 a total of 80 ells (ell = 59,38 cm, ca.47,5 m), and in 1829 a total of 84 ells (ca. 69,9 m).

name: Slagelse
Settlement_Description: Probably a permanent settlement with a certain urban character in the 11th century. At least several kings minted coins in Slagelse in the 11th century.
Town_Description: Slagelse was mentioned by the Danish chronicle Saxo Grammaticus in his Gesta Danorum from around 1208. The town also appeared in the so-called main piece of King Valdemars Cadastre from 1231, and in the same manuscripts registration of royal income from towns in the province of Zealand. Oldest known town privileges granted by king Eric Menved (1286-1319) in 1288 and later confirmed and expanded. Mayors are documented for the first time in 1385. At this time Slagelse was a significant town on western Zealand, and in general the town’s success continued into the 16th century, when Slagelse suffered from several devastating fires. Around 1160 the Knight Hospitaller founded Antvorskov monastery just outside Slagelse.

name: Estruplund
Settlement_Description: The village of Estruplund was first mentioned in 1632, but is significantly older. The parish church is from either the 12th or 13th century.

name: Assendelft
Settlement_Description: First mentioned in the first half of the 11th century, in a copy from 1063.

name: Wildemann
Settlement_Description: After mining activity had taken place in the area around 1200 and declined afterwards, the old mine shafts were reopened in 1524 and 1529. Between 1529 and 1532, the area was probably settled.
Town_Description: A mining town was founded that received mining privileges ('bergfreiheit') and a council in 1534. The privileges were confirmed in 1550.

name: Kurikka
Settlement_Description: <b>Inn:</b> An inn was established in Kurikka in 1627, and Erkki Pertunpoika from Kylmäjyrä farm was appointed as the innkeeper. He held the tavern rights until 1644, and his son Matti Erkinpoika continued to run the tavern in Kylmäjyrä. Matti is mentioned as the innkeeper in 1652. The winter and summer ways between Ostrobothnia and Northern Satakunta meet by Kurikka church.

name: Sankt Andreasberg
Settlement_Description: A first miner's settlement in this region existed in the late 13th century, but disappeared after the Black Death in the mid-14th century. In 1487, there are first indications of mining again, and the settlement acquired mining privileges ('bergfreiheit') in 1521.
Town_Description: Sankt Andreasberg acquired the privileges of a mining town ('bergstadt') in 1537.

name: Altenau
Settlement_Description: Ironworks in Altenau are mentioned in 1298 and 1311. Increased activity in silver mining led to the development of a settlement in the late 16th century.
Town_Description: A judge and council are mentioned in 1594. The settlement acquired a seal in 1617, and received mining town ('bergstadt') privileges in 1636.

name: null
Bridge_Description: A bridge must have replaced the ferry in the 16th century; it is drawn on a map of town by Jacob van Deventer in the second half of the 16th century.
Ferry_Description: A ferry existed across the Vecht in Hardenberg. According to an account of Duke Frederick of Schleswig-Holstein from ca. 1500, his servant had to pay a ferry fee in Hardenberg.

name: null
Ferry_Description: A ferry near Westervoort is first mentioned in an account of the count of Guelders of 1294/95. It is unclear whether it concerns a market ferry or a ferry for passengers. The ferry of Westervoort/IJsseloord thus probably dates from the thirteenth century or earlier. In 1765, it was replaced by a pontoon bridge.

name: Store Andst
Settlement_Description: The village of Andst was first mentioned in 1231, but is older. The parish church is from either the 12th or 13th century.

name: Bramdrup
Settlement_Description: The village of Bramdrup was first mentioned in 1231, but could be even older. The parish church is from either the 12th or 13th century.

name: Hald
Settlement_Description: The village of Hald was first mentioned in 1319, but is significantly older. The parish church is from either the 12th or 13th century.

name: Eldagsen
Settlement_Description: First mentioned at the end of the 11th century. An often-cited earlier mention of 826-876 is a falsification and cannot be linked to Eldagsen on linguistic grounds.
Town_Description: Eldagsen was mentioned as 'civitas' around 1300, in 1302 as 'oppidum' and in 1320 as borough ('weichbild'). It received town privileges from the counts of Hallermund with permission of the dukes of Brunswick in 1355.

name: Sorø
Settlement_Description: A Cistercian monastery founded in the middle of the 12th century. In the early modern period the former monastery was turned into an educational institution.
Town_Description: Sorø was granted town privileges by king Christian IV (1588-1648) in 1638.

name: Tøstrup
Settlement_Description: The village of Tøstrup was first mentioned in 1457, but is significantly older. The parish church is from either the 12th or 13th century.

name: Auning
Settlement_Description: The village of Auning was first mentioned in 1450, but is significantly older. The parish church is from either the 12th or 13th century.

name: Tauhardt
Toll_Description: Secondary station of safe conduct ('Beigeleitsstelle') of Eckartsberga, as mentioned in the regulations of safe conduct from 1550.

name: Nørre Galten
Settlement_Description: The village of Nørre Galten was first mentioned in 1407, but is significantly older. The parish church is from either the 12th or 13th century.

name: Hørning
Settlement_Description: The village of Hørning was first mentioned in 1407, but is significantly older. The parish church is from either the 12th or 13th century.

name: Rud
Settlement_Description: The village of Rud was first mentioned in 1445, but is significantly older. The parish church is from either the 12th or 13th century.

name: Rejsby
Settlement_Description: The village of Rejsby was first mentioned in 1294, but is significantly older. The parish church is from either the 12th or 13th century.

name: Hedemünden
Settlement_Description: First mentioned as royal farm in a 1017 donation charter. The settlement is listed as borough ('flecken') in 1460 and 1493-1494.
Town_Description: The town privileges of Hedemünden were confirmed in 1645.

name: Homeyenbrücke
Bridge_Description: First mentioned in 1216 (as new bridge), probably already mentioned in 1187. Later known as Homeyenbrücke. According to contracts between the old and new town from the 14th and 15th centuries, the bridge could be opened to let vessels with corn and flax pass.

name: null
Lock_Description: A pound lock at the margravial mill weir was built during the construction of the citadel after 1556. It is first mentioned in 1572. It replaced an earlier flash lock ('Flutrinne') that was probably located in a side canal that circumvented the mill weir.

name: null
Toll_Description: At places along the Havel and Spree in which locks had been constructed, a lock toll was collected for the maintenance of the locks. However, they were as high as other tolls which generated purely financial income.
Lock_Description: In 1548-1550 a round pound lock ('Kesselschleuse') was built at the Stone gate in Brandenburg. A reconstruction of the canal circumventing the new town ('Schiffahrt') and lock in Brandenburg is already mentioned in 1455, although the nature of the earlier construction is unknown.

name: null
Toll_Description: Toll-accounts (rotuli) of 'Termonde' are preserved for the years: 1364-1431.

name: Velling
Settlement_Description: The village of Velling was first mentioned in 1330-48, but is significantly older. The parish church is from either the 12th or 13th century.

name: Brejning
Settlement_Description: The village of Brejning was first mentioned in 1330-48, but is significantly older. The parish church is from either the 12th or 13th century.

name: Hæstrup
Settlement_Description: The village of Hæstrup was first mentioned in 1335, but is significantly older. The parish church is from either the 12th or 13th century.

name: Merum
Fair_Description: A fair on the first Tuesday of September was held in Merum until the 19th century; first evidence for this fair comes from a toll regulation from Roermond that probably dates from the 15th century. Inhabitants of Herten and Ool were freed of the road toll (pecunia viatica) levied at Roermond, because this town was exempted from the toll at the fair of Merum.

name: Malmø færge
Ferry_Description: A ferry between Malmö and Copenhagen was most likely founded by the middle of the 13th century.
Harbour_Description: Originally a natural harbour where ships anchored in the shallow water, and barges were used to transport people and goods into the town of Malmö. Later in the medieval period a jetty was constructed. The jetty was around 150 meters long. The harbour was frequently visited by foreign ships, in particular from Germany. In 1399, for example, ships from Lübeck sailed to Malmö.

name: Sønderby
Settlement_Description: The village of Sønderby was first mentioned in 1348, but is significantly older. The parish church is from either the 12th or 13th century.

name: Fangel
Settlement_Description: The village of Fangel was first mentioned in 1410, but is significantly older. The parish church is from either the 12th or 13th century.

name: Nexø
Town_Description: Oldest known town privileges was granted in 1346 by archbishop Peder Jensen Galen of Lund in Scania, who at the same time granted the neighboring settlement of Aakirkeby identical rights. Citizens first mentioned in 1404 and mayors in 1451. Nexø benefited from the rich fishing of herring in the Baltic Sea, and the town was also involved in the fishing and trading activities at the big markets at Skanør and Falsterbo in Scania. The fishing of herring attracted foreing traders; in Nexø a guilt for merchants from Kołobrzeg (German/Danish: Kolberg) was established in the late medieval period.

name: Kilen Bro
Bridge_Description: Around 1575 the steward (Danish: lensmand) of Ørum wished to build a bridge across Kilen. The bridge was not built before 1589. When the bridge collapsed in 1640, the ferry connection was reestablished.

name: Krouvi
Settlement_Description: Krouvi ('<b>Inn</b>') is one of the oldest villages in Marttila, established in the 14th century. It is located in the junction for Häme Oxen Road and the road leading south to Halikko. The name of the village ('inn') suggests a medieval place for an inn. In 1533, farmer "Hernic j Krogin" (Henry from the tavern house) is mentioned. In Jaakko Teitti's road description in 1556, the inn is located in the parish constable's farm in Juutila village 4 km southwest. In the 17th century, the constable office was moved to Krouvi.

name: Wintersdorf
Toll_Description: Secondary station of safe conduct ('Beigeleitsstelle') of Altenburg. Annual revenues are known from 1526/27 onwards. In the regulations for safe conduct ('Geleitsordnung') of 1548 fees are mentioned for wagons and carts only, no matter which cargo they carry.

name: Lobeda
Settlement_Description: Mention of a noble of Louede in 1156, but it is not entirely sure if this refers to Lobeda. In 1213 a parish priest of Lobeda is mentioned.
Town_Description: First mention of a town (civitas) in 1284, founded by the lords of Lobdeburg. In 1404 two mayors are mentioned, in 1407 the bylaws are confirmed (this record is lost, other bylaws remain from 1456).
Toll_Description: Wagon toll of the district Jena-Burgau, which is first mentioned in the accounts from 1481.

name: Christianshavn
Settlement_Description: Founded by king Christian IV (1596-1648) on the island of Amager as part of a general remodeling of the fortifications of Copenhagen, which lay on the opposite shore of a narrow strait of water. The foundation was also partly the result of an ambition to establish an international oriented urban community close to Copenhagen.
Town_Description: In 1639 king Christian IV (1596-1648) granted Christianshavn town privileges. Thus, Christianshavn was considered as an independent town until 1674, when the town privileges were revoked, and Christianshavn became a part of Copenhagen.

name: Frederikssund
Settlement_Description: Began as a ferry and slowly developed into a permanent settlement. The town of Frederikssund was not founded before the 18th century.
Toll_Description: Due to trading activities related to the ferry a toll station was established in 1573.
Ferry_Description: The age and character of the ferry across the most narrow part of Roskilde fjord is uncertain. Documented in 1516 but probably significantly older. In the 16th century two ferrymen were granted the ferry rights: one lived in Hornsherred on the western side of the shore and one near the settlement of Ude Sundby on the eastern shore. When king Frederick II (1559-1588) began building the castle of Frederiksborg in Hillerød the ferry was used for transporting building materials.

name: Zeilfeld
Toll_Description: Toll station of the district Heldburg, from which the oldest account dates from 1546.

name: Hurttala
Settlement_Description: <b>Inn:</b> Eero Mäntylä considers Herniäinen farm in Hurttala to be the oldest tavern in Hattula. The owner of the farm, Peter, is mentioned as a lay member of the King's court in 1385, and in 1405, Herniäinen farm hosted the Bishop's court gathering. Herniäinen is located close to the medieval Hattula church, and medieval churches often had a tavern nearby.

name: Svaneke
Settlement_Description: A permanent settlement based on fishing in the early middle ages. The settlement and later the town benefited from its location at the earstern tip of the island of Bornholm and the rich fishing, especially of herring, in the Baltic.
Town_Description: In the high medieval period the most important herring market on Bornholm was held in Svaneke. From around 1400 traces of trading relations between Svaneke and Hanseatic towns such as Stralsund. In 1491 “the town of Svaneke” (Danish: “Swanicke by”) was mentioned. Granted town privileges during the middle ages, perhaps around 1500. In 1543 a mayor and town bailiff were mentioned, and in 1555 older privileges were confirmed. In the period 1525-1576 the island of Bornholm was pawned to Lübeck, and apparently it was impossible for Svaneke to benefit from its privileges in this period.

name: Vejle
Settlement_Description: Founded in the end of the 11th century in the bottom of a fjord, Vejle Fjord, at an obvious place to cross a small river, Vejle Å, which runs into the fjord. The original version of the place name of Vejle presumably refers to a ford across the river.
Town_Description: Around the middle of the 12th century and perhaps even earlier Vejle had an urban character. The oldest known town privileges were granted by king Valdemar III (1326-1330) in 1327. Around 1310 a Dominican monastery was established. Town hall was mentioned in 1468 and presumably not much older. A royal castle was located near the town until the second half of the late medieval period.

name: Leiniälä
Settlement_Description: <b>Inn:</b> Reivilä farm in Leiniälä served as a parish constable (fi: nimismies, sw: länsman) and as a tavern in the early 17th c.

name: null
Harbour_Description: A natural harbour at Vindeboder near Sankt Jørgensbjerg from the Viking Age onwards. Sailing to Roskilde was, however, difficult, due to the shallow water in Roskilde Fjord, especially for larger medieval and early modern ships. The character of the harbour is not known.

name: null
Harbour_Description: Natural harbour in the fjord. A wharf existed in the harbour by 1328. In 1582 an existing wharf was expanded.

name: Aarhus
Settlement_Description: Aarhus is one of the oldest urban settlements of Denmark. Archeological excavations have shown how Aarhus was a permanent settlement with an urban character from around the year 800.
Town_Description: From the second half of the 10th century onwards Aarhus was a diocese, and one of the most significant towns of Denmark. Throughout the middle ages and early modern period Aarhus remained the clerical center of Eastern Jutland. At the turn of the 12th century at least three churches were built in Aarhus, and work on a new cathedral in the town center had begun. Soon after a town square, Store Torv, was established in front of the cathedral. A Dominican monastery was founded c. 1239. Around the middle of the 11th century the king issued coins in Aarhus, and later in the century the chronicler Adam of Bremen described Aarhus as “civitas”. Around 1300 Aarhus was given a town law by the king and a town hall was built at Store Torv. As in other towns in Jutland the town law was a copy of the law of Schleswig. The oldest preserved town privileges were granted by king Christoffer the Bavarian (1440-1448) in 1441, but the town was probably granted its first royal privileges in the 13th century. Already in the 10th century a rampart was built around most of the town, and the town continued to be fortified throughout the medieval period. Significant parts of the settlement, however, were located outside the fortification, especially from the 13th century onwards. During the late medieval period and early modern era Aarhus kept its status as one of the most important Danish towns. The town benefited from its central location in Jutland, and as an important junction for both land based and maritime transportation. The town was at its economic peak in the late 16th century, but in the following 17th century Aarhus stagnated, and the town was also damaged heavily during the Dano-Swedish wars.
Fair_Description: Market activities were essential already in the late 8th century, when craftsmen and traders gathered near the estuary of the river of Aarhus Å. During the medieval period at least one annual fair, the fair of Saint Olav, was held in Aarhus. Aarhus also held other annual fairs in the later middle ages and early-modern period. The age and character of these fairs is, however, uncertain. In the second half of the 17th century Aarhus only had one fair.
Toll_Description: The age and character of the toll in Aarhus is not known. Presumably, a royal toll was collected already in the Viking Age, and most certainly also in the early medieval period. In the 17th century a toll station was constructed, probably on the southern side of the river. But an even older toll station was presumably constructed on a piece of land owned by the king near the river in 1477. During the reign of king Hans (1481-1513) a specific toll on beer, wine and other goods was introduced in Aarhus as well as other Danish towns, the so-called ‘accise/sise’. This toll was collected by the town and on a regular basis handed over to the king. From Aarhus, registers of the sise-toll from the years around 1500 have been preserved.

name: Lübbersdorf
Settlement_Description: First mentioned in 1290 in a donation charter to Wanzka monastery.

name: Brandmühle
Settlement_Description: The water mill is already mentioned in 1309 and was in possession of Broda monastery, although it was at times partially privately owned.

name: Grenaa
Settlement_Description: Presumably a small settlement with an certain urban character around 1200. The settlement and later the town benefited from its location at the eastern tip of the peninsula of Djursland.
Town_Description: Grenaa is first mentioned in the so-called main piece in King Valdemar’s Cadastre from 1231. A royal estate is mentioned for the first time in 1327. Oldest preserved privileges were granted in 1440 by king Christoffer the Bavarian (1440-1448), but likely Grenaa was given its first town privileges in the 13th century. In 1433 members of the town council are mentioned. The first town hall was presumably built in the beginning of the 16th century.
Fair_Description: At least in the early modern period Grenaa held at least one annual fair. This was probably also the case in the late middle ages, but the character of the presumably medieval fair is unknown. In 1601 the fair originally held at Thorsager was relocated to Grenaa.
Harbour_Description: In 1270 a ship from Lübeck used the harbour in Grenaa. The remains of medieval harbour fortifications are believed to have been found south of the present outlet of a small river, Djursåen. The character of the medieval harbour is, however, uncertain. Throughout the late middle ages and early-modern period the harbour and town struggled with illegal harbours on the peninsula of Djursland.

name: Rosmus
Settlement_Description: The village of Rosmus was first mentioned in 1183, but is significantly older. The parish church is from either the 12th or 13th century.

name: Taps
Settlement_Description: The village of Taps was first mentioned in 1440, but is significantly older. The parish church is from either the 12th or 13th century.

name: Skanssi
Settlement_Description: <b>Inn:</b> Yrjö Luukkanpoika from Jämijärvi established an inn by Kyrö Skanssi fortlett in 1640.

name: Sint Anna ter Muiden
Settlement_Description: The settlement Mude is first mentioned in 1233 as part of a personal name Wilhelmus de Muda. "Sint Anna", after the patron saint of the town, was added to the name in the 16th century.
Town_Description: Mude was granted town privileges in March 1242 by Thomas (II) of Savoye, count of Flanders, and Joan of Constantinople, countess of Flanders. Initially important as an outport of Bruges on the Zwin estuary, it was troubled by silting of the Zwin and competition from Sluis in the 13th century and lost all economic significance in the middle of the 15th century.
Toll_Description: Mude was one of the stations where the toll on the Zwin of the counts of Flanders was levied. It is first mentioned as such in a toll account dated 1328/9, but probably installed shortly after 1252.

name: Manamansalo
Settlement_Description: <b>Inn:</b> An inn was established in Manamansalo in the 1640s.

name: Zuilichem
Toll_Description: A toll on sailing ships from the count of Gelre on the river Waal in Zuilichem is first mentioned in 1197, when the citizens of Tiel had rights as in the time of emperor Frederik († 1190). The farming out of the toll is found in the oldest account of the count of Gelre dated 1294 and in 1295 together with the tolls of Driel and Malsen.  The toll is last found in 1317. A undated tariff (before 1348) is preserved and edited for the citizens of Dordrecht. The toll must have been relocated before 1348 to Zaltbommel (oldest preserved toll-account there).

name: Huilu
Settlement_Description: <b>Inn:</b> 1st mention in 1472 as "Hwilo" (Swedish for resting place), which translated to Finnish as Huilu. Huilu village is first mentioned in 1540. By 1556 the 'resting place', possibly an inn, had moved to Lieto parish constable's farm in Pinomäki. An inn returned to Huilu in 1720s.

name: Neerpelt
Settlement_Description: Earliest mention in 815, in a copy dating from circa 1170. Next mention in 1107, in a thirteenth century copy.

name: Juva
Settlement_Description: <b>Inn:</b> Probably a place for king's estate (fi: kuninkaankartano, sw: kungsgård) before it was moved to Engesholm in 1559. Another possible place in Juttila, Marttila. King's estates were used as inns for officials. Juva village was first mentioned in 1566.

name: Ankka
Settlement_Description: <b>Inn:</b> Lieto parish constable was located in Ankka village in the 1630s. Parish constables (fi: nimismies, sw: länsman, eng. sheriff) were obliged to keep a tavern in the 16th c and 17th c.

name: Nahlendorf
Settlement_Description: Lunstädt and Nahlendorf are first mentioned in the tithe register of Hersfeld from the end of the 9th century. Both villages were hardly separated and can be seen as a double village ('Doppeldorf'). In 1937 Nahlendorf was incorporated into Lunstädt, which was in turn incorporated into Roßbach in 1950.

name: Köömilä
Settlement_Description: <b>Inn:</b> Kokemäki parish constable (fi: nimismies, sw: länsman) was located in Köömilä in 1635, when Klemetti Simonpoika Juupeli held the office. Constables were obliged to keep a tavern in late 16th c. - early 17th c.

name: Houten
Settlement_Description: First mentioned in a eleventh-century copy from a document from 918-948. Next mention in the tenth- eleventh century.

name: Pyrzyce
Settlement_Description: The beginnings as a fortification are dated back to the 9th century. Later in the 10th / 11th century a Slavic settlement developed. First mentioned in 1124. Close to the castle that was destroyed in 1283, Duke Barnim I founded an Augustianian nunnery before 1255. A mill existed in 1286.
Town_Description: First mentioned as town ('civitas') in 1248. In 1263 Barnim I granted Magdeburg town law and guild privileges.
Toll_Description: Pyrzyce acquired the right to levy a toll in 1301.

name: In den Ancker
Settlement_Description: This is an inn on the route between Zundert and Rucphen. This inn is part of one of the estates along the turfvaart channel.

name: Nispen
Settlement_Description: In the first half of the 12th century Arnulfus de Brabander donated an allodium to the abbey of Tongerlo. His son also donated the rights to two-thirds of the tithes within the parishes of Nispen and Zundert. Both these gifts were confirmed by the bishop of Liege in a charter from 1157, which is the first mention of Nispen.

name: Masia
Settlement_Description: <b>Inn:</b> A medieval guild hall was located in Masia in Munni farm. No exact date or location is known. Nearby hill is called Killanmäki ("Guild hill"). In 1639, an inn was established in nearby Kurittu, Heikki Vilpunpoika as the innkeeper. The inn moved to Haistila already the next year.

name: Koivisto
Settlement_Description: <b>Inn:</b> A medieval guild hall was located in Koivisto. No exact date is known, but in 1556, it is mentioned that the guild hall was by the rivermouth, which was at the time closer to Ulvila because of postglacial land uplift.

name: Děčín
Toll_Description: A salt toll of the duke of Bohemia is attested in 1146 and 1183, and in the 14th century. A toll on persons and horses on water and land is mentioned in 1359. According to a report of river merchants from Pirna in 1577, the tariffs of the toll of the Bünau family had been tripled in eight years time. In the 17th century two tolls are mentioned: a comital toll of the Thun family and a toll of the town council.

name: Kolding
Settlement_Description: Archaeological evidence of permanent settlement from around 1200. The settlement was located in the bottom of a fjord, Kolding Fjord, where a river, Kolding Å, runs into the fjord.
Town_Description: Kolding benefited from a location in the bottom of Kolding Fjord and near a section of Hærvejen/Ochsenweg, i.e. the historical system of roads running north-south that was concentrated on the watershed of the peninsula of Jutland. From Kolding there was also a relatively short distance across Jutland to the North Sea coast, in particular the town of Ribe. Also, Kolding was placed at the kingdom of Denmark's southern border to the duchy of Schleswig. In several ways, Kolding had a central location, and this gave the town an unique political and economical status. Kolding is mentioned for the first time in the so-called main piece in King Valdemar’s Cadastre from c. 1231, and probably had an urban character at this time. At least a town bailiff (Danish: Foged) and a town council are known from the 13th century. A Franciscan monastery was founded in 1288. It is unknown when Kolding was granted town privileges, but in 1321 king Christopher II (1320-1326 and 1330-1332) upheld previously granted privileges. A royal castle, Koldinghus, was built in the 13th century, and the castle remained one of the most important royal castles in Denmark throughout the middle ages and early-modern era. The town itself was fortified after 1313, perhaps around 1320. A town hall is mentioned for the first time in 1509. Although Kolding in general remained a dynamic and important town, it lost some of its momentum in the 17th century, when the nearby town of Fredericia was established. Kolding also suffered from the plague and several wars in the 17th century, for example during the Dano-Swedish wars 1657-1660 when the town was occupied by foreign forces.
Fair_Description: Due to its location at the border between the kingdom of Denmark and the Duchy of Schleswig, Kolding was an important market town with several annual fairs of both regional and international importance. The main commodity was oxen, which via the markets in Kolding were exported further south.
Toll_Description: Kolding was one of the most important royal tolls in Denmark. The age and character of the toll is, however, uncertain. Probably, it was introduced in the 14th century. The toll was collected near the bridge across the river. Toll registers from the early 16th century have been preserved in the court accounts of widow queen Christine, who then was granted the right to the toll (The National Archive/Rigsarkivet). As Kolding played a central role in the Danish export of oxen from the 15th century onwards, the toll on oxen was the most important. At the time of widow queen Christine in the early 16th century the toll was set at 2 shilling (Danish: skilling) per animal.
Staple_Description: Stable rights were granted by king Christian I (1448-1481) in 1475, who ordered that oxen were only allowed to be transported to Kolding as well as a few other towns (Assens, Ribe and the annual fairs in Skanør and Falsterbo). When Kolding lost its stable rights are uncertain.
Ferry_Description: Unregulated ferry between Kolding and Middelfart was mentioned in 1532.
Harbour_Description: The character of the medieval harbour is unknown. At first it was probably just a good natural harbour near the estuary of Kolding Å. Later a bulwark was built near the bridge across the river. The harbour was frequently used by German ships, for instance in 1399.

name: Præstø
Settlement_Description: Presumably a permanent settlement by the 13th century. The settlement and later town was located on a small island in the southern part of Præstø fjord. The character of the settlement, however, is uncertain.
Town_Description: Præstø was first mentioned in 1321. In 1353 king Valdemar IV (1340-1375) acquired Præstø from the Benedictine abbey of Saint Peder near Næstved. Præstø was apparently granted its first town privileges by king Eric the Pommerian (1396-1439) in 1403. A few years later, in 1406, a town council was documented. In 1470 the Antonines established an abbey in Præstø. Throughout the later middle ages and early modern era the town of Præstø struggled with illegal trade in the region, and in particular during the Dano-Swedish wars of the 17th century.

name: Wijchen
Settlement_Description: Earliest mention in 1155. Wijchen was a small, agrarian village. The castle is first mentioned in 1392, but probably dates from the fourteenth century.

name: Appeltern
Settlement_Description: The village and church of Appeltern are first mentioned in 1134, but the church is probably a little older. The castle of Appeltern is first mentioned in 1379.

name: Neu Krenzlin
Settlement_Description: First mentioned as Newen Crentzelein in 1534.

name: Bad Sulza
Settlement_Description: First mention in the tithe register of Hersfeld monastery from the late 9th century. Further mention in 1046, when a market was founded, which slowly developed into a town.
Town_Description: In 1353 referred to as oppidum, but until the 16th century referred to as borough ('Flecken') and little town ('Städtchen'). A council charter is only known since 1540.
Toll_Description: Secondary station of safe conduct ('Beigeleitsstelle') of Eckartsberga, as mentioned in a detailed list of safe conduct fees from 1550.

name: Delitzsch
Settlement_Description: The German Settlement probably had a Slavic predecessor. First written mention in 1200 in the name "Hermannus in Delicz". In 1207 a regional law court is mentioned.
Town_Description: Delitzsch became a town not before the second half of the 13th century. Market and town rights were probably granted around the same time. It is first referred to as town in 1306. In 1376 a (new?) town hall was constructed.
Fair_Description: A fair on St Gall in Delitzsch is mentioned in 1388, but later not anymore. In 1400 the market on St Peter and Paul is first mentioned. In 1428 an additional fair is founded on Sunday after the Assumption of Mary, which was moved to Sunday after All Saints in 1520.
Toll_Description: A fee for safe conduct was levied in Delitzsch on wagons and horses, with secondary stations of safe conduct in Landsberg and Zwochau. The surviving regulations of safe conduct in Delitzsch date from the 16th century, in a copy from 1668.

name: null
Bridge_Description: The first evidence for a bridge near the mill weir, the place of an old ford in the Ems, dates from 1362. With the extension of the town walls around 1450, the bridge must have been moved to the current location at the Emsstraße. The wooden bridge had to be repaired or rebuilt numerous times in the 17th century.

name: Schlotheim
Settlement_Description: First mentioned in 802-817. Mention of a castle in 974.
Town_Description: Referral to the town as "civitas" in 1277. The layout of the town is obviously planned. The bylaws of Schlotheim are recorded before 1408, at the beginning of the 14th century councillors, sheriffs and judges are mentioned.

name: Rheinsberg
Settlement_Description: A castle was built as a border fortress of the Ruppin dominion against Mecklenburg and later extended by the town complex. First mentioned in 1291.
Town_Description: Founded by the Lords of Ruppin. In 1368 the place was referred to as a civitas. Later the settlement is usually referred to as small town ('Städtlein'). After a fire in 1740 the town was rebuilt with a new street network.

name: null
Toll_Description: A fee was paid to cross the bridge (Danish: bropenge/brokorn). The exact age and character of the toll is, however, unclear.
Bridge_Description: The age of the bridge is uncertain. A bridge across the large river of Skjern Å was, however, built in the early 12th century. Wood from the oldest known medieval bridge has been dated to 1104/05 by dendrochronology. The bridge across Skjern Å was one of the longest bridges of medieval Denmark. In the late middle ages and early modern period a long wooden bridge of approx. 100 meters. At the end of the medieval period the bridge was moved c. 500 meters away from its original location, when Kongevejsbroen was built.

name: Helpt
Settlement_Description: First mentioned in 1298 in a donation charter to the monastery Wanzka.

name: Usadel
Settlement_Description: The village is first mentioned in 1310.

name: Nettesheim
Toll_Description: In 1386, the Archbishop of Cologne levied a land toll and/or road toll ('viaticum'). In 1386/87, 1392/93 and 1398/99, 8 mark were collected each year. In 1442/43 the annual revenue was 16 mark, in 1444/45 24 mark.

name: Rodenskrug
Settlement_Description: A tar kiln near Rollenhagen is mentioned in 1750. After its demise the tarmaker Tonnenberg built the inn Zechower Krug, later Rodenkrug, at the site.

name: Sakskøbing
Settlement_Description: The village of Sakstorp was located at a ford across a small river, Sakskøbing Å, and  probably founded in the 12th century.
Town_Description: A royal estate in “Sakstotp” is mentioned in the main piece of king Valdemar’s Cadastre from 1231. Another registration in the manuscript about the towns on the islands of Zealand, Lolland and Falster, which was written c. 1241, characterize Sakskøbing ("Saxakopingh") as a town. Thus, Sakskøbing was probably granted town rights in the 1230ties. Reconfirmed privileges from 1337 also indicate that the town was given town rights in the middle of the 13th century. The oldest preserved privileges, however, are from 1306. During the 13th and 14th centuries several kings issued documents in Sakskøbing, and the town also periodically functioned as a royal minting place. In 1423 mayors and members of the town council were mentioned for the first time. A town hall was first mentioned in 1449.
Fair_Description: In 1550 the fairs traditionally held in the village of Fjelde and in the village of Toreby were relocated to Sakskøbing. The character and date of both fairs are uncertain.

name: Karrebæk
Settlement_Description: The village of Karrebæk was first mentioned in 1231, but is significantly older. The parish church is from either the 12th or 13th century.

name: Elxleben
Settlement_Description: First mentioned in the Breviarium Sancti Lulli from 775/786-815.

name: null
Harbour_Description: Duisburg had been an important harbour on the Rhine river in the Early and High Middle Ages. Around 1200 or even earlier, the Rhine changed its course and Duisburg was now located on an old Rhine arm that silted up, leading to a decline of the harbour in the 14th century. On a 1566 view of the town, boats are still shown at the Dickelsbach (the former Rhine arm) in front of the Schwanentor, which indicate that the harbour could at this time still be reached with small vessels via the Ruhr river.

name: Tornow (Zehdenick)
Settlement_Description: First mentioned as small town ('oppidum') in 1348. A castle is mentioned in 1353. In 1428 the settlement is mentioned as village ('dörp').

name: Summa (Vehkalahti)
Settlement_Description: <b>Post house:</b> In 1638, the Royal Steward Bernhardt Steen von Steenhausen established a post house in the village of Summa in Vehkalahti. It also served as the constable's house.

name: Leidschendam
Settlement_Description: Leidschendam developed near a dam in the Vliet canal, which is first mentioned in 1434. The settlement is first mentioned in 1486.
Lock_Description: A dam in the Vliet canal in Leidschendam is first mentioned in 1434. The dam was pawned from the count of Holland by consecutively the families Van Wateringen, Van Naaldwijk and Van Arenberg. In 1580 the town of Delft became owner. Tariffs are known from 1435 (with priority for fish and wine) and 1562. The dam was built for regulating the water levels and prevented a free passage of ships. Cargoes therefore had to be transshipped here and small ships with flat bottoms dug over the dam. A flash lock was built in 1489, but destroyed by Gouda and Dordrecht in 1492 and 1493. During the Siege of Leiden in 1572, a flash lock was built, which remained in existence afterwards; in 1589 it was owned by Delft and opened six times a day to let small ships pass. The oldest account dated 1571/2 has 1971 pounds of revenues and a positive balance of almost 483 pounds.The development of the Vliet as a tow canal ('trekvaart') between Leiden and Delft in 1636-1638 increased the necessity of the construction of a pound lock, which was finally built in 1648. Ships could now pass the dam without unloading first.

name: Kirkkokari (Köyliö)
Settlement_Description: Site of late medieval pilgrimage and later sacrifical chapel associated with the cult of St Henrik of Finland (martyrized ca. 1164) with documented coins from 1364-87 to 1751-71.

name: Turun silta
Bridge_Description: King Erik of Pomerania confirmed on 22 November 1414 that the costs of the bridge in Turku (sw. Abo bro) were split between the town of Turku and peasant population and authorised the mayor and the burghers to negotiate a suitable deal in the matter. Whether the authorisation was about a completely new bridge or maintenance of an older one is not known. The bridge may have been preceded by a ferry. Since bishop Hemming of Turku donated in the 1340s the Cathedral a farm on the Southern side of Aurajoki river for the better access to the bishops to the church, no regular crossing of the river appears to have been existed all the year around at that time. The bridge and a plot of land next to it in the North is cited in 1420. The bridge was destroyed in the fire of Turku in 1827, and never rebuild. It was replaced with Tuomiokirkkosilta brigde some 100 meters upstream in 1831.

name: Stubbekøbing
Settlement_Description: Originally a fishing village at the strait of Grøndsund between the island of Møn and the island of Falster.
Town_Description: Stubbekøbing is listed as a town in King Valdemar’s Cadastre in a text within the manuscript originally written around 1240. Town seal known from around 1250, and in 1282 a town bailiff was mentioned for the first time. The oldest known town privileges, however, is from 1354. A few years later, in 1367, a town council was also mentioned, and in the following 15th century, in the year 1464, a town hall. Stubbekøbing was throughout the medieval period the largest and most important town on the island of Falster. In the 16th century, however, the town lost ground to the neighboring town of Nykøbing Falster. Stubbekøbing benefited from its location at the narrowest part of Grønsund, and trading with Hanseatic towns and merchants.
Fair_Description: Annual fair (Danish: Sankt Hansmarked) at the Feast day of Saint John the Baptist, i.e. June 24th. The fair was abolished in 1556, but reestablished in 1569. When the market originally was founded is not known.
Harbour_Description: Archaeological excavations have revealed the medieval harbour a bit south of the medieval town. Here it was possible for ships to use a natural harbour in a small fjord that no longer exists. During the medieval period in particular grain was exported from Stubbekøbing harbour. The harbour was used by Hanseatic merchants from the high medieval period onwards. In 1399, for example, ships from Lübeck sailed to Stubbekøbing.

name: null
Harbour_Description: The character of the medieval harbour is unknown. Presumably, the town only had a natural harbour. According to a map of Ærøskøbing in Resen’s Atlas Danicus from 1677 a harbour had a jetty.

name: Goedereede
Settlement_Description: Earliest mention of Goedereede is in 1312, when it was granted town rights.
Town_Description: Goedereede was granted town rights on 1 May 1312 by Gerard, lord of Voorne. The original charter has been lost; thanks to copies, the town rights are known.
Fair_Description: In the town-privilege of 1312 already was stated that seafaring inhabitants of Westvoorne had to attend the market in Goedereede. On August 19 1330 Gerard van Voorne, burgrave of Zeeland, granted a herringfair.
Toll_Description: Already before 1312 a comital fishtoll was levied. In 1475 an outpost for the toll of Geervliet was planned in Goedereede. In 1476 the six great towns opposed this outpost then named for the tolls of Geervliet and Iersekeroord.
Staple_Description: In the town privileges of 1312 it was stated that seafaring inhabitants of Westvoorne had to attend the market in Goedereede and a fish toll is found. On 8 February 1331 Gerard van Voorne granted a privilege for a weekly market on Thursday for the inhabitants of Westvoorne with compulsory market at Goedereede. In 1477 this regional staple right was confirmed.
Ferry_Description: A ferry between Schouwen (Brouwershaven) and West-Voorne (Goeree) was first mentioned in 1313. In the late 15th and 16th century, the ferry seems not to have functioned. Another ferry connected Goedereede with Strype near Rockanje, and from 1595 also with De Quack and Hellevoetsluis. A ferry with Zierikzee, first mentioned in 1391, seems to have disappeared by 1595, when no one could be found who was interested in operating it.
Harbour_Description: Already before 1312 a comital fishtoll was levied. In 1393 (Jan. 30) duke Albrecht renewed toll-exemption in Holland and Zeeland. In 1545 (June 11) emperor Charles V granted a fee during 20 years on fish- and ships with grain and catch of fish and grown grains (with a tariff). Yields were destined to deepen the harbour and restore the quays. In 1562 (May 13) an impost for another 20 years was granted on  seafaring fish-ships.

name: Geervliet
Settlement_Description: Geervliet is first mentioned in 1195. In the thirteenth century, the lords of Putten situated their court there. A chapter in the church is known for the years 1308-1571. A hospital is first mentioned in 1314.
Town_Description: Geervliet is granted town priviliges on 4 April 1381 by Sweder, lord of Abcoude-Gaesbeek, Putten and Strijen. During the reign of his successor and son, the town was surrounded by a stone wall.
Toll_Description: The Geervliet tol for sailing transport has its origin in the Carolingian period. It is the successor to a royal toll that was dependant of the former Dorestad toll. Originally the Geervliet tol was situated in Geervliet near the Bernisse river. It controlled the trafic coming from the North Sea towards the Netherlands going to Flanders, Brabant and Dordrecht via the rivers Meuse and Scheldt, moreover it controlled the traffic from the rivers Meuse, Waal and Rhine to Dordrecht, Flanders, Brabant and the North Sea. Because skippers tried to avoid the toll, outposts were situated in Sloecketers, Niervaert (Klundert), den Broeck, Hannekijnswairt, Rillant, Borsselshaec, Texel and Vlieland, and Enkhuizen. In the 16th century the toll was relocated to Dordrecht (the office was in the Joppens or Toll tower) because the Bernisse silted. Outposts were situated then in Geervliet, on the Spui river near Hekelingen, and in Delfshaven, Schiedam, Geertruidenberg, Steenbergen, 's-Grevelduin-Kapelle, Leur, Strijen, Gastel, Oudenbosch, Rosendaal, Brielle, Maassluis, Zwartewaal, Goeree and Breda. The toll was founded and owned by (a predecessor of) the Count of Holland and after the Rebellion against Spain it was owned by the States of Holland and West-Friesland. A tariff for those of Utrecht and for the lord of Putten is preserved and edited, dated 1357 or 1358.  A list with exempt places, abbeys and convents at the tolls of Dordrecht and Geervliet is s.d. (first half of 16th century).Accounts from the Geervliet toll are preserved for the years (probably) 1370, 1531/2, 1533/4 and (only for grain transports) 1544-46. Later tariffs and lists of exempt places are dated 1454 (Hansa), 1500, 1506, 1511, 1516, 1553.Later partly incomplete accounts for the years 1724 and 1769, 1780-1805 (complete toll),1771- 1795 (branch Rotterdam), 1729 – 1761 (branch Maassluis), 1621 (branch Pietershoek/land van Bonaventura).
Ferry_Description: Ferries to Abbenbroek and Heenvliet are first mentioned in 1379. The ferry-man at Heenvliet was also responsible for the beacons on the river Maas and levied a beacon-tax for this purpose.

name: null
Bridge_Description: In 1723 the wooden bridges at the Seehäuser gate were exchanged for stone bridges.

name: Kammerhof
Settlement_Description: In 1409 margrave Jost grants Seeburg the Kammerhof as fiefdom.
Ferry_Description: The establishment of a ferry in Kammerhof led to a conflict with Werben, which had held ferry privileges since 1360.
