Since Seeburg and Werben could not reconcile themselves, the margrave decided in 1448 that the ferry operation in Kammerhof had to be stopped. It was continued at a later date.

name: Woerden
Settlement_Description: Woerden is first mentioned in a fifteenth-century copy of a documented written after 786. Settlement history, however, dates back to the Roman period. The remains of a Roman Limes fortress have been found. In 1159 a castle is built at that spot by the bishop of Utrecht, Godfrey van Rhenen.
Town_Description: Town rights were granted on 12 March 1372 by Albert I, duke of Bavaria, governor ('ruwaard') of Holland. Woerden had been fortified with stone town walls and a moat before 1372.
Fair_Description: In 1410 (July 5) duke Jan van Beieren granted a free horse-fair and an oxen-fair. The buyer had to pay per horse 1 holl. herengroot on the free fair 3 days before St. Petersday advincula (August 1), and per cow 1/2 holl. herengroot on the free fair of St. Victorsday (October 10). The marketright on both fairs lasted 9 days. In 1596 the Estates of Holland granted a meager cattle-fair on the three Wednesdays before May 1. The town was well situated to fatten oxen in the surrounding meadows and had a lot of damage as a result of the 'Opstand' (raise against Spain).
Toll_Description: Prior to 1300 an episcopal toll on sailing ships existed, which circa 1300 was usurpated by the count of Holland. A tariff of about 1340 is preserved and edited. Around 1530 a new tariff is found in the accounts of the steward of the count with toll exemption for the Sticht Utrecht, the Land of Woerden and Nieuwkoop. Around 1540 Leiden is added. Probably this included also exemption from the tolls on the fairs as next to fishing vessels freight wagons are mentioned. In a charter concerning the lease of this toll dated 1542 (and later examples) the toll of Bodegraven is included.
Staple_Description: In 1396 Woerden obtained a staple-right from duke Albrecht. All hemp, grease and coats in the Land of Woerden had te be traded on the market in Woerden.

name: Nieuwpoort (Lek)
Settlement_Description: Nieuwpoort is first mentioned in a 1449 copy of a 1283 document.  A hospital is first mentioned in 1421.
Town_Description: Nieuwpoort was granted town rights in 1283, by Arnoud, lord of Liesveld, and Gijsbrecht, lord of Langerak. It thus became a codominium of the barons of Liesveld and the lords of Langerak. Possibly, earlier grants were made by their fathers. In 1489, the town walls and gates were destroyed. After have been besieged and burnt several times, Nieuwpoort is transformed into a fortress in 1672.
Fair_Description: In 1536 (Febr. 7) some inhabitants declared before the magistrate that after the fair in Nieuwpoort dated June 15-July 3, in Schoonhoven a free fair was on July 4-17 In 1614 it appears to be a horsemarket in June and a cattle-market in October, both for 14 days.
Harbour_Description: In 1283 Nieuwpoort obtained toll-exemption from the bishop of Utrecht for the tolls in the Sticht Utrecht.

name: Woudrichem
Settlement_Description: The first mention of Woudrichem dates from the tenth to eleventh century.
Town_Description: Woudrichem was granted town rights before 28 March 1283. Most likely, this grant took place in the period between 1272 and 1283 and was issued by William II of Horne (Huis Horne), lord of Altena. A hospital is first mentioned in 1359.

name: Leerdam
Town_Description: Leerdam is mentioned as a town ('stede') in 1371, but was granted town rights on 11 November 1382 by Otto, lord of Arkel.

name: null
Bridge_Description: Already in 1341 the monastery Clarholz acquired the permission to build a bridge across the Gellenbach, should the need arise, but it is unclear whether the bridge was actually built at the time. Later there existed a wooden bridge, which was replaced by a stone bridge in 1805.

name: Heusden
Settlement_Description: The name Heusden is first mentioned in 1108-1122, then spelled as 'Hysdene'. This, however, refers to present-day Oud-Heusden.In the thirteenth century, a new settlement originated near the local castle, which by 1250 had acquired the right of a fish market. A chapter in the church is known for the years 1355-ca. 1598. A hospital is first mentioned in 1397-1402.
Town_Description: Heusden was probably granted town rights between 1286 (when it is mentioned as a 'oppidulum') and 1296 (when it is described as a 'civitatem'). These rights may have been granted by Jan (John) III of Heusden.
Fair_Description: The toll-acounts dated 1391-93 mention a fair with 'Vastelavont' (eve before Ash Wednesday). Duke Willem ordained markettoll-exemption at Heusden (and Woudrichem) in 1407 for the following towns: Amsterdam, Middelburg, Zierikzee, Goes, Delft, Gouda, Haarlem, Rotterdam, Alkmaar, Geertruidenberg, Beverwijk, in 1408 for Leiden, in 1411 for Hoorn, in 1413 for Schiedam and finally in 1414 for Monnickendam and Dordrecht. In 1595 (July 10) the Staten of Holland ordained that as of old two free horse-fairs were permitted, next to the free fair.
Staple_Description: In 1357 Heusden obtained from duke Willem V of Holland a staple privilege regarding all fish traded upstream the rivers Meuse and Waal. Only herring from Scania was excepted and had to be marketed 'ten hoechsten marcten', i.e. in Venlo or Cologne. A tariff is preserved and edited. After the bend of the river on which Heusden is located was cut short north of town by Den Bosch in or shortly after 1480, much river traffic circumvented the town and the staple lost its importance.

name: Tholen
Settlement_Description: Tholen is first mentioned in 1261. It originates near a toll. In the early fourteenth century fortifications are added.
Town_Description: A hospital is first mentioned in 1312. Tholen was granted town rights on 7 December 1366 by John of Blois, lord of Beaumont, Schoonhoven and Tholen. On 16 May 1452, a large fire swept through Tholen. In 1291, the duke of Brabant grants toll freedom on the Honte and Schelde. In 1335, the duke of Holland grants stapel freedom for oats and corn to 'van der Tolnen in Zeeland dat men heyt Harderscoet'. In 1346, the countess of Holland and Zeeland grants toll freedom to 'Toelne en Scakersloe'.
Fair_Description: Count Jean de Blois granted Tholen in 1379 (Febr. 17) a free fair starting Monday after St. Johnsday Midsummer (June 24) during 8 days. In 1575 (August 2) king Philip II permitted, due to war-damage, relocation to the first Friday after the Nativity of the Virgin Mary (Sept. 8). This sooted better with the grain-trade.

name: Reimerswaal
Town_Description: Reimerswaal was granted town rights on 1 April 1375 by Albert ('Albrecht') of Bavaria, regent ('ruwaard') of Holland. In 1323 it obtained toll-exemption form the count of Holland. A hospital is first mentioned in 1348.In the sixteenth century Reimerswaal suffered from several storm surges, most notably the St. Felix's flood of 1530. Jacob van Deventer still drew the town as part of his town atlas around 1555, but in 1631, the remains of the city were deserted and claimed by the water.
Fair_Description: In 1355 (31 mei) gaf hertog WIllem van Beieren twee jaarmarkten: 1) maandag na vastenavond tot vrijdag daarna, 2) maandag na Bamis (1 okt.) tot vrijdag daarna, met vrijgeleide. Tegelijk gaf hij het privilege dat alle goederen die ter jaarmarkt werden gebracht uit Brabant en Vlaanderen vrij zouden zijn van de tol te Iersekeroord. In 1373 (24 jan.) bepaalde hertog Albrecht dat de marktvrede 14 dagen voor en na de jaarmarkt zou duren. In 1520 (8 jan) verlengde koning Karel op verzoek van het stadsbestuur van Reimerswaal de duur van beide vrije jaarmarkten en bepaalde dat de eerste voortaan op Aswoensdag zou beginnen. In 1575 ging de secretaris van Goes naar de centrale regering om de jaarmarkt van Reimerswaal te verkrijgen, de uitslag is onbekend.
Staple_Description: In 1315 (21 sept.) bepaalde graaf Willem van Henegouwen dat alle kooplieden die uit zijn landen op Brabant of uit Brabant op zijn landen varen hun goederen (uitgezonderd verse vis) eerst moeten brengen op de weekmarkt van de stad Reimerswaal op donderdag met vrijgeleide.

name: Goes
Settlement_Description: According to Van Berkel & Samplonius, Goes is first mentioned in 976. Cox seems to consider the subsequent mention in 1216 more trustworthy as a first mention.
Town_Description: From a juridical perspective, Goes became a town on 7 July 1405, via a statement of Willem VI, count of Holland en Zeeland. From a social-economic point of view, Goes may already be considered a town before that date. In 1417, Goes was granted the right to built fortifications.
Fair_Description: Jacoba van Beieren granted in 1417 (August 7) a fair with tariffs, starting 8 days before Lady Day (August 15) and 8 days after (August 8-22). The first showday was on August 14, but that caused problems as nobody showed up the day after the Assumption of the Virgin Mary. In 1441 (Sept. 12) the first showday was replaced to the Monday after August 15. In 1575 the secretary of Goes visited the central government to obtain the fair of Reimerswaal. A result is not known. King Philip II granted Goes a free fair in 1580 (Dec. 24) for all kind of commodities, in particular horses and cattle. Duration: ? CHECK

name: Sint Maartensdijk
Settlement_Description: Sint Maartensdijk is first mentioned in 1304.
Town_Description: Sint Maartensdijk was probably granted town privileges between 24 February and 9 June 1485 by Alienora van Borssele, lady of Sint Maartensdijk. A chapter in the church is known for the years 1428-ca. 1577.

name: Zierikzee
Settlement_Description: Zierikzee is first mentioned in a thirteenth-century copy of a document dated 1156. Zierikzee developed into a governmental centre of the count, and became a port and trading place. A meat house exists in 1248. A cloth hall is first mentioned in 1318. A hospital is first mentioned in 1271.  A chapter in the church is found for the years 1378-1573.
Town_Description: Zierikzee was granted town privileges some time around 1220 (before May 1217, or May 1220- February 1222) by William I, count of Holland. The charter, however, has not survived. The earliest surviving charter dates from 11 March 1248. In 1290 it obtained toll-exemption from the count of Holland. In 1304 Zierikzee was freed from the staple in Dordrecht. In 1368 Zierikzee received from the king of Sweden the rigt to have a 'vitte' (trading-post) on Schonen (southern point of Sweden) with its own guardian.
Fair_Description: In 1389 Zierikzee is supposed to have obtained a fair lasting 14 days by duke Albrecht. In 1421 (August 27) Philip of Burgundy granted a free fair. priv.boek op NA, HS 3e afd. inv.nr. 1436 fol.? DATA? In 1531 the emperor donated a second fair in the Lent and a staple for madder. In 1575 (June 22) the fair with St. Jacob (July 25) which was too early in the harvest as there was little grain, was relocated to the Monday before the Assumption of the Virgin (August 15). In 1583 (July 12) stadtholder William of Orange granted a fair the first Monday in September during six days.
Staple_Description: In 1304 the town obtained the right on the 'korenmaat' (measure for grain) and was ordained that all grain from the Land of Schouwen had to be traded on the market in Zierikzee. One year later all people working in the drapery Beoosten Schelde should only do that in Zierikzee. Emperor Charles V ordained in 1531 that all madder from Schouwen had to be inspected at Zierikzee and all grain had to be sold there. The guild-charter of the fishermen of St. Peter and Paul dated 1553 (August 21) said that alle fresh fish from Vlieland or from the sea transported along the harbour of Zierikzee had to be marketed and sold in the town for a fourth part.

name: Brouwershaven
Settlement_Description: According to Van Berkel & Samplonius, the first mention of Brouwershaven as 'Brijdorpersluis' dates from around 1305. Cox considers 1318 it's earliest mention, when the village is first called 'Brouwershavene'.Brouwershaven was founded on the initiative of the count of Holland and Zeeland from 1286 onward, in the 'ambacht' Brijdorp.
Town_Description: Brouwershaven was granted town privileges on 7 February 1403 by Albert I, duke of Bavaria, count of Holland and Zeeland. The charter mentions an earlier statute that must probably be dated before 1351. In 1342 (Juli 18) Willem (IV, count of Holland) gave toll-exemption to the inhabitants of 'Hurdzee ende nu hiet heren Aernoudshaven' (Brouwershaven).
Fair_Description: In 1344 (Nov. 24) Brouwershaven obtained a privilege for a free herringmarket from count Willem IV. In 1566 king Philip II purchased Brouwershaven out off the insolvent estate of Maximiliaan van Bourgondië. He thereupon donated a fair starting 27 August=Sept. 9 (duration 14 days) including a horsefair on the last day of August, with permission for a.o. a new fishmarket with saltworks.
Toll_Description: A fish-toll is first found in the accounts of the count in 1340. One undated herringtoll-account, dated probably 1477, is preserved and analysed.
Staple_Description: Brijdorp had a staple for beer from Holland. In 1288 the duke of Brabant gave exemption of his tolls to the inhabitants of the yet to be founded manor of Brijdorp. The placename Brouwershaven is first found in 1318. This gives the termini ante and post quem.
Ferry_Description: A ferry between the islands Schouwen and West-Voorne (Goeree) is first mentioned in 1313. In 1328 a ferry between Brouwershaven and Zierikzee is found. In 1433 and 1437 it is specified as sailing from Brouwershaven. The ferry sailed in both directions. It seems not to have existed in the late 15th and 16th century, but from 1600, a Brouwershaven ferryman on the ferry to Goedereede is mentioned again.
Harbour_Description: Possibly, a harbour was already located here before 1286, but from 1286 onward, it was further developed.  In 1342 (Juli 18) Willem (IV, count of Holland) gave toll-exemption to the inhabitants of 'Hurdzee ende nu hiet heren Aernoudshaven' (Brouwershaven).In 1440 Philip of Burgundy granted a spout in order by using the flood water to deepen the harbour. The village had to pay onethird of the costs. In 1519 there were 42 'stuurlieden' (steersmen of boats) in the village. In 1541 en 1554 Maximiliaan van Burgundy granted the levying of excises for several years to construct a new quay and harbour head. Around 1562 the village had 50 boats for the catch of salted fish (around 1600 37), in 1570 12 heringbusses. In 1570 when the neighbouring villages Bommenede and Goedereede as of flooding were inundated  Brouwershaven tried by giving tax-advantages to enlarge the harbour. Zierikzee was two hours away.
Lock_Description: Possibly, a lock was already located here before 1286, but from 1286, it was further developed.

name: Zevenbergen
Town_Description: In 1369, Zevenbergen is still mentioned as a village. The first mention of Zevenbergen as a town dates from 14 september 1396. Town rights were thus granted some time between 1369 and 14 September 1396. Possibly, these rights were granted by Hugeman of Strijen, lord of Zevenbergen.
Harbour_Description: The harbour is first mentioned in 1287. The harbour for peat ("turfthaven") was in the same location as the regular harbour.

name: Helmond
Settlement_Description: The earliest mention of Helmond can be found in a twelfth-century copy of documents dating from 1108. Archaeological evidence indicates that a new settlement came into being east of the river Aa near the castle 't Oude Huys around 1225.
Town_Description: According to Cox, Helmond probably received town rights between 1225 and 28 May 1241. He states that it is most likely that this happened some time around 1232. Around 1400 stone town walls and a castle were built.
Fair_Description: In 1376 duchess Johanna granted the lord of Helmond three fairs and a weekly markt on Tuesday. Dates fairs: 1) Sunday before Midlent, 2) Tuesday after Pentecost and 3) third Sunday before St. Dionisusday (Oct. 9). In 1382 toll-exemptions of Helmond at Grave, in the Land of Cuyk, Den Bosch, Lith, the Land of Breda and the Land of Turnhout are confirmed. Circa 1400 a cloth/breadhouse and meathouse are mentioned. In 1425 a weigh-house is known. In 1456 inhabitants of Helmond are first seen at the fairs of  Frankfurt. In 1457 (Febr. 7) the start of the three fairs was altered: 1) Tuedsay before Half Lent, 2) Tuesday before Pentecost, 3) Tuesday before St. Dionysius. Safe-conduct for all three fairs remainend three days before and after the days. An undated register from the abbey Tongerlo (Westerlo, B.) (circa 1556) contains a list of fairs in the region Kempen and Peel. 'Helmont' then still has three fairs: 1) the third Tuesday in the Lent, 2) Tuesday before Sinxten (Pentecost), 3) Sunday before St. Michael (Sept. 29) till the Tuesday after that.In 1592 (March 20) king Philip granted a fourth fair.

name: Strümp
Toll_Description: In Stümp, a land toll was levied from 1294 until about 1454/60. After that, the toll was transferred to the Brühl. The Count of Kleve held the toll until 1392, after which the toll fell to the Electorate of Cologne ('Kurköln').

name: null
Ferry_Description: See ferry Krimpen aan de Lek

name: Biervliet
Settlement_Description: Biervliet was probably founded around the same time as Damme, around 1180, by Philip of Alsace, count of Flanders. It is first mentioned in a 13th-century copy of a document dated 1183.
Town_Description: Town rights were granted before or in 1183 by Philip of Alsace, count of Flanders. Biervliet was located at the Braakman, which made it into a prosperous trading town. During storm surges in 1375 and 1404, it became located on a tiny island and entered into economic decline. In the 16th and 17th century, land reclaimations began. In 1702, a dike to IJzendijke reconnected Biervliet to the mainland.
Fair_Description: A fair on St Barnabas' Day (11 June) in Biervliet is mentioned in 1344. Due to the economic decline of the town, it must have ceased to exist in the 14th century.
Toll_Description: Revenues from a comital toll in Biervliet are mentioned in 1187. Toll-accounts are preserved for the years 1381-1492 (with lots of gaps), on beer for the years 1382-1492 (with lots of gaps) and on (cured)herring for the years 1412-'92 (also with lots of gaps). In 1471 it was leased for three years. The toll was abolished in 1502 by Philip the Handsome because of the construction of the canal Brugse Vaart.

name: Lathen
Settlement_Description: First mentioned in the possession of the monastery Corvey in 884.
Toll_Description: A toll of the bishop of Münster in Lathen is mentioned in 1613.

name: Ihrhove
Settlement_Description: The church was built in the mid-13th century.

name: Wiltshausen
Settlement_Description: A ferry house was built in 1562.
Ferry_Description: Ferry across the Leda river. A ferry house was built in 1562.

name: Terneuzen
Settlement_Description: According to Van Berkel & Samplonius, Terneuzen is first mentioned in 1340. Cox adheres to a slightly earlier date, 1325. The settlement originated near a waterway to Gent. During the Eighty Years War, Terneuzen became an important fortified town.
Town_Description: On 23 April 1584, Terneuzen was granted town privileges by William I, prince of Orange. Many of these privileges were granted because the inhabitants of Terneuzen could no longer go to the city of Axel for commerce and juridical matters, as Axel had become Spanish property. Afterwards, Terneuzen kept these privileges.Terneuzen was elevated to city rank by Royal Decree in 1816.
Toll_Description: A toll in Terneuzen was pawned together with the new lock in 1397. Owners of moorland around the Westvaart were exempted from the toll, against a payment of 12 lb. annually. One toll-account on hopped beer in the harbours of the Vier Ambachten and Terneuzen and a.o. Hulst dated 1439/'40 is preserved.
Harbour_Description: The Westervaart canal between Axel and Terneuzen was dug before 1309. In Axel, it was connected with the Oostervaart towards Gent. Terneuzen became an important harbour, among others for the export of peat from the Flemish moors.
Lock_Description: A new lock was constructed in Terneuzen in 1393.

name: null
Harbour_Description: In 1331 IJsselstein obtained toll-exemptiom from the bishop of Utrecht for the Sticht Utrecht. In 1584 William of Orange gave as tutor of his son Filips Willem, baron of IJsselstein, and his daughter Maria van Nassau, permission to the magisrtrate to levy a tax from the inhabitants up to 1000 guilders, to deepen the harbour.

name: Oerle
Settlement_Description: First mentioned in 1249. Oerle obtained market-rights for a weekly market in 1551 from the duke.

name: Oude Brug
Bridge_Description: The wooden "old bridge" across the harbour of Amsterdam was built in the 14th century.

name: Wöhrden
Settlement_Description: The settlement is first mentioned in 1281. It was built on an artificial mound ('wurt'), had a harbour and acquired market privileges in 1373. It was also known as Altenwöhrden to discern it from other settlements built on artificial mounds.
Fair_Description: In 1373 the parishes of Wöhrden, Neuenkirchen, Wesselburen, Weddingstedt and Hemmingstedt founded fairs in competition to those in Meldorf, on the Nativity of St John (24 June) and the Nativity of Mary (8 September).

name: Axel
Settlement_Description: Axel is first mentioned in a eleventh-century copy of a document dated between 987 and 994.
Town_Description: According to Cox, Axel was granted town privileges in 1183 by Philip of Alsace, count of Flanders. A charter does not exist. However, a later charter from 1532 attests that town rights were granted in 1213 by Ferdinand, count of Flanders, and Joan (of Constantinople), countess of Flanders.
Fair_Description: Count Philip the Good of Flanders confirmed the privileges of Axel in 1456, which included the right to hold two fairs in the beginning of August and October, and a weekly market on Saturday. The oldest town account from 1492/3 mentions an "old market" and two fairs with a horse toll. The town accounts of 1583/4 mention a flax and skin market.
Toll_Description: The toll in Axel might go back to the privileges from 1213. In 1227, it was owned by Willem van Beveren, who issued detailed toll regulations for various commodities, wagons and ships in 1235. Exemptions for monasteries and various villages are known for several years. The toll was acquired by the count of Flanders in 1315, who leased it out.
Staple_Description: Axel received a wool staple, possibly in 1297. Woollen cloth was not allowed to be sold within one mile around the town. Foreigners were only allowed to buy cloth that was fulled in Axel and received a specific mark.
Harbour_Description: Axel had shipping connections with the Westerschelde near Terneuzen via the Westervaart, and with Gent via the Oostervaart. The harbour was located at the east side of town. In the 14th-16th century, the canals and the harbour silted up, until large-scale inundations during the Dutch Revolt and the subsequent destruction and reconstruction of Axel as a border fortress in 1587 radically changed the situation.

name: Sas van Gent
Settlement_Description: Sas van Gent developed around a lock ('sas') in the canal Sassevaart that connected the city of Gent with the sea. The settlement must have come into existence around the time that building works on the lock were finished, in 1563. Sas van Gent was destroyed by the watergeuzen during the Dutch Revolt in 1572, but was rebuilt. After the conquest of the settlement by the Dutch Republic in 1644, it acquired a town-like character, although it was only elevated to a town in 1816 by William I, king of the Netherlands.
Harbour_Description: With the construction of the Sassevaart from 1547 onwards, Sas van Gent became the sea harbour of Gent.

name: Philippine
Town_Description: The earliest mention of Philippine dates from 1505/1506. In this period the walled town was founded in a newly constructed polder. At its foundation, Philippine was granted town rights. In the 1630s, it became a fortified town. From 1635 onwards, it also became a traders' town of some importance.

name: Kortgene
Settlement_Description: According to Van Berkel & Samplonius, Kortgene is first mentioned in 1247. Cox argues for a slightly earlier date, 1217. In 1413 town walls and gates were built.
Town_Description: Kortgene is first mentioned as a town on 6 December 1421. An official charter granting town rights has not survived. However, town privileges were probably granted by Philip of Borselen ('Filips van Borselen'), lord of Kortgene.During a flood in 1532, Kortgene was drowned. In 1681, the town was again reclaimed from the sea.
Fair_Description: A free fair and a weekly market were granted by Charles the Bold in 1474 for 'Cortekene', seigniory of knight Floris van Borsele.

name: Middelbeers
Settlement_Description: The settlement Beers, first mentioned in 1207, was divided into three parts, of which Middelbeers is first mentioned separately in 1542.

name: null
Bridge_Description: The bridge across the Wethau in the village of Wethau, formerly also known as the Zeitz bridge ('Zeitzische Brücke') belonged to the city council of Naumburg, and its annals mention that it had to be rebuilt or repaired multiple times, among others in 1402, 1454, 1470, 1499, 1503, 1508 and 1510. In the regulation of safe conduct of Eckartsberga, the bridge is mentioned as the end of the safe conduct of Eckartsberga and the beginning of the safe conduct of Weißenfels.

name: Domburg
Settlement_Description: In the vicinity of the modern town Domburg, another traders' settlement was located in the years around 200. This settlement, however, dissappeared into the sea. Archeological remains of a castle ('ringburcht') have been found. This castle was built shortly after 885. The first mention of Domburg in written records dates from the period 1181-1210.
Town_Description: 'Dumburgh infra castellum' (located in the east) was granted town rights between 25 December 1222 and 24 December 1223 by Floris IV, count of Holland, and Dirk, lord of Voorne and burgrave of Zeeland. 'Dumburgh extra castellum' (located in the west) was excluded from these town rights. In 1271 a hospital is mentioned. Domburg never fully developed into a town.
Fair_Description: In 1534 (16 nov.) verleende  stadsheer Adolf van Bourgondië een vrije weekmarkt. Blijkens de stadsrekening van 1545/'6 duurde de jaarmarkt 8 dagen. De stadsrekening van 1585/'6 noemt voor het eerst uitgaven voor een paardenmarkt.

name: Steenbergen
Settlement_Description: Steenbergen is first mentioned in 1267. The settlement is granted various privileges in the late thirteenth and early fourteenth century. The inhabitants also gained the right to build a stone wall around their settlement. In 1331, 'poorters' (burghers) were mentioned, but in 1337, Steenbergen is still called a 'dorp' (village).
Town_Description: Town privileges were granted between 1337 and 1345 by Mathilde ('Machtild'') of Wezemaal, lady of Bergen op Zoom, and John III, duke of Brabant and lord of Breda. A charter has not survived. 1345 is the first mention of Steenbergen as a town.
Fair_Description: In 1331 (Dec. 2) a fair on St. Petersday 'ingaande oest' (harvest) (August 1) was granted by the lord and wife of Bergen (op Zoom), with right and freedom as in the Antwerp of 'Sinxen' (Pentecost). Also granted was the construction of a harbour for trading vessels. In 1328 (Dec. 20) a permit was already granted by duke Jan III of Brabant and the lord of Bergen to levy a toll and 'weggeld' (road-tax) on the roads of Bergen and Wouw to Steenbergen. For the maintenance of this roads a 'wagen- en karregeld' (tax on coaches and carts) was installed.

name: Willemstad
Settlement_Description: The first mention of Willemstad dates from 2 March 1584. However, the settlement originated in 1565. Then, it was called De Ruigenhil. Later, it was transformed into a fortified town and became known as Willemstad.
Town_Description: On 12 August 1586, Willemstad is granted town rights by Maurice, prince of Orange, and Marquess of Bergen op Zoom.

name: Klundert
Settlement_Description: The earliest mention of Klundert dates from 1537 (according to Van Berkel & Samplonius; Cox takes 1525 as the earliest mention). However, this mention is probably related to the building of a dike in a polder, rather than an actual settlement. Cox states that in 1561 some families were living there.
Town_Description: Although no official grant of town privileges is known to have existed, Klundert developped into a town in the period 1578-1582 during the reign of William, prince of Oranje, lord of Niervaart. In 1582, the town is walled.
Fair_Description: In 1580 prince William of Orange granted a privilege for a horsefair, this was confirmed in 1588 by prince Maurits. The fair was organised twice a year: March 21 en August 1. In 1606 on request of the town the start was replaced to the first Friday of this months.

name: null
Harbour_Description: According to a falsified charter from 1188, Lübeck had the privilege of shipping on the Wakenitz and the Ratzeburg lake until Ratzeburg. These privileges were confirmed in 1226. A document from 1439 mentions the harbour to have been located west of the cathedral island; a view of the town from 1588, however, displays boats near the long bridge east of town.

name: null
Toll_Description: On the Merxleben bridge a bridge toll had been collected "for a long time" by the town of Langensalza until it was given to the town lord in 1668. A bridge house and a bridge tower existed.

name: Oosterhout
Settlement_Description: According to Van Berkel & Samplonius, Oosterhout is first mentioined in 1156. Cox takes 815 as the earliest mention (in a 1170 copy).In the seventeenth century, Oosterhout tried to claim town status. To this end, town grants from the 1100s-1300s were forged. These attempts, however, did not succeed.Oosterhout, was elevated to town rank on 3 May 1809 by Louis Bonaparte, king of Holland.
Fair_Description: In 1262 the lord of Breda granted  the 'villa' Oisterhout freedom of toll, roadtoll (pedagio) and a weekly market and a fair. In 1594 (April 2) the two existing fairs (the day after St. Jan Baptist and Monday before All-Saints) were enlenghtened. The council of the Spanish Government granted a duration for both fairs of three instead of one day. This would better accomodate the merchants who came from a distance of 6-8 or more miles.

name: null
Bridge_Description: A bridge across the river, Varde Å, was established in the medieval period. The bridge is mentioned for the first time in 1463, but is most certainly older. A bridge across Varde Å is shown on various maps of Varde from the 17th century. On the map of Varde in Resen’s Atlas Danicus, for example, it is located south of town at one of the main roads to Varde. Presumably, this was also the location of the medieval bridge. During the middle ages and early-modern era the bridge was extremely important to traffic in Western Jutland as it was one of the few places to cross Varde Å.
Harbour_Description: A river port mentioned for the first time in 1368, but presumably much older. Only smaller vessels could transport gods and people on Varde Å. Small boats and barges were used for transportation from Varde to a bay at the Northern Sea, Ho Bugt. From the 16th century onwards Hjerting at the coast functioned as a harbour for Varde.

name: Waalwijk
Settlement_Description: The first mention of Waalwijk dates from 1200 (in a 1305 copy of the document).
Town_Description: Town privileges were granted on 17 December 1303 by John II, duke of Brabant. However, it never fully developed into a town.
Fair_Description: In 1303 the count of Brabant granted three fairs: 1) Wednesday before Pentecost, 2) Wednesday before Maria assumptio (August 15), 3) Thursday after St. Remigius (Oct. 1). The last one was previously held in Gansoijen. In 1516 (Oct. 15) the lord of Waalwijk obtained permission for two years to organise a weekly market on Friday for economic benefits. He had asked however for a weekly market on Wednesday and a fourth fair. In 1542 (March 21) emperor Charles confirmed three free fairs: 1) Wednesday before Sinxen (Pentecost), 2) Wednesday before the Assumption of the Virgin Mary (August 15) and 3) Thursday after St. Baaf (Bavo: Oct. 1) and prohibited merchants from abroad, who marketed their horses and cattle at Baardwijk because of the dirty roads in Waalwijk where now a 'cautsie' or paved road was, to trade cattle during the three market-days at  Baardwijk.

name: null
Harbour_Description: A navigable waterway was created between the Schwerin lake and the Elbe river in 1568-1572.

name: Ravenstein
Settlement_Description: From 1355, a toll was levied along the river Meuse. In 1360, Walraven of Valkenburg built a castle near by the toll, and Ravenstein was being build.
Town_Description: Ravenstein was granted town rights on 4 May 1380 by Reinoud of Valkenburg, lord of Ravenstein.
Fair_Description: At the end of the 15th century three market-tolls are known: 1) one month after Good ('stille') Friday, 2) ten days before St. Johns bapt. nativ. (june 14), 3) one month after the third day before St. Lambertus eve (sept. 13).
Toll_Description: Walraven of Valkenburg levied a toll along the river Meuse from 1355 onwards. A small range of toll-accounts from the count of Gelre is preserved for the years 1390-96. The accounts for the years 1394/5 are edited. In 1394 halff the toll at Mook (Moudich) and Heerewaarden (Herwarden) were relocated to Ravenstein. The toll was then property of the lord of Born and Sittard. A tariff for the this toll and the one in Mook dated 1394 is edited. In 1395/6 halff the toll was relocated to Heerewaarden.
Harbour_Description: From 1355, a toll was levied along the river Meuse.

name: Kegelbrücke
Bridge_Description: Oldest crossing of the Ilm in Weimar. A wooden bridge was erected before 1430. In 1613 the wooden bridge was destroyed and replaced by a stone bridge in 1618, which was destroyed again in 1689, until it was re-erected in 1749.

name: null
Harbour_Description: River harbour on the Rhine. A ship crane is mentioned in 1585, which was replaced by a fixed crane before 1626.

name: null
Lock_Description: A lock in the canal between the Elbe and the Schwerin lake, which was built between 1568 and 1572, is displayed as "Heit sluse" on a map of the canal by Daniel Frese from 1605.

name: null
Lock_Description: A lock in the canal between the Elbe and the Schwerin lake, which was built between 1568 and 1572, is displayed as "Finde wi uns hir sluse" near the mill Findenwirunshier on a map of the canal by Daniel Frese from 1605.

name: null
Lock_Description: A lock in the canal between the Elbe and the Schwerin lake, which was built between 1568 and 1572, is displayed as "Snaken sluse" on a map of the canal by Daniel Frese from 1605.

name: null
Lock_Description: A lock in the canal between the Elbe and the Schwerin lake, which was built between 1568 and 1572, is displayed as "Walck sluse" on a map of the canal by Daniel Frese from 1605.

name: null
Lock_Description: A lock in the canal between the Elbe and the Schwerin lake, which was built between 1568 and 1572, is displayed as "Holt sluse" on a map of the canal by Daniel Frese from 1605.

name: Oostelbeers
Settlement_Description: The settlement Beers, first mentioned in 1207, was divided into three parts, of which Oostelbeers is first mentioned in 1312-1350.

name: Wessem
Settlement_Description: The earliest mention of Wessem can be found in an eleventh- to twelfth-century copy of a document dated 965.
Town_Description: Wessem was never officially granted town rights, but slowly developed into a town. It received several town(-like) privileges from the lords of Horne before 1329. On 27 April 1329, Wessem is first mentioned as a town.

name: null
Toll_Description: In 1213 the bishop of Liège enfeoffed Eijsden to Walram, the son of the duke of Limburg. He likely immediately installed a toll on the river Meuse. In 1221 the bishop made him declare that he owned no toll or road toll ('weggeld') here, but later the toll is mentioned again. A tariff dated from 1369 is preserved and edited, according to an 18th century copy. The toll was owned by the lord of Gronsveld at the time.

name: Niervaart
Settlement_Description: The exact location of the former village and town of Niervaart is unknown. It is assumed to have been located about 2 kilometers east of Klundert. Niervaart is first mentioned in 1290. In the 16th century after re-embanking called Klundert.
Town_Description: Niervaart was granted town(-like) privileges on 7 September 1357 by Aleid (Adelaide), lady of Putten en Strijen. Between 1421-1450, Niervaart ceased to exist as a consequence of several floods.
Fair_Description: In 1347 the lady of Strijen granted excises on beer and wine, the exchange, the weighing-house and the cloth-hall and the ferry to 'den Brooc' with the condition that yearly 10 pounds hollands should be donated to the hospital. In 1357 a privilege was obtained for a free fair eight days before and after the 'Nuvaertse kermis' (fair). Dates or duration unknown.
Toll_Description: Toll for sailing transport at the river Mark first mentioned in 1336, belonging to the lords of Strijen, later (since 1361?) to the count of Holland. Since 1389 leased as part of the comital toll at Geervliet.

name: Bockenheimer Warte
Settlement_Description: Watchtower in the enclosure ('landwehr') of Frankfurt, built in 1434/5.

name: Langenholzhausen
Settlement_Description: First mentioned as Holthusen in 1244. The settlement consisted of three parts: Langen-, Overen- and Nederenholthusen, of which the latter two later merged with the former.

name: Möllenbeck (Schaumburg)
Settlement_Description: A monastery of Augustianian Canonesses was founded shortly before 896. After having become Lutheran, the monastery was converted into a manor in 1649. An accompanying settlement, which is characterised as borough ('oppidum') in 1353 and 1355 and as village in 1361, seems to have been abandoned at multiple points in time in the late 14th and 15th centuries. The market church was demolished in 1448.

name: Bösingfeld
Settlement_Description: The first mention of 1224 indicates the existence of a castle of the count of Sternberg. A planned town was built around 1300, but it remained a borough ('flecken'). The settlement was destroyed and abandoned in a feud in 1424, and only resettled in 1492.

name: Furth (Neuss)
Toll_Description: Secondary toll station of the land toll of Neuss, first mentioned in 1386. It is last mentioned in 1789. 4 alb. per horse had to be paid.

name: Barntrup
Settlement_Description: The original settlement was located southeast of the current centre. Between 1225 and 1317, a new planned settlement was built by the count of Sternberg at the current location, where it is first mentioned in 1317 as "oppidum".
Town_Description: First characterised as town in 1366, Barntrup received Lemgo town privileges in 1376. However, it retained the character of a borough.

name: Humfeld
Settlement_Description: First mentioned in 1259, the settlement consisted of two parts: Overen- and Nederenhumvelde. It was partly abandoned in the 15th century, and resettled in 1467.

name: null
Ferry_Description: As a consequence of war activities, the location of the ferry moved from a more upstream location to a location in front of the town gate called 'Koepoort' ('Cow gate'). The ferry was owned by the land lord. In 1583, the ferry right was leased out on a long lease to the town of Doesburg.
Harbour_Description: After the construction of a new fortification in 1607, the strip of land between the IJssel river and the town ditch known as the Contre-Escarpe became the main landing place for river vessels.

name: null
Ferry_Description: The ferry near Dieren is one of the oldest ferries in the region. It is first mentioned in 1269. At least in the thirteenth century, it is owned by the Teutonic Order. Over the centuries, the Teutonic Order preserves ownership of half of the ferry rights. Originally, the ferry served long distance traffic, but after the establishment of a ferry in front of Doesburg in the fourteenth century, it must have lost this position and probably mainly served farmers.

name: null
Toll_Description: A bridge toll was levied at the bridge from the 14th century.
Bridge_Description: A wooden bridge across the Ruhr was first mentioned in 1282. It was replaced by a stone construction in the 14th century. The bridge was destroyed by the archbishop of Cologne in 1583, but restored before 1591. During the Thirty Years' War, the bridge was destroyed in 1635 and replaced by a ferry. A new bridge was only built in the 19th century.
Ferry_Description: After the destruction of the bridge in 1635, it was replaced by a ferry.

name: Nyborg færge
Ferry_Description: Around 1075 the German chronicler Adam of Bremen mentions a ferry between Funen and Zealand, and it is very likely that the ferry on Funen was located where Nyborg was founded a century later. In the 12th century the ferry sailed between Nyborg and Tårnborg on Zealand, but in the 13th century they probably began to sail to the place where the town of Korsør later developed. Throughout the medieval period and up until modern time the most used ferry route between the islands of Funen and Zealand was located at Nyborg. The importance of the ferry is reflected in a broad variety of written sources from both the Middle Ages and the early modern period.
Harbour_Description: The age and character of the medieval harbour is uncertain. However, due to Nyborg’s role as home to the ferry connection between Funen and Zealand and the town’s political importance a port must have been established at an early stage. Presumably when the castle and town was founded. In the late medieval period the port had a wharf, and in 1548 a new wharf was built. The harbour was frequently used by foreigners. In 1399, for example, ships from Lübeck sailed to Nyborg.

name: null
Harbour_Description: A harbour in Greifswald is first mentioned in 1254, but is probably older. It was located near the town in the river Ryck. In the following centuries the river silted up and the harbour was only usable by small vessels and was one of the causes for the decline of shipping from Greifswald. After 1279 the town built a new outport at the village Wieck near the mouth of the river. For the 16th century the fleet of Greifswald is estimated at 15-18 vessels.

name: Nahne
Settlement_Description: First mentioned in 1147. In Nahne there existed a watchtower of the enclosure ('landwehr') of the Neustadt of Osnabrück, which was under construction in 1406 and 1409.

name: Lange Brug
Bridge_Description: The wooden bridge across the Amstel is first mentioned in 1457, around the time that this area of the town was developed.

name: null
Ferry_Description: The ferry from Tiel to Wamel existed already in the Middle Ages. It was privately owned, but in 1680-1682 the town acquired possession of the ferry. The landing place was situated outside the town on the Echtelsedijk near Zandwijk, as shown on a painting by Jan van Goyen from 1646.

name: Nyborg
Settlement_Description: The settlement of Nyborg probably developed next to a castle, which was built around 1170. According to the Danish chronicler Saxo Grammaticus, who finished his Gesta Danorum c. 1208, the castle was built by Knud Prislavsen, a nephew to king Valdemar I the Great (1157-1182). The castle and later town of Nyborg benefited from its location in the bottom of Nyborg fjord, and at an obvious place to cross the strait of Storebælt, which separates the two larger main islands of Funen and Zealand.
Town_Description: Around 1200 the settlement around Nyborg castle had an urban character. According to the so-called main piece of King Valdemar’s Cadastre from 1231 Nyborg was private property of the royal family. In 1270 Nyborg was granted a town law by king Eric Glipping (1259-1286), and in 1292 king Eric VI Menved (1286-1319) confirmed the town’s privileges. When Nyborg was granted its first privileges is uncertain, most likely it was during the reign of king Valdemar II the Victorious (1202-1241). Citizens, mayors, as well as a town council and a town court are also documented in the late 13th century. By then the castle was one of the most important royal castles in Denmark, a status which continued into the late middle ages as well as in the early modern period. For example, the annual meeting between the king and the most influential political agents of the realm, the so-called Danehof, took place at Nyborg Castle from the late 13th century until the early 15th century. During the following 16th and 17th centuries members of the royal family often stayed at Nyborg Castle, which periodically was the main castle of the royal family. In the 16th century however, the political importance of Nyborg was stagnating, and both the castle and the town were damaged during the Count’s Feud (Danish: Grevens Fejde) 1534-1536 and the Dano-Swedish wars of the 17th century.
Fair_Description: Nyborg probably had one or several annual fairs before the middle of the 15th century, but this is uncertain. The first known annual fair was granted in 1446.
Toll_Description: Due to its locality at Storebælt, Nyborg was an important royal toll station already in the 13th century. The levying of the toll on people and goods crossing the strait is first mentioned during the reign of king Eric VI Menved (1286-1319), but is probably older. In the early 16th century Nyborg became the toll station for ships sailing through the strait of Storebælt. The character of this toll was, however, not formalized before 1560, when Nyborg became the official toll station for alle ships sailing through Storebælt (Danish: Storebæltstolden).

name: Ochten
Settlement_Description: Earliest mention probably dates from the second half of the ninth century, in a copy dated between 1150-1158.

name: Nakskov
Settlement_Description: Probably a fishing village in the period before c. 1200
Town_Description: Nakskov is listed as a town in King Valdemar’s Cadastre in a text within the manuscript originally written around 1240. King Christoffer I (1252-1259) probably granted the first town rights in the 1250ties. In 1266 a royal privilege issued by king Eric V Klipping (1259-1286) was given to the villani in Nakskov, and in 1274 king Eric granted Nakskov the same privileges as Næstved on the island of Zealand. The privileges were confirmed and extended in 1288, 1293 and 1320. A town council was mentioned for the first time in 1351. In 1590 a new town hall was built, presumably it replaced an older old town hall at the same spot. Nakskov benefited from a rich agricultural hinterland and fishing, as well as a dynamic trade with towns around the western Baltic Sea, especially Lübeck. In the 15th century Nakskov was among the important towns in Denmark. Economically, Nakskov was as big as all other towns on the islands of Lolland and Falster combined. Around 1510 king Hans (1481-1513) ordered the construction of a fortified naval shipyard on the island of Slotsø in Nakskov Fjord, which existed until 1688.
Fair_Description: Nakskov was granted the right to two annual fairs in 1539. In 1646 the fairs at Saltvig and Halsted were abolished, and instead a new fair in Nakskov was to be held yearly on October 5th. Three years later, in 1649, Nakskov was granted another annual summer fair. This fair began on the day of the feast of Saint Jacob (July 25), and lasted for three days.

name: Husholmen
Settlement_Description: Husholmen is a short-lived medieval castle consisting of masonry structures and wooden circular pilework surrounding a rocky island on a strategic location deep in Pieni Pernajanlahti (sw. Lillpernåviken) bay. According to the dendrochronological dating of the pilework and other finds the construction of the castle took place in the latter half of the 1380s. The castle was likely built by Jakob Abrahamsson (Djäkn) whom the king Albrekt of Mecklenburg of Sweden had in 1387 granted the right to hold to Porvoo bailiwick (sw. Borgå fögderi) and the castle of Turku with its underlying bailiwicks, and build fortifications in the area. Husholmen is also very likely Wartholm castle, which Jakob gave over together with Turku, Kastelholm, Aborch and Verghdenborch castles and their bailiwicks to Knut Bosson (Grip) and his Mecklenburgian mother Margareta Dume’s control in 1395. A surviving letter of the knight Johan Dume dated in Wardholm on 25 May some time in 1396-98 to the council of Reval mentions a harbour in connection of the castle. After Knut Bosson conceded Turku castle and his other wooden castles in Finland to queen Margaret in the spring of 1399, the castle was demolished for good in the early years of the 15th century. Another possible location of Wartholm is Sibbesborg in the near the medieval mouth of Sipoonjoki (sw. Sibbo å) river archaeologically dated to the late 14th century.

name: Greifswald
Settlement_Description: The settlement developed around saltworks that were first mentioned in 1193, since 1209 owned by the Cistercian monastery Eldena.
Town_Description: A market settlement is attested in 1241, mentioned as borough ('oppidum') in 1248. The town received the privilege of fortification in 1264. Wartislaw III of Pomerania granted Lübeck town privileges in 1250. A university was founded in 1456.
Fair_Description: A fair on St James's Day probably dates back to the foundation of the town. In 1524 dukes Georg I and Barnim IX granted the right to organise an additional fair on All Saints Day.
Toll_Description: The toll existed in connection to the staple, and is mentioned in 1275 when the town bought the toll from duke Barnim I. Tariffs are known from the same year, and show that the trade of the town was primarily directed towards Scandinavia and the Baltic.
Staple_Description: A staple in Greifswald is granted by Barnim I of Pomerania in 1274. At its confirmation in 1361, it was defined that all inhabitants of Pomerania who shipped corn or other commodities on the Peene through Wolgast or to Anklam, Gützkow or Ueckermünde, were obliged to offer their commodities on the Greifswald market and pay the toll there.

name: Wieck
Harbour_Description: In 1279 the town Greifswald acquired a strip of land on the northern shore of the mouth of the Ryck river, leading to a conflict with the monastery Eldena. On this land a new harbour, the "neuer Tief" was dug, which functioned as an outport for the harbour of the town, which was too shallow for larger vessels. In 1306 the bulwarks that fortified the new harbour are mentioned. From the late 16th century there stood a crane on the northern shore of the "neuen Tief", which was renewed around 1600.

name: Heger Turm
Settlement_Description: Watchtower in the enclosure ('landwehr') of Osnabrück, constructed around 1347.

name: null
Bridge_Description: A bridge across the narrow strait of Nakskov fjord between the town of Nakskov and Færgelandet to the south was built in 1646. Presumably, the bridge was built at the end of the modern street of Dronningestræde.
Ferry_Description: Prior to 1646 all traffic across the narrow strait of Nakskov fjord between the town of Nakskov and Færgelandet to the south had to be done by boat. Thus, a ferry connection was probably established at an early stage in the medieval period. The age and character of the ferry is, however, unknown.

name: null
Toll_Description: A toll was levied on ships passing the lock. Tariffs existed for butter, cheese, stockfish, herring, soap, tar, train oil, salt, barley, malt, linseed and wine.
Lock_Description: A wooden mill weir in the Ems is first mentioned in 1362, and replaced by a construction of stone in 1550. The existence of the weir forced the transshipment of cargoes on river barges. For this reason, a wooden pound lock ('verlaat') was constructed in the weir in 1579/80. The lock was in disrepair by 1621 and shipping on the river had largely come to a halt.

name: Krabbesholm
Harbour_Description: In the 17th century it was no longer possible to sail to the town of Skive by the river Karup Å, and therefore the bay at the manor of Krabbesholm a bit north of the town was used as a natural harbour. The harbour was mostly used by locals in the region, and throughout the middle ages and early-modern era the harbour of Skive struggled, especially due to competition with the town of Aalborg.

name: null
Bridge_Description: On the town seal of Skive from 1579 a bridge is depicted. This is probably a reference to the bridge across the river, Karup Å, close to the royal castle of Skivehus. The bridge across Karup Å is most likely much older. Probably a bridge was built around or shortly after 1200, when the royal castle of Skivehus and the town of Skive were established. The bridge was also mentioned in 1607, when it had to be rebuilt. Bridges across Karup Å close to the castle are also shown on a map of Skive in Resen’s Atlas Danicus from 1677.
Harbour_Description: Skive is located in the bottom of Limfjorden. During the middle ages it was possible to sail to the town by the river Karup Å. This was no longer possible in the 17th century, and therefore the bay at the manor of Krabbesholm a bit north of the town was used as a natural harbour. The harbour was mostly used by locals in the region, and throughout the middle ages and early-modern era the harbour of Skive struggled, especially due to competition with the town of Aalborg.

name: Bandholm
Settlement_Description: The settlement was first mentioned in 1360, but is probably much older. Functioned as Harbour for the town of Maribo.
Toll_Description: In 1632 the town of Maribo got its own toll office in Bandholm, the town's harbour, located north from the town.
Harbour_Description: In 1449 Maribo was granted the right to use Bandholm in northern Lolland as a harbour. Probably a natural harbour in the bay until the late 16th century, when a pier was built.

name: Thisted
Settlement_Description: Presumably founded during the high middle ages as a fishing village, that during the 1400s developed into a settlement with a town-like character. Thisted is first mentioned in 1367, and in 1374 it is labeled “villa”.
Town_Description: Thisted belonged to the bishop of Børglum, and was granted a law in 1454 (Danish: Birkeret). In 1459 town-dwellers (Danish: bymænd) are mentioned for the first time, and in 1497 a town bailiff (Danish: byfoged) was representing the bishop’s interests in Thisted. No later than 1522 a town council was established. On the initiative of bishop Stygge Krumpen of Børglum Thisted was granted town privileges in 1524 by king Frederik 1 of (1523-1533).
Fair_Description: It is uncertain if Thisted had a fair during the medieval period, as the market activities in the region of Thy were concentrated around the fairs held at Vestervig monastery After the Danish reformation in 1536, when the monastery was dissolved, the annual fairs previously held at Vestervig were relocated to Thisted in 1547. In 1573, however, the three annual fairs were once again moved back to Vestervig, which by then was a royal estate.

name: Masnedsund
Toll_Description: A royal toll was probably collected at the ferry, presumably from the 13th century onwards.
Ferry_Description: A ferry connecting Zealand with the island of Falster departed from Vordingborg, probably already in the early 13th century. The ferry sailed between Vordingborg and the settlement of Gåbense on Falster. In the 13th century the ferry departed from a bridge close to Vordingborg castle. In the following 14th century a ferry yard at Masnedsund was constructed.

name: null
Bridge_Description: The watermill of Mogenstrup is documented from the 15th century onwards. It was probably possible to cross the river of Fladså either by bridge or by a dam.

name: Przemyśl
Toll_Description: Mentioned as toll station in c. 1349, where 8 gr. had to be paid for each cart.

name: Borum
Settlement_Description: The village of Borum was first mentioned in the 14th century, but is much older. The parish church is from either the 12th or 13th century.

name: Pinen (Sallingsund)
Ferry_Description: The age and character of the ferry across the strait of Sallingsund is uncertain, but a ferry route was probably in place in the 13th century. In 1529 peasants on the island threatened to not pay taxes to either the bishop or the king before they got a new ferry, which the bishop in Viborg granted. In 1632 local nobles complained that that travelers had nowhere to seek shelter, so the ferry yard (Danish: færgegård) “Plagen” on the island of Mors and the inn “Pinen” on the Salling side must be after 1632. In the later medieval period and early modern era the ferry played an important role in the export of oxen from Mors to Salling.

name: Druten
Settlement_Description: First mentioned in 1076-1081 in a possibly falsified copy from the 12th century.

name: Teterow
Settlement_Description: Slavic castle, conquered by the Danes in 1171. Around 1200 a German settlement developed.
Town_Description: Lord Nikolaus of Werle founded a town around 1235 with Schwerin-Güstrow town law. In 1272, it is first referred to as 'oppidum'. The privileges have often been endorsed.

name: Tiel
Settlement_Description: Earliest mention dates from 850-865 (possibly 855), in a copy of 1170-1175. In 893, Tiel is mentioned as an 'oppidum'. It was an important trading settlement in the 9th and 10th century, and had a mint in the 11th century.
Town_Description: Tiel was probably granted town privileges by Holy Roman Emperor Henry VI between 1191 and 1197. It is first mentioned as a town in 1195. The town rights were confirmed by Reginald and Edward of Guelders in 1361.
Fair_Description: At least from 1447 onwards, fairs were organised in Tiel. From a source probably dating from the fifteenth century, it is known that four fairs were held in Tiel: one horse fair, a cattle fair, and two cloth fairs.

name: Vordingborg
Settlement_Description: A royal castle founded by king Valdemar I the Great (1157-1182) around 1160 as part of the protection of the realm against Slavic attacks. The castle was built near the natural crossing from Zealand to Falster.  Presumably, a settlement soon developed around the castle.
Town_Description: Vordingborg was first mentioned by the Danish chronicler Saxo in his Gesta Danorum from c. 1208 as part of a historical account about events in the second half of the 12th century. In the early 13th century Vordingborg had an urban character, and was also registered as a town in the so-called main piece in King Valdemar’s Cadastre c. 1231. A registration of towns on Zealand and the surrounding island (Danish: “Købstadslisten”) from 1241 also found in King Valdemar’s Cadastre counted Vordingborg among the towns of Zealand. The castle in Vordingborg was one of the most important royal castles in Denmark, and especially during the 13th and 14th centuries kings often used the castle. A Dominican abbey was probably founded in the middle of the 13th century, but for unknown reasons it only existed a few years. A town bailiff is documented in 1390, and in 1415 king Eric the Pommerian (1396-1439) upheld existing town  privileges; these were later confirmed and expanded several times. Mayors are also known from 1415. The political importance of the castle was declining during the later middle ages. The town’s development also stagnated, but still it remained one of the economical and political centres in the region. In the early modern period the castle was still periodically a royal residence, but in general Vordingborg had lost its importance. The town also suffered during the Count’s Feud (Danish: Grevens Fejde) 1534-1536 and Dano-Swedish wars in the 17th century.
Fair_Description: In the medieval period Vordingborg was an important market town on the island of Zealand, and the town held several annual fairs. During the early modern era, the number of annual fairs decreased. In 1651 only two annual fairs were allowed.
Harbour_Description: Originally a natural harbour near the castle. Later in the medieval period a jetty was constructed southeast of the castle.

name: Sæby
Settlement_Description: Around 1400 Sæby seems to have been a relatively small fishing village located at a river outlet on the Eastern coast of Vendsyssel. The settlement belonged to the bishop of Børglum.
Town_Description: Sæby developed into a town during the 15th century. In the 1460ties a Carmelite abbey was established and in the same decade a mayor and a town bailiff (Danish: byfoged) also appeared in textual sources. A town hall, which was placed at the town square west of the parish church, is mentioned in 1597. The oldest known town privileges were given by king Frederik 1. in 1524. The year after the town was granted a town law by bishop Stygge Krumpen of Børglum. The close relationship between the town and the dioceses of Børglum is reflected in the alternative name of the town “Mariested” (Mary's Place) until the Reformation in 1536.
Fair_Description: Apparently Sæby did not have any fair during the middle ages. This changed in the early 17th century, when king Christian IV (1596-1648) abolished all fairs in the region of Vendsyssel except four, one of these was the fair of Hundslund southwest of Sæby, and hereby secured Sæby a new status as marketown.

name: Megen
Settlement_Description: The earliest mention of Megen is a 1191 copy of a document dated 721-722. Archeological findings, however, indicate habitation during the Roman era.
Town_Description: Megen is already mentioned as a town in the period 1325-1350, but the earliest known granting of town rights dates from January 1357. These were granted by William, count of Megen, and Helwige, countess of Megen. Megen was surrounded by earth and stone walls. During the Eighty Years' War, the town and castle largely burned down in 1581. Both were rebuild.
Fair_Description: Karel van Bourgondië gaf in 1473 het recht tot het heffen van een markttol aan de stadhouder van Gelre. Drie markten waren vergund: 1) St. Servaes (13 mei), 2) St. Bartholomeus (24 aug.) en 3) Allerheiligen (1 nov.). Blijkens de tollijst uit 1473 moesten alle passerende schepen de drie dagen voor en na en drie dagen van de vrijmarkten zelf tol betalen. Brabantse en Gelderse schepen hoefden alleen roertol te betalen (de helft, alleen van het schip, niet van de lading).
Toll_Description: A toll for sailing transport on the Meuse river was granted to the counf of Megen together with town rights by the emperor on February 3, 1357. From ships going upstream the count was allowed to collect the tariff from the toll at Cuyk, from those going downstream the tariff known at Lith. In 1380 the duke of Gelre agreed with the duke of Brabant that the new tolls in Gennep, Grave, Megen and Batenburg should be abolished. The toll at Megen however would have been collected up to the end of the 16th century.
Ferry_Description: A ferry to Appeltern possibly already existed prior to 1500. It is first mentioned in 1519.

name: Egstedt
Settlement_Description: First mentioned in 833. Originally property of the family of Egstedt, which is still mentioned in 1308, but in the course of the 14th century it became property of the town of Erfurt.

name: Slangerup
Settlement_Description: The settlement of Slangerup probably developed in the 12th century around a royal estate, which was run by a royal official, a villicus (Danish: Bryde).
Town_Description: Slangerup was listed as royal property at the so-called main piece in King Valdemar’s Cadastre from c. 1231. According to another list in the same manuscript from 1241, a registration of towns of Zealand and surrounding islands (Danish: “Købstadslisten”), Slangerup was counted among the towns of Zealand. Citizens of Slangerup were mentioned for the first time in 1252, and members of the town council are documented in 1268. In 1301/1302 Slangerup was granted the right to use the same municipal law as the neighboring town of Roskilde. A Cistercian nunnery was founded in the 12th century. Throughout the medieval period Slangerup was one of the smallest and poorest towns in Zealand, and therefore the town asked the king for a reduction of the annual town tax in 1454. In 1569 Slangerup lost its town privileges, and the town's inhabitants were ordered to move to the town of Hillerød. Three years later, however, the town regained its privileges.
Fair_Description: Slangerup had at least one annual fair. The age, date and character of the medieval fair(s) is unknown. In 1516 king Christian II (1513-1523) allowed only four annual fairs on the island of Zealand. The fair in Slangerup was one of these legal fairs. The effect of the king’s initiative is, however, uncertain, as other fairs at least in time continued. In the second half of the 17th century Slangerup had four fairs, all of a local character.

name: Walschleben
Settlement_Description: First mention in 822. Formerly the settlement was given to the archbishopric of Magdeburg by Otto I, then became property of Fulda monastery and in the end of the counts of Gleichen.

name: Wundersleben
Settlement_Description: First mention at the end of the 8th or the beginning of the 9th century.
Toll_Description: Secondary station of safe conduct ('Beigeleistsstelle') of Weißensee, mentioned in 1558.

name: null
Harbour_Description: Up until the 18th century, when a proper port was built, Thisted probably only had a simple natural harbour. Functioned as an import/export center for the region of Thy.

name: Batenburg
Settlement_Description: Earliest mention in 1076-1081, in a possibly falsified copy dating from the second half of the twelfth century.
Town_Description: The earliest mention of Batenburg as a town dates from 1349. By then, Batenburg has been granted toll, mintage, and weekly market rights. The earliest preserved privilege dates from 1389, and enables the installation of a 'schepenbank'. In 1440 a chapter is installed (Batenburg is part of the archbishopric of Cologne).
Fair_Description: In 1254 the Roman king donated the two existing fairs to the lord of Batenburg as a wedding gift for his wife. Up till then the fairs were held in fief. In 1349 the Roman king pawned the lady of Batenburg with the seigniory, mint, 'gruit', fairs and weekly market. In 1443 there are three fairs: 1) 3 days before May-eve (April 30), 2) 3 days before Petri ad Vincula-eve (July 31) 3) 3 days before Catharina-eve (Nov. 24), duration 6 weeks and 3 days after the first Sunday. During 3 days before and after the fairs halff toll was levied. At the end of the 15th century: 1): 3 days before May-eve till the first Friday after Pentecost, 2): 3 days before St. Peterseve in the harvest= July 28 till the end of the harvest-month (end of August), 3): 3 days before St. Katrijneneve= Nov. 21 till Christmas= 23 dec. In 1566: 1) 3 days before St. Walbargavond (Walpurgis: May 1) till May-eve, 2) 3 days before St. Peterseve ad Vincula, 3): 3 days before St. Catharina-eve, each starting the first Sunday after St. Walbarg, St. Peter and St. Catharina, duration six weeks and 3 days with a tariff. A manual of the toll-keeper of Venlo dated early 16th century with the market-tolls on the Maas mentions as tariff: a 'sleeproer' 2 oude groot, a 'hangroer' 1 oude groot.

name: Pappila (Huittinen)
Settlement_Description: <b>Inn:</b> Huittinen vicarage (fi. pappila) served food and drinks to travellers. In 1640, farmers and soldiers were on their way to the inspection in Turku. They camped in the field next to the church and bought some ale from the vicarage.

name: Damrak
Harbour_Description: After the Amstel river was dammed around 1270 the former mouth of the river became known as Damrak and functioned as the sea port of Amsterdam. Quays are first mentioned around 1320. The harbour was only suitable for small ships; larger seagoing vessels had to anchor at the harbour front. The oldest shipyards and ropewalks were situated outside the Zeedijk and city wall in the nortwestern part of the town, but were relocated in the 15th century to the socalled Lastage. The outer harbour was protected by a stockade to floods and storms and by a tower (Montelbaanstoren), but remained outside the city walls. The oldest map of the town drawn by Cornelis Anthoniszoon dated 1538 shows this in detail. There existed a large crane in front of the Schreierstoren to put new masts in sailing vessels and load heavy cargo such as cannons and millstones; it was built in the 15th century and is first mentioned in 1498. Smaller cranes were spread throughout the quays of the city. In 1537 a new crane was built at the Montelbaanstoren. In the 16th century Amsterdam rapidly developed into the major harbour of the Netherlands. In 1565 governor Margaret ordained the town to deepen the Damrak and the Oudezijdswaal to give room for ships to reach the inner town. The 'Informacie' of 1514 mentions 27 seaworthy ships, 13 'boeiers' and 83 'binnenlandvaarders' (smaller ships for inland transport). In 1529 a market-boat ('beurtveer' with a regular connection) is found with Hoorn (using a caravel), in 1539 with Middelburg, in 1546 with Leiden, in 1547 with Antwerp and Harderwijk, in 1550 with Enkhuizen, in 1583 with Utrecht and in 1611 with Dordrecht, Rouen and London. In the mid-16th century some 12 or 13 caravels connected Amsterdam with Kampen across the Zuiderzee. Guicciardini estimated the fleet around 1566 at more then 500 ships, mostly hulks owned by citizens of Amsterdam. Twice a year some 200 or 300 ships from the Baltic were harboured. The registers of Sound toll levied at Elsinore in Denmark show a maximum in 1565 of 504 ships from Amsterdam out of a total of 2134 ships from Holland and a general totall of 3485 ships who passed the Øresund strait. A report made for the duke of Alva dated 1569 mentiones 150 small ships like 'boeiers' and 'heuden' belonging to inhabitants of Amsterdam. In 1586 an Englishman counted usually 1000 ships in the Amsterdam harbour.

name: Andisleben
Settlement_Description: First mention in 775/786-815. Seat of the noble family of Andisleben.

name: Straußfurt
Settlement_Description: First mentioned in 802. The name of the settlement likely refers to a ford, although this seems to be in direct contradiction with the name of Vehra on the opposite bank of the Unstrut river, which probably refers to a ferry.

name: Kokemäenkartanon silta
Bridge_Description: Kokemäenkartano bridge between the bailey area of Kokemäenkartano Royal Manor (sw. Kumo gård) south of the river Kokemäenjoki and the main residence and storage area of the manor on Isoluoto islet is cited in 1552–1640 when it was taken care by Loimaa, Alastaro and Ulvila parishes of Ala-Satakunta judicial district. The bridge may have been of 15th century origin. Its maintenance ended when the Crown sold the manor to private property in 1651.

name: null
Bridge_Description: The bridge was first mentioned in 1580 when it needed to be repaired. The age of the bridge is unknown. On a copper engraving of Slangerup in Resen’s Atlas Danicus (1677) a bridge is depicted in the background, perhaps a bridge across the river of Græse Å.

name: Skagen
Settlement_Description: Founded before 1300 on the top of the peninsula of Jutland as a fishing community. A hard and changing climate prevented a coherent structure of the settlement and later also the town.
Town_Description: Skagen was given town privileges in 1413 by king Erik the Pomeranian. In 1460 a mayor of Skagen appeared in the sources for the first time. King Hans of Denmark granted the first town law in 1507. In the 15th and 16th centuries Skagen was a relatively dynamic but also unusual town, as it was scattered and there were no streets and no town square. The permanent settlement appears to have been concentrated in two areas, modern day Skagen and Højen (modern day Gl. Skagen).
Toll_Description: The royal toll appears in sources from the 15th century onwards. A toll station is mentioned in 1514. The royal customs officer in Skagen was responsible for a lighthouse built in 1560. From the 15th century onwards the royal toll of Skagen was one of the most important in Jutland.
Harbour_Description: The character of the medieval harbour is unknown. But the harbour was important, especially for the trade with Norway. In 1327, for example, Skagen was mentioned as part of the route to either England or Norway from Poland. The harbour was used by Hanseatic ships, for example from Lübeck in 1399.

name: Randersbro
Bridge_Description: Around 1200 the Danish chronicler Saxo Grammaticus wrote about a battle in 1157 at a bridge in or near Randers, but the location of this bridge is uncertain. A bridge across the river Gudenåen leading to the town is mentioned in 1350, and again in 1496. The bridge is known from multiple sources, and presumably it had the same location throughout the medieval period. During the period 1626-1630 it was moved a little to the east.

name: Ærøskøbing
Settlement_Description: According to the so-called main piece of King Valdemar’s Cadastre from 1231 the whole island of Ærø was royal property. When the settlement of Ærøskøbing was established is uncertain, but it was before or during the second half of the 14th century.
Town_Description: Probably around 1400 Ærøskøbing had an urban character. Mayors and members of the town council are documented in 1442, and town privileges were granted during the reign of king Hans (1481-1513). The privileges were confirmed in 1525, 1542 and 1563. Presumably, a medieval town hall burned in 1629, and a new town hall was built in 1634. Throughout the middle ages and early modern era Ærøskøbing remained a small and relatively poor urban settlement.

name: Gebesee
Settlement_Description: First mentioned before 775/786. Originally a Carolingian royal court. Market rights were granted in 1334. Referred to as borough ('Flecken') since 1465.
Town_Description: Johann Georg of Saxony granted town rights in 1638, although the town continued to be called borough ('Flecken') until 1816.

name: Dragsminde
Toll_Description: Rødby was one of the most important royal toll stations throughout the late middle ages and early-modern period. The collection of toll was first mentioned in 1471 but appears to be older. Toll accounts are preserved from the period 1518-1522. The toll station was probably located at Dragsminde, where possible remains of a toll building have been found. The collecting of tolls declined in the 17th century.
Ferry_Description: It is not unlikely that relatively stable ferry routes were in place in the 13th century, but the first certain evidence is from the 15th century. From this point onwards Rødby was an important center for ferries to Germany, i.e. Fehmarn, Heiligenhafen, Lübeck and Rostock. The ferries probably departed from Dragsminde. The ferries remained very active until the 16th century, but diminished the following centuries.
Harbour_Description: Due to the character of the now drained Rødby Fjord the town of Rødby could only be used by small vessels. Hence a harbour was established closer to the shore at Dragsminde, and later harbours were also found at Kramnitse a bit further north and at Syltholm south of Rødby. These three legal harbours competed with several illegal harbours on Lolland. Both legal and illegal harbour were focusing on foreing trade, especially with Hanseatic towns and merchants. In 1399, for example, ships from Lübeck sailed to Rødby, i.e. probably Dragsminde. In the 16th century the harbour at Dragsminde benefited from a monopoly on the export of oxen from islands of Zealand, Lolland and Falster. In the following 17th century, however, the maritime traffic from the harbour declined.

name: null
Toll_Description: In 1380 the duke of Gelre agreed with the duke of Brabant that the new tolls in Gennep, Grave, Megen and Batenburg should be abolished. In 1443 however the lord of Batenburg granted Nijmegen here toll-exemption, in 1447 Roermond and in 1481 's-Hertogenbosch. In 1534 the duke of Gelre granted Venlo toll-exemption at Batenburg. Toll-accounts are preserved for the years 1572-76. In 1573 Batenburg was a temporary outpost for the toll of Zaltbommel instead of Heerewaarden.
Ferry_Description: In the oldest preserved and edited account dated 1294/'5 from the count of Gelre: nautis de Batinburg.

name: Haßleben (Erfurt)
Settlement_Description: Burial sites suggest the settlement of an early Thuringian noble family. First mention in a written record in 780-801.

name: Wusterhausen (Dosse)
Town_Description: Stendal town law was probably granted by the Lords of Plote before 1250. First mentioned as town ('civitas') in 1291.
Toll_Description: The town received the toll as fief by the Margraves of Brandenburg in 1320.

name: Rudkøbing
Settlement_Description: Presumably a permanent settlement in the 12th century when the town’s parish church was built. According to the main piece of King Valdemar’s Cadastre from 1231 Rudkøbing was kongelev, i.e. royal land.
Town_Description: Rudkøbing was granted town privileges in the 1250ties. The privileges were confirmed in 1296 and 1355. Townspeople from Rudkøbing are mentioned for the first time in 1345, when they were plundered in Gollwitz harbour. Mayors are documented in 1460, and a town hall in  1550. This medieval town hall burned down around 1600, and a new one was built in the period 1626-1643. As the only town on the island of Langeland Rudkøbing tried to control the trade on the island. In general, however, the town could not stop the illegal trading activities on Langeland. Throughout the medieval period and early modern era Rudkøbing remained one of the smallest towns in Denmark. The town suffered during the Count’s Feud (Danish: Grevens fejde), and was occupied by enemy forces during the Dano-Swedish war 1657-1660. At least in the 16th century the town was fortified.
Fair_Description: Apparently Rudkøbing did not have any annual fairs. In 1655, however, the peasants on Langeland were allowed to hold two annual fairs just outside Rudkøbing. When these fairs took place is not known.

name: Ename
Fair_Description: In 1273 a toll on the fair in Ename is mentioned. In that year and again in 1363 there were problems concerning this toll with the inhabitants of Geraardsbergen.

name: Nivå bro
Bridge_Description: The bridge is documented in 1580, but may be older. In 1616 king Christian IV (1596-1648) ordered the bridge built in stone.

name: Københoved
Settlement_Description: The village of Københoved was first mentioned in 1478, but is significantly older. The parish church is from either the 12th or 13th century.

name: Skodborg
Settlement_Description: The village of Skodborg was first mentioned around 1300, but is significantly older. The parish church is from either the 12th or 13th century.

name: Tamare
Settlement_Description: <b>Inn:</b> A medieval guild hall was located in Tamare. No exact date or location is known, but it could be close to the old church. There has also been an inn in Tamare in the 17th c.

name: Tårnborg
Settlement_Description: Presumably a royal castle built by king Valdemar I the Great (1157-1182) as part of his attempt to protect the Danish coasts against pirate attacks from the Slaves in the second half of the 12th century. The castle was built in the bottom of Korsør fjord, where there was a good natural harbour, that also was the place of one of the most important ferry routes between Zealand and Funen.
