Around 1200 an urban settlement had developed around the castle.
Town_Description: Tårnborg was royal property according to the so-called main list in King Valdemar’s Cadastre from c. 1231. Unknown when the first town privileges were granted, but most likely shortly after 1240. At this time, however, the settlement already had a clear urban character. This is reflected in archaeological finds, for example of more than 3000 coins from the 13th and 14th centuries. Around 1400 Tårnborg began to decline, and German merchants began to sail to Korsør at the outlet of the fjord. In 1425 king Eric the Pommerian (1396-1439) ordered Tårnborg demolished, and that the town’s inhabitants in the future should trade in Korsør. Hereby, the urban activities came to a stand at Tårnborg, and Korsør took over as the town in the region.
Toll_Description: Together with the royal castles on the island of Sprogø in the middle of the strait of Storebælt and the castle in  Nyborg on Funen at the opposite side of Storebælt the caste at Tårnborg made it possible to control the traffic in Storebælt. Hereby, it also became possible to collect toll from ships in the strait. The character of this early royal toll is, however, unknown. The first time there is strong evidence for a toll at Tårnborg is from 1316, when king Eric Menved (1286-1319) declared a lower royal toll on cloth in large quantities. This cloth came to Denmark via the big fairs at Skanør and Falsterbo in Scania, and then transported from Scania to Zealand and via Tårnborg to Funen and Jutland.
Ferry_Description: The German chronicler Adam of Bremen mentioned a ferry route between Zealand and Funen around 1075. It is possible that the ferry in Zealand was based at Tårnborg in the northeastern part of Korsør Fjord. During the 13th century, however, the ferries probably began to depart from the western outlet of the fjord, i.e. where the town of Korsør later developed.
Harbour_Description: The character of the medieval harbour at Tårnborg is unknown. The northeastern part of Korsør Fjord, however, must have functioned as a natural harbour. As the ships got bigger it became difficult to use the harbour in the fjord, and this probably contributed to the relocation of the town from Tårnborg to Korsør.

name: Helsingør
Settlement_Description: Probably a settlement with a certain urban character by the 12th century, which benefited from its location at the northern and most narrow part of the strait of Øresund (English: the Sound) between Zealand and Scania. According to the German chronicler Adam of Bremen a ferry connection between Helsingør and the town of Helsingborg was established in the second half of the 11th century.
Town_Description: Helsingør was registered as a town in a registration from c. 1241 of the towns of Zealand and surrounding islands (Danish: “Købstadslisten”) in King Valdemar’s Cadastre. By then Helsingør was a town, but when the first town privileges were granted is uncertain, presumably in the early 13th century. A town council and citizens are known from the following 14th century. The royal castle of Krogen was built east of town at the shore of Øresund by king Eric the Pommerian (1412-1439) in the early 15th century. King Eric also re-established the town of Helsingør, and granted the town new privileges as well as tax exemptions to new citizens. The new town is clearly reflected in the structural layout of the old parts of modern Helsingør, which before 1440 also was fortified by a moat and rampart. Up until the time of the Danish Reformation in 1536 the town had three monasteries. From the 15th century onwards Helsingør was in general a very prosperous urban community. The town benefited from the economical dynamics in the region around Øresund, and the royal toll on ships sailing through Øresund. The town attracted foreign merchants and craftsmen, many of whom even settled down in Helsingør. In 1574 king Frederik II (1559-1588) began a rebuilding of the medieval castle of Krogen into a modern renaissance castle, Kronborg Castle.
Fair_Description: During the late medieval period Helsingør probably held at least one annual fair. The date, age and character of the fair are uncertain. In 1549 king Christian III (1534-1559) moved the annual fair previously held in the settlement of Ludserød to Helsingør. The latter fair took place on Michaelmas (Danish: Sankt Mikkels dag) on September 29th. In the second part of the 17th century two annual fairs were held in Helsingør.

name: Skodborghus
Settlement_Description: A royal castle at one of the most obvious places to cross the river of Kongeåen. The castle is mentioned for the first time in 1368. Until the second half of the 16th century the royal castle played a central role in controlling the traffic across the river, especially the export of oxen from northern parts of Jutland. Around 1580, when the king gave up the castle, the crossing at Skodborghus had lost its importance. At this time illegal traffic of oxen across the river between Skodborghus and Kolding was a big problem.

name: Vamdrup
Settlement_Description: The village of Vamdrup was first mentioned in 1280, but is older. The parish church is from either the 12th or 13th century.

name: Takajärvi
Settlement_Description: <b>Inn:</b> Jaakko Yrjönpoika from Mikkola farm in Takajärvi is mentioned as a tavern in 1639, when Count Per Brahe travelled from Turku to Hämeenlinna. Takajärvi is located by the winter road. Mikkola farm served as a tavern for most of the 17th c., and it is mentioned as a tavern in 1706.

name: Sibbesborg
Settlement_Description: Sibbesborg is a site of a medieval castle on a rocky ridge in that time Sipoonjoki (sw. Sibbo å) rivermouth area. An island as late as in the late 17th century, the castle has been archaeologically dated to the latter half of the 14th century. It was likely built by Jakob Abrahamsson (Djäkn) whom the king Albrekt of Mecklenburg of Sweden had in 1387 granted the right to hold to Porvoo bailiwick (sw. Borgå fögderi) and the castle of Turku with its underlying bailiwicks and build fortifications in the area. After Jakob had in 1395 handed the castles of Turku, Kastelholm, Aborch and Verghdenborch and the castle of Wartholm in Nyland over to Knut Bosson (Grip) and his Mecklenburgian mother Margareta Dume, Knut ceded Turku castle and his other wooden castles to queen Margaret in 1399, who let several of the small new castles demolished in the opening years of the 15th century. Sibbesborg may have been the new castle of Wartholm in Nyland cited in two contemporary sources in 1395-98, but the more likely candidate for the fortification is Husholmen in Pikku Pernajanlahti bay east of Porvoo.

name: Vehra
Settlement_Description: First mention in 1208 as property of Pforta monastery. The name of the settlement alludes to a ferry, although this seems to be in direct contradiction with the name of Straußfurt on the opposite bank of the Unstrut river, which alludes to a ford.

name: Lindow (Mark)
Settlement_Description: Foundation of a convent of Cistercian nuns in 1230 in the vicinity, which moved to Lindow around 1240. A small market- and craftsmen-village developed at the monastery.
Town_Description: Mentioned as oppidum in 1373, later also called small town ('Städtchen'), founded by the lords of Ruppin. Town privileges may never have been granted.
Toll_Description: In 1525, Neubrandenburg complained that Elector Joachim I had started to levy a new large transit toll in Lindow, instead of the already existing minor wagon toll.

name: Neustadt (Dosse)
Settlement_Description: First mentioned in 1375. A castle is mentioned in 1407. The settlement was characterised as borough ('Städtlein'/'Flecken') in the 16th century.
Town_Description: Town privileges were granted in 1664 by the landgrave of Hessen-Homburg.

name: Bredsten
Settlement_Description: The village of Bredsten was first mentioned c. 1330, but is significantly older. The parish church is from either the 12th or 13th century.

name: Prenzlau
Settlement_Description: First mention of the name in 1187. Before it had already been a Slavic fortification. In 1188 it is already mentioned with a market and an inn.
Town_Description: Duke Barnim I granted Magdeburg town privileges in 1234, confirmed by the Margrave of Brandenburg in 1251.

name: Neuhaus (Wolfsburg)
Settlement_Description: The castle Neuhaus was first mentioned in 1354.

name: Horsens
Settlement_Description: Settlement most likely established in the 10th century. Archaeological excavations have revealed burials and traces of permanent production and trade in the late viking age.
Town_Description: Around 1100, perhaps earlier, Horsens had developed into a settlement with an urban character. Horsens was described as a “small town” by the Arab geographer al-Idrishi in 1138-1154. Coins were minted in the town under king Svend Grathe (1146-1157), and according to the so-called main piece in King Valdemars Cadastre, Horsens paid a relatively high annual tax to the king in the middle of the 13th century. A Franciscan monastery was founded in 1261. In 1313 king Eric VI Menved (1286-1319) fortified the town with a moat, which changed the town’s layout. King Eric also built a castle, probably the castle of Bygholm west of town. Horsens was granted its first town law, which was identical with the town law of Schleswig, around 1300. In 1350 a town hall was constructed, which was replaced by a new town hall in 1585. Oldest known privileges were granted by king Christopher the Bavarian (1440-1448) in 1442, but Horsens most certainly obtained town rights much earlier. In the 16th century the town experienced a positive development, and the settlement spread outside the fortification. But in the following 17th century the town began to decline.

name: Katerveer
Settlement_Description: The settlement Katen was first mentioned in 1243. It was swallowed by the river after 1570. The later still existing ferry was named after the former village.
Toll_Description: The "Cothentol" on shipping on the IJssel river is already mentioned in 973. It was leased to the town Deventer by the monastery Elten since 1241.
Ferry_Description: A ferry across the IJssel at the village Katen near Zwolle was probably installed by the bishop of Utrecht around 1200. In 1396 the bishop of Utrecht ordained that church and vicarage of Koten had to be maintained in their right on the ferry. The ferry was discontinued in 1930.

name: Venhuizen
Settlement_Description: Venhuizen is first mentioned around 1312. On 2 February 1414 Venhuizen, together with the village Hem, was granted town privileges by William (‘Willem’) VI, count of Holland. These settlements, however, never developed an urban character. The granting of town rights was part of an administrative reorganization in which a number of smaller settlements were granted town rights in order to provide them with a certain degree of self-government which replaced the need for the count of Holland's bailiffs ('baljuws'). The settlements kept their own separate settlement governments.

name: Sattula
Settlement_Description: <b>Inn:</b> Reko Heikinpoika from Rekola farm was appointed as the tavern in 1622. In 1637, the tavern rights were moved to Tuomas Matinpoika from Jaakkola farm in Sattula. There has been an alehouse also later in the 17th c. in Sattula village.

name: Bovenkarspel
Settlement_Description: Bovenkarspel is first mentioned in c.1312. Together with Grootebroek the village was granted town privileges on 2 August 1364 by Albert ('Albrecht'), governor ('ruwaard') of Holland. Together the settlements formed the 'stede' Broek. The villages Lutjebroek and Hoogkarspel were added to this 'stede' in 1402 and 1403, respectively. These settlements, however, never developed an urban character. The granting of town rights was part of an administrative reorganization in which a number of smaller settlements were granted town rights in order to provide them with a certain degree of self-governmen. The villages kept their own separate councils. The 'stede' lost its privileges in 1426, but these were partly regranted in 1429, and fully restored in 1436.

name: null
Bridge_Description: A bridge across the Widawa in Szymanów is first attested in 1337.

name: Köritz
Settlement_Description: The village is first mentioned in 1305.

name: Bremen
Settlement_Description: Around 780, there existed a settlement at the riverfront at the current street Tiefer at the shore of the Weser river, as well as a religious (episcopal) centre on a river dune.
Town_Description: The settlement acquired market, justice and mint privileges in 965. The first city wall was built after 1030 and a council is first mentioned in 1225. Older town privileges were confirmed by archbishop Gerhard I in 1217. It became an important trading city and member of the Hanse. The town expanded on the southern shore of the river after 1623, but more for defensive purposes than because of lack of space, as the Neustadt ('new town') remained sparsely populated for a long time.
Fair_Description: The fairs in Bremen went back at least to the market privileges of 965, probably even into the 9th century. The oldest fair took place in Autumn, to which a second Spring fair was added in a privilege of 1035. These two fairs both lasted a week and remained in place - with various alterations in the dates throughout the years - until 1638. In that year, the Spring fair was replaced by two three-day fairs, on Quasimodogeniti and Ascension Day; the Autumn market was prolonged to nine days. In the same 1638 privilege, four new horse fairs were installed.
Toll_Description: Various tolls were levied in the city of Bremen, of which the oldest have their roots in the toll rights of the archbishop from 888. The town levied tolls at each town gate, which were leased to Johan Cruse in 1373, who in return had to maintain the stone road from St Ansgar's bridge to St John's chapel. (Bremer UB III:431). Excluded was the toll on the Weser bridge, which was owned by the count of Hoya.<br/>The Akzise, import and export duties, accounted for about 86% for the entire income of the city in 1600. Moreover, from 1426 onwards a buoy toll ('tonnengeld') for maintenance of the traffic signs on the lower Weser river, a tidal area, was levied for each incoming and outgoing ship. Responsible for the levying of the latter toll were the eldermen of the common merchant. Akzise and Tonnengeld registers are extant from the year 1532 onwards (StAB, 2-R.2.A.o.2.b.).
Staple_Description: First signs of a staple can be found in the town rights of 1303/8, but only in 1360, a request from Lübeck shows that Bremen had installed a corn staple. In 1376, citizens of Hannover were allowed to ship all commodities freely, except corn, of which a third part had to be sold in Bremen. The town laws of the "Kundige Rolle" (1450, 1498) contain a three-day staple obligation for commodities coming from the sea and wood coming down the Weser, as well as a prohibition of the trade between non-citizens.<br/>Complaints from Minden on the Hanseatic Diets in 1506, 1507 and 1511 show that the staple could not be fully enforced. In 1541, the emperor confirmed the staple obligations, but revoked the charter in the same year. Minden citizens were exempted from the Bremen staple in 1552, but from 1611 there were renewed attempts to enforce the staple towards Minden merchants. The "Weddeordnung" of 1612 prohibited merchants from neighbouring towns to transport herring, butter, fish, tar, fish oil, tallow, corn, wine, beer and other commodities through Bremen. The staple was abolished with the "Weserschifffahrtsakte" of 1823.

name: Næstved
Settlement_Description: A Viking Age settlement near the mouth of the river of Suså into Karrebæk Fjord. The character of the settlement is unclear, but there is strong archaeological evidence of trade activities. At least in the 11th century, and perhaps earlier, the settlement had a permanent character. The settlement and later the town of Næstved benefited from its location near an easy place to cross Suså, and at an important junction for both land based and maritime transportation.
Town_Description: The town of Næstved is documented for the first time in the year 1135, when bishop Eskil of Roskilde confirmed the foundation of Saint Peder’s Abbey, a Benedictine house just outside the town. Five years later king Eric III Lamb (1137-1146) granted the monastery the right to the revenues from the market, the fines paid by criminals, and the annual town tax (Danish: midsommergæld) to the abbey of Saint Peder. The Benedictine monastery hereby became the town lord of Næstved, a status the monastery kept until the 15th century when king Eric the Pommerian (1396-1439) took control of the town. The monastery, however, continued to play a dominant role in Næstved; in 1530 at least 70 properties in Næstved belonged to the Benedictines. A town law was first mentioned in 1274, and town council and members of the council in 1280. At this point in time the town also had a municipal seal. In the 13th century Næstved was among the wealthiest towns in Denmark, something which is revealed in a registration of towns on the islands of Zealand, Lolland and Falster in King Valdemar’s Cadastre from c. 1241. Næstved’s status and wealth is also reflected in the foundation of both a Francican and Dominican monastery during the 13th century. In the late medieval period Næstved kept its status as one of the richests towns in the Danish kingdom, and had strong connections to Hanseatic towns. The latter is reflected in the foundation of a German guild in Næstved in the 15th century. The impressive late medieval town hall, built in the 15th and early 16th century, has been preserved to this day. The dissolution of the abbey of Saint Peder at the time of the Danish reformation in 1536 had a negative effect on Næstved. Apparently the town began to struggle with more illegale trade in the region, and also suffered heavily during the Dano-Swedish wars in the 17th century.

name: Rägelin
Settlement_Description: The village is first mentioned in 1358.

name: Grootebroek
Settlement_Description: According to Van Berkel & Samplonius, Grootebroek is first mentioned in 1288. Cox chooses a slightly later date, c1312.Grootebroek, together with Bovenkarspel, was granted town privileges on 2 August 1364 by Albert ('Albrecht'), governor ('ruwaard') of Holland. Grootebroek and Bovenkarspel combined formed the 'stede' Broek. The settlements Lutjebroek and Hoogkarspel were added to this 'stede' in 1402 and 1403, respectively. These settlements, however, never developed an urban character. The granting of town rights was part of an administrative reorganization in which a number of smaller settlements were granted town rights in order to provide them with a certain degree of self-government which replaced the need for the count of Holland's bailiffs ('baljuws'). The settlements kept their own separate settlement governments.The 'stede' lost its privileges in 1426, but these were partly regranted in 1429, and fully restored in 1436.
Fair_Description: In 1364 (Aug. 2) duke Albrecht granted a fair in 'Grote Broec and Boeven Kerspel' which then became the town Broec. The fair is dated St. James (July 25), duration: 14 days. Toll-exemption was also granted then.

name: Broekerhaven
Harbour_Description: A harbour on the Zuiderzee for the villages that were united into the "stede Broec" was constructed around 1449.

name: null
Harbour_Description: Located at Bygholm Å’s northern outlet. The harbour is mentioned in sources from the 14th century onwards, and was used by German merchants on a regular basis. In the late medieval period, maybe earlier, a pier was constructed. In the 17th century the pier was around 150 meters long.

name: Berkumer brug
Toll_Description: In 1569, the bishop of Münster complained about the levying of a bridge toll on the bridge near Berkum.
Bridge_Description: A bridge across the Vecht near Berkum was built by Zwolle in 1451.
Ferry_Description: A ferry must have existed before the construction of the bridge in 1451.

name: Hoym
Settlement_Description: First mentioned in a charter of Otto I in 961, in which the villa Hoym (Hahem) is confirmed as the property of Quedlinburg monastery. First mention of a castle Hoym in 1301, which guarded the crossing of the road from Braunschweig to Leipzig across the Selke river. Although the village was pawned several times, there is no mention of a road toll in the charters. However, it can be assumed that there had to be some kind of toll, especially at the Selke crossing.
Town_Description: In 1543 the settlement received town rights from duke Wolfgang of Anhalt.

name: Skanderborg
Settlement_Description: Originally a village (Skanderup) and a royal castle, which was amongst  the most important royal castles in Jutland from the late 12th century up until the 18th century.
Town_Description: The settlement around the castle developed into a town, and Skanderborg was given town rights in 1583 by king Frederik II (1559-1588).

name: Tjæreby
Settlement_Description: The village of Tjæreby is first mentioned in 1231. The settlement had no church but was part of Tårnborg parish.

name: Lutjebroek
Settlement_Description: Lutjebroek is first mentioned c1312.On 14 October 1402, Lutjebroek was added to the ‘stede’ Broek, which already consisted of Grootebroek and Bovenkarspel. These two settlements had been granted town privileges on 2 August 1364 by Albert ('Albrecht'), governor ('ruwaard') of Holland. In 1403, Hoogkarspel was also added to this ‘stede’. These settlements, however, never developed an urban character. The granting of town rights was part of an administrative reorganization in which a number of smaller settlements were granted town rights in order to provide them with a certain degree of self-government which replaced the need for the count of Holland's bailiffs ('baljuws'). The settlements kept their own separate settlement governments. The 'stede' lost its privileges in 1426, but these were partly regranted in 1429, and fully restored in 1436.

name: Schmölln
Settlement_Description: Already before 1066 a Benedictine monastery existed. It enjoyed market, coin and toll privileges.
Town_Description: Town and church are founded in 1238, but there might have been an earlier urban settlement on the opposite bank of the Sprotte river. In the 14th century Gera town rights are granted. In 1412 the town rights and privileges of the citizens are first confirmed.
Toll_Description: Secondary station of safe conduct ('Beigeleitsstelle') of Altenburg. Annual revenues are known from 1509/10 onwards, tariffs and regulations ('Geleitsordnung') date from 1548.

name: null
Harbour_Description: The river Zwarte Water connected Zwolle with the Zuiderzee and the Vecht. The oldes archaeological traces of a harbour date from the late 11th and 12th century and were located at the old course of the river Aa, around the Voorstraat and Melkmarkt. Later the harbour moved to the Rodetorenplein, where a harbour crane was located, which is shown on 16th- and 17th-century views of the city.

name: Altenburg
Settlement_Description: From approximately 800 centre of the Slavic area called Plisni (Pleißenland). A fortification was referred to as Altenburg, first mentioned in 976. A small village named Pauritz developed close to the castle's ramparts. From the 11th to the 13th century the castle was used as an imperial palace ('Kaiserpfalz') so that the village developed early urban structures in the 11th century.
Town_Description: From 1165 Altenburg consisted of an old and new town. In 1205 it was referred to as civitas. First record of town rights in 1256.
Fair_Description: Altenburg received the right to hold an eight-day fair from Sunday Rogate until Exaudi from margrave Wilhelm in 1419. A second fair on the Nativity of Mary is mentioned in 1437. The dukes of Saxony granted five new fairs in Altenburg in 1621, consisting of four horse fairs on Oculi, Vocem Jocunditatis, 8 days before St Michael and 8 days before All Saints and a fish fair on Sunday after St Vitus. However, these were revoked again after protests from Leipzig.
Toll_Description: A "small toll" in Altenburg is first mentioned in 1352 and was probably a market fee. The large toll was levied on transit traffic in connection to the safe conduct. Annual revenues of the safe conduct are known from 1464 onwards, accounts exist from 1504. The regulations of safe conduct ('Geleitsordnung') for Altenburg from 1515 and 1548 regulated the fees for several commodities and travel directions. Secondary stations of safe conduct ('Beigeleitsstellen') existed in Schmölln, Wintersdorf, Altmörbitz, Treben, Gerstenberg, Börten and Lucka.

name: Gerstenberg
Toll_Description: Secondary station of safe conduct of Altenburg on the road to Naumburg. Annual revenues are known from 1511/12 onwards, as well as detailed accounts. Tariffs and regulations ('Geleitsordnung') date from 1548. The accounts show that predominantly corn was transported on this route.

name: Vemmelev
Settlement_Description: The village of Vemmelev is first mentioned in 1182.

name: Rustenburg
Settlement_Description: The house Rustenburg is first mentioned in 1573. According to some authors, the name was derived from an inn.

name: Lucka
Settlement_Description: First mentioned in 1284. The village developed into a marketplace between 1307 and 1320.
Town_Description: Referred to as oppidum in 1324. First mentioned as town in 1331. In 1409 the settlement was granted privileges, bylaws and a municipal court, which were renewed in 1474.
Toll_Description: In 1347 the "house of Breitenhain, the small town of Lucka with their toll" are sold by the Wettins to the counts of Starkenberg. Even before it can be assumed that the settlement was a toll station for the castle of Breitenhain. Later it was a secondary station of safe conduct ('Beigeleitsstelle') of Altenburg, for which annual revenues are known from 1464 onwards. Curiously Lucka is not mentioned in the regulations for the safe conduct of Altenburg from 1548.

name: Treben
Toll_Description: The toll station in Treben is first mentioned in 1282 when it was given to the Teutonic Order. Later a secondary station of safe conduct ('Beigeleitsstelle') of Altenburg. Annual revenues are known from 1511/12 onwards, tariffs and regulations ('Geleitsordnung') date from 1548.

name: Ronneburg
Settlement_Description: First mention in 1209 as property of the lords of Weida.
Town_Description: The town was a planned foundation north-east of the castle in the second half of the 13th century. A citizen is first mentioned in 1301. It was probably granted Gera town rights in the beginning of the 14th century, which were confirmed in 1380.
Fair_Description: Since 1594 several fairs, especially cattle markets are known.

name: Sponholz
Settlement_Description: The village is first mentioned in 1496.

name: Frederiks Bro
Bridge_Description: The age and character of the first bridge in Aarhus across Aarhus Å is uncertain. In the 13th century a watermill and dam was mentioned for the first time, and in the middle of the 13th century a bridge was probably also built at Immervad, where there previously had been a ford across the river. The bridge at Immervad was first mentioned in 1477 and again in 1512.

name: Rühlow
Settlement_Description: The village is first mentioned in 1298. An inn in Rühlow is mentioned in 1496.

name: Voigtsdorf
Settlement_Description: First mentioned in possession of the bishop of Havelberg in 1267. An inn is mentioned in Voigtsdorf in 1614.

name: Petersdorf (Woldegk)
Settlement_Description: First mentioned in 1298 in a donation charter for the monastery Wanzka.

name: Nieuwebrug
Settlement_Description: Nieuwebrug is first mentioned as toll station in 1391. There existed an inn, where among others the Estates of Overijssel gathered in 1496. A village developed only in the 19th century.
Toll_Description: Toll station of the bishop of Utrecht, who exempted his servants in Twente and Ootmarsum from toll payments at Nieuwebrug and Hardenberg in 1391. In 1395 Oldenzaal was exempted from the toll here. The towns at the IJssel were also exempted. The toll was leased to Zwolle for 125 guilders annually.
Bridge_Description: The name Nieuwebrug refers to a new bridge across the Regge, which has to have existed already in 1391.

name: Genzkow
Settlement_Description: First mentioned in 1298 in a donation charter to Wanzka monastery.

name: Zwolle
Settlement_Description: Earliest mention in a donation charter of the bishop of Utrecht from 1040, the veracity of which is debated. The first certain mention dates from a confirmation of that charter from 1129 (in a 14th-century copy). Archaeological evidence points at continuous habitation since the 9th century.
Town_Description: Town privileges were granted by Wilbrand of Oldenburg, bishop of Utrecht, on 31 August 1230. These town privileges were renewed and extended in 1346.
Fair_Description: On 21 April 1265 Hendrik van Vianden, bishop of Utrecht, granted a nine-day fair on St Boniface (5 June) with safe conduct for the visitors within the bishopric of Utrecht. Probably the fair of St Michael (29 September) already existed at that point as well, which was probably the oldest fair as it is named after the patron of the town. In the late 13th century we also hear about fairs on the Assumption of the Virgin Mary (15 August) and Simon and Jude's Day (28 October). On 25 March 1309 the bishop granted a fifth fair of one week around Tuesday after Easter, with safe conduct. The charter also explicitly allows the trade of horses and cattle during all fairs. In the early 17th century, only three eight-day markets remained: on Palm Sunday, St James (25 July) and St Michael, of which the first two are already mentioned in an almanac from 1598 printed in Neudamm (Dębno).
Toll_Description: A toll was levied at the town gates. The oldest toll tariff from 1366 gives an impression of the range of commodities traded in the town via the land and water ways. The tariff of the road toll was heightened by the council in 1596, to fund repairs of the roads and bridges.
Staple_Description: The town claimed a staple right for rye, cattle and other agricultural products from Overijssel, which reached the town via the bridges Venebrugge and Nieuwebrug to the East. This right was confirmed by the bishop of Utrecht in 1438.

name: Grafhorst
Town_Description: Town privileges were granted by Jan III of Diest, bishop of Utrecht, on 20 April 1333. However, it remained a small settlement and never acquired an urban character.

name: Heringen (Helme)
Settlement_Description: First mention in a charter from 874 by Ludwig the German together with Nordhausen.
Town_Description: In 1339 a castle was built and the settlement was elevated to town by Dietrich IV of Honstein.
Fair_Description: Since the 14th century two fairs are known, on Mondag after St James and Tuesday before St Gall.

name: Harresø
Settlement_Description: The small settlement was first mentioned in 1499. The settlement had no church in the middle ages, but an inn was first mentioned in 1609.

name: Varde
Town_Description: Varde was counted among the towns of Denmark c. 1150, and in the early medieval period Varde was both an important town and a political center. According to the so-called main piece of King Valdemar’s Cadastre from 1231 the town belonged to the king. A royal castle was built around 1300 southwest of town. It was burned down and not rebuilt in 1439. In 1368-1370 town council men and citizens were mentioned, and the first known town privileges were granted by king Christopher the Bavarian (1440-1448) in 1442. Town hall first mentioned in 1620. In the late medieval period Varde played an important role in the export of oxen from Jutland, but through the years Varde lost ground to other towns in Jutland such as Viborg and in particular Ribe. The town also suffered heavily under the Count's Feud 1534-36, and during the wars of the 17th century.

name: Kongevejsbroen
Toll_Description: A fee was paid to cross the bridge (Danish: bropenge/brokorn). The exact age and character of the toll is, however, unclear.
Bridge_Description: At the end of the medieval period the bridge across Skjern Å was moved c. 500 meters away from its original location, when Kongevejsbroen was built. In 1619 it is mentioned that it was possible to use a ford next to the bridge. In 1632 the bridge had collapsed, but was soon rebuilt.

name: Følle
Settlement_Description: The village of Følle was first mentioned in 1313, but is significantly older. The settlement had no church but was part of the parish of Bregnet Church.

name: Stenalt
Settlement_Description: The village of Steenalt was first mentioned in 1375, but is significantly older. The settlement had no church but was part of the parish of Ørsted Church.

name: Pragsdorf
Settlement_Description: The village is first mentioned in 1381 as possession of the Helpte family. In 1547 the last male heir died, and the village was appropriated by the dukes of Mecklenburg. There were 26 families in the village in 1496.

name: Glienke
Settlement_Description: First mentioned in 1298 in a donation charter to the monastery Wanzka.

name: Kublank
Settlement_Description: The village is first mentioned in a donation charter to the monastery Wanzka in 1298. An inn in Kublank is mentioned in 1584.
Toll_Description: A toll station in Kublank is mentioned in 1584.

name: Schönhausen
Settlement_Description: First mentioned in 1266 in possession of the bishop of Havelberg. An inn in Schönhausen is mentioned in 1581.

name: null
Harbour_Description: A natural harbour with some man made constructions from the founding of Ribe onwards. According to the German chronicler Adam of Bremen, Ribe was an important harbour in the 11th century. The harbour connected Denmark with Friland, England, Saxony as well as other parts of western Europe. That Ribe continued as one of the most important ports of Denmark in the following period was emphasized by the Danish chronicler Saxo Grammaticus, who finished his Gesta Danorum c. 1208. The harbour lost some of its importance in the later middle ages and early modern period, but was still one of the most important to Danish export and import.

name: København
Settlement_Description: Large-scale archaeological excavations in the oldests parts of Copenhagen have revealed trading and craft activities in the late Viking Age, and that Copenhagen was a permanent settlement with an urban character in the 11th century. The settlement was located at one of the best natural harbors on eastern Zealand and at a place with overland routes across the large island of Zealand.
Town_Description: Copenhagen was first mentioned in a papal document from 1186, by which pope Urban III confirmed that king Valdemar I the Great (1157-1182) around 1167 had donated the castle of Copenhagen (“castrum de Hafn”) to archbishop Absalon of Lund, who was also bishop of Roskilde. The pope also confirmed that the castle and town of Copenhagen by the death of Absalon should be handed over to the diocese of Roskilde. Thus, when Absalon died in 1201, the town went to the church in Roskilde, and the bishops of Roskilde were town lords until 1417, when king Eric the Pommerian (1396-1439) took over the town. In the following decades Copenhagen developed into the most important town in Denmark; in time it came to be the Danish capital. Up until recently the papal document from 1186 was seen as the foundation document of Copenhagen, but thanks to archeological excavations it is now clear that Copenhagen had already an urban character, when archbishop Absalon took over the town. In his Gesta Danorum from c. 1208 the Danish chronicler Saxo Grammaticus touched upon the recent history of the town, which he described as  “urbs Absalonica” and “portus mercatorum”. Absalon established a strong castle on the small island of Slotsholmen near the coastline, where the settlement and later town also developed, and in the 13th century the town was also fortified. Both the castle and the town fortification were rebuilt several times. In the early modern era the castle was one of the most important royal castles in Denmark, and Copenhagen was surrounded by a strong town wall built of bricks. The town was granted its first town law by the bishop of Roskilde in 1254, which was replaced by the second town law in 1294. A town council and members of the council (consules) were also well-established by the end of the 13th century, as was a town hall. The latter was relocated in the later middle ages to the town’s main square (Danish: Gammeltorv). A Fransician monastery was founded around 1240. As an illustrative example of the growing importance of the town, the first university in Denmark was founded in Copenhagen in 1479, and at this time the town's main church, the Church of our Lady (Danish: Vor Frue), had also become the preferred place for royal coronations and weddings. Throughout the middle ages and early modern era Copenhagen grew in political and economic importance as well as size. The town benefited from its central location in the Danish realm and at the shore of the narrow strait of Øresund. By the 17th century Copenhagen was undisputedly the largest and in many ways most important town in Denmark.
Staple_Description: As part of his struggle with Lübeck king Christian II (1513-1523) established a staple in Copenhagen, as the king aimed to make his capital the leading entrepôt of the Baltic. The ambitious attempt failed, and Copenhagen only functioned as a staple town in a few years during the reign of Christian II.

name: Karrebæksminde
Harbour_Description: Mention as loading place ('ladeplads') in 1477. The place functioned as port for the town Næstved, which could only be reached with small vessels. Here transshipment took place between large sea-going vessels and small boats that could reach the town harbour at the Suså river. A canal was dug to Næstved in 1935-1938.

name: Kratzeburg
Settlement_Description: First mentioned in 1256. The village was originally called Werder, but became known after the castle Kratzeburg (first mentioned in 1314).

name: Düsterförde
Settlement_Description: The settlement consisted of two cottages ('büdnereien'), a tar kiln and an inn. It was allegedly founded by the Polish bear-leader Quarkowsky, who had been given the land by Duke Adolf Friedrich III (1707-1752). Hence it was also known as Quarkenkrug.

name: Duisburg
Settlement_Description: The settlement dates back to Roman times. Later it was a Frankish royal residence, which was first mentioned when it was plundered by Vikings in 883. It was enlarged to a royal palace in the 10th century.
Town_Description: Due to its location on the Rhine, Duisburg developed rapidly into a merchant centre that developed into a town in the 12th century. A privilege from 1129 to quarry stones for construction works in town still refers to the settlement as 'villa'. In 1145 a community of citizens is mentioned, and a document from 1165 implies that the settlement had become an Imperial Town. After the Rhine changed its course after 1200 and the Rhine arm on which Duisburg was located silted up, the town gradually lost its position as primary trade centre. Moreover, the town lost its status of Imperial town and became subjugated to the count of Cleves in 1290.
Fair_Description: Emperor Frederick granted two 14-day fairs on St Bartholomew (August 24) and Mid Lent (Sunday Leatare) in 1173. The fair of St Bartholomew was moved to Orsoy in 1428. Before 1276 there were three fairs, on Palm Sunday, August 29 and December 21. In 1577 three horse fairs were granted. A weekly market on Friday-Sunday is mentioned in 1408.
Toll_Description: 1) A river toll on the Rhine was levied here from 1184 to 1348/52. The toll changed hands frequently. Until 1248 it was held by the Empire, from 1248 to 1280 by Duke Walram of Limburg, from 1280 to 1288 by Count Renald of Geldern and from 1290 by the Count of Kleve. In addition, a (fair) market toll, which also applied to ships, has been documented since 1065. The Rhine toll was transferred to Kaiserwerth in 1348 by Count Gerhard von Berg. At the same time, the Count of Kleve continued to levy toll until he moved it to Büderich in 1352. The tariff in 1348 was 6 Turnosgroschen. 2) A land toll was also levied from 1280 onwards.
Staple_Description: Uncertain: a "jus stapulae" in Duisburg is first mentioned only in 1708, when it is moved to Wesel because of changes in the course of the Rhine. A charter of Duke Walram IV of Limburg from 1273 allows citizens of Cologne to transport their commodities unhindered through Duisburg, indicating that the town already claimed some kind of staple privileges in that period.

name: Friedland (Vorpommern)
Settlement_Description: Before the foundation of the town in 1244, there existed a village.
Town_Description: Margraves Johann and Otto of Brandenburg founded the town on 6 March 1244 with Stendal town privileges. The privileges were confirmed when the town was transferred to Mecklenburg in 1304.
Fair_Description: The mention of a market toll in 1282 suggests the existence of a fair in Friedland from that year. In 1625 a second cattle market on St Bartholomew was privileged. It is unknown when the first fair took place.
Toll_Description: The town Friedland possessed a toll in Friedland and Neubrandenburg since 1276. In 1282 a market toll was added. Neubrandenburg bought the toll there in 1366, but Friedland citizens would continue to be exempted from the toll.

name: Berga (Elster)
Settlement_Description: First mention in 1216. A mill is mentioned in 1306.
Town_Description: Referred to as opidum in 1378, in 1386 as town ('stat'). Town rights were granted in the 14th century, which were confirmed in 1427 by Henry of Weida.
Fair_Description: In 1427 three fairs and a weekly market are known in Berka, a fourth fair followed in 1653.

name: Woldegk
Town_Description: The town was founded between 1236 and 1250 by the Margraves of Brandenburg together with a castle (first mentioned in 1317) without preceding settlement. The foundation privileges have not survived. A council and citizens are mentioned in 1298. Duke Heinrich of Mecklenburg-Schwerin confirmed all privileges in 1471.

name: Lahti (Somero)
Settlement_Description:
<b>Inn:</b> A local official in Porras parish, <i>neljänneskuntamies</i> (sw. fjärdingsman), held a tavern by the common road in Lahti and received tax exemptions for it. Parish constable's house is mentioned in Jaakko Teitti's road description in 1556. 
Parish constables (fi: nimismies, sw: länsman) were obliged to keep a tavern in late 16th c.

name: Porras bridge
Bridge_Description: Bridge, or, more literally, 'steps' across Turpoonjoki river. The bridge gave its name to the village nearby. First mention in 1431.

name: Porras
Settlement_Description: The name Porras ('Step') comes from the bridge over Turpoonjoki. The village is first mentioned in 1431 and is also included in Jaakko Teitti's list in 1556 as a possible place for an official, Vogt (fi. vouti, sw. fogde)

name: null
Harbour_Description: A modest wharf is shown on a map in Resen’s Atlas Danicus from c. 1675. The character of the harbour in the middle ages is unknown. The harbour was difficult to use, especially for larger vessels, due to a sand reef close to the shore. Still, the harbour was used to export agricultural products to Germany.

name: Wildenbörten
Toll_Description: Secondary station of safe conduct ('Beigeleitsstelle') of Altenburg. Annual revenues are known from 1522/23 onwards. Curiously Wildenbörten is not mentioned in the regulations of safe conduct ('Geleitsordnung') of Altenburg from 1548.

name: Vaasa
Settlement_Description: Permanent agricultural settlement in Mustasaari area dates to the Swedish colonisation of the late 13th century and the beginning of the 14th. Mustasaari is cited as an independent parish together with Närpiö (sw. Närpes) and Pedersöre in 1348, when their inhabitants were given right to trade with victuals between themselves. The parish church and Mustasaari village were located east of Lågfjärden strait on an island to the southern end of which Korsholm castle was built before the year 1384. The castle and later Royal Manor served as the administrative centre of Gulf of Bothnia area north of Kvarken until 1441, and after that periodically and since 1525 to 1634 that of Ostrobothnia or the southern part of it. Originally attached to Satakunta province, Närpiö parish was placed under Korsholm in 1595. After the reorganisation of the provincial administration in 1635 the province of Pohjanmaa (sw. Österbottens län) was in 1642-48 split to Vaasa and Oulu provinces but the final partition took only place in 1776.
Town_Description:
The town of Vaasa (sw. Vasa) was established by king Karl IX in 1606. Originally named as Mustasaari (Mustsari) the town was after the reconfirmation and further specification of the privileges in 1611 named Wasa in honour of the Royal family. The town area was surveyed and measured in 1608. The original street network has survived in the new plans of 1651 and 1658. The old plan has survived in Originally centred around Mustasaari parish church, the town was after the fire of 1852 relocated to its present site. Mustasaari area is likely have hosted a haven and market site on the sailing route on Ostrobothnian coast already around the time of the founding of Korsholm castle in the third quarter of the 14th century. The weekly market day in Vaasa was in 1616 confirmed Saturday.
The trading area of Vaasa consisted since 1606 southern part of the province of Ostrobothnia, but was cut smaller in 1620 after the foundation of Nykarleby (fin. Uusikaarlepyy) and Gamlakarleby (fin. Kokkola) towns. Burghers of Vaasa held partial limited export rights in foreign trade in 1614-17, but were since 1617 alongside other towns in the Gulf of Bothnia area allowed to export their goods to Stockholm and Turku until 1765. In 1636 the crown prohibited all foreign shipping to towns, harbours, or other places north of Turku and Stockholm, including Åland. 
<b>Inn:</b> The first official inn in Vaasa town was established in 1627, and Didrich Spikernagell was appointed as the innkeeper. He also had a monopoly for the sale of communion wine. Vaasa town cellar, which traditionally had the monopoly over the sale of imported drinks, is mentioned in 1642, but in 1648 there were complaints that no one wants to take care of the cellar inn. Cellar rights were appointed to the burgher who offered the highest bid. In 1654, several alehouses and distilleries were appointed in Vaasa, and four wealthy burghers were appointed as town brewers. 
<b>Post office:</b> The Vaasa post office was likely established in 1644, as matters related to the hiring of a postmaster are mentioned in the provincial accounts from that time. The position was reportedly first held by Thomas Watsson, who was a customs officer, innkeeper, and rural police officer.
Fair_Description:
In the privileges of 1606 and 1611 Vaasa was confirmed two annual fairs, one on Candlemas (2 February) and one St Laurentius (10 August). The early autumn fair of St Laurentius was confirmed also in 1640 and is cited in 1708. Both fairs may date to the late 14th century.
In 1616 all trade in Ostrobothnia was centred to Oulu and Vaasa (sw. Vasa), but burghers of Stockholm, Turku, Rauma and Pori were granted the right for annual fair of two weeks in Pedersöre and Saloinen starting from St Olaf’s (29 July). Pedersöre fair was in 1624 translocated to Nykarleby and set to last for three days. The trading areas of Vaasa (1606) and Nykarleby (1620) towns hosted of old peasant fairs in three parishes of Lapua, Vöyri and Isokyrö, of which burghers of Vaasa were granted sole rights to St Henrik (20 January) and St Laurentius (10 August) fair in Isokyrö and Nykarleby, to Candelmas fair (2 February) in Lapua, and to St Margaret (20 July) and St Mary (8 September?) fairs in Vöyri. Burghers of Vaasa were further granted the right to visit St Margaret fair of Vöyri in 1624. In the early 17th century local fair was also held at St Michael (29 September) in Lapua. Since 1643 the right to attend fairs in Vöyri and Isokyrö were held by burghers of both towns. in 1650 burghers of Nykarleby were further granted sole right to hold a local fair on St Nicolaus (6 December) in Vöyri. After continuous litigation, fairs in Vöyri and Isokyrö were granted free for all towns in 1682. Since the late medieval chapel church of Vöyri was dedicated to St Margaret and St Anna (15 December), and the medieval parish church of Isokyrö to St Laurentius, St Margaret fair in Vöyri and St Laurentius fair in Isokyrö may have been of early 16th century or earlier medieval origin.
South of Vaasa early fairs were organised in Lapväärtti (sw. Lapfjärd), where the town of Kristiinankaupunki (sw. Kristinestad) was founded in 1649 and for which two annual fairs at the elevation of Holy Cross (14 September) and Candlemas (2 February) were confirmed in 1650-51. In 1624 burghers of Vaasa applied rights for two annual fairs on St Olaf (29 July) and St Barbara (4 December) in Långö (Närpiö parish), and in 1643 for annual fair on St Jakob (25 July) in either Närpiö or Lapväärtti, but none of these appear to have succeeded. Lapväärtti is cited as chapel of Närpiö in 1594 and was established as independent parish in 1607. Since Närpiö church was in 1398 dedicated to St Olaf and the Holy Cross, both the fairs in the area may date to the late 14th century. In 1680 a traditional fair in Närpiö was also held at Midsummer (24 June).

name: null
Harbour_Description: Due to the character of the now drained Rødby Fjord the town of Rødby could only be used by small vessels. Hence a harbour was established closer to the shore at Dragsminde, and later harbours were also found at Kramnitse a bit further north and at Syltholm south of Rødby. These three legal harbours competed with several illegal harbours on Lolland. Both legal and illegal harbour were focusing on foreing trade, especially with Hanseatic towns and merchants. In 1399, for example, ships from Lübeck sailed to Rødby, i.e. probably Dragsminde. In the 16th century the harbour at Dragsminde benefited from a monopoly on the export of oxen from islands of Zealand, Lolland and Falster. In the following 17th century, however, the maritime traffic from the harbour declined.

name: Wesenberg
Town_Description: Founded around 1250 by Lord Nikolaus of Werle-Güstrow without a former settlement. Founding privileges have not survived. The town is first mentioned in 1257. Schwerin town law endorsed in 1278 and 1300.

name: Bad Liebenwerda
Settlement_Description: In the 12th century a castle was built at a crossing of the Elster river, next to a probably Slavic settlement. A village, probably already a merchant settlement, developed around the same time. First mentioned in 1231.
Town_Description: Referred to as civitas in 1301. The town was fortified with a rampart and a ditch.
Toll_Description: Secondary station of safe conduct ('Nebengeleit') of Torgau in the system of safe conduct around Leipzig. Secondary stations of safe conduct existed in Wahrenbrück, Uebigau, Hohenleipisch, Dobra and Naundorf. It was the easternmost Ernestinian safe conduct. Annual revenues are known from 1464 onwards, and regulations and tariffs date from 1505.

name: null
Bridge_Description: A bridge across the Ilme between Einbeck and Salzderhelden is mentioned in 1463 and 1494.

name: Uusikaarlepyy
Settlement_Description: Permanent agricultural settlement in Nykarleby and Lapuanjoki river mouth area dates to the Swedish colonisation of the late 13th century and the beginning of the 14th. Nykarleby parish was established as an independent parish in 1607. <b>Inn:</b> Ture Pedersson Bielke, Swedish nobleman and castellan of St. Olaf's Castle in Savo, stopped in 1557 to change horses "by Lapua river". The place could be somewhere near the river mouth area, since there is one old Finnish mile (ca. 6 km) to the next waypoint, Soklot village.
Town_Description:
King Gustaf II Adolf ordained a town to be established in Leppo by in Lapuanjoki river mouth in 1617. The town of Nykarleby acquired privileges in 1620 when its trading area was specified to consist of Pedersöre, Nykarleby, Lapua and Vöyri (sw. Vörå) parishes, which had formerly made part of Vaasa’s trading area. Since 1617 towns in the Gulf of Bothnia area allowed to export their goods only to Stockholm and Turku. In 1636 the crown prohibited all foreign shipping to towns, harbours, or other places north of Turku and Stockholm, including Åland. The first plan of the town was made in the early 1620s, the two oldest surviving plans for enwidening the town area are from the years 1649 and 1651.
<b>Post office:</b> According to sources, the Uusikaarlepyy post office was likely established in 1642, as the court record from that time mentions the appointment of Klas Witting, a burgher, as the postmaster.
Fair_Description: The annual St Olaf summer fair (29 July) in Pedersöre was transferred to Nykarleby in 1624 and ordered to last for three days. The burghers of the town also continued to hold fairs in Pedersöre harbour area three times a year, two of which were in 1621 cited as St Peter (29 June) and St Laurentius (10 August). A traditional date for winter fair in the area may have been St Paul (25 January). The trading areas of Vaasa (1606) and Nykarleby (1620) towns hosted of old peasant fairs in three parishes of Lapua, Vöyri and Isokyrö, of which Nykarleby was in 1622 granted sole rights to Candelmas winter fair (2 February) in Lapua, and St Margaret (20 July) and St Mary (8 September?) summer and autumn fairs in Vöyri. In the early 17th century local fair was also held at St Michael (29 September) in Lapua. In the same year 1622 the sole right to St Henrik (20 January) and St Laurentius (10 August) fair in Isokyrö was granted to burghers of Vaasa, who also had the right to visit St Margaret fair of Vöyri since 1624. Since 1643 the right to attend fairs in Vöyri and Isokyrö were held by burghers of both towns. Burghers of Nykarleby were further granted sole right to hold a local fair on St Nicolaus (6 December) in Vöyri. After continuous litigation fairs in Vöyri and Isokyrö were granted free for all towns in 1682. Since the late medieval chapel church of Vöyri was dedicated to St Margaret and St Anna (15 December), and the medieval parish church of Isokyrö to St Laurentius, St Margaret fair in Vöyri and St Laurentius fair in Isokyrö may have been of early 16th century or earlier medieval origin.
Toll_Description: The 1/32 duty worth of all goods intended for sale in towns and fairs and brought to the site by peasants was collected in Nykarleby since 1622.

name: Pori
Settlement_Description: Permanent agricultural settlement in Kokemäenjoki rivermouth area dates to the Iron Age with additional layer of Swedish colonisation on the coast from the late 13th and early 14th centuries. The town of Pori was founded on the land of late medieval Pärnäinen (sw. Bärnäs) village.
Town_Description:
The town of Pori (sw. Björneborg) was established in 1558 by King Gustav I son Johan, who held Western Finland as a duchy in 1556–63. An important motive for the new site was postglacial land uplift, which hampered sailing to Ulvila, but also the lack of suitable site for fortification in Ulvila. King Erik XIV confirmed the privileges in 1564 and king Gustav II Adolf in 1627. The administrative centre of Kokemäenjoki river area was since 1558 Pori Royal manor, which was located outside the town area. The manor served as an administrative and economic node to the beginning of the 17th century, but its activities came to an end after the reorganisation of provincial administration in 1635 when the area was attached to the new Province of Turku and Pori. A short-lived Province of Pori existed in 1641–46. The oldest geographic survey of the town is from 1696, where the town area may reflect that purported in the lost town plan of ca. 1642.

Erik XIV barred export from Pori to foreign destinations in 1564. The trading area of the town consisted in the beginning of the 17th century Satakunta, where it competed in south with Rauma and in North-East inland with Turku. Burghers of Pori and Rauma held full export rights in foreign trade 1614–17, after that restricted rights to 1636 and right for foreign import to 1636. Together with Rauma and Uusikaupunki (sw. Nystad) Pori had special licence for exports to Germany in 1640. In 1636 the crown had prohibited all foreign shipping to towns, harbours, or other places north of Turku and Stockholm, which Pori had to follow until 1765.
<b>Post office:</b> Oluf Jönsson founded the Pori post office in 1644, and the office is mentioned in the postal tariff for the first time in 1645. The mail route from from Turku to Vaasa initially went through Kyrönkankaantie. The coastal road along the Gulf of Bothnia was established at a latter date. Since the offices at Pori and Rauma were initially mere secondary branch posts, mail could sit for a long time awaiting delivery.
Fair_Description: Pori was in 1602 and 1604 granted rights to three annual fairs, one of which took place in the town on apostle Bartolomeus (24 August) and is cited in almanacs in 1585 and 1598. The other two fairs took place in Pirkkala in Harju at Candlemas (2 February) and on St Laurentius (10.8.) in Ulvila (Nakkila) Lammainen (some 25 kms upstream from Pori and 20 kms downstream from Kokemäki). In 1616 burghers of Pori were together with Turku, Stockholm and Rauma granted free trade in Pedersöre and Saloinen annual fairs for two weeks after St Olof (28 July).
Toll_Description: The 1/32 duty worth of all goods intended for sale in towns and fairs and brought to the site by peasants was collected in Pori since 1622.

name: Traun
Toll_Description: Secondary station of safe conduct ('Beigeleit') of Triptis in the district ('Amt') Arnshaugk. Revenues are known for the years 1532-1541. In 1541 its role seems to have been taken over by Dreitzsch.

name: null
Bridge_Description: Bridge shown on the town's medieval seal, probably a reference to the bridge across the small river, Køge Å. The bridge is mentioned for the first time in 1439. The location of this medieval bridge is uncertain. Perhaps it was located at the same location as a new bridge was built in 1633, and where the present bridge is also found.

name: Pyhälahti
Settlement_Description: <b>Inn:</b> Eerola farm served as a local official (fi: nimismies, sw: länsman, eng. sheriff) and a tavern in Pyhälahti for a couple of years in the 1620s-30s.

name: Køge
Settlement_Description: Køge were first documented in a donation to Sorø Monastery by the powerful magnate Sune Ebbesens who died 1186. Presumably a permanent settlement at the end of the 13th century, but may be older.
Town_Description: Køge was founded on the marsh north of a small river, Køge å. It was a newly established settlement with a clear urban character when king Eric Menved (1286-1319) in 1288 granted Køge a town law. At the same time the king also granted the town-dwellers a tax-exemption for building on uninhabited parcels within the town. In the following period Køge developed rapidly. The town was soon surrounded by a rampart and a moat. A town court is documented in 1344, and during the 14th or 15th century a guild for Germans was established. The latter is evidence of Hanseatic interests not only in Køge but the whole region around the strait of Øresund. In 1454 a secular town scribe is mentioned for the first time, and a few years later, in 1461, a town hall also appears in the sources. In general Køge was a very dynamic town throughout the middle ages and early modern era. In many cases the town benefitted from royal support, as different Danish kings aimed to develop a rich and strong town on Zealand in the southern part of the region af Øresund. As many other towns or settlements along the coasts of Øresund, Køge benefited from the rich fishing in Øresund, in particular of herring. And as many other Danish towns, Køge suffered heavily during the Dano-Swedish wars 1657-1660.
Fair_Description: Køge was an important market town with at least one annual fair. The age, date and character of the fair is, however, unknown. An annual fair was probably held in the 14th century, if not earlier. In 1516 king Christian II (1513-1523) allowed only four annual fairs on the island of Zealand. A fair in Køge was one of these legal fairs. The effect of the king’s initiative is, however, uncertain, as other fairs at least in time continued to exist. In 1575 a fair previously held at the settlement of Snekkerup was moved to Køge. In the second part of the 17th century Køge still had two annual fairs.

name: Kristiinankaupunki
Settlement_Description: Permanent agricultural settlement in Närpes (fin. Närpiö) area dates to the Swedish colonisation of the late 13th century and the beginning of the 14th. Närpes is cited in 1331, and as an independent parish together with Mustasaari and Pedersöre in 1348, when their inhabitants were given right to trade with victuals between themselves. Lapväärtti is cited as a new colonisation in 1303. It was established as a chapel of Närpiö in 1594 and independent parish in 1607. A parish in Satakunta province since the early 14th century, Närpiö was placed under Korsholm and Ostrobothnia in 1595.
Town_Description: Governor-General Count Per Brahe the younger ordained a town to be established on Koppö peninsula in Lapväärtti in 1649. Two years later in 1651 he confirmed the first privileges of the foundation, where the new town was named Kristinestad (fin. Kristiinankaupunki) either after his wife Christina Stenbock or Queen Christina of Sweden. Three versions of the plan for the town area have survived from 1649–62, the earliest surviving geographical survey is from the year 1658. Towns in the Gulf of Bothnia were since 1617 allowed to export their goods to Stockholm and Turku only. In 1636 the crown prohibited all foreign shipping to towns, harbours, or other places north of Turku and Stockholm, including Åland.
Fair_Description: In 1650-51 two annual fairs were confirmed for Kristiinankaupunki; one at the elevation of Holy Cross (14 September) and the other at Candlemas (2 February). In 1624 burghers of Vaasa applied rights for two annual fairs on St Olaf (29 July) and St Barbara (4 December) in Långö (Närpiö parish), and in 1643 for annual fair on St Jakob (25 July) in either Närpiö or Lapväärtti, but none of these appear to have succeeded. Since Närpiö church was in 1398 dedicated to St Olaf and the Holy Cross, both the fairs in the area may date to the late 14th century.  In 1680 a traditional fair in Närpiö was also held at Midsummer (24 June).
Toll_Description: The 1/32 duty worth of all goods intended for sale in towns and fairs and brought to the site by peasants was collected in Kristiinankaupunki after its foundation.

name: Rauma
Settlement_Description: Permanent agricultural settlement in Rauma (r. Raumo) area goes back to the 13th century. The town of Rauma was founded on the farmland of three early villages. The first church on the site of the town church was built after 1410, stone church in 1495–1505. The church was attended both by the townspeople and the surrounding rural population who shared the same parish.
Town_Description:
The town of Rauma was founded by former regent Karl Knutsson (Bonde), who held western Finland as a fief, on 17 April 1442, when he granted the city's burghers the same privileges, rights and freedoms as the burghers of Turku. King Christopher of Bavaria confirmed the rights on 13 January 1444. Rauma was preceded by Unaja trading post and possible burgher community less than 10 km south of the town. Unaja is cited in 1413, when it paid the crown an annual tax of 50 marks. At the same time the tax for Ulvila was 20 and for Turku 600 marks. The city's privileges were further confirmed in 1461, 1476, 1527 and 1546. In 1550, King Gustav Vaasa ordered the burghers to move to the newly founded Helsinki, from which they received permission to return in 1557. Rauma made part of Gustav I son’s Johan's Duchy of Finland in 1556–63. The earliest town centre, market square, town hall and town church were located near the later Kalatori (Fish Market), from where the coastal road branched off to Turku and Ulvila. After the break in the 1550s, a new market square was established closer to that time harbour area. The Franciscan Friary and the Royal manor located on the north side of the Raumanjoki River were not part of the old city area. The Friary is first mentioned in 1449 and was abolished in 1538. Its stone church was built in 1515–20. The Rauma royal manor was established in 1556 in the convent buildings. The population of Rauma is estimated to have been around 1,000 before the move in the 1540s and around 630 after the burghers returned in the 1560s. The tax paid to the crown in the 1540s was around a third of the tax paid in Turku. The oldest surviving reliable geographic survey of Rauma is from the year 1756. The medieval and early modern town area has been defined by archeological surveys and source material.
Despite the opposition of Stockholm, Rauma burghers managed to maintain their right to direct merchant sailing to foreign destinations in the latter half 15th century as confirmed in the privileges of 1461 and 1476. Since 1502 the towns of Öregrund, Östhammar, Gävle, Ulvila and Rauma, located north of Stockholm, were only allowed to export their goods to Turku and Stockholm. The decree was renewed in 1504. The rights of Ulvila and Rauma were reaffirmed in the same form in 1512. Gustav Vasa restricted Ulvila's exports to Stockholm and Turku, banned Ulvila, Rauma and Turku from trading with countries other than Stockholm in 1531, but confirmed the rights again in 1533. The controversy over direct merchant sailing to foreign towns and cities continued throughout the 1540s. After the break, Rauma's rights to trade in the Gulf of Bothnia were confirmed in 1558, and privileges in 1594 and 1607. In 1616 burghers of Rauma were together with Turku, Stockholm and Pori granted free trade in Pedersöre and Saloinen annual fairs for two weeks after St Olof (28 July). After the introduction of the system of towns with staple rights (foreign export and import) in 1614, Rauma had full export rights in 1614–17, but then limited rights until 1636, and the right to imports from abroad until 1636. Together with Uusikaupunki and Pori, Rauma had a special permit for exports to Germany in 1640, after which Rauma's exports were only allowed to go to Stockholm and Turku.
<b>Post office:</b> Oluf Jönsson founded the Rauma post office in 1644, and the office is mentioned in the postal tariff for the first time in 1645. The mail route from from Turku to Vaasa initially went through Kyrönkankaantie. The coastal road along the Gulf of Bothnia was established at a latter date. Since the offices at Pori and Rauma were initially mere secondary branch posts, mail could sit for a long time awaiting delivery.
Fair_Description: The weekly market day in Rauma was confirmed as Saturday in 1616 and 1624, in 1640 together with Wednesday. Burghers of Rauma were confirmed in 1607 rights for two annual fairs in the town in 1607, one on Candlemas (2 February) and the other on Midsummer (24 June). Candlemas fair is mentioned in almanacs in 1585 and 1598. After the application of the burghers the dates were changed to the Conversion of ST Paul (25 January) and St Bartholomeus (24 August). Because ofthe many overlapping market days in the region, the burghers again requested a change in 1650 and 1660 after which the dates were 12 January and apostle Matteus (21 September).
Toll_Description: The 1/32 duty worth of all goods intended for sale in towns and fairs and brought to the site by peasants was collected in Rauma since 1622.

name: Husum
Settlement_Description: The bridge Husembro is first mentioned in 1252. After the "Mandränke" flood of 1362, a navigable connection with the sea was created, upon which the harbour settlement Husum developed in 1372; in 1398 divided into Oster- and Westerhusum.
Town_Description: In the 1430ies Husum had around 250 taxpayers. Market privileges were granted to the borough ('blek'/’flække’) Husum in 1465, and it acquired its own jurisdiction in 1472. Town privileges were granted in 1608. Throughout the late medieval period and early modern era Husum benefited from a lucrative trade, especially export of oxen from Denmark, with the Low Countries and Germany.
Fair_Description: Husum was an important market for oxen driven from Jutland. Markets are first attested in 1493 and took place each Thursday in May and April, with the main fairs taking place on the last Thursday in April and the first Thursday in May. In autumn, there was an oxen fair on St Simon and Jude. In 1607, two three-day cattle markets were granted in spring and autumn. Additionally, Heinrich Rantzau mentions two fairs on Trinity Sunday and St Matthew in his 1597 description of Schleswig and Holstein. These are also mentioned in an almanac from 1598, printed in Neudamm (Dębno).
Toll_Description: The exact age and character of the important royal transit toll at Husum is unknown. Toll registers are available for the years 1496-1497 and 1504-1506 (The National Archive/Rigsarkivet) and from 1553 (Landesarchiv Schleswig-Holstein).

name: Herzberg (Elster)
Settlement_Description: Probably originally a Slavic settlement. At the end of the 12th century the counts of Brehna built a castle, around which the settlement developed. First mentioned in 1238.
Fair_Description: According to the regulations of safe conduct for Dobra and Nauendorf from 1505, fees were levied on cattle during the fairs in Herzberg and Kirchhain.
Toll_Description: Secondary station of safe conduct ('Nebengeleit') of Wettin in the system of safe conduct around Leipzig.<br/>The regulations of safe conduct show that long-distance trade goods passed through here.

name: Buddemühlen
Settlement_Description: Originally a farmyard, became a manor in the late 15th century. First mentioned in 1482.

name: Katinala
Settlement_Description: <b>Inn:</b> Katinala had a parish constable (fi: nimismies, sw: länsman), who ran a tavern in his farm, Mäkelä, in the early 17th c.

name: Metsänkylä
Settlement_Description: <b>Inn:</b> Metsänkylä had a parish constable (fi: nimismies, sw: länsman), who ran a tavern in his house, for a couple of years in the 1620s-30s.

name: Roskilde
Settlement_Description: Established as a settlement with an urban character in the late 10th century.
Town_Description: The town was home to the diocese of Roskilde, also known as the diocese of Zealand. The diocese was founded around 1020, at a time when the newly founded settlement of Roskilde already had an urban character. Throughout the medieval period and into the early modern era, Roskilde was a religious centre of not only Zealand but the whole of Denmark. At the end of the 12th century, for example, there were at least ten churches within the town. The town also had several monasteries. Two of these were the Dominicans (established c. 1232) and the Franciscans (established c. 1237). In 1554 the bishopric was moved from Roskilde to Copenhagen. The many clerical institutions had a great influence on the town during the middle ages, when various bishops of Roskilde also were among the most powerful political agents of Denmark. The town lord, however, was the king of Denmark. And from an early stage the royal presence was also strong. King Swein Forkbeard (Danish: Svend Tveskæg) minted coins in Roskilde around 995, and royal minting was carried out in the town until the 14th century. A royal official (Danish: bryde) is encountered for the first time in 1145, and by the middle of the following 13th century the town had a town bailiff (Danish: byfoged). A municipal seal is known from 1250, and in 1268 king Eric Glipping (1259-1286) granted Roskilde a town law. Members of the town council (consules) as well as a town hall were mentioned for the first time in the 1270s and 1280s. At this time the town probably also had mayors, but this institution is not documented before 1349. According to a registration of royal taxes from the towns of Zealand and surrounding islands (Danish: “Købstadslisten”) in King Valdemar’s Cadastre from 1241, Roskilde was the wealthiest town on Zealand. Roskilde remained one of the political and economical centers of Zealand throughout the medieval period and into the early modern era, but during the late medieval period, however, it lost ground to other towns, such as Køge and in particular Copenhagen.
Fair_Description: Roskilde was an important market town on the island of Zealand, and several annual fairs were held in or near the town. However, the date, age and character of the fairs are uncertain. From the 13th century, and probably also before, Roskilde must have held at least one annual fair. In the 15th century, and probably also before, the most important fairs took place at Easter and on the feast of Saint Dionysius (October 1th). In 1516 king Christian II (1513-1523) allowed only four annual fairs on the island of Zealand. A fair in Roskilde was one of these legal fairs. The effect of the king’s initiative is, however, uncertain, as other fairs at least in time continued. In the second part of the 17th century Roskilde had three annual fairs.
Toll_Description: The age and character of the toll in Roskilde is not known. Presumably, a royal toll was collected already in the Viking Age, and most certainly also in the early medieval period. Different tolls are documented from the early 16th century onwards. One of these was a toll (sise) on imported German beer.

name: Lübeck
Settlement_Description: Downstream from today’s old town there was a Slavic settlement called Liubice (nowadays Alt Lübeck), where German merchants stayed. After the destruction of Liubice in 1138 the Bucu peninsula was settled, where a town was founded in 1143.
Town_Description: The town was founded by the Counts of Holstein in 1143, with the name of the Slavic settlement destroyed in 1138. After a failed relocation of the town after a fire in 1157, Duke Henry the Lion refounded the town with considerable privileges and made it the seat of a bishopric. In 1226 it became Free Imperial City. The town soon grew into one of the most important Hanseatic centres for long distance trade.
Toll_Description: According to the oldest toll regulations of the town from 1225, foreign merchants who wanted to trade in Lübeck had to pay a fare of 4 denarii each. Moreover, tolls were levied on the cargo of ships leaving the town, as well as for wagons, carts, cattle, pigs and sheep entering town at the town gates. Special regulations were made for Slavic people. In lists of town revenues from the 15th century, a "graventol" at the Holstentor and Mühlentor gates is mentioned as well, which was levied on the shipping on the Stecknitz canal ("graven"). Moreover, between 1492 and 1496, a "pound toll" for the suppression of piracy was levied on sea-going ships, of which extensive registers still exist.
Staple_Description: Lübeck's staple was defined by its role as transshipment point in the trade between the North and Baltic Sea, which allowed avoiding the long detour of circumventing the Danish peninsula. The Hanserecesse of 1417 and 1418 forbade the transport of grain through the Danish straits and outside of the Hanseatic towns. A prohibition for foreigners trading with each other is first attested in 1472. Hollanders were obliged to offer bacon, butter and oil from Scandinavia and wine for 4-7 days; the Treaty of Utrecht (1474) reduced the duration to three days on account of the perishable nature of the wares, with stockfish, herring, cod and seal blubber excepted. In the 16th century the east-west trade through the Sound increased, bypassing Lübeck. Negotiations with the Hollanders regarding this ended in 1532 to Lübeck’s disadvantage. The ordinance of 1607 codified the staple: trade among guests was forbidden, as well as the transit passage of commodities of Danish merchants (except for wine), and the same for copper, iron, pelts, oil, tar and other wares from Sweden and Finland; commdities from Russia (such as leather, tallow, wax and flax, among others) were exempted. After a legal decision arising from a dispute with Hamburg in 1625, Lübeck largely relaxed the compulsory sale of staple goods in the city. Renewed attempts at imposing the staple in the 18th century led once again to conflict, until the council implicitly let it fall into abeyance after 1728.

name: Rövershagen
Settlement_Description: First mentioned in 1305, but the village must have been older. The settlement was probably founded by the Rostock patrician family Röver. In 1305 two inns were founded by Rostock: one in the village itself, and one at the road to Ribnitz.

name: Bad Sülze
Settlement_Description: The settlement developed near the salt springs that were first mentioned in 1229, although most likely older than that. The settlement itself was first mentioned in 1243.
Town_Description: Founded with Lübeck town law by the lords of Rostock, likely with the support of Rostock merchants. Councillors are mentioned in 1262, the settlement is characterised as civitas in 1287. In 1298 the regional law court was moved from Marlow to Sülze.

name: Trzcińsko-Zdrój
Town_Description: Probably founded as a German town by the Margrave of Brandenburg before 1266. First mentioned as town ('civitas') in 1281.
Fair_Description: The town received the right to hold a fair on Sunday before St Simon and Jude in 1364, and a second fair on Monday after Judica in 1483. In 1541 two cattle fairs were granted on Saturday and Monday after St Lawrence.
Toll_Description: The right to levy a dam toll was granted in 1403. In 1483 a transit toll was granted from all wagons driving through town. In 1507 the Elector granted the right to levy a toll on horses that drew the wagons. Market tolls were also owned by the town.

name: Landkrug
Settlement_Description: In 1305 Rostock founded an inn at the road to Ribnitz near Rövershagen.

name: Kraak
Settlement_Description: First mentioned in 1275. In the beginning of the 14th century at the latest a commandery of the Knights Hospitaller was moved to Kraak.

name: null
Bridge_Description: The bridge at the village of Gevninge was first mentioned in 1574 because reparations were needed. The age of the bridge is unknown.

name: Undermalm
Settlement_Description: <b>Inn:</b> Undermalm is mentioned in Jaakko Teitti's list in 1556 as a possible place for a bailiff (fi. vouti, sw. fogde). Another possible place in Tenhola parish was Olsböle.

name: Kirchhain (Doberlug)
Settlement_Description: The German village was first mentioned in 1234 and was probably founded as market place by the monastery Dobrilugk. Characterised as oppidum in 1367.
Town_Description: Town privileges were not officially granted. Kirchhain is mentioned as town in 1473 and 1491. In 1582, the governor ('Landvogt') of Lower Lusatia declared, that Kirchhain was to enjoy the same privileges as other royal towns.
Fair_Description: According to the regulations of safe conduct for Dobra and Nauendorf from 1505, fees were levied on cattle during the fairs in Herzberg and Kirchhain.

name: Holbæk
