Settlement_Description: Holbæk was in 1198 an estate owned by the bishop Absalon of Roskilde, who donated the property to the Cistercian Monastery of Sorø. The settlement developed in the bottom of Isefjorden, a deeply branched arm of the sea into Zealand, at an obvious place for trading activity.
Town_Description: It is not possible to properly date the town’s age from written sources, but the town layout is similar to other urban settlements from the late 12th century or early 13th century. Also the original Saint Nicholas Church is probably from the late part of the 12th century. A registration of towns on Zealand and the surrounding island (Danish: “Købstadslisten”) from 1241 in King Valdemar’s Cadastre defined Holbæk as a town. In 1256 citizens (civis) and town council were mentioned for the first time, and in 1286 Holbæk was probably granted a town law by king Eric 6. Menved (1286-1319). Dominican monastery founded in 1275. In 1575 the town did not have a town hall, and therefore the king allowed a section of the newly dissolved monastery to be used as such. In the middle of the 13th century a royal castle was built in Holbæk, and it remained an important royal castle throughout the middle ages. During the Dano-Swedish wars in the late 1650ties a Swedish army demolished the castle and occupied the town.
Fair_Description: Up until the early 17th century Holbæk apparently only held one annual fair, which probably took place during Lent. The character and date of this fair is uncertain, but from 1650 the fair took place every Wednesday during Lent. In the 17th century, however, the town held at least two annual fairs. In 1609 Holbæk was granted a fair on the feast of Saint Gall (October 16th), and another annual fair was held a month earlier (September 16th). Both fairs may very well be older. All the fairs appear to have had a local character.

name: Malmö
Settlement_Description: In the early 13th century a seasonal herring market at the beach every autumn. A permanent settlement with an urban character began to develop west of the seasonal market.
Town_Description: Archaeological evidence of the development of an urban settlement during the 13th century. Around 1300 the previously market area to the east was covered by permanent structures. At this time Malmö was defined as a town. Throughout the late medieval period Malmö benefited from its central location in the region around the narrow strait of Øresund and the rich fishing of herring in Øresund. Around 1300 construction of the town's enormous parish church began, and in 1419 a Franciscan monastery was founded. Town privileges and a town council are documented from the 14th century onwards. Two town books from the 15th and 16th centuries have been preserved. Malmö belonged to the king of Denmark, and king Eric the Pommerian (1396-1439) built the castle of Malmöhus. The strong royal castle was rebuilt several times during the following centuries. The castle functioned as a royal residence and home to the royal steward. Malmö was also protected by a palisade and later a town wall. In the 1440ties Malmö became the most important royal mint place, and in the following period the town developed into the largest town in the Danish kingdom. Throughout the middle ages Malmö had strong connections to towns in northern Germany, in particular Stralsund. A German guild is documented from around 1330. The town of Malmö also played a central role in the process leading up to the Danish Reformation in 1536. When Scania was handed over to Sweden after the Dano-Swedish wars in the 1650ties Malmö stagnated up until the 19th century.
Fair_Description: In the 14th century the market activities in Malmö grew in importance, and the town developed into one of the most important of the international markets in Scania. Like the other annual fairs in Scania the fishing market in Malmö probably took place from August 15th to October 9th. As other Scania fairs, the one in Malmö lost its importance during the 16th century. The town also held another annual fair, which apparently took place during spring. This fair appears to have been a cattle market, and was first mentioned in 1360.

name: Glanerbrug
Bridge_Description: Bridge ('Glanerbrug') crossing the brook Glaner Beek, which formed the border between Westfalia and Overijssel. The bridge is first mentioned in 1665, but must have existed before. A settlement only developed in modern times.

name: Meldorf
Settlement_Description: First mentioned by Adam of Bremen in the late 11th century as location of the mother church of Dithmarschen in ca. 814-824.
Town_Description: Town privileges probably granted by the archbishop of Bremen between 1227 and 1259; in 1265 the settlement is first characterised as town. Town privileges were repealed in 1559 after the conquest of Dithmarschen.
Fair_Description: In 1336 a fair is founded on the Nativity of Mary. Heinrich Rantzau mentions a fair on Sunday Judica in his 1597 description of Schleswig and Holstein. The fair is also mentioned in an almanac printed in Neudamm (Dębno) in 1598.

name: Mierola
Settlement_Description: <b>Inn:</b> Mierola had a parish constable (fi: nimismies, sw: länsman), who ran a tavern in his farm, Mattila, for a couple of years in the 1620s-30s.

name: Koivunporras
Settlement_Description: <b>Inn:</b> Count Per Brahe travelled from Häme region to Turku in 1639-1640 and stayed in Koivunporras tavern by the winter road.

name: null
Ferry_Description: The ferry between Copenhagen and Amager was first mentioned in the early 16th century, but is most likely much older. It fell out of use when the bridge was built between Copenhagen and the newly founded Christianshavn in 1620.

name: Westerkappeln
Settlement_Description: First mentioned as Capellun in the 11th century. The addition "Wester" was added to discern the parish village from the settlement Ostercappeln east of Osnabrück.

name: Kevola
Settlement_Description: <b>Inn:</b> Kevola farm served as a parish constable (fi: nimismies, sw: länsman) and a tavern for a couple of years in the turn of the 16th and 17th c.

name: Ribe
Settlement_Description: Around AD 700 Ribe was a permanent settlement with an urban character. The settlement was located close to the outlet of a river, Ribe Å, and at a relatively easy place to cross the river.
Town_Description: From the 8th century Ribe was among the so-called emporia of northwestern Europe. The site was integrated in long distance trading networks, and stood under the production of the king of the Danes. Around 855 the missionary and bishop of Hamburg, Ansgar, built a church in Ribe, and from the 10th century Ribe was a diocese. This made the town the ecclesial centre of southwestern Jutland during the medieval period and early modern era, and several clerical institutions were founded. A Dominican monastery was established in 1228, and the Franciscans arrived in 1232. Various kings of Denmark also had great interests in Ribe, and the important town was frequently visited by the king. A royal castle was established at the crossing of the river, Ribe Å, in the 12th century, and relocated to the western part of the town in the middle of the 13th century. The citizens were granted their first royal privileges in 1202-1214. A town council is known from c. 1250, and the oldest town law is from 1269. Throughout the viking age and medieval period Ribe was counted among the most important Danish towns, especially concerning long distance trade. Although the town stagnated in the later middle ages, Ribe continued to be one of the most significant towns in Denmark. The town was, for example, an important centre in the export of oxen from Jutland.
Fair_Description: From the Viking age onwards Ribe was a very important market town. During the medieval period the town hosted several annual fairs, and became central to the export of horses and in particular oxen from western Denmark. The fairs of Ribe had either a regional or international character, and were among the most important in Denmark. By the middle of the 17th century the town only had two aanual fairs: one during summer and Our Lady Fair.
Toll_Description: The age of the first toll is unknown. But already during the Viking age the kings of Denmark must have collected some kind of toll in Ribe. In the medieval period Ribe was one of the most important royal tolls. In the late medieval period and early modern era the toll on oxen was an important royal income: around 6000 daler annually in the 1550ties. Toll registers from the early 16th century have been preserved in the court accounts of widow queen Christine, who then was granted the right to the toll (The National Archive/Rigsarkivet). As Ribe played a central role in the Danish export of oxen from the 15th century onwards, the toll on oxen was the most important. At the time of widow queen Christine in the early 16th century the toll was set at 2 shilling  Some of the known medieval and early modern tolls from Ribe are: 1) The first time a toll is documented in the written material is from shortly before 1230, when a royal toll on the export of horses was introduced. 2) In 1283 king Eric Glipping (1259-1286) introduced a toll on the export of herring and different agricultural products such as grain and horses. 3) As Ribe played a central role in the Danish export of oxen from the 15th century onwards, the toll on oxen was the most important in the late medieval period as well as the early modern era. In the early 16th century the toll was set at 2 shillings (Danish: skilling) per animal.
Staple_Description: Stable rights were granted by king Christian I (1448-1481) in 1475, who ordered that oxen were only allowed to be transported to Ribe as well as a few other towns (Assens, Kolding and the annual fairs in Skanør and Falsterbo). The stable rights to Ribe were emphasized a couple of times by king Christian II (1513-1523). In the middle of the 16th century Ribe lost its stable privilege.

name: Skive
Settlement_Description: Probably founded in the later part of the 12th century. Presumably in the beginning of the 13th century a royal castle, Skivehus, was built near a ford or perhaps even a bridge across a river, Karup Å, close to the river’s mount into Limfjorden.
Town_Description: Royal income from Skive and the castle of Skivehus, which was a royal castle from the 13th century until 1661, is registered in the so-called main piece of King Valdemars Cadastre from 1231. In 1326 previously granted town privileges were confirmed by king Valdemar III (1326-1330). A royal steward (Danish: Høvedsmand) is mentioned in 1328, and in 1468 a town court (Danish: byting). The town hall was described in 1685 as a very frail building, and also shown on a map in Resen’s Atlas Danicus from 1677. Both in the middle ages and the following period Skive benefited from the rich herring fishing in Limfjorden.
Fair_Description: Presumably, three annual fairs were held in Skive. The date, age and character of the fairs are unknown. Probably, they all had a local character. In the second half of the 17th century Skive only had one fair.

name: Landskrona
Settlement_Description: Originally a small fishing village named Södra Säby up until around 1400
Town_Description: Around 1400 king Eric of Pomerania (1396-1439) bought the village of Södra Säby and founded the town of Landskrona. The town was established near the coast of Øresund at a good natural harbour. A town council was first mentioned in 1405, and the oldest town privileges were granted by king Eric in 1413. Landskrona experienced a very dynamic growth during the 15th century, especially due to the newly founded town’s role in the fishing of herring in Øresund and the annual Scania fairs. An enormous church was built in the 15th century, when a Carmelite monastery was also established. The church was the biggest parish church in Denmark, but it was demolished in the middle of the 18th century. A royal citadel was built in the middle of the 16th century. After Scania was handed over to Sweden after the Dano-Swedish wars of the 17th century the citadel was rebuilt and expanded.
Fair_Description: In the 15th century the market activities in Landskrona grew in importance, and the town became one among the international markets in Scania. Like the other annual fairs in Scania the fishing market in Landskrona probably took place from August 15th to October 9th, and as the other Scania fairs, the one in Landskrona lost its importance during the 16th century.

name: Laage
Settlement_Description: In Slavic times a fortification. The settlement was first mentioned in 1216, its name refers to a bridge. A priest is mentioned in 1253, citizens in 1270. It was the seat of a small German bailiwick that was first mentioned in 1297.
Town_Description: First mentioned as oppidum in 1309, as civitas in 1336. The privileges were endorsed in 1441.
Fair_Description: A (horse) fair on Sunday after St John's day was privileged in 1549.

name: Tessin
Settlement_Description: A castle existed in Slavic times as centre of the land of Tessin, first mentioned in 1253. A bailiwick is mentioned in 1333.
Town_Description: A town was not founded before the settlement came to Mecklenburg in 1323. First mentioned as town in 1325, as oppidum in 1343. Schwerin law is attested from 1364, but no charters with priviliges remain. The town was usually characterised as civitas.
Fair_Description: The town council founded a new market on Saturday before St John's day in 1575. It might originally go back to the dedication day of St John's church in 1350 and was continued until 1845. Two fairs were confirmed by the duke in 1615.

name: null
Harbour_Description: A harbour for river vessels next to the Augustinian monastery is first mentioned in 1457, when a loading station for black coal from certain mines was installed here.

name: Demmin
Settlement_Description: Slavic fortification of the 10th century, mentioned in the chronicle of Adam of Bremen around 1075 as "very large town".
Town_Description: A town was founded around 1236 by Duke Wartislaw III of Pomerania. The Lübeck town law was ratified in 1292 and 1681.
Fair_Description: A fair on Sunday Invocavit in Demmin is mentioned in an almanac printed in Neudamm (Dębno) in 1598.
Toll_Description: In 1286 the town Malchin received a reduction of toll tariffs for the toll in Anklam and other tolls in Pomerania, which should not be higher than the toll in Demmin. In 1326 the town Altentreptow received excemption from the tolls in Anklam and Demmin from Duke Otto I of Pomerania.

name: Nykøbing Falster
Settlement_Description: Established around 1200, when a royal castle was built. Located at the most narrow part of the strait of Guldborgsund, which separates the island of Falster from the island of Lolland.
Town_Description: Nykøbing Falster is listed as a town in King Valdemar’s Cadastre in a text within the manuscript originally written around 1240. In 1255 the royal castle, which lay in the northern end of the town, was mentioned for the first time. According to Annales Lundenses Nykøbing Falster was attacked and burned by a Norwegian fleet in 1289. Town privileges were confirmed in 1451, and a document from 1488 declares that Nykøbing Falster was granted town rights by king Eric 6. Menved (1286-1319). In this period, in the year 1315, Nykøbing Falster was also characterized as a town. The oldest known town seal, a town hall and a town council are also first mentioned in the 14th century. Franciscan monastery established in 1419. Throughout the medieval and early-modern era Nykøbing Falster benefited from the rich agriculture on the island of Falster and fishing in Guldborgsund and surrounding waters. The town, however, as other towns on Lolland and Falster almost constantly struggled with the local peasantry’s unregulated trade with Hanseatic towns and merchants. The royal castle in Nykøbing was very important to the town as well as the crown. Several political events of a significant nature took place at the castle, for example a peace agreement between king Hans of Denmark and the Hanseatic League in 1507. The castle was the dowry or life estate of several queens of Denmark, for example queen Sophie who organized a modernization of the medieval castle in the late 16th century.

name: Rørvig Havn
Ferry_Description: The exact age and character of the ferry between Rørvig and the settlement of Hundested on the peninsula of Halsnæs is uncertain. It is, however, older than 1553, when it was mentioned for the first time.

name: Store Bro
Bridge_Description: In 1590 a bridge across a narrow part of the outlet of Stege Nor was mentioned for the first time. It probably replaced the ferry in the 16th century.
Ferry_Description: A ferry across the narrow outlet of Stege Nor is documented in 1551, but is with no doubt much older, probably from the 13th century.

name: Fuglse
Settlement_Description: The village of Fuglse was first mentioned in 1264, but is significantly older. The parish church is from either the 12th or 13th century.

name: Landskrone
Settlement_Description: The inn Landskrone in the dispersed hamlet ('bauernschaft') Schmedehausen was first mentioned by name in 1484, but probably already in 1317 negotiations took place in the establishment.

name: Halverde
Settlement_Description: First mentioned in the 11th century. The name of the settlement is derived from a ford.

name: Nykøbing Sjælland
Settlement_Description: Presumably a fishing village up until the 13th century. The settlement benefited from its protected location in the bottom of Nykøbing fjord in the northwestern corner of Isefjorden.
Town_Description: Nykøbing Sjælland was probably granted its first town privileges around 1250. The town’s name and original layout strongly indicates that it was established in the 13th century. The oldest preserved town privileges, however, are from 1443. During the 14th century Nykøbing was characterized as a town in several written sources. Townspeople first mentioned in 1413. The protected natural harbour and rich fishing in Isefjorden attracted German merchants.
Fair_Description: Whether Nykøbing Sjælland had any fairs in the middle ages is not known. During the early modern era, however, the town was granted the right to at least two annual fairs. The character and age of the fairs is uncertain, but all the fairs probably had a local character.

name: Plötzky
Settlement_Description: First mentioned in 1160 as the residence of an Ascanian ministerial family. Between 1220 and 1230 a Cistercian convent was founded. It was dissoluted in 1538.

name: null
Bridge_Description: A small bridge across the stream that flowed out of the mill pond of Pforta monastery near Altenburg is mentioned in the regulations of safe conduct of Eckartsberga from 1550. It served as the border of safe conduct between Naumburg and Eckartsberga/Auerstedt.

name: Stege
Settlement_Description: Presumably a fishing village in the 12th century.
Town_Description: The so-called main piece in King Valdemar’s Cadastre from c. 1231 registered Stege as royal property. According to another list in the same manuscript from 1241, a registration of towns of Zealand and surrounding islands (Danish: “Købstadslisten”), Stege was counted among the towns of Zealand. Thus, Stege was probably granted town privileges by king Valdemar II the Victorious (1202-1241), something which is probably also documented in a confirmation of the town’s privileges granted by the king Eric Glipping (1259-1286) from 1268. The document from 1268 is the first time citizens (“uillanis nostris”) are mentioned. During the 13th century the royal castle of Stegeborg was built, and in the 15th century the town of Stege was fortified with a surrounding moat and rampart as well as three town gates. One of the town gates (Mølleporten) has survived. During the later middle ages Stege played an important role in the rich fishing and export of herring from the regions around the strait of Øresund. The medieval town book of Stege, which was begun in 1418, has been preserved.
Fair_Description: Stege probably had at least one annual fair during the late medieval period. A fair is documented from the early 16th century. The date, age and character of the fair are unknown.

name: IJsselstein
Settlement_Description: IJsselstein is first mentioned in 1279. A chapter in the church is found in the years 1396-1577. A hospital is first mentioned in 1352.
Town_Description: IJsselstein developed several city-like features in the period 1279 - 1363. It was officially granted town rights on 23 June 1363 by Guyote van IJsselstein.
Fair_Description: In 1310 (Nov.) the bishop of Utrecht granted three fairs with safe-conduct: 1) first Thursday in Lent, 2) June 12 and 3) October 21, each for 8 days.In 1524 Floris van Egmond, lord of IJsselstein, granted a weekly market.In 1581 (Nov. 25) prince William of Orange as father and administrator of Philip Willem of Nassau, count of Buren granted two horse-fairs, each for 14 days. 1) Wednesday after the Sunday Midlent (called: the day of the rose) en 2) August 1.
Staple_Description: The lord of the seigniory IJsselstein stated in an undated decree (circa 1425-1451) that all goods in the Land of IJsselstein had to be brought in the weigh-house in IJsselstein. All corn had te be milled in the mill in IJsselstein. And all hemp had to be traded at the market there and not on those in Oudewater or Schoonhoven. In 1524 (March 6) the lord of IJsselstein granted a free weekly market on wednesday but ordained that all inhabitants of the town ('poorters') and those of the seignioriy had to bring all there goods first on this market.

name: Schale
Settlement_Description: First mentioned in the 9th or 10th century. A monastery was founded in 1278.

name: Liinmaan linna (Vreghdenborch)
Settlement_Description: <b>Liinmaa Castle (Vreghdenborch): </b> The Liinmaa castle mound on a former islet between the mouths of the Eura and Lapland rivers, has been linked in research to the Vreghdenborch castle mentioned at the end of the 14th century. Based on excavations, the activity on the mound dates to the end of the 14th century and the beginning of the 15th century. Vreghdenborch is only mentioned in sources in 1395, when Jakob Abrahamsson (Djäkn) who had since 1387 controlled the former fiefs of the seneschal and magnate Bo Jonsson (Grip) in western Finland and Uusimaa, handed it over together with the castles of Turku, Kastelholm, Wartholm and Aborch to Bo's son Knut Bosson and Bo’s widow Margareta Dume. In 1387, King Albrecht of Mecklenburg had granted Jakob the right to build fortifications and tower castles in the area under his control. The castle's fortifications were demolished at the beginning of the 15th century, when Knut had agreed with Queen Margareta in 1398 to hand over Turku Castle and his wooden castles in Finland by Easter 1399. The German name Vreghdenborch is either derived from the Middle High German word Frechte, an enclosure, or some form of the Middle Low German word Vrede (peace, security, protection). The name may go back to the former Mecklenburg privateer groups, the Victual Brothers (ger. Vitalienbrüder), who sojourned in the castles under the control of Knut Bosson and the Mecklenburgians in Finland and the Gulf of Bothnia area in 1395-1401.

name: null
Toll_Description: In 1454 known as an outpost of the toll of the count of Holland at Geervliet. Starting 1559 the estates of Holland situated in Rotterdam a toll-station for peat exported from the region Schieland outside Holland. Accounts from this toll are preserved for the years 1561-73 and for 1561/2 for the peat sold inside Holland south of the Meuse.
Harbour_Description: Wooden harbour heads were made in 1467. The Informacie dated 1514 said that these had to be repaired and names 13 buizen (herringboats) owned by inhabitants and another 50 most from Waterland skippers. The harbour needed deepening and protection which would cost 6000 pounds. Outside the walls ships harboured in peace-time in the Blaak and the Nieuwehaven. In 1544 a harbourmaster was installed and in 1546 plans were made to enlarge the harbour but not yet excecuted.

name: Kleinromstedt
Settlement_Description: Romstedt is first mentioned in 876, Kleinromstedt as separate village first in 1282.
Toll_Description: There existed a secondary station of safe conduct of Weimar in Romstedt, for which revenues are attested since 1532.

name: null
Harbour_Description: Originally a well protected natural harbour. In the medieval period a wharf was built.

name: null
Toll_Description: A comital toll on sailing ships belonging to the count of Holland, probably the continuation of the toll at Moordrecht, is first mentioned in 1325. The tollbooth situated at the entrance of the harbour is first mentioned in 1389. In the 15th century, the toll was combined with the Spaarndam toll: those who had already paid toll in Spaarndam were exempted from the toll in Gouda and the other way around. Toll tariffs for the German Hansa are preserved and edited for the years 1446, 1454 and 1455. A general tariff dates 1518. An incomplete toll account combined with the toll in Spaarndam is edited and is dated 1497-1500. Not edited are accounts for the years 1541-1544. Revenues are analysed for the years 1389-1433 and 1446-1600. Starting 1559 the Estates of Holland situated in Gouda a toll-station for peat exported from the region Rijnland outside Holland. Accounts of this toll are preserved for the years 1562/3, 1568-72 and for the peat sold in Holland south of the river Hollandse IJssel dated 1561/2.
Harbour_Description: At the waterfront at the Hollandse IJssel transshipment took place if ships were too big for the lock in the town.

name: Dömitz
Settlement_Description: Originally a Slavic castle and settlement, known from the end of the 12th century. A priest is first mentioned in Dömitz in 1230.
Town_Description: Dömitz is first characterised as civitas in 1259. The Lübeck town law was granted by the dukes of Dannenberg and confirmed in 1505. The town was reconstructed as a fortress in 1559-65.
Fair_Description: Dömitz acquired the right to hold three fairs and a weekly market in 1546. It might have been a confirmation of an older privilege.
Toll_Description: A toll in Dömitz is first mentioned in 1237. A toll on the Elbe of the dukes of Lüneburg in Dömitz and nearby Wehningen is clearly mentioned in 1372, when they were transferred to the duke of Mecklenburg. The river toll was specified at 4 Gulden, 1 rye bread, 1 loaf of bread and 2 buns for each passing ship in 1492. Toll registers exist for many years from 1431 onwards; these have been analysed by Nissen. A road toll was levied as well, as becomes clear from a report from 1688, in which it is stated that the road toll was levied at the mill Findenwirunshier when the road to Dömitz was flooded, which happened regularly.

name: Gronau (Westfalen)
Settlement_Description: The castle Bocholte at the bridge across the Dinkel near Spechtholte was first mentioned 1365. The name Gronau for the accompanying settlement first appears in 1371. It developed into a town-like settlement or borough ('wibbolde'), as it is first attested in 1487.
Toll_Description: The toll of Billerbeck was moved to Gronau at the beginning of the 16th century.

name: Enschede
Settlement_Description: Earliest mention in 1118 (in a thirteenth century copy, possibly a falsification).
Town_Description: Town privileges were granted by Jan III of Diest, bishop of Utrecht, on 15 December 1325.
Fair_Description: Bishop Philip of Utrecht granted Enschede two fairs after a fire in 1517, on Thursday after Easter and on the first working day after St Martin. Possibly this was a confirmation of older privileges.

name: null
Toll_Description:
Starting 1559 the Estates of Holland situated in Geertruidenberg a toll-station for peat exported from the regio called Langstraat outside Holland.
See also sub 2126
Harbour_Description: Geertruidenberg was a flourishing harbour town until a dam was built in the Maas near Heusden in 1271. However, a crane is mentioned in 1275 and 1355. After the flood of St Elisabeth in 1421, Geertruidenberg regained direct access to the Rhine and Meuse delta.

name: Losser
Settlement_Description: First mentioned in the late 10th century.

name: Bevergern
Settlement_Description: First mentioned around 1366 and located near a castle probably built around 1350.
Town_Description: Town privileges granted in 1366 by the dukes of Tecklenburg. Around 1400 it was called a town. The privileges were renewed in 1471.

name: Neuenkirchen (Münsterland)
Settlement_Description: First mentioned in 1022-1032, the settlement was originally called Snetwinkele or Suetwinkele. The name Neuenkirchen ('new church') first appears in 1269 and gradually replaced the old name of the village.

name: Karsdorf
Settlement_Description: The settlement came into being at a convenient Unstrut crossing and settlement can be attested since the Neolithic. First mentioned in 1109. Several monasteries earned property in Karsdorf in the Middle Ages.
Toll_Description: A bridge escort fee was collected in Karsdorf in 1573. In regulations of safe conduct from 1621 Karsdorf is mentioned as secondary station of safe conduct of Freyburg.

name: Laucha (Unstrut)
Town_Description: Before 1344 Laucha became a borough ('flecken') with market rights. It is mentioned as 'oppidum' in 1395. Town rights were granted in 1409 by margrave Friedrich of Meißen.
Fair_Description: Margrave Friedrich of Meißen granted two fairs in 1409, on Sunday after St Bartholomew and Sunday after Corpus Christi. In 1540 the dates were changed to Monday after Laetare and Friday before St Martin.

name: Jena
Settlement_Description: First mentioned in the tithe register of Hersfeld monastery from c. 830-850. The settlement benefitted from an advantageous position at a Saale river crossing.
Town_Description: Town rights were probably granted around 1230 by the lords of Lobdeburg. Citizens are attested in 1236. Gotha town rights were granted around 1332. Elector Johann Friedrich founded a university in the former Dominican monastery in 1548.
Fair_Description: Fairs in Jena are already mentioned in the 13th century. In 1354 there were three fairs, but their dates can only be inferred indirectly. One probably took place on Sunday Cantate, the second between 22 October and 3 November (possibly on St Simon and Jude), the third remains unknown. A cattle fair was granted on 20 June 1486, once again with unknown date, and a fair on St Giles on 10 December 1492. Weekly markets are first mentioned in 1406.
Toll_Description: A toll of the lords of Lobdeburg is first mentioned in 1316. The mint, toll and safe conduct rights were acquired by the town in 1352. The toll had to be paid by wagons and carts, for the maintenance of the roads around Jena. Furthermore, there existed toll for timber floated on the river, from which we only know the fees.

name: Rippach
Settlement_Description: The settlement is first mentioned in 1125-1147. It is named after the stream Rippach, which is first mentioned in 976.

name: Eckartsberga
Settlement_Description: A castle was erected on the Sachsenberg in 998, next to which a village (first mentioned as villa in 1074) developed into a borough ('Flecken') in the 12th and 13th century.
Town_Description: Probably between 1265 and 1292 Eckartsberga gained town rights, possibly in 1288 as reimbursment for resigning its church to the monastery of St. Moritz.
Fair_Description: Since 1431 two fairs are known on Ascension Day and St Giles. They are also mentioned in the regulations of safe conduct of 1550. They were moved to Easter and St Michael's day later.
Toll_Description: A safe conduct is known since 1291, which makes it one of the oldest stations of safe conduct on the Via Regia. Regulations of safe conduct from 1550 have survived.

name: Harras
Settlement_Description: Uncertain first mention in 1319. First certain mention in 1340.
Toll_Description: Toll station of the district Heldburg, from which the oldest account dates from 1546. Regulations of toll and safe conduct of Hildburghausen (which include Veilsdorf and Harras) remain from 1570.

name: Zeitz
Settlement_Description: First mention of Zeitz when a suffragan bishopric of the archdiocese of Magdeburg was founded here in 967. However, the settlement is probably older. The bishopric was moved to Naumburg in 1128/30.
Town_Description: Since 1147 the settlement is referred to as town. A town council constitution is first attested in 1322, which must have been older.
Fair_Description: A fair on the dedication day of the local church is first mentioned in 1252. At the end of the 15th century two fairs are granted, on Sunday Cantate in 1479 and on St Vitus in 1484. A third fair on Tuesday after St James was granted in 1593.

name: Schöneflieth
Settlement_Description: Castle, first mentioned in 1257 as byname of knight Dietrich von Schönebeck. The castle was destroyed around 1276 by the bishop of Münster, who acquired it in 1283. Dilapidated in the 17th and 18th century, the ruins were torn down in 1812.
Toll_Description: Bridge toll of the bishop and cathedral chapter of Münster, first mentioned in a toll tariff from the late 14th century (1399?). Permission of emperor Charles IV to raise the tariffs in 1521 led to protests from Münster. Attempts were also made to levy toll on ships and timber rafts on the Ems river from 1582 onwards. The toll was mainly levied on animals driven to the market of Greven.
Bridge_Description: A bridge across the Ems at Schöneflieth is first mentioned in bridge toll tariffs ('Bruggenghelt ton Schonenvlete') from the late 14th century (1399?). The bridge was often destroyed in the Thirty Years' War and by ice in the 17th century.
Ferry_Description: Before the bridge was constructed, a ferry must have operated here.

name: Stressenhausen
Toll_Description: Toll station of the district Heldburg, from which the oldest account dates from 1546.

name: Winzerla
Toll_Description: Secondary station of safe conduct of the district Jena-Burgau, as it is mentioned in an account from 1542.

name: Bad Kösen
Settlement_Description: The settlement developed from a Slavic settlement. It is first mentioned in 1040. Today's Kösen only became to a full town in the 1868. Before, the location at the Saale river was inhabited by a village called Wenzendorf, which later is deserted. In 1680 an inn is constructed in Kösen, which is owned by Pforte monastery. A farmyard named Cusne that was owned by Pforte monastery was located on the right bank of the Saale river and already existed before the monastery (before 1137).
Fair_Description: Kösen was an important handling station of rafted wood. It was traded on two wood markets every year and supplied Halle, Leipzig and Allstedt, among others.

name: Eckernförde
Settlement_Description: Developed from a fishing settlement on a sand bank. In the first few years mentioned in the context of the castle Ykaerneburg that belonged to "Godescalcus de Ekerenvorde", and "Nikolaus de Ekerenvorde". A royal castle according to the so-called main piece in King Valdemar’s Cadastre from 1231. The castle was located at a ford across the fjord to Windebyer Noor/Vindeby Nor and a part of the old fortification complex protecting the south border of Denmark, which also included Danevirke. A settlement with an urban character presumably developed in the shadow of the castle.
Town_Description: Systematically planned town of the 13th century, first mentioned as a town in 1302. King Christian III of Denmark confirmed the Schleswig town privileges in 1543.
Fair_Description: Heinrich Rantzau mentions a fair on St Michael's Day in his 1597 description of Schleswig and Holstein.

name: Roßla
Settlement_Description: First mentioned in 996. In 1341 the counts of Stolberg obtain the village.

name: Römhild
Settlement_Description: The settlement is first mentioned in 800.
Town_Description: Count Henry IV of Henneberg-Hartenberg founded the town between 1274 and 1317. In 1321 it is referred to as town.
Fair_Description: In 1498 Emperor Maximilian confirmed the already existing three fairs in Römhild, whose dates are moved from St Walpurga to the second day of Pentecost and St Burkhard's day, and from the second day of Pentecost to Monday after Letare. A weekly market was set on Monday. It is unknown how far back in time the original market right goes.

name: Tilleda
Settlement_Description: First mention in the register of property of Hersfeld monastery before 775/786. In 972 an Ottonian imperial palace is mentioned here. The palace was gradually abandoned after 1200. Later noble residences were located in the village in the valley under the palace.

name: Riestedt
Settlement_Description: In 777 Charlemagne donated the chapel in Riestedt to Hersfeld monastery. Also mentioned in the tithe register of the monastery (c. mid-9th century).

name: Thüsdorf
Settlement_Description: First mention in 1223. The settlement burned down in 1635 and was only rebuilt in 1652.

name: Pütte
Settlement_Description: The land and lake of Pütte is first mentioned in 1171, but the village itself only in 1287.

name: Schulpforte
Settlement_Description: In 1140 the Cistercian monastery that had been founded in Schmölln in 1137 was moved to this location and became known as the monastery Pforta. It was one of the richest monasteries in Central Germany. Abolished in 1540, a school was established on the former monastery grounds in 1543 by duke Moritz of Saxony, which exists to this day.

name: Helsinki
Settlement_Description: Permanent agricultural settlement in Vantaanjoki (sw. Vanda å) rivermouth area and Eastern Nyland (sw. Östra Nyland) coast dates to the Swedish colonisation in the latter half of the 13th century when new farms were founded amongst earlier 12th and 13th century area of usufruct and colonisation from inner Häme. The parish organisation of Eastern Nyland dates at the latest to the first quarter of the 14th century, in Porvoo (sw. Borgå) and Helsinga possibly already to the third quarter of the 14th century.
Town_Description: King Gustaf I founded Helsinki (sw. Helsingfors) at the mouth of Vantaanjoki (sw. Vanda å) river in 1550. In 1640 the town was relocated to its present site in Vironniemi. After the reorganisation of the provincial administration in 1634, Helsinki was the residence town of the Governor of Uusimaa and Häme province. The province was split temporarily in two in 1640-48. After regaining full staple rights for foreign export and import in 1628, Helsinki retained the staple rights also in the new location from 1640 to 1879, when the staple system was abolished. The area of the town is marked in a map from ca. 1645. The earliest geographical survey is from the years 1696/1707.
Fair_Description:
Burghers of Helsinki were in 1553 given rights to three annual fairs of which one was held in the town, and the two others in Pernaja and Pyhtää parishes. In older scholarship the fair in Helsinki was attributed to the feast of St Eusebia or Eusebius, but the misinterpretation is based on 19th century false reading of an 18th century source and the actual date of the 1553 fair is not known. When king Johan III in 1584 ordained the midsummer fair (24 June) at Sipoo (sw. Sibbo) to be relocated to Helsinki, he also confirmed a winter fair to be held in the town on 
Epiphany (6 January). In the 1650s the burghers applied the date of the winter fair to be changed first to Candlemas (2 February) and to Apostle Paul (25 January) in 1680. 

In 1584 king Johan III granted burghers of Porvoo and Helsinki joint rights for trading with peasants of the eastern half of Pernaja parish at the St Bartolomeus fair (24 August) in Pyhtää, whereas peasants from the western half of Pernaja were obliged to trade in Porvoo only. Previous traditional local fairs in Mustijoki (sw. Svartså) and Kulloonmäki (sw. Kullo) in Porvoo, Pikku Pernajanlahti (sw. Lillpernåviken) in Pernaja and elsewhere were prohibited. The king also relocated Sipoo Midsummer fair to Helsinki and confirmed a fair to be held on Michaelmas (29 September) in Espoo (sw. Esbå) Bobäck, where burghers of Helsinki were allowed to trade with peasants of the neighbouring province of Raasepori. Rights in Espoo were confirmed in 1594 when the date was cited as St Mary (8 September). Possibly an older local peasant fair, the Bobäck fair took place at the end of the Espoo bay alongside the Great Coastal Road. After relocation to Pikkala bridge on the same road in 1723, the fair was organised on Apostle Matteus (21 September). Burghers of Helsinki are also known to have held fair in Sipoo on St Mary (8 September) in the early 17th century.

After intense litigation throughout the last quarter of the 16th century Porvoo and Helsinki were in 1602 and in 1607 confirmed right to trade in the four annual fairs at Porvoo, Pernaja and Pyhtää. Burghers of Helsinki had free right to trade in confirmed fairs east of Porvoo and those of Porvoo west of Helsinki. Fair in Pyhtää took place in Vähä-Ahvenkoski and those in Pernaja at Koskenkylä (sw. Forsby) bridge on the Great Coastal Road, where they were held in 1708. In 1639 burghers of Helsinki were further granted the right to visit annual tar fair in Porvoo on 1 July. Already in 1614 Helsinki had seized the sole right to hold fair in Janakkala Turkhauta on 1 September, which were traditionally frequented by burghers from Porvoo. Since 1654 Turkhauta fair was organised on 14 September.
Toll_Description: The 1/32 duty worth of all goods intended for sale in towns and fairs and brought to the site by peasants was collected in Helsinki from the 1640s.

name: Stolberg
Settlement_Description: First mention of the settlement in 1210, even though it most probably existed before that. It must have been an important resting station on the way from Braunschweig to Erfurt through the Harz mountains.

name: Allstedt
Settlement_Description: First mentioned in a falsified charter from 777. Allstedt was a royal court and castle. A market settlement was founded between 1323 and 1330.
Town_Description: In 1425 Allstedt was granted town rights.

name: Anzefahr
Settlement_Description: First mentioned in 1226. Referred to as 'villa' in 1277.

name: Rudersdorf
Toll_Description: Secondary station of safe conduct ('Beigeleitsstelle') of Eckartsberga, as mentioned in the regulations of safe conduct from 1550.

name: Halikko
Settlement_Description: Permanent agricultural settlement in Halikko area goes back to the Iron Age. The medieval parish organisation in Finland Proper dates to the early 13th century with precursors in the latter half of the 12th century. First wooden church from early 13th century onwards, stone church (St. Bridget) was built between 1460 and 1475. Halikko central area has several large Viking Age and Crusading period burial fields around the church and South-West of the river in Rikalanmäki with a possible late Iron Age trading site. It is also cited as a one of the possible early destinations of the road from inland Häme to trading points in the coast of Southern Finland Proper. The Great Coastal Road crosses Halikonjoki river at Halikko Isosilta bridge some 400 meters South from the church.
Fair_Description: In Finland Proper several local peasant fairs existed in the 17th century, most of which consisted of trade with fish, grain, and other necessities amongst the population. Most of the fairs are apparently of medieval origin and took place on the feasts of local parish church such as the fair of St James in Paimio. Another of such fairs was since the late 15th century organised on the feast of St Bridget (10 October) at Halikko church from where it was some time in the early modern era relocated to Salo bridge where peasants from Uskela and Halikko parishes traded with burghers of Turku on St Bartholomeus (24 August) and apostle Matteus (21 September) in the 17th century.

name: Kloster Veilsdorf
Settlement_Description: First mention of the settlement Veilsdorf in 802-817. A Benedictine nunnery near the village is first mentioned in 1189, it was turned into a male convent in 1446. After the Peasants' War it was abolished and turned into the administrative seat of a region ('Amt').
Toll_Description: Toll station of the district Heldburg, from which the oldest account dates from 1546. Regulations of toll and safe conduct of Hildburghausen (which include Veilsdorf and Harras) remain from 1570.

name: Delfshaven
Settlement_Description: Delfshaven is first mentioned at the end of the fourteenth century. The settlement originated near the canal Delfshavense Schie from Delft to the river Meuse dug in 1389, meant to facilitate the transport of Delft's ale. By Royal Decree of 31 July 1825 (issued by William I of the Netherlands), it was decided that Delfshaven would be allowed to call itself a town.
Toll_Description: In 1454 ('Op die Nuwe Haven') known as an outpost of the toll of the count of Holland at Geervliet. Starting 1559 the Estates of Holland situated in Delfshaven a toll-station for peat exported from the region Delfland outside Holland.
Harbour_Description: In 1389 the Delftse Schievaart was dug towards the Meuse. The dike north of Schiedam was dug and at the end of a new canal towards the dike at the river Meuse a sluice was built. So Delfshaven became an outport of Delft. In 1451 permission of the landlord was granted to built a second harbour called the Achterhaven which doubled the surface. In 1492 the magistrate of Delft installed a market-boat ('beurtvaart') between the harbours of Delfshaven and Steenbergen. In the course of the 15th century this harbour was used by herringskippers from Waterland and from the coast of Zuidholland. It was also a place for hibernating ships. Likewise the relation between Arnemuiden and Middelburg, Delft was also scared for further growth of her outport. New buildings were prohibited here in 1537. Furthermore there were tensions between the beerskippers from Delft and the skippers from Waterland. A process was terminated in 1548 with a compromise and Delft had to consent in further improvements of the harbour. However some 30 skippers moved mid 16th century to the harbour of Rotterdam. Around 1600 some 75-100 'buizen' (herringboats) harboured here. At the mouth of the Nieuwe haven a new Buizenwaal was made.The numbers of hibernating ships for the years 1632-87 are edited.

name: Oberreißen
Toll_Description: A secondary station of safe conduct of Rudersdorf was installed in Oberreißen in 1585, for those circumventing the main road through Rudersdorf.

name: Tammerkoski
Settlement_Description: Tammerkoski village is first cited in 1405, but 11th century finds from the area hint to permanent settlement at the end of the Finnish Iron Age. At the time of the first tithing in the mind 13th century, the village had two large farmsteads who controlled the area on both sides of Tammerkoski stream. In 1540 the hamlet consisted of nine farms: five on the village plot west of the bridge and four scattered in the east. In the cadasters further three smaller farms further in the west are included to the hamlet. In 1466 the stream had at least three mills owned by large villages east of Tammerkoski, in 1585 nine. In 1637–60 the village was formed into a noble estate on the site of which the town of Tampere was established in 1778. <b>Inn:</b> Duke Johan of Finland stayed in Tammerkoski during his travel in 1556. From the 1530s to 1615 and 1618–22 the sessions of the parish court of Pirkkala parish were held at Vaininen farm, the owners of which served as parish constables and held the rights for an inn since 1585. In 1622–44 the parish constable and the inn were in Nalkala area, although Mauno Jokipii mentions Vaininen as the tavern in 1639-1640.
Fair_Description: The Harju annual fair in Pirkkala parish were transferred to Tammerkoski village in 1638 when the winter fair was ordained to be held for three days on St. Matthew (24 February) and the autumn fair for three days on St Bartholomew (24 August). The winter fair was changed to Epiphany (6 January) in 1639. Both fairs were relocated again in 1708 to Harju and in 1750 to Pispala where they were held until the founding of Tampere town in 1778. In Tammerkoski the site of the fair was alongside the common road in the former village plot west from the bridge. Burghers of Turku had the right to use 14 days before and after the fair for transporting their goods.
Toll_Description: The so called 1/32 duty of “small toll” (små tullen, pikkutulli) of all goods intended for sale in towns and fairs since 1622 was collected by officials temporarily transferred for the task form Rauma or another maritime town. The toll was located next to the bridge.

name: Auerstedt
Settlement_Description: First mentioned in 822-842. In the 13th century, the village was property of a family with the same name as the village and in the 14th century it became property of Pforta monastery.
Toll_Description: Secondary station of safe conduct ('Beigeleitsstelle') of Eckartsberga, as mentioned in a detailed list of fees from 1550. The safe conduct of Eckartsberga ended at the end of the village.

name: 's-Gravenzande
Settlement_Description: 's-Gravenzande is first mentioned in 1200. The settlement originated on a sandbank. The counts of Holland built a house there. A hospital is first mentioned in 1255.
Town_Description: 's-Gravenzande was granted town rights in May 1246 by Willem II, count of Holland, on the request of his widowed mother Mathilda ('Machteld') of Brabant. She also founded a beguinage in 's-Gravenzande (before 1255). 's-Gravenzande, however, did never really developed into a town.
Fair_Description: In 1317 fairs with Easter ('paesch Sand-market') and wit St. Victor (Oct. 10). Initial farmed as comital market-tolls together with the cloth-hall during the fairs, later (starting 1463) together with the 'straatgeld' (tax on the streets, probably money collected of market-stalls). In the comital account dated 1484/'5: combined fair- and a tax on the streets with: 1) Palm-Sunday, 2) Bamis (Oct. 1).

name: Zwartenbergs Veer
Ferry_Description: First mentioned in 1590. The ferry crossed the Mark river, to facilitate travel to and from Holland, and played a role during the Dutch Revolt. The ferry is displayed on a 1656 map of Brabant by C.J. Visscher.

name: Sangerhausen
Settlement_Description: A settlement probably already existed in the 6th or 7th century, in the 8th century develoment of a borough ('oppidum'), first mentioned in 780-802.
Town_Description: According to Niemeyer town privileges were granted in 1194. Referral to the settlement as "oppidum" in 1204. A town wall must have existed before the 1260s.
Toll_Description: Annual revenues of the safe conduct in Sangerhausen are known from 1482-1485. The fees are recorded in the regulations of safe conduct ('Geleitsordnung') from 1517.

name: Bergedorf
Settlement_Description: First mentioned in 1162 as a church town with the parish church of St Peter und Paul, but it already existed before as a parish of Hamburg. Bergedorf castle was first mentioned in 1212. It was acquired by Hamburg in 1420.
Town_Description: Town privileges were granted in 1275 by Duke John I of Saxony-Lauenburg after the Mölln-Lübeck model.
Toll_Description: A toll of the duke of Saxony-Lauenburg on timber floated down the Bille and transported on wagons through Bergedorf was agreed upon in a 1410 agreement between the duke and Hamburg. It is likely that this was a general toll on wagons, which came to Hamburg when it acquired Bergedorf castle in 1420.
Harbour_Description: After the Schleusenkanal was dug in 1443/45, Bergedorf acquired a navigable waterway via the Dove Elbe with Hamburg. The waterway mainly served the transport of wood from the surrounding forests.

name: Mahndorf (Halberstadt)
Settlement_Description: First mentioned in 1084, when the settlement consisted of two parts Beffen-Mandorp and Biscopa-Mandorp.

name: Milz
Settlement_Description: First mentioned in 784, when abbess Ermhilt donated her inherited property in a wide range of places to her monastery in the village Milz. In 799-800 the monastery became subjugated to the monastery in Fulda. The village enjoyed market rights, the beginnings of which are unknown.

name: Heppeneert
Toll_Description: A toll at 'Heppenert' is one of the six small tolls of Maastricht in 1357, when these were enfeoffed by the duke and duchess of Limburg to Thierri de Hornes, lord of Perwez. A toll in 'Heppenart' is also found in 1362. In 1396 the lord of Sittard and Born declared that the lord of Heinsberg should have the yields of the rivertolls in Buggenum, Linne and Heppenert.
Ferry_Description: A ferry-man ('naute') of 'Heppenart' is mentioned in the oldest account of the count of Gelre, dated 1294/5.

name: Zevenaar
Town_Description: Town privileges granted on 24 January 1487 by John II, duke of Cleves and count of Mark. Zevenaar is considered a minor town ('minderstad').
Fair_Description: In 1487 two fairs are mentioned, without dates, but with a duration of 2 days before until 6 days after. A weekly market took place on Thursday-Saturday.
Toll_Description: The oldest reference for a toll of the count of Cleves in Zevenaar dates from ca. 1355. In the town privileges from 1487, the Duke of Cleves donated revenues from the land and road toll in Zevenaar for the fortification of the town.
Staple_Description: With the city charter of 1487, the citizens of Zevenaar were given the right to force freight traffic and carts with 'provisions' that passed the Liemers to first offer their cargo on the market in Zevenaar. This served as compensation for the damage the roads and bridges suffered from the continuous flow of traffic.

name: Gützkow
Settlement_Description: Seat of the Slavic ruler Mitzlaw and site of a temple, which was demolished by missionary Otto of Bamberg in 1128 and a Christian church was founded.
Town_Description: A town was founded in the 13th century by the counts of Gützkow with Lübeck town rights.

name: Heinsberg
Toll_Description: The lord of Heinsberg levied a land toll in 1241. In addition to the land toll, safe conduct was also provided. In 1422 the toll rights were confirmed. Since 1483, the Lordship of Heinsberg was purchased by Jülich, with which the rights fell to the Duke of Jülich.

name: Weimar
Settlement_Description: First mentioned in 899. Residence of the lords of Weimar with a castle borough ('Burgflecken') in Carolingian times.
Town_Description: Foundation of the town around 1250 by the counts of Orlamünde. In 1254 first mention as civitas. In 1410 acquisition of town rights of Weißensee.
Fair_Description: In 1456 two three-day fairs on Pentecost and in the first half of October were confirmed, which meas that they had existed before. Three days before the fairs a cattle market took place. In 1729 a third fair was granted.
Toll_Description: Although Weimar is not considered to have been located on any major long-distance trade route, the accounts of safe conduct show that there was a considerable long-distance traffic through the town, bypassing Erfurt. The oldest account dates from 1505-1506. The fees are recorded in regulations from 1580, but these were already valid in 1505.

name: Berlin
Settlement_Description: A Slavic settlement is attested from the 6th to 8th century, but it was not necessarily the immediate predecessor of the German settlement that was first mentioned in 1244, then already a town.
Town_Description: The first indication of Berlin is given in the mention of its provost in 1244, who was already mentioned as provost of Cölln in 1237; both towns were closely associated. Since its first mention, Berlin can be seen as a town, it is referred to as civitas in 1251. The exact date of the acquisition of town rights has not survived. Participation at the Hanseatic Diets in 1359, 1430 and lastly 1443; in 1518 they were forced by their territorial lord to quit the alliance.
Fair_Description: The date of the awarding of the fairs in Berlin is not mentioned.
Toll_Primary_Owner: Stadt Berlin, ab 1448 der Kurfürst von Brandenburg
Toll_Description: In 1298 Berlin acquired the river toll of Köpenick. The privileges referred to as "Nedderlage" (entrepot / staple) were tolls for merchants who travelled through the town; they were transferred to the prince electorate in 1448.
Staple_Description: A record, in which Berlin was granted staple rights in 1297, turned out to be a forgery. Especially the mention of the staple therein is insecure. The first secure confirmation of the staple right in Berlin is granted in 1337, even though a fee was probably already collected in the 13th century.

name: Teteringen
Settlement_Description: First mentioned in 1303. It was a small village, mostly consisting houses along the two roads that come together here.

name: Burgsteinfurt
Settlement_Description: The castle Stenvorde was first mentioned in 1129, next to which a settlement developed, which was first mentioned in 1222.
Town_Description: An exact year in which the first town rights were granted is not known, but it must have been before 1299. From 1310 to 1337 the place is characterised as an 'oppidum'. In 1347 it was granted town rights of Munster.

name: Uusikaupunki
Settlement_Description: Uusikaupunki (sw. Nystad) town was in 1617 established on the land of three medieval villages (Ruokola, Pietilä Mähölä) in Kalanti (before 1936 Uusikirkko, sw. Kaland, Nykyrka) parish. Independent town parish 1622.
Town_Description:
King Gustaf II Adolf ordained a town to be established in Männäinen in Uusikirkko (Kalanti) parish, where the weekly Saturday market attracted burghers from towns and surrounding hinterland as far as Häme. Focused on the trade of wooden vessels made in the area. Männäinen Saturday market is the only weekly market known from Early modern rural Finland. The location of the new town of Uusikaupunki (sw. Nystad) was soon changed to a more suitable site by the sea, where e the town was officially established on 19 April 1617. The weekly market remained in Männäinen, which was frequented by the burghers of Uusikaupunki until 1642. The oldest map of the town area is included in the 1649 plan for the town.
Peasant shipping and trade from Kalanti and Vakka-Finland area to Stokholm, Tallinn and other major destinations in the Baltic Sea area goes back to the 13th century. The most important export was since the 14th century wooden drinking and storage vessels. King Gustav I forbid peasant shipping from Vakka-Finland to Germany in 1531, but it was again allowed after complaints in 1533 to Tallinn and Riga. The right to export wooden vessels was also confirmed in 1550. Uusikaupunki had limited active export rights in 1617–36, passive import rights to 1636, and together with Pori and Rauma special licence for exports to Germany in 1640 after which the burghers were only allowed to export their goods via Turku and Stockholm.
Fair_Description: The annual winter and autumn fairs of Mynämäki on Candlemas (2 February) and St Laurentius (10 August) were in 1623 moved to Uusikaupunki (sw. Nystad), where the Candlemas fair was further in 1625 combined with three Lokalahti and Vehmaa area fairs into a single fair on the second Sunday of Lent (15 February - 21 March). Because of the spring thaw, the burghers applied in 1654 the fair of the second Sunday of Lent to Conversion of St Paul s (25 January) and the autumn market to St Bartolomeus (24 August), but only the latter was granted. Winter fair was moved to St Paul in 1689.
Toll_Description: The 1/32 duty worth of all goods intended for sale in towns and fairs and brought to the site by peasants was collected in Uusikaupunki since 1622.

name: Brójce
Town_Description: In 1428, Wladislaw II granted Petrus Rorczbok the right to found a town with Magdeburg town law in the forest Brodcza. In 1458 the town did not exist yet, because of a lack of settlers. The founding privileges were confirmed in 1603 by Sigismund III.

name: Olsböle
Settlement_Description: <b>Inn:</b> Olsböle is mentioned in Jaakko Teitti's list in 1556 as a possible place for a bailiff (fi. vouti, sw. fogde). Another possible place in Tenhola parish was Undermalm.

name: Svenskby
Settlement_Description: <b>Inn:</b> An inn was established in Finby a couple kilometers northeast in 1585, where it was run by Jören Jönsson for five years. In 1590, the inn moved to Svenskby, since it was closer to the common road, and Erik Thomasson was appointed as the innkeeper. Svenskby is one of the traditional inn villages by the Great Coastal Road.

name: Dodendorf
Settlement_Description: First mention in a record by Otto II from 973 in which estates are exchanged between the monastery of Fulda and archbishop Adalbert of Magdeburg (MGH DD OII, nr. 64, S. 74-77).

name: Nederhorst den Berg
Settlement_Description: The castle Nederhorst and the adjoining village Den Berg were first mentioned in 1326. Both names were combined to the current placename in modern times.

name: Oulu
Settlement_Description:
Permanent settlement in Liminka and Oulu area dates at the latest to the turn of 13th and 14th centuries. Liminka is cited as an independent parish in 1477. Oulu was established as a chapel in 1592 and was made into and independent parish in 1610. The strategic rivermouth hosted two castles of the Swedish crown, the first one in Kastelli in ca. 1375-1400, and the second one in two phases from 1590 to 1715. The permanent settlement of town area is set here to ca. 1420.

<b>Inn:</b> Medieval trading posts likely had private alehouses and taverns to serve travelling merchants and farmers.Ture Pedersson Bielke, Swedish nobleman and castellan of St. Olaf's Castle in Savo, stopped to change horses in Oulujoki harbour in 1557
Town_Description: Trade in the most important traditional trading posts at major river mouths in the Gulf of Bothnia area was regulated at the latest in 1420, when the crown furnished them with storage houses, started to collect toll, and prohibited other traditional trading sites alongside the Bothnic coastline. In 1459 all trade in these legal trading posts was restricted to Stockholm and Turku only, but without any result. The trading rights of Ulvila and Rauma in the legal trading posts of Oulu, Ii, Kemi and Tornio were confirmed together with those of Stockholm and Turku in 1531, and in 1542 the crown rented shops and storage facilities in Oulu, Ii and Kemi. In January 1605 king Karl IX ordered a castle to be built on an island at Oulujoki rivermouth and licenced a town in the mainland opposite it. The town privileges were given in April same year. In June 1605 the king granted the merchants in Oulu, Mustasaari (Vaasa), Tornio, Kemi and Umeå trading rights in Finland and in Sweden and duty free export to Narva. The town privileges were reconfirmed in April 1606, when merchants in Ostorobothnian countryside were ordained to move to Oulu, the burghers were given ten years of tax freedom, and the import toll was ordained full value for goods without the clearance from exporting town, half a toll with the clearance. Export was possible to Stockholm only. In 1608 Russian Karelian merchants frequenting the Bothnic rivermouths since the Middle Ages were banned to travel further than Oulu. The town privileges were again reconfirmed in September 1610, after which Oulu burghers had the sole right of trading in all harbours between Kemi and Kokkola (Karleby) and the right to sail with their goods to Narva, Reval (Tallinn), and other towns under Swedish crown in Livonia. In 1616 the weekly market day in Oulu was confirmed Saturday. After the shipping ordinance of 1614 Oulu had limited active staple rights for export to the year 1617 and passive staple rights for import to 1636. Between 1617 and 1765 export was allowed only to Stockholm and Turku. The two oldest geographical surveys of the town area are from the year 1648. After the reorganisation of the provincial administration in 1634 the province of Pohjanmaa (r. Österbottens län) was in 1642-48 split to Vaasa and Oulu provinces when the administration of the latter was in Oulu. The final partition of the area took only place in 1776. <b>Post office:</b> The Oulu post office was likely established in 1644, as matters related to the hiring of a postmaster are mentioned in the provincial accounts from that time. The position was reportedly first held by Carl Camroun, who was a shipowner, innkeeper, magistrate, customs officer, and parliament member.
Fair_Description: The beginnings of annual fairs in Oulujoki rivermouth area are not known. Burghers of Oulu had since 1610 the sole right of trading between Kemi and Kokkola (Karleby). In 1616 all trade in Ostrobothnia was centred to Oulu and Vaasa (sw. Vasa). One of the most important annual fairs were held in Saloinen (later Raahe) at St Olaf’s feast (29 July) where burghers of Stockholm, Turku, Rauma and Pori were granted rights for two weeks in 1616. Burghers of Turku and Oulu disputed each other’s rights until 1642, when the fair was relocated to Oulu and set to St Laurentius (10 August), which may also have been an older date of fairs in Oulu rivermouth. The fair was confirmed to last eight days in 1650 and lengthened to twelve days in 1652. Burghers of Kokkola were in 1621 granted the right to trade at two annual fairs in Kalajoki. In 1622 the two annual fairs in Kalajoki were granted as the right of Kokkola and Oulu burghers, who also were granted together with other towns in Ostrobothnia to trade at two annual fairs in Kemi and Ii parishes. The rights remained heavily disputed. Burghers of Tornio were granted similar rights for Kemi and Ii fairs in 1627 and 1636. Burghers of Oulu blocked their rivals in Kemi in 1641 after which the trading rights were contested between the two towns to the 1680s and again in the 18th century. The burghers of Oulu were also granted the right of two annual fairs in Kajaneborg parish in 1625. Of these the summer fair was to be held at midsummer (24 June) in Paltaniemi and the winter fair on 15 December in Särismäki. Paltaniemi midsummer fair was relocated to Kajaani in 1650 where annual winter fair was ordained to Candlemas (2 February).
Toll_Description: The Swedish crown started to collect toll from the new regulated harbours and market posts in Bothnian river mouths in the beginning of the 1420s. In 1606 the import toll was ordained full value for goods without the clearance from exporting town, half a toll with the clearance. The 1/32 duty worth of all goods intended for sale in towns and fairs and brought to the site by peasants was collected in Oulu since 1622.

name: Haminasaari (Kemi)
Fair_Description: Trade in the most important traditional trading posts at major river mouths in the Gulf of Bothnia area was regulated at the latest in 1420, when the crown furnished them with storage houses, started to collect toll, and prohibited other traditional trading sites alongside the Bothnic coastline. In 1459 all trade in these legal trading posts was restricted to Stockholm and Turku only, but without any result. The trading rights of Ulvila and Rauma in the legal trading posts of Oulu, Ii, Kemi and Tornio were confirmed together with those of Stockholm and Turku in 1531, and in 1542 the crown rented shops and storage facilities in Oulu, Ii and Kemi. In 1622 Kokkola and Oulu burghers were granted together with other towns in Ostrobothnia to trade at two annual fairs in Kemi and Ii parishes. Burghers of Tornio were granted similar rights for Kemi and Ii fairs in 1627 and 1636, but the rights of other towns than Oulu remained heavily disputed. Burghers of Oulu blocked their rivals in Kemi in 1641 after which the trading rights were contested between the two towns to the 1680s and again in the 18th century. In Kemi, site of annual fair was since the early 16th century in Haminasaari, an island in river Kemijoki opposite the parsonage and Keminmaa early 16th century stone church where the parish church was relocated from Valmarinniemi sometime between the 1450s and 1517. According to local tradition the oldest market site in Kemi was close to Valmarinniemi. Kemi is first cited in 1329, when it was together with Saloinen a chapel of Pedersöre parish. Independent parish was established in the beginning of the 15th century. Haminasaari market site was in use until 1821 when it was destroyed by fire. Haminasaari island was left under the reservoir of Isohaara hydro energic power plant in the late 1940s. Finds from the archaeological excavations on the island in 1947 include a mint of Sten Sture the Elder (1471–1503), at least 27 foundations of market shops and storage facilities and material from the early 17th century to the 19th. Market sites and fairs in Tornio, Kemi, Ii and Oulu were also frequented by Russian Karelian merchants to 1608, when they were banned to travel further than Oulu.
Toll_Description:
The Swedish crown started to collect toll from the new regulated harbours and market posts in Bothnian river mouths in the beginning of the 1420s. 

The 1/32 duty worth of all goods intended for sale in towns and fairs brought to the site by peasants was collected in Haminasaari since 1622.

name: Vyborg
Settlement_Description: Permanent agricultural settlement in Viipuri (sw. Viborg, rus. Vyborg) area dates back at the latest to the 13th century, but apart from scattered 10th to 12th Century finds from the castle island and the favourable location of the site next to land and maritime routes, no straightforward evidence of permanent pre 1293 settlement has been found. The first documented activity on the site only starts with the building of the castle and the formation of the medieval town in the late 14th century. Viborg parish was established in the first quarter of the 14th century and consisted alter of both the town and land congregations. A stone church was built on the site of the former wooden churches in 1435–45. Originally under the Diocese and bishop of Turku, plans for an independent diocese emerged already in the 1360s, but the bishopric of Viipuri was first established only in 1554 and was in 1574–1618 subjugated to bishop of Turku. After the Great Northern War the diocese administration and see of the bishop was re-established in Porvoo (sw. Borgå) in 1723.
Town_Description:
Founded in 1293, Viborg castle emerged already in the first quarter of the 14th century as one of the most important strongholds in the Swedish realm with the castellan’s extensive powers over the economy, jurisdiction, and defence of the area. The earliest information on the organisation of the trade in the bailiwick is from 1336 when the castellan granted the burghers of Reval (Tallinn) the right to trade freely in three towns (in tribus civitatis) in his dominion, named Viipuri (Wyborch), Vehkalahti (Weckelax) ja Virolahti (Wyrlax). Apparently a community of merchants under the jurisdiction of the castellan located or frequenting a fixed trading site in the area, the town was developed into a sworn community of burghers at the end of the 14th century and was granted town privileges by king Erik of Pomerania in 1403. The oldest wooden constructions excavated in the town area date to the beginning of the 15th century. The only Finnish town ever to be enclosed by walls, characteristic of the relationship of the castle and the town was, that the initiative for building the wall in the 1470's was not taken by the town council but by the castellan. The town area was enwidened in the East in 1553–94 with new fortifications and regulated after 1638 to the third quarter of the 17th century in several stages. Th eoldest geographical survey of the town are is from 1637–38. The weekly market day of Viipuri was in 1616 coinfirmed Saturday. The town was in 1621 granted the right to mint. Viipuri and its surroundings were annexed by Russia after the Great Northern War in the peace of Nystad in 1721. Apart from the town and parish church, the town area hosted a Dominican church and friary after an Apostolical dispense from 1392, and an active Franciscan church and friary in 1403. Both convents had stone churches built after the town was levelled in a fire in 1477. After the dissolution in the 1530s Dominican church served the Finnish speaking congregation of the town and surrounding countryside.
An important turn in the trading privileges of towns of the Swedish realm took place in 1614, when a system of towns with staple rights (sw. stapelstad, fi. tapulikaupunki) and inland towns (sw. uppstad, fi. maakaupunki, ylämaakaupunki) was created in the new trading and shipping ordinance. Towns with staple rights were divided to first- and second-class staples. The burghers of both classes had the right to export, i.e. to sail to foreign towns and destinations (active rights in foreign trade), whereas only towns of the first class had the right of imports, i.e. the right of receive and unload foreign vessels in their harbours (passive rights in foreign trade). Modified in 1615 and 1617 the ordinance restricted the trade of foreigners in Swedish towns and searched to bar the traditional peasant trade to regional hubs in the realm. In Finland only Turku and Viipuri held the status of a first-class staple (active and passive rights) continuously from 1614.
Fair_Description:
Viipuri did not have significant annual fairs of its own in the Middle Ages and the beginning of the Early Modern era. Instead, the burghers entertained sole rights to several fairs located in the bailiwicks subjucated to the castle and, since 1635, in the province of Viborg and Nyslott, which belonged to the trading area of the town to the beginning of the 18th century. The most important of these was held in Lapvesi, where the burghers of Viipuri travelled every autumn for several weeks and where the peasants of Savo brought their products. In 1643 and 1647, the peasants of the Viipuri and Käkisalmi (sw. Kexholm) provinces and the eastern part of Häme applied for the establishment of a common free market in Viipuri, to which the government agreed, but the project fell through due to burghers’ opposition. In 1647 the town was granted an annual cattle fair to be held on St Bartholomeus (24 August), but its popularity remained low.

Burghers of Viipuri were in 1542 granted the sole right for four annual fairs in their trading area of which Vehkalahti St Olaf’s fair (29 July) were also allowed to take place in Viipuri town. The other thre fairs were held on apostle Peter (29 June) in Jääski, on the Nativity of Mary (8 September) in Lapvesi and on the Elevation of the Holy Cross (14 September) in Äyräpää. In 1585 the fair in Vehkalahti was held on apostle Bartholomeus (24 August). Sole right to all four fairs was confirmed in 1594, when the fair in Vehkalahti was held on St Laurentius (10 August). Burghers of Viipuri were granted the sole rights to St Laurentius fair (10 August) in Korkeakoski in 1600 and 1606. The burghers were in 1606 said to have held of old annual fair at Saijanjoki river on the old border between Sweden and Russia. The right was confirmed 1606. Viipuri burghers were in 1616 granted the rights to trade in Käkisalmi province. In 1621 the burghers were granted the right of annual Michaelmas (29 September) fair for two weeks in Lapvesi together with the traditional one week fair of the Nativity of Mary. The two fairs were combined into a continuous three week fair in 1675. In 1627 burghers of Viipuri were confirmed the right for two annual fairs in Muolaa and in Nyenskans, of which the right to the latter was called back in 1663.
Toll_Description: The 1/32 duty worth of all goods intended for sale in towns and fairs and brought to the site by peasants was collected in Viipuri since 1622. The toll stations were located at the town gates in the town wall, in Siikaniemi and in harbour areas.

name: Helsingborg
Settlement_Description: Helsingborg was originally a royal castle located at the most narrow part of Øresund. A settlement with an urban character developed next to the castle. During the middle ages the settlement gradually moved from the area near the castle to the flat land along the shore.
Town_Description: The German chronicler Adam of Bremen characterized Helsingborg as a town around 1075, which was located at the best place to sail across the strait of Øresund between Zealand and Scania. A few years later, in 1085, an annual royal tax from towns in eastern Denmark (Danish: Midsommergæld) was collected in Helsingborg. Thus, Helsingborg was considered as a town in the late 11th century. According to the so-called main piece of King Valdemar’s Cadastre from c. 1231 the town was royal institutional property (Danish: ‘kongelev’). The town was administered by the king’s governor at the strong castle, which was rebuilt several times during the middle ages. Early in the medieval period Helsingborg had four parish churches and a A Dominican monastery was founded in 1275. From its foundation in the 11th century and throughout the medieval period Helsingborg benefited from the rich fishing of herring in Øresund, and home to the most popular ferry connection between the provinces of Zealand and Scania. During the 15th and 16th centuries Helsingborg suffered from a decline in the annual fishing of herring and newly founded towns in western Scania (Landskrona and Luntertun).

name: Driebergen
Settlement_Description: Earliest mention of 'Thriberge(n)' in 1159, in a falsification which probably dates from the fourteenth century. Near the village stood the castle Rijsenburg, first mentioned in 1270. After the castle was demolished in 1809, a new village with the name Rijsenburg was founded, which was merged with Driebergen in 1931.

name: Szczecinek
Settlement_Description: First mentioned in 1295. The settlement probably developed around a fortress on the Trzesiecko lake.
Town_Description: The town was founded in 1310 by Duke Wartislaw IV with Lübeck town privileges as a security against Waldemar II of Brandenburg.

name: Rixtel
Settlement_Description: Oldest mention from 1179, in a thirteenth century copy. Merged with nearby Aarle into Aarle-Rixtel during the twentieth century.

name: Stenberga
Settlement_Description: Permanent agricultural settlement in Masku goes back to the Iron Age. The parish is first mentioned in 1234. <b>Stenberga castle: </b> Stenberga castle at the mouth of Maskunjoki river was built by the castellan of Turku Jakob Abrahamsson (Djäkn) whom the king Albrekt of Mecklenburg of Sweden had in 1387 granted the right to build fortifications in the area under his control. The castle is mentioned in 1398, when Jakob gave it temporarily to Viburd Kortumme, from whom it came to the possession of the crown in the same year and was partially demolished. <b>Naantali Bridgettine Abbey:</b>  The council of the Swedish realm founded in 1438 a Bridgettine abbey in Finland, for which the crown donated Stenberga manor with all its possessions. The abbey was in 1441 moved to the premises of an old Royal Manor in Pyhäjoki (Helgå) in Perniö but was finally located to Ailoinen in Raisio in 1442. King Christopher of Bavaria confirmed the relocation in 1443.

name: Falsterbo
Settlement_Description: Falsterbo was first mentioned in 1268 as the southern herring market on the peninsula Falsterbonäset with Skanör to the north. A permanent settlement in the second half of the 13th century.
