Town_Description: The royal castle of Falsterbohus was built in the middle of the 13th century, and soon the settlement next to the castle got an urban character.Falsterbo was described as a town (villa) in 1367, and in the following year mayors, a town council and citizens were mentioned. The town had several parish churches. One church was known as ‘the German church’, and is a reflection of the strong German presence, so is the existence of a German guild. The town of Falsterbo was relatively small and was dependent on the rich fishing of herring in Øresund. When the fishing began to decline the town also stagnated.
Fair_Description: The annual fair at Falsterbo sprung from the rich fishing in Øresund during autumn, when schools of herring passed through the Sound. As the other Scania fairs the one in Falsterbo began August 15th and ended October 9th. International trade related to the fishing of herring probably began in the 12th century, and around 1200 the market was concentrated at the town of Skanör. In the early 13th century the fishing and trading spread from Skanör to Falsterbo and from around 1300 also to other towns in the region around Øresund. During the 14th and 15th century towns such as Malmö, Ystad, Landskrona, Trelleborg and Dragør (on the island of Amager) came to dominate the annual fairs of Scania. In the 13th century both fairs on the peninsula of Falsterbo had an international character, and were visited by merchants from towns across northern Europe, especially from northern Germany. Merchants from Lübeck and other German towns came to Skanör and Falsterbo to sell their own products such as salt, cloth and beer and to buy salted herring. At the fairs both Danish and foreign towns were given their own plots (Danish: fed; German: Vitten), where they could implement their own jurisdiction, conduct trade and where the herring was processed. At Skanör towns such as Rostock, Stralsund, Wismar, Kiel and Lübeck had their plots, and at Falsterbo western merchants from England and Netherlands concentrated. In the late 14th century, however, the Germans forced the English and Dutch traders out of the fairs, and even more than before, German merchants now dominated the fairs. In the year 1399, for example, toll records from Lübeck revealed that 1218 ships from Lübeck visited the different fairs in Scania. During the period 1398-1400 the town of Lübeck imported c. 76.000 barrels of salted herring from the fairs. The fairs also attracted fishers and traders in large numbers from Denmark, in particular from the region around Øresund, and from the middle of the 13th century onwards many Danish towns were granted specific rights at the fairs. The fairs were controlled by the king of Denmark, but during the 14th century they were periodically in the hands of the king of Sweden as well as German political agents. The most important commodity was herring, but a broad variety of goods were bought and sold at the Scania fairs, as the fairs functioned as transit markets for products from the North Sea regions and the Baltic areas. The fairs of Scania were an important source of income for the king of Denmark, who collected various tolls at the different markets, and tried to regulate the market activity by legislation, the so-called ‘Motbogen’/’Modbogen’. During the 15th century the Scania fairs began to decline. Fishing and export of herring was still important, but the fairs lost their function as a place of exchange of goods between the Baltic and the North Sea. By the end of the 16th century the Scania fairs were no longer among the most important annual fairs of northern Europe.
Toll_Description: Toll on the export of herring, imported German beer and several other goods are known from the 13th century onwards. In general foreigners (i.e. in general Germans) had to pay a higher toll on herring as well as other goods than Danes. The toll was probably collected by the royal steward at Falsterbo castle. Toll registers from the year 1494 have been preserved (Rigsarkivet/The Danish National Archive).
Staple_Description: Stable rights were granted by king Christian I (1448-1481) in 1475, who ordered that oxen were only allowed to be transported to Skanör as well as a few other towns (Kolding Assens, Ribe and the annual fairs in Skanør and Falsterbo). When Skanör lost these stable rights are uncertain.

name: Myllykylä
Settlement_Description: <b>Inn:</b> Myllykylä (Qwerneby) is mentioned in Jaakko Teitti's list in 1556 as a possible place for a bailiff (fi. vouti, sw. fogde).

name: Immula
Settlement_Description: <b>Inn:</b> An inn is mentioned in Immula village southeast from the road in 1584, when it was run by Eskeli Paavonpoika. In 1591 the inn hosted travelling soldiers.

name: Veromies
Settlement_Description: <b>Inn:</b> A man named Lasse run an alehouse in Veromies village (sw. Skattmansby) north from the crossing. The alehouses in Helsinki parish paid in 1543 their taxes for ale selling in natura by delivering hops to the king's estate in Porvoo. In late 16th c., there was also an inn in Veromies.

name: Teutari
Settlement_Description: <b>Inn:</b> Teutari village south from the road had a transport organiser (fi. kyytirättäri, sw. skjutsrättare) in 1556. It was moved in 1624 at the latest to Kokkila, Siuntio. Transport organiser could also serve accommodation to travellers, like in 1592, when transport organiser Eskeli and Lasse Tuomaanpoika accommodated 50 travelling soldiers and their horses for three nights.

name: Scheepsdalebrug
Bridge_Description: A stone bridge was built by Jan van Oudenaerde across the river Ieperleet in 1397. It was located on the road from Bruges towards Blankenberge, which was already paved in 1291.

name: null
Bridge_Description: A fixed crossing of the Unstrut is mentioned in 1288. Before that date there probably existed a ferry or ford.

name: Siuntio
Settlement_Description: <b>Inn:</b> Siuntio Krögarby ("Tavern village") is mentioned in 1538. It is close to Siuntio church, as is Tjusterby (Tyyskylä) village, where the parish constable (fi: nimismies, sw: länsman) was located and where he kept a tavern. Siuntio parish constables served as innkeepers until 1702. Siuntio vicarage provided also food, drinks, and accommodation. In 1562, parish constable Hans Grelsson had noble guests, when duke Johan of Finland and his newly married wife, Catherine Jagiellon, had to come ashore in Pikkala harbour in the south, and were transported to the parish constable's house.

name: Kokkila
Settlement_Description: <b>Inn:</b> Siuntio parish constable (fi: nimismies, sw: länsman) was usually located in Kokkila, and the constable ran a tavern in his house. In 1584, Tuomas Tuomaanpoika held the office, and he was granted tax exemptions in return for serving and accommodating travellers. This was common by the busy Great Coastal road and also elsewhere. From early 17th c. to 1624 or 1635, the parish constable office and the inn were located in Myrans village ca. 3 km northeast. The office and the inn moved back to Tuomola farm and continued to operate there from 1635 to 1702 and also later during the 18th and 19th c.

name: Roermond
Settlement_Description: Earliest mention in 1130. The count of Guelders acquired a domain in Roermond before 1189 and founded the Cistercian monastery Munsterabdij there shortly before 1218. A hospital is found in 1259.
Town_Description: Earliest mention as a town ('oppidum') in 1224. The exact year in which town privileges have been granted is unknown, but this must have been between 16 June 1224 and 22 October 1229 by Gerard IV, count of Guelders. A burgomaster and town council is first mentioned in 1329.
Fair_Description: Roermond had three fairs: on Tuesday after Pentecost (known since 1294/5), St. Remi and St. Barbara (since 1351). A weighing house for wool (libramentum lane) is mentioned in 1294/5, a cloth hall in 1347. From 1354 onwards inhabitants of Roermond are found on the fairs of Frankfurt. A ducal charter of 1372 extended all fairs in Roermond to 16 days and introduced a fourth fair, of which the date is however unknown.In 1562 king Philip II granted three fairs with three days safeconduct because of the townfire in 1554: 1) Wednesday before mid-lent, 2) June 12 and 3) Nov. 7. In 1589 he consented another two fairs on Jan. 25 jan. and July 20. In 1596 there are six fairs: another one on the Tuesday and Wednesday after Pentecost.
Toll_Description: Next to the safe conduct on the Meuse, the Count of Guelders also levied a fee for safe conduct on land in 1226/53. Tariffs are not known. In 1284, 8 mark a year were collected.
Staple_Description: Roermond was granted an eight-day staple in 1372 for those outside Gelre and Julich on goods transported through the Maas river, which was moved to Venlo in 1523. It is being questioned whether this staple right has been effective. In 1578 king Philip II granted a privilege that in the 'ambt' (region) Montfort all lime, marl and coal in Roermond had to be transshipped.

name: null
Harbour_Description: It is unknown where the harbour for shipping on the Oker river in Braunschweig was located. For the shipping to Celle and Bremen in the late Middle Ages, a location in the northern part of town is assumed, probably around the former river island Werder in the borough Hagen, with an additional landing place on the opposite shore in the borough Neustadt around the former street Nickelnkulk. However, there is no written or archaeological evidence for a harbour in Braunschweig. The (un)loading of ships might also have taken place outside the town.

name: Sipoo
Settlement_Description:
Permanent agricultural settlement in Sipoo (sw. Sibbo) area and Eastern Nyland (sw. Östra Nyland) dates to the Swedish colonisation in the latter half of the 13th century when new farms were founded amongst earlier 12th and 13th century area of usufruct and colonisation from inner Häme. The parish organisation of Eastern Nyland dates at the latest to the first quarter of the 14th century. King Magnus Eriksson donated the rights of patronate of Porvoo parish and its two chapels of Sipoo (sw. Sibbo) and Pernaja to the Cistercian Abbey of Padise in present Estonia in 1351. The bishop and Cathedral Chapter of Turku reclaimed the rights in 1428. Independent parish 1425. Stone church on the likely site of earlier wooden church or churches was built in the early 1450s. Sipoonjoki (sw. Sibbo å) rivermouth was in ca. 1395-1400 protected by a short lived castle on Sibbesborg island.
<b>Inn:</b> The alehouses in Sipoo and Helsinki parishes paid in 1543 their taxes for ale selling in natura by delivering hops to Wiborg castle and the king's estate in Porvoo. Later, an inn was established in Sipoo in the 1580s, and Stor-Olof Larsson was appointed as the innkeeper.
<b>Post house:</b> In 1638, the Royal Steward Bernhardt Steen von Steenhausen established a post house in Sipoo. Specific information about the village is not available.
Fair_Description:
In 1584 burghers of the newly re-established Porvoo complained to the authorities, that right after the sea and rivers were free of ice, burghers of Helsinki arrived to trade with peasants of the region at the Old Royal Manor (in Saksala) and elsewhere despite of the official fair dates which were Midsummer in Sipoo (sw. Sibbo), Visitation of Mary (2 July) and Excaltation of the Cross (14 September) in Porvoo, St Michael (29 September) in Pernaja (sw. Pernå) and St Laurentius (10 August) at Pyhtää (sw. Pyttis) church. Apparently of older tradition Sipoo Midsummer fair is cited as a right of Helsinki burghers together with Pernaja and Pyhtää fairs in a confirmation of King Johan III in 1576. In 1616 at the latest the burghers of Helsinki also had rights to another fair in Sipoo on St Mary (8 September), the duration of which was in 1682 ordained to be two days. The 17th century autumn fair was held somewhere close to the Sipoonjoki rivermouth.

Annual summer and early autumn fairs in Sipoo, Pernaja and Pyhtää and the summer fair in Porvoo Saksala may have been organised in the context of ecclesiastical feasts of respective parish churches. In addition to the tar which had a growing status as an export article since the latter half of the 16th century, all the summer fairs were also connected to spawning seasons of Salmon, whitefish and Baltic herring, where summer fairs of Sipoo (24 June) and Porvoo in Saksala (1-2 July) of Julian calendar corresponded July the 4th and 12th in Gregorian calendar which was the high season of Salmon and right after the early spawning of Baltic herring which took place in the inner archipelago of the Gulf of Finland. Julian dates for autumn fairs at Pyhtää parish church (10 August), Vähä-Ahvenkoski (24 August), Sipoo (8 September), Porvoo (14 September), and Pernaja (29 September) correspond Gregorian calendar dates of 20 August, 3, 18 and 24 September and 9 October, all of which occurred during the high season of whitefish migration and the autumn spawning of Baltic herring in the outer archipelago.

name: null
Toll_Description: A toll station in the region ('Amt') Mahndorf on the street between Halberstadt and Derenburg is mentioned in 1657, when it was to be moved to the Brockenstedt mill between Derenburg and Quedlinburg.

name: Vik
Settlement_Description: <b>Inn:</b> Vik had a transport organiser (fi. kyytirättäri, sw. skjutsrättare) serving Siuntio parish constable.

name: Porvoo
Settlement_Description: Permanent agricultural settlement in lower Porvoonjoki (sw. Borgå å) area and Eastern Nyland (sw. Östra Nyland) dates to the Swedish colonisation in the latter half of the 13th century when new farms were founded in an area previously part of usufruct and emerging colonisation settlement from inner Häme. The parish organisation of Eastern Nyland dates at the latest to the first quarter of the 14th century, in Porvoo (sw. Borgå) possibly already to the third quarter of the 14th century. The parish and rector of Porvoo is first cited in 1327. The name of the parish (Borgå – Castle river, i.e. the one of the rivers in the area where there is a castle) implies that the castle should be older than the name of the parish in use in 1327. King Magnus Eriksson donated the rights of patronate of Porvoo parish and its two chapels of Sipoo (sw. Sibbo) and Pernaja (sw. Pernå) to the Cistercian Abbey of Padise in present Estonia in 1351. The bishop and Cathedral Chapter of Turku reclaimed the rights in 1428. The first parish church was built in the latter half of the 13th century, amended with first stone structures in 1410s and the present much larger medieval stone church in the 1440s. <b>Inn:</b> All the inns in Porvoo parish paid taxes to the king and bailiff (fi. vouti, sw. fogde). In 1543, Porvoo inns paid 4½ öre to the king and 13½ öre to the bailiff.
Town_Description:
Porvoo town was established either in the turn of the 1370s and 1380s or in the late 1340s. The town is first cited in 1387. The earliest plots centred around the parish church and an adjacent marketplace from where the inhabited area spread to downstream alongside the ridge and the eastern bank of the river where the later town hall and marketplace was located since the mid-15th century. The bridge of the Great Coastal Road crossing the river is first recorded in a sketchy map of the town from 1652. Originally maintained by Porvoo parish, the western half of bridge was in 1772 in the care of the parish and eastern half in that of the town. The town area is marked in a map from 1652. A detailed geographical survey of the town exists from the year 1696. All medieval charters of the town were very likely lost in the sack and subsequent burning of Porvoo by Danish forces in 1508. King Gustav I confirmed the privileges of the town in 1546. In 1550 the king ordered all the burghers of Ulvila (sw. Ulfsby), Rauma (sw. Raumo), Tammisaari (sw. Ekenäs) and Porvoo move to the newly established town of Helsinki (sw. Helsingfors) and annulled Porvoo as a town in 1551. The town was established anew in 1579, was again annulled because of the complaints of Helsinki in 1594 but received new privileges from king Karl IX in 1602. In 1616 the weekly market day in the town was confirmed as Wednesday.
The inhabitants and later burghers of Porvoo had since the late 1340s close contacts to Reval (Tallinn), through which much of the foreign export and import of the town may have taken place to the first half of the 16th century. In order to bar Revalian influence the 1546 privileges of Porvoo allowed foreign trade via Stockholm only. The annulation of the town rights in 1551 and its disputed status in 1579-1602 affected the trade gravely. An important turn in the trading privileges of towns of the Swedish realm took place in 1614, when a system of towns with staple rights (Sw. stapelstad, Fin. tapulikaupunki) and inland towns (Sw. uppstad, Fin. maakaupunki, ylämaakaupunki) was created in the new trading and shipping ordinance. Towns with staple rights were divided to first- and second-class staples. The burghers of both classes had the right to export, i.e. to sail to foreign towns and destinations (active rights in foreign trade), whereas only towns of the first class had the right of imports, i.e. the right of receive and unload foreign vessels in their harbours (passive rights in foreign trade). Modified in 1615 and 1617 the ordinance restricted the trade of foreigners in Swedish towns and searched to bar the traditional peasant trade to regional hubs in the realm. In Finland only Turku (sw. Åbo) and Viipuri (sw. Viborg) held the status of a first-class staple (active and passive rights) continuously from 1614. Other towns with provisional first-class rights from 1614 were Helsinki and Porvoo. Both enjoyed full first-class staple to 1623, when their toll was rented to the city Reval and foreign import shipping in the Gulf of Finland area was only allowed to Reval and Viipuri. Helsinki and Porvoo regained their full staple rights in 1628 with a continuation in 1636. After being relocated to the present site in 1640 Helsinki retained its full rights, but Porvoo lost its position and sunk into a status of an inland town.
<b>Post office:</b> The Porvoo post office is one of the first five post offices in Finland. In the year the office was established, Porvoo had about 500 residents. The first postmaster was Herman Raaf, who was known as a burgher, magistrate, and churchwarden.
Fair_Description:
The earliest information on annual fairs in Porvoo are from the year 1584 when king Johan III confirmed the town its two traditional fairs on Visitation of Mary (2 July, apparently in Saksala) and Exaltation of the Holy Cross (14 September, in town). The latter fair is cited in almanacs in 1598. Both days were again confirmed in 1594. In 1650 an annual winter fair in Porvoo was confirmed to be hold at Epiphany (6 January).

Annual summer and autumn fairs in Porvoo and in Saksala (sw. Saxby) village close to the medieval Royal Manor (sw. Gammelgård) less than 10 kms upstream from the town were in the first half of the 17th century part of a wider system of fairs in Eastern Nyland rivermouth areas going back to the late 14th century or even earlier. In 1584 burghers of the newly re-established Porvoo complained to the authorities, that right after the sea and rivers were free of ice, burghers of Helsinki arrived to trade with peasants of the region at the Old Royal Manor (in Saksala) and elsewhere despite of the official fair dates which were Midsummer in Sipoo (sw. Sibbo), Visitation of Mary (2 July) and Excaltation of the Cross (14 September) in Porvoo, St Michael (29 September) in Pernaja (sw. Pernå) and St Laurentius (10 August) at Pyhtää (sw. Pyttis) church. The same year burghers of Porvoo and Helsinki were granted joint rights for trading with peasants of the eastern half of Pernaja parish at the St Bartolomeus free fair in Vähä-Ahvenkoski in Pyhtää, whereas peasants from the western half of Pernaja were obliged to trade in Porvoo only. Previous traditional local fairs in Mustijoki (sw. Svartså) and Kulloonmäki (sw. Kullo) in Porvoo, Pikku Pernajanlahti (sw. Lillpernåviken) in Pernaja and elsewhere were prohibited. After intense litigation over local fairs throughout the last quarter of the 16th century both Porvoo and Helsinki were in 1602 and in 1607 respectively confirmed right to trade in the four annual fairs at Porvoo, Pernaja and Pyhtää so that burghers of Helsinki had free right to trade in confirmed fairs east of Porvoo and those of Porvoo west of Helsinki. Pyhtää Bartholomeus fair is cited in an almanac in 1616, but Pernaja Michaelmas fair not. Fair in Pyhtää was held in Vähä-Ahvenkoski and those of Pernaja at Koskenkylä (sw. Forsby) bridge on the Great Coastal Road, where they were held in 1708. In 1639 burghers of Helsinki were further granted the right to visit annual tar fair in Porvoo on 1 July. Already in 1614 Helsinki had seized the sole right to fair in Janakkala Turkhauta on 1 September traditionally been frequented by burghers from Porvoo. Since 1654 Turkhauta fair was organised on 14 September.

The 1584 trading site close to the 15th century Royal Manor in Saksala can be attached to much later local peasant fair in the same village organised on the feast of St Peter (29 June) as late as in the early 19th century. Close to the traditional fair day of the visitation of Mary (2 July) of 1584 and the tar fair of 1 July in 1639 in Porvoo, the early modern fair in Saksala appears to have focused on fresh tar, which inland peasants brought to the markets soon after its production. Of special interest is, that in a 1616 almanac the tar fair of the burghers of Helsinki in Porvoo on 1 July was called as St Enewalds fair (sw. Enewaldsmässan). A local saint of medieval Danish origin and unknown feast day from Blekinge, the shrine and well of St Enewald in Sölvesborg is cited three times as a destination of a pilgrimage in 1405-21. The emerging of his feast as a fixed fair of July the 1st and 2nd in Saksala may tell about the well known influence of the Danish high nobility active in Finland in the first two decades of the 15th century and the early Union era, when they took care of reorganisation of the regional and local administration of bailiwicks, taxation and jurisdiction.

Annual summer and early autumn fairs in Sipoo, Pernaja and Pyhtää and the summer fair in Saksala may have been organised in the context of ecclesiastical feasts of respective parish churches. In addition to the tar which had a growing status as an export article since the latter half of the 16th century, all the summer fairs were also connected to spawning seasons of Salmon, whitefish and Baltic herring, where summer fairs of Sipoo (24 June) and Porvoo in Saksala (1-2 July) of Julian calendar corresponded July the 4th and 12th in Gregorian calendar which was the high season of Salmon and right after the early spawning of Baltic herring which took place in the inner archipelago of the Gulf of Finland. Julian dates for autumn fairs at Pyhtää parish church (10 August), Vähä-Ahvenkoski (24 August), Porvoo (14 September), and Pernaja (29 September) correspond gregorian calendar dates of 20 August, 3 and 24 September and 9 October, all of which occurred during the high season of whitefish migration and the autumn spawning of Baltic herring in the outer archipelago.
Toll_Description: The 1/32 duty worth of all goods intended for sale in towns and fairs and brought to the site by peasants was collected in Porvoo since 1622. The two toll stations were located alongside the Great Coastal Road at the western end of Porvoo bridge and in east on the common road to Viborg.

name: Ilola
Settlement_Description: <b>Inn:</b> Porvoo parish inn moved in 1616 from Vekkoski to Ilola village and a farm, which came later known as Gästgivars ("Inn"). Ilola village had an inn until early 20th c., also in other farms than Gästgivars.

name: Oulun linna
Settlement_Description: Permanent settlement in Liminka and Oulu area dates at the latest to the turn of 13th and 14th centuries. In 1375 a castle of Swedish Crown was built to that time rivermouth in Kastelli. Novgorod laid siege to the castle in 1377. The castle did not establish itself as an administrational centre and it was either destroyed, demolished or left in oblivion in the turn of the 14th and 15th centuries. A new wooden fortification was built on Linnansaari (Castle’s Island) after the orders of king Johan III in 1590 and was active to the year 1599. The site was refortified with a masonry castle according to the orders of king Karl IX in 1605-18. The castle was burned down by Russian army in 1715, and the structures were abandoned altogether in 1795.

name: null
Toll_Description: The Count of Guelders levied a fee for safe conduct on the Meuse here from 1226/53. A special tariff of 1396 is known for people from Venlo, which determined 3 old stuivers per piece of wine. A river toll was also levied here, which was either synonymous with the safe conduct or at least closely connected to it.
Ferry_Description: The ferry of the steward in Roermond left from the area known as Buitenop outside the city walls, and consisted of two ferries after 1342, across the old and the new branch of the Meuse river (Oude Maas and Nieuwe Maas). With a road via Hoembergen it was connected to Horn. The ferry over the Oude Maas was located on Horn territory, the ferry over the Nieuwe Maas on Guelders territory. These ferries were located in the floodplain of the river, which flooded regularly. In that case the ferry in Ool was used, located about one kilometre south of the city.

name: Koski (Piikkiö)
Settlement_Description: <b>Inn:</b> An inn was established in Koski farm in 1638.

name: Porvoon silta
Bridge_Description: The bridge of the Great Coastal Road crossing Porvoonjoki river west of the town of Porvoo (sw. Borgå) is first recorded in a sketchy map of the town from 1652. The earliest bridge on the site may however date to the first organisation of the maintenance of the Great Coastal Road as a uniform land route between Turku and Viborg in the 1340s and 1360s. Originally maintained by Porvoo parish, the western half of bridge was in 1772 in the care of the parish and the eastern half in that of the town.

name: Sollstedt
Settlement_Description: First mention in 1221 in a charter about grain tolls, which are donated to Walkenried monastery.

name: Karjalohja
Settlement_Description: Permanent agricultural settlement in Karjalohja (sw. Karislojo) goes back to the Middle Ages. Karjalohja chapel church is mentioned in 1467. The earliest church was located close to the lake, but the church site was moved to the ridge before 1634. The 17th century fair site was next to the church on the ridge.
Fair_Description: Karjalohja's fair was held in 1627 on the feast of Apostle Paul (25 January). Karjalohja fair and Lohja fairs on Candlemas (2. February) and Saturday before Mid-Lent Sunday (28./29 February – 3 April) were moved to Tammisaari in 1627 to be held as one Candlemas fair. The fairs were returned to Karjalohja and Lohja before 1634.
Toll_Description: The 1/32 duty worth of all goods intended for sale in towns and fairs and brought to the site by peasants was collected in Karjalohja in 1622–27 and after 1634.

name: Oostende
Settlement_Description: Count Robert the Frisian of Flanders confirmed the foundation of the church of St Peter on the eastern end of the coastal island Testerep in 1072.
Town_Description: After the drainage of the surrounding coastal plain in the 12th century, Oostende developed into a town in the 13th. It received privileges, a market place and a fish market in 1267. The town was continuously threatened by storm surges, and in 1397 it was moved further inland. The town suffered heavily during the Dutch revolt, when it was taken by the Sea beggars in 1572 and besieged and recaptured by the Spanish in 1604. In this period, the town was completely destroyed and the surrounding countryside flooded and fundamentally changed. Afterwards it was rebuilt and became an important harbour town due to the construction of a canal to Bruges in the 17th century.
Fair_Description: Emperor Charles granted in 1518 the relocation of the fair the day after St. Peter and Paul (June 29) to St. Catherine (Nov. 25 or July 5?).

name: Ieper
Settlement_Description: In 1166 Ieper was freed from the tolls on the Ieperlee, when paying 1 denarius per boat. The Ieperlee connected Ieper to the Northsea via Nieuwpoort, Diksmuide en Schipstal (Scheepsdale near Bruges).
Fair_Description: A fair is known in 1127. Around 1200 it was part together with Bruges, Torhout (Thourout), Rijsel (Lille) and Mesen (Messines) of the famous Flemish cycle of fairs who took over the one previous found in the Champagne-region. In the 13th century the fair in Ypres lasted from Febr. 28 till March 28.

name: Görlitz
Settlement_Description: By the 11/12th century a borough with a Bohemian castle. Previously settled by Slavs, it was an important junction for long distance trade.
Town_Description: The old town was laid out around 1200, and expanded with the addition of a new town around 1250.
Staple_Description: A staple for woad was granted in 1339 and confirmed in the Golden Bull of 1356, but was probably enjoyed earlier. Woad traders in the Margraviate of Bautzen needed to travel through Görlitz and were not allowed to bypass the city. In a settlement of 1340 the length of the staple right was set at four weeks.

name: Destelbergen
Settlement_Description: Earliest mention probably in 962, in a mid-eleventh century copy.

name: Melle (Gent)
Settlement_Description: Earliest mention in 830, in a tenth century copy.

name: null
Harbour_Description: Philipp the Bold permitted the construction of a harbour in a remainder of the creek that separated the former island Testerep from the mainland in 1445-1446. This harbour was accessible from the west. During the reconstruction of the city into a fortress and the ensuing siege of Oostende by Spanish troops (1601-1604) the dunes were dug through and a new harbour developed east of the town.

name: Middelharnis
Fair_Description: In 1567 (April 8) Middelharnis obtained from king Philip II a fair during eight days, starting the second day after St. Laurens (August 10) and a free weekly market on Saturrday. A fine harbour is also mentioned. In 1569 (June 26) the lords of Middelharnis ('de heeren en heerschappen van Sinte Michiels in Putte dat men noempt Middelhernisse') got thes rights from the king but the fair is now dated Saturday after St. Laurensday, during eight days.

name: Kirkkonummi
Settlement_Description: <b>Inn:</b> The priest, Lars, was compensated from the yearly taxes because he had served food, drink and accommodation to travellers.

name: Piikkiö
Settlement_Description:
Piikkiö parish was established in the 2nd quarter of the 13th c., and the church area has had some activity also in the late iron age. Medieval wooden church was located southeast from the present church built in 1753-1755. 

<b>Inn:</b> An inn might be located by the church. Churches usually had taverns in the Middle Ages and 16th-17th-centuries. Most likely both the Piikkiö viicar and the parish constable (fi: nimismies, sw: länsman) offered food, drink, and accommodation to travellers. An official inn is mentioned in 1646 in Hadvala village close to the church.

name: null
Lock_Description: A second lock in Plassendale was built in connection to the newly dug canal Plassendale-Nieuwpoort in 1638-1641.

name: null
Toll_Description: The toll of Greifswald formerly levied on the flooded bridge between Gristow and Frätow was moved to the bridge between Kowall and Mesekenhagen, that was newly built in 1397. Citizens from Anklam were exempted from the toll in 1549.
Bridge_Description: The bridge between Kowall and Mesekenhagen was constructed in 1397 as part of a new road between Greifswald and Stralsund, after the previous connection between Gristow and Frätow had been flooded.

name: Wiehe
Settlement_Description: Probably a Frankish castle or domain around which a village developed, first mentioned in 775/786. Mention around 998 in the Breviarium Sancti Lulli. It is referred to as civitas in 998, which doesn't make it a town at this time, but shows its importance and possible fortification.
Town_Description: Mention of citizens of Wiehe in 1297. Market and other town-like privileges are granted in 1320. In 1394 the town rights are confirmed by landgrave Balthasar, so they may have existed as early as the beginning of the 14th century. The town right was based on that of Eisenach.
Toll_Description: Secondary station of safe conduct ('Beigeleitsstelle') of Eckartsberga, as mentioned in the regulations of safe conduct from 1550.

name: Paimio
Settlement_Description:
Permanent agricultural settlement in Paimio (sw. Pemar) area goes back to the Iron Age. The medieval parish organisation in Finland Proper dates to the early 13th century with precursors in the latter half of the 12th century. The earliest parish church of St James was located on the western bank of the river opposite the mouth of Vähäjoki river. A new church was built in the 1680s on the route of the Great Costal Road. The graveyard of St James remained in use until the 1720s.

<b>Inn:</b> First Paimio parish constable (fi: nimismies, sw: länsman) is mentioned in year 1553. Parish constables were obliged to keep a tavern in late 16th c. and early 17th c. Also the Paimio priest could offer food, drink, and accommodation to travellers. Paimio parish constables were usually appointed from wealthy farms by the Great Coastal road. In the 16th and 17tn c., they usually lived in the eastern parts of the parish, since they were inbetween Piikkiö and Halikko parish constables.
Fair_Description: In Finland Proper several local fairs existed in the 17th century, most of which consisted of trade with fish, grain, and other necessities amongst the peasants, occasionally of cattle sold to Turku merchants. When the burghers of Turku applied for their closure in 1672 such annual fairs were organised on Midsummer (24 June) in Masku, on St James the younger (25 July) in Rymättylä (sw. Rimito), Paimio (Sw. Pemar) and Kemiö (sw. Kimito), on St Olaf (29 July) in Nauvo (sw. Nagu), Lemu (sw. Lemo) and Sauvo (sw. Sagu), on Assumption of Mary (15 August) in Nousiainen (sw. Nousis) and on St Matteus (21 September) in Taivassalo (sw. Töfsala). Most of the fairs are apparently of medieval origin and took place on the feasts of local parish church such as the fair of St James in Paimio.

name: Eupen
Fair_Description: In 1544 (June 15) emperor Charles V granted two free fairs to the village Eupen in the Land of 'Lemborch'.
Toll_Description: A toll station belonging to the duchy of Limburg appears in accounts from 1389 onwards. The revenues were low at the time due to warfare. A fee of 2 sol. for each horse for safe conduct is attested in 1468.

name: null
Toll_Description: A ducal toll levied on the bridge near Gristow was acquired by Greifswald in 1375. In 1397, it was moved to the new bridge near Kowall because the old bridge had been flooded.
Bridge_Description: A bridge and causeway between Gristow and Frätow had been flooded before 1397: in that year, a new bridge was built near Kowall.

name: Monschau
Toll_Description: A toll station of the duke of Jülich is attested in 1492. Tariffs or revenues are not known.

name: Gernrode
Settlement_Description: In 960 margrave Leo founded a convent, which is first mentioned in 961. A settlement developed next to it and is first mentioned in a charter in 1136. Characterised as borough ('Weichbild') in 1416.
Town_Description: Town rights were granted in 1519 by abbess Anna of Plauen.

name: Vehmaa
Settlement_Description: <b>Inn:</b> A tavern might be located by the medieval church. Churches usually had taverns in the Middle Ages and 16th-17th-centuries. Vehmaa vicarage also served travellers. Villagers complained in the late 16th c. that there were a lot of soldiers travelling by the road. During <i>kelirikko</i>, the "breaking" of the road in muddy seasons in spring and autumn, the soldiers stay for tens of days and wait for good travelling conditions, and the villagers have to give them food during the wait.

name: Kaitarainen
Settlement_Description: <b>Inn:</b> An inn was established in Kaitarainen in 1634, and Tuomas Heikinpoika Sipilä was appointed as the innkeeper. Tuomas was old at the time, and he had served as a parish constable (fi: nimismies, sw: länsman) in 1603-1611. The Nousiainen inn stayed in Kaitarainen village until the 18th c., the office circulating between farms.

name: Rheinbach
Toll_Description: In 1343, Beatrix von Schleiden, as Lady of Rheinbach, levied a land toll and a fee for safe conduct on land. In 1345, the toll fell to the Archbishop of Cologne. Horse toll and fee for safe conduct are recorded in 1389/93. In 1396, 2 to 3 alb. per horse had to be paid, depending on the load. In 1422, an additional 1 gulden had to be paid for each foder of wine. In 1389/93, the horse toll and the fee for safe conduct brought in an average of about 497 mark annually. For further tariffs and revenues see source. In 1457 Hilberath was a secondary toll station.

name: Vuolijoki
Settlement_Description: <b>Inn:</b> An inn was established in Vuolijoki in 1634, and Simo Tirinen from Tirilä was appointed as the innkeeper. The inn might have later been relocated in Piipponen farm.

name: Lieto
Settlement_Description:
Lieto parish dates from the early 13th c., and the first wooden church was likely constructed soon after that. 

<b>Inn:</b> A tavern might be located by the church. Churches usually had taverns in the Middle Ages and 16th-17th-centuries. Teijula and Krouvi ("tavern") farms hosted the tavern by the church.

In 1550s, the parish constable's house was located in Pinomäki village in the east. Parish constables (fi: nimismies, sw: länsman, eng. sheriff) were obliged to keep a tavern in late 16th c. The parish constable is mentioned in Jaakko Teitti's road description in 1556 as a possible place for a bailiff (fi. vouti, sw. fogde). 

In 1642, an inn was established in Karvala village, which is located south from the road. Nuutti Niilonpoika was then the innkeeper.

name: Pursinen
Settlement_Description: <b>Inn:</b> An inn was established in Pursinen in 1650.

name: Nummi
Settlement_Description: <b>Inn:</b> Nousiainen parish constable was periodically located in Nummi. Parish constables (fi: nimismies, sw: länsman) were obliged to keep a tavern in late 16th c. and early 17th c. Other places for the office were Kaitarainen village in the north and Sontamala (Santamala) village ca. 1 km upstream. The first known parish constable from Nousiainen is Pentti Eerikinpoika Vehka from Sontamala, mentioned in 1583.

name: Laitila
Settlement_Description: <b>Inn:</b> Laitila vicarage served travellers by the common road. In 1569, travellers were accommodated at vicar Erik's. In the early 1630s, the vicar Petrus Bartholomae complained how he had to serve travellers every day, also those who travelled on their own account and not the crown's. He was given an abandoned farm for his troubles. There was also a transport organiser (sw. skjutsrättare, fi. kyytirättäri) in Laitila in the 1630s.

name: Kuloinen
Settlement_Description: <b>Inn:</b> An inn was established in Kuloinen in 1634, and Mikko Niilonpoika was appointed as the innkeeper. He lived in Lukkarla farm, which had served earlier as a parish constable (fi: nimismies, sw: länsman). Kuloinen remained a traditional place for Raisio inn.

name: Pyöli
Settlement_Description: <b>Inn:</b> Pyöli inn might date from earlier, but in the late 16th c., Klemetti Heikinpoika was the innkeeper. He was appointed later as the parish constable (fi: nimismies, sw: länsman) as well. Also Mikko Antinpoika held a tavern in Pyöli in 1600-1602.

name: null
Harbour_Description: When Ostend was reconstructed into a fortress during the Dutch revolt and the Spanish siege of the city (1601-1064), the dunes were dug through and the sea flooded the land around the city, creating a sea arm east of town: the Geule. Here a new harbour developed, replacing the old harbour northwest of town.

name: Wilster
Settlement_Description: Settlement on the shore of the Wilsterau, where a church belonging to the Hamburg cathedral chapter is first mentioned in 1164.
Town_Description: Count Gerhard II of Holstein granted Lübeck town law in 1282. The town became a significant sea trade centre in the 16th century.
Fair_Description: At the end of the 14th century one annual fair is mentioned in Wilster. Heinrich Rantzau mentions two fairs on the days of St Bartholomew (24 August) and St Dionysius (9 October) in his 1597 description of Schleswig and Holstein. Of these fairs, the one on St Bartholomew was probably the oldest, being the feast day of the patron saint of the local church. Two additional horse fairs on 23 May and 6 December were granted in 1680.

name: null
Harbour_Description: Soon after the foundation of the town, it developed into an important harbour on the Baltic Sea. Harbour regulations remain from 1278, which among others mention connections with England and Flanders. From the mid-13th century, the roads leading from the town towards the waterfront were extended by wooden piers that served the (un)loading of ships. After construction of a stone town wall in 1372, an 80m wide harbour district developed between the wall and the waterfront.

name: Poitsila
Settlement_Description: <b>Inn:</b> Vehkalahti parish constable was in Poitsila village from mid-16th century. It is mentioned as a place for overnight accommodation in the travel account of Duke Johan of Finland from 1555. In 1598, the parish constable was moved to Salmenkylä village in the north of Savilahti bay. Poitsila is located by the winter road.

name: Stralsund
Settlement_Description: Fishing settlement in Slavic times, German settlers since ca. 1200. First mentioned when it became a town in 1234.
Town_Description: Prince Wizlaw I of Rügen granted the same town privileges as Rostock (Lübeck town law) in 1234. A new town is already mentioned in 1256, and both parts of town were fortified with a wall between 1261 and 1300. The town quickly became significant as a trading centre on the Baltic Sea and as member of the Hanse.
Toll_Description: A toll was levied at the town gates and in the harbour. Originally in hands of the lord of Rügen, it was leased by the town in 1272 and in later years.
Staple_Description: Staple for stockfish from Bergen; in 1446 it was stipulated that members of the Hanse were only allowed to export flour, malt, and other victuals to Bergen if they brought fish from Bergen back with them to Lübeck, Wismar, Rostock or Stralsund.

name: null
Bridge_Description: In the regulations of safe conduct of Colditz, a bridge fee is mentioned. The station of safe conduct is especially important for cattle trade from Poland; every year toll was paid on thousands of cows and oxen.

name: Puotila
Settlement_Description: <b>Inn:</b> Vehmaa parish constable was periodically located in Puotila. Parish constables (fi: nimismies, sw: länsman) were obliged to keep a tavern in late 16th c. and early 17th c. In 1584, the office moved permanently to Vinkkilä.

name: Worbis
Settlement_Description: First mentioned in 1162. In 1238 the village next to the castle is mentioned as market settlement (Forense Worueze).
Town_Description: First mentioned as civitas around 1255. The acquisition of town rights possibly already occurred before that year. Between 1381 and 1574 the town rights were restricted, when the town was pawned.
Fair_Description: Archbishop Daniel Brendel of Homburg granted the town two fairs and a cattle fair in 1576. In 1660 the town was granted another fair on Sunday after St. Margaret's day.
Toll_Description: Worbis has been a toll station and station of safe conduct since the 13th century. According to toll regulations from 1661, the toll was collected at the lower town gate ('Untertor').

name: Saaresmäki
Settlement_Description:
Permanent agricultural settlement in Paltamo and Oulunjärvi area dates to the colonisation from Savolax in the 1550s. The administrative centre of the area was Royal Manor close to Vuohenginkoski stream in Kajaaninjoki river in 1555–58. Oulujärvi parish was founded in 1559.
Winter and portage way from Savo to Oulujärvi and Oulu via Vieremä and Saaresmäki is mentioned in 1557
<b>Inn:</b> An inn was established in Saaresmäki in 1642, and Perttu Pussinen was appointed as the innkeeper.
Fair_Description: The burghers of Oulu were granted the right of two annual fairs in Kajaneborg parish in 1625. Of these the summer fair was to be held at midsummer (24 June) in Paltaniemi and the winter fair on 15 December in Saaresmäki (Särismäki). It is unknown if the Saaresmäki fair took place.

name: Plassendale
Settlement_Description: After Ostend was taken by the Sea Beggars in 1572, the Spanish authorities built a fortress around the lock in Plassendale in 1585, the "Sterckte van Plassendale". A small hamlet developed inside the fortress, which housed among others a garrison, a lock master and his servants, and a brewery.
Lock_Description: In Plassendale there existed a boat ramp ('overdracht') that facilitated the shipping between the harbour of Ostend, which was built in 1445-1446, and the Ieperlee river between Bruges and Ypres. Here vessels could be hauled over the dam that separated both waterways. In 1623, when a new canal was built between Plassendale and Ostend, the boat ramp was replaced by a large lock.

name: Vahantaka
Settlement_Description: <b>Inn:</b> Laitila parish constable was located in Vahantaka after the 1620s. Parish constables (fi: nimismies, sw: länsman) were obliged to keep a tavern in late 16th c. and early 17th c. Erkki Tapaninpoika served as the parish constable and innkeeper, and his son Tapani Erkinpoika and sonson Erkki Tapaninpoika both continued innkeeping.

name: Koivuniemi
Settlement_Description: <b>Inn:</b> An inn was established in Koivuniemi in 1639, and Simo Jaakonpoika Isoperä was appointed as the innkeeper. The inn served travellers by the winter road across Längelmävesi lake.

name: Mäkiäinen
Settlement_Description: <b>Inn:</b> Mäkiäinen farm was appointed as the parish constable (fi: nimismies, sw: länsman) and inn in 1636. It served as an inn until 1680s.

name: Naumburg (Saale)
Settlement_Description: A castle was built by margrave Ekkehard around 1000, it is first mentioned in 1012. Naumburg was given to the bishopric of Zeitz in 1028, soon after which the episcopal residence moved to Naumburg and formed the basis for the town’s initial development.
Town_Description: In 1033, merchants who moved from Kleinjena to Naumburg were granted the freedom of trade and the inheritable possession of their homesteads. This record is regarded as the oldest record of a German town foundation. Referred to as civitas in 1142. A privilege for fortification of the town was granted in 1287, a council is attested in 1305. The town developed into an important market for the long-distance trade in the 14th and 15th century. A trading house was built in 1379. Jews were allowed to settle in the city in 1410. Between 1432 and 1433 Naumburg was a member of the Hanse. The council bought judicial sovereignty in 1486.
Fair_Description: Fairs in Naumburg are first mentioned in 1278, but probably date back to the early days of the town in the 11th century. The most important fair was the fair on St Peter and Paul's Day, which attracted an interregional public since the 15th century. In the 16th century, the Naumburg fairs led to heavy resistance from Leipzig, who had acquired an exclusive fair privilege within 15 miles around the city in 1507, inside which the city of Naumburg was located. The Peter and Paul's fair survived these quarrels, but not a second fair on Holy Thursday, which was intended to be moved to Sexagesima in 1514. Heavy resistance from Leipzig led to its ultimate revocation in 1667. Instead another fair on Monday after Palm Sunday was allowed, but without extended privileges for foreign merchants. It is known until today as the Topfmarkt and was moved to Friday after Easter in 1894.
Toll_Description: In 1397 the bishop abstained from the toll in Naumburg in favour of the town. Twenty years later the salt toll was given to the town by the bishop. The extensive toll registry of Naumburg from 1567 lists all the wares for which one had to pay a fee on the market.

name: Ellrich
Settlement_Description: First mentioned in 876. The oldest part of the settlement is probably to be found in the North, where a church was built in the 9th century and remains of fortifications were found. East of it the current town developed.
Town_Description: In the 13th century the settlement was probably fortified and had a town-like character. It is mentioned as 'opidum' in 1229, and as town in 1292. In 1315 a town wall is attested.

name: Längelmäki
Settlement_Description: <b>Inn:</b> Count Per Brahe the Younger, Governor-General of Finland, stopped in Längelmäki village when returning to Turku in winter 1640.

name: Wehnder Warte
Settlement_Description: Watchtower in the defensive enclosure ('landwehr') of Duderstadt near Wehnde, built in 1413.

name: Siemerode
Settlement_Description: The settlement was first mentioned in 1055. In the 15th and 16th century the settlement was deserted, it is unclear when it was resettled. In 1693 the "parochia in Simeroda" is mentioned, which probably means that it was resettled before that year.

name: Dornburg
Settlement_Description: The settlement developed from a Carolingian castle at the border with Slavic territories in the 9th century. In the 10th and 11th century a royal court with village, first mentioned in 937.
Town_Description: In the course of the 13th century Dornburg developed into a town with Saxonian rights. Referred to as town ('stat') in 1343. Merchants are mentioned in 1344, but the economic significance of the town remained limited to a local level.

name: Apolda
Settlement_Description: First mention in 1119. The settlement consisted of a castle and adjoining village.
Town_Description: First referred to as civitas in 1308. Elevation to town by the nobles of Apolda, who died out in the 14th century. Afterwards the Wettin family were the town lords, although the archbishop of Mainz held some claims to it until 1666.

name: Kirchhasel (Saale)
Toll_Description: In the 1530ies, merchants coming from Saalfeld are taken into schwarzburgish safe conduct at the border to Schwarza an accompanied through Rudolstadt up to the border stone at Kirchhasel/Etzelbach.

name: null
Bridge_Description: A bridge across two branches of the Saale river at Dorndorf was built after 1257, when indulgences were granted to those who made donations for the building of a bridge in Dorndorf, upon request of the abbot and convent of Pforte.

name: Nienburg (Saale)
Settlement_Description: First mentioned in 961. Attested as the centre of a castle district ('Burgward') in 975. In the same year Thankmarsfelde monastery was relocated to Nienburg. In the Early Middle Ages already an important place on the road between Magdeburg and Halle.
Town_Description: Mention as "urbs" in 1233. The mint of Hagenröde and the market of Staßfurt, both in possession of Nienburg monastery, had already been moved here in 1035. In 1560 the monastery was secularised.
Toll_Description: According to regulations of safe conduct ('Geleitsordnung') from 1563, a fee was due in Nienburg for animals, barrels, wine, beer from Zerbst and wagons of corn. Bernburg was exempted from safe conduct payments.

name: Triptis
Settlement_Description: First mention in 1212 when a nunnery was moved from Triptis to Zwickau. The counts of Lobdeburg-Arnshaugk can be seen as the founders of the market settlement which developed next to a castle.
Town_Description: Triptis acquired market rights with a weekly market in 1367. First mention as civitas in 1378. The counts of Lobdeburg-Arnshaugk probably elevated the village to town at the end of the 13th century.
Toll_Description: A station of safe conduct was based in Triptis. Revenues are known from 1484, mostly together with the safe conduct of Mittelpöllnitz. They indicate a limited regional traffic. From 1568 until 1688 the town owned the rights of safe conduct.

name: Schwarza
Fair_Description: 1495 Schwarza is granted the privilege to hold three fairs and to fortify the town by Emperor Maximilian.
Toll_Description: In the 1530s, merchants coming from Saalfeld are taken into safe conduct of Schwarzburg at the border to Schwarza and accompanied through Rudolstadt up to the border stone at Kirchhasel/Etzelbach.

name: Kaustio
Settlement_Description: <b>Inn:</b> An inn was established in Kaustio in 1650.

name: Camburg
Settlement_Description: Camburg is first mentioned (uncertainly) in 1030, but was probably already a castle in Carolingian times. Since the 10th century it became a comital manor with an adjoining village, which developed into a market borough. It was located at the road from Nuremberg to Naumburg via Jena. In the 12th century, there was a chapter of canons in Camburg.
Town_Description: Foundation of a planned town in the first half of the 12th century. Citizens ('cives') are mentioned in 1149, and in 1349 the settlement was characterised as oppidum. In 1373 Camburg had Naumburg town rights. In 1378 it is first characterized as town.
Fair_Description: Since the 13th century a fair on St Lawrence's day (8th August) is known in Camburg.
Toll_Description: Since 1259 a toll station for rafting is known on the Saale. Revenues for safe conduct are recorded since 1479, with the revenues of the rafting toll separately indicated since 1547.

name: Asselt
Toll_Description: A toll on sailing ships is attested here in 1275. In 1381 it was sold as part of the seigniory Swalmen held by a canon of St. Servaas in Maastricht to his cousin Diderick van Oost. In 1416 it was leased by the town Roermond.  In 1445 it is said that the toll on the Meuse in Asselt, belonging to the family Van Oest, is now levied at Kessel. In 1464-77 the toll is back in Asselt. In 1501 and 1545 the toll is a fief of the count of Buren. In 1555 the town-toll of Hampssen (belonging to Roermond) and half the toll of Kessel were levied here. The toll of Kessel was then said not to be property of the emperor but over hundreds of years of Roermond.

name: Monninkylä
Settlement_Description: <b>Inn:</b> Monninkylä alehouse served travellers by the road. In 1622, a farmer from Askola attacked the parish constable (fi: nimismies, sw: länsman) Yrjö Lappi, when he came to get horses. In 1697, an official inn was established.

name: Hyvinkää
Settlement_Description: <b>Inn:</b> In 1585, Nurmijärvi assistant priest complained how five farmers from Hyvinkää have become poor and cannot pay their taxes, since they have to give rides and food to travellers and soldiers. Hyvinkää inn might have been established after the complaint or in 1622 at the latest.

name: Linnansilta
Bridge_Description: The Castle bridge of the Great Coastal Road traversing the sound at Viborg Castle is first cited in 1563 when it was rebuilt. The earliest bridge on the site may date to the first organisation of the maintenance of the Great Coastal Road as a uniform land route between Turku and Viborg in the 1340s and 1360s. Since 1563 the bridge was maintained by Äyräpää and Jääski judicial districts, in 1600 also Ranta. The bridge was rebuild in 1600 and again in the 1670s.The bridge later also known as Turku bridge was the longest bridge in the entire route of the Great Coastal Road. The bridge is included in the 1655 map over the surroundings of Viipuri town in the range of two Swedish mil (ca. 21,4 km).

name: Holstenbrücke
Bridge_Description: A bridge across the Trave near the gate Holstentor is first mentioned in 1216, but possibly already existed in 1191. It was renewed around 1550 with four arches and steep slopes. In 1853/4 a new flatter bridge was built and widened in 1934.

name: Merikarvia
Settlement_Description: <b>Inn:</b> Until mid-17th c., Merikarvia church and its predecessor, St. Birgitta chapel, was located very close to the shore. There has probably been a tavern near the church in the junction of winter and summer ways of the Northern Coastal Road. Farmers in Ylikylä and Alakylä villages organised transports during the Middle Ages. Sten Sture sr, regent of Sweden, stayed in Merikarvia in 1491 when travelling through Ostrobothnia. Also Ture Pedersson Bielke, Swedish nobleman and castellan of St. Olaf's Castle in Savo, stopped to change horses by the St. Birgitta chapel in 1557. In the 17th century, the vicar provided accommodation for travellers, and in 1642, vicar Olavi was appointed as the innkeeper.

name: Vartsala
Settlement_Description: <b>Inn:</b> An inn might be located by the St. John Chapel at the seashore. Churches and chapels usually had taverns in the Middle Ages and 16th-17th-centuries. In 1650, an inn was established in Southern Vartsala by the Great Postal Road.

name: Pikkalan silta
Bridge_Description: The Pikkala bridge, which led over the Siuntiojoki river (sw. Sjundeå) on the Great Coastal Road, is mentioned in 1555, when there was a farm next to it (wid Landzbroen) in the village of Sillanpäby (Bridge-end village). The bridge and the village existed as early as 1472, when "Herman j Broo" was a member of the jury in Siuntio parish court. The bridge existed in 1561, but it had been replaced with ferry some time before 1573 and possibly as late as 1612. The bridge is mentioned again in 1617. The length of the bridge was in 1782 a total of 97,25 ells (ca. 57,8, m). In the 17th century the maintenance of the bridge was split with, Inkoo (sw. Ingå), Lohja (sw. Lojo) and Kirkkonummi (sw. Kyrkslätt) parishes. After 1693 Lohja was replaced with Siuntio. Since Lohja made in the 1550s part of the Eastern judicial district of Raasepori bailiwick while the other two were in the western judicial district, the organisation of the maintenance of the bridge goes back to the 1550s, possibly even to the first half of the 15th century when Siuntio was split from Lohja into an independent parish. From 1584 at the latest, the Bobäck Market, which had been held at the end of Espoonlahti along the Great Coastal Road, was moved in 1723 to the Pikkala Bridge, where the market day was the Apostle Matthew (21 September).

name: Burgtorbrücke
Bridge_Description: A wooden draw bridge across the ditch in front of the castle gate (Burgtor) existed in 1241. The current much larger bridge of the same name was only built in 1900, when a canal was dug through the peninsula that separated the Wakenitz and Trave rivers.

name: Crimmitschau
Settlement_Description: First mentioned in 1221. The settlement was founded as a planned settlement around 1200.
Town_Description: The settlement was expanded into a town at the end of the 13th century. It received Schmölln town privileges in 1414.

name: Svébořice
Toll_Description: The toll station of Niemes/Mimoň was moved to Svébořice/Schwabitz in the 17th century, when wagoners started circumventing Mimoň on the route between Zittau and Prague. A toll house is first attested in 1659.

name: null
Harbour_Description: The harbour for sea-going vessels in Lübeck was located along the shore of the Trave river north of the Holsten bridge (Untertrave). The oldest harbour remains date from the 12th century and were located between the Braun- and Mengstraße. In the 13th century the harbour area was extended along the entire western edge of town. A crane for loading vessels did not exist until the 19th century, but a crane on the opposite shore was used in shipbuilding in the 16th century.

name: Rudolstadt
Settlement_Description: First mentioned in 775-786. It developed from a Slavic settlement. 2 castles are attested in 1264.
Town_Description: The foundation of the town probably took place at the end of the 13th century or at the beginning of the 14th century by the counts of Orlamünde. The denomination 'town' can be found since 1326.
Fair_Description: Two fairs are known before 1404, another since 1465.
Toll_Description: First mention of a street toll in 1397, which is probably collected at the old gate. Count Günther of Schwarzburg is permitted to collect two pennies from each wagon and one Meißen groschen of a heavy wagon with merchants for the protection of the roads.</br>A toll table from 1638 remains, when the toll was already Schwarzburgian. (ThStA Rudolstadt, Kanzlei Arnstadt 1129, p. 91 f.)

name: Sarvilahti
Settlement_Description: <b>Inn:</b> There were two alehouses in Sarvilahti in 1556. Their owners were Envald Andersson and Bertil Larsson Sparff, whose alehouse was located in the Krogars farm (Tavern). It continued to serve as a tavern until 1847.

name: Pitkäsilta (Viipuri)
Bridge_Description: The Long bridge (fi. Pitkäsilta) on the Great Coastal Road between later Sorvali and Neitsytniemi suburban areas in Viipuri is first cited in 1548. The earliest bridge on the site may however date to the first organisation of the maintenance of the Great Coastal Road as a uniform land route between Turku and Viborg in the 1340s and 1360s. The bridge was in the 17th century maintained by Lapvesi and Jääski judicial districts. The bridge is included in the 1655 map over the surroundings of Viipuri town in the range of two Swedish mil (ca. 21,4 km).

name: Kuukaupin lautta
Ferry_Description: The ferry site at Vuoksi river (Kuukauppi) is first cited in 1626 together with another ferry next to Jääski church. A third ferry is cited 1638 in Siitola. Annual tax collected from Jääski judicial district for the Vuoksi ferryman is cited in 1565-66 and 1580. Apparently of late 14th century or 15th century origin, the oldest of the three ferry sites was Kuukauppi, which was maintained by the whole judicial district and located on an important common road between Viipuri and Saviniemi Royal Manor. The road led eventually already in the Middle Ages to Käkisalmi (sw. Kexholm, r. Korela) town and fortress on the Novgorodian and Russian side of the border in the South-West corner of Ladoga lake. The road was improved several times after the peace of Stolbova in 1617 when the Swedish realm annexed Käkisalmi province.

name: Bad Blankenburg
Settlement_Description: First mention in 1148. First mention of the castle in 1280.
Town_Description: The settlement is first referred to as opidum in 1323, and as civitas in 1330, but it probably already developed as a town in the middle of the 13th century. A council constitution is attested since the end of the 14th century.

name: Schleiz
Settlement_Description: The village originated from a Slavic settlement. It is first mentioned in 1232.
Town_Description: Next to the old settlement, a new town with a castle developed after 1284. In 1297 it is first characterised as town ('civitas'). A fortification of the new town is mentioned in 1359, a city hall in 1397. The old and new town were united in 1482 and received common statutes in 1492, which were predominantly based on the town law of Gera.
Fair_Description: A free fair on Wednesday after St James's day was granted in 1505.

name: Saalfeld (Saale)
Settlement_Description: Saalfeld developed from several settlements. A Carolingian royal manor is first mentioned in 899, which had its origins probably in the 8th century and was followed by an Ottonian castle. A Benedictine monastery was founded in 1071, to which belonged a market settlement around the Alter Markt ('old market'); a market toll is mentioned here in 1125. Another market settlement with a church of St Nicholas developed next to a manor of the archbishop of Cologne in the 12th century.
Town_Description: A planned town was founded in the late 12th century and first mentioned in 1198 as "villa regia". In 1208 it is first referred to as "civitas". A town seal appears in 1286, and a council is mentioned in 1289. The oldest known town privileges date from c. 1326. Market rights were transmitted from the old market to the new town in 1350, and inhabitants of the old market settlement received citizen rights of Saalfeld in 1363, although the settlement was only officially merged with the town in 1863.
Toll_Description: A market and a market toll are mentioned in the records in 1125. </br>An extensive regulation of safe conduct of 1728 remains, which also mentiones the toll on the Saale river.

name: Schalkau
Town_Description: As early as 1317 Schalkau is referred to as town. In 1441 also referred to as borough ('Flecken'). In 1362 landgrave Frederick the Stern granted Schalkau town and market rights modelled after Rodach and Neustadt rights.

name: Keltin lautta
Ferry_Description: The Northern and Southern routes of Upper Viipuri Road were organised into a common road between Viipuri and Häme castles at the latest in the first quarter of the 15th century, but the organisation of the maintenance may date to mid-14th century. The Northern route via Vuolenkoski appears to have been more important in the 16th century, whereas in the 17th the Southern road via Keltti was the main route. The ferry site in Keltti dates very likely to the early 15th century or late 14th. In 1556 king Gustaf I ordered either of the routes demolished, apparently without consecutions. A winterway crossed the river at the Keltti ferry site in 1617. The site was in use until 1812, when a new ferry site was introduced in Valkeala Alakylä.

name: Crock
Settlement_Description: The settlement of Crock is first mentioned (uncertainly) in 1152. On the Irmelsberg north of the village stood the church of St. Vitus, which was a destination of pilgrimage since the early Middle Ages. A late Gothic church replaced the original chapel in 1489.

name: Ranis
Settlement_Description: First mention in 1167-1180. The settlement consisted of a castle from Frankish times with suburbium.
Town_Description: The exact date of acquisition of town rights is not known, probably during the reign of the counts of Schwarzburg (1206-1389). First mention as town in 1381. Bylaws are known from 1590.

name: Gehren (Ilmenau)
Settlement_Description: Church village with knightly manor in the 13th and 14th century, first mentioned in 1299. Market borough ('Marktflecken') in the 16th century. Later Gehren owned town-like rights and facilities, it was granted town status in 1855.
Toll_Description: Regulations of safe conduct remain for the district of Gehren from the 16th century (ThStA Rudolstadt, Kanzlei Arnstadt 1129, p. 93).

name: Gräfenthal
Settlement_Description: First uncertain mention in 1182, first certain mention in 1248. The counts of Orlamünde owned a castle in Gräfenthal.
Town_Description: First mentioned as town in 1337. Town privileges are known from 1378, and bylaws were granted by the counts of Orlamünde in 1412. Metal works ('Saigerhütte') were founded in 1462, which confirms the town's significant location at the so-called copper road ('Kupferweg').
Toll_Description: A toll station at the route of safe conduct Coburg - Saalfeld is attested since 1446. It was a secondary station of safe conduct of Saalfeld. The regulations of safe conduct for Saalfeld from 1728 explicitly mention a road toll that had to be paid in Gräfenthal together with the fees of safe conduct.

name: Raseborg
Settlement_Description: The permanent agricultural settlement in the Karjaa (sw. Karis) region dates back to the Iron Age with additional intense Swedish colonisation on the coast in the late 12th and early 13th centuries. The parish organisation in Western Nyland dates to the early 13th century. The location of the earliest parish church is unknown. The later location, less than a kilometre northeast of Karjaa Maansilta bridge, dates to the beginning of the 15th century. A stone church was built in the late 1460s. <b>Raseborg Castle (sw. Raseborg)</b> is first mentioned in surviving sources in 1378, but it did not exist in 1373. The castle was founded as a new administrative centre of Western Uusimaa (sw. Västra Nyland) by the seneschal and magnate Bo Jonsson (Grip) who was ordained as the headman of Finland in 1371 and controlled all castles and bailiwicks in Finland and in large part of Sweden proper in 1374–86. The castle was expanded and modernized several times from the second quarter of the 15th century to the beginning of the 16th century. The castle suffered damage during the Danish occupation in 1521-23 but remained an administrative centre until 1553. The castle again served as the centre of a small bailiwick assembled from the parishes of Karjaa, Tenhola (sw. Tenala) and Pohja (sw. Pojo) in 1556–58. Originally located on a rocky islet deep in the archipelago, the site emerged unfavourable became difficult already in the early 16th century because of land uplift. Abandoned in 1558, the administration of the bailiff was first transferred from the castle to the nearby Royal manor of Raseborg and from there to the new Royal manor of Tammisaari (sw. Ekenäs) in 1560. <b>The Royal manor of Raseborg</b> active in 1558–60 was a former grange of the castle. From 1569 to 1680, Western Nyland made part of the County of Raseborg, the centre of which was in Tammisaari. A community of merchants and burghers attached to the castle and in the supervision of its castellans living in Snappertuna and Karjaa existed as early as in 1414 and is cited as a <b>town</b> in 1451 but appears never to have established a magistrate of its own and did not develop into a town proper in the Middle Ages. In 1528 the castellan Erik Fleming translocated the merchant community to Tammisaari (r. Ekenäs), where he founded a town which then got its privileges from King Gustav I in 1546. In 1682, a local annual fair was held in Snappertuna, the day of which was in 1694 Apostle Bartholomeus (24 August). Before Raseborg, the possible administrational centre of Western Nyland may have been <b>Junkarsborg Castle</b> some 15 km northeast of Maansilta bridge in Karjaa on an island in Mustionjoki (sw. Svartå) river with documented activity from the second quarter of the 14th century to the beginning of the 15th.

name: Großbreitenbach
Town_Description: Since the 16th century the settlement was a market borough ('Marktflecken'). By the end of the 16th century it was also sometimes referred to as town, but town rights were only acquired in 1855.
Fair_Description: In 1586 three fairs and cattle markets are mentioned.

name: Jutilan eli Saarelan silta
Bridge_Description: Jutila aka Saarela bridge in Viipuri parish on the common road between Viipuri town and Saviniemi Royal Manor was of old maintained by Ranta judicial district, but after the bridge was destroyed by flooding in 1599, Jääski judicial district was ordained to help with the rebuilding. After a judicial process in 1645 the duty of Jääski remained and the parishes of Jääski, Kirvu and Antrea took part of the maintenance of the bridge as late as in the end of the 19th century. The bridge is included in the 1655 map over the surroundings of Viipuri town in the range of two Swedish mils (ca. 21,4 km).

name: Kirkonkylän silta (Pyhtää)
Bridge_Description: Pyhtää Church bridge over Pyhtäänhaara on the Great Coastal Road is first cited in 1555, when Jakob Teitt included it in his map of the bridges in Kymijoki delta area. The earliest bridge on the site may date to the first organisation of the maintenance of the Great Coastal Road as a uniform land route between Turku and Viborg in the 1340s and 1360s. In the late 17th century Pyhtää Church bridge was together with Ahvenkoski Greater bridge (fi. Isosilta), Sutela Larger bridge (fi. Isosilta) and Kymijoki Huumanhaara bridge financed by a money tax from the judicial districts of Viipuri province and Porvoo area.

name: Turku
Settlement_Description: Permanent agricultural settlement in Aurajoki river area goes back to the Iron Age. According to the recent archaeological excavations and historical research the town of Turku was established as a sworn community of burghers with a permanent town council in the beginning of the 14th century on the site of an 13th century farm or small village in the area.
Town_Description:
The town of Turku (sw. Åbo) was established in ca. 1310 as a sworn community of burghers with a permanent town council through a joint project of the bishop, the crown and merchants, in which the bishop's seat was moved from Koroinen to Turku, the crown let built a castle at the mouth of the Aurajoki River, and a merchant town was founded in the area downstream of the Cathedral. The founding of Turku Castle dates to the 1280s and it is first mentioned in 1308. The consecration of the cathedral took place either in the year 1300 or 1292–96, but the years 1309–20 are also possible. The community of burghers its seal are first mentioned in 1309, the town council and its seal in 1324. The church of the Dominican convent at the downstream end of the town area existed in 1309. When Novgorod invaded Turku in 1318, they called the city Ljuderev after the then castellan Lyder van Kyren, which may tell that the name of the city was not yet widely known. According to a Dutch merchant who visited Turku in 1681, the town was founded in 1310, which may be based on some information about the early privileges of the town. King Gustav I confirmed the privileges in 1525, but the charter together with older charters and all registers of the town were destroyed in fire after that. The privileges were again confirmed in 1569 and 1607. The town area had expanded to the north side of the Aurajoki River already in the early 1400s and grew towards the castle during the 17th century. The bridge over Aurajoki river is first mentioned in 1414. The earliest surviving geographical survey of the town area dates to 1638. The old street network is also included in the town plans of 1639 and 1652. The Court of Appeal (fi. Hovioikeus, sw. Hovrätt), established in Turku in 1623, operated first in Turku Castle, then in the town and got its own building in 1671. The Academy of Turku was founded in 1640. From 1635 onwards, Turku was the capital of the province of Turku. The provincial administration was located at the castle until 1698.
From the early 15th century onwards, Turku and Stockholm sought to dominate trade in the Gulf of Bothnia region so that in 1459 an attempt was made to limit trade in the area's legal trading posts to the exclusive right of the burghers of Turku and Stockholm. In 1531, only Stockholm, Turku, Ulvila and Rauma had the right to trade in Tornio, Kemi, Ii and Oulu. When new towns had been established in the area in the early 17th century, their export and import rights were limited in the trade and sailing ordinances of 1614 and 1617 so that from 1617 onwards, all exports of the area had to pass through Turku or Stockholm. The towns were divided into staple towns that controlled export and import rights, and into inland towns that remained outside them, so that only Turku, Viipuri, Porvoo and Helsinki in 1614–23 and 1628–40, and Helsinki with Turku and Viipuri from 1640 onwards had active export and import rights in foreign trade. All foreign sailing to the towns north of Stockholm and Turku and to the Åland Islands was banned in 1636.
<b>Post office:</b> In 1638, when the post office was founded, Turku had around 6000 to 7000 inhabitants. The Turku post office is one of the first five post offices established in Finland. Lyttke Caloander was appointed as the first postmaster. 1638, there were reportedly eight post houses connected between Turku and Helsinki. Starting in 1642 the postmaster of Turku received extra payment for delivering mail to destinations other than the Uusimaa region. In 1643, a mail route to the north of Turku was mandated, and the deputy postmaster Oluf Jönsson was assigned to organize this route.
Fair_Description: From the 14th century onwards, the largest annual fairs in Western Finland were held in Turku, where the winter fair coincided with the feast of the martyrdom of St. Henrik on 20 January and the summer fair on the day of the translation of his relics on 18 June. Both have been documented as market days in 1531, but they most likely date back to the early 14th century. The feast of 20 January became established in the 1290s at the latest, when the Legend of St Henrik was compiled to support his cult, the feast of 18 June in connection with the consecration (i.e. the Church Mass) of Turku Cathedral, when the relics were moved f to Turku. Since the Church Mass on 17 June was the day before the translation, the time of the celebration may have been related to the annual fair held at the mouth of the Aura River. The year of consecration of the cathedral took place in 1300 or 1292–96, but the years 1309–20 are also possible. The timing of Turku's annual summer market and church celebrations are also related to other gatherings. In 1435, the Union King Erik of Pomerania established the Turku Lands Court (fi. Maanoikeus, sw. Landsrätt), which was set to meet in the week before the translation (11–18 June). The celebration is also mentioned as an event that brought the people together in 1457, when the Bishop of Turku, both high Judges of Finland and representatives of the church, the nobility, the burghers of Turku and the province of Finland Proper agreed on 24 June 1457 in the guild house of St. Gertrud in Turku that they supported the election of King Christian I of Denmark as King of Sweden. Finland's representatives were unable to attend the elections held in Stockholm on Midsummer's Eve, because the Feast of Corpus Christi (16 June) and the most important celebrations of the diocese (17–18 June), had prevented them from leaving for Stockholm. The summer fair on 18 June is mentioned in the almanacs 1585 and 1598. Turku's third annual fair was an annual free fair of two weeks ordained in 1636 and starting on the Nativity of Mary (8 September). Even this fair may date back to the Middle Ages, as the annual synod of the diocesan clergy was already in 1322 held on the day after and the Feast of the Nativity of the Virgin Mary (9–10 September). The celebration of the relics of the diocese (festum reliqiuarum) founded in 1396 to take place on 20 January was moved to 8 September some time before 1488.
Toll_Description:
The Turku Roadsted, i.e. the unloading and loading place of large ships, was from the Middle Ages to the 18th century in front of the castle, from where goods were transported forward by barges. According to the 1352 town law of Magnus Eriksson, the castellan of Turku had a three-day right of pre-emption on the cargo of ships arriving in the town. From 1525 onwards, ships were allowed to sail to the town and the bailiff's right was reduced to one day. Upstream of the castle in the river there was a customs barrier that closed traffic in the 16th century at the latest, which was ordered to be removed in 1576, but is mentioned again in 1594, when entry was free, but exports to Germany had to be cleared through customs. The customs barrier and the customs house on the north bank of the river are marked on 17th and 18th century maps. Turku, like other towns, was granted occasional exemptions from customs duties.

The 1/32 duty worth of all goods intended for sale in towns and fairs and brought to the site by peasants was collected in Turku since 1622. The customs stalls and gates of the customs fence surrounding the town were located on the entrance routes.

name: Meiningen
