Settlement_Description: Old Thuringian settlement and a royal Frankish court in the 8th/9th century. First mentioned in 982, in a copy from 1293. In the 11th century there existed a moated castle of the bishop of Würzburg, next to which the town developed.
Town_Description: Development of a town around 1200. Referred to as "civitas" in 1230. Acquisition of Schweinfurt town privileges in 1344.
Fair_Description: The oldest fairs in Meiningen date back to the foundation of the settlement. By 1565, their number had grown to eight, which were confirmed in that year by the counts of Henneberg and in 1612 by elector Johann Georg of Saxony. The latter also established two additional cattle markets on St Francis and St Martin and one horse market on Monday after Reminiscere. The cattle markets soon disappeared again, but the horse market prevailed until the 20th century. In 1662 it was decreed that all markets were to be held on the Tuesdays after the respective holidays. In 1676 another fair was granted, the Christ fair on Tuesday after St Lucia. The confirmation of the fairs in 1565 also mention a weekly market held on Thursdays.
Toll_Description: Bridge toll, which was taken, among others, from pilgrims to the "miracle of Grimmenthal" ('Wunder von Grimmenthal'). The toll helped finance stone bridges at the end of the Middle Ages.

name: Kuppis (Pyhtää)
Settlement_Description:
<b>Inn:</b> An inn was established in Kuppis in 1621. 

<b>Post house:</b> In 1638, the Royal Steward Bernhardt Steen von Steenhausen established a post house in the village of Kuppis ri Pyhtää. According to research literature, Kuppis is known as a traditional post house village along the coastal road.

name: Isosilta (Ahvenkoski)
Bridge_Description: The Greater (Isosilta) and Smaller (Pikkusilta) bridges at the westernmost branch of Kymijoki river in Ahvenkoski are first cited in 1555, when Jakob Teitt included them in his map of the bridges in Kymijoki delta area. The earliest bridges on the site may date to the first organisation of the maintenance of the Great Coastal Road as a uniform land route between Turku and Viborg in the 1340s and 1360s. Isosilta bridge was in the beginning of the 17th century maintained by the early 14th century parishes of Swedish colonisation in Central and Eastern Uusimaa, but in the 1720 also by the Western Uusimaa parishes of Inkoo and Espoo because of their old duty in the bridge. The organisation of the maintenance goes back to the period from the 1340s to the 1360s when the area was part of uniform administration under Viipuri castle. The smaller bridge in Ahvenkoski was on the Swedish Russian border in 1743-1809. The maintenance of the supporting stone structures of Isosilta were heavily disputed in 1608 and the bridge was in bad condition in 1638. In the late 17th century Isosilta was together with Pyhtää Church bridge (fi. Kirkonkylän silta) Sutela Larger bridge (fi. Isosilta) and Kymijoki Huumanhaara bridge financed by a special tax collected from the judicial districts of Viipuri province and Porvoo area. Pikkusilta and Isosilta were demolished in 1928 after a new bridge was built over Savukoski. The opening of Merikoski hydroenrgic power plant in 1933 raised the water level in the area for several meters.

name: Suhl
Settlement_Description: Salt and natural resource deposits facilitated early settlement in the region. Suhl is first mentioned around 1225. In 1445 it became a borough ('Flecken').
Town_Description: Town rights were granted in 1527 by William VI, count of Henneberg.
Fair_Description: In 1544 emperor Charles V granted the privilege to hold three fairs, upon instigation by Wilhelm IV. of Henneberg-Schleusingen. A fourth fair was added in 1599. In 1661 the day of the fairs were moved from Sunday to Tuesday.
Toll_Description: Toll registries show the tolls that had to be paid in Suhl in 1502 and 1524. (ThStA Meiningen, Sekt. III Nr. 510 (1502); ThStA Meiningen, Sekt. III 510 (A 14b) Nr. 3).)

name: Isosilta (Sutela)
Bridge_Description: Sutela Greater bridge (fi. Isosilta) on the Great Coastal Road is first cited in 1555, when Jakob Teitt included it in his map of the bridges in Kymijoki delta area. The earliest bridge on the site may date to the first organisation of the maintenance of the Great Coastal Road as a uniform land route between Turku and Viborg in the 1340s and 1360s. In 1606 Pernaja parish made an agreement with the tenants of Kymi Royal Manor over the maintenance of their part in the bridge. In the late 17th century the bridge was together with Pyhtää Church bridge, Ahvenkoski Greater bridge (fi. Isosilta), and Kymijoki Huumanhaara bridge financed by a special tax collected from the judicial districts of Viipuri province and Porvoo area. The bridge was relocated to its later place during the fortification of Kyminlinna in 1791-1809.

name: Huumanhaaran silta
Bridge_Description: A bridge in Kymijoki Huumanhaara stream on the Great Coastal Road is first cited in 1555, when Jakob Teitt included it in his map of the bridges in Kymijoki delta area. The earliest bridge was located close to the Kymi Royal Manor and may date to the first organisation of the maintenance of the Great Coastal Road as a uniform land route between Turku and Viborg in the 1340s and 1360s. The bridge was relocated to its later site some 200 m upstream some time before 1692, when a sconce (sw. skantz, fi. skanssi, kantti) was attached to protect it. The In the late 17th century the bridge was together with Pyhtää Church bridge, Ahvenkoski Greater bridge (fi. Isosilta) and Sutela Greater bridge financed by a special tax collected from the judicial districts of Viipuri province and Porvoo area.

name: Ohrdruf
Settlement_Description: Foundation of a missionary station by St Boniface in 725, property of Hersfeld monastery in the 9th century.
Town_Description: Developed into a town in the mid-14th century by the counts of Gleichen. Councillors are mentioned in 1356. The settlement is mentioned as borough ('Flecken') in 1375, and as town on the town seal from 1399.

name: Arnstadt
Settlement_Description: Originally an acient Thuringian settlement located at a traffic route across the Thuringian Forest. First mentioned as residence of the duke of Thuringia in 704.
Town_Description: The settlement developed into a market town between the 10th and 12th century. In 1220 it was first referred to as civitas and a trading place. Acquisition of town privileges in 1266.

name: Friedrichroda
Settlement_Description: First mention in 842. A market is attested in 1209 when landgrave Hermann I of Thüringen wanted to destroy the market in Friedrichroda, because it allegedly competed with his own towns.
Town_Description: The settlement was granted town rights in 1597. It was characterised as mining town ('Bergstadt') into the 19th century, after the main economic activity in town.

name: Tambach
Settlement_Description: First mention of the settlement Tambach in 1265. The roads that joined in Tambach and Dietharz were controlled by several castles, whose exact location is not verified in all cases. Evidence of markets in the year 1500. In 1919 Tambach and Dietharz were merged into one town.
Toll_Description: Important station of safe conduct on the way between Erfurt ans Schmalkalden. A table of safe conduct ('Geleitstafel') shows the fees due. (ThHStA Weimar, Reg. Bb 171, Capitalrechnung der Ämter zu Thüringen, Vogtland und Franken 1535/36.) <br/> In 1637 the safe conduct of Tambach is moved to Georgenthal.

name: Crawinkel
Toll_Description: The Knights Hospitaller were allowed to maintain a toll station and an inn in Crawinkel, which they sold to the counts of Gleichen in 1470.

name: Wasungen
Settlement_Description: First mentioned as village in 874. A castle is mentioned in 1189-90.
Town_Description: The settlement at the castle developed into a borough ('burgflecken') and is characterised as "oppidum" in 1301. The acquisition of Schweinfurt town privileges took place in 1308.

name: Leiden
Settlement_Description: Leiden was first mentioned in the ninth century register of property of the chapter of St Martin in Utrecht (in a copy from the tenth or late eleventh century). The settlement developed around a castle on the confluence of two branches of the Rhine river.
Town_Description: Town rights were confirmed on 19 December 1266 by Floris V, count of Holland. Four grants of privileges predate the 1266 confirmation, the earliest of which could have been given during the reign of Dirk VII, count of Holland (r. 1190-1203) or even Floris III, count of Holland (r. 1157-1190). A hospital is first mentioned in 1276. A chapter in the church of St Pancratius is known for the years 1366-1574. The city gained prosperity due to its cloth industry and was one of the largest cities in Holland in the Middle Ages.
Fair_Description: In the town rights of 1266 fines on the disturbing of markets (fairs?) are mentioned. On 4 June 1303 count John granted a fair on the eve of St Margaret (July 12). The fair must have decayed later, because it was re-installed by archduke Philip with a duration of 8 days in 1497. A second fair existed on the day of the Holy Cross (14 September), the consecration day of St. Peter's church. The burgrave levied a toll on the fair, which is mentioned around 1360 in a list of his possessions. In 1546 it was leased to the town. The revenues are found in the oldest preserved account of the steward of the lord of Wassenaar (burgrave of Leiden) from 1554. Exempted were Haarlem, Gouda, Amsterdam, Delft and the subordinate villages. Others payed a fee of 1%. In 1565 (May) king Philip II granted the town two free leather- and fill-fairs both for 8 days, to compensate the decaying drapery. The dates: 1) Friday before Oculi (Lent Sunday) and 2) Monday after St. Lambert (Sept. 17). The town is a good place for tanning as there was plenty of water and meadows with cattle in the surrounding Rijnland. In 1599 the dates were altered with permission of the Estates of Holland. In 1573 William of Oranhe granted a free horse-fair in September as of old. On 12 January 1577 the town requested stadtholder William of Orange to have a free fair between 1 and 15 October, in memory of the relief of Leiden. Later this year king Philip II granted this free fair for alle commodities and relocated the leather-fair. In 1624 (March 23) the mayors asked the Estates of Holland for two free meager cattle fairs. The granted dates were April 27 and November 21 with 4 days before and after safe-conduct.

name: Dalen
Settlement_Description: Earliest mention in probably in the twelfth century.

name: Korkeakoski
Settlement_Description: Permanent agricultural settlement in Kymi (sw. Kymmene) area dates to the Swedish colonisation in the latter half of the 13th century when new farms were founded amongst earlier 12th and 13th century area of usufruct and colonisation from Häme and Karelia. The parish organisation dates at the latest to the first quarter of the 14th century. Kymi is cited as a chapel of Pyhtää in 1440, independent parish in 1624.
Fair_Description: Burghers of Viipuri were granted the sole rights to St Laurentius fair (10 August) in Korkeakoski in 1600 and 1606.
Bridge_Description: A bridge in Korkeakoski (sw. Högfors) on the Great Coastal Road is first cited in 1555, when Jakob Teitt included it in his map of the bridges in Kymijoki delta area. The earliest bridge may date to the first organisation of the maintenance of the Great Coastal Road as a uniform land route between Turku and Viborg in the 1340s and 1360s. The site of the bridge was slightly altered in the beginning of the 20th century.

name: Ilttula
Settlement_Description: <b>Inn:</b> The inn was moved to Sievola in 1653, but there is no information on when it was established. The location by the Great Coastal Road has been good for lodging since the Middle Ages: see Kevola village ca 500 m northwards.

name: Wagenbrug
Bridge_Description: The bridge Wagenbrug must have been built in the 1610s when a defensive canal was dug around Den Haag.

name: Zuidlaren
Settlement_Description: Earliest mention of 'Lare' in 1232-1233. Earliest mention of 'Suethlare' in 1262.
Fair_Description: The earliest mention of a well-attended horse and cattle fair in Laren dates from around 1232 in the cronicle Quedam Narracio. This horse fair took place on Saint Michael (29 September), but might also have been held in May in its beginning. In 1633 the States of Drenthe instituted a two-day fair on Saint Matthew (21 September), which might have replaced the fair on Saint Michael, but the date may not have been a success. In 1655, the fair was replaced to Monday after the initial date (Saint Michael); in later years in was shifted to the Tuesday after Saint Michael. Since 1700, the fair takes place on the third Tuesday in October, which is still the date for the international horse fair that takes place in Zuidlaren each year.

name: Stadtilm
Town_Description: The village developed into a town in the late 13th century. It is characterised as 'oppidum' in 1274 and as town in 1282. In 1350 the town received renewed bylaws, which go back to the 13th century. New bylaws were granted in 1596.

name: Eteläinen
Settlement_Description: <b>Inn:</b> An inn was established in Eteläinen in 1637, and Matti Eskonpoika Paakkala was appointed as the innkeeper. The inn is mentioned also in 1639, and continued to operate until 1647.

name: Kymin kuninkaankartano
Settlement_Description:
Kymi Royal manor was established by the Earl Erengisle Sunesson (Bååt) in ca. 1350. The foundation was very likely based on an older landed property of his uncle Peder Jonsson, castellan of Viborg in 1324–36. The activities of the manor were expanded by seneschal and headman of Finland Bo Jonsson (Grip) who donated it to Vadstena Abbey in 1380, which then placed the manor and its salmon fisheries to the custody of castellans of Viborg. Abbey’s ownership was contested by the castellans until the Reformation. In 1556–70 the manor served as the centre of Kyminkartano bailiwick. A private property since 1617 the manor was relocated in 1791 because of the construction of Kyminlinna fortress.
<b>Inn:</b> Teitti

name: Sairiala
Settlement_Description: <b>Inn:</b> Sairiala ("Sarela") is mentioned in Jaakko Teitti's list in 1556 as a possible place for a bailiff (fi. vouti, sw. fogde). The place has previously been interpreted as "Saarela", but there is no such village in Tuulos, and Sairiala is by the road and close church. An inn might be located by the medieval Tuulos church. Churches usually had taverns in the Middle Ages and 16th-17th-centuries.

name: Pyhäjoki bridge (N)
Bridge_Description: The two bridges on the Bothnian Coastal Road over Pyhäjoki river are included in an early 1650s map. The northern bridge had stone foundations already in the 17th centruy.

name: Siikajoki
Ferry_Description: Ferry over Siikajoki river on the Bothnian Coastal road is mentioned in 1640 and 1646 as out of maintenance.

name: II
Ferry_Description: A ferry over Iijoki river was ordained to be built in 1641 and again 1647. In 1658 the ferry was already rotten and was replaced with a new one.

name: Kemijoki
Ferry_Description: A ferryman was ordained to take care of ferry over Kemijoki river in 1650.

name: Hauho
Settlement_Description: <b>Inn:</b> Parish constable (fi: nimismies, sw: länsman) Olli Pekanpoika hosted soldiers in his house in 1564. Parish constables were obliged to keep a tavern in late 16th c. and early 17th c. Hauho parish village inn is mentioned also in 1637. In 1640s, vicar Johannes Röökman owned an alehouse in Toppola farm, where he received extra income from aleselling. In 1651, Mikko Joakiminpoika Wargentin run an alehouse in his farm in Hauho parish village, which received the name Kapakka ("alehouse/inn"). Kapakka farm belonged to Kyttälä Manor. Kapakka had official tavern rights, since Mikko reported illegal alesellers in court. Mikko Joakiminpoika Wargentin ran the tavern until 1666, and there has been an inn in Hauho parish village also later.

name: Helsingin kuninkaankartano
Settlement_Description: Helsinki Royal Manor (fi: kuninkaankartano, sw: kungsgård) was established in 1550 and served as the centre for a bailiwick consisting of Western Nyland and Helsinki and Sipoo parishes in 1553-55, Espoo, Sipoo and Helsinki parishes in 1555-57 and later only Helsinki parish in 1561-63. In the latter year the administration was moved to Porvoo Royal Manor. The acitivities of the Manore were moved to nearby Viikki before 1571. The two bridges over Vantaanjoki river north of the Manor were built in 1550-51. <b>Inn:</b> Royal manors  were obliged to provide accommodation for travelling officials.

name: null
Harbour_Description: A landing place for river vessels on the river branch La Sauvenière, close to the Pont d'Île, is first mentioned in 1331. In 1487 a loading station for firewood was installed here.

name: Engesholm
Settlement_Description: <b>Inn:</b> Engesholm was established as a royal manor (sw. kungsgård, fi. kuninkaankartano) in 1559, and it became the administrative centre for Paimio, Marttila, Lieto and Piikkiö. Previously the centre was by the Great Oxen Road (Turku-Hämeenlinna) in Juva (Nyby) or Marttila. Engesholm royal manor was active only for a couple of years, but during that, it served accommodation for traveling officials.

name: Båtvik (Kirkkonummi)
Settlement_Description: <b>Inn:</b> An alehouse is mentioned in Kirkkonummi in the 1545-1550 list. It served travellers both by land and sea. Exact location is unknown.

name: Magdeburg
Settlement_Description: Originally a trading point with Slavs east of the Elbe. A castle built by Charlemagne is mentioned in 805, later an Ottonian palace. The settlement gained importance as a political and commercial centre in the 9th and 10th century. The Benedictine monastery of St Maurice was founded in 937. Archbishopric since 968.
Town_Description: In 1188 the Magdeburg town law is first securely attested, but must have been granted at an unknown date before that year. It would become the model for the foundation of numerous other town rights in Central and Eastern Europe. The old town was fortified in the second half of the 12th century. Magdeburg became a Hanseatic town in the 13th century. Together with the independent towns Neustadt and Sudenburg Magdeburg formed a conglomerate. During the Thirty Years' War in 1631 the city was completely destroyed and remained in ruins for decades.
Fair_Description: Magdeburg acquired market rights in 937. The most important and oldest fair in Magdeburg is the so-called "Herrenmesse" (lord's fair), which is first mentioned in a charter from 1179, but might be connected with an earlier mention from 1010. In 1448, two new three-day fairs were granted, but afterwards we don't hear about them anymore. Again in 1497, two three-day fairs were established, but these were forbidden only two years later by the Duke of Saxony, due to competition with the Leipzig fairs.
Toll_Description: A toll in Magdeburg is first mentioned in 937, when it was acquired by the monastery of St Maurice, although it is unclear what character it had. In 1208 Otto IV relinquishes his right of toll and mint in favour of the archbishop. New tolls were not to be collected without the confirmation of the archbishop. In 1309 and 1324 the archbishop relinquishes some tolls, like the wine and bridge toll. Several tolls in the course of the Elbe river are also mentioned within the oldest fief records of the town of Magdeburg.In 1463 an agreement between archbishop Frederick and Magdeburg settles that the council may collect part of the toll for the maintenance of the roads and bridges. The oldest toll tariffs date from 1478. A regulation of safe conduct remains from 1519, as well as a report on the practice of the regulations of safe conduct from 1571.
Staple_Description: Exclusive shipping rights on grain ('Kornverschiffungsrecht') for the archbishopric of Magdeburg are granted in 1309, which leads to decade-long conflicts with the archbishop. A contract from 1463 confirms Magdeburg town rights as well as free shipping rights on grain for the prelate, the clergy and knights, which was confirmed again in 1497. In the 16th century, the staple right were threatened by Leipzig, since Magdeburg was located in its zone of influence. This led to a contract with Hamburg concerning the protection of the staple rights of both towns in 1538. During the imperial ban 1547-1567 the staple in Magdeburg was revoked, but later re-established as a three-day depot right and mandatory turnover. In 1571 this is changed into a depot fee. Starting from 1596 it was handled as a depot and turnover right again. The destruction of the town during the Thirty Years' War (1631) meant an end of the staple, but soon thereafter there were several attempts to re-establish it. Shipping rights on grain were confirmed in 1638. The staple was finally abolished with the 'Elbschiffahrtsakte' in 1821.

name: Pont d'Avroy
Bridge_Description: Bridge across the Sauvenière river branch.
Harbour_Description: Next to the Avroy bridge, there existed a landing place for river vessels, which is first mentioned in 1350. It is also shown on early modern views of the city.

name: Yli-Vekkoski
Settlement_Description: <b>Inn:</b> An inn is mentioned in Yli-Vekkoski village in 1592. It was located in Jonnas farm, which might also be the place for the parish constable. The summer and winter roads of the Great Coastal Road met in Yli-Vekkoski, and there has been a horse changing station there in the late 16th century.  In 1616, the inn is no longer mentioned: the constable moved to Monninkylä village and the inn to Ilola village.

name: Svetton
Settlement_Description: <b>Inn:</b> Svetton alehouse is mentioned in 1543. It was owned by Matts Olsson. Alehouses in Pernaja paid taxes to the king and Vogt (fi. vouti, sw. fogde), 4½ and 13½ öres respectively.

name: Torsby (Pernaja)
Settlement_Description:
<b>Inn:</b> Torsby alehouse is mentioned in 1543, when it was owned by Anders Jopsson. Alehouses in Pernaja paid taxes to the king and Vogt (fi. vouti, sw. fogde), 4½ and 13½ öres respectively.

<b>Post house:</b> The post house in the village of Torsby in Pernaja, was established in 1666, and its is known to have operated there until the 1720s.

name: Bolagha keldo (Högbenkrogen)
Settlement_Description: <b>Inn:</b> Bolagha keldo (mentioned in 1424) might be a place for a medieval tavern. It is located between the villages Sannainen and Högben, no exact location is known. "Bol" means both an area for collecting taxes and a tax-like obligation to host travelling officials. The inn could be the same place that is in 1636 referred to as "Krogarekällan" ("Tavern spring"), and later known as Högbenkrogen ("Högben tavern").

name: Gesterby
Settlement_Description: <b>Inn:</b> In Jaakko Teitti's list in 1556, Gesterby is mentioned as a possible place for an official, Vogt (fi. vouti, sw. fogde). Another option for Vogt would be Massby, which is ca 4 km south by Sipoonjoki river.

name: Kroggård
Settlement_Description: <b>Inn:</b> Kroggård ("Alehouse") might be a medieval tavern in Karjaa, but it is first mentioned in 1556. According to a tax listing, there were then three alehouses in Karjaa.

name: Helsinga
Settlement_Description: <b>Inn:</b> In 1543, there were 19 alehouses in Helsinge parish, six of them in the church village (Jacob Sigfridsson, Knut Hansson, Per Olsson, Knut Jönsson, Olof Rute and Michel Larsson). The alehouses in Sipoo and Helsinki parishes paid their taxes for ale selling in natura by delivering hops to Wiborg castle and the king's estate in Porvoo. In mid-16th century, a man named Hindrich run an alehouse in Helsinga church village. In 1620, an inn was established in Helsinga church village, and it continued to operate for centuries. Another inn was established in 1660s to Hakkila, which is the other traditional inn village in Helsinga.

name: Majala
Settlement_Description: <b>Inn:</b> Majala farm got its name from medieval lodging ("Maja" = cabin, a place for accomodation). "Peder i Maiala" is mentioned in 1410, and in the following century, Majala served as parish constable. Parish constables (fi: nimismies, sw: länsman) were obliged to keep a tavern in late 16th c. Majala is also mentioned in Jaakko Teitti's list in 1556 as a possible place for a bailiff (fi. vouti, sw. fogde).

name: Krootila
Settlement_Description: <b>Inn:</b> The village got its name from a medieval tavern (Bondhekrogen in Perniö parish?).

name: Kevola
Settlement_Description: <b>Inn:</b> Kevola village has a house named Krouvi ("tavern"). Since there are no mentions of a tavern in 16th and 17th centuries, the name must be older. In the first half of the 17th century, the tavern was in Ilttula village 500 m south. In 1653, the tavern was moved to Sievola.

name: Pohja
Settlement_Description: <b>Inn:</b> There has been an alehouse in Pohja village at least from the late 15th-century, since it gave its name to the Krog farm. In 1500, the town council of Tallinn received a letter which stated that Margaretha Kroges from Raseborg and her two sisters authorise Hinrik Kroch to take care of their matters in Tallinn. According to a list from 1545-1550, there was an alehouse in Pohja village, serving travellers both by land and sea. Alehouse tax list from 1556 states that there were two alehouses in Pohja, one of them owned by Erik i Krogen. In 1599, Mrs. Elin served accommodation to two Russian ambassadors in Brödtorp village, ca. 3km northwest. In 17th c., the Pohja vicarage served food, drink, and accommodation to travellers. In 1623, two farmers who stayed in the vicarage during the fair, got into fight there.

name: Myllymäki
Settlement_Description: <b>Inn:</b> Jöns Persson owned an alehouse in Myllymäki village in 1543. The alehouses in Sipoo and Helsinki parishes paid their taxes for ale selling in natura by delivering hops to Wiborg castle and the king's estate in Porvoo.

name: Böle
Settlement_Description: <b>Inn:</b> An inn was established in Böle in 1602, and Jacob Jacobsson was appointed as the innkeeper.

name: Masku
Settlement_Description: <b>Inn:</b> "Jönis Krogh" from Masku is mentioned as a lay member of the court in 1442. The exact location of his tavern is not known, but it might be located by the church. Churches usually had taverns in the Middle Ages and 16th-17th-centuries, and an area near Masku church is still called "Krouvi" (tavern). In 1559, there was a farmer called Matti Krouvila ("tavern") in Humikkala village, ca. 2 km southeast. The name suggests a medieval tavern, and he could be a descendant of Jönis Krogh. Masku vicarage also served food, drink, and accommodation to travellers, like in 1569, when vicar Johannes Paavalinpoika hosted 30 Russian delegates. In 1632, an inn is mentioned in Kankainen village close to the church.

name: Eijsden
Settlement_Description: The first mention of Eijsden probably dates from 870 (in a sixteenth-century copy of the document). From the eleventh to the thirteenth century, Eijsden and neighbouring settlement Breust were central to the cultivation of the Plateau of Margraten. The history of several villages there can be traced back to either Eijsden or Breust.
Town_Description: Whether Eijsden was officially granted town rights remains a matter of historical debate. Eijsden itself was never called a 'stad' (town), but has always been referred to as a 'vrijheid'. On the other hand, Eijsden did have a town-like character. The 'vrijheidsboek', the document containing the rights of Eijsden, is interpreted by some as a town rights charter. Hans van Hall dates this book to 1321, Jan Hartmann states that it originated in the middle of the thirteenth century. In 2011 Van Hall argued that Eijsden should be seen as a minor town or borough ('dwergstadje' / 'Minderstadt'). Eijsden was fortified with an earth wall  and a moat. In 1632 a castle was built.

name: Mäenkylä
Settlement_Description: <b>Inn:</b> The court gathering of 1432 was held in the house of Antti the tavern keeper ("Anti krogx gordh").

name: Gulpen
Settlement_Description: Mentioned as royal property or fiscus around 1007, donated by the Ottonian King Henry II to the Collegiate Church of St Mary in Aachen (recorded in a confirmation from 1226 and the necrology of the chapter). Situated on a crossroads of the roads Maastricht-Aachen and Cologne-Liège. In 1375 a hospital is mentioned.
Fair_Description: On Easter Saturday 1544 emperor Charles V granted a fair on St. Hubert (November 3), lasting three days, upon request of the inhabitants of Gulpen.
Toll_Description: In 1161 the Duke of Limburg exempted the abbey of St. Trond from the toll in Herzogenrath and Gulpen for wine from the abbey. In 1242 the abbey of Burtscheid near Aachen was freed from the 'pedagium' (road toll) in Gulpen. In 1266 it appeared that inhabitants of Aachen were also exempted from the toll in Gulpen. In 1334 the lord of Valkenburg received the toll in Gulpen as a fief from the duke of Limburg and Brabant. The old tariffs of the margrave of Julich, which were renewed in 1343, state that 12 den. were levied from wagons. Wagons with wine on the way to Liège had to pay more than those on the road to Maastricht. In 1397 780 waggons with wine were taxed in Gulpen.

name: Vättilä (Marttila)
Settlement_Description: <b>Post house:</b> Two post houses were established along the mail route from Turku to Hämeenlinna between 1639-1640, one of which was in the in the village of Vättilä in Marttila.

name: Eys
Settlement_Description: The settlement was originally called 'Hanson', which is first mentioned around 1185.

name: Närpiö
Settlement_Description: <b>Inn:</b> Närpiö parish village is mentioned in Jaakko Teitti's list in 1556 as a possible place for a bailiff (fi. vouti, sw. fogde). In 1557, Ture Pedersson Bielke, Swedish nobleman and castellan of St. Olaf's Castle in Savo, stopped to change horses in Närpiö vicarage. In 1634, a company travelling from Ostrobothia to Turku stayed the night in Närpiö vicarage, where the vicar's widow offered them food, drink, and accommodation. There has also been a tavern in nearby Näsby village in 1620s, and in Närpiö parish village in 1624. In 1624, Mickel Andersson was the innkeeper in Näsby village. The tavern moved in mid-17th c. to Finby village nearby, when the parish constable Samuel Persson was appointed as the innkeeper.

name: Mühlhausen/Thüringen
Settlement_Description: First mentioned in 967, when Otto II issued a charter here. There was a royal/imperial court in Mühlhausen, which was destroyed in 1256.
Town_Description: Acquisition of town privileges in 1135. The Mühlhausen law was recorded in c. 1224 and is the oldest town law code in the German language. Since 1348 Mühlhausen can be considered a free imperial city. The original old town was expanded with a new town north of it since the early 13th century. Together they were fortified with a wall. A second wall was erected in the 14th century, which also included the suburbs.
Fair_Description: Three fairs with a duration of one week are recorded for Mühlhausen in 1317: On the feastdays of St Michael and St Kilian, and on Monday after Exaudi. In 1638 an additional fair is mentioned which took place on the Blobach square outside the gate of Our Lady (Frauentor).
Toll_Description: Emperor Konrad IV granted toll and mint rights for five years in 1251. The collection of a gate and road toll can be derived from the instructions for the guards in the chamberlain accounts of 1407 and 1409.

name: Porvoo Iso Linnanmäki
Settlement_Description: Permanent agricultural settlement in lower Porvoonjoki (sw. Borgå å) area and Eastern Nyland (sw. Östra Nyland) dates to the Swedish colonisation in the latter half of the 13th century when new farms were founded in an area previously part of usufruct and emerging colonisation settlement from inner Häme. The parish organisation of Eastern Nyland dates at the latest to the first quarter of the 14th century, in Porvoo (sw. Borgå) possibly already to the third quarter of the 14th century. The parish and rector of Porvoo is first cited in 1327. The name of the parish (Borgå – Castle river, i.e. the one of the rivers in the area where there is a castle) implies that the castle should be older than the name of the parish in use in 1327. Porvoo town was established either in the turn of the 1370s and 1380s or in the late 1340s. The town is first cited in 1387. <b>Porvoo Iso Linnanmäki castle mound</b> and its structures were since the early 1990s dated to the 1380s, but archaeological excavations in the summer of 2024 showed that the original earthworks must go back to the colonisation period in the late 13th century after which more permanent activity again took place on the site in the last quarter of the 14th century at the time of Bo Jonsson (Grip) in 1370-86, Jakob Abrahamsson (Djäkn) 1386-95, and Knut Bosson (Grip) in 1395-99. In the late 14th century, the actual administrative centre of the bailiwick may have been Wartholm castle (possibly Husholmen in Pikku-Pernajanlahti) cited in 1395 and demolished after it was given over to Union administration in 1399. Iso Linnanmäki was apparently abandoned permanently around the same time. The bailiwick of Porvoo (sew. Borgå fögderi) was since the beginning of the 15th century placed permanently under Viipuri castle (sw. Viborg) and administered by a bailiff of a new Royal Manor (sw. Gammelgård) first cited in 1413. The new Manor was founded separate of the possessions of an older Crown Manor in the area possibly established in the combination of the first castle, or after it. The oldest Crown Manor and the new 15th century Royal Manor may have also controlled the Saksala (sw. Saxby) fair located upstream of the castle and the later medieval town, and frequented by inland peasants and merchants of Porvoo and Helsinki as late in the 17th century.

name: Dierentuinbrug
Bridge_Description: The bridge must have been built in the 1610s when a defensive canal was dug around Den Haag. The name Dierentuinbrug dates from a later period.

name: Vejans (Siuntio)
Settlement_Description: <b>Post house:</b> In 1638, the Royal Steward Bernhardt Steen von Steenhausen established a post house in the Postis house, located in the village of Vejans in Siuntio. The post houses located on the coastal road typically served their purpose for a long time. In the village of Vejans, there was postal service activity throughout the entire period of the post house system from 1638 to 1816.

name: Salo
Settlement_Description:
Permanent agricultural settlement in Uskela and Salo area goes back to the Iron Age. The medieval parish organisation in Finland Proper dates to the early 13th century with precursors in the latter half of the 12th century. Uskela parish church was until 1827 located alongside Hiidentie road on the Western bank of Uskelanjoki river some 3,5 kms North from Salo bridge of the Great Coastal Road. St Anna’s chapel of Salo was established some time before 1490 on a hill East of the bridge alongside the Great Coastal Road.

<b>Inn:</b> A tavern might have be located by the St. Anna's chapel. Churches and chapels usually had taverns in the Middle Ages and 16th-17th-centuries. There was also an alehouse by the bridge in the 17th and 18th centuries. It was called "Moisio tavern" since it belonged to Moisio farm, and later "Sahlå tavern" (fi. Salonjoki, eng. Salo river). These taverns could have been located also on the other side of the Salonjoki river.
Fair_Description: In Finland Proper several local peasant fairs existed in the 17th century, most of which consisted of trade with fish, grain, and other necessities amongst the population. Most of the fairs were apparently of medieval origin and took place on the feasts of local parish churches next to the church. Larger fairs were in the 17th century organised in Kalanti (Männäinen), Mynämäki, Perniö and Salo all of which were frequented and dominated by the burghers of Turku. The fair at Salo bridge is first mentioned in 1606. The site of the fair was at the eastern end of the bridge alongside the Great Coastal Road on the property of Halikko Joensuu (sw. Åminne) manor. The fair days were of old Apostle Bartholomeus (24 August) and Apostle Matteus (21 September), in addition to which the local peasant fair of St Bridget (7 October). According to an ordinance of 1796, the fair at Salo bridge was to take four days starting from 7 October. Since information exists on local 17th century peasant fair in Salo on the Assumption of Mary (15 August), the early modern fairs at the bridge appear to have formed a kind of continuum from late August to mid-October similar to fairs in the Bothnian rivermouths.
Toll_Description: The 1/32 duty worth of all goods intended for sale in towns and fairs and brought to the site by peasants was collected in Salo fair since 1622.

name: null
Bridge_Description: The bridge must have been built in the 1610s when a defensive canal was dug around Den Haag.

name: Torkkola (Ylistaro)
Settlement_Description: <b>Post house:</b> Oluf Jönsson appointed Matti Sipinpoika as the postmaster of the Ylistaro Torkkola village and granted him the postmaster's mandate in the year 1643.

name: Finby (Sund)
Settlement_Description: <b>Post house:</b> In 1638, the Royal Steward Bernhardt Steen von Steenhausen established six post houses in Åland, along the route from Stockholm to Turku. One of the post houses was located in the village of Finby in Sund.

name: Serkele (Pernaja)
Settlement_Description: <b>Post house:</b> In 1638, the Royal Steward Bernhardt Steen von Steenhausen established a post house in the village of Serkele (Särkilahti?) in Pernaja.

name: Garpgård
Settlement_Description: <b>Inn:</b> Garpgård alehouse is mentioned in 1543, owned by Mats Jönsson. The alehouse gave its name to the bridge nearby (Krogbro = Tavern bridge). Alehouses in Pernaja paid taxes to the king and Vogt (fi. vouti, sw. fogde), 4½ and 13½ öres respectively.

name: Herzogenrath
Settlement_Description: Located near the abbey Rode (Rolduc), founded in 1104, and the village Afden, first mentioned in 1108, the castle Rode was first mentioned in 1137, when it was inherited by the dukes of Limburg.
Town_Description: The settlement adjoining the castle was granted privileges by duke Henry III of Limburg in 1219, town privileges followed in 1282. At the latter occasion, the settlement was first called Herzogenrath.
Toll_Description: 1) The Duke of Limburg levied a land toll in 1161. In 1389, 2 groschen per wine cart with two horses had to be paid, 4½ groschen per wine cart with 4 horses. In 1356/57 1188 cologne mark 8 denarii were collected, in 1374/75 2866 cologne mark and in 1377/78 1951 cologne marks. For further annual revenues see source. 2) The Duke of Limburg also levied a fee for safe conduct in 1249. For Flemings, a tariff of 27 denarii per barrel of wine applied in 1249. After the Land Peace of 1375, 2 to 3 white pennies ('Weißpfennig/Albus) per horse were paid, depending on the load. Horse fee and land toll merged with each other over time.

name: Leikola
Settlement_Description: <b>Inn:</b> Leikola parish constable is mentioned as an accommodation in the travel account of Duke Johan of Finland from 1555.

name: Korpi
Settlement_Description: <b>Inn:</b> Lappi parish constables (fi: nimismies, sw: länsman) lived in (Iso)Korpi village in the early 16th c. Parish constables were obliged to keep a tavern at the time. Local court gathered in Isokorpi in 1516. The village is located by the winter road connecting Lappi church and Hinnerjoki village.

name: Kortela
Settlement_Description: <b>Inn:</b> Mats van Kleven run a tavern in Kortela in 1584.

name: Pöytyä
Settlement_Description: <b>Inn:</b> Pöytyä vicarage is mentioned as an accommodation in the travel account of Duke Johan of Finland from 1556. There were also plans to establish a bailiff in Pöytyä parish village in 1556. In 1566, there were four tax-paying alehouses in Pöytyä parish, but their locations are not known. Most likely some of them served by the church.

name: Kulhua
Settlement_Description: <b>Inn:</b> Bishop of Turku Maunu Tavast acquired the abandoned farm Kulhua in the early 15th c. for lodging. Turku bishops still used it in 1556 for accommodation during their travels.

name: Irjanne
Settlement_Description: <b>Inn:</b> Eurajoki parish constables (fi: nimismies, sw: länsman) kept a tavern in Irjanne in the late 16th and early 17th c. First constable in Irjanne, Antti Antinpoika Kauppi, is mentioned in 1582. In 1631, the tavern was run by constable Fallentin Martinpoika, who lived in Mullila village nearby, but after him, the tavern returned to Irjala and Kauppi farm. After 1659, the tavern moved to Eurajoki parish village, and after 1679 to Antti Simonpoika Isopere in Tarvola village, where it stayed also during the 18th c.

name: Wagenstedter Brücke
Bridge_Description: Originally a ford across the Unstrut. A bridge at this place was probably built in the 13th century.

name: Kaukola
Settlement_Description: <b>Inn:</b> Niilo Pentinpoika Juutti, who was the stable master for Duke John of Finland, stayed at Olavi Balk, Laitila parish constable (fi: nimismies, sw: länsman). Parish constables were obliged to keep a tavern in late 16th c. and early 17th c. During the 1580s, the parish constable and the inn were located in Seppälä, which is not by the Ostrobothnian Coastal Road. The office moved back to Kaukola, and in 1639, parish constable Sipi Perttelinpoika Luukas ran a tavern in his house.

name: Isosilta (Halikko)
Bridge_Description: Halikko Great bridge (fi. Isosilta) over Halikonjoki river may date to the first organisation of the maintenance of the Great Coastal Road as a uniform land route between Turku and Viborg in the 1340s and 1360s. The bridge is included in the 1650s map of the Piikkiö and Halikko districts. It was maintained by the peasants of Halikko judicial district until 1831. The bridge was repaired in 1626 and completely rebuilt in 1674–76 and after 1713. The length of the bridge was in 1792 a total of 128 ells (ell = 59,38 cm, ca.76,0 m), and in 1798 and 1829 a total of 109 ells (ca. 64,7 m). The present bridge was built in 1865–66. It is one of the 54 bridges and sections of historical roads protected by the Finnish National Road Administration in 1982.

name: Mäntlahti (Vehkalahti)
Settlement_Description: <b>Post house:</b>In 1638, the Royal Steward Bernhardt Steen von Steenhausen established a post house in the village of Mäntlahti in Vehkalahti, where it operated until 1709. According to research literature. Mäntlahti is recognized as a traditional post house village along the coastal road.

name: Pirttikylä
Settlement_Description: <b>Inn:</b> There was a transport organiser (sw. skjutsrättare, fi. kyytirättäri) in Pirttikylä village in the late 16th c. Ture Pedersson Bielke, Swedish nobleman and castellan of St. Olaf's Castle in Savo, stopped to change horses there in 1557. An inn was established in 1632.

name: Noormarkku
Settlement_Description: <b>Inn:</b> An inn was established in Noormarkku in 1642, and Heikki Matinpoika was appointed as the innkeeper.

name: Petolahti
Settlement_Description: <b>Inn:</b> Ture Pedersson Bielke, Swedish nobleman and castellan of St. Olaf's Castle in Savo, stopped to change horses  in 1557 in "Palulax", which probably refers to Petolahti (sw. Petalax). There are no known inns in the village in the 17th c.

name: Södermark?
Settlement_Description: <b>Inn:</b> Ture Pedersson Bielke, Swedish nobleman and castellan of St. Olaf's Castle in Savo, stopped to change horses in Södermark in 1557. The name is no longer in use, but the location is approximately one old Finnish mile (ca 6 km) north from the previous stop, Närpiö vicarage.

name: Töjby
Settlement_Description: <b>Inn:</b> An inn was established in Töjby in 1632.

name: Härkmeri
Settlement_Description: <b>Inn:</b> Ture Pedersson Bielke, Swedish nobleman and castellan of St. Olaf's Castle in Savo, stopped to change horses in Härkmeri in 1557. In 1637, farmers from Siipyy, Skaftung and Härkmeri complained that they live near busy winter and summer roads, and they must give rides for 16-17 old Finnish miles (ca. 80-100 km). When they get back home, they must go again, which makes them very weary and poor. Farmers got some tax exemptions but complained again in 1641. Erik Pedersson was appointed as the innkeeper in 1656.

name: Siipyy
Settlement_Description: <b>Inn:</b> Ture Pedersson Bielke, Swedish nobleman and castellan of St. Olaf's Castle in Savo, stopped to change horses in Siipyy in 1557. In 1632, Mats Hansson was appointed as the innkeeper. He is mentioned in 1654-1656 as a parish constable (fi: nimismies, sw: länsman). In 1637, farmers from Siipyy, Skaftung and Härkmeri complained that they live near busy winter and summer roads, and they must give rides for 16-17 old Finnish miles (ca. 80-100 km). When they get back home, they must go again, which makes them very weary and poor. Farmers got some tax exemptions but complained again in 1641.

name: Turun linna
Settlement_Description: The founding of Turku Castle (r. Åbo hus, Åbo slott), located on an island at the mouth of the Aurajoki River, has been dated to the 1280s or the very beginning of the 1300s on the basis of coin finds and masonry structures. The castle is first mentioned in 1308. The castle was expanded several times during the Middle Ages and especially in the 1550s, when it served as the administrative centre and court of Duke John, who ruled western Finland as a duchy in 1556–63. The Court of Appeal, established in Turku in 1623, operated first in Turku Castle, then in the city and in its own building from 1671. When Turku became the administrative centre of the province of Turku in 1635, the provincial administration was located at the castle until 1698. In 1637–40 and 1648–50, the castle also housed the residence of the Governor-General of Finland, Pietari Brahe. The castle was connected to the mainland by a bridge through which the road led along the northern bank of the River Aura to Turku. From the Middle Ages to the 18th century, the Turku Roadsted, i.e. the unloading and loading place of large ships, was located in front of the castle, from where goods were transported forward by barges. Upstream from the castle a customs barrier closed the river at the latest in the 16th century.

name: Hooge Mierde
Settlement_Description: The settlement Mierde (Myrtha) is first mentioned in ca. 1200. The addition "Hooge" was added later to discern it from neighbouring Lage Mierde.

name: Ahlainen
Settlement_Description: <b>Inn:</b> Ahlainen is mentioned as an accommodation in the travel account of Duke Johan of Finland from 1556. Also Ture Pedersson Bielke, Swedish nobleman and castellan of St. Olaf's Castle in Savo, stopped to change horses and dine in Ahlainen in 1557. In 1634, Alakylä villagers were ordered to drive travellers from Ahlainen inn instead of paying money to the tavern hostess. In 1642, Niilo Olavinpoika is mentioned as the innkeeper.

name: Tiukka
Settlement_Description: <b>Inn:</b> Tiukka village had an transport organiser (sw. skjutsrättare, fi. kyytirättäri) in the late 16th c. In 1575, Hans Olsson paid fines for hitting the transport organiser Olof Persson by the common road. Transport organisers changed often: in 1584 Erik Jönsson, 1586 Lasse Ersson, and 1587 Andres Persson. An inn was established in Tiukka in 1634, and Jacob Olsson was appointed as the innkeeper. He died in 1639, but his widow Kirstin continued to run the tavern, and in return, she got tax exemptions to two of her farms. In 1649, Augustinus Eriksson was appointed as the innkeeper.

name: Maalahti
Settlement_Description: <b>Inn:</b> Maalahti is mentioned in Jaakko Teitti's list in 1556 as a possible place for a bailiff (fi. vouti, sw. fogde). Ture Pedersson Bielke, Swedish nobleman and castellan of St. Olaf's Castle in Savo, stopped to change horses in Maalahti in 1557. An inn was established in 1633.

name: Harrström
Settlement_Description: <b>Inn:</b> An inn was established in Harrström in 1624, and Matts Mickelsson was appointed as the innkeeper.

name: Krogbro
Bridge_Description: There has probably been a bridge here since the Middle Ages, but the Krogbro bridge is first mentioned in a map from 1777. There have been many bridges over the gully, and the present one was build short after 1875. The name "Tavern bridge" comes from the Garpgård tavern nearby.

name: Grelsby Kungsgård
Settlement_Description: King Magnus Eriksson confirmed in 1351 the bishop of Turku the ownership of an older Royal manor in Saltvik and established a new manor in Finström in Gregorisby. The manor was in private ownership in the 15th century. A Royal manor proper was founded in the late 1540s. It served as the administrative centre of Lemland, Jomala, Hammarland and Föglö parishes in 1556-62, and again in 1564–1621.

name: Moikipää
Settlement_Description: <b>Inn:</b> An inn was established in Moikipää in 1632.

name: Monå
Settlement_Description: <b>Inn:</b> Ture Pedersson Bielke, Swedish nobleman and castellan of St. Olaf's Castle in Savo, stopped to change horses in Monå in 1557.

name: Soklot
Settlement_Description: <b>Inn:</b> Ture Pedersson Bielke, Swedish nobleman and castellan of St. Olaf's Castle in Savo, stopped to change horses in Soklot in 1557. The village had a transport organiser (sw. skjutsrättare, fi. kyytirättäri), and in 1586, a local farmer had to pay fines for hitting him.

name: Sundby
Settlement_Description: <b>Inn:</b> An inn was established in Sundby in the early 17th c., although it is mentioned first in 1650.

name: Katternö
Settlement_Description: <b>Inn:</b> An inn was established in Katternö in 1642, and Anders Jönsson i Kråknäset was appointed as the innkeeper.

name: Hopsala
Settlement_Description: <b>Inn:</b> Ture Pedersson Bielke, Swedish nobleman and castellan of St. Olaf's Castle in Savo, stopped to change horses in Hopsala in 1557.

name: Sulva
Settlement_Description: <b>Inn:</b> An inn was established in Sulva in 1641.

name: Peitso
Settlement_Description: <b>Inn:</b> An inn was established in Peitso in 1650, and Per Mickelsson was appointed as the innkeeper.

name: Parkhauta
Settlement_Description: <b>Inn:</b> An inn was established in Parkhauta in 1630s. In 1646, Juho Laurinpoika Isoperhe was confirmed as the innkeeper, since he had already served in the position. Isoperhe farm continued to serve as an inn for a long time.

name: Åminne
Settlement_Description: <b>Inn:</b> An inn was established in Åminne in 1650, and Hans Olofsson was appointed as the innkeeper.

name: Isosilta
Bridge_Description: Paimio (sw. Pemar) Great bridge (fi. Isosilta, sw. Stora bro) over Paimionjoki river may date to the first organisation of the maintenance of the Great Coastal Road as a uniform land route between Turku and Viborg in the 1340s and 1360s. Sillankorva (Bridge end) farm close to the bridge is cited as a property of Turku Cathedral Chapter in 1407. A skirmish between Duke Charles and the Supporters of king Sigismund took place near the bridge in 1599. Since the peasants of the judicial districts (fi. kihlakunta, sw. härad) of Piikkiö and Halikko are known to have taken care of the bridge in the 17th century, its maintenance may have been organised in the beginning of the 15th century to that time South-Finland. The bridge is cited in bad condition in the 16720s and 1630s. It was rebuilt in 1653. In 1829 the bridge was 156 ells (ell = 59,38 cm, i.e. ca. 92,6 m) long. Paimio Small bridge (fi. Vähäsilta, sw. lilla bro) east of the Great bridge was in 1829 60 ells (ca. 35,6 m) long. Both bridges are included in a 1650s map of Piikkiö and Halikko districts.

name: Ylimarkku
Settlement_Description: <b>Inn:</b> Ylimarkku village is located by the winter road from Närpiö to Mustasaari (Vaasa). Ture Pedersson Bielke, Swedish nobleman and castellan of St. Olaf's Castle in Savo, stayed overnight in Ylimarkku in 1557. In 1624, an inn was established in Ylimarkku, and Bärndt Persson Nisuls was appointed as the innkeeper. In 1626, Gustav II Adolf of Sweden stayed the night in "Markeby", which could mean Ylimarkku. The inn is mentioned again in 1634 and continued to operate also in the late 17th c.

name: Eura
Settlement_Description:
The Eura parish village was likely formed before the 14th century. There are many famous Bronze and Iron Age archaeological findings in the area, so Eura river valley is one of the key areas in Satakunta. Eura church has been located in the same place since the Middle Ages, although there have been three church buildings in the site. 

<b>Inn:</b> An alehouse might have be located by the medieval church already . Churches usually had taverns in the Middle Ages and 16th-17th-centuries. Eura parish village is known to had an official inn from 1646 onwards with many owners. In 1646 the inn was hosted by Sipi Markunpoika Lukkala, in 1655 Sigfrid Markusson, and 1657 Anders Larsson.

name: null
Harbour_Description: Since the construction of the new bridge across the Meuse, the harbour was located on both sides (up- and downstream) of the bridge. In the years 1391-1525 the guild of the 'Schoense verderen' is found, who transported cloth to and herring from the markets in Scania. Market ferries ('marktschepen') to Liège and Roermond already existed in the 15th century. On the sketch of the town by S. de Bellomonte from 1587, there are three gates that give access to the harbour front: the 'porta carbonaria inferior/superior' (lower and upper coal gates) and a gate to the fish market. The quay on this side of the Meuse was called 'het Bat'.

name: Kaustari
Settlement_Description: <b>Inn:</b> An inn was established in Kaustari in 1640s, but it is first mentioned in 1656. Karl Simonsson was then the innkeeper, and he might have inherited the inn via his wife. His son, Mickel Karlsson, continued as an innkeeper.

name: Pohjankylä
Settlement_Description: <b>Inn:</b> An inn was established in Pohjankylä in 1627, and Mikko Juhonpoika Änkilä was appointed as the innkeeper. In 1637, Pentti Ollinpoika Hannila was appointed as the innkeeper. The parish constable (fi: nimismies, sw: länsman) Olli Sipinpoika Laurila hosted the inn in his farm Marttila in 1661-1673.

name: Yppäri
Settlement_Description: <b>Inn:</b> An inn was established in Yppäri in 1631, and Antti Matinpoika Pirkola was appointed as the innkeeper. Many new inns were established in the same year because of clearing and renovating work in the Ostrobothian Coastal Road. In 1653, Tuomas Erkinpoika Pisilä was appointed as the innkeeper, and Pisilä farm hosted the inn until 1796.

name: Ruotsalo
Settlement_Description: <b>Inn:</b> Ture Pedersson Bielke, Swedish nobleman and castellan of St. Olaf's Castle in Savo, stopped to change horses in Ruotsalo in 1557.

name: Isokylä (Kaarlela)
Settlement_Description: <b>Inn:</b> Kaarlela parish constable lived in Isokylä village at least from 1550s onwards. Parish constables (fi: nimismies, sw: länsman) were obliged to keep a tavern in late 16th c. Kaarlela parish constable had a transport organiser (sw. skjutsrättare, fi. kyytirättäri) in Lohtaja.

name: Kokemäen linna
Settlement_Description: Permanent agricultural settlement in Kokemäki (sw. Kumo) goes back to the Iron Age. The medieval parish organisation in Satakunta dates to the early 13th century with precursors in the latter half of the 12th century. The remains of a moated rectangular <b>Castle on Forsby Linnaluoto (literally Castle islet)</b> in Kokemäenjoki river has been identified as the castle in Satakunta, which king Albrecht of Mecklenburg ordained to be demolished and removed to another place after the complaints of Satakunta province in 1367. The charter has survived as a copy in the Cartulary of Turku Cathedral where it is in the late 15th century titled as “on the demolition of the castle in Kumo (Kokemäki)”. When the castle was founded is not known, but it may date to the headmanship of Matias Kettilmundson over Finland and Satakunta in 1324–25, or to the duchy of Halland and Finland of Bengt Algotsson in 1353–55, if the castle in question was not totally new and under construction. Archaeological excavations date the activity on the islet to the 13th and 14th centuries, partially to the 12th century. In the context of the demolition, the crown surrendered or exchanged the islet to the possession of bishop of Turku, who had in the mid-1350s established a manor opposite the castle on the Northern bank of the river.

name: Meerssen
Settlement_Description: Earliest mention in 847, in a ninth century copy.
Toll_Description: In the comital accounts at Meerssen an outpost of the toll of Valkenburg is mentioned since 1395, sometimes combined with a horse tax, although the latter is usually combined with the toll in Rode. Revenues of the road toll in Meerssen are found in the town accounts of Valkenburg, preserved (with lacunae) from 1452/3 onwards. In 1525 the comital toll of Valkenburg was farmed out with the tolls in Meerssen, Geulle, Cathagen, Bemelen and Weerde and the small toll of Klimmen.

name: Liikistö
Settlement_Description: The archaelogical site of Liikistö consists of a flat earthenwork with 13th to 14th century cemetery and a stone foundation of possibly later date. Together with Anola island and the site of Ulvila town Liikistö also hosted one of the earliest churches in the rivermouth area dating to the 13th century and mentioned in 1311. The church appears to have been abandoned after the merchants who had previously settled alongside the Kokemäenjoki river were ordained to move to the new town of Ulvila in the 1340s and 1350s. Finds of 15th coins from Liikistö witness about continuation of activities in the area even later. <b>Inn:</b> Ulvila is first cited in 1344 in a confirmation of land transaction, which in 1347 was said to have been corroborated in the presence of parishioners, townspeople, and rector of the parish in the Guild house of St Gertrud of Ulvila. The site of the guild house is unknown, possible places are Liikistö or the later town area of Ulvila. St. Gertrud's guild served especially travelling merchants and the cult came to the area with German traders.

name: Saijanjoki
Fair_Description: Viborg burghers were in 1606 said to have held of old annual fair at Saijanjoki river on the old border between Sweden and Russia. The right was confirmed 1606. The date of the fair is unknown.

name: Finby
Settlement_Description: <b>Inn:</b> Finby inn might have been established already in 1632. In 1650s, parish constable (fi. nimismies, sw. länsman) Samuel Persson was the innkeeper. A court record from 1650 tells about his guests: tailor Johan Eriksson and Pär Knutsson sat with the innkeeper. There was also another group with student Mathias Simonis and a sailor, as well as some other men. Parish constables served as innkeepers also in the late 17th. c.

name: Nieuwstadt
Settlement_Description: Nieuwstadt is first mentioned in 1242. It was founded on the location of an earlier settlement called (H)elsene.
Town_Description: Nieuwstadt is first mentioned in 1242, which is also its earliest mention as town (15 July). There is no known charter of town rights, but rights were probably granted by Otto II, count of Guelders. Nieuwstadt was walled between 1277 and 1573. Its importance diminished in the sixteenth century.
Fair_Description: Two fairs of 14 days each were granted in 1312. However, it is unknown whether they were ever organized at all.

name: Pitkäsilta (Hämeen linna)
Bridge_Description: Pitkäsilta-bridge over Vanajavesi stream on the common road between Häme and Viipuri Castles mas maintained by the entire late medieval and 16th century bailiwick of Häme Castle. The bridge is mentioned in 1583, but its maintenance had been very likely organised before the end of the 14th century or in the first half of the 15th. In 1738 the length of the bridge was 396 ells (ca. 23,5 m). In 1741 the bridge was relocated in the narrow stream between Häme Castle and the opposite Varikonniemi headland.

name: Kello
Settlement_Description: <b>Inn:</b> Ture Pedersson Bielke, Swedish nobleman and castellan of St. Olaf's Castle in Savo, stopped to change horses in Kello in 1557. Kello village had a transport organiser (fi. kyytirättäri, sw. skjutsrättare) serving Ii parish constable. In 1592, an inn was established, and Pietari Sipinpoika was appointed as the innkeeper. The Crown paid him 14 <i>spann</i> (ca. 1000 litres) barley for feeding and accommodating soldiers between Liminka and Ii. In 1640s, Kokkare farm served as an inn.

name: Skaftung
Settlement_Description: <b>Inn:</b> Skaftung is mentioned in Jaakko Teitti's list in 1556 as a possible place for a bailiff (fi. vouti, sw. fogde). Ture Pedersson Bielke, Swedish nobleman and castellan of St. Olaf's Castle in Savo, stayed overnight in Skaftung in 1557. In 1637, farmers from Siipyy, Skaftung and Härkmeri complained that they live near busy winter and summer roads, and they must give rides for 16-17 old Finnish miles (ca. 80-100 km). When they get back home, they must go again, which makes them very weary and poor. Farmers got some tax exemptions but complained again in 1641.

name: Sint Servaasbrug
Bridge_Description: A bridge crossing the Meuse river in Traiectum (Maastricht) on the Roman road Cologne-Bavay existed from the Roman period onwards. This bridge was located slightly further south from the modern Sint Servaasbrug. This was the only permanent bridge crossing the Meuse river between Liège and the North Sea. In 1139 the bridge was granted by the Emperor to the chapter of St. Servatius, with the right to levy a toll. In 1267 it was destroyed in warfare. In 1275 the restored wooden bridge collapsed during a religious procession, causing many people to drown in the Meuse. After this a new stone bridge was built: the present-day Sint Servaasbrug. Construction works started in 1281 and were finished before 1300. In 1646 the bridge was obtained by the city.

name: Vehkalahti (Hamina)
Settlement_Description:
Permanent agricultural settlement in Vehkalahti (sw. Veckelax) area dates to the Swedish colonisation in the latter half of the 13th century when new farms were founded amongst earlier area of usufruct and colonisation from Häme and Karelia. The parish organisation dates at the latest to the first half of the 14th century. Vehkalahti church is mentioned in 1396. Stone church from between 1430–70.
The earliest information on the organisation of the trade in the bailiwick of Viborg is from 1336 when the castellan granted the burghers of Reval (Tallinn) the right to trade freely in three towns (in tribus civitatis) in his dominion, named Viipuri (Wyborch), Vehkalahti (Weckelax) and Virolahti (Wyrlax). Instead of medieval towns proper with independent magistrates and sworn community of burghers, all the towns mentioned in 1336 had a form of fixed trading site with small merchant communities under the jurisdiction of the castellan located or frequenting the area. In 1653 a new town of Vehkalahti (sw. Veckelax Nystad) was chartered next to Vehkalahti church. A plan of the town was drawn already in 1649. Destroyed in the Great Northern War the town was re-established as Hamina (sw. Fredrikshamn) in 1721. 

<b>Inn:</b> An alehouse is mentioned in Vehkalahti in the 1545-1550 list. It served travellers both by land and sea. Vehkalahti parish constable's (fi: nimismies, sw: länsman) farm is mentioned as a place for accommodation in the travel account of Duke Johan of Finland from 1556.
Fair_Description: Burghers of Viborg were in 1542 granted sole right for four annual fairs in their trading area of which Vehkalahti St Olaf’s fair (29 July) were also allowed to take place in Viborg town. The other thre fairs were held on apostle Peter (29 June) in Jääski, on the Nativity of Mary (8 September) in Lapvesi and on the Elevation of the Holy Cross (14 September) in Äyräpää. Sole right to all four fairs was confirmed in 1594, when the fair in Vehkalahti was held on St Laurentius (10 August). In 1585 the fair in Vehkalahti was held on apostle Bartholomeus (24 August). The new town of Vehkalahti was in 1654 granted the right for three fairs on apostle Paulus (25 January), Laurentius (10 August) and Matteus (21 September).
Toll_Description: The 1/32 duty worth of all goods intended for sale in towns and fairs and brought to the site by peasants was collected in Vehkalahti since 1622.

name: Kokemäenkartano
Settlement_Description:
Permanent agricultural settlement in Kokemäki (sw. Kumo) goes back to the Iron Age. The medieval parish organisation in Satakunta dates to the early 13th century with precursors in the latter half of the 12th century. <b>Kokemäki Royal manor (sw. Kumo gård)</b> was established by the seneschal and magnate Bo Jonsson who was ordained as the headman of Finland in 1371, controlled all the castles and bailiwicks in Finland and much of Sweden proper in 1374–86, and sojourned ten weeks in the manor (in manerio regali dicto Kuma) in the winter of 1374. The manor replaced an older Royal castle on Forsby Linnaluoto islet demolished in 1367. Kokemäenkartano manor stabilised its position as the administrative centre of Satakunta at the time of Klaus Lydekesson (Djäkn), bailiff of Turku castle in 1411–35, and remained as such until the administration of the province was taken over by a new Royal manor in Ulvila in 1552. From 1553 to 1562 the manor served as the centre of small bailiwick consisting of Kokemäki, Huittinen and Loimaa parishes. It was included in the duchy of Johan in 1556–63. After sinking to the status of local manor, Kokemäenkartano was in the control of the nobility and was finally sold to Arvid Forbus in 1651. The main residence and storage area of the manor was located on Isoluoto islet opposite of the bailey area on the southern bank of the river accessed through a costly bridge maintained by three parishes of Ala-Satakunta district. The buildings on the islet and the bridge were abandoned after a new manor was completed on the southern side of the river in 1664.

<b>Inn:</b> Kokemäki manor is mentioned as a place for accommodation in the travel account of Duke Johan of Finland from 1556. Also Ture Pedersson Bielke, Swedish nobleman and castellan of St. Olaf's Castle in Savo, stayed in Kokemäki manor in 1557. Royal manors were obliged to provide accommodation for travelling officials.

name: Tornio
Settlement_Description:
Trade in the most important traditional trading posts at major river mouths in the Gulf of Bothnia area was regulated at the latest in 1420, when the crown furnished them with storage houses, started to collect toll, and prohibited other traditional trading sites alongside the Bothnic coastline. In 1459 all trade in these legal trading posts was restricted to Stockholm and Turku only, but without any result. The trading rights of Ulvila and Rauma in the legal trading posts of Oulu, Ii, Kemi and Tornio were confirmed together with those of Stockholm and Turku in 1531. Market sites and fairs in Tornio, Kemi, Ii and Oulu were also frequented by Russian Karelian merchants to 1608, when they were banned to travel further than Oulu. The oldest market site in Tornio area was very likely on Pirkkiö island in the river mouth, from where it was relocated to South-West side of Suensaari island to the area where the first market place of the town was.

<b>Inn:</b> Medieval trading posts likely had private alehouses and taverns to serve travelling merchants and farmers. Tornio parish constable (fi: nimismies, sw: länsman) was located in different villages by the Tornionjoki river mouth from 1540s onwards. Parish constables were obliged to keep a tavern in the 16th century. An inn is also mentioned in the 1640s.
Town_Description: The town of Tornio (sw. Torneå) was got its first privileges from Gustaf II Adolf in 1621. The town had no rights for foreign trade (active or passive staple rights), but the burghers had to ship their goods to Stockholm and Turku. Tornio was part of Sweden proper before 1809, when Tornionjoki river was set as the border between Sweden and Finland. The first church of the town was built near the marketplace in 1647 but was destroyed by fire in 1682 after which the new church was build outside the town at its present site in 1682-84. The oldest geographical surveys of the town area were made in 1638–42, the first map in 1642. In 1622 Kokkola and Oulu burghers were granted together with other towns in Ostrobothnia to trade at two annual fairs in Kemi and Ii parishes. Burghers of Tornio were granted similar rights for Kemi and Ii fairs in 1627 and 1636, but the rights of other towns than Oulu remained heavily disputed.  <b>Post office:</b> The founding year of Tornio post office is unsure, but according to the available sources the office was established at the latest in 1642.
Fair_Description: The summer fair in Tornio started in the Middle Ages and in 1519 at Midsummer (24 June). In 1649 the town applied the relocation of the fair to start on the eight day before midsummer. The market site was since the 1420s on the site of the oldest market place of the town where it was moved from Pirkkiö island in the rivermouth around that time.
Toll_Description: The Swedish crown started to collect toll from the new regulated harbours and market posts in Bothnian river mouths in the beginning of the 1420s. The 1/32 duty worth of all goods intended for sale in towns and fairs by the peasants was collected in Tornio since 1622.

name: Nieuw-Mude
Harbour_Description: Due to the silting of the Zwin, merchants from Mude (Sint Anna ter Muiden) founded the harbour and trading quarter Nieuw-Mude in the 14th century. After English soldiers had sacked Mude and Nieuw-Mude and used their buildings as a base to attack Sluis in 1405 and 1436, Duke Philipp the Good ordered in 1445 that Nieuw-Mude should never be rebuilt. The decision was confirmed in 1451, which meant the end of Mude as a harbour town.

name: Lapvesi (Lappeenranta)
Settlement_Description: Permanent agricultural settlement in Lapvesi and Lappeenranta (sw. Villmanstrand) area goes back to the Iron Age. Kauskila Kappelinmäki (Chapel hill) rich 12th and 13th century inhumation ground hosted the first church of the parish from the 14th century to the mid-16th and was in use until the early 17th century. The church was relocated closer to the fair site in Lapvesi in the mid-16th century. Lapvesi parish is first mentioned in 1415 but is likely to have been formed in the early 14th century.
Town_Description: Queen Christina founded Lappeenranta (sw. Vilmanstrand) town and gave the first town privileges in 1649. The town was founded on the site of the older fair site in Lapvesi north of the late 16th century parish church. The oldest surviving town plan is from the year 1649.
Fair_Description: Burghers of Viborg were in 1542 granted sole right for four annual fairs in their trading area of which Vehkalahti St Olaf’s fair (29 July) were also allowed to take place in Viborg town. The other thre fairs were held on apostle Peter (29 June) in Jääski, on the Nativity of Mary (8 September) in Lapvesi and on the Elevation of the Holy Cross (14 September) in Äyräpää. The right to all four fairs was confirmed in 1594. The burghers are known to have had permanent trading booths at the fair site since 1616. In 1621 the burghers of Viborg were granted the right of annual Michaelmas (29 September) fair for two weeks in Lapvesi together with the traditional one week fair of the Nativity of Mary. The two fairs were combined into a continuous three week fair in 1675.
Toll_Description: The 1/32 duty worth of all goods intended for sale in towns and fairs and brought to the site by peasants was collected in Lapvesi since 1622.

name: Tammisaari
Settlement_Description: Tammisaari (r. Ekenäs) was founded in 1528 by Erik Fleming, who held the bailiwick of Raseborg as a fief in 1528–40 and translocated an older community of merchants from around Raseborg castle or Snappertuna to a more suitable place on a promontory protruding into the bay of Pohja parish.
Town_Description: King Gustav I confirmed the privileges of the town of Tammisaari in 1546 but ordered in 1550 the burghers to move to the newly founded Helsinki, from where they received permission to return in 1557. Tammisaari belonged to Johan’s Duchy of Finland in 1556–63. The old privileges were confirmed in 1614. The oldest surviving geographical survey of the town area is from 1696. Since 1569 the town made part of the County of Raseborg with the parishes of Karjaa (sw. Karis) and Inkoo (sw. Ingå). In 1649 the County was further enlarged with the parishes of Pohja (sw. Poho), Karjalohja (sw. Karislojo), Lohja (sw. Lojo), Siuntio (sw. Sjundeå) and Vihti (sw. Vichtis), but was then cancelled altogether in the Great Reduction of 1680. Tammisaari was independent parish in 1603–95. In 1556 Johan established <b>Tammisaari Royal manor</b> (sw. Ekenäs gård) which served as the administrative centre of the bailiwick in 1560–69 and the County since 1569. The town of Tammisaari had active rights for export in 1614–17, limited in 1617–36, and passive rights for import to 1636. <b>Inn:</b> Tammisaari town council granted licences for the selling of drinks. Town alehouses sold mostly ale and distilled spirits (in the 17th c.), wine is mentioned only seldom. In the late 17th c., there was an inn serving accommodation to travellers as well as a transport organiser, which could date also from earlier.
Fair_Description: The burghers of Tammisaari complained in 1614 that the burghers of Turku and merchants’ apprentices from Tallinn and Sweden proper traded in Tenhola, which was prohibited in 1616. In 1627, Lohja Candlemas (2 February) and Saturday before Mid-Lent Sunday (28/29 February – 3 April) fairs were moved together with the Apostle Paul's (25 January) fair of Karjalohja to Tammisaari to be held as a single Candlemas (2 February) fair in the town. The fairs were returned to Lohja and Karjalohja before 1634, about which the merchants of Tammisaari unsuccessfully complained in 1636. Smaller annual fairs focused on the exchange of victuals were held in Lohja on fest of St Mary (15 August or 8 September). Local fairs are known to have been held in the late 17th Century at Pohja Church on 22 June and 14 September, and at Snappertuna Chapel on Apostle Bartholomeus (24 August).
Toll_Description: The 1/32 duty worth of all goods intended for sale in towns and fairs and brought to the site by peasants was collected in Tammisaari since 1622. The customs fence surrounding the town was, however, only built in 1695 and the town did not have separate house for the customs in the 17th century. The crown income from the duty was in 1637–39 in all 175 silver Dalers (Helsinki 250, Porvoo 540). The duty was since 1642 rented out.

name: Stocksudden
Settlement_Description: Permanent agricultural settlement in Tenhola (sw. Tenala) goes back to the 12th century. The parish organisation in Western Nyland dates to the early 13th century, Tenhola parish is first mentioned in 1329. The stone church was built between 1460 and 1480.
Fair_Description: Stocksudden local annual autumn fair some half a kilometre west from the Great Coastal road was ordained in 1747 to be held on 1 October, i.e. one week before the Nativity of Mary. Since the burghers of Tammisaari (sw. Ekenäs) complained as early as 1614 that the burghers of Turku and merchants’ apprentices from Reval (Tallinn) and Sweden proper traded in Tenhola, the fair at Stocksudden or Tenhola church may have been of older tradition. The fair was discontinued in 1822.

name: Jämsä
Settlement_Description: <b>Inn:</b> First inn was established in Jämsä in 1580s to Hyppölä farm. In 1595-1608 Saari-Penttilä farm served as the inn. In 1600, the assistant priest and parish constable (fi: nimismies, sw: länsman) in Jämsä, Matti Yrjönpoika from Auvila farm, served as the innkeeper. Count Per Brahe the Younger, Governor-General of Finland, stopped by Jämsä vicarage when returning to Turku in winter 1640.

name: Thorn
Settlement_Description: Thorn developed around a Benedictine nunnery that was founded in 992. It was situated near the old Roman road connecting Tongeren and Maastricht to Nijmegen. In the 13th century the monastery developed into a secular ladies' convent with far-reaching autonomy.
Fair_Description: In 1007 (June 4) the abby Thorn obtained market- and tollright from the German king with consent of the bishop of Liege in whose jurisdiction Thorn was situated. This was confirmed in 1292 by the king of the Roman empire.

name: Naantalin luostari
Settlement_Description: <b>Naantali Bridgettine Abbey:</b> The council of the Swedish realm founded in 1438 a Bridgettine Abbey in Finland. After an initial phase in Karinkylä Stenberga in Masku, the Abbey was in 1441 moved to the premises of an old Royal Manor in Pyhäjoki (Helgå) in Perniö but was finally located to Ailoinen in Raisio, where the knight Herik Klasson (Djäkn) and his wife Lucia Olofsdotter (Skelge) donated a farm for the foundation in 1442. King Christopher of Bavaria confirmed the relocation to Ailoinen in 1443. Active since 1444 the Abbey was consecrated in 1462. The Abbey’s landed property was confiscated in 1557, but the convent remained partially active until 1591. The Swedish name of the foundation is first cited in 1440 (Naadhennedal, sw. Nådendal), the Latin name Vallis Gracie in 1444. King Karl IX ordered the convent buildings to be demolished in 1608. The bridge connecting the Abbey and the town is mentioned in 1452. The road between Naantali and Raisio existed in 1454.

name: Hämeen linna
Settlement_Description: <b>Hämeen linna (sw. Tavastehus):</b> Hämeen linna Castle (Tauestahus) is first mentioned in 1308 in the division of the kingdom of Sweden between King Birger Magnusson and his brothers, Dukes Erik and Valdemar, when it came under Valdemar. The castle was preceded by an earlier base on the Hakoinen castle hill in Janakkala, where a coin from the time of King Birger Magnusson (1290–1318) has been found, and which Novgorod tried to conquer in 1311. The earliest coin finds at Häme Castle date back to the 1320s or 1330s. The castle and its fortifications were expanded and modernised several times from the second half of the 14th century to the mid-16th century, and it served as the administrative centre of Häme (sw. Tavastland) bailiwick and province even after the establishment of the provincial administration in 1635 until 1648, when the administration of the province of Uusimaa and Häme was transferred to Helsinki. The castle consists of three building complexes: the medieval main castle and the forecourt, the surrounding bastion system, built in the 1770s, and the brick buildings built in the 1740s and 1790s that served as an army depot. The castle served as a prison from the 1830s to the 1950s, after which it was restored.

name: Inkoo
Settlement_Description: Permanent agricultural settlement in Inkoo (sw. Ingå) goes back to the 12th century. The parish organisation in Western Nyland dates to the early 13th century. The stone church was built and expanded in three stages from the 1430s to the 1510s. The church was plundered by the Danes in 1509.
Fair_Description: Burghers of Helsinki were in 1594 granted rights to annual Apostle Matteus (21 September) fair in Inkoo. In 1614, the burghers of Tammisaari (sw.
