Ekenäs) tried unsuccessfully to relocate the fair to their town. Since Apostle Matteus was the consecration day of some of the stages of the stone church, the fair was of medieval origin. The fair site was located in the area between the Great Coastal road, the church and the harbour in the mouth of Inkoonjoki river. In the 1730s, Inkoo also held annual summer fair on the feast of apostle Jakob (25 July).
Toll_Description: The 1/32 duty worth of all goods intended for sale in towns and fairs and brought to the site by peasants was collected in Inkoo since 1622.

name: Pyhäjoki
Settlement_Description:
Permanent agricultural settlement in Perniö (sw. Bjärnå) dates to the Iron Age. Independent parish was established in the early 13th century and is mentioned in 1350. The earliest church was very likely located in Yliskylä, whereas the site of the later church along the Great Coastal Road dates to the early 14th century. The stone church was built between 1460 and 1480.
<b>Pyhäjoki Royal Manor</b> (sw. Helgå kungsgård) is first mentioned in 1347, when it was said to have existed already in the beginning of the 14th century. The manor was established in the late 13th or the beginning of the 14th century in the area of the Perniönjoki and Kiskonjoki rivermouths to support a settlement colonized from Sweden. The manor was either donated or pawned from 1354, but ownership remained with the crown until 1441, when it was donated as the basis for the planned Bridgettine Abbey in Finland. The monastery, founded in 1438, was initially planned for Masku's Stenberga, but was eventually located in 1442 in Raisio's Ailoinen. King Gustav I relocated the older medieval manor from Vanhakartano to Muntolannokka (Näse) at the confluence of the Perniönjoki and Kiskonjoki rivers in 1556. The manor came into possession of the nobility in 1640 and was moved to its later location near Latokartano in 1690. The route of the Great Coastal Road passed through the Näse and Vanhakartano area until the first quarter of the 17th century, when a new section of the road was built from Pakapyöli to Perniö Maansilta bridge.

name: Beek (Sittard)
Settlement_Description: Earliest mention in the mid-eleventh century, in an eighteenth century copy.

name: Maastricht
Settlement_Description: Maastricht originated as a Roman settlement in 50 C.E. It was located on the road between Cologne and Tongeren. In the third century Maastricht became seat of a bishopric, which was moved to Liège in the eighth century. Maastricht is first mentioned in written records in 535 (in a ninth-century copy). In 643 a leper house is mentioned. The chapter of St. Servatius is first attested in 889, that of Our Lady in 1096. Both were abolished in 1797.
Town_Description: In the twelfth century Maastricht developed into an important trade town. Most likely town rights were granted before 12 November 1204. The so-called 'Alde Caert' from 1243 contains the rights of the bishop of Liège in Maastricht. Statutes for the weavers and fullers are found in 1276. The oldest city account from the year 1399/1400 mentions three weigh houses, for fat, yarn and cloth ('vetwaag, garenwaag en gewantwaag'). Until 1794 Maastricht was a condominium of the dukes of Brabant and the Prince-Bishops of Liège.
Fair_Description: In 919 a weekly market is first mentioned. In 1243 three fairs and multiple daily markets are mentioned. In the first half of the 13th century the 'forum lignorum' (wood market) is mentioned. According to the steward accounts from the 14th/15th century a fair toll was levied in Maastricht on wagons from Aachen and Nuremberg. The fairs took place on the days of St. Servatius (May 13), St. Remaclus (September 3) and St. Remigius (October 1), with a duration of eight days before and after the fair days. A road toll ('Wegehegelt') was levied at the town gates during the fairs, according to the only surviving medieval city account from 1399/1400.
Toll_Description: In 779 Charlemagne confirmed the gift by his father Pepin († 768) to the abbey of St. Germain-des-Prés in Paris, concerning toll exemption in his lands, among others in Dorestad and Maastricht. In 908 the bishop of Liège received the rights on toll and mint in Maastricht. In 1332 the emperor confirmed the toll exemption of Nuremberg in Maastricht. In 1346 the bishop of Liège confirmed the existing privileges of Nijmegen at the toll of Maastricht. Toll accounts from 1324/25 and 1379-1382 are preserved. The revenues of the so-called 'Doorvarende Zwijgende (land)tol' belonged to the duke of Brabant, probably since the 14th century. It was probably levied at two places in the Vroenhof, the Brabant territory in Maastricht, both in and outside the town walls.
Staple_Description: Around 1500 Maastricht obtained the staple for raw wool imported from Hesse and Thuringia. It remained in place for most of the 16th century. The only surviving medieval city account from 1399/1400 already suggests a staple for wool from Cologne in Maastricht.

name: Turkhauta
Settlement_Description: Permanent agricultural settlement in Turkhauta area goes back to the 13th century. Originally a chapel of Janakkala parish, Hausjärvi was established as an independent parish in 1611.  <b>Inn:</b> An inn was established in Torttila, Turkhauta in 1642, and it remained in use until 1681.
Fair_Description: The burghers of Helsinki were in 1614 granted the sole right to the annual fair held in Turkhauta on 1 September, i.e. a week before Nativity of St Mary. The fair had been previously attended also by burghers of Porvoo (sw. Borgå) Helsinki's exclusive right was confirmed in 1616. In 1654, the fair day was changed to 14 September, so that the burghers returning from St Bartolomeus fair in Vähä-Ahvenkoski (24 August), could also make it to Turkhauta.
Toll_Description: The 1/32 duty worth of all goods intended for sale in towns and fairs and brought to the site by peasants was collected in Turkhauta since 1622.

name: Virolahti
Settlement_Description:
Permanent agricultural settlement in Virolahti (sw. Vederlax) area dates to the Swedish colonisation in the beginning of the 14th century when new farms were founded amongst possible earlier area of Finnish usufruct and colonisation. The parish organisation dates at the latest to the first half of the 14th century. Virolahti parish is mentioned 1370, stone sachristy from the first third of the 16th century. 
The earliest information on the organisation of the trade in the bailiwick of Viborg is from 1336 when the castellan granted the burghers of Reval (Tallinn) the right to trade freely in three towns (in tribus civitatis) in his dominion, named Viipuri (Wyborch), Vehkalahti (Weckelax) ja Virolahti (Wyrlax). Instead of medieval towns proper with independent magistrates and sworn community of burghers, all the towns mentioned in 1336 had a form of fixed trading site with small merchant communities under the jurisdiction of the castellan located or frequenting the area. Possible locations for the site of the trading activity in 1336 are the surroundings of Virolahti old church or Munkkiniemi (sw. Munkenäs) goods mentioned in 1370 in the area between Hailila and Ala-Pihlaja alongside the Great Coastal road. <b>Inn:</b> An alehouse is mentioned in Virolahti in the 1545-1550 list. It served travellers both by land and sea.

name: Iin Hamina
Settlement_Description:
Trade in the most important traditional trading posts at major river mouths in the Gulf of Bothnia area was regulated at the latest in 1420, when the crown furnished them with storage houses, started to collect toll, and prohibited other traditional trading sites alongside the Bothnic coastline. In 1459 all trade in these legal trading posts was restricted to Stockholm and Turku only, but without any result. The trading rights of Ulvila and Rauma in the legal trading posts of Oulu, Ii, Kemi and Tornio were confirmed together with those of Stockholm and Turku in 1531, and in 1542 the crown rented shops and storage facilities in Oulu, Ii and Kemi. Market sites and fairs in Tornio, Kemi, Ii and Oulu were also frequented by Russian Karelian merchants to the beginning of the 17th century. In 1622 Kokkola and Oulu burghers were granted together with other towns in Ostrobothnia to trade at two annual fairs in Kemi and Ii parishes. Burghers of Tornio were granted similar rights for Kemi and Ii fairs in 1627 and 1636, but the rights of other towns than Oulu remained heavily disputed. In the 1640s Oulu burghers arrived every year to Ii in the beginning of salmon season at midsummer, held fairs close to the parish church and stayed until St James (25.7.) or St Olaf (29.8.). Ii is cited as a chapel of Kemi in 1375, administrative parish in 1445 and ecclesiastic parish in 1477. In the archaeological excavations on the site of the oldest parish church next to the Hamina market area in 2009 a total of 70 graves were documented, the majority of which dated to the 15th and 16th centuries. The last wooden church on the site was destroyed by fire in the 1580s after which a new one was built in 1620 on the site of the later Ii church.

<b>Inn:</b> Medieval trading posts likely had private alehouses and taverns to serve travelling merchants and farmers.
Fair_Description: In 1622 the annual winter and summer fair in Ii Hamina was set to New Year’s day (1 January) and St John the Baptist (24 June). In 1660 annual fairs were held in summer starting from the feast of apostle Peter (29 June) for 14 days.
Toll_Description: The Swedish crown started to collect toll from the new regulated harbours and market posts in Bothnian river mouths in the beginning of the 1420s. The 1/32 duty worth of all goods intended for sale in towns and fairs and brought to the site by peasants was collected in Ii Hamina since 1622.

name: Lumijoki
Settlement_Description: <b>Inn:</b> Ture Pedersson Bielke, Swedish nobleman and castellan of St. Olaf's Castle in Savo, stopped to change horses in Lumijoki in 1557. Lumijoki village had a transport organisator (fi. kyytirättäri, sw. skjutsrättare) serving Liminka parish constable. In 1640s, an inn was established in the village, and Paavo Markuksenpoika Jakku was appointed as the innkeeper. Jakku farm served as an inn for a long time.

name: Siikajoki
Settlement_Description: <b>Inn:</b> Ture Pedersson Bielke, Swedish nobleman and castellan of St. Olaf's Castle in Savo, stopped to change horses in Siikajoki in 1557. Siikajoki village had a transport organisator (fi. kyytirättäri, sw. skjutsrättare) serving Salo parish constable. An inn was established in Siikajoki in 1640s, and Jaakko Sipinpoika Kerttula was appointed as the innkeeper. Kerttula farm continued to serve as an inn until early 18th c. and periodically also later.

name: Ii
Settlement_Description: <b>Inn:</b> Ture Pedersson Bielke, Swedish nobleman and castellan of St. Olaf's Castle in Savo, stayed overnight at Ii parish constable Tuomas Leistoinen in 1557. The vicar in Ii usually served as a parish constable as well, and was thus obliged to keep an inn. The parish constable had transport organisers (fi. kyytirättäri, sw. skjutsrättare) in Kello, Haukipudas, Olhava, Kuivaniemi, Simo, Simoniemi and Maksniemi. From 1630 onwards, there were exceptionally two parish constables in Ii: one by the church and another in Kuivaniemi. In 1631, an inn was established in Ii parish village. Many new inns were established in the same year because of clearing and renovating work in the Ostrobothian Coastal Road.

name: Saviniemi
Settlement_Description: Permanent agricultural settlement in Saviniemi area dates to the late Iron Age. <b>Saviniemi Royal Manor</b> was very likely established already in the mid-14th century on a strategic location on the eastern bank of Vuoksi river. The manor is first cited in 1523 and served as the administrative centre of Äyräpää bailiwick in 1552-61. <b>Inn:</b> Royal manors were obliged to provide accommodation for travelling officials. In 1660s, there was an alehouse by the manor, owned by Anton Borchardt, a magistrate in Vyborg, who also run an alehouse in Vyborg.

name: Oulunsalo
Settlement_Description: <b>Inn:</b> Oulunsalo village had a transport organiser (fi. kyytirättäri, sw. skjutsrättare) serving Liminka parish constable. An inn was established in 1650s, and Olli Antinpoika Anttila was appointed as the innkeeper. The winterway from Oulu to Lumijoki went through Oulunsalo, which was an island at the time, since it was faster to travel on ice rather than taking the road through Liminka.

name: Haukipudas
Settlement_Description: <b>Inn:</b> Haukipudas village had a transport organiser (fi. kyytirättäri, sw. skjutsrättare) serving Ii parish constable. In 1650, villagers told that since there was no inn in the village, their assistant vicar, Carolus Henrici, had to serve food and accommodation to travellers. The priest appealed for tax reduction, but its outcome is not known.

name: Jokipii
Settlement_Description: <b>Inn:</b> An inn was established in Jokipii farm in 1612. Jaakko Pertunpoika Jokipii complained how he had to give food and drinks to travellers, so he was given tavern rights together with tax exemptions and freedom from military service.

name: Harju
Fair_Description: Burghers of Pori were granted the rights of annual Candlemas winter fair in Pirkkala parish at Harju in 1602 and again in 1604. The actual status of the fair since the 1610s is unknown and it appears to have become part of the interest area of Turku after 1614. The fair was relocated in 1638 to Tammerkoski village from where the annual winter (6 January) and autumn (24 August) fairs were transferred back to Harju in 1708. In 1750 both fairs were relocated to Pispala where they were held until 1778. Harju chapel was established in 1639, the first chapel church was built in 1645. The site of the fair was East or South from the chapel church alongside the common road and several winterways. The oldest site of the possible medieval fair in the region may have in the same location or close to Käräjätörmä south of Vaakkolammi pond. The surrounding area had in 1540 six villages of which at least two, Tohloppi and Hyhky were established as farmsteads already before the first tithing in ca. 1250. Both of them and Pispala are also known from late 15th century sources, when the Bishop of Turku owned tennant farms in Hyhky and Pispala. The sessions of Pirkkala parish court were held in 1507-14 in Hyhky where some of the yeoman farmers acted as the parish constable.
Toll_Description: The 1/32 duty worth of all goods intended for sale in towns and fairs and brought to the site by peasants was likely to be collected in Harju from 1622 to 1637.

name: Heerlen
Settlement_Description: Earliest mention in circa 300, in an eighth and tenth century copy.
Toll_Description: A road toll ('winage appellé weghelt') in Heerlen first appears in the comital accounts of Valkenburg in 1399-1400. In 1439 it was collected by the steward of Valkenburg. Each wagon or cart paid 1 'alt morken'.

name: Toijala
Settlement_Description: <b>Inn:</b> Toijala village was in the intersection of two summer roads and a winterway to Turku, so it was a good place for a tavern. The first tavern owner is mentioned in 1561: Jussi Sipinpoika Koiweri (surname is a local version of the word for tavern). In 1575-1578 two brothers, Jussi and Heikki Sipinpoika Köyväri (another dialectal version) are mentioned as the owners of the tavern. Next mention of Toijala tavern is from the 1688, when the host was Martti Marinpoika from Kottila farm. Köyväri farm ran the tavern again in the 18th c. Köyväri farm, that got its name from "the tavern", could have served as such also during the 17th c.,  given the central location of the village.

name: Bemelen
Settlement_Description: Earliest mention in 1096, in a fifteenth-century copy. Bemelen is located on the old route between Maastricht and Aachen.
Toll_Description: In the comital account of Valkenburg from 1396-97 a toll in Bemelen in mentioned. Annual revenues are also recorded. It was subordinated to the 'big' toll of Valkenburg. The inhabitants of Aachen were exempt, at least they claimed so in 1404.

name: null
Ferry_Description: A ferry between Geulle and Uikhoven is first mentioned in 1381. It was a fief of the lord of Valkenburg. At that time the ferry must have crossed the Geul river. Around 1410 the river Meuse shifted its course to the former riverbed of the Geul.

name: null
Bridge_Description: The bridge crossing the river Geul next to the Geulpoort gate was improved with pillars made of stone instead of wood in 1477.

name: Valkenburg (Geul)
Settlement_Description: The castle Valkenburg is first mentioned in 1041, but this refers to present-day Oud-Valkenburg. A new castle with the same name was built around 1100 at the site of the current town Valkenburg and is first mentioned in 1121.
Town_Description: An urban trade settlement developed in the thirteenth century near the castle, which was surrounded with a stone wall. Valkenburg is first mentioned as a town before 1 May 1353. A charter has not survived. Possibly, town privileges were granted by Reinald, lord of Monschau and Valkenburg. A hospital is found in 1396. In 1473 some 1500 hearths were counted.
Toll_Description: A toll in Valkenburg is first mentioned in 1249. In 1284 citizens from Aachen were freed of this toll, against payment of 500 Mark at once and 50 Mark annually. The comital 'big' toll of Valkenburg had outposts in Bemelen, Meerssen, Geulle, Weert, Cathagen, Heerlen and a small toll in Klimmen since the late 14th century. Accounts containing the toll and the 'weggeld' (road toll) are preserved for the years 1452-1467, 1478, 1483-1490, and 1611-1792. The account from 1453/4 is the oldest which records the number of passing wagons: 176, which each paid 1/2 stuiver as 'weggeld'. A quarter of this income, called the 'little toll', belonged to the lord of the town. Only 16 wagons paid the actual toll that year, each 6 boddragers. Possibly these were the wagons who visited the local market. In 1460 the numbers were much higher: 388 and 33. According to Slanghen the tolls in Uikhoven and Geulle, both levied on the river Meuse, were also part of the domain of the lord of Valkenburg.

name: Kauskila
Settlement_Description: Kauskila has a chapel and pre-Christian cemetary, which might have been in use until the 17th c. <b>Inn:</b> Kauskila is located in the intersection of local roads, and there has most likely been a tavern by the chapel, serving travellers and pilgrims.

name: null
Ferry_Description: A ferry between Uikhoven and Geulle is first mentioned in 1381. It was a fief of the lord of Valkenburg. At that time the ferry must have crossed the Geul river. Around 1410 the river Meuse shifted its course to the former riverbed of the Geul.

name: Hemminki
Settlement_Description: <b>Inn:</b> Hemminki had a natural ford for crossing the Kauhavanjoki river, so the first tavern and the first church were established there in 1650. During dry season, one could cross the river with a full carriage in Hemminki.

name: Maksniemi
Settlement_Description: <b>Inn:</b> Maksniemi village had a transport organiser (fi. kyytirättäri, sw. skjutsrättare) serving Ii parish constable.

name: Limbourg
Fair_Description: In 1336 the duke of Brabant and Limburg granted Limbourg two fairs (with St. Martin: Nov. 11 and St. George: April 23) and a weekly market on Monday with a forced staple. In 1532 and 1548 emperor Charles V confirmed this privileges for the inhabitants of the Land of Herve.
Staple_Description: In 1336 the duke of Brabant and Limburg granted Limbourg two fairs and a weekly market on Monday with a forced staple. In 1532 and 1548 emperor Charles V confirmed this privileges for the inhabitants of the Land of Herve. Excepted from the staple are now workmen in the leadmines and inhabitants who lived less then a mile around Liège, Aix-la-Chapelle (Aachen) and Maastricht.

name: Echt
Settlement_Description: The first mention of Echt dates from 950, which might be a forgery from the tenth century. The first certain mention dates from 1050.
Town_Description: Councillors ('schepenen') are first mentioned in 1259. A hospital is mentioned in 1307. Around 1397 the town is fortified with a wall. A cloth hall is mentioned in 1481. However, the settlement is still referred to as 'villa' in 1342 and is listed as a town of minor importance in 1343. On 18 August 1494 Echt is first mentioned as town. However, no charter of town rights is known to exist. If town rights wereever granted officially, this was possibly done by Charles II, duke of Guelders.
Fair_Description: It is stated that Echt had the right to hold a fair before 1294, but this is questionable.
Toll_Description: According to the forged charter from 950, the Roman king Otto I gave his vassal Ansfried market and mint rights and the toll in Kessel ('Cassalo sito in pago Masalant'), which had to be relocated from Echt ('in villa Ehti').

name: Alsdorf
Toll_Description: A toll of the duke of Brabant is first mentioned in 1312/52. In that year the revenues were 7 Mark, in 1356/57 9 Mark and in 1389-1391 10 Mark. In 1389 also a fee for safe conduct of 2 alb per horse was levied.

name: Järvenkylä
Settlement_Description: <b>Inn:</b> An inn was established in Järvenkylä in Hollo farm in 1650. It served until the turn of the century.

name: Raeren
Toll_Description: A toll in 'Roderen' is mentioned in accounts of the duchy of Brabant-Limbourg from 1389 onwards. The revenues were low at the time, due to warfare. A tariff is known from 1468.

name: Ikaalinen
Settlement_Description: <b>Inn:</b> Ikaalinen vicar Abraham Jacobi established an inn in 1653, which continued to serve until the end of 1660s. The vicar's son, Abraham Ikalensis, continued as the innkeeper and complained in 1666, how drinks are served illegally in the village, and people come to the church drunk. The court reminded people of the tavern statute, which stated that only official taverns are allowed to serve drinks, and the 40 <i>marks</i> fine for illegal serving. After this, one of the local farmers, Paavo Ollinpoika from Talonen farm in Vatsiainen, said that the peasants would never agree to that, and he was fined for his words.

name: Muhos
Settlement_Description: <b>Inn:</b> An inn was established in Muhos in the 1640s, and Simo Tikkanen was appointed as the innkeeper. Tikkanen farm continued to serve as an inn for decades.

name: Tiistenjoki
Settlement_Description: <b>Inn:</b> An inn was established in Tiistenjoki, and Matti Yrjönpoika was appointed as the innkeeper. According to Luukko 1945, he ran his inn in Toppari farm, but Lehtinen & Luho 1963 claim that Matti was from Ämmälä farm, and the inn moved to Toppari farm in 1647. In 1663, officials in stated that only the inns in Härsilä, Stroka and Ylijepua are needed in Lapua area, and tried to close the inns in Kuhalammi, Toppari, Hemminki and Ylinurmo. It was thought that their owners had established inns only to receive tax exemptions and freedom from military service.

name: Lautiosaari
Settlement_Description: <b>Inn:</b> An inn was established in Lautiosaari in the 1640s.

name: Mäyry
Settlement_Description: <b>Inn:</b> An inn was established in Mäyry in 1615, and Heikki Mäyry was appointed as the innkeeper. Heikki had complained that he had to accommodate travellers between Ruovesi and Lapua, and in compensation he got some meat and hay, as well as an official tavern status. The inn later moved to Kuhalampi, which is in the southern end of Kuhajärvi lake. In 1663, officials in stated that only the inns in Härsilä, Stroka and Ylijepua are needed in Lapua area, and tried to close the inns in Kuhalammi, Toppari, Hemminki and Ylinurmo. It was thought that their owners had established inns only to receive tax exemptions and freedom from military service.

name: Haapakoski
Settlement_Description: <b>Inn:</b> Yrjö Matinpoika Krouvari ("Tavern keeper") had an alehouse in Haapakoski by Lapuanjoki river. He married into Tuomaala farm and continued to run the alehouse there. Since there was an official tavern in Lapua, who at this time had a monopoly in selling drinks, they wanted to close down the private alehouse, and succeded in 1663. Yrjö continued to sell drinks in secret, and in 1680s he war suspected of illegal tobacco trade.

name: null
Harbour_Description: In 1449 the monastery of Mariager was granted the right to establish a harbour. The character of the harbour is, however, unknown.

name: Tyrväänkylä
Settlement_Description: <b>Inn:</b> Tyrvää parish constable's (fi: nimismies, sw: länsman) farm is mentioned in Jaakko Teitti's list in 1556 as a possible place for a bailiff (fi. vouti, sw. fogde). Ture Pedersson Bielke, Swedish nobleman and castellan of St. Olaf's Castle in Savo, stopped in Tyrväänkylä in 1557. Olavi Eskelinpoika Eskola is mentioned as an innkeeper in Tyrväänkylä in 1586.

name: Lohja
Settlement_Description:
Permanent agricultural settlement in Lohja (sw. Lojo) goes back to end of the Iron Age. The parish organisation in Western Nyland dates to the early 13th century, Lohja parish is first mentioned in 1323. The stone church was built between ca. 1470 and 1490.

<b>Inn:</b> Lohja vicarage served food, drinks, and accommodation to travellers. In 1591, a group of soldiers from Sweden proper stayed at vicar Thomas for two nights. In 1600, Thomas certified that villagers who lived close to the church had served food, drink and lodging to soldiers who had gathered for muster.
Fair_Description: The annual winter fair in Lohja was held in 1627 on Candlemas (2 February) and on the Saturday before Mid-Lent Sunday (28/29 February – 3 April). In the early 1600s the fairs were attended by burghers of Turku and peasants from as far as Kalanti. In 1627, the Lohja fair was moved together with the Apostle Paul's (25 January) fair in Karjalohja to Tammisaari as a single Candlemas (2 February) fair. The fair returned to Lohja before 1634, which the merchants of Tammisaari unsuccessfully complained about in 1636. The Candlemas fair was confirmed to be held in Lohja in 1650. The Lohja fair is mentioned in almanacs in 1592 and 1618 and dates back to the Middle Ages. The site of the winter fair was located south of Lohja Church. Another old market day in the area was very likely the Conversion of Apostle Paul (25 January), when a donation to Lohja Church was confirmed at a parish meeting held at the church in the presence of the Bishop of Turku, the Provost of Lohja, the Rector of Karjaa, and the district judge. No annual fairs are known to be held in Tammisaari before 1627 or after the 1630s until the 18th century. Smaller annual fairs focused on the exchange of victuals were held in Lohja on fest of St Mary (15 August or 8 September). Local fairs are known to have been held in the late 17th Century at Pohja Church on 22 June and 14 September, and at Snappertuna Chapel on Apostle Bartholomeus (24 August).
Toll_Description: The 1/32 duty worth of all goods intended for sale in towns and fairs and brought to the site by peasants was collected in Lohja in 1622-27 and after 1634.

name: Metsäkylä
Settlement_Description: <b>Inn:</b> Archbishop of Uppsala Laurentius Petri, Bishop of Turku Mikael Agricola, and member of the royal council of Sweden Sten Eriksson Lejonhufwud travelled to Moscow to negotiate a peace between Sweden and Russia. They stayed in Metsäkylä, where they continued to the border.

name: Montfort
Settlement_Description: First mentioned in 1258, but it is not certain that this document refers to Montfort. First certain mention in 1272. The settlement originated near a castle built around 1260.
Town_Description: Town rights were granted between 1277 and 1294 by Reginald I, count of Guelders. These rights were granted to stimulate the development of the town, but Montfort never fully developed into a town. In 1310, Montfort lost its town privileges, but these were re-granted in 1312. Montfort is last mentioned as a town in written sources in 1421. However, Jacob van Deventer drew a map of Montfort for his series of town maps in 1545. The castle of Montfort last served military purposes in the 1630s.
Fair_Description: As stated in 1312 by Reginald (Reinald) I, count of Guelders, a fair and weekly market should have been given to Montfort before 1294. Most likely, however, this fair has never become effective.

name: null
Toll_Description: The Count of Guelders levied a bridge toll in Vlodrop for the first time in 1294/95. Tariffs are not known. In the 16th century the toll is known as the Wassenberg toll, which appears in accounts from 1389 onwards without specification. This toll was levied at three other places in the 16th century: Wassenberg, south of the church of Wildenrath and Orsbeck. In 1573 the stadtholder requested Roermond to act against the bridge of Vlodrop.

name: Ahmasjärvi
Settlement_Description: <b>Inn:</b> An inn was established in Ahmasjärvi in the 1640s, and Paavo Pekanpoika Kolehmainen was appointed as the innkeeper. The farm got the name Kivari ("Inn") and continued to serve until the end of the century.

name: Päntäne
Settlement_Description: <b>Inn:</b> An inn was established in Päntäne, and Antti Yrjönpoika from Keturi farm was appointed as the innkeeper in 1648. Antti had complained, that his house was commonly used as an inn, and in return he got official tavern rights.

name: Ikola
Settlement_Description: <b>Inn:</b> An inn was established in Ikola in 1650, and Pietari Gumse was appointed as the innkeeper. Two years later, the governor ordered the farmers in Isokyrö to transport logs to the tavern and help in building rooms for travellers.

name: Vlodrop
Settlement_Description: Earliest mention in 943, in an eleventh century copy.

name: Lempola (Ylistaro)
Settlement_Description:
<b>Inn:</b> An inn was established in Lempola farm in 1630, when Erkki Tapaninpoika and Sipi Sylvesterinpoika were appointed as innkeepers for "this year", so the tavern might have moved elsewhere later. There was a tavern in the 1640s in nearby Torkkoila village.

<b>Post house:</b> Oluf Jönsson appointed Yrjö Jaakonpoika as the postmaster of the Ylistaro Lempola village and granted him the postmaster's mandate in the year 1643.

name: Vittinki
Settlement_Description: <b>Inn:</b> Inspector for tobacco trade Jaakko Ångerman applied for a permission to establish a tavern in the uninhabited forest between Ilmajoki and Isokyrö. His project was unsuccesful, but a couple of years later, Matti Witting established a tavern next to Hopeavuori silver mine. Witting gave his name to the area.

name: Kaukjärvi
Settlement_Description: <b>Inn:</b> The road between Vyborg and Kaukjärvi is sometimes called "The Road of St. Bridget", which tells of its medieval origin. In Talpola (3 km south) there was a chapel dedicated to St. Bridget of Sweden. In the 16th c., Kaukjärvi villagers received tax exemptions since they accommodated and gave transports to so much people on the busy road. The road might have been used only during winter, since it is not visible in 17th c. maps. Knuutila farm was the traditional place of the inn, and its inhabitants got the surname Krouvari (=innkeeper).

name: Haistila
Settlement_Description:
Haistila village was settled in mid-13th century. It was among the westernmost Finnish-speaking settlements at the rivermouth area before the Swedish colonisation. The village had possessions on both sides of the river. The neighbouring Ragvaldsby (Ravani) was founded at the latter half of the 13th century or early 14th. Haistila was the site of the parish court in Ulvila in 1470, 1473 and 1550–52, when one of the farmesrs must have served as the Parish Constable (fi. Ninimsmies, sw. Länsman) of Ulvila. Parish Constablulary is also documented in Haistila in 1576–80, 1585–90, 1614–29, 1637–39 and 1643–56, in Ravani in 1583. 

<b>Inn:</b> The first inns in Haistila may date to the 15th century. Those Ulvila parish constables, who lived in Haistila, most likely served as innkeepers as well. Mikko Antinpoika from Haistila is mentioned as a parish constable in 1586. From 1637 onwards, Jaakko Matinpoika served as a parish constable and innkeeper in Haistila. In 1640s, Heikki Lauttamies ("Ferryman") served drinks by the ferry.

name: Ruosniemi
Settlement_Description: <b>Inn:</b> An inn was established in Ruosniemi in 1642, and Juho Pietarinpoika Tervaselkä was appointed as the innkeeper. In 1646, Erkki Juhonpoika Tervaselkä ran the inn.

name: Vähäkyrö
Settlement_Description: <b>Inn:</b> Vähäkyrö is located near the crossing of Kyröjoki river. The village and its parish constable might have been established already in the Middle Ages, although they are mentioned first in 1540s. Ture Pedersson Bielke, Swedish nobleman and castellan of St. Olaf's Castle in Savo, stopped to change horses and dine in Kyrö parish constable farm in nearby Ojaniemi village in 1557. The river and the common road had a lot of traffic, and in 1566, Kyrö parish constable had seven transport organisers (sw. skjutsrättare, fi. kyytirättäri) to help him. One of them was in Ylistaro, others in Ilmajoki and Lapua, but not all of their posts are known. It was ordered in 1624 that a bridge should be built across Kyröjoki river, where there previously had been a ferry. In 1650, parish constable Jaakko Grelsson was appointed as the innkeeper. A couple of years later, the governor ordered Vähäkyrö farmers to transport logs to the tavern and help in building rooms for travellers.

name: Torkkola
Settlement_Description: <b>Inn:</b> An inn was established in Torkkola in 1641, and Tapani Torkkoinen was appointed as the innkeeper. There might have been another tavern across the Kyröjoki river in Holkkola farm (or Torkkola inn was housed at Holkkola farm), since bailiff Arvid Simonpoika Hållfast was given rights to establish a tavern there in 1640.

name: Villiö
Settlement_Description:
Permanent agricultural settlement in Kokemäki (sw. Kumo) goes back to the Iron Age. The medieval parish organisation in Satakunta dates to the early 13th century with precursors in the latter half of the 12th century. Villiö village hosted German merchants by Kokemäenjoki river already from the 13th c. onwards. In 1362, there were three farms in <i>Villaby</i>, and <i>villa Kwmo</i> (Kuumo) mentioned in 1345 might also refer to Villiö. The area has many place names stemming from Middle Low German and/or connected to medieval craftmanship. Trading post might have been in Villiö or in Ylistaro, which is located about 1 km upstream (see also).

<b>Inn:</b> There has been a guild hall for the merchants in Villiö probably already in the 14th century. The hall would host travelling merchants, and it also served as a place for gathering. In the late 15th c., Villiö guild hall was a popular place for court gatherings, and sessions were organised there at least in 1482, 1492, and 1500. Medieval guild halls could also have served as an alehouse or an inn, serving food, drink, and accommodation also to non-members.

 In mid-15th c. and late 16th c., the parish constable (fi: nimismies, sw: länsman) was located in Villiö. Parish constables were obliged to keep a tavern in late 16th c. In 1586, Jaakko Olavinpoika Hyörä served as the parish constable and innkeeper.

name: Suosmeri
Settlement_Description: <b>Inn:</b> A medieval guild hall was located in Suosmeri. No exact date is known, but in 1556, it is mentioned that the guild hall was by the rivermouth, which was at the time closer to Ulvila because of postglacial land uplift.

name: Äyräpää (Muolaa)
Settlement_Description:
Permanent agricultural settlement in Muolaa and Äyräpää area goes back to the Iron Age. Äyräpää was together with Savilahti and Jääski one of the three pogosts Novgorod handed over to the Kingdom of Sweden in the peace of Nöteborg in 1323. In 1352 it is cited as one of the ten parishes under Royal patronage in Finland. In the Middle Ages the parish was also called as that of the Holy Cross (fi. Pyhäristi), which was the patron of the earliest church in the area. The earliest centre of the parish was in Muolaa region, the later Äyräpää parish was established in 1925.

<b>Inn:</b> Parish constable (fi: nimismies, sw: länsman) Nuutti Manninen ran a tavern in his house in 1600. In 1649, Reijo Hotokka ran a tavern in his farm in Kangaspelto, which is ca. 1 km east.
Fair_Description: Burghers of Viborg were in 1542 granted sole right for four annual fairs in their trading area of which Vehkalahti St Olaf’s fair (29 July) were also allowed to take place in Viborg town. The other thre fairs were held on apostle Peter (29 June) in Jääski, on the Nativity of Mary (8 September) in Lapvesi and on the Elevation of the Holy Cross (14 September) in Äyräpää. The burghers sole right to all four fairs was confirmed in 1594. Holy Cross was the medieval patron of Äyräpää church. In 1627 burghers of Viborg were confirmed the right for two annual fairs in Muolaa and in Nyenskans. The exact fair site in Muolaa is not clear.
Toll_Description: The 1/32 duty worth of all goods intended for sale in towns and fairs and brought to the site by peasants was collected in Äyräpää since 1622.

name: Säkylä
Settlement_Description: <b>Inn:</b> There has been a medieval tavern in Säkylä already before mid.-15th c. In 1458, Henrik and Jönis Kroghe ("Tavern") from Iso-Säkylä village (Säkylä major) served as lay members of court in Köyliö and Säkylä. Krouvila farm is also mentioned later in 1546 and 1552. Säkylä is located by a busy road between Virttaa and Eura, so it has been a good place for a tavern. First official inn is mentioned in 1586 in Vähä-Säkylä (Säkylä minor), when Tapani Klemetinpoika from Mäkitalo or Sonna farm was the innkeeper. Markus Sipinpoika from Perttula farm in Iso-Säkylä was the innkeeper in 1630, and Sipi Markunpoika (his son?) in 1641. They both served also as the paris constable (fi: nimismies, sw: länsman). The inn was located later in the 1640s in Nikkari farm by the church.

name: Köyliö
Settlement_Description:
Presumed site of Köyliö church before 1751. Köyliö, Säkylä and Yläne may have formed one parish in the 13th century. <b>Köyliö manor</b> belonged to the bishops of Turku in 1365. The church existed in 1378 and the area is cited as a chapel and quarter of a tax parish in the 15th century. Chapel in Kokemäki parish in 1541, independent parish since 1587. First wooden churches with late medieval stone sacristy were located south of the manor on lake bank. South from the church stood a separate chapel 1688, possibly memorial chapel of St Henrik. The church and the manor burned down in 1751 after which the new church was built more south in 1752.

<b>Inn:</b> Köyliö manor has been used for accommodation, first by the bishop (perhaps serving food, drink and lodging to pilgrims and other travellers) and later by the crown. Köyliö manor is mentioned in Jaakko Teitti's list in 1556 as a possible place for a bailiff (fi. vouti, sw. fogde)

name: Kokemäki
Settlement_Description:
Permanent agricultural settlement in Kokemäki (sw. Kumo) goes back to the Iron Age. The medieval parish organisation in Satakunta dates to the early 13th century with precursors in the latter half of the 12th century. 

<b>Inn:</b> A medieval guild hall was located by Kokemäki Church in the Middle Ages. Medieval guild halls could also have served as an alehouse or an inn, serving food, drink, and accommodation also to non-members.

name: Onkijoki
Settlement_Description: <b>Inn:</b> An inn was established in Onkijoki in 1646, but it was mentioned, that the Rynkö farm had served as the inn also earlier. Rynkö farm continued to serve as a tavern also when the farm was owned by assistant priest Mathias Rungius. The bishop forbade his innkeeping in 1679, after which the inn moved to Hirvikoski to Jaakko Sipinpoika from Uotila farm.

name: Hälvälä
Settlement_Description: <b>Inn:</b> An inn was established in Hälvälä in 1604.

name: null
Ferry_Description: A ferry across Mariager Fjord most likely existed prior to the foundation of the monastery. However, the ferry is first mentioned in 1451, when the monastery was given the right to a ferry across the fjord. The ferrying was maintained through the middle ages and into the 17th century, but traffic seems to have significantly decreased during the later parts of the period.

name: null
Toll_Description: In 1368 a toll on the Meuse ofthe lord of Rekem is found (location uncertain). It was opposed by Maastricht and likely not levied for an uncertain period. In the years 1661-1663 the toll was levied in Maaseik.
Harbour_Description: Hypothetical location of a harbour on the Meuse river. Around 1410 the river shifted its course to the former bed of the Geul river, 2km to the East, making Rekem lose its access to the river.

name: Korpi
Settlement_Description: <b>Inn:</b> An inn was established in Korpi in 1642, and Tuomo Yrjönpoika Isoperhe was appointed as the innkeeper. The inn was located by the winter road.

name: null
Harbour_Description: The bay of Ebeltoft (Danish: Ebeltoft Vig) functioned as a well protected natural harbour. At the latest from the 16th century the harbour contained a wharf.

name: Waldfeucht
Toll_Description: A toll station of the duke of Brabant-Limburg is first mentioned in 1396. In 1420 it was property of the lord of Heinsberg, and since 1483 of the duke of Jülich. Tariffs and revenues are not known.

name: Vaanii
Settlement_Description: <b>Inn:</b> Martti Tapaninpoika, the parish constable (fi: nimismies, sw: länsman), ran a tavern in his house in 1640s.

name: Kankaanpää
Settlement_Description: <b>Inn:</b> Köyliö parish constable (fi: nimismies, sw: länsman) was located in Kankaanpää village in 1540-42 and in 1556-1557. Parish constables were obliged to keep a tavern in late 16th c and early 17th c. Kankaanpää is mentioned as a place for accommodation in the travel account of Duke Johan of Finland from 1556. Also Ture Pedersson Bielke, Swedish nobleman and castellan of St. Olaf's Castle in Savo, stayed overnight in Kankaanpää in 1557. His host was parish constable Olavi Jaakonpoika, who is mentioned in office already in 1540. Torkkeli farm served as parish constable in 1640s and again in 1685.

name: Sampu
Settlement_Description: <b>Inn:</b> A medieval guild hall was located in Sampu. No exact date or location is known, but the district court gathered in Sampu guild hall in 1487-89 and 1514. The hall may have hosted St. Catherine's guild, since Huittinen church is dedicated to her, but also St. Gertrud's and St. Olaf's guilds were popular in medieval Satakunta region. Tuomas Takku, Sampu parish constable (fi: nimismies, sw: länsman) hosted Duke Johan of Finland in his travels in 1556, and Jaakko Teitti's list from the same year mentiones Takkula farm in Sampu as a possible place for a bailiff (fi. vouti, sw. fogde). Tuomas Takku hosted also Ture Pedersson Bielke, Swedish nobleman and castellan of St. Olaf's Castle in Savo, in 1557. Takku family continued to serve as parish constables and innkeepers into the 17th c.: in 1586, Sipi Tuomaanpoika Takku was the constable and the innkeeper, and Matti Sipinpoika Takku in 1639.

name: Kangasala
Settlement_Description: <b>Inn:</b> Kangasala is mentioned as a place for accommodation in the travel account of Duke Johan of Finland from 1556. Parish constable (fi: nimismies, sw: länsman) Hannu Hannunpoika Hannula ran a tavern in his house in Tursola village in 1639.

name: Punola
Settlement_Description: <b>Inn:</b> An inn was established in Punola in 1646, when Puno farm was given tavern rights. Puno farm also armed and maintained a cavalryman for the army.

name: Lempoinen
Settlement_Description: <b>Inn:</b> An inn was established in Killiäinen by Lempäälä church in 1585, and Lassi Erkinpoika was appointed as the innkeeper. Tuomas Laurinpoika Sulkola was the innkeeper in Lempoinen in 1639.

name: Kaharila
Settlement_Description: <b>Inn:</b> Kaharila farm served as a parish constable (fi: nimismies, sw: länsman) and a tavern for a couple of years before 1646, when the inn moved to Lauttakylä. In 1674, the inn moved back to Kaharila.

name: Mommola
Settlement_Description: <b>Inn:</b> Bailiff (fi. kruununvouti, sw. kronofogde) Henrik Påwalsson Callia kept an alehouse in Mommola. Bailiff's scribe and court scribe fought there in 1649.

name: null
Harbour_Description: The character of the medieval harbour is uncertain. It was, however, probably located at Nexø Red. In 1661 the harbour probably consisted of two short stone piers, just as it is shown on a map of Nexø in Resen’s Atlas Danicus from around 1675.

name: Virrat
Settlement_Description: <b>Inn:</b> An inn was established in Virrat in 1624, and Antti Herrainen was appointed as the innkeeper.

name: Vehoniemi
Settlement_Description: <b>Inn:</b> Juho Tiitola ran an inn in Vehoniemi in 1586.

name: null
Toll_Description: In 1119 the archbishop of Cologne gave the curtis 'Wesheim', including toll- and fishrights, and the portus (harbour) to the church of St. Pantaleon. Prior to 1240 the toll on the Meuse in Wessem was relocated to Weert by the lord of Horn. A toll in Wessem however is named again in 1362 when the steward of the duke of Brabant leased out seven tolls on the river Meuse.
Ferry_Description: A ferryman ('nautis') in 'Wisheym' is mentioned in the oldest account of the count of Gelre, dated 1294/5.
Harbour_Description: A harbour in Wessem is first mentioned in 1119 (see toll). In the heyday of the Meuse trade Wessem was the most northern harbour of importance. When the landroutes from Cologne westwards, which crossed the Meuse river north of Wessem, became of more importance, the development of Wessem declined and that of Weert and Roermond increased.

name: Keikyä
Settlement_Description: <b>Inn:</b> Matti Peevola, member of the Diet and a lay member of the district court, ran a tavern in his house until mid. 1640s. After that, there were no economic possibilities for running a tavern. Although Keikyä was located by a busy road, the village had only two farms.

name: Lahti
Settlement_Description: <b>Inn:</b> Lahti is mentioned as a place for accommodation in the travel account of Duke Johan of Finland from 1556. It is said to be by the same lake (Vesijärvi) than Hollola church, which might tell about water connection and winterway. In 1585, there was an official inn in Lahti village, hosted by Jaakko Ollinpoika. Lahti village has been by Vesijärvi lake in the present Kartano (Manor) area.

name: Mälläinen
Settlement_Description: <b>Inn:</b> Mälläinen is mentioned in Jaakko Teitti's list in 1556 as a possible place for a bailiff (fi. vouti, sw. fogde). In 1643, an official tavern was established, and Matti Markkula was appointed as the innkeeper. Markkula farm continued to serve as an inn also in the 18th c.

name: Laitila bridge
Bridge_Description: There are no records of Laitila bridge in the 16th c., so the bridge might be from early 17th c. It is first mentioned in 1650.

name: null
Ferry_Description: The age of the ferries connecting Svendborg with the islands to the south (Ærø, Langeland and Tåsinge) is uncertain. Ferries to these larger islands were probably established in the 13th century. The ferries are, however, not documented before the 15th and 16th centuries.
Harbour_Description: The character of the medieval harbour is unclear. But clearly Svendborg was an important harbour on the island of Funen, which was often used by foreign merchants. In 1399, for example, ships from Lübeck used the harbour. A wharf is mentioned several times during the 16th century, and is also shown on the map of Svendborg in Resen’s Atlas Danicus from around 1670.

name: null
Harbour_Description: Harbour at the confluence of two Rhine branches. A crane is first mentioned in 1391.

name: null
Bridge_Description: A small bridge ('Schem') across the Ems in Greven must have existed in 1498 at the latest. It could only be used for foot passengers; heavier traffic had to use the toll bridge at Schöneflieth. Only in 1777 a larger bridge was constructed.
Harbour_Description: After the construction of a weir in the Ems in Rheine in 1550, the river became navigable until Greven. Merchants from Münster initiated shipping on the Ems between Rheine and the castle Schöneflieth in 1582. In Greven the cargo was transshipped onto the land route to Münster.

name: null
Bridge_Description: The 'Long Bridge' connected Malchow with Old Malchow and was given to the town in 1292. Due to high maintenance costs, the bridge was destroyed in 1637.
Ferry_Description: After the destruction of the bridge in 1637, a ferry became indispensable for reaching the town. This existed until a dam was built in 1848.

name: null
Bridge_Description: The bridge across the river Pleißnitz was built by the town Görlitz in 1385.

name: null
Bridge_Description: In the early and high Middle Ages the only bridged crossing across the Werra between Vacha and Kreuzberg.

name: null
Bridge_Description: A river crossing of the Werra is first attested in 1186, it was situated further to the West than the current bridge (under the mouth of the Oechse). In 1346 a stone bridge was constructed, after a wooden bridge was carried away by floods in 1342.

name: null
Lock_Description: The map of Mecklenburg included in the atlas of Janssonius from 1622 shows a lock near Bennin in the Schaale canal, which was built in 1564.

name: Ruotsila
Settlement_Description: <b>Inn:</b> An inn was established in Ruotsila in 1600, and Jaakko Olavinpoika was appointed as the innkeeper. The inn was located by the winter road.

name: null
Harbour_Description: The character of the medieval harbour is unknown. A wharf is shown on a map of Bogense in Resen’s Atlas Danicus from 1677.

name: null
Bridge_Description: A bridge is shown on the municipal seal known from 1421. Thus, a bridge across Vejle Å must have existed prior to this year. The location of the medieval bridge is, however, uncertain. 18th century maps depict a bridge across Vejle Å south of town, and this was most likely also the location of the medieval bridge.

name: null
Ferry_Description: Ferry across the narrow strait of Virksund near the inlet to Hjarbæk Fjord. According to a document from 1452 the ferry belonged to the diocese in Viborg, and this has also been the case in the past. The exact age and character of the ferry is, however, uncertain. Presumably the ferry existed early in the medieval period. In 1514 a certain Niels Clementsen was granted the right to the ferry for the rest of his life.

name: null
Ferry_Description: Around 1075 the German chronicle Adam of Bremen mentions a ferry between Funen and Zealand. It is very likely that the ferry on Zealand was located at Tårnborg. During the 13th century, however, the ferry probably was relocated to the place, where the town of Korsør later developed. Throughout the medieval period and up until modern time the most used ferry route between the islands of Funen and Zealand was located at Korsør. The importance of the ferry is reflected in a broad variety of written sources from both the middle ages and early modern period.
Harbour_Description: The natural harbour at the fjord estuary was more accessible for larger ships than the bottom of the fjord at Tårnborg, and this fact probably motivated the founding of the town of Korsør in the 15th century. The harbour was from around 1400 used by ships from Lübeck. The oldest harbour in Korsør was close to the royal castle, but the character of this medieval harbour is unknown. In 1576 a new wharf was constructed, presumably a replacement for an older one.

name: null
Harbour_Description: The harbour in the bottom of the fjord was one of the most important in Denmark for trade with Germany, and many Hanseatic ships, in particular from Lübeck used the harbour. There was an ongoing struggle between the town and the peasants of Lolland, who benefited from irregular maritime trade with Hanseatic towns, and therefore tried to avoid using the harbour of Nakskov. In 1445 it was clarified that peasants were not allowed to trade directly with Germany; that this trade belonged to Nakskov. Only four years later this demand was repeated. However, the peasants on Lolland continued to trade with Germans. In 1682 the harbour consisted of several wharfs and bulwarks along the modern street of Havnegade.

name: null
Toll_Description: An imperial toll on sailing ships in Tiel at the river Waal existed since 896. It was moved to Kaiserswerth in 1174. However, a toll was also owned by the dukes of Brabant before 1339, when Tiel became part of Guelders, including the toll. Toll accounts are preserved for a range of years between 1382-1463. An outpost was situated at Heerewaarden on the river Meuse. The accounts for 1394-5 are edited. A tariff of the old toll in Tiel is preserved in a booklet from Venlo with market tolls on the Meuse from the early 16th century. The account of 1565 is analysed. Unedited accounts are preserved from the years 1563 onwards. In the years 1572-78 the toll was collected at Nijmegen. Another toll called the 'Meurschen' toll was owned by the dukes of Gelre of old.
Harbour_Description: Tiel was an important harbour on the Waal river especially in the 9th and 10th century. The harbour was located at the open waterfront of town, as can be seen on various town maps from the 17th century.

name: null
Harbour_Description: From the late medieval period onwards Sæby functioned as a harbour in Eastern Vendsyssel as a small river, Sæby Å, mouth was the only natural harbour between Skagen and Limfjorden. The harbour was plagued by storms, currents and high tides as well as ice during winter. This ment repairs were often needed. The king financed harbour repairs multiple times during the 1500s.

name: null
Toll_Description: In the 1420s king Eric the Pomeranian (1396-1439) introduced a toll on ships passing through the strait of Øresund between Zealand and Scania: Øresundstolden or the Sound toll. At first the toll was 1 nobel per ship. Up until the 18th century the toll was a very important source of income for the king of Denmark. In the 16th century a toll station was built near the shore close to the castle, but later the toll station was moved into the town of Helsingør. Toll registers from Øresundstolden have been preserved for the years 1497, 1503, 1528, 1536-1548. From 1574 up until 1857, when the toll was given up, toll registers have been preserved for almost every year (Rigsarkivet/The Danish National Archives).
Ferry_Description: The ferry Helsingør-Helsingborg was probably mentioned by the  German chronicler Adam of Bremen c. 1075. As this was the most narrow part of the strait of Øresund between Zealand and Scania, the ferry connection was very important throughout the medieval period and early modern era. With the introduction of the toll of Øresund in the beginning of the 15th century the ferry grew in importance. A guild of ferrymen was formed in Helsingør in the 1630ties, who was granted monopoly on crossing to Scania.
Harbour_Description: After the introduction of the toll of Øresund in the early 15th century, the harbour of Helsingør was one of the most important in Denmark. At this time the port had at least two wharfs. Another smaller harbour was located at the castle of Kronborg.

name: null
Harbour_Description: Around 1200 the Danish chronicler Saxo Grammaticus wrote that the river, Suså, earlier had been navigable, but now was overgrown and full of mud, and therefore difficult for larger vessels to use. Hence, only smaller vessels could be used on the river, and an area at Karrebæksminde at the river outlet was used for transhipment from smaller to larger vessels. Further up the river, archaeological excavations have revealed bulwarks in the port of Næstved, which have been dated to the 1220ties. At least from this point onwards the port had several wooden constructions. In the middle of the 15th century the bulwark or pier was more than 150 meters long. The port of Næstved was one of the most important on the island of Zealand; the gateway to the south. Hence, there were strong connections between Næstved and German/Hanseatic towns throughout the medieval period.

name: Salmentaka
Settlement_Description: <b>Inn:</b> An inn was established in Salmentaka in 1580-90s, and Heikki Juhonpoika Tauranen was appointed as the innkeeper. The inn was located by the winter road.

name: null
Harbour_Description: In 1554 Hjerting was described as harbour (ladeplads) for the town of Varde. Throughout the 16th and 17th centuty Hjerting was an important export harbour.

name: null
Ferry_Description: According to the two oldest versions of the town law, granted by the bishop of Roskilde in 1254 and 1294, the town had to ferry the bishop across the Sound (Danish: Øresund) to Scania without payment. This is a strong indication that ferries between Copenhagen and Scania, most likely the town of Malmö, were well established by the middle of the 13th century. Throughout the middle ages and early-modern era ferries connected Copenhagen and Scania, in general Malmö. Another ferry connected Copenhagen with the island of Amager. This ferry departed from a bridge called “Myndrikkebroen”, the possible precursor to the bridge called “Holmens Bro”, which probably was located at the eastern outlet at the harbour. The ferry between Copenhagen and Amager was first mentioned in the early 16th century, but is most likely much older.
Harbour_Description: Protected by the larger island of Amager and several smaller islands such as Slotsholmen Copenhagen was one of the best natural harbors on eastern Zealand and from the beginning of the settlement this was of great importance. A jetty is mentioned for the first time in the town law from 1294, and the port was also mentioned during the 14th century. This medieval port was located in the narrow strait between the small island of Slotsholmen and the coastline with the town. The port was constantly improved and expanded. In the 15th century this central part of the port was dominated by a long wharf. In the early 16th century a naval shipyard was established on the island of Bremerholmen near the eastern outlet of the harbour, and Copenhagen soon became the most important naval port in Denmark. During the reign of king Christian IV (1596-1648) the naval shipyard was relocated to Holmen, and the port of the town was also expanded. A copper engraving of Copenhagen seen from Amager in Civitates orbis terrarum by Georg Braun and Frans Hogenberg (1588) shows a large and advanced eastern end of the harbour. Throughout the medieval period and early modern era the port of Copenhagen was important to both regional and international trading networks, and was often used by both German as well as other foreing merchants.

name: null
Harbour_Description: The first harbour was placed inside the semi circle rampart surrounding the earliest settlement near the bridge across Køge Å. In the late middle ages the harbour was moved to the river estuary. The harbour of Køge was frequently used by German ships. Around 1400, for example, merchants from Lübeck sailed to Køge. Throughout the middle ages and also the early period there was sea trade between Køge and Hanseatic towns, in particular Lübeck.

name: null
Toll_Description: The dam toll in Tessin was moved to Laage in 1333, as part of a treaty between the lord of Mecklenburg (the owner of the toll) and the abbot of Dargun about the renovation of the dam. In 1436 it was moved back to Tessin.
Bridge_Description: A dam across the Recknitz marsh with four bridges over the branches of the river was built before 1333. In that year the abbot of Dargun and the lord of Mecklenburg agreed upon renovation of the dam.

name: null
Toll_Description: In 1333 the dam toll of Tessin was moved by the lord of Mecklenburg to Laage. In 1436 it was moved back to Tessin.
Bridge_Description: The name of the town, first mentioned in 1216, refers to a bridge and dam across the Recknitz river.

name: null
Bridge_Description: A water mill in Malchin is first mentioned in 1247. It was located on the eastern branch of the Peene river, and must have had a bridge across the river.

name: null
Ferry_Description: The ferry across the sea of Kattegat between Aarhus and Kalundborg on the island of Zealand was one of the most important ferry routes in Denmark throughout the middle ages and early-modern period. The ferry connection between Aarhus and Kalundborg in Zealand is apparently first mentioned by the German chronicler Adam of Bremen c. 1075. According to Adam it was also possible to take a ferry to Norway from Aarhus. The ferry to Zealand often went via the island of Samsø. Ferry accounts from the 1640ties have been preserved. The registry reveals that 10-15 smaller vessels were used as ferries between Aarhus and Kalundborg, and that these ferries annually transported between 700 and 1400 passengers across Kattegat.
Harbour_Description: In the Viking age and early medieval period the harbour was placed by the town fortification on the northern bank of the river, Aarhus Å, and near the river’s outlet into the sea. In the 15th century a new harbour was built on the opposite southern side of the river. Throughout the Middle Ages and the early modern era the port was one of the most important in Jutland.

name: null
Bridge_Description: The canal Nieuwe Vecht was dug around 1497. The bridge on the road between Zwolle and Almelo must also have been constructed at this time.

name: Lammi
Settlement_Description:
Permanent agricultural settlement in Lammi area goes back to the Iron Age. The parish is mentioned in 1374 together with Porkkala and Evo villages. Stone church dates from 1510. 

<b>Inn:</b> An inn might be located by the church. Churches usually had taverns in the Middle Ages and 16th-17th-centuries. In 1555 and 1557, the Porkkala manor north from Lammi church hosted respectively Duke Johan of Finland and Ture Pedersson Bielke, Swedish nobleman and castellan of St. Olaf's Castle in Savo. Porkkala manor has also hosted an alehouse, but it might date only from the 18th c.

name: Pont d'Arches
Bridge_Description: The bridge across the Meuse on the north side of town is first mentioned in 1245.

name: Saksala
Settlement_Description: Permanent agricultural settlement in lower Porvoonjoki (sw. Borgå å) area and Eastern Nyland (sw. Östra Nyland) dates to the Swedish colonisation in the latter half of the 13th century when new farms were founded in an area previously part of usufruct and emerging colonisation settlement from inner Häme. The parish organisation of Eastern Nyland dates at the latest to the first quarter of the 14th century, in Porvoo (sw. Borgå) possibly already to the third quarter of the 14th century. Porvoo town some 10 kms downstream from Saksala (sw. Saxby) was established either in the turn of the 1370s and 1380s or in the late 1340s. The town is first cited in 1387. King Gustaf I confirmed the privileges of the town in 1546. In 1550 the king ordered all the burghers of Ulvila (sw. Ulfsby), Rauma (sw. Raumo), Tammisaari (sw. Ekenäs) and Porvoo move to the newly established town of Helsinki (sw. Helsingfors) and annulled Porvoo as a town in 1551. The town was established anew in 1579, was again annulled because of the complaints of Helsinki in 1594 but received new privileges from king Karl IX in 1602.
Fair_Description:
The earliest information on annual fairs in Porvoo are from the year 1584 when king Johan III confirmed the town its two traditional fairs on Visitation of Mary (2 July) and Exaltation of the Holy Cross (14 September). The latter fair is cited in almanacs in 1598. Both days were again confirmed in 1594. In 1650 an annual winter fair in Porvoo was confirmed to be hold at Epiphany (6 January). Of the three fairs, the fair of Visitation of Mary was apparently organised in Saksala. 
In 1584 burghers of the newly re-established Porvoo complained to the authorities, that right after the sea and rivers were free of ice, burghers of Helsinki arrived to trade with peasants of the region at the Old Royal Manor (in Saksala) and elsewhere despite of the official fair dates in the bailiwick. The 1584 trading site close to the 15th century Royal Manor in Saksala can also be attached to much later local peasant fair in the same village organised on the feast of St Peter (29 June) as late as in the early 19th century. Close to the traditional fair day of the visitation of Mary (2 July) of 1584 and the tar fair of 1 July in 1639 in Porvoo, the early modern fair in Saksala appears to have focused on fresh tar, which inland peasants brought to the markets soon after its production. Of special interest is, that in a 1616 almanac the tar fair of the burghers of Helsinki in Porvoo on 1 July was called as St Enewalds fair (sw. Enewaldsmässan). A local saint of medieval Danish origin and unknown feast day from Blekinge, the shrine and well of St Enewald in Sölvesborg is cited three times as a destination of a pilgrimage in 1405-21. The emerging of his feast as a fixed fair of July the 1st and 2nd in Saksala may tell about the well-known influence of the Danish high nobility active in Finland in the first two decades of the 15th century and the early Union era, when they took care of reorganisation of the regional and local administration of bailiwicks, taxation and jurisdiction.
Toll_Description: The 1/32 duty worth of all goods intended for sale in towns and fairs and brought to the site by peasants was liable also in Saksala since 1622.

name: Vreeswijk
Toll_Description: The toll of the bishop of Utrecht on shipping on the Vaartsche Rijn was partially moved from Oudegein to Vreeswijk when the "nieuwe vaart" was constructed in 1289.
Lock_Description: The "nieuwe vaart" between the Lek and the Vaartsche Rijn was dug in 1289. Two wooden locks were built in 1373. Before that year there was a portage ('overtoom').

name: Lüneburg
Settlement_Description: A place called Hliuni was first mentioned in 795. In 951 a castle was founded next to the settlement. A monastery of St Michael is attested in Ottonian times before 956, in combination with the local saltworks, which would be the backbone of the local economy for centuries.
Town_Description: Henry the Lion destroyed the neighbouring settlement Bardowick in 1189, after which Lüneburg gained prominence as an important centre of trade and acquired town privileges. Duke Otto the Child confirmed the rights in 1247; from 1273 Lüneburg held the privilege of being the sole salt producer in the duchy.
Fair_Description: Regulations for the cloth trade from the early 14th century show that two fairs were taking place in Lüneburg, on St Michael and on Sunday Jubilate. According to a document from 1360, the St Michael's market attracted visitors from Stade, Hamburg, Braunschweig, Hannover, the Rhineland, Hesse and Holland.
Staple_Description: According to ducal privileges from 1365, 1367 and 1369 one could only ship grain and wood out of town with permission of the council; the regulation included Winsen, Harburg, Bleckede and other places in the duchy from where grain and wood was shipped. The prescription to use the roads leading through Lüneburg followed in 1392 and was extended to include the drift of cattle in 1467 and 1497. It was compulsory to offer corn, hops, wood, cattle and fish for sale on the local market for 3 days. This compulsion was extended to all commodities in the 16th century. In addition, trading between foreign merchants was prohibited. The town also sought to extend the staple claims to the trade on the Aller and Elbe river systems, with limited success. In the 16th ships on the Elbe were increasingly forced to unload their goods in Bleckede and carry them to market in Lüneburg, which led to a conflict with Hamburg and Magdeburg, and in 1574 the stopping of the traffic on the Elbe was limited to ships carrying boy salt (from the Bay of Biscay) upstream. The staple was limited to the payment of a fee in the 18th century, and finally abolished in 1843.

name: Maansilta (Perniö)
Bridge_Description: Perniö (sw. Bjärnå) Maansilta (Lands bridge, sw. Landsbro, 1792) over Kiskonjoki river is included in the early 1650s map of Piikkiö and Halikko judicial districts. The earliest bridge on the site may date to the first organisation of the maintenance of the Great Coastal Road as a uniform land route between Turku and Viborg in the 1340s and 1360s. The bridge was until 18739 maintained by Tenhola (sw. Tenala) parish of Uusimaa province and Perniö parish of Finland Proper, after that by Perniö only. The bridge weas demolished after the relocation of the road and new bridge some 100 meters upstream in 1935.

name: Kivisilta
Bridge_Description: The Stone bridge (sw. Stenbro, fi. Kivisilta) on the Great Coastal Road between Tienhaara crossroads and later Sorvali suburban area in Viipuri is first cited in 1560 (Steenn bro). The earliest bridge on the site may date to the first organisation of the maintenance of the Great Coastal Road as a uniform land route between Turku and Viborg in the 1340s and 1360s. The stone structures were repaired in between 1602-17. In 1661 the bridge was said to have of old been entirely of stone. In the early 17th century, the bridge was maintained by all the judicial districts of pre 1470s medieval bailiwick of Viipuri Castle except Porvoo bailiwick (Savo, Kymenkartano, Lapvesi, Jääski, Äyräpää and Ranta). Savo was exempted from the maintenance in the 1640s and Kyminkartano in 1661. The bridge is included in the 1655 map over the surroundings of Viipuri town in the range of two Swedish mil (ca. 21,4 km).

name: null
Harbour_Description: Around 1300 Sluis became the most important harbour on the Zwin waterway to Bruges, which was silting up. From 1387, Sluis was the main harbour for the fleet of the Burgundian dukes. Pilots were stationed here, who helped ships navigate the Zwin; pilot ordinances are known from 1448/1449 and 1484. In the 15th century, the harbour of Sluis started to silt up as well and lost its significance. Around 1500, it was predominantly centred on fishing. Guicciardini however mentions this around 1560 one of the finest and savest harbours in Europe with room for more then 500 ships.

name: null
Harbour_Description: Harbour at the canal between Brussels and Willebroek, built shortly after 1560. From 1618, regular barge services operated on the canal.

name: null
Harbour_Description: A crane was built at the bridge of St John in the late 13th century, it is first mentioned in 1282. Although the crane was demolished in the 18th century, its location still lives on in the name of the square Kraanplein.

name: IJzendijke
Settlement_Description: A first mention from 1046 is a forgery made in the second quarter of the 12th century. The subsequent mention dates from 1127.
Town_Description: Town rights were probably granted around 1238 by Joan of Constantinople, countess of Flanders. After an uproar of Flemish towns, IJzendijke lost its privileges in 1328, but these were regranted by 1330. IJzendijke ceased to exist due to a storm surge in 1404. The area was only gradually reclaimed from the sea. Present-day IJzendijke was built as a fortress at the approximate location of the drowned town in 1587 and was elevated to town by Royal Decree in 1816.
Harbour_Description: A harbour in IJzendijke on the eastern side of town is first mentioned in 1348. It was connected to the Westerschelde (Honte) via the stream Elmare.

name: Apenburg
Settlement_Description: First mention in 1264, but this early settlement was destroyed before 1344.
Town_Description: The new settlement is moved and referred to as civitas, later it is usually called little town ('stedtchen'). In 1402 town rights are recorded.
Fair_Description: In 1445 three fairs with cattle trade are known.

name: null
Lock_Description: The lock was located at the end of the Sassevaart, which ensured a connection with the sea for the town of Gent. Permission for construction of the Sassevaart was granted in 1547 by Emperor Charles V. In 1549, permission for building the lock followed. Construction works on the lock were completed in 1563.

name: Güsten
Settlement_Description: First mentioned in 970 as property of the archbishopric of Magdeburg through a donation of Otto I.
Town_Description: Granted town rights in 1373, which were confirmed in 1459 and 1551. However, the settlement never developed to be more than a farming town.

name: Harzgerode
Settlement_Description: Otto III granted market, mint and toll rights to the settlement of Hagenrode in 993. At the end of the 13th century the dukes of Anhalt constructed a castle in Harzgerode.
Town_Description: In 1338 Harzgerode is the first settlement in Anhalt that was elevated to a town.

name: Oudkarspel
Settlement_Description: According to Van Berkel & Samplonius, Oudkarpsel is first mentioned in 1094 (then spelled as ‘Aldenkercha’). The subsequent mention dates from 1289. On 12 May 1415, Oudkarspel, together with the villages Noord-Scharwoude, Zuid-Scharwoude, and Broek op Langedijk, was granted town privileges by William (‘Willem’) VI, count of Holland. Oudkarspel, Noord-Scharwoude, Zuid-Scharwoude and Broek op Langedijk combined formed the ‘stede’ Langedijk. These settlements, however, never developed an urban character. The granting of town rights was part of an administrative reorganization in which a number of smaller settlements were granted town rights in order to provide them with a certain degree of self-government which replaced the need for the count of Holland's bailiffs ('baljuws'). The town privileges were withdrawn on 13 and 20 August 1426.

name: Noord-Scharwoude
Settlement_Description: According to Van Berkel & Samplonius, Noord-Scharwoude is first mentioned in 1094 (then spelled as ‘Bernardeskercha’). The subsequent mention dates from 1289. On 12 May 1415, Noord-Scharwoude, together with the villages Oudkarspel, Zuid-Scharwoude, and Broek op Langedijk, was granted town privileges by William (‘Willem’) VI, count of Holland. Noord-Scharwoude, Zuid-Scharwoude, Oudkarspel and Broek op Langedijk combined formed the ‘stede’ Langedijk. These settlements, however, never developed an urban character. The granting of town rights was part of an administrative reorganization in which a number of smaller settlements were granted town rights in order to provide them with a certain degree of self-government which replaced the need for the count of Holland's bailiffs ('baljuws'). The town privileges were withdrawn on 13 and 20 August 1426.

name: Zuid-Scharwoude
Settlement_Description: According to Van Berkel & Samplonius, Zuid-Scharwoude is first mentioned in 1094 (then spelled as ‘Sudrekercha’). The subsequent mention dates from 1289. On 12 May 1415, Zuid-Scharwoude, together with the villages Oudkarspel, Noord-Scharwoude, and Broek op Langedijk, was granted town privileges by William (‘Willem’) VI, count of Holland. Zuid-Scharwoude, Noord-Scharwoude, Oudkarspel and Broek op Langedijk combined formed the ‘stede’ Langedijk. These settlements, however, never developed an urban character. The granting of town rights was part of an administrative reorganization in which a number of smaller settlements were granted town rights in order to provide them with a certain degree of self-government which replaced the need for the count of Holland's bailiffs ('baljuws'). The town privileges were withdrawn on 13 and 20 August 1426.

name: Harmelen
Settlement_Description: Earliest mention in 1202 is a falsification. Next mention is from circa 1220.

name: Budel
Settlement_Description: First mentioned in 779, in a 12th-century copy.

name: Ziegenrück
Settlement_Description: First mention in 1222, noble property since the 13th century. According to legend, Charlemagne built the castle as a defense against the Sorbs, but there are no remains of this castle.
Town_Description: In 1328 house and town of Ziegenrück are first mentioned, town rights were possibly granted at the beginning of the 13th century. In 1527 all town privileges were revoked due to participation in the Peasant's War. After that it is referred to as borough ('Flecken'). It only acquired new bylaws in 1853.

name: Broek op Langedijk
Settlement_Description: According to Van Berkel & Samplonius, Broek op Langedijk is first mentioned in the 1420 copy of a document dating from the twelfth century. The subsequent mention dates from 1216. On 12 May 1415, Broek op Langedijk, together with the villages Oudkarspel, Noord-Scharwoude, and Zuid-Scharwoude, was granted town privileges by William (‘Willem’) VI, count of Holland. Broek op Langedijk, Noord-Scharwoude, Zuid-Scharwoude and Oudkarspel combined formed the ‘stede’ Langedijk. These settlements, however, never developed an urban character. The granting of town rights was part of an administrative reorganization in which a number of smaller settlements were granted town rights in order to provide them with a certain degree of self-government which replaced the need for the count of Holland's bailiffs ('baljuws'). The town privileges were withdrawn on 13 and 20 August 1426.

name: Wijdenes
Settlement_Description: Wijdenes is first mentioned around 1312. Together with the village Oosterleek, the settlement was added to the ‘stede’ Schellinkhout in 1414. These settlements, however, never developed an urban character. The granting of town rights was part of an administrative reorganization in which a number of smaller settlements were granted town rights in order to provide them with a certain degree of self-government which replaced the need for the count of Holland's bailiffs ('baljuws'). name: Oosterleek

name: Aartswoud
Settlement_Description: Earliest mention in circa 1312. Next mention in circa 1338. On 2 February 1414, Aartswoud, together with Hoogwoud, was granted town privileges by William VI, count of Holland. Aartswoud and Hoogwoud combined formed the ‘stede’ Hoogwoud. These settlements, however, never developed an urban character.
