The settlements kept their own separate settlement governments. The stede lost its town privileges on 13 August 1426, but these were re-granted on 29 March 1450.

name: Oude-Niedorp
Settlement_Description: The first mention of Oude-Niedorp occurs in a circa 1420 copy of a document that probably dates from the end of the eleventh century. The subsequent mention dates from 1180 (in a twelfth century copy). Oude-Niedorp, together with Nieuwe-Niedorp, was granted town privileges on 12 May 1415 by William VI, count of Holland. The original document has not survived. Oude-Niedorp and Nieuwe-Niedorp combined formed the ‘stede’ Niedorp. These settlements, however, never developed an urban character. The granting of town rights was part of an administrative reorganization in which a number of smaller settlements were granted town rights in order to provide them with a certain degree of self-government which replaced the need for the count of Holland's bailiffs ('baljuws'). The settlements kept their own separate settlement governments. As a result of the Hook and Cod wars, the ‘stede’ lost its town privileges in August 1426. The town rights were re-granted on 8 May 1452.
Fair_Description: In 1395 (12 sep.) verkrijgen Schagen en Niedorperambacht vrijheid om met hun zuivel e.a. goederen ter wage en ter markt te gaan waar het hun belieft. In 1452 krijgen Oude en Nieuwe Niedorp en Winkel hun stadsrecht terug (ontnomen in 1426 i.v.m. steun aan Jacoba van Beieren). Filips de Goede geeft dan ook twee jaarmarkten en een weekmarkt, maar die dienen gehouden te worden in het aan de Zuiderzeekust gelegen Winkel. In 1557 (24 juli) krijgt Nydorp van koning Filips II een weekmarkt op maandag en twee vrije jaarmarkten: 1) de eerste maandag na Pinksteren tot de zaterdag als vanouds, 2) maandag na St. Victor (10 okt.) tot de zaterdag, steeds met drie dagen er voor en erna vrij marktgeleide. Dit omdat er veel zuivel werd verhandeld in omliggende plaatsen van 'vazallen', waardoor de koninklijke waag in Niedorp achteruit ging.

name: Westwoud
Settlement_Description: Earliest mention in circa 1312. In 1414, Westwoud, Oosterblokker and Westerblokker were granted town privileges by William VI, count of Holland. Together, these settlements became the ‘stede’ Westwoud. These settlements, however, never developed an urban character. The settlements kept their own separate settlement governments. In 1493, the administrative region (‘banne’) Westwoud was split into Westwoud and Binnenwijzend. Binnenwijzend then got its own village government and representatives within the ‘stede’ Westwoud.

name: Oberschledorn
Settlement_Description: The settlement Sledere is first mentioned in 1245, but is impossible to discern if it concerns Oberschledorn or neighbouring Niederschleidern. First certain mention of Oberschledorn in 1386.

name: Opmeer
Settlement_Description: Opmeer is first mentioned around 1312. In 1414, the settlements Opmeer, Hensbroek, Spanbroek and Obdam were granted town privileges by William VI, count of Holland. Together, these settlements formed the ‘stede’ Spanbroek. These settlements, however, never developed an urban character. The settlements kept their own separate settlement governments. For political reasons, the ‘stede’ lost its privileges in 1426. By 1434, the territory was divided between several lords.

name: Kroppenstedt
Settlement_Description: First mention in 934, when it is given by Heinrich I.
Town_Description: In 1254 a council constitution can be proven, so it can be assumed that Kroppenstedt was given town rights when it was given to the bishopric of Halberstadt in 1253.

name: Obdam
Settlement_Description: According to Cox, Obdam is first mentioned around 1312. Van Berkel and Samplonius take a slightly later early date, referring to a 1420-copy of an early thirteenth century text. In 1414, the settlements Obdam, Opmeer, Spanbroek and Hensbroek were granted town privileges by William VI, count of Holland. Together, these settlements formed the ‘stede’ Spanbroek. These settlements, however, never developed an urban character. The granting of town rights was part of an administrative reorganization in which a number of smaller settlements were granted town rights in order to provide them with a certain degree of self-government which replaced the need for the count of Holland's bailiffs ('baljuws'). The settlements kept their own separate settlement governments. For political reasons, the ‘stede’ lost its privileges in 1426. By 1434, the territory was divided between several lords. In 1456, Obdam and Hensbroek received their own town privileges as ‘stede’ Obdam-Hensbroek, separate from the ‘stede’ Spanbroek.

name: Hoornbrug
Settlement_Description: A chapel of the Holy Cross was built south of the bridge in 1502 by Comen Gheryt van Leyden as gratitude for the safe return from his pilgrimage to Jerusalem. The chapel was probably destroyed during acts of war in 1572-1575.
Bridge_Description: The bridge is first mentioned in 1340. Probably this was a wooden bridge with a foundation of bricks. A new bridge with two arches was built entirely from bricks in 1601-2.

name: Hensbroek
Settlement_Description: Hensbroek is first mentioned around 1312. In 1414, the settlements Hensbroek, Opmeer, Spanbroek and Obdam were granted town privileges by William VI, count of Holland. name: Benningbroek
Settlement_Description: Earliest mention in circa 1338. In 1414, Benningbroek and Sijbekarspel were granted town rights by William VI, count of Holland. The settlements kept their own separate settlement governments. For political reasons, the town rights were withdrawn in 1426. The privileges were temporarily regranted in 1428 and 1452, before they were permanently restored in 1456.

name: Wadway
Settlement_Description: Earliest mention in 1256, in a copy dating from circa 1300. In 1414, the settlements Wadway, Hauwert, Nibbixwoud and Wognum were granted town privileges by William VI, count of Holland. Together, these settlements formed the ‘stede’ Wognum. These settlements, however, never developed an urban character. The granting of town rights was part of an administrative reorganization in which a number of smaller settlements were granted town rights in order to provide them with a certain degree of self-government which replaced the need for the count of Holland's bailiffs ('baljuws'). The settlements kept their own separate settlement governments. The ‘stede’ Wognum lost its town rights in 1426 and is permanently added to the jurisdiction of Hoorn in 1436. On the level of village government, they kept their independence.

name: Wognum
Settlement_Description: Wognum is first mentioned in the first half of the eleventh century. name: Twisk
Settlement_Description: Earliest mention probably in 1243-1245. The subsequent mention dates from 1311. In 1414, Twisk, Lambertschaag, Abbekerk and Midwoud were granted town rights by William VI, count of Holland. Together, these settlements formed the ‘stede’ Abbekerk. name: Mücheln
Settlement_Description: First mention in the Hersfelder Zehntverzeichnis.
Town_Description: Friedrich the Stern elevated the settlement to town in 1350.

name: Midwoud
Settlement_Description: Earliest mention in circa 1312. In 1414, Midwoud, Lambertschaag, Twisk and Abbekerk were granted town rights by William VI, count of Holland. name: Barsingerhorn
Settlement_Description: Barsingerhorn is first mentioned in 1289. Barsingerhorn and Haringhuizen were granted town rights on 12 May 1415 by William VI, count of Holland and Zeeland. Together, these settlements formed the ‘stede’ Barsingerhorn. These settlements, however, never developed an urban character. The granting of town rights was part of an administrative reorganization in which a number of smaller settlements were granted town rights in order to provide them with a certain degree of self-government which replaced the need for the count of Holland's bailiffs ('baljuws'). The settlements kept their own separate settlement governments. Many of the town privileges granted in the West-Friesland area (in which Barsingerhorn and Haringhuizen are situated) were withdrawn in 1426. New town privileges were granted to Barsingerhorn in 1427. However, as the lord granted these rights did not have the authority to do so, the privileges were again withdrawn in 1436.

name: Haringhuizen
Settlement_Description: Haringhuizen is first mentioned in 1338, then called 'Die Niewekerc'. It is first mentioned as Haringhuizen in 1344. Haringhuizen and Barsingerhorn were granted town rights on 12 May 1415 by William VI, count of Holland and Zeeland. Together, these settlements formed the ‘stede’ Barsingerhorn. These settlements, however, never developed an urban character. The granting of town rights was part of an administrative reorganization in which a number of smaller settlements were granted town rights in order to provide them with a certain degree of self-government which replaced the need for the count of Holland's bailiffs ('baljuws'). The settlements kept their own separate settlement governments. Many of the town privileges granted in the West-Friesland area (in which Haringhuizen and Barsingerhorn are situated) were withdrawn in 1426. New town privileges were granted to Barsingerhorn in 1427. However, as the lords who granted these rights did not have the authority to do so, the privileges were again withdrawn in 1436.

name: Prettin
Settlement_Description: First mentioned in 966, in an 11th-century copy. It appears as castle district ('burgward') in the 11th century.
Town_Description: In 1523 probably Magdeburg town rights are confirmed, it is unclear when they were first granted (possibly in the middle of the 12th century). Market rights were granted in 1565.

name: Raguhn
Town_Description: First referred to as town in 1395, granted an own jurisdiction. Town rights may have been granted as early as 1259.

name: Schildau
Settlement_Description: First mention in 1184 in the Petersberg chronicle.
Town_Description: Town rights were possibly granted in the 15th century, the settlement has its own seal in 1445. Citizens are mentioned in 1528.
Fair_Description: In the 17th century the town gains some wealth through three fairs.

name: Schraplau
Settlement_Description: First mention in the tithe register of Hersfeld in the late 9th century. The castle was constructed around 1200. In 1497 referred to as oppidum, soon after that administrated by a mayor and a council. Town rights were probably only granted in the 1740s.

name: Wegeleben
Settlement_Description: First mention in a family name, who probably constructed the castle in the 12th century.
Town_Description: Settlement counts as town since 1267, when it already has a wall. It is referred to as civitas in 1288. In 1354 a mayor and a council are mentioned, but Wegeleben is still referred to as borough ('Flecken') most of the time.

name: Teuchern
Settlement_Description: First mention in 976, in 981 mentioned as a district ('Gau'), 1140 referred to as villa.
Town_Description: Teuchern developed town-like features in the 13th century and is mentioned as "oppidum" in 1238 and as town in 1342. In 1480 fairs and weekly markets are granted and probably town rights as well.

name: Seulinger Warte
Settlement_Description: The so-called Mägdebergswarte, first mentioned in 1437, was a watchtower ('Warte') of the enclosure ('Landwehr') of Duderstadt. In the same year a barrier ('Schlagbaum') was set up next to the tower. In the 16th century the name Sulinger Warte caught on. In 1535 a guard house ('Warthus boven Sulingen') was built. In 1589 a new one was erected. It is possible that the watchtower was already in ruins by then.

name: Hellevoetsluis
Settlement_Description: The fortress ('vesting') Hellevoetsluis was built in the early 17th century as a navy harbour.
Ferry_Description: Since 1581 a ferry made Hellevoet a chain in the traffic between Holland and Zeeland. In 1595 the ferry between Goedereede and Strype was also extended to De Quack and Hellevoetsluis. The ferry of Oudenhoorn was also relocated to Hellevoetsluis between 1594 and 1596. It was pawned to the city of Brielle. Ferries operated to Sommelsdijk, Dirksland, Melissant, Bommenede, Maye and Goedereede. Detailed instructions for the ferry to Bommenede date from 1605.
Harbour_Description: As the Meuse mouth was silting up the Goereese Gat got growing importance as a gateway to the harbours along the 'Beneden-Maas'. In 1595 and 1604 the harbour was improved, partly as a 'winterlaag' (place for hibernating skips). In 1619 a sluice with a width of 9 meters and a harbour with a length of 650 meters and width of 39 meters was ready.
Lock_Description: A sluice was built in the dike around the polder Struijten (1533) for the water management of the polder Nieuw Helvoet (1394).

name: null
Ferry_Description: Ferry connections existed between Dirksland and Oudenhoorn (possibly in one direction only). Between 1594 and 1596, the ferry destination was relocated from Oudenhoorn to Hellevoetsluis. A ferry to Zierikzee is found in 1456.

name: Herkingen
Ferry_Description: A ferry from Dreischor to Overflakkee is mentioned in 1431-42, sailing to Dirksland. From 1470/71, the ferries sailed to Herkingen and/or Oude-Tonge.

name: Katendrecht
Settlement_Description: First mentioned in 1199, in a copy from 1371.
Ferry_Description: The ferry in Katendrecht is first mentioned in 1323.

name: null
Ferry_Description: According to Horsten, the ferry was located on the site of the former 'Veerbrug', a bridge first mentioned in 1752.

name: null
Ferry_Description: According to Horsten, the ferry was located on the site of the former 'Veerbrug', a bridge first mentioned in 1752.

name: Damme (Brugge)
Settlement_Description: Earliest mention in 1180, when a dam was built here in the Zwin, hence the name.
Fair_Description: Already in 1252, a fair on Pentecost is mentioned. A weekly market was organised on Thursday. In 1551 (June) emperor Charles granted a free horse fair for two days: 26 and 27 Oct. Guicciardini mentions in 1567 an important horse-fair in May.
Toll_Description: Damme was the main toll station where the toll on the Zwin of the counts of Flanders was levied (see also Bruges). In 1228, inhabitants of Aardenburg were exempted from the toll in Damme. Toll regulations from 1252 give a detailed insight in the shipping between Damme and Bruges. Toll-accounts (rotuli) are preserved for the years: 1364-1433.
Staple_Description: In 1323 count Lodewijk van Nevers reorganised the Zwin-staple and gave Bruges a separate staple at Damme for casked-herring. In 1324 the staple for herring from Scania (Schonen) was here. In 1331 the same count granted Damme the staple for wine from La Rochelle and St. Jean d'Angely.
Harbour_Description: Since the construction of a dam and sluice in the Zwin in 1180, only smaller ships could sail on to Bruges via the Reie river. Larger ships had to transship their cargoes onto lighter boats. Damme therefore developed into the primary outport of Bruges, which position it held until c. 1250, when ongoing silting of the Zwin favoured the use of other Zwin harbours, predominantly Sluis. In 1269 a crane was built, granted by countess Margaretha.
Lock_Description: The dam in the Zwin from 1180 was constructed with a sluice ('grote speye') that only allowed smaller ships that were not higher than 7 ft and with a draught of less than 6 ft with a removable mast to pass and sail on to Bruges via the Reie river.

name: Drie Fonteinen
Lock_Description: The locks of Drie Fonteinen south of Vilvoorde were constructed in the canal Brussel-Willebroek between July 1560 and September 1561.

name: null
Bridge_Description: Earliest mention in 1333, location likely in between Alphen and Koudekerk where the toll was situated (see: Gouwsluis). Probably replacing a ferry. Toll and ferry were rights belonging to the viscount of Leiden, who gave them in subfief to the lord of Wassenaar. The seignorial rights on the (Oude) Rijn stretched between Rijnsoever (near Katwijk in the dunes where the river Rijn originally flowed into the North Sea) and Swademburdam (Zwammerdam).

name: Nikolausberg
Settlement_Description: The settlement was originally called Olredeshusen or Adelradeshusen and was first mentioned in 1162, when a monastery of Augustinian canonesses was founded here. The monastery was moved to Weende before 1184, but the former monastery church of St Nicholas became a pilgrimage destination, probably in the late 14th century. Since then, the name Nikolausberg gradually replaced the old name of the village.

name: Zwammerdam
Settlement_Description: Earliest mention in 1165. Zwammerdam is named after a dam that the count of Holland built in the Rhine in the 12th century.

name: null
Harbour_Description: In 1299 (July 21) the count granted the inhabitants a dam with a lock in order to improve the harbour. He donated his toll to pay for the earth to construct a dike. Citizens also had to pay according to their ability. In 1336 the count gave permission to reconstruct the silted up mouth of the Schie into a harbour. But the permission given by him to Rotterdam in 1340 to dug a canal from the Schie to the Meuse obstructed the further development of the harbour in Schiedam. However in the Informacie of 1514 the town said that herringcatch was the most important mean of subsistence. They then had 20 fish-ships (10 year earlier 26) and seven ships for trade. But the costs for maintaining the long harbour were high.

name: null
Toll_Description: The comital toll on sailing ships at Woudrichem was relocated to Gorinchem at the opposite bank of the river Merwede in 1420. The tollbooth was part of the castle of the count of Holland. Toll accounts (some incomplete and some combined with the toll in Schoonhoven) are preserved and edited for the years 1422, 1478-1481 en 1518. Unedited accounts exist for the years 1573-1580. A manual of the toll-keeper at Venlo, dated early 16th century, with the market-tolls on the river Maas has a tariff for the 'great' and the 'new' toll at Gorinchem. A not edited tariff for the toll at Gorinchem and the toll in Schoonhoven dates from the first half of the 16th century. The socalled 'Arkelse tol' was a watertoll levied on the river Merwede during 14 days: 8 days before and after the fair with Pentecost. In 1556 are exempt: Dordrecht, Den Haag, Vlaardingen, Worcum (=Woudrichem), Heukelum, Asperen, Rotterdam, Heusden, Meeuwen, Eethen, Waalwijk and 's-Hertogenbosch.

name: null
Toll_Description: Accounts of the outpost here from the Grote Zeeuwse Tol dated 1591/2, 1600, 1625vv are digitalised.
Harbour_Description: In 1344 beaconage already amounted to 160 lb., as the comital account shows. The town-account of 1495/'6 mentions the construction of a new harbour. In 1555, the magistrate of Tholen declared that the ‘raveyere van Eendracht’ (see the current Eendrachtsdijk), running passed Tholen through the domain of Vossemeer, had always been a natural and safe harbour; therefore, the magistrate declared to be against plans to block off this waterway by means of a dam. Shippers of Amsterdam, Gorcum and Brussels also declared that the water of Vossemeer (‘gat van Vossemeer’) made an important port of refuge on the way to Flanders or Brabant. Toll freedom granted in 1335 and 1346 points at a harbour, and schipmasters and merchants from Tholen in the first half of the fourteenth century.

name: Bodenwerder
Settlement_Description: Bodenwerder came into existence as a trading place on a river island ('werder') in the Weser river. It was first mentioned in 1150.
Town_Description: Bodenwerder acquired town privileges after Holzminden model in 1287.

name: null
Toll_Description: In 1454 found in a tariff for the Hansa as tollplace from the count of Holland, together with Iersekeroord and Kats. Usually in the 14th and 15th century as an outpost of the toll at Iersekeroord. In the toll-accounts dated 1470-'75 as an outpost of this toll next to Middelburg, Arnemuiden, Veere, Vlissingen and Kats. Toll-accounts on alum are dated 1471 and 1473-'75, then also collected at Bruges and Antwerp. A toll-account dated 1497/'8 has the impost collected in Bergen op Zoom on cloth from England destinated for Antwerp. Accounts of the outpost here of the Grote Zeeuwse tol dated 1584-92 and 1628vv are digitalised.
Ferry_Description: Ferry connections existed between Bergen op Zoom and Reimerswaal (first mentioned in 1360, but already existing at that time, and disappeared with the abandonment of Reimerswaal in 1631), Yersekendam (first mentioned in 1351), Schakerloo on the island of Tholen (mentioned in 1418), and various places on the opposite shore of the Oosterschelde on Zuid-Beveland, such as Yersekeroord (first mentioned in 1330-1333) and Steenvliet. The latter connections disappeared after this part of Zuid-Beveland was flooded in 1530. Since circa 1480 a ferry to Dordrecht is known. In 1494 ferries to Antwerp and Arnemuiden are found.
Harbour_Description: In 1439 the harbour was ameliorated with piers at the mouth. In 1474 a new harbour was made for bigger ships and the staple for English cloths was situated here. In 1503 the lord of Bergen op Zoom extends the jurisdiction of the town to include all of the port. As a result of the silting up because of the floods of 1530 and 1532 access to the harbour deteriorated.

name: null
Harbour_Description: The harbour is presumed to have existed from the start of the settlement as a brook which connected the town to the Streine (a branch of the river Schelde). Duke John III of Brabant granted Steenbergen the right to build a harbour dike in 1331, making this the earliest mention of the harbour for trading vessels. Between 1539 and 1581 the harbour was closed off from open water during the construction of the Graaf Hendrikspolder.

name: null
Harbour_Description: In 1224 toll-exemption in Holland was certified, in 1393 again including the toll at Heusden. In 1288 the duke of Brabant granted the lord of Gorinchem toll-exemption from land- and watertolls. A harbour crane is found circa 1395.

name: null
Toll_Description: The comital river toll at Niemandsvriend near Sliedrecht was moved to Woudrichem in 1354. The input of grains, woad and coal and the output of salt en herring during the years 1380-85 via the toll at Woudrichem to or from Dordrecht is edited. Yields of the farming out of the toll are edited for the years 1395-1420. In 1420 the toll station was relocated to Gorinchem at the opposite bank of the river Merwede.
Ferry_Description: The ferry from Dalem is first mentioned in 1417. Woudrichem is first mentioned as destination in 1504. According to an account dated 1474/5 this ferry belonged to the lord of Altena. According to accounts dated 1556/7 en 1565/6 half of the right of this ferry from the lord of Altena belonged to the caste keeper of Loevenstein, but already in 1469 the count of Holland had usurpated this half. In 1590 the seigniory of Altena was expired to the Estates of Holland and the accounts of his steward mention two ferries: the socalled Penninxveer from Woudrichem via Loevestein to Dalem and the ''grote' (big) ferry of Woudrichem.

name: null
Toll_Description: A toll on sailing ships in 'Bommel' is donated in 999 by emperor Otto II to the church of Utrecht. Prior to 1348 the toll at Zuilichem was relocated to Zaltbommel. A wide range of toll-accounts from the count of Gelre is preserved for the years 1294-1499. The accounts of 1294/5 and 1394/5 are edited. In 1394/'5 there was an old and a new toll. The last one ('de novo') was levied from all goods from abroad coming upstream and from all salt coming upstream. In 1371 Nijmegen obtained toll-exemption. A tariff for Utrecht dated 1399 is edited. Later accounts are preserved from the years 1542 onwards. An outpost was situated at Heerewaarden on the river Meuse but in 1573 and succeeding years it was temporarily collected in Batenburg. In the years 1572-'78 the toll of Zaltbommel was collected for the benefit of the prince of Orange and the audit office in Nijmegen. In 1577 Nijmegen requested to move back the toll.
Harbour_Description: Skippers from Zaltbommel (Boumela) are found in the toll-tariff of Koblenz dated 1104.

name: Lügde
Settlement_Description: First mentioned in 784. After the town Lügde developed on the opposite shore of the Emmer, the old settlement became known as Oldenlude and was abandoned in the 14th century.
Town_Description: Opposite the original settlement, a town developed, which is characterised as "civitas" in 1195. Around 1240, it became a town with Lippstadt town privileges.

name: Sint Maarten
Settlement_Description: First mentioned in 1289. The settlement was originally called Nieuwland, but soon became known as Sint Maarten, after the patron saint of the local church St Martin.

name: null
Harbour_Description: Dommel (vanuit het zuiden) en Aa (vanuit het oosten) kwamen hier samen in de Dieze, die enkele kilometers noordelijker in de Maas uitmondde en verbinding gaf met de Rijn. Via de Dommel en Aa was er verbinding met de Meierij rond de stad. Den Bosch verkreeg in 1196 tolvrijdom op de Rijn van de keizer. In 1203 volgde tolvrijdom in Gelre in een verdrag tussen de hertog van Brabant en graaf van Gelre, al lag de tollenaar te Hedel (en Batenburg) later vaak dwars. In 1213 kwam de stad met Geertruidenberg overeen dat wederzijds zonder tol kon worden gehandeld. Tot en met de 14e eeuw is er overigens heel weinig bewijs voor een omvangrijke handel. In 1405 werd van oude voorrechten in Holland en Zeeland gesproken tussen Den Bosch en Vlaanderen, behalve te Geervliet (hele tol) en Niemandsvriend (halve tol) en in Woudrichem (slechts de vier jaarmarkttollen). Maar deze beweerde rechten gaven aanhoudend problemen met de tollenaars te Woudrichem en Gorinchem. Over de te betalen tol in het Sticht van Utrecht bestonden problemen in 1488/'9, 1514 en nog in 1589. In 1563 bevestigde koning Filips II echter de tolprivileges in Holland en Zeeland en in Gelre en Zutphen. De oudste stadsrekening uit 1399 noemt al een kraanaccijns. In 1442 kwam er een nieuwe kraan en in 1448 werden twee torens gebouwd in de havenmond die met een stenen brug verbonden waren.

name: null
Ferry_Description: In 1396 the bishop of Utrecht leased to the aldermen of Hasselt for the benefit of the town a.o. the ferrry during 16 years. In 1403 he donated this in long lease to the town. The bishop and his servants should be taken across without costs. In 1522 the bishop granted to complete the bridge across the Zwarte Water, in order that ships could only pass there with consent. In the 16th century, Zwolle prevented the replacement of the ferry across the Zwarte Water in Hasselt with a bridge. In 1532 a 'beurtveer' (market-boat) with carvels is found between Hasselt and Amsterdam across the Zuiderzee.

name: null
Toll_Description: A toll on sailing ships belonging to the lord of Heusden is first mentioned in 1251. In 1317 the count of Kleef gave the toll and seigniory in fief to the son of the lord of Heusden, like his ancestors did. In 1357 the toll was usurpated together with the seignory by the count of Holland. Accounts are preserved and edited for the years 1378-1380 and 1391-1393. There is a special administration for the tolls of drapery (lakentol), wine and from the merchants from Gorinchem, Katwijk (fish), The Hague (fish) and from the tolls levied during the fairs (in 1391-93 with 'Vastelavont': eve before Ash Wednesday) and there traded horses. Tolls were also collected at the gate called Oudheusden and at outposts in Baardwijk and Giessen and at landtolls situated in Doeveren and Hedikhuizen. In 1391-93 it is called the watertoll and a 'wagentol' (toll on chariots) is levied. Yields of the farming out of the toll are presented in a graph for the years 1360-1505. In 1419 outposts are found in Engelen, Vlijmen and Baardwijk.
Ferry_Description: In 1503 the steward of the Land of Heusden stated that the ferry of Heusden half was property of the count of Holland and half of the lord of Hemert (at the Guelders bank of the river Meuse).
Harbour_Description: A crane was built in 1392 by the citizen militia with permission of the count of Holland. They also received the yields of the cranage levied there. After the meander of the Meuse river on which Heusden is located was cut short north of town by Den Bosch in or shortly after 1480, much river traffic circumvented the town and the harbour deteriorated quickly.

name: Strienemonde
Toll_Description: A toll for sailing transport belonging to the count of Holland on the Striene river at Strienemonde is first mentioned in 1274 or 1275. Submerged by the Eisabethsfloods in 1421 and 1424. In 1330 it obtained toll-exemption form the count of Holland. A tariff for the count of Holland and for the lord of Putten, dated 1357 or 1358, is preserved and edited. One account is preserved and edited, dated 1388/89.

name: null
Harbour_Description: Perhaps as old as 1250, but certainly from 1327 onwards. Incoming and outgoing ships to and from Antwerpen and their cargo are analysed for the years 1567-'78 as registrated in the registers of the 'Brabantse watertol'.

name: null
Ferry_Description: A ferry belonging to the count of Holland to Volewijc is first mentioned in the oldest account of the bailliff of the count of Amstelland in 1308, in 1346 another ferry is found to Sosenerdam (later: Nieuwendam/Zunderdorp). In 1556 Amsterdam bought the rights of the comital ferry to Waterland for 550 guilders. A market-boat ('beurtveer' with regular connection) with Hoorn is first mentioned in 1529, with Middelburg in 1539 and with Enkhuizen in 1550.

name: null
Toll_Description: In 1298 Beverwijk obtained toll-exemption from the count of Holland. A non dated tariff for the toll levied in Beverwijk en Wijk op Zee is copied in 1489 from an old 'roll'. The account of the count of Holland dated 1316 already mentions a 'sciptol' in Wijk, which was levied all year except when the fairs were organised. In 1399 Muiden and Weesp, in 1412 Edam and in 1415 Brielle obtained toll-exemption at the tolls of Beverwijk (Brielle: and: Ter Wijck optie zee) and Spaarndam. In 1512 an agreement was made by the publican (tollenaar) of Beverwijk and Spaarndam with merchants from Groningen and East-Friesland selling oxen and horses. They only had to pay in Spaardam, except when the market in Beverwijk was organised.

name: null
Ferry_Description: The ferry is first mentioned in 1463.

name: Grohnde
Settlement_Description: A settlement is first mentioned in 1237-1247, a castle in 1395.

name: null
Toll_Description: The toll for shipping on the river Lek in Rhenen is probably the continuation of the early medieval (Carolingian) toll of Dorestad. It is first mentioned in Rhenen in 1220, but it is plausible that is was established there already earlier. The toll was owned by the Bishop of Utrecht. Around 1470 Utrecht Bishop David of Burgundy moved the toll to his residency Wijk bij Duurstede. A long term conflict about the location of the toll resulted in a temporary displacement of the toll back to Rhenen from 1546-1557, but after the last year the toll was definitively levied in Wijk bij Duurstede.
Ferry_Description: A ferry crossing the Rhine in Rhenen is first mentioned in 1350.

name: null
Bridge_Description: Imperial chancellor Dietrich von Portitz (1361-1367) built a bridge across the Saale near the castle Giebichenstein.

name: Bottrop
Fair_Description: Bottrop was granted a retail and cattle fair on St Michael's Day in 1423.

name: Gåbense
Ferry_Description: Ferry between the island of Falster and the town of Vordingborg on Zealand. Probably established in the 13th century. In 1523 a man named Jens was granted the right to the ferry in Gåbense for an annual tax to the royal castle in Nykøbing Falster. From the middle of the 17th century part of the postal rute from Zealand.

name: Ool
Toll_Description: A toll at Ool is one of the six small tolls of Maastricht in 1357, when they were enfeoffed by the duke and duchess of Limburg to Thierri de Hornes, lord of Perwez. Three of these (including Ool) were situated on the Meuse above Roermond, and probably had their origin in the claims of Brabant on the former county of Kessel. The toll in Ool is mentioned in 1362 when the steward of the duke of Brabant leased out seven tolls on the river Meuse. In 1393 Reinald of Valkenburg gave his part in the toll to his half-brother Godfried II. The toll is mentioned again in 1545, but seems to have lost its significance by the 18th century.
Ferry_Description: A ferry across the Maas river in Ool is already mentioned in 1293 (and still in 1560). It was situated 1 kilometre south of Roermond and of great importance for the town, as the road to the ferry in Roermond was regularly flooded, in which case traffic used the ferry in Ool.

name: Locht
Settlement_Description: First mentioned as toll station in 1356. Also known as 'in via lapidae' or 'up deme Steinwege': a paved road, probably dating back to the Roman road. Locht was divided into two settlements, Bovenste ('highest') and Onderste ('lowest') Locht, according to their place in the landscape.
Toll_Description: A toll station of the duke of Brabant and Limburg was first mentioned in 1356. In that year, the revenues were 15 Aachen mark, in 1374-1384 and 1389/90 10 mark, and in 1390/91 5 mark.

name: Årøsund
Toll_Description: The age and character of the toll at Årøsund is uncertain. Probably a toll on the ferry and maybe also in the harbour was collected from around 1200 onwards. The royal taxes collected in Haderslev herred according to the so-called main list in King Valdemar’s Cadastre from c. 1231 was probably partly from the ferry in Årøsund. According to the town law of Haderslev from 1292 a personal toll was collected at Årøsund, in other words merchants and others had to pay for the right to cross Lillebælt. From this point onwards a toll on agricultural products from Funen, in particular oxen, was probably also collected at Årøsund.
Ferry_Description: Ferry connection across the strait of Lillebælt between Årøsund and the town of Assens on Funen is first mentioned in the town law of Haderslev from 1292, but is probably older, perhaps from around 1200. Throughout the middle ages and early modern era the ferry between Assens and Årøsund was one of the most important across Lillebælt, especially from the 15th century onwards when this particular route became central to the export of oxen from Funen. In the years around 1500 about 1500 oxen were exported from Funen using the ferry, and in early years of the following 17th century the annual numbers had increased to 9000-10.000 oxen. In 1561 duke Hans den Ældre (German: Johann der Ältere or Hans der Ältere) granted Nils Halsen the right to the ferry as his family had been ferryman at Årøsund for generations. In return Nils Halsen had to pay an annual tax to the duke and make sure travelers had a place to sleep and eat, when the ferry was unable to cross the strait due to bad weather. In 1640 the newly established royal postal service between Copenhagen and Hamburg began using the ferry between Årøsund and Assens.
Harbour_Description: The age and character of the medieval harbour is uncertain. Due to the importance of the ferry between Årøsund and Funen the medieval harbour most likely had a pier. In 1651, when Årøsund had become the port used by larger ships from Haderslev, the pier was extended.

name: Tranekær Færge
Ferry_Description: Ferry from Tranekær on Langeland to Svendborg on Funen mentioned in 1498, when queen Christine used to Tranekær from Svendborg. Most likely to be older.

name: Saka
Settlement_Description: The area 'Saccze' was mentioned in a treaty ('Kurenvetrag') in 1230. In 1253 it fell to the Teutonic Order. At the end of the 14th century, Sacken was given as a fief several times. Sackenhausen was a complex of goods made up of several farms and an inn.

name: null
Bridge_Description: A "grote brugge" ('large bridge') across the Venta is mentioned in 1438, when it was restored.

name: Binnenwijzend
Settlement_Description: Binnenwijzend is first mentioned around 1312. It was part of the administrative region (‘banne’) of Westwoud until 1493, when this administrative region (‘banne’) was split into Westwoud and Binnenwijzend. Binnenwijzend then got its own village government and representatives within the ‘stede’ Westwoud. This 'stede' (consisting of Westwoud, Oosterblokker and Westerblokker) had been granted town privileges in 1414 by William VI, count of Holland. These settlements, however, never developed an urban character. The granting of town rights was part of an administrative reorganization in which a number of smaller settlements were granted town rights in order to provide them with a certain degree of self-government which replaced the need for the count of Holland's bailiffs ('baljuws'). The settlements kept their own separate settlement governments.

name: Knollendam
Settlement_Description: A dam that closed off the Zaan river from the Starnmeer lake was built in the late 13th century. It was first mentioned in 1347. A village developed around it. After the dam was demolished in 1641, the settlement was divided into Oost- and West-Knollendam on both shores of the Zaan.
Ferry_Description: After the dam was demolished in 1641, a ferry connected both shores of the river.
Lock_Description: A lock in the dam was constructed around 1360 and a second one in 1558. In 1567, the locks were permanently opened and in 1641, the entire dam was removed.

name: Yersekendam
Ferry_Description: The ferry of Yerseke was located at Yersekendam, where it is first mentioned when it was enfeoffed by the count of Holland in 1351. Connections existed with Zierikzee, Bergen op Zoom and Antwerp. A ferry to the island of Tholen (Gorishoek) is only known from the middle of the 18th century.

name: Kuivezand
Settlement_Description: A small community harvested peat here since 1280, but the first mention of Kuivezand is from 1384. Once all the peat was extracted, sand drifts started appearing.

name: null
Ferry_Description: A ferry between Oudenbosch and Dordrecht probably dated back to shortly after the flood of St. Elisabeth of 1421. In 1514 a ferry (or possibly market boat ['beurtveer']) to Oudenbosch is mentioned in Dordrecht.
Harbour_Description: The canal connecting Oudenbosch with the Mark river was dug in 1300. The harbour was used predominantly as transshipment harbour for peat transports.

name: Westelbeers
Settlement_Description: The settlement Beers, first mentioned in 1207, was divided into three parts, of which Westelbeers is first mentioned separately in 1542.

name: null
Ferry_Description: Ferry from Sleeuwijk to Gorinchem, first mentioned in 1327, when it was donated to the count of Holland.

name: Oirschot
Settlement_Description: First mentioned in the 10th or early 11th century, in an 11th-century copy.
Fair_Description: Before 1340 Oirschot had a fair and in 1340 a cloth-hall. Admission by emperor Charles V on August 20 1524 for a fair on Monday and Tuesday after Low Sunday (Sunday after Eastern) to compensate the damage of the billeting of soldiers. They have to pay the steward in Den Bosch a long lease and during the fair the land-toll and smal cattle-tolls should be collected. An undated register from the abbey Tongerlo (Westerlo, B.) (circa 1556) contains a list of fairs in the region Kempen and Peel. 'Oerschot' has then three fairs: 1) first Tuesday after St. Anthonis (Jan. 17?), 2) first working day post festum St. Servatii (May 13) in May, 3) first working day  post festum Huberti (Nov. 3).

name: Hedel
Settlement_Description: First mentioned in 815-816, in a copy from 1170-1175.

name: null
Ferry_Description: The ferry across the Meuse river in Hedel is first mentioned in 1390. See Hedel for details.

name: Bouvignes-sur-Meuse
Fair_Description: In 1499 a free fair and a weekly market were granted by Philip the Handsome.

name: Drunen
Settlement_Description: First mentioned in the first quarter of the 13th century.

name: Geyen
Toll_Description: 1) From 1389, the Duke of Jülich levied a fee for safe conduct and a land toll here. Depending on the load, 2 to 3 white pfennigs ('Weißpfennige'/Albus) per horse had to be paid as escort fee. In 1389/93 the annual amount averaged about 316 mark per year, in 1398/99 about 192 mark. 2) In addition, the duke levied a road toll in 1500. Unfortunately, tariffs have not been preserved.

name: Lövenich
Toll_Description: The Archbishop of Cologne levied a land toll in 1449. Tariffs are not known. The annual revenue amounted to about 200 guilders with the toll in Merheim. In 1455 Lövenich was a secondary toll station of Königsdorf.

name: null
Ferry_Description: A ferry between the islands Schouwen and Duiveland is first mentioned in 1313. In 1368, Zierikzee is mentioned as place of departure in Schouwen. Ferry services were stopped when a dam was built between the two island in 1610. Other connections existed among others with Dreischor, Goes, Middelburg, Yerseke and Stavenisse. A ferry to Dirksland is mentioned in 1456.

name: null
Toll_Description: A ferry toll of the count of Holland appears a few years after 1415; in 1496 it was owned by the lord of Vlissingen. This was not a fee for using the ferry, but a separate toll. It was discontinued in 1582.In the toll-accounts of Iersekeroord dated 1470-'75 Vlissingen is an outpost of this toll next to Middelburg, Arnemuiden, Kats, Veere and Bergen op Zoom.In 1444 count Philip of Burgundy confirmed a privilege for a herringtoll (see sub staple), which was granted by his predecessors on a unknown date. From the years 1474/'5 and 1481/1483 herringtoll-accounts are preserved. The oldest two are analysed. In 1541 the privilege of 1444 was once more confirmed by the lord of the town. Meanwhile Biervliet had lost its herringtrade to Vlissingen. Income from the outpost here from the toll at Iersekeroord dated 1470-73, 1518 and 1524/5 are edited. Accounts of the outpost here from the Grote Zeeuwse toll dated 1584-1592 and 1628vv are digitalised.
Ferry_Description: Count Willem III of Holland appointed Pape Roelofssoone as ferryman on the ferry to Flanders in 1312. The ferry already existed at that time, and must date back to the foundation of the town around 1300. The ferry was always owned by the count, who enfeoffed it.
Harbour_Description: A harbour was constructed around 1300, which formed the core around which the town developed. In 1443 a new harbour basin was constructed south of the old town to accommodate the growing herring fishing fleet: the current Vissershaven. In 1549 there were plans to enlargen the harbour again, which led to resistance from Middelburg. The Pottekaaihaven was constructed in 1582, which was connected with a sluice with the town canal. In 1610 the harbour was extended again, making Vlissingen one of the largest harbours in the Dutch Republic. The city had a significant herring fishing and trading fleet.

name: null
Ferry_Description: A ferry crossing the Rhine in Rhenen is first mentioned in 1350.

name: Salzderhelden
Settlement_Description: The saltworks in Salzderhelden are first mentioned in 1305, the castle in 1306, but it was possibly built in the 13th century. The settlement was characterised as borough ('blek' / 'flecken') since 1480, which received market privileges in 1509.
Toll_Description: A toll in Salzderhelden is first mentioned in 1422.

name: null
Bridge_Description: The bridge across the Leine river in Salzderhelden was first mentioned in 1482. Next to the bridge was a watchtower of the town of Einbeck.

name: null
Toll_Description: A toll on shipping on the Oste river at Neuhaus is mentioned in 1502.

name: Schlachte
Harbour_Description: Jever was originally located on direct waterways with the North Sea via the Harlebucht and the Hooktief. The waterways silted up in the later Middle Ages. The connection with the Harlebucht was given up, and in 1546 Hooksiel became the new sea harbour of Jever, which could be reached with smaller boats via the Hooktief.

name: Hooksiel
Settlement_Description: First mentioned in 1479. A sluice ('siel') was probably built in 1546, at the current location in 1588, around which the harbour settlement developed.
Toll_Description: Count Anton Günther of Oldenburg installed a toll station on harbour traffic in Hooksiel in 1603.
Harbour_Description: After the direct waterways that connected Jever with the sea silted up in the late Middle Ages, Hooksiel became the sea harbour of Jever from 1546 onwards. Commodities were transshipped here on smaller boats that sailed to Jever via the Hookstief.

name: Greetsiel
Settlement_Description: Greetsiel developed around a sluice ('siel') that was first mentioned in 1388. A castle was built here by the Cirksena family in the 14th century; it was demolished in 1778.
Toll_Description: A toll was introduced in Greetsiel by count Johann II of East Frisia around 1576, which led to complaints from merchants from Emden and abroad. Cargo for which toll in Greetsiel already had been paid was exempted from toll in Emden.

name: Stekene
Settlement_Description: First mention in 1223, in a copy from c.1544.

name: Sint-Gillis-Waas
Fair_Description: Emperor Charles granted in 1555 a free fair on Wednesday after St. Matthew (Sept. 21).

name: null
Harbour_Description: Hulst was located on the Saxhaven, a navigable stream that connected the town with the Westerschelde. Since 1314, the Stekense Vaart also provided a connection with Gent and Rupelmonde. Moreover, there were canals that transported peat from Saaftinge (the Lieve) and Hulsterloo (Moervaart). The harbour was the reason for the town's prosperity as trading town, but in the 14th century, it started to silt up. A tolltariff dated is 1317 is edited. In 1326 a crane was built. In 1358, a temporary harbour tax was levied to pay for the construction of a lock to improve the water level. Harbour-tax income for the years 1482-92 are edited.The Stekense Vaart must have fallen out of use by the 16th century, as it is not shown on maps anymore. With the inundations of 1585, the Hellegat came into existence, which became the new harbour of Hulst on the southern side of town.

name: null
Bridge_Description: A bridge was built across the Vecht in Ommen in 1492.
Ferry_Description: Before construction of the bridge in 1492, a ferry operated probably at the same location. In 1447 the ferry was pawned by the bishop of Utrecht to the town during his life and another 6 years. In 1462 the ferry was pawned by the steward of Sallant for 6 years.

name: null
Toll_Description: In 1432 the villages of Wolmirstedt, Rogätz and Jerichow are mentioned as toll stations on the Elbe in a conflict between the council of Magdeburg and the archbishop. Further mentions of the toll in 1460 and 1492. The toll is also mentioned in four travel accounts of the merchant Gottfried Kleeditz from Pirna from 1671 to 1674.

name: null
Harbour_Description: The Saale river must have been used by ships until Halle. In the 18th century, a wood and coal landing place was located opposite the royal saltworks, but for earlier centuries the location of a harbour is unknown.

name: null
Ferry_Description: In 1394 the bishop of Utrecht ordained that he and his men had to be taken across. The bishop pawned the ferry to the town in 1460 and again in 1517.

name: null
Toll_Description: In 1018 the count of Holland Dirk III had a castle and toll on the river Merwede in Vlaardingen on the route from Cologne to England. After complaints of merhants from Tiel the emperor ordained that the duke of Neder-Lotharingen and the 'Reichs'-bishops had to take action but they lost the battle. In 1289 the lord of Wassenaar renounced eternally the hulktol ('huelec tolne') at Dordrecht on in- and outgoing seaships on the Maas, which was a fief from the count of Holland. Dordrecht however on order of the count had to pay a fee starting 1289 for the toll the lord of Wassenaar used to have at Vlaardingen. According to the oldest register with the fiefs of the count the toll ('hulctolne') was indeed in Vlaardingen. In 1454 Vlaardingen ('Vlerdingen') is found as an outpost of the toll of the count of Holland at Geervliet.
Harbour_Description: In 1470 the harbour was enlarged from the Spuidam up to the Maas and a pier was built ont the westside of the mouth of the harbour to prevent the silting up of te harbour. In the 16th century continuous deepening was necessary and the pier was enlenghtend. The 'Hoogheemraadschap' (district waterboard) of Delfland gave also attention and money to deepen the harbour. In 1555 the town had 13 or 14 herringboats ('buizen'). The Opstand against Spain had devastating results. Only at the end of the 16th century the harbour was useful again. In 1625 a crane was built. A sandbank hampered the entrance to the harbour in 1633. The heads were enlengtend in 1640.

name: null
Ferry_Description: A ferry between Schoonhoven and Gelkenes crossing the river Lek is first mentioned in 1317. Yields for the farming out of this right for the second half of the 14th century are published. It was then owned by the count of Blois, who was lord of the town and had a castle in Schoonhoven. One account of the ferry survived and is dated 1497. Citizens of Schoonhoven and Nieuwpoort paid a special tariff per year and inhabitants of the villages of Goudriaan and Ottoland and those living within a mile (circa 6,5km.) of Schoonhoven on both sides of the river Lek as well per traverse.

name: null
Ferry_Description: A ferry from Dordrecht to the seigniory Merwede (Papendrecht) is first mentioned in 1330. A ferry to Brielle in 1394. Circa 1480 a market-boat ('beurtveer') Dordrecht-Bergen op Zoom was set up. In 1514 market-boats are mentioned to Rotterdam and Oudenbosch.

name: null
Lock_Description: Possibly in the twelfth century, the water Delf was dug as a connection between the waters Fivel and Eems. The Delf got a dam with a lock near the current Vlintenbrug.

name: Oldenzijl
Lock_Description: A sluice ('zijl') between the Winsumer- and Reitdiep was first mentioned here in 1323. After a new connection was dug between both waterways more to the west in 1458-9, with a new sluice in Shaphalsterzijl, it became known as the old sluice (Oldenzijl). The sluice was demolished in 1636 after the Reitdiep was straightened.

name: Übach
Toll_Description: A toll of the duke of Brabant-Limburg is first attested in 1356. In 1356/57 and 1389-91 the annual revenues were 1 mark.

name: null
Bridge_Description: A bridge was constructed across the IJssel in Zutphen in 1485.
Ferry_Description: Before the construction of the bridge in 1485, a ferry crossing must have existed at this place.

name: null
Ferry_Description: A ferry south of Oostburg must have existed since the construction of the canal Brugse Vaart in 1502-1505. It is first mentioned in a request by Oostburg to the States General in 1615. The ferry had been owned by Oostburg for a long time before, but was acquired by the States General during the Dutch Revolt.

name: Großsoltbrück
Bridge_Description: Bridge near the village Großsolt, first mentioned in 1615-1616.

name: null
Lock_Description: After the water mill in Keppel had been demolished in 1582 to facilitate shipping on the Oude IJssel, the Lord of Keppel constructed a new mill in the southern arm of the river in 1537. The construction did not contain a lock, but the weir was built in such a way that ships could pass it with normal water levels. However, since the weir changed the water levels, it hindered shipping nevertheless. A court case between Doesburg and Keppel at the Guelders court did nothing to change the situation.

name: null
Lock_Description: After the mouth of the Oude IJssel into the IJssel was moved south of town in 1605, a new pound lock complex was constructed around 1615 to regulate the shipping on both rivers.

name: 's Hertogenmolens
Lock_Description: Duke Willem II of Croÿ, lord of Aarschot, ordered the construction of new water mills in the Demer near the beguinage before 1520. Between the two mills, there was a lock through which ships could be dragged.

name: Niederlage
Harbour_Description: A harbour on the Oder developed around the town foundation of 1253. The landing place was indicated as Niederlage - after the Frankfurt staple - on early modern views of town.

name: Zichem
Fair_Description: Roman king Charles IV granted in 1362 a fair 8 days  before St. Remigius (Oct. 1) and during 8 days. In 1499 the count of Nassau granted, in order to restore war damage, a free fair during 3 days on the Tuesday before Pentecost and a free weekly market.

name: Oldemarkt
Settlement_Description: Originally called Dodovene, first mentioned in 1336. The name Oldemarkt is first attested in 1438, named after the markets of the parish Paasloo that took place there. The markets gave the settlement a near urban character, although it always remained a village.
Fair_Description: In 1438 the bishop of Utrecht granted the parishioners of Paasloo a weekly market on Tuesday and two fairs in Oldemarkt in the same parish. They took place on St Lambert's day (17 September) and Tuesday after Pentecost, with a duration of both 8 days before and after these dates. In 1478 he relocated the latter fair from Tuesday to Thursday after Pentecost and granted a new fair with Mid-Lent. In 1492 the weekly market was moved from Tuesday to Saturday. In 1618 the Pentecost fair, which had been cancelled due to the war, was reinstated on the 1st of May. The markets were especially important for the trade in butter.

name: null
Lock_Description: The count of Holland built a dam in the Rhine (Oude Rijn) at the Zwade shortly before 1165, in order to regulate water levels in Holland, but it led to water problems in Utrecht. Emperor Fredrick Barbarossa ordered the demolition of the dam in 1165, but to no avail: the dam remained, with an opening for ships to pass.

name: Ede
Settlement_Description: First mentioned in 838, in an 11th-century copy.

name: Wamel
Settlement_Description: First mentioned in 893, in a copy from 1222.

name: Breust
Settlement_Description: Breust is first mentioned in a seventeenth-century copy of a manuscript from 965. From the eleventh to the thirteenth century, Breust and the neighbouring settlement Eijsden were central to the cultivation of the Plateau of Margraten. The history of several villages there can be traced back to either Breust or Eijsden.

name: null
Harbour_Description: Due to the existence of three sluices between the Haarlem Lake and the IJ, the tow canal ('trekvaart') between Amsterdam and Haarlem, which was built in 1631, was interrupted in Halfweg. Passengers had to change barges here.

name: Ouderkerk aan de Amstel
Fair_Description: From 1308 onwards a comital market-toll in Ouderamstel (1355: Ouderkerk) is collected by the steward of Amstelland. In 1450 described as decayed. Possibly earlier because the accounts of the steward are lacking for the years 1369-1450.

name: Baambrugge
Bridge_Description: Baambrugge is named after a bridge across the Angstel.

name: null
Lock_Description: The Hinderdam on the border of Holland and the Nedersticht, a dam with locks, was built in the Vecht river by the bishop and Estates of Utrecht in 1437, to protect the land from floods from the Zuiderzee. It replaced a dam built near Vreeland in 1326, which had replaced the Otterspoor dam near Breukelen. The Hinderdam was demolished around 1672, when new locks were built in Muiden.

name: Otterspoor
Lock_Description: Somewhere between 1244-1259 a dike at Otterspoor near Maarssen in the river Vecht on the parish border with Breukelen was made. In 1259 merchants from Cologne obtained a safeconduct between Gein and Maarssen. In 1323 it is called the 'meerdam' ('seadike') with a lock, which suggests a function in stemming floods from the Zuiderzee. Here transshipment on the route to Utrecht in smaller boats was necessary, as a result of the shallowness of the river Vecht. The dam was replaced by a new one near Vreeland in 1326.

name: Gronsveld
Settlement_Description: Gronsveld is first mentioned in a document from 673-690, which is a falsification from 1024-1031. The subsequent mention dates from around 1089 in a thirteenth-century copy.

name: Rijckholt
Settlement_Description: The first mention of Ryckholt dates from 1330.

name: Amstelveen
Fair_Description: A horse- and horned cattle-fair was granted by king Charles V to the lord of the manor Amstelveen Reinout van Brederode in 1523, as his subjects were hampered while visiting outside his jurisdiction the nearby horse-fair in Aboude in the Sticht of Utrecht by the Guelders and Frisians. Fair-days were the last two days of August, just before the fair started in Abcoude. In 1529 the fair was part of the purchase of the seigniory of Amstelveen by Amsterdam. Yields of the fair in the city-accounts of Amsterdam preserved since 1531 are low and the fair expired. This was probably caused by the fame of the ancient horse-fair in Aboude and the fact that king Charles became temporal lord of the Sticht of Utrecht in 1528.

name: Leimuiden
Settlement_Description: First mentioned in the first half of the 11th century.

name: Castricum
Settlement_Description: First mentioned probably in the late 11th century, in a copy from ca. 1420.

name: Everstein
Toll_Description: A toll on sailing ships at the river Lek levied at the castle Everstein belonging to the lord of Arkel is mentioned in 1398/1399 en 1402. Then goods belonging to citizens of Cologne were taken in custody. The castle was built by the lord of Arkel around 1380 but was burnt down in 1405.

name: null
Ferry_Description: Found in the oldest preserved and edited account of Gelre dated 1294/'5: nave nautica: 14lb.

name: null
Ferry_Description: A ferry in Asperen at the river Linge to Acquoy, fief of the lord of Voorne, is found in 1316. A comital ferry likely to Leerdam, is found in 1504.  In 1556 the account of the steward of the count of Holland mentions five fair-tolls and a watertoll, which is then leased together with two ferrys, one at Asperen and one crossing the river Linge.

name: null
Ferry_Description: Ferry from Sleeuwijk to Gorinchem, first mentioned in 1327, when it was donated to the count of Holland.

name: null
Ferry_Description: Found in the oldest preserved and edited account of the count of Gelre dated 1294/'5: nave nautica... apud Rinsewich.

name: Langscheid
Settlement_Description: A first mention from the late 13th century is uncertain. In 1307, the settlement is mentioned as <q>novella plantatio</q> and <q>nova villa</q>, founded by count Ludwig of Arnsberg, who made the settlement into a borough ('freiheit') after the Lippstadt town right. The original settlement was located south of modern Langscheid, and disappeared in the Sorpetalsperre reservoir, built in 1928-1935.

name: Ravenswaaij
Settlement_Description: First mentioned in 1139, in a 14th-century copy.

name: Goldberg
Settlement_Description: Mentioned in 1227 as village in possession of the monastery Dobbertin.
Town_Description: Made into a town in 1248 by Pribislaw I of Parchim with Parchim town law.

name: null
Ferry_Description: The ferry from Tiel to Wamel existed already in the Middle Ages. It was privately owned, but in 1680-1682 the town acquired possession of the ferry.

name: Penzlin
Settlement_Description: Originally a Slavic village, first mentioned in 1170.
Town_Description: A town must have been founded before 1226. The Schwerin town privileges were confirmed by Lord Nikolaus of Werle in 1263.

name: Serrahn
Settlement_Description: The village with a mill is first mentioned in 1296.

name: Marlow
Settlement_Description: First mentioned in 1179. Originally a Slavic fortification and market village, mentioned as borough ('flecken') in 1210. East of it a German village developed. Characterised as 'oppidum' in 1298. In the same year the regional law court was moved from Marlow to Sülze.
Town_Description: Lübeck town privileges were confirmed in 1459, but the town was mostly referred to as borough ('oppidum').
Toll_Description: A transit toll is mentioned in 1286.

name: null
Ferry_Description: The ferry across the Nederrijn near Opheusden is mentioned in 1406. It had great significance for the town of Wageningen.

name: Reuterstadt Stavenhagen
Settlement_Description: Foundation of a castle in the 13th century by the knights of Stove, first mentioned in 1230.
Town_Description: Dukes Barnim I and Wratislaw III of Pomerania-Stettin granted town privileges between 1252 and 1264; the privileges and the Lübeck town law were confirmed in 1282. The town remained very small.

name: null
Lock_Description: After farmers from Diepenheim and Goor had destroyed the "old lock" (Oude Sluis) in the Schipbeek in a conflict about water levels in the region in 1630, the town of Deventer decided to build an additional "new" lock (Nieuwe Sluis) to regulate the water levels better.

name: null
Toll_Description: In 950 (10th century forging) Roman king Otto I gave his vassal Ansfried market- and mintrights and the toll in Kessel ('Cassalo sito in pago Masalant'), which had to be relocated from Echt ('in villa Ehti'). There is no proof for an actual established market. Two tolls were levied on the river Meuse in Kessel. On the one hand, a river toll was established by the Count of Guelders in 1279, which he enfeoffed to the Lord of Kessel from 1350. In 1348 this toll was arranged by Matthijs van Kessel, Deddrick Oest and the town Roermond. On the other hand, the Duke of Brabant established a toll station in 1357, which he granted as a fief: in 1357 to Dietrich von Hornes, Lord of Perwez, in 1414 to Konrad, Lord of Schleiden and in 1480 to Count Kuno von Manderscheid. Only special tariffs for citizens from specific towns, such as Roermond and Venlo, are known. The annual revenue of the Guelders toll in 1294/95 was 25 Cologne mark. Around 1500 Nijmegen should have been declared toll-exempt. In 1579 the oldest preserved city-account of Roermond states that half the toll of Kessel and all the toll of Hanssum belonged to the city.
Ferry_Description: A ferry-man ('nautis') in Kessel is first attested in the oldest account of the count of Gelre dated 1294/5.

name: null
Lock_Description: A lock in the mill weir in Lochem already existed in 1591. It could only be passed by small vessels; larger ships had to be hauled over the weir. The lock was pawned for 35 guilders in 1595, in 1600 for a reduced price. The lock was renewed in 1610, with 1/3 of the construction costs paid by the town of Lochem and the rest by Zutphen, and once again in 1644. An installation for hauling ships across the weir ('overtoom') was constructed in 1629. Tariffs for using the lock were set in 1646.

name: null
Lock_Description: Between 1644 and 1646, a lock was built in the mill weir of Borculo, as part of attempts to make the Berkel river navigable. Tariffs for using the locks were set in 1646.

name: null
Lock_Description: Between 1644 and 1646, a lock was built in the mill weir of Mallem, as part of attempts to make the Berkel river navigable. Tariffs for using the locks were set in 1646.

name: null
Harbour_Description: Until 1646, attempts to make the Berkel river navigable had advanced so far that ships from Zutphen could reach a landing place at the confluence of Berkel and Ölbach near Vreden.

name: Oostendorper watermolen
Harbour_Description: The Oostendorp water mill near Haaksbergen was the end point of the navigable waterway that was created when the Schipbeek was connected to the Diepenheimer Molenbeek and Buurserbeek in or shortly after 1611. It served as a transshipment point for the land traffic. A canal circumventing the mill with a lock was built in 1663, allowing shipping past the mill until the Dutch-German border near Alstätte. However, the lock fell into disrepair in 1687 and was not repaired, so that the Oostendorp mill once again became the end point of the Schipbeek water way.

name: Brück (Brandenburg)
Settlement_Description: First mentioned in 1249 as part of the name Walterus de Brugge. Originated near a castle, that was still mentioned in 1441.
Town_Description: Town privileges were granted by Duke Rudolf II of Saxony between 1360 and 1374. In 1459, however, the place is still mentioned as oppidum (borough).
Toll_Description: Brück appears as secondary station of safe conduct ('Nebengeleit') in accounts of the district ('Amt') Belzig from 1489 onwards.

name: null
Harbour_Description: The entire waterfront of town was used as sea harbour for Rostock. Landing piers (usually seven, in some years less) stretched out into the water for mooring ships. These are first attested on an image from 1420/1430. On a view of town from 1585, a luffing crane is first displayed in front of the Burgwall gate. It was replaced by a rotary crane in 1622.

name: Glasewitzer Burg
Settlement_Description: Watchtower with boom barrier in the enclosure ('landwehr') of Güstrow. The enclosure is first mentioned in 1270, the year of construction of the tower is unknown. Later converted into a farm that was leased from the town.

name: null
Lock_Description: Oude Sluis ('old lock') in the section of the Schipbeek between the Regge and Diepenheimse Molenbeek. This section of the canal was dug in or shortly after 1611. The lock was a flash lock, which resulted in a flood of water when it was opened. This was a problem for farmers in the area during the haymaking period, who therefore claimed the right to build a dam in front of the lock in summer. Although it was contested by the town of Deventer, this seems to have been common practice, and the lock must have been usable for ships only in winter.

name: null
Lock_Description: A connection between the Schipbeek and the Regge river at Westerflier must have been dug before 1547. Due to the different water levels, such a connection required a pound lock. The pound lock at Westerflier is first explicitly mentioned in 1633, when it was destroyed. To prevent unwanted flooding, the lock was permanently closed; the keys were kept by the burgomaster of Diepenheim. Only with his permission, the lock could be opened for ships.

name: Æbelholt
Settlement_Description: The Order of Saint Augustine Monastery founded c. 1170.

name: null
Harbour_Description: According to a letter of the lord of Almelo Otto van Rechteren from 1476, the canal Nieuwe Graven had been dug on his orders shortly before, which created a navigable connection with the Exooshe Aa and Regge rivers. Almelo functioned as a transshipment point for the transport between Twente and Zwolle. In town regulations from 1489, it is stipulated that ships were not allowed to stay longer at the harbour quays than three days. Before the construction of the canal, shipping was probably possible via the old stream, but of minor importance.

name: null
Lock_Description: A large weir ('schutstal') in the Regge river for the two water mills near Schuilenburg manor was reconstructed around 1400, and must therefore already have existed before. The weir could be opened as a flash lock for ships, but skippers had to wait until evening when the milling was done because opening the lock caused temporary low water levels. Waiting times amounted to multiple days in dry times, which led to many conflicts between skippers and millers in the 16th-18th centuries. According to regulations from 1550, there also existed a ship hauling installation ('overtoom') for transporting empty ships across the barrier without having to open the lock.

name: null
Toll_Description: In order to fund the maintenance of the Schipbeek canal, the town of Deventer started levying a toll on the canal near Holten in 1637: 4 stuivers for each vessel and 10 stuivers for each piece of timber (or for four pieces of timber of bad quality). Tariffs were raised in 1744. The toll was abolished in 1799.

name: Schwabstedt
Settlement_Description: The bishop of Schleswig built a castle in Schwabstedt on the Treene river after 1268, which is first mentioned in 1318. A settlement developed next to it; a church is mentioned in 1491. Mentioned as borough ('blek') in the 16th century.
Toll_Description: A wood and wagon toll is mentioned in Schwabstedt already in 1378. A toll of the bishop of Schleswig is also mentioned in a register of revenues from 1509.

name: null
Harbour_Description: Hollingstedt is mentioned in the Schleswig town law of ca. 1200 as North Sea harbour of Schleswig at the Treene. Archaeological finds show that there was a transshipment point here since the 11th century. Although Hollingstedt lost much of its importance as harbour place later, the Treene tolls of Schwabstedt and Treia suggest that the Treene was still used as waterway in the 16th century.

name: null
Toll_Description: A toll of the bishop of Schleswig in Treia is mentioned in a 1436 register: for each wagon 3 Scherf, each animal 1 penny, and for a stighe (=10) lambs 4 albos, as well as tariffs for various commodities. Tariffs for the river traffic are not specifically mentioned, but from later sources it is known that the toll was levied on traffic that crossed the river as well as on the river.
Harbour_Description: The existence of a river toll in Treia suggests that the Treene was used as a waterway at least until Treia.

name: Fürstenwerder
Settlement_Description: Founded as an Ascanian border fortress when Stargard became part of Mecklenburg in 1304.
Town_Description: In 1323 the settlement was first mentioned as town ('civitas'). In the 15th century it was mentioned as a noble town ('adliges Städtlein').

name: Greiffenberg
Settlement_Description: The castle and the associated settlement already existed in the Pomeranian period, i.e. before 1250.
Town_Description: The settlement was owned by the knight Johann de Grifenberg in 1261 and was referred to as town ('civitas'). In 1349, Duke Barnim allowed the knights of Gryphenberg to establish a new town with town rights, markets and a market toll.

name: null
Toll_Description: In 1389 count Albrecht granted Hoorn to collect a toll on each oxen or horses supplied ashore by the Danish. This comital toll was at first farmed out together with the weigh-house and 'wissel' but starting 1467 separate. The outputs over the years 1389-1722 are analysed.
Ferry_Description: A market-boat ('beurtveer') to Amsterdam is first mentioned in 1529.
Harbour_Description: The Old- en 'Doelen'-harbour are medieval and dated 1341. Early 16th century the Doelenhaven is widend and deepend. Probably around 1560 a start was made with the outlet of the harbour towards sea. In 1567 a new harbourtax is collected from the hibernating ships who sailed to other countries (1 stuiver per last), in order to maintain the harbour and guard the ships. Vitelli counted in his report for the duke of Alva in 1569 20 'navires a gabie' (with a crow's-nest), 30  'buizen' (herringboats), 40 boyers, and ships from Denmarkt named 'bencrayen' of less then 30 last for horses, cattle and other merchandise. In 1576 the new harbour is realised but the debouch is in one of the new harbours at the eastside of the town.

name: Dam
Lock_Description: A dam was built in the Krommenie in 1357. It remained passable until shortly after 1544.

name: Altlandsberg
Settlement_Description: Since Slavic times a fortification with village. South of it a German market settlement developed.
Town_Description: The town must have been founded before 1257, because in that year the town "new" Landsberg (Landisberg Nova - Gorzów Wielkopolski) was founded. A foundation charter of Altlandsberg has not been preserved; it is first mentioned as town in 1308.

name: Köpenick
Settlement_Description: The Slavic Lord Jaxa de Copnic, owned a fortification in the mid-12th century, but a settlement already existed before that. In 1245 Köpenick was the seat of a bailiff.
Town_Description: A town charter has not survived, but Köpenick probably had Brandenburg-Magdeburg law. In 1298 the place was referred to as an oppidum, in 1325 as civitas. Mentioned as a town in 1381.

name: Biesenthal
Settlement_Description: The village originates from a Slavic fortification and fishing village. There was an Ascanian castle nearby, probably built at the beginning of the 13th century. A German village developed there, which evolved into a market place. A bailiff is mentioned in 1258 and a parson in 1265.
Town_Description: Margrave Johann confirmed already existing privileges in 1315. In 1317 the place was referred to as oppidum and in 1337 as town. In 1375 and 1451, however, it was again mentioned as a village.

name: Buckow (Märkische Schweiz)
Settlement_Description: Ancient fishing settlement. There probably existed a Silesian border fortress with a Slavic village, which was mentioned as a castrum in 1249. From 1405, the place was referred to as borough ('oppidum').

name: Stüvete Burg
Settlement_Description: Watchtower with boom barrier in the enclosure ('landwehr') of Güstrow. The enclosure is first mentioned in 1270, the tower itself in 1394. However, it was built on a piece of land belonging to the village Gutow, that is known to have been in possession of the town already in 1371. Having fallen out of use, the tower was repaired in 1592, but demolished in 1613.

name: Putlitz
Settlement_Description: In 948, the place was mentioned in the foundation charter of the bishopric of Havelberg as the main town of a district. Since the 13th century, the castle served as the centre of the noble family of Gans.
Town_Description: The town was founded by the lords Gans, first mentioned as a town in 1319. New town privileges were granted in 1492.

name: Rhinow
Town_Description: Probably founded by the Ascanian Konrad (1281-1310). In 1333 the settlement was referred to as oppidum, in 1443 as Stad.

name: Senftenberg
Settlement_Description: The village was built on the site of a fortification. First mentioned in 1279, already as town.
Town_Description: First mentioned as civitas in 1279, as oppidum In 1301. Date of foundation unknown, the town probably possessed Magdeburg law.

name: Lubsko
Settlement_Description: Originally a German castle with a market settlement. There is no evidence of Slavic traces, but the German fortress was built between two originally Slavic villages. First mentioned in 1253, after it had become a town.
Town_Description: The town received its first town charter from Margrave Dietrich around 1220. Further economic privileges followed in 1283. In 1253 the town was first mentioned as oppidum. In 1422, Magdeburg town rights were confirmed.

name: Trzciel
Settlement_Description: Earthen ramparts indicate early fortifications and castles. The old town originated from a Polish village that was mentioned in 1252.
Town_Description: The town was listed in 1458 among the towns that had to provide armed men for the war with the Knights' Order.

name: Kargowa
Settlement_Description: The place originated as a German refugee colony next to a village.
Town_Description: The foundation of the town between 1641 and 1653. Christoph von Unruh acquired the village in 1641. The oldest privilege of the town dates from 1653. In 1655 Unruh calls himself the founder of the town in a document. Since 1661 in possession of Magdeburg law.

name: Oldenswort
Settlement_Description: First mentioned in 1252. The local church dates from the second quarter of the 13th century.

name: Kalfsteert
Ferry_Description: The polder Kalfsteert was reclaimed from the sea by the monastery of Ter Duinen before 1355. A ferry existed here to Hansweert in Zuid-Beveland, which is mentioned in 1591, but must have existed earlier. Around 1600, the area was flooded and the ferry moved to Walsoorden.

name: Waarde
Settlement_Description: First mentioned in 1219. The local church was founded between 1222 and 1251.
Ferry_Description: Waarde became a destination for the ferry from Walsoorden that replaced the ferry Hansweert-Kalfsteert after the latter settlement disappeared in the water around 1600. In 1646 Waarde is first mentioned as destination, when the ferry was pawned. From the 18th century, the ferry from Walsoorden sailed to Hansweert again.

name: null
Ferry_Description: A ferry in Sint Maartensdijk is first found in 1324. A ferry between Sint Maartensdijk, Scherpenisse and Duiveland is first mentioned in 1360.

name: null
Harbour_Description: The peat canal Schipgracht or Burggraven between Gent and Ertvelde is first mentioned in 1228. The canal was built by the burgrave of Gent.

name: null
Harbour_Description: After military inundations in 1585 had caused the development of a new sea inlet, the Hellegat, a new harbour developed on the southern side of town.

name: Overslag
Settlement_Description: The village developed near a transshipment place ('overslagplaats') on the water route between Axel and Gent. It is mentioned in 1465/66, when the canal between Overslag and Kalve was in a dilapidated state.
Harbour_Description: A system of peat canals (Moervaart, Oostvaart, Westvaart) connected the town of Gent with Axel and the Westerschelde estuary in Terneuzen. In Overslag, these canals were not directly connected so that commodities had to be transshipped here. There might also have existed a barge-hauling installation ('overtoom'). The connection lost importance after the opening of the Sassevaart canal in 1547.

name: null
Toll_Description: A road toll ('weghelt') between Biervliet and Boekhoute existed before 1375-1404, when storm surges flooded the countryside and Biervliet became located on an island. The location of the toll house is unknown.

name: null
Harbour_Description: Through its harbour, that was located on the eastern side of town, Biervliet was connected to the Westerschelde (Honte), probably originally via a small river. In the 16th century, the harbour silted up. A new anchoring place was created outside the entrance of the old harbour.

name: Kahldenbrücke
Bridge_Description: The Kahldenbrücke was one of the most important bridges across the Peene in Demmin, and is first attested in the 17th century, but must have been much older.

name: Saaftinge
Settlement_Description: The land of Saaftinge is first mentioned in 1231. It was a lordship ('heerlijkheid') of the count of Flanders. The settlement Saaftinge is mentioned as a town in the late 13th century, but was destroyed by flooding in 1334. Although the land was reclaimed from the sea and the settlement refounded, it remained a mere village. It finally disappeared during a storm surge in 1570 and subsequent inundations in 1584.
Toll_Description: The herring toll of Saaftinge was a toll of safe conduct on shipping on the Honte (Westerschelde) between Honteoord and Wulpe. It appears as fief of the count of Flanders in a register from 1365. A part of the cargo had to be paid, dependent on the direction, destination and cargo of the ship. Ships that tried to evade the toll had to pay four times the amount, and even nine times if the ship had to be followed until Antwerp.

name: Assenede
Settlement_Description: First mentioned in 1120. The village was an important regional market centre, but was never raised to a town.
Toll_Description: A market toll of the count of Flanders in Assenede is mentioned in 1323. In 1349, when the weekly market was moved from Sunday to Tuesday, toll tariffs were set for animals. In 1398/99 no-one could be found who wanted to lease the toll because of its low revenues, but in the 15th century it was leased every six years.

name: Sint Jansteen
Settlement_Description: First mentioned in 1248, in a copy from ca. 1800. Sint Jansteen was a separate lordship ('heerlijkheid') as fief of the Burgrave of Gent.
