Settlement_Description: The small settlement of  Høve was first mentioned c. 1370, but is significantly older. The settlement had no church but was part of the parish of Asnæs.

name: Grønsund Færge (Møn)
Ferry_Description: The ferry across the narrow strait of Grønsund between Møn and Falster is mentioned in 1509 but is most likely to be older, presumably from the 13th century.

name: Boeslunde
Settlement_Description: The village of Boeslunde was first mentioned in the so-called main piece of King Valdemars’ Cadastre from c. 1231.

name: Even Bro
Bridge_Description: The bridge is mentioned in 1614, but is most likely to be older.

name: Tuse
Bridge_Description: In the 16th century the village of Tuse was an important road station for traffic across Zealand, between Copenhagen and Kalundborg. The peasants in Tuse regularly complained over the problems caused by the many travelers passing through the village. A bridge across the nearby river of Tuse Å was first mentioned in 1630, but is probably from the 16th century or even older.

name: Køge Kro
Settlement_Description: An inn used by travelers between the towns of Copenhagen and Køge. Documented from 1556, but is probably older.

name: Roskilde Kro
Settlement_Description: An inn used by travelers between the towns of Copenhagen and Roskilde. Presumably, the inn was established in the 15th century, but is not mentioned before the 16th century. In 1659 it was destroyed by occupying Swedish troops.

name: Mogenstrup
Settlement_Description: The village of Mogenstrup at the river of Fladså was first mentioned around 1300.

name: Eggeslevmagle
Settlement_Description: The village of Eggeslev was first mentioned in 1140. A ford across the river of Bjerge Å was located north from the village.

name: Erdrup Bro
Bridge_Description: Documented in 1618-1619, but is likely to be older. In the early 17th century the royal governor of Korsør Castle was responsible for the bridge, and a fee (Danish: brokorn/bropenge) had to be paid to the governor to cross the bridge.

name: Havelse Mølle
Bridge_Description: A watermill and bridge or dam across the river of Havelse Å is known from around 1500.

name: Faxe
Settlement_Description: The village of Faxe was first mentioned in 1280, but is significantly older. The first stone church was built in either the 12th or 13th century, and replaced by a new parish church in the late middle ages.

name: Værebro
Bridge_Description: A bridge across the river of Værebro Å was first mentioned in the early 13th century by the chronicler Saxo Grammaticus. Apparently a stone bridge in the late medieval period and into the early modern era. The bridge collapsed in the 18th century. Originally the bridge was placed c. 500 meters west of the modern bridge.

name: Tvolm
Settlement_Description: The village of Tvolm was first mentioned in 1457 and again in 1512, but is significantly older. The parish church is from either the 12th or 13th century.

name: Dragør
Settlement_Description: A fishing village first mentioned c. 1333.
Fair_Description: The rich fishing of herring each autumn attracted people and trade to  Dragør. In the 14th century the market activities in Dragør grew in importance, and by 1342 the town was one of the Scania fairs, although it was located on the island of Amager in the province of Zealand. Like the other annual fairs of Scania the fishing market in Dragør probably took place from August 15th to October 9th. And as the other fairs, the one in Dragør lost its importance during the 16th century.
Staple_Description: Stable rights were granted by king Christian I (1448-1481) in 1475, who ordered that oxen were only allowed to be transported to Dragør as well as a few other towns (Kolding Assens, Ribe and the annual fairs in Skanör and Falsterbo). When Dragør lost these stable rights are uncertain.
Harbour_Description: The character of the medieval harbour is unknown. Probably a natural harbour.

name: Øksenvad
Settlement_Description: The village of Øksenvad was first mentioned in 1390 but is significantly older. The parish church is from either the 12th or 13th century.

name: Odden
Settlement_Description: Odden was an important manor in Vendsyssel from the middle of the 15th century onwards.

name: Mygdal
Settlement_Description: The village of Mygdal was first mentioned in the 15th century, but is significantly older. The parish church is from the 13th century.

name: Astrup
Settlement_Description: The village of Astrup was first mentioned in 1474 but is significantly older. The parish church is from the early 13th century.

name: Skibsby
Settlement_Description: The settlement of Skibby was first mentioned in 1347, but is significantly older.

name: Gerdrup
Settlement_Description: The village of Gerdrup was first mentioned in 1170.
Bridge_Description: Probably a late medieval bridge across the river of Hove Å north of the village. Another possibility is that the bridge was located about 1 kilometer south of the village, or that there were two bridges near the village of Gerdrup.

name: Dommerby
Settlement_Description: The village of Dommerby was first mentioned in 1409 and again in 1524, but is significantly older. The parish church is from either the 12th or 13th century.

name: Resen
Settlement_Description: The village of Resen was first mentioned in 1330-48 and again in 1492, but is significantly older. The parish church is from either the 12th or 13th century.

name: Sjørup
Settlement_Description: The village of Sørup was first mentioned in 1504. The name indicates that the village is older than 1504.

name: Kvosted
Settlement_Description: The village of Kosted was first mentioned in 1525, but is significantly older. The parish church is from either the 12th or 13th century.

name: Ravnholt
Settlement_Description: The small settlement of Ravnholt was first mentioned in 1496, but is probably older.

name: Øster Marup
Settlement_Description: The village of Øster Mårup was first mentioned in 1498 and again in 1597.

name: Finderup
Settlement_Description: The village of Finderup was first mentioned in 1277, but is older. The parish church is from either the 12th or 13th century. In 1286 the Danish king Erik was stabbed to death in Finderup.

name: Nørre Knudstrup
Settlement_Description: The village of Nørre Knudstrup was first mentioned in 1410, but is significantly older. The parish church is from either the 12th or 13th century.

name: Rerup
Settlement_Description: The village of Rerup was first mentioned in 1467, but is significantly older. The parish church is from either the 12th or 13th century

name: Harre
Settlement_Description: The village of Harre was first mentioned in 1386 and again in 1488, but is significantly older. The parish church is from either the 12th or 13th century.

name: Tøndering
Settlement_Description: The village of Tøndering was first mentioned in 1420 and again in 1437 and 1474, but is significantly older. The parish church is from either the 12th or 13th century.

name: Asp
Settlement_Description: The village of Asp was first mentioned in 1330-48, but is significantly older. The parish church is from either the 12th or 13th century.

name: Bajlum
Settlement_Description: The village of Ballum was first mentioned in 1420 and again in 1474, but is significantly older. The parish church is from either the 12th or 13th century.

name: Vium
Settlement_Description: The village of Vium was first mentioned in 1400, but is significantly older. The parish church is from either the 12th or 13th century.

name: Vester Grønning
Settlement_Description: The village of Vester Grønning was first mentioned in 1403, but is significantly older. The parish church is from either the 12th or 13th century.

name: Østerild
Settlement_Description: The village of Østerild was first mentioned in 1268, but is older. The parish church is from the second half of the 12th century.

name: Sindal
Settlement_Description: The village of Sindal was first mentioned in 1419, but is significantly older. The parish church is probably from the 13th century.

name: Ålbæk
Settlement_Description: The small settlement of Ålbæk was first mentioned in 1638. The settlement had no church before the modern era.

name: Lem
Settlement_Description: The village of Lem was first mentioned in 1440 and again in 1487, but is significantly older. The parish church is from either the 12th or 13th century.

name: Koldby
Settlement_Description: The village of Koldby was first mentioned in 1556 and again in 1664 and 1688, but is significantly older. The parish church is from either the 12th or 13th century

name: Flovlev
Settlement_Description: The village of Flovlev was first mentioned in 1408, but is significantly older. The parish church is from either the 12th or 13th century.

name: Langerhuse
Settlement_Description: The settlement of Langerhuse was first mentioned in 1610 and again in 1664.

name: Snejbjerg
Settlement_Description: The village of Snejbjerg was first mentioned in 1330-48, but is significantly older. The parish church is from either the 12th or 13th century.

name: Vemmenæs færge
Ferry_Description: Documented from the early 16th century, but may be older.

name: Borris
Settlement_Description: The village of Borris was first mentioned in 1330-48, but is significantly older. The parish church is from either the 12th or 13th century.

name: Skrydstrup

name: Luntertun
Settlement_Description: The settlement was located near the royal estate of Rönneholm. A chapel is dated to the 13th century.
Town_Description: In 1481 king Hans (1481-1513) granted Luntertun town privileges, and the chapel was rebuilt into a church. Already in 1516, however, king Christian II (1513-1523) ordered the inhabitants to move the newly founded town of Ängelholm further down the river of Rönne Å, and Luntertun lost its town privileges.
Fair_Description: Luntertun held at least one annual fair. However, the date, age and character of the fair is not known. At a common meeting in 1504 the towns of Scania decided only to allow a limited number of annual fairs in the province. One of these legal annual fairs of Scania was held in Luntertun. Apparently the fair was declared illegal by king Christian II (1513-1523) in 1516.
Harbour_Description: Access to the sea via the river of Rönne Å. A harbour was established at the river bank. The character of the medieval harbour is uncertain.

Three of these (including Buggenum) situated on the Meuse above Roermond probably have their origin in the claims of Brabant regarding the old county of Kessel. A toll at 'Buggenheym' is named in 1362 when the steward of the duke of Brabant leased out seven tolls on the river Meuse. In 1393 the lord of Horn and Sittard stated that the toll was owned by the count of Kleef and the lord of Heinsberg and his son. In 1417 the widow of Berle transferred her rights on the seigniory of Haeps and the toll of Kuyc to the duke of Julich and Gelre. In 1488 Nijmegen is toll-exempt. In 1529 there is conflict between the towns of Venlo and Roermond regarding the relocation of this toll to Grave. The duke of Gelre then stated that the toll was moved to Middelaar (at the opposite site of the Meuse). An account of the toll dated 1572-'75, then collected at Grave is preserved.<li> The first record of the Hapse Maastol (Toll on the Meuse river of the lord of Haps) dates from 1383. It probably originated as one toll in Cuijk but at some point, half of the toll went to the lord of Haps. This toll on the Meuse river moved to Grave in 1574, like the one from the lord of Cuijk had did before. An account of the Haepschen toll dated 1572 (juli 1-nov. 30) is preserved. The toll of Grave moves to Venlo from 1606 to 1648. It is unclear if the toll of Haps, located in Grave, did the same thing. What happens next is not known. In the 18th century the rivertoll of Haps is found in Katwijk, close to Cuijk.

name: Lith
Toll_Description: The toll was situated at the junction of the rivers Meuse and Waal. In 1272 the toll duty of Venlo at 'Litthe' is stated, with a tariff. A tariff from the duke of Brabant dated 1274 for the citizens of Dordrecht is preserved and edited. In 1444 the tariffs for citizens of Venlo and Roermond are given. Toll exempt are then Grave, Nijmegen, Tiel, Zaltbommel, Gorinchem and 'Tricht' (Maastricht). Nijmegen obtained that right earlier in 1372. In a toll manual of the toll-keeper of Venlo dated early 16th century with the market-tolls on the Meuse river, the tariff at 'Liet' is found.Between 1551 and 1671 the yearly average number of passing ships increased from about  200 to 1800. Between 1551-'75 most ships come from Venlo (more then 1/3), between 1601-'30 about an equal number from Venlo and Liège, but between 1659-'71 Liège is at the top (almost 1/3).

name: null
Toll_Description: Since 1536 a bridge toll was collected.

name: null
Ferry_Description: The ferry across the IJssel in Doesburg must originally have been located near the Veerpoort ('ferry gate'; the name is first attested in 1389) in the town walls. Due to the shifting of the riverbed in two branches in front of the town, the ferry was later moved downstream near the manor ('havezathe') Oldenhave, where the two river branches merged. Here it is at least attested in the 16th century. In 1583 the ferry was moved in front of the Koepoort for defensive reasons.

name: Driel
Fair_Description: The duke of Gelre promised a fair in Driel in 1449, after he relocated the rivertoll from Hedel to Driel.
Toll_Description: A toll on sailing ships from the count of Gelre in Driel is first mentioned in 1197, when the citizens of Tiel had rights as in the time of emperor Frederik († 1190). The farming out is found in the oldest account of the count of Gelre dated 1294, in 1295 together with the tolls of Malsen and Zuilichem. A undated tariff (before 1348) is preserved and edited for the citizens of Dordrecht. Nijmegen obtained toll-exemption in 1372. The toll was relocated in 1444 to Hedel. But in 1448/'9 the duke of Gelre ordained that the toll would be put back to Driel, where he also granted a fair. The account of the seigniory of Hedel dated 1552/'3 states that the toll formerly was replaced to Driel and now was pawned to the lord of van den Berge by the duke of Gelre. But in 1564 the toll was back in Hedel. Still there in 1574, although without income as a result of the uprising against Spain. Toll-accounts are preserved for the years 1294/5 (edited), 1404-1406 and 1444/5 (with a tariff and list of toll-exempt towns).

name: Heerewaarden
Fair_Description: Shorty before 1394 a landtoll was installed on horses and cattle. Two market-tolls at the river Meuse are known at the end of the 15th century. The first 14 days starting Mid Lent, the second also 14 days after St. Remeysday (Oct. 1). Another (later?) source dates the first market the Wednesday before or after Mid Lent. In 1501 the 'Moirsche' markettol is levied here with Bamis (Oct. 1) and Mid Lent. Freed from this toll are then Nijmegen, Tiel, (Zalt)Bommel, Culemborg and 's-Hertogenbosch, as is proved with a toll-book of about 100 years old. In 1532 Roermond and Venlo are complaining by the duke that there toll-exemption is denied here. An early 16th century toll-book states that Venlo has to pay here like at the toll of Liett (Lith).
Toll_Description: Skippers of Heerewaarden (Herewerde) are found in the toll-tariff of Koblenz dated 1104. A toll on sailing ships from the duke of Gelre is found in 1351 in 'Herwarden' on the river Meuse, when he leased it together with the toll in 'Tyele'. In 1359 the duke of Gelre and his brother pawned this toll together with the toll at Tiel and the tollbooths to the count of Meurs. Toll-accounts are preserved for a range of years between 1390-1500. The accounts of 1394/5 are edited. In 1394 the duke of Gelre and Julich gave the citizens of Roermond toll-exemption regarding the halff of this toll and the one at Mook, with a tariff (edited). In 1395/6 half the toll of Ravenstein was relocated to Heerewaarden. A tariff for Utrecht dated 1399 is edited.
Ferry_Description: In 1301 geeft de hertog van Lotharingen de veren tussen Herwarden en Bergerstade en tussen Herwarden en Coestade in erfpacht.

name: Oijen
Toll_Description: A toll on sailing ships from the count of Gelre at the castle in Oijen on the river Meuse was reinstalled by the roman emperor Charles IV in 1366 (Oct. 17). Tollrights were of old. Only inhabitants of Brabant were exempt. A treaty dated 1380 between the dukes of Limburg and Brabant and of Gelre regarding the tolls on the river Meuse stated that the people from Gelre would be exempt at the toll of Ooien, levied by the duchess of Gelre. One toll-account is preserved dated 1408/9. In 1434 Zaltbommel got toll-exemption here from the duke of Gelre.

name: null
Bridge_Description: The "long bridge" between the old and new town in Brandenburg was constructed in the mid-13th century.

name: null
Lock_Description: The mill weir in Rathenow is first mentioned in 1288. In the same year also the town canal is mentioned, which was made navigable for shipping with a flash lock and circumvented the obstacle of the mill weir. It is characterised als "Flutrinne" in the 14th century.

name: null
Bridge_Description: When the ferry across the IJssel was moved to a location in front of the Koepoort (cow gate) in Doesburg, the small branch of the IJssel directly at the town (the Nieuwe Kanaal) was crossed with a small bridge. Around 1602 it was replaced by a ferry. After relocation of the river branches in 1629 and the silting up of the main branch in the 1630s, the Nieuwe Kanaal became the main arm of the river, over which a pontoon bridge was constructed in 1642.
Ferry_Description: The small bridge across the Nieuwe Kanaal was replaced by a ferry around 1602 (the new or little ferry). The ferry must have disappeared when a pontoon bridge was constructed in 1642.

name: null
Bridge_Description: Because of the silting up of the former main branch of the IJssel in the 1630s (from then on: Lamme IJssel), a dam with a small bridge was constructed to replace the ferry in or shortly after 1640.
Ferry_Description: The ferry across the IJssel river was moved in front of the Koepoort (cow gate) in Doesburg in 1583. Since the river was divided into two branches at this place, the ferry crossed the wider main branch, whereas a small bridge (later also a ferry) crossed the small branch (het Kanaal) near the town. The main branch of the river silted up in the 1630s, so that the ferry became unusable and was replaced by a dam in or shortly after 1640.

name: Kats
Toll_Description: In 1454 found ('Cats') in a tariff for the Hansa as tollplace from the count of Holland, together with Iersekeroord en Bergen op Zoom. Usually in the 14th and 15th century as an outpost of the toll at Iersekeroord. In the toll-accounts of 1470-'75 as an outpost of this toll next to Middelburg, Arnemuiden, Veere and Vlissingen and Bergen op Zoom.

name: null
Toll_Description: Income from the outpost here from the toll at Iersekeroord are edited for 1524/5. Accounts of the outpost here from the Grote Zeeuwse toll dated 1591/2 en 1600 are digitalised.

name: null
Ferry_Description: A ferry between Reimerswaal and Bergen op Zoom is mentioned in 1360, but already existed before that year. A ferry to the island of Tholen was first mentioned in 1371, belonging to the count of Holland. Both ferries changed hands often during the following centuries. They disappeared when the town was abandoned in 1631.

name: Biezelinge
Settlement_Description: The village was first mentioned in 1246. It received the privilege to hold a weekly market just as in Goes and Yerseke in 1339.
Harbour_Description: Biezelinge was one of the most important harbours on the island of Zuid-Beveland, located on a creek that connected to the Westerschelde. In 1431 the harbour was silted and had to be dredged.

name: null
Lock_Description: A lock was built during the construction of a canal between the Havel and Finow rivers, that started in Liebenwalde in 1605. By 1609 it was possible to sail from Liebenwalde to Schöpfurt; a lock fee was determined in 1620. The canal dilapidated in the Thirty Years' War.

Harbour_Description: In 1609 the construction of the Finow canal had advanced so far, that a ship could travel from Liebenwalde to Schöpfurth. The canal detoriated in the Thirty Years' War.
Lock_Description: Lock in the canal between the Havel and Finow rivers. The section between Liebenwalde and Schöpfurth was finished in 1609, a lock fee was set in 1620. The canal dilapidated during the Thirty Years' War.

Lock_Description: A flash lock near Woltersdorf was constructed in 1550 to facilitate the shipping of limestone from the quarry near Rüdersdorf. It detoriated in the Thirty Years' War, but was renovated and replaced by a pound lock in 1640.

name: Kalkberge
Harbour_Description: The limestone quarries near Rüderstorf, belonging to the monastery Zinna, were first mentioned in 1375, but must have been older. The limestone was transported on the waterway.

name: Kleckewitz
Settlement_Description: The village is first mentioned in 1220.

name: Seegrehna
Settlement_Description: The village is first mentioned in 1377.

Ferry_Description: In the 1566 regulations of safe conduct, the ferry fees are mentioned as well.

Bridge_Description: In 1689 the bridge is first mentioned when it was destroyed by a flood, but it can be assumed that there existed a stone bridge much earlier.

name: Galchoirt
Ferry_Description: A ferry south of the town of Tholen in the district ('ambacht') Schakerloo to Bergen op Zoom, also known as Galchoirt and Stakelberch, is first mentioned in 1418. It was eternally pawned to the town Tholen in 1462. The ferry sailed from the southern tip of the Brodeloospolder, which was claimed from the sea in 1403, but inundated in 1570.

name: Oelbroeck
Settlement_Description: Oelbroeck originated around 1250 as a small agricultural settlement. It is first mentioned in 1312. Around the second half of the fifteenth century, the name Sint Anthonis starts to be used for this place. In the course of the sixteenth century, the name Sint Anthonis became dominant.

name: Lamgats veer
Ferry_Description: The ferry probably existed from 1282 and definitely between 1483-1572. The ferry was temporarily disrupted in 1573/1574 due to the Sea Beggars ('Geuzen'). After 1574 the ferry operated until after 1650. From 1282 St. Bernards' abbot owned the ferriage right up to the middle of the river. The other half was in possession of the lord of Bergen op Zoom. From 1564 the rights were completely owned by the house of Bergen op Zoom.

name: Hamersleben
Settlement_Description: A royal court is mentioned in 1021, when it was donated to the bishopric Merseburg. A monastery of Augustinian canons was moved to Hamersleben from Osterwieck in 1112.

name: Bytów
Settlement_Description: The land of Bytów is first mentioned in 1321, a castle in 1329. Next to it a Slavic settlement existed.
Town_Description: Kulm town privileges granted by the Teutonic Knights in 1346.

name: Monnikerede
Settlement_Description: Monnikerede is first mentioned in 1226 in the name Lambekinus de Munekerede, a merchant in England in the service of Bruges.
Town_Description: Aldermen are first mentioned in 1266, suggesting that the settlement must have received urban privileges in the mid-13th century. The town served as one of the outports of Bruges on the Zwin estuary, mainly for the fish trade. It deteriorated in the late Middle Ages due to the silting of the Zwin, the construction of the new canal the Verse Vaart (1548-1566) that circumvented the town, and the Dutch Revolt. The town formally merged with Damme in 1594 and was subsequently abandoned.
Toll_Description: Monnikerede was one of the stations of the Flemish Zwin toll in the 13th century (see Bruges).
Staple_Description: In 1323 count Lodewijk van Nevers reorganised the Zwin-staple and gave Bruges a separate staple at Monnikerede for dried fish.
Harbour_Description: Monnikerede was one of the outports of Bruges at the Zwin estuary, mainly for the fish trade.

name: Giersbergen
Settlement_Description: Giersbergen was a monastic grange which was given to the Cistercian abbey of Ter Kameren in 1244. It was gifted by Hendrik van Herentals on behalf of Henry II, Duke of Brabant. At the end of the fourteenth century the monastic grange was leased and in 1614 it was sold.

name: Ginnekense Brug
Bridge_Description: A footbridge existed here since 1531. In 1613 a larger bridge was built by Jan Baptist Keermans, the lord of the nearby Bouvigne castle. During sieges of Breda in 1624/5 and 1637 the bridge was destroyed, but rebuilt in roughly 1640.

Bridge_Description: From at least the fifteenth century, but probably earlier, a bridge crossed the brook the Rips.

Bridge_Description: In the fifteenth century there is a bridge here crossing the brook the Rips. In 1540 it is mentioned to be a stone bridge.

Bridge_Description: The bridge was probably completed along with the city walls and gates around 1320, to allow entrance to the city. The bridge connects to the Koepoort.

name: null
Bridge_Description: An early version of the bridge might have existed from approximately 1190. The first mention of the bridge is from 1354-5. The Lord of Breda was responsible for its upkeep, and collected a toll for this at the bridge. The bridge and gate were the main western entrances to Breda.

name: null
Bridge_Description: A bridge across the Drawa is first mentioned in 1273.

name: Złotów
Settlement_Description: First mentioned in 1370, when it was already a town. Archaeological evidence attests Stone Age settlement and a Pomeranian castle mound around 700. Later the Pomeralian dukes built a castle with adjoining settlement.
Town_Description: Mentioned as town in 1370. The oldest surviving charter of town rights from 1665 confirms Magdeburg town law.

name: Police
Settlement_Description: The Slavic fishing village was property of the knight Bartholomeus de Poliz around 1249-1254.
Town_Description: The town was founded by Duke Barnim I in 1260, who granted Magdeburg town privileges.

name: null
Bridge_Description: A bridge across the Barycz in Milicz is first mentioned in 1249.

Bridge_Description: Two bridges are mentioned in Kalisz in 1258.

Bridge_Description: The bridge across the Widawa near Psie Pole is already mentioned in 1206.

name: Banie
Settlement_Description: First mentioned as town in 1234. There might have existed a Slavic fortification and settlement before, but this is not confirmed by archaeological finds yet.
Town_Description: The settlement is first mentioned as already existing town in a donation charter to the Knights Templar in 1234, which also involved market privileges and the Brandenburg town law. Confirmed in 1251.

name: Bobolice
Settlement_Description: Already in Pomeranian-Slavic times a small administrative centre; the castle, town and land Bublitz is mentioned in 1339.
Town_Description: Bishop of Kamień Friedrich von Eickstädt founded the town with Lübeck town privileges in 1340, although the charter was only issued in 1350. Confirmed in 1614.

name: Dobra (Nowogard)
Settlement_Description: The castle Dobra is first mentioned in 1295.
Town_Description: First mentioned as town in 1331. The year of acquisition of Lübeck town rights is unknown, but they were confirmed in 1461.

name: Widuchowa
Settlement_Description: The castle Viduchow is first mentioned in 1159. A borough ('oppidum') developed before 1283.
Town_Description: Town privileges were granted by Duke Barnim III of Pomerania in 1347.

name: Chociwel
Settlement_Description: A German settlement came into existence near an old Slavic fortification in the second half of the 13th century. It is first mentioned in 1321.
Town_Description: Brandenburg town privileges were granted in 1338. Around 1600 the town acquired the Lübeck town law.

name: Dobrzany
Town_Description: The town was founded before 1336, probably by the Güntersberg family. However, in 1491 it was referred to as village ('villa'), in 1567 as borough ('städtlein').

name: Krajenka
Settlement_Description: Originally a Slavic fortification, later a castle of the lords of Danaborski.
Town_Description: Foundation of a town by Andreas of Danaborski in 1420. The privilege was endorsed in 1654, 1732 and 1751. The town had Magdeburg town law.

name: Łobez
Settlement_Description: Probably already a settlement in Slavic times. First mentioned in 1271 as castle in possession of the noble Borcke family.
Town_Description: Town privileges probably granted before 1295 by the Borcke family, who also confirmed the privileges in 1460. Lübeck town law is explicitly mentioned in 1348.

name: Łeba
Town_Description: Lübeck town rights were granted by Gdańsk commander Wilhelm von Baldersheim in 1357. Later the Kulm town law was used. A new town was founded in 1373; town rights were transferred from the old to the new town in 1575.

name: null
Harbour_Description: The manor Osiecznica / Güntersberg was in possession of the monastery of Leubus (Lubiąż), who were active in shipping on the Oder river, according to a charter from 1211. The manor was used as a waystation and transshipment point.

name: Drawno
Settlement_Description: First mentioned in 1313 as a castle of the Wedell family, next to which a settlement developed.
Town_Description: The town was founded by the lords of the castle, allegedly in 1315 or 1347. It is first referred to as town in 1363.

name: Ińsko
Settlement_Description: A German settlement developed in the second half of the 13th century, around 1250 the region was still largely deserted.
Town_Description: A town was founded and first mentioned around 1300.

name: null
Bridge_Description: A stone bridge across the Nidda near Nied is first mentioned in 1362.

name: Węgorzyno
Settlement_Description: Slavic fortification, later a castle that is mentioned as residence of the Borcke family in 1348.
Town_Description: Lübeck town privileges were probably granted before 1460.

name: Polanów
Settlement_Description: Mentioned in 1307 as castle of Peter of Neuenburg. The castle might have already existed in the 13th century.
Town_Description: Peter of Pollnow allegedly granted town privileges in 1313. The Lübeck town law was endorsed in 1613.

name: Miastko
Settlement_Description: The village was first mentioned as fief of the Massow family in 1478. Mentioned as small town ('stedeken') in 1506. The court in Szczecin granted town privileges in 1617, but the Massow family refused. The town status was finally granted in 1721 by the King in Prussia Friedrich Wilhelm I.

name: Biały Bór
Settlement_Description: Mentioned in 1386 as a castle of the Teutonic Order. It developed from a Slavic fishing village.
Town_Description: An unnamed "village before the town" is mentioned in 1410/1411.

name: Lange Brücke

Ferry_Description: The ferry across the Nogat is among others mentioned in an itinerary from 1603.

Bridge_Description: A bridge across the Łyna is first mentioned in the town privileges of 1351.

Bridge_Description: A bridge across the river Działdówka is already mentioned in the town privileges of 1349.

Toll_Description: Together with the right to build a bridge, the town acquired the right to levy a passing fee. In the 17th century, there was a royal toll station at the bridge.
Bridge_Description: Bydgoscz received permission to build a bridge across the Brda in 1362.

Bridge_Description: A bridge across the Notec between Tur and Samoklęski is mentioned in 1337.

Bridge_Description: A bridge across the Vistula in Toruń was built in 1433.
Ferry_Description: A ferry existed before the construction of the bridge in 1433, but is still mentioned in 1457.

Bridge_Description: A bridge in Kruszwica is mentioned as early as 1252.

name: Karlsfried
Settlement_Description: The castle Karlsfried was built by Charles IV to secure the road between Zittau and Bohemia in 1357. It was demolished in 1442.
Toll_Description: The street in front of the castle was blocked with a wall with a gate. Here wagons had to pay a safe conduct toll.

Toll_Description: The town Mladá Boleslav acquired the right to levy a bridge toll in 1502, next to the already existing road toll in the town itself, to fund the maintenance of the bridge.

Bridge_Description: The bridge across the Seltenrein had to be repaired in 1533, so must have existed before. In 1584 it is named Spittelbrücke.

Toll_Description: Because the road through Ebersdorf was hard to pass, the town Löbau had built a road circumventing the village with permission of Emperor Charles IV. In 1367 he granted permission to levy a toll of two Heller for each wagon on the road until the expenses were covered. However, the toll remained in existence and was even raised in 1616. It was only abolished in 1686.

Ferry_Description: The ferry in Tammiste is mentioned in 1530. Its exact location is not known.

name: Berlicum
Fair_Description: King Philip II granted in 1575 Bilt to have two free fairs in St. Anneparochie. The first fair was dated April 28, three days after the fair in Bellecum (Berlicum). In 1579 (Nov. 11) Philip II gave permission to move the fair in Anneparochie from April 28 to May 14, so the merchants of horses and cattle had more time to come to Berlicum.

Harbour_Description: Soltsy was a transshipment point between land and river traffic on the route between Pskov and Novgorod.

name: Zoutleeuw
Settlement_Description: First mentioned in 1136. An earlier mention of Leuua from 980 probably refers to another place. Originally called Leeuw, the addition "Zout" was added in the 16th century when it became important as a harbour for salt imports.
Fair_Description: Duke Hendrik I of Lotharingen donated Zoutleeuw a fair (forum generale) in 1213 in the nabourhood Dalhem, the day before Pentecost during 8 days (Verkooren: 8 days before the Sunday for Ascencion), The location was next to the Leonardus church, on a junction of traderoutes between Tienen and St. Truiden and between Cologne and Bruges and as last stop on the river Kleine Gete. In 1328 the date was altered from Pentecos to St. Gillisday (Sept. 1), in order to connect better to the fairs in Antwerp. A second fair was obtained in 1383 from duke Wenceslas, also attuned to those in Antwerp, but with little success.

name: null
Toll_Description: In 1213 Zoutleeuw was freed from all tolls by duke Henry I of Lotharingen. Merchandise aboard of ships passed beyond Haelen were forbidden to unload then and had to be sold in Zoutleeuw. A fee ('werfgeld') was levied on shipping on the river Kleine Gete.
Harbour_Description: The river Kleine Gete has been navigable until Zoutleeuw since times of old.

name: null
Toll_Description: In 1517 Tienen also received the right to levy a fee on shipping on the river. Accounts from 1531-1532 show that this 'werfgeld' was 7 stuiver for each ship; there also existed detailed tariffs for various commodities. A fee ('zakgeld') was additionally levied on grain exported through the harbour.
Harbour_Description: Tienen received permission to make the Grote Gete river navigable in 1517, but it was only operable from 1528/1529. Shipping on the river came to a halt during the Dutch revolt.

name: Nistelrode
Settlement_Description: First mentioned in a text from the first quarter of the 13th century.

name: null
Bridge_Description: Although there are some clues that the bridge is much older, the oldest verifiable mention is from 1425.

name: null
Bridge_Description: 1464 is the first mention of a bridge in this location.

name: Budingen
Settlement_Description: First mentioned in 1080, in a mid-thirteenth-century copy.

name: Diegem
Toll_Description: When the road through Diegem was improved in 1517, the local church acquired the right to levy a road toll ('weggeld'). Precise tariffs for wagons, carts and various animals are known from 1517, 1617 and 1627. The toll was abolished in 1742, but re-introduced in 1765.

name: null
Bridge_Description: The bridge and road through Diegem were improved in 1517.

name: null
Lock_Description: A lock was built during a project to make the Grote Gete river navigable, which was finished in 1528/1529.

name: null
Lock_Description: A lock was built during a project to make the Grote Gete river navigable, which was finished in 1528/1529.

name: null
Lock_Description: A lock was built during a project to make the Grote Gete river navigable, which was finished in 1528/1529.

name: Ibbrugge
Bridge_Description: Bridge that used to be called Ibbruge. Attested from at least 1242.

name: Gilze
Toll_Description: A tollpost from Breda is mentioned being in Gilze in 1436.

name: null
Harbour_Description: Jaunjelgava served as a transshipment point between land and water traffic.

name: null
Harbour_Description: Before establishment of the town, the place already was a transshipment point from water to land in the 16th century.

name: Lennisheuvel
Settlement_Description: Lennisheuvel was inhabited from the Neolithic period onwards, but was first mentioned in 1352. The place was situated along a frequently travelled road, but remained small throughout the Middle Ages.

name: Den Engel
Settlement_Description: The inn originated from the early 13th century, but was first mentioned in 1492. It contained a farm for hops, a brewery, and an inn. They grew hops since at least 1527, used that to brew beer, and then sold it in the inn to travelers and locals. The inn used to have a hanging sign depicting an angel.

name: Hoogerheide
Settlement_Description: Hoogerheide was first mentioned as a town in 1339. The place developed slowly and got its first chapel around 1500.

name: Wouw
Settlement_Description: Wouw was inhabited since the late Iron age, but was first mentioned in 1232. Whilst surrounding settlements developed from peat extraction, Wouw developed due to its natural forests.

name: Bouvigne
Settlement_Description: At first a large farmstead, around 1500 it was fortified and expanded over the centuries. Now a castle.

name: Oud Gastel
Settlement_Description: The settlement was first mentioned in 1275. It possibly originated as a 'vroenhof' or 'herenhof'. The region was worked for peat from 1289 onward.

name: null
Bridge_Description: Attested firstly in 1624 on a map of the siege of Breda.

name: Essen (Brabant)
Settlement_Description: First mention of Essen is in a charter from 1159 in which Berner of Rijsbergen donates his land in and around Essen to the abbey of Tongerlo.

name: Stampersgat
Settlement_Description: Stampersgat probably came into existence in the 15th century, populated later by refugees from the drowned village Nieuw Gastel. It developed thanks to a ferry which crossed the Dintel. The first mention of the settlement is in 1639.
Ferry_Description: The ferry between Stampersgat and Fijnaart is first mentioned in 1632.

name: null
Bridge_Description: Bridge over a small river that no longer exists but is depicted on a 1624 map of the siege of Breda, as well as the 1656 Roman-Visscher map.

name: null
Harbour_Description: Although there existed natural waterways in earlier times, in 1451 a harbour was built and the Roosendaalse Vliet was extended to accommodate more water traffic. In the 16th century Roosendaal became an important peat harbour. In 1525 a peat canal to Roosendaal was planned with financial help of the abbot of Tongerlo, who could use it for its adjacent peatlands and farms. In 1552 the magistrate requested the prince of Orange to deepen and widen the harbour and creek with the help of a sluice.

name: Putte
Settlement_Description: Earliest mention from 1277. Today, the town is split in two by the Belgian-Dutch border. The Dutch part is known as Putte, while the Belgian part is known as Putte-Kapellen.

name: Huijbergen
Settlement_Description: First mentioned in 1246, in a sixteenth century copy.

name: De Stockvis
Settlement_Description: De Stockvis ("The Stockfish") was an inn which is drawn by Jacob van Deventer on his map of 's-Hertogenbosch from 1545.

name: Kalmthout
Settlement_Description: First attested in 1338 when the bishop of Liege gives the town the permission to build a chapel.

name: null
Toll_Description: Between 1309 and 1314 archbishop Burchardt III founded a castle in Hohenwarthe and extracted toll on the Elbe, whereupon Magdeburg citizens destroyed the castle. In 1391 a toll on the Elbe in Neuhof, near Hohenwarthe, is mentioned, but it is unclear whether this is still the same toll.

name: null
Harbour_Description: The town of Burg established a landing place ('Schifsstätte') here. Citizens of Magdeburg violently forced a ship to sail to Magdeburg from here in 1632, in order to withhold other skippers from landing in Burg.

name: null
Harbour_Description: The use of the river Ucker as waterway from Prenzlau is first attested in 1282, but was probably older. It was mainly used to export corn to the Baltic Sea in the 13th and 14th century. The harbour fell out of use in the Early Modern period.

name: null
Bridge_Description: Oldest mention from 1501: "d'brugge, aen de tongelreep". Probably older.

name: null
Ferry_Description: A ferry from Geertruidenberg towards Raamsdonk.

name: Giessen (Land van Altena)
Fair_Description: In 1259 three days in July. In 1388 three days before St. Margareth-eve. Exempt are only the burghers of Woudrichem and Heusden. The toll-accounts of Heusden dated 1378-93 have an outpost in Giessen. In 1408 Leiden obtained exemption of the market-toll from duke William. The edited tariff of the markett-tolls at Woudrichem dated 1408 is also destined for those of Giessen. Later the date of the fair is: the seventh day before St. Margarethday (July 6) till seven days after that or with St. Mary Magdalena-eve. In 1569: starting St. Margareth-eve during 14 days on the land and on the Meuse. The king had half the toll both levied on land and on water.

name: null
Harbour_Description: Ueckermünde was a transshipment port between river and sea traffic on the Ucker river between Prenzlau and the Szczecin Lagoon.

name: null
Harbour_Description: Pasewalk was mentioned as transshipment point on the Ucker river in 1282 and 1320. Transport on the river came to a halt in the early modern period.
Lock_Description: According to a charter from 1282, the mill weir in Pasewalk had a construction to let ships pass ('Vlütrenne'), for which the miller was allowed to levy a fee.

name: null
Lock_Description: According to a 1282 charter, the mill weir in the Ucker river in Nieden had a construction to let ships pass ('Vlütrenne'), for which the miller was allowed to levy a fee.

name: Deurne
Settlement_Description: Oldest mention found in 1191 copy from a text from 721.

name: Bakel
Settlement_Description: Oldest mention found in a copy from 1191 of a text from 715.

name: Vlierden
Settlement_Description: Earliest mention found in an 1191 copy of a 721 text.

name: null
Toll_Description: A river toll on the Elbe in Wehningen was first mentioned in 1372 when the castle came into the possession of the duke of Mecklenburg. In 1492, the toll fees are specified at 4 Gulden and 1 loaf of bread for each passing ship.

name: Zuidland
Settlement_Description: Originally called the lordship ('heerlijkheid') Westenrijk. The name Zuidland is first mentioned in 1340 and gradually became the name of the village.

name: Akersloot
Settlement_Description: First mentioned in 1083, in a falsification from 1125-c.1150.
Fair_Description: Een jaarmarkt met St. Jacobsdag (25 juli) met een grafelijke tol is bekend sinds 1367. Hier werden veel kazen en boter verhandeld, zoals blijkt uit de tolrekening van Spaarndam uit 1391/'2. De plaats zelf verkreeg al in 1277 tolvrijdom in Holland en Zeeland. In 1447 (mei 27) klaagt Keulen hier (en in de steden Haarlem, Amsterdam, Alkmaar en Hoorn) over de dikte en zwaarte van de botertonnen.

name: null
Bridge_Description: A stone bridge across the Fulda near Leimbach is mentioned in 1446. It dilapidated later.

name: null
Toll_Description: Road toll for the maintenance of the Nidda bridge, granted in 1342.
Bridge_Description: Bridge across the Nidda, for which the settlement was allowed to levy a road toll in 1342.

name: null
Bridge_Description: A stone bridge across the Ohm near Kirchhain is attested in 1270.

name: Giessenburg
Fair_Description: In 1516 (June) the seigniory Nieuw(er)kerk and Giessenburg was granted by Charles V a free horse-and cattle-fair as an immortal fee from the count of Holland. Of old here was a market-toll of cattle found, which was decayed by the wars. The horse-fair would be the day after St. Margareth on July 14 juli, the cattle-fair on St. Simon and Jude-eve (Oct. 27). The period of safeconduct used to be 8 days before and after, but will be now 3 days. With a toll-tariff. The yields would be half for the king, via his steward of Zuidholland.

name: Katwijk aan den Rijn
Settlement_Description: A charter of 1224 mentioned 'apud Renum Catwijch': Katwijk aan de Rijn. In 1340 the 'burggraafschap' of Leiden, including Katwijk aan Zee, came to the family Van Wassenaer. In 1295, the lepers have their own chapel in Katwijk. A hospital is found in 1343; in 1388 also the hospital of St. Mary at Katwijk aan de Rijn.
Fair_Description: See sub toll and staple. In 1388 duke Albrecht granted the burgrave to relocate the fishmarket of Katwijk aan de Rijn towards Katwijk aan Zee. Per pound fish those of Katwijk aan Zee had to pay the burgrave 1 groot. In 1393 the burgrave was banned and the market was put back to Katwijk aan de Rijn by the count of Holland. In 1394 his comital income from both the Katwijken out of 'pondgeld, hofvis en jaartollen' amounted no fewer than 1000 hollandse guilders. In 1398 the markt was again relocated to Katwijk aan Zee, in 1408 back to Katwijk aan de Rijn en in 1413 again back to Katwijk aan Zee. In 1447 Cologne complained to the comital council of Holland and the governments of Katwijk, Noordwijk, Harderwijk en Egmond about the size of the baskets in which the salted fish was traded. The socalled Informacie dated 1514 tells that there are five (herring)boats in Katwijk aan Zee, of which three belong to inhabitants of Delft, Gouda, Leiden en Amsterdam. Katwijk itself has two big seeworthy boats and 18 of 19 'pinken', 10 or 11 jaar earlier there were 11 of 12 boats and 21 or 22 pinken.
Toll_Description: See sub fair and staple. Around 1355 a toll at Katwijk is collected all year starting St. Jansdag decollacio (August 29). The tariff is: per boat 1 schelling, a 'pink' 6 schelling, 'hofvis' starting St. Martijns (Nov. 11) until Palm Sunday per ship 4 schelling. An undated list of the goods of the lord of Wassenaer dated around 1360 mentions a toll from the burgrave in 'Catwic' which he yearly farmes out, 'riemgeld' per steersman (12s. per 'scene') and his 'hofvis'. According to a statement for the emperor the right of the 'pondgeld and hofvis' was over 300 years in 1542. Between St. Maarten in de winter (Nov. 11) en O.L.V. Lichtmis (Febr. 2) per barge or 'pink' with100 or more haddock 4 of the best were taken. From O.L.V. Lichtmis to Palm Sunday per barge of ship with 20 or more cod 1 as 'hofvis' was taken. Each barge or scip with 1 'tal' or more plaice had to give 1 of the best 'snees'. Between Low Pentecost (Sunday after Pentecost) and Lambertsday (Sept. 17) no 'pondgeld' had to be paid, except from the 'dogge- or korfvaart'. With 'doggers and corvers' herring was catched, which was taxed per three barrels 60 carolus guilders.
Staple_Description: See sub fair and toll. For each chariot (two carts for one chariot) with fish passing Katwijk aan Zee or aan de Rijn the seaman has to pay 'hofvis'. The fish catched and brought ashore in Egmond or Zandvoort is excluded. This exemption is known for Egmond in 1443, and for Zandvoort in 1544, when it was stated that this was of old. Scheveningen was also exempt, as appears in statements dated 1533 and 1560.

name: Ober-Wegfurth
Settlement_Description: First certain mention from 1015-1100. Earlier mentions from 744-747 and 852 are falsifications from c. 1160. The settlement is named after a ford in the river Fulda.

name: Lauterbach
Settlement_Description: A chapel in Lauterbach is first mentioned in 812.
Town_Description: Elevated to town rank by abbot Bertho II of Leipoltz during the "Fuldaer Stiftsfehde" of 1261-1270. In 1266, the settlement is first characterised as town ('municionem sive opidum').

name: Geldermalsen
Toll_Description: In 1294 the toll on sailing ships of Malsen at the river Linge is leased by the count of Gelre, together with those the tolls of Zuilichem and Driel.

name: Poortugaal
Harbour_Description: In 1558 (2 febr.) kreeg Portegael toestemming van koning Filips II een nieuwe haven te maken (aan de Maas). In 1568 (16 dec.) kregen zij octrooi voor een nieuwe impost op ijzer, kolen, kalk, steen etc. voor drie jaar.

name: Sint Annaparochie
Fair_Description: King Philip II granted in 1574 (March before Eastern) Bilt to have two free fairs in St. Anneparochie. They had a lot of damage because of rebels and inundation. A fair did not exist then and the distance to other towns was considerable and it was located in the middle of them. A weekly market was granted on Monday when there was no other organised in the neighbourhood. The dates of the fairs: 1) April 28, three days after the fair in Bellecum (Berlicum), 2) Monday after the Nativity of the Virgin in September (Sept. 8). In 1579 (Nov. 11) Philip II gave permission to move the fair from April 28 to May 14, so the merchants of horses and cattle had more time to come to Berlicum. A yearly fee of 40gr.vl. had to be paid to the steward-general of Friesland (in stead of 3 pounds before).

name: null
Toll_Description: Malchin levied a bridge toll, for which the monastery Dargun was exempted in 1283, because of help with the construction of the bridge. The toll is also mentioned in a report from 1561.
Bridge_Description: Bridge and causeway across the Peene, first mentioned in 1283 when the monastery Dargun was exempted from the bridge toll because of assistance with the construction of the bridge.

name: null
Ferry_Description: The ferry across the Lippe in Ahsen is first mentioned in 1276.

name: null
Bridge_Description: The bridge across the Lippe in Dorsten is mentioned in 1444.

name: haven Harlingen
Harbour_Description: Harlingen lijkt pas in de loop van de 16e eeuw tot ontwikkeling te zijn gekomen. In 1546/'7 wordt het een 'principale' haven genoemd, maar op de kaart van Van Deventer is de haven gelegen ten noorden van de dwangburcht nog zeer beperkt en lijkt meer op een vluchthaven. Na 1550 is een sterke toename te zien van het aantal schippers op de Oostzee. In 1552 is er een controleur ofwel havenmeester. In 1559 wordt de stad verantwoordelijk voor het leggen van de bakens in de Jetting: de vaargeul naar de Noordzee. Daartoe mocht het bakengeld heffen, wat toekwam aan de armenvoogden.

name: Hinderdam Delft
Lock_Description: Just north of Delft mid 12th century, after floodings, the Delftse Vliet was dug. Together with it a Hinderdam was built to redirect water around the Hof van Delft via the Kerstanjewetering and Lookwetering. Via the Kickert or Buitenwatersloot it was also possible to discharge water in the Delftse Schie. Possibly the oldest dam was situated more south closer to the comital court. After the construction of the Nieuwe Delf before 1246 this dam was unnecessary and demolished. Next to the Kampveld a new dam was built. In 1316 grain was transhipped here in smaller ships and the dam was then first called 'Hinderdam' (a dam which hampered the passage). Small ships with a flat bottom were pulled over the dam with an 'overhaal'. Around the dam a small settlement arose. Till 1376 revenues were for the heemraden (magistrates of the water drainage board of Delfland), after that for the count of Holland. His yields tripled in the eighties of the 14th century. The passage from Delft to Den Haag and Leiden improved strongly. Together with the construction of a canal to the Maas and the seaharbour in Delfshaven Delft became a trading city. In 1449 the toll was collateral to Delft because of a loan and a tariff was formulated. Raising this tariff was prohibited, to lower it not. The count and his court were exempt. In 1464/'5 however the Court of Holland tried to raise the tariff. In 1471 Delft got the dam in a perpetual leasehold while paying 240 pounds yearly, a new tariff was formulated and the dam appeared to be replaced by a sluice (verlaat). The municipal account dated 1573/4 of Delft shows a positive balance for the dam of over 1050 pounds.

name: null
Toll_Description: In 1518, 1529/1530 and from 1542 onwards a toll on peat was levied, as established in a charter of bishop Philip of Burgundy. Accounts are preserved for the years 1565/1566 and combined with the toll at Blokzijl for 1568. Steenwijk was exempted from toll payments. Yields of the toll are edited starting 1609 and of a peat-impost starting 1634.
Lock_Description: Zwartsluis is named after the lock that was built here when the Meppelerdiep was dammed here at its confluence with the Zwarte Water shortly before 1398. The lock was mainly important for ships transporting peat.

name: null
Harbour_Description: A harbour is known to have existed in the tenth century, functioning as export port for salt. It gained real importance in the eleventh century, when Stavoren participated in trade on the Rhine and IJssel. Stavoren flourished in the fourteenth century, but as the Zuiderzee expanded, the harbor became shallow. As a result, it declined in importance. At least in the 16th century, the sea harbour was located north of town.

name: null
Bridge_Description: In 1492 the bishop of Utrecht granted a bridge in the parish Rijssen where the family Van Rutenberge of old had the ferry as a fief.
Ferry_Description: n 1492 the bishop of Utrecht granted a bridge in the parish Rijssen where the family Van Rutenberge of old had the ferry as a fief.

name: null
Ferry_Description: In 1403 the duke of Guelders returned the ferry to 'Wyel', which he had appropriated illegally, to the lord of Abcoude and Duurstede.

name: null
Harbour_Description: Bunschoten had a small harbour which connected to the Zuiderzee via a canal. It is mentioned in the privileges from 1383. In later centuries the harbour and fishing activities moved to the more northerly Spakenburg (first mentioned in 1435).

name: Cathagen
Toll_Description: In the comital account of Valkenburg dated 1395 called 'winage de Cathagen'. In the remainder of the 14th century without revenues as a result of the wars. In 1452 farmed out with the 'big' toll (of Valkenburg).
Bridge_Description: The account of the steward of Valkenburg dated 1454 mentions a bridge at Cathagen (at the Geleenbrook), which was maintained with money out of the toll of Valkenburg. In 1531/'2 the bridge was repaired after a huge flood with wood from the seignorial forest.

name: Weilburg
Settlement_Description: First mentioned in 906 as Frankish manor, which went back into Merovingian times.
Town_Description: Mentioned as 'civitas' as early as 913 and 915, as 'oppidum' in 1195. King Adolf of Nassau granted Frankfurt town privileges in 1295, which were confirmed in 1302.

name: Urmond
Toll_Description: In Urmond the duke of Gulik had a toll. The trade route from Gulik reached the Maas here. In 1598 Maastricht, Roermond and Luik declared that they never payed toll at Urmond. In 1616 an attempt was made to abolish this toll and the toll at Gennep on the Maas. But the toll was still there in the French period.

name: Ulrichstein
Settlement_Description: First mentioned in 1279. The settlement developed next to a castle.
Town_Description: Emperor Ludwig granted Friedberg town privileges in 1347.

name: tol Gennep
Toll_Description: Situated between the Niers and the Maas rivers. In 1361 the German emperor granted the lord of Gennep (then named an oppidum) a toll on the Maas in his castle Gen- or Immenhage, also known as Genneperhuis. The duke of Brabant and Limburg and the duke of Gelre made an agreement in 1380 about the tolls on the Maas. The new tolls at Gennep, Grave, Megen and Batenburg should be abolished. Only those over 50 years old would be maintained. In 1385 the lord of Gennep however stated that he held his castle in fief of the duke of Gelre and that all inhabitants of Gelre were toll-exempt while passing there, with the exception of the market-toll. From 1442  Gennep belongs to the duke of Kleef, who stimulated transshipment in the harbour. In 1499 the roman king Maximiliaan stated that the inhabitants of Geldern had to pay the toll at Gennep to the count of Kleef as proprietor of the toll. In 1616 an effort was made to abolish this toll and the one at Urmond.

name: Aalst (N-B)
Toll_Description: In 1380 the duke of Brabant and Limburg and the duke of Gelre made an agreement regarding the tolls at the Maas. The new toll of Gelre at Aalst was abolished, just likt the tolls at Gennep, Grave, Megen and Batenburg. Only those over 50 years old would be maintained.

name: null
Bridge_Description: A bridge across the Lahn is first mentioned in 1568.

name: Balduinbrücke
Toll_Description: The Archbishop of Trier levied bridge fee from 1359, although the Moselle bridge was not completed until 1363. This suggests that it was already usable in 1359. In the same year, 1 heller per person and 2 heller per large animal had to be paid. In the 15th century, 6 heller per carriage had to be paid.
Bridge_Description: The bridge across the Moselle was finished after 1363, but apparently already usable in 1359, when the tariffs for the bridge toll were set.

name: null
Harbour_Description: A harbour with a crane is shown on the view of Ehrenbreitstein by Merian (1636).

name: Kastre
Settlement_Description: The castle Kastre (German: Warbeck) is first mentioned in 1392 in the "Niebur" peace treaty between the Hanse and Novgorod. Dendrochronological evidence indicates that the castle was built around 1377, probably as a consequence of border war between Pskov and the bishopric of Tartu. The castle was destroyed by the Russians in 1558, came into Polish hands in 1582, and was conquered by the Swedes in 1656, who carried out repairs. Despite Swedish plans to rebuild the castle, it was still in ruins in 1704. Next to the castle existed a settlement, where 21 households were recorded in 1601, and an inn for travellers on the waterway.
Toll_Description: First mentioned as toll station on the Emajõgi river between Tartu and Novgorod in 1392 in the "Niebur" peace treaty between the Hanse and Novgorod. The treaty mentions a barrier ('baum') across the river to force ships to halt. Novgorodians were exempted from toll payment. The toll was especially important for local fisheries, upon which a tithe was levied at the castle.

name: tol Hardinxveld
Toll_Description: In 1518 an outpost of the toll on sailing ships at Gorinchem is found here (in the toll-account dated 1478-'81 not mentioned). The toll was levied from not exempt places on vegetables, fruit and cattle brought via the ferry in Holland. In 1573 and 1580 an outpost is still here.In 1399 the inhabitants of Hardinxveld, subjects of the lord of Brederode, obtained toll-exemption from the count of Holland.

name: null
Toll_Description: The lord of Arcen claimed to have older rights on transshipment then Venlo and to be an older toll-place. Possibly remnants of an old tollbooth are preserved.

name: dam Gennep
Lock_Description: Een dam in de Niers die tevens als molenstuw diende bestond in de 16e eeuw.

name: Warmonderhek
Toll_Description: The lord of Warmond levied a toll at the bridge to fund its construction and maintenance.
Bridge_Description: The lord of Warmond acquired permission of the States of Holland in 1639 to build a bridge across the Poel and to levy a toll for its construction and maintenance. A license for the construction of a stone bridge of 12-13 feet wide was issued in 1642.
Ferry_Description: The ferry across the Poel is first mentioned around 1400. It consisted of two parts, of which the Oegstgeest half was probably owned by the abbey of Egmond, which was also in possession of the nearby manor Abtspoel. The other part belonging to Warmond was owned by the Van Teylingen family, who lived on the nearby manor Teylingen. They sold their part of the ferry to the lord of Warmond in 1430, who pawned it eternally to the monastery of Warmond in 1487. The ferry was replaced by a bridge in 1642.

name: Neeritter
Settlement_Description: First mentioned as "new" Itter in 1143 (in a 13th century copy) to make a distinction to Opitter. It was a seigniory of the chapter of St. Lambertus in Liège. As free village ('vrijdorp') it was exempted from taxes. Local measures and a hospital are mentioned in 1451.
Fair_Description: Two fairs are mentioned, but details are not known.

name: Schotten
Settlement_Description: The village is first mentioned in 1293.

name: Altenstadt
Settlement_Description: The village is first mentioned in 767.

name: Bergen (Frankfurt)
Settlement_Description: The village is first mentioned in 1057. The village developed an urban character and was later referred to as borough ('Flecken'), but never received town privileges.

name: null
Bridge_Description: The bridge is first mentioned in 1330.

name: Linz am Rhein
Toll_Description: 1) A Rhine toll of the Archbishop of Cologne is first mentioned in 1365. Before that year it was levied in Andernach, as well as after 1475, but then a new toll was installed in Linz, with the same tariffs as in Bonn. In 1424/25 it was shortly levied in Königswinter. 2) A fee for safe conduct is mentioned in 1448. 3) A land toll was also levied by the archbishop of Cologne, first mentioned in 1418. This was referred to as the "small toll". For fees and revenues, see Pfeiffer.

name: Nidda
Settlement_Description: First mentioned in 802-817. In 1218 the settlement is characterised as "villa".
Town_Description: The settlement is called "oppidum" in 1234. Town privileges were acquired in 1311, confirmed in 1450.

name: Birstein
Settlement_Description: First mentioned with a castle in 1279.

name: Kollum
Settlement_Description: First mention probably dates from 822-ca. 825 in a copy from 1150-1158. In 1383, Kollum is mentioned in a contemporary source.
Fair_Description: Emperor Charles V granted two free fairs in Kollum in 1538/'9 (or 1549?): a horsemarket the day before St Marcellinus & Peter (June 1) and a free fair with St Giles (September 1), both for four days.Around 1500 there was already an excise collector of the duke of Saxony who taxed beer, wine and cloth. A (butter)weigh-house is also known then.

name: Nieuwerkerk (Zeeland)
Fair_Description: King Charles granted in 1516 a fair to the seigniory Nieukerke of Jan van Wena.

name: Overloon
Settlement_Description: First mentioned as 'Loon' in 1308, in a seventeenth century copy. Mentioned as 'Loen' in 1527.

name: null
Ferry_Description: A ferry across the Werra is first mentioned in 1349/1350.

name: Esch
Settlement_Description: First mentioned in 773-774 as 'Hesc', in a thirteenth-century copy. Another mention in the first quarter of the thirteenth century as 'in Escho'.

name: null
Bridge_Description: On the map of Geertruidenberg made by Jacob van Deventer between ca. 1545 and 1575, a bridge connects the town gate with a little island, on which a ferry was located.

name: Kollum haven
Harbour_Description: In 1547 there is a collector of the emperor in the harbours of Kollum and Achtkarspel. The harbour of Kollum is unknown before. Trade in corn and beer was most important.

name: Veer Schagen
Ferry_Description: In 1514 Maximilian and Charles V granted a privilege to the lord of Schagen to give the ferry between Schagen, Callantsoog, Petten en Huisduinen with its revenues to the parish-church of Schagen at the benefit of the socalled 'Zeven Getijden'. In 1552 Charles V stated that an appointment had to be made with the churchmasters regarding the ferry crossing the Zijpe, as it was now a road, for which construction had been paid by the church (after embanking of the Zijpe).

name: Kolhorn
Settlement_Description: The settlement is first mentioned in 1518.
Harbour_Description: The Enqueste of 1494 mentions Colhorn as the harbour of Schagen, of which before 1477 12 'rijn'ships sailed to Deventer with cheese and butter.

name: null
Toll_Description: A Rhine toll is levied by the Lords of Falkenstein from c. 1250 until 1269, and from 1310 by the Counts Palatine. The castle Pfalzgrafenstein was constructed on an island in the river to enforce the levying of the toll. For annual revenues and fees, see Pfeiffer.

name: Berne
Settlement_Description: First mentioned in the mid-12th century, but the settlement probably existed since the 9th century. The count of Oldenburg constructed a castle here after 1234, but gave it up after the new castle in Delmenhorst was built in 1259. The settlement gained the character of a market borough ('Marktflecken') as centre of the land of Stedingen.

name: Hasbergen (Delmenhorst)
Settlement_Description: The settlement is first mentioned in 1142.
Toll_Description: A toll was levied in Hasbergen from 1390 at the latest, although we find first mentions of it in 1527, when inhabitants of the Vieland tried to circumvent the toll. Documents from 1532 mention an "irregular" toll in Hasbergen.

name: Huntebrück
Toll_Description: The count of Oldenburg levied a bridge toll in Huntebrück.
Bridge_Description: A bridge across the Hunte is first mentioned in 1250. It must have disappeared afterwards, as a ferry is mentioned in 1428. Count Anton I of Oldenburg constructed a new "beautiful" bridge in 1569, which is described as a wooden bridge with 12 segments and two stone bridge houses at both ends in 1613. The bridge was given up in 1638 and replaced by a ferry again. Newer bridges existed in 1869-1895 and from 1908 onwards.
Ferry_Description: A ferry in possession of the Count of Oldenburg is first mentioned in 1428. It operated until 1569, when a new bridge was built, from 1638 until 1869 and in 1895-1908.

name: Varel
Settlement_Description: First mentioned in 1124 as farm of the monastery Rastede. Seat of a Frisian chieftain in 1386. A castle was built in 1506. The borough ('flecken') was only raised to town status in the 19th century.
Fair_Description: Two fairs were granted in 1597, on Monday after Judica and Monday after St Giles.

name: Rastede
Settlement_Description: The church of St Ulrich was dedicated in 1058. A Benedictine monastery was founded in 1091 and secularised by the counts of Oldenburg after 1539, who transformed it into a summer palace.

name: null
Bridge_Description: The earliest mention from a bridge in Onderdendam dates from 1464, but a bridge might have existed before.

name: Thedinghausen
Settlement_Description: The village Dettenhusen is first mentioned in 1168. In 1285 the archbishop of Bremen built the moated castle Thedinghausen here, which came to be the name of the village as well. The archbishop and the count of Hoya fought frequent battles  over the castle, which remained in ruins after 1681.
Toll_Description: The toll in the village Dettenhusen is first attested in 1260. As the castle changed hands often, so did the toll. It consisted of a road and a water toll, of which the latter was levied in Eißel until 1612.

name: Blexen
Settlement_Description: First mentioned in 789 in the Vita Sancti Willehadi from the 9th century. Blexen was a parish and became an important trade centre and harbour in the land of Rüstringen, albeit under strong control from Bremen. Mentioned as borough ('oppidum') in 1318. Since 1933 part of the town Nordenham.
Fair_Description: A Walpurgis market is mentioned in 1318. It is still mentioned in the ordinances of the Oldenburg skipper's guild from 1529.
Harbour_Description: The sluice of Blexen was used as harbour.

name: Atens
Settlement_Description: First mentioned in 1312 as place of negotiations between Bremen and the Frisians. Bremen built the castle Friedeburg here in 1407, to control the Frisian chieftains and allied pirates. The castle was conquered by the chieftains in 1424 and demolished in 1425. Renamed into Nordenham and elevated to town rank in 1908; the old settlement is since part of Nordenham.

name: Harpstedt
Settlement_Description: A person "Volchardus de Harpenstede" is mentioned in the Livonian chronicle of 1203. The settlement itself is first mentioned in a charter in 1242. A moated castle is mentioned in 1291. The counts of Hoya granted borough ('weichbild') privileges on 5 March 1396, but the settlement never developed into a full town.

name: Hude
Settlement_Description: Hude is first mentioned in 1236. In or shortly before 1232, the Cistercian monastery "Portus S. Mariae" was moved here, destroyed and rebuilt after 1234. The monastery was abolished in 1536. The count of Oldenburg later rebuilt it into a hunting palace.

name: Brake (Unterweser)
Settlement_Description: A "Brake to Harghen" is first mentioned in 1384 as site of a dike burst ("brake") near the village Harrien. The area consisted of various islands between arms of the Weser river, the Lockfleth and Harrierbrake, which were dammed in 1516/1531. Afterwards the settlement Harrierbrake or Braksiel came into being, which began to be called Brake by the end of the 16th century.

name: null
Toll_Description: Toll on the Weser river, which was levied by the Count of Oldenburg from 1623 onwards, initially in Brake. In 1624, the toll was moved to Elsfleth, although a secondary toll station remained in Brake. The town of Bremen did not accept the levying of the toll and managed to avoid toll payment of Bremen ships with naval and diplomatic measures, until the town was finally forced to acknowledge the toll in 1653. Toll registers for the years 1624-1627, 1653-1661, 1663-1668 and single years in the 1670s are kept in the Niedersächsisches Landesarchiv Oldenburg.

name: null
Toll_Description: The Oldenburg Weser toll was originally levied in Brake, but only after a year it was moved to Elsfleth (see there). A secondary toll station of Elsfleth remained in Brake.
Harbour_Description: The sluice Braker Siel served the drainage of the newly reclaimed land in 1531 and also served as harbour for Brake.

name: Onderdendam
Settlement_Description: First mentioned in 1252 as 'ulderna domme' in a thirteenth-century copy. A mention as Onderndamme dates from around 1323. The place was named after a dam, which was probably located in the water Deelstermaar, east of the place where the Boterdiep flows into the Deel. On historical maps, which are available from the seventeenth century onward, there is no lock drawn near Onderdendam. Probably during the thirteenth century there was no human habitation yet near the lock, but it functioned as a meeting place, for example for the annual court day of the region Hunsingo. The earliest mention of residences dates from 1464, when among others an inn is mentioned. In 1620, an inn called 'De Moriaan' is named on the location of the later 'waterschapshuis' at present-day Bedumerweg 2.<br>Onderdendam was a node in the drainage of water in the region. In the seventeenth century, it became a node in the developing barge-canal system between Hunsingo and the town of Groningen. Several watercourses were deepened, and in 1664, Warffum was connected to Groningen city by means of the barge-canal Boterdiep.
Fair_Description: In the fourteenth century (probably already in the thirteenth century) a eight-day fair is mentioned in Onderdendam during the Translation of St Walfried (June 22).

name: Borgerhout
Settlement_Description: First mentioned in 1214, in a 14th-century copy.

name: null
Bridge_Description: A stone bridge across the Anger between Ratingen and Lintorf is first mentioned in 1301.

name: null
Toll_Description: In 1475 Amsterdam as most important member of Amstelland claimed to have toll-exemption 200 or 300 or even more years in Vollenhoven as part of the Sticht-Utrecht. The toll on sailing ships from the bishop of Utrecht is only found in a privilege granted in 1461 by the bishop where a.o. the toll in the freedom of Vollenhove and the 'ruddertoll' (roertol) outside the freedom of Vollenhove is farmed out for fifty years to the magistrate. However the toll is found in the only surviving accounts of the bishop dated 1504/5 en 1507/8 and then of little meaning. The tariff is: a ruddertoll per boat, little or big, with a hanging rudder: 1 oude Vlaams and the 36st 'penning' from the goods aboard 'te wetten van scepe ind guet in den ampte van Vullenhoe tolber wesende'. After 1528 this yields belonged to the landlord and quickly perished.

name: null
Bridge_Description: A bridge across the Weser is mentioned in 1573. It was destroyed by floods in 1582 and rebuilt in 1587.

name: Neubruchhausen
Settlement_Description: Neubruchhausen was created by the partition of the county Bruchhausen in Alt- ('old') and Neu- ('new') Bruchhausen in 1259. The settlement is first mentioned in 1308. In 1384 Neubruchhausen was sold to the count of Hoya. It is characterised as borough ('Vleck') in 1521.

name: Dietharz
Settlement_Description: First mention of the settlement Dietharz in 1246. In 1919 Tambach and Dietharz were merged into one town.

name: veer Kortgene
Ferry_Description: A ferry in Kortgene is first found in 1334.

name: Haamstede
Fair_Description: A fair is found in an ordinance from the lord of the seigniory Haamstede dated 1300.

name: Mierlo
Fair_Description: An undated register from the abbey Tongerlo (Westerlo, B.) (circa 1556) contains a list of fairs in the region Kempen and Peel. 'Mierloe' has then two fairs: 1) the second Tuesday in the Lent, 2) Sunday for St. 'Katlijne' (Nov. 25) till the next Tuesday.

name: Pamelsche Warte
Settlement_Description: Around 1400, the surrounding area belonging to the city of Paderborn was completely surrounded by an enclosure. About 700 m south of this node was the watchtower, the so-called Pamelsche Warte and guarded not only the passage of the Hellweg but also a valley cutting coming from Dahl. Shortly before the end of the World War in 1945, the tower was blown up because it was in the way of an alternative airport. Today, the ruins still exist.

name: Gansoijen
Fair_Description: Until 1303 a fair was known in Oijen, which was then relocated to Waalwijk.

name: Makkum
Settlement_Description: First mentioned in 944, in a copy from 1150-1158.

name: Schleusenpriel
Harbour_Description: Ships could sail until the sluice in the tidal creek (Schleusenpriel) of Ritzebüttel, which was located at the modern Kämmererplatz. A harbour developed here in the 16th century, and is mentioned as such between 1568 and 1618. Before the 17th century the main harbour for Ritzebüttel was located at Altenbruch, which was easier to navigate due to sandbanks near the mouth of the Schleusenpriel. The construction of a new lock some 100m to the north in 1889/90 prevented ships from sailing to old the sluice.

name: null
Toll_Description: A landtoll was raised near Hedikhuizen at the Hoge Maasdijk on the road to Den Bosch. This was an outpost of the toll at Heusden, found in accounts dated 1378-93.

name: Hoeke
Harbour_Description: Hoeke was located at the point where the Zwin widened. It was one of the outports of Bruges.

name: Waterhalle
Harbour_Description: In the 13th century it was possible to reach the market square directly with a ship via the river Reie. A crane is mentioned here in 1288, but must have disappeared shortly after. A new hall (Waterhalle) was constructed before 1295 above the Reie that allowed ships to sail directly under the building and (un)load there. The hall also consisted of storage and trading spaces. It was demolished in the 18th century.

name: null
Toll_Description: A bridge toll is mentioned in 1086.
Bridge_Description: A bridge toll is mentioned in 1086. Two bridges are mentioned in 1345.

name: null
Toll_Description: A bridge toll for draught horses is mentioned in 1287. Citizens of Nymburk were exempted, which was confirmed in 1327.

name: Karlův most
Toll_Description: A bridge toll on draught horses and exported commodities is mentioned in 1332. Persons living within 2 miles around the city were exempted.
Bridge_Description: A bridge across the Vitava is first mentioned in 1159. In 1342 it was destroyed by floods, after which the current bridge was constructed, which eventually became known as the Charles Bridge.

name: Radeberg
Settlement_Description: A German village was founded in the 12th century. The settlement is first mentioned with a castle in 1219.
Town_Description: First mentioned as "Städtchen" (small town) in 1344. Town privileges were granted in 1412.
Toll_Description: A toll in Radeberg is mentioned in 1394.

name: Gruna (Dresden)
Settlement_Description: First mentioned around 1370. Since 1901 the village is part of Dresden.
Toll_Description: A toll in Gruna is mentioned in 1394.

name: Pulsnitz
Settlement_Description: A German village came into being around 1200. It is first mentioned in 1225.
Town_Description: In 1355, Pulsnitz received market and in 1375 town privileges from Emperor Charles IV.

name: Elstra
Settlement_Description: First mentioned in 1248 as part of the name Johannes de Elstrowe.

name: null
Bridge_Description: The causeway and the corresponding bridges are first mentioned in 1287. However, the more important roads used crossed the lowlands of the Großes Bruch at Hadmersleben or Neudamm – Neuwegersleben.

name: Ballenstedt
Settlement_Description: Originally a castle of the counts of Ballenstedt, who first appear in 1030. A collegiate church was founded in 1043, consecrated in 1046 and turned into a Benedictine monastery in 1123.
Town_Description: The monastery was destroyed by peasants in 1525 and consequently acquired by lord Wolfgang of Anhalt, who secularised it. He granted the settlement town privileges in 1543.

name: null
Bridge_Description: In the description of safe conduct from 1736 a small wooden bridge near the ferry at Roßbach is mentioned. It can be assumed to have existed before.
Ferry_Description: In 1300 the ferry is bought by Pforte monastery. It is mentioned again in 1303. In the description of safe conduct from 1736 the ferry near Roßbach is mentioned as well. The safe conduct from Freyburg ended here in the middle of the Saale river.

name: Gebrannte Brücke
Bridge_Description: In a border description from 1162 a "burned bridge" is mentioned at this site, which might have been a small wooden bridge or a log road through the marshy area.

name: Stößen
Settlement_Description: First mentioned in 968, but archaeological finds suggest a significant settlement already in the 5th-7th century.
Town_Description: Stößen became a town in the 13th century and is first attested as "oppidum" in 1287 and as "civitas" in c. 1300. However, the economy depended mostly on agriculture.
Fair_Description: Two fairs are attested since the 15th century.

name: Osterfeld
Settlement_Description: First mentioned in 1232. A German castle was probably built in the 13th century, possibly on the basis of an older Slavic fortification.
Town_Description: Osterfeld probably became a town in the middle of the 13th century, but the economy depended on agriculture and it was never fortified. It acquired renewed Magdeburg town privileges in 1523 and market privileges in 1565.

name: Lehmannsbrücke
Bridge_Description: The Lehmannsbrücke was built at the location of a former ford in the river Gera and is the oldest bridge in Erfurt, first mentioned as Liepwinisbrucca in 1108.
